target_language_example: Los domingos voy a la iglesia con mi familia.
native_language_example: On Sundays I go to church with my family.

meaning: to the left; on the left (side).
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or location. Common with movement verbs and instructions like “girar” (to turn) and “seguir” (to continue): “Gire a la izquierda” = “Turn left.” Also pairs with “a la derecha” (to the right).
target_language_example: La farmacia está a la izquierda del banco.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is to the left of the bank.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen over time after a long period, often meaning that the final result will be seen later (similar to “in the long run” or “eventually”). Common with verbs like ser, pagar, pasar, resultar: "A la larga, todo se arregla."
target_language_example: A la larga, este esfuerzo valdrá la pena.
native_language_example: In the long run, this effort will be worth it.

meaning: into the light; to light (as opposed to darkness). Also: “to light” = revealed/known (in phrases like “salir a la luz”).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: “to the light” (direction/return: Regresa a la luz). Very common in the fixed expression “salir a la luz” = “to come to light / to be revealed” (a secret, truth, scandal). Also used with “la luz” meaning “light” in general (e.g., “al calor y a la luz” = “to heat and light”).
target_language_example: La información salió a la luz después de la investigación.
native_language_example: The information came to light after the investigation.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information that helps you interpret something (“in light of these facts…”). It can also be literal when talking about actual light (often with candles): “a la luz de una vela / de las velas” = “by candlelight.”
target_language_example: A la luz de lo que pasó ayer, vamos a cambiar el plan.
native_language_example: In light of what happened yesterday, we’re going to change the plan.

additional_notes: A common regional alternative to “por la mañana.” It’s used for general time (“a la mañana tomo café”) and also with specific days/dates (“el martes a la mañana” = Tuesday morning; “los domingos a la mañana” = on Sunday mornings).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a la mañana para desayunar.
native_language_example: See you in the morning for breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens the morning after a previous event (often mentioned just before). It commonly appears at the start of a sentence to set the time. You may also see it without the first “a”: “la mañana siguiente” (“the next morning”).
target_language_example: A la mañana siguiente, llamé al médico.
native_language_example: The next morning, I called the doctor.

additional_notes: This is a nonstandard variant you may hear in some regions or in casual speech. The most common and widely accepted form is **a lo mejor** (also meaning “maybe/perhaps”). It’s used to express possibility or uncertainty and often goes at the beginning of the sentence.
target_language_example: A la mejor llego tarde.
native_language_example: Maybe I’ll arrive late.

meaning: to the table; at the table.
additional_notes: Used for going to sit/eat at the table (often as a call like “A la mesa.” = “Dinner’s ready / To the table!”). Common with verbs like “sentarse a la mesa” (to sit down at the table), “estar sentado a la mesa” (to be seated at the table), and “modales a la mesa” (table manners). With movement verbs it can also mean onto the table, e.g., “subir a la mesa” (to climb up onto the table).
target_language_example: Los niños ya están a la mesa.
native_language_example: The kids are already at the table.

additional_notes: A very strong, vulgar expression used to reject something (“A la mierda con…”, “A la mierda + noun”) or to insult/dismiss someone (“Vete/Váyase a la mierda”). Stronger than “al diablo” and not appropriate in polite situations. Often appears with verbs like “mandar a la mierda” = “to tell someone to fuck off / to send someone to hell.”
target_language_example: ¡A la mierda con este plan! Nos vamos.
native_language_example: To hell with this plan! We’re leaving.

meaning: to half; halfway; in the middle.
additional_notes: Used to show that something is reduced to 50% (reducir a la mitad, bajar a la mitad) or that something is located at the halfway point (estar a la mitad de esa distancia). You’ll often see it with "de" + a noun or amount: "a la mitad de la ciudad" (in the middle of the city), "a la mitad de ellos" (half of them).
target_language_example: Corté el pastel a la mitad.
native_language_example: I cut the cake in half.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar", "verse" (to look), and "vestirse" (to dress) to say someone/something is trendy or up-to-date in fashion or style. You can negate it: "no está a la moda" (it’s not in style).
target_language_example: Ese corte de pelo está muy a la moda este año.
native_language_example: That haircut is very fashionable this year.

meaning: 'death' (as the object of a verb, often after verbs like 'fear' or 'escape').
additional_notes: Uses the personal “a” because death is treated like a person/agent in many expressions (especially with verbs like temer(le) a, escapar a, engañar a). Often appears as “le temer a la muerte” (“to fear death”) or “escapar a la muerte” (“to escape death”).
target_language_example: Mucha gente le teme a la muerte.
native_language_example: Many people fear death.

meaning: “to the woman” / “the woman” (with the personal a).
additional_notes: Used before a specific female person (la mujer = “the woman”). In Spanish, a is often required before a human direct object (the “personal a”): e.g., “Veo a la mujer” = “I see the woman.” It can also mark “to” after verbs like ayudar/saludar (help/greet someone).
target_language_example: Vi a la mujer en la estación.
native_language_example: I saw the woman at the station.

meaning: to the girl; (marking the girl as the direct object) the girl.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" + "la" to refer to a specific girl. It can mean "to the girl" (indirect object/recipient: "Le dio una rosa a la niña") or "the girl" as a direct object with the personal "a" (common with people/animals: "Atacó a la niña").
target_language_example: Vi a la niña en el parque.
native_language_example: I saw the girl in the park.

additional_notes: Common (especially in Argentina/Uruguay) to mean “in the evening/at night,” often contrasting with "a la mañana". In many other places you’ll also hear "por la noche" or "en la noche." It can refer to a specific night ("Ayer a la noche") or a general time ("los domingos a la noche").
target_language_example: ¿Venís a la noche o mañana a la mañana?
native_language_example: Are you coming tonight or tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used most often with verbs like volver / regresar (to return) to say that a situation is returning to the usual state after a change, problem, or interruption. You’ll commonly hear: volver a la normalidad (“to go back to normal”).
target_language_example: Después de las vacaciones, todo volvió a la normalidad.
native_language_example: After the vacation, everything went back to normal.

additional_notes: Used to express movement/direction toward a workplace office (a + la = “to the”). Common with verbs like ir, venir, llegar, llevar, enviar/mandar. If you’re talking about being in the office (location), you usually use “en la oficina” (in/at the office).
target_language_example: Voy a la oficina después de comer.
native_language_example: I’m going to the office after lunch.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (like ir, irse, llevar, llegar) to show destination. "A" = to, "la" = the (feminine singular), "oficina de correos" = post office. In directions you may also see "hasta la oficina de correos" (as far as the post office) or "en la oficina de correos" (at the post office).
target_language_example: Voy a la oficina de correos a enviar una carta.
native_language_example: I'm going to the post office to send a letter.

meaning: to the darkness / to the dark.
additional_notes: Often used after verbs that take the preposition “a,” like “acostumbrarse a” (to get used to) and “temer a” (to fear). In English you often translate it as “the dark” rather than “the darkness,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: Cuando se fue la luz, mis ojos se adaptaron a la oscuridad.
native_language_example: When the power went out, my eyes adjusted to the dark.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the other item/person in a pair or a previously mentioned set. It’s feminine singular (la), so it matches a feminine noun (e.g., la línea, la persona). With people, you may see the personal “a” (e.g., Vamos a atrapar a la otra = We’re going to catch the other one).
target_language_example: Esta camisa es bonita, pero prefiero a la otra.
native_language_example: This shirt is nice, but I prefer the other one.

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase to say something is done or goes perfectly. Often follows a verb (hacerlo a la perfección, dibujar algo a la perfección) or describes how things are going (Todo marchaba a la perfección). Also appears in the saying “La práctica lleva a la perfección” (“Practice makes perfect”).
target_language_example: El plan salió a la perfección.
native_language_example: The plan worked out perfectly.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to indicate destination (e.g., ir a la piscina, llevar a la piscina). With verbs like tirar/caer, it can mean into the pool. The feminine article changes with the preposition: a + la = a la (contrast: a + el = al).
target_language_example: Vamos a la piscina después de clase.
native_language_example: We’re going to the pool after class.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like ir, irse, venir, llevar, estar rumbo) to say someone is going/heading/taking someone to the beach. It’s “a” + “la playa” (feminine singular), so the literal idea is “to the beach.”
target_language_example: ¿Vamos a la playa este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Are we going to the beach this weekend?

meaning: to the police; the police (as the object of a verb like “call,” “tell,” “report to”).
additional_notes: "A" is a preposition meaning “to.” It’s commonly used before an indirect object, especially with verbs like llamar (a) (to call), informar a (to inform), decir a (to tell), reportar a / denunciar a (to report to). In these contexts, "a la policía" means you contact the police or give information to them. Note: "la policía" alone usually means “the police” as a group; adding "a" depends on the verb.
target_language_example: Si ves algo sospechoso, llama a la policía.
native_language_example: If you see something suspicious, call the police.

meaning: to the question (as in “answer the question”).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like responder/contestar (to answer) to mark what you are answering: responder/contestar a + la pregunta. Often translates as just “answer the question” in English, even though Spanish includes “to”.
target_language_example: No contestes todavía a la pregunta; primero escucha la explicación.
native_language_example: Don’t answer the question yet; first listen to the explanation.

meaning: at the door; on the door (e.g., knock/ring).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like llamar (to knock/ring), golpear (to knock/hit), and dirigirse (to head) to describe being at the door or doing something to the door. In this context, llamar a la puerta means “to knock/ring at the door.”
target_language_example: Están llamando a la puerta, ¿puedes abrir?
native_language_example: They’re knocking at the door—can you open it?

meaning: to the meeting; at the meeting.
additional_notes: “A” marks direction (“to”) and is also used with verbs like asistir a (“to attend”), faltar a (“to miss”), and ir a (“to go to”). “Reunión” means “meeting” and is feminine, so it takes “la”. In context it often corresponds to “(to/at) the meeting” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a la reunión mañana?
native_language_example: Are you going to the meeting tomorrow?

meaning: to the living room; into the room.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "a" to show movement toward a place (similar to “to/into”). "La" is the feminine “the,” because "sala" is feminine. In many Spanish-speaking countries, "la sala" commonly means the living room (the main sitting room), though it can also mean a hall/room depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos a la sala a ver una película.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the living room to watch a movie.

meaning: to the (room for) … / to the … room.
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement/direction to a specific room that has a purpose or function. It’s typically followed by a noun: a la sala de fumadores (to the smoking room), a la sala de masajes (to the massage room). Often used with verbs like ir (to go), volver/regresar (to return), llevar (to take), mandar (to send).
target_language_example: Por favor, llévalo a la sala de reuniones.
native_language_example: Please take him to the meeting room.

meaning: per week; a week later (with time words like "siguiente").
additional_notes: Most commonly means “per week” to express frequency: "tres días a la semana" (three days a week), "horas a la semana" (hours per week). With a time modifier like "la semana siguiente" it can mean “the following week / a week later.”
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio cuatro veces a la semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym four times a week.

meaning: to the lady; to Mrs. (polite, adult woman).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” to mark the person who receives an action (e.g., send something to her) or the person you address in commands. With names, “la señora + surname” means “Mrs. + surname” (polite/formal).
target_language_example: Por favor, entrégueselo a la señora García.
native_language_example: Please give it to Mrs. García.

meaning: in the shade; (figuratively) in the shadow of (someone).
additional_notes: Used literally for a place not in direct sunlight: "a la sombra" or "a la sombra de + [thing]" (in the shade of a tree/building). Figuratively, "vivir a la sombra de + [person]" means being overshadowed by someone’s fame or influence.
target_language_example: Vamos a sentarnos a la sombra de la pared porque hace mucho calor.
native_language_example: Let’s sit in the shade of the wall because it’s very hot.

meaning: to temptation (in the phrase “ceder a la tentación” = “to give in to temptation”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb “ceder” (to give in/yield): “ceder a la tentación” means you couldn’t resist and you did the tempting thing. You can also say “no ceder a la tentación” = “not to give in to temptation.”
target_language_example: Quise comer más pastel, pero no cedí a la tentación.
native_language_example: I wanted to eat more cake, but I didn’t give in to temptation.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes/goes over to a shop. "A" indicates direction (to/toward), and "la" is "the" (feminine singular). Often used with verbs like ir (to go), venir (to come), correr (to run): "Voy a la tienda" (I’m going to the store).
target_language_example: Voy a la tienda a comprar pan.
native_language_example: I’m going to the store to buy bread.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement, especially "ir": "ir + a + [place] + a + infinitive" = “to go to [place] to do [verb]”. You can add what you’re buying after "comprar" (e.g., "a comprar pan").
target_language_example: Voy a la tienda a comprar leche y vuelvo enseguida.
native_language_example: I’m going to the store to buy milk and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Uses "a" to show movement/direction (ir/venir/llegar a la universidad) and also commonly to talk about attending university (ir a la universidad = to go to/attend college). In many contexts it can be translated as "to college" in American English.
target_language_example: Voy a la universidad en autobús todos los días.
native_language_example: I go to university by bus every day.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to say something is available to be bought: *Está/No está a la venta.* You’ll also see **salir a la venta** for when tickets/products become available for purchase (go on sale).
target_language_example: ¿Está a la venta esta casa?
native_language_example: Is this house for sale?

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more things happen together. Very common with "todo/todos" (all at once) and in the pattern "uno/una ... a la vez" meaning "one ... at a time" (e.g., "Una pregunta a la vez").
target_language_example: No podemos hacer dos cosas a la vez.
native_language_example: We can't do two things at the same time.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **a** + **la vida** (“life”). It often appears with adjectives and verbs that take **a** (e.g., *indispensable a la vida* = “essential to life”, *darle sentido a la vida* = “to give meaning to life”). It can also be part of set phrases like **Gracias a la vida** (“Thanks to life”) or with a modifier: *a la vida escolar* (“to school life”).
target_language_example: El amor le da sentido a la vida.
native_language_example: Love gives meaning to life.

additional_notes: Used to say that something can be seen (often in reports like “¡Objetivo a la vista!” = “Target in sight!”). Common with verbs like "estar" (estar a la vista = to be visible), "tener" (tener algo a la vista = to have it in view), and "aparecer" (aparecer a la vista = to come into view).
target_language_example: Ya está el hotel a la vista.
native_language_example: The hotel is already in sight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is visible and not hidden. Very common with people/words like todos (everyone), cualquiera (anyone), or a person: "a la vista de todos" = where everyone can see it; "a la vista de cualquiera" = where anyone can see it. Often implies it’s exposed or left out openly.
target_language_example: No dejes el pasaporte a la vista de todos.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the passport in plain sight (where everyone can see it).

a la vuelta de la esquina

target_language_multi_word_term: a la vuelta de la esquina
meaning: 'just around the corner' (very near; sometimes 'coming soon').
additional_notes: Commonly used to say a place is very close: "Vivo a la vuelta de la esquina". It can also be used figuratively to mean something is imminent or about to happen: "Veo la muerte a la vuelta de la esquina" (I feel death is near). Often intensified with "justo" (right/just): "Justo a la vuelta de la esquina".
target_language_example: La farmacia está a la vuelta de la esquina.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is just around the corner.

additional_notes: Often used with words like "moda" to mean "in the latest fashion" ("vestido a la última moda"). Depending on context, it can also mean "to the last (one)" when followed by a noun (e.g., "a la última sesión" = "to the last showing/session").
target_language_example: Quiere estar a la última, así que siempre compra ropa nueva.
native_language_example: She wants to be up-to-date, so she always buys new clothes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about effects, consequences, or plans that matter over a long period of time. It can modify a verb (Pensar a largo plazo = to think long-term) or a noun (un plan a largo plazo = a long-term plan).
target_language_example: A largo plazo, esta decisión nos ayudará.
native_language_example: In the long term, this decision will help us.

meaning: “to the” (feminine plural), or “(to) + the” before certain direct objects.
additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns (las + noun). Common uses: (1) direction/movement toward a place: "a las cuevas" = "to the caves"; (2) the “personal a” before direct objects that are people (and sometimes animals): "veré a las familias" = "I’ll see the families". Also commonly used with time: "a las tres" = "at three o’clock."
target_language_example: Voy a las tiendas después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m going to the stores after work.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "jugar": "jugar a las cartas" = to play cards (card games in general, not a specific one). "Las cartas" can also mean the physical playing cards; in that case you may still see "a las cartas" if it refers to what someone did to the cards (depending on the verb/context).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres jugar a las cartas conmigo esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to play cards with me tonight?

meaning: 'to the girls' / 'the girls' (with the marker a).
additional_notes: Used with **a** before a person/people who are the **indirect object** (often with **les**: *A las chicas les gusta...* = 'The girls like...') or the **direct object** when the verb acts on people (the 'personal a': *Estás asustando a las chicas* = 'You’re scaring the girls'). **Chicas** usually means 'girls/young women.'
target_language_example: A las chicas les encanta esa canción.
native_language_example: The girls love that song.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. Use **a la** with 1 o’clock (*a la una*) and **a las** with other hours (*a las dos, a las cinco*).
target_language_example: La reunión es a las cinco.
native_language_example: The meeting is at five.

additional_notes: This phrase is normally completed with a time-of-day word like "mañana" (morning), "tarde" (afternoon), or "madrugada" (very early morning/before dawn). In the examples, "a las cinco de la madrugada" means around 5 a.m. Use "a las" + hour for telling time (except 1: "a la una").
target_language_example: Llegamos a las cinco de la mañana.
native_language_example: We arrived at five in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "A las" is used with most clock times (except 1:00, which is "a la una"). You can add "en punto" to mean exactly (e.g., "a las cuatro en punto").
target_language_example: La reunión empieza a las cuatro.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at four o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It uses **a** + **las** + hour for most times (because *hora* is feminine plural in this expression). For 1 o’clock you say **a la una** (singular). In some contexts it can imply a meeting/reservation time: *Mesa cuatro, a las diez* = “Table four, (for) 10:00.”
target_language_example: Te llamo a las diez.
native_language_example: I’ll call you at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say what time something happens. With specific clock times, Spanish uses **a + la/las + hour**: **a la una** (at 1:00) but **a las dos/tres/cuatro** (at 2/3/4). You can add minutes: **a las dos y media** (at 2:30). **como a las dos** means “around/about 2:00.”
target_language_example: La reunión es a las dos.
native_language_example: The meeting is at two o’clock.

meaning: to women; by women (as the people affected).
additional_notes: "A" often marks an indirect object (who something happens to / who someone appeals to): "gustar a las mujeres" = "to be liked by women" (literally, "to please women"). "Las" is "the" (plural, feminine).
target_language_example: Le gusta contar historias a las mujeres.
native_language_example: He likes telling stories to women.

meaning: "to the women" + "(to) them" (indirect object: to/for women).
additional_notes: Used to mark who something happens to, who likes/loves something, etc. It commonly appears with verbs like gustar/encantar/interesar. Structure: A + group/person + les + verb. Example: A las mujeres les gusta X = Women like X (literally, 'X is pleasing to the women').
target_language_example: A las mujeres les interesa el deporte.
native_language_example: Women are interested in sports.

meaning: 'women like' / 'women enjoy' (literally: 'to women, it is pleasing').
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to express what women like. The thing liked can be a person, an activity (gusta + infinitive), or a singular noun/idea. For plural things, use: "a las mujeres les gustan ..." (e.g., "A las mujeres les gustan los zapatos"). "A las mujeres" can be replaced (a mí, a ti, a él/ella, a nosotros, etc.), but "les" stays because the subject is plural (women).
target_language_example: A las mujeres les gusta viajar.
native_language_example: Women like to travel.

meaning: "to the girls" / "the girls" (with the personal or indirect-object "a").
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun (las niñas = “the girls”) when it’s an indirect object (often translates as “to the girls”): A las niñas les gusta… (“The girls like…”). It’s also used with the “personal a” before a direct object that is a specific person: Buscaron a las niñas (“They looked for the girls”). In the idiom la niña de mis ojos (“the apple of my eye”), you can see it in comparisons like Lo cuidaré como a las niñas de mis ojos (“I’ll take care of him like the apple of my eye”).
target_language_example: Voy a darles un regalo a las niñas.
native_language_example: I’m going to give the girls a present.

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. With hours other than 1, Spanish uses **a las + number** (e.g., *a las nueve*). With 1 o’clock, it’s **a la una**. You can add parts of the day like *de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche* to be more specific.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las nueve.
native_language_example: See you at nine o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. Use **a las + [hour]** for times from 2:00 to 12:00 (a las dos, a las nueve). For 1:00, use **a la una** (singular). You can add **de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche** if you need to specify AM/PM.
target_language_example: La reunión es a las ocho.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eight o’clock.

a las ocho de la mañana

target_language_multi_word_term: a las ocho de la mañana
meaning: at eight in the morning (8:00 a.m.).
additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "a las" is used with times except 1:00 ("a la una"). "de la mañana" clarifies it’s in the morning; you can also hear "a las ocho" if the context already makes it clear.
target_language_example: La reunión es a las ocho de la mañana.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eight in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to state the time when something happens. With times (except 1 o’clock), Spanish typically uses "a las + [hour]": a las once (11:00). You can add precision with phrases like "en punto" (exactly) or minutes: "a las once y cuarto" (11:15).
target_language_example: La reunión es a las once.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eleven o’clock.

additional_notes: Commonly used as the indirect object with verbs like gustar/encantar/interesar ("to/for people"): A las personas les gusta… It can also mark a direct object when the verb is about acting on people, using the personal “a”: humillar a las personas, ver a las personas. Here, “las personas” means “people” in general.
target_language_example: A las personas les preocupa el futuro.
native_language_example: People worry about the future.

meaning: at the first opportunity; as soon as something starts.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very early or at the first sign of trouble/possibility. Often appears in longer expressions like “a las primeras de cambio” (= at the first chance / right away).
target_language_example: A las primeras, se cansó y se fue a casa.
native_language_example: At the first opportunity, he got tired and went home.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "A las" is used with all clock times except 1:00 ("a la una"). You can add parts of the day for clarity: "a las seis de la mañana/tarde/noche".
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las seis.
native_language_example: See you at six.

a las seis de la mañana

target_language_multi_word_term: a las seis de la mañana
meaning: at six in the morning (6:00 a.m.).
additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "A las" is used with most clock times (except 1:00, which is "a la una"). "De la mañana" specifies that it’s in the morning (a.m.).
target_language_example: Tengo que salir de casa a las seis de la mañana.
native_language_example: I have to leave the house at six in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. With times, Spanish uses "a las" + hour (plural), and "y media" means “and a half” (= :30). You can add context like "de la mañana" (in the morning), "de la tarde" (in the afternoon), or "de la noche" (at night).
target_language_example: La clase empieza a las seis y media.
native_language_example: The class starts at six thirty.

meaning: “(to) the snakes” (used after verbs like “to fear/be afraid of”).
additional_notes: Used with verbs/expressions that take the preposition **a**, especially **temer a** (“to fear”) and **tener miedo a** (“to be afraid of”). In English you usually translate it as “of snakes” rather than “to the snakes.” **Las** is feminine plural because **serpiente** is feminine.
target_language_example: Mi hermana le tiene pánico a las serpientes.
native_language_example: My sister is terrified of snakes.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. Use **a la** + hour for 1:00 (a la una) and **a las** + hour for 2:00–12:00 (a las dos, a las siete). You can add details like **en punto** (exactly) or **y media** (half past): *a las siete en punto*, *a las siete y media*.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las siete.
native_language_example: See you at seven.

a las siete de la mañana

target_language_multi_word_term: a las siete de la mañana
meaning: at seven in the morning (7:00 a.m.).
additional_notes: Used to say the exact time something happens. "A las" is used with most clock times (a la una = at 1:00), and "de la mañana" specifies it’s in the morning (AM).
target_language_example: Tengo una reunión a las siete de la mañana.
native_language_example: I have a meeting at seven in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to give a specific time on the clock. With times other than 1:00, Spanish typically uses plural: a las + number (a las dos, a las cuatro). For 1:00, it’s a la una. You can add parts of the day (de la mañana/tarde/noche) or minutes (y media = :30, y cuarto = :15).
target_language_example: La reunión es a las tres.
native_language_example: The meeting is at three.

meaning: to clean the house (used after verbs like “help” or “ready”).
additional_notes: Often appears with verbs that take “a + infinitive,” especially when someone helps or is ready/available to do something: “ayudar a + infinitive” (to help to do), “estar listo/a para + infinitive” (to be ready to do). You can also say “limpiar la casa” without “a” depending on the main verb.
target_language_example: ¿Me ayudas a limpiar la casa esta tarde?
native_language_example: Will you help me clean the house this afternoon?

meaning: 'to call' (used after another verb, like 'volver' or 'venir').
additional_notes: Spanish often uses **a + infinitive** after certain verbs to link to the next action. Common patterns: **volver a llamar** = “to call again,” **ir a llamar** = “to go/going to call,” **venir a llamar** = “to come to call (e.g., come by and call/knock).” With object pronouns: **volveré a llamarte / la volveré a llamar** = “I’ll call you / her again.”
target_language_example: Te voy a llamar cuando llegue a casa.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you when I get home.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a bigger structure: (1) "volver a llegar tarde" = "to be late again" (volver a + infinitive = to do something again). (2) "ir a llegar tarde" = "to be going to be late" (ir a + infinitive = going to). (3) Often followed by "para" + event/place: "llegar tarde para la escuela" = "to be late for school". On its own you’ll most often hear "llegar tarde" without the initial "a".
target_language_example: No quiero volver a llegar tarde al trabajo.
native_language_example: I don't want to be late for work again.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **a** + infinitive **llevar**. It often appears after verbs like **acompañar (a)**, **acostumbrar (a)**, **preferir**, etc. **Llevar** is flexible: it can mean to take/bring someone or something somewhere (*llevar a las niñas a la escuela*), to wear clothing (*llevar zapatos*), or to carry a burden (*llevar el peso del mundo*).
target_language_example: ¿Me acompañas a llevar estas cajas al coche?
native_language_example: Will you come with me to carry these boxes to the car?

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like empezar a, ponerse a, and echarse a to mean “to start crying.” The preposition a + infinitive marks the start/beginning of an action (e.g., Empezó a llorar = “He/She started to cry”). By itself, llorar means “to cry.”
target_language_example: Cuando escuché la noticia, me eché a llorar.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I burst into tears.

meaning: to rain (used after another verb, especially about starting).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like empezar (to start), volver (to rain again), ponerse (to begin suddenly), and ir (to be about to): empezar a llover (to start raining), volver a llover (to rain again), ponerse a llover (to start raining), ir a llover (to be going to rain). The "a" here is part of the common pattern "verb + a + infinitive" (not the location word "to"/"at").
target_language_example: Creo que va a empezar a llover en unos minutos.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to start raining in a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used mainly in two ways: (1) with "de" to mean "along" a place/line/route (a lo largo del río/la calle/el cielo); (2) with time expressions to mean "throughout/over the course of" (a lo largo de la vida/del año/de la semana). Often corresponds to English “along” or “throughout,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Hay muchos cafés a lo largo de esta calle.
native_language_example: There are many cafés along this street.

meaning: over the course of; throughout; along.
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) time: "a lo largo de los años / de mi vida" = "over the years / over my life"; (2) place: "a lo largo de la calle / de todo el país" = "along the street / throughout the whole country". Often followed by a noun (e.g., "a lo largo de + el/la/los/las + noun").
target_language_example: A lo largo de la semana, tengo tres reuniones.
native_language_example: Over the course of the week, I have three meetings.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or location following the length of the river (next to it as it continues). More generally, you can say "a lo largo de + [place/thing]" = "along" / "throughout" (e.g., a lo largo de la calle, a lo largo del camino).
target_language_example: Hay cafeterías a lo largo del río.
native_language_example: There are cafés along the river.

meaning: "to what" / "to that which" (introduces a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used with expressions like "nada" or "algo" to mean "nothing/something to + verb" (e.g., "nada a lo que volver" = "nothing to go back to"). It can also be used to transition back to the main topic: "Y luego, a lo que sigue" = "And then, on to what comes next."
target_language_example: No tengo nada a lo que aferrarme.
native_language_example: I have nothing to hold on to.

additional_notes: Used to clarify or point back to an idea you just mentioned. Very common after verbs like saber/entender: "¿Sabes a lo que me refiero?" (= "Do you know what I mean?"). You’ll often see it with demonstratives: "A eso/Esto es a lo que me refiero" (= "That/This is what I mean").
target_language_example: ¿Entiendes a lo que me refiero cuando digo que necesitamos más tiempo?
native_language_example: Do you understand what I mean when I say we need more time?

meaning: to what… / about what… / regarding (that thing).
additional_notes: Used with the neuter article **lo** to refer to an idea or an unspecified thing. Very common in **a lo que + verb** (“to what…”, “about what…”): *Presta atención a lo que dice* (“Pay attention to what he says”). It can also refer back to a situation already mentioned: **a lo de + noun** (“about the [topic/thing] of…”): *¿Te refieres a lo del puente?* (“Do you mean the bridge thing?”).
target_language_example: No le hagas caso a lo que dicen los demás.
native_language_example: Don’t pay attention to what other people say.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something on a large scale or in an extravagant/impressive way (spending, traveling, celebrating, etc.). With feelings, it can mean “a lot” or “seriously” (e.g., enamorarse a lo grande = to fall hard).
target_language_example: Para su cumpleaños, lo celebraron a lo grande.
native_language_example: For her birthday, they celebrated in a big way.

meaning: 'throughout' / 'over the course of' (often: "a lo largo de" = "throughout/along").
additional_notes: Most commonly used as "a lo largo de" + a time period or place. With time it means "throughout/over" (a lo largo del año = throughout the year). With space it means "along" (a lo largo de la calle = along the street).
target_language_example: A lo largo del día, beberé mucha agua.
native_language_example: Throughout the day, I will drink a lot of water.

meaning: along; throughout; over the course of.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that extends along a place/route (a lo largo de la costa = along the coast) or continues through a time period (a lo largo de todo el año = throughout the year / over the whole year). Often used with "todo/a" for emphasis: "a lo largo de todo el país" (throughout the whole country).
target_language_example: A lo largo del día, reviso mis correos varias veces.
native_language_example: Throughout the day, I check my emails several times.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or can be seen/heard far from where you are. It often goes with verbs like ver (to see) and oír/escuchar (to hear): "Vimos... a lo lejos", "Oí... a lo lejos".
target_language_example: Se ve una montaña a lo lejos.
native_language_example: You can see a mountain in the distance.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a guess about what might be true. It’s common at the start of a sentence: "A lo mejor + verb". With "a lo mejor no..." it means "maybe not". It can also follow an imperative or suggestion to mean "maybe" something will happen: "Sigue, a lo mejor...".
target_language_example: A lo mejor llegamos tarde si hay tráfico.
native_language_example: Maybe we’ll arrive late if there’s traffic.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a guess about what could be true. Very common in spoken Spanish and often followed by the indicative (e.g., “A lo mejor es…”). It can also appear mid-sentence after a comma.
target_language_example: A lo mejor llego tarde porque hay tráfico.
native_language_example: Maybe I’ll arrive late because there’s traffic.

meaning: "to what" / "to that which" (referring to a thing or idea).
additional_notes: Used before a clause introduced by "lo que" to point to the specific thing being talked about. Common in phrases like "a lo que sigue" (to what comes next) and "a lo que me refiero" (what I mean / what I’m referring to).
target_language_example: No entiendo a lo que te refieres.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit on a number, amount, or degree (the maximum possible). It often appears between commas after the quantity: "tres, a lo sumo, cuatro semanas". It can also limit a statement more generally ("a lo sumo lo sospecha" = he can only suspect it at best).
target_language_example: Llegaré en una hora, a lo sumo.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in an hour, at most.

meaning: "to the" (a + los); also used in "a los + number + años" = "at (age) ...".
additional_notes:
It’s the contraction of **a** + **los** (plural masculine “the”). Common uses:
- **Direction/recipient**: *Voy a los baños.* (“I’m going to the bathrooms.”)
- **Personal a** before a male/mixed plural direct object (often people/animals): *Obedece a los profesores.*
- **Age/time expression**: **a los + number + años** = “at … years old”: *Empezó a trabajar a los dieciséis años.*
target_language_example: Llegué a los 20 años a esta ciudad.
native_language_example: I arrived in this city at age 20.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" to mark who is affected or receives an action (often an indirect object), e.g., "Les da miedo a los animales" = "It scares the animals." It can also appear after a verb like "dar de comer" (to feed) to show who gets something. In these cases you’ll often also see the indirect object pronoun "les" referring back to "los animales."
target_language_example: No debes gritarles a los animales.
native_language_example: You shouldn't yell at the animals.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" to mark who something is directed to (often an indirect object with verbs like "decir" or "encantar"). It can also be the direct object with the personal "a" when referring to people (e.g., "Traigan a los chicos..."). "Chicos" can mean "boys" specifically, or more generally "kids/guys" depending on context.
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a los chicos para que vengan.
native_language_example: I'm going to call the boys/kids so they come.

meaning: to the customers / to the clients.
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object (often translated as “to” in English), like decir, mentir, explicar. It can also appear with the “personal a” before a direct object that is a person/group, especially with verbs like recibir or atender (e.g., “Recibimos a los clientes” = “We welcome/receive the customers”).
target_language_example: Voy a explicarles el problema a los clientes.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain the problem to the customers.

meaning: to the others; to everyone else.
additional_notes: Used to include other people besides the one already mentioned. It often contrasts with “a ti/a mí” (you/me): “No solo a ti, también a los demás” (“Not just you, but the others too”). “A” is the preposition “to/for,” and “los demás” means “the others/rest (of them).”
target_language_example: No se lo digas solo a él; díselo también a los demás.
native_language_example: Don’t tell only him; tell the others too.

meaning: to/for both of them; to the two (people).
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking to or about two people at the same time (usually masculine or mixed-gender; for two females you typically say “a las dos”). Often appears with indirect object pronouns like “les” (A los dos les gusta...) or as a greeting (Buenos días a los dos).
target_language_example: Les di las gracias a los dos.
native_language_example: I thanked both of them.

meaning: to the students; (sometimes) the students (as a direct object with “a”).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” to mark an indirect object (recipient) like in “enseña… a los estudiantes” and “provee… a los estudiantes.” It can also appear with the “personal a” before a direct object when the direct object is a specific group of people: “asustó a los estudiantes,” “engañó a los estudiantes.” Often replaced or doubled by the pronoun “les” (to them).
target_language_example: Voy a explicar la tarea a los estudiantes mañana.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain the homework to the students tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "gustar" to show who likes something (e.g., "A los gatos les gusta..."). It’s also used after adjectives/phrases like "ser alérgico a..." ("allergic to..."). "A" + "los" = "to the" (plural masculine), and "gatos" means "cats".
target_language_example: A los gatos les gusta dormir al sol.
native_language_example: Cats like sleeping in the sun.

additional_notes: In Spanish, when the direct object is a specific group of people, you usually use the personal "a": veo a los hombres (I see the men), teme a los hombres (she fears men). Here, "los hombres" can mean "the men" (specific men) or "men" in general, depending on context.
target_language_example: No entiendo a los hombres a veces.
native_language_example: I don't understand men sometimes.

meaning: (to) humans / the humans (often marking the direct object).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **a** + **los humanos** (“the humans”). In Spanish, **a** is often used before a **person or person-like being** when it is the direct object (the **personal a**): *Entiendo a los humanos* = “I understand humans.” It can also mean literal “to the humans” after verbs like *dar/dejar/mandar* (“to give/leave/send”).
target_language_example: No quiero hacerles daño a los humanos.
native_language_example: I don’t want to harm humans.

additional_notes: Often means “to the children” after verbs like dar (to give) or llevar (to take): “Doy… a los niños” = “I give… to the children.” It can also mark a direct object when the people affected are specific (personal a): “Adoro a los niños” = “I adore (the) children.”
target_language_example: Voy a leerles un cuento a los niños.
native_language_example: I'm going to read a story to the children.

a los niños a la escuela

target_language_multi_word_term: a los niños a la escuela
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "llevar" (to take/bring) or "acompañar" (to accompany) to say you take the children to school. The first "a" is the personal "a" before a person (a los niños), and the second "a" marks the destination (a la escuela).
target_language_example: Siempre llevo a los niños a la escuela antes de ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I always take the kids to school before going to work.

additional_notes: Used to mark the indirect object (who something is for/pleases/happens to). Very common with verbs like gustar/encantar: the thing liked is the grammatical subject (e.g., Los pasteles les encantan), and a los niños tells you who likes it. The “les” usually appears even when you already say a los niños (this is normal in Spanish). You can swap in other groups: a mis amigos les, a tu mamá le, etc.
target_language_example: A los niños les gustan mucho los juegos de mesa.
native_language_example: The children really like board games.

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern "(A + person) + le(s) encanta(n) + thing" to express that someone loves something. "A los niños" marks who feels the love; "les" matches plural (niños). Use "encanta" with a singular thing (e.g., Halloween) and "encantan" with plural things (e.g., los cuentos). Often followed by a noun or an infinitive verb (e.g., "cavar", "escuchar").
target_language_example: A los niños les encantan los helados en verano.
native_language_example: Kids love ice cream in the summer.

additional_notes: This is the common Spanish structure with gustar: "A + [people] + les gusta + [thing/verb]". Use "les" because it’s plural (to them). Use "gusta" (singular) with one thing or an infinitive verb (e.g., "jugar"); use "gustan" with plural things (e.g., "A los niños les gustan los helados"). You can add "más" to compare: "les gusta más X que Y".
target_language_example: A los niños les gusta leer antes de dormir.
native_language_example: The kids like reading before bed.

meaning: in the eyes; (figuratively) to one’s view/notice.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like mirar (to look) or ver (to see): mirar a alguien a los ojos = “to look someone in the eyes” (direct eye contact). It can also be figurative with expressions like saltar a los ojos (“to jump out at you,” be obvious) or invisible a los ojos (“invisible to the eye/to our sight”).
target_language_example: Mírame a los ojos cuando me hablas.
native_language_example: Look me in the eyes when you talk to me.

meaning: the others (used with "a" before a person/people).
additional_notes: Often includes the personal "a" when the others are people/animals and are the direct object of the verb (e.g., "amar a los otros", "alcancé a los otros", "trae a los otros"). In English, this "a" usually isn’t translated as “to.”
target_language_example: No escuches a los otros; confía en ti.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to the others; trust yourself.

meaning: to the dogs / (with people or animals) the dogs.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" + "los" ("the") + "perros" ("dogs"). Often appears with the "personal a" before a specific person/animal after verbs like "odiar" and "preferir" (e.g., "Odio a los perros", "Prefiero a los perros"). It can also mark an indirect object (who receives something): "Di el agua a los perros" = "I gave the water to the dogs."
target_language_example: No les des chocolate a los perros.
native_language_example: Don’t give chocolate to the dogs.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people who receive the action of the verb: "a" marks an indirect/direct object person, "los" = "the (ones)", and "que" introduces a relative clause. Commonly translated as "to those who..." / "to the ones that...". For other forms: "a las que" (feminine plural), "a los que" can also mean "to whom" in some contexts; singular is often "a quien" or "a la que / al que" depending on usage.
target_language_example: Ayuda a los que no tienen dónde dormir.
native_language_example: Help those who don’t have anywhere to sleep.

meaning: by force; the hard way (not willingly).
additional_notes: Common in the expression "a buenas o a malas" (“one way or another”). It means someone will do something even if they have to use pressure or force, or if it happens in an unpleasant way. It’s informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Si no quieres hablar, hablaremos a malas.
native_language_example: If you don’t want to talk, we’ll do it the hard way.

additional_notes: Used after another verb (often with "ir" or "aprender") to mean "to send" or "to order". With a thing: "mandar una carta" = to send a letter. With a person + destination/action: "mandar a mi hijo a la universidad" = to send my son to university; it can also mean to order someone to do something (a stronger, commanding sense).
target_language_example: Voy a mandar un mensaje ahora.
native_language_example: I'm going to send a message now.

meaning: 'as' / 'in the manner of'; 'as a kind of'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something done as an imitation, style, or approximate substitute of something else (“in the style of”). Very common with nouns: “a manera de + noun” (e.g., a manera de ejemplo = as an example; a manera de broma = as a joke). It can often be translated as “like” or “sort of,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Lo dijo a manera de broma.
native_language_example: He said it as a joke.

meaning: (1) even/quit (no one owes anything); (2) by hand/handmade.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) "estar a mano" = to be even/settled after a favor, debt, or argument ("So we’re even"). (2) "hecho a mano" = made by hand (handmade), often for crafts, food, or artisanal products.
target_language_example: Te presté mi libro y me ayudaste con la mudanza; estamos a mano.
native_language_example: I lent you my book and you helped me move; we’re even.

additional_notes: Common in Spain and informal/colloquial. Used to emphasize that there is a large quantity of something (often with verbs like haber/tener: “Hay/Tengo … a mares”).
target_language_example: En verano hay turistas a mares en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: In the summer there are tons of tourists in this city.

meaning: 'to kill' / 'to kill (someone)' (with the intention of killing).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "disparar" (to shoot), "ir" (to go), or "venir" (to come) to show purpose or intent: "disparar a matar" = to shoot to kill (not just to scare or wound). Often implies lethal intent.
target_language_example: Los soldados recibieron la orden de disparar a matar.
native_language_example: The soldiers were given the order to shoot to kill.

additional_notes: You’ll often see this when Spanish uses the structure **ir/venir + a + infinitive** to express purpose: *vino a matar...* = “he came to kill...”. The second **a** is the **personal a**, used before a **person (or personified being/pet)** who is the direct object: *matar a Mary*, *matar a mi padre*. With a thing, you usually don’t use the personal **a**: *matar el tiempo* (“kill time”).
target_language_example: Vinieron al pueblo a matar a un hombre.
native_language_example: They came to the town to kill a man.

meaning: around the middle of (a time period).
additional_notes: Used with months, years, seasons, or other time periods to say something happens roughly halfway through that period. Common in dates and schedules: "a mediados de mayo" (mid-May), "a mediados de año" (mid-year).
target_language_example: Voy a viajar a mediados de julio.
native_language_example: I'm going to travel around mid-July.

additional_notes: Used with clothes and products/services made specifically for a person: Un traje a medida (a tailored suit), Se lo hacemos a medida (We’ll make it to your specifications). Also appears in the common expression “a medida que” = “as/while” (A medida que pasa el tiempo… = As time goes by…).
target_language_example: Quiero un vestido a medida.
native_language_example: I want a custom-made dress.

additional_notes: Used to show that one thing happens or changes gradually as another thing happens or progresses. It often goes with verbs like avanzar, pasar, crecer, mejorar/empeorar. Similar to “conforme” or “según” in meaning, but it strongly suggests a process over time.
target_language_example: A medida que practicas, te sientes más seguro.
native_language_example: As you practice, you feel more confident.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an exception or condition that must happen for the main clause to be false. It is followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "a menos que tengas"). Often similar to "except if" / "unless" in English.
target_language_example: No salgo a menos que deje de llover.
native_language_example: I’m not going out unless it stops raining.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly. It commonly goes before the verb (A menudo llega...), but it can also appear after the verb (sale a menudo) or at the start of a sentence for emphasis (Y a menudo,...).
target_language_example: A menudo vamos a este café los sábados.
native_language_example: We often go to this café on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Usually used with a verb like **ir**: **ir a menudo a pescar** = “to often go fishing.” **A pescar** literally means “to fish,” but after movement verbs (ir, venir, salir) it commonly means “to go fishing.” Word order can vary: **A menudo iba a pescar** / **Iba a pescar a menudo**.
target_language_example: Los sábados vamos a menudo a pescar al lago.
native_language_example: On Saturdays we often go fishing at the lake.

meaning: "often" (with an impersonal/passive "se": "people are often... / people often...").
additional_notes: "A menudo" means "often" and it commonly appears with "se" to make an impersonal statement (no specific subject): "A menudo se dice..." = "People often say..." / "It is often said...". The verb agrees with what comes after in passive-style uses (e.g., "A menudo se comparan..." if the noun is plural).
target_language_example: A menudo se habla de este tema en clase.
native_language_example: People often talk about this topic in class.

meaning: at the mercy of; at the whim of.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is defenseless and controlled by an outside force (nature, circumstances, or another person). Often implies lack of control and vulnerability: "estar/quedar a merced de...".
target_language_example: Sin frenos, el coche quedó a merced de la gravedad.
native_language_example: With no brakes, the car was at the mercy of gravity.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" before a noun with the possessive "mi" (my): "a mi casa" = "to my house." Don’t confuse it with "a mí" (with an accent), which means "to me" and is used with pronouns: "A mí me gusta" = "I like."
target_language_example: Voy a mi casa después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m going to my house after work.

meaning: to my grandmother; my grandmother (as a person-object).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "a" before an indirect object (often with "le": "Le di un regalo a mi abuela") and also as the "personal a" before a direct object that is a specific person (common with verbs like "querer": "Quiero a mi abuela"). Word order can vary, especially with pronouns ("Le compré un regalo a mi abuela").
target_language_example: Le escribí a mi abuela una carta.
native_language_example: I wrote my grandmother a letter.

meaning: “to my grandfather” / “my grandfather” (when he’s the person affected).
additional_notes: Spanish often uses **a** before a person: (1) as an **indirect object** (“to/for”) like in *A mi abuelo le gusta…* and *A mi abuelo le dan miedo…*; and (2) as the **personal a** with a direct object who is a person, like *satisfacer a mi abuelo* (“to satisfy my grandfather”). **mi abuelo** means “my grandfather.”
target_language_example: Quiero llamar a mi abuelo esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to call my grandfather tonight.

meaning: my friend (as the direct object, with the “personal a”).
additional_notes: Spanish often uses the preposition “a” before a specific person who is the direct object (the “personal a”): “Vi a mi amigo” = “I saw my friend.” It can look like English “to,” but here it doesn’t mean “to.” (It *does* mean “to my friend” when the friend is an indirect object: “Le di el libro a mi amigo.”)
target_language_example: Hoy voy a ver a mi amigo después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to see my friend after work.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or direction (ir, venir, entrar, volver, caminar) to indicate going toward your place. Often translated as “to my house,” and in many contexts “to my place/home.” Contrast: “en mi casa” = “at/in my house.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir a mi casa después de clase?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my place after class?

meaning: "my wife" (often preceded by "a" because she is the object of the verb).
additional_notes: Spanish often uses "a" before a person when they are the direct object ("personal a"), especially with verbs like ver, encontrar, llamar, extrañar, presentar. With indirect objects, you may also see "A mi esposa le..." meaning "To my wife / My wife (indirect object)...".
target_language_example: Quiero invitar a mi esposa a cenar.
native_language_example: I want to invite my wife to dinner.

meaning: “my family” (often used with “a” to mark the person/people affected or the direct object).
additional_notes: Common in Spanish because people are often introduced with the personal “a” (a + person/people): e.g., “Extraño a mi familia” = “I miss my family.” You may also see it as an indirect object with verbs like “irle (bien/mal) a alguien”: “A mi familia le va bien” = “My family is doing well.”
target_language_example: Extraño a mi familia cuando viajo.
native_language_example: I miss my family when I travel.

meaning: to my cat; my cat (when marked with “a”).
additional_notes: “A mi gato” can mean literally “to my cat” (often with an indirect object pronoun like *le*: *A mi gato le encantará…*). It’s also used as the **personal a** before a specific animal/person that is the direct object: *Tengo que alimentar a mi gato*; *Extraño a mi gato*. In those cases, English usually doesn’t translate the “a”.
target_language_example: Le compré un juguete a mi gato.
native_language_example: I bought my cat a toy.

additional_notes: Uses "a" to show movement/direction toward a place (going/coming/bringing someone or something). Often used with verbs like entrar (to enter), subir (to go up), llevar (to take/bring), venir (to come), regresar (to return). For location without movement, Spanish usually uses "en mi habitación" (in my room).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes subir a mi habitación un momento?
native_language_example: Can you come up to my room for a moment?

meaning: “my sister” as the object of a verb (to/at my sister).
additional_notes: Spanish uses the personal “a” before a direct object that is a specific person/animal: ver a mi hermana, matar a mi hermana, observar a mi hermana. Also used for an indirect object meaning “to my sister” (e.g., Le doy un regalo a mi hermana).
target_language_example: Le escribí a mi hermana ayer.
native_language_example: I wrote to my sister yesterday.

meaning: “to my brother” / “my brother” (with the preposition a).
additional_notes: Used with **a** in two very common ways: (1) as an **indirect object** meaning “to/for my brother” (often with **le** too): *A mi hermano le encanta…* (“My brother loves…”). (2) as the **personal a** before a person as a direct object: *Conocía a mi hermano* (“She knew my brother”).
target_language_example: Le compré un regalo a mi hermano.
native_language_example: I bought my brother a gift.

meaning: "to my daughter" / "my daughter" (as an indirect object or after "querer").
additional_notes: Often used with the personal "a" before a person, and commonly appears with indirect object pronouns like "le" (e.g., "A mi hija le gusta..."). It can also mean "my daughter" as a direct object with verbs like "querer" ("quería a mi hija" = "he loved my daughter").
target_language_example: Le compré un regalo a mi hija.
native_language_example: I bought my daughter a gift.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "a" before an indirect object (the person affected). Very common with "gustar"-type verbs: "A mi hijo no le gusta..." = "My son doesn't like..." (literally, "To my son, it isn't pleasing"). Often paired with the indirect object pronoun "le".
target_language_example: A mi hijo le encanta jugar al fútbol.
native_language_example: My son loves playing soccer.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is beside you (physically) or with you in a supportive way. Common with verbs like estar, sentarse, dormir, pasar. You can change the possessive: a tu lado (next to you), a su lado (next to him/her/you formal), a nuestro lado (next to us).
target_language_example: ¿Te puedes sentar a mi lado?
native_language_example: Can you sit next to me?

meaning: to my mother; (direct object) my mother.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., dar, decir, avisar): *Le di... a mi madre* (“I gave... to my mother”), *Le diré... a mi madre* (“I’ll tell... my mother”). It can also mark a person as the direct object with *a* (the “personal a”): *presentarte a mi madre* (“introduce you to my mother”).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi madre esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my mother tonight.

meaning: to/for my mom; my mom (as the person affected by the verb).
additional_notes: “A” is used before a person as an indirect object (e.g., “Le di el libro a mi mamá” = “I gave the book to my mom”) and also as the personal “a” before a direct object that is a person (e.g., “Vi a mi mamá” = “I saw my mom”). Often you can replace it with a pronoun: “a mi mamá” ↔ “le” (to her) or “la” (her), depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi mamá esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my mom tonight.

meaning: my way; in my own way.
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something the way you want, following your own style or rules. Often appears with verbs like hacer (to do), ser (to be), and with things like las cosas (things): “hacer las cosas a mi manera” = “do things my way.” It can sound firm or insistent in disagreements (“será a mi manera” = “it’ll be my way”).
target_language_example: Déjame intentarlo a mi manera.
native_language_example: Let me try it my way.

meaning: "to my husband" (often used as the object: "my husband").
additional_notes: "a" + person is used with the personal "a" when the person is the direct object (e.g., "A mi marido no le interesan..." / "No amaba a mi marido"). With verbs like "gustar" and "interesar," "a mi marido" commonly marks who is affected/concerned (roughly "as for my husband" / "to my husband"). "Mi marido" alone means "my husband"; "marido" can also mean "spouse" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi marido esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my husband tonight.

meaning: “to my wife” / “my wife” (as an indirect object).
additional_notes: Literally “to my wife.” Very common with indirect-object verbs like encantar, decir, dar, avisar: “A mi mujer le…” = “My wife…” (you often also add the pronoun le). If it follows the preposition a, it can also mean “(to) my wife” as a direct object with a personal a: “Engañé a mi mujer” = “I cheated on my wife.”
target_language_example: A mi mujer le dije que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: I told my wife I would arrive late.

meaning: to my girlfriend / my girlfriend (as an indirect object or after certain verbs).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" before "mi novia" (my girlfriend). You often see it when she is the indirect object (recipient) with verbs like "comprar" or "mentir": "Le compré flores a mi novia" (I bought my girlfriend flowers), "Le mentí a mi novia" (I lied to my girlfriend). It’s also used as the personal "a" with direct objects that are people: "Echo de menos a mi novia" (I miss my girlfriend), "Mis padres conocen a mi novia" (My parents know my girlfriend).
target_language_example: Quiero invitar a mi novia a cenar esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to invite my girlfriend to dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Uses "a" to show movement or direction toward a place (answering “where to?”). Often with verbs like ir, venir, pasar, llevar, llamar (to call to a number/location), etc. For a static location (“in/at my office”), Spanish usually uses "en mi oficina".
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a mi oficina a las tres?
native_language_example: Can you come to my office at three?

meaning: to my dad / my father (as an object after verbs like 'help', 'love', 'know', 'see').
additional_notes: Often appears with verbs that take a direct object: e.g., "Ayudé a mi padre" (I helped my dad), "Conocía a mi padre" (I knew my dad). The "a" here is the personal "a" used before a specific person as the direct object (not the same as indirect-object "to").
target_language_example: Llamé a mi padre anoche.
native_language_example: I called my dad last night.

meaning: to my dad / my dad (as an object).
additional_notes: Literally “to my dad.” It’s used when “papá” is an indirect object (often with the pronoun le): “A mi papá le gusta…” = “My dad likes…”. It’s also used after certain verbs that take “a” before a person (personal a), like oír/escuchar, ver, llamar: “Oigo a mi papá…” = “I hear my dad…”. If the dad is the subject, you usually just say “mi papá” (no “a”): “Mi papá quiere café.”
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi papá esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my dad tonight.

meaning: "my dog" (as a direct object, marked with personal "a").
additional_notes: In Spanish, you often put "a" before a person or pet when it is the direct object of the verb (called the "personal a"): "Llevé a mi perro..." / "Alimento a mi perro...". In English you usually just say "my dog" without "to".
target_language_example: Veo a mi perro desde la ventana.
native_language_example: I see my dog from the window.

additional_notes: Uses the personal "a" to mark an indirect object with verbs like contestar/responder (often: "contestar a" / "responder a"). In English you can usually drop "to" and just say "answer my question". Also common: "en respuesta a mi pregunta" = "in response to my question."
target_language_example: ¿Puedes responder a mi pregunta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you answer my question, please?

meaning: "to my uncle" / "my uncle" (as the object of a verb).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "a" before a person. It can mark an indirect object (recipient) as in "Le mandé esta carta a mi tío" (= I sent this letter to my uncle), often together with "le". It can also be the "personal a" before a direct object when the person is being seen/visited/taken somewhere: "Veré a mi tío" (= I’ll see my uncle), "dejaron a mi tío" (= they dropped my uncle off).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi tío esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my uncle tonight.

meaning: Often intended as “to me” / “for me” (nonstandard spelling of the correct form “a mí”).
additional_notes: When Spanish means “to me/for me” after the preposition “a”, the correct spelling is **a mí** (with an accent). Writing **a mi** without the accent is very common in informal texting, but it’s considered incorrect in standard writing. Note: **a mi** (without accent) can also be correct when **mi** is possessive (“my”), e.g., “a mi casa” = “to my house,” but in that case it’s not the pronoun “me.”
target_language_example: A mi tambien.
native_language_example: Me too.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" + the plural possessive "mis" + a plural noun (e.g., "a mis gatos"). Very common for marking an indirect object, especially with verbs like "gustar/encantar" ("A mis gatos les va a encantar" = "My cats are going to love it"). Also appears in set phrases like "a mis espaldas" (“behind my back”).
target_language_example: Le mandé un mensaje a mis padres.
native_language_example: I sent a message to my parents.

meaning: "to my friends" / "my friends" (as the object of a verb).
additional_notes: "mis amigos" means "my friends." The "a" is used in a few common ways: (1) as the personal "a" before a person/people who are a direct object (Busco a mis amigos; He perdido a mis amigos), (2) to show an indirect object meaning "to" (Siempre escribo a mis amigos), and (3) after some verbs like presentar (Te presentaré a mis amigos) and dedicar (Dedico esta victoria a mis amigos).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mis amigos esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my friends tonight.

additional_notes: Often used to mean someone did something secretly or without telling you, especially gossiping or criticizing you (hablar/reírse de alguien a sus espaldas). It can also be literal for physical position (“behind me”), especially with location clues like “a mis espaldas” in descriptions.
target_language_example: Me enteré de que tomaron la decisión a mis espaldas.
native_language_example: I found out they made the decision behind my back.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **a**. Very commonly, **a** marks the person who receives an action (an indirect object): *Les compré regalos a mis hijos* (“I bought gifts for my kids”). It can also appear with verbs like *visitar* or *ver* when the direct object is a person (the “personal a”): *Voy a ver a mis hijos* (“I’m going to see my children”).
target_language_example: Quiero llamar a mis hijos esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to call my kids tonight.

meaning: my parents (as the object of the verb).
additional_notes: Use the personal "a" before a direct object that is a specific person/people: "Veo a mis padres". With verbs like "decir" or "contar", it can mark the indirect object: "Les dije a mis padres" (= I told my parents). Often replaced by object pronouns: "los" (them, direct object) or "les" (to them, indirect object).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a llamar a mis padres.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to call my parents.

meaning: as; by way of; in the form of (used to introduce an example or approximation).
additional_notes: Used before a noun/phrase to indicate something is being used as an example, approximation, or substitute (similar to “as a kind of…” or “by way of…”). Common patterns: “a modo de ejemplo” (by way of example), “a modo de resumen” (as a summary), “a modo de introducción” (as an introduction).
target_language_example: A modo de ejemplo, te muestro dos opciones.
native_language_example: By way of example, I'll show you two options.

additional_notes: Common in informal speech as an intensifier after a verb: e.g., “querer a morir” = “love (someone) to death,” “asustarse a morir” = “be scared to death,” “doler a morir” = “hurt like crazy.” Don’t confuse this with the literal verb phrase “(ir/empezar/estar dispuesto) a morir” meaning “(to be going/to start/to be willing) to die.”
target_language_example: Me duele a morir la cabeza.
native_language_example: My head hurts like crazy.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., gustar, dar, tomar el pelo) or a direct object when the object is a person (personal “a”), meaning the action affects many people. Often followed by a pronoun like le/les to refer back to “gente” (treated as singular in Spanish: a mucha gente le…).
target_language_example: A mucha gente le encanta el café.
native_language_example: Many people love coffee.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "condenar/sentenciar" (to sentence) or in expressions like "pelea/lucha a muerte" to mean a death sentence or a fight where someone is expected to die. In informal speech it can also be used figuratively to mean "a lot" or "really intensely" (e.g., "Me gusta a muerte" = "I love it so much").
target_language_example: Dicen que fue una pelea a muerte.
native_language_example: They say it was a fight to the death.

meaning: extremely; to the limit (as much as possible).
additional_notes: Common idiom used to intensify an adjective or describe doing something with maximum intensity. Often appears after the word it emphasizes: "cansado a más no poder" (extremely tired), "trabajar a más no poder" (work as hard as possible).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado a más no poder.
native_language_example: I’m extremely tired.

additional_notes: Used to set the latest possible time/date for something to happen. It often follows a specific deadline: a más tardar el domingo / a más tardar a las diez / a más tardar antes del fin de mes. Common in instructions and schedules.
target_language_example: Envíame el formulario a más tardar el viernes.
native_language_example: Send me the form no later than Friday.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize who is affected or involved, often contrasting with someone else (e.g., “a ti … y … a mí”). Common after verbs like gustar/encantar and in contrasts: “A mí me gusta…, pero a él no.” Often goes with the indirect object pronoun “me” in the same sentence (“A mí me…”).
target_language_example: A mí me gusta el café, pero a mi hermana le gusta el té.
native_language_example: I like coffee, but my sister likes tea.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens or applies specifically to you, often for contrast (e.g., “to me, it seems…”, “I (personally)…”). It commonly appears with verbs that take an indirect object (me), like gustar-type verbs (sonar, caer bien), and in experiences (“me pasó…”). You can drop “a mí” in many cases (“Me caes bien”), but adding it makes it more emphatic.
target_language_example: A mí me da igual; podemos ir mañana.
native_language_example: I don’t mind; we can go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that *you* (not someone else) like something. The basic pattern is: **A mí me gusta + noun/infinitive** (e.g., *A mí me gusta el pescado* = I like fish; *A mí me gusta trabajar* = I like working). Spanish uses an indirect-object pronoun (**me**) with **gustar**, and the thing you like is the grammatical subject, so **gusta** is used for singular things/activities. (Plural: *A mí me gustan…*)
target_language_example: A mí me gusta esta música.
native_language_example: I like this music.

meaning: “I like” (for plural things), with extra emphasis on “me / as for me.”
additional_notes: Use with things you like that are plural (or one singular noun that’s treated as plural, like “los mariscos”). The structure is: a mí (to me) + me (to me) + gustan (they please) + [thing(s) you like]. You can drop “a mí” in neutral statements (“Me gustan los sábados”), but keep it for contrast or emphasis (“A mí me gustan, pero a él no”). For a singular thing, use “a mí me gusta …”.
target_language_example: A mí me gustan las películas de terror, pero a mi hermana no.
native_language_example: I like horror movies, but my sister doesn’t.

additional_notes: Used to give your personal view. With "a mí" it emphasizes that it’s *your* perspective (often contrasted with someone else: "a ti... a mí..."). You can use it alone as a short reply meaning "That’s what I think". Common follow-ups: "a mí me parece bien/mal", "a mí me parece que + clause".
target_language_example: A mí me parece que esta idea es mejor.
native_language_example: It seems to me that this idea is better.

additional_notes: Emphatic form of the indirect object pronoun: you use it to stress that the action is directed at yourself. It’s often used with verbs that already have me (e.g., me digo a mí misma, me culpo a mí misma, me sorprendí a mí misma). Use a mí mismo if the speaker is male.
target_language_example: A veces tengo que recordarme a mí misma que todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: Sometimes I have to remind myself that everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis or to make it clear that the action is directed at the speaker. It often appears with reflexive verbs (e.g., encontrarse) and can be added even when the verb already has a reflexive pronoun (me) to stress “myself.” Variations: a ti mismo/a (yourself), a sí mismo/a (himself/herself/themselves).
target_language_example: No puedo culpar a nadie: me equivoqué a mí mismo.
native_language_example: I can’t blame anyone: I made the mistake myself.

meaning: "I don't" / "it doesn't to me" (emphatic: "not to me").
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not apply to you, or that you personally don’t think/feel/experience something. Often followed by a verb like parece (seems), pasó (happened), engaña (fools), basta (is enough). You can swap the person: a ti no te, a él/ella no le, a nosotros no nos, etc.
target_language_example: A mí no me gusta ese plan.
native_language_example: I don't like that plan (me, personally).

additional_notes: Used to say you feel/think the same as someone else. Often appears with a verb: "A mí también me gusta..." = "I like it too." It can also stand alone after a statement: "A él le gusta... y a mí también" = "He likes it... and I do too." You can swap the pronoun for other people: "a ti también" (you too), "a él también" (him too), "a ella también" (her too).
target_language_example: A mí también me gusta esta canción.
native_language_example: I like this song too.

meaning: “Me too” (same for me), used before verbs like gusta/cae bien/pasa/ocurre.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something also applies to you. Often appears with verbs that take an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le…), especially likes/dislikes and things that happen to someone: “A mí también me gusta…” = “I like it too.” You can swap in other people: “A ti también te…”, “A ella también le…”.
target_language_example: A mí también me pasa a veces.
native_language_example: That happens to me too sometimes.

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone about liking something. Literally “to me also it pleases,” and it commonly appears with the thing you like: “A mí también me gusta esa película.” You can drop the object if it’s clear: “A mí también me gusta.” Often paired with “A mí me gusta…” (“I like…”).
