additional_notes: Used to state that a situation is a fact and can’t (or won’t) be changed; it can sound resigned or matter-of-fact. Often said after an explanation: “...y así son las cosas.”
target_language_example: No me gusta la decisión, pero así son las cosas.
native_language_example: I don’t like the decision, but that’s how things are.

additional_notes: A common medical phrase. Often used with verbs like: “tener un ataque al corazón” (to have a heart attack) and “dar(le) un ataque al corazón” (to have/get a heart attack; literally “to give (someone) a heart attack”). With “casi” it can be used exaggeratively to mean “I almost had a heart attack” from shock or fear.
target_language_example: Cuando escuché la noticia, pensé que me iba a dar un ataque al corazón.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I thought I was going to have a heart attack.

additional_notes: A medical emergency when the heart suddenly doesn’t get enough blood. Often written with an accent as “ataque cardíaco.” In everyday Spanish, you may also hear “infarto” or “infarto de miocardio.”
target_language_example: Mi abuelo tuvo un ataque cardiaco y lo llevaron al hospital.
native_language_example: My grandfather had a heart attack and they took him to the hospital.

additional_notes: A common medical/mental-health term for a sudden episode of intense fear/anxiety with physical symptoms (e.g., fast heartbeat, shortness of breath). Use with the verbs tener/estar teniendo: "Tuve un ataque de pánico" (I had a panic attack), "Está teniendo un ataque de pánico" (He/She is having a panic attack).
target_language_example: Creo que estoy teniendo un ataque de pánico.
native_language_example: I think I'm having a panic attack.

additional_notes: Used to politely get a group’s attention, especially before making an announcement (e.g., in meetings, presentations, on speakers). Common patterns: “Presten atención, por favor” (plural ‘pay attention, please’) and “Su atención, por favor” (‘your attention, please’).
target_language_example: Atención, por favor: vamos a empezar la reunión.
native_language_example: Attention, please: we’re going to start the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" to introduce what you pay attention to. Very commonly appears in the set phrases "prestar atención a" (to pay attention to) and "poner atención a" (to pay attention to). With people, you typically use an indirect object pronoun too: "prestarle atención a alguien".
target_language_example: Presta atención a las instrucciones, por favor.
native_language_example: Pay attention to the instructions, please.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle (atropellado/atropellada/atropellados/atropelladas) to describe someone who was hit by a vehicle. Often appears with ser (passive): "fue atropellado por un coche" = "he was run over by a car". You can also see it with estar to describe the resulting condition: "estaba atropellado" (less common). "por" introduces the thing causing the action (e.g., por un coche/un auto/un camión).
target_language_example: El peatón casi murió después de ser atropellado por un vehículo.
native_language_example: The pedestrian almost died after being run over by a vehicle.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said and show that something remains true despite it (similar to “even so” or “still” at the start of a sentence). Often follows a negative or limiting idea: “It’s difficult/expensive/late… aun así…” In writing it’s commonly spelled “Aun así,” with a comma.
target_language_example: No tengo mucho tiempo; aun así, puedo ayudarte un momento.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time; even so, I can help you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession or a minimum condition. It’s followed by the subjunctive (sea = subjunctive of ser). Commonly means “even if it’s…” (aunque sea en el último día = even if it’s on the last day) or “at least…” (aunque sea un minuto = at least a minute). It can also mean “even” in emphatic phrases: Los encontraré aunque sea debajo de la tierra = I’ll find them even if it’s under the earth.
target_language_example: Ven aunque sea un ratito.
native_language_example: Come even if it’s just for a little while (at least for a bit).

additional_notes: Common phrase meaning a car that is brand new (not used). In many countries you’ll also hear "coche nuevo" or "carro nuevo" with the same meaning. Adjective agreement: "auto nuevo" (masc. singular), "autos nuevos" (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy ahorrando para comprarme un auto nuevo.
native_language_example: I’m saving up to buy myself a new car.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a toy airplane folded from paper. Plural: aviones de papel.
target_language_example: Hice un avión de papel y lo lancé por la ventana.
native_language_example: I made a paper airplane and threw it out the window.

meaning: "Yesterday I went to the..." (to a masculine singular place).
additional_notes: Used to say you went somewhere yesterday. "Fui" is the preterite (simple past) of "ir" (to go). "Al" is the contraction of "a + el" and must be followed by a masculine singular noun (ayer fui al parque, al médico, al zoo). For feminine singular places, use "a la" (ayer fui a la tienda).
target_language_example: Ayer fui al supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say you unexpectedly met someone. Literally “yesterday I found myself with,” but in everyday Spanish it means “I ran into (someone)” or sometimes “I met up with (someone).” Conjugation changes with the subject and time: “Hoy me encontré con…”, “Me encontré con…”, “Ayer nos encontramos con…”.
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré con mi profesora en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my teacher at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the morning of the previous day. Common placement is at the start or end of the sentence (e.g., “Ayer por la mañana…” / “…ayer por la mañana”). You can also hear “ayer en la mañana” in some regions.
target_language_example: Ayer por la mañana tuve una reunión temprano.
native_language_example: Yesterday morning I had an early meeting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the night between yesterday and today. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Ayer por la noche vi..." / "Vi... ayer por la noche." In many contexts it’s interchangeable with "anoche" (last night).
target_language_example: Ayer por la noche cenamos en casa.
native_language_example: Last night we had dinner at home.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened in the afternoon of the previous day. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Vino ayer por la tarde"), but it can also appear in the middle to describe a person or thing ("la chica que conocí ayer por la tarde").
target_language_example: Nos vimos ayer por la tarde en el café.
native_language_example: We saw each other yesterday afternoon at the café.

meaning: “Yesterday I saw …” (with the personal ‘a’ used before a person).
additional_notes: Use it to say you saw someone yesterday. In Spanish, you normally put **a** before a **specific person** you saw: *Ayer vi a Bill / a tu mujer / a la señora Smith*. You can also use **a** with **un/una + person** when the direct object is a person: *Ayer vi a un hombre…*. With things (not people), there’s usually no **a**: *Ayer vi un coche.*
target_language_example: Ayer vi a mi profesor en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw my teacher at the supermarket.

additional_notes: "Ayuda" is the third-person singular present form of "ayudar" (to help). It is commonly followed by "a" + infinitive to express that something/someone helps to do an action: "X ayuda a aliviar" (X helps to relieve). If a person is being helped, Spanish often includes an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les ayuda a..." (helps me/you/him-her/us/them to...).
target_language_example: Este medicamento ayuda a aliviar el dolor muscular.
native_language_example: This medication helps to relieve muscle pain.

additional_notes: Used before an indirect object (a person/animal) introduced with **a**: *ayudar a + person*. With object pronouns it becomes *ayudarme/ayudarte/ayudarle/ayudarnos/ayudarles* (often without **a**). You can also add a second action with **a + infinitive**: *ayudar a alguien a hacer algo* (“help someone (to) do something”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ayudar a mi hermana a estudiar esta noche?
native_language_example: Can you help my sister study tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ayudar" + "a" + the person being helped. "Los demás" means "the others" / "everyone else" (people other than yourself). You can replace it with a specific person: "ayudar a mi amigo" (help my friend).
target_language_example: Siempre intento ayudar a los demás cuando puedo.
native_language_example: I always try to help others when I can.

additional_notes: “Ayudé” is the preterite (past, completed action) of *ayudar* = “to help.” It’s commonly followed by **a + person** (often with the personal *a*): *Ayudé a Tom…* = “I helped Tom…”. You can then add **a + infinitive** to say what you helped them do: *Ayudé a Tom a subirse…* = “I helped Tom (to) get on…”. You can also say *ayudé a + infinitive* when the object is understood: *Ayudé a cargar las bolsas* = “I helped carry the bags.” Another common pattern is **ayudar a alguien con algo**: *Ayudé a mi padre con el trabajo* = “I helped my father with the work.”
target_language_example: Ayudé a mi amiga a encontrar su teléfono.
native_language_example: I helped my friend find her phone.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of **ayudar**: **yo ayudé**. **Ayudar** is usually followed by **a** + a person: *ayudar a mi madre*. You can also add the indirect object pronoun **le** for emphasis/clarity (*Le ayudé a mi madre*), but in many contexts it’s optional: *Ayudé a mi madre en la cocina*.
target_language_example: Ayer ayudé a mi madre con la cena.
native_language_example: Yesterday I helped my mother with dinner.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "ayudar": "(he/she/you formal) helped". Use "ayudó a + person" to say who was helped: "Ayudó a la chica." When you add what you helped with, use "ayudó a + person + con + noun" (helped with): "Ayudó a su padre con el jardín." You can also use "ayudó a + infinitive" to mean "helped to do" something: "Le ayudó a entrar." Often "a" is required before a specific person (the personal "a").
target_language_example: Mi hermano me ayudó a estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: My brother helped me study for the exam.

additional_notes: Command form of "ayudar" (to help) + "me". It’s used to ask someone to help you do an action: "Ayúdame a" + infinitive (cocinar, enviar, salir, etc.). You can add politeness with "por favor" or soften it with "¿de acuerdo?".
target_language_example: Ayúdame a estudiar para el examen, por favor.
native_language_example: Help me study for the exam, please.

additional_notes: Refers to the period of the year when classes are in session (as opposed to summer/holiday breaks). It’s commonly used with verbs like empezar (to start) and terminar/acabar (to end), and can appear in schedules or legal contexts (e.g., custody arrangements “during the school year”).
target_language_example: El año escolar termina en junio.
native_language_example: The school year ends in June.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the start of a new calendar year and plans, wishes, or goals for it. Often appears in greetings like “Feliz Año Nuevo” (Happy New Year). Capitalization varies: “Año Nuevo” is common in greetings/holiday references; “año nuevo” is fine in general text.
target_language_example: Este año nuevo voy a ahorrar más dinero.
native_language_example: This new year I’m going to save more money.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the previous calendar year, or more generally to a point starting one year ago. Often used with prepositions like “el” (desde el año pasado = since last year) and “del” (del año pasado = from last year).
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español el año pasado.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish last year.

meaning: year after year; every year for a long time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize repetition or something continuing over many years (often with a sense of persistence, frustration, or gradual change). Common with verbs like repetir, seguir, volverse, and tener que tratar con.
target_language_example: Me promete lo mismo año tras año, pero nunca cambia.
native_language_example: He promises me the same thing year after year, but he never changes.

meaning: a year and a half (18 months).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time period. Often appears with time expressions like "hace" (ago), "en" (in), and "después" (later/after): "hace un año y medio" = a year and a half ago; "en un año y medio" = in a year and a half; "un año y medio después" = a year and a half later. You can also use it alone as a short answer to "¿Cuánto tiempo?".
target_language_example: Viví allí un año y medio.
native_language_example: I lived there for a year and a half.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened a certain number of years before now. It often appears after a time expression: “dos/tres/unos años atrás.” You may also hear it combined with “hace” (e.g., “hace unos años atrás”); that’s common in speech, though many style guides consider it redundant—“hace unos años” or “unos años atrás” is enough.
target_language_example: Nos conocimos muchos años atrás.
native_language_example: We met many years ago.

additional_notes: Used after a number to specify someone’s age: "tengo 20 años (de edad)". "De edad" is optional and a bit more formal/emphatic than just "años". You’ll often see it in biographies, news, or official contexts. You can also use it in comparisons: "Me lleva dos años de edad" = “She/He is two years older than me.”
target_language_example: El niño tenía ocho años de edad cuando se mudó a México.
native_language_example: The boy was eight years old when he moved to Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to express that something remains true or happens in spite of what was just said. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence and followed by a comma: "Aún así, ...". Also commonly written as "aun así"; with the accent (aún) it can emphasize the idea of "still/yet."
target_language_example: Estaba muy cansado; aún así, salí a caminar.
native_language_example: I was very tired; even so, I went out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison or increase (“more than before/than expected”). Often appears with comparisons: “aún más … que …” = “even more … than …”. You may also see it without accents as “aun más” in some texts.
target_language_example: Si sigues practicando, hablarás español aún más rápido.
native_language_example: If you keep practicing, you'll speak Spanish even faster.

additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened or become true up to the present moment (or up to a specific time in the past). Often followed by a verb: "Aún no + verbo". It emphasizes that it may happen later. Also commonly written "aun no" (without the accent) in many contexts, but "aún" is standard when it means "still/yet."
target_language_example: Aún no he terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: I haven’t finished the homework yet.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** + an adjective or past participle to say something hasn’t reached a state yet (not finished, not ready, not ripe, etc.). Often followed by an adjective/participle: *aún no está listo/terminado/maduro*.
target_language_example: El informe aún no está listo.
native_language_example: The report isn’t ready yet.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened up to now. It’s most often followed by a past participle to form the present perfect: “aún no ha + participle” (e.g., aún no ha respondido = hasn’t responded yet). “Ha” is the he/she/it/you (formal) form of the auxiliary verb “haber.”
target_language_example: Aún no ha llegado el doctor.
native_language_example: The doctor still hasn’t arrived / hasn’t arrived yet.

meaning: 'I haven’t … yet' / 'I still haven’t …' (with the present perfect).
additional_notes: Used before a past participle to say something has not happened up to now: aún no he comido (I haven’t eaten yet). Often interchangeable with "todavía no he". Common with verbs like acabar (to finish), empezar (to start), llegar (to arrive), and with "sabido" to mean "I still haven’t found out / I don’t know yet".
target_language_example: Aún no he visto esa película.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen that movie yet.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to say something hasn’t happened yet. "Lo" is an object pronoun meaning “it” (a specific thing already mentioned or understood): Aún no lo sé = “I still don’t know it.” Often followed by a verb like creo (believe), sé (know), decidí (decided), encontramos (found).
target_language_example: Aún no lo he terminado, pero voy a seguir.
native_language_example: I still haven’t finished it, but I’m going to keep going.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund bajando (from bajar, “to go down/descend”) to describe an action in progress: Está bajando las escaleras = “He is going down the stairs.” It can also work like a direction in conversation, similar to “down the stairs”: El baño está bajando las escaleras = “The bathroom is downstairs (down the stairs).” You may also hear: subiendo las escaleras (“going up the stairs”).
target_language_example: Te vi bajando las escaleras cuando llegué.
native_language_example: I saw you going down the stairs when I arrived.

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to talk about weight loss. Uses the verb "bajar" (to go down) + "de" + "peso" (weight). Often used with phrases like "quiero/tengo que/necesito bajar de peso" (I want/have to/need to lose weight) or "para bajar de peso" (in order to lose weight).
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de bajar de peso, así que camino todos los días.
native_language_example: I'm trying to lose weight, so I walk every day.

meaning: to lower your head; to bow your head (often showing shame, submission, or respect).
additional_notes: Used both literally (moving your head downward) and figuratively ("not standing up for yourself," "accepting something without protest"). Common in instructions: "Baja la cabeza". Also appears as "bajar la cabeza ante" (to bow your head to/before someone or something).
target_language_example: Cuando el profesor me regañó, tuve que bajar la cabeza.
native_language_example: When the teacher scolded me, I had to lower my head.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation is being managed and isn’t out of hand. Very common with the verb "tener": "Lo tengo bajo control" = “I’ve got it under control.” You can also use it with "estar": "Todo está bajo control" = “Everything is under control.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes, ya está bajo control.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s already under control.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is physically under something else (location), or is below a level/threshold (like temperature). It’s also used in set phrases like “bajo el nombre de” (“under the name of”). The noun is masculine singular (“el”); with feminine you’ll often see “bajo la”.
target_language_example: Guardé el dinero bajo el colchón.
native_language_example: I hid the money under the mattress.

additional_notes: Used to describe being or doing something beneath the surface of the water. Common with verbs like nadar (to swim), estar (to be), vivir (to live), and viajar (to travel). Often contrasts with sobre el agua (“on/above the water”).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar bajo el agua.
native_language_example: I can’t talk underwater.

meaning: under your arm; tucked under your arm.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "llevar" (to carry) to say someone is carrying something by holding it between their arm and their body. Often refers to objects like a book, bag, folder, umbrella, etc.
target_language_example: Salió de casa con una carpeta bajo el brazo.
native_language_example: He left the house with a folder under his arm.

additional_notes: A location phrase: **bajo** = “under/beneath,” followed by **el árbol** (“the tree”). Used to say where someone/something is (sleeping, waiting, a bench, Christmas presents, etc.). You can swap in another noun: *bajo la mesa* (under the table), *bajo el puente* (under the bridge).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos bajo el árbol para tener sombra.
native_language_example: We sat under the tree to have shade.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (la) to talk about being physically under something (bajo la alfombra, bajo la sombra) or figuratively under an influence/control (bajo la influencia). With masculine nouns, use “bajo el”.
target_language_example: Nos sentamos bajo la lluvia unos minutos.
native_language_example: We sat under the rain for a few minutes.

meaning: in the rain; under the rain.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like caminar, marchar, jugar, cantar, dejar, etc. to say something happens while it’s raining (often with the idea of being outside/exposed to the rain). You can also use it more literally for something left outside where rain falls on it.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos esperando el autobús bajo la lluvia.
native_language_example: We waited for the bus in the rain.

meaning: locked up; under lock and key.
additional_notes: Used to say something is kept locked (in a room, safe, cabinet, etc.) so other people can’t access it. Common with verbs like "guardar" (to keep/store) and "tener" (to keep/leave), e.g., "guardar algo bajo llave" = to keep something locked up.
target_language_example: Guardo mi pasaporte bajo llave.
native_language_example: I keep my passport locked up.

additional_notes: Literally “under the earth/ground.” Used for things physically below ground (tunnels, facilities, roots) and also as a common way to say someone is buried/dead (“Está bajo tierra”). Often appears with verbs like “estar” (to be) and “enterrar” (to bury).
target_language_example: El búnker está bajo tierra.
native_language_example: The bunker is underground.

meaning: “got off/out of the” or “came down from the”.
additional_notes: This is the past tense (él/ella/usted) of **bajar de + el = del** (“to go down from”). Very commonly used with the reflexive form **bajarse de** to mean **to get off** a bus/train or **to get out of** a car/taxi: *Se bajó del autobús / del carro*. It can also be literal “came down from” a place or object: *bajó del séptimo piso*, *se bajó del árbol*.
target_language_example: Después de la parada, se bajó del metro.
native_language_example: After the stop, he got off the subway.

additional_notes: "Bajó" is the preterite (simple past) of "bajar" for él/ella/usted. It’s used for a completed action in the past. You can add details like how/when: "bajó las escaleras apurado" (in a hurry), "bajó las escaleras en pijama" (in pajamas).
target_language_example: Anoche bajó las escaleras en silencio.
native_language_example: Last night, he/she went down the stairs quietly.

additional_notes: A raised area of sand (usually underwater or just at the surface) that can make a boat run aground (encallar / encallarse). Common in rivers, lakes, and near the coast. Also heard as "banco de arena" for sandbars that appear at low tide.
target_language_example: Tuvimos que cambiar de ruta porque había un banco de arena cerca de la orilla.
native_language_example: We had to change route because there was a sandbar near the shore.

meaning: brass band (a music group with brass instruments).
additional_notes: Used for a musical group made up mainly of brass instruments (like trumpets, trombones, tubas), often playing in marches, parades, or on the street. In many contexts you can also hear simply "una banda de bronce" or "banda de metales".
target_language_example: La banda de bronces toca en el desfile del pueblo.
native_language_example: The brass band plays in the town parade.

additional_notes: Used for a collection of information stored electronically (or organized records). Common with verbs like buscar en (to search in), estar en (to be in), and subir/cargar a (to upload/add to). Often refers to a company/system database: La base de datos de clientes (the customer database).
target_language_example: Voy a buscar tu nombre en la base de datos.
native_language_example: I’m going to look up your name in the database.

meaning: 'it's enough to' / 'all you need is to'.
additional_notes: Used to say that doing one thing is sufficient to achieve a result. It’s often followed by an infinitive (basta con + infinitive): "Basta con leer" = "You just have to read." It can also be followed by a noun: "Basta con tu apoyo" = "Your support is enough."
target_language_example: Para abrir la puerta, basta con usar esta llave.
native_language_example: To open the door, all you need is to use this key.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop or to say you’ve had enough. Common patterns: "¡Basta de + infinitive!" (Basta de hablar = Stop talking) and "¡Basta de + noun!" (Basta de tonterías = Enough nonsense). It can sound firm or impatient; you can also say "¡Basta!" on its own.
target_language_example: Basta de discutir; vámonos a casa.
native_language_example: Enough arguing; let’s go home.

meaning: pretty well; quite well; fairly well.
additional_notes: Used to say something works/looks/turns out well enough, often meaning “better than okay” but not necessarily “excellent.” With skills or ability, it means you can do something reasonably well. Word order: usually after the verb (hablar bastante bien, funciona bastante bien).
target_language_example: Hoy me siento bastante bien, gracias.
native_language_example: I feel pretty well today, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to say something is good to a noticeable degree, but not necessarily “excellent.” Often corresponds to “pretty good” in English. It can describe things (un sitio web), skills (su inglés), or people (un jugador bastante bueno).
target_language_example: Su inglés es bastante bueno.
native_language_example: His/Her English is pretty good.

meaning: quite a long time; enough time.
additional_notes: Often means “a long time” in phrases like “hace bastante tiempo” (a long time ago / it’s been quite a while) or “desde hace bastante tiempo” (for quite a while). With context like “Tienes bastante tiempo”, it can also mean you have plenty of time (no rush).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todavía tenemos bastante tiempo para llegar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we still have plenty of time to get there.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of beber: bebió = “drank” (completed action). Un sorbo = “a sip” (a small amount of liquid). Common pattern: beber/tomar + un sorbo de + [drink] (agua, vino, cerveza, etc.).
target_language_example: Ella bebió un sorbo de café antes de salir.
native_language_example: She drank a sip of coffee before leaving.

additional_notes: A simple sentence using **poder** (“can/to be able to”) + an infinitive (**caminar** = “to walk”). In real use, **bebé** is often preceded by a determiner or possessive (e.g., **mi/tu/nuestro/vuestro**), but the core term remains **bebé puede caminar**. You can add **ya** (“already”) to emphasize a newly acquired ability: **Mi bebé ya puede caminar.**
target_language_example: Mi bebé puede caminar.
native_language_example: My baby can walk.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of *besar* (“to kiss”): **besó** = “(he/she) kissed.” **en la mejilla** means “on the cheek.” Often used for a friendly or polite greeting/goodnight kiss. Object pronouns like **lo/la/me/nos** show who was kissed (him/her/me/us).
target_language_example: Mi abuela me besó en la mejilla antes de irse.
native_language_example: My grandma kissed me on the cheek before leaving.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "bicicleta" (bicycle) + the adjective "nueva" (new). In Spanish, adjectives usually go after the noun, and "nueva" changes for gender/number: "bicicleta nueva" (feminine singular), "bicicletas nuevas" (plural).
target_language_example: Quiero una bicicleta nueva para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I want a new bicycle to go to work.

additional_notes: Used to comfort or reassure someone you care about. "Cariño" is an affectionate term like “honey/sweetheart/darling,” so it’s common with partners, kids, or close family. Often said after (or as part of) phrases like "Vas a estar bien" or "Todo va a estar bien."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, vas a estar bien, cariño.
native_language_example: Relax, you’ll be okay, honey.

additional_notes: Common polite reply when someone asks how you are (or how someone/something is doing): “¿Cómo estás?” → “Bien, gracias.” It can also be used to confirm that something is OK: “Está bien, gracias.” Often you’ll hear “Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?” (“Fine, thanks. And you?”).
target_language_example: —¿Cómo estás? —Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?
native_language_example: —How are you? —Fine, thanks. And you?

additional_notes: Often used to emphasize or upgrade an evaluation: you say something was/ is “bien” and then add “muy bien” to stress that it was actually very good. Also common as a brief response about how someone is doing (Estoy bien, muy bien = “I’m fine, very well”). Intonation matters: it can sound enthusiastic (genuinely praising) or matter-of-fact (confirming that everything is okay).
target_language_example: La presentación estuvo bien, muy bien.
native_language_example: The presentation was good—very good.

additional_notes: Used in conversation to acknowledge what was said (“bien/okay”) and then add a disagreement, concern, or different point (“pero/but”). Often appears with a pause/comma: “Bien, pero…” You’ll also see it without a comma: “Bien pero…”.
target_language_example: Bien, pero no tengo tiempo ahora.
native_language_example: Okay, but I don’t have time right now.

additional_notes: Used to agree or move the conversation forward and introduce the next action. Often follows “(está) bien” and is then followed by an infinitive: “Bien, vamos a intentar… / llevar… / probar…”. In speech it can sound like a decision or a practical next step: “Alright then, let’s…”.
target_language_example: Bien, vamos a empezar con lo más fácil.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s start with the easiest thing.

meaning: “okay / alright, (fine)…”; “you’ll see” (with ya verás/ya lo verá).
additional_notes: “Bien, ya…” is very common in speech to accept something, end a discussion, or show mild impatience (“Okay, okay, I get it.”). Often used as a transition before the next action. In “ya verás / ya lo verá,” it means “you’ll see” (reassuring or insisting). “Ya” here suggests “soon / now / already,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Bien, ya voy; solo déjame terminar esto.
native_language_example: Okay, I’m coming now; just let me finish this.

meaning: 'Nice, huh?' / 'Good, eh?' (tag used to check/seek agreement).
additional_notes: Used informally after a comment with bien to invite the listener to agree or confirm (sometimes teasing or emphasizing). Common with things like looks, smell, health, or how something suits you: Te queda bien, ¿eh? = 'It looks good on you, huh?'
target_language_example: Quedó bien, ¿eh?
native_language_example: It turned out well, huh?

meaning: "..., right?" / "..., isn’t it?" (seeking confirmation, often like "well, right?").
additional_notes: Used at the end (or in the middle) of a sentence as a tag question to check that the other person agrees or to confirm something you believe is true. It often adds a conversational "well" tone (bien) plus "no?" = "right?". Common in casual speech.
target_language_example: Estás listo para salir, bien, ¿no?
native_language_example: You’re ready to go out, right?

meaning: "...right?" / "..., isn't it?" (asking for confirmation that something is OK or done well).
additional_notes: Used as a tag question after a statement with bien (“well/OK”) to check that the other person agrees. Often translated as “right?” or “isn’t it?” depending on context. In speech, the voice usually rises on ¿verdad? to show you’re asking, not stating.
target_language_example: Lo hice bien, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: I did it well, right?

additional_notes: Used mainly in two common patterns: (1) comparisons: "(tan / así de) bien como ..." = "as well as ..." (often with a verb), e.g., doing something as well as someone else. (2) "Está bien como está" = "It’s fine the way it is" (no change needed).
target_language_example: No hablo inglés tan bien como mi hermano.
native_language_example: I don’t speak English as well as my brother.

meaning: well with (getting along with / matching / looking good with).
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- "llevarse bien con + person" = to get along well with someone: "Me llevo bien con mis compañeros."
- "(no) llevarse bien con + thing/situation" = to do well with / cope well with something (often used with "nunca/no").
- "combinar bien con + clothing/thing" = to match/go well with.
- "verse/quedar bien con + clothing" = to look good with / suit (an outfit or item).
In these uses, "con" means "with"; "bien" works like "well".
target_language_example: Me llevo bien con mi jefa, pero esta chaqueta no combina bien con esos pantalones.
native_language_example: I get along well with my boss, but this jacket doesn’t match those pants well.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone (often said alone: “¡Bien hecho!”). It can also describe something that is correctly/skillfully done: “un trabajo bien hecho” (“a job well done”). You can intensify it with “muy”: “Muy bien hecho.”
target_language_example: ¡Bien hecho! Terminaste el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: Well done! You finished the project on time.

meaning: 'well what…' / 'carefully what…' (i.e., do something carefully/well with what follows).
additional_notes: Used when *bien* (well/carefully) intensifies a verb and *lo que* introduces a clause meaning “what/that which.” Common with verbs like *entender* (understand), *escuchar* (listen), *leer* (read), *elegir* (choose), *recordar* (remember): *Escucha bien lo que te digo* = “Listen carefully to what I’m telling you.”
target_language_example: Piensa bien lo que vas a hacer antes de decidir.
native_language_example: Think carefully about what you're going to do before deciding.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as an interjection: “Bien por + [person/pronoun]” to congratulate or show approval (Bien por ti/él/ella/nosotros). Tone can be genuinely supportive or mildly sarcastic depending on context and intonation. In other contexts, “bien” + “por” may appear with different meanings (e.g., pagar bien por algo = “pay well for something”), but the congratulatory use is the most common fixed phrase.
target_language_example: ¡Bien por ti! Te lo mereces.
native_language_example: Good for you! You deserve it.

meaning: “how well” (often in **lo bien que…**) / “really; indeed” (emphasis, sometimes sarcastic).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as **lo bien que + verb** to comment on the degree/quality of an action: *Es increíble lo bien que canta* (“It’s incredible how well she sings”). It can also be used as an emphatic **bien que + verb** meaning “(you/he/she) sure does…”—often to underline a contrast or to sound ironic: *Bien que te quejas, pero no ayudas* (“You sure complain, but you don’t help”).
target_language_example: Ya veremos lo bien que te sale el plan.
native_language_example: We’ll see how well your plan turns out.

meaning: 'Okay, okay' / 'alright' (used to agree, acknowledge, or reassure).
additional_notes: Repeating bien adds emphasis and often sounds like you’re calming someone down, showing you understand, or moving the conversation along (similar to “okay, okay”). Depending on tone, it can also mean “fine, fine” (a bit impatient). Often followed by gracias when answering “How are you?” or by information (e.g., giving directions).
target_language_example: Bien, bien, no te preocupes; ya lo tengo.
native_language_example: Okay, okay, don’t worry; I’ve got it.

meaning: "Well, then" / "OK, so" (to move the conversation forward or conclude).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational transition. It can introduce a next step ("Bien, entonces espere") or signal agreement/closing ("Bien, entonces estamos de acuerdo"). Often said with a pause: "Bien, entonces..."
target_language_example: Bien, entonces vamos a empezar.
native_language_example: Well then, let's start.

additional_notes: Used to start a question after a pause or to move the conversation along (similar to English “Well, what do you say/decide?”). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral or a bit impatient/challenging (“So, what?” / “Well, what?”). Often followed by a verb: “Bien, ¿qué decides?” / “Bien, ¿qué dices?” It can also be used alone: “Bien, ¿qué?” = “Well, what?”
target_language_example: Bien, ¿qué vamos a hacer ahora?
native_language_example: Well, what are we going to do now?

additional_notes: Common in legal and financial contexts. It refers to property that belongs to a person individually, often contrasted with "bienes gananciales" (marital/community property). "Bienes" here means assets/property (not “goods” in a shopping sense).
target_language_example: Antes de casarse, hicieron una lista de sus bienes propios.
native_language_example: Before getting married, they made a list of their own assets.

additional_notes: Used to greet someone when they arrive at a place, group, or situation. It agrees with the person being welcomed: bienvenido (male), bienvenida (female), bienvenidos/bienvenidas (plural). You may also hear the more formal “Bienvenidos sean a…”.
target_language_example: Bienvenido a nuestra casa; siéntete como en casa.
native_language_example: Welcome to our home; make yourself at home.

meaning: "Welcome to" (addressing a group, or at least one man).
additional_notes: Used to greet people when they arrive somewhere or to introduce a place/event. "Bienvenidos" is the masculine plural form; it’s also used for mixed-gender groups. For all women, use "bienvenidas a". For one person: "bienvenido a" (man) / "bienvenida a" (woman). The preposition "a" is followed by a place or event (often with an article: "a la", "al").
target_language_example: Bienvenidos a nuestra casa.
native_language_example: Welcome to our house.

meaning: black and white; (figuratively) oversimplified, with no gray areas.
additional_notes: Used literally for colors or for media (photos, movies, images) that aren’t in color: "en blanco y negro" = "in black and white." Also used figuratively to say something isn’t just one extreme or the other: "No todo es blanco y negro" = "Not everything is black and white."
target_language_example: Prefiero las fotos en blanco y negro.
native_language_example: I prefer black-and-white photos.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person's position (lying on their stomach) or the position of an object turned so the front/top faces downward. Often used with verbs like estar/estar echado, dormir, dejar, and poner.
target_language_example: Por favor, pon el papel boca abajo.
native_language_example: Please put the paper face down.

meaning: face up; on your back (lying with your face toward the ceiling).
additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like estar/tumbarse/dormir to describe someone lying on their back, or with poner to place something with the front/top side facing up. Common contrast: “boca abajo” = face down.
target_language_example: Si te mareas, acuéstate boca arriba y respira despacio.
native_language_example: If you feel dizzy, lie on your back (face up) and breathe slowly.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: a nuclear weapon (“an atomic bomb”). In casual speech it can be used figuratively to describe something that’s very powerful or impressive (e.g., a phone, a computer, a speaker), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ese altavoz es una bomba atómica: suena increíble.
native_language_example: That speaker is an atomic bomb: it sounds amazing.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of borrar (“to delete/erase”) + su cuenta (“his/her account”). Used when someone permanently removes an account (often on a website/app): borró su cuenta de Facebook / de Instagram. You can change the person: borré mi cuenta (I deleted my account), borraste tu cuenta (you deleted your account), borraron su cuenta (they deleted their account).
target_language_example: Ayer borró su cuenta porque ya no usaba la app.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she deleted his/her account because he/she no longer used the app.

meaning: a rowboat (a small boat moved with oars).
additional_notes: Often used with the article: "un/el bote de remos". "Remo" = oar, so it’s literally “boat of oars.” You’ll commonly see it with verbs like "cruzar" (to cross), "alejarse" (to move away), or "atravesar" (to go across) when talking about crossing a river or moving away from shore.
target_language_example: Alquilamos un bote de remos para cruzar el lago.
native_language_example: We rented a rowboat to cross the lake.

meaning: "a bottle of" (used to say what’s inside the bottle).
additional_notes: Used before a drink or liquid to specify the contents: una botella de agua, una botella de vino. With quantities, you can also say: Tengo una botella de whisky (I have a bottle of whisky).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes comprar una botella de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you buy a bottle of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for, buy, or refer to a quantity/container of wine. You can change the amount: una botella (one bottle), otra botella (another bottle), media botella (half a bottle). Often appears after verbs like dame (give me), compramos (we bought), tráigame (bring me), or with prepositions like de: beber de la botella (drink from the bottle).
target_language_example: ¿Nos trae una botella de vino, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring us a bottle of wine, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a quantity of wine measured in bottles. The number comes before the phrase (e.g., dos/tres botellas de vino). You can add adjectives after it (e.g., botellas de vino vacías = empty wine bottles).
target_language_example: ¿Cuántas botellas de vino necesitamos para la cena?
native_language_example: How many bottles of wine do we need for dinner?

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the body part (your right arm). Figurative meaning: someone you rely on a lot at work or in life—your most trusted helper. In the figurative sense, it often appears with possessives like "mi/tu/su brazo derecho".
target_language_example: En la oficina, Ana es mi brazo derecho.
native_language_example: At the office, Ana is my right-hand person.

additional_notes: Often used literally to talk about the physical left arm (e.g., tattoos, numbness). It can also be used idiomatically in expressions like “Daría mi brazo izquierdo por…” meaning “I’d give my left arm for…” to emphasize you really want something or it’s very valuable (not meant literally).
target_language_example: Daría mi brazo izquierdo por dormir ocho horas seguidas.
native_language_example: I’d give my left arm to sleep eight hours straight.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as a loyal, trustworthy friend. It’s the common shortened form of “bueno” before a masculine singular noun (bueno amigo → buen amigo).
target_language_example: Gracias por estar conmigo; eres un buen amigo.
native_language_example: Thanks for being with me; you’re a good friend.

additional_notes: Used as a mealtime wish, like “Enjoy!” You can say it on its own (“Buen apetito.”) or to a group (“Buen apetito para todos.”). It can also be used literally to describe appetite: “tener buen apetito” (to have a good appetite) or “comer con buen apetito” (to eat heartily).
target_language_example: ¡Buen apetito! La cena está lista.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal! Dinner is ready.

meaning: "good appearance"; (about a person) "to look well" / "to look good".
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone or something looks, often as a quick judgment (healthy, attractive, or in good condition). Common patterns: "tener buen aspecto" (to look good/well), "no tener buen aspecto" (to not look good / look worrying), and intensifiers like "muy" ("tiene muy buen aspecto").
target_language_example: Después de dormir bien, tengo muy buen aspecto.
native_language_example: After sleeping well, I look really good.

meaning: "good boy" / "good kid" (a well-behaved or kind boy/guy).
additional_notes: Often used to praise someone’s behavior or character. With "un" it describes yourself or someone else ("Soy un buen chico" = "I’m a good guy"). Without an article it can be used as advice/encouragement ("Sé buen chico" = "Be a good boy"). "Buen" is the shortened form of "bueno" before a masculine singular noun ("buen chico").
target_language_example: Es un buen chico y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: He’s a good guy and he always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character (they are kind, generous, well-intentioned). Common patterns: “tener buen corazón” (to have a good heart) and “ser de buen corazón” (to be good-hearted). You can intensify it with “muy”: “de muy buen corazón.”
target_language_example: Sé que cometió un error, pero tiene buen corazón.
native_language_example: I know he made a mistake, but he has a good heart.

meaning: “good day” (as a greeting) / “nice day” (about the weather).
additional_notes: Used as a daytime greeting in many Spanish-speaking regions (often more formal than “hola”). With weather, it means the day turned out pleasant: “hizo buen día” = “it was a nice day / the weather was good.” Also used with titles like “Don/Doña” to be polite.
target_language_example: Buen día, ¿cómo está usted?
native_language_example: Good day, how are you?

meaning: good taste (literal taste, or good judgment/style).
additional_notes: Used both for flavor (food/drink tastes good) and for having refined taste or good judgment in choices (clothes, art, people, etc.). In sentence 2, it means he has good taste in women.
target_language_example: Tiene muy buen gusto para elegir ropa.
native_language_example: He has very good taste in choosing clothes.

meaning: a good man; an honorable/kind man.
additional_notes: Used to describe a man’s character (kind, decent, honorable). Often expresses respect or admiration. It can also be used directly to refer to someone politely ("el buen hombre" = "the good man" / "that good fellow"). Note: "buen" is the shortened form of "bueno" before a masculine singular noun ("buen hombre").
target_language_example: Dicen que mi abuelo era un buen hombre y siempre ayudaba a los demás.
native_language_example: They say my grandfather was a good man and he always helped others.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (“to have”) or with estar + de (“to be in”): tener buen humor (“to be in a good mood”), estar de buen humor / de muy buen humor (“to be in a good/very good mood”). You can add muy to emphasize.
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de buen humor porque descansé bien.
native_language_example: Today I'm in a good mood because I slept well.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place is suitable/ideal for an activity. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ganar, tener, pasar). You’ll also see it with the article: “un buen lugar para…”.
target_language_example: Este parque es un buen lugar para relajarse.
native_language_example: This park is a good place to relax.

meaning: a good eye; good judgment (for noticing/choosing things well).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is good at noticing details or judging/choosing well. Very common with "tener": "tener buen ojo". You can add "para" + infinitive or noun to specify what: "buen ojo para juzgar" / "buen ojo para estas cosas".
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene buen ojo para elegir ropa.
native_language_example: My sister has a good eye for choosing clothes.

additional_notes: Used to say someone would make a desirable romantic partner (for their looks, personality, job, status, etc.). It can describe a man or a woman: «Tom es buen partido». Don’t confuse «partido» here with «partido» meaning “game/match” (sports) or “political party.”
target_language_example: Dicen que Marta es muy buen partido.
native_language_example: They say Marta is a great catch.

meaning: "Enjoy your meal!" (said to someone who is about to eat).
additional_notes: A common polite phrase used right before someone starts eating (similar to French “bon appétit”). You can say it to one person or a group: “Buen provecho” / “Caballeros, buen provecho.” In a different structure, “sacar buen provecho de (algo)” means “to get good use/benefit out of (something)” (e.g., “Espero sacar buen provecho de ello.”).
target_language_example: ¡Que disfrutes la cena, buen provecho!
native_language_example: Enjoy dinner—enjoy your meal!

meaning: a good while; quite some time.
additional_notes: Usually used with an article: "un buen rato". It can mean you spent a long time doing something (often longer than expected): "Estuve esperando un buen rato." It can also mean you had a nice time: "Pasamos un buen rato" (= we had a good time).
target_language_example: Te estuve esperando un buen rato.
native_language_example: I waited for you for quite a while.

additional_notes: Used to talk about pleasant weather (sunny, mild, not rainy). Common with the verbs hacer and haber: “Hace buen tiempo” / “Hizo buen tiempo” = “The weather is/was nice,” and “Habrá buen tiempo” = “There will be good weather.” You can also use it with tener: “Tener buen tiempo” (especially when talking about a day, trip, or event having good weather).
target_language_example: Si hace buen tiempo, vamos a la playa.
native_language_example: If the weather is nice, we’re going to the beach.

meaning: a nice guy; (with "tener buen tipo") good-looking / with a good figure.
additional_notes: With "ser un buen tipo", it means someone is kind, decent, or friendly (often a man). With "tener buen tipo", it refers to physical appearance: being attractive or having a good body/figure. It’s fairly informal and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Mi vecino es un buen tipo y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: My neighbor is a nice guy and he always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for what they did. You can say it directly to someone (¡Buen trabajo!) or refer to their work with an article: “el buen trabajo” (Keep up the good work = Sigue con el buen trabajo / Sigan con su buen trabajo). In everyday Spanish, you’ll also hear “¡Buen trabajo!” and “¡Buen trabajo, chicos!”; “hombre” can be used like “man”/“buddy” in a friendly way.
target_language_example: ¡Buen trabajo! Lo hiciste muy bien.
native_language_example: Good job! You did it really well.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well when they’re about to travel or as they leave. Often said directly as “Buen viaje” or in the more formal/subjunctive form “Que tengas/tenga buen viaje” (you/usted have a good trip). You can also use it after the trip with verbs like “Espero que hayas/hayan tenido un buen viaje” (“I hope you had a good trip”).
target_language_example: Buen viaje, ¡nos vemos pronto!
native_language_example: Have a good trip—see you soon!

meaning: a good deed; an act of kindness.
additional_notes: Used for a concrete helpful or kind thing someone does. Very common in the set phrase "hacer una buena acción" (to do a good deed), and also "mi buena acción del día" (my good deed for the day). Can be singular or plural: "buenas acciones".
target_language_example: Voy a hacer una buena acción y ayudar a mi vecino con las bolsas.
native_language_example: I’m going to do a good deed and help my neighbor with the bags.

additional_notes: Informal expression (common in Latin America) used to praise or approve what someone just did/said, or to react positively to a suggestion, joke, or idea. Often said on its own as a quick response.
target_language_example: —Voy a llevar paraguas por si llueve. —¡Buena esa!
native_language_example: —I’m going to bring an umbrella in case it rains. —Nice one!

additional_notes: Used to describe someone (or a group) as kind, decent, and well-intentioned. It’s very common in everyday Spanish. It usually stays in the singular form "gente" even when talking about several people: "Son buena gente" (They’re good people). You can add intensifiers like "muy": "muy buena gente".
target_language_example: Mis vecinos son muy buena gente y siempre ayudan.
native_language_example: My neighbors are really nice people and always help.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good suggestion/plan. Often said on its own to agree (“Buena idea.”). You’ll also hear it with emphasis: “¡Qué buena idea!” = “What a good idea!” You can add an article depending on context: “una buena idea” (a good idea) or “la buena idea” (the good idea).
target_language_example: Es una buena idea salir temprano.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to leave early.

meaning: skill/a good touch (at something); also: a good coat/layer (of paint, etc.).
additional_notes: With "tener buena mano para/con + noun" it means you’re naturally good at something or good with someone: "Tiene buena mano para la pintura" / "buena mano con los niños". With "una buena mano de + noun" (especially "de pintura") it means a good, generous coat/layer: "una buena mano de pintura" = “a good coat of paint.” By itself, "Buena mano" can be a brief compliment meaning “Nice work / Good job.”
target_language_example: Necesito alguien con buena mano para arreglar esto.
native_language_example: I need someone with a good touch/skill to fix this.

additional_notes: Used to say someone remembers things well (names, facts, events). With the verb tener: "Tener buena memoria" = "to have a good memory."
target_language_example: Mi abuela tiene buena memoria para los nombres.
native_language_example: My grandmother has a good memory for names.

additional_notes: Used to announce or react to something positive. Often appears with an article: una buena noticia (“some good news”) or la buena noticia (“the good news”). Common patterns: “Tengo una buena noticia” (I have good news) and “La buena noticia es que…” (The good news is that…).
target_language_example: Tengo una buena noticia: mañana no hay clase.
native_language_example: I have good news: there’s no class tomorrow.

meaning: a good person; a kind/nice person.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character (that they’re kind, decent, well-intentioned). Often said with the verb "ser" (permanent quality): "Es buena persona". It can also be used about yourself: "Soy una buena persona".
target_language_example: Mi vecino es buena persona y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: My neighbor is a good person and always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck, often on its own ("¡Buena suerte!") or in the phrase "Que tengas buena suerte" ("I hope you have good luck"). It can also refer to luck as a thing ("para la buena suerte", "te dará buena suerte").
target_language_example: ¡Buena suerte en tu examen!
native_language_example: Good luck on your exam!

additional_notes: Means a life that is pleasant/satisfying (health, happiness, comfort, etc.). It can also refer to a comfortable or enjoyable lifestyle ("living well"). In phrases like “Que tengas / Ten una buena vida”, it can sound like a warm wish, or (depending on tone/context) a “goodbye” meaning “have a nice life.”
target_language_example: Después de tantos años de trabajo, por fin vive una buena vida.
native_language_example: After so many years of work, he finally lives a good life.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting in the evening and as a farewell at night (often when people are going to bed). Common in polite speech; you can add a name or title after it (e.g., “buenas noches, Don…”) or address a group (“buenas noches, todos”).
target_language_example: Buenas noches, ¿cómo estuvo tu día?
native_language_example: Good evening, how was your day?

additional_notes: Used to talk about positive information or a favorable update. Often appears with verbs like traer (to bring), tener (to have), escuchar (to hear), or ser (to be): “Ella vino con buenas noticias” / “Esas son buenas noticias.” You can also exclaim it: “¡Qué buenas noticias!”
target_language_example: Tengo buenas noticias: mañana no hay clase.
native_language_example: I have good news: there’s no class tomorrow.

meaning: 'Good afternoon' (also used as a polite 'hello' in the afternoon/evening).
additional_notes: A common greeting used from around midday until nighttime (often until dinner time). It can be used when arriving or when leaving, especially as a polite sign-off (like “good day”). Often followed by a name or title: “Buenas tardes, señor/señora”, “Buenas tardes a todos”.
target_language_example: Buenas tardes, ¿cómo está usted?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how are you?

additional_notes: Common patterns: **ser bueno/a para + infinitive** = to be good at doing something ("Es bueno para cocinar" = "He’s good at cooking"). **ser bueno/a para + noun** = to be good for / useful for / suitable for something ("Bueno para la salud" = "Good for your health"). In phrases like **demasiado bueno para ser verdad**, it means "too good to be true."
target_language_example: No soy muy bueno para hablar en público.
native_language_example: I’m not very good at speaking in public.

additional_notes: With skills or activities, **bueno/a para + (el/la) + noun** often means **good at** (ability), even though a literal translation is “good for.” You can change the activity: *bueno para el fútbol / la natación*. You may also hear **hacerse bueno/a para...** = “to become good at...”.
target_language_example: Tom es bueno para el tenis, sin duda.
native_language_example: Tom is good at tennis, without a doubt.

additional_notes: Used to say something benefits someone or is suitable for them. It can describe health/choices (“Eso no es bueno para ti”) or how someone treats you (“Es demasiado bueno para ti” = he’s too good for you). Note the difference from sarcastic “Good for you!”—in Spanish that’s more often “¡Qué bien por ti!” or “¡Bien por ti!”.
target_language_example: Creo que hacer ejercicio es bueno para ti.
native_language_example: I think exercising is good for you.

additional_notes: Used to react to new information (often like English “good to know”). In real conversations it’s very common to add an object: “Bueno saberlo” (good to know it) or “Es bueno saberlo” (it’s good to know). You may also hear “Qué bueno saberlo” (how good to know that).
target_language_example: Ah, bueno saberlo. Gracias por avisarme.
native_language_example: Oh, good to know. Thanks for letting me know.

additional_notes: Commonly used in the pattern “(Es) bueno verte” or “Qué bueno verte” to greet someone you’re happy to see. Literally “good (to) see you.” You can also say “Es bueno verte también” = “It’s good to see you too.”
target_language_example: ¡Qué bueno verte otra vez!
native_language_example: It’s so good to see you again!

meaning: "Well, now..." (a transition to the next step or what happens next).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to move the conversation forward: introducing the next instruction, conclusion, or new situation. "Bueno" here works like English "well" (a discourse marker), not literally "good." Often followed by what to do next ("Bueno, ahora vas a...") or by something the speaker has just realized/confirmed ("Bueno, ahora lo sabes").
target_language_example: Bueno, ahora vamos a empezar con la primera pregunta.
native_language_example: Well, now we're going to start with the first question.

meaning: “Well, I think…” (used to start a sentence and give your opinion/guess).
additional_notes: Common conversational opener. "Bueno" works like “well/so” to introduce what you’re about to say, often with a slight pause. "Creo que" means “I think (that)…” and is often used to soften what you say (it sounds less direct than stating it as a fact). You can also drop "que" before an infinitive: "Creo ir" is uncommon; more natural: "Creo que voy a ir".
target_language_example: Bueno, creo que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: Well, I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "Well, then…" (a transition to a conclusion or next step).
additional_notes: Common in conversation to wrap up what was just said and move on. It can introduce a decision (“Well then, let’s go”), a conclusion (“Well then, I guess…”), or a change of topic. Often said with a pause after "bueno".
target_language_example: Bueno, entonces quedamos mañana a las ocho.
native_language_example: Well then, we’re meeting tomorrow at eight.

meaning: "Well, it's..." (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational filler at the start of a sentence, often to soften an opinion, react to something, or give an explanation. It’s very common in speech. You’ll usually hear it with a pause after bueno: “Bueno, es…”.
target_language_example: Bueno, es un poco tarde, ¿no?
native_language_example: Well, it’s a bit late, isn’t it?

meaning: "Well, that’s…" / "Well, that is…" (introducing a conclusion or comment).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to react and then state what something is (often summing up, clarifying, or acknowledging a point): “Bueno, esa es la cuestión” = “Well, that’s the question/issue.” You’ll typically finish it with a noun phrase (la cuestión, una teoría, una forma, etc.).
target_language_example: Bueno, esa es la razón por la que no fui.
native_language_example: Well, that’s the reason I didn’t go.

meaning: "Well, that…" (a conversational way to react, introduce a comment, or wrap up a point).
additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker in speech. Often expresses a pause or transition before commenting on something just mentioned (agreement, mild surprise, evaluation, or moving the story along). You’ll also hear it when someone is concluding or summarizing: “Bueno, eso es todo…” (“Well, that’s all…”).
target_language_example: Bueno, eso ya lo sabía.
native_language_example: Well, I already knew that.

meaning: "Well, that's…" / "Well, that is…" (often reacting or concluding).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to react to what someone said (sometimes with a positive/negative opinion), or to wrap up a point. You’ll often hear it before an adjective or phrase: "Bueno, eso es fantástico." It can also stand alone as "Bueno, eso es." meaning "Well, that’s it" / "Well, that’s that."
target_language_example: Bueno, eso es todo por hoy.
native_language_example: Well, that’s all for today.

meaning: “Well, thanks for…” (a polite way to begin thanking someone).
additional_notes: Used to start a thank-you, often when wrapping up a conversation or meeting. "Bueno" works like “well/okay,” softening the transition, and "gracias por" introduces what you’re thankful for: a noun ("gracias por su tiempo" = “thanks for your time”) or an infinitive ("gracias por venir" = “thanks for coming”).
target_language_example: Bueno, gracias por ayudarme hoy.
native_language_example: Well, thanks for helping me today.

additional_notes: "Bueno," is a very common way to start a response (like “well…” in English), often to show a pause, a decision, or mild hesitation. "Lo" is the direct object pronoun meaning “it/that,” and it normally goes before the verb: "Bueno, lo entiendo" = “Well, I understand it.” In the examples, "lo haré" = “I’ll do it,” and "lo sé" = “I know it.”
target_language_example: Bueno, lo entiendo, pero no puedo hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: Well, I understand it, but I can't do it today.

additional_notes: Bueno is often used as a conversational filler/transition meaning “well…/so…”. It’s followed by whatever you’re about to say. The "me" is the pronoun that goes with the next verb (common with reflexive verbs like "me voy" = “I’m leaving”, or with verbs where someone does something to you: "me salvó" = “(he/she) saved me”).
target_language_example: Bueno, me tengo que ir ya.
native_language_example: Well, I have to go now.

meaning: “Well, look…” (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used in conversation as a filler/discourse marker to get someone’s attention or to soften/prepare an explanation, correction, or refusal. Note: in natural Spanish you’ll much more often hear the conjugated form “Bueno, mira, …” (to one person) or “Bueno, miren, …” (to several people); the fixed form “bueno, mirar” is unusual outside of listings/labels.
target_language_example: Bueno, mirar, hoy no puedo quedar.
native_language_example: Well, look, I can’t meet up today.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to disagree gently, correct someone, or backtrack/qualify what was said. Often followed by an explanation: “Bueno, no es que…”, “Bueno, no, no es mi novio.” In speech, the pause/comma matters: “Bueno, no” sounds less blunt than a plain “No.”
target_language_example: —¿Te gustó la película? —Bueno, no… me pareció un poco aburrida.
native_language_example: —Did you like the movie? —Well, no… I thought it was a bit boring.

additional_notes: A very common, casual way to end a conversation. "Bueno" here means something like “well/alright,” and "nos vemos" literally means “we’ll see each other,” used like “see you.” It’s often followed by a time expression: después/luego/mañana/más tarde.
target_language_example: Bueno, nos vemos el lunes.
native_language_example: Alright, see you on Monday.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Spanish to start a response, change the topic, move things along, or wrap up a point. It can signal acceptance/resignation (“well then…”) or simply introduce what comes next. Often followed by another idea: “Bueno, pues vamos.”
target_language_example: Bueno, pues nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Well then, see you tomorrow.

meaning: “Well, if…” (used to introduce a condition or soften what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to sound more polite, hesitant, or to acknowledge what someone said before adding a condition. Common in spoken Spanish: “Bueno, si no es mucha molestia…” = “Well, if it’s not too much trouble…”, “Bueno, si tú lo dices” = “Well, if you say so.”
target_language_example: Bueno, si quieres, podemos hablar mañana.
native_language_example: Well, if you want, we can talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hesitant conclusion, mild resignation, or an uncertain opinion. "Bueno" works like English "well" to start a response or soften what you’re about to say, and "supongo que" expresses that you’re not 100% sure. Often followed by a verb ("...iré", "...podría", "...será mejor") or by "sí/no" ("Bueno, supongo que sí").
target_language_example: Bueno, supongo que podemos intentarlo mañana.
native_language_example: Well, I guess we can try tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to soften or qualify “sí,” often when admitting something, correcting yourself, or agreeing but with reservations. It can be followed by an explanation or a contrast (e.g., “pero…”).
target_language_example: Bueno, sí, tienes razón, pero quería intentarlo de todas formas.
native_language_example: Well, yes, you’re right, but I wanted to try anyway.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying and show uncertainty or reluctance. Often introduces a suggestion, a possibility, or a polite disagreement/hedge (similar to “well, perhaps…”). Can also stand alone as a hesitant reply: “Bueno, tal vez.”
target_language_example: Bueno, tal vez podamos ir mañana si no llueve.
native_language_example: Well, maybe we can go tomorrow if it doesn’t rain.

meaning: “Well, I…” / “Okay, I…” (leading into something addressed to you).
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence in conversation. "Bueno" works like a soft transition (“well/okay”), and "te" is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to you” (e.g., te dije = “I told you”, te dejo = “I’ll leave you / I’m heading out”, te veo luego = “I’ll see you later”). Often sounds like you’re wrapping up, explaining, or emphasizing what you said/will say.
target_language_example: Bueno, te llamo mañana.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll call you tomorrow.

meaning: "Okay, let's..." / "Alright, we're going to..." (to start doing something).
additional_notes: Very common conversational way to introduce the next step or an action you’re about to do. Literally it’s “well, we’re going to…”, but it often works like English “okay, let’s…”. You can follow it with an infinitive: "Bueno, vamos a explicar...", "Bueno, vamos a terminar...".
target_language_example: Bueno, vamos a empezar la reunión.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s start the meeting.

meaning: “Alright, (then)…” / “Okay, now…” (used to move on, wrap up, or show “enough/already”).
additional_notes: A very common conversational opener: **bueno** = “well/alright” and **ya** often means “already/now,” but together they usually work as a discourse marker. It can signal (1) a transition to the next thing (*Bueno, ya llegamos*), (2) that something is enough/should stop (*Bueno, ya es suficiente*), (3) closing a conversation (*Bueno, ya nos veremos*), or (4) “as you already know” (*Bueno, ya sabes...*). Tone depends on context: it can sound neutral or slightly impatient.
target_language_example: Bueno, ya me voy a casa; mañana hablamos.
native_language_example: Alright, I’m going home now; we’ll talk tomorrow.

meaning: "Well, I…" (used to start your response, often emphasizing what *you* think/do).
additional_notes: Used as a conversation opener before stating your point, memory, decision, or opinion. It can also signal a mild contrast with what someone else said ("Well, *I*..."). Common in spoken Spanish; you’ll often hear it with a pause: "Bueno, yo..."
target_language_example: Bueno, yo prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: Well, I’d rather stay home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question, often to move the conversation along, show impatience/surprise, or get to the point (similar to “So, what…?” or “Well then, what…?” in English). You’ll usually see it followed by another clause: “Bueno, ¿qué hacemos?”
target_language_example: Bueno, ¿qué vamos a hacer ahora?
native_language_example: So, what are we going to do now?

meaning: "Well, and…?" / "So…?" (used to ask what happens next or for more details).
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a question to keep the conversation going, shift to the next point, or ask for clarification: "Bueno, ¿y ahora qué?" (So what now?), "Bueno, ¿y después...?" (And after that?), "Bueno, ¿y qué le pasó?" (So what happened to him/her?). It can also show mild surprise or impatience depending on tone ("Pero bueno, ¿y esto?").
target_language_example: Bueno, ¿y entonces qué hacemos?
native_language_example: So, what do we do then?

additional_notes: Used to say people have a friendly relationship. Often appears as “muy buenos amigos” (“very good friends”). It can also imply “just friends” in some contexts, depending on tone.
target_language_example: Somos buenos amigos desde la escuela.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends since school.

additional_notes: A common, polite greeting used in the morning (often until around lunchtime). Written correctly as "buenos días" (with an accent on "días"), but this entry keeps the exact term as provided: "buenos dias". You can use it with strangers, in shops, at work, etc. Often paired with "Hola": "Hola, buenos dias."
target_language_example: Hola, buenos dias. ¿Cómo está?
native_language_example: Hello, good morning. How are you?

additional_notes: Used as a polite greeting in the morning and often up to early afternoon in many Spanish-speaking places. Capitalized at the start of a sentence: “Buenos días”. In sentence 4, “los buenos días” is used as a noun phrase meaning “the good days” (good times) from long ago, not the greeting.
target_language_example: Buenos días, ¿cómo está?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about being polite and showing respect in social situations (for example, greeting people, saying “please/thank you,” not interrupting). It’s often used with the verb tener: “tener buenos modales” = “to have good manners.”
target_language_example: En esta casa, se esperan buenos modales en la mesa.
native_language_example: In this house, good manners at the table are expected.

meaning: “looked for (someone/something) everywhere / all over the place.”
additional_notes: Past participle phrase commonly used with haber (he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han) to form the present perfect: (yo) he buscado…, etc. It often takes an object pronoun (la/lo/los/las/le/te/os) indicating who/what you’ve been searching for; in Spain, le for a male person is also common (leísmo). The phrase is largely compositional: buscado (looked for) + por todas partes (everywhere).
target_language_example: Te he buscado por todas partes, pero no te encontraba.
native_language_example: I’ve looked for you everywhere, but I couldn’t find you.

additional_notes: "Buscando" is the gerund of "buscar" and is used with estar to mean "to be looking for". Use "a" before a direct object that is a specific person (and often pets): "buscando a su hermana", "buscando a Tom". For things/objects, you usually drop "a": "Estoy buscando mi teléfono".
target_language_example: Estoy buscando a mi amigo por toda la casa.
native_language_example: I'm looking for my friend all over the house.

meaning: looking for (someone/something) everywhere; searching all over.
additional_notes: Often used after a form of "estar" (e.g., "he estado", "estuve", "estábamos") to emphasize an ongoing or extensive search across many places, often implying difficulty finding the person/thing. Common with object pronouns before the auxiliary: "lo/la/los/las" (him/her/it/them), "te" (you).
target_language_example: Lo he estado buscando por todas partes.
native_language_example: I’ve been looking for him/it everywhere.

additional_notes: Use "buscar a" when the direct object is a person (or sometimes a pet). The "a" is the personal "a" used with specific people: "Voy a buscar a Ana." With things, you usually drop the "a": "Voy a buscar las llaves."
target_language_example: Voy a buscar a mis hijos a la escuela.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up / look for my kids at school.

meaning: to look for a job; to job hunt.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "buscar" (to look for) + "trabajo" (work/job). Common with "empezar a" (to start) as in "empezar a buscar trabajo" and with movement/purpose expressions like "venir/ir a" (to come/go) to explain why someone goes somewhere: "vino a ... para buscar trabajo".
target_language_example: Tom ha empezado a buscar trabajo.
native_language_example: Tom has started looking for a job.

additional_notes: Used for a phone’s voicemail service/inbox. Common with verbs like ir/mandar/entrar: "Ir/mandar al buzón de voz" = to go/send to voicemail (the call isn’t answered); "Entrar el buzón de voz" = voicemail picks up.
target_language_example: Si no contesto, deja un mensaje en el buzón de voz.
native_language_example: If I don’t answer, leave a message in the voicemail.

meaning: a loose end; an unresolved detail.
additional_notes: Used for a remaining detail or issue that hasn’t been explained or finished. Very common in the phrase “atar cabos sueltos” (to tie up loose ends), especially when talking about investigations, stories, plans, or paperwork.
target_language_example: Antes de entregar el informe, quiero resolver cada cabo suelto.
native_language_example: Before turning in the report, I want to resolve every loose end.

additional_notes: Often used when talking about finishing something completely (a plan, story, investigation, project). Common with the verb "atar": "atar los cabos sueltos" = "to tie up loose ends." You can also say "sin cabos sueltos" to mean "with no loose ends."
target_language_example: Antes de cerrar el caso, tenemos que atar todos los cabos sueltos.
native_language_example: Before closing the case, we have to tie up all the loose ends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or repeats year after year. Often goes at the beginning or end of the sentence: “Cada año…” / “…cada año.”
target_language_example: Cada año viajamos a la misma playa.
native_language_example: Every year we travel to the same beach.

meaning: each person; everyone (individually) — “to each their own.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about people one by one, emphasizing individual responsibility, preference, or situation. Common patterns: “Cada cual + verb” (Cada cual que haga lo suyo = Each person should do their part), “Cada cual a su manera” (each in their own way), “Allá cada cual” (up to each person / to each their own). Often takes singular verbs because it refers to each person individually.
target_language_example: En mi casa, cada cual prepara su desayuno.
native_language_example: In my house, each person makes their own breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens daily as a routine or repeated frequency. It can also emphasize regularity ("day after day"). Often paired with a present tense verb to describe habits: "Vengo aquí cada día".
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio cada día antes del trabajo.
native_language_example: I exercise every day before work.

meaning: with each passing day; as days go by.
additional_notes: Used to show that something changes (often increases or gets worse) over time. It frequently goes with comparisons like “más/menos + adjective/adverb” (e.g., “más guapa”) or with “me duele más”. You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Cada día que pasa me siento más seguro hablando español.
native_language_example: With each passing day, I feel more confident speaking Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens repeatedly once per hour (a schedule: “Toma la medicina cada hora”) or to emphasize that something changes hour by hour (“Empeora a cada hora” = “It’s getting worse every hour”). Often appears as “a cada hora” meaning “every hour / hour by hour.”
target_language_example: El autobús pasa cada hora.
native_language_example: The bus comes every hour.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each morning. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Cada mañana,") or after the verb ("... cada mañana").
target_language_example: Cada mañana voy al trabajo en autobús.
native_language_example: Every morning I go to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency or repetition (something happens every minute), or to emphasize how valuable/urgent time is ("Every minute counts"). Often appears in lists like "cada segundo, cada minuto" for emphasis. With "por" ("por cada minuto") it means "for each minute" when counting or measuring.
target_language_example: Me llama cada minuto para saber si llegué bien.
native_language_example: He calls me every minute to see if I arrived safely.
