additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you mean all the words one by one, not just the general idea. Often appears with translation instructions (Traduce/Traduzca/Traduzcan) or for emphasis like “every word you say…”.
target_language_example: Escuché cada palabra que dijiste.
native_language_example: I listened to every word you said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to people individually in a group (“each person”). Very common with verbs like recibir, tener, dar: “Cada quien recibió…”, “Le dio … a cada quien.” It can also imply “each to their own/each one separately,” especially with actions: “Mejor vamos cada quien a casa” = “Let’s each go home (separately).” Often interchangeable with “cada uno/a,” depending on region and context.
target_language_example: Aquí cada quien paga lo suyo.
native_language_example: Here each person pays for their own.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens continuously or very frequently, or to emphasize that time is extremely important (often with "cada segundo cuenta" = "every second counts"). You can also chain it with other time units for emphasis: "cada segundo, cada minuto, cada día".
target_language_example: En una emergencia, cada segundo cuenta.
native_language_example: In an emergency, every second counts.

additional_notes: Used to describe a repeating schedule or frequency. Common in instructions and routines (especially medical advice): "Toma este medicamento cada seis horas" = take it, then take it again 6 hours later (repeatedly). You can swap the number: "cada cuatro horas" (every four hours), "cada dos días" (every two days).
target_language_example: Pon una alarma: tienes que tomar la pastilla cada seis horas.
native_language_example: Set an alarm: you have to take the pill every six hours.

additional_notes: Used to talk about individuals within a group (“each of them”). It often goes with singular verbs and with possessives like “su” or “propio/a” to show something belongs to each individual: “Cada uno tiene su propio…”. It can also be used after quantities to mean “to each”: “Les di mil yenes a cada uno.”
target_language_example: En el examen, cada uno debe trabajar solo.
native_language_example: In the exam, each person must work alone.

additional_notes: Used to talk about individuals within a group one by one (not the group as a whole). It’s often followed by a plural noun or pronoun: “cada uno de los…” (each of the…), “cada uno de sus…” (each of their…), “cada uno de vosotros/ustedes” (each of you). The verb usually matches “cada uno” (singular): “cada uno de ellos tiene…”.
target_language_example: Cada uno de mis amigos tiene una opinión diferente.
native_language_example: Each of my friends has a different opinion.

meaning: each one of them / each of them.
additional_notes: Used to talk about people or things in a group individually. You can also say “cada una de ellas” for an all-female group, or “cada uno de ellos/ellas” depending on the group. Often followed by a singular verb: “Cada uno de ellos tiene…”. By itself (“Cada uno de ellos.”) it can be a short answer meaning “Each one of them.”
target_language_example: Cada uno de ellos tiene su propia llave.
native_language_example: Each of them has their own key.

additional_notes: Used to talk about every individual person or thing within a specific group, followed by a plural noun: cada uno de los + (plural noun). It agrees in gender/number: cada uno de los (masc. group or mixed), cada una de las (fem. group). Often used with a singular verb because it focuses on each individual: “Cada uno de los niños tiene…”.
target_language_example: Cada uno de los estudiantes tiene su propio libro.
native_language_example: Each of the students has their own book.

meaning: each one of us / each of us.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the members of a group that includes the speaker. Often followed by a verb in the singular: "Cada uno de nosotros tiene..." You can change it to match other groups: "cada uno de ustedes" (each of you), "cada uno de ellos" (each of them).
target_language_example: Cada uno de nosotros tiene una opinión diferente.
native_language_example: Each of us has a different opinion.

additional_notes: Used to address a group directly and refer to them individually. It’s common after verbs like conocer (to know), estar orgulloso de (to be proud of), or trabajar con (to work with). It agrees with the group: for an all-female group you may also hear “cada una de ustedes,” and in informal Spain Spanish you’ll hear “cada uno de vosotros.”
target_language_example: Quiero hablar con cada uno de ustedes después de la reunión.
native_language_example: I want to talk with each one of you after the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that varies from person to person (preferences, ways of doing things, a place, etc.). Literally “each one has his/her…”, but Spanish commonly uses singular "su" even when meaning "their" in English. The noun after "su" shows what each person has (e.g., "cada uno tiene su forma", "cada uno tiene su lugar").
target_language_example: No te preocupes: cada uno tiene su ritmo para aprender.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everyone has their own pace for learning.

additional_notes: Used in two very common patterns: (1) **cada vez que + verb** = “every time/whenever” (e.g., *Cada vez que te escribo...*). (2) **cada vez + más/menos + adjective/adverb** or **cada vez + comparative** = “more and more / less and less / increasingly” (e.g., *cada vez más fuerte, cada vez mejor*). By itself (*Cada vez.*) it can mean “every time” (often implying “as usual/again”).
target_language_example: Cada vez que lo pienso, me parece más importante.
native_language_example: Every time I think about it, it seems more important.

additional_notes: Used to say that something changes gradually over time in the direction of “more” (greater intensity, quantity, frequency, popularity, etc.). Common with verbs like ponerse/hacerse/volverse + adjective (e.g., “cada vez más oscuro”), and with gustar: “Me gusta cada vez más” = “I like it more and more.”
target_language_example: Cada vez más personas trabajan desde casa.
native_language_example: More and more people work from home.

additional_notes: Used to show that something is increasing over time or with each passing occasion (“cada vez” = each time, “más” = more). Often followed by a noun or by an adjective/adverb: “Cada vez más gente…”, “hace cada vez más calor”.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay cada vez más tráfico.
native_language_example: In this city there is more and more traffic.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that happens repeatedly. It’s followed by a verb clause (often in the present tense to talk about a habitual situation).
target_language_example: Cada vez que llamo, no contestas.
native_language_example: Every time I call, you don’t answer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens repeatedly whenever a certain situation occurs. "Cada vez que" = "every time (that)". "La" means "her" (direct object: the woman/girl), and "veo" is "I see" (from "ver"). You can change the pronoun and verb: "cada vez que lo veo" (every time I see him/it), "cada vez que te veo" (every time I see you).
target_language_example: Cada vez que la veo, me pongo nervioso.
native_language_example: Every time I see her, I get nervous.

meaning: “every time I …” / “whenever I …” (introduces something that happens repeatedly).
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause about a repeated situation: "cada vez que" + verb. "Me" is an object/reflexive pronoun that goes with the verb (e.g., me veo = I see myself; me muevo = I move; me pide = asks me). Often followed by the main clause: "Cada vez que me llama, contesto" (Every time he calls me, I answer).
target_language_example: Cada vez que me llama, estoy ocupado.
native_language_example: Every time he calls me, I’m busy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about who reports to whom in an organization (workplace, military, government, etc.). Often appears with verbs like “respetar” (to respect/follow) or “seguir” (to follow) and with “hay”/“existe” to say there is an established hierarchy.
target_language_example: Tienes que respetar la cadena de mando y hablar primero con tu supervisor.
native_language_example: You have to respect the chain of command and talk to your supervisor first.

additional_notes: Common legal term meaning a prison sentence for the rest of someone's life. Often used with verbs like "condenar a" / "sentenciar a" (to sentence to): "Fue condenado a cadena perpetua". In some places it can allow parole after many years, but it generally means "life in prison."
target_language_example: Lo condenaron a cadena perpetua por el crimen.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to life in prison for the crime.

meaning: to like someone; to get along (with someone).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone gives you a good impression or you find them pleasant. It’s commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "me cae bien" (I like him/her / he/she seems nice to me), "te cae bien", "le cae bien", "nos cae bien", "les cae bien". For the opposite, use "caer mal" (to dislike / to rub someone the wrong way).
target_language_example: María me cae bien, pero todavía no la conozco mucho.
native_language_example: I like María (she seems nice to me), but I still don’t know her very well.

meaning: to rub someone the wrong way; to be (un)liked (to give a bad impression).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person (or something they did) causes a negative impression. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: “Me cae mal” = “I don’t like him/her” (literally, “He/She falls badly to me”). You can also use it in past tense for a first impression: “Me cayó mal” = “I didn’t like him/her (when I met them / at that moment).” Opposite: “caer bien” (to be liked).
target_language_example: Ese chico me cae mal porque siempre interrumpe a los demás.
native_language_example: I don’t like that guy because he always interrupts other people.

meaning: to like each other; to get along (to find someone likable).
additional_notes: Used to describe interpersonal chemistry/how well people get along. It commonly appears conjugated with indirect-object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/os/les): “Me caes bien” = “I like you / You seem nice to me.” The infinitive “caerse bien” is often used after verbs like “poder,” “deber,” or “querer,” or when speaking generally (e.g., “Es importante caerse bien”). It’s about personal impression/compatibility, not romantic love.
target_language_example: Es importante caerse bien en el trabajo.
native_language_example: It’s important to get along at work.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "caer bien (a alguien)". It’s used to say you have a good impression of someone or that you find them pleasant (not necessarily romantic). Common patterns: "Me caes bien" (I like you), "Le caes bien" (They like you), and with emphasis "A mí me caes bien" (I like you).
target_language_example: Me caes bien; ¿quieres tomar un café algún día?
native_language_example: I like you; do you want to have coffee sometime?

additional_notes: A polite, common way to order coffee in a café or restaurant. Often said by itself (“Café, por favor.”) or after a request (“Dame un café, por favor.”). You can swap in other items: “Agua, por favor.”
target_language_example: Dame un café, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me a coffee, please.

additional_notes: A very common drink, especially at breakfast. In cafés, you can order it hot; the exact milk/coffee ratio can vary by country or place, but it generally means regular coffee mixed with milk.
target_language_example: ¿Me pone un café con leche, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I have a coffee with milk, please?

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase for talking about your morning routine. "Por la mañana" means "in the morning" (during the morning time). You can swap in other things: "té por la mañana" (tea in the morning), "ejercicio por la mañana" (exercise in the morning).
target_language_example: Siempre necesito café por la mañana para empezar el día.
native_language_example: I always need coffee in the morning to start the day.

additional_notes: Used when ordering coffee to specify no milk (and usually no foam). It can still be served with sugar on the side; say “sin azúcar” if you want it unsweetened. In many places, “un solo” is a common shorthand for “un café solo.”
target_language_example: Para mí, un café solo, sin azúcar, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a black coffee, no sugar, please.

additional_notes: Used to say what kind of box it is or what’s inside: caja de galletas (box of cookies), caja de clavos (box of nails), caja de zapatos (shoebox). Often used when buying or grabbing a packaged box of items: una caja de dulces (a box of candy).
target_language_example: Voy a comprar una caja de té para la oficina.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy a box of tea for the office.

additional_notes: A container/box used to store and carry tools (e.g., a hammer, screwdriver). Often used with verbs like guardar (to store), dejar (to leave), necesitar (to need), or estar en (to be in).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está mi caja de herramientas?
native_language_example: Where is my toolbox?

meaning: music box (a small box that plays music).
additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a small, often decorative box with a mechanism that plays a tune when opened or wound up. Used with articles like "una" or "la": "una caja de música", "la caja de música".
target_language_example: Encontré una caja de música antigua en el ático.
native_language_example: I found an old music box in the attic.

additional_notes: A common noun for a lockable metal box/cabinet used to store money, jewelry, documents, etc. Often used with verbs like guardar (to store), abrir (to open), and poner (to put). Also used in set phrases like combinación de la caja fuerte (the safe’s combination).
target_language_example: Guardé el pasaporte en la caja fuerte del hotel.
native_language_example: I stored my passport in the hotel safe.

meaning: “black box” (a device/record, or something mysterious with hidden contents).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to an airplane’s flight recorder (“la caja negra del avión”). More broadly, it can mean something whose internal workings or information are unknown/hidden (like “a black box in someone’s mind”), or a box/container that’s literally black in color depending on context.
target_language_example: Todavía no saben qué pasó hasta que analicen la caja negra del avión.
native_language_example: They still don’t know what happened until they analyze the plane’s black box.

additional_notes: Used in stores and restaurants for the machine where the cashier enters purchases and takes payment. You’ll often hear it with verbs like "pagar en la caja" (pay at the register) or "abrir/cerrar la caja" (open/close the register).
target_language_example: Puede pagar con tarjeta en la caja registradora.
native_language_example: You can pay by card at the cash register.

meaning: to shut up; to silence someone.
additional_notes: Often used as a strong command (e.g., “¡Calla la boca!”) or to emphasize forcing someone to stop talking (e.g., “Le hicieron callar la boca”). It’s rude/harsh, so avoid using it with strangers or in polite situations; “cállate” or “guarda silencio” are softer alternatives depending on context.
target_language_example: ¡Calla la boca y escucha un momento!
native_language_example: Shut up and listen for a moment!

meaning: a dead end (street); a dead end / no way out (situation).
additional_notes: Literally “alley/street without an exit.” Used both for a real dead-end street and, figuratively, for a situation with no solution or escape ("I'm stuck / there's no way out"). In speech it can also be said alone to mean “dead end.”
target_language_example: Seguimos caminando y terminamos en un callejón sin salida.
native_language_example: We kept walking and ended up at a dead end.

meaning: the calm before the storm (a quiet moment before trouble or intense activity).
additional_notes: Used literally for weather, but more often as a metaphor: a peaceful or quiet period right before an argument, crisis, busy time, or other difficult situation. Often appears with ser/estar: «Es/era la calma antes de la tormenta».
target_language_example: Disfrutemos este rato; es la calma antes de la tormenta.
native_language_example: Let’s enjoy this moment; it’s the calm before the storm.

meaning: to change (from one thing to another).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to show what you’re switching: cambiar de + noun (often without an article). Common with things like clothes (cambiar de chaqueta), rooms (cambiar de habitación), passwords (cambiar de contraseña), habits, plans, etc. It emphasizes switching to a different one, not just modifying the same thing.
target_language_example: Voy a cambiar de número de teléfono.
native_language_example: I’m going to change my phone number.

additional_notes: Used when someone decides differently than before (e.g., after thinking more or getting new information). Conjugate "cambiar" to match the subject (puedo/puedes/puede/podemos/pueden cambiar de idea). Often used with "todavía" (“still”) to suggest there’s still time to decide differently.
target_language_example: Lo pensé mejor y decidí cambiar de idea.
native_language_example: I thought about it more and decided to change my mind.

additional_notes: Used when someone stops thinking/feeling one way and decides or believes something different. Very common with verbs like “hacer” (to make someone change their mind): “me hizo cambiar de opinión” = “it made me change my mind.” Often used with “no” to say someone won’t change their mind: “No le harás cambiar de opinión.”
target_language_example: Lo pensé mejor y decidí cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: I thought about it again and decided to change my mind.

additional_notes: Used for big ambitions or plans to make society/life better (or sometimes to radically transform things, even negatively, depending on context). It often implies making a major impact beyond just personal change.
target_language_example: Quiero cambiar el mundo, aunque sea poco a poco.
native_language_example: I want to change the world, even if it’s little by little.

meaning: to change things (to improve a situation).
additional_notes: Often used when talking about changing a situation, how something works, or the current state of affairs—not just switching one object for another. You can add context with phrases like "en mi país" (in my country), "aquí" (here), or "para mejor" (for the better).
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando para cambiar las cosas en nuestra comunidad.
native_language_example: We’re working to change things in our community.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say what is being changed: cambio de ropa (change of clothes), cambio de planes (change of plans), cambio de ambiente (change of scenery/atmosphere), cambio de ritmo (change of pace). It often implies switching to something different or making an adjustment.
target_language_example: Tuvimos un cambio de planes y nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: We had a change of plans and stayed home.

meaning: on the way to; heading to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about movement toward a destination (literal or figurative). Often appears as “(ir/estar/venir) camino a + place” (e.g., “Voy camino a mi casa”) and can also be used like “camino a + noun” in a metaphorical sense (“camino a la felicidad”).
target_language_example: Estamos camino al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We’re on the way to the airport.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while you are traveling/heading home. You’ll also see it as “de camino a casa” or “ir/venir camino a casa” (to be on the way home).
target_language_example: Te llamo camino a casa.
native_language_example: I'll call you on my way home.

additional_notes: Most commonly used like "camino de + place/person" to mean you are going toward a destination: "camino de casa" = "on my way home". In more descriptive writing, "un camino de + noun" can mean "a path/road of ..." (e.g., "un camino de oscuridad" = "a path of darkness").
target_language_example: Compré pan camino de casa.
native_language_example: I bought bread on the way home.

meaning: "field of" / "(sports) field"; sometimes "camp of" (e.g., a prison/concentration camp).
additional_notes: Used to build common nouns with de: campo de juego (playing field), campo de fútbol/hockey (soccer/hockey field), campo de maíz/girasoles (corn/sunflower field), campo de concentración (concentration camp), campo de visión (field of view/vision). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Hay un campo de fútbol cerca de mi casa.
native_language_example: There’s a soccer field near my house.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the area where a battle is fought (often with the verb "salir/ir al campo de batalla" = "to go out to the battlefield"). It’s also used figuratively to mean a place or situation of intense conflict (e.g., "El amor es un campo de batalla").
target_language_example: Después de la explosión, la calle parecía un campo de batalla.
native_language_example: After the explosion, the street looked like a battlefield.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a prison camp where large groups of people are detained, often in wartime and especially associated with Nazi Germany in World War II. It’s a very serious, historical term. Plural: campos de concentración.
target_language_example: Los prisioneros huyeron del campo de concentración.
native_language_example: The prisoners escaped from the concentration camp.

additional_notes: A very common, neutral phrase. Use it after verbs like escuchar (to hear/listen to), oír (to hear), empezar a/comenzar a (to start to), and seguir (to follow/continue). In Spanish you often say: escuchar/oír a + person + infinitive (e.g., Escuché a Tom cantar una canción).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes cantar una canción conmigo?
native_language_example: Can you sing a song with me?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about how much of something there is. It often comes with adjectives like cierta (a certain), mucha (a lot of), inmensa (a huge), or una gran (a great/large).
target_language_example: Necesito una pequeña cantidad de dinero para el autobús.
native_language_example: I need a small amount of money for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how much money there is, usually with an adjective (una pequeña/gran/fuerte cantidad de dinero) or with “cualquier” (“any amount of money”). In sentence 4, “esa cantidad de dinero” means “that amount of money” (referring to a specific sum mentioned or understood).
target_language_example: Necesito una cierta cantidad de dinero para el viaje.
native_language_example: I need a certain amount of money for the trip.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of cantar (“to sing”): cantó = “sang” (completed action). Often followed by details like the type of song or language (una canción japonesa / en inglés). You can replace the subject: Yo canté una canción, Nosotros cantamos una canción.
target_language_example: Anoche cantó una canción en la cena.
native_language_example: Last night, he/she sang a song at dinner.

additional_notes: Used as part of the structure "ser capaces de + infinitive" to express ability, capability, possibility, or managing to do something. It agrees in number and gender with the subject: "capaz de" (sing. masc.), "capaz de" (sing. fem. is also "capaz"), "capaces de" (plural), "capaces de" (plural fem. also "capaces"). Often used in various tenses: "somos/eran/seremos capaces de..."; "fuimos capaces de..." can imply a concrete achievement (similar to "we managed to").
target_language_example: Finalmente fuimos capaces de resolver el asunto.
native_language_example: In the end we were able to resolve the matter.

meaning: "ability/capacity to" (do something); also "a capacity of" (amount it can hold).
additional_notes: Often followed by an infinitive: capacidad de + verb (e.g., capacidad de hacer/pensar). With containers/limits, it’s followed by a number + unit: capacidad de treinta litros / capacidad de mil (places, people, etc.).
target_language_example: No tengo la capacidad de hacerlo solo.
native_language_example: I don't have the ability to do it alone.

meaning: ability/capacity to (do something); room for (a number of people/things).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean someone’s ability to do something (capacidad para + infinitive: "capacidad para hablar"). It’s also used with quantities to mean how many people/things something can hold ("capacidad para treinta personas"). Common with verbs like tener/adquirir/perder and nouns like falta de.
target_language_example: No tengo la capacidad para hacer todo esto solo.
native_language_example: I don't have the ability to do all of this alone.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having the ability or skill to do something. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (capaz de + infinitive): "capaz de responder", "capaz de cruzar". In some contexts it can also suggest "likely to" (especially with the future), but the basic meaning is ability.
target_language_example: No soy capaz de abrir esta botella.
native_language_example: I can't manage to open this bottle.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability or what they might do in a situation. It’s often followed by an infinitive (capaz de + infinitive): capaz de hacer, capaz de entender, capaz de venir. In negative form: no soy capaz de hacerlo = “I’m not able to do it.” You can also use it for emotional extremes: no sabes de lo que soy capaz (de hacer) = “you don’t know what I’m capable of (doing).”
target_language_example: No me sentía capaz de hacerlo solo, pero lo intenté.
native_language_example: I didn’t feel able to do it alone, but I tried.

meaning: "capital of" (the capital city of a place).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to identify a country/region’s capital city: “Madrid, capital de España.” Note that “capital” can also mean “money/assets” (e.g., “un capital de un millón de dólares”), but in that sense it’s usually not the fixed phrase “capital de” meaning “capital of.”
target_language_example: Bogotá es la capital de Colombia.
native_language_example: Bogotá is the capital of Colombia.

additional_notes: Used to name the leader of a team. Often appears with the verb elegir (“to choose/select”): "Elegimos a X capitán de nuestro equipo" / "Lo elegimos capitán de nuestro equipo" (we chose him as captain). "Capitán" is masculine; the feminine form is "capitana".
target_language_example: ¿Quién es el capitán de nuestro equipo este año?
native_language_example: Who is the captain of our team this year?

additional_notes: Used to name the leader/representative of a team (often in sports). You can use it with the verb "ser" (Soy el capitán del equipo) or with "nombrar" (Lo nombraron capitán del equipo = They named him team captain).
target_language_example: Nuestro capitán del equipo habla con el árbitro.
native_language_example: Our team captain speaks with the referee.

additional_notes: Used to show orientation or position relative to something, similar to "frente a". It’s usually followed by a noun (often with an article): "cara a la puerta" (facing the door). Common in the fixed expression "cara a cara" = "face to face."
target_language_example: Se puso cara a la pared para que no lo vieran.
native_language_example: He stood facing the wall so they wouldn’t see him.

meaning: face to face; in direct confrontation.
additional_notes: Used for meeting or seeing someone in person (not online/over the phone), or for confronting something directly (a person, an enemy, reality, a problem). It can also be used as a noun phrase: "el cara a cara" = a face-to-face meeting or showdown.
target_language_example: Prefiero hablarlo cara a cara.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk about it face to face.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does not have good practical judgment. It often sounds critical. The verb is usually "carecer de" (to lack), conjugated: "carezco", "careces", "carece", "carecemos", "carecéis", "carecen". You can add the subject for clarity: "Él/Ella carece de sentido común".
target_language_example: Aunque es muy inteligente, carece de sentido común.
native_language_example: Although he’s very intelligent, he lacks common sense.

additional_notes: Used in science/physics to talk about the property of particles or objects that can be positive or negative (e.g., electrons = negative, protons = positive). Often appears with verbs like tener (“to have”) or with adjectives like positiva/negativa, and with intensity words like enorme (“enormous”).
target_language_example: Este objeto tiene carga eléctrica positiva.
native_language_example: This object has a positive electric charge.

meaning: "responsibility for / in charge of" (often in *hacerse cargo de*), or "the position/role of".
additional_notes:
Very common in these patterns:
- **hacerse cargo de + noun** = to take care of / take responsibility for something or someone. (e.g., *Tom se hará cargo de todo*.)
- **estar a cargo de + noun** = to be in charge of. (e.g., *Ella está a cargo del proyecto*.)
- **el cargo de + job title** = the position/role of. (e.g., *el cargo de locutor* = the announcer position.)
Be careful: **cargo** is a false friend with English **cargo** (freight). Here it usually means “responsibility/position,” not “freight.”
target_language_example: ¿Quién se hace cargo de los niños esta noche?
native_language_example: Who’s taking care of the kids tonight?

additional_notes: A common food term. It can be used generally (La carne de cerdo tiene mucha grasa) or to specify what you want in a dish (Quiero carne de cerdo). Often contrasted with other meats like pollo (chicken) or res/vacuno (beef).
target_language_example: ¿Tienen tacos de carne de cerdo?
native_language_example: Do you have pork tacos?

additional_notes: Commonly used for ground beef/pork, etc. You’ll hear it when shopping or cooking (e.g., for meatballs, burgers, or meatloaf). Also used as an adjective phrase: "pastel de carne picada" = a pie/loaf made with ground meat.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes carne picada de ternera?
native_language_example: Do you have ground beef?

additional_notes: Refers to meat like beef (carne de res/vaca), pork (cerdo), or lamb (cordero), as opposed to white meat (carne blanca) like chicken (pollo) or turkey (pavo). Often used when talking about diet, nutrition, or restaurant menus.
target_language_example: En este restaurante sirven mucha carne roja.
native_language_example: At this restaurant they serve a lot of red meat.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for a romantic letter written to someone you love. You can also say "una carta de amor" (a love letter) or "cartas de amor" (love letters).
target_language_example: Le escribí una carta de amor.
native_language_example: I wrote him/her a love letter.

meaning: a country house; a house in the countryside (often a weekend/summer home).
additional_notes: Used for a house outside the city, typically in a rural area. It can be a second home for weekends or vacations; in some contexts it may be quite simple (even a small house on a plot of land). Often used with verbs like ir a / estar en / pasar el fin de semana en la casa de campo.
target_language_example: Este verano vamos a pasar un mes en la casa de campo.
native_language_example: This summer we’re going to spend a month at the country house.

additional_notes: Used to say that a house is believed to have ghosts or a supernatural presence. Common with "dicen que..." (they say that...), "se dice que..." (it’s said that...), or "según la leyenda..." (according to legend...). Often appears as "La casa está embrujada" or "Esta casa está embrujada".
target_language_example: No quiero entrar; la casa está embrujada.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go in; the house is haunted.

meaning: new house (a newly bought or newly built home).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a house that is new to the owner (recently purchased or moved into), not necessarily newly constructed. The adjective typically goes after the noun: casa nueva.
target_language_example: Estamos muy contentos con nuestra casa nueva.
native_language_example: We’re very happy with our new house.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine subject (ella, mi hermana, etc.): «estar casada con + un/una + person» = current marital status (“is married to”). With «estar» it focuses on the state; with «ser/era» it can sound more descriptive and is common in narration. Change «un» to «una» depending on the person: «casada con una mujer». For a man: «casado con».
target_language_example: Mi tía está casada con un médico.
native_language_example: My aunt is married to a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the range of things is very broad, but not 100% (there are a few exceptions). Often appears with verbs like ver (to see), comer (to eat), poder (can), and estar dispuesto/a a (to be willing to).
target_language_example: Con suficiente tiempo, puedo aprender casi cualquier cosa.
native_language_example: With enough time, I can learn almost anything.

meaning: "I almost..." / "I nearly..." (something almost happened to me, or I almost did something).
additional_notes: Use "casi" before an object pronoun like "me" when the verb affects you (or you’re the one who would have done it): "Casi me desmayo" = I almost fainted; "Casi me pega" = He/She almost hits me. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the past: "casi me morí", "casi me matan") and expresses that it did NOT actually happen, but came close.
target_language_example: Casi me caigo en la calle.
native_language_example: I almost fell in the street.

additional_notes: Used to say that very few people (almost none) do something or know something. It’s a common combination of "casi" (almost) + "nadie" (nobody) and is followed by a verb: "Casi nadie + verb".
target_language_example: En mi clase, casi nadie llega temprano.
native_language_example: In my class, hardly anyone arrives early.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to talk about something that happens very infrequently. It often goes right before the verb ("casi nunca como..."), but it can also come at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Casi nunca como...").
target_language_example: Casi nunca salimos entre semana.
native_language_example: We almost never go out during the week.

meaning: almost never (with “se” before a reflexive/reciprocal verb).
additional_notes: Use **casi nunca** to say something happens very rarely. The **se** is the reflexive/reciprocal pronoun that goes before the verb: **casi nunca se ríe** (she almost never laughs), **casi nunca se enferma** (he almost never gets sick). With plural subjects it can be reciprocal: **casi nunca se veían** = “they almost never saw each other.”
target_language_example: Mis padres casi nunca se pelean.
native_language_example: My parents almost never argue.

additional_notes: Used before a verb with **se** (often reflexive or in accidental constructions) to say an event nearly occurred: **casi se muere** = “he almost died,” **casi se cae** = “he almost fell,” **casi se me olvida** = “I almost forgot.” Word order is typically **casi + se + verb** (with any extra pronouns like *me/le* in between: *casi se me olvida*).
target_language_example: Casi se me cae el teléfono.
native_language_example: I almost dropped my phone.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of reflexive verb ahogarse (“to drown; to choke”). Used for accidents or near-accidents, often involving water (drown) or something stuck (choke). You can change the subject and keep the same form: Yo casi me ahogué, tú casi te ahogaste, él/ella casi se ahogó.
target_language_example: En la piscina, mi primo casi se ahogó.
native_language_example: In the pool, my cousin almost drowned.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to say something happens most of the time, but not 100%. It commonly goes before the main verb (e.g., “casi siempre voy…”) or right after the subject (“Yo casi siempre…”).
target_language_example: Yo casi siempre desayuno en casa.
native_language_example: I almost always eat breakfast at home.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to say that nearly all of them are included. It agrees with feminine plural nouns: casi todos los (masculine), casi todas las (feminine). Often followed by “otras” (other), e.g., “casi todas las otras…” = “almost all the other…”.
target_language_example: Casi todas las tiendas están cerradas hoy.
native_language_example: Almost all the shops are closed today.

additional_notes: Used before a plural masculine noun to say that nearly the whole group is included. It agrees with the noun: for feminine plural use "casi todas las" (e.g., "casi todas las personas"). You can also use it with time expressions: "casi todos los viernes" = "almost every Friday".
target_language_example: Casi todos los días salgo a caminar.
native_language_example: I go out for a walk almost every day.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very frequently, but not literally daily. Often placed after the verb (e.g., "Voy casi todos los días") or at the beginning/end of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio casi todos los días.
native_language_example: I exercise almost every day.

additional_notes: Often used as "un/una caso de + noun" to describe an incident or medical/legal situation: "un caso de asesinato" (a murder case), "un caso de muerte" (a case involving a death). Also appears in the common expression "hacer caso de" = "to pay attention to / heed" (e.g., "Haz caso de su consejo" = Heed his/her advice).
target_language_example: Es un caso de fraude muy grave.
native_language_example: It’s a very serious case of fraud.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something) is unlikely to improve, change, or succeed. It’s often said jokingly or as a criticism: “Eres un caso perdido” = “You’re a lost cause.” You can use it with ser (eres/soy) or about a situation: “Esto es un caso perdido.”
target_language_example: No intentes convencerlo; es un caso perdido.
native_language_example: Don’t try to convince him; he’s a lost cause.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as **en caso que + verb** to introduce a possible situation and what to do if it happens. It often appears with the subjunctive (e.g., *en caso que llueva*). Similar to **por si** (“just in case”), but **en caso que** is a bit more formal and explicit.
target_language_example: En caso que llegues tarde, llámame.
native_language_example: In case you arrive late, call me.

additional_notes: Most often used to talk about the reason something happens: *la causa de + noun* (“the cause of + noun”). It can sometimes refer to a cause/campaign someone supports (*la causa de la ciencia*, *la causa de Morales*), meaning “the cause/campaign for…”. In many contexts you’ll also hear **a causa de** (“because of / due to”), which is very similar but more explicitly means “due to.”
target_language_example: La causa del problema fue un error en el sistema.
native_language_example: The cause of the problem was an error in the system.

additional_notes: Usually used as **a causa del** or **por causa del** + a noun to give the reason for something. **Del** = **de + el** (“of the”). With feminine nouns: **a causa de la** / **por causa de la**.
target_language_example: No salimos a causa del tráfico.
native_language_example: We didn’t go out because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of caer (“to fall”). It’s commonly used for a person or an object falling from a tree. Very often you’ll also hear/see it with the reflexive pronoun: “se cayó del árbol,” which is the most natural way to say someone fell (accidentally). For objects like fruit, “cayó del árbol” is common without “se.”
target_language_example: El niño se cayó del árbol y se lastimó la pierna.
native_language_example: The boy fell from the tree and hurt his leg.

additional_notes: This is a common storytelling pattern: **cayó** (“(he/she) fell”) + **y se + verb**. The **se** is reflexive and is often used with injury/accident verbs like **golpearse** (to hit/strike oneself), **hacerse daño** (to hurt oneself), **darse con** (to hit oneself against). Subject pronouns are usually omitted in Spanish, so you’ll often just see **cayó y se…** in the past tense. (Also very common: **se cayó** = “(he/she) fell down”.)
target_language_example: María cayó y se lastimó la muñeca.
native_language_example: María fell and hurt her wrist.

additional_notes: Uses the vosotros form (Spain) in the simple past (pretérito) of **ceder**: **cedisteis** = “you all gave in/yielded.” It’s commonly followed by **a** + a noun: **ceder a la tentación** (“to give in to temptation”). You can negate it with **nunca/jamás** (“never”).
target_language_example: Al final, cedisteis a la tentación y comisteis el postre.
native_language_example: In the end, you all gave in to temptation and ate dessert.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **ceder a** = “to give in to / to yield to” something. **Cedió** is the simple past (pretérito) form, so it describes a finished action in the past. You can change the subject: **Yo cedí**, **tú cediste**, **ella/él cedió**, etc. Often used with **la tentación** (temptation) but also with other things: *ceder a la presión* (give in to pressure).
target_language_example: Al final, cedió a la tentación y comió el pastel.
native_language_example: In the end, he gave in to temptation and ate the cake.

additional_notes: A common place word meaning a large building/area with many stores. Often used with ir a (to go to): ir al centro comercial. Uses masculine articles (el/al).
target_language_example: Vamos al centro comercial esta tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to the shopping mall this afternoon.

meaning: "center" or "facility" for a specific activity (e.g., a control center).
additional_notes: Used to form common nouns: "centro de" + noun = a place dedicated to that purpose (centro de control, centro de detención, centro de investigación, centro de llamadas). It’s often translated as “(something) center” or “(something) facility.”
target_language_example: Hay un centro de salud en mi barrio.
native_language_example: There’s a health center in my neighborhood.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun (me) because the action is done to yourself. You can change it depending on the subject: cepillarme (myself), cepillarte (yourself), cepillarse (himself/herself/yourself formal/themselves). Also common with time expressions like después de comer (after eating) or después de despertar (after waking up).
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, tengo que cepillarme los dientes.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, I have to brush my teeth.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun because it’s something you do to yourself: cepillarte (to brush yourself). You can swap the pronoun for other people: cepillarme/cepillarte/cepillarse/cepillarnos/cepillaros/cepillarse los dientes. Common with commands and routines: "Andá a..." (Go...) and "Tienes que..." (You have to...).
target_language_example: No se te olvide cepillarte los dientes antes de dormir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to brush your teeth before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Common everyday item. Often used with possessives (mi/tu/su) and verbs like usar (to use), cambiar (to change/replace), and olvidar (to forget). You can specify the type, e.g., “cepillo de dientes eléctrico” (electric toothbrush).
target_language_example: ¿Trajiste tu cepillo de dientes?
native_language_example: Did you bring your toothbrush?

additional_notes: An informal command (tú) telling one person to brush their teeth. It uses the reflexive form of cepillar: cepillarse (to brush oneself). Often followed by cuándo (when) or después de... (after...).
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, cepíllate los dientes.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, brush your teeth.

additional_notes: Used to express physical proximity. It’s often followed by a person, place, or object (cerca de mí, cerca de la casa). It can also be used with numbers to mean “about/approximately” (cerca de 10 minutos), but here it’s about being nearby.
target_language_example: Mi teléfono está cerca de la cama.
native_language_example: My phone is near the bed.

additional_notes: Used to say something is nearby your current location. Often with verbs like estar, quedar, haber, vivir, or to describe where something happened (e.g., I lost it near here). You can also use it alone as a short answer: “Cerca de aquí.”
target_language_example: ¿Hay algún restaurante cerca de aquí?
native_language_example: Is there a restaurant near here?

additional_notes: Used to talk about physical proximity to a feminine noun (la + noun): cerca de la biblioteca, cerca de la estación. With masculine nouns, use cerca del (cerca de + el). It can also be used for things passing near something: Pasó cerca de la Tierra.
target_language_example: Hay un café cerca de la plaza.
native_language_example: There’s a café near the plaza.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located close to a station (often a train or metro station). You can replace “la estación” with another place: “cerca del hotel” (near the hotel), “cerca de aquí” (near here). “Cerca de” can also be used with time/amounts (e.g., “cerca de las seis” = around six), but in these examples it’s about location.
target_language_example: Hay un café cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: There’s a café near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located a short distance from the beach. You can swap in other places: cerca de la escuela (near the school), cerca del centro (near downtown). Note: cerca de is often followed by de; when the next word is el, it becomes del (cerca del hotel).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos en un apartamento cerca de la playa.
native_language_example: We’re staying in an apartment near the beach.

additional_notes: Used to describe a location close to a window. Often follows verbs like estar (to be), poner (to put), or quedar (to be located). You can swap the noun: cerca de la puerta (near the door), cerca de la mesa (near the table).
target_language_example: Quiero sentarme cerca de la ventana.
native_language_example: I want to sit near the window.

meaning: near my house (close to where I live).
additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happened in the area around your home. Often used with "hay" (there is/are): "Hay un parque cerca de mi casa." You can swap the possessive to match the person: cerca de tu/su/nuestra casa.
target_language_example: Hay un supermercado cerca de mi casa.
native_language_example: There’s a supermarket near my house.

additional_notes: Used to say something is at a short distance from a place or thing: cerca del ascensor, cerca del puente. It can also be used with times to mean “around/about” a time: cerca del mediodía (“around noon”). It’s the contraction of cerca de + el → cerca del. With feminine nouns, use cerca de la (e.g., cerca de la estación).
target_language_example: La farmacia está cerca del hotel.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is near the hotel.

meaning: near the sea; close to the ocean.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located not far from the sea. You can also hear: "cerca de la playa" (near the beach) or simply "cerca del océano" (near the ocean). It often goes with verbs like "vivir" (to live) or "estar" (to be located).
target_language_example: Nos hospedamos cerca del mar para ir a la playa todos los días.
native_language_example: We’re staying near the sea so we can go to the beach every day.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located close to the park. "cerca de" = "near/close to" and it’s often followed by a place (cerca de la escuela, cerca del centro). "del" is a contraction of "de + el" (so: cerca de + el parque → cerca del parque).
target_language_example: Hay una cafetería cerca del parque.
native_language_example: There’s a café near the park.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located close to a river. Often follows verbs like estar (Su casa está cerca del río) or is used as a place description (La batalla tuvo lugar cerca del río...). You can also say cerca de + [place]: cerca de la casa (near the house), cerca del parque (near the park).
target_language_example: Vamos a caminar cerca del río esta tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to walk near the river this afternoon.

additional_notes: A noun for the animal that eats ants and termites. Despite the literal words (“pig” + “ant”), it refers specifically to an aardvark (not a pig). Usually used with the article: el/la cerdo hormiguero.
target_language_example: En el zoológico vimos un cerdo hormiguero comiendo hormigas.
native_language_example: At the zoo we saw an aardvark eating ants.

additional_notes: Used to describe a door, gate, room, etc. that has been locked. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: cerradA con llave (fem. singular, e.g., la puerta), cerradO con llave (masc. singular, e.g., el portón), cerradAS con llave, cerradOS con llave. Often with estar: "La puerta está cerrada con llave" = "The door is locked."
target_language_example: La puerta del garaje está cerrada con llave.
native_language_example: The garage door is locked.

additional_notes: Literally “to close the beak.” It’s an insulting, informal way to tell someone to stop talking, often used as an imperative: “¡Cierra el pico!” You’ll also hear “Cierra el pico, por favor” (still rude despite “please”). A more neutral alternative is “cállate” (still direct) or “guarda silencio” (more formal).
target_language_example: Mejor cierra el pico y déjame hablar.
native_language_example: You’d better shut up and let me talk.

meaning: to shut up; to close your mouth.
additional_notes: Literally “to close the mouth.” In everyday speech it often means “to stop talking,” and can sound rude or like a strong command depending on tone (similar to “shut up”). It commonly appears conjugated (e.g., “cierra la boca”), but the base multi-word term is “cerrar la boca.” A frequent alternative is “cállate.”
target_language_example: Tienes que cerrar la boca un momento y escucharme.
native_language_example: You have to shut up for a moment and listen to me.

meaning: 'to close the door' (sometimes 'to lock the door' if "con llave" is added).
additional_notes: Used for physically shutting a door. Add "con llave" to specify locking it: "cerrar la puerta con llave" = "to lock the door." Often used in reminders and requests (e.g., "Asegúrate de..." = "Make sure to...").
target_language_example: Asegúrate de cerrar la puerta cuando te vayas.
native_language_example: Make sure to close the door when you leave.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) of "cerrar": "cerró" = "(he/she/it) closed". Subject is often implied in Spanish (él/ella/eso). Used for a completed action, including when something non-human causes it: "La corriente de aire cerró la puerta" = "The draft closed the door."
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, cerró la puerta.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, he/she closed the door.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of “cerrar los ojos” (to close one’s eyes). Used to describe a completed action, often to listen better, pretend to sleep, or fall asleep. You can change the subject pronoun or add a name: “Tom cerró los ojos”.
target_language_example: Cerró los ojos por un momento para relajarse.
native_language_example: He/She closed his/her eyes for a moment to relax.

meaning: a scapegoat; someone blamed for a problem (often unfairly).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a person who takes the blame so others don’t have to. Often appears with verbs like ser (to be) or necesitar (to need): “X es el chivo expiatorio” / “Necesitan un chivo expiatorio.”
target_language_example: No me culpes a mí; no soy tu chivo expiatorio.
native_language_example: Don’t blame me; I’m not your scapegoat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of 100 years, often in historical context (e.g., events that happened “hace cien años” = “100 years ago,” or that lasted “cien años” = “for 100 years”). Related phrase: “un siglo” = “a century.”
target_language_example: Mis bisabuelos llegaron a este país hace cien años.
native_language_example: My great-grandparents arrived in this country 100 years ago.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money. It can appear alone as a short answer (e.g., “¿Cuánto cuesta?” — “Cien dólares.”). Before a noun, Spanish uses the shortened form “cien” (not “ciento”): “cien dólares”, “cien personas”. With a specific noun like “billete” (bill/banknote), Spanish often uses “de”: “un billete de cien dólares”.
target_language_example: ¿Cuánto cuesta la entrada? Cien dólares.
native_language_example: How much is the ticket? One hundred dollars.

additional_notes: Used to state the number 100,000. It can be part of a longer phrase (e.g., "cien mil hombres") or said by itself as an answer. Before a noun, Spanish typically doesn’t add “of” like English does (“cien mil calles” = “one hundred thousand streets”).
target_language_example: Vendieron cien mil entradas en un día.
native_language_example: They sold one hundred thousand tickets in one day.

additional_notes: A common genre label for books, movies, and TV. Often used with "de": "una novela de ciencia ficción" (a science-fiction novel). It can also be said on its own as an exclamation or label (e.g., reacting to something that seems unreal or futuristic).
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta la ciencia ficción o prefieres la fantasía?
native_language_example: Do you like science fiction, or do you prefer fantasy?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to give an approximate large number (not necessarily exactly 200, 300, etc.). Often appears in bigger expressions like "cientos de miles" (hundreds of thousands). With time expressions it can mean "for hundreds of...": "en cientos de años" = "in hundreds of years" / "for hundreds of years."
target_language_example: Recibimos cientos de mensajes en un solo día.
native_language_example: We received hundreds of messages in a single day.

additional_notes: An aggressive command (imperative) telling someone to stop talking. Literally “close your beak,” where pico means “beak” and, informally, “mouth.” Common in Spain and often appears with insults (as in the examples). Use with caution—it can easily start a fight.
target_language_example: ¡Cierra el pico y déjame en paz!
native_language_example: Shut up and leave me alone!

additional_notes: This is the tú imperative of cerrar (to close) + la ("the" for feminine nouns). It’s used to tell someone to close something: cierra la ventana (window), cierra la puerta (door), cierra la persiana (blind/shutter). With body parts it can mean “shut”: cierra la boca = “shut your mouth.” Adding insults (e.g., “puta”) makes it very rude/offensive.
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta, por favor.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

additional_notes: Imperative command using (tú): cerrar = to close, la boca = the mouth. Usually rude or aggressive; in arguments it can be a direct insult or threat. In calmer contexts it can mean “be quiet” (often to listen), but it still sounds harsh—"cállate" is similar, and "guarda silencio" is more polite.
target_language_example: Por favor, cierra la boca y escucha un momento.
native_language_example: Please, be quiet and listen for a moment.

additional_notes: Command (tú) form of **cerrar** used to tell one person informally to close the door. Often used with suggestions or urgency (e.g., **mejor** = “you’d better”, **rápidamente** = “quickly”). For a more formal command to one person, use **cierre la puerta**.
target_language_example: Por favor, cierra la puerta cuando salgas.
native_language_example: Please close the door when you leave.

additional_notes: An instruction/command using the tú form (from cerrar). It can be used literally (to shut your eyes) or as a calming/imagining prompt (e.g., before counting or listening). For other people: “cierre los ojos” (usted), “cierren los ojos” (ustedes).
target_language_example: Cierra los ojos un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Close your eyes for a moment, please.

additional_notes: This is the formal usted imperative of cerrar (“to close”), used in polite requests or instructions (often with por favor). For an informal command to a friend/family member, you’d say: Cierra la puerta. You may also hear: Cierre la puerta detrás de usted (“close the door behind you”).
target_language_example: Por favor, cierre la puerta al salir.
native_language_example: Please close the door when you leave.

additional_notes: Used to refer to particular things without naming them, often because they’re unknown, not specific, or you don’t want to say them directly. Common in the pattern “hay ciertas cosas que…” (“there are certain things that…”). “Ciertas” agrees with the feminine plural noun “cosas.”
target_language_example: Hay ciertas cosas de las que no quiero hablar ahora.
native_language_example: There are certain things I don’t want to talk about right now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the highest point of a specific mountain. Often appears with prepositions like "en" (at/on) and "desde" (from): "en la cima de la montaña", "desde la cima de la montaña". "Cima" can also be used in other contexts meaning "top" or "peak" (e.g., "la cima de un árbol" = the top of a tree).
target_language_example: Hicimos una foto en la cima de la montaña.
native_language_example: We took a photo at the top of the mountain.

additional_notes: A sequence of numbers used when counting aloud (often in exercises, songs, or to keep rhythm). Note spelling: cinco (5), seis (6), siete (7), ocho (8).
target_language_example: Vamos a contar: cinco, seis, siete, ocho.
native_language_example: Let’s count: five, six, seven, eight.

meaning: five years (a duration or an age).
additional_notes: Used to talk about (1) a length of time: "por/en cinco años" = for/in five years; "desde hace cinco años" = for the past five years; and (2) someone’s age: "a los cinco años" (at age five) or "de cinco años" (five-year-old). With comparisons: "cinco años mayor/menor que" = five years older/younger than.
target_language_example: Viví en México cinco años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for five years.

additional_notes: A time expression used to talk about a duration (durante cinco días = for five days), a deadline/amount of time you need (Dame cinco días = Give me five days), or a point in time relative to now/another event (cinco días después = five days later; dentro de cinco días = in five days). Use "día" (singular) with 1 (un día) and "días" (plural) with 2+ (dos/tres/cuatro/cinco días).
target_language_example: Necesito cinco días para terminarlo.
native_language_example: I need five days to finish it.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in a typical week (a frequency). Often answers “¿Con qué frecuencia...?” (“How often...?”). You can swap the number: “tres días a la semana”, “seis días a la semana”.
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio cinco días a la semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym five days a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money in dollars (USD). Often appears after verbs like pagar (to pay), deber (to owe), and with fines: una multa de cinco dólares (a five-dollar fine).
target_language_example: ¿Me prestas cinco dólares?
native_language_example: Can you lend me five dollars?

additional_notes: Used to state a duration or an amount of time. With durations, Spanish often uses "tardar + (time) + en + infinitive" (e.g., "Tardé cinco horas en manejar...") or "por" (e.g., "por cinco horas" = for five hours).
target_language_example: La película dura cinco horas.
native_language_example: The movie lasts five hours.

additional_notes: Used to express the number 5,000 before a noun (cinco mil años, cinco mil euros) or on its own as a number. Spanish uses a space between the words; it’s not written as one word.
target_language_example: Necesito cinco mil dólares para el coche.
native_language_example: I need five thousand dollars for the car.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or give a brief amount of time. Very common with verbs like dar (Dame cinco minutos.) and tener (Tienes cinco minutos.) to mean “give me five minutes” / “you have five minutes.” It can also indicate how much earlier/later something happens: cinco minutos antes/después (five minutes before/after).
target_language_example: Solo necesito cinco minutos para terminar.
native_language_example: I only need five minutes to finish.

additional_notes: Used as a number on its own (answering a question), for quantities and measurements (liters per minute, etc.), in prices (often said without a currency word, e.g., “Dos, cincuenta y cinco” = $2.55/€2.55 depending on context), and for ages with “a los … años” (at … years old).
target_language_example: El autobús llega a las cincuenta y cinco.
native_language_example: The bus arrives at fifty-five.

additional_notes: Used for the safety belt in cars, planes, etc. Common with verbs like ponerse (to put on), usar (to wear/use), and abrocharse (to fasten). You may also hear it with the article: el cinturón de seguridad.
target_language_example: Antes de arrancar, ponte el cinturón de seguridad.
native_language_example: Before starting, put on your seat belt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about surgical procedures to change or repair appearance (for example, after an accident) or for cosmetic reasons. It’s a general term; specific procedures are often mentioned with verbs like “hacerse” (to get/have done): “hacerse una cirugía plástica.”
target_language_example: Mi prima se hizo cirugía plástica el año pasado.
native_language_example: My cousin had plastic surgery last year.

additional_notes: Used with a person to say you have a scheduled meeting (often professional/medical) or a romantic date. Context usually makes it clear: "una cita con el director" = appointment/meeting; "una cita con María" = (romantic) date.
target_language_example: Tengo una cita con el dentista mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with the dentist tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used with tener (to have): Tengo cita con el médico / Tengo una cita con el médico. Both are common; adding una makes it more clearly “an appointment.” You can change the tense (tengo/tenía) depending on when it happens.
target_language_example: Mañana tengo cita con el médico a las diez.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a doctor’s appointment at ten.

meaning: 'the biggest/largest city in/of' (used with rankings like first, second, fifth, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to talk about city size rankings: "la (primera/segunda/quinta) ciudad más grande de + country/region". "más grande" agrees with "ciudad" (feminine singular), so it stays "más grande" here. Often translates as "in" in English ("the second largest city in Spain"), even though Spanish uses "de" ("of").
target_language_example: Guadalajara es la segunda ciudad más grande de México.
native_language_example: Guadalajara is the second largest city in Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the town or city where someone was born or grew up. Often appears with a possessive: "mi/tu/su ciudad natal". You can use it with "ser" (Mi ciudad natal es...) or with "recordar" (me recuerda a mi ciudad natal).
target_language_example: Siempre vuelvo a mi ciudad natal en verano.
native_language_example: I always go back to my hometown in the summer.

additional_notes: Used to stress certainty or to make something explicit. Common patterns: **dejar (bien) claro que + clause** = “to make it (very) clear that…”, and **que quede claro que + clause** = “let it be clear that…”. In replies, you’ll often hear **claro que sí/no** = “of course (yes/no)”.
target_language_example: Que quede claro que no es una excusa.
native_language_example: Let it be clear that it’s not an excuse.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is obvious, expected, or goes without saying. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence (“Claro está, …”) or as a parenthetical aside (“…, claro está.”). You may also see it as “claro está que …” = “of course/clearly …”.
target_language_example: Claro está que no puedo ir si tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Of course I can’t go if I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize what follows (often like an emphatic “yes”). It can sound reassuring (“Of course you can”) or insistent (“Of course I know him”). Sometimes it also means “clearly/obviously,” especially when giving a reason: “Si fue un lunes, claro que vino” (“If it was a Monday, of course he came”).
target_language_example: Claro que te ayudo mañana.
native_language_example: Of course I’ll help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something, usually followed by a verb that takes the object pronoun **lo** (“it,” “him” in some contexts). Common patterns: **Claro que lo sé** (Of course I know), **Claro que lo conozco** (Of course I know him/it), **Claro que lo soy** (Of course I am), **Claro que lo están** (Of course they are). **Lo** must agree with what you’re referring to; you may see **la/los/las** instead depending on gender/number.
target_language_example: —¿Sabes la respuesta? —Claro que lo sé.
native_language_example: —Do you know the answer? —Of course I do.

additional_notes: Used to give a strong, emphatic “no,” often in response to a question or suggestion. It can sound neutral or reassuring (“Claro que no, cariño.” = “Of course not, darling.”). You may also hear it with filler words like “pues”: “Pues claro que no.”
target_language_example: —¿Te molesta si abro la ventana? —Claro que no.
native_language_example: —Do you mind if I open the window? —Of course not.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm something (often as a friendly, emphatic "yes"). It can sound a bit insistent depending on tone. Often interchangeable with "por supuesto" or "claro". In some contexts it can be ironic/sarcastic, like "yeah, sure".
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Claro que sí.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: Used in conversation to show quick agreement or acknowledgement. Repeating claro can sound more emphatic; depending on tone it can be friendly and reassuring, or a bit impatient/dismissive (like "yeah, yeah"). Often followed by "que sí" to reinforce agreement: "Claro, claro que sí."
target_language_example: —¿Puedes ayudarme ahora? —Claro, claro, en un minuto.
native_language_example: "Can you help me now?" "Sure, sure, in a minute."

meaning: “Of course” / “clearly” (often used to emphasize yes or agreement).
additional_notes: Common in conversation to strongly confirm something: “Claro que sí” = “Of course (yes).” It can also introduce an explanation or contrast, similar to “of course/however”: “Claro que quiero ir, pero no puedo.” Literally “clear that,” but in practice it often functions like “of course.”
target_language_example: Claro que sí, puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: Of course, I can help you.

additional_notes: Used to say what subject someone has a class or lesson in: clase de + noun (clase de piano, clase de español). In Spanish you usually say "clase de X" (not *"clase en X"*).
target_language_example: Tengo clase de español los lunes.
native_language_example: I have Spanish class on Mondays.

additional_notes: Refers to the social/economic group between the working class and the upper class. Often used with "de" to describe a person or place ("un barrio de clase media"), and can be modified: "clase media baja" = "lower middle class".
target_language_example: Ella es de clase media y vive en las afueras de la ciudad.
native_language_example: She is middle class and lives on the outskirts of the city.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: (1) With plural things (often with "muchas"/"diferentes"), it means categories: "muchas clases de juegos" = many kinds of games. (2) With a subject you study, it means lessons: "tomar clases de berebere" = to take Berber classes. Often followed by a noun.
target_language_example: Hay muchas clases de comida aquí, y también doy clases de español.
native_language_example: There are many kinds of food here, and I also teach Spanish classes.

meaning: 'club of' (a club for a specific activity or group).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say what kind of club it is: club de fútbol (soccer club), club de golf (golf club), club de comedia (comedy club/venue). It can refer to an organization/association (pertenecer a un club de golf) or a place/venue (ir a un club de comedia).
target_language_example: Se apuntó a un club de lectura para conocer gente.
native_language_example: She joined a book club to meet people.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a car powered by electricity (often rechargeable). You’ll often hear it with verbs like cargar (to charge) or comprar (to buy). Also: carro eléctrico (more common in much of Latin America).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde puedo cargar mi coche eléctrico?
native_language_example: Where can I charge my electric car?

additional_notes: A noun phrase: coche (car) + nuevo (new). Adjectives usually go after the noun in Spanish (coche nuevo). It agrees in gender/number: coche nuevo (masc. singular), coches nuevos (plural). With a feminine noun (e.g., casa), it would be nueva.
target_language_example: Me compré un coche nuevo la semana pasada.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new car last week.

additional_notes: Used when you want to get on the earliest train available (often because you woke up early or are in a hurry). In many places, "coger" is the normal verb for catching a train/bus; in some Latin American countries people may prefer "tomar" ("tomar el primer tren") because "coger" can sound vulgar there.
target_language_example: Si queremos llegar a tiempo, tenemos que coger el primer tren.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive on time, we have to catch the first train.

meaning: to answer the phone; to pick up the phone.
additional_notes: Used when someone answers a ringing phone (“pick up”). In much of Spain, coger is common, but in several Latin American countries coger can be vulgar, so alternatives like contestar el teléfono, atender el teléfono, or levantar el teléfono are safer there.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes coger el teléfono, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you answer the phone, please?

additional_notes: A common, literal phrase: "colección" = collection and "sellos" = (postage) stamps. Often used with verbs like "ordenar" (to organize), "mostrar" (to show), "enseñar" (to show someone), and "echar un vistazo" (to take a look). You’ll usually see a possessive before it: "mi/tu/su colección de sellos".
target_language_example: Tengo una colección de sellos desde que era niño.
native_language_example: I’ve had a stamp collection since I was a kid.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) form of "comenzar" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes". It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "comenzaron a + infinitive" (e.g., "comenzaron a hablar" = they started to talk). Similar in meaning to "empezaron a".
target_language_example: Cuando llegó el profesor, comenzaron a estudiar.
native_language_example: When the teacher arrived, they started to study.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "comenzar": "comenzó" = he/she/it began. It’s followed by "a" + infinitive (e.g., "comenzó a estudiar", "comenzó a toser"). Use it to talk about the moment someone started doing something.
target_language_example: Cuando llegó la lluvia, comenzó a hacer frío.
native_language_example: When the rain arrived, it started to get cold.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "comenzar": "comenzó" = "(it/he/she) began." Very common pattern: "comenzar/empezar a + infinitive" to say something started to happen (e.g., "comenzó a nevar" = it started to snow). "Llover" is an impersonal verb, so you don’t name a subject; in English we use "it."
target_language_example: Estábamos caminando y de repente comenzó a llover.
native_language_example: We were walking and suddenly it started to rain.

additional_notes: A very common, flexible phrase for when you want to eat but don’t specify what. Often used to suggest grabbing a bite: "Vamos a comer algo" (Let’s get something to eat). You can add adjectives or details: "algo delicioso" (something delicious), "algo dulce" (something sweet).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres comer algo antes de salir?
native_language_example: Do you want to eat something before we go out?

meaning: to eat food (often followed by an adjective or cuisine type).
additional_notes: In Spanish this phrase can sound a bit repetitive (like “eat food”), but it’s common in learner sentences and is used when you add details: comer comida + adjective (comida caliente/blanda/chatarra) or comida + nationality (comida coreana/italiana/francesa). Often you can simply say “comer” when the context already makes “food” obvious.
target_language_example: No puedo comer comida muy picante.
native_language_example: I can’t eat very spicy food.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "cometer errores" = "to make mistakes" (literally, "to commit errors"). "Comete" is the present tense for él/ella/usted; plural: "cometen errores". Very commonly used in general statements like "Todo el mundo comete errores" (Everyone makes mistakes).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo el mundo comete errores.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everyone makes mistakes.

additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase. Use it to talk about making mistakes in general or in a specific activity: “cometer errores en inglés/en el trabajo.” Often used with “puede(n)”, “temer”, or “tener miedo de” (to be afraid of) as in the examples.
target_language_example: Es normal cometer errores cuando aprendes un idioma nuevo.
native_language_example: It’s normal to make mistakes when you learn a new language.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **cometer** (“to commit”) plus **un error** (“a mistake”). You’ll often see it in the **present perfect** (**he/has/ha/habemos cometido un error**) meaning “have made a mistake,” or in the **past perfect** (**había/habías cometido un error**) meaning “had made a mistake.” In everyday Spanish, **cometer un error** is fairly formal; **cometer un error fatal** means “make a fatal mistake.”
target_language_example: Creo que he cometido un error con la dirección.
native_language_example: I think I’ve made a mistake with the address.

meaning: "made a mistake" (simple past / preterite, third-person singular).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "cometer" (to commit) with "un error". It’s a common, neutral way to say someone made a mistake. "Cometió" is the simple past (pretérito perfecto simple), typically for a completed action in the past. You can change the subject and verb form as needed: "Yo cometí un error", "Ella cometió un error", "Cometimos un error".
target_language_example: Creo que Tom cometió un error.
native_language_example: I think Tom made a mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the verb phrase "cometer un error" (to make/commit a mistake). Use it to admit a specific mistake you made. Often followed by a reason or explanation: "por hacerlo con prisa" (for doing it in a hurry) or a type of mistake: "un error de novato" (a beginner/rookie mistake).
target_language_example: Perdón, cometí un error con la cuenta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake with the bill.

additional_notes: Common phrase for unhealthy, highly processed food (e.g., fast food, chips, candy). Often used with verbs like comer (to eat) and with quantities like demasiada (too much). It’s usually uncountable in Spanish: comer comida basura.
target_language_example: Los fines de semana como menos comida basura.
native_language_example: On weekends I eat less junk food.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: comida (food) + china (Chinese). Used with verbs like comer (to eat), pedir/ordenar (to order), and cenar (to have dinner). You can also say comida china para llevar (“Chinese takeout”).
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a pedir comida china.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to order Chinese food.

additional_notes: A common, neutral noun phrase. Use it to talk about the type of food you eat or like. You’ll often see it with verbs like comer (to eat), gustar (to like), and acostumbrarse a (to get used to).
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta la comida japonesa?
native_language_example: Do you like Japanese food?

additional_notes: "Comiendo" is the gerund (-ing form) of "comer" (to eat). It’s commonly used with "estar" to talk about an action in progress (present: "está comiendo" = is eating; past: "estaba comiendo" = was eating). You may also see "comerse" (as in "se está comiendo"), which often emphasizes eating it up/finishing it, but in many cases it can simply mean "to eat."
target_language_example: Estoy comiendo un sándwich ahora.
native_language_example: I’m eating a sandwich now.

additional_notes: “Comiendo” is the gerund (-ing form) of “comer” (to eat). It’s often used with “estar” to talk about what someone/something is doing right now: “estar comiendo…”. In sentence 2, “Me estoy comiendo una manzana” adds the pronoun “me”, which commonly emphasizes that you’re eating it up/yourself (often implying the whole apple).
target_language_example: Estoy comiendo una manzana en el parque.
native_language_example: I’m eating an apple in the park.

meaning: "(he/she/it) starts to" / "begins to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (comienza a + verb) to say an action or process is starting. It’s the él/ella/usted form of "comenzar" in the present tense; for "I start to" you’d say "comienzo a". Similar to "empieza a" (more common in everyday speech in many places).
target_language_example: La clase comienza a las ocho, así que comienza a prepararte ahora.
native_language_example: Class starts at eight, so start getting ready now.

meaning: “like a” / “as a” (treat/see someone as if they were a certain type of person).
additional_notes: Used to compare how someone is treated or perceived: *tratar a alguien como a un…* (to treat someone like a…), *ver a alguien como a un…* (to see someone as a…). The **a** is the personal **a** used with direct objects that are people. With feminine nouns, it becomes **como a una** (*como a una reina*).
target_language_example: No me hables como a un niño; ya soy adulto.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like I’m a child; I’m an adult now.

meaning: as usual; as always (as is typical).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the normal/typical way. It can appear at the beginning of the sentence (often followed by a comma) or at the end. In conversation it can be slightly ironic or complaining depending on tone: "Llegó tarde, como de costumbre" (= he was late again, as usual).
