target_language_example: Como de costumbre, me desperté temprano y tomé café.
native_language_example: As usual, I woke up early and had coffee.

meaning: "how to put it" / "so to speak" (a filler used when searching for words).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to introduce a rewording or a less direct way of saying something, often when you’re hesitating or trying to be polite. It can appear alone ("Como decir…") or inside a sentence ("Es, como decir, complicado").
target_language_example: Es, como decir, un poco incómodo hablar de eso.
native_language_example: It’s, how to put it, a bit uncomfortable to talk about that.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun with the definite article (el) to make comparisons: "X es como el Y" (X is like the Y). It can also be part of "tan ... como el ..." or with adjectives for strong comparisons: "duro como el acero" (hard as steel). For feminine nouns you use "como la" instead.
target_language_example: Este color es como el del cielo.
native_language_example: This color is like the color of the sky.

meaning: like at home; (make yourself) at home.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like sentirse/estar (“to feel/be”) or as an invitation (Siéntete como en casa) to tell someone to relax and be comfortable in your home or space. In the phrase “No hay lugar como en casa” it means “There’s no place like home.”
target_language_example: Pasa, siéntate y ponte cómodo: estás como en casa.
native_language_example: Come in, sit down, and get comfortable: you’re at home here.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to the present situation or object, often meaning “a day/place/one like this.” It agrees with the noun: como este (masc. sing.), como esta (fem. sing.), como estos (masc. plural), como estas (fem. plural). Often follows a noun (un día como este) or stands in for one (uno como este = one like this).
target_language_example: Nunca había visto un reloj como este.
native_language_example: I had never seen a watch like this.

como la palma de mi mano

target_language_multi_word_term: como la palma de mi mano
meaning: very well; like the back of my hand.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like conocer/saber to say you know a place, area, topic, or even a person extremely well. You can change the possessive to match the speaker (como la palma de tu mano, de su mano, etc.).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: conozco el camino como la palma de mi mano.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I know the way like the back of my hand.

additional_notes: Used to give an upper limit or maximum estimate (often with numbers or time). It can go before or after the phrase it limits: “Como mucho, tiene seis dólares” / “tiene seis dólares, como mucho.”
target_language_example: Tardaremos dos horas, como mucho.
native_language_example: It’ll take us two hours, at most.

additional_notes: Used to give a deadline or the latest acceptable time something can happen. Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Te lo envío mañana, como muy tarde." You can also hear "a más tardar" with the same meaning. It’s not about doing something 'late' on purpose—it's about the latest limit.
target_language_example: Necesito el informe el viernes, como muy tarde.
native_language_example: I need the report by Friday at the latest.

additional_notes: Used to set a lower limit or minimum expectation. It can stand alone as a short reply meaning “at least” (often implying “that’s the bare minimum,” sometimes with mild criticism).
target_language_example: Necesito dos días, como mínimo, para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: I need at least two days to finish the project.

meaning: like new; as good as new.
additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) will be restored to an almost-new condition after cleaning, fixing, resting, etc. Often used with verbs like estar (to be), quedar (to end up/turn out), or dejar (to leave/make): “Quedará como nuevo” = “It’ll be as good as new.”
target_language_example: Después de limpiarlo, el coche quedó como nuevo.
native_language_example: After cleaning it, the car looked as good as new.

meaning: '(so/too/enough) ... to' (indicating a degree sufficient to do something).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective/adverb or quantity phrase to introduce an infinitive: "tan/lo bastante/muy + (adj./adv.) + como para + infinitivo". It expresses that something is to such a degree that it would lead to (or justify) an action/result, often with a critical tone: "muy salada como para comerla" = "too salty to eat".
target_language_example: Estoy demasiado cansado como para salir hoy.
native_language_example: I'm too tired to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the consequence of an action or situation. Common patterns: “como resultado de + noun” (as a result of + noun) and “como resultado,” (as a result / consequently).
target_language_example: Como resultado de la tormenta, cancelaron el vuelo.
native_language_example: As a result of the storm, they canceled the flight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause of a situation or outcome. It’s followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., “como resultado de la lluvia”). With a verb clause, Spanish often uses “como resultado de que…”. Common in formal or neutral writing.
target_language_example: Como resultado de la tormenta, no hay clases hoy.
native_language_example: As a result of the storm, there are no classes today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the same as it usually is. It can describe a situation/state (Está como siempre = “He/She/It is the same as always”) or introduce a comment about a repeated pattern (Como siempre, … = “As always, …”).
target_language_example: Como siempre, llegas tarde.
native_language_example: As always, you arrive late.

meaning: like his/her father; as his/her father.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to their father (appearance, personality, behavior) or to say something is the same as the father’s (e.g., a name). With names, it often means “named after his/her father” (e.g., “Le pusieron Robert, como su padre” = “They named him Robert, like his father”). “Su” can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Habla mucho como su padre.
native_language_example: He/She talks a lot like his/her father.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something in its role or category ("as X"), often to clarify that you mean the thing itself and not something related to it. Common in more formal explanations: "No es un problema como tal" = "It’s not a problem as such (in itself)."
target_language_example: No tengo nada en contra de la idea como tal, pero no me convence el plan.
native_language_example: I have nothing against the idea as such, but the plan doesn’t convince me.

meaning: as such; like that (in that role).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a role/identity just mentioned (e.g., “a man,” “a professional,” “a leader”) and say someone should act accordingly. Often appears after verbs like comportarse (to behave) or actuar (to act).
target_language_example: Eres el jefe, así que actúa como tal.
native_language_example: You're the boss, so act like it (as such).

additional_notes: Very informal/colloquial, common in texting or casual speech. Often written without accents or punctuation (proper: “¿Cómo estás?”). You can answer with “Bien, ¿y tú?” (Good, and you?).
target_language_example: Hola, ¿como tas? Hace tiempo que no te veo.
native_language_example: Hi, how are you? I haven’t seen you in a while.

meaning: like everyone else; like all the others.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the rest of a group, often implying being ordinary, typical, or the same as others. It can be neutral or carry a critical/complaining tone depending on context (e.g., 'You’re just like everyone else'). You’ll also hear variations like "como las/los demás" (agreeing with gender/number) and "como todo el mundo" (like everybody).
target_language_example: No tienes que actuar como todos los demás.
native_language_example: You don’t have to act like everyone else.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the person you’re speaking to. Common patterns: "alguien/un(a) ... como tú" = “someone/a ... like you”; "(tan) + adjective + como tú" = “(as) + adjective + as you”; and in negatives "no (ser) como tú" = “not like you.” "Tú" is informal (used with friends/family); with "usted" you’d say "como usted."
target_language_example: No conozco a nadie como tú.
native_language_example: I don’t know anyone like you.

additional_notes: Used to make comparisons or analogies ("as/like a …"): Está ciego como un murciélago. It can also mean “as a” to describe a role or function: Te traje aquí como un recurso temporal (“as a temporary resource/backup”). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun; the feminine form is "como una".
target_language_example: Trabaja como un traductor en una empresa.
native_language_example: He works as a translator at a company.

meaning: like a baby; (often) like a baby = in a childish way.
additional_notes: Used after a verb to compare someone’s behavior to a baby’s. It can be literal (e.g., sleeping/crying like a baby) or insulting/critical (acting childish, whining, making noise). Often appears with verbs like llorar (to cry), dormir (to sleep), comportarse/portarse (to behave).
target_language_example: Deja de quejarte; estás actuando como un bebé.
native_language_example: Stop complaining; you’re acting like a baby.

meaning: “like a pig” (very messily / a lot; can be insulting).
additional_notes: Used after a verb to compare someone’s behavior to a pig, often criticizing them for eating a lot or without manners: Come como un cerdo. It can also intensify other actions, especially sudar: Estoy sudando como un cerdo (“I’m sweating a lot”). It’s informal and can sound rude depending on context.
target_language_example: Después de correr, estoy sudando como un cerdo.
native_language_example: After running, I’m sweating like a pig.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "tomar" (to take) to say you interpret something—often a comment that could be negative or teasing—as a compliment. Common patterns: "(Yo) lo tomo como un cumplido" / "Tómalo como un cumplido".
target_language_example: Aunque suene raro, lo digo en serio: tómalo como un cumplido.
native_language_example: Even if it sounds weird, I mean it seriously: take it as a compliment.

meaning: “like a man”; often used like “man up.”
additional_notes: Literally means “like a man.” It can be used as a comparison (Me siento como un hombre nuevo = “I feel like a new man”) or as an encouragement/command to be brave, responsible, or tough (Acéptalo como un hombre = “Accept it like a man”). This use is common but can sound macho/old-fashioned or sexist depending on context.
target_language_example: Tienes que enfrentarlo como un hombre.
native_language_example: You have to face it like a man.

meaning: like a native (speaker); with native-like fluency.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s language ability to that of a native speaker. Often appears with verbs like "hablar" and can be softened with words like "casi" (almost): "casi como un nativo".
target_language_example: Después de vivir en México, habla español como un nativo.
native_language_example: After living in Mexico, he speaks Spanish like a native.

meaning: like a child; like a little kid.
additional_notes: Used after a verb to compare someone’s behavior, reactions, or state to that of a child. It can be neutral (innocent, carefree, sleeping soundly) or critical (acting immature). Also appears as “como una niña” depending on the person being described.
target_language_example: Cuando no consigue lo que quiere, se pone a llorar como un niño.
native_language_example: When he doesn’t get what he wants, he starts crying like a child.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has played a fatherly role in your life (support, guidance, care), even if they aren’t your biological father. Common with verbs like ser/estar: “Es/Era/Ha sido como un padre para mí.” You can swap roles: “como una madre para mí”, “como un hermano para mí”, etc.
target_language_example: Mi tío fue como un padre para mí cuando era niño.
native_language_example: My uncle was like a father to me when I was a kid.

meaning: like a fish (very well/easily, especially about swimming; or drinking a lot).
additional_notes: Used after a verb to compare someone to a fish. Most commonly: **nadar como un pez** = “to swim like a fish” (very well). With **beber**, it often means “to drink like a fish” (to drink a lot, usually alcohol). Related expression: **como un pez fuera del agua** = “like a fish out of water” (feeling uncomfortable/out of place).
target_language_example: Mi hermana nada como un pez.
native_language_example: My sister swims like a fish.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons. Common with verbs like volar/correr/moverse to mean “like a bird.” In the set phrase “libre como un pájaro,” it means “free as a bird.” With comer (“come como un pájaro”), it means someone eats very little (like a bird).
target_language_example: Después del examen, me sentí libre como un pájaro.
native_language_example: After the exam, I felt free as a bird.

additional_notes: Used to say something works very well, reliably, and often with exact timing. Common with verbs like "funcionar" (to work), "ir" (to go), "marchar" (to run), and "ser" (to be) for punctuality: "Funciona como un reloj" = "It works like clockwork." "Tan ... como un reloj" emphasizes someone is extremely punctual.
target_language_example: El autobús pasa a las ocho, como un reloj.
native_language_example: The bus comes at eight, like clockwork.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that feels unreal, magical, or too good to be true. Often appears with verbs like ser/estar (e.g., “Fue/Es/Se siente como un sueño”) and can be intensified with “casi” (“almost”). Can also be used as a compliment (“tan hermosa como un sueño” = “as beautiful as a dream”).
target_language_example: Ganar el viaje gratis fue como un sueño.
native_language_example: Winning the free trip was like a dream.

meaning: like an angel (very beautifully, sweetly, or kindly).
additional_notes: Used as a compliment, especially with verbs like cantar (to sing) or hablar (to speak), to say someone sounds extremely beautiful, gentle, or good. It can also refer to someone’s appearance or character (e.g., ser/verse como un ángel = to be/look like an angel).
target_language_example: Bailas como un ángel.
native_language_example: You dance like an angel.

meaning: like a; as a (used to compare or describe something).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to make a comparison or describe a role/way of treating someone: "como una prisión" (like a prison), "como una señal" (as a sign), "tratar como una princesa" (treat like a princess). If the noun is masculine, use "como un". Often appears in similes ("feliz como una pulga").
target_language_example: Me miró como una loca.
native_language_example: He looked at me like I was crazy.

additional_notes: Usually used with estar ("está/estás como una cabra") to say someone is acting crazy, silly, or a bit out of control. It’s an informal idiom. Literally it means "like a goat"; in some contexts it can also be literal (e.g., "huele como una cabra" = "he smells like a goat").
target_language_example: Mi hermano está como una cabra: salió en camiseta con nieve.
native_language_example: My brother is nuts: he went out in a T-shirt while it was snowing.

meaning: like an arrow (very fast and/or very straight).
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an arrow, emphasizing speed (e.g., moving/shooting off quickly) or direction/shape (e.g., going straight). Often appears with verbs like "ir" (to go) or "salir" (to shoot out).
target_language_example: El coche pasó como una flecha por la autopista.
native_language_example: The car sped by like an arrow on the highway.

meaning: like a (little) girl; in a childish/immature way.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like hablar (to talk), actuar (to act), vestirse (to dress), or estar (to be/act) to compare someone’s behavior to that of a girl. Depending on context, it can be neutral (describing something childlike) or insulting/derogatory—especially when said about a boy/man to criticize him as childish, weak, or overly feminine.
target_language_example: Deja de quejarte; estás actuando como una niña.
native_language_example: Stop complaining; you're acting like a little girl.

meaning: “like a stone” (very heavy, cold, silent, or sinking).
additional_notes: Used as a simile with "como" to emphasize that something is extremely heavy (or feels heavy), very cold, completely silent/without speaking, or (with swimming) that someone sinks easily. You can also hear similar phrases like "como una roca" (“like a rock”).
target_language_example: Después de la noticia, se quedó callado como una piedra.
native_language_example: After the news, he stayed as silent as a stone.

additional_notes: Used to compare yourself to someone/something. Often follows a noun: "una persona como yo" (a person like me), "un hombre como yo" (a man like me). You can also use it after "ser": "Es como yo" (He/She is like me).
target_language_example: No conozco a nadie como yo.
native_language_example: I don’t know anyone like me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is correct/appropriate or done the right way. Often said by itself as an approving comment (“Como debe ser.”). It can also mean “properly” when telling someone how to do something (e.g., do it neatly/correctly).
target_language_example: Hazlo con calma y bien, como debe ser.
native_language_example: Do it calmly and well, the way it should be.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done (or should be done) correctly, in the right way, or to an acceptable standard. Often appears with verbs like comer, cuidar, trabajar, vestir, etc. It can also describe something that meets expectations (“a proper/real one”), especially in phrases like “un X como es debido.”
target_language_example: No descansé como es debido anoche.
native_language_example: I didn’t rest properly last night.

additional_notes: Very polite/formal; typically addressed to someone as “usted.” Often used to let the other person choose or to show you’re flexible. You may also hear it as “como guste usted” or “como usted guste.”
target_language_example: Podemos reunirnos mañana o el viernes, como guste.
native_language_example: We can meet tomorrow or on Friday—whatever you prefer.

additional_notes: Used to compare two situations or to say something is the same way as before. The "lo" refers back to an idea or action already mentioned (often followed by a verb: "como lo era", "como lo hacemos"). Very common in comparisons like "tan ... como lo ..." (“as ... as ...”).
target_language_example: Hice el café como lo haces tú.
native_language_example: I made the coffee the way you do.

meaning: like never before; as (someone) never has.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens in an unusually strong or exceptional way, compared to any previous time. Often appears with verbs like "ver" (to see), "jugar" (to play), "divertirse" (to have fun), and can be expanded as "como nunca (antes)" = "like never before."
target_language_example: Trabajó como nunca para terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: He worked like never before to finish the project on time.

meaning: “(so)… as to” / “enough to” (to show degree + result).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives or adverbs (often with tan / lo bastante) to express that someone/something has a certain degree or quality, with the consequence in the infinitive clause: “tan + adj/adv + como para + infinitive” (so … as to), “lo bastante + adj/adv + como para + infinitive” (enough … to). It can also mean “as if to” to express purpose/gesture (e.g., “Respire hondo, como para cantar” = as if to sing).
target_language_example: No estoy tan cansado como para irme a dormir ahora.
native_language_example: I’m not so tired as to go to sleep now.

additional_notes: Used after words like tan/tanto/tanta/tantos ("so/as") to express the maximum you’re able to do. It uses the present subjunctive of poder (pueda) because it refers to an unknown limit or ability: tan rápido como pueda (as fast as I can). You can also change it for other people: como puedas (you can), como pueda él/ella (he/she can), como podamos (we can).
target_language_example: Llámame tan pronto como puedas.
native_language_example: Call me as soon as you can.

meaning: as ... as you can (as best you can).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives/adverbs (often with "tan" or "tanto/a/os/as") to express the maximum possible degree: "tan + adjective/adverb + como puedas" or "tanto/a/os/as + noun + como puedas". Very common in instructions/commands: "ven tan rápido como puedas" = come as fast as you can. Verb agrees with the subject: "como pueda/puedas/puedan".
target_language_example: Por favor vuelve a casa tan rápido como puedas.
native_language_example: Please come back home as fast as you can.

additional_notes: Used to point out something that is obvious or visible in the situation, often to support what you’re saying. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence; in speech it may also be used alone to emphasize the point.
target_language_example: Como puedes ver, no tengo tiempo ahora.
native_language_example: As you can see, I don’t have time right now.

meaning: "as you like / as you wish"; "however you want".
additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive of querer (quiera). Common in polite responses meaning “as you wish” (e.g., Como quiera, señor.). It can also mean “however/whatever you want” about names or choices (Puede llamarme como quiera.), and it appears in comparisons like tanto… como quiera = “as much/long as (someone) wants.”
target_language_example: Hazlo como quiera; yo confío en ti.
native_language_example: Do it however you want; I trust you.

meaning: "since / given that"; also "however it may be / in any case" (formal).
additional_notes: A fairly formal connector used in writing (legal, academic). It can introduce a reason: “Como quiera que no había tiempo, salimos.” (= Since there wasn’t time…). It can also mean “however it may be / anyway” to move the conversation forward or add a conclusion. Often interchangeable with “puesto que” (since) or “en cualquier caso” (in any case), depending on context.
target_language_example: Como quiera que ya es tarde, nos vamos a casa.
native_language_example: Since it’s already late, we’re going home.

meaning: "however you want" / "whatever you prefer"; also "fine, if you say so".
additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom to choose how to do/say something (Dilo/Hazlo como quieras). Said alone, it can mean agreement or indifference (“Okay, whatever you want”), and depending on tone it can sound a bit dismissive.
target_language_example: —¿Pizza o pasta? —Como quieras.
native_language_example: —Pizza or pasta? —Whatever you prefer.

additional_notes: Used after words like tan/tanto/tanta/tantos/tantas to express the maximum degree or amount: tan + adjective/adverb + como sea posible (“as [adjective/adverb] as possible”) and tanto/a/os/as + noun + como sea posible (“as much/many [noun] as possible”). Often appears in requests or goals (e.g., “as clearly as possible”).
target_language_example: Necesito terminarlo lo antes posible y tan bien como sea posible.
native_language_example: I need to finish it as soon as possible and as well as possible.

meaning: "anyway" / "in any case"; also "however you can" ("no matter how").
additional_notes: Often used to change topic or conclude something: "Como sea, ..." = "Anyway, ...". It can also mean doing something by whatever method is possible: "Hazlo como sea" = "Do it however you can / no matter how." In the second use, it can sound forceful depending on tone.
target_language_example: Como sea, tengo que terminarlo hoy.
native_language_example: Anyway, I have to finish it today.

additional_notes: Used to compare a real situation with an imagined or unreal one (often after verbs like actuar, hablar, ver). It’s very common with the imperfect subjunctive (como si + fuera/estuviera/volviera...), especially when the comparison is not true or is hypothetical. It can also be used for vivid description: “as if I were there.”
target_language_example: Me miras como si no me conocieras.
native_language_example: You look at me as if you didn’t know me.

additional_notes: Used to qualify what you just said, often to mean it’s an approximate label, a metaphor, or not the exact word. Common in conversational Spanish to soften or clarify an expression.
target_language_example: Es el jefe, como si dijéramos, del equipo.
native_language_example: He’s the boss, so to speak, of the team.

meaning: "as if (I/he/she) were" (describing an unreal or imagined situation).
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an unreal/imaginary situation. It’s followed by the imperfect subjunctive of estar (estuviera/estuviese). The subject depends on context: como si estuviera = as if I/he/she were; como si estuviéramos = as if we were, etc.
target_language_example: Hablaba en voz baja, como si estuviera en una biblioteca.
native_language_example: He spoke quietly, as if he were in a library.

additional_notes: Used to compare a real feeling/situation to an imagined one. It uses the imperfect subjunctive (estuviera) after como si to show something unreal or hypothetical. Change the noun after en: como si estuviera en casa (at home), en un sueño (in a dream). You can also change the verb for other people: como si estuvieras en… (you), como si estuviéramos en… (we).
target_language_example: Estoy tan relajado, como si estuviera en la playa.
native_language_example: I’m so relaxed, as if I were at the beach.

meaning: as if it were; as though it were.
additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an unreal, doubtful, or imagined situation. It often implies that something is not really true (or is unlikely), like English “as if…”. After "como si", Spanish typically uses the imperfect subjunctive: fuera (from ser) is common, but you’ll also see other verbs (e.g., "como si tuviera", "como si estuviera"). You can also change it for number/gender: "como si fueran", "como si fuera".
target_language_example: Me miró como si fuera un extraño.
native_language_example: He looked at me as if I were a stranger.

meaning: "as if it were yesterday" (I remember it very clearly).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you remember something vividly, even if it happened a long time ago. Often follows verbs like "recordar" or "acordarse": "Lo recuerdo/me acuerdo como si fuera ayer."
target_language_example: Nuestro primer día en esta ciudad lo recuerdo como si fuera ayer.
native_language_example: I remember our first day in this city as if it were yesterday.

meaning: “as if (he/she/it) were a …” (used for comparisons that are not real).
additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to another thing in an unreal or hypothetical way. It uses the imperfect subjunctive of ser: "fuera" (common in Spain/Latin America). Change for gender/number: "como si fuera una" (feminine), "como si fueran unos/unas" (plural).
target_language_example: Habla como si fuera un médico, pero no ha estudiado medicina.
native_language_example: He talks as if he were a doctor, but he hasn’t studied medicine.

meaning: “as if they were” (talking about more than one thing/person).
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an unreal or exaggerated situation: “as if X were Y.” It’s very often followed by a noun or description. "Fueran" is the imperfect subjunctive of "ser" and agrees with a plural subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes/las cosas). Singular version: "como si fuera".
target_language_example: Me miras como si fueran culpables.
native_language_example: You look at me as if they were guilty.

meaning: “as if you were” (talking to or about someone).
additional_notes: Used to compare reality to an imaginary or unreal situation. It introduces a hypothetical idea, and in Spanish it typically uses the imperfect subjunctive: fueras (from ser). Often used to criticize or exaggerate (“You act/talk as if you were…”), or to show strong affection (“…as if you were his/her own child”).
target_language_example: Me miras como si fueras a decirme algo importante.
native_language_example: You look at me as if you were going to tell me something important.

meaning: as if it were / as though it were.
additional_notes: Used to compare reality to an imaginary or unreal situation, or to describe something that feels like it’s true. It’s common with the imperfect subjunctive: "como si + fuese" (from "ser"). Often followed by a noun or time expression ("como si fuese mío", "como si fuese ayer").
target_language_example: Me mira como si fuese culpable.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if I were guilty.

meaning: 'as if (someone) had…' (introduces an unreal/improbable comparison in the past).
additional_notes: Used after "como si" + imperfect subjunctive (here, "hubiera" from "haber") to talk about something that seems true but probably isn’t, or to make a dramatic comparison. Very often followed by a past participle to form the pluperfect subjunctive: "como si hubiera sido / hubiera estado / hubiera ocurrido…". English usually translates it with "as if" + past perfect: "as if he had…".
target_language_example: Me habló como si hubiera visto un fantasma.
native_language_example: He spoke to me as if he had seen a ghost.

meaning: "as if it had been" / "as though it had been."
additional_notes: Used after "como si" to introduce an unreal or hypothetical comparison (often in expressions like "como si hubiera sido ayer" = "as if it were yesterday"). "Hubiera sido" is the past perfect subjunctive of "ser" ("to be"), commonly used to talk about something in the past that’s not literally true, or to guess/speculate based on evidence ("Suena como si hubiera sido..." = "It sounds like it was...").
target_language_example: Me habló como si hubiera sido mi profesor.
native_language_example: He talked to me as if he had been my teacher.

meaning: “as if (he/she) knew everything” (i.e., speaking/acting like a know-it-all).
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone’s attitude or tone, implying arrogance or overconfidence. Grammar: "como si" + imperfect subjunctive ("supiera", from "saber"). The subject can vary by context (él/ella/usted), and it’s often preceded by a verb like "hablar" (e.g., "Hablas como si lo supiera todo").
target_language_example: Él habla como si lo supiera todo, pero en realidad no tiene idea.
native_language_example: He talks as if he knew everything, but in reality he has no idea.

meaning: “as if (to/for) me …” (introduces an unreal or imagined situation).
additional_notes: Used to compare reality with something hypothetical: **como si + imperfect subjunctive** (e.g., *como si me conociera* = “as if he knew me”). The **me** is an object pronoun (“me”), and the verb that follows is often in the imperfect subjunctive (*conociera, importara, dejara*). It can also be used sarcastically: *Como si me importara* = “As if I cared.”
target_language_example: Me miró como si me conociera de toda la vida.
native_language_example: He looked at me as if he’d known me his whole life.

meaning: as if nothing (had) happened; like it’s no big deal.
additional_notes: Used to describe acting or continuing normally, without showing any reaction, concern, or emotion—often after something surprising, awkward, or serious. Common patterns: “como si nada (hubiera ocurrido / pasara)” and “seguir + gerundio + como si nada”.
target_language_example: Me miró y siguió hablando como si nada.
native_language_example: He looked at me and kept talking as if nothing had happened.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to say someone continues or acts normally, pretending there was no problem or event. Very common with verbs like seguir (to keep), actuar (to act), volver (to return). The verb is usually in the past subjunctive: como si nada hubiera pasado / como si nada pasara.
target_language_example: Me saludó como si nada hubiera pasado.
native_language_example: He greeted me as if nothing had happened.

meaning: "as if ... not" / "as though ... not"; also "whether ... or not" (in tanto si... como si no).
additional_notes: Often followed by the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., como si no fuera / tuviera / hubiera...). Used to describe an unreal, hypothetical, or pretended situation: "actúa como si no..." = "he acts as if he doesn't...". In the pattern "tanto si X como si no", it means "whether X or not".
target_language_example: Me habló como si no me conociera.
native_language_example: He talked to me as if he didn't know me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is treated as if it never existed or happened. It’s normally followed by a past participle (past perfect subjunctive): como si nunca hubiera existido/pasado/sido/estado. After “como si,” Spanish uses the subjunctive because it describes something unreal or hypothetical.
target_language_example: Lo borraron de la lista como si nunca hubiera existido.
native_language_example: They erased him from the list as if he had never existed.

meaning: “as if I had” / “as though I had”.
additional_notes: Used to describe an unreal, hypothetical, or perceived situation (often a comparison to how something feels/seems). It’s part of the pattern “como si + imperfect subjunctive” (tuviera, fuera, estuviera, etc.). Often followed by a noun (“como si tuviera resaca”) or by “que + verb” (“como si tuviera que hacer más” = as if I had to do more). Subject changes with context: “como si tuviera” (I/he/she had), “como si tuvieras” (you had), “como si tuviéramos” (we had).
target_language_example: Me habló como si tuviera la culpa de todo.
native_language_example: He talked to me as if I were guilty of everything.

additional_notes: Used to say something is typical or happens every time. It can be neutral (“as usual”) or slightly critical/ironic depending on tone and context (e.g., “wrong, as always”). Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear earlier.
target_language_example: Llegas tarde, como siempre.
native_language_example: You’re late, as always.

additional_notes: Used to comment on the sound or impression of words/ideas. Often follows adjectives like "raro" ("Extraño como suena...") meaning "Strange as it sounds...". It can also be used to acknowledge something might sound bad/strange: "Sé como suena" = "I know how it sounds."
target_language_example: Raro como suena, es la verdad.
native_language_example: Strange as it sounds, it’s the truth.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the person you’re speaking to (tú). Often means “as you do” with the verb understood: "Nadie me entiende como tú (me entiendes)". Also used in comparisons with "tan/tanto... como": "tan bien... como tú", "tanta... como tú".
target_language_example: Nadie me escucha como tú.
native_language_example: No one listens to me like you do.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison word like "como" to mean "like me" or "as I do". Often appears in comparisons with "tan... como yo" ("as... as me") or in expressions like "Nadie... como yo" ("No one... like I do").
target_language_example: No cocines como yo; siempre se me quema algo.
native_language_example: Don’t cook like me; I always burn something.

meaning: female roommate (a woman you share a room with).
additional_notes: Used to talk specifically about a female person you share a room with (often in a dorm or shared housing). The masculine form is “compañero de cuarto.” In some places people also say “compañera de piso/de apartamento” for a roommate who shares the apartment (not necessarily the same bedroom).
target_language_example: Mi compañera de cuarto llega tarde casi todos los días.
native_language_example: My (female) roommate arrives late almost every day.

meaning: roommate (person you share a room with).
additional_notes: Used for someone you share a bedroom/dorm room with (common in dorms, shared apartments, etc.). In everyday Spanish, people often also say "compañero de piso" for someone you share an apartment/flat with (even if you don’t share the same bedroom).
target_language_example: Mi compañero de habitación llega mañana.
native_language_example: My roommate arrives tomorrow.

meaning: “Comrade, Senior Lieutenant” (a formal way to address someone with that rank).
additional_notes: Used as a respectful form of address in a military/police setting, often in contexts influenced by socialist/communist terminology where compañero (“comrade”) is used instead of “sir/ma’am.” Teniente mayor is a rank roughly meaning “senior/first lieutenant” (not “major” in the English-rank sense).
target_language_example: Compañero teniente mayor, el informe está listo.
native_language_example: Comrade, Senior Lieutenant, the report is ready.

additional_notes: Refers to people who are in the same class/course as you. You can say "mi(s) compañero(s) de clase" (my classmate(s)) or "nuestros compañeros de clase" (our classmates). Can also be feminine: "compañeras de clase" for a group of all women, or mixed groups often use the masculine plural "compañeros".
target_language_example: Mis compañeros de clase y yo estudiamos juntos para el examen.
native_language_example: My classmates and I study together for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something/someone is not just a little different, but totally unlike another thing, situation, or past version of a person. Often appears with "ser" ("es/era completamente diferente") and can be followed by "de" to compare: "completamente diferente de...".
target_language_example: Este plan es completamente diferente del que teníamos ayer.
native_language_example: This plan is completely different from the one we had yesterday.

meaning: “bought a” (used after a form of *haber* in the perfect tenses).
additional_notes: You’ll usually see it in phrases like **he/has/han comprado un…** (“I have/you have/they have bought a…”) or **había comprado un…** (“had bought a…”). With the reflexive form **comprarse**, it means “to buy oneself”: **Me he comprado un par de guantes** = “I bought myself a pair of gloves / I’ve bought myself a pair of gloves.”
target_language_example: ¿Has comprado un regalo para tu mamá?
native_language_example: Have you bought a gift for your mom?

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: comprar un camión/un computador/un apartamento/un microondas. For feminine nouns, use "comprar una" (e.g., comprar una casa). With plural, use "comprar unos/unas" (e.g., comprar unos zapatos). Often followed by adjectives like "nuevo/a".
target_language_example: Quiero comprar un libro nuevo.
native_language_example: I want to buy a new book.

additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase. Uses the verb "comprar" (to buy) + the direct object "un coche" (a car). Often appears with expressions about ability or affordability, like "poder" (can), "permitirse" (to afford), or "no me alcanza" (I don’t have enough money).
target_language_example: Estoy ahorrando para comprar un coche este año.
native_language_example: I’m saving to buy a car this year.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "comprar" (to buy) + "un coche" (a car) + adjective "nuevo" (new). Very common with verbs like "pensar en" (to think about) and "acabar de" (to have just done). You can change the article and adjective to match what you mean: "comprar el coche nuevo" (buy the new car), "comprar una coche nuevo" (incorrect; "coche" is masculine).
target_language_example: Estoy ahorrando para comprar un coche nuevo este año.
native_language_example: I’m saving up to buy a new car this year.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is feminine (una medicina, una almohada, una correa, una alfombra). Often the noun comes right after: “comprar una medicina.” It can also mean “buy one” if the item is already understood from context.
target_language_example: No tengo paraguas; voy a comprar una esta tarde.
native_language_example: I don’t have an umbrella; I’m going to buy one this afternoon.

additional_notes: "Comprar" means "to buy." You can swap in other items (e.g., "comprar un coche nuevo"). With "irse a comprar" or "se va a comprar," it often means someone is going to buy it (sometimes implying “for themself”). "Permitirme" in "No puedo permitirme..." means "I can't afford...".
target_language_example: Voy a comprar una bicicleta nueva este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy a new bicycle this weekend.

additional_notes: Used for the action/plan/idea of purchasing a home. Often appears after verbs like querer/gustar (to want/would like), pensar en (to think about), investigar la posibilidad de (to look into the possibility of), or with la idea de (the idea of) + infinitive: "la idea de comprar una casa".
target_language_example: Estamos pensando en comprar una casa el próximo año.
native_language_example: We’re thinking about buying a house next year.

additional_notes: An everyday phrase: comprar = “to buy”, una casa = “a house”, nueva = “new” (feminine singular to match casa). In Spanish, nueva usually comes after the noun: una casa nueva. You can change the tense around it: vamos a comprar una casa nueva (we’re going to buy), quiero comprar una casa nueva (I want to buy).
target_language_example: Estamos ahorrando para comprar una casa nueva.
native_language_example: We’re saving to buy a new house.

additional_notes: Uses an indirect object pronoun before the verb to show who receives the gift: comprarle = “to buy for him/her/you.” Then use a + the person: comprarle un regalo a Tom. You can also replace a + name with a pronoun: comprarle un regalo a él/a ella/a ti. (Pronoun + a + person is common for clarity: comprarle a él.)
target_language_example: Voy a comprarle un regalo a mi mamá para su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy my mom a gift for her birthday.

meaning: to buy oneself a car (to get a car).
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) to emphasize the purchase is for oneself: "me compré un coche" = "I bought myself a car." Very common in Spanish for personal purchases. Often appears with "acabar de" (just did) and with details like "nuevo" (new), "usado" or "de segunda mano" (used).
target_language_example: Él acaba de comprarse un coche usado.
native_language_example: He just bought himself a used car.

additional_notes: Used to say you purchased something in the past. "Compré" is the preterite (completed past) of "comprar" = "to buy" for "yo" (I). It’s usually followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., "un reloj", "un auto"). For feminine nouns, use "compré una" (e.g., "compré una camisa").
target_language_example: Ayer compré un regalo para mi mamá.
native_language_example: Yesterday I bought a gift for my mom.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of comprar: compré = “I bought.” Use it for a completed action in the past. You can add details like time/place (Ayer compré un libro; Compré un libro aquí) or type (Compré un libro de chistes). With an indirect object, it means you bought it for someone: Le compré un libro a Tom = “I bought Tom a book.”
target_language_example: Hoy fui a la librería y compré un libro para mi hermana.
native_language_example: Today I went to the bookstore and bought a book for my sister.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: compré una casa/bolsa/chaqueta. "Compré" is the preterite (simple past) of comprar, so it refers to a completed purchase in the past. With masculine nouns, use "compré un" (e.g., compré un libro).
target_language_example: Ayer compré una entrada para el concierto.
native_language_example: Yesterday I bought a ticket for the concert.

additional_notes: "Compré" is the simple past (pretérito) of "comprar" (to buy), used for a completed action in the past. "Una cámara" usually means a (photo/video) camera; you can also say "una cámara de fotos" to be extra clear. You can add time expressions like "el otro día" (the other day), "hace dos días" (two days ago), or "hace poco" (recently).
target_language_example: Hace poco compré una cámara para mi viaje.
native_language_example: I recently bought a camera for my trip.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of **comprar**: **(él/ella/usted) compró** = “bought.” **Un** is the masculine singular “a/an” (use **una** for feminine nouns). You can add an indirect object to show who it was bought for: **le compró un suéter** = “he bought him/her a sweater,” **me compró un reloj** = “he bought me a watch.” You may also see **se compró** to emphasize buying something for oneself: **ella se compró un peine** = “she bought herself a comb.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano compró un regalo para mi mamá.
native_language_example: My brother bought a gift for my mom.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of comprar: compró = “bought.” It often implies a completed action at a specific time. You’ll also see the reflexive form “se compró un coche,” meaning “(he/she) bought himself/herself a car.”
target_language_example: El año pasado compró un coche nuevo.
native_language_example: Last year, he bought a new car.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite (simple past) of comprar to talk about a completed purchase in the past. Subject pronouns are often omitted (e.g., Compró un perro = He/She bought a dog). You may also see se compró un perro, which emphasizes buying it for oneself ("bought himself/herself a dog"). Word order can vary (Ayer compró un perro / Compró un perro ayer).
target_language_example: Mi hermana compró un perro la semana pasada.
native_language_example: My sister bought a dog last week.

additional_notes: "Compró" is the preterite (simple past) of "comprar" (to buy). "Una" is the feminine singular form of "a/an" and is used before feminine nouns (una camisa, una falda, una piña). With masculine nouns, use "compró un" (un pato, un libro).
target_language_example: Ayer compró una entrada para el concierto.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she bought a ticket for the concert.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of comprar for él/ella/usted: compró. In context it often matches English “bought.” You may also see the reflexive version “se compró una cámara,” which usually means “bought himself/herself a camera” (emphasizing it was for them).
target_language_example: Mi hermana compró una cámara nueva ayer.
native_language_example: My sister bought a new camera yesterday.

additional_notes: Common term for a laptop, especially in Latin America. Often used with possessives: mi/tu/su computadora portátil. In Spain, you’ll also hear “ordenador portátil” or simply “portátil”.
target_language_example: Voy a llevar mi computadora portátil al trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m going to take my laptop to work.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person or thing as normal/typical, without special qualities. Often follows the noun ("un hombre común y corriente") or is used after "ser/parecer" ("parece común y corriente"). It can be mildly dismissive depending on tone, like saying someone is 'just an ordinary' person.
target_language_example: No quiero una vida común y corriente; quiero hacer algo diferente.
native_language_example: I don't want an ordinary life; I want to do something different.

additional_notes: A religious phrase. Used literally to talk about someone/something being connected to God, and commonly as a blessing or farewell ("Ve con Dios" = "Go with God"). It can also be a respectful way to say someone has died ("Ya está con Dios" = "He/She is with God now").
target_language_example: Que descanses en paz; ahora estás con Dios.
native_language_example: Rest in peace; you are with God now.

additional_notes: "Ud." is the written abbreviation of "usted" (formal "you"). "Con Ud." is used to mean "with you" when addressing someone politely (e.g., a customer, stranger, or someone in authority). In speech, you normally say "con usted" rather than pronouncing the abbreviation.
target_language_example: Quisiera hablar con Ud. un momento.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak with you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say something contains water or is filled/covered/served using water (e.g., llenar algo con agua = to fill something with water). It can also indicate the cause or means of something happening (me quemé con agua hirviendo = I burned myself with boiling water; apagar el fuego con agua = to put out the fire with water).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes traer un vaso con agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used after a verb to indicate the person you’re doing something with or involving (e.g., "probarlo con alguien" = try it with someone, "acostarme con alguien" = sleep with someone, "salir con alguien" = date someone, "ponerme en contacto con alguien" = get in touch with someone). "Alguien" is an indefinite person (not a specific name).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de eso con alguien que no conozco.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that with someone I don’t know.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is done with affection/care, or as a sign-off in messages (like “With love,”). Also appears in contrasts like “confundir X con amor” (“to confuse X with love”), where it means the feeling of love/affection.
target_language_example: Te lo digo con amor, pero tienes que descansar más.
native_language_example: I’m telling you this with love, but you need to rest more.

meaning: calmly; in a relaxed way; take it easy.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something without rushing or getting upset (e.g., hablar con calma, esperar con calma, actuar con calma). Very common in advice/commands with verbs like tomar: Tómalo con calma = “Take it easy / Don’t get worked up.”
target_language_example: Respira hondo y habla con calma.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath and speak calmly.

additional_notes: Used in banking, invoices, and expense reports to indicate which account, card, budget, or person will pay the cost. Often followed by an account, card, department, or name: “con cargo a la tarjeta”, “con cargo a la cuenta”, “con cargo a Marketing”. Similar to “a cargo de” (“paid for by”), but “con cargo a” emphasizes the account/source the charge is applied to.
target_language_example: Los gastos del hotel serán con cargo a la tarjeta de la empresa.
native_language_example: The hotel expenses will be charged to the company card.

additional_notes: Often used in letters/messages as a warm sign-off (like “With love,”). It can also describe doing or remembering something in a loving, caring way: leer algo con cariño (read it lovingly/carefully), recordar a alguien con cariño (remember someone fondly).
target_language_example: Te lo digo con cariño: cuídate mucho.
native_language_example: I’m telling you this with love: take good care of yourself.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing an action in a careful way, often to avoid danger, damage, or mistakes. It can modify a verb (Hazlo con cuidado.) and it’s also common as a warning/advice (Vayan con cuidado. = “Be careful.”).
target_language_example: Abre la caja con cuidado, es frágil.
native_language_example: Open the box carefully; it’s fragile.

additional_notes: A required contraction of **con + el → con el** (you can’t say *con el* as two separate words). It usually means "with the" in a literal sense (e.g., *con el pie* = "with your foot"), but it can also appear in common verb phrases where the meaning depends on the verb: **quedarse con el** = "to keep / end up with" (something), **estar con el** = "to be with / side with" (someone), **estar ocupada con el cuidado de...** = "to be busy with the care of...".
target_language_example: Voy con el profesor al museo.
native_language_example: I’m going with the teacher to the museum.

additional_notes: A formal, polite set phrase used before (or after) disagreeing, correcting someone, giving an order, or saying something that could sound rude. Often used when addressing someone with authority (señor/señora). It can sound stiff or even slightly sarcastic depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Con el debido respeto, creo que está equivocado.
native_language_example: With all due respect, I think you're wrong.

meaning: with the money; (run off/keep it) taking the money.
additional_notes: Often used after verbs like escapar/huir/correr (“to escape/flee/run”) to mean someone leaves while carrying the money (i.e., stole it). With quedarse, it means “to keep the money” (often unfairly). With hacer … con el dinero, it means “to do something with the money” (use/spend/invest it).
target_language_example: No te vayas con el dinero; tenemos que pagar la cuenta.
native_language_example: Don’t leave with the money; we have to pay the bill.

meaning: in order to; with the goal of.
additional_notes: Introduces the purpose/goal of an action and is followed by an infinitive (con el fin de + verbo en infinitivo): con el fin de estudiar, construir, conocer. It’s a fairly formal way to say purpose; in everyday speech you’ll often hear para or para que instead.
target_language_example: Reservé una mesa con el fin de celebrar tu cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I booked a table in order to celebrate your birthday.

meaning: with the manager; (in some contexts) to/with the manager (to complain or speak).
additional_notes: Literally means “with the manager.” After certain verbs like "quejarse" (to complain), "hablar" (to talk), or "discutir" (to argue), "con el gerente" often means you are addressing the manager directly (similar to “to the manager” / “with the manager” in English).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar con el gerente, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak with the manager, please.

meaning: over time; as time goes by.
additional_notes: Used to say that something changes gradually as time passes. It often appears with verbs like mejorar (to improve), cambiar/transformarse (to change), desvanecerse (to fade), crecer (to grow).
target_language_example: Con el paso del tiempo, me acostumbré a vivir en otra ciudad.
native_language_example: Over time, I got used to living in another city.

meaning: "with whom" / "with which" (refers back to a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer to a person or thing mentioned earlier, after the preposition "con" (with). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to: con el que (masc. singular), con la que (fem. singular), con los que (masc. plural), con las que (fem. plural). Often used after a noun: "un hombre con el que..." / "un lugar con el que...".
target_language_example: Necesito a alguien con el que pueda practicar español.
native_language_example: I need someone with whom I can practice Spanish.

meaning: "with the result" / "with the outcome" (often: satisfied or not satisfied with it).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives/phrases like satisfecho/a, contento/a, (in)satisfecho/a to say how someone feels about the outcome of something (an exam, test, project, etc.). It’s commonly followed by “de + [thing]” to specify what the result is from: “con el resultado del examen”.
target_language_example: No estoy satisfecho con el resultado de la reunión.
native_language_example: I'm not satisfied with the outcome of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens gradually as time passes, often meaning "eventually" (e.g., healing, getting used to something). It can appear at the start of the sentence or after the verb: "Con el tiempo..." / "...con el tiempo." Not to confuse with "a tiempo" (on time) or "en el tiempo" (in time/within time).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, me acostumbré a vivir aquí.
native_language_example: Over time, I got used to living here.

meaning: with the work; (busy/occupied) with work; about work (tasks).
additional_notes: “Con” often means “with” in the sense of being involved in something. “Con el trabajo” can mean (1) helping someone with a job/task (“Ayudé… con el trabajo”), (2) being busy/occupied with work (“estoy ocupado con el trabajo”), or (3) being satisfied/happy with the work done (“contento/satisfecho con el trabajo”). The article can change: con el trabajo (the work / work in general), con mi/tu/su trabajo (my/your/their work), con un trabajo (a job/task).
target_language_example: Estoy ocupado con el trabajo y no puedo salir hoy.
native_language_example: I’m busy with work and I can’t go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with a woman/girl, or that you do something accompanied by her. It can also mean doing something using something feminine previously mentioned (e.g., “con ella” = “with it” when referring to a feminine noun), but most often it means “with her.”
target_language_example: Voy al cine con ella esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with her tonight.

meaning: 'with them' (referring to a group of males or a mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something together with a group, or dealing/communicating with that group. In Spanish, "ellos" is used for a group of men or a mixed-gender group; for a group of women only, use "con ellas".
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar con ellos mañana?
native_language_example: Can you talk with them tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun to refer to a specific thing already known from context: con esa cantidad (with that amount), con esa sonrisa (with that smile), con esa máquina (with that machine). For masculine nouns, use con ese; for plural, con esas / con esos.
target_language_example: No puedo con esa música tan alta.
native_language_example: I can’t deal with that music being so loud.

meaning: "with that" / "using that" (referring to something masculine: "that one").
additional_notes: "Ese" means "that" (masculine singular), usually followed by a noun: "con ese cuchillo" = "with that knife." It can also stand alone if the noun is understood: "No me vengas con ese" = "Don’t come at me with that (excuse/line)." For feminine use "con esa"; plural: "con esos / con esas."
target_language_example: No puedo cortar esto con ese cuchillo; necesito uno más grande.
native_language_example: I can’t cut this with that knife; I need a bigger one.

meaning: with that; about that (referring to “that” situation/thing).
additional_notes: Used with verbs/nouns to talk about an issue or reaction to something previously mentioned: "No tengo problema con eso" = "I have no problem with that." In common set phrases it can sound idiomatic: "Ya basta con eso" = "Enough of that," "No empieces con eso" = "Don’t start with that," and "Suerte con eso" = "Good luck with that" (often a bit sarcastic depending on tone).
target_language_example: No empieces con eso, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t start with that, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something close in context (“this”): a task, object, plan, or situation. Very common after verbs like acabar (con esto) “finish/end this”, lidiar (con esto) “deal with this”, poder (más) con esto “handle this”, tener problema (con esto) “have a problem with this”, and ir (con esto) in expressions like “Ya veo a dónde vas con esto” = “I see where you’re going with this.”
target_language_example: No puedo seguir con esto; necesito un descanso.
native_language_example: I can’t keep going with this; I need a break.

additional_notes: Used to describe that an action is done without effort or problems. It often comes after the verb (e.g., "lo hizo con facilidad"), and it can be used with many verbs like hacer, resolver, aprender, encontrar, etc.
target_language_example: Aprendí la canción con facilidad.
native_language_example: I learned the song easily.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like hablar, leer, or escribir to say you can do something easily and naturally, especially a language: hablar español con fluidez. It can also be used humorously or exaggeratedly (e.g., Hablo Google Translate con fluidez).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar español con fluidez antes de viajar.
native_language_example: I want to speak Spanish fluently before traveling.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens regularly or many times. It can go at the beginning of the sentence ("Con frecuencia se dice...") or after the verb ("Lo hago con frecuencia").
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio con frecuencia.
native_language_example: I go to the gym often.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something with physical force or with strong intensity/energy. Often answers “how?” (¿Cómo?) and can modify many verbs: hablar con fuerza (speak firmly/loudly), empujar con fuerza (push hard), llover con fuerza (rain heavily).
target_language_example: Empuja la puerta con fuerza.
native_language_example: Push the door hard.

meaning: with enthusiasm; really wanting to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express strong desire, motivation, or eagerness. Common patterns: "tener ganas de + infinitive" (to feel like / to want to do something) and "hacer algo con ganas" (do something with effort/energy). "Lo espero con ganas" = "I’m really looking forward to it."
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo español con ganas.
native_language_example: I’m learning Spanish with enthusiasm.

additional_notes: Used to express willingness or pleasure in doing something (“I’d be happy to”). Common in polite offers and responses: “Con gusto puedo…” / “Vendré con gusto.”
target_language_example: Con gusto te ayudo con la tarea.
native_language_example: I’ll gladly help you with the homework.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: con la experiencia (“with the experience”), con la tripa llena (“with a full belly”). For masculine singular, use con el; for plural, con las / con los. Often introduces what you use, who you’re with, or the condition/circumstance something happens in.
target_language_example: Voy a salir con la profesora.
native_language_example: I’m going to go out with the (female) teacher.

meaning: with the help of; thanks to (someone/something’s help).
additional_notes: Used to say you do something using another person’s or thing’s assistance. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: con la ayuda de ella / de mi amigo / de un auto. Common in both formal and everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Terminé el proyecto con la ayuda de mis compañeros.
native_language_example: I finished the project with the help of my classmates.

meaning: with your head; using your head (e.g., to nod, to think).
additional_notes: Literally “with the head.” Common with verbs like asentir/mover (to nod/move) to show the action is done by moving your head: “asentir con la cabeza” = “to nod your head.” It can also mean “using your head/mind,” as in “pensar con la cabeza” (think rationally). In some contexts it means hitting something with your head: “darse con la cabeza (en…)” = “to hit your head (on…).”
target_language_example: Me dijo que sí con la cabeza.
native_language_example: He/She signaled yes by nodding.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like hablar (to talk), charlar (to chat), socializar (to socialize), juntarse (to hang out/get together), ser bueno/malo con (to be good/bad with). Often refers to people in general or a specific group depending on context (e.g., con la gente de su laboratorio = with the people from his lab).
target_language_example: Me gusta trabajar con la gente.
native_language_example: I like working with people.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using your hand (as the instrument). Common with actions like holding or carrying something ("sostener con la mano"), feeding an animal directly ("darle de comer ... con la mano"), or greeting by waving ("saludar con la mano").
target_language_example: Escribí la nota con la mano porque no tenía computadora.
native_language_example: I wrote the note by hand because I didn't have a computer.

additional_notes: Used to say which hand someone uses to do an action (write, eat, hold something). You can swap izquierda/derecha depending on the hand. Common pattern: "(verb) con la mano izquierda".
target_language_example: No puedo cortar con la mano izquierda; soy diestro.
native_language_example: I can't cut with my left hand; I'm right-handed.

meaning: with the police; (sometimes) the police, please.
additional_notes: Literally “with the police.” It’s used in a few common ways: (1) to mean being involved with/alongside the police (e.g., “problemas con la policía” = trouble with the police; “ir con la policía” = go with the police). (2) In phone or emergency contexts, it can mean “put me through to the police / get the police” (often with a verb like “Póngame…”). In insults like “A la mierda con la policía,” it’s a strong, rude expression.
target_language_example: Póngame con la policía, por favor; es una emergencia.
native_language_example: Put me through to the police, please; it’s an emergency.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a feminine singular person or thing after a preposition: con + la + que. Common in relative clauses: la mujer con la que hablaste (the woman you spoke with). With things/abstract nouns it often means “with which/how”: la facilidad con la que contestó (the ease with which / how easily she answered).
target_language_example: La escuela con la que colaboramos está cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: The school we collaborate with is near here.

meaning: with his/hers (with theirs); in “salirse con la suya”: to get one’s way.
additional_notes: “La suya” is a possessive pronoun meaning “his/hers/its/theirs” (feminine singular), used when the noun is understood (e.g., *tu traducción* vs. *la suya* = “yours” vs. “his/hers”). After prepositions like *con*, it becomes *con la suya* (“with his/hers”). Very commonly appears inside the fixed expression *salirse con la suya* (“to get away with it / to get one’s way”).
target_language_example: No voy a dejar que se salga con la suya.
native_language_example: I’m not going to let him/her get his/her way.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dormir (to sleep) or quedarse dormido (to fall asleep) to describe doing something while the window is open. You can change the article/number depending on the situation: con una ventana abierta (with an open window), con las ventanas abiertas (with the windows open).
target_language_example: No puedo dormir con la ventana abierta en invierno.
native_language_example: I can't sleep with the window open in winter.

meaning: "with life" (used after many verbs to mean "with life / with someone’s life").
additional_notes:
Very common with different verbs:
- seguir con la vida = to go on with life / keep living
- acabar con la vida (de alguien) = to end someone’s life (to kill)
- jugar con la vida (de alguien) = to risk someone’s life / play with someone’s life
- confundir X con la vida = to confuse X with real life
It’s usually literal in meaning, but the exact English translation depends on the verb.
target_language_example: No juegues con la vida de nadie.
native_language_example: Don’t play with anyone’s life.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns to mean "with" in the sense of accompaniment, having/holding something, or using something (e.g., con las tijeras = with the scissors). It can also mean "regarding/with" in expressions like "concuerda con las..." (it matches/lines up with the...).
target_language_example: Voy con las llaves en la mano.
native_language_example: I'm going with the keys in my hand.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something using your hands, or in physical contact with your hands. Often appears with an adjective: "con las manos mojadas" (with wet hands), or in set phrases like "con las manos en alto" (with your hands up).
target_language_example: No abras la botella con las manos sucias.
native_language_example: Don’t open the bottle with dirty hands.

con las manos en la masa

target_language_multi_word_term: con las manos en la masa
additional_notes: Used when someone is discovered while doing something wrong or illegal. Very common with verbs like "pillar" (to catch), "coger" (to catch), and "atrapar" (to catch). Literally "with (your) hands in the dough"—like being caught while still doing it.
target_language_example: Lo pillaron con las manos en la masa cuando copiaba en el examen.
native_language_example: They caught him in the act when he was cheating on the exam.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like ir/irse/volver (to go/leave/come back) to mean you leave without buying, receiving, or bringing something (e.g., no gift, no purchase, no results). Can be literal (no items in your hands) or figurative (no gain).
target_language_example: Fui a la tienda, pero volví con las manos vacías.
native_language_example: I went to the store, but I came back empty-handed.

additional_notes: Uses "con" (= with) + "las mujeres" (= the women). It can mean being physically together with women ("Quédate con las mujeres") or how someone deals/gets along with women ("Es bueno con las mujeres", "exitoso con las mujeres").
target_language_example: No es tímido con las mujeres, pero con los hombres sí.
native_language_example: He isn’t shy with women, but he is with men.

additional_notes: Used to say something includes milk (especially drinks like coffee or tea). In food-making contexts, it can mean “made with milk” (e.g., se hace con leche). Often contrasts with other options like sin leche (“without milk”).
target_language_example: Quiero un café con leche, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with milk, please.

additional_notes: Used with "cerrar" or "estar" to say something is locked: "cerrar con llave" = to lock (with a key), "estar cerrada con llave" = to be locked. It can describe doors, drawers, rooms, etc. Word order varies: "cerrar con llave la puerta" / "cerrar la puerta con llave".
target_language_example: ¿La puerta está cerrada con llave?
native_language_example: Is the door locked?

meaning: “with what” / “with the thing that” (used before a clause to mean “what…”).
additional_notes: Used to refer to “what” someone says/does/has/feels, etc., often after verbs like tener cuidado, seguir, estar, ser, or expressions like con lo que + verb (“with what/how much…”). In some contexts it conveys intensity: con lo que pica… = “given how much it itches…”. Also appears in ironic remarks like Con lo que me interesa… (“As if I cared…”).
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con lo que dices.
native_language_example: Be careful what you say.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of someone’s words (“what you say”). Very common after expressions like: tener cuidado / ten cuidado / ojo (“be careful”), estar de acuerdo / no estar de acuerdo (“(not) agree”), etc. Literally “with what you say,” but in English it’s often just “what you say.”
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con lo que dices en la reunión.
native_language_example: Be careful what you say in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the relative pronoun "lo que" after "con". It can refer to (1) an amount or resources: "con lo que cuesta..." = "with what it costs..." / "for the price of..."; (2) the thing/activity to continue or deal with: "Sigan con lo que estaban haciendo" = "Keep doing what you were doing"; (3) a comparison or match: "coherente con lo que piensa" = "consistent with what they think".
target_language_example: No puedo pagar con lo que tengo ahora.
native_language_example: I can’t pay with what I have right now.

additional_notes: "Con" means "with" and "los" is the masculine plural definite article ("the"). It’s used before masculine plural nouns: con los baches (with the potholes), con los diamantes (with the diamonds), con los peregrinos (with the pilgrims). It can mean accompaniment/association ("with"), involvement (working with someone), or having something in your possession (leaving with the diamonds). Compare: con la (feminine singular), con las (feminine plural), con el (masculine singular).
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con los coches cuando cruces la calle.
native_language_example: Be careful with the cars when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Describes someone sitting or standing with their arms crossed across their chest. It can be purely physical/neutral, but depending on context it may suggest a closed, defensive, impatient, or unimpressed attitude.
target_language_example: No te quedes con los brazos cruzados; ayúdame, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t just stand there with your arms crossed; help me, please.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ayudar (to help), estar (to be), quedarse (to stay), or terminar (to finish) to say someone is dealing with homework. Also common as "con mis/tus/sus deberes" (with my/your/his/her homework). In some countries you may also hear "la tarea" for homework.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes ayudar con los deberes de matemáticas?
native_language_example: Can you help me with my math homework?

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using your fingers rather than a tool (like a fork, brush, or comb). It often implies doing it by hand: eating finger food (comer con los dedos), combing hair (peinarse con los dedos), counting on your fingers (contar con los dedos), or finger-painting (pintar con los dedos).
target_language_example: No toques la pantalla con los dedos, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t touch the screen with your fingers, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone behaves in relation to other people in general. It often follows adjectives or verbs like ser amable, ser considerado/a, tener paciencia, or tratar a alguien (e.g., “Sé amable con los demás”).
target_language_example: No seas tan duro con los demás; todos cometemos errores.
native_language_example: Don’t be so hard on others; we all make mistakes.

meaning: with the children; with the kids.
additional_notes: Uses "con" (with) + "los niños" (the children). It can mean being together/doing an activity together ("salir con los niños"), or being good at dealing with children ("ser genial/paciente con los niños"). "Niños" can refer to boys specifically or to children in general; "los" makes it "the" (specific children, often your/their kids).
target_language_example: Voy al parque con los niños después de la escuela.
native_language_example: I'm going to the park with the kids after school.

additional_notes: Used with "con" to say you do something using your eyes (i.e., by watching/looking). Often appears in set phrases like "con los ojos abiertos" (with eyes open) and "con los ojos vendados" (blindfolded), and in contrasts like "con el oído... con los ojos" (by ear… by eye).
target_language_example: Reconocí el edificio con los ojos, no con el nombre.
native_language_example: I recognized the building by sight, not by its name.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: having your eyes open. Used literally (e.g., “sleep with your eyes open”) and figuratively to mean staying alert/cautious and paying close attention (similar to “with your eyes open” / “with your eyes wide open”). Often follows an action: “dormir/besar/estar con los ojos abiertos”.
target_language_example: Tienes que caminar con los ojos abiertos en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: You have to walk with your eyes open in this city.

additional_notes: Literally “with the eyes closed.” Used to describe someone doing something while their eyes are shut (resting, listening, sitting). It can also be used figuratively to mean “easily / without thinking,” but in your examples it’s physical.
target_language_example: Respira hondo con los ojos cerrados.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath with your eyes closed.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is together with the other people or things in a group. Often appears with verbs like ir (go), estar (be), reunirse (meet up), llevarse bien (get along), or poner (put): "Ve con los otros" (Go with the others), "Ponlo ahí con los otros" (Put it there with the others).
target_language_example: Si terminas antes, espera con los otros.
native_language_example: If you finish early, wait with the others.

additional_notes: Describes someone who is about to cry or is already crying a little (from sadness, emotion, or even joy). Used as an adverbial phrase to describe how someone looks, speaks, or does something: "mirar/hablar/estar" con lágrimas en los ojos.
target_language_example: Me despedí con lágrimas en los ojos.
native_language_example: I said goodbye with tears in my eyes.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with or using something that belongs to you. It’s followed by a singular noun: con mi teléfono (with my phone), con mi hermano (with my brother). For plural, use con mis (with my + plural noun).
target_language_example: Voy al trabajo con mi computadora.
native_language_example: I go to work with my computer.

additional_notes: Use it to say you are accompanied by your family or doing something together with them. It often answers “Who are you with?” (¿Con quién estás?) or adds context to an activity (hablar con mi familia = to talk with my family). You can swap in other possessives: con tu familia (with your family), con su familia (with his/her/their family).
target_language_example: Voy al parque con mi familia.
native_language_example: I’m going to the park with my family.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "con" (with) + "mi hermana" (my sister). It can mean being together/working alongside someone ("trabaja con mi hermana") or being involved with someone ("tuvo una relación ... con mi hermana").
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi hermana esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your brother (going somewhere, being with him, doing an activity). It can describe companionship (“I went with my brother”) or who someone is currently with (“He’s with my brother”).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi hermano esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my brother tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your daughter, spending time with her, or doing an activity involving her. "Con" can mean "with" in the sense of accompaniment (being together) or involvement (doing something with/for someone).
target_language_example: Estoy en el parque con mi hija.
native_language_example: I’m at the park with my daughter.

additional_notes: Used to say you are with your mother (doing an activity together) or that something happens in her company. It can also mean “with” in the sense of living together (e.g., Vivo con mi madre = I live with my mother). The preposition con usually becomes conmigo only with the pronoun mí (“with me”), not with nouns like mi madre.
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi madre.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my mother.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your father or doing an activity alongside him. "Con" usually means "with" (in the sense of accompaniment): con mi madre (with my mother), con mi amigo (with my friend).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi padre esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my father tonight.
