additional_notes: Used to talk about staying awake late into the night. Often appears with the verb “quedarse” (to stay/remain): “quedarse despierto hasta tarde” = “to stay up late.” You can adjust for gender/number: despierto (m.), despierta (f.), despiertos/despiertas (plural).
target_language_example: Los fines de semana me quedo despierto hasta tarde.
native_language_example: On weekends I stay up late.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does not sleep during the whole night. Often appears with the verb phrase “quedarse” (to stay): “quedarse despierto toda la noche” = to stay awake all night. “Despierto” changes for gender/number: despierta, despiertos, despiertas.
target_language_example: Me quedé despierto toda la noche estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: I stayed awake all night studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than another event/time. Before a noun/pronoun: "después de la tormenta", "después de mi divorcio", "después de medianoche". Before a clause, Spanish usually uses "después de que" + subjunctive: "Después de que se hayan ido..."
target_language_example: Después de cenar, vamos al cine.
native_language_example: After dinner, we’re going to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to give a routine instruction that should be done every time you eat (common in health advice and medication directions). "Después de" = "after" + "cada" = "each" + "comida" = "meal/food."
target_language_example: Recuerda lavarte las manos después de cada comida.
native_language_example: Remember to wash your hands after each meal.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the action of having dinner. It’s a time expression: después de + infinitive (después de comer, después de estudiar, etc.).
target_language_example: Vamos a dar un paseo después de cenar.
native_language_example: We’re going to go for a walk after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens once the lesson/school period ends. It can refer to a specific class session or more generally to the end of the school day (depending on context). Often used with routines: "después de clase suelo..."
target_language_example: Vamos a tomar un café después de clase.
native_language_example: Let’s go have a coffee after class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once the school day or a class period is finished. Common in school-related plans and routines: "después de clases, voy a…" (after class, I’m going to…). You can also hear "después de la clase" (after the class) for one specific class.
target_language_example: Nos vemos después de clases para estudiar.
native_language_example: See you after class to study.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than eating. It can be followed by nothing (after eating/after the meal) or by an object: «después de comer mi comida» (after eating my food). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence, with a comma when it starts the sentence.
target_language_example: Después de comer, vamos a dar un paseo.
native_language_example: After eating, we're going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens once 10 minutes have passed from a starting point (often from the beginning of an action or situation). You can replace the number/time: después de cinco minutos (after five minutes), después de una hora (after an hour).
target_language_example: Después de diez minutos, empezó a llover.
native_language_example: After ten minutes, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens next in time, referring back to an action or event already mentioned. It’s common in storytelling and giving instructions: Primero..., y después de eso.... Also often shortened to "después" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Terminamos de comer y después de eso fuimos al cine.
native_language_example: We finished eating and after that we went to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to say one action happened after a completed earlier action. It’s followed by a past participle: después de haber + participio (haber encontrado, haber leído, haber terminado). In everyday speech you can often also say: después de + infinitivo (Después de leer la carta...).
target_language_example: Después de haber cenado, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: After having dinner, we went out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say that one event happens later in time than another. It’s the feminine form of “después de” + the article “la”; use it before a singular feminine noun (e.g., “después de la clase”). Before a masculine noun, use “después del” (de + el).
target_language_example: Después de la cena, vamos a dar un paseo.
native_language_example: After dinner, we’re going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the meal (cena = dinner). Often placed at the start or end of the sentence: “Después de la cena, …” / “… después de la cena.”
target_language_example: Después de la cena, hago la tarea.
native_language_example: After dinner, I do my homework.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens following the end of the school day. It can be followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "después de la escuela + jugamos/estudio/trabajo").
target_language_example: Después de la escuela, hago mi tarea y luego salgo con mis amigos.
native_language_example: After school, I do my homework and then hang out with my friends.

meaning: 'after the war' (in the period following a war).
additional_notes: Used to place an event in time after a specific war that both speakers understand from context (often a major war). It can refer to immediately after or generally in the years following: e.g., "dos años después de la guerra" = "two years after the war."
target_language_example: Después de la guerra, mucha gente tuvo que empezar de nuevo.
native_language_example: After the war, many people had to start over.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once it has rained. It commonly introduces a time clause at the beginning of a sentence (followed by a comma), but it can also appear later in the sentence. You can swap in other events: después de la clase (after class), después de cenar (after dinner).
target_language_example: Después de la lluvia, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: After the rain, we went out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once a person has died (often in discussions about the afterlife: "la vida después de la muerte" = "life after death"). It can describe a time period (“after death”) or beliefs (“after death there is nothing”).
target_language_example: Muchas religiones hablan de lo que pasa después de la muerte.
native_language_example: Many religions talk about what happens after death.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause (subject + verb) that happens first, followed by the main action: "después de que + verb". With completed/past actions it’s very commonly followed by the subjunctive in many dialects (e.g., "después de que regresara"), though you’ll also hear the indicative ("después de que regresó"). If there’s no verb (just a noun/infinitive), use "después de" (e.g., "después de la cena", "después de comer").
target_language_example: Te llamo después de que termine la reunión.
native_language_example: I’ll call you after the meeting ends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens later than an event or time period that belongs to someone/something. It’s "después de" + the possessive adjective "su" (his/her/its/your formal). With plural possessions use "después de sus" (after his/her/their...).
target_language_example: Después de su cena, se fue a casa.
native_language_example: After his/her dinner, he/she went home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing events, words, or actions that happened before, often implying contrast, surprise, or a complaint (like “considering everything that…”). It’s commonly followed by a verb: “después de todo lo que + ha pasado / habíamos dicho / he hecho…”.
target_language_example: Después de todo lo que hiciste por mí, no puedo decir que no.
native_language_example: After everything you did for me, I can’t say no.

additional_notes: Used to (1) correct or update a conclusion: "It wasn’t X, after all" / "He’s going after all"; and (2) give a reason or reminder that supports what you’re saying: "After all, she’s the judge." Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence, and it’s common with commas in writing.
target_language_example: Parece que vamos a salir después de todo.
native_language_example: Looks like we’re going to go out after all.

additional_notes: Used to say that one event happens later than another: después de + noun. Here, "un" is the masculine singular indefinite article; with feminine nouns use "después de una" (e.g., después de una pausa). With plural nouns: "después de unos/unas". Often followed by an event or period of time (e.g., un descanso, un golpe).
target_language_example: Después de un buen desayuno, salimos de casa.
native_language_example: After a good breakfast, we left the house.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than an event or time period: "después de una lluvia" (after a rain), "después de una década" (after a decade). It must be followed by a feminine singular noun; with a masculine singular noun you usually say "después de un". With "el" it becomes "después del" (after the).
target_language_example: Después de una reunión larga, me fui a casa.
native_language_example: After a long meeting, I went home.

meaning: “after a long …” (often followed by a noun like wait/absence).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens following a long period of time. It’s typically completed with a feminine noun because of “una” (e.g., una espera = a wait, una ausencia = an absence). Common pattern: “Después de una larga + [noun], …” or “… después de una larga + [noun].”
target_language_example: Después de una larga espera, por fin nos atendieron.
native_language_example: After a long wait, they finally helped us.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than an event or time. It’s the contraction of “después de + el” (de + el = del). With feminine nouns, use “después de la” (no contraction): “después de la clase”. With plural nouns: “después de los / de las”.
target_language_example: Después del almuerzo, voy a llamar a mi mamá.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to call my mom.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens later than (and usually as a consequence of) a specific accident. Often followed by a result or change: "Después del accidente, ..." or used with a time expression: "tres horas después del accidente".
target_language_example: Después del accidente, tuvo que ir al hospital.
native_language_example: After the accident, he had to go to the hospital.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than lunchtime. Often followed by an action or a time (e.g., “después del almuerzo, …”). In Spanish, “después de” becomes “después del” before a masculine singular noun like “almuerzo” (de + el = del).
target_language_example: Nos vemos después del almuerzo.
native_language_example: See you after lunch.

meaning: after work; after getting off work.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you do once your workday ends. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence or set off with commas, and can be emphasized with words like "inmediatamente" (immediately) or "directo" (straight).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, vamos a cenar.
native_language_example: After work, we're going to have dinner.

additional_notes: Refers to a detective hired by an individual or company (not the police) to investigate something (e.g., surveillance, finding information). Often used with contratar (to hire): «contratar a un detective privado».
target_language_example: Contratamos a un detective privado para encontrar a la persona desaparecida.
native_language_example: We hired a private investigator to find the missing person.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position at the back of something/someone (detrás de la casa, detrás de María) or movement following someone/something (correr detrás de la pelota = run after/chase the ball). It can also be figurative: leer detrás de las palabras = read between the lines/understand the hidden meaning.
target_language_example: El perro corre detrás del gato.
native_language_example: The dog runs after the cat.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically located behind something else (place/position), or figuratively hidden “behind” an appearance or explanation (e.g., detrás de la fachada = behind the facade). Use it before a feminine singular noun: detrás de la puerta, detrás de la cómoda. With a masculine noun, use detrás del (de + el).
target_language_example: El gato está detrás de la silla.
native_language_example: The cat is behind the chair.

additional_notes: A location phrase using detrás de (“behind”) + la cortina (“the curtain”). Used literally for something physically hidden or positioned behind a curtain; it can also suggest something happening secretly/out of sight (like “the men behind the curtain”). You can also say de detrás de la cortina (“from behind the curtain”).
target_language_example: El gato está detrás de la cortina.
native_language_example: The cat is behind the curtain.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) is located on the far side of a door from where you are. Common with verbs like estar (to be), esconderse (to hide), colgar (to hang), esperar (to wait). You can also use it more figuratively (as in “Detrás de la puerta, la riqueza lo esperaba”) to mean something is “just out of sight” or “right around the corner.”
target_language_example: El gato está detrás de la puerta.
native_language_example: The cat is behind the door.

additional_notes: Used to say something (the sun, moon, etc.) is hidden/covered by clouds and not visible. Often appears with verbs like "desaparecer" (to disappear) and "ser" (to be): "desapareció detrás de las nubes", "está/es invisible detrás de las nubes". You can also say "desde detrás de las nubes" = "from behind the clouds".
target_language_example: El sol salió de detrás de las nubes.
native_language_example: The sun came out from behind the clouds.

additional_notes: Literally refers to the area on your head just behind your ears. Common with verbs like rascar (to scratch), lavar (to wash), or describing haircuts (e.g., corto detrás de las orejas = short behind/around the ears).
target_language_example: A mi perro le encanta que le acaricien detrás de las orejas.
native_language_example: My dog loves it when they pet him behind the ears.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something/someone is located or moves behind the speaker. Often with verbs like estar (to be), ponerse (to stand/get), ir/venir (to go/come): "Está detrás de mí" = "He/She is behind me."
target_language_example: No te pongas detrás de mí; no puedo verte.
native_language_example: Don’t stand behind me; I can’t see you.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position/movement at your back (often as a warning: “Behind you!”). It can also mean “following you” (walking/driving after you): “Iremos detrás de ti.” In some contexts, “estar detrás de alguien” can imply support or pursuit (“backing you” / “after you”), but the basic meaning is physical location. Also note: “ti” is used after prepositions (de, a, para, etc.).
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado, hay un perro detrás de ti!
native_language_example: Careful, there's a dog behind you!

meaning: behind him; (also) after him / pursuing him.
additional_notes: Most literally it means physical position (“behind him”). In some contexts, especially with verbs like andar/ir/estar detrás de, it can mean someone is “after him” (chasing, following, or trying to get him). In phrases like “cerró la puerta detrás de él,” it describes an action done as he passes (he closed the door behind him).
target_language_example: Había alguien detrás de él, pero no se dio la vuelta.
native_language_example: There was someone behind him, but he didn’t turn around.

additional_notes: "Detrás de" means "behind" in a physical sense. "Del" is the contraction of "de + el" (used with masculine singular nouns: detrás del sofá, detrás del arbusto). It can also mean "after" in the sense of pursuing or looking for someone/something: La policía va/anda detrás del asesino = The police are after the killer.
target_language_example: El gato está escondido detrás del coche.
native_language_example: The cat is hiding behind the car.

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase "darse cuenta" (to realize/notice), most often with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/se/nos/os di(o) cuenta". It commonly takes "de" + noun ("me di cuenta de eso") or "de que" + clause ("me di cuenta de que..."), and can be emphasized with "ya" ("Ya me di cuenta" = "I already realized").
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten the keys.

additional_notes: This is the preterite (past) form of the reflexive verb phrase **darse cuenta de** (“to realize/notice”). It’s commonly followed by **de** + a noun (**Me di cuenta de su ausencia**) or **de** + a clause (**Me di cuenta de que la amaba**). In negative, **No me di cuenta de...** means “I didn’t realize/notice...”.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que olvidé las llaves.
native_language_example: I realized I forgot the keys.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to say whatever follows: *Di lo que quieres decir* (“Say what you want to say”). Often appears with the subjunctive (*di lo que sea*, *di lo que tengas que decir*) to mean “say whatever…”. It’s a command using **di** (tú imperative of *decir*).
target_language_example: Di lo que piensas, sin miedo.
native_language_example: Say what you think, without fear.

meaning: "I assumed" / "I took it for granted that".
additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular preterite of the expression "dar por sentado que" (literally "to give for seated," but meaning to assume something is true without checking). You can change the verb to match the subject and tense: "doy por sentado que..." (I assume), "dio por sentado que..." (he/she assumed), "dimos por sentado que..." (we assumed). It’s commonly followed by a clause with "que".
target_language_example: Di por sentado que la reunión era a las seis.
native_language_example: I assumed the meeting was at six.

meaning: “the doctor says that…” / “the doctor tells me to…”
additional_notes: Used to report a doctor’s advice or instructions. It’s often followed by the present subjunctive (camine, coma, deje, etc.) because it expresses what the doctor recommends or tells someone to do.
target_language_example: Dice el médico que descanse más y que beba agua.
native_language_example: The doctor says I should rest more and drink water.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says or claims. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., “Mamá dice que…”, “Tom dice que…”), and it’s followed by a full clause (usually with a verb): “dice que + [sentence]”.
target_language_example: Mi hermano dice que mañana no trabaja.
native_language_example: My brother says that he isn’t working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says or claims. "Dice" is the third-person singular of "decir" (to say), and it’s often followed by "que" (that). "El" is "the" (masculine singular), so it’s followed by a masculine noun (e.g., "el zorro"). You can change the subject: "dicen que el..." = "they/people say that the..."
target_language_example: Dice que el restaurante está cerrado hoy.
native_language_example: He/She says that the restaurant is closed today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says about a woman/girl. "Dice" is the 3rd-person singular of *decir* (he/she/you-formal says). "Que" introduces the reported clause. "Ella" (she) is often optional in Spanish unless you want emphasis or clarity: *Dice que sabe dónde están* is more common than *Dice que ella sabe…*. Related: *Se dice que ella…* = “It’s said that she…” (impersonal/rumor).
target_language_example: Dice que ella no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: He/She says that she doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or says. The subject of dice is often implied (él/ella/usted). What follows after que is a statement with es (“is”). You can change the verb to match the person/tense: digo que es (I say it’s), dicen que es (they say it’s), dijo que era (he said it was).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dice que es urgente.
native_language_example: My boss says it’s urgent.

meaning: "(he/she) says no" or "(he/she) says that ... not".
additional_notes: Used with a subject understood from context (often él/ella/usted). "Decir que no" can mean refusing (saying no) or denying something (saying it didn’t happen): e.g., "Dice que no" = "He/She says no"; "Dice que no lo hizo" = "He/She says he didn’t do it."
target_language_example: Le ofrecí ayuda, pero dice que no.
native_language_example: I offered him/her help, but he/she says no.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or states they want. The subject is usually implied from context (él/ella/usted), and the verb that follows is in the present tense: "dice que quiere + infinitive" (e.g., quiere ser/ir/hacer). Note that Spanish "dice" means "says" (it’s not related to English "dice").
target_language_example: María dice que quiere viajar a México este verano.
native_language_example: María says she wants to travel to Mexico this summer.

meaning: "(He/She) says that…" (introduces what someone claims; the clause uses "se").
additional_notes: Used to report what someone says. After "dice que", the "se" belongs to the following verb and can be: (1) reflexive ("se iba" = he left, "se recuperará" = he’ll recover), or (2) impersonal/passive "se" ("se venden" = they are sold). In speech you often add a subject: "Él/Ella dice que…"
target_language_example: Ella dice que se siente mejor hoy.
native_language_example: She says that she feels better today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or says about a male person. In Spanish, the subject pronoun (él) is often optional, so you’ll also commonly hear "dice que…" (e.g., "Dice que quiere hablar con usted"). Using "él" adds emphasis or clarity about who is being talked about.
target_language_example: Mi hermano dice que él no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: My brother says that he doesn’t have time today.

meaning: “they say that…” / “it’s said that…” (reporting what people say or believe).
additional_notes: Used to introduce hearsay, rumors, or general opinion without saying exactly who said it. It’s the present tense of "decir" (to say) in 3rd person plural: "(ellos) dicen" + "que". Similar meaning to "se dice que…". Often implies the speaker is not fully confirming the information.
target_language_example: Dicen que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: They say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "they say that the..." / "people say that the..."
additional_notes: Used to report rumors, common beliefs, or what people say in general. The verb is 3rd person plural (dicen = “they say”) with an unspecified subject (“people”). Often followed by a noun with el (masculine singular): "Dicen que el + noun + ...". For feminine nouns, you’ll hear: "Dicen que la..."; for plural: "Dicen que los/las...".
target_language_example: Dicen que el café ayuda a concentrarse.
native_language_example: They say that coffee helps you concentrate.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people say or what’s commonly believed, without saying who exactly (“they/people”). Very common for rumors, reputation, or general opinions. Usually followed by a description with "ser" (e.g., "Dicen que es honesto").
target_language_example: Dicen que es muy bueno, pero no lo conozco.
native_language_example: They say he’s very good, but I don’t know him.

additional_notes: Past participle of decir used with haber (e.g., he/has/had) or with modals/conditionals: debiste haber dicho la verdad (you should have told the truth), si me hubieras dicho la verdad (if you had told me the truth). More generally, the base phrase is decir la verdad = “to tell the truth.”
target_language_example: Deberías haber dicho la verdad desde el principio.
native_language_example: You should have told the truth from the beginning.

meaning: 'told/said that' (as part of a past tense with haber).
additional_notes: Used after a form of **haber** to make compound past tenses of **decir**: **he/has/ha/hemos/han dicho que...** (have/has said that) and **había/habías... dicho que...** (had said that). Often implies you communicated information to someone: **Te he dicho que...** = “I told you that...”.
target_language_example: Te había dicho que hoy no podía.
native_language_example: I had told you that I couldn’t today.

additional_notes: Past participle of *decir* used in perfect tenses (*he/has/había dicho...*) to report that someone refused or didn’t allow something. Often appears as *decirle a alguien que no* (to tell someone no): *Te he dicho que no* = “I’ve told you no / I said no.”
target_language_example: Ya le he dicho que no puedo ir.
native_language_example: I’ve already told him/her that I can’t go.

meaning: “said and done” / “no sooner said than done.”
additional_notes: Used to show that something was done immediately after it was said, often to emphasize quick action or that someone kept their word. Common pattern: “Dicho y hecho: …” or “Y dicho y hecho.”
target_language_example: —¿Vamos por un café? —Dicho y hecho: en cinco minutos salimos.
native_language_example: “Shall we go for a coffee?” “Said and done: we’re leaving in five minutes.”

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (diciendo) to describe an action in progress, often with estar: está/estaba diciendo la verdad = 'is/was telling the truth.' You can also use it after modal/auxiliary verbs like podría estar: podría estar diciendo la verdad = 'might be telling the truth.'
target_language_example: No te enojes: te lo estoy diciendo la verdad.
native_language_example: Don’t get mad: I’m telling you the truth.

meaning: 'saying that' (introducing what someone claims, reports, or uses as an excuse).
additional_notes: Uses the gerund (diciendo) + que to introduce the content of what someone said. Very common after a main verb to add a message, claim, or reason/excuse: "Me llamó diciendo que..." (He/She called me saying that...), "Se fue diciendo que..." (He/She left saying that...). Often corresponds to English "saying that" or sometimes "claiming that."
target_language_example: Me escribió diciendo que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: He/She wrote to me saying that he/she would arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about age. With the verb "tener" it means "to be 18": "Tengo dieciocho años" (I’m 18). In comparisons, you’ll often see it with "desde que" (since) or "no… más de" (not more than / no older than).
target_language_example: Cumplo dieciocho años este mes.
native_language_example: I turn eighteen this month.

additional_notes: Used either for age (often with "tener": "Tengo dieciséis años" = "I’m sixteen") or for a period of time ("dieciséis años después" = "sixteen years later"). With ages, it commonly appears as "a los dieciséis años" meaning "at (the age of) sixteen".
target_language_example: A los dieciséis años me mudé a otra ciudad.
native_language_example: At sixteen, I moved to another city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time (duration) or someone’s age. Often appears with time expressions like "hace diez años" (ten years ago), "a los diez años" (at age ten), "tardó diez años en..." (it took [someone] ten years to...), or "pasó diez años..." (spent ten years...).
target_language_example: Viví en México diez años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of 10 days (duration) or something that happened 10 days ago with "hace" ("hace diez días" = "ten days ago"). You can also use it with "en" to mean within a 10-day period ("en diez días" = "in ten days" / "within ten days").
target_language_example: Voy a estar de viaje diez días.
native_language_example: I’m going to be traveling for ten days.

additional_notes: Used to state a price, a payment amount, wages, or money owed. With amounts of money, Spanish often uses the verb + amount directly: “cuesta diez dólares” (it costs ten dollars), “me debe diez dólares” (he owes me ten dollars), “son diez dólares” (it’s ten dollars). In many contexts you’ll also hear “por diez dólares” (for ten dollars) and “a diez dólares al día” (at ten dollars a day).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes cambiar un billete de diez dólares?
native_language_example: Can you break a ten-dollar bill for me?

additional_notes: Used to talk about quantities (people, money, etc.). It can be literal or used for exaggeration/strong emphasis ("not even with ten thousand men..."). In numbers: 10.000 (often written with a dot in many Spanish-speaking countries).
target_language_example: El coche cuesta diez mil dólares.
native_language_example: The car costs ten thousand dollars.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration (e.g., a delay) or frequency (e.g., something happens every ten minutes). You can use it with time expressions like “en diez minutos” (in ten minutes) and “cada diez minutos” (every ten minutes).
target_language_example: Vuelvo en diez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to compare two (or more) things and point out how they are not the same. It’s often used with verbs like "hay" (there is/are) and adjectives like "gran" or "clara": "Hay una gran/clara diferencia entre A y B". You can also use it in definitions or explanations: "Es la diferencia entre A y B".
target_language_example: Hay una gran diferencia entre estudiar un poco y estudiar todos los días.
native_language_example: There’s a big difference between studying a little and studying every day.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say an action is hard: "difícil de + infinitive" (difícil de aprender/creer/prever/leer). It agrees in gender and number with what it describes: "difícil" (masc. sing.), "difíciles" (plural), "difícil" (fem. sing. too), e.g., "preguntas difíciles de responder".
target_language_example: Es difícil de entender cuando hablan tan rápido.
native_language_example: It's hard to understand when they speak so fast.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation or decision is hard for a particular person/group. Usually appears with **ser**: *Es/Debe de ser difícil para + pronoun/name* (e.g., *difícil para mí/ti/él/ella/nosotros/ustedes*), or *una decisión difícil para + alguien*.
target_language_example: Sé que es difícil para ti, pero vamos a encontrar una solución.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard for you, but we’re going to find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for you personally. It often follows a form of ser (“es/era/fue”) and can be followed by an infinitive: “Es difícil para mí + infinitive” (e.g., entender, hablar). You can swap “mí” for another person: “difícil para ti/para él/para nosotros.” Note: “mí” (with an accent) is the object pronoun after “para”; “mi” (no accent) means “my.”
target_language_example: Es difícil para mí levantarme temprano los lunes.
native_language_example: It’s difficult for me to get up early on Mondays.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for the person you’re speaking to. Common with verbs like ser/estar: “(Debe) ser difícil para ti” = “(It must) be difficult for you.” You can also add intensity: “demasiado difícil para ti” (too difficult for you).
target_language_example: Entiendo que es difícil para ti hablar de eso.
native_language_example: I understand that it's difficult for you to talk about that.

meaning: "let’s say" / "let’s suppose" (used to introduce an explanation or an approximate/softened statement).
additional_notes: Used to frame what you’re about to say as a way of explaining, giving an example, or speaking approximately rather than 100% precisely. Often softens the statement (like “so to speak” or “kind of”). Common in speech: “Digamos que…” + clause.
target_language_example: Digamos que hoy no tengo muchas ganas de salir.
native_language_example: Let’s say I don’t really feel like going out today.

meaning: "(you) say anything"; usually in "No digas nada" = "Don’t say anything."
additional_notes: Used most often with "no" as a negative command to tell someone to stay quiet or not reveal information: "No digas nada" (Don’t say anything), "No les digas nada" (Don’t tell them anything). "Nada más" means "anything else" in this context: "No digas nada más" (Don’t say anything else).
target_language_example: Por favor, no digas nada hasta que lleguemos a casa.
native_language_example: Please, don’t say anything until we get home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something merits a quality or treatment. Pattern: **ser + digno/a + de + noun/infinitive** (e.g., *digno de orgullo*, *digno de admiración*). It agrees in gender/number: *digno, digna, dignos, dignas*. Often sounds formal or literary.
target_language_example: No es digno de confianza.
native_language_example: He/She isn’t trustworthy (literally: “worthy of trust”).

meaning: “I’m telling the truth.” / “I tell the truth.”
additional_notes: Often used to insist you’re not lying: “Digo la verdad.” With “si te digo la verdad,” it commonly means “to be honest / truthfully” and introduces a frank opinion or confession.
target_language_example: Te prometo que digo la verdad.
native_language_example: I promise I’m telling the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re stating or expressing an opinion about. It can also be used with an indirect object to mean “I tell (someone) that...”, e.g., "Le digo que..." (I tell him/her that...) or "Me digo que..." (I tell myself that...).
target_language_example: Sólo digo que no es tan fácil.
native_language_example: I’m just saying it’s not that easy.

meaning: 'I say' / 'I’m the one saying it' (often: 'if you ask me' or 'that’s what I’m saying').
additional_notes: Used in conversation to emphasize that something is your opinion or your words. It can also show agreement (“Eso/Lo mismo digo yo” = “That’s what I’m saying / Same here”) or add insistence/authority (“Se lo digo yo” = “I’m telling you (trust me)”). Word order matters: “digo yo” often sounds more emphatic than plain “yo digo”.
target_language_example: Está carísimo; digo yo que deberíamos esperar.
native_language_example: It’s really expensive; if you ask me, we should wait.

meaning: "I told" / "I said to" (past tense, used with a person).
additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of decir: dije = “I said/I told.” With people, Spanish often uses the personal a: dije a Tom = “I told Tom.” Very commonly it appears with indirect-object pronouns: le dije a Tom (“I told Tom”), se lo dije a Tom (“I told it to Tom”), se lo dije a ella (“I told it to her”).
target_language_example: Le dije a mi hermana que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: I told my sister that I would arrive late.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of decir (“to say”) + que (“that”), used to introduce reported speech: what you said in the past. What comes after que can vary (e.g., estaba, volvería, fuéramos) depending on the time frame or mood you need.
target_language_example: Dije que no podía ir hoy.
native_language_example: I said that I couldn’t go today.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of decir: dije = “I said/told.” Used to report what you stated earlier. Usually followed by an identity/description (ateo, enfermera, suplente) or an evaluation (posible). Often continues with a verb in the imperfect: “Dije que era…” = “I said that it was/that I was…”.
target_language_example: Dije que era estudiante, pero en realidad ya había terminado la carrera.
native_language_example: I said I was a student, but actually I had already finished my degree.

meaning: 'I said that I would (do) it' / 'I told you that (about) it.'
additional_notes: "Dije" is the simple past of "decir" (to say/tell). "que" introduces what you said (“that…”). "lo" is an object pronoun meaning “it” or “that,” referring to something already known from context (e.g., conseguirlo = get it, pensarlo = think about it, dejarlo = leave/quit it). Often used to remind someone of what you previously said: "Dije que lo haría" = “I said I would do it.”
target_language_example: Dije que lo iba a hacer, pero no tuve tiempo.
native_language_example: I said I was going to do it, but I didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Past tense of "decir" (to say/tell) + "que no". Often used to remind someone you already refused or set a boundary. It can stand alone (Dije que no.) or introduce a clause: "Dije que no pagamos nada" = "I said we aren’t paying anything."
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero dije que no voy a ir.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I said I'm not going to go.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of decir (dijeron) to report what “they” said at a specific moment in the past. It’s often followed by a statement (que + clause) or by “sí/no” as a short answer: “Dijeron que sí/no.”
target_language_example: Dijeron que no tenían tiempo.
native_language_example: They said that they didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of “decir” for “they”: “dijeron”. Use it to report what a group of people said. It can stand alone to mean they refused (“Dijeron que no.”), or be followed by a clause: “dijeron que no + verb” (e.g., “dijeron que no podían venir” = they said they couldn’t come). In everyday English you often translate it as “they said they didn’t…” rather than the very literal “they said that not…”.
target_language_example: Les pedí ayuda, pero dijeron que no.
native_language_example: I asked them for help, but they said no.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite (past) of decir: dijiste = "you said" (informal singular tú). "Que" introduces what the person said. Common for reminding someone of their words, asking for clarification, or pointing out a contradiction.
target_language_example: Dijiste que ibas a llamarme hoy.
native_language_example: You said that you were going to call me today.

additional_notes: Used to report or remind someone of what they previously said about something. Common in conversations to correct, confirm, or challenge earlier information. Often appears with an object pronoun too: “me dijiste que era…” = “you told me it was…”.
target_language_example: Pensé que dijiste que era hoy.
native_language_example: I thought you said it was today.

additional_notes: Used to quote or remind someone of what they previously said. Often followed by a verb phrase: “dijiste que no tenías…/que no estaban…” (= “you said you didn’t have…/that they weren’t…”). By itself (“Dijiste que no.”) it means “You said no.”
target_language_example: Dijiste que no querías ir, ¿te acuerdas?
native_language_example: You said you didn’t want to go, remember?

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a past statement. "Dijiste" is the simple past of "decir" (you said), and "querías" is the imperfect of "querer" (you wanted/you used to want). Often followed by an infinitive (querías hablar/irte/hacer) or by another clause with "que" (querías que + subjunctive).
target_language_example: Dijiste que querías cambiar de trabajo, ¿todavía lo estás pensando?
native_language_example: You said you wanted to change jobs—are you still thinking about it?

additional_notes: “Dijo” is the preterite (simple past) of **decir** (“to say/tell”). It’s often followed by **a + person** to show *who* was told: **Le dijo a su madre...** = “He/She told his/her mother...”. Very commonly you’ll also see object pronouns with it: **se lo dijo a María** (“he/she told it to María”), where **lo** = “it” and **se** replaces **le** before **lo/la/los/las**.
target_language_example: Se lo dijo a Ana ayer.
native_language_example: He/She told it to Ana yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. It’s the past tense of “decir” (él/ella dijo) + “que” (“that”) to introduce the reported information. You can add an indirect object pronoun when needed: “le dijo que …” = “(he/she) told him/her that …”. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb).
target_language_example: María dijo que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: María said that she would arrive late.

additional_notes: Past tense of "decir" ("dijo" = "he/she said"). Used to report what someone said: "X dijo que era…". After "que", Spanish typically uses the imperfect "era" to describe what something/someone was (reported speech). The subject of "era" is understood from context (it can refer to he, she, you, or it).
target_language_example: María dijo que era su hermano.
native_language_example: María said it was her brother.

meaning: 'he/she said (that) he/she was…' (reported speech in the past).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a past state or condition. You can add a noun/adjective after "estaba" (bien, triste, ocupado, cansada, etc.). The verb form changes with the speaker: "me dijo" (told me), "le dijo" (told him/her), "dijeron" (they said). In English you may or may not include "that."
target_language_example: Mi hermano dijo que estaba enfermo ayer.
native_language_example: My brother said he was sick yesterday.

additional_notes:
Used in reported speech to introduce what someone said about how they were feeling or what condition they were in. 
- dijo = “(he/she) said” (pretérito/past)
- que = “that”
- estaba = “was” (temporary state, from estar)
- muy = “very”
You normally add an adjective after muy (e.g., ocupado/a, aburrido/a, emocionado/a, satisfecho/a). The subject (“he/she”) is often understood from context and not stated.
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: My boss said that he was very tired.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said ("dijo que" = “said that”) followed by the past perfect ("había" + past participle) to talk about something that happened before another past moment. Subject pronouns (él/ella/usted) are often omitted in Spanish: “Dijo que había…” can mean “He said…” or “She said…”. You can change "dijo" to other people: "dije que había" (I said), "dijeron que había" (they said).
target_language_example: María dijo que había perdido las llaves.
native_language_example: María said that she had lost the keys.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they planned or intended to do in the past. The verb changes with the speaker (dije/dijiste/dijo/dijimos/dijeron) and you can change the subject after “que” (e.g., “dijo que yo iba a…”). In reported speech about the past, “va a” often becomes “iba a”.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que iba a llamarme después.
native_language_example: She said she was going to call me later.

meaning: "(he/she) said that (to him/her)" / "(he/she) said that (it) happened to him/her".
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (indirect speech): "X dijo que..." = "X said that...". The pronoun "le" often refers to the person affected or involved (him/her/you formal), especially with verbs like "robar" (they stole from him/her), "seguir" (they were following him/her), or expressions like "le daba sueño" (he/she felt sleepy). In English you may translate it as "said that he/she..." or "said that to him/her..." depending on context.
target_language_example: El policía dijo que le iban a ayudar.
native_language_example: The police officer said they were going to help him/her.

meaning: "(he/she) said that (he/it/him)…" (reported speech + direct object pronoun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone said in the past: dijo que… = “(he/she) said that…”. The "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it,” referring to something already known from context (e.g., "dijo que lo intentaría" = “said he would try it”; "dijo que lo sentía" = “said he was sorry [about it]”). Often followed by an imperfect or conditional verb to reflect a future-in-the-past idea (intentaría, podría, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que lo revisaría mañana.
native_language_example: My boss said that he would look it over tomorrow.

meaning: "(He/She) said that I..." / "(He/She) told me that I..."
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, introducing a clause with que (“that”). Often followed by a verb in the imperfect (e.g., me amaba, me extrañaba) for reported feelings, or by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., me lavara) when reporting a command or suggestion. You’ll also see the order flipped as: “Me dijo que…” = “(He/She) told me that…”.
target_language_example: Dijo que me ayudaría mañana.
native_language_example: He/She said that he/she would help me tomorrow.

meaning: "(he/she) said no" or "(he/she) said that ... not".
additional_notes: Used with reported speech. It can mean a direct refusal/denial ("He said no"), or it can introduce a negative statement: "dijo que no + verb" ("said that he/she didn’t..."). In commands/advice it often appears as "me dijo que no + imperfect subjunctive": "Me dijo que no condujera..." = "He told me not to drive...".
target_language_example: Le pregunté si venía, pero dijo que no.
native_language_example: I asked if he was coming, but he said no.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., "Él dijo…" / "Ella dijo…"). After "que," Spanish often uses the imperfect: "tenía" = "had" / "didn’t have" at that time. Commonly followed by a noun or by an expression like "dónde + infinitive" ("dónde ir" = "where to go").
target_language_example: Ana dijo que no tenía tiempo para venir.
native_language_example: Ana said that she didn’t have time to come.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said and what they believed at the time. After "dijo" and "pensaba," Spanish often uses "que" (“that”) to introduce the next clause. The subject can change with context: "Tom dijo…" = “Tom said…”, "Ella dijo…" = “She said…”. You’ll also see the present version: "dice que piensa que" (“says he/she thinks that”).
target_language_example: Ella dijo que pensaba que era demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: She said she thought it was too late.

additional_notes: Common reporting structure: **decir (pretérito)** + **que** + verb. Here **podía** is the imperfect of **poder** (“could/was able to”), often used to report what someone said they were able/allowed to do. The subject is often understood from context: **Dijo que podía hacerlo** = “(He/She) said (he/she) could do it.” You can add the subject for clarity: **Él/Ella dijo que podía…**
target_language_example: Ella dijo que podía ayudarme mañana.
native_language_example: She said that she could help me tomorrow.

additional_notes:
Used to report what someone said they wanted. 
- "dijo" is the simple past of "decir" (he/she said) and "quería" is the imperfect past of "querer" (he/she wanted/was wanting).
- Often followed by an infinitive: "dijo que quería ir" (said he wanted to go), or a noun: "dijo que quería un coche" (said he wanted a car).
- Subject is often clear from context; you can add it: "Él dijo que quería..." / "Ella dijo que quería..."
target_language_example: Ella dijo que quería hablar contigo.
native_language_example: She said that she wanted to talk to you.

meaning: “(he/she/it) said that (he/she/it) …” (often followed by a verb with se).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: dijo que + a clause. The subject of dijo (he/she/it) may be a person (Ella le dijo…) or a thing like a newspaper (El periódico dijo…). The word se is a pronoun that often appears with pronominal/reflexive verbs (irse = to leave, alejarse = to move away, divorciarse = to get divorced) or in passive/impersonal uses (se aproximaba = was approaching).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que se iba a retrasar.
native_language_example: My boss said that he was going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to report that someone agreed or accepted something. It’s the past tense (preterite) of “decir”: dijo = “said,” and “que sí” = “that yes.” You can also use the same pattern with an object: “me dijo que sí” = “(he/she) told me yes / said yes to me.”
target_language_example: Le ofrecieron el trabajo y dijo que sí.
native_language_example: They offered him/her the job and he/she said yes.

meaning: 'he/she said (that) he/she had' (reported speech in the past).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "Dijo" is the simple past of "decir" (he/she said), "que" means "that," and "tenía" is the imperfect of "tener" (had/was having). Often introduces information, a state, or an obligation: "dijo que tenía sed" (said she was thirsty), "dijo que tenía prisa" (said he was in a hurry), "dijo que tenía que + infinitive" (said he had to...).
target_language_example: Mi hermano dijo que tenía una reunión.
native_language_example: My brother said he had a meeting.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to introduce what a male subject said about himself. Often appears as “X dijo que él…”. In everyday Spanish, the pronoun “él” is frequently omitted when it’s clear who you mean: “Tom dijo que estaba…”
target_language_example: Ella dijo que él no podía venir hoy.
native_language_example: She said that he couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said about his condition/state. Common in indirect (reported) speech: **dijo que** + clause. **estaba** is the imperfect of *estar* (“was”), often used for temporary states, feelings, or conditions (bien, desorientado, enamorado, dispuesto, etc.). In Spanish, **él** is often optional (e.g., *Dijo que estaba bien*).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que él estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: My boss said that he was very tired.

additional_notes: "Dile a" is used to give a command meaning “Tell [person] …”. It comes from the verb "decir" (to say/tell): "di" = tell (tú command), and "-le" = to him/her/you (formal). Then "a" introduces the person you’re telling: "Dile a Tom..." = “Tell Tom...”. Often followed by "que" + a sentence: "Dile a Tom que no" = “Tell Tom no.”
target_language_example: Dile a tu hermano que llegue temprano.
native_language_example: Tell your brother to arrive early.

meaning: Tell your… (informal command, to one person).
additional_notes: "Dile" is the tú imperative of "decir" (to tell), with "le" = "to him/her/you (formal)". It’s commonly followed by "a + [person]" to name who you’re telling (e.g., "Dile a tu jefe…" = "Tell your boss…"). "Tu" is the informal possessive "your" (your boss / your husband / your girlfriend).
target_language_example: Dile a tu hermana que llego en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: Tell your sister I’ll arrive in five minutes.

meaning: “tell your mother” (informal command to one person).
additional_notes: Uses the informal tú command: dile = “tell (him/her/you formal)” + a tu madre = “to your mother.” Often followed by que + a sentence (“Tell your mother that…”) or de/acerca de + a noun (“Tell your mother about…”).
target_language_example: Dile a tu madre que llegaremos tarde.
native_language_example: Tell your mother that we’ll arrive late.

additional_notes: "Dile" is the informal (tú) command form of "decir" + an indirect object pronoun (le = to him/her/you formal/them). It’s commonly followed by "que" + a clause to report a message: "Dile que…" = “Tell (someone) that…”. Often the person you’re telling is understood from context; if needed, you can add a name: "Dile a Marta que…".
target_language_example: Por favor, dile que llego en diez minutos.
native_language_example: Please tell him/her that I’ll arrive in ten minutes.

meaning: “tell him/her/them that I’m …” (when you can’t talk).
additional_notes: Used to pass a message through someone else: **dile** = “tell (him/her/them)” (informal tú command of *decir*), and **que estoy** introduces what you want them to say about you (usually what you’re doing right now). If you need “tell you (formal)” use **dígame**; if you’re talking to multiple people, **digan**.
target_language_example: Dile que estoy ocupado ahora y que lo llamo más tarde.
native_language_example: Tell him I’m busy right now and that I’ll call him later.

meaning: “Tell him/her that I…” (used to pass on a message about yourself).
additional_notes: "Dile" is the tú command form of "decir" + the indirect object pronoun "le" (= to him/to her/to you formal). "Que" introduces what you want them to say, and "me" means “me” (the subject of the message is usually "yo"). Common pattern: "Dile que me + verb" (e.g., "dile que me espere" = tell him/her to wait for me).
target_language_example: Dile que me llame más tarde, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to call me later, please.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction to someone to pass on a message to a group ("them"). It’s an affirmative tú command: di + les (“tell” + “to them”), followed by que to introduce what you want said. You can add pronouns after que (me, te, lo, etc.): “Diles que me ayuden.”
target_language_example: Diles que llego en diez minutos.
native_language_example: Tell them I’ll be there in ten minutes.

meaning: "Tell me, what..." (used to introduce a question).
additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention before asking a question. Depending on tone and context, it can sound neutral (“Tell me, what happened?”) or confrontational/accusatory (“Tell me, what do you think you’re doing?”). Often followed by a full question: “Dime, ¿qué pasa?” / “Dime, ¿qué quieres?”
target_language_example: Dime, ¿qué quieres comer hoy?
native_language_example: Tell me, what do you want to eat today?

meaning: “tell me how…” (ask for instructions or a description).
additional_notes: “Dime” is the informal command form of “decir” (to tell) used with tú. “Cómo” introduces an indirect question meaning “how” (how to do something, how to get somewhere, what something/someone is like, or how something went). Often followed by an infinitive: “Dime cómo llegar / usar / hacerlo…”, or by a clause: “Dime cómo se llama / cómo es…”.
target_language_example: Dime cómo lo hiciste.
native_language_example: Tell me how you did it.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for a location or place. Often followed by a verb: “Dime dónde vives” (where you live), “Dime dónde está …” (where … is). “Dime” is the informal (tú) command form of “decir” (to tell/say). You can add “por favor” to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Dime dónde está el baño, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell me where the bathroom is, please.

additional_notes: An informal (tú) command: di (tell) + me (to me) = dime. Used to press someone to be honest, often with words like ahora (now), mejor (better), por favor (please), or solo/sólo (just). For a formal (usted) version, say: "Dígame la verdad."
target_language_example: Por favor, dime la verdad: ¿qué pasó anoche?
native_language_example: Please tell me the truth: what happened last night?

additional_notes: "Dime" is the informal (tú) command form of "decir" (to tell/say). "Lo que" means "what" / "that which" and introduces the information you want the other person to tell you (dime lo que + verb). In formal speech, use "Dígame lo que...".
target_language_example: Dime lo que necesitas y te ayudaré.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need and I’ll help you.

additional_notes:
Used to ask someone directly what they want (an object, a plan, a choice, etc.).
- dime = “tell me” (informal tú command of decir)
- lo que = “what / that which”
- quieres = “you want” (tú)
Often said with emphasis (Solo/Sólo dime...) to mean “Just tell me…”.
target_language_example: Dime lo que quieres comer esta noche.
native_language_example: Tell me what you want to eat tonight.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for an explanation or reason. "Dime" is the informal (tú) command of "decir" (to tell/say). You can soften it with "por favor" or make it more formal with "Dígame por qué".
target_language_example: Dime por qué estás enojado conmigo.
native_language_example: Tell me why you’re mad at me.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to give you information or instructions. It’s a common way to start a question or request, often followed by a verb (e.g., “dime qué pasó / qué hacer / qué quieres”). Written with an accent in “dime” (from decir).
target_language_example: Dime qué necesitas para mañana.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to specify that the money comes specifically from a store’s cash register (often in contexts like stealing or taking cash). "Caja registradora" = cash register; "dinero de" = money from.
target_language_example: No toques el dinero de la caja registradora.
native_language_example: Don’t touch the money from the cash register.

meaning: 'money on' / 'money in' (used with en to say where money is spent or placed).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like gastar (to spend) + dinero en + noun: Gasto dinero en ropa (I spend money on clothes). It’s also used for physically putting money somewhere: Puso su dinero en la caja (He/She put the money in the box). In phrases like por tu dinero en esta tienda, it can suggest “value for your money” in that place/store.
target_language_example: No quiero gastar dinero en cosas que no necesito.
native_language_example: I don't want to spend money on things I don't need.

meaning: money in the bank (money you have in a bank account).
additional_notes: Used to talk about money you have saved or deposited at a bank, meaning it’s in your account (not cash you’re carrying). Often used with verbs like tener (to have), depositar (to deposit), and poner (to put).
target_language_example: No tengo mucho dinero en el banco ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I don’t have much money in the bank right now.

meaning: “easy money” (money obtained with little effort, often too good to be true).
additional_notes: Used to talk about money that seems quick or effortless to get. It often has a negative tone, suggesting there’s a catch, risk, or moral cost (e.g., “easy money always comes with a price”). You can also use it sarcastically: “Dinero fácil, ¿verdad?”
target_language_example: No te metas en eso solo por el dinero fácil.
native_language_example: Don’t get into that just for the easy money.

additional_notes: Used to say what the money is intended to be used for, often with verbs like ahorrar (to save), tener/no tener (to have/not have), dejar (to leave), or necesitar (to need): dinero para el viaje / para pagar / para la universidad. With an infinitive, it expresses money needed in order to do something: dinero para pagar un taxi, dinero para hacer cualquier cosa.
target_language_example: No tengo dinero para comprar un billete.
native_language_example: I don’t have money to buy a ticket.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having (or not having) enough money for a purchase. It’s usually followed by what you want to buy: “dinero para comprar un coche / una casa”. You can add “algo de” to mean “some”: “algo de dinero para comprar…”.
target_language_example: No tengo dinero para comprar entradas para el concierto.
native_language_example: I don’t have money to buy tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: "Que tenía" is a relative clause meaning "that (someone) had" and it describes "dinero". It often appears with "el poco" to mean "the little money (someone) had," emphasizing it wasn’t much. The subject is understood from context (yo tenía, él tenía, ella tenía, etc.).
target_language_example: Gasté el poco dinero que tenía en comida.
native_language_example: I spent the little money I had on food.

additional_notes: Used to say you have (or don’t have) the amount of money needed to purchase something. Often appears with verbs like tener (“to have”) or necesitar (“to need”): “tener dinero suficiente para comprar…” You can add the item after it (una casa, pan y leche, etc.).
target_language_example: No tengo dinero suficiente para comprar un coche.
native_language_example: I don’t have enough money to buy a car.

additional_notes: Used to say someone gave something to a person/being: "dio" = "gave" (completed past action), and "a" introduces the recipient (often with an indirect object pronoun like le/les/se). Note: in the fixed phrase "dio a luz" it means "gave birth."
target_language_example: Le dio a su hermano el libro.
native_language_example: He/She gave his/her brother the book.

additional_notes: Form used inside the reflexive construction "darse cuenta de que" (to realize/notice that). "dio" is the 3rd-person singular preterite of "dar"; it typically appears as "se dio cuenta de que" (he/she/you-formal realized that) and is followed by a clause introduced by "que". Common patterns: "Me di cuenta de que...", "Te diste cuenta de que...", "Se dio cuenta de que...", "Nos dimos cuenta de que...".
target_language_example: Al fin, él se dio cuenta de que estaba equivocado.
native_language_example: At last, he realized that he was wrong.

meaning: "gave a" (often used like "took/made/did" with an action noun).
additional_notes: "Dio" is the preterite (simple past) of **dar** = "to give." In Spanish, **dar + un/una + noun** is very common with nouns that describe actions: *dio un bote* = "jumped" (literally "gave a jump"), *dio un respiro* = "took a breath," *dio un discurso* = "gave/delivered a speech." The exact English verb changes depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Al escuchar el ruido, dio un salto.
native_language_example: When he heard the noise, he jumped.

dio un puñetazo en la cara

target_language_multi_word_term: dio un puñetazo en la cara
additional_notes: "Dar un puñetazo" means "to throw/land a punch" (literally, "to give a punch"). "Dio" is the simple past (preterite) of "dar" for he/she/you (formal). You can swap the indirect object pronoun to show who got hit: "me" (me), "te" (you), "le" (him/her/you formal), "nos" (us), "les" (them/you all).
target_language_example: El hombre le dio un puñetazo en la cara al ladrón.
native_language_example: The man punched the thief in the face.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "dar": "(él/ella/usted) dio" = "he/she/you (formal) gave". Often used with an indirect object pronoun for who receives it: "me/te/le/nos/les dio un regalo" (gave me/you/him-her/ us/ them a gift). You can also add "a + person" for clarity: "Le dio un regalo a su novia". In "A todos los niños se les dio un regalo", the "se les" is a common way to mean "they were given" (impersonal/passive-style).
target_language_example: Ayer mi abuela me dio un regalo.
native_language_example: Yesterday my grandmother gave me a gift.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite (completed past) of **dar**: **dar → dio**. It often appears with an indirect object pronoun showing *to whom* it was given: **me** (to me), **te** (to you), **le** (to him/her/you formal), **nos** (to us), **les** (to them/you all). **Reloj** can mean a wristwatch or a clock; context tells you which.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo me dio un reloj por mi cumpleaños.
native_language_example: My grandpa gave me a watch for my birthday.

meaning: 'gave a' (used with a noun to express an action or effect).
additional_notes: It’s the past tense of "dar" (él/ella/usted dio) + "una". Spanish often uses "dar" + a noun where English uses a different verb: "dio una carcajada" = "laughed", "dio una ojeada" = "took a look", "dio una patada" = "kicked", "dio una paliza" = "beat up". With light/sound it can mean "gave off" or "emitted": "dio una luz tenue" = "gave off a dim light".
target_language_example: El niño dio una vuelta y volvió corriendo.
native_language_example: The kid took a turn around and came back running.

dio una palmada en el hombro

target_language_multi_word_term: dio una palmada en el hombro
additional_notes: A common physical gesture meaning encouragement, reassurance, congratulations, or getting someone’s attention. Uses the verb phrase "dar una palmada" (to give a pat/slap) + "en el hombro" (on the shoulder). The form "dio" is the simple past (pretérito) of "dar" for él/ella/usted; you can also say "me dio..." (patted me), "le dio..." (patted him/her).
target_language_example: Cuando terminé el examen, el profesor me dio una palmada en el hombro.
native_language_example: When I finished the exam, the teacher patted me on the shoulder.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "dar una patada" = "to kick" (literally "to give a kick"). Often followed by "a" + person ("Le dio una patada") or "en" + body part ("en la pierna"). "En las pelotas / en los huevos" are vulgar ways to say "in the balls".
target_language_example: Me dio una patada en la pierna y me caí.
native_language_example: He/She kicked me in the leg and I fell.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for an address (home/business) or to indicate the delivery/destination address. Often said when sending something, filling out a form, or telling a driver/taxi where you want to go (e.g., Lléveme a esta dirección, por favor).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es la dirección, por favor?
native_language_example: What’s the address, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s email address. Common in formal contexts (forms, customer service, official emails). Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have), "dar" (to give), "anotar" (to write down), or "perder" (to lose). In casual speech it may be shortened to "correo" or "email" depending on region, but the full term is widely understood.
target_language_example: He perdido tu dirección de correo electrónico.
native_language_example: I’ve lost your email address.

additional_notes: Future tense of "decir" (to say/tell): "yo diré" = "I will say/tell." It’s often used as a lead-in to what you’re about to say, similar to “Look, I’ll tell you something…” or “Let me tell you something…”. Common with an indirect object pronoun: "te diré algo" (I’ll tell you something), "le diré algo" (I’ll tell him/her/you-formal something).
target_language_example: Te diré algo: no me gusta ese plan.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you something: I don’t like that plan.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re going to say or explain next. "Diré" is the simple future of "decir" (to say/tell). It’s commonly followed by a full clause: "Diré lo que pienso" (I’ll say what I think). With "tú quieras" it can mean “whatever you want”: "Diré lo que tú quieras" (I’ll say whatever you want).
target_language_example: Te diré lo que pasó mañana.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you what happened tomorrow.

meaning: “I’d say…” / “I would say that…” (a tentative opinion or guess).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of decir (“to say”) to sound less certain, more polite, or to estimate. Often followed by a number or a yes/no opinion. You can also change the subject: Él/Ella diría que… (“He/She would say…”).
target_language_example: Diría que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I’d say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of decir (“diría” = “I would say”) to give a cautious or tentative yes—often meaning “probably” or “I think so,” rather than a firm commitment. You can also use it about someone else: “Tom diría que sí” = “Tom would say yes.”
target_language_example: ¿Crees que va a llover? Diría que sí.
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain? I’d say so.

additional_notes: Used for a computer’s storage unit, either internal or external (e.g., “disco duro externo”). You’ll often see it with verbs like guardar (to save), borrar (to erase), and llenar/estar lleno (to be full).
target_language_example: Necesito más espacio porque mi disco duro está lleno.
native_language_example: I need more space because my hard drive is full.

meaning: “Excuse me, where is…?” (polite way to ask for a location).
additional_notes: Use this to politely get someone’s attention and ask where a place is. “Disculpe” is formal/polite (often used with strangers). After “¿dónde está…?”, use “el/la” for a specific place: “el baño”, “la estación”, or no article with some place names/business types depending on context (e.g., “¿dónde está Correos?”).
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿dónde está la parada de autobús?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (dispuesto a + infinitive) to show willingness or readiness: "Estoy dispuesto a ayudar." Also commonly used in the negative: "no estar dispuesto a" = "to be unwilling/not prepared to." It agrees in gender and number: dispuesto, dispuesta, dispuestos, dispuestas.
target_language_example: No estoy dispuesto a esperar más.
native_language_example: I'm not willing to wait anymore.

meaning: to tell right from wrong; to distinguish good from evil.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "distinguir" (to distinguish) with "el bien" (good/right) and "el mal" (evil/wrong). Often used in moral contexts (kids, ethics, knowing what’s right vs. wrong). You can change the subject and tense: "puedo distinguir...", "sabe distinguir...", "no es fácil distinguir...".
target_language_example: No siempre es fácil distinguir el bien del mal.
native_language_example: It’s not always easy to tell right from wrong.

meaning: twice as much/many as; double (the amount) of.
additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or degree: "el doble de X" = double X. With adjectives, it often appears as "el doble de + adjective + que" (e.g., "el doble de fuerte que yo" = twice as strong as me). It can also describe a person who is a "stand-in" or "body double" for someone ("el doble de Rick Dalton").
target_language_example: Este café cuesta el doble de lo que costaba antes.
native_language_example: This coffee costs twice what it used to cost.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an age or a length of time. For age, it often appears with phrases like “a los doce años” (at age 12) or “tenía doce años” (I was twelve). For duration, it can mean a period of twelve years (“Doce años es mucho…”).
target_language_example: Viví en esa ciudad doce años.
native_language_example: I lived in that city for twelve years.

additional_notes: Used when buying or talking about quantities of eggs. “Una docena” = 12; you can change the number (e.g., “dos docenas”). Often used with other items too: “una docena de …”. Related: “media docena de huevos” = half a dozen (6 eggs).
target_language_example: ¿Me das una docena de huevos, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a dozen eggs, please?

additional_notes: Used to say what body part hurts: "dolor de" + body part (dolor de cabeza, dolor de muelas/dientes, dolor de espalda). You can use it with "tener" (Tengo dolor de cabeza) or "estar con" (Estoy con dolor de cabeza).
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de cabeza desde ayer.
native_language_example: I’ve had a headache since yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally “pain in the head.” Common with tener: Tengo dolor de cabeza / Tengo un dolor de cabeza. You can add adjectives like leve (mild) or fuerte (bad/severe). It can also be used figuratively to mean something annoying or complicated (like “a headache” in English).
target_language_example: Este papeleo es un dolor de cabeza.
native_language_example: This paperwork is a headache (a hassle).

additional_notes: Used to talk about pain in your stomach area. Often used with tener (to have): “Tengo dolor de estómago.” You can add an adjective like fuerte (strong/severe): “un fuerte dolor de estómago.”
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de estómago, así que no voy a comer mucho.
native_language_example: I have a stomachache, so I’m not going to eat much.

additional_notes: Common way to say you have a toothache. Often used with tener (to have): "Tengo dolor de muelas". You can also use it with llevar + time to say it has been going on for a while: "Llevo dos días con dolor de muelas".
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de muelas; necesito ir al dentista.
native_language_example: I have a toothache; I need to go to the dentist.

additional_notes: Plural of “dolor de cabeza” (a headache). Often used with verbs like “tener” (to have) and “sufrir (de)” (to suffer from): “Tengo dolores de cabeza” / “Sufro de dolores de cabeza”. You may also hear “me duele la cabeza” for “my head hurts.”
target_language_example: Últimamente tengo dolores de cabeza casi todos los días.
native_language_example: Lately I’ve been getting headaches almost every day.

meaning: to master English; to be fluent in English.
additional_notes: Uses the verb dominar (“to master/to have a strong command of”) with a language. It often implies a high level (very good control), more than just “to learn.” You can also say dominar + el español / el francés, etc.
target_language_example: Quiero dominar el inglés para conseguir un mejor trabajo.
native_language_example: I want to master English to get a better job.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent Sunday in the past. Very often appears with “desde” (“since”) to show something started then and continues until now: “desde el domingo pasado…”. It agrees with “domingo” (masculine): “el domingo pasado”.
target_language_example: No lo veo desde el domingo pasado.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him since last Sunday.

meaning: a nobody; an insignificant person (often insulting).
additional_notes: Used with ser (e.g., «Eres/Es/Soy un don nadie») to say someone has no importance, status, or influence. It’s usually rude/derogatory, similar to calling someone “a nobody” in English.
target_language_example: No le hagas caso; es un don nadie.
native_language_example: Don’t pay attention to him; he’s a nobody.

meaning: “Where is …?” (asking for the location of something/someone).
additional_notes: In correct Spanish spelling and punctuation, this is usually written as “¿Dónde está …?” (with accents and opening question mark). “Dónde” takes an accent in questions, and “está” (from “estar”) takes an accent. The unaccented form “donde esta” is common in informal texting or when accents are omitted.
target_language_example: Donde esta mi padre.
native_language_example: Where is my father?

meaning: “where (someone/something) is / where it is” (relative ‘where’ referring to a location).
additional_notes: Most commonly, Spanish uses the accented form «dónde está» in direct questions: «¿Dónde está el mando?» = “Where is the remote?”. Without the accent («donde está»), it’s typically a relative/embedded ‘where’: «Se quedará donde está» = “It will stay where it is.” The only difference in writing is the accent: «dónde» = interrogative/exclamatory “where”, «donde» = relative “where.”
target_language_example: Si no le identifica nadie, se quedará donde está.
native_language_example: If nobody identifies him, he will stay where he is.

meaning: Literal: “where to want” / intended meaning in context: “where (someone) wants” or “wherever (someone) wants.”
additional_notes: **Nonstandard / unusual phrasing.** Spanish normally conjugates the verb **querer** (to want), so you would typically see **donde quieres** (“where you want”) or **donde quieras** (“wherever you want / anywhere you want”). Also note spelling: **dónde** (with accent) is used in direct/indirect questions (e.g., «¿Dónde quieres ir?» / «No sé dónde quieres ir.»); **donde** (no accent) is used in statements/relative clauses (e.g., «Vamos donde quieras.»).
target_language_example: En algunos apuntes aparece «donde querer», pero lo normal es decir «donde quieras».
native_language_example: In some notes you might see “donde querer,” but normally you would say “donde quieras.”

meaning: wherever you want; anywhere you like.
additional_notes: Uses subjunctive (quieras) to mean an open choice: “wherever you want.” Often used by itself to mean “wherever you want/anywhere is fine.” With movement verbs, it’s common to add "a": "ir a donde quieras", "llevarte a donde quieras" (“go/take you wherever you want”).
target_language_example: Puedes quedarte donde quieras.
native_language_example: You can stay wherever you want.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified place: “any place” or “no matter where.” Often appears as **donde sea que...** (“wherever...”), and can be used alone as a short answer: **Donde sea.** = “Anywhere.” Also common with **a** after verbs of movement: **ir a donde sea** (“go anywhere”).
target_language_example: Podemos comer donde sea, pero que sea cerca.
native_language_example: We can eat anywhere, but it has to be nearby.

additional_notes: Used to talk about any place, without specifying which one. It often introduces a clause in the subjunctive because the location is unknown or not important: “Donde sea que vaya…” = “Wherever she goes…”. Also common with estar/suceder/vivir: “Donde sea que esté…”, “Donde sea que suceda…”, “Donde sea que viva…”.
target_language_example: Donde sea que estés, llámame cuando puedas.
native_language_example: Wherever you are, call me when you can.

additional_notes: Used to talk about any place or every place that fits the situation (“no matter where”). Often followed by a verb: “Dondequiera que esté…” = “Wherever he/she is…”. You may also see the variant “adondequiera que” when emphasizing movement/destination (“wherever (to)”).
target_language_example: Dondequiera que vayas, te llamaré.
native_language_example: Wherever you go, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens in any place someone goes. The verb can change to match the subject and tense: dondequiera que vayas (you go), dondequiera que va (he/she goes), dondequiera que vayamos (we go), dondequiera que fueran (they went). Often followed by another verb in the present (or matching tense): Dondequiera que vaya, encuentro...
target_language_example: Dondequiera que vaya, siempre termino hablando con alguien.
native_language_example: Wherever I go, I always end up talking to someone.

meaning: to sleep a little; to get some sleep.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or say you need a short rest or some sleep. Very common with verbs like necesitar (to need), tener que (to have to), deberías (you should), and trata de (try to).
target_language_example: Después del viaje, necesito dormir un poco.
native_language_example: After the trip, I need to get some sleep.

meaning: "two, three"; often means "a couple" / "two or three" (approximately).
additional_notes: Used in casual speech to say an approximate small number: "Lo hice dos, tres veces" = "I did it a couple of times." It can also be used literally when counting out loud (often in music, dance, exercise, etc.). Sometimes you’ll hear it with a pause: "dos… tres" or as part of a count like "una, dos, tres".
target_language_example: He ido a ese restaurante dos, tres veces.
native_language_example: I’ve been to that restaurant two or three times (a couple of times).

meaning: 'two, three, four' (often said out loud to count or keep rhythm).
additional_notes: Used when counting in sequence, especially as a cue for timing: starting an activity, keeping a beat in music/dance/exercise, or counting repetitions. You’ll often hear it repeated or preceded by “uno/una” (“one”).
target_language_example: ¡Preparados? Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, ¡vamos!
native_language_example: Ready? One, two, three, four—go!
