Agreement: **pequeña** is feminine singular; change it to match the subject: **pequeño** (masc. sing.), **pequeñas** (fem. pl.), **pequeños** (masc. pl.).
target_language_example: Esta habitación es demasiado pequeña para nosotros.
native_language_example: This room is too small for us.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t fit or isn’t suitable because it’s not big enough. It can be followed by a person (para mí, para nosotros) or by an action with an infinitive (para nadar). You can change the adjective for gender/number: es demasiado pequeña / son demasiado pequeños.
target_language_example: Este abrigo es demasiado pequeño para mí.
native_language_example: This coat is too small for me.

additional_notes: Used to say that there isn’t enough time left to do something, or that an opportunity has already passed. Often followed by **para + infinitive**: *Es demasiado tarde para llamar* (“It’s too late to call”). You can add **ya** (“already”) for emphasis: *Es demasiado tarde ya*. The opposite idea is *nunca es demasiado tarde* (“it’s never too late”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, es demasiado tarde para cambiar la reserva.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s too late to change the reservation.

additional_notes: Used to say an action can no longer be done in time ("too late to" + infinitive: Es demasiado tarde para llamar) or that it’s too late for someone/something ("too late for" + person/thing: Es demasiado tarde para mí). Often appears with "Nunca" to express that it’s not too late: "Nunca es demasiado tarde para aprender" (“It’s never too late to learn”).
target_language_example: Es demasiado tarde para cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: It’s too late to change your mind.

additional_notes: Used to compare things or situations. Often followed by "de" to say what something differs from: "es diferente de..." (different from...). Can also react to new information: "Bueno, eso es diferente."
target_language_example: Para mí, esta situación es diferente.
native_language_example: For me, this situation is different.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is hard to do: Es difícil convencer..., Es difícil decir.... You can also use it with a noun/verb phrase as the subject: Dominar el inglés es difícil. Often implies a general statement (not tied to a specific person).
target_language_example: Es difícil aprender un idioma sin practicar.
native_language_example: It’s hard to learn a language without practicing.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something is not easy to do/understand: Es difícil de + infinitive (describir, entender, explicar, creer, etc.). In everyday Spanish you’ll also hear "Es difícil" without "de" (Es difícil entenderlo), but both are common.
target_language_example: Es difícil de creer, pero es verdad.
native_language_example: It’s hard to believe, but it’s true.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is not easily satisfied and has high expectations. Often said about a boss, customer, or anyone who complains easily. You can change the subject: "Soy difícil de complacer" (I’m hard to please), "Mi jefe es difícil de complacer" (My boss is hard to please).
target_language_example: A mi profesora le cuesta quedar satisfecha; es difícil de complacer.
native_language_example: My teacher has a hard time being satisfied; she’s hard to please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not easy to understand (because it’s complex, confusing, or unclear). You can use it by itself (Es difícil de entender.) or specify the subject: X es difícil de entender. Also common: Es difícil de entender, pero… (“It’s hard to understand, but…”).
target_language_example: Lo que dijo el profesor es difícil de entender.
native_language_example: What the teacher said is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult for a particular person or group. Pattern: "Es difícil para + [person/group] + [infinitive/thing]". With pronouns: "para mí, para ti, para él/ella, para nosotros/as". Note the accent: "mí" (me) vs "mi" (my).
target_language_example: Es difícil para mí levantarme temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: It’s hard for me to get up early every day.

additional_notes: Used with ser (es) + adjective (divertido) to describe something as fun or entertaining: Es divertido bailar. It can describe an activity/thing (Esto es divertido) or a person (Tom es divertido = Tom is fun/funny). In the negative, ya no es divertido means 'it’s not fun anymore.' You may also see a similar structure with an indirect object: Me es divertido (less common than Es divertido para mí or Me resulta divertido) = 'It’s fun for me / I find it fun.'
target_language_example: Ya no es divertido jugar así.
native_language_example: It’s not fun to play like that anymore.

meaning: "is where" (used to say/define the place where something happens or exists).
additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize a location. Often follows a place phrase for emphasis (e.g., "En mi casa es donde...") or starts a sentence to define a place ("Es donde vivo"). It can also be used in general definitions: "Una mina es donde...".
target_language_example: Aquí es donde nos conocimos.
native_language_example: This is where we met.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: **ser + number of years + mayor que + person**. The verb changes with the subject (e.g., *soy / eres / es / somos / son*). You can replace *dos* with any number: *es tres años mayor que…*. For “younger,” use *menor que*: *es dos años menor que…*.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es dos años mayor que yo, pero parece más joven.
native_language_example: My sister is two years older than me, but she looks younger.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** (to be): **es** = “is” and **el** = “the” (masculine singular noun). Common in definitions and statements of identity: *X es el Y* (“X is the Y”). Use **es la** for feminine singular (*la casa*), and **son los/son las** for plural.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es el médico de la familia.
native_language_example: My brother is the family doctor.

meaning: 'it is love' / 'love is' (used when defining or identifying love).
additional_notes: Literally "is the love," but in Spanish the article (el) is often used in definitions or general statements: "X es el amor" = "X is love" / "That’s what love is." Very common inside the question "¿Qué es el amor?" ("What is love?") or in phrases like "Sé lo que es el amor" ("I know what love is").
target_language_example: Para mí, ayudar a los demás es el amor.
native_language_example: For me, helping others is love.

additional_notes: Use this pattern to say it’s a family member’s (or someone’s) birthday: **Es el cumpleaños de mi + [person]**. **cumpleaños** = “birthday” (always masculine: **el cumpleaños**). **de** means “of,” and **mi** means “my.” In English you usually switch to **’s**: “my mom’s birthday.”
target_language_example: Es el cumpleaños de mi hermana.
native_language_example: It’s my sister’s birthday.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, prices, or sizes. Often followed by a number (Ocho es el doble de cuatro) or by a clause/noun phrase (Es el doble de lo que pagamos ahora). With adjectives like grande, you commonly add “que” to compare: “es el doble de grande que …” = “is twice as big as …”.
target_language_example: Este apartamento es el doble de caro que el otro.
native_language_example: This apartment is twice as expensive as the other one.

meaning: "it’s the day" (used to say what day it is, or that a particular day is for something).
additional_notes: Used with a specific day ("Mañana es el día…" = "Tomorrow is the day…") or with "de" to name an occasion ("es el día de mi boda" = "it’s my wedding day"). It can also introduce a relative clause: "es el día en el que…" ("it’s the day when/on which…").
target_language_example: Hoy es el día para descansar.
native_language_example: Today is the day to rest.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has finished or is over. Often followed by a noun phrase: es el fin de la historia (the story is over), es el fin de la diversión y los juegos (the fun and games are over). You can also use it in a bigger sentence (e.g., La muerte es el fin de...).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: no es el fin del mundo.
native_language_example: Relax: it’s not the end of the world.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has reached its endpoint (a path, a season, a period of rest, a championship, etc.). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: Es el final del camino / del otoño. With a feminine noun, you use: “es el final de la …” (e.g., Es el final de la película).
target_language_example: Lo siento, es el final del viaje.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s the end of the trip.

meaning: 'he is the man' / 'you’re the man' (the right person).
additional_notes: Used to identify someone as the person you mean (e.g., “He’s the man in the photo”) or to say someone is the right person for a job/role (“He’s the man for the job,” “the man of the house,” “the man of my dreams”). It can also be used as praise, especially in direct address: “Usted eres el hombre” ≈ “You’re the man.”
target_language_example: Si alguien puede arreglarlo, él es el hombre.
native_language_example: If anyone can fix it, he’s the man.

additional_notes: Used to say that somewhere is the right/ideal place for something. Often followed by an adjective or a superlative: "es el lugar perfecto" (the perfect place), "es el lugar más..." (the most...). You can also add "para" + infinitive to say what it’s a good place for: "es el lugar perfecto para criar niños".
target_language_example: Este café es el lugar perfecto para estudiar.
native_language_example: This café is the perfect place to study.

additional_notes: Used to say that a particular place is the safest option. The structure is: es = “it is”, el lugar = “the place”, más seguro = “safest/more safe” (masculine singular). You can add details with para… (“for…”) or specify the place: “El sótano es el lugar más seguro.”
target_language_example: En una tormenta, es el lugar más seguro.
native_language_example: In a storm, it’s the safest place.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is the best (the top choice) in a group or category. It agrees with the subject: for a woman you usually say “es la mejor”; for more than one, “son los/las mejores.” You can add “en + [activity/field]” (e.g., “es el mejor en lo que hace”) or use it with other superlatives like “el más barato es el mejor” (“the cheapest is the best”).
target_language_example: Para mí, este restaurante es el mejor de la ciudad.
native_language_example: For me, this restaurant is the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is identical to another, or unchanged. Often appears with context that makes the comparison clear (e.g., “but the game is the same”). For people, it can mean “it’s him/the same guy” or “he’s back to being himself again” (e.g., “Tom es el mismo de nuevo”). Changes for gender/number: es la misma, son los mismos, son las mismas.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: este cargador es el mismo que el tuyo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: this charger is the same as yours.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right time has arrived to do something, often followed by **de + infinitive**: *Es el momento de + verbo* ("It’s time to + verb"). You can add words like *ahora* (now), *perfecto* (perfect), or *apropiado* (appropriate) to emphasize timing.
target_language_example: Es el momento de irnos.
native_language_example: It’s time for us to go.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something has the highest degree of a quality in a group. Pattern: "[Subject] es el más + adjective" (masculine singular). Change it to match what you’re talking about: "es la más" (feminine), "son los más / son las más" (plural). You can add "de..." to specify the group: "es el más alto de la clase".
target_language_example: Este restaurante es el más barato del barrio.
native_language_example: This restaurant is the cheapest in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to compare one person (or thing) with a group. Structure: [person/thing] + es + el/la más + adjective + de + [group]. With "alto" it typically refers to height (tall). Adjust gender/number as needed: "es la más alta de…" for a female subject; or swap the adjective: "es el más rápido de…" (the fastest of…).
target_language_example: Tom es el más alto de la clase.
native_language_example: Tom is the tallest in the class.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is the biggest in size or the greatest in importance/ability. Often followed by “de…” (of…) to compare within a group: “Es el más grande de los dos” (the bigger of the two), “Es el más grande de los artistas vivos” (the greatest of the living artists). “Grande” can mean physical size (big) or figurative greatness (great).
target_language_example: Para mí, este edificio es el más grande de la ciudad.
native_language_example: For me, this building is the biggest in the city.

meaning: "is the name of" (used to identify what something/someone is called).
additional_notes: Used to state that a person, place, or thing is called something. Often followed by a name or noun: "Es el nombre de + [person/thing]". You can also use it in questions: "¿Es el nombre de tu madre?"
target_language_example: Carlos es el nombre de mi hermano.
native_language_example: Carlos is my brother’s name.

additional_notes: Used to state that someone is another person’s father. It can also be used figuratively to mean “the source/origin of” something (e.g., “Time is the father of truth”). For plural children, you can say “es el padre de mis niños / de tres niños.”
target_language_example: Juan es el padre de Sofía.
native_language_example: Juan is Sofía’s father.

additional_notes: Used to say a country has the highest degree of an adjective within a group. Structure: [Country] + es el país más + adjective (+ de/del + group). The adjective usually agrees with “país” (masculine): más pequeño/chico, más grande, más occidental, etc.
target_language_example: Canadá es el país más grande de América del Norte.
native_language_example: Canada is the largest country in North America.

additional_notes: Used to compare countries by size. It’s a full statement: **es** (“is”) + **el país** (“the country”) + **más grande** (“biggest/largest”). Often followed by **de** or **del** (“of the”) + a region/group (**de Escandinavia**) or **del mundo** (“in the world”). You can swap the subject before it: *Rusia es el país más grande…*
target_language_example: Canadá es el país más grande de América del Norte.
native_language_example: Canada is the largest country in North America.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person/thing is number one in order or rank. It comes before a masculine singular noun: "es el primer día / es el primer presidente / es el primer lugar". Before a masculine singular noun, "primero" shortens to "primer".
target_language_example: Este es el primer día de clases.
native_language_example: This is the first day of classes.

additional_notes: Used to point out that something is starting now (the first day of school, a new job, a new period of life, etc.). Often followed by “de…” (of) to say what it’s the first day of: “Es el primer día de clases.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es el primer día y todo es nuevo.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s the first day and everything is new.

meaning: "is the one who/that" (used to identify the person/thing that does something).
additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize who/what fits a description or performed an action. Typically followed by a verb clause: "Tom es el que pagó las entradas." You may also see it in superlatives/comparisons: "es el que más/menos...". It changes for gender/number: "es la que", "son los que", "son las que".
target_language_example: Tom es el que pagó las entradas.
native_language_example: Tom is the one who paid for the tickets.

meaning: "he's the one who told me" / "he's the one who said (to me)".
additional_notes: Used to identify who gave you information or an instruction. Typically followed by what the person told you (e.g., qué hacer, cómo hacerlo, cuándo sería la reunión, a quién dárselo). You can change it for gender/number: Ella es la que me dijo… / Ellos son los que me dijeron… / Ellas son las que me dijeron…
target_language_example: Tom es el que me dijo cuándo sería la reunión.
native_language_example: Tom is the one who told me when the meeting would be.

es el que más me gusta

target_language_multi_word_term: es el que más me gusta
meaning: “It’s the one I like the most.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is your favorite among several options. Literally: “it is the one that I like the most.” You can change it to match gender/number: **es la que más me gusta** (feminine), **son los que más me gustan** (plural masculine/mixed), **son las que más me gustan** (plural feminine). Often used after mentioning a group: **De todos…, es el que más me gusta.**
target_language_example: Me gustan todos los colores, pero el verde es el que más me gusta.
native_language_example: I like all the colors, but green is the one I like the most.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is the longest river in a place. Structure: **[X] es el río más largo de/en [place]**. Use **de** with continents/countries/regions (de África, de Europa) and **en** to mean “in” a place (en Japón). **más largo** is the superlative “longest” (literally “more long”).
target_language_example: El Amazonas es el río más largo de Sudamérica.
native_language_example: The Amazon is the longest river in South America.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the final one in an order or sequence (time, list, warnings, etc.). It can also mean “the latest/newest model” in product contexts ("el último modelo"). Changes with gender/number: "es la última" (fem.), "son los últimos/las últimas" (plural).
target_language_example: Este es el último tren a Madrid.
native_language_example: This is the last train to Madrid.

meaning: “is the last refuge” (the final excuse or fallback).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern “X es el último refugio de Y” to criticize something as a desperate last resort (often a moral judgment). It’s a set, quote-like expression; you can also say “el último refugio” on its own.
target_language_example: Decir que no te importa es el último refugio de quien no quiere admitir que está herido.
native_language_example: Saying you don’t care is the last refuge of someone who doesn’t want to admit they’re hurt.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is the only one in a group. It agrees with gender/number: es el único (masc.), es la única (fem.), son los únicos / son las únicas (plural). Often followed by a noun (modo, testigo) or by “de + place/group” (de aquí).
target_language_example: Tom es el único testigo del crimen.
native_language_example: Tom is the only witness to the crime.

additional_notes: Used to say that just one person/thing does something or has a quality. It’s followed by a verb clause: es el único que + verb. It can change for gender/number: es la única que (female), son los únicos que / son las únicas que (plural). In negative sentences you’ll often see: no es el único que… (“he/she isn’t the only one who…”).
target_language_example: Tom es el único que da de comer al perro.
native_language_example: Tom is the only one who feeds the dog.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize that something matches perfectly or is precisely correct. Often followed by a noun phrase ("Es exactamente la misma idea") or by "lo que…" ("Es exactamente lo que quiero"). For plural subjects you use "son exactamente" ("Son exactamente iguales").
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que necesitamos.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what we need.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm that something matches your meaning, plan, or expectation. It’s followed by a verb phrase: “Es exactamente lo que quiero decir” (what I mean), “Eso es exactamente lo que voy a hacer” (what I’m going to do). Often appears after “eso” (“that”): “Eso es exactamente lo que…”.
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que necesito ahora.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to intensify an adjective: "Es extremadamente + adjetivo". It’s a formal/neutral way to say something is very intense (peligroso, aburrido, despistado, etc.). Often followed by an adjective, not a noun.
target_language_example: Este examen es extremadamente difícil.
native_language_example: This exam is extremely difficult.

meaning: "is famous for its/her" (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to say a place or person is well-known because of something. The adjective changes for gender/number: es famoso por su (masc. singular), es famosa por su (fem. singular), son famosos/as por su. Use "por" + "su" + noun; "su" agrees with what is owned, and the owned thing is often singular here (e.g., su vino, su arquitectura).
target_language_example: La región es famosa por su queso.
native_language_example: The region is famous for its cheese.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe something as easy: **[subject] + es fácil** (El examen es fácil). You can also use it impersonally with an infinitive to mean “it’s easy to…”: **Es fácil + infinitive** (Es fácil viajar).
target_language_example: Es fácil aprender español con práctica.
native_language_example: It’s easy to learn Spanish with practice.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb after de: Es fácil de + usar/aprender/decir/hacer. You can change the subject (e.g., Esta cámara es fácil de usar) and gender/number to match it: es fácil (singular), son fáciles (plural).
target_language_example: Este programa es fácil de entender.
native_language_example: This program is easy to understand.

additional_notes: Used to react positively to something (an idea, news, a plan, a situation). Often appears as “Esto es genial” (“This is great”) or “Eso es genial” (“That’s great”). “Genial” in Spanish usually means “great/awesome/brilliant,” not “genius.”
target_language_example: ¡Tu idea es genial!
native_language_example: Your idea is great!

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe size (a general characteristic). **Es** is for singular subjects (El lago/La habitación). For plural: **son grandes**. **Grande** stays the same for masculine/feminine singular (el coche es grande / la casa es grande), and becomes **grandes** in plural. Watch out: **grande** can look like English **grand**, but it usually just means **big/large**.
target_language_example: Tu casa es grande, pero muy acogedora.
native_language_example: Your house is big, but very cozy.

additional_notes: Used to say that the moment has come to do an action: Es hora de + infinitive (Es hora de cerrar). With a noun, it can mean “it’s time for…” (Es hora de mi inyección). You’ll also see Es hora de que + subjunctive (Es hora de que nos vayamos). Ya es hora de… adds emphasis: “it’s (about) time to…”.
target_language_example: Es hora de irnos a casa.
native_language_example: It’s time to go home.

meaning: “it’s time for us to go / leave.”
additional_notes: Used to say it’s time to leave. Often appears with a lead-in like “Bueno/Bien,” and can be softened with “Creo que…” (“I think…”). Literally “it’s the hour of leaving (ourselves),” where “irnos” = “to go/leave” + “nos” (“us”), meaning “for us to leave.”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; es hora de irnos.
native_language_example: It’s already late; it’s time for us to go.

meaning: "it’s time to leave" / "it’s time to go."
additional_notes: Used to say that the moment to leave has arrived. Often followed by a place or destination: "irse a casa" (to go home) or "irse de aquí" (to get out of here). "Irse" is the reflexive form of "ir" and emphasizes leaving/going away from the current place.
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; es hora de irse.
native_language_example: It’s already late; it’s time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say the moment has come for someone to do something, often as a suggestion, insistence, or a sense of urgency. After "es hora de que," Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive: "Es hora de que vayas," "…salgamos," "…sepas." You can also use "ya" for emphasis: "Ya es hora de que…".
target_language_example: Ya es hora de que empecemos a trabajar.
native_language_example: It’s (really) time for us to start working.

es hora de que nos vayamos

target_language_multi_word_term: es hora de que nos vayamos
additional_notes: Used to say (often politely or firmly) that the moment has come to go. After “es hora de que…”, Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive: “nos vayamos” (from “irse” = to leave/go away). You can add where you’re leaving for/going: “Es hora de que nos vayamos a casa / de aquí / de este lugar.”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; es hora de que nos vayamos.
native_language_example: It’s already late; it’s time for us to leave.

meaning: “it’s time for you to…” (often with the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone (you) should do something now, or that the moment has come. It’s typically followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: “Es hora de que te marches / te perdones / te decidas.” Can be firm or urging depending on tone (e.g., “Vamos, es hora de que te…”).
target_language_example: Es hora de que te vayas a casa.
native_language_example: It’s time for you to go home.

es hora de que te vayas

target_language_multi_word_term: es hora de que te vayas
meaning: “it’s time for you to leave / go.”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (often firmly) that the right time has come for them to go. After “es hora de que…”, Spanish typically uses the present subjunctive: “te vayas” (from “irse,” to leave/go away). You can add a destination: “Es hora de que te vayas a casa / al colegio.”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; es hora de que te vayas.
native_language_example: It’s late; it’s time for you to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t change or is identical/similar. Very common in comparisons: **es igual que** (same as), **es igual al/a la** (same as + noun). It can also imply “it’s always the same” when talking about repeated situations (e.g., *Siempre es igual*).
target_language_example: Para mí, es igual si vamos en coche o en tren.
native_language_example: For me, it’s the same whether we go by car or by train.

meaning: “is equal to” / “is the same as” / “is like.”
additional_notes: Used to state equality in math (A es igual a B) and also to compare things or people (“Mi respuesta es igual a la tuya” = my answer is the same as yours; “Es igual a su padre” = he/she is like his/her father, very similar). You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: “son iguales a” (they are equal to), “era igual a” (was equal to).
target_language_example: Este número es igual a veinte.
native_language_example: This number is equal to twenty.

additional_notes: Used to say that something matters or is significant. Common patterns: "Es importante + infinitive" (Es importante aprender…), and "Es importante que + subjunctive" (Es importante que todos sepan…). You can also say "Esto es importante" = "This is important."
target_language_example: Es importante que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s important that you arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has value or importance for a person, group, or thing. Follow it with a noun or pronoun: es importante para la economía, para mí, para nosotros. You can also put a subject before it (El turismo es importante para...) or use an infinitive as the subject (Estudiar inglés es importante para...).
target_language_example: Dormir bien es importante para tu salud.
native_language_example: Sleeping well is important for your health.

additional_notes: Use it to express that something matters to you personally. It can be followed by a noun ("La música es importante para mí") or by "que" + a verb to say that a situation/action is important ("Es importante para mí que estés ahí"). You can change the person: "para ti" (to you), "para él/ella" (to him/her), "para nosotros" (to us).
target_language_example: Es importante para mí pasar tiempo con mi familia.
native_language_example: It’s important to me to spend time with my family.

meaning: "it’s important that" (used to stress the importance/necessity of something).
additional_notes: Often followed by the subjunctive because it expresses a recommendation, importance, or necessity: "Es importante que estudies." (not *"estudias"*). You can change the verb to match tense: "Fue/era/será importante que...". You can also add an indirect object: "Es importante que me llames" (It’s important that you call me).
target_language_example: Es importante que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s important that you arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say something cannot happen or cannot be done. Very common pattern: **Es imposible que + subjunctive** (Es imposible que termine / llegue). You can also use **imposible de + infinitive** to mean “impossible to…” (imposible de cumplir).
target_language_example: Lo siento, es imposible que te lo entregue hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s impossible for me to deliver it to you today.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** + **incapaz de** + infinitive to say someone cannot do something due to lack of ability, skill, capacity, or self-control. Often sounds strong/critical; in many situations **no puede** is a softer, more neutral way to say “can’t.” You can change the verb to match the subject: **soy/eres/es/somos/son incapaz(ces) de**. It agrees in number (and sometimes gender): **incapaz** (singular), **incapaces** (plural).
target_language_example: Parece obvio que él es incapaz de nadar.
native_language_example: It seems obvious that he is unable to swim.

additional_notes: Used to express strong surprise or admiration about a situation or a person. Common patterns: “Es increíble que + (subjunctive)” (It’s unbelievable that...) and “Es increíble lo que + verb” (It’s incredible what...). Can be positive (amazing) or negative (hard to believe). Often used with “¡Dios mío!” for emphasis.
target_language_example: Es increíble lo rápido que aprendes.
native_language_example: It’s incredible how fast you learn.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is required for a person, goal, or situation. Structure: [Thing] + es indispensable para + [person/thing/verb in infinitive]. Example with an action: "Es indispensable para aprender español."
target_language_example: Dormir bien es indispensable para estar sano.
native_language_example: Sleeping well is essential to be healthy.

additional_notes: Used to state that someone did not do something wrong or is not guilty (often in a legal/crime context, but it can also mean someone is naïve). You can change the subject: "Soy inocente" (I’m innocent), "Eres inocente" (you’re innocent).
target_language_example: No cabe la menor duda de que Tom es inocente.
native_language_example: There isn’t the slightest doubt that Tom is innocent.

additional_notes: Used to say something won’t work or isn’t worth doing. Common pattern: “Es inútil + infinitive” (Es inútil discutir / esperar / leer…). Can also describe a thing as not useful: “La televisión … es inútil.”
target_language_example: Es inútil intentarlo otra vez; no hay tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s pointless to try again; there’s no time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly what you need, wanted, expected, or mentioned. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the past or present: Es justo lo que necesitaba / necesito. Similar in meaning to "es exactamente lo que".
target_language_example: ¡Es justo lo que estaba buscando!
native_language_example: It’s exactly what I was looking for!

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to identify/define something: **Es la + [feminine noun]**. Common for explanations or emphasis (e.g., **Es la regla** = “That’s the rule.”). It can also introduce the main point: **…es la falta de privacidad** (“…is the lack of privacy”).
target_language_example: No es una idea; es la verdad.
native_language_example: It’s not an idea; it’s the truth.

additional_notes: Used to state that a city is the capital city of a country/region. Structure: [City] + es la capital de + [place]. You can change tense/person: “fue la capital de” (was), “será la capital de” (will be).
target_language_example: Madrid es la capital de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

additional_notes: Used to state that a place is the political/administrative capital of a country, region, or territory: “X es la capital de la Y.” It can also be used figuratively to mean a place is famous for something: “París es la capital de la moda.” The article changes with the noun that follows (de la / del / de los / de las): “del” = “de + el”.
target_language_example: Buenos Aires es la capital de la Argentina.
native_language_example: Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina.

meaning: 'it is the house/home' (often: 'this is the house/home').
additional_notes: Uses the verb ser (es = 'is') with la casa ('the house/home') to identify a place, often followed by de + person/people to say who it belongs to: Es la casa de mis padres. You’ll also hear it when introducing or pointing out a place: Ésta es la casa de mi primo.
target_language_example: Ésta es la casa de mi abuela.
native_language_example: This is my grandmother’s house.

additional_notes: Used to say that a girl is number one in a quality (smartest, prettiest, coolest, etc.). Put an adjective after "más" (e.g., inteligente, guapa, bonita) and often add "de/del" + group ("de la escuela", "del mundo"). Can also describe "la chica más" + adjective without "es" (e.g., "la chica más simpática").
target_language_example: Ella es la chica más inteligente de la clase.
native_language_example: She is the smartest girl in the class.

es la ciudad más grande de

target_language_multi_word_term: es la ciudad más grande de
additional_notes: Used to compare cities by size (usually population): “X es la ciudad más grande de + place/region/country.” Note: “más grande” can mean “largest” or “biggest”; if you mean physical size (area), you may hear “la de mayor superficie.”
target_language_example: Madrid es la ciudad más grande de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is the largest city in Spain.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the most important factor for achieving a result. Often followed by: de + noun (La paciencia es la clave del éxito = Patience is the key to success) or para + infinitive/noun (La práctica es la clave para mejorar = Practice is the key to improving). You can also use the plural: Son la clave = They are the key.
target_language_example: La constancia es la clave para aprender español.
native_language_example: Consistency is the key to learning Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to form a superlative, often followed by an adjective (importante, preciosa, hermosa, interesante, tonta, dulce, bonita). You can add context with “del mundo” (in the world) or with a clause like “que he visto” (that I’ve seen). Very common in speech; you can also say “Es lo más + adjective” (e.g., “Es lo más bonito”).
target_language_example: Ese libro es la cosa más divertida que he leído este año.
native_language_example: That book is the funniest thing I’ve read this year.

additional_notes: Used to say that the appropriate or scheduled time has arrived. Very common with **de + noun/verb**: *Es la hora de la cena* (dinner time), *Es la hora de dormir* (time to sleep). With **del/de la** before a noun: *Es la hora del almuerzo / de la siesta*. It can also be used on its own to mean “it’s almost time” or “it’s time (to go/do it).”
target_language_example: Vámonos; ya es la hora.
native_language_example: Let’s go; it’s time.

additional_notes: Used to identify what language something/someone uses: “X es la lengua de Y” (X is the language of Y), “X es la lengua oficial de Y” (X is the official language of Y). You’ll also see it used metaphorically: “la matemática es la lengua del universo” (“math is the language of the universe”). In many contexts, *lengua* and *idioma* both mean “language.”
target_language_example: El español es la lengua principal en muchos países de América Latina.
native_language_example: Spanish is the main language in many Latin American countries.

meaning: “is the mother of” (the main cause/origin of).
additional_notes: Used in proverb-like statements to say that one thing produces or leads to another: “X es la madre de la Y.” Common with abstract nouns (la necesidad, la experiencia, la repetición). English often uses “X is the mother of Y” or “X is the root/driver of Y.” Note: in actual Spanish, the preposition often contracts with masculine singular nouns (de + el = del), but this entry focuses on the fixed substring “es la madre de la”.
target_language_example: La necesidad es la madre de la invención.
native_language_example: Necessity is the mother of invention.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best within a group or category. "Mejor" = "better/best"; with "la" it agrees with a feminine noun (la lengua, la medicina, la opción). For a masculine noun, you usually say "es el mejor" (El café es el mejor). You can also add "de" to specify the group: "Es la mejor de la clase" (She/It’s the best in the class).
target_language_example: Para mí, esta película es la mejor.
native_language_example: For me, this movie is the best.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or proportions: X es la mitad de Y = “X is half of Y.” It can be literal (numbers, size, time) or figurative (“half the answer”). Often followed by a noun, number, or pronoun: es la mitad de diez mil / es la mitad de su vida. You may also see a comparison with an adjective: “es la mitad de + adjective + que …” (e.g., “es la mitad de grande que …” = “is half as big as …”).
target_language_example: Este precio es la mitad del precio original.
native_language_example: This price is half of the original price.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to say that a female person/thing is the most (superlative) in a group: “X es la más + adjective”. Use **el más** for masculine singular (e.g., *Él es el más alto*). Often followed by **de** + group (*la más inteligente de la clase*) or **de todas/de todos** (“of all”).
target_language_example: Ana es la más rápida del equipo.
native_language_example: Ana is the fastest on the team.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the most (adjective) person in a group. It’s often followed by an adjective (rica, aburrida, genial, valiente, inteligente) and then either “del/de la …” (of the …) or “que conozco” (that I know). You can negate it with “no”: “No es la persona más …”.
target_language_example: Ella es la persona más amable de la oficina.
native_language_example: She is the kindest person in the office.

additional_notes: Used to say something comes first in an order, list, or ranking. It agrees with a feminine noun (la primera): *letra, cosa, noticia, persona, puerta, condición*. For a masculine noun, use *es el primero*; for plural, *son los/las primeros/as*. You can also use it in a fixed way to emphasize importance: *X es lo primero* (“X is the most important thing / comes first”).
target_language_example: Para mí, la seguridad es la primera prioridad.
native_language_example: For me, safety is the number one priority.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening for the first time. Very often followed by **que** + verb: *Es la primera vez que lo oigo* (“It’s the first time I’ve heard it”). You can add context with **desde que** (“since”): *Es la primera vez desde que…*.
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que vengo aquí.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come here.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening for the first time. It’s followed by a verb; in everyday speech you’ll usually hear the present tense after "es la primera vez que" (e.g., "Es la primera vez que vengo"). You can change the tense to match the situation: "Fue/Era la primera vez que..." = "It was the first time that..."
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que visito México.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve visited Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something for the first time. It’s followed by a verb clause; in Spanish you’ll often hear the verb in the present (e.g., "Es la primera vez que veo...") even though in English we often use the present perfect ("it’s the first time I’ve seen...").
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que viajo solo.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve traveled alone.

es la razón por la que

target_language_multi_word_term: es la razón por la que
additional_notes: Used to explain the cause of something. It’s often followed by a verb phrase: “Es la razón por la que + (verb/clause) …”. You can change it for gender/number: “Es la razón por la que…” (la razón, feminine singular) stays the same, but you can also hear “Esa es la razón por la que…”. In more casual speech, “Por eso…” is a common shorter equivalent.
target_language_example: Esa es la razón por la que no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: That’s the reason why I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening again for the second time (often with a time expression: “en/esta semana”, “hoy”, etc.). Very commonly followed by **que** + verb: **Es la segunda vez que...** (“It’s the second time that...”/“I’ve ... for the second time”).
target_language_example: Es la segunda vez que pierdo las llaves esta semana.
native_language_example: It’s the second time I’ve lost my keys this week.

additional_notes: Used to say something has happened three times. Often followed by a time period ("en tres meses", "esta semana", "este mes") or by "que" + verb to specify the action: "Es la tercera vez que lo veo" (“It’s the third time I see him”). If you’re pointing to the present situation, you can also say "Esta es la tercera vez" (“This is the third time”).
target_language_example: Es la tercera vez que me llamas hoy.
native_language_example: It’s the third time you’ve called me today.

additional_notes: Used to insist that something is true, often as a justification or defense ("Sorry, but it’s the truth"). In your examples it can also mean “what I need is the truth / the truth is the first victim,” where la verdad = “the truth.” Literally “it is the truth.”
target_language_example: No te va a gustar, pero es la verdad.
native_language_example: You’re not going to like it, but it’s the truth.

additional_notes: Literally “is the life.” Used (1) literally to say what something is (“X es la vida” = “X is life” / “X is the life…”), and (2) very commonly in the fixed expression “Así es la vida” to mean “That’s life,” said when you accept that something bad or unfair happens.
target_language_example: Así es la vida: a veces las cosas no salen como quieres.
native_language_example: That’s life: sometimes things don’t go the way you want.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (la + última). It can mean the most recent/newest in a series (e.g., news, fashion, version) or literally the final/last one. With people, it often means “the last person” in a sequence or “the least expected person” (as in: “the last woman I expected to see”). Not to be confused with English “ultimate” (which often means “the best”); Spanish última mainly means “last” or “latest.”
target_language_example: Esta es la última versión de la app.
native_language_example: This is the latest version of the app.

meaning: "it’s the last time" (this won’t happen again).
additional_notes: Used to insist that something is happening for the final time, often as a promise, warning, or firm statement. It can stand alone ("Es la última vez.") or be followed by "que" + verb ("Es la última vez que...").
target_language_example: Es la última vez que llego tarde al trabajo.
native_language_example: It’s the last time I’m late to work.

additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re talking about is feminine and singular (la forma, la manera, la solución). For a masculine noun, use “es el único” (e.g., “Es el único camino”). “Única” looks like “unique,” but here it usually means “only (one).”
target_language_example: Es la única opción que tenemos.
native_language_example: It’s the only option we have.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is just one possible or effective method to achieve a result. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive verb: es la única forma de + infinitive (hacer, aprender, salir, etc.). You can change the subject/tense as needed: Es/Fue/Será la única forma de…
target_language_example: Es la única forma de llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s the only way to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the sole option or method to achieve a goal. Typically followed by an infinitive verb (de + infinitive): Es la única manera de escapar / ir / poder quedarme. You can change the verb for tense/person: Fue/Será la única manera de…
target_language_example: Lo siento, es la única manera de llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s the only way to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that one person is the only one who does something or can do something. It’s followed by a verb clause (often with que) describing the action/ability: “Tom es la única persona que puede ayudarme.” In the past/future you change “es” (e.g., “era la única persona que…”, “será la única persona que…”).
target_language_example: Ella es la única persona que entiende este problema.
native_language_example: She’s the only person who understands this problem.

meaning: "it’s the …" (with neuter *lo*, often before an adjective: "the worst," "the minimum").
additional_notes: Spanish uses the neuter article *lo* with adjectives to talk about something in a general/abstract way: *es lo mejor/peor* = “it’s the best/worst (thing).” It also appears in fixed patterns like *lo primero es lo primero* (“first things first”) and in emphasis structures like *qué es lo que…* (“what is it that…?”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero es lo mejor para todos.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s the best thing for everyone.

meaning: “it’s the best” / “it’s the best thing to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is the best option or decision in a situation. Often followed by context like “si crees que es lo mejor” (“if you think it’s best”). You can also add “de + noun” to mean “the best part of …” (e.g., “lo mejor de la excursión” = “the best part of the trip”).
target_language_example: Creo que es lo mejor para todos.
native_language_example: I think it’s the best thing for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to point to the specific thing being referred to (“that is what we’ll do / what we need / what you want”). Often follows another clause for emphasis: “...eso es lo que...”. It can also appear in indirect questions meaning “what”: “saben qué es lo que sigue” = “they know what comes next.”
target_language_example: Si es lo que necesitas, puedo ayudarte mañana.
native_language_example: If that’s what you need, I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: "that’s what you want" / "if that’s what you want."
additional_notes: Used to confirm or emphasize someone’s preference/decision. Often appears inside the pattern “(si) es lo que + verb” (e.g., “si es lo que quieres”) meaning “(if) that’s what you want.” It can also be part of a longer question: “Dime qué es lo que quieres” = “Tell me what it is that you want,” where “lo que” means “what/that which.”
target_language_example: Si es lo que quieres, podemos hacerlo mañana.
native_language_example: If that’s what you want, we can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is just one thing (and no other) that someone needs/does/has, etc. Often followed by a verb: “Es lo único que necesito / tienes que hacer / ha habido…”. You can change the verb (es/era/será) to match the time.
target_language_example: Es lo único que quiero ahora.
native_language_example: It’s the only thing I want right now.

meaning: "is the" (used with neuter "lo" + an adjective/superlative: "the first/last/most...").
additional_notes: "Lo" is the neuter article in Spanish. In patterns like "es lo primero/último" or "es lo más + adjective", it means “the (thing) that is most/first/last…”. It’s commonly followed by: primero, último, mejor, peor, or "más" + adjective (e.g., "es lo más importante").
target_language_example: Para mí, tu familia es lo más importante.
native_language_example: For me, your family is the most important thing.

meaning: "it’s the best" / "it’s the best option (to do)."
additional_notes: Used to say something is the best choice or solution in a situation (often with context like "por ahora" = "for now"). It can also mean something is the best you’ve ever seen/experienced ("Es lo mejor que he visto..."). Common pattern: "Es lo mejor para + infinitive" (best for doing something) and "Es lo mejor que + verb" (the best that...).
target_language_example: Creo que es lo mejor que podemos hacer ahora.
native_language_example: I think it’s the best thing we can do now.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the best option or decision for a person or group. Very common with pronouns or nouns after para: para mí/ti/él/ella/nosotros/ellos; para los niños; para ambos/los dos.
target_language_example: Creo que es lo mejor para ti.
native_language_example: I think it’s best for you.

meaning: "it’s the best (thing) that…" / "it’s the best I/we/you can do."
additional_notes: Used to say something is the best among options or the best you can do in a situation. Often followed by a verb in the present perfect (he/has hecho, he/has visto) or by poder (es lo mejor que puedo/podemos/puedes hacer). In Spanish, a verb after "lo mejor que" is commonly in the subjunctive when it refers to an uncertain/ideal option (e.g., "Es lo mejor que puedas hacer"), though in everyday speech you’ll also hear the indicative ("puedes").
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero es lo mejor que puedo hacer por ahora.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s the best I can do for now.

es lo mejor que puedo hacer

target_language_multi_word_term: es lo mejor que puedo hacer
additional_notes: Use it to say you’re doing as much as you’re able to, given limits (time, money, skill, situation). It can sound apologetic (when you can’t do more) or matter-of-fact (when setting expectations). You can add context with phrases like “en este momento” (right now) or “por ahora” (for now).
target_language_example: Lo siento, es lo mejor que puedo hacer por ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s the best I can do for now.

meaning: “it’s the least (that)…” / “it’s the least I/he/she can do.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is a minimal effort, often as a small favor, thanks, or basic responsibility. Commonly followed by a verb phrase like “puedo hacer” (I can do) or “puede hacer” (he/she/you can do): “Es lo menos que puedo hacer por ti.”
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme; es lo menos que puedo hacer.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me; it’s the least I can do.

meaning: 'It’s the same' / 'it’s all the same (to me)' (no difference).
additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t change or there’s no difference. Common with "para mí" to mean "I don’t mind / it makes no difference to me" (e.g., "Es lo mismo para mí"). You can also add "que" to compare: "Es lo mismo que..." = "It’s the same as...".
target_language_example: Da igual: para mí es lo mismo.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter: it’s all the same to me.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say something is the most (e.g., “Es lo más lindo…” = “It’s the prettiest…”). The pattern is: **ser + lo más + adjective**. **Lo más** doesn’t change, but the adjective usually agrees in gender/number (lo más **bonito/bonita/bonitos/bonitas**). In some countries, **¡Es lo más!** can also be a casual way to mean “It’s the best!”
target_language_example: Este consejo es lo más útil para empezar.
native_language_example: This advice is the most useful for getting started.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the top priority. Often follows a noun with “ser”: “La salud es lo más importante” (“Health is the most important thing”). “Lo más + adjective” means “the most + adjective,” with “lo” turning the adjective into “the … thing” (an abstract idea).
target_language_example: Para mí, pasar tiempo con mi familia es lo más importante.
native_language_example: For me, spending time with my family is the most important thing.

additional_notes: Used to say what should be prioritized above everything else. Very common in the set phrase “Lo primero es lo primero”, meaning “First things first.” You can also replace it with a noun: “La familia es lo primero” (Family comes first).
target_language_example: Antes de salir, la seguridad es lo primero.
native_language_example: Before going out, safety comes first.

additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize something (a cleft structure): "X es lo que..." = "X is what...". Often followed by a verb phrase: "Es lo que eres" (It's what you are). You may also see it inside a question: "qué es lo que..." = "what is it that..." (adds emphasis).
target_language_example: Esto es lo que necesito ahora mismo.
native_language_example: This is what I need right now.

meaning: "It is what it is" / "that’s how it is" (accepting a situation).
additional_notes: Used to express resignation or acceptance when something can’t be changed, or when the available options are limited (similar to “that’s all there is”). Often said in a matter-of-fact tone; can sound a bit blunt.
target_language_example: No hay más entradas; es lo que hay.
native_language_example: There are no more tickets; it is what it is.

meaning: “is … enough / sufficiently …” (usually followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say something has enough of a quality to do something or for something to be true. Very often followed by an adjective + “como para” + infinitive: “es lo suficientemente + adj. + como para + verb” (“is + adj. + enough to + verb”). You can also place it before the adjective: “es suficientemente + adj.”
target_language_example: No es lo suficientemente importante como para discutirlo ahora.
native_language_example: It isn’t important enough to discuss it now.

additional_notes: Used to say something was the final thing said/done/remembered, or (often with querer/necesitar) to emphasize that something is the least wanted/needed ("the last thing we need/want"). Usually followed by a verb phrase: "Es lo último que dije / me dijo / necesito / quiero / recuerdo."
target_language_example: Es lo último que quiero ahora mismo.
native_language_example: It’s the last thing I want right now.

meaning: 'it's the only thing that…' (the only one/thing that…).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is just one option, one fact, or one thing that matters. It’s followed by a clause (usually a verb phrase): “Es lo único que sé” = “It’s the only thing I know.” You can also switch person/tense as needed: “Fue lo único que…” (It was the only thing that…), “Será lo único que…” (It will be the only thing that…).
target_language_example: Es lo único que puedo decir ahora.
native_language_example: It’s the only thing I can say right now.

meaning: "it's what" / "it is what" (introduces what something is or was).
additional_notes: Used to identify or clarify something: **Es lo que + verb/phrase** (“It’s what + verb/phrase”). Very common for explanations (**Es lo que creo** = “It’s what I think”) and for correcting misunderstandings with **no es lo que...** (“it’s not what...”): **No es lo que parece** (“It’s not what it looks like”).
target_language_example: No es lo que quería decir.
native_language_example: It’s not what I meant to say.

additional_notes: Used to point to the exact words of a source (a sign/label, a person, the law, “people,” etc.). Often implies “I’m just repeating what it says,” sometimes to end an argument or emphasize that you’re following the wording. You can add who/what says it after: "Es lo que dice la ley" (the law), "Es lo que dice mi madre" (my mom), "Es lo que dice" can stand alone when the source is understood.
target_language_example: No me culpes; es lo que dice el contrato.
native_language_example: Don’t blame me; that’s what the contract says.

additional_notes: Used to report what people (or the news, rumors, etc.) say, often with a neutral or slightly skeptical tone (“supposedly”). It can refer to a specific group: *en las noticias* (on the news), *algunos* (some people), *todos* (everyone).
target_language_example: Mañana va a llover, es lo que dicen.
native_language_example: They say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **Es lo que hacen los + plural noun** to say something is typical/expected behavior for that group: *Es lo que hacen los amigos* (“That’s what friends do”). Use **los** for masculine or mixed groups, and change to **las** for all-female groups: *Es lo que hacen las hermanas*. You can also change the verb to match: *Es lo que hace mi mamá* (singular), *Es lo que hacemos nosotros* (we do).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es lo que hacen los buenos vecinos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: that’s what good neighbors do.

es lo que hay que hacer

target_language_multi_word_term: es lo que hay que hacer
meaning: “it’s what has to be done” / “it’s what you have to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary or the right/expected thing to do. Often expresses obligation in a general sense (not aimed at a specific person), using the structure “hay que + infinitive” (“one has to / you have to”). Can also be used firmly to justify an action: “Because it’s what needs to be done.”
target_language_example: No me apetece, pero es lo que hay que hacer.
native_language_example: I don’t feel like it, but it’s what has to be done.

meaning: “that’s what I wanted” / “that’s what I was looking for.”
additional_notes: Used to confirm that something matches what you wanted or expected. Often followed by an infinitive to specify what (“Es lo que quería oír” = “That’s what I wanted to hear”). It can also introduce what you wanted to show/say (“Esto es lo que quería mostrarte” = “This is what I wanted to show you”).
target_language_example: Perfecto, es lo que quería.
native_language_example: Perfect, that’s what I wanted.

meaning: “it’s what you want” / “if that’s what you want.”
additional_notes: Used to agree to someone’s preference or choice. The subject pronoun is usually omitted in Spanish, so quiere can mean “you want” (usted, formal), “he wants,” or “she wants,” depending on context. You’ll also see it extended: Es lo que quiere oír. = “It’s what you want to hear.”
target_language_example: Está bien, lo haré si es lo que quiere.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll do it if that’s what you want.

meaning: "it’s what you want" / "is that what you want?"
additional_notes: Used to state or (with question intonation or punctuation) ask whether something matches what the other person wants. Very common in emphatic questions like “¿Es lo que quieres?” (= “Is that what you want?”). You can also see it in longer forms like “dime qué es lo que quieres” (“tell me what it is you want”).
target_language_example: ¿Esto es lo que quieres, sí o no?
native_language_example: Is this what you want, yes or no?

meaning: 'it’s what I/you/he/she always…' (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is habitual or consistently true. It’s typically followed by a conjugated verb: "Es lo que siempre digo" = "That’s what I always say." You can change the subject implied by the verb (digo, haces, ha querido, etc.). Often used like "Eso es lo que siempre…" (“That’s what I always…”).
target_language_example: Eso es lo que siempre hago cuando estoy nervioso.
native_language_example: That’s what I always do when I’m nervous.

meaning: "it’s what you …" (talking about something that affects you).
additional_notes: Used to identify something as the exact thing that applies to you. After this phrase, Spanish often uses a verb where **te** is an object pronoun (“to you / for you”), e.g., **te hace falta** (you need), **te mereces** (you deserve), **te gusta** (you like).
target_language_example: Es lo que te conviene ahora.
native_language_example: It’s what’s best for you right now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what *you* (yo) said, would do, would have done, or can do. It’s often followed by a verb phrase: “Es lo que yo decía” (that’s what I was saying), “Es lo que yo haría” (that’s what I would do). You can also add emphasis by contrasting with someone else: “Es lo que yo quiero, no lo que tú quieres.”
target_language_example: Es lo que yo necesito ahora.
native_language_example: That’s what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to say something has a negative effect on someone or something. Structure: **[Thing/action] + es malo para + [person/thing]**. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: *mi salud, el medio ambiente, ti, vosotros*. Contrast with **es bueno para** (“is good for”).
target_language_example: Dormir poco es malo para tu concentración.
native_language_example: Sleeping too little is bad for your concentration.

meaning: 'it/he/she is wonderful' (talking about a thing or a person).
additional_notes: Use "es maravilloso" to say something is wonderful/amazing in a general or lasting way (using "ser"). It can describe a situation ("Es maravilloso que...") or praise a person ("Tom es maravilloso" / "Él es maravilloso con nosotros"). For a feminine noun/person, use "es maravillosa"; plural: "son maravillosos/as".
target_language_example: Es maravilloso que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: It’s wonderful that you came today.

additional_notes: Used to compare age: "X es mayor que Y" = “X is older than Y.” It can also be used for numbers/amounts/sizes to mean “greater than” (e.g., "Cinco es mayor que tres"). For the opposite, use "es menor que" (“is younger/smaller than”). Note: "mayor" also appears in phrases like "hermano/a mayor" (“older brother/sister”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano es mayor que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is older than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities like population, area, size, etc. The phrase “la de” means “that of (the other place/thing)” and avoids repeating the noun: “La población de China es mayor que la de la India” (= “…than India’s [population]”). Use “la de” when the repeated noun is feminine (la población, la superficie); use “el de” with masculine nouns (e.g., “El tamaño de X es mayor que el de Y”). Note: “mayor” is a false friend of English “major”; here it means “greater/bigger” (or “older” in other contexts).
target_language_example: La superficie de España es mayor que la de Portugal.
native_language_example: Spain’s area is bigger than Portugal’s.

additional_notes:
Used to say one option is preferable. Very common with:
- “Es mejor + infinitive”: advice/recommendation (Es mejor evitar… = It’s better to avoid…)
- “Es mejor que + subjunctive”: suggestion about what someone should do (Es mejor que te quedes… = It’s better that you stay…)
It can also compare people/things: “X es mejor que Y” (Tom es mejor nadador que yo = Tom is a better swimmer than I am). In the fixed phrase “y lo que es mejor,” it means “and what’s more / even better,” adding extra good information.
target_language_example: Es mejor que salgamos temprano para no llegar tarde.
native_language_example: It’s better that we leave early so we don’t arrive late.

additional_notes: Used in two main ways: (1) + subjunctive to give advice or say what would be preferable: Es mejor que + (yo/tú/él...) + present subjunctive (e.g., hables, vuelva). (2) + noun/infinitive to compare: “X is better than Y” (e.g., Esta casa es mejor que la otra; Es mejor que jugar a los bolos). In comparisons, it often means “better than,” while before a clause with a conjugated verb it usually means “it’s better that…”.
target_language_example: Es mejor que descanses hoy.
native_language_example: It’s better that you rest today.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things: **X es mejor que el Y** (“X is better than the Y”). **el** is the masculine singular article (“the”); use **la** for feminine (**es mejor que la película**). If you mean “than him,” it’s **que él** (with an accent), not **que el**.
target_language_example: Este restaurante es mejor que el de la esquina.
native_language_example: This restaurant is better than the one on the corner.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things: **X es mejor que la Y** = “X is better than the Y.” Here **la** is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), so it must match a feminine noun (e.g., *la alternativa, la arcilla, la riqueza*). You can swap **la** for **el/los/las** depending on the noun: *Es mejor que el plan A / que las otras opciones.*
target_language_example: Este café es mejor que la otra marca.
native_language_example: This coffee is better than the other brand.

additional_notes: Used to compare something someone else has with something you have. The possessive pronoun “la mía” means “mine” (feminine), so it refers back to a feminine noun already mentioned (e.g., la bicicleta, la guitarra). For a masculine noun, use “el mío” (“mine”). You can also swap “la mía” for other possessives: “la tuya” (yours), “la suya” (his/hers/theirs), etc.
target_language_example: Tu chaqueta es mejor que la mía.
native_language_example: Your jacket is better than mine.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a warning that someone should avoid doing something. Often followed by the present subjunctive (e.g., entres, comas, hables, diga). It can also stand alone as “It’s better not (to).”
target_language_example: Es mejor que no salgas tan tarde.
native_language_example: You’d better not go out so late.

meaning: "You’d better leave" / "It’s better that you leave."
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a strong suggestion (sometimes a warning) that someone should leave. It commonly appears as **Es mejor que + subjunctive**: *vayas* is the present subjunctive of *irte* (to leave/go away). You can add details like *ahora* (now) or *de la ciudad* (from the city).
target_language_example: Es mejor que te vayas antes de que llegue la policía.
native_language_example: You’d better leave before the police arrive.

additional_notes: Used with a singular subject + singular noun to say something belongs to you or describes something of yours: “X es mi Y” (X is my Y). “Mi” changes to match the noun you own/describe: mi (singular), mis (plural). If the subject is plural, use “son”: “Ellos son mis amigos.”
target_language_example: Este libro es mi favorito.
native_language_example: This book is my favorite.

meaning: "she is my friend" / "(someone) is my friend" (female friend).
additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your friend. You can change the subject depending on who you mean: “Ella es mi amiga” (She is my friend) or just “Es mi amiga” when the subject is clear. For a male friend, say “es mi amigo.” To say someone is no longer your friend: “ya no es mi amiga.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes; ella es mi amiga.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; she’s my friend.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is your friend. Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so “Es mi amigo” can mean “He’s my friend” or “She’s my friend” depending on context. For a female friend, say “Es mi amiga.” You can add a name after it: “Es mi amigo Suzuki.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es mi amigo.
native_language_example: Relax, he’s my friend.

additional_notes: Used to state that a place is your home (ownership or where you live). Often appears in contrasts like “No la compré ni la alquilé, pero es mi casa” (“I didn’t buy it or rent it, but it’s my home”). Related welcoming expression: “Tu casa es mi casa” = “Make yourself at home” (literally “Your house is my house”).
target_language_example: Puede que no sea grande, pero es mi casa.
native_language_example: It might not be big, but it’s my home.

additional_notes: Used to take responsibility or blame for something. Often said with an apology: “Lo siento, es mi culpa.” To deny responsibility, use “No es mi culpa” (“It’s not my fault”). “Culpa” = “fault/blame,” so you can change the person: “Es tu culpa” (it’s your fault), “Es su culpa” (it’s his/her/their fault).
target_language_example: Perdón por el retraso; es mi culpa.
native_language_example: Sorry for being late; it’s my fault.

additional_notes: Used to say something is (or isn’t, with “no es mi especialidad”) your area of expertise or what you’re best at. Often used to describe skills, work, or knowledge areas. You can also emphasize with “Esa es mi especialidad.”
target_language_example: La clasificación es mi especialidad.
native_language_example: Classification is my specialty.

additional_notes: Used to identify a woman as your spouse. Often said when introducing someone: “Ella es mi esposa” is a slightly fuller version (explicit “she”), but “Es mi esposa” is very common when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Mucho gusto: es mi esposa, Laura.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you: this is my wife, Laura.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your sister. Since Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, "es mi hermana" commonly means "she is my sister" (or "that person is my sister") based on context. You can add a name: "Es mi hermana Sue."
target_language_example: ¿La conoces? Es mi hermana.
native_language_example: Do you know her? She’s my sister.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your brother. Often followed by extra information: “Es mi hermano el que…” = “It’s my brother who…”. In Spanish you can drop the subject (“él”) because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: No, no es un amigo: es mi hermano.
native_language_example: No, he’s not a friend: he’s my brother.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your daughter. Often said when introducing her (“Ella es mi hija”) or when pointing her out (“Es mi hija”). You can also use it with a name: “Gloria es mi hija.”
target_language_example: Ella es mi hija; se llama Sofía.
native_language_example: She is my daughter; her name is Sofía.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your son. The subject can be a person’s name (“Tom es mi hijo”) or a pronoun (“Él es mi hijo”). Often said by itself (“Es mi hijo.”) when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Perdón, es mi hijo; se perdió un momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, he’s my son; he got lost for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say that a language is the one you learned first (your first language). Structure: [Language] + es mi lengua materna. You can also say “mi idioma materno” or “mi lengua nativa.”
target_language_example: El inglés es mi lengua materna, pero estoy aprendiendo español.
native_language_example: English is my native language, but I’m learning Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your mother. It’s the verb ser (es = “is”) + mi (“my”) + madre (“mother”). Often appears after a name or description: “Alice/Mary es mi madre” (Alice/Mary is my mother) or “La señora de allí es mi madre” (The lady over there is my mother).
target_language_example: Ella es mi madre.
native_language_example: She is my mother.

additional_notes: Use it to say a male person is your best friend. Spanish often includes the name first ("Juan es mi mejor amigo"). For a female best friend, say "es mi mejor amiga". You can add "pero..." to contrast: "Es mi mejor amigo, pero..."
target_language_example: Carlos es mi mejor amigo, pero a veces es muy impaciente.
native_language_example: Carlos is my best friend, but sometimes he's very impatient.

additional_notes: Used to identify a female romantic partner. You can say it with or without the subject (e.g., “Ella es mi novia” / “Es mi novia”). For a male partner: “es mi novio.”
target_language_example: No, no es solo una amiga: es mi novia.
native_language_example: No, she’s not just a friend: she’s my girlfriend.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your father. Spanish often drops the subject pronoun (“él/ella”), so “Es mi padre” can mean “He is my father” or “She is my father” depending on context (usually “he”). You can replace “padre” with other family members: “Es mi madre” (my mother), “Es mi hermano” (my brother).
target_language_example: —¿Quién es él? —Es mi padre.
native_language_example: —Who is he? —He is my father.

additional_notes: Use it to say you’ve never done something before. It’s often followed by a gerund (Es mi primera vez + verb-ing: "Es mi primera vez donando sangre") or by "en" + place/situation ("Es mi primera vez en la cárcel"). You can add "también" for "this is also my first time."
target_language_example: Perdón, es mi primera vez aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s my first time here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is your responsibility or part of what you do for a living. Often followed by an infinitive: “Es mi trabajo + infinitive” (e.g., “Es mi trabajo saber…” = “It’s my job to know…”). Word order can vary: “X es mi trabajo” (“X is my job”).
target_language_example: Es mi trabajo ayudarte con esto.
native_language_example: It’s my job to help you with this.

meaning: 'is much bigger/greater than' or 'is much older than.'
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or people with a strong difference. "mayor" can mean larger/greater (size, quantity, speed, importance) or older (age); context tells you which. Structure: "X es mucho mayor que Y". With nouns, you can avoid repeating the noun: "La población de Japón es mucho mayor que la de Australia" (= than Australia's).
target_language_example: Mi hermano es mucho mayor que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is much older than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people or things. Put what you’re describing before it, and the person/thing you’re comparing to after que. You can change es to other forms of ser to match the subject (e.g., son mucho mejores que, era mucho mejor que).
target_language_example: Este restaurante es mucho mejor que el de la esquina.
native_language_example: This restaurant is much better than the one on the corner.

meaning: “it is much more …” (used to make a stronger comparison).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective/adverb to say someone/something has a quality to a much greater degree than another. Often followed by “que” (than): “Es mucho más + adjetivo + que …” or by “de lo que …” (than what …): “Es mucho más inteligente de lo que parece.” The verb changes with the subject (e.g., “son mucho más …”).
target_language_example: Este examen es mucho más difícil que el anterior.
native_language_example: This exam is much harder than the previous one.

additional_notes: Used to compare height: **ser + mucho más + alto + que + (person/thing)**. *Mucho* intensifies the comparison (“much”). You can swap **alto** for other adjectives: *mucho más grande que* (much bigger than), *mucho más joven que* (much younger than). In some regions you may hear **tú** instead of **vos**.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es mucho más alto que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is much taller than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare sizes: **A es mucho más grande que B** (“A is much bigger than B”). You can replace **grande** with other adjectives: **mucho más rápido que** (much faster than), **mucho más caro que** (much more expensive than).
target_language_example: Este cuarto es mucho más grande que el otro.
native_language_example: This room is much bigger than the other one.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **ser + muy + adjective** to say something/someone has a quality to a high degree: *Es muy importante / Es muy difícil*. You can replace **es** with other forms of **ser** depending on the subject and tense (e.g., *soy muy*, *eres muy*, *son muy*, *era muy*).
target_language_example: Esta tarea es muy fácil.
native_language_example: This task is very easy.

additional_notes: Used to describe something you find pleasant or enjoyable (a temperature, a taste, a feeling, an experience, or seeing someone). It can also be a polite way to say you’re happy to meet or see someone: “Es muy agradable verte.”
target_language_example: El clima hoy es muy agradable.
native_language_example: The weather today is very pleasant.

additional_notes: "Alto" means "tall" for people and "high" for prices, numbers, levels, etc. Use "es" (from "ser") for a general/lasting description: "El precio es muy alto" (the price is very high), "Mi hermano es muy alto" (my brother is very tall). For temporary physical location/height you’d more often use "está": "El avión está muy alto" (the plane is very high up).
target_language_example: Ese edificio es muy alto, pero el alquiler también es muy alto.
native_language_example: That building is very tall, but the rent is also very high.

meaning: "(He/She/You) are very kind" / "That’s very kind (of you)."
additional_notes: Used to describe someone as kind/nice, or as a polite response to a compliment, offer, or help (similar to “That’s very kind of you”). With people: "Es muy amable conmigo" = “He/She is very kind to me.” In set polite phrases you may hear "Es/Usted es muy amable" or "Ud. es muy amable". Can also appear as "Es muy amable por su parte" (“That’s very kind of you/It’s very kind on your part”) and "Es muy amable en decirlo" (“That’s very kind of you to say”).
target_language_example: ¿Me puede ayudar? Gracias, es muy amable.
native_language_example: Can you help me? Thanks, that’s very kind of you.

es muy amable de su parte

target_language_multi_word_term: es muy amable de su parte
additional_notes: A polite, fairly formal way to thank someone for an offer, help, or a kind gesture. Uses the formal possessive “su” (your), so it fits situations where you address someone as “usted” (e.g., a stranger, an older person, a customer/service context). You can also say “Muy amable de su parte” after “Gracias.”
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por su ayuda; es muy amable de su parte.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help; that’s very kind of you.

es muy amable de tu parte

target_language_multi_word_term: es muy amable de tu parte
meaning: “That’s very kind of you.” / “It’s very kind of you.”
additional_notes: Used to thank someone and say they’re being kind. Literally “it is very kind on your part.” Often followed by a clause with que: “Es muy amable de tu parte que me ayudes” (“It’s very kind of you to help me”). You can intensify it with “muy” or say “Es amable de tu parte” (less strong).
target_language_example: Es muy amable de tu parte traerme un café.
native_language_example: It’s very kind of you to bring me a coffee.

meaning: “is very pretty/beautiful” (describing a feminine person or thing).
