native_language_example: Madrid is a very beautiful city.

meaning: “is a very … city” (used to describe a city with an adjective).
additional_notes: Use this pattern to describe a city: [Place] es una ciudad muy + adjective. The adjective agrees with “ciudad” (feminine singular), so many adjectives end in -a (segura, cara, bonita). With adjectives that don’t change for gender (e.g., moderna, interesante), the form stays the same. You can also drop “una” in some contexts, but “es una ciudad muy…” is very common and natural.
target_language_example: Barcelona es una ciudad muy bonita.
native_language_example: Barcelona is a very beautiful city.

meaning: “is one thing” (used to contrast with something else).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the pattern “X es una cosa, Y es otra” to highlight a contrast: one action/idea is different from another (often implying “they’re not the same” or “one doesn’t automatically lead to the other”). In English it’s usually “X is one thing; Y is another.”
target_language_example: Decirlo es una cosa; hacerlo es otra.
native_language_example: Saying it is one thing; doing it is another.

meaning: “it’s a matter of …”; “it’s an issue/question of …”
additional_notes: Used to say what something mainly depends on or what kind of issue it is (money, trust, principles, public health, conscience, etc.). Very common in formal or serious contexts. Often followed by a noun: Es una cuestión de dinero/confianza/principios. You can also change the tense/person: Fue una cuestión de tiempo; No es una cuestión de suerte.
target_language_example: No es una cuestión de talento; es una cuestión de práctica.
native_language_example: It’s not a matter of talent; it’s a matter of practice.

meaning: 'it's kind of / sort of' (a type of).
additional_notes: Used to compare or classify something by saying it is similar to, or a type of, something else. Common in definitions and explanations. You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: "son una especie de..." (they are), "era una especie de..." (it was).
target_language_example: Este aparato es una especie de cámara, pero también graba audio.
native_language_example: This device is kind of a camera, but it also records audio.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser to identify someone or something as a star. Literally it means an astronomical star (El Sol es una estrella). Figuratively, it can mean someone famous or outstanding, often with an extra description like “una estrella del rock” (a rock star). You can also say “Es una estrella” by itself when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Para mí, ella es una estrella.
native_language_example: To me, she’s a star.

meaning: "it’s a way of" (doing something); "it’s a form/type of" (something).
additional_notes: Used to define or describe something by comparing it to a broader category ("X es una forma de Y") or to explain a purpose/approach ("es una forma de + infinitive"). Very common for giving explanations: "Es una forma de decir(lo)" = "It’s a way of saying it" (not meant literally).
target_language_example: Para mí, viajar es una forma de aprender.
native_language_example: For me, traveling is a way to learn.

additional_notes: Used to identify something as a phrase (often in grammar, writing, or when quoting someone). You can add a description or source: “Es una frase de Sonny” (It’s a phrase/quote from Sonny), “Es una frase obvia” (It’s an obvious phrase). For negation: “Eso no es una frase” (That’s not a phrase).
target_language_example: Es una frase muy común en español.
native_language_example: It’s a very common phrase in Spanish.

meaning: “it’s a great…” / “he’s a great…” / “she’s a great…”
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something positively. In Spanish, the adjective "grande" shortens to "gran" before a singular noun (gran chica, gran película, gran manera). You can change "es" to match the subject: "soy" (I’m), "eres" (you are), "es" (he/she/it is), "somos" (we are), "son" (they are).
target_language_example: Es una gran idea.
native_language_example: It’s a great idea.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a very good chance/possibility (often for work, study, travel, etc.). You can add “para + [person/thing]” to specify who it’s for: “Es una gran oportunidad para mí/ti.” Also commonly followed by “para + infinitive” to say what it’s an opportunity to do: “Es una gran oportunidad para aprender/mejorar.”
target_language_example: Es una gran oportunidad para aprender español.
native_language_example: It’s a great opportunity to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to describe what something is: a story, tale, or narrative. Very often followed by “de …” (es una historia de amor = it’s a love story) or by a relative clause (es una historia que… = it’s a story that…). In more formal/academic contexts, “una historia de…” can mean “a history of…” (e.g., human history is a history of ideas).
target_language_example: Es una historia de amor muy bonita.
native_language_example: It’s a very beautiful love story.

additional_notes: Used to say something is an idea (a thought, concept, or suggestion). Often followed by an adjective (Es una idea interesante) or by a clause with que (Es una idea equivocada que...). It can also be used casually to acknowledge a suggestion (Es una idea, claro), similar to “That’s an idea.”
target_language_example: Podemos ir en tren; es una idea buena y barata.
native_language_example: We can go by train; it’s a good, cheap idea.

meaning: "it’s an illusion" (something that seems real but isn’t).
additional_notes: Used to say that a belief, feeling, or appearance is misleading or not real. Often used in philosophical or dramatic statements (e.g., “La seguridad es una ilusión”). You can also use “Todo es una ilusión” = “It’s all an illusion.”
target_language_example: Pensé que tenía el control, pero es una ilusión.
native_language_example: I thought I had control, but it’s an illusion.

additional_notes: Used to classify or describe what something is (often a language): “X es una lengua + adjective” (difficult, beautiful), or “X es una lengua + type” (bereber, construida). You can also use it figuratively, as in “La música es una lengua común…”. Note: “lengua” can mean both “language” and the physical “tongue”; in these examples it means “language”.
target_language_example: El español es una lengua muy hablada en muchos países.
native_language_example: Spanish is a language that is widely spoken in many countries.

additional_notes: Used to classify a language: "[Language] es una lengua eslava". You can add a subgroup after it, e.g. "es una lengua eslava occidental/oriental" (“a West/East Slavic language”). "Lengua" and "idioma" are often interchangeable here.
target_language_example: El polaco es una lengua eslava occidental.
native_language_example: Polish is a West Slavic language.

additional_notes: Used to say something is wild, unbelievable, chaotic, or unreasonable. Can describe a situation (¡Adentro es una locura! = It’s crazy in there!) or an activity (Es una locura leer esa revista = It’s crazy to read that magazine). Often said with emphasis; can be negative (too much, dangerous) or playful/exaggerated.
target_language_example: Ir sin dormir al trabajo es una locura.
native_language_example: Going to work without sleeping is crazy.

additional_notes: Used to express regret or disappointment about a situation. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive because it comments on a fact rather than stating it neutrally (e.g., “Es una lástima que no puedas venir”). You can also say “Qué lástima que…”.
target_language_example: Es una lástima que no puedas quedarte más tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s a shame you can’t stay longer.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to say something is bad: es una mala broma (a bad joke), es una mala costumbre (a bad habit), es una mala traducción (a bad translation), es una mala influencia (a bad influence). For masculine nouns, use: es un mal + noun (e.g., es un mal ejemplo).
target_language_example: Mentir es una mala idea.
native_language_example: Lying is a bad idea.

meaning: "it’s a damn/ freaking ..." (strong, rude emphasis before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to intensify a negative opinion or frustration: *Es una maldita redada / película / lástima / tortura.* The adjective *maldita* agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., *una maldita idea*). With a masculine noun, you’d say *es un maldito ...* (e.g., *un maldito problema*). It’s vulgar/insulting in many contexts; use with caution.
target_language_example: Es una maldita pérdida de tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s a damn waste of time.

additional_notes: Used to explain how something is done or understood, or to soften/rephrase what you’re saying (like “it’s a way of saying it/looking at it”). Common patterns: “Es una manera de decirlo” (a way to put it), “Es una manera de verlo” (a way to see it). Often followed by an infinitive (decir, hacerlo, verlo, etc.).
target_language_example: Es una manera de explicarlo sin entrar en detalles.
native_language_example: It’s a way to explain it without going into details.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement is false. You can add an adjective for nuance: “una mentira blanca” = “a white lie” (a small lie meant to avoid hurting someone). Word order is flexible in speech: “Es una mentira” / “Eso es una mentira” / “¡Es mentira!”
target_language_example: No le creas: es una mentira.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him: it’s a lie.

meaning: "is a mixture of" / "is a mix of".
additional_notes: Used to describe what something is made up of or composed of. It’s often followed by a plural noun (es una mezcla de gases) or by two things joined with y (es una mezcla de verdad y error). You can add qualifiers like varios/muchos/diferentes: es una mezcla de varios gases.
target_language_example: Este té es una mezcla de hierbas y especias.
native_language_example: This tea is a mix of herbs and spices.

additional_notes: Strong, vulgar way to say something is very bad, disappointing, or terrible. Often used with a specific subject: “X es una mierda” (“X sucks”). You can intensify it: “es una mierda enorme” (“it’s huge crap / it really sucks”). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Este trabajo es una mierda, pero tengo que terminarlo.
native_language_example: This job sucks, but I have to finish it.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es = “is”) to identify someone’s gender/identity. Often followed by an adjective: “Es una mujer guapa” (“She’s a pretty woman”). You can add “Sí, por supuesto” to strongly confirm something: “Sí, por supuesto que es una mujer.”
target_language_example: Es una mujer muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very smart woman.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es) to describe a woman’s general/lasting qualities. You normally add an adjective after muy (e.g., rica, atractiva, elegante, obstinada, ocupada, talentosa). For temporary states, Spanish often uses estar instead (e.g., Está muy ocupada = She is very busy).
target_language_example: Ana es una mujer muy inteligente.
native_language_example: Ana is a very intelligent woman.

additional_notes: Used to praise or evaluate something/someone with a feminine noun: Es una muy buena idea/elección/persona/pregunta. For masculine nouns, use: Es un muy buen … (Es un muy buen libro). With professions/nationalities you usually drop “una”: Es muy buena tenista.
target_language_example: Es una muy buena idea.
native_language_example: It’s a very good idea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es) to identify someone as a girl/young female (niña). Often followed by an adjective (e.g., es una niña encantadora). Negative form: no es una niña. Can also be used as an announcement like “¡Es una niña!” (It’s a girl!).
target_language_example: Es una niña muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very smart girl.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as artistically impressive or beautifully made. It can be literal (a real artwork) or figurative for things like a garden, a conversation, a performance, etc. You can change the subject (e.g., “Tu pastel es una obra de arte”).
target_language_example: Tu dibujo es una obra de arte.
native_language_example: Your drawing is a work of art.

meaning: “It’s an order.” (a command that must be obeyed).
additional_notes: Used to give a firm command, often from someone with authority (a boss, officer, etc.). You can say it strongly as “¡Es una orden!” In legal contexts, “una orden” can also mean an official order/warrant (e.g., “una orden de la corte” = “a court order”).
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta ahora mismo: es una orden.
native_language_example: Close the door right now: it’s an order.

meaning: “is a person” (used to describe what someone is like).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or description to talk about someone’s character or qualities: “X es una persona + adjective” (agradable, complicada, decente, honesta, inteligente). In polite/formal contexts, you may see “usted es una persona…”. Often interchangeable with “X es + adjective” (e.g., “Tom es honesto”), but “es una persona…” can feel a bit more descriptive/reflective about the person overall.
target_language_example: Mi jefe es una persona muy justa.
native_language_example: My boss is a very fair person.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s personality or qualities. It’s followed by an adjective (independiente, gentil, ocupada, sabia, sensible, trabajadora, simpática). The adjective agrees in gender and number with persona (feminine singular), so you typically use the feminine form: persona muy ocupada / simpática, even if the person is male. For a group: son personas muy amables.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es una persona muy amable.
native_language_example: My brother is a very kind person.

meaning: “it’s a pigsty” (a very dirty, filthy place).
additional_notes: Used to criticize a place as extremely dirty or messy (a room, a house, a neighborhood, etc.). It’s insulting/derogatory in tone. You can also hear: “Esto parece una pocilga” (“This looks like a pigsty”).
target_language_example: No puedo invitar a nadie: mi departamento es una pocilga.
native_language_example: I can’t invite anyone over: my apartment is a pigsty.

additional_notes: Used to point out that something is a question (often to clarify tone or intent). You can add an adjective after “pregunta” (e.g., “Es una pregunta interesante.”). With “sólo/solo” it can mean “It’s just a question,” to downplay it or say you’re not accusing or insisting.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, sólo es una pregunta.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a question.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity, plan, or place isn’t worth doing because it doesn’t bring results or value. Common pattern: "[Something] es una pérdida de tiempo" (e.g., Estudiar eso es una pérdida de tiempo). You can also hear the plural: "son una pérdida de tiempo" for plural subjects.
target_language_example: Discutir otra vez es una pérdida de tiempo.
native_language_example: Arguing again is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a good moral quality or admirable trait. Often follows an abstract noun (La honestidad es una virtud.) or an infinitive phrase acting as a noun (Aprender de tus errores es una virtud.). You can add emphasis with adjectives: es una gran virtud / es una virtud muy valiosa.
target_language_example: La paciencia es una virtud, especialmente con niños.
native_language_example: Patience is a virtue, especially with kids.

meaning: "is one of" (refers to a female noun; for a male noun: "es uno de").
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to a group: "Es una de mis amigas" = she is one of my friends. Very common before plural nouns with an article/possessive: "una de las...", "una de mis...". Often used with superlatives: "una de las más..." (one of the most...).
target_language_example: Sofía es una de mis profesoras favoritas.
native_language_example: Sofía is one of my favorite teachers.

meaning: “it is one of the” (feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a group: “It’s one of the + [plural noun].” Use **es uno de los** with a masculine plural noun, and **son uno/una de los/las** for plural subjects. Often followed by a superlative or description: **una de las + más + adjective + noun** (e.g., “one of the most beautiful capitals”).
target_language_example: Es una de las mejores razones para aprender español.
native_language_example: It’s one of the best reasons to learn Spanish.

es una de las ciudades más grandes

target_language_multi_word_term: es una de las ciudades más grandes
additional_notes: Used to describe something as belonging to a group of the largest cities. Often followed by a place: del mundo (in the world), de Japón (in Japan). You can swap the noun and adjective to fit other things: es uno de los países más grandes (one of the biggest countries).
target_language_example: Madrid es una de las ciudades más grandes de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is one of the biggest cities in Spain.

es una de las cosas que

target_language_multi_word_term: es una de las cosas que
additional_notes: Used to introduce one item from a list of reasons, characteristics, habits, etc. After "que" you usually add a verb clause describing the thing: "Es una de las cosas que me gustan" (one of the things I like). Often followed by emphasis like "más" (most): "una de las cosas que más me gusta".
target_language_example: Es una de las cosas que más me gustan de este lugar.
native_language_example: It’s one of the things I like most about this place.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (a feminine noun, or something understood from context) is among the top/best in a group. Often followed by a feminine plural noun: “Es una de las mejores cosas…”. You can also leave the noun implied: “Es una de las mejores.” For a masculine noun, use “es uno de los mejores” (e.g., “uno de los mejores restaurantes”).
target_language_example: Esta playa es una de las mejores de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This beach is one of the best in the city.

meaning: “it’s one of my …” (used with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Use this to say something belongs to a group of your favorites/best/etc. The noun after it is typically plural: "Es una de mis canciones favoritas" = one of my favorite songs. Use "Es uno de mis" with masculine nouns ("Es uno de mis amigos"). With plural subjects, use "Son una(s) de mis…" ("Son unas de mis películas favoritas").
target_language_example: Es una de mis comidas favoritas.
native_language_example: It’s one of my favorite foods.

meaning: "is one of" (indicates membership in a group).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to a larger group: es uno de + plural noun (often with an article/possessive). Very common with superlatives: es uno de los más + adjective ("one of the most..."). It agrees in gender/number: es uno de (masc. singular), es una de (fem. singular), son uno(s) de / son una(s) de (plural).
target_language_example: Este lago es uno de los más profundos del país.
native_language_example: This lake is one of the deepest in the country.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone/something as belonging to a group. For people, Spanish often uses the masculine plural pronoun “ellos” for mixed-gender groups; for an all-female group you’d say “es una de ellas.” You can also change the verb: “soy uno de ellos” (I’m one of them), “eres uno de ellos” (you’re one of them), “somos uno de ellos” (we’re one of them).
target_language_example: Se nota que él es uno de ellos.
native_language_example: You can tell that he’s one of them.

meaning: “is one of the” (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a group: “X is one of the + plural noun.” Often followed by a superlative like “más…” (most/more) or “peores/mejores” (worst/best): “es uno de los más hermosos,” “es uno de los peores.” For feminine singular subjects, use “es una de las” before a plural feminine noun.
target_language_example: Madrid es uno de los destinos más visitados de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is one of the most visited destinations in Spain.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to the top group. It often continues with a plural noun: “Es uno de los mejores países/lugares/restaurantes…”. You can make it feminine/plural depending on what you’re describing: “Es una de las mejores (ciudades/opciones)”, “Son unos de los mejores (equipos)”, “Son unas de las mejores (películas)”.
target_language_example: Este restaurante es uno de los mejores de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This restaurant is one of the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to your personal group of favorites or choices. It’s followed by a plural noun phrase: es uno de mis lugares/autores/platos favoritos. For feminine groups, use: es una de mis … (e.g., es una de mis películas favoritas).
target_language_example: Este café es uno de mis sitios favoritos para estudiar.
native_language_example: This café is one of my favorite places to study.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone belongs to your group of friends. It agrees with the person being described: for a female, use “es una de mis amigas.” You can add modifiers after “amigos,” such as “más cercanos” (closest) or “más íntimos” (very close/intimate), or add “también” (also): “También es uno de mis amigos.”
target_language_example: Tom es uno de mis amigos más cercanos.
native_language_example: Tom is one of my closest friends.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true, agree with someone, or insist on a fact (often like “that’s true”). You can also use it to politely correct or emphasize: “No quiero…, pero es verdad” (“I don’t want to…, but it’s true”). Related: “¿Es verdad?” = “Is it true?” and “Es verdad que…” = “It’s true that…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero es verdad: no hay más entradas.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s true: there are no more tickets.

additional_notes: Used to confirm a statement or acknowledge a fact, often introducing a clause with a slight contrast or concession ("It’s true that…, but…"). It can refer to facts, general truths, or information about someone.
target_language_example: Es verdad que no tengo tiempo, pero puedo ayudarte mañana.
native_language_example: It’s true that I don’t have time, but I can help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific shirt that’s not right next to the speaker (often “that one” rather than “this one”). "Esa" agrees with the noun: camisa is feminine singular, so you say "esa camisa" (not *ese camisa*). Often used when choosing between items: "Esa camisa no, la otra."
target_language_example: ¿Dónde compraste esa camisa?
native_language_example: Where did you buy that shirt?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "esa" to point to a particular song that’s known from context (for example, one you just mentioned, heard, or are referring to). "Esa" often implies the song is not right here with the speaker (e.g., over there, or already known), but in many conversations it simply means “that” vs. “this.”
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta esa canción que está sonando?
native_language_example: Do you like that song that's playing?

meaning: that house (over there / not this one).
additional_notes: "Esa" points to something not close to the speaker (often near the listener, or at some distance). It’s used with feminine singular nouns like "casa" (house). Contrast: "esta casa" = this house; "aquella casa" = that house over there (far away).
target_language_example: ¿Quién vive en esa casa?
native_language_example: Who lives in that house?

meaning: "that girl" (a girl you’re pointing out or referring to).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "esa" (feminine singular of "ese") + "chica" (girl). It points to a specific girl (often someone not very close to the speaker, or already identified in the conversation). In Spanish it can also refer back to someone mentioned earlier: "esa chica" = "that (aforementioned) girl."
target_language_example: ¿Quién es esa chica que está hablando con Luis?
native_language_example: Who is that girl who is talking to Luis?

meaning: "that girl" (a specific girl, not close to the speaker).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "esa" with "chica" to point out a particular girl. "Esa" usually refers to someone/something at some distance from the speaker (often near the listener or just not "here"). It can sound neutral or slightly dismissive depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: ¿Quién es esa chica de la foto?
native_language_example: Who is that girl in the photo?

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific kind of person/thing/comment/etc., often with an implied opinion (“that kind of people/comments”). It agrees in gender/number with *clase*: *esa clase de* (feminine singular) is very common as a fixed phrase; also possible: *ese tipo de* (“that type of”).
target_language_example: No me gusta esa clase de películas.
native_language_example: I don’t like that kind of movies.

meaning: “that thing” (used when you don’t know or don’t want to name it).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative “esa” (“that”, feminine) + “cosa” (“thing”). Common for pointing something out or asking what it is: “¿Qué es esa cosa?” You can use it when the object/person isn’t identified yet, or when you’re being vague. For masculine nouns you’d usually say “ese (algo/objeto)” or name the noun (e.g., “ese perro”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes quitar esa cosa de la mesa?
native_language_example: Can you remove that thing from the table?

meaning: "that story" (referring to a specific story/claim already mentioned or understood).
additional_notes: "Esa" is the feminine singular form of "that" (for something not right here, often already mentioned). "Historia" can mean "story" (an anecdote, explanation, or even a made-up excuse) and can also mean "history" depending on context; in these examples it means "story."
target_language_example: No me creo esa historia.
native_language_example: I don’t believe that story.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific way of doing or thinking, usually already mentioned or clear from context. Very common in the pattern "de esa manera" = "in that way". Also used as "esa manera de + infinitive" (e.g., "esa manera de hablar" = "that way of speaking").
target_language_example: No me gusta esa manera de hablar.
native_language_example: I don't like that way of speaking.

meaning: “that shit” (a very vulgar, dismissive way to refer to something).
additional_notes: Used to express anger, contempt, or frustration about a thing, situation, or what someone is talking about. It can refer to a specific object (“Turn that shit off”) or a whole series of events (“All that crazy shit happened…”). Strong profanity—avoid in polite/formal contexts; with friends it can be common but still harsh.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de esa mierda ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that shit right now.

meaning: “that woman” (a specific woman, not here or not the closest one).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective “esa” + “mujer” to point out a particular woman. Often refers to someone previously mentioned or identified in context. Contrast: “esta mujer” = this woman (near/just mentioned), “aquella mujer” = that woman over there / more distant (in space or time).
target_language_example: No conozco a esa mujer, pero parece amable.
native_language_example: I don’t know that woman, but she seems kind.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular night that both people know about or that was mentioned before. It can point to the recent past (“that night I didn’t sleep”) or to a memorable event (“that night when…”). Often appears at the start of a sentence for emphasis: “Esa noche, …”.
target_language_example: Esa noche no pudimos dormir por el ruido.
native_language_example: That night we couldn’t sleep because of the noise.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific word that has been mentioned, is understood from context, or is being singled out (sometimes because it’s important, offensive, or very precise). It agrees with the feminine noun palabra: esa (that) + palabra (word).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se escribe esa palabra?
native_language_example: How do you spell that word?

additional_notes: "Esa" is a demonstrative meaning "that" (usually something not right here, or something you and the other person can identify). It agrees with the feminine noun "película". You can also hear "ese" (masculine) and "eso" (neuter for "that" idea/thing).
target_language_example: ¿Has visto esa película?
native_language_example: Have you seen that movie?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective “esa” (feminine singular) to refer to a specific question that’s already known from context or was mentioned before. Often used with verbs like contestar/responder (“to answer”) and can sound a bit pointed depending on tone (e.g., refusing to answer).
target_language_example: No entiendo esa pregunta; ¿puedes repetirla?
native_language_example: I don’t understand that question; can you repeat it?

meaning: 'that door' (a specific door over there/previously mentioned).
additional_notes: "Esa" is a demonstrative meaning "that" (near the listener or not right next to the speaker). Use it to point out or refer back to a particular door: "Cierra/abre esa puerta". "Puerta" is feminine, so it’s "esa" (not "ese").
target_language_example: ¿Puedes cerrar esa puerta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you close that door, please?

additional_notes: "Esa" is the feminine singular demonstrative meaning "that" (not "this"), used for something not right next to you—often near the listener or a bit farther away. "Tienda" means "store/shop" and is feminine, so it takes "esa" (not "ese"). Used to point out or refer back to a specific store: "Esa tienda está cerrada" = "That store is closed."
target_language_example: No me gusta esa tienda porque es muy cara.
native_language_example: I don’t like that store because it’s very expensive.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative “esa” (“that”, usually not right here/now) + “época” (“era/period”). Common for referring back to a particular period already mentioned or understood from context, often something from the past: “en esa época” = “at that time / in those days.”
target_language_example: En esa época vivíamos en Madrid.
native_language_example: At that time, we lived in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something feminine (esa = 'that' feminine; es = 'is'). Often followed by a noun: "Esa es la verdad". For masculine, use "ese es"; for plural, "esas son" / "esos son".
target_language_example: Esa es mi mochila.
native_language_example: That is my backpack.

meaning: “that is the” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to point out, identify, or emphasize something: “That is the + [feminine noun].” It agrees with a feminine singular noun (la noticia, la excepción, la belleza). For a masculine noun you’d use “ese es el.”
target_language_example: Esa es la razón por la que no fui.
native_language_example: That is the reason why I didn’t go.

additional_notes: Used to highlight the key issue or the main thing everyone wants to know. It can be said on its own (“Esa es la pregunta.”) or followed by more detail (e.g., “Esa es la pregunta correcta / del millón / que hacemos todos”). Often implies uncertainty or that the answer isn’t clear yet.
target_language_example: ¿Va a funcionar el plan? Esa es la pregunta.
native_language_example: Is the plan going to work? That’s the question.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify something that belongs to you. "Esa" = "that" (feminine, singular) and "mi" = "my"; the noun that follows is feminine (e.g., cama, chica, especialidad, oferta, teoría). For a masculine noun, use "ese es mi" (e.g., Ese es mi coche).
target_language_example: Esa es mi mochila.
native_language_example: That is my backpack.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a different issue or to say that something is separate from what you were just talking about. Often followed by a noun or clause: “Esa es otra cosa” (That’s another thing) or “Esa es otra historia” (That’s another story). You may also hear “Eso es otra” when referring to something with eso instead of esa.
target_language_example: Podemos ir mañana, pero hoy no puedo; esa es otra.
native_language_example: We can go tomorrow, but I can’t today; that’s another matter.

additional_notes: Used to point something out (“esa” = “that” for feminine nouns) and identify who it belongs to or relates to (“su”). “Su” can mean his, her, your (formal), or their, so context matters; you can clarify with “de él / de ella / de usted / de ellos(as)”. Often followed by a noun: “Esa es su firma” (That’s his/her signature).
target_language_example: Esa es su casa, no la nuestra.
native_language_example: That is their house, not ours.

additional_notes: Used to point out, identify, or comment on something: “Esa es una teoría / una idea / una pregunta.” It agrees with gender and number: esa (feminine singular) + es (is) + una (a/an, feminine). For masculine nouns, use “ese es un …” (e.g., “Ese es un macho”).
target_language_example: Esa es una buena opción para mañana.
native_language_example: That is a good option for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used as an incomplete sentence where the noun is implied: *Esa es una buena (idea/pregunta/broma)*. With a noun, you’ll usually see: *Esa es una buena noticia/pregunta/señal.* In speech it can sound like you’re praising what someone just said, or reacting as if something is clever or funny.
target_language_example: —¿Y si vamos mañana temprano? —Esa es una buena.
native_language_example: —What if we go early tomorrow? —That’s a good one.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened for the final time (often followed by “que” + a verb: “Esa fue la última vez que la vi” = “That was the last time I saw her”). You can change “esa” to “esta” (this) or “aquella” (that over there/that one long ago), and “fue” to “era” depending on context.
target_language_example: Esa fue la última vez que hablamos.
native_language_example: That was the last time we talked.

esa fue la última vez que

target_language_multi_word_term: esa fue la última vez que
additional_notes: Used to say something happened for the final time in the past. It’s often followed by a verb in the past (e.g., vi, estuve, habló) describing what happened that last time. You can also hear it as "esa fue la última vez que + [verb]" in storytelling or explanations.
target_language_example: Esa fue la última vez que fuimos al cine juntos.
native_language_example: That was the last time we went to the movies together.

additional_notes: Refers to things not near the speaker (physical or abstract). Common when you don’t want to name something directly or when it’s understood from context (habits, actions, events): No hago esas cosas. Can be negative or dismissive (“that stuff”), but can also be neutral (“those things did happen”).
target_language_example: No me gusta hablar de esas cosas.
native_language_example: I don’t like talking about that kind of thing.

meaning: 'those photos' (photos over there or ones already mentioned).
additional_notes: “Esas” is the feminine plural form of “ese/esa” (that), used with feminine plural nouns like “fotos.” It often refers to photos that are not right next to the speaker (closer to the listener, farther away, or just previously mentioned). Contrast: “estas fotos” = these photos; “aquellas fotos” = those photos over there/far away.
target_language_example: No borres esas fotos, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t delete those photos, please.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify multiple feminine things at some distance (or already known in context). "Esas" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., noticias, cosas, órdenes, opciones) or can stand alone as a pronoun. Contrast: "estos son" (masculine), "esas son" (feminine), "esos son" (masculine).
target_language_example: Esas son mis llaves.
native_language_example: Those are my keys.

additional_notes: Used in police/investigation contexts to refer to the place where a crime happened. Often appears with prepositions like en (at/in), hasta (to), or de la (of the): en la escena del crimen, los archivos de la escena del crimen.
target_language_example: La policía acordonó la escena del crimen.
native_language_example: The police cordoned off the crime scene.

additional_notes: Used in instructions on forms, documents, sign-in books, etc. “Escriba” is the formal usted command of “escribir,” and “su” refers to the person being addressed (your, formal). Often followed by where/how: “en esta hoja” (on this sheet), “con lápiz” (in pencil).
target_language_example: Por favor, escriba su nombre aquí.
native_language_example: Please write your name here.

additional_notes: An affirmative tú command (informal singular) using "escribir". Common in instructions on forms, exams, or notes. You can add where/how: "al final" (at the end), "con lápiz" (in pencil), "junto al mío" (next to mine). For a formal command to one person, use "Escriba su nombre".
target_language_example: Por favor, escribe tu nombre aquí.
native_language_example: Please, write your name here.

additional_notes: "Escribiendo" is the gerund (-ing form) of "escribir" (to write). This phrase is commonly used with "estar" to talk about something in progress right now or at a specific time in the past: "está/estaba escribiendo una carta". You may also see it after "estar ocupado/a" to mean "to be busy writing a letter."
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; estoy escribiendo una carta.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m writing a letter.

additional_notes: Literally “to write his/her own name.” Used to talk about a basic skill (often emphasizing that someone can’t do something simple: “ni siquiera puede escribir su propio nombre”). Change the possessive to match the person: escribir mi propio nombre (my), escribir tu propio nombre (your), escribir su propio nombre (his/her/your formal/their).
target_language_example: Ni siquiera sabe escribir su propio nombre.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t even know how to write his/her own name.

additional_notes: A common phrase meaning to create a book (fiction or non-fiction). It’s often used with verbs like querer (to want), comenzar (to start), poder (can/could), or deber (should) + infinitive: “Quiero/comencé/podríamos escribir un libro.” In “Deberías escribir un libro,” it can also be a suggestion or compliment meaning “You have so much to say/so many stories that it could be a book.”
target_language_example: Algún día voy a escribir un libro sobre mis viajes.
native_language_example: Someday I’m going to write a book about my travels.

additional_notes: Used for writing a (usually formal or traditional) letter, typically on paper. You can add who it’s for with "a": "Escribirle una carta a María" = “to write Mary a letter.” In everyday speech, people may also say "mandar/enviar una carta" (to send a letter) once it’s written.
target_language_example: Voy a escribir una carta a mi abuela esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to write a letter to my grandmother tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say what the subject of a book is. The verb is in the simple past (pretérito): escribió = “wrote.” Change the subject as needed: Yo escribí…, Tú escribiste…, Él/Ella escribió…, Nosotros escribimos…, Ellos escribieron…. After sobre you can use a noun (sobre animales), a topic (sobre el tema), or a clause with cómo (“about how…”).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo escribió un libro sobre su infancia.
native_language_example: My grandfather wrote a book about his childhood.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "escribir": "escribió" means "wrote" (completed action). Often used with an indirect object for the recipient: "Le escribió una carta a su amiga" = "She wrote a letter to her friend" (literally, "She wrote her a letter"). You can also use "a + [person]" to make the recipient clear.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo me escribió una carta cuando yo era niño.
native_language_example: My grandpa wrote me a letter when I was a kid.

additional_notes: "Escribí" is the simple past (preterite) of "escribir" for "yo" (I). Use it for a completed action in the past. With an indirect object, you often say "le escribí una carta" = "I wrote him/her a letter" (literally, "to him/her I wrote a letter").
target_language_example: Le escribí una carta para agradecerle su ayuda.
native_language_example: I wrote him/her a letter to thank them for their help.

additional_notes: This is a past participle phrase and is normally used with the auxiliary verb **haber** to form perfect tenses: **he escrito una carta** (I have written a letter), **habrá escrito una carta** (will have / probably has written a letter), **habría escrito una carta** (would have written a letter). You’ll often see an indirect object pronoun before the auxiliary to show who you wrote to: **le he escrito una carta** (I wrote him/her a letter), **te he escrito una carta** (I wrote you a letter).
target_language_example: Ya le he escrito una carta a mi abuela.
native_language_example: I’ve already written my grandmother a letter.

additional_notes: Used to specify the language something is written in ("escrito en francés"), or the medium/surface/location where it appears ("escrito en la pizarra", "escrito en la última página"). It’s the past participle of escribir (“to write”) and commonly appears with estar: "está/estaba escrito en...".
target_language_example: El artículo estaba escrito en francés.
native_language_example: The article was written in French.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (escuchando) to describe an action in progress or happening at the same time as another action. Often appears with estar (están/estaban escuchando la radio) or after another verb to show simultaneous action (Me dormí escuchando la radio = I fell asleep while listening to the radio).
target_language_example: Estoy escuchando la radio mientras cocino.
native_language_example: I'm listening to the radio while I cook.

additional_notes: "Escuchando" is the gerund of "escuchar" (to listen). It’s used to describe an action in progress, often with "estar" ("está/estamos escuchando música" = "is/are listening to music"). It can also be used after another verb to say how/when something happens: "Me levanté el ánimo escuchando música" ("I cheered myself up by listening to music").
target_language_example: Estoy en casa escuchando música.
native_language_example: I'm at home listening to music.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "escuchar" (to listen) + "la radio" (the radio). Common with verbs like "gustar" (Me gusta escuchar la radio), "preferir" (Prefiero escuchar la radio a...), and in the past/habitual (Solía escuchar la radio...).
target_language_example: Cuando cocino, me gusta escuchar la radio.
native_language_example: When I cook, I like to listen to the radio.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the content of what someone says or what happened: escuchar lo que + clause (e.g., “escuchar lo que dijo”, “escuchar lo que pasó”). Typically followed by a verb in a subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Quiero escuchar lo que dice Tom.
native_language_example: I want to hear what Tom says.

additional_notes: A common verb phrase: escuchar = “to listen (to)” and música = “music.” Use it after verbs like gustar (Me gusta escuchar música), ser (Mi hobby es escuchar música), and disfrutar (Disfruto escuchar música). You may also hear the variant “escuchar la música,” meaning “to listen to the music” (a specific music).
target_language_example: Me gusta escuchar música cuando estudio.
native_language_example: I like to listen to music when I study.

additional_notes: Used to express that you want (or are happy) to hear someone speaking—often on the phone, in a voice message, or in person. You can change the possessive: escuchar mi/su/nuestra voz (“to hear my/his/her/your(pl)/our voice”).
target_language_example: Me alegra escuchar tu voz después de tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m glad to hear your voice after so long.

meaning: “I listen to this song” / “I’m listening to this song.”
additional_notes: “Escucho” is the 1st-person singular present tense of “escuchar” (to listen/to hear). It’s often used with a direct object: “escucho + [thing]”. In context, it can mean either actively listening (“I listen to…”) or simply hearing (“I hear…”). “Esta” = “this” (feminine), matching “canción” (song).
target_language_example: Ahora mismo escucho esta canción y me relaja.
native_language_example: Right now I’m listening to this song and it relaxes me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you heard from someone else (a rumor or report). It often implies you’re not stating it as a confirmed fact. Uses the preterite tense of escuchar (escuché = I heard).
target_language_example: Escuché que mañana no hay clases.
native_language_example: I heard that there are no classes tomorrow.

additional_notes: A place (or organization) where people go to learn foreign languages. It’s a straightforward noun phrase: escuela (school) + de (of) + idiomas (languages). Common with verbs like trabajar en (to work at), ir a (to go to), or estudiar en (to study at).
target_language_example: Voy a una escuela de idiomas para aprender francés.
native_language_example: I go to a language school to learn French.

meaning: high school (or middle school, depending on the country).
additional_notes: In many Latin American countries, "escuela secundaria" usually refers to secondary school/high school (roughly ages 12–18), sometimes split into lower and upper levels. In Spain, it often matches "educación secundaria" (ESO), closer to middle school/junior high (roughly ages 12–16). You’ll also hear "secundaria" by itself: "Estoy en secundaria."
target_language_example: Mi hermana está en la escuela secundaria este año.
native_language_example: My sister is in high school this year.

additional_notes: Very offensive and vulgar in most contexts. Used to insult or express anger toward a man (“that jerk/bastard”), and sometimes (depending on region and relationship) jokingly among friends—but it’s risky and can start a fight. Often refers to someone specific already known in the conversation. In some places it can also mean someone tough or crafty, but as a beginner it’s safest to treat it as an insult and avoid using it.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con ese cabrón.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to that asshole.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "ese" (“that”) to refer to a specific case or situation already known from context (e.g., a legal/police case, a file, a particular example, or a scenario being discussed). Often appears with verbs like "abrir" (open a case), "cerrar" (close a case), or "investigar" (investigate a case).
target_language_example: En ese caso, no podemos hacer nada.
native_language_example: In that case, we can’t do anything.

meaning: "that boy" / "that guy" (a male person you’re pointing out or referring to).
additional_notes: "Ese" is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective meaning “that” (near the listener or previously mentioned). It agrees with "chico" (male singular). Often used to identify someone specific: "Ese chico que..." = “That boy/guy who...”. In some contexts "chico" can mean “guy” (not necessarily a child), depending on age and tone.
target_language_example: ¿Quién es ese chico que está en la puerta?
native_language_example: Who is that guy at the door?

meaning: "that day" (a specific day, usually already mentioned or understood).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "ese" to point to a particular day that isn’t today—often one already referred to in the conversation/story. It can refer to a day in the past or future ("that day"), and it often contrasts with "este día" (this day) or "aquel día" (that day over there / more distant in time).
target_language_example: No voy a olvidar ese día nunca.
native_language_example: I’m never going to forget that day.

additional_notes: "Ese" points to something not right next to the speaker (often closer to the listener) or something both people can identify. It agrees with the noun: ese edificio (masculine singular). Contrast: "este edificio" = this building (near me), "aquel edificio" = that building over there (far away).
target_language_example: ¿Ves ese edificio de la esquina?
native_language_example: Do you see that building on the corner?

meaning: "that time" / "back then" (a specific point or period in the past or future).
additional_notes:
Used to refer to a particular moment or period already known from context. Very common with prepositions: 
- "hasta ese entonces" = "until that time"
- "para ese entonces" = "by then" / "for that time"
- "de ese entonces" = "from back then" / "from that period". 
Similar to "en ese entonces" ("at that time").
target_language_example: Para ese entonces, ya habré terminado el trabajo.
native_language_example: By then, I’ll have finished the work.

meaning: “that son of a bitch” (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Very offensive, vulgar, and aggressive. Used to insult or show intense anger/contempt toward a man (or someone referred to as “he”); it can also be said about a person regardless of gender, but it’s still gendered/derogatory. Often said alone as an exclamation (“¡Ese hijo de puta!”). “Ese” = “that” (masculine), pointing to a specific person.
target_language_example: ¡Ese hijo de puta me robó la cartera!
native_language_example: That son of a bitch stole my wallet!

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify a particular man the speaker has in mind (often someone visible, already mentioned, or known from context). "Ese" is the masculine singular demonstrative (“that”), used with a noun: ese + hombre. It can sound neutral or carry emphasis depending on tone (e.g., admiration, suspicion, annoyance).
target_language_example: No confío en ese hombre.
native_language_example: I don’t trust that man.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a specific man who’s at some distance, not the speaker (“that man”). It’s often followed by a name (Ese hombre es Raúl.), an adjective (Ese hombre es fuerte.), or a noun phrase (Ese hombre es escocés.). In Spanish you usually keep the subject pronoun out (you don’t say “él” here).
target_language_example: Ese hombre es mi profesor de español.
native_language_example: That man is my Spanish teacher.

meaning: 'that book' (a specific book, not here/near you).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "ese" before a noun to point out a specific thing, usually closer to the listener or not very near either person (contrast: "este libro" = this book; "aquel libro" = that book over there/far away). It agrees in gender/number: "ese libro" (masc. sing.), "esa casa", "esos libros", "esas casas".
target_language_example: ¿Puedes prestarme ese libro cuando termines?
native_language_example: Can you lend me that book when you’re done?

meaning: “that place” (a specific place not here, often already known or mentioned).
additional_notes: “Ese” is the masculine singular demonstrative meaning “that” (usually not close to the speaker). Use it with a masculine noun: ese lugar. It often refers to a place that both people know about or that was mentioned before. With “ir a ese lugar,” it can also mean “go to that place” (sometimes implying a particular institution or destination in context).
target_language_example: No quiero volver a ese lugar.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go back to that place.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "ese" (“that”) + "momento" (“moment”) to point to a specific time, usually one already mentioned or understood from context. Often appears after prepositions like "hasta ese momento" (“until that moment”) or "en ese momento" (“at that moment”).
target_language_example: En ese momento, no sabía qué decir.
native_language_example: At that moment, I didn’t know what to say.

meaning: that boy (near you or previously mentioned).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "ese" to point out or refer back to a specific boy: something/someone near the listener, or already known in the conversation. Feminine: "esa niña"; plural: "esos niños" / "esas niñas".
target_language_example: ¿Quién es ese niño que está en la puerta?
native_language_example: Who is that boy who is at the door?

meaning: "that name" (the name you mentioned / that specific name).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "ese" to point to a specific name that’s known from context or has been mentioned before. Common when correcting someone (“Me llamaste por ese nombre”), identifying someone (“No hay nadie con ese nombre aquí”), or referring to a surname/name someone keeps (“se quede con ese nombre”). You can also hear "por ese nombre" = "by that name."
target_language_example: No me gusta ese nombre; prefiero otro.
native_language_example: I don’t like that name; I prefer another one.

meaning: “that dog” (near you or already known in context).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective **ese** + noun: **ese perro** = “that dog.” It often points to a specific dog the speaker and listener can identify (e.g., the dog you’re talking about or the one you both see). Feminine version: **esa perra**. Plural: **esos perros / esas perras**.
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con ese perro.
native_language_example: Be careful with that dog.

meaning: “that problem” (a specific problem, not this one).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective **ese** (“that”) with **problema**. **Ese** usually points to something not close to the speaker (often something already mentioned or known in the conversation). Note: **problema** is masculine: **ese problema**, **el problema**.
target_language_example: No entiendo ese problema; ¿me lo explicas?
native_language_example: I don’t understand that problem; can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: (1) With things/ideas/events, it means “that kind/type (of thing)” (often used like “something like that”): "algo de ese tipo". (2) Referring to a person (usually a man), it means “that guy” and can sound a bit informal or dismissive depending on tone. The feminine form is "esa tipa" (often more negative/colloquial); more neutral: "esa persona" / "ese hombre".
target_language_example: No me gusta ese tipo; siempre está criticando a los demás.
native_language_example: I don’t like that guy; he’s always criticizing other people.

additional_notes: Used to classify or describe something/someone as belonging to a category: ese tipo de cosa (that kind of thing), ese tipo de juegos (those kinds of games). It agrees in gender/number with the word tipo: ese tipo de (singular), esos tipos de (plural). You can also use este tipo de (this kind of) and aquel tipo de (that kind over there).
target_language_example: No me gusta ese tipo de música.
native_language_example: I don't like that kind of music.

meaning: “that kind of thing / those sorts of things.”
additional_notes: Used to refer vaguely to things like the ones being talked about, often to avoid listing details (similar to “and stuff like that”). It can sound slightly dismissive depending on tone/context. Singular: “ese tipo de cosa.”
target_language_example: No me interesan ese tipo de cosas.
native_language_example: I’m not interested in that kind of thing.

meaning: “that job” / “that work” (referring to a specific one).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular job/task already known from context (or being discussed). Often contrasts with otro trabajo (“another job”). In Spanish, ese/esa is “that” (near you or previously mentioned), while aquel/aquella is “that over there.”
target_language_example: No puedo aceptar ese trabajo ahora.
native_language_example: I can’t accept that job right now.

meaning: 'that dress' (near you / the one we’re talking about).
additional_notes: "Ese" points to something not right next to the speaker (often near the listener) or something already known in the conversation. It agrees with the noun: "ese" (masculine singular) + "vestido" (dress). Contrast: "este vestido" = this dress (near me), "aquel vestido" = that dress over there (far away).
target_language_example: ¿Cuánto cuesta ese vestido?
native_language_example: How much does that dress cost?

meaning: "that was the" (referring to a specific masculine thing/person).
additional_notes: Used to point back to something already mentioned or understood from context. "Ese" = "that" (masculine singular), and "era" is the imperfect of "ser" meaning "was" (often used for descriptions/identifying what something was). For feminine nouns, you’d say "esa era la".
target_language_example: Ese era el problema; ahora lo entiendo.
native_language_example: That was the problem; now I understand it.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something: “Ese es + noun” = “That is the …”. It agrees with masculine singular nouns (ese). For feminine use “esa es”, for plural “esos son / esas son”. Often used when you’re clarifying or confirming what/who something is.
target_language_example: Ese es el problema.
native_language_example: That is the problem.

additional_notes: Used to identify something masculine-singular (el + noun): Ese es el desafío / punto / motivo. For feminine nouns, use: Esa es la... Also common for emphasis: Precisamente ese es el motivo...
target_language_example: Ese es el problema que tenemos ahora.
native_language_example: That is the problem we have right now.

meaning: “That is my …” (introducing your masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify something as yours: “Ese” = “that” (masculine singular), “es” = “is,” “mi” = “my.” It’s typically followed by a noun: “Ese es mi número.” For feminine nouns, use “Esa es mi …” (e.g., “Esa es mi casa”).
target_language_example: Ese es mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: That is my passport.

meaning: “that is his/her/your …” (pointing out something that belongs to someone).
additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize something as belonging to someone: **Ese** = “that” (masculine singular), **es** = “is”, **su** = “his/her/your (formal)/their”. **Su** is ambiguous in Spanish, so context tells you whose it is. Often followed by a noun: *Ese es su problema / secreto / pan*.
target_language_example: Señor, ese es su asiento.
native_language_example: Sir, that is your seat.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something masculine singular that’s not close to the speaker (“ese”). It matches a masculine noun/adjective phrase: Ese es un bote / un escritor. For feminine, use “esa es una …”. In speech it can also introduce a comment about a situation: “Y ese es un tema delicado…”.
target_language_example: Ese es un problema serio.
native_language_example: That is a serious problem.

additional_notes: Used to say something is good, usually followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., plan, vino, punto). It’s the masculine form: **un buen** (short for *un bueno*) comes before the noun. For feminine nouns, you use **esa es una buena …** (e.g., *Esa es una buena idea*). In speech, it’s often contracted as **Ese es** → **Ese’s** not written, but you’ll commonly hear **Ese es un buen…** as **Es un buen…** when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Ese es un buen restaurante; vamos allí.
native_language_example: That’s a good restaurant; let’s go there.

additional_notes: Used to add emphasis or to specify identity: it means it’s exactly that person/thing/time you’re talking about. It agrees in gender/number: "esa misma" (f.), "esos mismos" (m. pl.), "esas mismas" (f. pl.). Common with nouns: "ese mismo día" = "that very/same day"; can also stand alone as a pronoun: "Ese mismo" = "That very one."
target_language_example: ¿Ves ese coche? Ese mismo es el que quiero comprar.
native_language_example: Do you see that car? That very one is the one I want to buy.

meaning: 'that is not' (for a masculine singular thing/person).
additional_notes: Used to deny or correct an identification: you’re saying something/someone isn’t the one being talked about. "Ese" is a masculine singular demonstrative (“that one/that”), and "es" is the verb "ser" (to be) in the present tense. For feminine, use "esa no es"; for plural, "esos no son / esas no son".
target_language_example: Lo siento, ese no es mi nombre.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s not my name.

meaning: the weakest link (the most vulnerable part).
additional_notes: Used both literally (a chain link that breaks first) and figuratively (the person/step/part in a team or process most likely to fail). Often appears in the saying: “Una cadena no es más fuerte que su eslabón más débil.”
target_language_example: En este proyecto, la comunicación es el eslabón más débil.
native_language_example: In this project, communication is the weakest link.

meaning: "..., right?" / "..., isn't it?" (asking for confirmation about that).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a statement to check that the other person agrees or to invite them to confirm. It’s very common in casual conversation. Similar to adding “right?” or “isn’t that so?” in English; you can also hear just “¿no?” without “eso”.
target_language_example: Te gusta la música, eso, ¿no?
native_language_example: You like the music, right?

meaning: Nonstandard/unnatural as written. In correct Spanish you would normally say **«Eso creo.»** (“I think so.” / “That’s what I believe.”).
additional_notes: **«eso creer»** is not an idiomatic multi-word term in Spanish; it reads like an error or a literal word-for-word mapping from English. If you mean “I think so,” use **«Eso creo.»** or **«Eso es lo que creo.»**. The sequence **«eso creer»** could only appear in contrived contexts (e.g., quoting someone’s mistake, a headline fragment, or a grammar exercise).
target_language_example: El estudiante escribió en su redacción: «eso creer», pero la forma correcta es «eso creo».
native_language_example: The student wrote in his essay: “eso creer,” but the correct form is “eso creo.”

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an idea or expectation in the past ("eso" = that; "era" = was; "lo que" = what/that which). Common after verbs like creer/pensar/decir to clarify what someone wanted, thought, or meant: "Creí/Pensé que eso era lo que...".
target_language_example: Eso era lo que necesitábamos para terminar el trabajo.
native_language_example: That was what we needed to finish the job.

meaning: "That is" / "that's" (pointing something out, explaining, or confirming).
additional_notes: Often used to identify or describe something ("Eso es fácil" = "That is easy"), to comment on what someone said ("Eso es fácil de decir" = "That's easy to say"), or to confirm/encourage someone in the moment ("Eso es" = "That's it / Exactly"). The standalone "Eso es" can mean "That's it" or "That's right."
target_language_example: Eso es lo que quería decir.
native_language_example: That's what I meant.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific fact or characteristic about what was just mentioned. Often followed by a verb clause: "Eso es algo que + (verb...)". Common in comparisons or pointing out shared traits: "Eso es algo que tenemos en común" (that's something we have in common).
target_language_example: Eso es algo que me gusta de ti.
native_language_example: That's something I like about you.

additional_notes: Used to react positively to a situation or piece of information. It can reassure someone ("That's good") or reframe something as a positive ("...but that's good"). Often said with a confirming tone, sometimes followed by a tag like "¿cierto?" (right?).
target_language_example: ¿Ya encontraste trabajo? Eso es bueno.
native_language_example: Did you already find a job? That's good.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that specifies precisely what someone said, did, needed, wants, etc. It’s a strong, emphatic way to confirm or point out an exact match. Often followed by a verb phrase: “Eso es exactamente lo que + (verb)” (e.g., dijiste, necesito, queremos).
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que estaba pensando.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I was thinking.

meaning: 'that's exactly what…' (to emphasize a perfect match with what someone said/thought/needs).
additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or to point out that something matches precisely what you mean/expected/needed. It’s often followed by a verb phrase: "Eso es justo lo que + (verb)" (e.g., "eso es justo lo que necesitamos"). In speech, you can also hear "Eso es exactamente lo que…" with the same idea.
target_language_example: Eso es justo lo que quería escuchar.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I wanted to hear.

meaning: 'that is the…' (starting the phrase “That is what…/That’s the…”).
additional_notes: Used before a clause with **que**: **Eso es lo que + verb** = “That’s what + verb.” It points back to something already mentioned or understood. Common patterns: **Eso es lo que hago/dije/necesito/sé**. Note: by itself, **eso es lo** is incomplete—you normally need **que** after it.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que estaba buscando.
native_language_example: That’s what I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used to point back to something just mentioned or understood from context, and then introduce a clause with lo que + verb: “That is what I think/hope/love.” Often translated as “That’s what…” in natural English. lo que means “what/that which,” referring to an idea or action (not a specific person).
target_language_example: Eso es lo que necesito ahora.
native_language_example: That’s what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to explain or justify someone’s typical behavior: “That’s what X do.” The verb changes with the subject (e.g., “eso es lo que hago” = that’s what I do; “eso es lo que hacemos” = that’s what we do). Often followed by who you mean: “Eso es lo que hacen los niños” (That’s what kids do).
target_language_example: No te sorprendas: eso es lo que hacen los adolescentes.
native_language_example: Don’t be surprised: that’s what teenagers do.

eso es lo que me gusta

target_language_multi_word_term: eso es lo que me gusta
meaning: "That's what I like" / "That's what I like about (it/someone)."
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific thing you like. Very common pattern: "Eso es lo que me gusta de + persona/cosa" (That’s what I like about + person/thing). You can also use it before an infinitive: "Eso es lo que me gusta escuchar/oír" (That’s what I like to hear). Often said to show approval: "¡Eso es lo que me gusta!" = “That’s what I’m talking about!”
target_language_example: ¡Eso es lo que me gusta de este lugar: la tranquilidad!
native_language_example: That’s what I like about this place: the peace and quiet!

additional_notes: Used to explain a result or consequence: “That’s what happens (when/with…)”. Often followed by **cuando** (“when”) or **con** (“with/about”), as in *Eso es lo que pasa cuando...* / *Eso es lo que pasa con...*. Can sound matter-of-fact or mildly critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: No estudió para el examen; eso es lo que pasa cuando dejas todo para el último momento.
native_language_example: He didn’t study for the exam; that’s what happens when you leave everything until the last minute.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you (yo) say/think/would do, usually followed by a verb: “Eso es lo que yo digo/pienso/haría…”. The “yo” is optional in Spanish (often just “Eso es lo que digo”), but including it adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., “that’s what *I* would do”).
target_language_example: Eso es lo que yo pienso.
native_language_example: That’s what I think.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that one thing is the only important/relevant/remaining thing. It’s often followed by a verb like cuenta (counts), importa (matters), necesito saber (I need to know), nos queda (we have left), quiero (I want), or sé (I know). In speech it can also appear as “es lo único que…”.
target_language_example: Para mí, eso es lo único que importa ahora.
native_language_example: For me, that’s the only thing that matters now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains or specifies something: “That’s what I’m saying/looking for/wanting.” Often followed by a verb phrase (e.g., “eso es lo que quiero”). In speech, you may also hear the shortened form “es lo que…”.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que necesito ahora mismo.
native_language_example: That’s what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone (or a text) claims or states. Often implies “according to that person/source,” and can be neutral or slightly skeptical depending on tone/context. You can swap in the source: “Eso es lo que dice mi abogado / el contrato / ella.”
target_language_example: No sé si es verdad, pero eso es lo que dice el informe.
native_language_example: I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s what the report says.

meaning: "That's what I..." / "That's what ... to me" (used before a verb).
additional_notes: A very common sentence frame: **Eso es lo que me + verb**. It points back to something already mentioned and then adds your reaction/thought/and feelings. Often followed by verbs like **preocupa** (worries me), **preguntaba** (I was wondering), **imaginaba** (I imagined), **gustaría** (I’d like). You can also add an object after the verb: *Eso es lo que me dijiste* (“That’s what you told me”).
target_language_example: Eso es lo que me preocupa ahora.
native_language_example: That’s what worries me now.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific thing you want (often something already mentioned or understood). Very common as a lead-in to an infinitive: “Eso es lo que quiero + infinitive” (That’s what I want to do/find out/say). Also used to clarify or emphasize your choice/request: “Eso es lo que quiero, por favor.”
target_language_example: No necesito más opciones: eso es lo que quiero.
native_language_example: I don’t need more options: that’s what I want.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a repeated or habitual action and is usually followed by a verb (e.g., dices, hago, le digo). “Eso” = “that,” “es” = “is,” “lo que” = “what/that which,” “siempre” = “always.” You’ll often hear it with pronouns or names after the verb: “Eso es lo que siempre le digo (a mi mamá).”
target_language_example: Eso es lo que siempre digo cuando estoy nervioso.
native_language_example: That’s what I always say when I’m nervous.

meaning: “That’s what … you” / “That’s the thing that … to you.”
additional_notes: Used to point back to something and introduce the information that follows: “That’s what (someone) told/promised/wanted to say to you.” You normally add a verb phrase after it (e.g., contó, prometo, quería decir). Here, **te** is the indirect object pronoun meaning **“to you”**.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que te dije ayer.
native_language_example: That’s what I told you yesterday.

meaning: "that’s what I…" / "that is what I…" (emphasizing what *I* said/did/want).
additional_notes: Used as the start of a sentence: **Eso es lo que yo + verb**. It points back to something (eso = “that”) and emphasizes the speaker (**yo**). Often translated as “That’s what I said/did/want,” “That’s what I would have done,” etc. You’ll also see it without **yo** when emphasis isn’t needed: **Eso es lo que dije**.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que yo necesito ahora.
native_language_example: That’s what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to describe something with an adjective (or an adjective phrase): Eso es muy + adjective (común, típico, poco, tierno, etc.). Often appears as a reaction or comment meaning “That’s very…” or “That’s so…”. For people, it can also mean “That’s very [adjective] in a man/him.”
target_language_example: Eso es muy importante para mí.
native_language_example: That’s very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation for what was just said. Often followed by a full clause: “Eso es porque + [reason]”. In casual speech you may also hear “Es porque…” when the “eso” is understood.
target_language_example: No quiere venir; eso es porque está muy cansado.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to come; that’s because he’s very tired.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly with what follows. It introduces a clause (often with a verb) describing what the thing is/does/was: "Eso es precisamente lo que quiero" = "That’s exactly what I want." Often you can drop "precisamente" for a less emphatic "Eso es lo que..."
target_language_example: Eso es precisamente lo que necesitábamos para terminar el trabajo.
native_language_example: That is exactly what we needed to finish the work.

meaning: “That’s all that …” (everything that; no more than that).
additional_notes: Used to say something is the complete amount or the only thing available/necessary before adding a verb or clause: “Eso es todo lo que + verb.” Often implies limitation or finality (e.g., “that’s all I’ll say / all you’ll need / all we can give you”). In speech it’s also common to hear “Es todo lo que…” without “eso.”
target_language_example: Eso es todo lo que necesito por ahora.
native_language_example: That’s all I need for now.

eso es todo lo que sé

target_language_multi_word_term: eso es todo lo que sé
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have any more information. Often followed by extra details like "por ahora" (for now) or a topic with "sobre..." (about...). You can also add a tag like "¿de acuerdo?" (okay?) to emphasize that the conversation should move on.
target_language_example: Lo siento, eso es todo lo que sé por ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, that's all I know for now.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing needed, said, asked for, etc. It’s often followed by a verb phrase or clause: "Eso es todo lo que + (verb/clause)". In English you can often omit “that”: “That’s all I need.”
target_language_example: Eso es todo lo que necesito por ahora.
native_language_example: That’s all I need for now.

additional_notes: Used to say there is nothing more to add or that the information is complete. Often followed by a relative clause: “Eso es todo lo que sé” (“That’s all I know”). Can also be used alone to end an explanation.
target_language_example: Lo siento, eso es todo lo que puedo decir.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s all I can say.

additional_notes: Used to wrap up a class, meeting, presentation, video, etc. You’ll often hear it with fillers like “bien/muy bien/y” at the beginning. “Eso” = “that,” “es” = “is,” “todo” = “all,” “por hoy” = “for today.”
target_language_example: Bueno, eso es todo por hoy; nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Alright, that’s all for today; see you tomorrow.

meaning: "That’s a/an" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or label something: “Eso” = “that,” “es” = “is,” and “un” = “a/an.” It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., “un coche”). For feminine nouns, use “eso es una …”.
target_language_example: Eso es un problema.
native_language_example: That’s a problem.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something: **Eso es una + [feminine singular noun]**. It’s the feminine version of **eso es un** (masculine). Often you’ll hear it pointing at something or giving an opinion (e.g., *Eso es una porquería* = “That’s garbage”).
target_language_example: Eso es una buena idea.
native_language_example: That is a good idea.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; it’s an ungrammatical form people sometimes produce when they mean **“Eso espero”** = “I hope so.”
additional_notes: **Esperar** means “to wait” or “to hope,” but it must be conjugated in a sentence. To say “I hope so,” Spanish uses **Eso espero** (literally “That, I hope”). The sequence **eso esperar** mixes a demonstrative (**eso**) with an infinitive (**esperar**) and does not work as a normal expression.
target_language_example: En su mensaje escribió: «eso esperar», pero quería decir: «Eso espero».
native_language_example: In his message he wrote “eso esperar,” but he meant “I hope so.”

additional_notes: Used to show agreement or acceptance about what someone said or a situation. It can also mean “that’s good” depending on context and tone. Often said on its own (“Eso está bien.”) or as a reaction like “Ah, eso está bien.” Similar to “Está bien,” but with eso (“that”) referring back to a specific thing just mentioned.
target_language_example: —No puedo ir hoy. —Bueno, eso está bien.
native_language_example: —I can’t go today. —Okay, that’s fine.

meaning: "that was" (referring to something in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the preterite of ser (fue) to talk about a completed past event or situation. "Eso" refers back to something already mentioned ("that/that thing"). Common in phrases like "Eso fue todo" = "That was all."
target_language_example: Eso fue increíble.
native_language_example: That was incredible.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened far in the past, often to dismiss it as no longer relevant. You can change it to match what you’re talking about: “eso” (that), “eso” → “eso”/“eso”, or “eso” → “eso”, and the tense can change (e.g., “eso era hace mucho tiempo” in some contexts).
target_language_example: No te preocupes; eso fue hace mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; that was a long time ago.

meaning: “that’s what (it) was/that’s what …” (referring back to what happened or what someone said).
additional_notes: Used to point back to a specific thing already mentioned or understood (“eso” = that; “fue” = was; “lo que” = what/that which). Very common before a verb like “dije/dijo/pasó”: “Eso fue lo que dije” = “That’s what I said.” You can change tense/person as needed (e.g., “eso es lo que…” = that’s what…, “eso era lo que…” = that was what…).
target_language_example: Eso fue lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: That’s what happened yesterday.

meaning: 'that’s what' (that’s the thing that… / that’s what happened).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned, emphasizing that it was exactly that thing. Very common in storytelling/explanations: “Eso fue lo que pensé/dijeron/hice/le dije…”. It’s essentially “Eso” (that) + “fue” (was) + “lo que” (what/that which). Also appears in other tenses: “Eso es lo que…” (that’s what…), “Eso era lo que…” (that was what…), “Eso será lo que…” (that will be what…).
target_language_example: Eso fue lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: That’s what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to point to the exact thing just mentioned or understood from context. Very common as a standalone agreement/confirmation meaning “Exactly.” or “That’s exactly what I mean/was thinking.”
target_language_example: —¿Quieres decir que debemos ir ahora? —Sí, eso mismo.
native_language_example: —Do you mean we should go now? —Yes, exactly.

meaning: “not that” / “that’s not …” (used to negate or reject something).
