native_language_example: Here you go, this is for you.

meaning: “this is so…” (used to emphasize an adjective).
additional_notes: Use it to strongly describe what something is like, followed by an adjective: “Esto es tan + adjective.” You can also add “que…” to express a result: “Esto es tan hermoso que…” = “This is so beautiful that…”. In speech, “tan” is often strengthened with “tan” + “tan” or “tan, tan”, but the basic pattern is the same.
target_language_example: Esto es tan interesante que no puedo dejar de verlo.
native_language_example: This is so interesting that I can’t stop watching it.

meaning: “This is all that …” / “This is everything that …”
additional_notes: Used to say that the following action/thing is the only one needed or the only one remaining. It’s usually followed by a verb phrase: “esto es todo lo que + (debes/tienes que/puedes) + infinitive” (this is all you have to do), or “esto es todo lo que + verb” (this is all that remains/that we have). Often implies “nothing more than this.”
target_language_example: Esto es todo lo que tienes que hacer: espera aquí.
native_language_example: This is all you have to do: wait here.

meaning: “this is a …” (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something: Esto (this) + es (is) + un (a/an). Use before singular masculine nouns (un negocio, un peligro) and some masculine singular nouns starting with stressed a- also take un (un auténtico logro). For feminine nouns, use “esto es una …”. You can add an adjective after “un”: “Esto es un auténtico logro.”
target_language_example: Esto es un problema serio.
native_language_example: This is a serious problem.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something you’re pointing at or talking about. Because it uses “una,” the next noun is feminine: “Esto es una catástrofe / una caverna / una farsa / una maravilla.” For masculine nouns, use “Esto es un …” (e.g., “Esto es un problema.”).
target_language_example: Esto es una buena idea.
native_language_example: This is a good idea.

additional_notes: Uses **ir a + infinitive** in the imperfect (**iba a pasar**) to talk about something that was expected/inevitable from a past point of view. Often used after verbs like **saber**: *Sabía que...* = “I knew that...”.
target_language_example: No me sorprende; esto iba a pasar.
native_language_example: I’m not surprised; this was going to happen.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (esto = “this”) does not have a certain quality or identity. It’s commonly followed by a noun (“esto no es un accidente” = “this is not an accident”), an adjective (“esto no es importante” = “this is not important”), or a comparison (“esto no es lo mismo” = “this is not the same”).
target_language_example: Esto no es lo que esperaba.
native_language_example: This is not what I expected.

meaning: 'this is not a' (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to deny or correct what something is (or what someone thinks it is). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: Esto no es un combate. For feminine nouns, use “esto no es una” (Esto no es una broma).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: esto no es un examen, es una práctica.
native_language_example: Relax: this isn’t a test; it’s a practice.

meaning: "this is not a..." (used to say something isn’t a particular thing).
additional_notes: Used to deny or correct a classification/label. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (una + noun): “Esto no es una clínica.” With masculine nouns, use “esto no es un ...” (e.g., “Esto no es un problema.”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, esto no es una tienda.
native_language_example: Sorry, this is not a store.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen next (a prediction or near-future result). It’s "esto" (this) + "va" (goes) + "a" + infinitive (arruinar, doler, estar, llevar, ser). Very common in spoken Spanish as an alternative to the simple future.
target_language_example: Esto va a salir bien.
native_language_example: This is going to turn out well.

meaning: "this is going to be" (talking about the future).
additional_notes: Used to make a prediction about what something will be like. It’s the near-future structure: **ir (va) + a + ser**. Often followed by an adjective or noun: *Esto va a ser divertido / un problema.* You can also say **va a ser...** if it’s clear what you mean.
target_language_example: Esto va a ser increíble.
native_language_example: This is going to be incredible.

additional_notes: Used to point out exactly two people or things that are close, visible, or already mentioned. It agrees in gender and number: estos dos (masc./mixed), estas dos (fem.). Often followed by a noun (estos dos computadores), but it can also stand alone (cuida de estos dos = “take care of these two [guys/ones]”). In time expressions it can mean “these last two …”: estos dos últimos días = “these last two days.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llevarte estos dos a casa?
native_language_example: Can you take these two home?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the present period of time in a general way (“lately/nowadays”), not necessarily literally “today and yesterday.” It can also mean “one of these days” when used with "uno de" (Uno de estos días...).
target_language_example: No he dormido bien estos días.
native_language_example: I haven’t slept well these days / lately.

additional_notes: Plural demonstrative phrase used to point to books that are near the speaker or being discussed. Use with masculine plural nouns like "libros" (singular: "este libro" = "this book").
target_language_example: ¿Puedes guardar estos libros en la mochila?
native_language_example: Can you put these books in the backpack?

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a group of books that are near the speaker (estos = “these”). Follow it with an adjective (caros, nuevos, los mejores) or with a possessive (nuestros, tuyos) to say who they belong to. "Son" is the verb "ser" for "they are."
target_language_example: Estos libros son interesantes.
native_language_example: These books are interesting.

meaning: “these guys” / “these people” (often with a slightly informal tone).
additional_notes: Tipo literally means “type,” but in everyday Spanish un tipo / unos tipos can mean “a guy / some guys” (sometimes “some people,” especially when you don’t know them well or don’t want to name them). You can use it neutrally or with a negative/annoyed tone depending on context.
target_language_example: No confíes en estos tipos.
native_language_example: Don’t trust these guys.

additional_notes: Demonstrative phrase: "estos" = "these" (masculine plural) + "zapatos" = "shoes." Used to point out specific shoes near the speaker or in the current context. Often used with possession (me pertenecen), opinions (son cómodos), or complaints (me molestan).
target_language_example: No me gustan estos zapatos; prefiero los otros.
native_language_example: I don't like these shoes; I prefer the other ones.

meaning: “these are” (talking about masculine/mixed plural things or people).
additional_notes: Used to identify or introduce multiple items/people. It matches plural masculine (or mixed-gender) nouns: Estos son mis abuelos. For plural feminine nouns, use “estas son” (less common; often you’ll hear “estas son mis amigas”). For singular, use “este es / esta es”. You can also add “para…” to show who something is for: Estos son para ti.
target_language_example: Estos son los documentos correctos.
native_language_example: These are the correct documents.

additional_notes:
Used to point out or present items: “These are the …”. 
- estos = “these” (masculine plural)
- son = “are”
- los = “the” (masculine plural)
Commonly followed by a plural noun: “Estos son los originales.” For feminine plural, use “Estas son las …”.
target_language_example: Estos son los documentos correctos.
native_language_example: These are the correct documents.

meaning: “these are my …” (introducing things/people you own or are responsible for).
additional_notes: Used when presenting or pointing to multiple masculine (or mixed-gender) items/people that belong to you. Structure: Estos son mis + plural noun (e.g., mis CD, mis lápices, mis chicos). For feminine plural, use “Estas son mis …” (e.g., estas son mis llaves). For singular, use “Este es mi …” / “Esta es mi …”.
target_language_example: Hola, estos son mis amigos.
native_language_example: Hi, these are my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say something is going to happen very soon (in the next moment). It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: “Estoy a punto de salir” = “I’m about to leave.” You can change the subject/tense: “estás a punto de…”, “está a punto de…”, “estábamos a punto de…”.
target_language_example: Estoy a punto de empezar la reunión.
native_language_example: I’m about to start the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something is familiar/normal for you because you do it often or have experienced it a lot. Follow it with an infinitive (estoy acostumbrado a + dormir, ir, vivir) or with a noun (estoy acostumbrado a + las bajas temperaturas). Agree with the speaker: estoy acostumbrado (male) / estoy acostumbrada (female); plural: estamos acostumbrados/as.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: estoy acostumbrado a trabajar bajo presión.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m used to working under pressure.

additional_notes: Used to express appreciation for a person, help, or a thing. It agrees with the speaker: a woman usually says “estoy agradecida por”. You can also commonly use “estar agradecido/a por” in other persons (p. ej., “estamos agradecidos por…”).
target_language_example: Estoy agradecido por tu apoyo durante este año.
native_language_example: I’m grateful for your support this year.

additional_notes: Used with **por + infinitive** (action): *Estoy ansioso por leer* = “I’m looking forward to reading.” It can also be used with **por + noun**: *Estoy ansioso por las vacaciones* = “I’m looking forward to the vacation.” Depending on context, **ansioso** can sometimes mean “anxious/nervous,” but in these examples it’s closer to “excited/eager.”
target_language_example: Estoy ansioso por verte este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m looking forward to seeing you this weekend.

additional_notes: Present progressive: **estar (yo estoy)** + **aprendiendo** (gerund of *aprender*). Used for something you’re learning **right now / these days**. For a more general statement, you can also say **aprendo** (“I learn / I’m learning”). You can add a language after it: *Estoy aprendiendo español.*
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo español, pero todavía cometo muchos errores.
native_language_example: I’m learning Spanish, but I still make a lot of mistakes.

additional_notes: Used to explain why you are here, followed by an infinitive (e.g., ayudar, llevar, informar). It’s a common, neutral phrase; you can change the subject: "estamos aquí para" (we’re here to), "está aquí para" (he/she is here to), "estoy aquí para ayudarte" (I’m here to help you).
target_language_example: Estoy aquí para ayudarte con la tarea.
native_language_example: I'm here to help you with the homework.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel okay or that everything is okay. Very common as a reply to “¿Cómo estás?” (“How are you?”) or when someone asks if you’re okay. Tone depends on context: it can be reassuring (“I’m okay”) or, with repetition/“¿eh?”/a certain tone, it can mean “I’m fine (stop asking).”
target_language_example: No te preocupes, estoy bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m fine.

additional_notes: Present progressive of **buscar** (to look for/search for): **estar + buscando**. Use it for something you’re trying to find right now (an object, a person, or something abstract like the truth). Often followed by **un/una**, **mis/tus**, or **a + person**: *Estoy buscando a Juan.* In questions: *¿Qué estoy buscando?*
target_language_example: Perdón, estoy buscando el baño.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’m looking for the bathroom.

additional_notes: Used when you’re trying to find a specific person or group. It’s the verb phrase "estoy buscando" (I’m looking for) plus the personal "a", which is used before a direct object that is a person (e.g., "a mis amigos", "a Mía"). For things/objects, you usually drop "a": "Estoy buscando mi teléfono."
target_language_example: Perdón, estoy buscando a mi hermana.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’m looking for my sister.

additional_notes: Used to express frustration or that you’ve had enough of something. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (Estoy cansado de esto.) or by an infinitive (Estoy cansado de luchar.). If what follows is a clause with a conjugated verb, use "de que" + subjunctive (Estoy cansado de que pienses...). For a female speaker: "estoy cansada de".
target_language_example: Estoy cansado de esperar; vámonos.
native_language_example: I'm tired of waiting; let's go.

additional_notes: Present progressive of comer (to eat): estar (estoy) + gerund (comiendo) to talk about what you’re doing right now. You can also hear it with a reflexive pronoun for emphasis or “eating it up,” especially with the whole item: Me estoy comiendo una manzana (I’m eating a whole apple / I’m eating up an apple).
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; estoy comiendo.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m eating.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree with someone. It’s often followed by "con" + a person/pronoun: "con usted" (formal you), "con ustedes" (you all), "con vosotros" (you all, Spain), "con él/ella" (with him/her). You can also shorten it to "Estoy de acuerdo" (I agree).
target_language_example: Estoy completamente de acuerdo contigo: es la mejor opción.
native_language_example: I completely agree with you: it’s the best option.

additional_notes: Used to express strong certainty about a belief or opinion. It’s the 1st-person singular present of “estar convencido” + “de que” + a clause (typically in the indicative): “Estoy convencido de que tengo razón.” You can change the person/tense and gender agreement when needed: “Estoy/estás/está convencido(a) de que…”.
target_language_example: Estoy convencido de que tengo razón.
native_language_example: I’m convinced that I’m right.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with an idea or person. Often followed by **con** + noun/pronoun: *Estoy de acuerdo con la propuesta / con ella / con vosotros*. You can also use it without **con** when the context is clear: *En eso estoy de acuerdo.*
target_language_example: Estoy de acuerdo contigo; es una buena idea.
native_language_example: I agree with you; it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with a person or with an idea/statement. Follow it with a person/thing (Estoy de acuerdo con Ana / con esa idea) or with a clause using "lo que" (Estoy de acuerdo con lo que dices). Often matches English directly; you can also hear "Estoy de acuerdo" by itself when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Estoy de acuerdo con tu plan.
native_language_example: I agree with your plan.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with a man (“él” = him). You can add details with "en" + topic: "Estoy de acuerdo con él en eso" (“I agree with him on that”). To change who you agree with, swap the pronoun: "con ella" (her), "contigo" (you), "con usted" (you, formal), "con ellos/ellas" (them). Negative: "No estoy de acuerdo con él" (“I don’t agree with him”).
target_language_example: No estoy de acuerdo con él en esto.
native_language_example: I don’t agree with him about this.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with someone. You can soften it by adding phrases like “hasta cierto punto” (“to a certain extent”) or “en ese sentido” (“in that sense”). You can also swap “contigo” for “con usted” (more formal) or “con ustedes” (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy de acuerdo contigo, pero creo que podríamos intentarlo de otra manera.
native_language_example: I agree with you, but I think we could try it in another way.

additional_notes: From the verb decir (“to say/tell”) in the present progressive (estar + gerund). Use it to emphasize what you’re explaining or insisting on: Es/eso es lo que estoy diciendo (“That’s what I’m saying”), Sabes lo que estoy diciendo (“You know what I’m saying”), Te lo estoy diciendo (“I’m telling you”). Often used to stress a point; can sound a bit insistent depending on tone.
target_language_example: ¡Eso es lo que estoy diciendo!
native_language_example: That’s what I’m saying!

additional_notes: Used to insist that what you’re saying is true, often to defend yourself or reassure someone. You can add an indirect object pronoun to say who you’re telling: “Te/Le/Les estoy diciendo la verdad” = “I’m telling you (informal)/you (formal)/you all the truth.” More emphatic versions include “Te juro…” (I swear…) or “Dios sabe…” (God knows…).
target_language_example: Créeme, estoy diciendo la verdad.
native_language_example: Believe me, I’m telling the truth.

additional_notes: Used to say you are ready and willing to do an action, often implying commitment or readiness to accept the consequences. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (ayudar, hacer, pagar, etc.). For a woman, say “estoy dispuesta a”; for more than one person, “estamos dispuestos/as a”.
target_language_example: Estoy dispuesto a intentarlo otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m willing to try again.

additional_notes: Uses the verb estar (temporary state): estoy = “I am.” Embarazada means “pregnant” (not “embarrassed”—that’s avergonzada). You can add emphasis or uncertainty: Creo que estoy embarazada (“I think I’m pregnant”), Probablemente estoy embarazada (“I’m probably pregnant”). A man would say: Estoy embarazado (rare in everyday use; usually you’d avoid it and say Mi pareja está embarazada “My partner is pregnant”).
target_language_example: No se lo he dicho a nadie todavía, pero estoy embarazada.
native_language_example: I haven’t told anyone yet, but I’m pregnant.

additional_notes: Used to say a change is just beginning to happen to you (a feeling, understanding, doubt, etc.). It’s the present continuous: estar (estoy) + gerund (empezando) + a + infinitive. You can change the subject: “estás empezando a …” (you’re starting to), “está empezando a …” (he/she is starting to).
target_language_example: Estoy empezando a cansarme de esperar.
native_language_example: I’m starting to get tired of waiting.

meaning: "I’m in / I’m at" (location), or "I’m in" (a situation/condition/field).
additional_notes: Used with “estar” to say where you are physically (Estoy en el bar, en un hotel), or what situation/condition/state you’re in (Estoy en la cárcel, en la ducha, en una silla de ruedas, en el máximo). It can also be used to talk about what area you work in or are involved in: Estoy en transporte. With abstract expressions like “estar en lo cierto” it means “to be right.”
target_language_example: Ahora mismo estoy en casa, pero luego estoy en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Right now I’m at home, but later I’m at work.

meaning: "I’m in contact with" (I communicate with / I keep in touch with).
additional_notes: Used with a person, group, or organization to say you are communicating with them (by phone, email, messages, etc.) or you maintain a relationship. You can change the subject and tense: estoy / estás / está / estamos… en contacto con; also commonly "estar en contacto" and "mantenerse en contacto".
target_language_example: Estoy en contacto con mi jefe por WhatsApp.
native_language_example: I’m in contact with my boss on WhatsApp.

meaning: "I’m in/on the …" (followed by a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with "estar" to say where you are or what situation/state you’re in. It must be followed by a noun phrase with feminine singular "la" (e.g., "Estoy en la celda" = I’m in the cell; "Estoy en la guía" = I’m in the guide; "Estoy en la lista negra" = I’m on the blacklist; "Estoy en la ruina" = I’m ruined/broke). For masculine nouns you usually use "estoy en el".
target_language_example: Estoy en la puerta de entrada.
native_language_example: I’m at the front door.

meaning: “I’m in love with you.” (said by a woman)
additional_notes: Used to express romantic love. Enamorada agrees with the speaker’s gender: a man says “estoy enamorado de ti.” You can also use “de ti” (to you) or “de ti” after other forms (e.g., “no estoy enamorada de ti” = “I’m not in love with you”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no estoy enamorada de ti.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I’m not in love with you.

additional_notes: Used to confess romantic love. Literally “I am in love of you,” but in English you say “in love with you.” For a woman speaking: “estoy enamorada de ti.” In the negative: “No estoy enamorado/a de ti” = “I’m not in love with you.” You can also use “estar enamorado/a de + (person)” for “to be in love with (someone).”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero estoy enamorado de ti.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I’m in love with you.

additional_notes: Present progressive of esperar (“to wait for/expect”). Often followed by what you’re waiting for: Estoy esperando una entrega (I’m expecting a delivery). With a direct object pronoun: Lo estoy esperando (I’m waiting for him/it). For people, you can add a to make it clearer: Te estoy esperando (a ti) = I’m waiting for you.
target_language_example: Estoy esperando el autobús.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to express that you feel pleased about something. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "Estoy feliz de verte" (I’m happy to see you). You’ll also often see "Estoy feliz de que…" + subjunctive to talk about a situation/event: "Estoy feliz de que estés aquí" (I’m happy you’re here).
target_language_example: Estoy feliz de ayudarte con la tarea.
native_language_example: I'm happy to help you with the homework.

additional_notes: Present progressive of hablar: estar + hablando. Often followed by **de** to say what you’re talking about (**Estoy hablando de tu hija.** = “I’m talking about your daughter.”). With a person as the listener, use **a** (**Le estoy hablando a mi hermana.** = “I’m talking to my sister.”). You can also use it in emphasis like **De eso es lo que estoy hablando** (“That’s what I’m talking about.”).
target_language_example: Estoy hablando con el profesor ahora.
native_language_example: I’m talking with the teacher now.

additional_notes: Used with the present progressive (estar + hablando) to emphasize that the conversation is happening right now. Follow it with a person (or even a thing, jokingly) you’re addressing: Estoy hablando con Tom / con el señor / con mi hijo. "Hablar con" can mean either "talk to" or "talk with" in English.
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo; estoy hablando con mi mamá.
native_language_example: I can’t right now; I’m talking to my mom.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or clarify the topic you’re discussing. It’s the present progressive of hablar: estoy + hablando + de + noun/idea. You can add emphasis like “Estoy hablando de X, de Y.” (I’m talking about X, about Y.) Often used to correct or focus what you mean.
target_language_example: No estoy hablando de dinero; estoy hablando de tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m not talking about money; I’m talking about time.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (estoy) + gerund (haciendo) to talk about an action in progress at the moment, or around now (temporary/ongoing). Often followed by what you’re doing: "Estoy haciendo un proyecto", "Estoy haciendo la tarea". With an object pronoun it can become: "Lo estoy haciendo" = "I’m doing it."
target_language_example: Ahora mismo estoy haciendo la cena, ¿puedes esperar un momento?
native_language_example: Right now I’m making dinner—can you wait a moment?

meaning: "I’m fed up with" / "I’m sick and tired of."
additional_notes: Used with **estar + harto/a + de** to express strong annoyance or that you’ve had enough of something. **Harta** is feminine (a woman speaking); masculine is **harto**. You can follow it with a **noun** (Estoy harta de tu familia), a **pronoun** (Estoy harta de él), or an **infinitive** (Estoy harta de llorar).
target_language_example: Estoy harta de esperar.
native_language_example: I’m sick and tired of waiting.

additional_notes: Used to express strong annoyance or frustration with something that keeps happening or that you’ve had too much of. It agrees with the speaker: estoy harto (male speaker) / estoy harta (female speaker). You can also use plural: estamos hartos/hartas de (we’re fed up with). Commonly followed by a noun (de este trabajo) or an infinitive (de esperar, de trabajar tanto).
target_language_example: Dile que estoy harto de sus mentiras.
native_language_example: Tell him/her that I'm fed up with his/her lies.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb after para: “Estoy listo para hablar/irme/ayudarte.” You can change the subject/tense: “Estoy/estás/está/estamos listos para…” Also common without para: “Estoy listo.” (“I’m ready.”).
target_language_example: Ya estoy listo para salir.
native_language_example: I’m ready to leave now.

meaning: "I am very…" (used to intensify a feeling or condition).
additional_notes: Used with temporary states/feelings (estar + adjective). The adjective must agree with the speaker: cansado/cansada, contento/contenta, orgulloso/orgullosa, etc. Often followed by an adjective like cansado/a (tired), emocionado/a (excited), hambriento/a (hungry), contento/a (happy), satisfecho/a (satisfied).
target_language_example: Estoy muy nervioso por el examen.
native_language_example: I’m very nervous about the exam.

additional_notes:
Used to express strong gratitude. It often appears with:
- "por" + noun/infinitive: "Estoy muy agradecido por su ayuda" (for your help).
- "de" + infinitive (common, though "por" is often preferred in many contexts): "Estoy muy agradecido de ser su aprendiz".
You can also add an indirect object pronoun to say who you’re grateful to: "Le estoy muy agradecido" (I’m very grateful to you/him/her). If the speaker is female: "Estoy muy agradecida".
target_language_example: Estoy muy agradecido por todo lo que has hecho.
native_language_example: I’m very grateful for everything you’ve done.

meaning: "I’m very happy to / I’m very glad to (about)."
additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness/pleasure about something. Common patterns: (1) "Estoy muy contento de" + infinitive: "Estoy muy contento de estar aquí" (I’m very happy to be here). (2) "Estoy muy contento de que" + subjunctive when a different subject is involved: "Estoy muy contento de que estés aquí" (I’m very happy that you’re here). Change "contento" to match the speaker: "contenta" (female speaker), "contentos/contentas" (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy muy contento de que hayas venido.
native_language_example: I’m very happy that you came.

additional_notes: Used to express your current feeling (temporary state). Common patterns: estoy muy feliz de + infinitive (estoy muy feliz de verte / de estar aquí), estoy muy feliz por + person (happy for you), and estoy muy feliz porque + reason (because…). You can also say it alone as a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Estoy muy feliz porque hoy es mi cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I’m very happy because today is my birthday.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or an infinitive (verb) after en: Estoy muy interesado en la música / en aprender chino. You can change the subject and level of interest: estoy/estás/está... interesado/a; muy/bastante/poco. Match gender and number with the person: interesado (male), interesada (female), interesados/interesadas (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy muy interesado en conocer tu ciudad.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in getting to know your city.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have time for something right now. You can add what you’re too busy for with “para + [thing]” (e.g., “Estoy muy ocupado para eso” = “I’m too busy for that”). You’ll also hear “Estoy muy ocupada” if the speaker is female.
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy estoy muy ocupado.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m very busy today.

additional_notes: Used to express strong pride in a person or a situation. Follow it with a noun/pronoun (de ella, de él, de ustedes) or with "de que" + a clause (de que todos estén aquí). Change "orgulloso" to "orgullosa" if the speaker is female (estoy muy orgullosa de).
target_language_example: Estoy muy orgulloso de ti por tu esfuerzo.
native_language_example: I’m very proud of you for your effort.

additional_notes: Uses the verb estar to describe a temporary state right now. You can add what you’re busy doing with a gerund: “estoy ocupado cocinando” (I’m busy cooking). To say you’re not busy: “no estoy ocupado/a”. If the speaker is female, it’s often “estoy ocupada”.
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; estoy ocupado.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m busy.

additional_notes: Used to express pride in a person, thing, or action. It’s feminine; a man would say “estoy orgulloso de”. Follow it with (1) a noun: “Estoy orgullosa de mi proyecto.” (2) an infinitive: “Estoy orgullosa de ser brasileña.” or (3) “de que” + subjunctive when the next part is a full clause: “Estoy orgullosa de que te hayas enfrentado a él.”
target_language_example: Estoy orgullosa de ti.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you.

additional_notes: Used to express pride in a person, thing, or action. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (Estoy orgulloso de ustedes/ti/él) or an infinitive verb (Estoy orgulloso de ser/trabajar). Agree gender/number: orgulloso (male speaker), orgullosa (female speaker), orgullosos/orgullosas (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy orgulloso de lo que lograste.
native_language_example: I’m proud of what you achieved.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone you feel proud about what they did or who they are. You can change it for gender/number: “estoy orgullosa de ti” (speaker is female); “estamos orgullosos/orgullosas de ti” (we’re proud of you). For more than one person: “estoy orgulloso de ustedes” (I’m proud of you all).
target_language_example: Estoy orgulloso de ti por todo tu esfuerzo.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you for all your effort.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what’s on your mind or something you’re considering doing. It’s the present progressive of pensar: estoy pensando (I’m thinking) + en (about). Common patterns: “estoy pensando en + noun” (thinking about something) and “estoy pensando en + infinitive” (considering doing something), e.g., “estoy pensando en ir / mudarme / comprar…”.
target_language_example: Estoy pensando en cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m thinking about changing jobs.

additional_notes: Used with estar + preocupado/a + por + person/thing. Change "preocupado" to "preocupada" if you’re a woman, and you can change the subject: "estás preocupado/a", "está preocupado/a", "estamos preocupados/as", etc. Note: "preocupado" usually means "worried" in Spanish (it looks like English "preoccupied," which can be misleading).
target_language_example: Estoy preocupado por el examen de mañana.
native_language_example: I'm worried about tomorrow's exam.

additional_notes: Used to express certainty about something. Common patterns: "De eso estoy segura" = “I’m sure about that”; "Estoy segura de que..." (or sometimes "Estoy segura que...") = “I’m sure that...”. Negatives like "No estoy segura" / "Ya no estoy segura" mean “I’m not sure” / “I’m not sure anymore.” For a man, say "estoy seguro."
target_language_example: Estoy segura de que todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: I’m sure everything will turn out fine.

additional_notes: Used to express strong certainty about what follows. The verb agrees with the speaker: a man says “estoy seguro de que.” You can also use it before “sí/no”: “Estoy segura de que sí/no.”
target_language_example: Estoy segura de que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I’m sure it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Expresses certainty about what follows. In more formal or prescriptive Spanish, many speakers prefer “Estoy segura de que…”. “Estoy segura que…” is common in everyday speech in many regions. For a man: “Estoy seguro que / Estoy seguro de que…”. You can omit “yo” because it’s already implied in “estoy”.
target_language_example: Estoy segura que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I’m sure it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express confidence about a fact or situation. Common patterns: **estoy seguro de + noun/pronoun** (Estoy seguro de eso / de ello = “I’m sure about that”), and **estoy seguro de que + clause** (Estoy seguro de que vendrá = “I’m sure that he’ll come”). With a person, **estoy seguro de ti** means “I believe in you / I’m confident in you.”
target_language_example: Estoy seguro de que todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: I’m sure everything will turn out fine.

additional_notes: Used to express certainty or strong confidence. Usually followed by **que + verb**: *Estoy seguro de que vendrá* (“I’m sure he’ll come”). It can also be followed by **infinitive**: *Estoy seguro de tener éxito* (“I’m sure I’ll succeed”). You can change the subject/person: *estás seguro de*, *está seguro de*, *estamos seguros de*, etc. (agree **seguro/segura/seguros/seguras**).
target_language_example: Estoy seguro de que todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: I’m sure everything will work out.

additional_notes: Used to express confidence or certainty about a statement. Follow it with a full clause (subject + verb): “Estoy seguro de que va a ganar.” You may also hear “Estoy segura de que” (speaker is female) or plural “Estamos seguros/as de que.”
target_language_example: Estoy seguro de que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I’m sure it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "I’m sure that he..." / "I’m confident that he..."
additional_notes: Used to express certainty about what a male person (él) will do or what will happen. The pattern is: "Estoy seguro/a de que + [subject] + [verb]". Use "seguro" if the speaker is male, and "segura" if the speaker is female: "Estoy segura de que él llegará". Often you can drop the subject pronoun: "Estoy seguro de que aprobará".
target_language_example: Estoy seguro de que él vendrá mañana.
native_language_example: I’m sure that he’ll come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express strong confidence about a fact or prediction. In more formal Spanish, many speakers prefer **estoy seguro de que…** (with *de*), but **estoy seguro que…** is very common in everyday speech. It can refer to the present/past (*Estoy seguro que lo hace / lo hizo*) or the future (*Estoy seguro que lo hará*).
target_language_example: Estoy seguro que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I'm sure it's going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to emphasize a feeling or state: “Estoy tan cansado / tan feliz.” Often followed by “que” to show a result: “Estoy tan cansado que…” (“I’m so tired that…”). The adjective usually agrees with the speaker (cansado/cansada). “Tan” is used before adjectives/adverbs; don’t confuse it with “tanto/a(s),” which is used with nouns (e.g., “tanto trabajo” = “so much work”).
target_language_example: Estoy tan nervioso que no puedo hablar.
native_language_example: I’m so nervous that I can’t speak.

additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness about something. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., estés, vinieras, volvieras) because it expresses an emotional reaction. In many contexts you’ll also hear the variant "estoy tan feliz de + infinitive" (e.g., "Estoy tan feliz de verte" = "I’m so happy to see you").
target_language_example: Estoy tan feliz de que hayas venido.
native_language_example: I’m so happy that you came.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (estoy) + gerund (trabajando) to describe something happening right now or currently in progress. Often followed by: en + noun/verb idea (Estoy trabajando en algo nuevo = I’m working on something new) or con + people (Estoy trabajando con ellos = I’m working with them). Negation: No estoy trabajando = I’m not working.
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; estoy trabajando en un proyecto.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m working on a project.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to + verb” form) to say you’re making an effort: "Estoy tratando de ayudar". In everyday speech you may also hear "trato de" (I try to).
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de aprender español, pero necesito más práctica.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn Spanish, but I need more practice.

meaning: "I’m a bit / a little" (used before an adjective or state).
additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying or make it sound less strong: Estoy un poco + adjective/state (borracho, sorprendido, resfriado, celoso/a, etc.). You can change the verb for other people: estoy/estás/está/estamos… un poco.
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy estoy un poco cansado.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I’m a bit tired.

additional_notes: Present progressive of **ver**: **estar + gerundio (viendo)** to talk about an action in progress. Common with TV/movies/news (**watching**), but it can also mean **seeing/looking at** something or someone: *Estoy viendo la casa* (I’m looking at the house), *Te estoy viendo* (I see you / I’m watching you). You can add **lo/la**: *Lo estoy viendo ahora* (I’m watching/seeing it now).
target_language_example: Estoy viendo una película ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I’m watching a movie right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you are physically present or available. Often used for reassurance or support: “Estoy aquí si me necesitas” (“I’m here if you need me”). You can add emphasis with “yo”: “Yo estoy aquí.” The opposite idea is “No estoy aquí” (“I’m not here”) or “Imagina que no estoy aquí” (“Imagine I’m not here”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, estoy aquí si me necesitas.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m here if you need me.

meaning: "I'm here to" (to say your purpose/reason for being here).
additional_notes: Used to explain what you came to do. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: "estoy aquí para + infinitive" (e.g., ayudar, trabajar, verte). You can change it by person/tense: "estoy" (I am), "estás" (you are), "está" (he/she is), "estamos" (we are).
target_language_example: Estoy aquí para ayudarte con la tarea.
native_language_example: I'm here to help you with the homework.

meaning: “I’m with …” / “I’m busy with …”; also “I’ll be right with you.”
additional_notes: Used with estar + con + noun/person. It can mean (1) being together with someone: “Estoy con amigos.” (2) being occupied with a task/assignment: “Estoy con (un) encargo.” (3) being affiliated/working with an organization: “Estoy con una organización…”. In customer-service contexts, “Ya estoy con usted/ustedes” means “I’ll be right with you.”
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar: estoy con trabajo, pero luego te llamo.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now: I’m busy with work, but I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (temporary state/location) + en to say where you are physically (en casa, en el mercado, en la India, en el auto) or what situation/event/level you’re currently in (en una cena, en el primer año de instituto). Often translates as “at” for places/events, “in” for countries/rooms/vehicles, and sometimes “on” with transport like en el auto/bus/tren (also common: “in the car”).
target_language_example: Ahora mismo estoy en el trabajo, pero luego estoy en casa.
native_language_example: Right now I’m at work, but later I’m at home.

meaning: "I am in/on the" (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** to talk about your **location** (e.g., *en el décimo piso* = on the 10th floor) or **being part of a group/place** (e.g., *en el escuadrón* = in the squad). **en + el** contracts to **en el** (you don’t say *en el el*). For feminine nouns, use **estoy en la**.
target_language_example: Estoy en el tren ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I'm on the train right now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a famous actor/actress in movies. Often with an article (la/una) or as a profession/goal with ser: "Quiere ser estrella de cine." You can add adjectives like "gran" (great) or "famosa" (famous).
target_language_example: De niño, soñaba con ser una estrella de cine.
native_language_example: As a child, I dreamed of being a movie star.

additional_notes: A common, literal phrase for talking about stars you can (or can’t) see at night. Often used with negatives like "no había" / "no se veía" and emphasis like "ni una sola" (not a single one) or "ninguna" (none).
target_language_example: No había ni una sola estrella en el cielo.
native_language_example: There wasn’t a single star in the sky.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("estudiando") to say someone is in the process of studying French, often with forms like "estar" ("está/estaba/ha estado... estudiando") to emphasize an ongoing activity. It’s also common with "llevar + time + gerund" to mean "to have been doing something for (time)": "Llevo tres años estudiando francés".
target_language_example: Estoy estudiando francés este semestre.
native_language_example: I’m studying French this semester.

meaning: to study law (as a university major).
additional_notes: In Spanish, "Derecho" (capitalized) commonly refers to the academic field/degree in Law. Without capitalization ("derecho"), it often means "right" (a right/entitlement) or "straight/upright" depending on context. You can also say "estudiar leyes" in a more general sense, but "estudiar Derecho" is the standard way to talk about the major.
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a estudiar Derecho en la universidad.
native_language_example: My sister is going to study law at university.

meaning: to study abroad (in a foreign country).
additional_notes: Used to talk about studying in another country, often as part of a university exchange program, scholarship (beca), or time living overseas. You can also say "ir a estudiar al extranjero" (to go study abroad).
target_language_example: El año que viene quiero estudiar en el extranjero.
native_language_example: Next year I want to study abroad.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like decidir (to decide), comenzar (to start), querer (to want), deber (should), and tener que (to have to). You can swap francés for other subjects/languages: estudiar español, estudiar matemáticas. Note: to say “learn French” in general, Spanish often uses aprender francés, but estudiar francés focuses on studying (classes, books, practice).
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar francés esta noche.
native_language_example: I have to study French tonight.

additional_notes: A very literal, compositional phrase: "estudiar" = "to study" and "inglés" = "English." You can conjugate "estudiar" (e.g., "estudio/estudiaba/estudiaré inglés") or use it after another verb (e.g., "empecé a estudiar inglés" = "I started studying English").
target_language_example: Voy a estudiar inglés esta tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to study English this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about learning music in a formal way (classes, school, conservatory) or seriously practicing it. After verbs of movement like "ir" or "irse" + "a" (e.g., "ir a Italia"), it often expresses purpose: going somewhere in order to study music.
target_language_example: Me mudé a Madrid para estudiar música.
native_language_example: I moved to Madrid to study music.

additional_notes: Used to say something nearly happened (but didn’t), or you were on the verge of doing it. It’s the preterite (past) form of "estar a punto de". You can change it for other people/tense: "estuve/estuviste/estuvo... a punto de" + infinitive (e.g., "rendirme", "venir", "ser").
target_language_example: Estuve a punto de llamarte, pero era muy tarde.
native_language_example: I was about to call you, but it was very late.

meaning: "I was thinking about" (earlier / for a while).
additional_notes: "Estuve" is the preterite of "estar" and signals a completed period of time in the past: you were thinking about something for a while (often earlier today or at some point before now). It’s often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause: "en eso", "en ti", "en lo que dijiste". (Contrast: "estaba pensando en" suggests an ongoing background action: "I was thinking about" in progress.)
target_language_example: Ayer estuve pensando en cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was thinking about changing jobs.

additional_notes: “Estuve” is the preterite (simple past) of **estar** for **yo**. Use **estuve en + place** to say you were somewhere for a finished period of time (even if it was weeks): *Estuve en el hospital por unas semanas.* It can also be used more figuratively: *Una vez estuve en tu lugar* (“I was in your place / I’ve been in your shoes”).
target_language_example: Estuve en casa todo el día ayer.
native_language_example: I was at home all day yesterday.

meaning: 'were here' / 'was here' (hypothetical, wished-for, or expected situation).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect subjunctive of **estar** (**estuviera**) + **aquí** (“here”). Common after **si** (“if”) for hypothetical situations: *Si (yo) estuviera aquí…* = “If I were here…”. Also appears after expressions of expectation or desire like **esperar que**, **querer que**, **suponerse que** when talking about something that isn’t true/confirmed at the moment: *Esperaba que Tom estuviera aquí* = “I was hoping Tom would be here.”
target_language_example: Si yo estuviera aquí, te ayudaría.
native_language_example: If I were here, I would help you.

meaning: "(he/she) almost"; "was about to" (something nearly happened, but didn’t).
additional_notes: Used to say something nearly happened. It’s the 3rd-person singular preterite of "estar a punto de" (él/ella/usted). After "de" you typically use an infinitive: "estuvo a punto de + infinitive" (e.g., ahogarse, morir, perder). For other people/tenses: "estuve/estuviste/estuvimos… a punto de"; "estaba/estaban a punto de"; "ha estado a punto de".
target_language_example: Ella estuvo a punto de ahogarse.
native_language_example: She almost drowned.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of **estar** (*estuvo*) to talk about someone being here at a specific moment in the past (often a completed, finished time). Common with time expressions like **hace un momento** (a moment ago) or **la semana pasada** (last week).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor estuvo aquí hace unos minutos.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor was here a few minutes ago.

additional_notes: Pretérito (simple past) of "estar de acuerdo con" for a he/she/you-formal subject (él/ella/usted). Use it to say someone agreed with a person (Ella estuvo de acuerdo con él), an idea/thing (Él no estuvo de acuerdo con eso), or an action/verb (Ella estuvo de acuerdo con pagar...). In negative: "no estuvo de acuerdo con...". For plural subjects use "estuvieron de acuerdo con".
target_language_example: Ella estuvo de acuerdo con mi idea.
native_language_example: She agreed with my idea.

additional_notes: Preterite form of **estar**: **él/ella/usted estuvo** + **en** to say someone was in a place at a specific time in the past. Use **en** for locations like cities/countries (**estuvo en Los Ángeles / en Estados Unidos**) and also for being on TV (**estuvo en la TV**). For background/ongoing past situations, Spanish often uses **estaba en** instead.
target_language_example: Mi hermano estuvo en Madrid la semana pasada.
native_language_example: My brother was in Madrid last week.

additional_notes: Used with estar + a dieta to say someone is following a diet, usually to lose weight or for health reasons: "Ella está a dieta". Can also be used jokingly or figuratively (e.g., "La luna está a dieta").
target_language_example: Mi madre está a dieta, así que hoy no va a comer postre.
native_language_example: My mom is on a diet, so she’s not going to eat dessert today.

está a la vuelta de la esquina

target_language_multi_word_term: está a la vuelta de la esquina
meaning: “It’s just around the corner” (very nearby; sometimes “coming very soon”).
additional_notes: Used for locations to mean something is very close—often the next street/corner. It can also be used figuratively for time/events to mean something is about to happen soon (e.g., “La primavera está a la vuelta de la esquina”). You can change the verb for other subjects/tenses: “estaba / estará / están a la vuelta de la esquina.”
target_language_example: El supermercado está a la vuelta de la esquina, podemos ir caminando.
native_language_example: The supermarket is just around the corner; we can walk there.

additional_notes: Used with a conjugated form of estar + a punto de + infinitive to say something will happen very soon (imminently). The specific form "está a punto de" is third-person singular (he/she/it/you-formal). Other forms include: "estoy/estás/está/estamos/están a punto de".
target_language_example: El tren está a punto de llegar.
native_language_example: The train is about to arrive.

meaning: 'is about to start' / 'is just about to begin'.
additional_notes: Used to say something will start very soon (imminently). It’s the structure: estar + a punto de + infinitive (e.g., Está a punto de empezar/comenzar). Change está to match the subject: estoy/estás/estamos/están a punto de…
target_language_example: La película está a punto de comenzar, así que apaga el celular.
native_language_example: The movie is about to start, so turn off your phone.

meaning: “is about to end / is almost finished.”
additional_notes: Used to say something will finish very soon. It’s the structure “estar a punto de + infinitive” (“to be about to + verb”). Change “está” to match the subject: “estoy/estás/está/estamos/están a punto de terminar.” Often used with events, activities, or processes (a meeting, construction, a presentation, etc.).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero la película está a punto de terminar.
native_language_example: Sorry, but the movie is about to end.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say someone/something is safe or protected. Often appears with “de” to mean “safe from” (Está a salvo de un ataque). It can also mean something (like a secret) is secure with someone: “Tu secreto está a salvo conmigo” = “Your secret is safe with me.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: tu hijo está a salvo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: your son is safe.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., la tienda, la puerta, la ventana). It’s the present tense of estar + abierta (past participle used as an adjective) to describe a state. For masculine: “está abierto”; for plural: “están abiertos/abiertas”.
target_language_example: La puerta está abierta, pasa por favor.
native_language_example: The door is open; come in, please.

meaning: “she is used to” / “she is accustomed to” (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular subject (ella). It’s the verb phrase estar acostumbrado/a a + infinitive (or a + noun) to talk about a habit or something that feels normal because it’s familiar. For other people: estoy acostumbrado/a a, estás acostumbrado/a a, está acostumbrado/a a, etc.
target_language_example: Ella está acostumbrada a levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: She is used to getting up early.

additional_notes: Used with a person + estar + acostumbrado/a(s) + a + infinitive (habit/action) or noun (something you’re used to). It describes a habitual situation that feels normal to the person. Change gender/number as needed: está acostumbrada a…, están acostumbrados a….
target_language_example: Tom está acostumbrado a hablar en público.
native_language_example: Tom is used to speaking in public.

meaning: “it’s at the end of the hallway.”
additional_notes: Used to give directions to a place or object inside a building. Literally “(it) is at the end of the corridor/hallway.” Often said without the subject because Spanish can drop it when it’s clear (e.g., a room, door, bathroom). You can change the verb for other subjects: “están al final del pasillo” (they are).
target_language_example: La oficina está al final del pasillo, a la derecha.
native_language_example: The office is at the end of the hallway, on the right.

additional_notes: Use it to say where something is located: [thing] está al lado de [place]. Here, "de la" is used before a feminine singular noun (la farmacia, la oficina). For a masculine noun, use "está al lado del" (e.g., del banco). You can also drop the article and say "está al lado de" when it’s not followed by "el/la".
target_language_example: Mi casa está al lado de la escuela.
native_language_example: My house is next to the school.

meaning: “is next to the / is beside the”.
additional_notes: Used to say one thing is immediately next to another. It’s the verb estar (location) + al lado de (“next to”). Before a masculine singular noun, use del (= de + el): está al lado del teatro. With a feminine noun, use de la: está al lado de la casa. You can also use plural: están al lado de los/las…
target_language_example: Mi casa está al lado del parque.
native_language_example: My house is next to the park.

additional_notes: Used to say something is across from you, on the opposite side of a boundary or area (a river, street, city, etc.). Often followed by “de” + place/thing: “Está al otro lado del río / de la calle / de la ciudad.”
target_language_example: El supermercado está al otro lado de la calle.
native_language_example: The supermarket is across the street.

meaning: “is on the other side of” (across from).
additional_notes: Used to say where something is located relative to something else. Common with places like la calle (the street), la ciudad (the city), las montañas (the mountains). Structure: estar + al otro lado de + noun. You can change está to match the subject (están, estoy, etc.).
target_language_example: El supermercado está al otro lado de la avenida.
native_language_example: The supermarket is on the other side of the avenue.

additional_notes: Used with estar + ansioso/a + por + infinitive (or sometimes a noun) to express eagerness or anticipation: “Está ansioso por verte”. In some contexts “ansioso” can also mean “anxious” (worried), but with “por” + an action it often means “eager.”
target_language_example: Está ansioso por conocer el resultado.
native_language_example: He’s eager to find out the result.

meaning: “is learning” / “is in the process of learning.”
additional_notes: From the verb "aprender" (to learn) in the present progressive: "estar" (conjugated: está) + gerund "aprendiendo". Use it to emphasize that the learning is happening right now or is ongoing. Often followed by what is being learned (e.g., "está aprendiendo español"); you can also add adverbs like "rápidamente" (quickly) or "todavía" (still).
target_language_example: Mi hermana está aprendiendo a conducir.
native_language_example: My sister is learning to drive.

additional_notes: Used with the present progressive: estar (conjugated) + aprendiendo + a + infinitive to say someone is in the process of learning how to do something (e.g., manejar/conducir, bailar, escribir). You can change está to estoy/estás/están, etc., depending on the subject.
target_language_example: Mi hermana está aprendiendo a cocinar comida mexicana.
native_language_example: My sister is learning to cook Mexican food.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive (estar + gerund) to emphasize an ongoing change happening these days/now. Common with numbers, prices, rates, and population. You can also use the more neutral present: “aumenta” = “increases.”
target_language_example: La temperatura está aumentando poco a poco.
native_language_example: The temperature is increasing little by little.

meaning: 'is under' (under someone’s control, influence, surveillance, care, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with "estar" + "bajo" + a noun to show that someone/something is under authority, influence, protection, supervision, or responsibility: "está bajo mi mando" (under my command), "bajo la influencia" (under the influence), "bajo vigilancia" (under surveillance), "bajo su cuidado" (in their care). The form changes with the subject ("estoy/estás/está/estamos/están bajo...").
target_language_example: El edificio está bajo control de la policía.
native_language_example: The building is under police control.

additional_notes: Used to say a story, movie, book, idea, etc. comes from a source (real events, someone’s life, another work). Often followed by a noun: “está basada en hechos reales / una historia real / su experiencia”. You can also use other forms: “está basado en” (masculine), “están basadas en” (plural).
target_language_example: La serie está basada en un libro famoso.
native_language_example: The series is based on a famous book.

meaning: “It’s okay / alright / fine.” (also: “that’s good” depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to accept something, reassure someone, or say something is fine/acceptable (“Okay, I’ll do it”; “Don’t be mad, it’s okay”). It can also mean “it’s good/nice” when describing something: “Está bien el barrio” = “The neighborhood is nice/pretty good.” In “Está bien que + subjuntivo”, it means “It’s good/okay that…” or “It’s fine that…”.
target_language_example: —¿Te parece si lo hablamos mañana? —Está bien.
native_language_example: —Is it okay if we talk about it tomorrow? —Okay.

additional_notes: "Está bien" is a very common way to accept or agree (“okay/alright/fine”). The "lo" is an object pronoun meaning “it” or “him” (and sometimes “that”), referring to something already known from context: e.g., "Está bien, lo atraparé" = “Okay, I’ll catch him/it.” In "Todo está bien, lo tengo", "lo tengo" means “I’ve got it/him.”
target_language_example: Está bien, lo haré ahora.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll do it now.

meaning: “It’s okay / alright, don’t …” (used to calm someone down or reassure them).
additional_notes: Often said to stop or soften what someone is doing (e.g., yelling, worrying, blaming themselves): “Está bien, no grite” = “Okay, don’t yell.” It can also mean “It’s fine, there’s no need…” or “Don’t worry.” You may hear it repeated (“Está bien, está bien”) for emphasis.
target_language_example: Está bien, no te enojes; podemos hablar mañana.
native_language_example: It’s okay, don’t get angry; we can talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to accept something or agree up to a point, then introduce a reservation, objection, condition, or warning. Very common in conversation. It can refer to a thing (“El texto está bien, pero…”) or to agreeing to a request (“Está bien, pero rápido”). Often followed by a negative ("pero no...") or a condition ("pero solo si...").
target_language_example: Está bien, pero no puedo quedarme mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: Okay, but I can’t stay very long.

additional_notes: Present progressive of "buscar" (to look for/search for): "estar" + "buscando". Often used with "a" before a specific person or pet: "está buscando a Tom"; with things, usually no "a": "está buscando sus zapatos". Pronouns can go before "está" ("Te está buscando") or attached to the gerund ("Está buscándote").
target_language_example: Mi mamá está buscando su teléfono.
native_language_example: My mom is looking for her phone.

meaning: 'is changing' / 'is in the process of changing.'
additional_notes: This is the present progressive: **estar (conjugated) + gerund**. It emphasizes an action happening now or a change currently in progress: *El mundo está cambiando.* With a reflexive pronoun (**se está cambiando**), it can mean “is changing clothes” (*Tom se está cambiando de ropa*), but that extra **se** changes the meaning.
target_language_example: Todo está cambiando muy rápido.
native_language_example: Everything is changing very fast.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (he) is married to a woman. "Está" is from estar (temporary/current state), and "casado" agrees with a male subject; for a female subject you’d say "está casada". The "una" introduces a feminine noun/profession/nationality: "una actriz", "una canadiense", "una profesora". You can also say "está casado con + name": "Está casado con Ana".
target_language_example: Mi hermano está casado con una enfermera.
native_language_example: My brother is married to a nurse.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is nearby. Often followed by “de” + place/person: “está cerca de aquí” (it’s near here), “está cerca de ti” (it’s close to you). With masculine singular nouns, “de + el” becomes “del”: “cerca del río” (near the river).
target_language_example: El restaurante está cerca del hotel.
native_language_example: The restaurant is near the hotel.

meaning: “is close to / near” (location) or “is about to” (almost happening).
additional_notes: Used with a place or object to talk about physical proximity: “La silla está cerca de la puerta” = “The chair is near the door.” With an infinitive verb (e.g., entrar, salir, empezar), it can mean “is about to / is close to (doing something)”: “Está cerca de entrar…” = “It’s close to entering…”. Changes with the subject (estoy/estás/está/estamos/están cerca de).
target_language_example: La silla está cerca de la puerta.
native_language_example: The chair is near the door.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located. “está” is from *estar* (location/state). “cerca de” means “near/close to,” and it contracts to “cerca del” before a masculine singular noun with *el* (del = de + el). You can swap the place: *está cerca del banco/del hospital/del centro*.
target_language_example: El hotel está cerca del parque.
native_language_example: The hotel is near the park.

meaning: “it/she is closed” (feminine; also used for a place being closed).
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (la puerta, la botella, la cocina, la oficina, la tapa). It’s the verb estar (a temporary state/condition) + the adjective cerrada (“closed”). Often appears with details like desde el interior (“from the inside”) or con llave (“locked”). For masculine nouns, use está cerrado.
target_language_example: Lo siento, la oficina está cerrada hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, the office is closed today.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a temporary state: a place/service isn’t open, a road is blocked, or something like a valve/tap is shut. It agrees with the thing that’s closed: **está cerrado** (masc. singular), **está cerrada** (fem. singular), **están cerrados/cerradas** (plural). Common for shops/restaurants (**El restaurante está cerrado**) and roads (**El camino está cerrado**).
target_language_example: El restaurante está cerrado.
native_language_example: The restaurant is closed.

additional_notes: Used to say something is evident or certain. Common patterns: “No está claro” = “It’s not clear (yet)”; “Está claro que + [sentence]” = “It’s clear that…”; by itself (“Está claro.”) it can mean “Of course.” or “Clearly.”
target_language_example: No está claro si va a llover mañana.
native_language_example: It’s not clear whether it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you consider evident based on facts or the situation. Very common in spoken and written Spanish. You can also hear variations like “está claro” (it’s clear) or “queda claro que” (it becomes clear that).
target_language_example: Está claro que no entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: It’s clear that he doesn’t understand the question.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (conjugated) + gerund (-ando/-iendo) to talk about an action in progress at the moment. Here, "está" matches he/she/it/you (formal) in the present tense; for other subjects: estoy comiendo, estás comiendo, estamos comiendo, están comiendo.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está comiendo en la cocina.
native_language_example: My brother is eating in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Uses the verb estar (“to be,” for states/conditions) + the adverb completamente (“completely”) to strongly emphasize an adjective or past participle: está completamente solo (completely alone), está completamente equivocado (totally wrong), está completamente desconectado (completely disconnected). It’s often translated as “totally,” “completely,” or “entirely,” depending on context.
target_language_example: El teléfono está completamente apagado.
native_language_example: The phone is completely off.

meaning: “is buying” (is in the process of purchasing).
additional_notes: Present progressive: "estar" (conjugated) + gerund (-ando/-iendo). "Está comprando" is third-person singular (he/she/it is buying; you formal are buying). Often followed by what’s being bought ("flores", "leche") and/or where ("en el mercado", "en la tienda").
target_language_example: Mi hermano está comprando pan en la panadería.
native_language_example: My brother is buying bread at the bakery.

additional_notes: Present progressive of crecer (to grow). Used for people/animals growing up (babies, hair), and also for things that increase or rise over time (the economy, unemployment, the tide, population). Often followed by details like “día a día” (day by day) or “a pasos gigantes” (by leaps and bounds).
target_language_example: La planta está creciendo muy rápido.
native_language_example: The plant is growing very fast.

additional_notes: Used with estar + past participle to describe a current state: something has a layer of something on it. Agree the participle with the thing covered: está cubierto de (masc. sing.), está cubierta de (fem. sing.), están cubiertos de (masc. pl.), están cubiertas de (fem. pl.). Often used for weather, dirt, snow/ice, etc.
target_language_example: El camino está cubierto de hielo.
native_language_example: The road is covered in ice.

additional_notes: It’s the present progressive of dar (to give): estar (present) + dando (gerund). Used for actions happening right now. Often appears in set phrases with dar, where the natural English translation may not be literally “give” (e.g., dar una paliza = to beat someone up).
target_language_example: Me está dando una oportunidad.
native_language_example: He/She is giving me a chance.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say someone agrees with an idea, plan, or decision. You can add “con” to say what they agree with: “Está de acuerdo con el plan.” (In questions, it’s common to ask: “¿Está de acuerdo?”).
target_language_example: ¿Está de acuerdo con la propuesta?
native_language_example: Do you agree with the proposal?

additional_notes: Used with estar + de + mood noun (humor) to describe someone’s current, temporary mood. You can change the subject: Estoy de mal humor (I’m in a bad mood), Estamos de mal humor (we’re in a bad mood).
target_language_example: No le hables ahora; está de mal humor.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to him now; he’s in a bad mood.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a temporary state/condition that’s excessive: **está demasiado + adjective** (e.g., oscuro, salado, débil). Often followed by **para + infinitive** to say “too … to …”: *está demasiado salada para comerse* = “it’s too salty to eat.”
target_language_example: El café está demasiado caliente para tomarlo ahora.
native_language_example: The coffee is too hot to drink right now.

additional_notes: Used to describe where something is. It’s the verb estar (for location) + detrás de (“behind”). Change está to other forms as needed: está (he/she/it), están (they/you plural), estoy (I), etc. Can also mean “is after/chasing” someone (e.g., La policía está detrás de Tom = The police are after Tom).
target_language_example: La estación está detrás del museo.
native_language_example: The station is behind the museum.

meaning: 'is willing to' / 'is prepared to' (ready to do something).
additional_notes: Used with a person or organization + estar + dispuesto/a/os/as + a + infinitive to express willingness or readiness. Agree in gender/number: está dispuesto a (he/it), está dispuesta a (she), están dispuestos a (they, masc/mixed), están dispuestas a (they, fem).
target_language_example: Tom está dispuesto a hablar.
native_language_example: Tom is willing to talk.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (conjugated) + gerund (durmiendo) to talk about an action in progress at this moment. Often used with time words like ahora (“now”) or with a place: está durmiendo en el sofá (“is sleeping on the sofa”).
target_language_example: No hagas ruido; mi hermana está durmiendo.
native_language_example: Don’t make noise; my sister is sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say that something has just started or is in the early stages (a change, a process, the weather, feelings, etc.). It’s the present progressive of empezar (estar + empezando), so you can change the subject: estoy empezando a (I’m starting to), estás empezando a (you’re starting to), etc.
target_language_example: Creo que está empezando a llover.
native_language_example: I think it’s starting to rain.

meaning: “is in / is at” (location) or “is in” (a state like “in session”).
additional_notes: “Está” is the present tense of “estar” (used for location and temporary states), and “en” means “in/on/at.” Use “está en + place” for where someone/something is: “Está en Inglaterra.” It can also be used with certain situations or states: “está en sesión” = “is in session.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: My brother is at home now.

meaning: is on the way; is coming.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently traveling toward a place, or that something is expected to arrive soon (help, a person, a season, the next one in a series). Often used with "ya" for emphasis: "ya está en camino" (it’s already on the way).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: tu pedido ya está en camino.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: your order is already on the way.

additional_notes: Used with laws, rules, ideas, actions, or people to say something goes against them or that someone opposes them. With laws/rules it often means “is illegal/forbidden” (e.g., “está en contra de la ley”). Changes with the subject: estoy/estás/está/estamos/están en contra de.
target_language_example: Fumar en la oficina está en contra de nuestras reglas.
native_language_example: Smoking in the office is against our rules.

meaning: "is in the" / "is on the" (for a masculine singular place or object).
additional_notes: Used with the verb estar to say where someone or something is located. "En" can mean "in" or "on" depending on the context. "El" is the masculine singular "the" (for feminine, you use "está en la"). Often followed by a noun like "el bolso" (the bag) or "el aula" (the classroom).
target_language_example: Mi teléfono está en el coche.
native_language_example: My phone is in the car.

additional_notes: Used to say that something important could be lost or affected by what happens next (often someone’s life, safety, reputation, money, etc.). It commonly follows the thing that’s at risk: "La vida de mi padre está en juego" (My father’s life is at stake). You can also start with "Está en juego..." to emphasize what’s at risk.
target_language_example: Si fallamos, nuestro trabajo está en juego.
native_language_example: If we fail, our job is on the line.

meaning: "is in the" / "is on the" (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with locations (cities, countries, bays, etc.) or to indicate something is listed/contained somewhere (e.g., in a directory/guide). Use it before feminine singular nouns that take the article "la" (e.g., la India, la bahía, la guía). With "estar" it usually describes where something/someone is or where it appears (not a permanent characteristic).
target_language_example: El restaurante está en la esquina.
native_language_example: The restaurant is on the corner.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the kitchen. "Está" is the present tense of "estar" (to be, for location/state). Change the subject by changing the verb: "estoy en la cocina" (I’m), "estás" (you), "están" (they).
target_language_example: El gato está en la cocina.
native_language_example: The cat is in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person or thing (singular) is located on top of the table. It uses estar (temporary/location) + en (on/in/at) + la mesa (the table). For plural, use “están en la mesa.”
target_language_example: Tu vaso está en la mesa, no en el suelo.
native_language_example: Your glass is on the table, not on the floor.

additional_notes: Used with estar + en + peligro to say someone or something is in danger right now or in a risky situation. You can add what is in danger: “Su vida está en peligro” = “His/Her life is in danger.” (Plural: “están en peligro.”)
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! El niño está en peligro.
native_language_example: Careful! The child is in danger.

additional_notes: Used with a location/position noun to say someone or something is in its proper place or at a specific spot: está en su casa, en su escritorio, en su puesto, etc. Note that su can mean his, her, your (formal), their, or its depending on context. Common fixed phrase: estar en su derecho = “to be within one’s rights.”
target_language_example: El gerente está en su oficina ahora.
native_language_example: The manager is in his/her office now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + enamorado + de to say someone is (currently) in love with a person. Change it for gender/number: está enamorada de (she is in love with), están enamorados/as de (they are in love with). After de, use a person or pronoun: de ella (with her), de él (with him), de mí (with me), de ti (with you), de vos (with you, voseo), de nosotros/as (with us).
target_language_example: Creo que él está enamorado de ti.
native_language_example: I think he’s in love with you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (temporary condition) + "enferma" (feminine form of "enfermo"). It refers to a woman or girl who is ill. For a man, say "está enfermo"; for more than one person, "están enfermos/enfermas". Often followed by details like symptoms: "está con fiebre" (she has a fever).
target_language_example: Lo siento, Ana no viene hoy porque está enferma.
native_language_example: Sorry, Ana isn’t coming today because she’s sick.

additional_notes: Uses estar (temporary state) + enfermo (sick). You can use it for people (“Tom está enfermo”) and also metaphorically for things or situations (“El mundo está enfermo” = “The world is sick/broken”). For seriousness, you may hear “está enfermo de gravedad” (“is seriously ill”).
target_language_example: Mi papá está enfermo, así que no va a trabajar hoy.
native_language_example: My dad is sick, so he’s not going to work today.

additional_notes: Present progressive: estar (está) + gerund (escribiendo) to describe an action in progress right now or around this time (e.g., “this year”). You can change the subject or tense: “Estoy escribiendo un libro” (I am writing a book), “Están escribiendo un libro” (They are writing a book).
target_language_example: Mi hermana está escribiendo un libro sobre su viaje.
native_language_example: My sister is writing a book about her trip.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: estar (conjugated) + gerund (escribiendo) to emphasize an action happening right now. Add the recipient with "a": "Está escribiendo una carta a María." You can add "ahora" to make the 'right now' meaning extra clear.
target_language_example: Está escribiendo una carta para su abuela.
native_language_example: He/She is writing a letter for his/her grandmother.

meaning: "is written in" (a language/format/medium or a document/location).
additional_notes: Passive construction with "estar" + past participle ("escrito"). Used to state the language something is written in ("El Corán está escrito en árabe") or where it is written/recorded ("Está escrito en el documento"). It agrees with the subject in number/gender: "está escrito" (masc. sing.), "está escrita" (fem. sing.), "están escritos" (masc. pl.), "están escritas" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: El texto anterior está escrito en euskera.
native_language_example: The previous text is written in Basque.

additional_notes: Used to describe the language a text/document is written in. You can swap the language: “está escrito en español / francés / alemán”. Often followed by an adjective to describe the level: “en inglés sencillo/fácil/simple” = “in simple/easy English.”
target_language_example: El manual está escrito en inglés, pero también hay una versión en español.
native_language_example: The manual is written in English, but there’s also a Spanish version.

additional_notes: Present progressive of **esperar**: **estar + esperando**. Use it for (1) waiting for someone/something: **Está esperando a María.** (2) waiting in a place: **Está esperando en la sala.** (3) expecting/hoping that something happens: **Está esperando que María haga algo.** Note: **esperar** can mean “to wait” and also “to hope/expect,” so don’t confuse it with English “to expect” in all cases.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está esperando el autobús.
native_language_example: My brother is waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Present progressive: **estar** (conjugated) + **estudiando**. Use it for an action in progress or a temporary ongoing situation. The subject can be included (**Ella está estudiando**) or omitted (**Está estudiando**) when it’s clear. Often followed by what someone is studying (**Está estudiando derecho**) or where (**Está estudiando en Harvard**) or for what purpose (**Está estudiando para ser...**).
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; está estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; he/she is studying for the exam.

meaning: “is out / is outside” (not here; not within; not included).
additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t at home/available (Está fuera), or that something is outside a limit/area/authority, often with “de” (Está fuera de tu jurisdicción = outside your jurisdiction). It can also mean “off course” (El cohete está fuera de su rumbo) or “out/removed/eliminated” in contexts like rules, sports, or being fired (Está fuera).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el gerente está fuera ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the manager is out right now.

meaning: "is outside/out of" (not within; beyond; away from).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to show that something/someone is not within a limit, range, place, or category. Common uses: **fuera de alcance** (out of reach), **fuera de la ciudad** (out of town), **fuera de curso / fuera de rumbo** (off course), **fuera de tu jurisdicción** (outside your jurisdiction), **fuera de sospecha** (above suspicion / beyond suspicion). Often implies being beyond control or no longer contained (e.g., *El genio está fuera de la botella*).
target_language_example: Lo siento, eso está fuera de mi control.
native_language_example: Sorry, that's out of my control.

meaning: “It’s out of the question.” / “It’s not up for discussion.”
