additional_notes: Used in legal/crime contexts to say a judge gave someone a specific punishment. It’s the past tense (pretérito) passive form: "fue" + "condenado" (masculine; "fue condenada" for a woman) + "a" + the penalty (e.g., "muerte", "prisión", "cinco meses de prisión").
target_language_example: Después del juicio, fue condenado a dos años de prisión.
native_language_example: After the trial, he was sentenced to two years in prison.

additional_notes: Used to admit responsibility or blame for something that happened. It’s in the past tense (fue = “was”). You can soften it with phrases like “En parte fue culpa mía” (“It was partly my fault”) or emphasize it with “todo” (“everything”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, fue culpa mía llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, it was my fault for arriving late.

meaning: 'was the' / 'it was the' (preterite of *ser* + masculine singular definite article *el*).
additional_notes: Used to identify what something/someone was in the past: *Ayer fue el último día...* = “Yesterday was the last day...”. In questions about past events: *¿Cuál fue el acuerdo?* = “What was the agreement?”. Very common in the emphatic structure **fue el que + verb** to highlight who did something: *Tom fue el que cocinó* = “Tom was the one who cooked.” (Feminine equivalent: **fue la**.)
target_language_example: Tom fue el que cocinó la cena.
native_language_example: Tom was the one who cooked dinner.

meaning: “was the first” (masculine singular, before a noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was the first to do something or the first in a series/group. "Fue" is the preterite of "ser" (he/she/it was). "El primer" is the shortened form of "el primero" used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., "el primer presidente"). For feminine, use "fue la primera"; for masculine without a following noun, "fue el primero".
target_language_example: Neil Armstrong fue el primer astronauta en caminar sobre la luna.
native_language_example: Neil Armstrong was the first astronaut to walk on the moon.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did an action before anyone else. Pattern: [Name] fue el primero en + infinitive (hacer, irse, llegar). For a woman: fue la primera en. For plural: fueron los/las primeros/as en. In other tenses: es/era/será el primero en.
target_language_example: Tom fue el primero en hacer una pregunta.
native_language_example: Tom was the first to ask a question.

additional_notes: Used to say that just one person (masculine singular, or mixed/unspecified group) did something. It uses the preterite of ser (fue = was). Variants: feminine singular “fue la única que”; plural “fueron los/las únicos/as que”.
target_language_example: Tom fue el único que limpió la habitación.
native_language_example: Tom was the only one who cleaned the room.

meaning: “was expelled from / was kicked out of (the)” (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Past passive form of **expulsar**. Used when someone/something is forced to leave a group, place, or vehicle. **Del** = **de + el** (“from the”). For a woman you’d say **fue expulsada del**; for plural **fueron expulsados/as del**.
target_language_example: Juan fue expulsado del partido por gritarle al árbitro.
native_language_example: Juan was kicked out of the game for yelling at the referee.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened: *Fue hace + time period* (e.g., *fue hace dos años* = “it was two years ago”). Often appears after a noun phrase too: *La última vez… fue hace…* (“The last time… was … ago”). In everyday speech, you can also hear *hace + time* by itself (*Hace dos años* = “Two years ago”).
target_language_example: Fue hace seis meses cuando empezamos a vivir aquí.
native_language_example: It was six months ago when we started living here.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened far in the past. Often appears with emphasis words like “pero” (but) or “sí” (yes). You may also hear the redundant “fue hace mucho tiempo atrás”; “atrás” isn’t necessary because “hace… (ago)” already implies the past.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero fue hace mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it was a long time ago.

meaning: “was injured/wounded in …” (in an event/place) or “was injured/wounded in/on …” (a body part).
additional_notes: This is the passive in the past (preterite): **ser + herido** (“to be injured/wounded”). Use **en** for the context/event/place (**en la batalla**, **en un accidente**, **en un robo**) and also for the body part (**en la pierna**, **en la cabeza**). Note: **herido** agrees in gender/number with the subject (e.g., *fue herida* for a woman).
target_language_example: El soldado fue herido en la pierna.
native_language_example: The soldier was wounded in the leg.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of ser (fue) + “la primera” to say someone/something was the first one. The subject is often understood from context (it can mean “she was the first” or “it was the first,” if the noun is feminine). Common patterns: “fue la primera en + infinitive” (was the first to do something) and “fue la primera + noun / que + clause.” Variations: “fue el primero” (masc.), “fueron los/las primeros/as” (plural).
target_language_example: María fue la primera en llegar a la fiesta.
native_language_example: María was the first to arrive at the party.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a first-time experience in the past. Very often followed by "que" + a verb: "Fue la primera vez que..." (It was the first time that...). You can also use it alone to confirm something: "Esa fue la primera vez."
target_language_example: Fue la primera vez que viajé solo.
native_language_example: It was the first time I traveled alone.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened for the first time in the past. You can change the tense depending on the context: "es la primera vez que" (it’s the first time that) or "era la primera vez que" (it was the first time that, describing a past situation). In Spanish, after "es la primera vez que" you typically use present perfect ("he visto"), while after "fue/era la primera vez que" you typically use past perfect ("había visto")—though simple past is also common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Fue la primera vez que probé comida mexicana.
native_language_example: It was the first time I tried Mexican food.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was the final one in a sequence. It agrees with the noun it refers to: **fue el último** (masc.), **fue la última** (fem.), **fueron los/las últimos(as)** (plural). Common patterns: **fue la última en + infinitive** (“was the last to + verb”) and **fue la última + noun** (“was the last + thing/event/person”). Note: **último/a** means “last/final,” not “ultimate” in the usual English sense.
target_language_example: Mi hermana fue la última en salir de la casa.
native_language_example: My sister was the last to leave the house.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened for the final time (it won’t happen again). Often followed by **que** + a clause: *Fue la última vez que le vi* (“It was the last time I saw him”). Can also appear as *Esta fue la última vez* (“This was the last time”) to refer to the current/just-mentioned moment.
target_language_example: Fue la última vez que hablamos antes de mudarme.
native_language_example: It was the last time we talked before I moved.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb to say someone/something had enough of a quality to do something: “fue lo suficientemente + adj./adv. + para + infinitive” (e.g., “Fue lo suficientemente rápido para ganar”). It’s the preterite (past) form with “ser” (fue). For negatives, use “no fue lo suficientemente + adj.” (“He wasn’t fast enough”).
target_language_example: No fue lo suficientemente cuidadoso para leer las instrucciones.
native_language_example: He wasn’t careful enough to read the instructions.

meaning: “that was what …” / “it was … that …” (past; used for emphasis).
additional_notes: Used in cleft sentences to emphasize the information that follows. Common pattern: “X fue lo que + verb/clause” = “X was what + clause” / “It was X that + clause.” In questions you’ll often see “¿Qué fue lo que…?” meaning “What was it that…?” (more emphatic than just “¿Qué…?”). It’s the past tense of “ser” (fue = it was); you may also see “era lo que” depending on context.
target_language_example: Fue lo que necesitaba oír.
native_language_example: That was what I needed to hear.

meaning: “that’s what I said” / “it was what I said.”
additional_notes: Past tense of "es lo que dije". Used to confirm or clarify what you said before, often correcting a misunderstanding ("Eso no fue lo que dije" = “That’s not what I said”). It can also appear in questions like "¿Qué fue lo que dije?" (“What was it that I said?”).
target_language_example: No me malinterpretes: fue lo que dije, nada más.
native_language_example: Don’t misunderstand me: that’s what I said, nothing more.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** in the **preterite** (**fue**) to talk about a completed past fact: *X fue mi primer Y* (“X was my first Y”). **Primer** is the shortened form of **primero** used before a masculine singular noun (*mi primer amor/viaje/novio*). With feminine nouns, use **mi primera** (*mi primera vez, mi primera idea*).
target_language_example: Ese fue mi primer trabajo.
native_language_example: That was my first job.

additional_notes: "Fue" is the preterite (completed past) of "ser" (“to be”). Use "fue muy" + adjective to describe how something/someone was on a specific occasion or completed event: "El viaje fue muy largo". Often refers to a situation/event (“It was very…”), but can also describe a person’s behavior in that moment: "Tom fue muy grosero". For plural subjects, use "fueron muy".
target_language_example: La película fue muy interesante.
native_language_example: The movie was very interesting.

additional_notes: "Fue" is the simple past (pretérito) of "ser" and is used for completed events or a person’s behavior in a specific situation. "Amable" means kind/polite. You can add a subject if needed: "Él/Ella fue muy amable." With an indirect object pronoun it means “was very kind to (someone)”: "Les fue muy amable" = “He/She was very kind to them.”
target_language_example: La recepcionista fue muy amable conmigo.
native_language_example: The receptionist was very kind to me.

fue muy amable de tu parte

target_language_multi_word_term: fue muy amable de tu parte
additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely for something they did. It literally means “it was very kind on your part.” You can follow it with an infinitive to say what the person did: “Fue muy amable de tu parte ayudarme/invitarme.” (For more than one person you’re speaking to: “de su parte” (formal) or “de vuestra parte” (Spain).)
target_language_example: Fue muy amable de tu parte venir a verme al hospital.
native_language_example: That was very kind of you to come see me at the hospital.

additional_notes: Used with the preterite of ser (fue) + the masculine singular article (un) to describe what something/someone was at a specific time in the past. Common in definitions/explanations: "Lo que pasó fue un...". For feminine nouns use "fue una"; for plural use "fueron" (e.g., "fueron unos/unas").
target_language_example: La reunión fue un éxito.
native_language_example: The meeting was a success.

additional_notes: Common for explaining or insisting that something happened by mistake (often to deny responsibility or intent). Past tense (pretérito) of ser: "fue" = "it was." You’ll often hear it with emphasis: "Te dije/Ya te dije que fue un accidente" ("I told you / I already told you it was an accident").
target_language_example: Perdón, fue un accidente; no quería romperlo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was an accident; I didn’t mean to break it.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to say something was good in the past: Fue un buen + sustantivo (comienzo, espectáculo, salto, etc.). For feminine nouns, use “fue una buena …” (Fue una buena idea). Often “fue” means “it was” or “that was,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Fue un buen día para caminar por la ciudad.
native_language_example: It was a good day to walk around the city.

meaning: “it was a day” (used to describe how a day was).
additional_notes: Past tense of "ser" (fue = "was") + "un día" ("a day"). It’s commonly followed by an adjective or description: "Fue un día horrible/ideal/divertido". You can also specify the day with "El lunes fue un día…" or "Hoy fue un día…".
target_language_example: Ayer fue un día muy largo, pero productivo.
native_language_example: Yesterday was a very long day, but productive.

meaning: “it was a mistake / it was an error.”
additional_notes: Past-tense phrase (pretérito of ser: fue) used to say something was wrong or a bad decision. Common patterns: “Fue un error + infinitive” (Fue un error visitar a Tom. = It was a mistake to visit Tom) and “Fue un error de…” (de dedo = a typo / slip of the finger; de su parte = on his/her part). You can also add an adjective: “Fue un error imperdonable” (an unforgivable mistake).
target_language_example: Lo siento: fue un error.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: it was a mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense phrase used to say something didn’t succeed. Uses the verb "ser" in the preterite (fue) + "un fracaso" (a failure). You can swap in another subject: "La reunión fue un fracaso".
target_language_example: La entrevista fue un fracaso.
native_language_example: The interview was a failure.

meaning: "was a great" (or sometimes "was a big") [masculine singular].
additional_notes: Uses the preterite of **ser** (*fue*) to describe what someone/something **was** in the past. **Gran** is a shortened form of *grande* used **before** a singular noun (typically meaning “great/important,” sometimes “big”). It agrees with the noun: **fue una gran** (feminine), **fueron un gran/unos grandes** (plural; commonly **grandes**).
target_language_example: Beethoven fue un gran compositor.
native_language_example: Beethoven was a great composer.

additional_notes: Used to say that an event, project, or product turned out very well and was popular or achieved its goals. It’s the past tense (pretérito) of "ser": "fue" = "was". You can change the subject: "La fiesta fue un gran éxito" / "El proyecto fue un gran éxito".
target_language_example: La inauguración fue un gran éxito.
native_language_example: The opening event was a great success.

additional_notes: A polite, formal-sounding phrase used to close a conversation after meeting or interacting with someone. Common patterns: “Fue un placer + infinitive” (Fue un placer conocerla = It was a pleasure to meet you) and “Fue un placer + [object pronoun]” (Fue un placer verla = It was a pleasure to see you). You can adjust formality with pronouns: conocerla/verla (formal you, fem.), conocerlo/verlo (formal you, masc.), conocerlos/verlos (you all / them), verte (informal you).
target_language_example: Fue un placer hablar con usted.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure talking with you.

meaning: “It was a pleasure to meet you.”
additional_notes: A polite phrase used when saying goodbye after meeting someone. "Fue" is past tense of "ser" (it was), "un placer" = a pleasure, and "conocerte" = to meet you (informal/singular "tú"). For a more formal version, say "Fue un placer conocerle" (to meet you, formal). You can also use present tense "Es un placer conocerte" when meeting someone.
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; fue un placer conocerte.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; it was a pleasure to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to say that something turned out well. It’s the preterite (completed past) of “ser”: “fue” = “was,” and “un éxito” = “a success.” You can negate it with “No fue un éxito” (“It wasn’t a success”).
target_language_example: La presentación fue un éxito, gracias a tu ayuda.
native_language_example: The presentation was a success, thanks to your help.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** in the **preterite** to describe what something **was** (a completed event or experience). **Una** agrees with a **feminine singular** noun: *Fue una mañana perfecta.* For masculine nouns, use **fue un**: *Fue un día perfecto.* Often followed by a noun phrase or an adjective + noun.
target_language_example: Fue una decisión difícil.
native_language_example: It was a difficult decision.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past situation/event with a feminine singular noun: Fue una gran + noun (fiesta, decepción, pérdida, idea). With masculine nouns: Fue un gran + noun (día, éxito). With plural: Fueron una(s) gran(des) + noun(s). Note: "gran" is the short form of "grande" used before a noun.
target_language_example: Fue una gran sorpresa verte aquí.
native_language_example: It was a big surprise to see you here.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in the plural: “fuegos artificiales” = “fireworks.” In the singular, “fuego artificial” can refer to a single firework or the concept in general. Often appears with verbs like “ver” (to watch) or “lanzar”/“tirar” (to set off).
target_language_example: Ese fuego artificial explotó muy cerca.
native_language_example: That firework exploded very close by.

meaning: crossfire; being caught in the middle of conflicting sides.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “crossed fire.” Used for gunfire coming from two or more directions, and also figuratively for being trapped between opposing people/groups (e.g., an argument, conflict, or political dispute). Often appears as “quedar/estar en medio del fuego cruzado” (to end up/be in the crossfire).
target_language_example: No quiero que los niños queden en medio del fuego cruzado.
native_language_example: I don’t want the kids to get caught in the crossfire.

additional_notes: Refers to the explosive devices used in celebrations and shows. Common with verbs like ver (to watch), comprar (to buy), and phrases like una exhibición de fuegos artificiales (a fireworks display). Usually plural.
target_language_example: En Año Nuevo, vimos fuegos artificiales en la playa.
native_language_example: On New Year’s, we watched fireworks on the beach.

additional_notes: Used to indicate location outside a place (fuera de casa = outside the home), to tell someone/something to stay away (Mantén a Tom fuera de aquí = Keep Tom out of here), or to mean 'except for/beyond' in set phrases like fuera de lo ordinario ('out of the ordinary'). Often followed by a noun or a place expression (fuera de aquí/ahí).
target_language_example: Deja el vaso fuera de la mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the glass off the table, please.

additional_notes: Used with estar/parecer to say a person, situation, or thing is no longer being controlled or managed. Often implies things are getting worse or chaotic: «Esto está fuera de control» (This is getting out of hand).
target_language_example: El tráfico hoy está fuera de control.
native_language_example: Traffic today is out of control.

meaning: outside of the; out of the.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to mean something is not inside, not part of, or away from something: fuera de la casa (outside the house), fuera de la estructura (outside the structure), fuera de la Tierra (outside the Earth). It’s the phrase fuera de + the article; change the article to match the noun: fuera del (de + el), fuera de los, fuera de las.
target_language_example: Deja los zapatos fuera de la casa.
native_language_example: Leave the shoes outside the house.

meaning: outside the city; out of town.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not in the city (often traveling) or is located beyond the city limits. Common with estar (temporary: traveling) and vivir (permanent location).
target_language_example: Este fin de semana voy a estar fuera de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This weekend I'm going to be out of town.

additional_notes: Used both literally (things not in their usual position: "everything was out of place") and figuratively (a person looks/feels like they don’t fit in, or a remark is inappropriate: "that comment was out of place"). Often used with "estar", "sentirse", or "verse/lucir".
target_language_example: Creo que mi ropa está fuera de lugar para esta fiesta.
native_language_example: I think my clothes are out of place for this party.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something is not in your space, view, or ability to affect it: fuera de mi camino (out of my way), fuera de mi vista (out of my sight), fuera de mi propiedad (off my property), fuera de mi control (out of my control). Note: in writing, "mí" takes an accent when it means "me" (fuera de mí).
target_language_example: Por favor, mantente fuera de mi habitación.
native_language_example: Please stay out of my room.

meaning: out of danger; no longer at risk.
additional_notes: Used especially for health or emergencies to say someone is safe now (often after an accident or illness). It usually goes with estar: "Está fuera de peligro". You can also say "ya está fuera de peligro" (= already out of danger) or "se encuentra fuera de peligro" (more formal).
target_language_example: Después de la operación, el doctor dijo que mi mamá ya está fuera de peligro.
native_language_example: After the operation, the doctor said my mom is already out of danger.

meaning: out of order; not working; out of service.
additional_notes: Used for things like phones, elevators, machines, or systems that aren’t functioning (often seen on signs: “Fuera de servicio.”). It can also describe people who are “off duty” (e.g., personal fuera de servicio = staff who are not currently working).
target_language_example: El cajero automático está fuera de servicio; vamos a otro.
native_language_example: The ATM is out of order; let’s go to another one.

meaning: 'beside oneself' (out of control from strong emotion).
additional_notes: Used with estar to describe someone overwhelmed by emotion (often anger, but also shock, fear, etc.): «Está fuera de sí». It can also be used in the causative pattern «poner a alguien fuera de sí» = 'to drive someone crazy / to make someone lose control': «Esto puso al alcaide fuera de sí».
target_language_example: Cuando oyó la noticia, se quedó fuera de sí.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she was beside herself.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not inside a place/object or is removed from it. It’s also used in the idiom “como un pez fuera del agua” = “like a fish out of water” (feeling uncomfortable or out of place). Grammar note: it’s the contraction of “fuera de + el” (with masculine singular nouns). With feminine singular: “fuera de la”; plural: “fuera de los/las”.
target_language_example: Saca el teléfono fuera del bolsillo, por favor.
native_language_example: Take the phone out of your pocket, please.

additional_notes: Literally “out of the path/road.” Used to describe someone/something being removed so it doesn’t block or interfere (e.g., “Con Linda fuera del camino…” = “With Linda out of the way…”). Very common as an urgent command: “¡Fuera del camino!” = “Out of the way!”
target_language_example: ¡Ponte fuera del camino! Viene un coche.
native_language_example: Get out of the way! A car is coming.

meaning: "were going to" / "was going to" (subjunctive form, often about a possible or imagined future action).
additional_notes: This is the imperfect subjunctive of **ir** used in the structure **fuera a + infinitive** (e.g., *fuera a llover*). It often appears after phrases like **no creí/no pensé que...**, **parece como si...**, or in hypothetical **si**-clauses (**Si él fuera a llegar tarde...**). It talks about something that was expected/feared/imagined to happen (often with doubt or unreality), not a simple past plan.
target_language_example: No esperaba que el examen fuera a ser tan difícil.
native_language_example: I didn’t expect the exam to be so difficult.

additional_notes: Used after triggers like **que** (e.g., *esperaba que...*), **el hecho de que...**, **suerte de que...**, etc., to talk about a situation that is hypothetical, uncertain, or simply being stated from someone’s perspective. It’s the **imperfect subjunctive** form of *ser* for **él/ella/usted** (and also *yo*): *que él fuera un...* = “that he were/was a...”. Negative: *no fuera un...* = “weren’t/wasn’t a...”.
target_language_example: Me sorprendió que fuera un médico tan joven.
native_language_example: I was surprised that he was such a young doctor.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ir: ellos/ellas/ustedes fueron + a + place/destination. Used for completed trips or movements to a destination (a la playa, a la escuela, a Chicago). You can add how they traveled: “Fueron a Chicago en coche.”
target_language_example: Mis amigos fueron al museo ayer.
native_language_example: My friends went to the museum yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense of the passive voice: "ser" (fueron) + past participle (asesinados). Used to say that some people were murdered, without focusing on who did it. "Asesinar" implies an intentional killing (murder), stronger than "morir" (to die). Can change for gender/number: "fue asesinado" (one man), "fue asesinada" (one woman), "fueron asesinadas" (women).
target_language_example: Dos periodistas fueron asesinados anoche.
native_language_example: Two journalists were murdered last night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about mental strength to resist temptation, keep habits, or continue despite difficulties. Often appears with verbs like “tener” (to have) and “necesitar” (to need), or with possessives like “su fuerza de voluntad” (his/her willpower).
target_language_example: Necesito mucha fuerza de voluntad para dejar de fumar.
native_language_example: I need a lot of willpower to quit smoking.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of **ir**: **yo fui** = “I went.” Use **fui a + place** (fui a la tienda = I went to the store) or **fui a + infinitive** to mean “I went to do something” (fui a comprar = I went to buy).
target_language_example: Ayer fui a la tienda.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the store.

meaning: "I went home." / "I went to the house."
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ir in the yo form: fui = “I went.” With a casa it usually means “home” (not necessarily “to my house”). You can add a + infinitive to say why you went: Fui a casa a descansar = “I went home to rest.”
target_language_example: Fui a casa a buscar mis llaves.
native_language_example: I went home to get my keys.

meaning: "I went to sleep" / "I went to bed."
additional_notes: Past tense (yo) of "ir" + "a" + infinitive. Often used as "me fui a dormir" = "I went off to sleep / I went to bed" (leaving what you were doing). With a place, it can mean you went somewhere in order to sleep there/spend the night: "fui a dormir a Londres" (I went to London to sleep / I slept in London).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, me fui a dormir temprano.
native_language_example: After dinner, I went to bed early.

meaning: "I went to the" (past; with a feminine destination/place).
additional_notes: Used with the preterite of **ir** (to go): **yo fui** = “I went.” **a** means “to,” and **la** is the feminine singular “the,” so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., *la librería, la zapatería, la ópera*). It can refer to going to a place or an event/venue. With masculine **el**, Spanish contracts **a + el = al** (e.g., *fui al cine*).
target_language_example: El sábado fui a la playa con mis amigos.
native_language_example: On Saturday I went to the beach with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you went to bed (usually to sleep). In everyday Spanish you very often hear the reflexive form instead: "me fui a la cama" (“I went to bed / I headed to bed”), especially when describing a sequence of actions (ate, showered, said good night, then went to bed).
target_language_example: Estaba cansado, así que fui a la cama temprano.
native_language_example: I was tired, so I went to bed early.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of ir: yo fui = “I went.” Used to say you went to school on a specific occasion/time (often with a time word like ayer, esta mañana). You can add details with con (with), porque (because), or no to make it negative: no fui a la escuela = “I didn’t go to school.”
target_language_example: Hoy no fui a la escuela porque estaba enfermo.
native_language_example: Today I didn’t go to school because I was sick.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ir: yo fui = “I went.” Used for a completed action in the past. “La estación” usually means a train/subway/bus station; you can add details like the station name (Fui a la estación Osaka), the reason (para despedir a un amigo), or how you got there (en taxi).
target_language_example: Ayer fui a la estación para tomar el tren.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the station to take the train.

additional_notes: "Fui" is the simple past (preterite) of "ir" (to go) for "yo". Use it for a completed action in the past. "A la" = "to the" (a + la). "Tienda" means a store/shop, and you can specify the type: "la tienda de libros" (the bookstore). You can also add a purpose with "a" + infinitive: "Fui a la tienda a comprar..." (I went to the store to buy...).
target_language_example: Ayer fui a la tienda a comprar leche.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the store to buy milk.

additional_notes: Past tense of **ir a + infinitive**: **fui a ver** = “I went to see / I went to watch.” Use **fui a ver a + person** when you go to see/visit someone (e.g., *fui a ver a mi amigo*). With events or things, you usually don’t add the extra **a** (e.g., *fui a ver el partido*).
target_language_example: El sábado fui a ver una película con mis amigos.
native_language_example: On Saturday I went to see a movie with my friends.

additional_notes: "Fui" is the simple past (pretérito) of "ir" (to go) for "yo". "Al" = "a" + "el" and is used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., "al supermercado"). With feminine nouns, use "a la" (e.g., "fui a la oficina").
target_language_example: Ayer fui al parque con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the park with my friends.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of ir: "yo fui" = "I went." Used to say you went to the hospital (for treatment, an appointment, or to visit someone). Often followed by a purpose: "a ver / a visitar" + person (e.g., "Fui al hospital a visitar a mi esposa").
target_language_example: Fui al hospital por la mañana para una cita.
native_language_example: I went to the hospital in the morning for an appointment.

additional_notes: “Fui” is the past tense (preterite) of “ir” (to go) for “yo” (I). “Al” is the contraction of “a + el” and is used with masculine singular places like “el supermercado.” Commonly followed by “con…” (with…) or “y…” (and…) to add details.
target_language_example: Ayer fui al supermercado y compré leche.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the supermarket and bought milk.

meaning: It was me / I was the one (who did it).
additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as the person responsible for something (often in answers or clarifications). It uses the preterite of "ser" (fui = I was) plus "yo" for emphasis, similar to saying “It was ME.” Often appears in negatives: "No fui yo" = “It wasn’t me.”
target_language_example: Perdón, fui yo quien rompió el vaso.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was me who broke the glass.

meaning: "It was me who..." / "I was the one who..." (emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that YOU did the action (often to admit, take credit, or deny responsibility). It’s in the past because "fui" is the preterite of "ser" ("I was"). Pattern: "Fui yo quien" + verb in the past (e.g., "fui yo quien lo robó"). You can negate it: "No fui yo quien..." = "It wasn’t me who...". Similar structures: "fui yo el/la que...".
target_language_example: No fui yo quien rompió el vaso; fue él.
native_language_example: It wasn’t me who broke the glass; it was him.

meaning: “we went to” / “we went to (do something)” (past tense).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of **ir** for **nosotros**: *ir → fuimos*. Use **fuimos a + place** (destination): *Fuimos a Barcelona.* Use **fuimos a + infinitive** (purpose/activity): *Fuimos a nadar.* With specific places you often add **a + el = al**: *Fuimos al lago.*
target_language_example: Anoche fuimos a cenar a un restaurante nuevo.
native_language_example: Last night we went to eat dinner at a new restaurant.

meaning: “we went to the movies / we went to the cinema.”
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ir: fuimos = “we went.” Used to say that you and others went to a movie theater, often with a time word like ayer, el sábado, luego, etc. Very common in storytelling about completed actions.
target_language_example: Después de cenar, fuimos al cine con unos amigos.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went to the movies with some friends.

meaning: "it was you" / "you were the one" (informal singular past).
additional_notes: Uses the past tense of "ser" (fuiste) + "tú" for emphasis, often to identify or blame/praise someone: "Fuiste tú" = "It was you." Common pattern: "Fuiste tú quien..." = "You were the one who..." (talking to one person you address as "tú").
target_language_example: Fuiste tú quien me avisó a tiempo.
native_language_example: You were the one who warned me in time.

meaning: "it was you who" (emphasizing that you were the one who did it).
additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize responsibility/credit for an action in the past. It uses the preterite of ser (fuiste) + tú + quien + verb: “Fuiste tú quien lo sugirió.” You can negate it: “No fuiste tú quien…”. (For other people: “fui yo quien…”, “fue él/ella quien…”, “fuimos nosotros quienes…”.)
target_language_example: Fuiste tú quien olvidó las llaves en la mesa.
native_language_example: It was you who forgot the keys on the table.

fumar es malo para la salud

target_language_multi_word_term: fumar es malo para la salud
meaning: Smoking is bad for your health.
additional_notes: A general statement about the harmful effects of smoking. Very common in health warnings and formal/informative contexts (news, doctors, campaigns). Structure: infinitive as the subject (fumar = “to smoke/smoking”) + es + malo para + noun (“is bad for …”). You can swap in other activities or nouns: “Beber mucho es malo para la salud” (Drinking a lot is bad for your health).
target_language_example: Todo el mundo sabe que fumar es malo para la salud.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that smoking is bad for your health.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is easy to do: **es fácil de + infinitive** (e.g., *Es fácil de arreglar*). The thing that is easy can be the subject (*Esto es fácil de hacer*) or a person can be described as easy to deceive/convince, etc. (*Él fue fácil de engañar*).
target_language_example: No es fácil de entender.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to understand.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is easy for a particular person (here, "you"). Often followed by an infinitive: "Es/será/fue fácil para ti + verbo" (e.g., "será fácil para ti entenderlo"). It can also appear as part of "hacerlo más fácil para ti" = "make it easier for you."
target_language_example: Será fácil para ti encontrar el hotel con el mapa.
native_language_example: It will be easy for you to find the hotel with the map.

additional_notes: Used when someone gives advice or downplays a problem, and you want to point out that it’s easier for them because they’re not in your situation. Often said on its own (“Fácil para ti decirlo.”). You can change the person: “fácil para él/ella/usted decirlo.”
target_language_example: ¿Que no me preocupe? Fácil para ti decirlo; tú no tienes este problema.
native_language_example: Not to worry? Easy for you to say; you don’t have this problem.

additional_notes: Tú imperative of the reflexive verb "fijarse en". It’s used to direct someone’s attention to something (a person, object, detail, etc.). Common in spoken instructions: "Fíjate en este mapa" (pay attention to this map), "Fíjate en mí" (watch me). It can also imply “notice” a detail: "Fíjate en ese charco de sangre" (look/notice that pool of blood).
target_language_example: Fíjate en la señal: dice que está prohibido estacionar.
native_language_example: Look at the sign: it says parking is forbidden.

additional_notes: Used to specify the sport (as opposed to fútbol, which usually means soccer in Spanish). Often appears with verbs like jugar (to play) and ver (to watch), and with nouns like partido/juego (game/match).
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta el fútbol americano?
native_language_example: Do you like American football?

additional_notes: Common everyday term for sunglasses. Typically used in the plural (las gafas de sol). Often appears with verbs like llevar (to wear) or ponerse (to put on): Llevo gafas de sol / Me pongo las gafas de sol.
target_language_example: No olvides tus gafas de sol; hace mucho sol.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your sunglasses; it’s very sunny.

additional_notes: Used to talk about earning income through work or an activity. Often followed by details like how/where ("ganar dinero trabajando") or contrasted with other goals ("no se trata de ganar dinero").
target_language_example: Quiero ganar dinero este verano para pagar mis estudios.
native_language_example: I want to earn money this summer to pay for my studies.

meaning: to buy time; to save time.
additional_notes: Commonly means “to buy time” (delay something to have more time to act or decide): Solo queda ganar tiempo. In more practical contexts it can also mean “to save time” by choosing a faster option: Para ganar tiempo viajamos en avión.
target_language_example: Llamé al técnico para ganar tiempo mientras buscaba la factura.
native_language_example: I called the technician to buy time while I looked for the receipt.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about supporting yourself financially (making money to live), usually through work. It often appears with verbs like tener que (have to), intentar/tratar de (try to), or preferir (prefer), and it changes with the person: ganarme (me), ganarte (you), ganarse (him/her/themself), ganarnos (us), ganaros (you all), ganarse (them/you all).
target_language_example: Me fui a la ciudad para ganarme la vida.
native_language_example: I went to the city to earn a living.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone supports themselves financially, often implying work or a job. Common patterns: “ganarse la vida como + profesión” (to make a living as a + profession) and “ganarse la vida + gerundio” (to make a living doing something). Conjugates as a reflexive verb: me/te/se/nos/os/se gano, ganas, gana, etc., + “la vida”.
target_language_example: La mayoría de las personas tiene que trabajar para ganarse la vida.
native_language_example: Most people have to work to earn a living.

meaning: like / feel like (doing something); desire to (do something).
additional_notes: Used most often with the verb "tener": "tener ganas de + infinitive" = to feel like doing something / to want to do something. In negative form, "no tengo ganas de..." means you don’t feel like it. "Quitar(se) las ganas de" means to take away someone’s desire/motivation (e.g., "me quitó las ganas de vivir").
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de comer algo caliente.
native_language_example: I feel like eating something warm.

meaning: like / feel like dancing; desire to dance.
additional_notes: Used with (tener) ganas de + infinitive to express wanting to do something. "Tengo ganas de bailar" = "I feel like dancing / I want to dance." You can add intensity: "muchas ganas" (really want to) or "pocas ganas" (don’t feel much like it).
target_language_example: Hoy tengo muchas ganas de bailar, aunque sea un rato.
native_language_example: Today I really feel like dancing, even if it’s just for a little while.

meaning: feel like crying; have the urge to cry.
additional_notes: "Ganas de + infinitive" expresses a desire/urge to do something. With "llorar," it means you’re on the verge of tears. Often used with verbs like "tener" or "sentir" ("tener/sentir ganas de llorar") and also with "entrarle" to emphasize the feeling suddenly starting ("le entraron ganas de llorar" = 'they suddenly felt like crying').
target_language_example: Al escuchar la noticia, me dieron ganas de llorar.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I felt like crying.

meaning: feeling like throwing up; nausea (urge to vomit).
additional_notes: Used with tener or dar (to feel/experience): Tengo ganas de vomitar = “I feel like throwing up.” / Me dio ganas de vomitar = “It made me feel like throwing up.” You can intensify it with unas/muchas: Tengo unas/muchas ganas de vomitar = “I really feel like throwing up.”
target_language_example: Después de la montaña rusa, me dieron ganas de vomitar.
native_language_example: After the roller coaster, I felt like throwing up.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of ganar: “(he/she) won.” Used for competitions, contests, tournaments, etc. You’ll often see it with “en” (in a competition/tournament) or “de/del” (of/from a particular event): “ganó el primer premio en…” / “ganó el primer premio del…”.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ganó el primer premio en el concurso de dibujo.
native_language_example: My sister won first prize in the drawing contest.

additional_notes: Used to say someone spends a lot of money on a specific thing. The verb is "gastar" (to spend), and it usually goes with "en" + a noun (or "en" + infinitive). You may also hear the reflexive form "gastarse" ("se gasta mucho dinero en..."); it means the same idea in everyday use.
target_language_example: Ella gasta mucho dinero en zapatos.
native_language_example: She spends a lot of money on shoes.

additional_notes: This is a very common pattern: **[noun] + está + [adjective / place / gerund]** to talk about a cat’s **current state** (mojado, educado), **location** (en la cocina), or **what it’s doing right now** (**está maullando**, **está tumbado**). In Spanish you usually include an article: **El gato está… / Un gato está…** (not just *gato está* by itself).
target_language_example: El gato está dormido en el sofá.
native_language_example: The cat is asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: gato = cat, persa = Persian. It usually refers to the long-haired cat breed. Use with articles like el/un and it agrees in number: gato persa / gatos persas.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene un gato persa muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: My sister has a very calm Persian cat.

meaning: a genie in a lamp (magic being that grants wishes).
additional_notes: Usually refers to the magical character from stories (like Aladdin) who lives in a lamp and can grant wishes. Commonly used with verbs like conceder (to grant) and pedir (to ask for): "El genio de la lámpara concedió..." / "Le pidió al genio de la lámpara...".
target_language_example: Si encontrara un genio de la lámpara, le pediría un deseo.
native_language_example: If I found a genie in a lamp, I would ask him for a wish.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes a group of people. Very common in speech and writing: "gente que + verb" (e.g., gente que habla, gente que puede ayudar). It’s singular in form (gente) but usually refers to multiple people.
target_language_example: Busco gente que me ayude con la mudanza.
native_language_example: I'm looking for people who can help me with the move.

additional_notes: A common direction/instruction (often in the tú command form). Used when giving driving or walking directions: “Gira a la derecha en el cruce / al llegar al semáforo.” You may also hear the more formal/plural command: “Gire a la derecha” (usted) or “Giren a la derecha” (you all).
target_language_example: Sigue todo recto y luego gira a la derecha en la esquina.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and then turn right at the corner.

additional_notes: Common in directions and navigation. Often used as an informal command (tú): “Gira a la izquierda (en la esquina / en el semáforo / después de dos cuadras)”. You may also hear the formal/usted command: “Gire a la izquierda”.
target_language_example: En el próximo cruce, gira a la izquierda.
native_language_example: At the next intersection, turn left.

additional_notes: Used for giving directions. It’s the formal command form (usted) of "girar" (to turn). In casual speech you may also hear "gira a la derecha" (tú) or "giren a la derecha" (plural). Often followed by a place or landmark: "en el banco" (at/by the bank) or "en el tercer semáforo" (at the third traffic light).
target_language_example: En la próxima esquina, gire a la derecha.
native_language_example: At the next corner, turn right.

meaning: thanks to; because of (usually for a positive cause).
additional_notes: Used to point to the person/thing responsible for a result. Often expresses gratitude or credit (“thanks to you”), but it can also be sarcastic (“Yeah, thanks to him, not you”). For negative causes, Spanish often uses “por culpa de” (“because of / due to”).
target_language_example: Llegué a tiempo gracias a ti.
native_language_example: I arrived on time thanks to you.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude or relief (often like an exclamation: “Thank God!”). It can also literally mean giving thanks to God ("We gave thanks to God"). You’ll often see it at the start of a sentence followed by a comma: "Gracias a Dios, ..."
target_language_example: Gracias a Dios, llegamos a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank God, we arrived on time.

meaning: 'thanks to you' (because of you; due to you).
additional_notes: Used to give credit to someone for a positive result (“Thanks to you, I can…”). Depending on context and tone, it can also be sarcastic/blaming (“…and it’s all thanks to you” meaning “because of you” in a negative way). Similar to “por tu culpa” when clearly blaming, but “gracias a ti” can be either sincere or sarcastic.
target_language_example: Lo logré, gracias a ti.
native_language_example: I did it, thanks to you.

meaning: 'Thanks, but…' (often to politely disagree or refuse).
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge something (help, advice, an offer, a suggestion) and then introduce a contrast with pero. Very common for soft refusals: "Gracias, pero no" = "Thanks, but no." You can also hear "No, gracias" (same idea, just different word order).
target_language_example: Gracias, pero ya tengo planes para esta noche.
native_language_example: Thanks, but I already have plans for tonight.

additional_notes: Used to thank a group of people for a specific action. Put an infinitive after por (por venir, por participar) or a noun/thing (por esto). Common in speeches, meetings, and events.
target_language_example: Gracias a todos por ayudarme con el proyecto.
native_language_example: Thanks to everyone for helping me with the project.

additional_notes: Use it to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It’s typically followed by a noun (Gracias por el espectáculo; Gracias por vuestra atención) or by an infinitive verb (Gracias por estar aquí; Gracias por llamarme de vuelta; Gracias por explicarme...). You can also use it in set phrases like Gracias por todo (“thanks for everything”).
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme hoy.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me today.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for helping you. You can add details after it (e.g., ayer “yesterday”, siempre “always”) or continue with pero… (“but…”) to add a contrast.
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme con la tarea.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with the homework.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing introduced by the masculine singular definite article el (e.g., el apoyo, el consejo). If the noun is feminine, use “gracias por la …”; if it’s plural, “gracias por los/las …”. You can also say “gracias por + [noun]” without an article in some cases.
target_language_example: Gracias por el regalo.
native_language_example: Thanks for the gift.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an invitation. After **a**, you can add a place or event (**a tu casa**, **a la fiesta**) or an action in the infinitive (**a sentarme**, **a comer**). Choose **tu** with friends/family and **su** (or **usted**) for more formal/polite situations.
target_language_example: Gracias por invitarme a cenar con ustedes.
native_language_example: Thanks for inviting me to have dinner with you (all).

additional_notes: Use this to thank someone for a specific thing or action, followed by a feminine noun: Gracias por la información / ayuda / explicación. For masculine nouns, use “gracias por el …” (Gracias por el café). You can also use it to thank someone for an abstract thing like a conversation or correction.
target_language_example: Gracias por la ayuda, de verdad.
native_language_example: Thanks for the help, really.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely in formal situations. "Su" is the formal singular "your" (usted). It’s typically followed by a noun: gracias por su tiempo (your time), su atención (your attention), su confianza (your trust). For informal "your," use "gracias por tu …".
target_language_example: Gracias por su ayuda, doctora.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, doctor.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely for assisting you. "Su" is the formal "your" (usted), common in customer service, speaking to strangers, or professional settings. With friends/family you’ll usually hear "gracias por tu ayuda".
target_language_example: Gracias por su ayuda; fue muy amable.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help; that was very kind.

meaning: “Thanks for your …” (to thank someone for something they did/are doing).
additional_notes: Use it before a masculine singular noun to say what you’re thankful for: Gracias por tu + [noun] (e.g., tu ayuda, tu tiempo). If the noun is feminine, use “Gracias por tu” + noun too (tu works for both genders), but the noun changes (e.g., gracias por tu ayuda). In very formal situations, you may see “Gracias por su …” (your = su).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for showing up or attending. You can add details with "a + place/event" (Gracias por venir a nuestro cine) or "hasta aquí" to emphasize they came a long way (Gracias por venir hasta aquí). Often said when greeting someone or at the end of a meeting.
target_language_example: Gracias por venir a mi fiesta.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming to my party.

additional_notes: Used when talking about temperature that is below zero, especially with Celsius in Spanish-speaking contexts. Common patterns: “hace X grados bajo cero” (it’s X degrees below zero), “está/estuvo a X grados bajo cero” (it is/was at X below zero), “bajar/descender a X grados bajo cero” (to drop to X below zero). You can also say “menos de X grados bajo cero” (less than X below zero).
target_language_example: Mañana por la noche vamos a estar a cuatro grados bajo cero.
native_language_example: Tomorrow night it will be four degrees below zero.

meaning: department store; large store (often selling many types of products).
additional_notes: Common in Spain to refer to big multi-department retail stores (often with clothing, cosmetics, home goods, etc.). It literally means “big warehouse/store,” but it’s usually used like “department store.”
target_language_example: Voy a ir al gran almacén para comprar ropa y un regalo.
native_language_example: I’m going to the department store to buy clothes and a gift.

meaning: “a big deal”; something important or impressive (often sarcastic).
additional_notes: Often used with ser: “Es una gran cosa” = “It’s a big deal / It’s a great thing.” In the negative it downplays something: “No es gran cosa” = “It’s not a big deal / It’s nothing special.” With article “la gran cosa” (or without in some regions) it can be ironic, meaning someone thinks they’re very important: “Se cree la gran cosa” = “She thinks she’s a big deal.”
target_language_example: No es gran cosa, pero me alegra que hayas venido.
native_language_example: It’s not a big deal, but I’m happy you came.

meaning: a great day; the big day (an important, awaited day).
additional_notes: Gran is the shortened form of grande used before a singular noun (gran día, gran momento). In context, el gran día often means “the big day” for a special event (wedding, exam, trip).
target_language_example: ¡Mucha suerte en tu entrevista mañana: es tu gran día!
native_language_example: Good luck on your interview tomorrow: it’s your big day!

additional_notes: Gran is a shortened form of grande used before a singular noun (gran error, gran idea). It emphasizes importance or severity. Common patterns: Fue un gran error. / Ese fue mi gran error. / Cometer un gran error (“to make a big mistake”).
target_language_example: Decir eso en la reunión fue un gran error.
native_language_example: Saying that in the meeting was a big mistake.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened or was true for most of a period or a big portion of something. It’s typically followed by a noun: "gran parte de su vida" (a large part of his/her life), "gran parte de su trabajo" (a large part of his/her work). "Su" can mean his, her, your (formal), or their—context tells you which.
target_language_example: Pasé gran parte de su visita hablando con él sobre el viaje.
native_language_example: I spent a large part of his visit talking with him about the trip.

meaning: “(as) big/large as” in comparisons like “X times bigger than …”.
additional_notes: Used in size comparisons, especially with quantities: **el doble de grande que** (twice as big as), **el triple de grande que** (three times as big as), **la mitad de grande que** (half as big as). It normally appears as **de grande que + [noun/pronoun]** after a number/amount, not by itself. In everyday Spanish you’ll also hear **más grande que** (“bigger than”).
target_language_example: Este apartamento es el doble de grande que el mío.
native_language_example: This apartment is twice as big as mine.

additional_notes: Used to talk about large urban areas, often implying more people, traffic, services, or “city life.” It’s simply the plural of “gran ciudad” (a big city). Depending on context, it can mean physically large cities or important/major cities (e.g., “the world’s major cities”).
target_language_example: Prefiero vivir en un pueblo pequeño, no en grandes ciudades.
native_language_example: I prefer to live in a small town, not in big cities.

meaning: a small contribution (to help a cause/effort).
additional_notes: Used especially in the phrase "poner/aportar tu grano de arena" to mean doing your small part to help. Literally "grain of sand," and it often refers to contributing time, money, or effort, even if it seems minor.
target_language_example: Cada uno puede poner su grano de arena para cuidar el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: Everyone can do their small part to take care of the environment.

additional_notes: Used to specify the historical form of the Greek language (as opposed to "griego moderno" = Modern Greek). "Antiguo" agrees with "griego" (masculine singular). You’ll often see it after the language name: "inglés antiguo", "español antiguo".
target_language_example: Estoy estudiando griego antiguo en la universidad.
native_language_example: I’m studying Ancient Greek at university.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the contemporary Greek language, often to contrast it with "griego antiguo" (Ancient Greek). It can appear in language-learning contexts (classes, books, translations): "estudio griego moderno" / "un diccionario de griego moderno".
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo griego moderno para mi viaje a Grecia.
native_language_example: I’m learning modern Greek for my trip to Greece.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say what the group is made up of or what kind of group it is: grupo de gente (a group of people), grupo de rescate (rescue team), grupo de apoyo (support group), grupo de amigos (group of friends). Often followed by a plural noun, but can also be followed by a singular noun that names a category or type (e.g., grupo de rescate).
target_language_example: Somos un grupo de estudiantes de intercambio.
native_language_example: We are a group of exchange students.

meaning: to keep quiet; to remain silent.
additional_notes: Used to talk about deliberately not speaking, often as a rule, order, or personal decision (e.g., in class, during an operation, or as a vow). Also common as an instruction in the plural: «¡Guarden silencio!» = “Be quiet!”
target_language_example: Los estudiantes deben guardar silencio durante la clase.
native_language_example: Students must keep quiet during class.

additional_notes: Used to say you will not tell other people private information. It often appears with verbs like poder (can) and saber (know how to): «No puedo guardar un secreto» / «Sé guardar un secreto». Also common with «Debo guardar un secreto» (I must keep a secret).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: sé guardar un secreto.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can keep a secret.

additional_notes: A job title for someone who protects a place (a store, warehouse, building, event). Often used with ser/estar (Soy/Es guardia de seguridad) or trabajar como (Trabaja como guardia de seguridad). The article is optional when talking about someone’s profession (Soy guardia de seguridad).
target_language_example: Mi hermano trabaja como guardia de seguridad en un centro comercial.
native_language_example: My brother works as a security guard at a mall.

meaning: civil war (a war within a country).
additional_notes: Used to describe an armed conflict between groups in the same country (not a war between different countries). Often appears with articles like "la guerra civil" or "una guerra civil" and in phrases like "el comienzo de otra guerra civil" (the start of another civil war).
target_language_example: La guerra civil duró varios años y dividió al país.
native_language_example: The civil war lasted several years and divided the country.

additional_notes: Refers to a large war involving many countries (often specifically World War I/II: "la Primera/Segunda Guerra Mundial"). It’s usually used with an article ("la") and can be modified with ordinal numbers (primera, segunda) or "otra" (another).
target_language_example: Mi bisabuelo luchó en la Segunda Guerra Mundial.
native_language_example: My great-grandfather fought in World War II.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: guitarra = “guitar” + eléctrica = “electric.” Uses feminine agreement (una guitarra eléctrica). In Spanish, you can say Tengo una guitarra eléctrica; adding Yo is optional and usually only for emphasis.
target_language_example: Quiero aprender a tocar la guitarra eléctrica.
native_language_example: I want to learn to play the electric guitar.

meaning: '(he/she/you) likes the' (used with gustar + a singular masculine noun).
additional_notes: With **gustar**, the thing you like is the grammatical subject, so Spanish literally works like “**the X is pleasing to (someone)**.” In real Spanish you’ll almost always see this with an indirect object pronoun: **me/te/le/nos/os/les gusta el + singular masculine noun**. To say who likes it, you can add **a mí, a ti, a Tom, a ella**, etc. For plural nouns use **gustan**: *Me gustan los tacos.*
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gusta el chocolate.
native_language_example: My sister likes chocolate.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "gustar," which works like "to be pleasing" in English: the thing liked ("el helado") is the grammatical subject, and the person is an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/os/les." Often you add "A + person" for clarity or emphasis: "A Tomás le gusta el helado." Use "gusta" (singular) with a singular noun like "el helado," and "gustan" with plural nouns ("Me gustan los helados"). To say you don’t like it: "No me gusta el helado."
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gusta el helado de fresa.
native_language_example: My sister likes strawberry ice cream.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar + infinitive: (A mí) me gusta estar…, (A él/ella) le gusta estar…, (A nosotros) nos gusta estar… to say someone likes being in a certain state or situation (alone, wet, surrounded by people, etc.). The person is often introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Tom le gusta…").
target_language_example: A mí me gusta estar en casa los domingos.
native_language_example: I like being at home on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gustar**, which works differently from English: the thing liked is the grammatical subject. So **A María le gusta la música** literally means “Music pleases María,” but in natural English it’s “María likes music.” You’ll almost always see it with an indirect object pronoun (**me/te/le/nos/os/les**) and sometimes **a + person** for clarity or emphasis. **La** is the feminine singular article; for masculine you’d use **gusta el**; for plural things: **gustan los/las**.
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gusta la pizza.
native_language_example: My sister likes pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to express strong liking. The thing/person liked is the grammatical subject: “Me gusta mucho esta sopa” = “I like this soup a lot” (literally: “This soup pleases me a lot”). You’ll often see it with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les) and sometimes an explicit person: “A María no le gusta mucho el fútbol.” Note: “Ella me gusta mucho” means “I like her a lot” (often with a romantic sense).
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho esta canción.
native_language_example: I like this song a lot.

meaning: “(they) like the …” (used with plural feminine nouns).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar" to talk about things people like. The person is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/os/les" (e.g., "A ella le gustan las fresas" = she likes strawberries). Because "las" is feminine plural, it’s followed by a feminine plural noun (las verduras, las fresas, las minifaldas). For masculine plural, use "gustan los"; for singular, use "gusta el/la".
target_language_example: A mí me gustan las películas de comedia.
native_language_example: I like comedy movies.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar. What is liked (“las chicas”) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les. Often appears as: “Me/Te/Le/Nos/Les gustan las chicas.” Use “gusta” (singular) if what you like is one thing (e.g., “Me gusta la chica”).
target_language_example: A mí me gustan las chicas inteligentes.
native_language_example: I like smart girls.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **gustar**. In Spanish, the thing you like (**las manzanas**) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is **plural**: *gustan*. The person who likes them is shown with an **indirect object pronoun**: *me/te/le/nos/les* (often with emphasis: *a mí, a ti, a él/ella, a nosotros, a ellos*). Example: *Me gustan las manzanas* = “I like apples” (literally, “Apples are pleasing to me”).
target_language_example: A ella le gustan las manzanas, pero a mí no.
native_language_example: She likes apples, but I don't.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like gustar to say someone likes things. In Spanish the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les): “Me gustan los pasteles” = “I like cakes.” Use “gustan” with plural nouns; with a singular noun you use “gusta” (e.g., “Me gusta el café”). “Los” is the masculine plural “the”; for feminine plural use “las” (“Me gustan las flores”).
target_language_example: ¿Te gustan los videojuegos?
native_language_example: Do you like video games?

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say that beans are pleasing to someone. The thing liked (los frijoles) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is plural: gustan. Add an indirect object pronoun for who likes them: me (I), te (you), le (he/she/you formal), nos (we), les (they/you all). Often you can add “a + name/pronoun” for clarity: A Mary le gustan los frijoles. (Note: a literal translation like “Beans please me” matches the grammar, but in English you usually say “I like beans.”)
target_language_example: A mí me gustan los frijoles, pero a mi hermano no le gustan.
native_language_example: I like beans, but my brother doesn’t.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar" to say someone likes cats. The person who likes them is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les. "Los gatos" is the thing liked, so the verb is plural: "gustan". You can add "a + person" for clarity/emphasis: "A ella le gustan los gatos."
target_language_example: ¿Te gustan los gatos?
native_language_example: Do you like cats?

additional_notes: Uses the verb **gustar**: the thing you like (**los hombres**) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes them is shown with an indirect object pronoun (**me/te/le/nos/os/les**). So you’ll often see it as **me gustan los hombres** (I like men) or **no me gustan los hombres** (I don’t like men). If you see **No es que...**, it often triggers the subjunctive: **No es que me gusten los hombres** (“It’s not that I like men”).
target_language_example: A mí me gustan los hombres altos.
native_language_example: I like tall men.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar". In Spanish, the thing being liked ("los mariscos") is the grammatical subject, so the verb is usually plural here: "gustan". Add an indirect object pronoun to say who likes it: me (I), te (you), le (he/she/you formal), nos (we), les (they/you all). You can also add "a + person" for clarity: "A Mary le gustan los mariscos."
target_language_example: A mí me gustan los mariscos, pero a mi hermano no le gustan.
native_language_example: I like seafood, but my brother doesn’t.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "gustar" with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les). The thing liked ("los perros") is the grammatical subject, so the verb is plural: "gustan". Common patterns: "Me gustan los perros" = I like dogs; "No me gustan los perros" = I don’t like dogs; "A él/ella le gustan los perros" = He/She likes dogs.
target_language_example: A mi hermana no le gustan los perros, pero a mí sí me gustan.
native_language_example: My sister doesn’t like dogs, but I do.

meaning: “would like (that) …” (to express a wish or preference about someone doing/being something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar in the conditional (gustaría) plus que to introduce what you’d like to happen. It usually triggers the subjunctive in the following clause: “Me gustaría que vinieras” = “I’d like you to come.” The subject of gustar is the thing/event you would like (e.g., “que fueras…”), and the person who wants it is an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les).
target_language_example: Me gustaría que me ayudaras mañana.
native_language_example: I’d like you to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when meeting someone (or after meeting them) to express pleasure at knowing them. Very common variants: «(Mucho) gusto conocerte» and «Qué gusto conocerte». You’ll also hear it in longer phrases like «Es un gusto conocerte», «Fue un gusto conocerte» (nice meeting you / it was a pleasure meeting you), and «Me dio gusto conocerte» (it made me happy to meet you). In many places it’s also common to say «Encantado/a» as a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: Mucho gusto conocerte, soy Laura.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, I’m Laura.

meaning: Nice to see you. / Glad to see you.
additional_notes: Common greeting (and sometimes a friendly closing) when you see someone. Often used as: «(Fue) un gusto verte» (It was nice to see you), «Qué gusto verte» (So nice to see you), or «Me dio gusto verte» / «Le dio mucho gusto verte» (I’m/He’s/She’s happy to see you; literally “It gave me/him/her pleasure to see you”). You can add a name or «amigo/a».
target_language_example: ¡Qué gusto verte otra vez, Ana!
native_language_example: So nice to see you again, Ana!

additional_notes: Written to show laughing in text or in dialogue. It can be genuine laughter or used sarcastically to mock or tease. Often repeated (“ha ha ha”) and usually separated by commas or exclamation marks depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ha ha, qué gracioso eres.
native_language_example: Haha, you’re so funny.

additional_notes: Used to say something is over or finished. It’s the present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (acabado), often translated as “has ended/has finished.” Common with events, periods of time, games, wars, negotiations, etc. Word order can vary: “El juego ha acabado” / “Ha acabado el juego.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, la reunión ya ha acabado.
native_language_example: Sorry, the meeting has already ended.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + past participle (**cambiado**) to talk about a change that has happened already, often with a result that matters now. Used with a subject (*El mundo ha cambiado*) or with a direct object using **a** for people/countries (*La guerra ha cambiado a Japón* = “The war has changed Japan”).
target_language_example: Desde que te fuiste, todo ha cambiado.
native_language_example: Since you left, everything has changed.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (haber + participle) to talk about a change that has happened up to now: someone/something is different now compared to before. Often followed by "desde..." (since...) or "ya no..." (no longer...). You can change the subject/pronoun: "he/has/hemos/han cambiado mucho".
target_language_example: Mi ciudad ha cambiado mucho en los últimos diez años.
native_language_example: My city has changed a lot in the last ten years.

additional_notes: Present perfect of caer (“to fall”). Used for physical falling (often with se: Se te ha caído algo = “You dropped something / Something fell from you”), for decreases (La temperatura ha caído = “The temperature has dropped”), and for institutions/regimes collapsing (El régimen ha caído = “The regime has fallen”). Also in the expression caer en desgracia = “to fall from favor.”
target_language_example: Se me ha caído el vaso al suelo.
native_language_example: I dropped the glass on the floor.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **haber (ha)** + past participle (**comenzado**) to say something has already started up to now. Often appears with **ya** (“already”) or **ni siquiera** (“not even yet”). Used for events, shows, battles, eclipses, etc.
target_language_example: La reunión ya ha comenzado.
native_language_example: The meeting has already started.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: "ha" (from haber) + "comprado" (past participle). It’s followed by "un" because the noun is masculine singular (e.g., un abrigo, un ordenador). With "se ha comprado un…", it often means "has bought (himself/herself) a…" (for their own use).
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha comprado un coche usado.
native_language_example: My brother has bought a used car.

additional_notes: Present perfect (he/she/it/you formal) of crecer (to grow). Used for physical growth (a person, hair, a plant) and for things that increase or expand (size, amount, a city). Often used with intensifiers like mucho/tanto/demasiado and with measurements (p. ej., tres centímetros). In "Cómo ha crecido, ¿eh?" it’s an exclamation meaning “Wow, look how much (someone) has grown.”
target_language_example: Parece que Yuki ha crecido desde la última vez.
native_language_example: It looks like Yuki has grown since the last time.

meaning: "has/have given" (present perfect of "dar"); often used in set phrases like "has begun" or "had/got" (an attack, etc.).
additional_notes: "Ha" is from "haber" and "dado" is the past participle of "dar". It forms the present perfect: "él/ella/usted ha dado" = "he/she/you (formal) has given". In idioms, "ha dado comienzo" means "has begun/has started", and "le ha dado un ataque" means "he/she had/got an attack" (something happened to them).
target_language_example: El profesor ha dado la respuesta.
native_language_example: The teacher has given the answer.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + past participle (**decidido**). Used with a third-person singular subject (él/ella/usted) or a singular noun/name (e.g., *Tom*). Often implies the decision is relevant now or has just been made.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ha decidido cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister has decided to change jobs.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **dejar** (él/ella/usted): **ha dejado**. Common patterns: **ha dejado + objeto** = “has left (something/someone)”, **ha dejado de + infinitive** = “has stopped (doing something)”, and **se ha dejado + objeto** = “has forgotten/left behind (something)” (often unintentionally), e.g., *Se ha dejado el cambio*. With body/hair: **se ha dejado la barba** = “has grown/let his beard grow.”
target_language_example: Tom ha dejado de hablarme.
native_language_example: Tom has stopped talking to me.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (dejar de + infinitive) to say an action has stopped. “Ha” is the present perfect (he/she/it has), so it often implies it stopped recently or by now: ha dejado de llover (it has stopped raining). Change the person as needed: he dejado de, has dejado de, hemos dejado de, etc.
target_language_example: Mi móvil ha dejado de cargar.
native_language_example: My phone has stopped charging.

additional_notes: Present perfect of desaparecer (“to disappear”): ha (has) + desaparecido (disappeared). Used for something that is no longer there or has gone away, often with a result that matters now. The subject can come after the verb: Ha desaparecido el dolor (“The pain has disappeared”).
target_language_example: Mi cartera ha desaparecido.
native_language_example: My wallet has disappeared.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + **dicho** (past participle of *decir*). Used for what **he/she/it has said** (often recently or with relevance now). It can also mean **has told** when there’s a person receiving the message: *Me ha dicho...* = “He/She has told me...”.
target_language_example: Mi jefe ha dicho que mañana no hay clase.
native_language_example: My boss has said that there’s no class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: "[someone] ha dicho que + clause". It's the present perfect of "decir" (he/she/it has said). Often corresponds to English "said (that)" or "has said (that)" depending on context. You can change the subject and tense: "He dicho que..." (I said...), "dijo que..." (he/she said...).
target_language_example: El guía ha dicho que el museo abre a las diez.
native_language_example: The guide said that the museum opens at ten.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "empezar" + "a" + infinitive. Used to say someone/something has recently begun doing an action: "ha empezado a + infinitive" (ha empezado a nevar, a cantar, a buscar...). Often implies a new change or recent development. Other persons: he empezado a (I’ve started to), has empezado a (you’ve started to), hemos/han empezado a (we/they’ve started to).
target_language_example: Últimamente, mi hermano ha empezado a levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: Lately, my brother has started getting up early.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "haber" (ha) + past participle (escrito) to talk about something someone has done, often with a result or relevance now. It can also be used to talk about life experience (e.g., how many books someone has written). Common with quantities like "tres", "muchos", "cientos de".
target_language_example: María ha escrito un artículo para el periódico.
native_language_example: María has written an article for the newspaper.

meaning: "has been" (often used as part of "ha estado" + gerund = "has been doing").
additional_notes: "Ha estado" is the present perfect form of **estar** (3rd person singular: "he/she/it has been"). Very commonly it’s followed by a **gerund** (verb ending in -ando/-iendo) to form **ha estado + gerund**, meaning an action has been happening recently or up to now: *ha estado mirando* = "has been looking/staring." With indirect object pronouns it becomes *me/te/le/nos/os/les ha estado...* (e.g., *te ha estado mirando* = "has been looking at you").
target_language_example: Mi jefe ha estado hablando de ese proyecto toda la semana.
native_language_example: My boss has been talking about that project all week.

meaning: "has been in / has been to" (has spent time in a place or situation).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **ha** (has) + **estado** (been) + **en** (in/on). It often talks about life experience or repeated visits (**Ha estado en Australia dos veces** = he’s been to Australia twice). It can also mean being in a situation/activity for some time: **ha estado en el teléfono por horas** = he’s been on the phone for hours. With media/activities, it can mean participation: **ha estado en películas** = he has been in movies.
target_language_example: Ella ha estado en España varias veces.
native_language_example: She has been to Spain several times.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (haber + estado) to talk about a period up to now or a recently relevant situation: Ha estado enfermo durante mucho tiempo (“He has been sick for a long time”). Often followed by time expressions like durante…, por…, desde…. You can add en cama (“in bed”) to say someone has been sick in bed. Note: with a finished past time like la semana pasada, Spanish more naturally uses the simple past (Estuvo enfermo la semana pasada).
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha estado enfermo desde el viernes.
native_language_example: My brother has been sick since Friday.

additional_notes: It’s the present perfect: **haber (ha)** + past participle **ganado**. Use it for something that has happened (often recently or with a result in the present): *Ha ganado el premio.* With **se ha ganado**, it often means **“has earned/deserved”** something (*Se ha ganado el derecho a pedir más*) or **“has won (someone) over”** (*Me ha ganado* = “it/he/she won me over”). **Ganado** doesn’t change for gender/number in this tense.
target_language_example: Mi equipo ha ganado el partido.
native_language_example: My team has won the match.

additional_notes: It’s the present perfect of gustar: ha gustado = “has been pleasing.” In Spanish, the thing you like is the grammatical subject, and the person is shown with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les. Examples: Me ha gustado el libro. (I liked the book.) / Le ha gustado el concierto. (He/She liked the concert.) Often used with a + person for emphasis: A mí también me ha gustado.
target_language_example: ¿Te ha gustado la película?
native_language_example: Did you like the movie?

meaning: “there has been / there have been” (it has existed/occurred).
