target_language_example: Conduce hacia el sur y verás el mar.
native_language_example: Drive south and you’ll see the sea.

meaning: "toward the" / "in the direction of" (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to show movement or orientation in the direction of something feminine: *hacia la casa* (toward the house), *hacia la estación* (toward the station). It can also be figurative: *hacia la salvación* (toward salvation). For masculine nouns, use **hacia el**.
target_language_example: Vamos hacia la playa.
native_language_example: We’re going toward the beach.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward the right side. Common in giving directions (often after verbs like girar/voltear “to turn”) and with mirar “to look.” In politics, it can mean leaning toward the right (conservative ideas).
target_language_example: Sigue todo recto y luego gira hacia la derecha.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and then turn to the right.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement/orientation (where to look, turn, or head). Often follows verbs like mirar (to look) or girar (to turn). You can also hear it alone as an instruction: “Hacia la izquierda.”
target_language_example: Gira hacia la izquierda en la próxima calle.
native_language_example: Turn left at the next street.

additional_notes: "Hacia" means "toward" (movement or direction), and "mí" is the object pronoun "me" used after a preposition. It’s used with verbs of movement or gestures: "venir/caminar/correr hacia mí" (come/walk/run toward me), "mirar hacia mí" (look toward me), "tender la mano hacia mí" (reach a hand toward me). Note the accent: "mí" (me) vs. "mi" (my).
target_language_example: El perro corrió hacia mí cuando abrí la puerta.
native_language_example: The dog ran toward me when I opened the door.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an -ing action with a follow-up clause using "lo que" (= "what/that which"): "haciendo lo que + verb...". It can describe what someone is in the middle of doing ("Sigue haciendo lo que...") or how/why something happens ("murió haciendo lo que...").
target_language_example: Aprendí mucho haciendo lo que me dijiste.
native_language_example: I learned a lot by doing what you told me.

additional_notes: Used to describe past weather. "Hacía" is the imperfect of "hacer" used for general conditions (especially weather): "hace frío" (it’s cold), "hacía frío" (it was cold). "Mucho" intensifies it: very/really cold. Often followed by a time expression: "ayer", "por la noche", "durante...".
target_language_example: En la montaña hacía mucho frío, así que nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: In the mountains it was very cold, so we stayed home.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "hacer" to describe past weather/background conditions. Often followed by "que" + a result: "Hacía tanto calor que..." (It was so hot that...). You’ll also see it without "que" when giving the reason for an action: "Como hacía tanto calor, ..." (Since it was so hot, ...).
target_language_example: Ayer hacía tanto calor que nos quedamos en casa con el aire acondicionado.
native_language_example: Yesterday it was so hot that we stayed home with the air conditioning.

additional_notes: Used to describe the weather in the past (imperfect: hacía) and introduce a consequence with que. Common pattern: “Hacía tanto + noun + que …” (e.g., hacía tanto calor que…). Often followed by a verb in the past describing what happened as a result.
target_language_example: Hacía tanto frío que se me quedaron las manos heladas.
native_language_example: It was so cold that my hands got freezing cold.

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask someone to do something; it uses the usted command form (haga). Often followed by an infinitive (haga el favor de + verb). Common in service situations or when you want to sound extra courteous; with the wrong tone it can also sound a bit stern.
target_language_example: Haga el favor de cerrar la puerta, por favor.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

additional_notes: Uses the usted command form of **hacer** (*haga*). Common patterns: **Haga lo que + verb (subjunctive)** = “Whatever you do…” (*Haga lo que haga…*), **Haga lo que pueda** = “Do what you can,” **Haga lo que tenga que hacer** = “Do what you have to do,” and **Haga lo que + clause** = “Do what…” (*Haga lo que le han dicho*).
target_language_example: Haga lo que haga, no se rinda.
native_language_example: Whatever you do, don’t give up.

meaning: “do whatever you want / let him (or her) do whatever (he or she) wants.”
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive (haga, quiera). Often said as a permissive/indifferent response meaning “Fine—let him/her do whatever he/she wants.” Common with dejar/deja/deja que (“let”) or alone: “Que haga lo que quiera.” You can change the person: haga (usted/él/ella), hagas (tú), hagan (ustedes/ellos/ellas); quiera/quieras/quieran.
target_language_example: Si no quiere escuchar, que haga lo que quiera.
native_language_example: If he doesn’t want to listen, let him do whatever he wants.

additional_notes: Used with the ustedes command hagan (“do”) followed by lo que (“what/whatever”). It often introduces something like “hagan lo que les digo” = “do what I tell you.” The verb after lo que can change (digo/diga) depending on meaning and grammar, but the overall idea is giving instructions to a group (or to one person in some regions where ustedes is used).
target_language_example: Por favor, hagan lo que les pido.
native_language_example: Please do what I’m asking you.

meaning: “Do whatever you want.” (to more than one person)
additional_notes: Uses the ustedes command form of hacer: hagan. lo que quieran means “whatever you want,” referring to an unspecified action. Often said to give permission or show indifference (“Fine, do what you want”). You may also see it after que: Que hagan lo que quieran (“Let them do whatever they want”).
target_language_example: Si no les gusta el plan, hagan lo que quieran.
native_language_example: If you don’t like the plan, do whatever you want.

additional_notes: Formal plural command (ustedes) of hacer: “make/do.” Used by an announcer or dealer to tell a group to bet (e.g., in a casino, game, or competition). Can also be used humorously before revealing an outcome: “Place your bets (and let’s see what happens).”
target_language_example: ¡Hagan sus apuestas, que el juego va a empezar!
native_language_example: Place your bets—the game is about to start!

meaning: “no matter what you do” / “whatever you do”.
additional_notes: Used to introduce advice, instructions, or a warning that applies in every case. It uses the present subjunctive of hacer (hagas) in a fixed pattern: “Hagas lo que hagas, …”. You can also say it alone for emphasis, like “Whatever you do.”
target_language_example: Hagas lo que hagas, no abras esa puerta.
native_language_example: Whatever you do, don’t open that door.

meaning: "I do things" (how I do tasks / handle things).
additional_notes: "Hago" is the "I" form of "hacer" (to do/make). "Hago las cosas" is often followed by an adverb or phrase that explains *how* you do things: "bien" (well), "a mi manera" (my way), "de la misma manera" (the same way). It can refer to tasks, habits, or your way of doing things in general.
target_language_example: Perdón, hago las cosas despacio, pero las hago bien.
native_language_example: Sorry, I do things slowly, but I do them well.

meaning: “I do what …” (followed by a verb or phrase).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you do, often with a following expression like quiero (I want), debo hacer (I must do), es mejor (is best), etc. It’s the first-person singular present of hacer (to do/make) + lo que (“what/that which”).
target_language_example: Hago lo que puedo para ayudarte.
native_language_example: I do what I can to help you.

additional_notes: From the verb cambiar (“to change”) in the present perfect: haber (han) + past participle (cambiado). Used to say that something has changed up to now, often with time expressions like “en los últimos…”, “desde entonces”, or “nunca”. The subject is plural: ellos/ellas/ustedes, or a plural thing (las reglas, las circunstancias).
target_language_example: Desde el año pasado, las cosas han cambiado mucho.
native_language_example: Since last year, things have changed a lot.

meaning: “they have given” / “they gave” (present perfect of dar).
additional_notes: Used with an implied subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes). Common with object pronouns: me/te/le/nos/les han dado… (“they’ve given me/you/him/us/them…”). With "dar a" it can mean “to hit / to shoot (and hit)”: ¿Le han dado a X? = “Did they hit X?”
target_language_example: Me han dado la llave del cuarto.
native_language_example: They gave me the room key.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decidir (to decide): ellos/ellas/ustedes han decidido + infinitive (han decidido no comprar…) or + que + clause (han decidido que…). In many contexts it can be translated as either “have decided” or simple past “decided,” depending on how recent/relevant the decision is.
target_language_example: Mis padres han decidido mudarse a otra ciudad.
native_language_example: My parents have decided to move to another city.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "decir" with an implied subject "ellos/ellas/ustedes". Often used when the speaker doesn’t specify exactly who said it ("they" = people, authorities, others). The object can be explicit with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les han dicho" = "they told me/you/him/her/us/them". Frequently followed by "que" to report information: "Han dicho que..." = "They said that...". Negative: "no han dicho" = "they haven’t said/told".
target_language_example: Me han dicho que mañana no hay clase.
native_language_example: They told me that there’s no class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to describe an activity that has been happening recently or up to now: "Han estado rastreando..." = "They've been tracking...". It can also mean "have been" in a state/situation: "Han estado juntos" (have been together), "han estado casados" (have been married), "nunca han estado con una mujer" (have never been with a woman). Sometimes it's used in set phrases like "ha(n) estado a la venta" = "has/have been on sale".
target_language_example: Últimamente han estado trabajando hasta tarde.
native_language_example: Lately, they've been working late.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **haber** (**han**) + past participle **hecho** to talk about something **they** did at an unspecified time in the past that matters now (often used like English “have done”). The subject can be explicit (**ellos/ellas/ustedes**) or implied by context.
target_language_example: No sé qué han hecho, pero están muy felices.
native_language_example: I don’t know what they’ve done, but they’re very happy.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **ir** for **ellos/ellas/ustedes**: **han ido** = “they/you (plural) have gone.” With **las cosas han ido bien/mal/a peor**, it often means “things have gone/been going well/badly/gotten worse” (more about how something turned out than physical movement). With **se** (**se han ido**), it means “they have left / everyone has gone.”
target_language_example: Últimamente, las clases han ido mejor.
native_language_example: Lately, the classes have been going better.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "llegar" (to arrive): haber (han) + past participle (llegado). Used with a plural subject (they/you all). Often followed by "a" + place: "Han llegado a Madrid." You can negate it: "No han llegado todavía" = "They haven't arrived yet."
target_language_example: Ya han llegado los invitados.
native_language_example: The guests have already arrived.

additional_notes: Present perfect of pasar (to pass) with an implied subject like el tiempo / los años / los meses (“time/years/months have passed”). Often used with a time expression (Han pasado cinco años) or with desde que / desde (“since”) to say how much time has passed since something happened. It can also be used more generally with cosas (“things/events have happened”).
target_language_example: Han pasado dos semanas desde que empezé el trabajo.
native_language_example: Two weeks have passed since I started the job.

meaning: “It’s been ten years since…” / “Ten years have passed since…”
additional_notes: Used to say how much time has elapsed since an event. Very common pattern: **Han pasado + [amount of time] + desde + ...**. Use **desde que + verb clause** (Desde que la vi / Desde que murió) or **desde + noun** (Desde su muerte). You can change the time: *Han pasado dos meses desde…*, *Han pasado muchos años desde…*.
target_language_example: Han pasado diez años desde que nos mudamos aquí.
native_language_example: It’s been ten years since we moved here.

meaning: two years have passed / it’s been two years.
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (han pasado) to say that two years have elapsed up to now. Very common with "desde que" (since) to mark the starting point: "Han pasado dos años desde que…" You can swap the number: "Han pasado tres meses", "Han pasado cinco días". Also used alone as a full sentence: "Han pasado dos años."
target_language_example: Han pasado dos años desde que me mudé a esta ciudad.
native_language_example: It’s been two years since I moved to this city.

additional_notes: Present perfect of ser: haber (han) + past participle (sido). Used with plural subjects (ellos/ellas/ustedes) to talk about states or situations that have happened up to now or have present relevance. Often followed by an adjective or past participle (e.g., han sido intensas, han sido leídos).
target_language_example: Este año las clases han sido interesantes.
native_language_example: This year the classes have been interesting.

meaning: "have been" (they/you all have been) — present perfect of *ser*.
additional_notes: Formed by **han** (present of *haber*) + **sido** (past participle of *ser*). It’s used to talk about what someone/something **has been** up to now or in a recent past with relevance to the present: *Han sido muy amables* (They’ve been very kind). It can also appear in impersonal/time expressions: *Han sido necesarias casi dos semanas...* (“It has taken/almost two weeks have been necessary...”). In some contexts it can mean “it was/they were” when identifying who did something: *Seguro que han sido esos delincuentes* (“I’m sure it was those criminals”).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde han sido tus vacaciones este año?
native_language_example: Where have your vacations been this year?

additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (han) + past participle (visto). Used for experiences or things seen up to now. Often means “they have seen” (ellos/ellas/ustedes), with the subject understood from context.
target_language_example: ¿Ya han visto la película?
native_language_example: Have you all seen the movie yet?

additional_notes: Used with **estar**: **estar harto/a/os/as de + noun** or **de + infinitive**. It agrees with the subject (**harto, harta, hartos, hartas**) and expresses strong annoyance or having had too much of something/someone.
target_language_example: Estoy harto de esperar; vámonos ya.
native_language_example: I’m sick of waiting; let’s go now.

additional_notes: Future tense of hacer (“to do/make”): haré = “I will do.” Used to promise or emphasize willingness to do whatever is necessary, often with por (“for”) or para (“in order to”), or followed by que + subjunctive: “haré cualquier cosa que me digas (que haga)” = “I’ll do anything you tell me (to do).”
target_language_example: Haré cualquier cosa para ayudarte a salir de aquí.
native_language_example: I’ll do anything to help you get out of here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with what you will do, often followed by subjunctive (e.g., "haré lo que me pidas"). Common extensions: "haré lo que sea necesario" (I’ll do whatever is necessary), "haré lo que tenga que hacer" (I’ll do what I have to do), "haré lo que usted quiera" (I’ll do what you want).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: haré lo que haga falta.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll do whatever is needed.

meaning: I’ll do whatever it takes / I’ll do anything.
additional_notes: Expresses strong determination or willingness to do anything to achieve a goal or help someone. Often followed by para + infinitive (purpose): “Haré lo que sea para salir…”. Also common with por + someone (for someone’s sake): “Haré lo que sea por ti.” The verb is future tense (haré = “I will do”) and lo que sea means “whatever (it may be)”.
target_language_example: Haré lo que sea para recuperar mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I’ll do whatever it takes to get my job back.

meaning: “I’ll do everything I can…” / “I’ll do all that’s (within my power)…”.
additional_notes: Used to promise you’ll make your best effort. It’s typically followed by phrases like “a mi alcance” (within my reach), “en mi mano” (in my hands), or “en mi poder” (within my power) to emphasize you’ll do whatever is possible.
target_language_example: Haré todo lo que esté en mi poder para resolverlo hoy.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to solve it today.

meaning: I’ll do everything I can / I’ll do my best.
additional_notes: A promise to make a strong effort. Uses the future tense (haré = “I will do”) plus the subjunctive (pueda = “I can / may be able to”) after lo que (“what/whatever”). Often followed by para + infinitive (“in order to…”) or por + someone (“for you”).
target_language_example: No puedo garantizarlo, pero haré todo lo que pueda para ayudarte.
native_language_example: I can’t guarantee it, but I’ll do everything I can to help you.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional tense (haría = “would do”) to express willingness/hypothetical devotion. Follow it with an object pronoun or person: por ti (for you, informal), por usted (for you, formal), por ustedes (for you all), por vosotros (for you all, Spain), por él/ella (for him/her).
target_language_example: Haría cualquier cosa por mi familia.
native_language_example: I would do anything for my family.

meaning: “I’d do anything for …” / “I’d do whatever it takes for …”
additional_notes: Uses the conditional haría (“I would do”) plus lo que fuera (“whatever it might be”) to express willingness to do anything to help someone or to achieve a goal. Often followed by a person (por ti, por ella) or an objective/idea (por amor, por ganar dinero). You can change the subject: Yo haría…, Él/Ella haría…, Haríamos…
target_language_example: Haría lo que fuera por ayudarte.
native_language_example: I’d do anything to help you.

additional_notes: Present perfect of cambiar, used to say someone has changed from before to now. Often appears with adverbs like mucho (“a lot”) or nada (“at all”): No has cambiado nada = “You haven’t changed at all.” You can add the subject for emphasis: Tú has cambiado.
target_language_example: Has cambiado mucho desde el año pasado.
native_language_example: You’ve changed a lot since last year.

meaning: “you have left” / “you have let (allowed)” (present perfect of *dejar*).
additional_notes: *Has dejado* = **haber (has) + past participle (dejado)**. It’s used for past actions with a connection to the present (“you’ve left/you’ve allowed/you’ve stopped/you’ve abandoned”). Common patterns: **has dejado entrar** (you let [someone] in), **has dejado a alguien** (you left someone / broke up with someone), **has dejado atrás** (you left behind), **has dejado reposar** (you let [it] rest), **te has dejado X** (you left/forgot X), **has dejado plantado** (you stood [someone] up).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has dejado la puerta abierta?
native_language_example: Why did you leave the door open?

meaning: 'you have said' / 'you said' (present perfect of *decir*, informal singular).
additional_notes: Used with **tú** to talk about what someone has said, often with **que**: *Has dicho que...* (“You said that…”). In many contexts it translates as simple past in English (“you said”), especially when referring to something just said or relevant now. Negative: *No has dicho...*; also common in questions/complaints: *Aún no me has dicho...* (“You still haven’t told me…”).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has dicho eso?
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

additional_notes: Used with tú to say someone has been in a place or state up to now (or at some time before now that matters in the present). Often followed by an adjective (ausente, enfermo), a place (ahí, en casa), or a gerund to show an ongoing/repeated action (has estado dando vueltas = “you’ve been hanging around/going around”).
target_language_example: ¿Has estado en México alguna vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Mexico?

meaning: “you have been in/to …” (you’ve visited or spent time somewhere).
additional_notes: Present perfect (tú): haber (has) + estado (past participle of estar) + en. Used to talk about life experience or something that happened at an unspecified time in the past, often with “alguna vez” (ever) or “ya” (already). With places it usually means “have been to,” but it can also mean “have been in” (present in) a situation or group for a period of time (e.g., “has estado en mi familia…”).
target_language_example: ¿Has estado en Madrid alguna vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Madrid?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about actions that are completed but connected to the present (results, experience, or recent past). It agrees with “tú” (informal singular “you”): has = you have; hecho = done/made. Common patterns: “¿Qué has hecho?” (What have you done?), “Has hecho una promesa” (You’ve made a promise).
target_language_example: ¿Qué has hecho con las llaves?
native_language_example: What have you done with the keys?

meaning: you did the right thing; you did well.
additional_notes: Used to approve or reassure someone about something they already did. Often followed by an action with "al + infinitive": "Has hecho bien al llamar..." (You did well to call...). Can also be said on its own: "Has hecho bien."
target_language_example: Has hecho bien al decir la verdad.
native_language_example: You did the right thing by telling the truth.

additional_notes: Present perfect of oír (“to hear”), used to ask if someone heard something or to say they have. Often appears with a direct object: ¿Lo has oído? (“Did you hear it?”) / Has oído lo que he dicho (“You heard what I said”). Can also be followed by de to mean “have you heard from/about”: ¿Has oído de él? / No has oído nada de ella (“You haven’t heard anything from/about her”).
target_language_example: ¿Has oído la noticia?
native_language_example: Have you heard the news?

additional_notes: Second-person singular present perfect of perder (haber + perdido). Used to say someone has lost a game/competition (“Has perdido”), or that they’ve lost/missed something or a step in a process (“has perdido un paso”). It can also be followed by what was lost: “has perdido la cabeza” = “you’ve lost your mind/head.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, has perdido la llave otra vez.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’ve lost the key again.

meaning: “you have put/placed” (also, with a reflexive pronoun: “you’ve gotten / you’ve put on”).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect: haber (has) + past participle (puesto). It’s used for things you’ve done recently or that matter now. Common patterns: **has puesto + object** (“you’ve put X”): *Has puesto a mamá muy enferma* (“You’ve made Mom very sick”); **te has puesto + adjective** (from *ponerse* = “to become/get”): *Te has puesto celosa* (“You’ve gotten jealous”); **te has puesto + clothing** (“to put on”): *Ya te has puesto el uniforme* (“You’ve already put on your uniform”).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde has puesto las llaves?
native_language_example: Where have you put the keys?

meaning: "you have been" (present perfect of ser, tú).
additional_notes: Used to describe what someone has been like up to now (often with adjectives or nouns): Has sido muy amable / Has sido una buena amiga. It uses the tú form: has + sido. For usted, use ha sido; for vosotros, habéis sido.
target_language_example: Has sido muy paciente hoy.
native_language_example: You’ve been very patient today.

additional_notes: Present perfect (tú) of tener: haber (has) + past participle (tenido). Used to talk about something you’ve had/experienced up to now, often with words like alguna vez (ever), ya (already), nunca (never). Depending on context, it can mean having an illness/fever, having time/work, having enough of something, or having had an experience before.
target_language_example: ¿Has tenido tiempo para comer hoy?
native_language_example: Have you had time to eat today?

additional_notes: Present perfect of "venir" (venir → venido) with "tú": "haber" (has) + past participle (venido). It’s used to say that someone has arrived or came (often with a sense of a recent or relevant past), and it can be followed by extra details: "has venido aquí", "has venido en coche", "has venido a + infinitive" (you came to do something), "has venido al lugar adecuado" (you came to the right place).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has venido tan temprano?
native_language_example: Why did you come so early?

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb haber (has) + past participle (visto) to talk about something you’ve seen at an unspecified time up to now. Common in questions like "¿Has visto...?" and in statements like "Has visto miles de ellos" (You’ve seen thousands of them).
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mis llaves?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

meaning: "you’ve come back / you’ve returned"; also "you’ve done (something) again" (with a + infinitive).
additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (has) + past participle (vuelto). It can mean you have returned (often implied: to a place or situation): "¡Qué bien que has vuelto!". Very commonly it’s followed by "a" + infinitive to mean “you’ve ___ again” (repetition): "Has vuelto a cometer el mismo error" = “You made the same mistake again.”
target_language_example: Has vuelto a llegar tarde otra vez.
native_language_example: You’ve arrived late again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what has happened or what is true from the past up to the present moment. It often implies things could change later. Common as a short reply: “Hasta ahora, bien” = “So far, so good.”
target_language_example: No he tenido problemas hasta ahora.
native_language_example: I haven’t had any problems so far.

meaning: up to there; as far as that point; (figuratively) that’s enough / stop there.
additional_notes: Refers to a limit or endpoint in space, progress, or action. It’s common in directions ("Go up to there...") and also used to set a boundary or stop something: "Hasta ahí está bien" = "That’s fine up to that point" / "That’s enough." Said alone ("Hasta ahí") it can mean "Up to there" or "Stop right there," depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: No sigas discutiendo: hasta ahí.
native_language_example: Don’t keep arguing: that’s enough.

additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching a place or point (physical or figurative): coming all the way here (“venir/llegar hasta aquí”), something extending/reaching here (“llegar hasta aquí”), or to mark a stopping point in a story/presentation (“Hasta aquí…” = “That’s it up to here / So far…”). Often implies effort or distance when used with venir/llegar.
target_language_example: Lo siento por hacerte venir hasta aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry for making you come all the way here.

meaning: to a certain extent; up to a point.
additional_notes: Used to say you agree with something or that something is true/possible, but only partially (not completely). It can go at the end of a sentence or at the beginning for emphasis (Hasta cierto punto, ...). Often contrasted with “pero no del todo” (but not completely).
target_language_example: Me gusta el trabajo, pero solo hasta cierto punto.
native_language_example: I like the job, but only up to a point.

additional_notes: Used to mark a limit or extent (distance, ability, etc.): "hasta donde pude" = "as far as I could." Very common in the expression "hasta donde sé" / "hasta donde yo sé" = "as far as I know" (based on the information I have).
target_language_example: Te acompaño hasta donde pueda.
native_language_example: I’ll come with you as far as I can.

additional_notes: Used to limit what you’re saying to your current knowledge or information (often implying it could be wrong or incomplete). Common at the start of a sentence: “Hasta donde sé, …”.
target_language_example: Hasta donde sé, la reunión es mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting is tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement as being based on your current knowledge (you’re not 100% sure). It often comes at the beginning of a sentence and is followed by a comma. You can change the person: “hasta donde yo sé” (I know), “hasta donde él/ella sabe” (he/she knows), “hasta donde sabemos” (we know).
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, la reunión es mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting is tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used to give information with some uncertainty, meaning “based on what I know.” Often followed by a statement about someone/something. You can swap the subject: “Hasta donde yo sé, ella… / ellos… / usted…” or omit it: “Hasta donde yo sé, es honesto.”
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, él trabaja aquí desde 2020.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he has worked here since 2020.

meaning: 'until the' or 'to the' (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with destinations or limits (physical or figurative): *hasta el asiento trasero* = 'as far as the back seat', *hasta el fin del mundo* = 'to/until the end of the world'. It also appears in farewells and scheduling: *Hasta el jueves* = 'See you on Thursday' / 'Until Thursday'. Use **hasta la** before feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Camina hasta el parque y luego vuelve a casa.
native_language_example: Walk to the park and then come back home.

meaning: up to your neck; neck-deep (overwhelmed/in deep).
additional_notes: Used literally for a physical level (e.g., water reaching your neck) and very often figuratively to mean you have too much of something or you’re deeply involved/in trouble (work, debt, problems). Common patterns: "estar hasta el cuello de + noun" ("Estoy hasta el cuello de trabajo") and "estar hasta el cuello con + noun" ("Está hasta el cuello con deudas").
target_language_example: Esta semana estoy hasta el cuello de exámenes.
native_language_example: This week I’m up to my neck in exams.

meaning: until the end; all the way (to the end).
additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to the last moment or the last part of something (a game, meeting, movie, etc.), or up to the end point of a route. Often answers “How long?” (stay until the end) or “How far?” (go all the way to the end of the street). Can also imply persistence: insistir hasta el final (“keep insisting to the very end”).
target_language_example: Me quedé hasta el final de la película.
native_language_example: I stayed until the end of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything that has happened up to the present time (or up to a specific time you mention). Very common at the start of a sentence: "Hasta el momento, ...". It can also be followed by "de + event" to mean "up to the time of ..." (e.g., "hasta el momento del crimen").
target_language_example: Hasta el momento, no hemos tenido ningún problema.
native_language_example: So far, we haven’t had any problems.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize going all the way to the end, without leaving anything out: time (hasta el último segundo), effort/life (hasta el último aliento), completeness (hasta el último detalle), or money (hasta el último dólar). It agrees with what follows: hasta el último segundo/detalle/dólar; hasta la última vez; hasta los últimos minutos; hasta las últimas consecuencias.
target_language_example: Lo revisaré hasta el último detalle antes de enviarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll check it down to the very last detail before sending it.

meaning: until then; up to that time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the period of time leading up to a specific moment in the future or past that was just mentioned or is understood from context. Often works as a transition at the start of a sentence ("Hasta entonces, ...") or can stand alone as a short goodbye/closing meaning "until then."
target_language_example: Nos vemos el viernes; hasta entonces, cuídate.
native_language_example: See you on Friday; until then, take care.

meaning: up to today; until today (so far).
additional_notes: Used to mark the time limit ending today (up to the present moment). Often implies that something was true/unknown before now, and may change from today onward (e.g., “Nunca había visto uno hasta hoy” = you’re seeing it for the first time today). Can also be a short standalone phrase meaning “Up to today/So far.”
target_language_example: Hasta hoy, no hemos tenido ningún problema.
native_language_example: Up to today, we haven’t had any problem.

additional_notes: Used to mark an end point in time, distance, or limit: hasta la una (until 1 o’clock), hasta la mitad (up to halfway). Also common in set phrases like Hasta la próxima (until next time). It’s the same as hasta el, but with feminine nouns (la).
target_language_example: El restaurante está abierto hasta la medianoche.
native_language_example: The restaurant is open until midnight.

additional_notes: Used to mark an end time: something continues up to nighttime. Often appears in the pattern “desde … hasta la noche” (“from … until nighttime”). By itself, it can be a short goodbye meaning “See you tonight.”
target_language_example: Tengo clase hasta la noche.
native_language_example: I have class until nighttime.

additional_notes: A common friendly way to say goodbye, implying you expect to see the person again. Often used at the end of conversations, in person, on the phone, or in messages. You can also hear/see the shorter version: "hasta la próxima" or "hasta la próxima vez" (until the next time).
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. ¡Hasta la próxima!
native_language_example: Well, I’m going. See you next time!

additional_notes: A common farewell used when leaving, often implying you’ll see the person again. You can say it by itself or with someone’s name ("Hasta la vista, Sara"). It’s a set phrase; literally it’s “until the sight/view,” but it’s used like “see you.”
target_language_example: Me tengo que ir; hasta la vista.
native_language_example: I have to go; see you later.

meaning: to the last drop; completely (leaving nothing).
additional_notes: Used literally with drinks/liquids (drinking/using every last bit), and figuratively to mean taking or squeezing every last bit of something (time, money, effort, etc.). Often follows verbs like "beber" (to drink), "exprimir" (to squeeze), or "aprovechar" (to make the most of).
target_language_example: Aproveché mis vacaciones hasta la última gota.
native_language_example: I enjoyed my vacation to the fullest.

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say goodbye, often implying you may see the person again later (today or another time). Used in both formal and informal situations. Often said by itself or after phrases like “bien” (okay) or “de nada” (you’re welcome).
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; hasta luego.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; see you later.

additional_notes: Most often means "until tomorrow" when talking about how long something lasts (e.g., quedarse hasta mañana = to stay until tomorrow). It can also be used as a goodbye meaning "see you tomorrow". Literally "until tomorrow."
target_language_example: Nos vemos; hasta mañana.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow.

meaning: 'until further notice' (until you hear a new update/instruction).
additional_notes: Used in announcements to say something will continue indefinitely, and will only change when someone informs you. Common with closures, freezes/suspensions, policies, or temporary arrangements.
target_language_example: La reunión queda pospuesta hasta nuevo aviso.
native_language_example: The meeting is postponed until further notice.

additional_notes: A common, polite goodbye used when you expect to see the person again in the near future. Often used on its own ("Hasta pronto.") or with thanks ("Hasta pronto y muchas gracias.").
target_language_example: Me tengo que ir; hasta pronto.
native_language_example: I have to go; see you soon.

additional_notes: Introduces a time limit and is followed by an action/event: something continues up to the moment that happens. Very common with past actions ("...hasta que se rompió") and with "No fue hasta que..." = "It wasn’t until...".
target_language_example: Me quedé despierto hasta que llegaste.
native_language_example: I stayed awake until you arrived.

additional_notes: Used to mark an endpoint in time: an action continues up to the moment when something happens. The "se" is often part of a reflexive verb (e.g., acostarse = to go to bed) or a change-of-state verb (e.g., oscurecerse/oscurecer = to get dark), and it can also appear with passive/impersonal ideas (e.g., hasta que se demuestre = until it is proven). After "hasta que", Spanish often uses the subjunctive when the event is not yet known/hasn’t happened, and the indicative when it’s a completed/past fact.
target_language_example: Esperamos aquí hasta que se abra la tienda.
native_language_example: We’ll wait here until the store opens.

additional_notes: Used to set a condition that lasts up to the moment you do something. It’s often followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (vuelva, llegue, diga, baje) because it refers to a future/unknown moment. In commands, it can sound firm or authoritative: "Nadie sale… hasta que yo lo diga."
target_language_example: Quédate aquí hasta que yo vuelva.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back.

additional_notes: A strong, often emotional or dramatic goodbye implying you won’t see the person/place again. It’s also used in titles/dedications (e.g., to a country or someone who has died). Less common in everyday casual goodbyes than "hasta luego" or "hasta mañana".
target_language_example: Me voy a otra ciudad; hasta siempre.
native_language_example: I’m moving to another city; farewell forever.

additional_notes: Used to say someone stays awake or something lasts until a late time. Often with verbs like "quedarse" (to stay) and "estar" (to be): "quedarse despierto/a hasta tarde" = "to stay up late."
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; me quedé despierto hasta tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I stayed up late.

additional_notes: Used to say an action continues late into the night. Common with ongoing activities (trabajar, estudiar, escuchar música) and often implies “later than usual.” You can also hear the shorter version “hasta tarde” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos despiertos hasta tarde por la noche hablando.
native_language_example: We stayed up until late at night talking.

meaning: "even you" (used to express surprise or emphasis).
additional_notes: Uses "hasta" with a person/pronoun to mean “even …,” often implying “if even you (of all people)…” It’s common in spoken Spanish for emphasis, and it can sound a bit teasing or shocked depending on tone. Often used with exclamations: "¡Hasta tú...!"
target_language_example: ¡Hasta tú lo entiendes!
native_language_example: Even you understand it!

additional_notes: Uses "hay" (from haber) to say something exists or is present. Often followed by a place: "Hay algo aquí" (There’s something here), or by a relative clause with "que": "Hay algo que necesito decirte" (There’s something I need to tell you). In questions, intonation (or "¿") makes it mean "Is there something…?": "¿Hay algo que pueda hacer?"
target_language_example: ¿Hay algo que te preocupe?
native_language_example: Is there something that’s worrying you?

meaning: 'there's something that' (I/we need/want to talk about).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic you want or need to discuss. Structure: "hay algo" (there is something) + "de lo que" (about which/that) + a verb like "hablar" (to talk). Often followed by "debemos/tenemos que/quiero" + "hablar" + "contigo/te".
target_language_example: Hay algo de lo que quiero hablar contigo cuando tengas un momento.
native_language_example: There’s something I want to talk to you about when you have a moment.

meaning: "is there anything else that" / "there is something else that".
additional_notes: Used to introduce an additional thing (a question, fact, or task) beyond what was already mentioned. It often comes before a verb in the subjunctive after a question (e.g., "¿Hay algo más que quieras?") and before an infinitive or obligation phrase (e.g., "hay algo más que debo hacer").
target_language_example: ¿Hay algo más que necesites hoy?
native_language_example: Is there anything else that you need today?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified thing you want to say/do/show/mention. Often followed by a verb phrase: "Hay algo que quiero decirte" (something I want to tell you) or "Hay algo que debes ver" (something you should see). "Hay" is the common way to say "there is/there are" in Spanish.
target_language_example: Hay algo que necesito preguntarte.
native_language_example: There’s something I need to ask you.

meaning: “There’s something I need to / I must …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce something important you feel obligated to say, do, show, or know. It’s followed by an infinitive: hay algo que debo + decirte (tell you), decirle (tell you—formal/you/he/she), mostrarte (show you), saber (know). Common for serious or sensitive topics.
target_language_example: Hay algo que debo preguntarte antes de irme.
native_language_example: There’s something I need to ask you before I leave.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you want to say/show/teach/protect, etc. It’s often followed by an infinitive: "Hay algo que quiero decirte/mostrarte/enseñarte". You can also add an indirect object: "Hay algo que quiero decirle" (to you/formal you).
target_language_example: Hay algo que quiero preguntarte.
native_language_example: There’s something I want to ask you.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone exists or is present in a place/situation. "Hay" is the impersonal form of "haber" meaning "there is/there are" (it doesn’t change for singular/plural), and it’s often followed by a location: "Hay alguien aquí / ahí / en casa". You can also add "más" for “someone else”: "Hay alguien más".
target_language_example: ¿Hay alguien en casa?
native_language_example: Is there anyone at home?

additional_notes: Used to put something in perspective and say you shouldn’t focus too much on one issue because other things matter more. Often followed by “que + noun/infinitive”: “Hay cosas más importantes que el dinero” (…than money), “Hay cosas más importantes de las que preocuparse” (…to worry about).
target_language_example: No te enojes por eso; hay cosas más importantes.
native_language_example: Don’t get mad about that; there are more important things.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about certain tasks, facts, or situations. Often followed by a verb clause: "Hay cosas que necesito hacer" (There are things I need to do). In negative statements it’s common with "no se pueden" / "no se pueden dejar": "Hay cosas que no se pueden dejar al azar" (There are things you can’t leave to chance).
target_language_example: Hay cosas que no puedo explicar ahora.
native_language_example: There are things I can’t explain right now.

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (from *haber*) to say that something exists/there is/there are. **Estaciones** here means the seasons of the year (primavera, verano, otoño, invierno). Often used with a place or time: *En Japón hay cuatro estaciones* / *Hay cuatro estaciones al año*.
target_language_example: En mi país hay cuatro estaciones, pero el invierno es muy corto.
native_language_example: In my country there are four seasons, but winter is very short.

additional_notes: Used to say that two of something exist or are present. “Hay” is used for existence/presence (not *estar*). Often followed by a noun or by “que + verb” to describe which two: “Hay dos que…”.
target_language_example: En mi clase hay dos estudiantes nuevos.
native_language_example: In my class there are two new students.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about some people (not everyone). It’s common for talking about habits, opinions, or beliefs. Verb agreement: "hay" is always singular, but the following verb changes depending on the people mentioned (e.g., "hay gente que cree" / "hay gente que creen").
target_language_example: Hay gente que prefiere caminar en vez de tomar el autobús.
native_language_example: There are people who prefer to walk instead of taking the bus.

meaning: "there are thousands of" / "there are lots of".
additional_notes: Used to say that a very large number of something exists. It’s built with: hay (there is/are) + miles de (thousands of) + a plural noun. For emphasis you may also see bigger numbers, e.g., "hay miles de millones de" = "there are billions of".
target_language_example: En esta playa hay miles de conchas.
native_language_example: There are thousands of shells on this beach.

meaning: "there is/are a lot of" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that a large amount or quantity exists. "Hay" is the verb form meaning "there is/there are". "Mucha" agrees with a feminine singular noun (e.g., comida, agua, demanda). For other forms: masculine singular "hay mucho" (tiempo), feminine plural "hay muchas" (personas), masculine plural "hay muchos" (problemas). You can also add "más" for comparison: "hay mucha más..." = "there is much more...".
target_language_example: Hoy hay mucha gente en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Today there are a lot of people at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal verb phrase "hay" (from "haber") to say that people exist/are present somewhere. Common with a place: "Hay mucha gente en..."; and with "aquí/allí" (here/there). "Hay" stays the same even if the noun is plural (not *hayn*).
target_language_example: Hoy hay mucha gente en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Today there are a lot of people at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., ventanas, razones, flores, pinturas) to say that many of something exist/are present. It’s the phrase "hay" (there is/are) + "muchas" (many, fem. pl.). You can also use "hay muchos" with masculine plural nouns.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay muchas cosas que ver.
native_language_example: In this city there are many things to see.

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (from *haber*) to say that something exists/there is/there are. **Hay muchas cosas + adjective** = “There are many things that are …” (e.g., *hay muchas cosas raras*). **Hay muchas cosas por + infinitive** means “There are many things to + verb” (*por concluir/descubrir*).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: hay muchas cosas que podemos intentar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are many things we can try.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a list or general idea of many things, followed by a verb phrase. "Hay" means "there is/there are" (from haber). After "cosas que", you add a clause describing those things: "Hay muchas cosas que + verb" (e.g., "puedes hacer", "no entiendes", "quiero decirte").
target_language_example: Hay muchas cosas que necesitamos hablar hoy.
native_language_example: There are many things we need to talk about today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about a group of people, followed by a verb clause with **que** (“who/that”). Often appears as **No hay muchas personas que…** = “There aren’t many people who…”. **Hay** comes from **haber** (“there is/are”).
target_language_example: Hay muchas personas que no entienden la situación.
native_language_example: There are many people who don’t understand the situation.

meaning: “there is a lot (of) / there are many.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb haber (hay = “there is/are”) to say a large amount exists. Usually followed by a noun: hay mucho espacio (“there is a lot of space”), hay mucho trabajo (“there is a lot of work”). With a plural noun you typically say hay muchos/muchas (hay muchos libros, hay muchas personas).
target_language_example: Aquí hay mucho ruido por la noche.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of noise here at night.

meaning: 'there’s a lot to…' / 'there’s a lot that…'.
additional_notes: Used with **hay** (“there is/are”) + **mucho** (“a lot”) + **que**. Often followed by an **infinitive**: *Hay mucho que comprar/ver/aprender* (“There’s a lot to buy/see/learn”). It can also be followed by a **clause**: *Hay mucho que no sabes* (“There’s a lot you don’t know”).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay mucho que hacer por la noche.
native_language_example: In this city there’s a lot to do at night.

additional_notes: Used to say that a lot of something exists or is present. “Hay” comes from “haber” and is used for “there is/there are” (it doesn’t change for singular/plural): Hay muchos libros / Hay muchas casas. Use “muchos” with masculine plural nouns (muchos árboles) and “muchas” with feminine plural nouns (muchas flores).
target_language_example: Aquí hay muchos estudiantes.
native_language_example: There are many students here.

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (from *haber*) to say something exists or is found in a place. Often followed by an optional description (e.g., *hay muchos edificios altos*) and/or a location phrase (e.g., *en el centro*, *por acá*). Word order is typically **Hay + quantity + noun (+ adjective) (+ location)**.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay muchos edificios nuevos.
native_language_example: In this city there are many new buildings.

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (“there is/there are”) to say something exists/are present. **Peces** = fish (plural). **En** = in (usually followed by a place): *en el mar* (in the sea), *en ese/este lago* (in that/this lake), *en la laguna* (in the lagoon).
target_language_example: Hay muchos peces en este lago.
native_language_example: There are many fish in this lake.

additional_notes: Used to say a larger quantity exists, often in comparisons with **que** (“than”): **hay más X que Y** = “there are more X than Y.” Can refer to countable things (personas, nubes) or uncountable things (agua).
target_language_example: En este barrio hay más restaurantes que tiendas.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood there are more restaurants than shops.

additional_notes: In Spanish you normally use this with a negative: **no hay nada** (“there’s nothing / there aren’t any”). It’s also common before a clause: **No hay nada que pueda hacer** (“There’s nothing I can do”). For “something,” Spanish uses **algo**: **No hay nada** (nothing) vs. **Hay algo** (something).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada que pueda hacer ahora.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, there’s nothing I can do right now.

meaning: “there is nobody / there isn’t anyone” (normally: “no hay nadie”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **hay** (“there is/are”) to say that nobody is present. In standard Spanish you almost always say **no hay nadie** (double negative): *Aquí no hay nadie.* The affirmative **hay nadie** is generally not used (you’d say **hay alguien** = “there is someone”).
target_language_example: Lo busqué por todas partes, pero no hay nadie en la oficina.
native_language_example: I looked everywhere, but there isn’t anyone in the office.

meaning: 'there is a need to' / 'it’s necessary to'. Often used as 'no hay necesidad de' = 'there’s no need to'.
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "hay" (from "haber") to express existence: "hay necesidad de + infinitive". Very commonly appears in the negative to calm someone down or say something isn’t required: "No hay necesidad de gritar" = "You don’t need to yell" / "There’s no need to yell." You can also say "No hay necesidad de que + subjunctive" (e.g., "No hay necesidad de que vengas") for a full clause.
target_language_example: No hay necesidad de explicar todo ahora.
native_language_example: There’s no need to explain everything right now.

meaning: “there is a problem” (often used as part of “no hay problema” = “no problem”).
additional_notes: From haber (“hay” = “there is/are”) + problema. In everyday speech you’ll most often hear it as “No hay problema,” meaning “No problem,” “It’s fine,” or “No worries,” as a reassuring response or to say something is not an issue. You can also use “¿Hay problema?” to ask “Is there a problem?”.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no hay problema; lo hacemos mañana.
native_language_example: Relax, no problem; we’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation in a general/impersonal way. It’s followed by an infinitive: hay que + verbo (hay que irse, hay que contarlo). Often corresponds to English "we have to" or "you have to," but without naming a specific person.
target_language_example: Hay que estudiar un poco cada día.
native_language_example: You have to study a little every day.

meaning: you/we must change (or replace) something; it needs to be changed.
additional_notes: “Hay que + infinitive” expresses an impersonal obligation (like “you have to / we have to / one must”). With “cambiar,” it often means “to replace” a part/object (una válvula, la chapa) or “to change” a method/habit (la manera de hacer las cosas). The subject isn’t stated; the context tells who should do it.
target_language_example: Hay que cambiar las pilas del control remoto.
native_language_example: We have to change the remote’s batteries.

meaning: "you/we/one must do"; "it needs to be done".
additional_notes: An impersonal way to talk about obligation or necessity (like English “you have to…” in a general sense). It doesn’t say who specifically must do it. Very common in phrases like “lo que hay que hacer” (= what needs to be done / what must be done). You can also use it with any infinitive: “Hay que estudiar” (You have to study / Studying is necessary).
target_language_example: Hay que hacer la tarea hoy.
native_language_example: We have to do the homework today.

meaning: "you have to have" / "one must have" (it’s necessary to have).
additional_notes: Impersonal expression of necessity/obligation: "hay que" + infinitive. "Hay que tener + noun" means that having that thing/quality is required in general (not aimed at a specific person). Often used for advice or general rules: "Hay que tener paciencia" = "You have to be patient."
target_language_example: Para aprender un idioma, hay que tener constancia.
native_language_example: To learn a language, you have to be consistent.

meaning: you have to be careful / one must be careful.
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal structure “hay que + infinitive” to give general advice or a warning (not aimed at a specific person). Often followed by “al + infinitive” (when doing something) or “con + noun/person” (be careful with/about).
target_language_example: Hay que tener cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement followed by a clause that explains what you can’t do, want to do/say/ask/know, etc. Structure: hay + tantas cosas + que + verb/clause. Often expresses feeling overwhelmed or that there’s a lot to cover.
target_language_example: Hay tantas cosas que tengo que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: There are so many things that I have to do today.

meaning: “there is a” (used to say something exists or is present).
additional_notes: "Hay" is the impersonal form of "haber" meaning “there is/are.” Use "hay un" before a singular masculine noun (hay un río, hay un agente). For feminine singular use "hay una". For plural, use "hay" + plural noun (no article needed, but you can add one in some contexts: "hay unos/unas..."). It’s commonly followed by a place expression: "hay un ___ en/al lado de/entre...".
target_language_example: En esta calle hay un banco cerca de la plaza.
native_language_example: On this street there is a bank near the square.

additional_notes: Used to say something exists in a place. "Hay" means “there is/there are,” and "un gran" is “a great/big” (gran is used before a singular noun: "un gran supermercado". For feminine nouns: "una gran pared"). Often followed by a location phrase like "en" or "cerca de".
target_language_example: Hay un gran problema con el plan.
native_language_example: There is a big problem with the plan.

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (from *haber*) to say that someone exists/is present somewhere. Often followed by a place: **hay un hombre aquí/en la puerta/abajo**. For emphasis or clarity you can add **aquí/ahí/allí** (“here/there”).
target_language_example: Hay un hombre afuera que quiere hablar contigo.
native_language_example: There’s a man outside who wants to talk to you.

meaning: 'there are a lot of' / 'there are tons of'.
additional_notes: Used to say there is a large quantity of something. It’s common and informal-ish (more casual than 'hay muchos/muchas' or 'hay mucha/mucho'). 'Hay' is from 'haber' meaning 'there is/there are', and 'un montón de' literally means 'a pile/heap of' + noun.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hay un montón de restaurantes buenos.
native_language_example: In this city there are a lot of good restaurants.

meaning: 'there is a small …' (introducing a small thing).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something exists/is present: “Hay un pequeño + sustantivo” (e.g., “Hay un pequeño perro…”). “Hay” means “there is/there are” and doesn’t change for plural, but the article/adjective do: “Hay una pequeña casa”, “Hay pequeños problemas”. Adjective agreement: pequeño (masc. sing.), pequeña (fem. sing.), pequeños/pequeñas (plural).
target_language_example: Hay un pequeño problema con la reserva.
native_language_example: There’s a small problem with the reservation.

additional_notes: Used to say that a small amount of something exists or is present. "Hay" is the form of "haber" meaning "there is/there are" (not "tener"). Often followed by an uncountable noun (hay un poco de agua) or an idea/quality (hay un poco de verdad).
target_language_example: Aquí hay un poco de pan si tienes hambre.
native_language_example: There’s a bit of bread here if you’re hungry.

additional_notes: Used to state that an issue exists. Very common with a location or topic: "Hay un problema en..." (There’s a problem in/at...) or "Hay un problema con..." (There’s a problem with...). You can add emphasis like "Todavía hay un problema" (There’s still a problem).
target_language_example: Perdón, hay un problema con mi reserva.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s a problem with my reservation.

additional_notes: Used with a singular feminine noun to say something exists or is present: hay una universidad, hay una batalla. In questions/negatives: ¿Hay una…? / No hay una…. Often translates as “there is/there’s a…”.
target_language_example: ¿Hay una farmacia cerca de aquí?
native_language_example: Is there a pharmacy near here?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific (often important) point or topic before adding more information with a clause starting with que. Very common in speech and writing to emphasize “one thing” among others. You can change una cosa to algo (“hay algo que…”) or add emphasis with solo (“solo hay una cosa que…”).
target_language_example: Hay una cosa que tenemos que hablar hoy.
native_language_example: There’s one thing we need to talk about today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that two things (or situations) are not the same. Common patterns: "Hay una gran diferencia entre A y B" (between A and B) and "Hay una gran diferencia en..." (in/when it comes to...).
target_language_example: Hay una gran diferencia entre hablar español y hablarlo con fluidez.
native_language_example: There’s a big difference between speaking Spanish and speaking it fluently.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is needed immediately. Very common in formal contexts (news, reports, announcements). Pattern: Hay una necesidad urgente de + noun/infinitive (e.g., de ayuda, de actuar).
target_language_example: Hay una necesidad urgente de más médicos en esta zona.
native_language_example: There is an urgent need for more doctors in this area.

additional_notes: This is the present perfect subjunctive of hacer: haya (subjunctive of haber) + hecho (past participle). It’s used after triggers like que, no creo que, nadie ha dicho que, me parece bien que, perdona que, etc., when talking about an action that happened before now (often recently) but is viewed with doubt, emotion, opinion, denial, or as a reaction. Contrast: lo ha hecho = “he/she has done it” (indicative, stating it as fact) vs. no creo que lo haya hecho = “I don’t think he/she has done it” (subjunctive).
target_language_example: Dudo que él lo haya hecho.
native_language_example: I doubt that he has done it.

meaning: "has been" / "may have been" (subjunctive, about the past).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect subjunctive of **ser**: **(que) haya sido**. It’s used after triggers like **espero que** (I hope), **no creo que** (I don’t think), **tal vez** (maybe), **ojalá** (I hope/wish) to talk about something in the past with uncertainty, doubt, or a wish. Often translates as “may have been” or “has been,” depending on context.
target_language_example: No creo que haya sido mi culpa.
native_language_example: I don’t think it was my fault.

additional_notes: This is the present perfect subjunctive of "ver" (to see): haya visto, hayas visto, haya visto, hayamos visto, hayáis visto, hayan visto. It’s used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive—often with uncertainty, possibility, or non-specific references—such as "puede que", "quizá", or in clauses like "nada que..." / "lo que..." (e.g., "No se parece a nada que haya visto"). In English it often translates as "may have seen" or "(that) ... has/have seen."
target_language_example: Puede que ya lo haya visto, pero no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: He may have already seen it, but I’m not sure.

meaning: "let there be peace" / "let’s have peace" (a call for calm, no arguing).
additional_notes: Used to ask people to stop fighting or arguing and calm down. It often appears as a short, emphatic phrase (sometimes with exclamation marks), similar to saying “peace, everyone” or “let’s keep the peace.”
target_language_example: Ya, por favor, haya paz: podemos hablarlo sin gritar.
native_language_example: Okay, please, let’s have peace: we can talk about it without shouting.

additional_notes: Uses the tú imperative of hacer (haz) + exactamente (“exactly”) + lo que (“what/that which”). It’s followed by a clause like “te diga” (I tell you) or “digo” (I say). Often used to emphasize strict obedience or precision.
target_language_example: Por favor, haz exactamente lo que te expliqué.
native_language_example: Please do exactly what I explained to you.

additional_notes: An instruction using the tú imperative of hacer (haz). lo mismo means “the same (thing)”. Often followed by que + clause to say who/what to copy: Haz lo mismo que yo (“Do the same as me”). It can also refer back to something already done: haz lo mismo de antes (“do the same as before”).
target_language_example: Si yo apago la luz, haz lo mismo.
native_language_example: If I turn off the light, do the same.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do a specific thing, often followed by a clause: haz lo que + verb (haz lo que creas / haz lo que te dije). It can also appear in set phrases like haz lo que tienes que hacer (“do what you have to do”) or haz lo que hay que hacer (“do what needs to be done”). Note the command form haz is from hacer (tú).
target_language_example: Haz lo que puedas y no te preocupes.
native_language_example: Do what you can and don’t worry.

additional_notes: Often used to give permission or to show indifference/resignation (“it’s up to you”). It can sound supportive in context, but it can also sound dismissive or a bit annoyed depending on tone. Uses the tú imperative: haz (from hacer) + lo que quieras (“whatever you want”).
target_language_example: Si no te gusta este plan, haz lo que quieras.
native_language_example: If you don’t like this plan, do whatever you want.

meaning: “do what you…” (as you were told / what you feel / what seems best).
additional_notes:
A very common command pattern: **haz** (tú command of *hacer*) + **lo que** (“what/whatever”) + **te** (“to you”), followed by more information. Often used with:
- **he dicho / te dije** = what I (have) told you
- **pido** = what I’m asking you to do
- **parezca / plazca** = whatever you think / whatever you want
- **mande tu corazón** = whatever your heart tells you
Because **te** needs something after it, it usually appears as **haz lo que te + verb/clause**.
target_language_example: Haz lo que te dije y todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: Do what I told you and everything will turn out fine.

additional_notes: An imperative command using the tú form (haz = “do”). Often said firmly to give instructions or orders. You can change the person: “haz lo que te diga él” = “do what he tells you,” “haz lo que te diga ella” = “do what she tells you.” In some regions you may hear it with “nomás/nomás” meaning “just/only”: “Nomás haz lo que te diga.”
target_language_example: Por favor, haz lo que te diga y no te muevas.
native_language_example: Please do what I tell you and don’t move.

additional_notes: A direct command using the tú imperative of hacer (haz). It’s often used to insist on obedience or urgency (“Just do what I say”). You can soften it with “por favor” or make it formal with “haga lo que le digo” (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, haz lo que te digo y no te preocupes: después te lo explico.
native_language_example: Please do what I’m telling you and don’t worry: I’ll explain it to you later.

haz lo que tengas que hacer

target_language_multi_word_term: haz lo que tengas que hacer
meaning: Do what you have to do.
additional_notes: An imperative used to tell someone to do whatever is necessary. It uses the present subjunctive ("tengas") because it refers to an unspecified thing you may need to do ("whatever you have to do"). Often implies acceptance or resignation ("go ahead, do it"). You can add emphasis with "solo" (just) or "tú" (you).
target_language_example: Si quieres irte, haz lo que tengas que hacer.
native_language_example: If you want to leave, do what you have to do.

haz lo que tienes que hacer

target_language_multi_word_term: haz lo que tienes que hacer
meaning: Do what you have to do.
additional_notes: Direct imperative (tú) telling someone to do what is necessary or required, often with a sense of “get it done” or encouragement. You may also hear it with emphasis: “Tú haz lo que tienes que hacer” (“You do what you have to do”). The more formal version is “Haga lo que tiene que hacer” (usted).
target_language_example: No te preocupes por mí; haz lo que tienes que hacer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about me; do what you have to do.

meaning: "do what I (say/do)" (used to introduce what you should follow).
additional_notes: This is an imperative phrase and it’s usually followed by a verb to complete the idea: "Haz lo que yo digo" (do what I say) or "Haz lo que yo haga" (do what I do). With "yo te diga", "te" means "to you": "do what I tell you." You’ll often see the verb after "yo" in the present (digo) or in the present subjunctive (haga / te diga), depending on the structure.
target_language_example: No discutas: haz lo que yo te diga.
native_language_example: Don’t argue: do what I tell you.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of *hacer*: **haz** = “do (you)”. Used to tell someone to focus and complete their responsibilities. You can add adverbs like *rápidamente* (“quickly”) or combine it with another command: *Ve y haz tu trabajo* (“Go and do your job”).
target_language_example: Por favor, haz tu trabajo antes de las cinco.
native_language_example: Please do your work before five.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for you. Very common in spoken Spanish; it can sound polite or a bit demanding depending on tone and what you ask next (e.g., “Hazme un favor y apaga…”). You can also say it alone (“Hazme un favor.”) when the request is implied or will follow. Variants: “hazme el favor (de + infinitive)” and more formal “hágame un favor”.
target_language_example: Hazme un favor y avísame cuando llegues.
native_language_example: Do me a favor and let me know when you arrive.

meaning: Move aside. / Step out of the way.
additional_notes: Command (tú) form of "hacerse a un lado". Used to tell one person to get out of the way; can sound firm or rude depending on tone. "Hazte" = "make yourself"; "a un lado" = "to one side". For formal "you" use: "Hágase a un lado" or "Hágase a un lado, por favor."
target_language_example: Perdón, hazte a un lado un momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, move aside for a moment.

additional_notes: Uses **haber** (he) + past participle (**aprendido**) to talk about something you learned at an unspecified time, often with relevance to the present. Common in Spain for recent/connected past; in much of Latin America, **aprendí** (simple past) is often used in the same situations. The participle **aprendido** does not change for gender/number here.
target_language_example: He aprendido mucho en este curso.
native_language_example: I’ve learned a lot in this course.

additional_notes: Present perfect of beber: haber (he) + past participle (bebido). Used to talk about something you drank at an unspecified time in the past, often connected to the present (e.g., "Ya he bebido café" = "I've already had coffee"). Also common with quantities and adverbs like demasiado (too much) and ya (already), and with sources like del grifo (from the tap).
target_language_example: No puedo conducir; he bebido vino.
native_language_example: I can't drive; I've drunk wine.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **haber (he) + past participle (cambiado)**. It can mean you have changed (as a person/situation) or, depending on context, that you have changed something. With **no... nada** it means “I haven’t changed at all.”
target_language_example: Desde el año pasado, he cambiado mucho.
native_language_example: Since last year, I've changed a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you ate at an unspecified time before now, or about experiences up to now. Common in Spain for recent past (e.g., "He comido mucho esta semana"), while in much of Latin America the simple past is often preferred ("Comí mucho esta semana"). Often appears with time expressions like esta semana, hoy, ya, nunca, todavía.
target_language_example: No me siento bien; creo que es algo que he comido.
native_language_example: I don’t feel well; I think it’s something I ate.

additional_notes: Form of the verb comprar in the pretérito perfecto: he + participle (comprado). Commonly used for recent past actions or actions connected to the present. With reflexive pronouns (me/te/se…), it often means “bought (something) for myself,” e.g., Me he comprado… = “I bought myself…”.
target_language_example: He comprado pan para la cena.
native_language_example: I bought bread for dinner.

additional_notes: This is the present perfect: **he** ("I have") + **conocido** (past participle of *conocer*). It’s used for experiences up to now (often like “I’ve met…”). With a person, you usually add **a**: *He conocido a alguien* (“I’ve met someone”). It can also mean “I’ve known (someone)” depending on context, but *conocer* often focuses on first meeting/getting acquainted rather than long-term knowing.
target_language_example: He conocido a tu hermana en la universidad.
native_language_example: I met your sister at the university.

additional_notes: This is the present perfect: "he" (I have) + "conocido" (met/known). Use it when you’ve met someone at some point in the past and it’s relevant now. With people, Spanish usually uses the personal "a": "he conocido a Juan". In negative sentences it becomes "no he conocido a..." (I haven’t met/known...).
target_language_example: He conocido a tu hermana, pero no a tu hermano.
native_language_example: I’ve met your sister, but not your brother.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **he** (I have) + **conseguido** (past participle of *conseguir*). Use it to say you’ve succeeded in doing something (*he conseguido verla* = “I’ve managed to see her”) or that you obtained something (*he conseguido dos* = “I’ve gotten two”). Often followed by an infinitive (**he conseguido + infinitive**) or a direct object (**he conseguido + noun/pronoun**).
target_language_example: ¡Por fin lo he conseguido!
native_language_example: I finally managed to do it!

meaning: 'I have told' / 'I told you (have told you)'.
additional_notes: Present perfect of **contar** (yo **he contado**). With people, **contar** often means **to tell** (a story/secret/information), not just **to count**. It commonly appears with object pronouns: **le he contado** (I’ve told him/her), **no le he contado esto a nadie** (I haven’t told this to anyone), **se lo he contado todo** (I’ve told him/her everything).
target_language_example: Ya te lo he contado, pero no me escuchaste.
native_language_example: I’ve already told you, but you didn’t listen.

additional_notes: Present perfect of dar (to give): haber (he) + past participle (dado). It’s used with direct/indirect objects (e.g., te he dado algo, no te he dado nada) and in fixed expressions like he dado mi palabra (“I gave my word”). In sentences like Me he dado de alta, the full verb is darse de alta (“to register/sign up; to get discharged”), where he dado is part of the reflexive present perfect (me he dado…).
target_language_example: Te he dado mi palabra.
native_language_example: I've given you my word.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decidir: he (I have) + decidido (decided). It’s used to say you’ve made a decision (often recently) about what you will do. Common patterns: “He decidido + infinitive” (He decidido renunciar.) and “He decidido que + clause” (He decidido que debemos quedarnos aquí.). Negative: “No lo he decidido todavía” = “I haven’t decided yet.”
target_language_example: He decidido que mañana voy a empezar a estudiar español.
native_language_example: I’ve decided that tomorrow I’m going to start studying Spanish.

meaning: "I have left" / "I’ve quit" / "I’ve let (someone)" (present perfect of *dejar*).
additional_notes:
The exact meaning depends on what comes after it:
- **he dejado de + infinitive** = “I’ve stopped/quit doing …” (*He dejado de fumar*).
- **he dejado + thing + en + place** = “I’ve left … (somewhere)” (*He dejado el pasaporte en alguna parte*).
- **he dejado + infinitive (e.g., entrar, pasar)** = “I let (someone) …” (*He dejado entrar al gato*).
- **Lo he dejado.** can mean “I left it” or, about a relationship, “I left him/her / I broke up with him/her,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Lo siento: he dejado mi móvil en casa.
native_language_example: Sorry—I left my phone at home.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decir (to say/tell). Often appears with object pronouns to show who you told: les he dicho (I told them), te he dicho (I told you), le he dicho (I told him/her). With que, it introduces reported speech: He dicho que lo dejes (I said to leave it).
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho que no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I already told you I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Almost always used with **no**: **(no) he dicho nada** = “I haven’t said anything / I didn’t say anything.” With an indirect object pronoun it becomes **no le he dicho nada** = “I haven’t told him/her anything,” and you can add who: **no le he dicho nada a ella**. In everyday speech, Spanish often uses the present perfect (**he dicho**) for recent past actions.
target_language_example: Todavía no le he dicho nada a mi jefe.
native_language_example: I still haven’t told my boss anything.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect of decir: he dicho = “I have said/told.” Common to introduce reported speech with que (“that”). Often used to insist or remind someone, especially with ya: ya te he dicho que… (“I’ve already told you that…”).
target_language_example: He dicho que no quiero ir hoy.
native_language_example: I said I don’t want to go today.

additional_notes: Present perfect of encontrar (to find): he encontrado = I have found. It’s used for finding a person or thing you were looking for, or for discovering something. Object pronouns often go before it: lo/la he encontrado = I found it (him/it, her/it). For people, Spanish often uses the personal “a”: He encontrado a Tony.
target_language_example: ¡Por fin he encontrado mis llaves!
native_language_example: I finally found my keys!

meaning: "I have understood" / "I understood" (present perfect: I’ve understood).
additional_notes: Used to say you understood what someone said or meant. Often appears with object pronouns: "lo he entendido" (I understood it), "te he entendido" (I understood you), or with "bien / muy bien" for emphasis. In many situations, English would just say "I understand" even though Spanish uses the present perfect (he + entendido). Negative forms are common: "No he entendido" (I didn’t understand) and "No he entendido nada" (I didn’t understand anything).
target_language_example: Perdón, ahora sí te he entendido.
native_language_example: Sorry, now I understand you.

additional_notes: "He escrito" is the yo form of the present perfect: haber (he) + past participle (escrito). It’s used to talk about what you have done up to now, often with words like hoy (today), ya (already), nunca (never), todavía no (not yet). In many parts of Spain it’s especially common for actions in a time period that includes the present (e.g., today/this week).
target_language_example: Esta semana he escrito tres correos importantes.
native_language_example: This week I have written three important emails.

meaning: "I have heard" / "I've heard" (present perfect of escuchar).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve heard something at least once up to now. Common patterns: he escuchado + [thing] (He escuchado mucho de ti. = I’ve heard a lot about you.); he escuchado a + [person] + [verb] (He escuchado a Roy cantar. = I’ve heard Roy sing.); no he escuchado nada / nunca he escuchado... (I haven’t heard anything / I’ve never heard...). Also used in comparisons like lo más... que he escuchado jamás (the most ... I’ve ever heard).
target_language_example: Ya he escuchado esa historia muchas veces.
native_language_example: I've already heard that story many times.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (haber + past participle): "he esperado" = "I have waited".
