native_language_example: I have to return these books to the library today.

meaning: 'the library is' (located/is in a temporary state).
additional_notes: Uses **estar** (not *ser*) to talk about the library’s **location** or a **temporary condition**. Common patterns: **está a + distance/time** (Está a cinco minutos), **está a la derecha/izquierda** (It’s to the right/left), **está en + place/floor** (in/on), **está temporalmente cerrada** (temporarily closed).
target_language_example: La biblioteca está cerca del parque.
native_language_example: The library is near the park.

additional_notes: A common noun with feminine gender, so it uses la/una (la bicicleta, una bicicleta). Often used with verbs like montar en (to ride), comprar (to buy), and robar (to steal). In everyday speech you may also hear la bici (“the bike”).
target_language_example: Voy al trabajo en la bicicleta.
native_language_example: I go to work on the bike.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dar/den/doy/darle: "dar la bienvenida a + person/group" = to welcome someone (often in a formal or public way, but can be personal too). The "a" introduces who is being welcomed.
target_language_example: Vamos a dar la bienvenida a nuestros invitados.
native_language_example: We’re going to welcome our guests.

meaning: the mouth; (in expressions) the act of speaking (“your mouth”).
additional_notes: Literal body part: *Abra la boca* (“Open your mouth”), *Respira por la boca* (“Breathe through your mouth”). Very common in commands and idioms about speaking: *cállate/cierra la boca* = “shut up / shut your mouth” (can sound rude or aggressive). *No abrí la boca* = “I didn’t say a word.” *Hablar con la boca llena* = “talk with your mouth full.” *Me has quitado las palabras de la boca* = “You took the words right out of my mouth” (you said what I was about to say).
target_language_example: No abras la boca hasta que termine de hablar.
native_language_example: Don’t open your mouth until I finish speaking.

meaning: 'your mouth shut' (be quiet; don’t say anything).
additional_notes: Most often used with verbs like mantener: “mantener la boca cerrada” = “keep your mouth shut.” It’s direct and can sound rude or like a strong warning. You can also see it in the past: “haber mantenido la boca cerrada” = “should have kept your mouth shut.”
target_language_example: Por favor, mantén la boca cerrada durante la reunión.
native_language_example: Please keep your mouth shut during the meeting.

additional_notes: A very common noun for a wedding ceremony/celebration. It’s feminine, so you say: la boda, una boda, mi/su boda. Common phrases: “La boda es mañana” (The wedding is tomorrow), “Nos vemos en la boda” (See you at the wedding), “la boda de mi hija” (my daughter’s wedding).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a venir a la boda el sábado?
native_language_example: Are you going to come to the wedding on Saturday?

additional_notes: Used to identify whose wedding it is. It’s often followed by a name (la boda de Jessica) or a possessive phrase (la boda de mi hermana). In questions about attending, you’ll often see: “¿Vas a ir a la boda de …?”
target_language_example: ¿Vienes a la boda de mi primo el sábado?
native_language_example: Are you coming to my cousin’s wedding on Saturday?

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a bag you can hold (e.g., a shopping bag) or a purse/handbag, depending on context. With “dame”, it’s a direct request: “Give me the bag/purse.”
target_language_example: Pon las manzanas en la bolsa.
native_language_example: Put the apples in the bag.

additional_notes: A feminine noun used for containers of liquids (water, wine, etc.). Common with verbs like abrir (to open), cerrar (to close), llenar (to fill), and verter (to pour/spill). Also appears in the expression "El genio está fuera de la botella" (“The genie is out of the bottle”), meaning something is already done and can’t be undone.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes pasarme la botella de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the water bottle, please?

meaning: the head; (figuratively) your mind/brain (common in advice).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the head (body part). Common with verbs like "sacudir/mover la cabeza" (to shake/nod your head). Figuratively, it can mean "your brain/common sense," especially in phrases like "Usa la cabeza" (Use your head).
target_language_example: Me duele la cabeza.
native_language_example: My head hurts.

additional_notes: A place where you go to buy/drink coffee and often snacks or light meals. It’s feminine, so you say: "la cafetería" and "a la cafetería" (to the café).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la cafetería después de clase.
native_language_example: See you at the café after class.

meaning: the box; the cash register/cash drawer.
additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical box/container (e.g., for a product or to store things). In shops and businesses, "la caja" can also mean the register area or cash drawer where money is kept (e.g., "poner dinero en la caja").
target_language_example: Deja el recibo en la caja, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the receipt at the register/cash desk, please.

meaning: the safe (a locked box for valuables).
additional_notes: Used for a secure container where you keep money, documents, jewelry, etc. Often appears with location phrases: en la caja fuerte (in the safe), de + place (the safe of a place): la caja fuerte del taller (the workshop’s safe). Note: fuerte literally means “strong,” but the whole phrase means “safe.”
target_language_example: Guarda el pasaporte en la caja fuerte.
native_language_example: Keep the passport in the safe.

meaning: 'the street' (also: 'outside' in the sense of being out in public).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a street/road in a town or city (La calle Fresno = Fresno Street). With verbs like salir (salir a la calle), it often means 'to go out (onto the street)/to go outside.' Used in everyday location directions and when talking about crossing the street (cruzar la calle).
target_language_example: No salgas a la calle sin abrigo; hace frío.
native_language_example: Don't go out without a coat; it's cold.

additional_notes: A common noun used for a peaceful, relaxed state (often after stress or danger). Frequently appears in set phrases and commands: "mantener la calma" / "conservar la calma" = "to stay/keep calm"; "la calma antes de la tormenta" = "the calm before the storm"; "después de la tormenta/tempestad, viene la calma" = "after the storm comes calm."
target_language_example: Respira hondo y mantén la calma.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath and stay calm.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar to say someone is in bed (often because they’re sick or resting): “estar en la cama”. Also common with “quedarse en la cama” (to stay in bed) and “volver a la cama” (to go back to bed).
target_language_example: Hoy me quedo en la cama porque no me siento bien.
native_language_example: Today I’m staying in bed because I don’t feel well.

meaning: the pickup truck; the van (depending on the region/context).
additional_notes: A common vehicle word. In many places, *camioneta* refers to a small truck/pickup; in others it can mean a van or SUV-type vehicle. Used with *en* to mean “in the vehicle” (*en la camioneta*) and with *de* to show possession (*la camioneta de mi mamá* = “my mom’s truck/van”).
target_language_example: Dejé las cajas en la camioneta.
native_language_example: I left the boxes in the truck/van.

additional_notes: A feminine noun for a (usually button-up) shirt. Use it when talking about clothing: ponerse/quitarse la camisa (put on/take off your shirt), llevar una camisa (wear a shirt). You can add details like limpia y seca (clean and dry), del revés (inside out), or la etiqueta del precio (the price tag).
target_language_example: Me voy a poner la camisa azul para la reunión.
native_language_example: I’m going to put on the blue shirt for the meeting.

additional_notes: Used for a bell that rings to signal something (especially a school bell) or a physical bell you can ring (e.g., in an emergency). Common with verbs like "sonar" (to ring/sound) and "tocar" (to ring).
target_language_example: Cuando suene la campana, todos entran a clase.
native_language_example: When the bell rings, everyone goes into class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability or skill to do an action. It’s followed by an infinitive (la capacidad de memorizar) or by a noun phrase (la capacidad de concentración). Often appears with tener: tener la capacidad de…
target_language_example: Ella tiene la capacidad de aprender idiomas muy rápido.
native_language_example: She has the ability to learn languages very fast.

meaning: the capital (main city of a country/state/region).
additional_notes: Used for the seat of government or most important administrative city. Often followed by "de" to say what it’s the capital of: "la capital de México", "la capital del estado". It can also be used in apposition after a place name: "Ciudad de México, la capital". Feminine noun: "la capital".
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es la capital de España?
native_language_example: What is the capital of Spain?

additional_notes: Used to name the main city where a country’s (or region’s) government is based. Structure: **La capital de + place + es/se llama + city**. The word **capital** is feminine, so it’s **la** capital.
target_language_example: La capital de España es Madrid.
native_language_example: The capital of Spain is Madrid.

additional_notes: Used with common verbs like lavarse la cara (to wash your face), cubrirse la cara (to cover your face), and mirar la cara / mírame la cara (to look at someone’s face). Spanish often uses a definite article with body parts (la cara) where English might use a possessive (“my/your face”).
target_language_example: Me lavé la cara antes de salir de casa.
native_language_example: I washed my face before leaving the house.

additional_notes: Usually refers to meat you eat (beef, pork, etc.). To be specific, Spanish often uses “carne de + animal”: “carne de cerdo” (pork), “carne de res” (beef), “carne de pollo” (chicken meat). In some contexts “carne” can mean “flesh” (human/animal body), but in everyday food talk it means “meat”.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres la carne bien hecha o al punto?
native_language_example: Do you want the meat well-done or medium?

additional_notes: Used for a competition where people (or animals/vehicles) try to finish first. Note: "carrera" can also mean "career" or "degree course" depending on context, so it can be confusing for English speakers.
target_language_example: Llegué tarde y me perdí la carrera.
native_language_example: I arrived late and missed the race.

additional_notes: A common noun for a roadway connecting places (often outside cities). Often used with "por" (along/on) and "a un lado de" (on the side of).
target_language_example: Hay mucho tráfico en la carretera hoy.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of traffic on the road today.

meaning: the letter (a written message); also "the menu" (restaurant), depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly means a written letter/message. In restaurants, "la carta" often means "the menu" (e.g., "¿Me trae la carta, por favor?"). The meaning is determined by context.
target_language_example: La carta es para ti.
native_language_example: The letter is for you.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a wallet (often a billfold) or a purse/handbag for carrying money, cards, and ID. In many places, you can also hear it for a briefcase, but the everyday meaning is wallet/purse, especially in phrases like “perder la cartera” (lose your wallet) or “robar la cartera” (steal your wallet).
target_language_example: No encuentro la cartera; ¿la has visto?
native_language_example: I can’t find my wallet; have you seen it?

additional_notes: Usually means a physical house/building, but it can also mean “home” depending on context (e.g., volver a la casa = go back home). Use "de" to show who it belongs to: "la casa de tu padre" = your father's house.
target_language_example: Voy a la casa después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m going home after work.

additional_notes: Used to show who a house belongs to or whose home you mean: **la casa de + person/name/pronoun**. Often shortened in speech to **casa de** (without *la*) when speaking generally, but **la casa de** is common when you mean a specific house. Example: *la casa de mis padres* = "my parents' house."
target_language_example: Vamos a la casa de mi abuela esta tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to my grandmother’s house this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the neighboring house (right next to where you are or where someone lives). Often said without extra details because the location is understood from context.
target_language_example: Los niños están jugando en la casa de al lado.
native_language_example: The kids are playing at the house next door.

meaning: “the house/home of (a male person)” or “at (a male person’s) house.”
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular person/title to show possession or destination: la casa del abuelo = “grandpa’s house.” It’s a contraction of de + el → del, so you don’t say *de el* here. With a feminine owner, use la casa de la (e.g., la casa de la abuela). It can refer to someone’s home, residence, or household/estate depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos a la casa del profesor después de clase.
native_language_example: We’re going to the teacher’s house after class.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with donde (“where”) that describes a specific house/place. Often followed by a verb in the past (nació, vivía, pasó su infancia) to say what happened there. You can also use “en la casa donde …” (“in the house where …”).
target_language_example: Visitamos la casa donde vivió mi abuela.
native_language_example: We visited the house where my grandmother lived.

meaning: “the house in which / where” (refers to a specific house).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes a particular house. "en la que" = "in which" (more formal) and often matches English "where". It agrees with "la casa" (feminine singular); with masculine/singular you’d use "el ... en el que" (e.g., "el lugar en el que"), and for plural "las/los ... en las/los que".
target_language_example: Visitamos la casa en la que se conocieron mis abuelos.
native_language_example: We visited the house where my grandparents met.

meaning: "the house is" (using *estar* for location or temporary state/condition).
additional_notes: Use **estar** (not **ser**) to talk about where the house is (**La casa está en la colina**) and how it is right now (**La casa está ardiendo / despejada**). For a more permanent description/identity (e.g., "The house is big"), you’d typically use **ser**: **La casa es grande**.
target_language_example: La casa está cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: The house is near here.

meaning: "the house" + "se" (used to say what happens to the house: "the house gets/is ..." or "the house ..." without naming who does it).
additional_notes: Here, **se** is often used in two common ways: (1) **passive se**: *La casa se calienta...* ≈ “The house is heated...” (focus on the result, not who heats it). (2) **unplanned/accidental event**: *La casa se derrumbó* ≈ “The house collapsed” (something happened; no agent is mentioned). It’s not a fixed expression—*se* changes with the verb (e.g., *se calienta, se derrumbó, se corresponde*).
target_language_example: La casa se pintó de blanco el año pasado.
native_language_example: The house was painted white last year.

additional_notes: Used to explain why something happened: "la causa de..." (the cause of...). It can also mean a cause you support or fight for (often political/social): "por la causa" (for the cause). Common pattern: "la causa principal" = the main cause.
target_language_example: La causa del retraso fue el tráfico.
native_language_example: The cause of the delay was traffic.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what made an accident happen. Often appears with verbs like ser (La causa del accidente es...), investigar (investigar la causa del accidente), and phrases like todavía/desconocida when the cause isn’t known yet.
target_language_example: La policía está investigando la causa del accidente.
native_language_example: The police are investigating the cause of the accident.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what started a fire. Often appears with verbs like ser (es/era) or with impersonal/passive-style phrases: No se conoce / No se sabe la causa del incendio (“The cause of the fire is not known”). You can swap tenses depending on whether you mean now (es) or in the past (era/se sabía).
target_language_example: Todavía no se conoce la causa del incendio.
native_language_example: The cause of the fire is still not known.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the main meal eaten in the evening/night. Common with verbs like "cenar" (to have dinner), "cocinar/preparar la cena" (to cook/prepare dinner), and "hacer(se) la cena" (to make dinner for oneself).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a preparar la cena temprano.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to make dinner early.

meaning: “dinner is…” (using **estar** to say where it is or what state it’s in).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the **current state or location** of dinner: *La cena está casi lista* (“Dinner is almost ready”), *La cena está en el horno* (“Dinner is in the oven”), *La cena está preparada* (“Dinner is prepared/ready”). Spanish uses **estar** (not *ser*) for temporary conditions and locations.
target_language_example: La cena está lista; ven a la mesa.
native_language_example: Dinner is ready; come to the table.

meaning: "dinner is ready" (the meal is prepared and you can eat now).
additional_notes: A very common home phrase. Use it to announce that dinner is prepared/finished cooking. You can address someone directly after it (e.g., “La cena está lista, Taro.”). "La cena" = dinner; "está" (from estar) describes a temporary state; "lista" agrees with the feminine noun "cena".
target_language_example: ¡La cena está lista! Vengan a la mesa.
native_language_example: Dinner is ready! Come to the table.

additional_notes: Used to announce that the meal is ready and people can come to the table. Very common in formal or polite announcements (e.g., addressing guests: “Damas y caballeros…”). Also said casually at home. You can swap in other meals: “El almuerzo está servido” (lunch is served).
target_language_example: Niños, la cena está servida; vengan a la mesa.
native_language_example: Kids, dinner is served; come to the table.

additional_notes: Refers to a barrier (usually wood/metal/wire) around a yard, field, or property. Common verbs with it: saltar/brincar la cerca (to jump over the fence), pintar la cerca (to paint the fence), subir la cerca (to climb the fence), revisar la cerca (to check the fence). You can also say "cerca eléctrica" for an electric fence.
target_language_example: No te acerques a la cerca eléctrica.
native_language_example: Don’t go near the electric fence.

additional_notes: A formal event (often with a set order/ritual), such as a wedding, graduation, or an opening ceremony. Common patterns: "la ceremonia de + noun" (la ceremonia de apertura = the opening ceremony) and "la ceremonia tendrá lugar" (the ceremony will take place).
target_language_example: La ceremonia empieza a las seis, así que llega temprano.
native_language_example: The ceremony starts at six, so arrive early.

additional_notes: A common clothing word. Often used with verbs like ponerse (to put on), quitarse/sacarse (to take off), and colgar (to hang up): Ponte la chaqueta. / Se sacó la chaqueta y la colgó. The article changes with number: la chaqueta (one), las chaquetas (more than one).
target_language_example: Hace frío: ponte la chaqueta, por favor.
native_language_example: It’s cold: put on your jacket, please.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "la" (the, feminine singular) + "chica" (girl/young woman). Often refers to a specific girl already known from context ("Conozco a la chica" = I know the girl). "Chica" can also mean "girl" in a casual way, but it’s not slang in these examples.
target_language_example: La chica está esperando afuera.
native_language_example: The girl is waiting outside.

additional_notes: "Chica" means "girl" or a "young woman," depending on context. "La" is the feminine singular definite article ("the"). You’ll often see it used to identify which person you mean: "la chica de la foto" (the girl in the photo), "la chica hablando con Jim" (the girl talking with Jim).
target_language_example: ¿Quién es la chica de la foto?
native_language_example: Who is the girl in the photo?

additional_notes: Used to describe a girl/woman as having the highest degree of a quality. Pattern: **la chica más + adjective + de...** (“the most … in/of...”) or **la chica más + adjective + que...** (“the most … that...”). Example: *la chica más inteligente de la clase* / *la chica más valiente que he conocido*.
target_language_example: Ella es la chica más inteligente de la clase.
native_language_example: She’s the smartest girl in the class.

additional_notes: Used to identify a specific girl/woman with a relative clause. It’s "la chica" (the girl/young woman) + "que" (who/that). In Spanish, "que" is used for both people and things, and it often matches English "who" (for people) or "that."
target_language_example: La chica que vive aquí es mi compañera de clase.
native_language_example: The girl who lives here is my classmate.

additional_notes: A feminine noun usually referring to science as a field of study or scientific knowledge in general. It’s often used with verbs like ser (La ciencia es...), gustar (Me gusta/no me gusta la ciencia), and in phrases like en la ciencia (“in science,” i.e., within the scientific world/field).
target_language_example: A mi hermano le encanta la ciencia, pero a mí me cuesta.
native_language_example: My brother loves science, but it's hard for me.

additional_notes: Used for the highest point of a mountain or hill: "la cima de la montaña". It can also be figurative for reaching the highest level of success, power, or achievement: "en la cima de su carrera/poder".
target_language_example: Cuando lleguemos a la cima, vamos a descansar un poco.
native_language_example: When we reach the top, we’re going to rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the highest point of a hill (often a specific, known hill). You’ll commonly see it with verbs like estar/encontrarse (to be located) and llegar/alcanzar (to reach).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos en la cima de la colina para ver el atardecer.
native_language_example: We sat at the top of the hill to watch the sunset.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the highest point of a mountain. You’ll often see it with verbs like llegar a / alcanzar (to reach) and with weather descriptions (e.g., cubierta de nieve = covered in snow). Also common: la cima (the summit) when the mountain is clear from context.
target_language_example: Por fin llegamos a la cima de la montaña antes del atardecer.
native_language_example: We finally reached the top of the mountain before sunset.

additional_notes: In these examples, "la cinta" refers to a recorded audio tape/cassette (something you can record, send, or take care of). Depending on context, "cinta" can also mean "ribbon" (decorative strip) or "tape" in general, and in some contexts it can refer to film/movie footage. It’s a feminine noun: la cinta / una cinta.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner la cinta otra vez, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you play the tape again, please?

additional_notes: Used with the definite article "la" to refer to a specific city, often the one everyone knows from context (e.g., the main city nearby). You can also say "en la ciudad" = "in the city".
target_language_example: Prefiero vivir en la ciudad porque hay más transporte público.
native_language_example: I prefer to live in the city because there is more public transportation.

meaning: "the city of" (used to name a specific city).
additional_notes: Used before a city name: la ciudad de Nueva York, la ciudad de San Pablo. It can also be used generically to mean “the city” in phrases like “la ciudad de norte a sur” (“the city from north to south”). Often you can drop it and just say the city name (e.g., “Vive en Nueva York”).
target_language_example: La ciudad de Barcelona es muy turística.
native_language_example: The city of Barcelona is very touristy.

meaning: the whole city; the entire city.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something involves all parts of the city, not just one area. It often appears after the noun ("ciudad entera" = "entire city"), and can be used with other nouns too (e.g., "el día entero" = "the whole day").
target_language_example: Después del apagón, la ciudad entera se quedó sin luz.
native_language_example: After the blackout, the whole city was left without power.

meaning: civilization (a developed society, culture, and way of life).
additional_notes: Used to talk about human society and its cultural, political, and technological development (often in history: "la cuna de la civilización" = "the cradle of civilization"). It can also be used more abstractly to contrast civilized values (laws, order, education) with violence or brute force ("el triunfo de la civilización sobre la fuerza").
target_language_example: La Media Luna Fértil es considerada la cuna de la civilización.
native_language_example: The Fertile Crescent is considered the cradle of civilization.

meaning: the class; the lesson (a period of instruction).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a school class session (the lesson/time period), not just the subject. It can also mean the group of students in that class (e.g., “La clase estaba compuesta por…”). Used in set phrases like “Después de la clase” (after class) and with verbs like “comenzar/empezar la clase” (to start class) and “interrumpir la clase” (to interrupt class).
target_language_example: Después de la clase, tengo que hacer la tarea.
native_language_example: After class, I have to do my homework.

additional_notes: “La clase de + noun” can mean either (1) “the kind/type of …” when talking about a category (la clase de música = the kind of music), or (2) “the … class/lesson” when talking about school subjects or activities (la clase de matemáticas = math class). Context usually makes it clear. In meaning (1), it’s often used like English “the kind of person who…”: Eres la clase de… (You’re the kind of…).
target_language_example: No soy la clase de persona que se rinde fácilmente.
native_language_example: I'm not the kind of person who gives up easily.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s personality or typical behavior, followed by a verb clause (often in the present tense): "Es la clase de persona que..." = "He/She is the kind of person who..." You can also use it to contrast what someone thinks vs. reality: "No es la clase de persona que crees".
target_language_example: No soy la clase de persona que se rinde fácilmente.
native_language_example: I'm not the kind of person who gives up easily.

meaning: the key; the key point/secret; a code/password.
additional_notes: Used both literally (a physical key) and figuratively (the key idea/solution or the secret behind something). In technology or security contexts it can also mean an access code/password. Common patterns: “Esa es la clave” (That’s the key), “La clave está en…” (The key is in…), “la clave de + noun” (the key to/for…).
target_language_example: La clave para aprender español es practicar todos los días.
native_language_example: The key to learning Spanish is to practice every day.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the kitchen” (a room): *Allí está la cocina.* It can also mean “cooking” or “cuisine,” especially when followed by an adjective or a nationality (*la cocina japonesa* = Japanese cuisine).
target_language_example: Voy a limpiar la cocina antes de que lleguen los invitados.
native_language_example: I'm going to clean the kitchen before the guests arrive.

additional_notes: Very common noun with two everyday meanings. 1) Animal “tail”: la cola del perro/gato. 2) A line of people waiting: hacer cola (to wait in line), estar en la cola (to be in the line), al frente de la cola (at the front of the line). Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Hay mucha gente en la cola para entrar al museo.
native_language_example: There are lots of people in the line to get into the museum.

additional_notes: A common noun for a smaller, rounded elevation (smaller than a mountain). Used with verbs like subir (to go up/climb), bajar (to go down), and with prepositions like sobre/encima de (on top of) and detrás de (behind).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos en la colina para ver el atardecer.
native_language_example: We sat on the hill to watch the sunset.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “food” in general (La comida se ve deliciosa). In many Spanish-speaking places, especially in Spain, la comida can also mean “lunch” (the main meal of the day), contrasting with el desayuno (breakfast) and la cena (dinner). It can refer to a type of cuisine too: la comida india = Indian food.
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora es la comida?
native_language_example: What time is lunch?

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning food from Chinese cuisine. Often used with the verb gustar: Me gusta la comida china. You can also use it without the article when speaking in general: Me gusta comida china (less common) or with some: Me gusta la comida china / Me gusta la comida china mucho. Note: comida is feminine, so it uses la.
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta la comida china?
native_language_example: Do you like Chinese food?

additional_notes: Used to talk about food from Japan as a general category. With verbs like gustar (Me gusta la comida japonesa) and probar (Quiero probar la comida japonesa). You can swap in another nationality: la comida italiana, la comida mexicana, etc.
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta la comida japonesa o prefieres la comida mexicana?
native_language_example: Do you like Japanese food, or do you prefer Mexican food?

additional_notes: Refers to a business/organization (often an employer). Very common in formal and business contexts. Don’t confuse with "compañía" meaning "company" in the sense of companionship (e.g., "Gracias por tu compañía" = "Thanks for your company").
target_language_example: La compañía va a abrir una nueva oficina el próximo mes.
native_language_example: The company is going to open a new office next month.

additional_notes: Usually means the act of competing (e.g., for a job: "la competencia por el puesto"). In business contexts it can also mean rival companies/people you compete against ("la competencia de proveedores extranjeros"). It’s feminine: "la competencia".
target_language_example: En este sector, la competencia es muy fuerte.
native_language_example: In this sector, the competition is very strong.

additional_notes: Common Latin American Spanish word for “computer.” In Spain, “el ordenador” is more common. Often used with verbs like prender/encender (to turn on) and apagar (to turn off), and phrases like “en la computadora” (on the computer) or “delante de la computadora” (in front of the computer).
target_language_example: No puedo abrir el archivo en la computadora.
native_language_example: I can’t open the file on the computer.

meaning: the community; a group of people with something in common.
additional_notes: Used for a local community (neighborhood/town), a broader group (la comunidad internacional), or people connected by identity, interests, or profession (la comunidad LGBT, la comunidad de submarinos). Also appears in set phrases like "servicios a la comunidad" (community service) and "cuotas de la comunidad" (membership dues/fees).
target_language_example: Esta biblioteca ofrece actividades para toda la comunidad.
native_language_example: This library offers activities for the whole community.

additional_notes: Used for an organized event where people meet to discuss a topic (“conference”), or for a formal presentation (“lecture/talk”), often in academic or professional contexts. With verbs like asistir a (to attend) and terminar (to end).
target_language_example: La conferencia empieza a las diez, así que lleguemos temprano.
native_language_example: The conference starts at ten, so let’s arrive early.

additional_notes: A feminine noun; usually refers to a spoken exchange of ideas or information. Common with verbs like empezar/iniciar (to start), interrumpir (to interrupt), continuar (to continue), and terminar/acabar (to end).
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo que terminar la conversación ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to end the conversation now.

additional_notes: Used for the flow of water or air (e.g., a current that drags someone, a draft that closes a door). It can also mean the mainstream or the prevailing trend/way of thinking ("la corriente principal"). Common expression: "nadar contra la corriente" = to go against the current / go against the grain.
target_language_example: La corriente estaba muy fuerte y casi me arrastra.
native_language_example: The current was very strong and it almost dragged me away.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the judicial court (the judge and legal system) or the courtroom where a case is heard: "en la corte" = "in court." In other contexts, "la corte" can also mean a royal court (the king/queen’s court), but the example sentences point to the legal meaning.
target_language_example: El caso se decidirá en la corte.
native_language_example: The case will be decided in court.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to make a superlative: la cosa más + adjective (+ de… optional). It means “the most [adjective] thing,” often in an emotional, exaggerated, or informal-sounding way. Example: La cosa más importante (the most important thing).
target_language_example: La cosa más importante es decir la verdad.
native_language_example: The most important thing is to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a superlative + relative clause: "la cosa más hermosa que (he/haya) visto" = “the most beautiful thing (I’ve) seen.” After "que," you’ll often see a verb phrase like "he visto" (present perfect) or "vi" (past). You may also hear "lo más hermoso que…" (“the most beautiful thing that…”) without "la cosa." Adding "jamás" (“ever/never”) emphasizes the idea: "la cosa más hermosa que jamás haya visto" = “the most beautiful thing I’ve ever seen.”
target_language_example: Este atardecer es la cosa más hermosa que he visto en mi vida.
native_language_example: This sunset is the most beautiful thing I’ve seen in my life.

additional_notes: Refers to the land next to the sea/ocean. Often used with directions: la costa norte/sur/oriental/occidental (“the north/south/east/west coast”). Common with en/a along with travel verbs: estar en la costa (to be on the coast), manejar por la costa (to drive along the coast).
target_language_example: Vamos a pasar el fin de semana en la costa.
native_language_example: We’re going to spend the weekend on the coast.

meaning: the habit of; the custom of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to talk about something someone usually does: "tener la costumbre de + infinitive" (I/you/he has the habit of...). In the past: "tenía la costumbre de..." = used to have the habit of....
target_language_example: Tengo la costumbre de tomar café después de comer.
native_language_example: I have the habit of drinking coffee after eating.

meaning: the bill/check; the account; the count.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: in restaurants, "la cuenta" is the bill/check ("Pido la cuenta" = "Can I get the check?"). In finance/online services it’s an account (e.g., "cuenta bancaria" = bank account). In phrases like "perder la cuenta", it means losing count (not keeping track of a number).
target_language_example: ¿Nos trae la cuenta, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you bring us the check, please?

additional_notes: A feminine noun used for a rope, cord, or thick string. Common with verbs like agarrar (to grab), tirar de (to pull on), sostener/mantener firme (to hold tight), and romperse (to break).
target_language_example: Agárrate de la cuerda y no la sueltes.
native_language_example: Hold on to the rope and don't let it go.

additional_notes: A common noun for a natural hollow in rock or a large underground space. It’s feminine, so it uses la/una (la cueva, una cueva). Typical prepositions: en la cueva (in the cave), dentro de la cueva (inside the cave), entrar a/en la cueva (to enter the cave), salir de la cueva (to leave the cave).
target_language_example: No entres en la cueva sin una linterna.
native_language_example: Don’t go into the cave without a flashlight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about responsibility for something bad that happened. Common patterns: **tener la culpa** (to be at fault), **la culpa fue mía/de X** (it was my/X’s fault), **echarle la culpa a alguien** (to blame someone), **ser culpa de...** (to be ...’s fault).
target_language_example: No fue mi intención, pero tengo la culpa.
native_language_example: It wasn’t my intention, but it’s my fault.

meaning: culture (the customs, arts, and way of life of a group).
additional_notes: A common noun used with the definite article: la cultura. It’s often followed by an adjective of place or group (la cultura local, la cultura americana, la cultura japonesa). You can also use it more generally without an adjective when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Me interesa mucho la cultura de España.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in the culture of Spain.

additional_notes: Used for a device that takes photos or records video. With the article (la), it usually refers to a specific camera in the context (“the camera”), and it can also be used alone as a short label/answer (e.g., when pointing something out).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la cámara?
native_language_example: Where is the camera?

additional_notes: Refers to the place where people are kept as punishment for crimes (or while awaiting trial). With the article: "la cárcel" = "the jail/prison"; without it you can also say "ir a cárcel" in some varieties, but "ir a la cárcel" is very common. Related phrases: "ir a la cárcel" (to go to jail), "estar en la cárcel" (to be in jail), "escaparse de la cárcel" (to escape from jail).
target_language_example: Si sigues robando, podrías ir a la cárcel.
native_language_example: If you keep stealing, you could go to jail.

meaning: the decision; a choice you make.
additional_notes: A common noun used for an important choice or final choice. Often appears with the verb phrase "tomar la decisión" (to make the decision), and with possessives: "mi/tu/su/nuestra decisión" (my/your/his-her/their/our decision). You can also say "la decisión no es definitiva" to mean it’s not final yet.
target_language_example: Necesito tiempo para tomar la decisión.
native_language_example: I need time to make the decision.

additional_notes: Used to say someone chose the best option. Often comes after verbs like tomar (to make/take a decision): Tomar la decisión correcta. You can also hear the plural: las decisiones correctas.
target_language_example: Sé que es difícil, pero creo que estás tomando la decisión correcta.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but I think you’re making the right decision.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position or direction (opposite of la izquierda). Often appears in phrases like a la derecha (to the right/on the right), de la derecha (on the right), or on signs/instructions: derecha sobre izquierda (right over left). Can also mean “the political right,” but in these examples it’s about physical direction/side.
target_language_example: El baño está a la derecha de la cocina.
native_language_example: The bathroom is to the right of the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how two things are not the same (ver la diferencia = “see the difference”). In expressions like hacer la diferencia, it means “to make a difference” (have a positive impact or change something). Noun: diferencia (feminine) → la diferencia.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ver la diferencia entre estos dos colores?
native_language_example: Can you see the difference between these two colors?

additional_notes: Used to compare two things or people. It’s followed by two items, often linked with “y” (and): “la diferencia entre tú y yo…”. Typically used with “ser” (is/are): “La diferencia entre A y B es…”. You can also say “la diferencia entre nosotros (dos)” to mean “the difference between us (two)”.
target_language_example: La diferencia entre este café y el otro es el precio.
native_language_example: The difference between this coffee and the other one is the price.

additional_notes: Most often means “address” (where someone lives or a business location): la dirección de casa, la dirección de mi negocio. It can also mean “direction” in the sense of where you’re going or a compass direction: en la dirección incorrecta, norte es una dirección. Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar la dirección, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me the address, please?

additional_notes: Used for the space between two things (often with "entre" = between) or from one place to another ("desde... a..."). The phrase "a la distancia" means "in the distance" (far away, but visible).
target_language_example: Se ve una montaña a la distancia.
native_language_example: You can see a mountain in the distance.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to illegal drugs (cocaine, heroin, etc.), especially in crime/police contexts: "la droga" = "the drugs" as the contraband. It can also mean a substance/medication in general, but for medicine Spanish more often uses "el medicamento" or "la medicina". With "droga" you may see: "tráfico de droga" (drug trafficking), "dinero de la droga" (drug money), "dependencia a la droga" (drug dependence/addiction).
target_language_example: La policía encontró la droga en la cocina.
native_language_example: The police found the drugs in the kitchen.

meaning: the shower (the shower stall/fixture, or the act of showering).
additional_notes: Used with estar/en to say someone is showering or in the shower: “estar en la ducha”. Can also refer to the shower fixture itself (e.g., “La ducha está rota” = the shower is broken).
target_language_example: Estoy en la ducha; te llamo en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I’m in the shower; I’ll call you in five minutes.

additional_notes: Refers to a country/region’s economic system and conditions (jobs, money, production, growth), or the field of study. Often used with “de” + place: “la economía de mi país/la región”. You can describe it with adjectives like “buena/mala/fuerte/débil” and talk about trends like “se recupera / se está acelerando”.
target_language_example: La economía del país está mejorando este año.
native_language_example: The country’s economy is improving this year.

additional_notes: Used for people and things. Common in phrases like "a la edad de..." (at the age of...), "para la edad que tiene" (for their age), "debido a la edad" (due to age), and "la edad mínima" (minimum age). Can also imply aging/catching up with you: "la edad me alcanzó".
target_language_example: A la edad de 18 años, ya trabajaba.
native_language_example: At the age of 18, I was already working.

additional_notes: A general, uncountable noun for the process/system of teaching and learning (school, training, formation). Often used with verbs like "recibir" (to receive/get), "tener" (to have), "mejorar" (to improve), and "consistir en" (to consist of).
target_language_example: La educación es importante para el futuro.
native_language_example: Education is important for the future.

additional_notes: Usually refers to an organization where people work (a company/employer). It can also mean a business venture or undertaking (especially in phrases like “fracasar con la empresa” = to fail in the venture). Gender/number: la empresa, las empresas.
target_language_example: Dejé la empresa porque encontré un trabajo mejor.
native_language_example: I left the company because I found a better job.

additional_notes: Usually refers to energy in general (physical or spiritual: "la energía que fluye", "se sentía la energía"), but in everyday contexts it can also mean electrical power/utility service ("se interrumpió la energía", "ahorro de la energía", "negocio de la energía"). Feminine noun: la energía.
target_language_example: Se fue la energía durante la tormenta.
native_language_example: The power went out during the storm.

additional_notes: Used to define or describe solar energy. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., "la energía solar es demasiado cara" / "una fuente limpia"). In writing you may see it without the article in general statements: "Energía solar es..." (less common than "La energía solar es...").
target_language_example: La energía solar es buena para el medio ambiente.
native_language_example: Solar energy is good for the environment.

additional_notes: A healthcare worker who cares for patients (e.g., gives injections, explains what to do). The masculine form is "el enfermero"; "la enfermera" can also be used when the nurse is a woman.
target_language_example: La enfermera me tomó la temperatura.
native_language_example: The nurse took my temperature.

meaning: the entrance; admission; a ticket/entry fee.
additional_notes: Often refers to the way in/doorway to a place (La entrada a la estación; Nos vemos en la entrada). It can also mean “admission/entry” as permission to enter (Se prohíbe la entrada) or the cost/ticket for entry (La entrada es gratis/gratuita). In phrases like “forzar la entrada,” it means breaking in/forcing entry. You may also see “la entrada al + place” for “the entrance to the…”.
target_language_example: La entrada al museo cuesta diez euros.
native_language_example: Admission to the museum costs ten euros.

meaning: the stairs; a staircase; a ladder (depending on context).
additional_notes: Usually means “stairs/staircase” in buildings (e.g., subir/bajar la escalera = to go up/down the stairs). In some contexts it can also mean “ladder” (like a stepladder), so the situation (house vs. worksite, etc.) helps. Common with prepositions: por la escalera (via/using the stairs), cuidado con la escalera (watch out for the stairs/ladder).
target_language_example: No uses el ascensor; sube por la escalera.
native_language_example: Don’t use the elevator; go up the stairs.

meaning: "the scene" (especially a crime/incident scene; also a scene in a movie/play).
additional_notes: Common in police/news contexts: "en la escena" = "at/on the scene" (where something happened). It can also mean a specific part of a story or performance: "la escena del balcón" = "the balcony scene". In some contexts, "estar metido en la escena" can mean being involved in what’s going on.
target_language_example: La policía ya está en la escena del accidente.
native_language_example: The police are already at the scene of the accident.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the location where a crime happened, especially in police/detective contexts. Often appears with verbs like llegar a (arrive at), estar en (be at), and ir a (go to).
target_language_example: La policía acordonó la escena del crimen.
native_language_example: The police cordoned off the crime scene.

meaning: the school; also a 'school' of thought/style (movement).
additional_notes: Most often means the physical school or the institution where students study (e.g., 'go to school', 'work at the school'). It can also mean an artistic/intellectual movement or style: "la escuela romántica" = the Romantic school/movement. Common verbs: ir a la escuela (to go to school), volver de la escuela (to come back from school), empezar/terminar (to start/finish).
target_language_example: Mis hijos van a la escuela en autobús.
native_language_example: My kids go to school by bus.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first years of formal schooling for children. You’ll often see it after verbs like ir a (“to go to”) or estar en (“to be in/attend”). In many Spanish-speaking countries, the exact grades covered can vary, but it generally matches “elementary school.”
target_language_example: Mis hijos van a la escuela primaria cerca de casa.
native_language_example: My kids go to the elementary school near our house.

additional_notes: Used for the stage of schooling after elementary/primary school (roughly ages 12–18, depending on the country). In many Latin American countries, this is the standard way to say “high school.” You’ll also hear “instituto” or “preparatoria” in some places. Often used with verbs like dejar/abandonar (to drop out/leave) and desde (since) to talk about that period of life.
target_language_example: Conocí a mi mejor amiga en la escuela secundaria.
native_language_example: I met my best friend in high school.

additional_notes: A common noun for a bladed weapon. Usually used with the article (la espada), and it often appears in set phrases like "con la espada en la mano" (with a sword in hand).
target_language_example: El caballero levantó la espada para defenderse.
native_language_example: The knight raised the sword to defend himself.

meaning: the back (part of the body); also used in phrases meaning “to turn one’s back.”
additional_notes: Usually refers to the human back: “me duele la espalda” (my back hurts). Common expressions: “dar la espalda a alguien” = to turn your back on someone / ignore someone; “rascarse la espalda” = to scratch your back.
target_language_example: Me duele la espalda desde ayer.
native_language_example: My back has hurt since yesterday.

additional_notes: Commonly means “hope” as a positive feeling or belief that something good will happen (Tener esperanza, Perder la esperanza). With "con la esperanza de + infinitive" it means “in the hope of / hoping to” do something: "Vino con la esperanza de verte" = “He/She came hoping to see you.” It can also be used more abstractly/symbolically (e.g., a color representing hope).
target_language_example: No pierdas la esperanza: todo va a mejorar.
native_language_example: Don’t lose hope: everything will get better.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you hope will happen. Very often you’ll see it in the fuller expression “tener la esperanza de que…” (“to have the hope that…”). The verb that follows is commonly in the subjunctive when referring to an uncertain future or desired outcome: “Tengo la esperanza de que todo salga bien.”
target_language_example: Tengo la esperanza de que puedas venir mañana.
native_language_example: I hope that you can come tomorrow.

meaning: the corner (of a street/block; a corner place).
additional_notes: Often used for street directions: “a la esquina” means “to the corner,” and “en la esquina” means “on/at the corner.” In many contexts it refers to the street corner at the end of the block.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la esquina.
native_language_example: See you at the corner.

meaning: the station (usually a train or bus station).
additional_notes: Used for transport hubs: most commonly la estación de tren(es) (train station) or la estación de autobuses (bus station). It can also mean “season” (la estación del año) or “station” in other contexts (e.g., a radio station), but in travel contexts like these examples it usually means a train/bus station.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la estación de tren?
native_language_example: Where is the train station?

additional_notes: Used with a place name to mean “the station in/of [place]”: la estación de Tokio. It can also be used with a type of transport: la estación de buses/autobuses (“the bus station”). With seasons, it’s followed by what the season is for, often a plural noun: la estación de lluvias (“the rainy season”).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la estación de tren a las seis.
native_language_example: See you at the train station at six.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you catch or arrive by train. In everyday speech you may also hear “la estación de trenes” or simply “la estación” when it’s clear you mean the train station. Common in directions with “¿dónde está…?” and locations like “cerca de / lejos de / en el centro”.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la estación de tren a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the train station at eight.

additional_notes: Refers to endless time (often in a religious, philosophical, or poetic sense). It can also be used more loosely to exaggerate how long something feels. Common with verbs like pasar (to spend) and durar (to last): pasar la eternidad = to spend eternity.
target_language_example: Es el lugar indicado para pasar la eternidad.
native_language_example: It’s the right place to spend eternity.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to talk about whether something exists or continues to exist. Common with verbs like demostrar (to prove), negar (to deny), creer en (to believe in), and amenazas a (threatens) + la existencia de…
target_language_example: No hay pruebas de la existencia de vida en ese planeta.
native_language_example: There is no proof of the existence of life on that planet.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something is missing or not enough of it: "la falta de + noun" (e.g., la falta de dinero = lack of money). It often points to a cause or reason for a problem (la falta de atención puede conducir a...).
target_language_example: La falta de tiempo me impide ir al gimnasio.
native_language_example: Lack of time keeps me from going to the gym.

additional_notes: Often refers to your relatives as a group, but it can also mean the people in your household (the ones you live with). It’s commonly used in set phrases like “Bienvenida a la familia” (“Welcome to the family”) and “La familia es la familia” (“Family is family”), meaning family bonds/loyalty matter even when things are complicated. With “en la familia,” it can mean “in the family” as in within the household or among relatives.
target_language_example: Este domingo vamos a cenar con la familia.
native_language_example: This Sunday we’re going to have dinner with the family.

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning “happiness” as a general state or ideal (often about life satisfaction). Common patterns: “encontrar la felicidad” (to find happiness), “camino hacia la felicidad” (the path to happiness), “Te deseo (toda) la felicidad” (I wish you (all) the happiness), and sayings like “La felicidad no puede comprarse / no tiene precio” (Happiness can’t be bought / is priceless).
target_language_example: Para mí, la felicidad es pasar tiempo con mi familia.
native_language_example: For me, happiness is spending time with my family.

additional_notes: Used for a social event where people get together to celebrate (often with food, music, and sometimes alcohol). You’ll often see it with verbs like "ir a" (to go to), "venir a" (to come to), or "empezar" (to start): "ir a la fiesta", "venir a la fiesta", "la fiesta empieza".
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza la fiesta?
native_language_example: What time does the party start?

additional_notes: Used to introduce who the party is hosted by (often a person) or what it is celebrating. With events/holidays it can mean a festival or celebration connected to something (e.g., "la fiesta de carnaval" = a carnival party/celebration). Often followed by a name, a holiday, or a type of party: "la fiesta de Ana", "la fiesta de cumpleaños", "la fiesta de despedida".
target_language_example: ¿Vas a venir a la fiesta de cumpleaños de Marta?
native_language_example: Are you going to come to Marta’s birthday party?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the woodwind instrument (aerophone). Common with the verb "tocar" (to play an instrument): "tocar la flauta" = "to play the flute." You may also hear "flauta dulce" for a recorder.
target_language_example: Mi hermana toca la flauta en la escuela.
native_language_example: My sister plays the flute at school.

additional_notes: Often refers to how something is done: "de la forma que..." = "the way that...". In "encontrar la forma de + infinitive", it means "to find a way to (do something)". It can also mean "form" in the sense of a new style, version, or shape ("la forma nueva").
target_language_example: Tenemos que encontrar la forma de hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: We have to find a way to do it today.

additional_notes: Has two common uses depending on context: (1) "find/figure out a way to do something" (often with verbs like encontrar, buscar: "la forma de + infinitive"). (2) "the shape/form of something" ("tener la forma de + noun").
target_language_example: No encuentro la forma de explicarlo.
native_language_example: I can't find a way to explain it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how something happens or how someone does something. It often introduces a clause: "la forma en la que + verb" ("the way (that) + verb"). In everyday Spanish it’s very common to also hear "la forma en que" (without "la").
target_language_example: No me gustó la forma en la que me hablaste.
native_language_example: I didn’t like the way you spoke to me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a description of someone’s actions, behavior, or manner of doing something: “la forma en que + verb”. It often has a critical or evaluative tone in context (e.g., “I don’t like the way you talk to him”), but it can also be neutral.
target_language_example: No me gusta la forma en que me miras.
native_language_example: I don’t like the way you look at me.

additional_notes: A very common noun for a photograph or picture (often from a camera or phone). Used with verbs like sacar/tomar una foto (to take a photo) and in phrases like la foto del perfil (profile photo) or en la foto (in the photo). Feminine: la foto, una foto; plural: las fotos.
target_language_example: Debo cambiar la foto del perfil.
native_language_example: I need to change the profile photo.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the boundary between two countries, regions, or areas. Common with prepositions like "entre" (between) and verbs like "cruzar" (to cross): "la frontera entre X e Y", "cruzar la frontera".
target_language_example: Tuvimos que mostrar el pasaporte en la frontera.
native_language_example: We had to show our passport at the border.

additional_notes: Used to describe rain that is very intense and often causes problems or delays. Common in phrases like "a causa de la fuerte lluvia" (because of the heavy rain), "por la fuerte lluvia" (due to the heavy rain), and "a pesar de la fuerte lluvia" (despite the heavy rain). Also: "lluvia fuerte" without the article when speaking more generally.
target_language_example: No pudimos conducir bien por la fuerte lluvia.
native_language_example: We couldn’t drive well because of the heavy rain.

additional_notes: Often refers to physical strength ("tiene mucha fuerza"), the concept of force/power in general ("la fuerza de la naturaleza"), or using violence/coercion ("por la fuerza"). In the examples, it contrasts inner strength found in calm and the idea of brute force opposed to civilization.
target_language_example: No todo se consigue por la fuerza.
native_language_example: Not everything can be achieved by force.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone's physical strength, a group's power, or the effectiveness of something (like an army, weapons, or an organization). It’s usually followed by a noun: la fuerza de Joe, la fuerza de una Luna Superior, la fuerza de las armas. In many contexts you can also translate it as “the force of,” but in everyday use it often means “strength” or “power.”
target_language_example: Con la fuerza de este equipo, podemos terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: With the strength of this team, we can finish the project on time.

additional_notes: Common meanings: (1) purpose/role of something: “La función del freno…” = what the brake is for. (2) a scheduled performance/show: “Empieza la función” (The show is starting), “la función de teatro” (the theater performance). In the show sense it’s often used with verbs like ir a, empezar, disfrutar.
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza la función?
native_language_example: What time does the show start?

additional_notes: Refers to a place where goods are made or assembled. Often used with "en" to mean "at/in the factory" (e.g., "en la fábrica"). In some contexts it can also mean a factory/company building (the plant) rather than the business itself.
target_language_example: Trabajo en la fábrica de coches.
native_language_example: I work at the car factory.

meaning: (in expressions like “me da la gana”) “feel like it / want to (do something)”—often with the sense of “because I can / whenever I want.”
additional_notes: Almost always used in fixed phrases with dar: “me/te/le/nos/les da la gana” = “(someone) feels like it / wants to.” With “hacer/ir/venir… cuando me da la gana” it means “whenever I want,” often sounding stubborn, defiant, or rude. You can also say “porque me dio la gana” (“because I felt like it / because I wanted to”).
target_language_example: No voy a explicarlo; lo hice porque me dio la gana.
native_language_example: I’m not going to explain it; I did it because I felt like it.

additional_notes: Refers to the throat area used for swallowing and speaking. Very common in health contexts: “Me duele la garganta” = “My throat hurts / I have a sore throat.” You can add detail with “al tragar” (when swallowing): “Me duele mucho la garganta al tragar.” It also appears in idioms like “(subirse) a la garganta” to express strong emotion or nervousness (something feels like it rises to your throat).
target_language_example: Me duele mucho la garganta al tragar.
native_language_example: My throat hurts a lot when I swallow.

additional_notes: A collective noun that usually takes a singular verb in Spanish: "La gente dice..." = “People say...”. It refers to people as a group (not specific individuals). For a specific crowd, Spanish often uses "las personas", "la gente de aquí", "esta gente", etc.
target_language_example: A veces la gente habla sin saber.
native_language_example: Sometimes people talk without knowing.

additional_notes: Used to refer to people belonging to a specific place, region, organization, or group: la gente de la isla (the people of the island), la gente de África (the people of Africa). It’s often followed by a location or noun phrase.
target_language_example: La gente de este barrio es muy amable.
native_language_example: The people in this neighborhood are very friendly.

meaning: the people here; the local people.
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about people from the place you’re in (a town, neighborhood, country, etc.). It’s a broad, general statement about locals and their habits or situation. Often contrasted with visitors/outsiders (e.g., "la gente de fuera").
target_language_example: La gente de aquí es muy amable con los turistas.
native_language_example: The local people here are very friendly with tourists.

meaning: the people from/of the (place, group, or organization).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group identified by where they are from or what they belong to. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: la gente del teatro (the theater people), la gente del este (people from the east). With a feminine noun, you use: la gente de la + noun (la gente de la ciudad).
target_language_example: La gente del barrio es muy amable.
native_language_example: The people from the neighborhood are very kind.

additional_notes: A poetic or story-like phrase. Depending on context, it can refer to heavenly beings (like angels) or to “people from the sky” (for example, aliens). Grammar: la gente (“people”) is singular in Spanish, so you may see singular verbs too (La gente del cielo piensa...).
target_language_example: Dicen que la gente del cielo nos protege.
native_language_example: They say the people from heaven protect us.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief, rumor, or general opinion without saying exactly who says it. Very common in conversation. You can swap in other subjects: “dicen que…” (they say that…), “mis amigos dicen que…” (my friends say that…).
target_language_example: La gente dice que va a llover mañana.
native_language_example: People say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: "La gente" is grammatically singular in Spanish, even though it refers to multiple people, so it takes singular verbs like "es" (not "son"). Use it for general statements: "La gente es..." = "People are..."
target_language_example: A veces, la gente es muy amable.
native_language_example: Sometimes, people are very kind.

meaning: “people are …” (talking about people in general in a current situation/state).
additional_notes: Used to describe what people (as a group, in general) are like/doing/feeling at a given moment, often followed by an adjective or a gerund: la gente está enfadada (people are angry), la gente está engordando (people are gaining weight). Note: “la gente” is singular in Spanish, so it takes singular verbs: la gente está (not *la gente están*).
target_language_example: En mi barrio, la gente está preocupada por la seguridad.
native_language_example: In my neighborhood, people are worried about safety.

meaning: "people talk/speak" (people in general speak, or are talking).
additional_notes: La gente = “people” (a general group), and it’s grammatically singular, so it takes singular verbs: la gente habla / la gente dice. It can mean (1) people literally speaking a language: “En Canadá, la gente habla inglés y francés”, or (2) people talking about someone/something (often like gossip or public opinion): “La gente habla del agua…”, “La gente habla bien/mal de…”. You can also use it to mean “people will talk” as a general idea: “La gente habla.”
target_language_example: No hagas eso; la gente habla.
native_language_example: Don’t do that; people will talk.

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to talk about young people as a group. It often contrasts with "la gente mayor" (older people). "Gente" is treated as singular in Spanish, so you often see singular verbs/adjectives with it (e.g., "La gente joven tiene...").
target_language_example: En esta ciudad, la gente joven busca trabajo en el centro.
native_language_example: In this city, young people look for work downtown.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people. Spanish uses the singular noun phrase “la gente” (literally “the people”) with a singular verb: “La gente no cambia.” The negation “no” goes directly before the conjugated verb: “La gente no siempre dice…”. If the verb is in the future, it often translates as “won’t”: “La gente no dejará…”.
target_language_example: La gente no entiende lo difícil que es.
native_language_example: People don’t understand how hard it is.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes a group of people. It’s singular in grammar (la gente) even though it refers to many people, so it often takes a singular verb in Spanish (e.g., La gente que vino…). You can also say "las personas que" (more explicitly plural).
target_language_example: La gente que vive aquí es muy amable.
native_language_example: The people who live here are very kind.

additional_notes: Used when talking about what people generally do. “La gente” is singular in Spanish (so verbs usually go in 3rd person singular: “la gente se equivoca”). The “se” is a pronoun that often marks a reflexive verb (people do something to themselves: “se lastima”), but it can also appear with other common patterns like “creerse” (to believe something) or “equivocarse” (to be mistaken).
target_language_example: En internet, la gente se enoja muy rápido.
native_language_example: On the internet, people get angry very quickly.

additional_notes: Used for a place where animals are raised or crops are grown (e.g., una granja de cerdos = a pig farm). It can also be used for other kinds of large production sites, like una granja solar (“a solar farm”). Common with de + owner/name: la granja de su padre (“her father’s farm”).
target_language_example: Compramos leche fresca en la granja.
native_language_example: We buy fresh milk at the farm.

additional_notes: A feminine noun (la guerra). Common in general statements (e.g., "La guerra no es inevitable") and with fixed expressions like "ganar la guerra" (to win the war) and the proverb "perder la batalla pero ganar la guerra" (lose the battle but win the war).
target_language_example: Ojalá que la guerra termine pronto.
native_language_example: I hope the war ends soon.

additional_notes: A feminine noun, so it uses "la" (singular) and "las" (plural: "las guitarras"). Very commonly used with the verb "tocar" (to play an instrument): "tocar la guitarra" = "to play the guitar."
target_language_example: ¿Tocas la guitarra o el piano?
native_language_example: Do you play the guitar or the piano?

meaning: the room (e.g., a room in a home, building, or hotel).
additional_notes: Feminine noun: la habitación / las habitaciones. Commonly used for any room (bedroom, living room, etc.), and also very often means “hotel room.” With verbs like estar/dejar/entrar/salir, it refers to being in or moving into/out of a room (e.g., “dejó la habitación” = “left the room”). Not the same as “cuarto,” which is a very common synonym in many countries.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes esperar en la habitación un momento?
native_language_example: Can you wait in the room for a moment?

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of **estar** (**estaba**) to describe how the room was at that time (dark, cold, locked, covered, etc.). Common pattern: **La habitación estaba + adjective / prepositional phrase** (e.g., *a oscuras*, *con llave*, *cubierta de...*).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, la habitación estaba muy desordenada.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the room was very messy.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe the room’s **location** (e.g., *al final del salón*) or a **state/condition** that can change (temperature, cleanliness, how it’s lit, etc.). Adjectives agree with *habitación* (feminine singular): *está fría/limpia/iluminada*. For more permanent descriptions, Spanish often uses **ser** (e.g., *La habitación es grande*).
target_language_example: La habitación está muy oscura por la noche.
native_language_example: The room is very dark at night.

additional_notes: Common in Argentina, Uruguay, and some other regions; in many other places you’ll hear "el refrigerador" or "la nevera". Used with "en la heladera" = "in the fridge". Feminine noun: "la heladera".
target_language_example: Guardé la comida en la heladera.
native_language_example: I put the food in the fridge.

additional_notes: Used for a physical injury on the body (a cut, gash, puncture, etc.), often when talking about bleeding, healing (curarse), bandaging (vendar), or leaving a scar (cicatriz). Can also be used figuratively for emotional pain, but the most common sense is a bodily wound.
target_language_example: Por favor, muéstreme la herida.
native_language_example: Please show me the wound.

meaning: history; the story (account of what happened).
additional_notes: Often means either (1) the school subject “history” or (2) “the story”/“the whole story” about an event. It can also refer to “history of…” a topic (e.g., la historia de las monedas). In Spanish, “historia” can cover both “history” and “story,” depending on context.
target_language_example: No conozco toda la historia, pero quiero saber qué pasó.
native_language_example: I don’t know the whole story, but I want to know what happened.

meaning: the full story; the whole story.
additional_notes: Used when you want all the details, not just part of what happened. Often said with verbs like contar (to tell) or saber (to know): "contar la historia completa" = "tell the whole story."
target_language_example: Cuéntame la historia completa, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell me the whole story, please.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to talk about either (1) historical events related to a place, country, topic, etc. (la historia de Nepal, la historia de América) or (2) a narrative/tale about someone or something (la historia de un monstruo). Context tells you whether it means "history" or "story."
target_language_example: ¿Conoces la historia de esta ciudad?
native_language_example: Do you know the history of this city?

meaning: "the story of my life"; often used to mean "that always happens to me."
additional_notes: Literally "the story of my life." In conversation it’s frequently an ironic/sarcastic comment after something typical (usually annoying or unlucky) happens again: "That’s the story of my life." It can also be used more literally when someone is going to tell their life story (often with verbs like contar). You’ll also hear it as a short standalone reaction: "La historia de mi vida."
target_language_example: Se me olvidan las llaves otra vez... la historia de mi vida.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys again... story of my life.

meaning: "the story/history of the" (about a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what the story or history is about. It’s made of: la historia (the story/history) + del (= de + el, “of the”). Use it before a masculine singular noun: la historia del pañuelo, la historia del cosmos. With a feminine noun, use "la historia de la" (e.g., la historia de la ciudad). With plural nouns, use "la historia de los/las".
target_language_example: ¿Conoces la historia del edificio?
native_language_example: Do you know the history of the building?

meaning: the time (the hour); the time for something.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current time on the clock (Decir la hora = to tell the time) or the time of an event (la hora exacta de tu partida = the exact time of your departure). With "la hora de + noun/infinitive" it often means "time for" (Es la hora del almuerzo = It’s lunchtime; Se acerca la hora del descanso = break time is coming). It can also mean a moment that will arrive in the future: "Llegará la hora en que..." = "The time will come when...".
target_language_example: ¿Qué hora es? Ya es la hora de irnos.
native_language_example: What time is it? It’s already time for us to leave.

meaning: 'time to' / 'time for' (the time to do something or for something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean “time to + verb”: La hora de almorzar = “time to eat lunch.” It can also be followed by a noun: la hora de la comida = “mealtime.” Common fixed expressions include Llegó la hora de la verdad (“the moment of truth has arrived”) and No veía la hora de… (“I couldn’t wait to…”).
target_language_example: Ya es la hora de irnos.
native_language_example: It’s time for us to go.

meaning: (Spain, slang) “awesome/amazing”; also an exclamation like “holy shit!”
additional_notes: Very informal and can be considered vulgar. Common in Spain. Used as: (1) a strong positive evaluation: “Es la hostia” = “It’s amazing.” (2) an exclamation on its own: “La hostia.” = “Holy shit.” Note: in other contexts, “hostia” can also literally mean the communion wafer, and in expressions like “dar una hostia” it can mean “to slap/punch.”
target_language_example: ¡Este concierto es la hostia!
native_language_example: This concert is awesome!

additional_notes: Refers to humans as a whole, often in a broad, universal sense (e.g., “the most important invention in human history,” “what’s left of humanity”). It can also mean “human nature” or “kindness/compassion,” but in these examples it’s mainly “humankind.”
target_language_example: Debemos proteger el planeta para el futuro de la humanidad.
native_language_example: We must protect the planet for the future of humanity.

additional_notes: Used for an idea, suggestion, or plan. Often appears in phrases like “La idea es + infinitive” (“The idea is to…”), and with verbs like tener (“have”), robar (“steal”), parecer (“seem”), or votar en contra de (“vote against”).
target_language_example: La idea es empezar temprano para evitar el tráfico.
native_language_example: The idea is to start early to avoid traffic.

meaning: "the idea of"; a plan, thought, or concept about something.
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive (la idea de + verb) or a noun to talk about a possible plan or concept: "la idea de comprar...". With "de que" + clause, it introduces a full statement: "la idea de que paguen...". It can also mean "the suggestion/proposal" when referring to whose idea it was ("Fue la idea de ustedes").
target_language_example: No me gusta la idea de mudarme tan lejos.
native_language_example: I don’t like the idea of moving that far away.

meaning: the church (building or the church as an institution).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a church building in location phrases (cerca de la iglesia, al lado de la iglesia, al otro lado de la calle). It can also mean the religious institution/organization (“La iglesia debe…”). With verbs like ir a, it often means attending a service: “ir a la iglesia” = “to go to church.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos después de la iglesia.
native_language_example: See you after church.

additional_notes: Used for an image in a book/screen/photo, or a mental image that something evokes ("La imagen me recuerda..."). Also appears in comparisons like "Es la imagen de su padre" meaning "He/She is the spitting image of his/her father" (very similar in appearance). Feminine noun: la imagen.
target_language_example: Mira la imagen, por favor.
native_language_example: Look at the image, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what is important: “la importancia de + noun” (la importancia de la paz) or “la importancia de + infinitive” (la importancia de hacer ejercicio). Very common in formal or neutral contexts like explanations, presentations, or advice.
target_language_example: No subestimes la importancia de dormir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t underestimate the importance of sleeping well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what something seems like or what you suspect is true, often without being 100% sure. Very common in: "Tengo la impresión de que..." (I have the impression/feeling that...) and "Da la impresión de que..." (It gives the impression that... / It seems that...).
target_language_example: Tengo la impresión de que hoy va a llover.
native_language_example: I have the feeling that it’s going to rain today.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning “information” in general (usually uncountable, like in English). Used with verbs like dar/pedir (“give/ask for information”) and in set phrases like “la era de la información” (“the information age”).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar la información sobre el horario?
native_language_example: Can you give me the information about the schedule?

meaning: the intention to; the plan to.
