additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone intends to do (their purpose/plan). Very common with verbs in the infinitive: "tener la intención de + infinitive" (to intend/plan to...). It can also be used in questions or statements about someone’s motives: "¿Tenía la intención de... ?".
target_language_example: Tengo la intención de estudiar español todos los días.
native_language_example: I intend to study Spanish every day.

additional_notes: Used for academic/scientific work ("research") and also for an official inquiry like a police investigation ("the investigation"). Often appears with verbs like "hacer" (to do research), "dedicarse a" (to devote oneself to), "estar en marcha" (to be underway), and "terminar" (to end).
target_language_example: La investigación continúa y todavía no hay resultados.
native_language_example: The research/investigation continues and there still aren’t any results.

additional_notes: Refers to an island (land surrounded by water). Often used with verbs like llegar a (to arrive at/reach), ir a (to go to), parecer (to seem/look), and estar (to be/located, to be in a state): "llegar a la isla", "ir a la isla", "la isla estaba desierta".
target_language_example: Fuimos a la isla en barco.
native_language_example: We went to the island by boat.

additional_notes: Used for direction or position (opposite of "la derecha"). It can also refer to the left hand/arm, especially in sports or when talking about which hand you use (e.g., "con la izquierda").
target_language_example: Gira a la izquierda en la próxima calle.
native_language_example: Turn left at the next street.

additional_notes: Used for a cage where animals or birds are kept. Often appears with prepositions like "en la jaula" (in the cage) and "de la jaula" (out of/from the cage).
target_language_example: El gato no quiere estar en la jaula.
native_language_example: The cat doesn’t want to be in the cage.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the idea of fairness/right and wrong (La justicia es lenta, pero definitiva) or to legal institutions like courts and law enforcement (Ha huido de la justicia; La justicia se encuentra en la corte). Common collocations: hacer justicia (to do justice), buscar justicia (to seek justice), huir de la justicia (to flee justice), sistema de justicia (justice system).
target_language_example: Solo quiero la justicia para las víctimas.
native_language_example: I only want justice for the victims.

additional_notes: Common noun used with the definite article: “la leche” = “the milk.” In everyday speech it often appears in contexts like buying, drinking, storing, or bringing milk (e.g., “La leche está en el refrigerador”, “Entré con la leche”).
target_language_example: La leche está en el refrigerador.
native_language_example: The milk is in the fridge.

additional_notes: Used with the article (la) to talk about reading in general as a pastime or practice: “Me gusta la lectura” = “I like reading.” Not the same as English “lecture” (that’s usually “conferencia” or “clase magistral”).
target_language_example: La lectura me ayuda a relajarme por la noche.
native_language_example: Reading helps me relax at night.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. With verbs like estirar (to stick out) or sacar (to stick out/pull out), it usually means the body part (tongue). When followed by an adjective or a nationality (árabe, coreana, española), it usually means a language. Also common in the phrase lengua materna = mother tongue/native language.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes sacar la lengua?
native_language_example: Can you stick out your tongue?

additional_notes: Refers to a law/legal system or a specific rule that is officially enforced. Often used with verbs like ser (Es la ley. = “That’s the law.”), cambiar (cambiar la ley = “change the law”), and cumplir (cumplir la ley = “follow/obey the law”).
target_language_example: Todos deben respetar la ley.
native_language_example: Everyone must respect the law.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning the state of being free (politically, personally, or physically). It’s feminine: la libertad. Often used in phrases like "libertad de expresión" (freedom of speech) or "en libertad" (free / at liberty).
target_language_example: La libertad es muy importante para mí.
native_language_example: Freedom is very important to me.

meaning: "the freedom to" / "the liberty to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about being allowed or able to do something: "tener la libertad de + infinitivo" (you are free to...). It also appears in the polite expression "tomarse la libertad de + infinitivo" meaning "to take the liberty of..." (often when you did something without explicitly asking first). It can also be used more literally as "the freedom of" a place or situation.
target_language_example: Me tomé la libertad de llamarte para confirmar la cita.
native_language_example: I took the liberty of calling you to confirm the appointment.

additional_notes: A common, formal phrase used in politics, law, and human rights. It’s usually used with verbs like apoyar (to support), estar a favor de (to be in favor of), and defender (to defend). Often used with para + group: "para todos" (for everyone).
target_language_example: Creemos en la libertad de expresión.
native_language_example: We believe in freedom of speech.

additional_notes: Used for a list of names, items, tasks, etc. Very common with verbs like agregar/añadir (to add), leer (to read), and tener (to have). In Spanish you usually include the article: la lista.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner mi correo en la lista?
native_language_example: Can you put my email on the list?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what the list contains: la lista de invitados (guest list), la lista de canciones (track list), la lista de libros prohibidos (list of banned books). Often appears with estar en la lista de… (“to be on the … list”).
target_language_example: ¿Estás en la lista de invitados?
native_language_example: Are you on the guest list?

meaning: 'the key' (for a lock); also 'the key' in a figurative sense (the solution).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a physical key that opens something: la llave de la puerta, la llave que abre el palacio. It’s also used metaphorically to mean something essential or the way to access/understand something: tener la llave de su corazón (“to have the key to his/her heart”). Feminine noun: la llave, una llave, las llaves.
target_language_example: No encuentro la llave del coche.
native_language_example: I can’t find the car key.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about rain or rainy weather. Uses the feminine article: la lluvia. In Spanish, weather phrases often use verbs like llover (to rain) and parar (to stop): Que pare la lluvia = “I hope the rain stops.”
target_language_example: No puedo salir sin paraguas por la lluvia.
native_language_example: I can’t go out without an umbrella because of the rain.

meaning: the lottery; (figuratively) a very rare stroke of luck.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ganar" (to win) and "(le) tocar" (to win / to get chosen by chance): "ganar la lotería" = to win the lottery; "A Fernando le tocó la lotería" = Fernando won the lottery. It can also be used figuratively to mean something extremely unlikely ("más difícil que ganar la lotería" = harder than winning the lottery).
target_language_example: Si ganara la lotería, viajaría por todo el mundo.
native_language_example: If I won the lottery, I would travel around the world.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article (la) to talk about Earth’s moon in general: Ha salido la luna. Also appears often in poetic descriptions (e.g., “the moon smiled at us”). In Spanish, “Tierra” is usually capitalized when referring to the planet Earth.
target_language_example: Esta noche la luna está muy brillante.
native_language_example: Tonight the moon is very bright.

additional_notes: Used for light in general (as a physical phenomenon) or a specific light source like a lamp/light in a room. Common with verbs like apagar (to turn off), encender (to turn on), and reflects/absorbs (se refleja / absorbe). Feminine noun: la luz; plural: las luces.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes encender la luz, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn on the light, please?

additional_notes: Used with a noun after de to say where the light comes from or what kind of light it is: la luz de las velas (candlelight), la luz de las estrellas (starlight). It can also be used figuratively to mean “guidance/clarity/truth” (la luz de la verdad). Note: “la luz” is feminine, so you’ll usually see la luz de…, and plural las luces de….
target_language_example: Prefiero la luz de la mañana para leer.
native_language_example: I prefer the morning light for reading.

meaning: daylight; (also) “the light of day” (to exist/be seen or made public).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: natural light during the day ("No vimos la luz del día"). It’s also used in the fixed expression "ver la luz del día" like English “see the light of day,” meaning something appears, becomes visible, or is released/published (and in the negative: "no volver a ver la luz del día" = never be seen/used/published again).
target_language_example: Ese informe nunca vio la luz del día.
native_language_example: That report never saw the light of day.

additional_notes: A common, literal phrase meaning the sun’s light. Often used when talking about warming/heating (calentar) or lighting up/illuminating a place (iluminar). You can also see it in comparisons/metaphors (e.g., “what sunlight is to flowers…”).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos afuera para disfrutar de la luz del sol.
native_language_example: We sat outside to enjoy the sunlight.

additional_notes: Used for a lamp or light fixture that gives light (e.g., a bedside lamp, desk lamp). Often followed by an adjective to describe it ("la lámpara vieja", "la lámpara gris"). Related verbs: "encender" (to turn on/light) and "apagar" (to turn off).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes apagar la lámpara, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the lamp, please?

meaning: the line (mark/row); the line (phone connection); a boundary/limit; a line of thought/approach (“in line with”).
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) a physical line or row on a form/page: "En la línea, sólo tu nombre." (2) a boundary you shouldn’t cross: "Cruzar la línea" = “to cross the line.” (3) telephone connection: "La línea se cortó" = “The line got cut / We got disconnected.” (4) "en la línea de" = “in line with / along the lines of,” often for plans, policies, ideas: "No va en la línea de nuestra política." Also "final de la línea" = “end of the line” (literal or figurative).
target_language_example: Lo que dices no está en la línea de lo que acordamos.
native_language_example: What you’re saying isn’t in line with what we agreed.

meaning: “the … line of” / “the … line” (used to name a specific type of line).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to specify what kind of line you mean: la línea de comandos (command line), la línea de montaje (assembly line), la línea de llegada (finish line), la línea de gol (goal line), la línea de tren/metro (train/subway line). It’s a very literal, common pattern: la + línea + de + [thing].
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la línea de metro que va al centro?
native_language_example: Where is the subway line that goes downtown?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mother and connect her to another person or thing. It’s typically followed by a noun or a possessive phrase: la madre de mi amigo (my friend’s mother), la madre de un amigo mío (a friend of mine’s mother).
target_language_example: La madre de mi hermano trabaja en un hospital.
native_language_example: My brother’s mother works in a hospital.

additional_notes: Used to talk about unlucky events or an unlucky situation. Often appears after "tener" (to have) or with "ser" to describe something as unlucky (e.g., "un número de mala suerte" = an unlucky number). Can also be used alone as an exclamation or short comment: "¡La mala suerte!"
target_language_example: Hoy tengo la mala suerte de perder el autobús.
native_language_example: Today I have the bad luck of missing the bus.

additional_notes: A common noun for a suitcase or piece of luggage (usually for travel). It’s feminine: la maleta, una maleta; plural: las maletas. Often used with verbs like llevar (to carry/take), cerrar (to close), cargar (to load/carry), and perder de vista (to lose sight of).
target_language_example: Puse la maleta en el maletero del coche.
native_language_example: I put the suitcase in the trunk of the car.

additional_notes: Used to introduce how something happens or is done. It’s often followed by a verb: "la manera en que + [someone] + verb". Very similar in meaning to "la forma en que".
target_language_example: No me gustó la manera en que respondió a la pregunta.
native_language_example: I didn’t like the way he/she answered the question.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a person’s hand (body part). Common with verbs like tener (to have), poner (to put), and in phrases like en la mano (in the hand). Sometimes used in fixed expressions (e.g., morder la mano que te da de comer = “bite the hand that feeds you”).
target_language_example: Me duele la mano derecha.
native_language_example: My right hand hurts.

meaning: "the right hand"; also "someone’s right-hand person" (main helper).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers literally to the right hand (often used in instructions: "Levante la mano derecha" = "Raise your right hand"). Figuratively, "ser la mano derecha de alguien" means to be someone’s main assistant or most trusted helper.
target_language_example: Ella es la mano derecha del director en la oficina.
native_language_example: She is the director’s right-hand person in the office.

additional_notes: Used for the left hand specifically (vs. “la mano derecha” = the right hand). With body parts in Spanish, you usually use the definite article (“la”), not a possessive (“my”), even when it’s your own body: “Me duele la mano izquierda” = “My left hand hurts.” It can also appear in fixed/religious expressions like “la mano izquierda de Dios” (“the left hand of God”).
target_language_example: Me duele la mano izquierda desde ayer.
native_language_example: My left hand has hurt since yesterday.

additional_notes: A common noun for the fruit. Uses the feminine singular article “la”; plural: “las manzanas”. You can describe it with adjectives like color ("La manzana es verde") or talk about cutting it ("partió la manzana en dos").
target_language_example: Quiero comerme la manzana después de la cena.
native_language_example: I want to eat the apple after dinner.

meaning: the sea; also (in “la mar de…”) ‘very’ / ‘a lot of’.
additional_notes: “Mar” is often masculine (“el mar”), but “la mar” is also common—especially in poetic or traditional sailor speech. In everyday colloquial Spanish, the fixed pattern “la mar de + adjective/adverb/noun” is used as an intensifier: “la mar de bien” = “very well,” “la mar de ocupados” = “very busy,” “la mar de gente” = “a lot of people.”
target_language_example: Hoy estoy la mar de cansado.
native_language_example: Today I’m very tired.

additional_notes: Used with de to mean “most of” a group or amount: la mayor parte de los casos (most cases), la mayor parte de los invitados (most of the guests). You can also use it with del/de la: la mayor parte del día (most of the day), la mayor parte del dolor (most of the pain). It can appear set off by commas to emphasize the idea of “for the most part/mostly.”
target_language_example: La mayor parte de la gente llega temprano.
native_language_example: Most people arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the biggest portion of something (time, people, things). It’s followed by a noun or by “lo que…” (e.g., “la mayor parte de lo que dijo” = “most of what he/she said”). Often paired with time expressions like “su vida” (his/her life) or “el día” (the day).
target_language_example: Pasé la mayor parte del día trabajando.
native_language_example: I spent most of the day working.

meaning: most of the / the majority of the.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the bigger portion of something (a group, a period of time, an amount). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun because of “del” (= de + el): la mayor parte del público/dinero/tiempo. With a feminine noun, use “la mayor parte de la …” (e.g., la mayor parte de la gente). Verb agreement can be singular or plural depending on whether you treat “parte” or the following noun as the main idea, but singular is very common (La mayor parte del dinero fue…).
target_language_example: La mayor parte del día estuve trabajando.
native_language_example: I spent most of the day working.

meaning: most of the time; the majority of the time.
additional_notes: Used to say what usually happens or what is true in general, not 100% of the time. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence (e.g., “La mayor parte del tiempo…, ” or “… la mayor parte del tiempo.”).
target_language_example: La mayor parte del tiempo trabajo desde casa.
native_language_example: Most of the time I work from home.

additional_notes: Used with **de** to mean “most of” (la mayoría de + noun/pronoun): *la mayoría de sus novelas* = “most of his/her novels.” It usually takes singular verb agreement when treated as a group (*La mayoría ha...*), though plural agreement is also common when emphasizing the people/things within the group (*La mayoría han...*). You can also use it alone as a short answer: *La mayoría.* = “Most of them.”
target_language_example: La mayoría de mis amigos vive cerca.
native_language_example: Most of my friends live nearby.

additional_notes: Used to talk about more than half of a group. It’s followed by a noun phrase: la mayoría de + los/las + plural noun (la mayoría de los alumnos), or a plural noun directly (la mayoría de pasajeros). The verb can be singular or plural depending on whether you treat it as “the majority” (singular) or “most people/things” (plural): La mayoría de la gente es... / La mayoría de los alumnos van...
target_language_example: La mayoría de mis amigos vive cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: Most of my friends live near here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the larger part of a group of males or a mixed-gender group (ellos = “they/them”). For an all-female group, use “la mayoría de ellas” (“most of them”). Often followed by a verb: “La mayoría de ellos se fue/se fueron…”.
target_language_example: La mayoría de ellos no entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: Most of them don’t understand the question.

meaning: most people; the majority of people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true for most people in general (a generalization). It’s often followed by a verb in the singular ("la mayoría ... está/es/hace") because "la mayoría" is the main subject, though plural agreement is sometimes heard in everyday speech.
target_language_example: La mayoría de la gente piensa que es una buena idea.
native_language_example: Most people think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say that more than half of a group of feminine plural nouns does something: "la mayoría de las escuelas" = "most of the schools". It can also appear as "La mayoría de las veces" = "most of the time".
target_language_example: La mayoría de las personas llegan temprano.
native_language_example: Most people arrive early.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “most of the …”. It agrees with the noun: la mayoría de las + feminine plural (la mayoría de las personas), and la mayoría de + a singular/uncountable noun (la mayoría del tiempo). It’s often followed by a plural verb (La mayoría de los estudiantes son…), though singular is sometimes used in formal contexts.
target_language_example: La mayoría de los estudiantes viven cerca de la universidad.
native_language_example: Most of the students live near the university.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true for most people in a group. Structure: "la mayoría de" + plural noun (e.g., "la mayoría de los estudiantes" = most students). It can be followed by a plural verb, as in the examples.
target_language_example: La mayoría de los japoneses hablan japonés.
native_language_example: Most Japanese people speak Japanese.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the morning period (roughly from sunrise until around noon). With clock times, Spanish often uses “de la mañana” to mean “a.m.”: “la una de la mañana” = 1:00 a.m. Common set phrases include “por la mañana” (in the morning), “pasar la mañana + gerund” (to spend the morning doing something), “la mañana del + day” (the morning of…), and “desde la mañana a la noche” (from morning to night).
target_language_example: Nos vemos por la mañana.
native_language_example: See you in the morning.

meaning: the next morning; the following morning.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the morning of the day after a previously mentioned day or event. Often appears with plans or actions that happen the day after something: "...la mañana siguiente" or "a la mañana siguiente" (= the next morning).
target_language_example: Nos fuimos a casa y volvimos la mañana siguiente.
native_language_example: We went home and came back the next morning.

additional_notes: Used for the prize for 1st place in a competition. Often appears with verbs like ganar (to win), obtener (to get), and with de + event: la medalla de oro de la competencia (the competition’s gold medal).
target_language_example: Ella ganó la medalla de oro en natación.
native_language_example: She won the gold medal in swimming.

additional_notes: Used with prepositions like a (at), hasta (until/by), and pasada (past/after): a la medianoche = at midnight; hasta la medianoche = until/by midnight; pasada la medianoche = after midnight. Usually refers to the transition between one day and the next.
target_language_example: Tenemos que entregar el trabajo hasta la medianoche.
native_language_example: We have to turn in the assignment by midnight.

additional_notes: Used to describe the best female person or a feminine noun (explicit or implied). Often followed by “de” (“la mejor de todas”) or a noun (“la mejor estrategia”). For masculine, use “el mejor”; for plural, “los/las mejores”. Accent matters: “mejor” (better/best) vs “mayor” (older/bigger).
target_language_example: Para mí, ella es la mejor del equipo.
native_language_example: For me, she’s the best on the team.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the most effective/ideal method for doing an action, typically followed by an infinitive: “la mejor forma de + infinitive” (la mejor forma de hacerlo / de aprender / de llegar). You can also use “la mejor manera de” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: La mejor forma de practicar español es hablar un poco cada día.
native_language_example: The best way to practice Spanish is to speak a little every day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the best method or approach for an action that follows, usually with an infinitive (e.g., "la mejor manera de aprender") or with "es" + gerund/infinitive ("la mejor manera de hacerlo es..."). Often interchangeable with "la mejor forma de".
target_language_example: La mejor manera de aprender español es practicar un poco cada día.
native_language_example: The best way to learn Spanish is to practice a little every day.

la mejor noche de mi vida

target_language_multi_word_term: la mejor noche de mi vida
additional_notes: A strong, emotional way to say a night was amazing or unforgettable. Often used after an experience (Fue/Anoche fue...), or dramatically about the present/future (Esta es/será...). You can swap the time (fue/es/será) and the possessive to match the person: la mejor noche de tu vida (your), de su vida (his/her/their), de nuestra vida (our).
target_language_example: ¡Fue la mejor noche de mi vida!
native_language_example: It was the best night of my life!

additional_notes: Common after verbs like tener/en la mente (to have in mind), venir a la mente (to come to mind), and quedarse la mente en blanco (for your mind to go blank). It refers to thinking, remembering, imagining, or mental strength/ability.
target_language_example: No puedo sacarlo de la mente.
native_language_example: I can’t get it out of my mind.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a piece of furniture (dining table, desk, etc.). In the phrase "poner la mesa," it means "to set the table" (put out plates, cutlery, glasses, etc.). Feminine noun: "la mesa"; plural "las mesas."
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la mesa del comedor?
native_language_example: Where is the dining table?

meaning: “shit” (vulgar); also “this/that shit” or “crap” (vulgar) in a more general sense.
additional_notes: Very vulgar/strong. Literally refers to feces (e.g., it smells bad, cleaning it). It’s also used to refer to something unpleasant or difficult (“la mierda ya es bastante difícil” = “this shit is hard enough”), or as an insult about someone/something (“eres la mierda…” = “you’re shit/you’re a piece of shit”). Often sounds stronger than English “crap.”
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de la mierda de ayer.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about yesterday’s shit.

meaning: the mission; a specific task or assignment (often official).
additional_notes: Used for an objective or operation someone must carry out (military, police, work, religious, etc.). Common with verbs like terminar/concluir (finish), llevar a cabo (carry out), cancelar/abortar (cancel/abort), and with phrases like tener luz verde (have the green light).
target_language_example: Tenemos que cumplir la misión antes del amanecer.
native_language_example: We have to complete the mission before dawn.

additional_notes: Feminine form of "el/la mismo/a" and agrees with a feminine noun (explicit or implied): "la misma persona" = "the same person." It can also stand alone like a pronoun when the noun is understood: "Quiero la misma" = "I want the same one."
target_language_example: Compramos la misma camiseta.
native_language_example: We bought the same T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people attend the identical class/course or are in the same class group. Agreement: same class = "la misma clase"; same classes (plural) = "las mismas clases".
target_language_example: ¿Estás en la misma clase que yo?
native_language_example: Are you in the same class as me?

additional_notes: Used to say two people/ideas/actions are identical, or to complain that something repeats again and again (often: "siempre es la misma cosa"). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: "la misma cosa" (feminine singular), "el mismo problema", "las mismas cosas", "los mismos días".
target_language_example: No quiero discutir la misma cosa otra vez.
native_language_example: I don’t want to argue about the same thing again.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people have an equal or very similar age. Often appears with comparison words like “más o menos” (more or less) or “aproximadamente” (approximately), and with “que” to compare: “tener la misma edad que…” = “to be the same age as…”.
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo tenemos la misma edad.
native_language_example: My sister and I are the same age.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: "ser/tener de la misma edad que..." = to be the same age as someone. You can also add approximations like "casi" (almost) or "aproximadamente" (approximately) before it.
target_language_example: Mi primo es de la misma edad que yo.
native_language_example: My cousin is the same age as me.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people attended (or attend) the identical school. It often appears in comparisons with "que" ("la misma escuela que...") or with a relative clause ("la misma escuela a la que...").
target_language_example: Nos conocimos porque íbamos a la misma escuela.
native_language_example: We met because we went to the same school.

additional_notes: Used when someone repeats an identical question again (and often often), or when you keep wondering the same thing. It’s feminine because pregunta is feminine (la misma). You can also change it for number/gender: el mismo problema (the same problem), las mismas preguntas (the same questions).
target_language_example: No me hagas la misma pregunta otra vez.
native_language_example: Don’t ask me the same question again.

additional_notes: Common patterns: **la mitad de + noun/pronoun** (“half of …”): *La mitad de ellos…* / *La mitad de las bananas…*. Also used with **por la mitad** (“in half / into two equal parts”): *Cortó el pastel por la mitad.* You can use it for amounts (*Dame la mitad* = “give me half”) and figuratively for something being cut in half (*casi te corta por la mitad*).
target_language_example: Si quieres, pagamos la mitad cada uno.
native_language_example: If you want, we’ll each pay half.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or pronoun to say 50% of a group/amount: "la mitad de los estudiantes" (half of the students), "la mitad de nuestras fuerzas" (half of our strength/forces). You can modify it with words like "casi" (almost) or "solo" (only): "casi la mitad de...", "solo la mitad de...". With comparisons, it can mean "half as ... as": "la mitad de grande que" (half as big as).
target_language_example: Solo comí la mitad de la pizza.
native_language_example: I only ate half of the pizza.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la + noun) to mean “half of the …”: *la mitad de la población*, *la mitad de la Tierra*. For masculine nouns, use **la mitad del** (*la mitad del tiempo*). It can also appear without **de** when you just mean “half”: *la mitad de la tarea* / *la mitad de la frase*.
target_language_example: La mitad de la clase llegó tarde.
native_language_example: Half of the class arrived late.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: la mitad del alquiler, la mitad del texto. (Before a feminine singular noun, you use “la mitad de la”: la mitad de la casa.) It commonly expresses quantities, portions, or percentages. With people it can be literal (“half the man you are”) or figurative.
target_language_example: Solo necesito la mitad del dinero hoy.
native_language_example: I only need half of the money today.

additional_notes: A common noun for a large natural elevation. Use it with the definite article: la montaña. Often used with verbs like subir (to go up/climb), escalar (to climb), and with prepositions like hasta (up to) and a mitad de (halfway up).
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a subir la montaña si hace buen tiempo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to climb the mountain if the weather is good.

additional_notes: Uses the superlative structure “más + adjective” = “most + adjective” (here, “más alta” = “highest,” feminine to match “montaña”). Often followed by “de/del …” to say “in/of …”: “la montaña más alta del mundo/de África/de Europa.” You can swap in other nouns and adjectives: “el edificio más alto” (the tallest building).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es la montaña más alta de este país?
native_language_example: Which is the highest mountain in this country?

additional_notes: Refers to a female, usually a girl or young woman (often a teenager or young adult). Similar to "la chica" (very common) and sometimes older than "la niña" (little girl). Can be used when you don’t know the person’s name: "la muchacha que…".
target_language_example: La muchacha que trabaja aquí es muy amable.
native_language_example: The young woman who works here is very kind.

additional_notes: A common noun used with the definite article (la). Often appears in comparisons and in the structure “la muerte de + person” (“the death of + person”). It can also be used more generally as the concept of death.
target_language_example: La muerte de su padre cambió su vida.
native_language_example: The death of her father changed her life.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s death, often followed by a name or a possessive phrase: la muerte de Neil Perry; la muerte de su madre. You’ll also see it in expressions like “desde la muerte de…” (“since the death of…”) and with verbs like llorar (to mourn) or superar (to get over).
target_language_example: Nunca olvidaremos la muerte de nuestro abuelo.
native_language_example: We will never forget the death of our grandfather.

meaning: 'death is' (used to define or describe death).
additional_notes: Common sentence starter: “La muerte es + noun/adjective” to say what death is like (e.g., “La muerte es permanente”). You can also add comparisons with “similar a” (“La muerte es similar al sueño”).
target_language_example: Para él, la muerte es parte de la vida.
native_language_example: For him, death is part of life.

additional_notes: Usually means “the woman.” In some contexts it can also mean “the wife” (often "mi mujer" = “my wife”). It can be used with a relative clause to identify which woman: "La mujer que...".
target_language_example: La mujer está esperando afuera.
native_language_example: The woman is waiting outside.

meaning: “the woman who/that …” (introduces information describing a woman).
additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause with que (“who/that”) to identify or describe a specific woman: La mujer que + verb/phrase. In Spanish, que is used for both “who” and “that” in this kind of sentence.
target_language_example: La mujer que trabaja aquí es mi profesora.
native_language_example: The woman who works here is my teacher.

additional_notes: Refers to a large group of people gathered in one place (e.g., at a game, concert, or in the street). Often used with verbs like "gritar/chillar" (to shout), "dispersarse" (to disperse), or "perder de vista" (to lose sight of someone) "en medio de la multitud".
target_language_example: Había tanta gente que no podía avanzar por la multitud.
native_language_example: There were so many people that I couldn’t move forward through the crowd.

additional_notes: Used for a physical machine/device (from small appliances to large machines). You’ll often see it with verbs like funcionar (“to work/run”): hacer que la máquina funcione = “make the machine work.”
target_language_example: La máquina no funciona, así que tengo que arreglarla.
native_language_example: The machine doesn’t work, so I have to fix it.

additional_notes: Used to avoid repeating a previously mentioned noun: *Tu idea es parecida a la mía* (= my idea). It agrees in gender and number with what you’re talking about: **la mía** (feminine singular), **el mío** (masculine singular), **las mías** (feminine plural), **los míos** (masculine plural). Often used in contrasts like *tu voluntad, no la mía* (“your will, not mine”).
target_language_example: Esa chaqueta no es tuya; es la mía.
native_language_example: That jacket isn’t yours; it’s mine.

additional_notes: A feminine noun, so it uses the article la (“the”): la música. It can refer to music in general (La música es un lenguaje universal.) or to the sound being played at the moment (Baja la música.). Often used with verbs like escuchar (to listen to) and bajar/subir (to turn down/up).
target_language_example: Me gusta la música, pero hoy prefiero el silencio.
native_language_example: I like music, but today I prefer silence.

additional_notes: A common genre label. Often used with verbs like gustar/encantar/preferir: "Me gusta la música clásica" (I like classical music), "Prefiero la música clásica" (I prefer classical music). Can be contrasted with other genres: "...mientras que yo prefiero el jazz" (while I prefer jazz).
target_language_example: Cuando necesito concentrarme, pongo la música clásica.
native_language_example: When I need to concentrate, I put on classical music.

meaning: 'music is' (used to describe or define music).
additional_notes: Common sentence starter: “La música” (music) + “es” (is). Use it to give an opinion (“La música es aburrida”), describe a quality (“La música es maravillosa”), or define what music means to someone (“La música es vida / mi pasión”). You can swap in other nouns too: “El café es…”.
target_language_example: Para mí, la música es muy importante.
native_language_example: For me, music is very important.

additional_notes: A common body-part noun. In Spanish, body parts usually use the definite article (la/ el) instead of a possessive: "Tienes algo en la nariz" (literally “You have something in the nose” = “in your nose”). Also appears in expressions like "tener la nariz enterrada en un libro" (“to have your nose buried in a book” = to be absorbed in reading).
target_language_example: Me duele la nariz.
native_language_example: My nose hurts.

additional_notes: Refers to the natural world in general: plants, animals, landscapes, and the environment. Often used with verbs like gustar (Me gusta la naturaleza) and with topics like protecting the environment (salvar/proteger la naturaleza). Also used in general statements (La naturaleza está llena de...).
target_language_example: Nos encanta pasar tiempo en la naturaleza los fines de semana.
native_language_example: We love spending time in nature on the weekends.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. In sci‑fi or travel contexts, it’s usually a ship/spacecraft (e.g., "Hay algo en la nave" = something is on/in the ship). In business/industry contexts, "una nave" often means a large industrial building/warehouse ("nave industrial"). It’s feminine: la nave, una nave.
target_language_example: Hay algo raro en la nave.
native_language_example: There’s something strange on the ship.

additional_notes: Refers to a vehicle designed to travel in space. It’s commonly used with verbs like "aterrizar" (to land), "despegar" (to take off), "volver" (to return), and "salir de" (to exit): "salir de la nave espacial" = "to leave the spaceship."
target_language_example: Los astronautas entraron en la nave espacial antes de despegar.
native_language_example: The astronauts went into the spaceship before taking off.

additional_notes: Used for the weather phenomenon that reduces visibility. Common with verbs like "haber" (hay la niebla / hay niebla), "aparecer" (to appear), "cubrir" (to cover), and in phrases like "en la niebla" (in the fog). Always feminine: "la niebla".
target_language_example: Nos perdimos en la niebla y tuvimos que volver atrás.
native_language_example: We got lost in the fog and had to turn back.

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning the white frozen precipitation (“the snow”). Common in comparisons like "blanco/a como la nieve" (“as white as snow”) and with verbs like "caer" (to fall) or "cubrir" (to cover).
target_language_example: En invierno, a veces cae la nieve en las montañas.
native_language_example: In winter, snow sometimes falls in the mountains.

meaning: 'the snow (it) …' (with **se** used to form an intransitive/“happens by itself” verb).
additional_notes: You’ll usually see this followed by a verb like **acumularse** (to pile up), **derretirse** (to melt), **tornarse** (to become). Here **se** doesn’t mean “herself/itself” in a literal sense; it often marks that the change/state happens on its own: **La nieve se derrite** = “The snow melts.” (not “Someone melts the snow”).
target_language_example: La nieve se acumuló durante la noche.
native_language_example: The snow piled up overnight.

additional_notes: "La" is the feminine singular "the." "Niña" means "girl" (often a child). Used for a specific girl already known in the situation or mentioned before. Plural: "las niñas" (the girls). Contrast: "la mujer" (the woman), "la chica" (the girl/young woman, often more casual).
target_language_example: La niña está jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: The little girl is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Often used for the time after sunset or the evening/night in general. Common patterns: "por la noche" (at night), "de noche" (at night/by night), "la noche del…" (the night of…), and "caer la noche" (night is falling / it’s getting dark).
target_language_example: Por la noche hace frío aquí.
native_language_example: At night it’s cold here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the night immediately before a certain day/event mentioned or understood from context. Often followed by “a + [event]” (e.g., “la noche anterior a un vuelo”).
target_language_example: Preparé todo la noche anterior al examen.
native_language_example: I prepared everything the night before the exam.

meaning: "the night in…" / "the night when…" (depending on what comes next).
additional_notes: Used in two very common patterns: (1) **pasar la noche en + place** = “to spend the night in + place” (location). Example: *Pasamos la noche en Hakone.* (2) **la noche en que + clause** = “the night when + sentence” (time). Example: *la noche en que se conocieron* = “the night when they met.” Here **en que** functions like “when,” so it’s not translated word-for-word as “in that.”
target_language_example: Lo vi la noche en que llegó al pueblo.
native_language_example: I saw him the night when he arrived in town.

meaning: a night in a hotel (staying overnight at a hotel).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like pasar (to spend) to talk about staying overnight at a hotel: pasar la noche en un hotel. You can add details after hotel (caro, barato, económico, de cinco estrellas). Also common in the plural: pasar las noches en un hotel.
target_language_example: Por el vuelo cancelado, tuvimos que pasar la noche en un hotel.
native_language_example: Because of the canceled flight, we had to spend the night in a hotel.

meaning: the news; a piece of news; the report.
additional_notes: Used for a specific news item or report: una noticia (a news story). It can also mean “news” in general in some contexts (e.g., ¿Cuál es la noticia? = What’s the news?). Often used with verbs like ser (to be) and llegar (to arrive): La noticia es falsa (The news/report is false).
target_language_example: Parece que la noticia era falsa.
native_language_example: It seems that the news was false.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the information/announcement that someone has died. "Su" means "his" or "her" (or sometimes "their" singular formal), depending on context. Common verbs with this phrase include: recibir (to receive), difundir/se difundió (to spread), sorprender (to surprise), and llorar por (to cry about).
target_language_example: Todavía no puedo creer la noticia de su muerte.
native_language_example: I still can’t believe the news of his/her death.

meaning: “the new” (feminine singular), often meaning “the new one.”
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la nueva película = “the new movie”), or by itself when the noun is understood from context (Ella es la nueva = “She’s the new one,” e.g., the new teacher/employee). It must agree with the noun: la nueva (fem. sing.), el nuevo (masc. sing.), las nuevas (fem. pl.), los nuevos (masc. pl.).
target_language_example: Ella es la nueva en la oficina.
native_language_example: She’s the new one in the office.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a recently introduced or recently passed law. Often appears with verbs like aprobar (to pass/approve), explicar (to explain), and afectar (to affect). Gender/number: la (feminine singular) + ley (law).
target_language_example: La nueva ley entrará en vigor el próximo mes.
native_language_example: The new law will take effect next month.

meaning: “the work” (a piece of art/music/literature, a play, or construction/work being done).
additional_notes: "La obra" is a common way to refer to a creative work (a novel, musical piece, painting, etc.) or specifically a theater play ("una obra de teatro"). It can also mean building/construction work or a job/task in progress, so the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: ¿Has visto la obra en el teatro todavía?
native_language_example: Have you seen the play at the theater yet?

meaning: 'the offer' (a proposal; also a deal/special price).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like aceptar (to accept) and rechazar (to reject). It can refer to an offer of help, an invitation, or a formal proposal (e.g., una oferta de trabajo = a job offer). In stores, una oferta can also mean a special deal/discount.
target_language_example: Acepté la oferta de trabajo.
native_language_example: I accepted the job offer.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a place where people do desk/administrative work: a company office, a department office, etc. Can also mean a specific office within an organization (e.g., la oficina del comandante = “the commander’s office”). With movement verbs it commonly appears as ir/venir a la oficina (“to go/come to the office”).
target_language_example: Hoy trabajo desde casa, pero mañana voy a la oficina.
native_language_example: Today I’m working from home, but tomorrow I’m going to the office.

additional_notes: A common place/building where you send mail and packages. Often used with location verbs like estar/quedar/ubicarse (to be located). You can also say "correos" in some countries to refer to the postal service.
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la oficina de correos para enviar un paquete.
native_language_example: I have to go to the post office to send a package.

additional_notes: Most commonly used for a medical/surgical operation (a procedure a doctor or surgeon performs). It’s feminine: la operación. You’ll often hear it with verbs like realizar/hacer (to perform/do) and suspender (to suspend/call off). It can also mean a more general “operation” (e.g., a police or military operation), but the examples here are medical.
target_language_example: La operación salió bien y ya está recuperándose.
native_language_example: The operation went well and he/she is already recovering.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the general attitude of society toward an issue, person, or policy—often in politics and the news. Common with verbs like reflejar (to reflect), cambiar (to change), estar a favor de (to be in favor of), and estar en contra de (to be against). Usually singular even though it refers to many people.
target_language_example: Según las encuestas, la opinión pública está en contra de la nueva ley.
native_language_example: According to the polls, public opinion is against the new law.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning a good moment or possibility to do something. Often used with verbs like tener (to have), dar (to give), aprovechar (to take advantage of), perder/dejar pasar (to miss/let pass), and phrases like si tienes la oportunidad (“if you get the chance”).
target_language_example: Si tengo la oportunidad, iré contigo.
native_language_example: If I get the chance, I’ll go with you.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (de + verb) to say someone has/gets/takes a chance to do something: "tener la oportunidad de..." (to have the chance to...), "darle la oportunidad de..." (to give someone the chance to...), "aprovechar la oportunidad de..." (to take advantage of the chance to...).
target_language_example: No tuve la oportunidad de hablar con el doctor.
native_language_example: I didn’t have the chance to talk to the doctor.

meaning: 'the order' (a command or an official instruction); also 'the order' (a purchase/order request).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a command given by someone in authority (e.g., a boss, officer, judge): "Dar la orden" = to give the order; "cumplir la orden" = to carry out/obey the order. In business/shipping contexts it can also mean an order you place (purchase order): "hacer la orden" = to place/make the order. Note: "orden" also exists as "el orden" meaning 'order/organization' (the opposite of chaos), but "la orden" is specifically a command or a purchase order.
target_language_example: El jefe dio la orden de cerrar la tienda.
native_language_example: The boss gave the order to close the store.

meaning: the orchestra (a large group of musicians who play together).
additional_notes: A feminine noun, so it takes "la" (singular) and "las" (plural: "las orquestas"). Used for ensembles that play classical music (symphonies, waltzes, etc.), but it can also refer more generally to a big instrumental group. Common verbs with it: "tocar" (to play), "interpretar" (to perform), "empezar a" (to start to).
target_language_example: La orquesta va a tocar esta noche en el teatro.
native_language_example: The orchestra is going to play tonight at the theater.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tener miedo de / temer ("to be afraid of") and estar en ("to be in"): tener miedo de la oscuridad, estar en la oscuridad. It can also be used figuratively in poetic or fantasy contexts (e.g., espíritus de la oscuridad = "spirits of darkness").
target_language_example: No puedo ver nada en la oscuridad.
native_language_example: I can't see anything in the dark.

meaning: "the other night" (a recent night in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past night that happened recently, but not necessarily last night (it could be a few nights ago). Often used when the exact date isn’t important or isn’t specified. Can also be understood as “the other evening,” depending on context.
target_language_example: La otra noche vi una película en casa.
native_language_example: The other night I watched a movie at home.

meaning: the other shore/bank (of a river, lake, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the opposite side of a body of water (especially a river). Often appears with "del río" (of the river) or with prepositions like "en" (on), "desde" (from), and "a" (to): "en la otra orilla del río" = on the other bank of the river.
target_language_example: Vamos a cruzar el puente para llegar a la otra orilla.
native_language_example: We’re going to cross the bridge to get to the other side/riverbank.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the second of two things already mentioned or understood from context. It agrees in gender and number: la otra (fem. sing.), el otro (masc. sing.), las otras (fem. pl.), los otros (masc. pl.). Often used to contrast choices or parts: "Esa camisa no, la otra" (= not that shirt, the other one) or "con la otra (mano)" (= with the other hand). Also appears in fixed patterns like "Una cosa llevó a la otra" (one thing led to another).
target_language_example: No quiero esta taza; prefiero la otra.
native_language_example: I don’t want this cup; I prefer the other one.

meaning: the word; also, the floor/turn to speak.
additional_notes: Most commonly means “the word” (a specific word or term): *No me viene la palabra* = “I can’t think of the word.” In more formal contexts, *tomar la palabra* means “to take the floor / begin speaking” (e.g., in a meeting). Expressions: *Esa es la palabra* = “That’s the word / Exactly,” and *Te/Le tomo la palabra* = “I’ll hold you to your word” (I accept your promise/offer).
target_language_example: No recuerdo la palabra exacta, pero sé lo que significa.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the exact word, but I know what it means.

additional_notes: Used for the display of a phone, computer, TV, etc.: la pantalla del ordenador (the computer screen). In some contexts it can also mean a projector/movie screen (la pantalla grande = the big screen).
target_language_example: No puedo leer nada en la pantalla porque está muy oscura.
native_language_example: I can’t read anything on the screen because it’s very dark.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the place where you wait for a bus. Often appears with location phrases like "está al lado de..." (it’s next to...), "al otro lado de la calle" (across the street), or "cerca de" (near).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la parada de autobús más cercana?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest bus stop?

additional_notes: Refers to a wall (usually an interior wall of a room or building). Commonly used with location phrases like "junto a la pared" (next to the wall), "contra la pared" (against the wall), or "en la pared" (on the wall).
target_language_example: Hay un cuadro en la pared.
native_language_example: There is a picture on the wall.

meaning: "the part" (a section, area, or side of something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a portion of something (la parte que...), a specific area or region (la parte norte), or a position/side (la parte de arriba = the top part; la parte delantera = the front part). Often followed by "de" + noun (la parte del edificio) or by an adjective (la parte norte).
target_language_example: Me gusta la parte del final de la película.
native_language_example: I like the ending part of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to point to the rear area of a place or object. Often followed by "de" + noun: "la parte de atrás del mercado" = "the back of the market". With vehicles it can mean the rear of a vehicle (e.g., where you would hit it from behind).
target_language_example: Los baños están en la parte de atrás del restaurante.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are in the back of the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used for peace in general, often in contexts like countries, treaties, or public order. Common with verbs like mantener la paz (“to keep/maintain the peace”) and desear la paz (“to wish for peace”).
target_language_example: Después de la guerra, todos querían la paz.
native_language_example: After the war, everyone wanted peace.

additional_notes: Used to talk about peace between countries/nations on a global scale. It commonly appears with verbs like lograr (achieve), conseguir (obtain), establecer (establish), and desear/querer (wish/want).
target_language_example: Todas las naciones desean la paz mundial.
native_language_example: All nations desire world peace.

additional_notes: A very common noun for a ball used in sports or games. It’s feminine singular, so you’ll usually see it with articles like "la" (the) or "una" (a).
target_language_example: ¿Me pasas la pelota, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the ball, please?

additional_notes: A feminine noun. You’ll often use it with verbs like ver (to watch/see) and with adjectives to describe it: La película fue interesante. Also used for a “film” in general, not just in a movie theater.
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza la película?
native_language_example: What time does the movie start?

meaning: the effort/trouble; in expressions like "valer la pena" = "to be worth it".
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like "valer la pena" (to be worth it) and "merecer la pena" (to be worth it / to be worth doing). It often introduces an infinitive: "Vale la pena leerlo" = "It’s worth reading." On its own, "pena" can also mean "sadness/pity" or a "penalty," but in these examples it refers to something being worth the effort.
target_language_example: No vale la pena discutir por eso.
native_language_example: It’s not worth arguing about that.

additional_notes: A formal/legal term for the punishment of executing someone for a serious crime. Often used with verbs like abolir (to abolish), imponer (to impose), and aplicar (to apply). Also appears in phrases like condenar a alguien a la pena de muerte (“to sentence someone to death”).
target_language_example: Muchos países han abolido la pena de muerte.
native_language_example: Many countries have abolished the death penalty.

additional_notes: Means the state of being perfect or without flaws. Common with verbs like alcanzar/lograr (to achieve), estar lejos de (to be far from), and in the phrase ir/funcionar a la perfección (“to go/work perfectly”). Also appears in the saying: La práctica hace la perfección (“Practice makes perfect”).
target_language_example: El plan no es la perfección, pero funciona muy bien.
native_language_example: The plan isn’t perfection, but it works very well.

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to refer to a person. It always uses the feminine article (la) even when talking about a man (e.g., “la persona adecuada” = “the right person”). Don’t confuse it with English “persona” (someone’s public image).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con la persona responsable.
native_language_example: I need to speak with the person in charge.

additional_notes: Used to make a superlative description of someone. It’s followed by an adjective (e.g., rica, pequeña, lista, perezosa, vieja) and often by extra information like "del mundo" (in the world) or "que conozco" (that I know). The adjective agrees with persona (feminine singular), even when talking about a man: "Él es la persona más rica".
target_language_example: Ella es la persona más amable de la oficina.
native_language_example: She is the nicest person in the office.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a specific person by adding a defining clause after que. It can refer to someone already known (“La persona que vive al lado…”) or to specify who did something (“La persona que me dio esa pintura…”). You’ll also see it in set phrases like “No soy la persona que solía ser” (“I’m not the person I used to be”).
target_language_example: La persona que llamó ayer quiere hablar contigo.
native_language_example: The person who called yesterday wants to talk to you.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine article la because piedra is a feminine noun. Often refers to a particular, known stone in the story or situation (like a magical stone): la piedra = 'the stone' (that everyone is talking about).
target_language_example: La piedra está escondida en la oficina.
native_language_example: The stone is hidden in the office.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a person’s skin (the organ covering the body). It can also mean an animal’s hide/skin, sometimes in contexts about materials or money (e.g., selling the hide). Often used with prepositions like en la piel (“on the skin”).
target_language_example: Me puse crema porque tengo la piel muy seca.
native_language_example: I put on cream because my skin is very dry.

additional_notes: A body-part noun. In Spanish, you often use the definite article (el/la/los/las) instead of a possessive (mi/tu/su), especially with pain or injuries: Me duele la pierna = “My leg hurts.” With indirect object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/les), it can show whose leg it is: Le mordió la pierna = “It bit his/her leg.”
target_language_example: Me lastimé la pierna jugando al fútbol.
native_language_example: I hurt my leg playing soccer.

additional_notes: Used to specify the leg on the right side of the body. Often appears with verbs like doler (to hurt), lesionarse (to injure oneself), romperse (to break), and with phrases like en la pierna derecha (in/on the right leg). In Spanish, body parts commonly use the definite article (la) instead of a possessive (mi/tu), especially after indirect object pronouns: Me duele la pierna derecha = “My right leg hurts.”
target_language_example: Me duele la pierna derecha desde ayer.
native_language_example: My right leg has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: In some Latin American countries (especially in the Southern Cone), "pieza" is commonly used to mean a bedroom or a simple room in a house (like a rented room). In other contexts, "pieza" can also mean "piece/part" (e.g., una pieza de pan = a piece of bread), so the meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Tengo que ordenar la pieza antes de que lleguen.
native_language_example: I have to tidy the room before they arrive.

additional_notes: Often refers to a painting as an artwork (una pintura famosa). It can also mean the activity/art of painting (tener buena mano para la pintura = to be good at painting) or paint as a substance depending on context.
target_language_example: Me gusta la pintura, pero no tengo mucha paciencia para pintar.
native_language_example: I like painting, but I don’t have much patience to paint.

additional_notes: A feminine noun, so it uses "la" (singular) and "las" (plural: "las piscinas"). It can refer to a public/community pool or a private pool at a house/hotel. Common with verbs like "abrir" (to open), "estar cubierta" (to be covered), and "meterse a/en la piscina" (to get into the pool).
target_language_example: En verano vamos a la piscina todos los días.
native_language_example: In summer we go to the pool every day.

meaning: the track; a clue/lead; a runway.
additional_notes: “Pista” is used both literally and figuratively. Literal meanings include a track (sports track, ski slope) or an airport runway (“pista de vuelo”). Figuratively, it can mean a clue/lead in an investigation: “poner a alguien sobre la pista (de…)” = to put someone on the trail of…, “seguir la pista (de/a…)” = to track/follow the trail of…, and “estar en la pista” = to be on the right track.
target_language_example: La policía está siguiendo la pista del sospechoso.
native_language_example: The police are tracking the suspect.

meaning: the blackboard / whiteboard (board at the front of a classroom).
additional_notes: Used for the board a teacher writes on in class (chalkboard or whiteboard). Common with verbs like escribir en la pizarra (to write on the board), apuntar/señalar a la pizarra (to point at the board), llamar a alguien a la pizarra (to call someone up to the board), and borrar/bajar de la pizarra (to erase/take something off the board).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes escribir la respuesta en la pizarra, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you write the answer on the board, please?

additional_notes: A very common noun. It’s feminine, so it uses the article la (la pizza). With gustar, what is liked goes after the verb: A todos les gusta la pizza. You can describe it with adjectives like fría (cold).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres la pizza con queso extra?
native_language_example: Do you want the pizza with extra cheese?

additional_notes: A feminine noun meaning the sandy (or rocky) shore by the sea or a large lake. It often appears with common prepositions like a la playa (to the beach), en la playa (at/on the beach), and de la playa (from the beach).
target_language_example: Vamos a la playa mañana.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach tomorrow.

additional_notes: Refers to an open public space in a town or city, often a central square where people meet, walk, sit, and events may happen. Common phrases: "plaza de la ciudad" (city square), "plaza central" (main/central square).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la plaza a las seis.
native_language_example: See you in the square at six.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how many people live in a place (a country, city, region, etc.). It often appears with comparisons (más/menos que) or with numbers/estimates (es…, aproximadamente…). You can also use it with singular verb agreement because it’s a singular noun phrase: “La población de esta ciudad está creciendo.”
target_language_example: La población de México es muy grande.
native_language_example: The population of Mexico is very large.

additional_notes: A noun meaning the condition of being poor or lacking money/resources. Often used with verbs like "vivir en" (to live in), "caer en" / "quedarse en" (to fall into / end up in), and "salir de" (to get out of).
target_language_example: Muchas familias viven en la pobreza en esta región.
native_language_example: Many families live in poverty in this region.

additional_notes: Refers to the police as an institution/force. It’s grammatically singular in Spanish ("La policía llegó"), but in English you may say "the police are...". Common with verbs like "venir/llegar" (to come/arrive), "hablar con" (to talk to), and "coger" (to catch/arrest).
target_language_example: Llama a la policía; hay un robo en la tienda.
native_language_example: Call the police; there’s a robbery in the store.

meaning: “the police are…” (police + a form of “to be”), used to say where they are or what they’re doing.
additional_notes: “La policía” is a collective noun, so it usually uses singular verb forms in Spanish (está), even though in English we often say “the police are.” It’s commonly followed by a location (allí, en la entrada, por todas partes) or by a gerund to describe an action: “la policía está + verb-ando/-iendo” (vigilando, persiguiendo, yendo).
target_language_example: La policía está buscando al sospechoso.
native_language_example: The police are looking for the suspect.

additional_notes: Used to say that the police are currently looking into a situation (an accident, a case, a matter). Present progressive: "está(n) + investigando". You can change the subject: "La policía está investigando..." / "Los agentes están investigando...".
target_language_example: La policía está investigando el robo en el barrio.
native_language_example: The police are investigating the robbery in the neighborhood.

meaning: politics; policy (a set of rules or principles).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “politics” in general (“Me interesa la política”). It can also mean “policy” in the sense of an organization’s rules or approach (e.g., “la política de la empresa” = “the company policy”). In Spanish, context usually makes clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: No entiendo mucho de la política, pero quiero votar.
native_language_example: I don’t understand much about politics, but I want to vote.

meaning: the possibility of; the chance to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that could happen or be true. Often followed by **de + infinitive** (la posibilidad de ser, de limpiar) or **de que + subjunctive** (la posibilidad de que sea cierto). Common with verbs like **existir**, **dar**, **tener**, **rechazar**, **considerar**.
target_language_example: No descartes la posibilidad de que lleguemos tarde.
native_language_example: Don’t rule out the possibility that we’ll arrive late.

additional_notes: A common noun for a question you ask or a question being discussed. It’s feminine, so it uses la/una: la pregunta (the question), una pregunta (a question).
target_language_example: La pregunta es: ¿a qué hora empieza?
native_language_example: The question is: what time does it start?

additional_notes: Used to refer to journalists and media organizations (TV, newspapers, websites) as a group. It can also mean “the printing press,” but in these examples it clearly means the news media (reporters).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con la prensa ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to the press right now.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine article "la". Common with time expressions like "en la primavera" (in spring) and with verbs about weather/season changes (e.g., snow melting, rain, flowers).
target_language_example: En la primavera los días son más largos.
native_language_example: In spring, the days are longer.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns or when “first” refers to a feminine person/thing (e.g., la primera persona, la primera edición, la primera fila). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood from context: “Esa es sólo la primera (frase)”. Often part of common phrases like “la primera víctima” (“the first victim”).
target_language_example: Esta es la primera vez que vengo aquí.
native_language_example: This is the first time I’ve come here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was the first in order (the first you met, the first to arrive, etc.). It often appears with relative phrases like “la primera persona a la que…” (“the first person that/who…”) or with “en + infinitive”: “la primera persona en llegar” (“the first person to arrive”). Don’t confuse with grammar “primera persona” (first person: I/we); in that sense it’s usually used without an article.
target_language_example: Ella fue la primera persona en ayudarme.
native_language_example: She was the first person to help me.

additional_notes: Used to identify the earliest person to do something or to be encountered in a situation. It’s often followed by a verb in the present, past, or subjunctive depending on context (e.g., "sea la primera persona que...").
target_language_example: Fui la primera persona que llamó para ayudar.
native_language_example: I was the first person who called to help.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an event happening for the first time. Very common in phrases like "la primera vez que..." ("the first time that...") and "por primera vez" ("for the first time"). It can also be used to mean "the first time around" in contexts like "Ya te oí la primera vez" (I heard you the first time).
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que visito Madrid.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve visited Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about someone’s first experience doing something. Commonly followed by a verb (often in the past: vine/estuviste; or present when talking about a first-time experience happening now: Esta es la primera vez que…).
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que pruebo la comida mexicana.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve tried Mexican food.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occasion when something happened. It’s followed by a verb phrase/clause: "La primera vez que + verb". Common patterns: "La primera vez que + past tense" (talking about a past first time) and "Esta/Ésta es la primera vez que + present" (Spanish often uses the present to mean "This is the first time I have...": "Esta es la primera vez que visito Portugal").
target_language_example: La primera vez que conduje de noche estaba muy nervioso.
native_language_example: The first time I drove at night, I was very nervous.

la primera vez que te vi

target_language_multi_word_term: la primera vez que te vi
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened the first time you met/saw someone. It often sets up a memory, realization, or mistake: “since/from the first time I saw you” (desde la primera vez que te vi). In this phrase, te = “you” (object) and vi = “I saw” (from ver).
target_language_example: Me enamoré de ti la primera vez que te vi.
native_language_example: I fell in love with you the first time I saw you.

meaning: “the princess” (a female royal, usually the daughter of a king/queen).
additional_notes: Used with the feminine definite article “la.” Often appears with “a” + indirect object pronoun when she is the receiver of an action: “A la princesa le gustaba…” = “The princess liked…” (literally, “To the princess, it was pleasing…”).
target_language_example: La princesa vivía en el palacio.
native_language_example: The princess lived in the palace.

meaning: "the test" / "the exam"; also "the trial" or "proof" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a test or exam: hacer la prueba (to take/do the test), repetir/volver a hacer la prueba (to retake the test), pasar/superar la prueba (to pass the test). It can also mean a trial/tryout (una prueba física = a physical test) or proof/evidence (una prueba de que... = proof that...).
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar para la prueba de mañana.
native_language_example: I have to study for tomorrow's test.

additional_notes: Feminine form of “the next.” Often used with a feminine noun that’s understood or stated: la próxima primavera (“next spring”), la próxima vez (“next time”). By itself it can mean “the next time” (common in goodbyes like Hasta la próxima / Nos vemos a la próxima) or “the next person/one” depending on context.
target_language_example: Hasta la próxima, hablamos mañana.
native_language_example: See you next time; we’ll talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Very common with future plans: "la próxima semana voy a..." It can also be used alone as a question to confirm timing: "¿La próxima semana?"
target_language_example: Nos vemos la próxima semana.
native_language_example: See you next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the next future occasion when something will happen. Common patterns: “La próxima vez que + present subjunctive” (e.g., La próxima vez que vengas…) and “Tal vez/quizás la próxima vez” (“maybe next time”). Also used alone as a short phrase: “La próxima vez, …” (“Next time, …”).
target_language_example: La próxima vez, avísame con tiempo.
native_language_example: Next time, let me know ahead of time.

additional_notes: A common noun for a door of a room, house, building, etc. Often used with location phrases like "junto a" (next to) or "al lado de" (beside). In "se me atascó", it means "the door got stuck on me" (an accidental situation that happened to the speaker).
target_language_example: Por favor, cierra la puerta al salir.
native_language_example: Please close the door when you leave.

meaning: the door open; the open door.
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like dejar (“to leave”) to say you left the door open: Deja/Dejé/Dejó la puerta abierta. Also appears with other verbs (e.g., regañar por haber dejado… “to scold for having left…”). Adjective agreement: abierta (feminine) matches puerta.
target_language_example: No dejes la puerta abierta, hace frío.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the door open; it’s cold.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to show which door you mean (possession or association): "la puerta de la casa" (the house’s door / the door to the house), "la puerta del auto" (the car door). "De" often contracts with "el" to form "del": "la puerta del auto".
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta de la habitación, por favor.
native_language_example: Close the bedroom door, please.

meaning: “the door of the …” / “the …’s door” (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to specify which door you mean by naming what it belongs to or leads to. Structure: la puerta + del (= de + el) + [masculine singular noun]. For feminine nouns, use “la puerta de la …” (e.g., la puerta de la casa).
target_language_example: No dejes abierta la puerta del coche.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the car door open.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the main entrance of a building or house. It’s commonly used with location phrases like en la puerta del frente (“at the front door”) or with verbs like abrir/cerrar (“to open/close”). You may also hear la puerta principal with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Deja el paquete en la puerta del frente, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the package at the front door, please.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (estaba) to describe a state/background situation in the past (the door’s condition). Often sets the scene for another past action: “La puerta estaba abierta y entré” (“The door was open and I went in”). You can swap the noun: “La ventana estaba abierta” (“The window was open”).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, la puerta estaba abierta, así que pasé.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the door was open, so I went in.

additional_notes: Uses imperfect past (estaba) to describe a state/background situation in the past (the door being closed). You can add details like con llave (“locked”), desde adentro/desde afuera (“from the inside/outside”), or por dentro (“on the inside”). In the present you’d say: La puerta está cerrada (“The door is closed”).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, la puerta estaba cerrada con llave.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the door was locked.

additional_notes: Uses estar + past participle (está cerrada) to describe a resulting state: the door is (currently) closed. Often said when you can’t enter; you may add details like con llave (“locked”) or no tenemos llave (“we don’t have a key”).
target_language_example: No puedo entrar: la puerta está cerrada.
native_language_example: I can't get in: the door is closed.

meaning: the main door; the main entrance door.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the primary entrance to a building (as opposed to a side or back door). Often used with prepositions like “por” (through) or verbs like “abrir/cerrar/dejar … abierta/cerrada” (open/closed).
target_language_example: Entra por la puerta principal, por favor.
native_language_example: Please go in through the main door.

meaning: 'the door (it) …' used with **se + verb** to mean the door closes/closed (often by itself or without saying who did it).
additional_notes: This is the start of a very common Spanish pattern: **[thing] + se + verb** (often called *se accidental* or *se impersonal/passive* depending on context). It’s used when something happens on its own (e.g., because of wind) or when the speaker doesn’t want/need to mention who did it. It’s frequently followed by verbs like **cerrar**: *La puerta se cerró* = “The door closed / got shut”; *La puerta se cierra…* = “The door closes / is closed…” (habitually or automatically).
target_language_example: La puerta se abrió sola.
native_language_example: The door opened by itself.

meaning: "the door opened" (often implying it opened by itself).
additional_notes: Uses the verb abrir in the preterite (se abrió = "opened"). The pronoun se is common when something happens without saying who did it, or when it seems to happen on its own (e.g., la puerta se abrió sola = "the door opened by itself"). You can add adverbs like lentamente (slowly) or automáticamente (automatically).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, la puerta se abrió automáticamente.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the door opened automatically.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the door at the back of a house/building/vehicle. Adjective agreement: trasero/trasera matches the noun (puerta is feminine, so trasera). Often used with estar + abierta/cerrada to say whether it’s open/closed (e.g., La puerta trasera está abierta).
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta trasera, por favor.
native_language_example: Close the back door, please.

meaning: "the door and" (often the start of "the door and then...").
additional_notes: This is simply the noun phrase "la puerta" (the door) followed by the conjunction "y" (and) to connect the next action/event: "llegó a la puerta y tocó" (he arrived at the door and knocked). Spanish often uses "y" to link two actions done one after the other.
target_language_example: Llegué a la puerta y llamé dos veces.
native_language_example: I got to the door and knocked twice.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the time and sight of the sun going down in the evening. Often used with verbs like ver (to see) and esperar (to wait for), and with superlatives like la más bella (the most beautiful).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos en la playa para ver la puesta de sol.
native_language_example: We sat on the beach to watch the sunset.

meaning: a very vulgar exclamation like “fucking hell!”; also used to intensify meaning (“a lot/like hell”).
additional_notes: Extremely offensive profanity. Often said alone to show anger, frustration, surprise, or pain (similar to “Fuck!” / “Fucking hell!”). In phrases like “duele como la puta madre” or “va a doler la puta madre,” it works as an intensifier meaning “it hurts like hell / a ton.” In insults you may hear “la puta madre que te parió,” which is even more aggressive.
target_language_example: ¡La puta madre! Se me cayó el celular.
native_language_example: Fucking hell! I dropped my phone.

meaning: the page (in a book, magazine, website, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a numbered page in printed material: "por/en la página nueve" = "to/on page nine." With websites, it can mean a web page (e.g., "la página web"), but in these examples it’s a page in a book or newspaper.
