target_language_example: Dime lo que realmente quieres.
native_language_example: Tell me what you really want.

additional_notes:
Used in relative clauses to talk about an action without naming who does it. Very common with verbs like pensar, imaginar, requerir, tratarse (de):
- “más de lo que se pensaba” = “more than was thought / more than people thought.”
- “lo que se requiere” = “what is required.”
If you see “se les …” (e.g., “lo que se les da la gana”), **les** shows who it applies to (“to them”), while **se** still keeps the subject general/unspecified.
target_language_example: No sabes lo que se aprende viajando solo.
native_language_example: You don’t know what you learn when you travel alone.

additional_notes: Used to label or define something in a typical or well-known way, often meaning “what people call…” or “what you’d call…”. Common patterns: **Es lo que se dice + noun** (“He’s what you call a…”), **no es lo que se dice + adjective** (“not exactly…”), or **Eso es lo que se dice** (“That’s what it’s called/That’s what people say”).
target_language_example: No es lo que se dice barato, pero vale la pena.
native_language_example: It’s not exactly cheap, but it’s worth it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize doing any needed action to reach a goal. Often follows verbs like hacer (“to do”), limpiar (“to clean”), or simply stands alone as a strong response meaning “whatever is needed.” The phrase uses the subjunctive (sea) because it refers to an unspecified thing.
target_language_example: Haré lo que sea necesario para ayudarte.
native_language_example: I’ll do whatever it takes to help you.

additional_notes: Used to mean “anything/whatever (it may be),” often with the subjunctive after it: "Haz lo que sea necesario" (“Do whatever is necessary”). It can also sound dismissive or uninterested in casual replies: "Sí, lo que sea" (“Yeah, whatever”).
target_language_example: Podemos ir a comer lo que sea, no tengo preferencia.
native_language_example: We can go eat whatever; I don’t have a preference.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unknown or irrelevant thing/action: “whatever it is that…”. It often expresses indifference or that the specific details don’t matter. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., *lo que sea que digas*). Similar forms: *lo que sea* (“whatever”) and *sea lo que sea* (“whatever it may be”).
target_language_example: Lo que sea que decidas, te voy a apoyar.
native_language_example: Whatever you decide, I’m going to support you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a noun clause with an implied idea like “the thing(s) that…”. It’s often followed by a verb in the present perfect or past to mean “what I/you/he/she have/has always done/wanted/said” (e.g., "lo que siempre he hecho" = "what I’ve always done").
target_language_example: Es lo que siempre he querido.
native_language_example: It’s what I’ve always wanted.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun phrase “lo que” (“what” / “the thing that”) to refer to an idea or thing without naming it. “He querido” is the present perfect (“I have wanted”), and with “siempre” it often means “I’ve always wanted (up to now).” You’ll often hear it after “Eso/Esto es…” (“That/This is…”) or as a sentence fragment for emphasis. You can also add “de ti” to mean “what I’ve always wanted from you.”
target_language_example: Este trabajo es lo que siempre he querido.
native_language_example: This job is what I’ve always wanted.

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of something. Often follows verbs like saber (to know) or mostrar/explicar (to show/explain): “Ya sé lo que significa” = “I already know what it means.” Can also be used after “Eso es…” to point back to something: “Eso es lo que significa…” = “That’s what … means.”
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que significa esta palabra.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what this word means.

additional_notes: Uses the neuter article "lo" + "que" to mean "that which/what". It introduces a clause describing an event in the past: "lo que sucedió" = "what happened". Often used after verbs like "decir" (to say/tell), "ver" (to see), "recordar" (to remember), "saber" (to know), "descubrir" (to find out). You can add details with "con" (to/with someone) or time expressions: "lo que sucedió con André", "lo que sucedió ese día".
target_language_example: Todavía no sé lo que sucedió anoche.
native_language_example: I still don't know what happened last night.

additional_notes: Uses the neuter article "lo" + "que" to mean "what" in a general sense: "lo que sé" = "what I know." Very commonly appears after "todo": "Eso es todo lo que sé" = "That’s all I know." You can add more information after it, e.g., "lo que sé sobre él" (what I know about him).
target_language_example: Lo que sé es que va a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: What I know is that he’s going to arrive late.

meaning: "what" + "to you" (used to introduce what affects you / what you need / what is good for you).
additional_notes: It combines the neuter relative "lo que" (“what/that which”) with the indirect object pronoun "te" (“to you”). It’s followed by a verb: "lo que te haga feliz" = “what makes you happy,” "lo que te conviene" = “what suits you / what’s best for you.” Often used in expressions like "no sabes lo que te conviene" (“you don’t know what’s best for you”).
target_language_example: Elige lo que te haga sentir mejor.
native_language_example: Choose what makes you feel better.

meaning: “what I tell you (to do)” / “whatever I tell you.”
additional_notes: Used to give an order or emphasize authority/control: *Harás lo que te diga* = “You’ll do what I tell you.” It’s built from **lo que** (“what/that which”) + **te diga** (subjunctive of *decir*, “I tell you”), often after verbs like *hacer* (to do) or in commands.
target_language_example: Si quieres jugar, primero haz lo que te diga.
native_language_example: If you want to play, first do what I tell you.

meaning: 'what I'm telling you' / 'what I said to you'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the exact words/instructions someone is giving the listener, often to emphasize that they should pay attention or obey. Common with commands like "Escucha..." (Listen...), "Haz..." (Do...), "Repite..." (Repeat...), and in statements like "Eso es lo que te digo" (That’s what I’m telling you).
target_language_example: Haz lo que te digo y todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: Do what I'm telling you and everything will be fine.

meaning: "what I told you" / "the thing I told you."
additional_notes: Used to refer back to information you already said to someone. Common after verbs like decir (to tell), recordar (to remember), pensar en (to think about), and can be followed by time words like ayer (yesterday).
target_language_example: Haz caso a lo que te dije.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what I told you.

meaning: “what I’ve told you” / “what I said (to you).”
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something the speaker already told the listener. Very common with verbs like escuchar (to listen), pensar (to think), recordar (to remember), and meditar (to reflect). Grammar: lo que = “what/that which,” te = “to you,” he dicho = “I have said/told” (present perfect).
target_language_example: Haz caso a lo que te he dicho y no salgas tan tarde.
native_language_example: Listen to what I’ve told you and don’t go out so late.

meaning: "what we have" (the things/resources/information we currently have).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the current state of resources, information, or results so far—often when evaluating, summarizing, or deciding what to do next. Common patterns: “Esto es lo que tenemos (hasta ahora)” = “This is what we have (so far)”; “Vamos a ver lo que tenemos” = “Let’s see what we have”; “Lo que tenemos es suficiente” = “What we have is enough.”
target_language_example: Por ahora, vamos a trabajar con lo que tenemos.
native_language_example: For now, let's work with what we have.

meaning: “what we have here …” (introducing or pointing out something).
additional_notes: Used when you’re about to examine, show, or comment on something in front of you. Often said as an opener: “Veamos/Vamos a ver/Miren lo que tenemos aquí…”. You can change the subject (tenemos) depending on who’s involved: “lo que tengo aquí” (I), “lo que tienen aquí” (they/you plural), etc.
target_language_example: Veamos lo que tenemos aquí: dos entradas para el concierto.
native_language_example: Let’s see what we have here: two tickets for the concert.

meaning: “what we have to do” / “what we need to do.”
additional_notes: Uses **lo que** (“what/that which”) to refer to an action or task. **Tenemos que** means “we have to / we must.” Often used to talk about responsibilities or the necessary next step: **Hacemos lo que tenemos que hacer** (“We do what we have to do”) or **Lo que tenemos que hacer es…** (“What we have to do is…”).
target_language_example: Lo que tenemos que hacer es terminar esto hoy.
native_language_example: What we have to do is finish this today.

meaning: "whatever I/you/he/she has to do" (what needs to be done).
additional_notes: Uses the structure "hacer lo que tener que hacer" to mean doing whatever is necessary. The person changes with the verb: "tenga" (I/you/he/she/it in the present subjunctive, often after "haré", "haga", "voy a"), and the implied subject comes from context (e.g., "Haré..." = I will; "Haga..." = you (formal) should). Often said with a determined tone: "Do what you must."
target_language_example: No me gusta, pero haré lo que tenga que hacer.
native_language_example: I don’t like it, but I’ll do whatever I have to do.

meaning: 'what I have to say' (what I need to say).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you want others to listen to. Often follows commands or requests like escucha (listen), oye (hey/listen), oigan (everyone listen), or escuche (formal 'listen'). Literally 'that which I have to say,' where lo que = 'what/that which,' tengo que = 'I have to,' decir = 'to say.'
target_language_example: Antes de irte, escucha lo que tengo que decir.
native_language_example: Before you go, listen to what I have to say.

meaning: what I have to do; what I need to do.
additional_notes: Uses **lo que** (“what/that which”) + **tener que** (“to have to”) to talk about an obligation or duty. Often used to emphasize that you’re doing what’s necessary, even if it’s difficult. Person/tense can change: *lo que tienes que hacer*, *lo que tenía que hacer*, etc.
target_language_example: No me gusta, pero voy a hacer lo que tengo que hacer.
native_language_example: I don’t like it, but I’m going to do what I have to do.

meaning: what I had to do / what I was supposed to do.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a duty or obligation in the past. Often appears after verbs like hacer (“to do”) or decir (“to tell”): e.g., “Hice lo que tenía que hacer” = “I did what I had to do,” and “Le dijo lo que tenía que hacer” = “He/She told him/her what to do.” You can change the tense/person: lo que tengo que hacer (what I have to do), lo que tendrás que hacer (what you will have to do).
target_language_example: Ya hice lo que tenía que hacer; ahora puedo descansar.
native_language_example: I already did what I had to do; now I can rest.

meaning: 'what you had to do' / 'what you were supposed to do'.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect "tenías que" to talk about a duty/obligation in the past. Often appears after verbs like "hacer" (you did what you had to do) or "decir" (I told you what you had to do). "Sólo" can add the sense of "only/just" (no more than that).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: hiciste lo que tenías que hacer.
native_language_example: Relax: you did what you had to do.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like escuchar/oír (“to listen/hear”) to refer to a person’s opinion or message. In context, “tiene” can refer to he/she/you (formal)/it, depending on who you’re talking about; you can also change it: “lo que tengo que decir” (what I have to say), “lo que tienes que decir” (what you have to say).
target_language_example: Escuchemos lo que tiene que decir antes de decidir.
native_language_example: Let’s listen to what they have to say before deciding.

meaning: what he/she/you (formal) has to do; what must be done.
additional_notes: Refers to a duty/obligation: **lo que** (“what/that which”) + **tener que** (“to have to”) + **hacer** (“to do”). **tiene** is 3rd person singular or formal **usted**; it changes with the subject: **lo que tengo que hacer** (what I have to do), **lo que tienes que hacer** (what you have to do), **lo que tenemos que hacer** (what we have to do). Often used in firm or matter-of-fact statements (e.g., giving advice, stating responsibility).
target_language_example: Él sabe lo que tiene que hacer.
native_language_example: He knows what he has to do.

meaning: what you have; the thing(s) you have.
additional_notes: Used to refer to whatever someone has (objects, resources, abilities, information). Common after verbs like "ver" (to see) or "usar" (to use): "Déjame ver lo que tienes" = "Let me see what you have." Often part of a longer structure like "haz/usa lo que tienes" (do/use what you have).
target_language_example: Si no puedes comprar otro, usa lo que tienes en casa.
native_language_example: If you can’t buy another one, use what you have at home.

meaning: what you have to do; what needs to be done.
additional_notes: Common in advice or when talking about obligations/necessity. Often used in phrases like “(hacer) lo que tienes que hacer” = “(do) what you have to do,” implying there may be no better option. You can change the person: “lo que tengo que hacer” (what I have to do), “lo que tiene que hacer” (what he/she has to do).
target_language_example: Haz lo que tienes que hacer y luego descansa.
native_language_example: Do what you have to do and then rest.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about something the other person thinks, wants, says, does, etc.: «Es lo que tú crees» (“It’s what you think”). Often followed by a verb: «lo que tú digas» (“whatever you say”). In comparisons it can imply “the same as you”: «quiere lo que tú» (“he wants what you want”).
target_language_example: Haré lo que tú me digas.
native_language_example: I’ll do what you tell me.

meaning: whatever you want; anything you like (it’s up to you).
additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive (quieras) to express an open choice: “whatever/anything you want.” It can follow verbs like ser, significar, ponerse, convertirse en, etc. On its own (“Lo que tú quieras.”) it often means “Whatever you want / Up to you.” You may also hear it without the subject pronoun: “lo que quieras.”
target_language_example: Podemos cenar donde tú quieras; lo que tú quieras.
native_language_example: We can have dinner wherever you want; it’s up to you.

additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun "usted" to mean “what you …” referring to a thing/idea rather than a person. It often introduces a clause: "lo que usted quiere/piensa/diga" = “what you want/think/say.” Common in set phrases like "Eso es lo que usted piensa" (“That’s what you think”) and "Lo que usted diga" (“Whatever you say,” often implying agreement or resignation).
target_language_example: Dígame lo que usted necesita.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an upcoming event or outcome (often something expected or inevitable). It can appear after verbs like saber (to know), decir (to tell), or mostrar/explicar (to show/explain): “No sé lo que va a pasar” = “I don’t know what’s going to happen.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: ya veremos lo que va a pasar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll see what’s going to happen.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer to a future event (often something you predict or explain). Literally "that which is going to happen". Often appears after phrases like "esto es..." (this is...), "te diré..." (I’ll tell you...), or in statements like "nunca se sabe..." (you never know...).
target_language_example: Nadie sabe lo que va a suceder mañana.
native_language_example: Nobody knows what is going to happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or explain a plan. Often follows phrases like “Esto es…” or “Eso es…”, meaning “This/That is what we’re going to do.” “Lo que” = “what/that which,” and “vamos a” is the near-future (“we’re going to”). You can change the verb: “lo que vamos a decir” (what we’re going to say).
target_language_example: Primero, te explico lo que vamos a hacer.
native_language_example: First, I’ll explain what we’re going to do.

additional_notes: Uses the relative structure "lo que" + verb to mean “the thing that …”. Here it refers to whatever is visible in a situation (often as the object of a verb like "describir" or in a question like "¿Te gusta lo que ves?").
target_language_example: Dime lo que ves por la ventana.
native_language_example: Tell me what you see through the window.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something you saw. "Lo que" means "what/that which" and introduces a clause; "vi" is the preterite of "ver" (I saw). Often appears after verbs like "saber" (to know), "recordar" (to remember), or in emphasis like "Eso fue lo que vi" (That’s what I saw).
target_language_example: No puedo olvidar lo que vi anoche.
native_language_example: I can’t forget what I saw last night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer to a plan or intended action. Often appears after verbs like saber (to know), decir (to tell), and contar (to explain/tell), as in: “te diré/contaré lo que voy a hacer” (I’ll tell you what I’m going to do).
target_language_example: Primero te explico el problema y luego te digo lo que voy a hacer.
native_language_example: First I’ll explain the problem, and then I’ll tell you what I’m going to do.

additional_notes: Used to start a clause that refers to an action or thing done by the speaker (often followed by a verb: "lo que yo haga/diga/quiero"). It adds emphasis by explicitly stating "yo" (I), and it can be contrasted with what others do.
target_language_example: Lo que yo diga es importante.
native_language_example: What I say is important.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what the speaker says, often for emphasis or insistence. Common after verbs like hacer (to do) and prestar atención/escuchar (to pay attention/listen): “Haz lo que yo digo” = “Do what I say.” You can also say it alone (“Lo que yo digo.”) to stress your point, like “See? That’s what I’m saying.”
target_language_example: Haz lo que yo digo y terminarás más rápido.
native_language_example: Do what I say and you’ll finish faster.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something matches your expectation or suspicion: "That’s what I thought." Often appears after Es/Era/Eso es: "Es/era lo que yo pensaba." The pronoun "yo" is optional in many contexts ("lo que pensaba"), but adding it can give emphasis: "what *I* thought."
target_language_example: Sí, era lo que yo pensaba.
native_language_example: Yes, that’s what I thought.

meaning: "what I … you" (introduces what I do/say/offer to you).
additional_notes: Used to start a clause with **lo que** = “what/that which,” plus **yo** (“I”) and **te** (“to you”). It’s usually followed by a verb: *lo que yo te decía* (“what I was telling you”), *lo que yo te ofrezco* (“what I offer you”), *con lo que yo te puedo ayudar* (“with what I can help you”).
target_language_example: Lo que yo te digo es importante.
native_language_example: What I’m telling you is important.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause about something he said, did, wants, etc. It’s a relative structure: lo que = “what/that which,” and él clarifies the subject (“he”). Often followed by a verb: lo que él dijo (what he said), lo que él empezó (what he started).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que él está diciendo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what he is saying.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun phrase “lo que” to mean “what/that which,” referring to the content of what he says. Often followed by a verb in the singular: “Lo que él dice es…” = “What he says is…”. You can swap the subject: “lo que ella dice,” “lo que dicen,” etc.
target_language_example: No creo lo que él dice.
native_language_example: I don’t believe what he says.

additional_notes: Uses the neuter relative pronoun phrase "lo que" to refer to the content of his words (the thing he said). It works like a noun phrase and can be the subject or object of a sentence: "No importa lo que él dijo" (It doesn’t matter what he said), "Repetí lo que él dijo" (I repeated what he said).
target_language_example: No entendí lo que él dijo en la reunión.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what he said in the meeting.

additional_notes: Uses **lo que** (“what/that which”) to refer to an unknown or specific thing, plus **él quiere** (“he wants”). It can follow verbs like *averiguar* (to find out) or *ser* (to be): *Averigua lo que él quiere* / *Esto es lo que él quiere*. Often used with another verb in the infinitive: *lo que él quiere comer* (“what he wants to eat”).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que él quiere.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what he wants.

additional_notes: `Lo` is an object pronoun meaning “it/that,” referring to something already known from context (a fact, name, event, etc.). Common when you suddenly remember: **Ahora lo recuerdo** (“Now I remember”). You can add emphasis with **sí**: **Sí, ahora lo recuerdo**.
target_language_example: Ah, ya lo recuerdo: tu cumpleaños es en marzo.
native_language_example: Ah, I remember now: your birthday is in March.

additional_notes: From the verb "rogar" (to beg/plead). It’s a very polite, strong way to ask for something. It often appears with an indirect object pronoun: "se lo ruego" (I beg you [formal]/him/her/them), "os lo ruego" (I beg you [Spain, plural]). The "lo" refers to what you’re asking for ("I beg it"), but in English you usually just say "I beg you" or "please".
target_language_example: Se lo ruego, no me deje aquí.
native_language_example: I beg you, don’t leave me here.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that” (a thing or fact already understood from context). "Sabe" is the present tense of "saber" (“to know” facts/information). Often used to confirm someone is aware of something: "Así que lo sabe" = “So you/he/she knows.”
target_language_example: No se lo digas; ya lo sabe.
native_language_example: Don’t tell him/her; he/she already knows.

additional_notes: Used with saber to say someone knows all the information about something. The "lo" is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it/that” (often not translated in English): Él lo sabe todo = “He knows it all.” Often appears in phrases like "cree que lo sabe todo" (“he thinks he knows everything”), suggesting someone is a “know-it-all.” You may also see "se lo sabe todo", which often means someone has learned/memorized everything (e.g., for an exam).
target_language_example: Él cree que lo sabe todo, pero se equivoca.
native_language_example: He thinks he knows everything, but he’s wrong.

additional_notes: "Lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it/that" (something already understood from context). "Sabemos" is the present tense of "saber" for "we". The word order can vary (e.g., "Aún no lo sabemos" / "No lo sabemos aún" = "We still don't know it").
target_language_example: Lo sabemos desde ayer.
native_language_example: We’ve known it since yesterday.

additional_notes: Form of **saber** (to know a fact) in **ellos/ellas/ustedes** present tense: **saben** = “they/you (plural, formal) know.” **Lo** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” or “that” (referring to something already mentioned or understood). Often the subject (“ellos/ellas”) is omitted: **Lo saben**.
target_language_example: No se lo digas a nadie; ya lo saben todos.
native_language_example: Don't tell anyone; everyone already knows it.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker assumes the listener already knows a fact or agrees with it. The object pronoun “lo” means “it/that” (referring to an idea, fact, or situation mentioned or understood). Often appears for emphasis at the end of a sentence: “..., y lo sabes” (“..., and you know it”).
target_language_example: No es tu culpa, y lo sabes.
native_language_example: It’s not your fault, and you know it.

additional_notes: “Lo” means “it/that” (referring to something already mentioned). “Sabía” is the imperfect past of “saber” (“to know”), often used for knowledge someone already had at that time. The subject (yo/él/ella, etc.) is understood from context. Common as an exclamation: “¡Lo sabía!” = “I knew it!”
target_language_example: ¡Lo sabía! Iba a llover.
native_language_example: I knew it! It was going to rain.

additional_notes: From saber (“to know”) in the imperfect tense: sabías = “you knew/you used to know.” Lo = “it/that,” referring to information already mentioned or understood from context. Often used in questions to check if someone knew something: “¿Lo sabías?” = “Did you know (that)?”
target_language_example: Yo pensé que lo sabías, pero nadie te lo dijo.
native_language_example: I thought you knew, but nobody told you.

meaning: "I'm sorry"; also "I feel it" (I sense it).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as an apology (“I’m sorry”), often followed by an explanation: “Lo siento, pero…”. In some contexts it literally means “I feel/sense it,” referring to something you can physically feel or notice (“Lo siento en el agua” = “I feel it in the water”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I can't go today.

meaning: “I’m sorry, I don’t…” (apology + saying no/that you don’t know, can’t, won’t, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to politely apologize and then give a negative response. Common patterns: “Lo siento, no sé…” (I’m sorry, I don’t know…), “Lo siento, no puedo…” (I’m sorry, I can’t…), “Lo siento, no tengo…” (I’m sorry, I don’t have…). Often sounds more polite than just starting with “No…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ayudarte ahora.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t help you right now.

meaning: “I’m sorry, but …” (polite way to introduce bad news, disagreement, or refusal).
additional_notes: Used to soften what comes next (e.g., a correction, refusal, or unpleasant truth). Often followed by a statement in the present (es, no puedo, no creo) or future (tendrás que…). Commonly implies “I understand, but I can’t change it.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no puedo ayudarte hoy.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I can’t help you today.

meaning: “I’m sorry, but no.” / “Sorry, but I can’t / I don’t.”
additional_notes: Used to apologize or soften a refusal or disagreement. Often followed by a reason (e.g., “Lo siento, pero no puedo…” = “I’m sorry, but I can’t…”). In “Lo siento, pero no.” it stands alone as a polite, firm “no.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to apologize or to express sympathy/condolences. Often followed by **por** + a noun/pronoun: **Lo siento mucho por tu pérdida** (“I’m very sorry for your loss”). **Lo siento** alone is also very common; **mucho** adds emphasis (“very/really”).
target_language_example: Lo siento mucho por lo que pasó.
native_language_example: I’m very sorry about what happened.

additional_notes: Used to apologize or express sympathy about a specific thing or situation. You can follow it with a noun, pronoun, or clause: lo siento por esto (about this), lo siento por lo de esta mañana (about what happened this morning). For apologizing directly to a person, you can also use “lo siento” alone or “lo siento mucho”.
target_language_example: Lo siento por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for arriving late.

additional_notes: Used in sentences that trigger the subjunctive (often with que), especially: after expressions like “sin que…” (without someone knowing), after wanting/preventing (“no quería que…”), after doubt/negation of belief (“no creo que…”), and in hypothetical “if” clauses (“Si él lo supiera…” = If he knew it). “Lo” refers to a thing/idea already mentioned (“it/that”).
target_language_example: Si ella lo supiera, no estaría tan tranquila.
native_language_example: If she knew it, she wouldn’t be so calm.

additional_notes: Used to say you already know the information. "Lo" is a pronoun meaning "it/that" (the thing being talked about), and "sé" is "I know" (from "saber"). Often used as a quick response: "Lo sé" = "I know". You can emphasize with "ya": "Ya lo sé" (I already know). It can also appear after the thing you know: "Eso lo sé (bien)" = "That I know (well)."
target_language_example: Ya lo sé, no te preocupes.
native_language_example: I know already—don’t worry.

additional_notes: Repetition of “lo sé” (“I know it”) is used to emphasize that you already understand or have heard it, often to reassure someone or to show mild impatience (“yes, yes, I get it”). Common in conversation; intonation can make it sound calm or annoyed.
target_language_example: Lo sé, lo sé, pero déjame terminar.
native_language_example: I know, I know, but let me finish.

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what someone just said (or a known fact) and then introduce an objection, concern, or different point of view. Very common in conversation; you’ll also hear it without the comma: “Lo sé pero…”.
target_language_example: Lo sé, pero no creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: I know, but I don’t think it’s a good idea.

meaning: “is/are going to (do) it” (near future with the object pronoun “lo”).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about the near future: **lo va a + infinitive** = “he/she/you (formal)/it is going to do it.” Here **lo** usually means “it” (a thing/idea already mentioned), but it can also mean “him.” The verb **va** comes from **ir** (to go): *yo voy a, tú vas a, él/ella/usted va a, nosotros vamos a, ellos van a*. You can swap the object pronoun: **la va a** (it/her), **los va a** (them masc.), **las va a** (them fem.).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo va a arreglar mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s going to fix it tomorrow.

meaning: “we’re going to (do it)” / “we’re going to (verb) it”.
additional_notes: Used with the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **vamos a + infinitive** (“we’re going to + verb”). **Lo** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that,” and it goes **before** the conjugated verb (**vamos**): *Lo vamos a encontrar* (“We’re going to find it”). It can combine with other pronouns: *Nos lo vamos a perder* (“We’re going to miss it”).
target_language_example: Lo vamos a resolver mañana.
native_language_example: We’re going to solve it tomorrow.

meaning: "they're going to (do it)" / "they're going to (do something to it/him)".
additional_notes: This is a common future construction: **ir a + infinitive**. Here **van** = "they (ellos/ellas/ustedes) are going to", and **lo** is an object pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him"). The infinitive comes next: *lo van a dar* (they're going to give it), *lo van a rastrear* (they're going to track it). With this structure, the pronoun usually goes **before** the conjugated verb (*lo van a...*), though it can also attach to the infinitive (*van a darlo*).
target_language_example: Lo van a hacer mañana.
native_language_example: They’re going to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when talking to someone (tú) about what they are going to do. Structure: **lo** (it/that) + **vas a** (you’re going to) + **infinitive**: *Lo vas a hacer*, *Lo vas a decir*. **Lo** refers to a thing/idea already known from context (“it/that”). The object pronoun can change: *la vas a…* (it/her), *los/las vas a…*, *me lo vas a…* (you’re going to … it to me).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo vas a entender.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re going to understand it.

meaning: "You’re going to do it" / "you will do it" (referring to something specific).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **vas a hacer** = “you’re going to do.” **Lo** is an object pronoun meaning “it/that” and refers to an action or task already known from context. Often used to encourage or emphasize responsibility: **Lo vas a hacer muy bien** (“You’ll do it very well”), **Lo vas a hacer tú** (“You’re the one who’s going to do it”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo vas a hacer bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re going to do it well.

meaning: "I see it/him"; also "I see" (= I understand).
additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him" (sometimes "that"). Use "lo veo" to say you literally see someone/something, or as a short response meaning you understand what was said. You can add words after it: "Lo veo bien" = "I see it as good / I think it’s fine."
target_language_example: —¿Entiendes el problema? —Sí, lo veo.
native_language_example: "Do you understand the problem?" "Yes, I see."

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him" (masculine singular, or a neutral "it" for an idea/situation). "Vi" is the preterite (simple past) of "ver" (to see): "I saw". You can add context after it, e.g., "Lo vi ayer" (I saw him/it yesterday) or "Lo vi en la calle" (I saw him/it on the street).
target_language_example: Ayer lo vi en el parque.
native_language_example: I saw him in the park yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say where you saw something. "Lo" usually means "it" (sometimes "him"), "vi" = "I saw" (preterite of ver), and "en" can mean "on" or "in" depending on the place/medium: en YouTube/en una revista (on/in), en una película (in a movie), en mi sueño (in my dream).
target_language_example: Lo vi en Instagram ayer.
native_language_example: I saw it on Instagram yesterday.

additional_notes: "Lo" is an object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (also "that"), depending on context. "Vi" is the preterite of "ver" (to see), used for a completed action in the past. You can add "solo/sólo" to emphasize "only once" (both spellings are seen). The pronoun can change: "la vi una vez" (I saw her/it once), "los vi una vez" (I saw them once, masc./mixed), "las vi una vez" (I saw them once, fem.).
target_language_example: Solo lo vi una vez, hace años.
native_language_example: I only saw him once, years ago.

additional_notes: Used with **ir a + infinitive** to talk about a near-future action. **Lo** is an object pronoun meaning “it/that” (sometimes “him,” formal), and it comes **before** the conjugated verb: **Lo voy a + infinitive** (e.g., *Lo voy a hacer* = “I’m going to do it”). In negative sentences: *No lo voy a + infinitive*.
target_language_example: Lo voy a hacer mañana.
native_language_example: I’m going to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you intend to do something (often soon). "Lo" = “it/that” (the thing already mentioned), and "voy a" + infinitive expresses the near future. You can add emphasis with "ya" (“right now/already”) or "yo" (“I will do it”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo voy a hacer esta tarde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m going to do it this afternoon.

meaning: “the cats”; also the name of a place (Los Gatos).
additional_notes: If it’s written with lowercase (los gatos), it usually just means “the cats” (los = “the” for masculine plural; gatos = “cats”). If it’s capitalized (Los Gatos), it’s often a proper noun (a town/city name, especially in California) and you typically don’t translate it.
target_language_example: Vivimos en Los Gatos, cerca de San José.
native_language_example: We live in Los Gatos, near San José.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to physical accidents (e.g., traffic or workplace accidents) or unexpected mishaps. In more formal/scientific contexts (e.g., evolution/history), it can refer to random or chance events (“accidents of nature/history”). Singular: “el accidente.”
target_language_example: Los accidentes han sido poco comunes este año.
native_language_example: Accidents have been uncommon this year.

additional_notes: Plural, masculine form of "el actor". Used for male actors or mixed-gender groups. For an all-female group, you may also hear "las actrices" (the actresses).
target_language_example: Los actores ensayan antes de la función.
native_language_example: The actors rehearse before the show.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Use it to talk about adults in general (often compared with kids): "los niños" vs. "los adultos". Singular is "el adulto" (male/unspecified) or "la adulta" (female).
target_language_example: En esta reunión solo pueden entrar los adultos.
native_language_example: Only adults can enter this meeting.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "los" (the) + "alemanes" (Germans). Used for a group of German people. In many contexts it can mean German soldiers/forces (as in historical or war settings). For mixed-gender groups, Spanish commonly uses the masculine plural "los alemanes".
target_language_example: Los alemanes viven en Alemania.
native_language_example: Germans live in Germany.

meaning: the students (pupils; usually at a school).
additional_notes: Used mainly for students in primary/secondary school (sometimes also in a class with a teacher). Singular: el alumno (male or generic), la alumna (female). In many places, university students are more commonly called los estudiantes.
target_language_example: Los alumnos escuchan al profesor y toman apuntes.
native_language_example: The students listen to the teacher and take notes.

meaning: the Americans (people from the Americas; often used to mean people from the U.S.).
additional_notes: "Los" is the plural masculine definite article (“the”). "Americanos" can refer broadly to people from North, Central, or South America, but in everyday Spanish it often refers specifically to people from the United States; to be specific, many speakers say "los estadounidenses" (U.S. Americans).
target_language_example: Esa tendencia es marcada entre los americanos.
native_language_example: That trend is noticeable among Americans.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article: el anciano (an elderly man), la anciana (an elderly woman), los ancianos (elderly people in general, often mixed gender). Used when talking about older people as a group, often in contexts of respect, care, or social issues.
target_language_example: En este barrio hay un centro para los ancianos.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood there is a center for the elderly.

additional_notes: Definite plural: "los" = "the" (masculine plural) + "animales" = "animals." Used to talk about animals in general or a specific known group. Singular: "el animal" (the animal).
target_language_example: A los niños les encantan los animales.
native_language_example: Kids love animals.

additional_notes: Plural of "el auto" (car). Common in Latin America; in Spain, "los coches" is more common. Use with articles: "los autos" = the cars; "unos autos" = some cars.
target_language_example: Los autos están estacionados afuera.
native_language_example: The cars are parked outside.

additional_notes: Used to talk about years in general or a period of time (often with an added phrase like "de la guerra" = "of the war"). It can also refer to the passing of time or what time has brought to someone ("Los años le han dado...").
target_language_example: Con los años, he aprendido a tener paciencia.
native_language_example: Over the years, I’ve learned to be patient.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: *el bombero* (firefighter) → *los bomberos* (the firefighters). Used for the fire department/emergency responders who put out fires and handle rescues. Often appears with verbs like *apagar* (to put out), *llamar a* (to call), and *esperar a* (to wait for).
target_language_example: Llama a los bomberos, hay humo en la cocina.
native_language_example: Call the firefighters; there’s smoke in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Plural of “el bosque” (forest/woodland). Used for real forests or as a setting (“in the woods”), and it can be followed by “de/del” to specify which ones (e.g., “los bosques de Lothlórien”, “los bosques del mundo”). Often used with “en” to mean “in the woods/forests”.
target_language_example: Nos perdimos en los bosques durante la caminata.
native_language_example: We got lost in the woods during the hike.

additional_notes: Plural of "el brazo" (arm). Common in instructions and commands: "Levante/Separa/Usa los brazos" (Raise/Separate/Use your arms). In the phrase "con los brazos en alto," it means “with (your) hands/arms up.” Also appears in the idiom "bajar los brazos" = “to give up / to stop trying.”
target_language_example: Levante los brazos, por favor.
native_language_example: Raise your arms, please.

meaning: "the good ones" / "the good guys" (the good people).
additional_notes: Uses the masculine plural article + adjective as a noun phrase. Commonly refers to a group of people seen as "the good side" (often contrasted with *los malos*). It can also refer more generally to "the good ones" among several options. For mixed-gender groups, Spanish typically uses the masculine plural (*los buenos*).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, nosotros somos los buenos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’re the good guys.

additional_notes: Plural definite noun phrase. Used to talk about horses in general or about a specific group of horses, depending on context. Singular is "el caballo" (the horse). "Los" is the masculine plural form of "the".
target_language_example: Los caballos corren muy rápido.
native_language_example: Horses run very fast.

additional_notes: A simple factual sentence using **ser** (“to be”) to classify something (X + son + animales). You can swap in other subjects or categories: *Los perros son animales* (Dogs are animals), *Los caballos son mamíferos* (Horses are mammals).
target_language_example: Los caballos son animales muy inteligentes.
native_language_example: Horses are very intelligent animals.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun, usually used with the definite article: los calcetines (“the socks”). Common with verbs like ponerse/quitarse/sacarse (to put on / take off). You can add adjectives after it: los calcetines mojados (wet socks), los calcetines al revés (inside out).
target_language_example: Me voy a poner los calcetines antes de salir.
native_language_example: I'm going to put on my socks before leaving.

additional_notes: Usually refers to open rural land used for farming or grazing animals. Often used with verbs like estar/encontrarse (to be located), mirar (to look at), or necesitar (to need): "Los campos necesitan lluvia". Can also contrast with other natural areas: "Los bosques, los campos".
target_language_example: En primavera, los campos se llenan de flores.
native_language_example: In spring, the fields fill up with flowers.

additional_notes: Definite plural noun phrase: "los" (the, masculine plural) + "cerdos" (pigs). Used to talk about pigs in general or a specific group of pigs, depending on context.
target_language_example: Los cerdos comen de todo.
native_language_example: Pigs eat everything.

additional_notes: Masculine plural of chico (“boy/young person”). It can refer specifically to boys, or more generally to a group of children or young people (mixed or all-male), depending on context.
target_language_example: Los chicos están jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: The boys are playing in the park.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase meaning people from China (masculine plural is used for mixed groups). Singular: "el chino" (male) / "la china" (female). In some regions, "los chinos" can also refer to curly hair or bangs, but in these examples it clearly means Chinese people.
target_language_example: Los chinos celebran el Año Nuevo Lunar.
native_language_example: Chinese people celebrate Lunar New Year.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "científico" (scientist). Used for groups of scientists, or for mixed-gender groups; for an all-female group, you can say "las científicas". Often appears as the subject of statements about research or expert opinion (e.g., "Según los científicos..." = "According to scientists...").
target_language_example: Los científicos dicen que necesitamos reducir la contaminación.
native_language_example: Scientists say we need to reduce pollution.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "el/la cliente". In shops, cafés, restaurants, and other businesses, it usually means "customers" (people who buy things). In professional services (law, consulting, etc.), it can also mean "clients" (people who hire a service).
target_language_example: Los clientes esperan en la fila para pagar.
native_language_example: The customers are waiting in line to pay.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: **los** = “the” (masculine plural) + **coches** = “cars.” Used to talk about cars in general or a specific group of cars. In some countries people may also say **carros/autos** for “cars.”
target_language_example: Los coches aquí son muy caros.
native_language_example: Cars here are very expensive.

additional_notes: Definite plural: "los" + "colores". Used when talking about specific colors in a set (in art, clothing, decoration, etc.). Common phrases: "los colores del arco iris" (the colors of the rainbow), "colores claros/oscuros" (light/dark colors). Singular is "el color" (the color).
target_language_example: Me gustan los colores de esta pintura.
native_language_example: I like the colors in this painting.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: **los** = “the” (masculine plural) + **conejos** = “rabbits.” Used to talk about rabbits in general or specific rabbits known from context. Singular: **el conejo** (the rabbit).
target_language_example: Los conejos comen verduras y necesitan espacio.
native_language_example: Rabbits eat vegetables and need space.

additional_notes: Used for factual information, figures, records, or details (often in documents, files, forms, or computer systems). Common in phrases like comprobar los datos (verify the information), borrar los datos (delete the data), and los datos del archivo (the file’s data). Singular: el dato (a data point/detail).
target_language_example: Necesito los datos para completar el formulario.
native_language_example: I need the data/information to complete the form.

additional_notes: Usually plural in Spanish: hacer los deberes = “to do (your) homework.” Very common with verbs like hacer (to do/make) and terminar (to finish): Estoy haciendo los deberes. / No he terminado los deberes.
target_language_example: No puedo salir; tengo que hacer los deberes.
native_language_example: I can’t go out; I have to do my homework.

additional_notes: Usually refers to fingers, but it can also mean toes when the context is feet. Often used with body-part actions: pasar los dedos por (run your fingers through/over), meter(se) los dedos en (put your fingers in), lamerse los dedos (lick your fingers), quemarse los dedos (burn your fingers). In expressions: cruzar los dedos / mantener los dedos cruzados = “keep your fingers crossed.”
target_language_example: Me duelen los dedos de tanto escribir.
native_language_example: My fingers hurt from writing so much.

additional_notes: Usually used with a possessive or indirect object when talking about someone’s toes: "me duelen los dedos de los pies" (my toes hurt), "se le helaron los dedos de los pies" (his/her toes got frozen). Can also appear as "dedos del pie" in singular or in more formal/medical contexts.
target_language_example: Me duelen los dedos de los pies después de caminar mucho.
native_language_example: My toes hurt after walking a lot.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite): *votaron* = “they voted” (completed action). *Los delegados* means “the delegates.” Often followed by details like how many times (*seis veces*), when (*inmediatamente*), or what they voted on (*votaron sobre el tema* = “they voted on the issue/topic”).
target_language_example: Los delegados votaron sobre la propuesta al final de la reunión.
native_language_example: The delegates voted on the proposal at the end of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to refer to other people or things in a group besides the one(s) already mentioned. Common patterns: "los demás + verb" (Los demás son rojos) and "como los demás" (like everyone else). For mixed groups it can refer to people in general; for objects it means "the remaining ones".
target_language_example: Yo me quedo aquí; los demás pueden irse.
native_language_example: I’m staying here; the others can leave.

additional_notes: Plural noun with the definite article: el deporte (a sport / sport as an activity) → los deportes (sports). Common with verbs like gustar (Me gustan los deportes), interesar (Me interesan los deportes), and with expressions like ser bueno/malo en (Soy malo en los deportes) or pasión por (pasión por los deportes).
target_language_example: A mi hermana le encantan los deportes, pero a mí no.
native_language_example: My sister loves sports, but I don't.

additional_notes: Often refers to legal rights or entitlements. In creative contexts it can mean rights to publish, distribute, translate, or perform a work ("los derechos de publicación", "los derechos para interpretar"). In social/political contexts it means human/civil rights ("los derechos trans").
target_language_example: La autora vendió los derechos de la película a un estudio.
native_language_example: The author sold the film rights to a studio.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to more specific information about something (what happened, how it works, etc.). Often appears with verbs like dar (to give), saber (to know), and estar (to be) and in the expression “Todo está en los detalles” (“It’s all in the details”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes darme los detalles del plan?
native_language_example: Can you give me the details of the plan?

additional_notes: Definite plural article: Spanish commonly uses "los" with body parts (e.g., "Me duelen los dientes" = "My teeth hurt"). Often used with reflexive verbs for personal care: "lavarse"/"cepillarse los dientes" (to wash/brush your teeth).
target_language_example: Me cepillo los dientes antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Plural of "el dios" (a god). Used for gods in mythology or religion. In phrases like "gracias a los dioses" it means "thank the gods" (an expression of relief).
target_language_example: Gracias a los dioses, llegamos a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank the gods, we arrived on time.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "los" (the, masculine plural) + "doctores" (doctors). Used to talk about doctors in general or a specific group of male or mixed-gender doctors. For an all-female group you may also hear "las doctoras"; for a mixed group, "los doctores" is commonly used.
target_language_example: Los doctores dicen que necesitas descansar unos días.
native_language_example: The doctors say you need to rest for a few days.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase (singular: el documento). Commonly used for official papers like IDs, forms, contracts, permits, etc. Often appears with verbs like traer (to bring), pedir (to request), firmar (to sign), mostrar/enseñar (to show), revisar (to review).
target_language_example: ¿Tiene los documentos a mano?
native_language_example: Do you have the documents handy?

additional_notes: Use the definite article (los) with a day of the week to talk about a habitual action: los domingos = on Sundays / every Sunday. For a specific upcoming Sunday, you often say “el domingo” (e.g., El domingo voy al cine).
target_language_example: Los domingos desayuno tarde.
native_language_example: On Sundays I eat breakfast late.

additional_notes: Used to refer to two people or things together. It agrees in gender and number: masculine/plural is most common as a mixed or unknown group (los dos). For two females, use "las dos". It can also be used with nouns: "los dos niños" = "both boys / the two boys."
target_language_example: Los dos queremos ir al cine esta noche.
native_language_example: Both of us want to go to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific pair of brothers. "Los" is "the" (masculine plural), "dos" is "two," and "hermanos" means "brothers" (or "siblings" in some contexts, but with "los" it normally means brothers).
target_language_example: Los dos hermanos viven en Madrid.
native_language_example: The two brothers live in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a specific pair of countries already known from context. "Los" is the plural masculine form of "the"; "país" becomes "países" in the plural. Often appears after prepositions like "entre" (between): "entre los dos países".
target_language_example: La frontera entre los dos países es muy larga.
native_language_example: The border between the two countries is very long.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article: "los" + "dulces". "Dulces" can refer to candy, desserts, and sweet snacks in general (depending on the context). You can also use it as an adjective: "comida dulce" (sweet food).
target_language_example: Yo en cambio prefiero los dulces.
native_language_example: I, on the other hand, prefer sweets.

additional_notes: Plural of "el día" (day). Used to talk about days in general (often in statements about seasons, routines, or how time feels), e.g., "los días son más cortos/largos". It can also mean "the days (we’re living/going through)," as in "pasar mejor los días" = "get through the days better."
target_language_example: En verano, los días son más largos y hace más calor.
native_language_example: In summer, the days are longer and it’s hotter.

meaning: the days become / the days get (longer/shorter).
additional_notes: Uses hacerse + adjective to describe a gradual change over time. It’s common with comparatives like más largos / más cortos (“longer/shorter”), and with expressions like cada vez (“more and more”) to emphasize the progression. Literally “the days make themselves,” but it means “the days get/become.”
target_language_example: En diciembre, los días se hacen más cortos.
native_language_example: In December, the days get shorter.

additional_notes: Plural of el edificio (“the building”). Used for any kind of buildings (apartment buildings, office buildings, industrial/research buildings). If you want to specify the type, you can add a phrase after de (e.g., los edificios de apartamentos = “the apartment buildings”).
target_language_example: Los edificios del centro son muy altos.
native_language_example: The buildings downtown are very tall.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Used to talk about elephants in general or a specific group, depending on context. "Los" is the masculine plural definite article (“the”).
target_language_example: En el zoológico, los elefantes comen mucho cada día.
native_language_example: At the zoo, the elephants eat a lot every day.

additional_notes: Plural of "el empleado". Used to talk about a company’s staff in general (often in workplaces, offices, stores, airlines, etc.). After "de" it means "employees of" (e.g., "los empleados de Air France"). Often contrasted with "clientes" (customers).
target_language_example: Solo pueden entrar los empleados por esta puerta.
native_language_example: Only employees can enter through this door.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Uses the masculine plural article "los," which is also the default for mixed-gender groups. Singular: "el estudiante" (the student). Often followed by an adjective or nationality: "los estudiantes americanos".
target_language_example: Los estudiantes tienen un examen mañana.
native_language_example: The students have an exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to talk about the students’ **current state/condition** (están felices, están ausentes), **location** (están en el salón), or what they’re doing right now (están preparando…). **Están** is the 3rd-person plural form of **estar** and matches the plural subject **los estudiantes**.
target_language_example: Los estudiantes están listos para empezar la clase.
native_language_example: The students are ready to start class.

meaning: 'the students' + 'se' (reflexive/indirect-object pronoun used in many verb patterns).
additional_notes:
You’ll see **se** after *los estudiantes* in two common ways:
1) **Reflexive/pronominal verbs** (the students do something involving themselves): *Los estudiantes se levantan* = “The students stand up / get up.”; *Los estudiantes se ofrecieron (voluntarios)* = “The students volunteered.”
2) **With an indirect object: se les** (often in passive/impersonal style): *A los estudiantes se les dijo...* = “The students were told...” and *A los estudiantes se les prohíbe...* = “The students are forbidden / are not allowed...”
Note: **se** changes to **les** to show “to them,” and *se* is used instead of *le/les* before another *le/les* (e.g., *se les dijo*, not *les les dijo*).
target_language_example: A los estudiantes se les pidió que trajeran sus tareas mañana.
native_language_example: The students were asked to bring their homework tomorrow.

additional_notes: Plural noun with the definite article "los" (= "the"). Used when talking about aliens as a group or idea: "Creo que existen los extraterrestres" (I think aliens exist). Singular is "el extraterrestre". The verb "abducir" means "to abduct" (often used in alien stories).
target_language_example: Mucha gente cree que los extraterrestres viven en otros planetas.
native_language_example: Many people believe that aliens live on other planets.

additional_notes: Plural of el examen. Used for school/university exams in general or a specific set/period of exams (e.g., end-of-term exams). Often appears with verbs like empezar (to start), continuar con (to continue with), and aprobar (to pass).
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar mucho para los exámenes finales.
native_language_example: I have to study a lot for the final exams.

additional_notes: Plural noun with the masculine plural article "los". Used for supernatural beings/spirits; in some contexts it can also be used figuratively for "ghosts" of the past (e.g., memories or unresolved problems), but the examples here are about literal ghosts.
target_language_example: Dicen que en esa casa viven los fantasmas.
native_language_example: They say ghosts live in that house.

additional_notes: A very common time expression meaning weekends in general (a habitual routine). Usually placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: «Los fines de semana descanso» / «Descanso los fines de semana». Often used with routines and rules (e.g., opening times): «Los fines de semana se entra por…».
target_language_example: Los fines de semana no trabajo y paso tiempo con mi familia.
native_language_example: On weekends I don’t work and I spend time with my family.

additional_notes: Plural masculine article + adjective used as a noun: los + franceses = “the French (people)”. It can mean French people in general or a specific group of French people, depending on context. For a mixed-gender group, Spanish commonly uses the masculine plural (los franceses).
target_language_example: Los franceses hablan francés.
native_language_example: The French speak French.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase used for fireworks as a general thing or a specific fireworks show. It commonly appears with verbs like ver (to see), empezar (to start), and with time expressions (e.g., a medianoche, “at midnight”). Although fuego means “fire,” the full phrase means “fireworks,” not “artificial fires.”
target_language_example: Vamos a ver los fuegos artificiales esta noche.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch the fireworks tonight.

additional_notes: Refers to money spent or required (business or personal). Common with verbs like calcular (calculate), disminuir/reducir (lower/cut), and with phrases like "los gastos van por mi cuenta" (= I’ll cover the expenses).
target_language_example: Yo pago los gastos del viaje.
native_language_example: I’ll pay the travel expenses.

additional_notes: Definite plural noun phrase: "los" = "the" (masculine plural) + "gatos" = "cats." Used to talk about cats in general or a specific group of cats, depending on context.
target_language_example: A mi hermana le encantan los gatos.
native_language_example: My sister loves cats.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about cats. "Los" is the plural definite article (“the”), "gatos" = “cats,” and "son" is the plural form of "ser" (“to be”) used for descriptions, general truths, and characteristics.
target_language_example: Los gatos son independientes, pero cariñosos.
native_language_example: Cats are independent, but affectionate.

additional_notes: Used to say what cats possess or what characteristics they have. "Los gatos" = "cats/the cats" (plural). "Tienen" is the present tense (they/you all have) of "tener". You can follow it with a noun ("los gatos tienen pulgas") or with "la capacidad de + infinitive" ("los gatos tienen la capacidad de ver...").
target_language_example: Los gatos tienen bigotes muy sensibles.
native_language_example: Cats have very sensitive whiskers.

additional_notes: Common, slightly informal way to contrast children with older people ("los niños" vs. "los grandes"). Literally "the big ones," but it usually means adults/older people in context.
target_language_example: Ahora están hablando los grandes, ¿vale?
native_language_example: The grown-ups are talking now, okay?

meaning: the guards; the security/police officers on duty.
additional_notes: "Guardia" means a guard or watchman. In many contexts it refers to official guards (e.g., border guards, prison guards, soldiers guarding an area) or security staff. Use "los" because it’s plural and masculine ("las guardias" would be feminine). If you mean police specifically, you’ll often hear "la policía" or "los policías," though "los guardias" can sometimes refer to police/guards depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Los guardias no nos dejaron entrar al edificio.
native_language_example: The guards didn’t let us enter the building.

additional_notes: Refers to real events or true information (often in contrast to opinions, stories, or theories). Very common in phrases like "la versión de los hechos" (someone’s account of what happened) and "basarse en los hechos" (to be based on facts).
target_language_example: Antes de discutir, revisemos los hechos.
native_language_example: Before arguing, let’s review the facts.

additional_notes: Plural definite noun phrase: "los" (the, masculine plural) + "hombres" (men). Used to talk about men in general as a group (e.g., "Los hombres son...") or about specific men known from context. In mixed-gender groups, Spanish often uses the masculine plural as the default ("los hombres" can sometimes mean "people/men" depending on context, but it literally means "the men").
target_language_example: Los hombres de mi familia viven cerca.
native_language_example: The men in my family live nearby.

meaning: “the men of …” (men belonging to/associated with someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with **de + person/organization/thing** to show affiliation, loyalty, or origin. Often refers to someone’s followers, guards, workers, or soldiers (**los hombres de Ramón** = Ramón’s men). It can also describe a category/type of men (**los hombres de uniforme** = men in uniform).
target_language_example: La policía detuvo a los hombres de la banda.
native_language_example: The police arrested the gang’s men.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about men as a group: **Los hombres** (the men/men) + **son** (are). Often followed by an adjective or noun. Depending on context it can sound like a stereotype or insult (e.g., *Los hombres son cerdos*). You can also use **los hombres son + más/mejores/peores + que...** for comparisons.
target_language_example: Los hombres son diferentes, pero todos merecen respeto.
native_language_example: Men are different, but everyone deserves respect.

additional_notes: Subject + verb phrase: **los hombres** (“men/the men”) + **tienen** (they “have,” from *tener*). It’s often followed by a noun (**tienen presión** = “have pressure”) or by **que + infinitive** to express obligation (**tienen que trabajar** = “have to work”).
target_language_example: Los hombres tienen que estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: Men have to study for the exam.

additional_notes: Refers to bones in the body. Often used in medical/injury contexts (e.g., bones being fragile or broken). In expressions like “la carne de los huesos,” it means the bones as what’s left after removing flesh (a very graphic/threatening phrase).
target_language_example: Me duelen los huesos cuando hace frío.
native_language_example: My bones hurt when it’s cold.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase used for eggs as food or ingredients. Singular is "el huevo" (the egg). Common with verbs like poner/colocar (to put), sacar (to take out), gustar (to like), and with food combinations like "jamón y huevos". Note: in some contexts "huevos" can be slang for "testicles," but in these examples it clearly means eggs.
target_language_example: ¿Compraste los huevos para el desayuno?
native_language_example: Did you buy the eggs for breakfast?

meaning: humans; human beings; people (as a species).
additional_notes: Uses the plural article "los" to talk about humans in general (like "humans" in English). Often used in general statements about human nature or what humans do: "Los humanos son...". You can also use "los seres humanos" for a more formal "human beings."
target_language_example: A veces, los humanos cometemos errores.
native_language_example: Sometimes, we humans make mistakes.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about humans (as a species) or people in general. "Los humanos" is plural and refers to humans; "son" is the plural form of "ser" (to be) for a permanent/general characteristic. It’s often followed by a noun or adjective: "Los humanos son mamíferos" (noun), "Los humanos son mortales" (adjective).
target_language_example: Los humanos son curiosos por naturaleza.
native_language_example: Humans are curious by nature.

additional_notes: Most often means “taxes” in general (money paid to the government). In some contexts—especially with verbs like preparar/hacer/presentar—“los impuestos” can refer to “tax returns” or “tax paperwork.” Common uses: “Los impuestos están incluidos” (tax included), “reducir los impuestos” (to lower taxes), “basarse en los ingresos” (based on income).
target_language_example: Este año tengo que hacer los impuestos antes del 15 de abril.
native_language_example: This year I have to do my taxes before April 15.

meaning: “the Indians”; often used to mean Indigenous (Native) peoples of the Americas (context-dependent).
additional_notes: In many modern contexts, calling Indigenous peoples “los indios” can sound outdated or offensive. A more respectful/common alternative is “los pueblos indígenas” or “los indígenas.” Also note that “indio(s)” can refer either to Indigenous peoples in the Americas or to people from India; the meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: En muchos países se prefiere decir “los pueblos indígenas” en lugar de “los indios”.
native_language_example: In many countries people prefer to say “Indigenous peoples” instead of “the Indians.”

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase used to talk about English people as a group. Often contrasts with other nationalities (e.g., los franceses). It can refer specifically to people from England, but in everyday speech it’s sometimes used loosely to mean people from the UK.
target_language_example: Los ingleses suelen tomar té por la tarde.
native_language_example: English people often drink tea in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Uses the masculine plural article (los). In everyday English, “bugs” is common, but in Spanish insectos refers specifically to “insects” (not all small creepy-crawlies). Often used as the object of verbs like atraer (to attract), odiar (to hate), oír (to hear).
target_language_example: Odio los insectos de cualquier tipo.
native_language_example: I hate insects of any kind.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: **los** (the, masculine plural) + **italianos** (Italians). Used to talk about Italians as a group in general. For a mixed or all-female group, Spanish still often uses the masculine plural (**los italianos**); for all women you can also say **las italianas**. Capitalization: **italianos** is usually lowercase in Spanish.
target_language_example: Los italianos comen pasta con frecuencia.
native_language_example: Italians eat pasta often.

additional_notes: Refers to Japanese people as a group. It’s the masculine plural form; it can also be used for mixed-gender groups. For women only, you can say “las japonesas.” Singular: “el japonés / la japonesa.”
target_language_example: Los japoneses son muy amables con los visitantes.
native_language_example: Japanese people are very kind to visitors.

meaning: 'the Japanese are' (talking about Japanese people in general).
additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about Japanese people as a group. "Los japoneses" = "the Japanese (people)" (masculine plural used generically for mixed groups); "son" is the plural form of "ser" (to be) for permanent/general characteristics. Often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase (e.g., "trabajadores", "un pueblo muy limpio").
target_language_example: Los japoneses son muy respetuosos en el transporte público.
native_language_example: The Japanese are very respectful on public transportation.

additional_notes: Definite plural noun phrase: **los** (the) + **judíos** (Jews). It refers to Jewish people as a group (religion/ethnicity), so use it neutrally and respectfully. In Spanish it’s usually written lowercase (**judíos**) unless part of a proper name; in English it’s often capitalized (**Jews**). You can also use **judío/judía** as an adjective: *una familia judía* (“a Jewish family”).
target_language_example: En este barrio viven muchos de los judíos.
native_language_example: Many of the Jews live in this neighborhood.

meaning: the games of / the (type of) games (of).
additional_notes: Used to talk about games of a specific sport or category. It’s usually followed by a noun (los juegos de béisbol = baseball games; los juegos de destreza = skill games). Note: for sports, you’ll also often hear "los partidos de" (matches/games), especially for soccer, basketball, etc.
target_language_example: Hoy hay los juegos de baloncesto en la tele.
native_language_example: Today there are basketball games on TV.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase meaning “young people” in general (often teenagers/young adults). It’s the masculine plural form, which is also used for mixed-gender groups. You can also say “la juventud” for “youth” as a concept.
target_language_example: Los jóvenes de mi barrio se reúnen en el parque los fines de semana.
native_language_example: Young people in my neighborhood meet in the park on weekends.

additional_notes: Refers to the lips of the mouth. Used in common expressions like "besar en los labios" (to kiss on the lips) and "salir de los labios" (to come from someone’s lips = to be said). It can also describe putting something to your lips when drinking: "llevar(se) algo a los labios".
target_language_example: Se pintó los labios antes de salir.
native_language_example: She put on lipstick before going out.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase (el ladrón → the thief/robber; los ladrones → the thieves/robbers). Commonly used when talking about people who steal, especially in crime contexts (police, break-ins, robberies).
target_language_example: La policía atrapó a los ladrones después del robo.
native_language_example: The police caught the thieves after the robbery.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase: **los** = “the” (plural, masculine) + **libros** = “books.” Use it to talk about specific books that are known from context (e.g., the books we mentioned, the books on the table).
target_language_example: Los libros están en la mesa.
native_language_example: The books are on the table.

meaning: 'the books of' / 'the books about' (a topic or place).
additional_notes: Used to identify which books you mean by adding a topic or origin after de: los libros de animales (books about animals), los libros de historia (history books), los libros de la biblioteca (the library's books / books from the library). In sentence 6, de allí means 'from there' (take the books from there).
target_language_example: Necesito los libros de matemáticas para estudiar.
native_language_example: I need the math books to study.

meaning: 'the books are…' (used to describe books or say what books are like).
additional_notes: "Los libros" = "the books" (plural). "Son" is the form of "ser" for "they are" (used for identity/description/general truths). Common in definitions, quotes, and general statements: "Los libros son nuestros" (ownership), "Los libros son el alimento del espíritu" (a general truth/metaphor).
target_language_example: Los libros son una buena forma de aprender español.
native_language_example: Books are a good way to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Using the plural day name with the article (los + day) usually means a repeated routine or general habit: los lunes = on Mondays / every Monday. For a single specific Monday, Spanish often uses "el lunes" (e.g., "El lunes tengo cita").
target_language_example: Los lunes trabajo desde casa.
native_language_example: On Mondays I work from home.

meaning: the means (resources/ways to do something) OR the media.
additional_notes:
Meaning depends on context. 
- **Means / resources / methods**: *No tiene los medios* = “He/She doesn’t have the means/resources.” Also used in contrasts like *El fin y los medios* (“the end and the means”). 
- **Media (press/TV/internet/news)**: *en los medios* = “in the media”; *los medios lo siguen* = “the media are following him.” 
Common fixed phrase: **los medios de transporte** = “means/modes of transportation.”
target_language_example: No tengo los medios para pagar el curso.
native_language_example: I don’t have the means to pay for the course.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the top people or things in a group (e.g., hotels, gifts, singers). It agrees in gender/number: los mejores (masc./mixed plural), las mejores (fem. plural). Common in compliments: "Ustedes son los mejores" = "You’re the best."
target_language_example: De todas las opciones, elegimos los mejores asientos.
native_language_example: Out of all the options, we chose the best seats.

los mejores años de mi vida

target_language_multi_word_term: los mejores años de mi vida
meaning: the best years of my life.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a period you remember as the happiest or most meaningful in your life (often in the past, sometimes about the present/future). The verb is often in the past: “Fueron…” / “Esos fueron…”. You can change the possessive to match the person: “de tu vida”, “de su vida”, “de nuestra vida”.
target_language_example: Siento que estos son los mejores años de mi vida.
native_language_example: I feel like these are the best years of my life.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the people who belong to a group (a band, club, sect, gang, team, etc.). Singular: "el miembro". Often followed by "de" + group: "los miembros de la banda / secta / pandilla".
target_language_example: Los miembros del club se reúnen todos los viernes.
native_language_example: The club members meet every Friday.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean the people who belong to a group or organization: los miembros del jurado (the jury members), del comité (of the committee), del club (of the club). It’s the plural of el miembro, and del = de + el.
target_language_example: Los miembros del equipo llegaron temprano.
native_language_example: The members of the team arrived early.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of “el mismo” (“the same”). It refers back to people or things already mentioned or understood from context. Common in phrases like “los mismos errores” (the same mistakes) or “los mismos hombres” (the same men), emphasizing identity or repetition. Use “los mismos” with masculine plural nouns; with feminine plural, use “las mismas.”
target_language_example: Matías seguía cometiendo los mismos errores.
native_language_example: Matías kept making the same mistakes.

meaning: "the monkeys" (male monkeys, or monkeys in general).
additional_notes: “Mono” means “monkey.” With “los” it’s plural and definite: “the monkeys.” In Spanish, the masculine plural (“los monos”) is also used for mixed groups or to talk about monkeys as a category in general. (Unrelated: “mono/mon(a)” can also mean “cute,” depending on context.)
target_language_example: En el zoológico, los monos siempre están jugando.
native_language_example: At the zoo, the monkeys are always playing.

meaning: "the boys" / "the guys" (a group of male kids or young men).
additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase. Often used for a group of boys, but in casual speech it can also mean “the guys” (a group of men) or even “the kids” depending on context. Singular: el muchacho; feminine: las muchachas.
target_language_example: Los muchachos ya llegaron a casa.
native_language_example: The guys already got home.

additional_notes: Plural noun (usually used in the plural) for household/office furniture like chairs, tables, sofas, etc. Often used with verbs like mover (to move), comprar (to buy), vender (to sell), and with de + place/owner: los muebles de la oficina (the office furniture).
target_language_example: Tenemos que limpiar los muebles antes de la visita.
native_language_example: We have to clean the furniture before the visit.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article: "los" + "muertos". It usually refers to dead people as a group ("the dead") and can sometimes imply dead bodies depending on context. In phrases like "el mundo de los muertos" it means "the world of the dead". In "los muertos vivientes" it means "the living dead" (zombies).
target_language_example: En esta historia, los muertos regresan para hablar con los vivos.
native_language_example: In this story, the dead return to speak with the living.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article. Singular: "el musulmán" (male) / "la musulmana" (female). Plural: "los musulmanes" (mixed group or masculine default) and "las musulmanas" (all-female group). Commonly used to refer to Muslims as a religious community in general.
target_language_example: El Corán es la escritura sagrada de los musulmanes.
native_language_example: The Qur'an is the sacred scripture of the Muslims.

meaning: "the most" / "the + superlative" (the ones that are the most…).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or sometimes a past participle) to form a superlative and refer to a masculine or mixed-gender plural group: "los más + adj." = "the most + adj." or "the + adj-est" (e.g., los más jóvenes = the youngest).
