It can also appear in the pattern "uno/una de los más + adj." = "one of the most + adj.". "Los" changes with gender/number: "los más" (masc. plural / mixed), "las más" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Este lago es uno de los más profundos del país.
native_language_example: This lake is one of the deepest in the country.

additional_notes: Plural definite noun phrase: "los" (the, masculine plural) + "médicos" (doctors/physicians). Used to talk about doctors in general or a specific group of doctors. Singular: "el médico"; feminine forms: "la médica" / plural "las médicas" (also "las doctoras" is common).
target_language_example: Los médicos dicen que necesito más descanso.
native_language_example: The doctors say I need more rest.

additional_notes: Used to refer to people connected to you when the noun is understood from context (e.g., my family, my friends, my teammates). Often translates naturally as “my folks/people.” It agrees in gender/number: los míos (masc./mixed plural), las mías (fem. plural). You can also say el mío / la mía for singular (“mine”).
target_language_example: Esta noche ceno con los míos.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m having dinner with my family/folks.

additional_notes: Usually refers to business in general or commercial matters (sales, clients, making money), not a single “business” as a company. Common in phrases like “ser bueno con los negocios” (be good at business), “los negocios están lentos” (business is slow), and “no es bueno para los negocios” (it’s bad for business). For a specific company/shop, you’ll often hear “la empresa” or “el negocio”.
target_language_example: Últimamente, los negocios van bien en mi tienda.
native_language_example: Lately, business has been going well at my store.

additional_notes: This is the masculine plural form used to refer to Black people as a group. In Spanish, using an adjective as a noun with an article ("los" + adjective) can sound blunt, objectifying, or dehumanizing in some contexts—especially when referring to race/ethnicity—so it may be perceived as offensive depending on tone, region, and situation. More neutral and generally preferred options are "las personas negras" or "la gente negra". If you need a respectful group reference in most contexts, choose one of those instead.
target_language_example: En muchos textos de historia se explica cómo los negros fueron discriminados durante siglos y cómo lucharon por sus derechos.
native_language_example: In many history texts, it explains how Black people were discriminated against for centuries and how they fought for their rights.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about feeling nervous or on edge (stress/tension), or about getting irritated. Common patterns: estar/tener los nervios de punta = “to be very nervous/on edge”; poner (a alguien) de los nervios = “to drive (someone) crazy / get on (someone’s) nerves”; perder los nervios = “to lose your temper / lose your nerve.”
target_language_example: Antes del examen, tenía los nervios de punta.
native_language_example: Before the exam, I was extremely nervous.

meaning: the children; the boys (depending on context).
additional_notes: Plural of el niño (“boy/child”). With mixed groups (boys + girls), Spanish often uses the masculine plural “los niños” to mean “the children.” You can also say “los niños y las niñas” to be extra specific.
target_language_example: Los niños están jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: The children are playing in the park.

meaning: “the children/boys of …” / “the … children (from/in …)” (often used to specify age, group, or origin).
additional_notes: Used with **de** to add identifying information about **los niños**: **de + age** (Los niños de diez años = ten-year-old kids), **de + group/role** (los niños de coro = choirboys), or **de + place** (los niños de Estados Unidos = children in/from the U.S.). In singular: **el niño de**.
target_language_example: Los niños de ocho años pueden entrar gratis.
native_language_example: Eight-year-old children can enter for free.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of estar (estaban) to describe an ongoing past situation or a past state/background: how the children were (asleep/awake), where they were (en fila), or their condition (bien, casi desnudos). Often followed by an adjective, a location phrase (en + place), or a gerund for a past continuous action (estaban durmiendo = were sleeping).
target_language_example: Cuando entré, los niños estaban jugando en el patio.
native_language_example: When I came in, the children were playing in the yard.

additional_notes: Used with estar (not ser) to talk about temporary states (e.g., sleeping), ongoing actions (estar + gerund: están soñando = are dreaming), or location (están en la escuela = are at school). Common adjectives after it: dormidos, cansados, contentos.
target_language_example: Los niños están cansados hoy.
native_language_example: The children are tired today.

additional_notes: "Los niños" = "the children" (masculine plural; can also refer to a mixed group of boys and girls). "Necesitan" is the "they" form of necesitar (to need). It’s commonly followed by a noun (amor, cariño) or an infinitive verb (dormir, jugar).
target_language_example: Los niños necesitan comer bien para crecer.
native_language_example: Children need to eat well to grow.

additional_notes: Refers to children who are still very young (often toddlers to early elementary age). The adjective "pequeños" agrees with "niños" (masculine plural). You can also say "los pequeños" when the context is clear, or use "las niñas pequeñas" for girls.
target_language_example: Este parque es perfecto para los niños pequeños.
native_language_example: This park is perfect for little kids.

additional_notes: This is not really a fixed phrase by itself—it's the subject (los niños = “the children”) followed by the pronoun se, which appears with many verbs in Spanish. In your examples it’s part of pronominal verbs like cansarse (to get tired), divertirse (to have fun), dormirse (to fall asleep), and merecerse (to deserve). English usually doesn’t translate se directly; you translate the whole verb phrase (e.g., “get tired,” “have fun,” “fall asleep,” “deserve”).
target_language_example: Los niños se levantan temprano para ir a la escuela.
native_language_example: The children get up early to go to school.

additional_notes: “Los niños” means “the children,” and “son” is the “they/you all are” form of **ser**. Use **ser** for identity, inherent characteristics, or general statements (e.g., *Los niños son nuestro futuro*). For temporary states (like being tired), Spanish often uses **estar** instead.
target_language_example: Los niños son muy curiosos.
native_language_example: The children are very curious.

additional_notes: “Los niños” = “the children/kids” (plural). “Tienen” is the present-tense “they have” form of **tener**. Used to state what children possess, experience, or are allowed/not allowed to do (e.g., *tienen miedo* = “are afraid,” *tienen prohibido + infinitive* = “are forbidden to…”).
target_language_example: Los niños tienen que dormir temprano.
native_language_example: The children have to go to sleep early.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a list of people’s/animals’/things’ names. It’s the plural form; singular is “el nombre de” (“the name of”). Often followed by a noun (“los nombres de sus amigos”) or a clause with “quienes” (“los nombres de quienes…” = “the names of those who…”).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes decir los nombres de tus compañeros de trabajo?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the names of your coworkers?

meaning: "ours" / "our people" (referring to people or things that belong to us).
additional_notes: Uses the definite article + a possessive pronoun: "los nuestros" = "ours" (masculine plural) or "our people/our side" depending on context. It can refer to people (family, group, team) or to things mentioned earlier (e.g., parents, plans, possessions). It agrees in gender/number: "los nuestros" (m. pl.), "las nuestras" (f. pl.), "el nuestro" (m. sg.), "la nuestra" (f. sg.).
target_language_example: Tenemos que apoyar a los nuestros en los momentos difíciles.
native_language_example: We have to support our people in difficult times.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (los) + an adjective (nuevos) as a noun phrase. It can refer to new items (e.g., shoes, furniture) or to people who are new in a group/situation ("the newcomers"). Often contrasts with "los viejos" (the old ones).
target_language_example: En la oficina, los nuevos todavía no conocen las reglas.
native_language_example: At the office, the newcomers still don’t know the rules.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase: **el número** (the number) → **los números** (the numbers). Used for quantities, digits, or statistics/data depending on context (e.g., *Los números hablan por sí mismos* = “The numbers speak for themselves”).
target_language_example: No entiendo los números en esta tabla.
native_language_example: I don’t understand the numbers in this table.

additional_notes: Used with body parts in Spanish (often with the definite article): me duelen los ojos (“my eyes hurt”). Common expressions: entre los ojos (“between the eyes”); abrirle/abrirme los ojos (to open someone’s/my eyes = make them realize something); sécate los ojos (wipe/dry your eyes); tener los ojos puestos en alguien/algo (to keep an eye on someone/something, watch closely).
target_language_example: Sécate los ojos y dime qué pasó.
native_language_example: Wipe your eyes and tell me what happened.

additional_notes: Often used in commands (Mantén/Mantengan los ojos abiertos) to tell someone to watch carefully or be on the lookout. Literally refers to having your eyes open, but it can also mean being attentive to danger, opportunities, or details.
target_language_example: Mantén los ojos abiertos cuando cruces la calle.
native_language_example: Keep your eyes open when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s eye color, often with the verb tener (to have): «tener los ojos azules». You can change the article/number to match the person: «los ojos» (most common) or «sus ojos», and plural contexts like «tienen los ojos azules».
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene los ojos azules, como mi mamá.
native_language_example: My brother has blue eyes, like my mom.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like **tener** (to have) or **mantener** (to keep): *Tenía/Mantén los ojos cerrados.* With **con** it can also be figurative, meaning “very easily / without effort”: *Podría hacerlo con los ojos cerrados* (“I could do it with my eyes closed”).
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta con los ojos cerrados si quieres, pero no hagas ruido.
native_language_example: Close the door with your eyes closed if you want, but don’t make noise.

additional_notes: Used literally to talk about someone’s eyes: “Los ojos de mi mamá” (“my mom’s eyes”). Also used figuratively with "ante" or "a": "ante los ojos de la ley" = “in the eyes of the law” (how the law sees/judges something). Often followed by a person or group: "los ojos de ella", "los ojos de un amigo".
target_language_example: Ante los ojos de mis padres, mentir está mal.
native_language_example: In my parents’ eyes, lying is wrong.

meaning: '(the) eyes and…' (used to link to another action or body part).
additional_notes: This is a common chunk you’ll see when Spanish connects two actions with the same subject (e.g., "Abrió los ojos y vio…" = "He opened his eyes and saw…") or when listing features ("los ojos y las cejas" = "the eyes and the eyebrows"). With body parts, Spanish often uses the definite article (los/las) where English uses a possessive (my/his/her).
target_language_example: Abre los ojos y mira la pizarra.
native_language_example: Open your eyes and look at the board.

additional_notes: Plural of el oso (“bear”). Used with the definite article los (“the”) to talk about bears in general or a specific group of bears. Often used with a + los (a los osos) after verbs like gustar (A los osos les gusta la miel).
target_language_example: En este parque hay muchos osos, pero normalmente los osos evitan a la gente.
native_language_example: In this park there are many bears, but bears usually avoid people.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group of masculine or mixed-gender people or things (plural). Often implies “the remaining” or “the different ones,” depending on context. Can also be followed by a number: “los otros dos” = “the other two.” For feminine plural, use “las otras.”
target_language_example: ¿Dónde están los otros? Ya es hora de salir.
native_language_example: Where are the others? It’s already time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group of children, excluding the child/children you’re focusing on. It can contrast one child with the others (e.g., “different from the other children”). You’ll also see singular forms like “el otro niño” (the other boy/child) and feminine “las otras niñas” (the other girls).
target_language_example: Ella no hablaba mucho con los otros niños en la escuela.
native_language_example: She didn’t talk much with the other kids at school.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "el otro"; often used for a group you’re comparing yourself to ("like the others", "than the others") or to refer to other people in general. It can include mixed-gender groups; for an all-female group you may also hear "las otras". Often appears in comparisons: "como/igual que los otros" (like the others) and "más ... que los otros" (more ... than the others).
target_language_example: No te preocupes por los otros; haz lo mejor que puedas.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about the others; do the best you can.

additional_notes: Plural of "el oído" (ear). Often used after prepositions: "para los oídos" (for the ears), "en los oídos" (in the ears). Common in health/sensation phrases like "un zumbido en los oídos" (a ringing in the ears) or "tapones para los oídos" (earplugs).
target_language_example: Después del concierto, me dolían los oídos.
native_language_example: After the concert, my ears hurt.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form used for a mixed group of parents (mother + father) or parents in general. Singular: el padre = the father. You’ll also see "los papás" as a more informal way to say "the parents."
target_language_example: Los padres de Ana viven en México.
native_language_example: Ana’s parents live in Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s mother and father (or parent(s)) followed by a name or noun: "los padres de Khadija". It’s plural and masculine by default even if the parents are mixed-gender. You can also say "los papás de" (more informal) or "los progenitores de" (more formal/technical).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a los padres de Marta para avisarles.
native_language_example: I’m going to call Marta’s parents to let them know.

additional_notes: Used for clothing you wear on your legs. In Spanish it’s very common to use the definite article (los) with clothing, especially with verbs like ponerse/quitarse (e.g., Me puse los pantalones = I put my pants on). Also appears in the idiom "llevar los pantalones" meaning "to be the one in charge / to call the shots" in a relationship or family.
target_language_example: Necesito comprarme los pantalones para el trabajo.
native_language_example: I need to buy pants for work.

meaning: 'the papers' (documents); in some expressions, 'your composure' or 'your role'.
additional_notes: Literally means “the papers” (documents). In common expressions it takes on idiomatic meanings: **perder los papeles** = to lose your temper/lose control; **cambiar los papeles** = to switch roles (each person does the other’s part).
target_language_example: No pierdas los papeles, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t lose your temper, please.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase used for people traveling in a vehicle (bus, train, plane, car, etc.). Singular: el pasajero / la pasajera. Often appears with verbs like subir (to get on), bajar(se) (to get off), and with safety topics like cinturón de seguridad (seat belt).
target_language_example: Los pasajeros ya están en el avión y deben abrocharse el cinturón.
native_language_example: The passengers are already on the plane and must fasten their seat belts.

additional_notes: Plural of "el país" (country). Used to talk about countries in general or a specific group of countries. Often appears in patterns like "la mayoría de los países" (most countries) and with adjectives: "países árabes" (Arab countries), "países extranjeros" (foreign countries).
target_language_example: Muchos de los países de Europa usan el euro.
native_language_example: Many of the countries in Europe use the euro.

additional_notes: Definite plural noun phrase: "los" + "peces". Used to refer to fish as a group in general or to a specific group of fish. Singular: "el pez" (the fish).
target_language_example: María les dio de comer a los peces.
native_language_example: María fed the fish.

meaning: (to have) your hair stand on end; to get goosebumps (from fear/shock).
additional_notes: Usually used with poner: "(Algo) me pone los pelos de punta" = “(Something) gives me goosebumps / makes my hair stand on end.” Very common with the reflexive pattern "Se me ponen/han puesto los pelos de punta" (literally “the hairs got stood up on me”), meaning you suddenly felt scared, shocked, or creeped out. Can also be used for strong emotion, but most often for fear or something unsettling.
target_language_example: Cuando escuché ese ruido en la noche, se me pusieron los pelos de punta.
native_language_example: When I heard that noise at night, my hair stood on end.

additional_notes: Plural of "el periódico" (newspaper). Used for reading the news ("leer los periódicos") or being featured in the press ("estar en los periódicos"). Often refers to newspapers in general, not specific ones, unless context specifies which.
target_language_example: Todas las mañanas leo los periódicos en la cafetería.
native_language_example: Every morning I read the newspapers at the café.

additional_notes: Definite plural article + noun: los (the, masculine plural) + perros (dogs). Used to talk about dogs in general or a specific group of dogs depending on context. Common in rules/signs like “Están prohibidos los perros” (= Dogs are not allowed).
target_language_example: A los niños les encantan los perros.
native_language_example: Kids love dogs.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about dogs. "Los" is the plural masculine article (“the”) and "son" is the present tense of **ser** for **they/you (plural)**. Adjectives that follow usually agree in plural: *Los perros son inteligentes/fieles/divertidos.* You can also say *Los perros son...* when you mean dogs in general (a whole category).
target_language_example: Los perros son muy cariñosos con sus dueños.
native_language_example: Dogs are very affectionate with their owners.

additional_notes: Plural of "el pie" (foot). Used for body parts (Me duelen los pies = My feet hurt). Also appears in common expressions: "al pie de" = at the bottom of (a page), as in "pies de página" (footnotes); "poner los pies en (un lugar)" = to set foot in (a place). In commands you may hear it with verbs like levantar/mover (lift/move your feet).
target_language_example: Después de caminar todo el día, me duelen los pies.
native_language_example: After walking all day, my feet hurt.

additional_notes: Often means “the dishes” in the sense of dirty dishes and dishwashing (e.g., lavar/fregar los platos). It can also literally mean the plates on the table that someone clears away (recoger los platos).
target_language_example: Hoy me toca lavar los platos.
native_language_example: Today it’s my turn to do the dishes.

additional_notes: Uses the plural article "los" + adjective "pobres" to talk about a whole group of people in general (the poor). It can be used as the object of a verb: "ayudar a los pobres" (to help the poor) or with feelings like "dar pena" (to make you feel sorry). Depending on context, it can sound generalizing; you may also hear "personas pobres" as a more explicit alternative.
target_language_example: Muchas organizaciones trabajan para apoyar a los pobres.
native_language_example: Many organizations work to support the poor.

additional_notes: Plural with the definite article: "los" = "the" (masculine plural). Refers to police officers as people (not the institution in general). In many places you can also say "la policía" for "the police" as an institution/force. "Policía" can be singular (policía) or plural (policías).
target_language_example: Los policías llegaron rápido y hablaron con los testigos.
native_language_example: The cops arrived quickly and talked to the witnesses.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase with the definite article: los + políticos. Used to talk about politicians as a general group (often in opinions or criticisms). Singular: el político; feminine: la política / las políticas (also means “politics” in some contexts).
target_language_example: A veces los políticos prometen mucho y cumplen poco.
native_language_example: Sometimes politicians promise a lot and deliver little.

additional_notes: Plural of "el precio". Used to talk about the cost of goods/services in general, often with verbs like "subir" (to go up/raise), "bajar/caer" (to go down/fall), and phrases like "estar altos" (to be high) or "ir/van en aumento" (to be rising).
target_language_example: Los precios han subido mucho este año.
native_language_example: Prices have gone up a lot this year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about people or things that come first in order, time, or rank. Often followed by a number ("los primeros seis" = "the first six"). It can also mean "early" in expressions like "en los primeros días" (in the early days) or "en los primeros cursos" (in the first/earliest grades). As a noun phrase, it can refer to the first people to do something ("Fueron los primeros en subir" = They were the first to get on).
target_language_example: Llegué tarde, pero mis amigos fueron los primeros en entrar.
native_language_example: I arrived late, but my friends were the first to go in.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Used to talk about people who are being held (in prison, a jail, a camp, etc.). Singular: el prisionero / la prisionera. Common verbs with it: llevar (take), liberar (free/release), huir (escape), regresar (return).
target_language_example: Los prisioneros fueron liberados al amanecer.
native_language_example: The prisoners were released at dawn.

additional_notes: Plural of "el profesor". In Spanish, "profesor" can mean a school teacher or a university professor; context tells you which. The masculine plural "los" is used for an all-male group or a mixed-gender group (men + women). For an all-female group you’d say "las profesoras".
target_language_example: Los profesores de español son muy pacientes.
native_language_example: The Spanish teachers are very patient.

additional_notes: Used with a time period to mean the period starting now: "los próximos dos días" = "the next two days." It agrees in gender/number with the noun: "los próximos" (masc. plural), "las próximas" (fem. plural). Often followed by a number: "los próximos diez segundos."
target_language_example: Voy a estar ocupado los próximos tres días.
native_language_example: I’m going to be busy for the next three days.

additional_notes: Refers to the two organs in your chest used for breathing. Usually used in plural in Spanish (even when talking generally about lung health): "Me duelen los pulmones" (My lungs hurt). Can appear in comparisons/metaphors (e.g., parks as the "lungs" of a city). Often used with "llenarse de" (to fill with) or descriptions of damage from smoking/pollution.
target_language_example: Después de correr, me dolían los pulmones.
native_language_example: After running, my lungs hurt.

additional_notes: Plural noun with the definite article. Used to talk about birds in general or a specific group of birds. Singular: el pájaro (the bird).
target_language_example: En el parque, los pájaros vuelan sobre los árboles.
native_language_example: In the park, the birds fly over the trees.

additional_notes: A simple present-tense sentence: subject (los pájaros = the birds) + verb (cantan = sing). Often used to describe nature sounds or what happens regularly (e.g., in the morning, in the countryside).
target_language_example: En primavera, los pájaros cantan temprano.
native_language_example: In spring, the birds sing early.

additional_notes: A simple present-tense sentence: **los pájaros** (“the birds”) + **vuelan** (they fly, from *volar*). Used to state a general fact or describe what birds are doing; you can add details with phrases like **al sur** (to the south), **por el cielo** (through the sky), or **bajo** (low).
target_language_example: En primavera, los pájaros vuelan más alto.
native_language_example: In spring, the birds fly higher.

meaning: "those who" (refers to a group of people).
additional_notes: Used to point to people who meet a condition, often followed by a verb: "los que + verb". It’s the plural masculine/mixed form; for an all-female group use "las que". Often appears after expressions like "solo"/"sólo" (only): "Solo los que..." = "Only those who...".
target_language_example: Los que llegan temprano pueden escoger mejor asiento.
native_language_example: Those who arrive early can choose a better seat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the outcome of something like a test, game, vote, or experiment. Often followed by “de” + what it’s from: “los resultados de la prueba” (the test results). You can also describe them with adjectives: “Los resultados fueron negativos.”
target_language_example: Todavía no tenemos los resultados del examen.
native_language_example: We still don't have the exam results.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (los) + adjective (ricos) to refer to a whole group of people: “the rich.” Often contrasted with "los pobres" (“the poor”). You can also use it for other groups, e.g., "los jóvenes" (young people), "los españoles" (Spanish people).
target_language_example: Los ricos y los pobres deberían tener las mismas oportunidades.
native_language_example: The rich and the poor should have the same opportunities.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "los" (the) + "romanos" (Romans). Used for the people of ancient Rome; it also appears in the proverb "Cuando en Roma, haz como los romanos" (“When in Rome, do as the Romans do”).
target_language_example: Los romanos construyeron muchas carreteras.
native_language_example: The Romans built many roads.

additional_notes: Definite article + nationality in plural. Used to refer to Russian people as a group (e.g., in conversation, news, or stories). Singular: el ruso / la rusa; plural feminine: las rusas. In Spanish, nationalities are not capitalized unless part of an official name.
target_language_example: Dicen que los rusos van a llegar mañana.
native_language_example: They say the Russians are going to arrive tomorrow.

additional_notes: A general, formal/neutral way to talk about people as a species (often in science, philosophy, or general statements). Singular: "el ser humano" = "a human being" / "the human being" (humanity in general).
target_language_example: Los seres humanos necesitan agua para vivir.
native_language_example: Human beings need water to live.

additional_notes: Plural definite noun phrase (soldado = soldier). Used to talk about a specific group of soldiers. Often appears as the subject (Los soldados cumplieron.) or after the preposition a to mark an indirect object (A los soldados se les ordenó...).
target_language_example: Los soldados llegaron temprano al campamento.
native_language_example: The soldiers arrived early at the camp.

meaning: 'dreams' (things you see while sleeping, or hopes/goals).
additional_notes: Usually plural. It can mean (1) sleeping dreams: "los sueños" you have at night, or (2) life dreams/aspirations: goals you want to achieve. Common collocations: "el mundo de los sueños" (the dream world), "hacer realidad los sueños" (make dreams come true), "diccionario de los sueños" (dream dictionary).
target_language_example: Cualquier cosa puede pasar en el mundo de los sueños.
native_language_example: Anything can happen in the world of dreams.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive pronoun suyos with the article los to replace a noun already mentioned. It can refer to things (e.g., books) or people (“his men,” “her family”). The form matches what is possessed (plural, masculine or mixed group): los suyos (plural), las suyas (plural feminine), el suyo / la suya (singular). Which meaning (his/her/their/your formal) depends on context.
target_language_example: Yo llevé mis documentos y ella llevó los suyos.
native_language_example: I brought my documents and she brought hers.

additional_notes: Use the article + day of the week (los + sábado) to talk about a habitual action that happens every week on that day: Los sábados trabajo / descanso. You can add a time: los sábados por la mañana (on Saturday mornings). To be more specific, for a single, specific Saturday you often say este sábado (this Saturday) or el sábado (on Saturday).
target_language_example: Los sábados por la tarde salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: On Saturdays in the afternoon we go out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about life conditions in a certain period (“hard times”), or how society and circumstances change (“times are changing / have changed”). Often appears with adjectives like difíciles/duros (difficult/hard) or with verbs like cambiar (to change).
target_language_example: En los tiempos de mi abuelo, no había internet.
native_language_example: In my grandfather’s time, there wasn’t any internet.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase (singular: el trabajador / la trabajadora). Often refers to workers as a group, especially in jobs and labor contexts (salaries, working conditions, strikes: estar de huelga). You can also use it for employees in a company: los trabajadores de la empresa.
target_language_example: Los trabajadores de este restaurante tienen un buen horario.
native_language_example: The workers at this restaurant have a good schedule.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "el tren" (train). Used to talk about trains in general or specific trains already known from context. Often followed by a location phrase with "en" (e.g., "los trenes en Serbia") and can be the subject of sentences like "Los trenes son..." or "Los trenes van...".
target_language_example: Los trenes aquí llegan tarde con frecuencia.
native_language_example: The trains here often arrive late.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine plural article (los) for a group of three, including mixed-gender groups. Often followed by a noun (los tres vasos = “the three glasses”) or used alone when the noun is understood (por los tres = “for the three of us/them”).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde están los tres libros que compraste?
native_language_example: Where are the three books you bought?

additional_notes:
"Los tuyos" is the masculine plural possessive pronoun for "tú". It replaces a noun that’s understood from context:
- Things: "Mis zapatos... los tuyos" = “my shoes… yours.”
- People (common): "por ti y los tuyos" = “for you and your loved ones/your family.”
It agrees with what’s being replaced: feminine plural = "las tuyas"; singular = "el tuyo / la tuya".
target_language_example: Cuida de ti y de los tuyos.
native_language_example: Take care of yourself and your family/loved ones.

additional_notes: Plural, masculine form of "el vecino". Often refers to people living in the same building, on the same street, or in the surrounding area. You’ll commonly hear it in situations involving shared spaces (e.g., the main door/entrance) or when neighbors complain/call authorities.
target_language_example: Los vecinos hacen mucho ruido por la noche.
native_language_example: The neighbors make a lot of noise at night.

additional_notes: Used to talk nostalgically about the past, often implying things were better or simpler then. Common in phrases like “recordar los viejos tiempos” (to remember the old days), “como/igual que los viejos tiempos” (like old times), and “hablar de/sobre los viejos tiempos” (to talk about the old days).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos a mirar fotos y a recordar los viejos tiempos.
native_language_example: We sat down to look at photos and remember the old days.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Often used with verbs like ponerse (to put on), quitarse/sacarse (to take off), and with parts like los cordones de los zapatos (shoelaces). In Spanish, clothing items are commonly talked about with the definite article (los/las), where English might use a possessive (my/your).
target_language_example: Quítese los zapatos, por favor.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes.

los zapatos antes de entrar a

target_language_multi_word_term: los zapatos antes de entrar a
meaning: 'your/the shoes before entering (a place)' (usually in the phrase 'quitarse/sacarse los zapatos antes de entrar a...').
additional_notes: Used when asking or telling someone to remove their shoes before going into a place (a house, temple, etc.). Most commonly you’ll hear it as: "Quítate/Quítese/Sácate/Sáquese los zapatos antes de entrar a + lugar." Note the change for informal vs. formal commands: "quítate" (tú) vs. "quítese" (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, quítate los zapatos antes de entrar a mi departamento.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes before entering my apartment.

additional_notes: Plural of "el árbol" (tree). Used with the definite article "los" to talk about specific trees or trees in general (as a group). Common with verbs like cortar (to cut down), subir(se) a (to climb up), and with location phrases like entre los árboles (among/between the trees).
target_language_example: En otoño, las hojas de los árboles cambian de color.
native_language_example: In autumn, the leaves on the trees change color.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun (often omitted) to refer to the final ones in a sequence or the most recent period: los últimos años/meses/momentos. Can also contrast with los primeros ('the first ones'). Often followed by a time expression like tres meses, dos semanas, etc.
target_language_example: He estado muy ocupado los últimos días.
native_language_example: I've been very busy the last few days.

meaning: the last few years; recent years.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of years leading up to now (or up to another reference time in the past). Often appears as “en los últimos años” = “in recent years,” but it can also be used without “en” after a time-related verb or expression.
target_language_example: En los últimos años, he trabajado desde casa.
native_language_example: In recent years, I’ve worked from home.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "el único". Used to say that just those people/things (and nobody/nothing else) did something or exist in that situation. Often followed by "que" + verb ("los únicos que..."). It can refer to mixed groups too; feminine is "las únicas" and singular is "el/la único/a".
target_language_example: Nosotros fuimos los únicos que llegamos temprano.
native_language_example: We were the only ones who arrived early.

additional_notes: Used to say that a specific (masculine or mixed-gender) plural group are the only people/things that do something. It’s typically followed by a clause (que + verb). It changes for gender/number: el único que, la única que, los únicos que, las únicas que. Common with ser: Son los únicos que entienden.
target_language_example: Nosotros fuimos los únicos que encontramos el tesoro.
native_language_example: We were the only ones who found the treasure.

meaning: "those from" / "the ones of" (refers to a specific group or set).
additional_notes: Used to talk about "the people/things that belong to" or are "from" a place, group, category, or situation. It often avoids repeating a noun: "Los de la limpieza" = "the cleaning staff"; "los de arriba" = "the ones upstairs"; "idénticos a los de otros" = "identical to other people’s (symptoms)". The feminine form is "las de"; singular is "el/la de".
target_language_example: ¿Ya llegaron los de mantenimiento?
native_language_example: Have the maintenance guys arrived yet?

meaning: “those who” / “the ones who” (plural, masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by a relative clause (what comes after que). It often appears at the start of a sentence (“Los que…”) or after a verb as the subject (“…los que…”). For an all-female group, use “las que”. In Spanish you can’t usually drop this the way English sometimes drops “those who” (e.g., Spanish needs “Los que entiendan…”).
target_language_example: Los que tengan preguntas pueden quedarse al final.
native_language_example: Those who have questions can stay at the end.

meaning: “I now pronounce you husband and wife.”
additional_notes: A formal phrase said by the officiant at the end of a wedding ceremony. The pronoun “los” refers to the couple (them), and “declaro” is “I declare/pronounce.” Often appears with “Ahora” or “Y ahora” (“Now/And now…”).
target_language_example: Y ahora los declaro marido y mujer.
native_language_example: And now I pronounce you husband and wife.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (haber + past participle): "he visto" = "I have seen." "Los" is a direct object pronoun meaning "them" (usually masculine plural, or a mixed group). In Spanish, object pronouns like "los" go before the conjugated verb ("he"). You can also attach the pronoun to an infinitive: "Voy a verlos" ("I’m going to see them").
target_language_example: No te preocupes: los he visto hoy por la mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ve seen them this morning.

additional_notes: “Los” is an object pronoun meaning “them” or “you (plural, formal in Spain; in Latin America it can refer to people you address as ustedes).” “Veo” means “I see.” Depending on context, it can mean (1) literally seeing people/things (“Los veo abajo.” = “I see them downstairs.”) or (2) a goodbye meaning “See you (all) …” (“Los veo mañana.” = “I’ll see you tomorrow.”).
target_language_example: Los veo el lunes.
native_language_example: I’ll see you on Monday.

meaning: to fight against; to struggle against.
additional_notes: Used for fighting an enemy/opponent (literal) or resisting something abstract like bad luck, illness, temptation, etc. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun: luchar contra el mago (fight the wizard), luchar contra ello (fight against it).
target_language_example: Tenemos que luchar contra el miedo.
native_language_example: We have to fight against fear.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s appearance in a way that suggests an unreal or uncertain cause. After **como si** (“as if”), Spanish uses the **subjunctive**: **hubiera** is the imperfect subjunctive of *haber* and is often followed by a past participle (e.g., *hubiera visto / hubiera estado*) to mean “had seen / had been.” You can change **lucía** to match the subject/tense: *lucía* (he/she looked), *lucían* (they looked), *luzco* (I look), etc.
target_language_example: María lucía como si hubiera llorado toda la noche.
native_language_example: María looked as if she had cried all night.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that one event happens after another, or that something happens after a period of time. It’s common in more formal or written Spanish; in everyday speech you’ll often hear “después de” with the same meaning. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (“luego de unos minutos”) or an infinitive (“luego de dar a luz”).
target_language_example: Luego de la reunión, vamos a tomar un café.
native_language_example: After the meeting, we’re going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used mainly in Latin America as a conjunction meaning “after” or “once/as soon as.” It’s similar to "después de que" or "en cuanto". It usually introduces an action that happens first: "Luego que termine, ..." (= After/Once I finish, ...).
target_language_example: Luego que termine el trabajo, te llamo.
native_language_example: After I finish the work, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to describe a place associated with something: a category/type of place (lugar de pollo frito = a fried chicken place), a specific location belonging to something (lugar de la Tierra Media = a place in Middle-earth), or a familiar spot (el lugar de siempre = the usual place). The noun after "de" is what the place is connected to.
target_language_example: Busquemos un lugar de café tranquilo para hablar.
native_language_example: Let’s look for a quiet coffee place to talk.

additional_notes: Used to refer to where someone works (an office, store, factory, etc.). Often appears with possessives: mi/tu/su lugar de trabajo (“my/your/his/her workplace”), and in set phrases like en el lugar de trabajo (“at the workplace”).
target_language_example: No se permite fumar en el lugar de trabajo.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed in the workplace.

meaning: “place where” (a place in which something happens or someone does something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a description of what happens in that place (often followed by a verb in the infinitive or a conjugated verb): “un lugar donde sentarme” = “a place where I can sit / to sit.” It works like “donde” = “where” after “lugar” (place).
target_language_example: Busco un lugar donde estudiar en paz.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place where I can study in peace.

additional_notes: Used to say there is (or isn’t) space, opportunity, or suitability for something: "hay/no hay lugar para + noun/infinitive". It can be literal (a physical place) or figurative (no room for excuses, miracles, etc.).
target_language_example: En esta casa no hay lugar para discusiones.
native_language_example: In this house, there’s no room for arguments.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a city, neighborhood, or home as somewhere you can live. Very common with verbs like ser (Es un buen lugar para vivir) and necesitar/encontrar (Necesito/Encontraremos un lugar para vivir).
target_language_example: Boston es un buen lugar para vivir.
native_language_example: Boston is a good place to live.

additional_notes: Refers to the trip or period right after a wedding when a couple celebrates (often by traveling). Usually used with possessives like "mi/tu/su luna de miel" or with "de" (e.g., "viaje de luna de miel").
target_language_example: Vamos a pasar nuestra luna de miel en México.
native_language_example: We’re going to spend our honeymoon in Mexico.

additional_notes: Refers to the moon when its whole face appears illuminated. Common with the verb haber (Hay luna llena = “There’s a full moon”) or with estar/ser to describe conditions (La luna llena está brillando = “The full moon is shining”). You can also use it for upcoming dates/events: la próxima luna llena (“the next full moon”).
target_language_example: Con luna llena, la playa se ve increíble por la noche.
native_language_example: With a full moon, the beach looks incredible at night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about natural sunlight in a room or outdoors. Often appears with verbs like llegar/entrar (“to reach/come in”) and with prepositions like a la luz del sol (“in/by the sunlight”) or de la luz del sol (“from the sunlight,” e.g., to protect your eyes).
target_language_example: Las plantas necesitan luz del sol para crecer.
native_language_example: Plants need sunlight to grow.

meaning: “green light”; permission/approval to start or continue.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is the green traffic light. Figuratively, it means authorization or go-ahead (often used with “dar luz verde (a algo/a alguien)” = “to give the green light (to something/someone)”). You can also say “tener luz verde” = “to have the green light.”
target_language_example: El proyecto ya tiene luz verde, podemos empezar hoy.
native_language_example: The project already has the green light; we can start today.

meaning: tears in your eyes (about to cry / crying).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone whose eyes are teary—because of sadness, emotion, laughter, pain, wind, etc. Often appears with the verb "tener": "tener lágrimas en los ojos" (to have tears in your eyes).
target_language_example: Cuando escuchó la noticia, tenía lágrimas en los ojos.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he had tears in his eyes.

additional_notes: An affirmative command (imperative) to one person, using the reflexive pronoun "te" (lavarse = to wash oneself). Common with time words and polite markers: "ahora mismo" (right now), "a menudo" (often), "antes de" (before), "después de" (after), and "por favor" (please). In Latin America you’ll also hear "lávense las manos" for a group.
target_language_example: Antes de comer, lávate las manos con jabón.
native_language_example: Before eating, wash your hands with soap.

meaning: bad things about other people (speaking negatively about them).
additional_notes: Most often used with the verb phrase “hablar mal de …” (to speak badly about / criticize someone), especially when talking behind someone’s back (“a sus espaldas”). You can replace “los demás” with a person or group: “hablar mal de ella/de mis compañeros”.
target_language_example: No me gusta cuando la gente habla mal de los demás.
native_language_example: I don’t like it when people speak badly about others.

meaning: '(it’s) bad that…' / 'too bad that…' / 'it’s a shame that…'.
additional_notes: Used with **que** to introduce a clause you’re judging negatively. Common patterns: **Qué mal que + verb** = “How bad that…” / “It’s a shame that…”, **No está mal que + subjunctive** = “It’s not bad that…”, **No vendría mal que + subjunctive** = “It wouldn’t be a bad idea if…” / “It wouldn’t hurt if…”.
target_language_example: Qué mal que no puedas venir hoy.
native_language_example: It’s a shame you can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe someone’s mood: "Estoy de mal humor" (I’m in a bad mood). You can also say "tener mal humor" (to be in a bad mood / to be irritable).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de mal humor, mejor hablamos mañana.
native_language_example: I’m in a bad mood today; we’d better talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to bad weather (rain, storms, etc.), often used with por: "por el mal tiempo" (because of the bad weather). In some contexts it can also mean a difficult period in life ("atravesar por un mal tiempo" = to go through a hard time). With hacer: "hace mal tiempo" / "sigue haciendo mal tiempo" = the weather is still bad. With tener: "tuvimos mal tiempo" = we had bad weather (lately).
target_language_example: No podemos ir a la playa porque hace mal tiempo.
native_language_example: We can’t go to the beach because the weather is bad.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how others see a person or thing. Common patterns: "tener mala fama" (to have a bad reputation) and "dar (mala) fama a alguien/algo" / "darle mala fama a..." (to give someone/something a bad reputation; to make them look bad).
target_language_example: Ese restaurante tiene mala fama, pero a mí me gusta.
native_language_example: That restaurant has a bad reputation, but I like it.

meaning: a bad kid; a troublemaker (“bad seed”).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone (often a child/teen) who behaves badly, causes problems, or is considered delinquent. It’s a negative, judgmental label. Literally means “bad weed,” but the idiomatic meaning is closer to “bad seed.”
target_language_example: No te juntes con esos chicos; dicen que son mala hierba.
native_language_example: Don’t hang out with those guys; people say they’re troublemakers.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a poor choice or plan. Very common in short comments ("Mala idea.") and in softer/less direct forms like "No es mala idea" / "No sería mala idea" (“It’s not a bad idea” / “It wouldn’t be a bad idea”), which often mean it’s actually a pretty good suggestion.
target_language_example: Salir ahora es mala idea; está lloviendo mucho.
native_language_example: Leaving now is a bad idea; it’s raining a lot.

additional_notes: Common in Spain. Often used with estar/tener: estar de mala leche = to be in a bad mood; tener mala leche = to have a nasty/mean streak or bad temper. Strongly negative and fairly colloquial; tone can be harsh depending on context.
target_language_example: No le hables ahora; está de mala leche.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to him now; he’s in a bad mood.

additional_notes: Used to judge someone’s character or behavior as mean, cruel, or immoral. Often said with the verb ser (e.g., Es una mala persona). It’s a strong, insulting statement, so use carefully.
target_language_example: No creo que seas una mala persona, pero eso estuvo mal.
native_language_example: I don’t think you’re a bad person, but that was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to talk about unlucky events (often with "tener": "tener mala suerte" = to have bad luck). It can also be a dismissive response meaning “too bad” or “tough luck.”
target_language_example: Hoy tengo mala suerte: perdí mis llaves otra vez.
native_language_example: I have bad luck today: I lost my keys again.

additional_notes: Used for unwanted plants that grow where you don’t want them (often in a garden). Common with verbs like quitar/sacar/arrancar malas hierbas (“pull/remove weeds”) and deshacerse de malas hierbas (“get rid of weeds”).
target_language_example: Cada primavera tenemos que arrancar malas hierbas del jardín.
native_language_example: Every spring we have to pull weeds in the garden.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or describe unpleasant information. Often said as a short announcement (“Malas noticias...”) before explaining what happened, or in the common pattern “Tengo malas noticias para ti” (“I have bad news for you”).
target_language_example: Tengo malas noticias: el vuelo está cancelado.
native_language_example: I have bad news: the flight is canceled.

additional_notes: Used to show anger, frustration, or annoyance, often at the start of a sentence. Literally means “may it be cursed,” but in everyday Spanish it works like “damn it.” Considered strong language (swearing); avoid in polite or formal situations. You can also hear it shortened to “¡Maldita!” or “¡Maldita sea la cosa!”
target_language_example: ¡Maldita sea! Se me olvidaron las llaves otra vez.
native_language_example: Damn it! I forgot my keys again.

additional_notes: A strong curse used to show anger, impatience, or frustration. It can stand alone ("¡Maldita sea!") or be added for emphasis in a sentence ("Lo tengo, maldita sea"). It’s also commonly said before a person’s name ("Maldita sea, Nick") when scolding or snapping at someone. Considered rude/vulgar in many situations—use with caution.
target_language_example: ¡Maldita sea! Se me olvidaron las llaves otra vez.
native_language_example: Damn it! I forgot my keys again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about repeated behaviors that are negative or unhealthy. Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have), "deshacerse de" (to get rid of), and "curarse de" (to be cured of).
target_language_example: Estoy intentando dejar mis malos hábitos y comer más sano.
native_language_example: I’m trying to quit my bad habits and eat healthier.

meaning: "Mom, why...?" (asking your mother for a reason/explanation).
additional_notes: Used to address your mom directly (mamá) and then ask a "why" question (¿por qué...?). Often used by children. Write it with an accent: mamá. Also note the difference between ¿por qué? ("why?") and porque ("because").
target_language_example: Mamá, ¿por qué tenemos que irnos ahora?
native_language_example: Mom, why do we have to leave now?

additional_notes: A common, family/childlike way to refer to your parents together. You can use it with possessives (mi mamá y papá = my mom and dad) and after prepositions (con mamá y papá = with mom and dad; por mamá y papá = about mom and dad).
target_language_example: Esta noche voy a cenar con mamá y papá.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to have dinner with mom and dad.

additional_notes: Used to express how something is done or a style/habit: "una manera de + infinitive" (a way to do something). It can also imply behavior: "No es manera de + infinitive" = “That’s no way to …” / “You shouldn’t … like that.” With "pensar", it often means a viewpoint: "su manera de pensar" = “their way of thinking.”
target_language_example: Es una buena manera de aprender español.
native_language_example: It’s a good way to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to introduce how something happens or is done, often followed by a verb: "la manera en que + verb" (the way that...). It can refer to a method (“the only way I can…”) or to someone’s behavior (“the way Tom behaved”). You’ll also see it after prepositions like "por": "por la manera en que…" (because of the way…).
target_language_example: Me gusta la manera en que explicas las cosas.
native_language_example: I like the way you explain things.

additional_notes: Most literally it means the right hand (often used for directions or instructions: “gira a mano derecha” = “turn right”). In the figurative sense, “ser mi mano derecha” means to be someone’s most trusted helper (their “right-hand man/person”).
target_language_example: Gira a mano derecha en la próxima esquina.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next corner.

additional_notes: Used to specify the hand on the left side of your body (opposite of "mano derecha"). Often appears with possessives ("mi/tu/su mano izquierda") and with verbs like "agarrar" (to grab/hold), "atrapar" (to catch), "mostrar" (to show), and "girar" (to turn).
target_language_example: Sostén el vaso con la mano izquierda, por favor.
native_language_example: Hold the glass with your left hand, please.

additional_notes: Common expression used to start working on something right away. Often said after agreeing on a plan (like “OK, let’s begin”). Literally “hands to the work,” but it’s used like an idiom in English.
target_language_example: Ya tenemos todo listo; manos a la obra.
native_language_example: We have everything ready; let’s get to work.

meaning: to stay calm; to keep calm.
additional_notes: Common advice or instruction in stressful situations. Uses the verb "mantener" (to keep/maintain) + "la calma" (calm). Often said with "tenés que" (vos, common in Argentina/Uruguay) or "tienes que" (tú) to mean "you have to". Also appears with "Pase lo que pase" = "no matter what happens."
target_language_example: Respirá hondo y tratá de mantener la calma.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath and try to stay calm.

meaning: to stand firm; to hold your ground.
additional_notes: Used when someone doesn’t change their opinion/decision or doesn’t give in under pressure. Often followed by "en" + noun (e.g., "mantenerse firme en su decisión").
target_language_example: Aunque lo criticaron, decidió mantenerse firme en su decisión.
native_language_example: Even though they criticized him, he decided to stand firm in his decision.

additional_notes: An imperative used to address more than one person (ustedes). Common in announcements or emergencies to tell a group to remain calm; often followed by instructions (e.g., “por favor…”, “permanezcan…”). For one person you can say “mantén la calma” (informal) or “mantenga la calma” (formal).
target_language_example: Por favor, mantengan la calma y sigan las instrucciones.
native_language_example: Please stay calm and follow the instructions.

additional_notes: Phrase in the simple past (pretérito) using the 3rd-person singular form of "mantener" (mantuvo). It expresses that someone did what they said they would do. "Su" can mean his/her/your/their depending on context; if you need to be explicit, you can use "su promesa" with a clarifying phrase (e.g., "su promesa a Ana"). Related forms: "mantuve mi promesa" (I kept my promise), "mantuviste tu promesa" (you kept your promise), "mantuvieron su promesa" (they kept their promise).
target_language_example: Él mantuvo su promesa, aunque fue difícil.
native_language_example: He kept his promise, even though it was difficult.

meaning: "rotten apple"; (figuratively) a bad influence/person who corrupts others.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a piece of fruit that has gone bad. It’s also used in the common saying "Una manzana podrida (lo) echa a perder todo" to mean that one bad person or element can spoil a whole group. Adjective agreement: manzana (feminine) → podrida.
target_language_example: En ese equipo, una manzana podrida estaba arruinando el ambiente.
native_language_example: On that team, a rotten apple was ruining the atmosphere.

meaning: reverse; go backward; no turning back.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dar": "dar marcha atrás" = to reverse/back up (a car) or to backtrack on a decision/plan. "No hay marcha atrás" means there’s no going back (it’s final).
target_language_example: Si no te gusta el plan, todavía podemos dar marcha atrás.
native_language_example: If you don’t like the plan, we can still back out.

additional_notes: Used to say that two people are married, or that they have just been declared married (e.g., in a wedding ceremony). You’ll often see it after verbs like ser (son marido y mujer), convertirse en (se convirtieron en marido y mujer), or declarar (los declaró marido y mujer).
target_language_example: Después de la ceremonia, todos sabían que ya eran marido y mujer.
native_language_example: After the ceremony, everyone knew they were already husband and wife.

additional_notes: Used with the verb haber to form the present perfect or past perfect: "he matado a..." = "I have killed..."; "hubiera/hubieran matado a..." = "would have killed...". The "a" is the personal "a" used before a direct object that is a person (or personified being): "He matado a Qiang". With "nadie" you also commonly see: "No he matado a nadie" = "I haven't killed anyone."
target_language_example: No he matado a nadie.
native_language_example: I haven't killed anyone.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object that is a person or animal. Spanish usually adds the “personal a” before people (and often pets): matar a Juan, matar a mi perro. Very strong/violent verb; avoid unless you mean literal killing.
target_language_example: No quiero matar a ningún animal.
native_language_example: I don’t want to kill any animal.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (while waiting).
additional_notes: Used when you do something just to stay busy until something else happens (often while waiting). Common with verbs like "estar" or "para": "Estoy matando el tiempo" / "Para matar el tiempo...". It’s a fixed expression; you’re not literally killing anything.
target_language_example: Para matar el tiempo, voy a leer un poco mientras espero.
native_language_example: To kill time, I’m going to read a little while I wait.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of "matar" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes"; the subject is often omitted in Spanish. The "a" is the personal "a" used before a specific person (and sometimes a specific animal) who is the direct object: "Mataron a André" = "They killed André."
target_language_example: Dicen que mataron a un hombre en el pueblo.
native_language_example: They say they killed a man in the town.

additional_notes: *Mató* is the simple past (preterite) form meaning “(he/she/it) killed.” Spanish uses the **personal a** (*a*) before a **direct object that is a specific person** (and often a pet): *mató a Bill*, *mató a su marido*. With things, you usually don’t use *a*: *Mató el insecto* (“He killed the insect.”).
target_language_example: El ladrón mató a la mujer.
native_language_example: The thief killed the woman.

additional_notes: Used to compare age ("older than") or size/amount/importance ("greater than"). It follows a comparative word like "mayor" and comes before the thing/person you’re comparing to: "Soy mayor que tú". For ages, you can add a number: "tres años mayor que".
target_language_example: Este problema es mayor que lo que imaginábamos.
native_language_example: This problem is bigger than what we imagined.

additional_notes: Used with numbers/ages to compare how many years older someone is than you: "Es + número + años mayor que yo". For "younger than me," say "menor que yo." You can swap "yo" for another person/pronoun: "mayor que ella/él" or "mayor que mí."
target_language_example: Mi hermana es dos años mayor que yo.
native_language_example: My sister is two years older than me.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to talk about more than half of a group: la mayoría de + plural noun (la mayoría de los chicos, la mayoría de personas). It usually takes a singular verb (La mayoría de los chicos les gusta...), but plural verbs are also heard in some contexts.
target_language_example: La mayoría de mis amigos vive cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: Most of my friends live near here.

meaning: tomorrow first thing (early in the morning).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something very early tomorrow, usually at the start of the day (e.g., as soon as work or school starts). It’s common with plans, appointments, departures, and tasks: "Tengo que irme mañana a primera hora".
target_language_example: Te llamo mañana a primera hora para confirmarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you first thing tomorrow to confirm it.

additional_notes: Used to specify that something will happen in the morning of the next day. It’s common in some regions to say “mañana en la mañana,” though many speakers also simply say “mañana por la mañana.” Often used with a specific time (e.g., “a las siete”).
target_language_example: Nos vemos mañana en la mañana antes del trabajo.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow morning before work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the evening/nighttime of the next day. In many places, especially in Latin America, people commonly say “en la noche” where English might say “at night” or “in the evening.” You can also hear “mañana por la noche.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamarme mañana en la noche?
native_language_example: Can you call me tomorrow night?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen tomorrow during the afternoon (often roughly from after lunch until early evening). In some regions people more commonly say "mañana por la tarde" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Nos vemos mañana en la tarde para tomar un café.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow afternoon to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to specify the morning (por la mañana) of the next day (mañana). Common in plans and appointments (e.g., Nos vemos mañana por la mañana). Often shortened in conversation to just “mañana” if the morning is understood from context.
target_language_example: Tengo una cita con el médico mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen tomorrow in the evening/nighttime. Common with plans and future events (e.g., "Te veré mañana por la noche"). You can also say "mañana en la noche" in some regions. Related: "mañana por la mañana" (tomorrow morning), "mañana por la tarde" (tomorrow afternoon).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamarme mañana por la noche?
native_language_example: Can you call me tomorrow night?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen tomorrow during the afternoon (roughly after lunch and before evening). In schedules and appointments, you can also hear/see "mañana en la tarde" in some regions, but "mañana por la tarde" is widely understood.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamarme mañana por la tarde?
native_language_example: Can you call me tomorrow afternoon?

meaning: "(someone/something) just (did something) to me" / "has just (done something) to me."
additional_notes: Used with the pattern **acabar de + infinitive** to talk about something that happened moments ago. **Me** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me” or “me” (e.g., *Me acaba de morder* = “It just bit me”). You can swap **me** for other pronouns: *te acaba de…* (to you), *le acaba de…* (to him/her/you formal), *nos acaba de…* (to us).
target_language_example: El perro me acaba de ladrar.
native_language_example: The dog just barked at me.

additional_notes: Used with the structure: (pronoun) + acabar de (conjugated) + infinitive to talk about the very recent past. The pronoun changes with the person: me acabo de (I), te acabas de (you), se acaba de (he/she/you formal), nos acabamos de (we), se acaban de (they/you all). Example: "Me acabo de casar" = I just got married.
target_language_example: Me acabo de dar cuenta de que dejé las llaves adentro.
native_language_example: I just realized I left the keys inside.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "acostarse con". In everyday Spanish it commonly means to have sex with someone (not just to sleep in the same bed). It’s typically used when talking about a past event; the base form is "acostarse con" (to sleep with), and it changes by person/tense (e.g., "me acuesto con", "se acostó con").
target_language_example: Anoche me acosté con mi novio.
native_language_example: Last night I slept with my boyfriend.

additional_notes: From the verb acordarse (reflexive). Common patterns: **me acuerdo de + noun/pronoun** (Me acuerdo de eso = I remember that) and **me acuerdo que + clause** (Me acuerdo que ella llevaba… = I remember that she was wearing…). Often used with **ya** (“already/now”): *Ya me acuerdo* = “Now I remember.” Negative: *No me acuerdo* = “I don’t remember.”
target_language_example: No me acuerdo de su nombre, pero me acuerdo de su cara.
native_language_example: I don’t remember his/her name, but I remember his/her face.

additional_notes: Used with the verb acordarse de (reflexive), so it takes a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) and is followed by de + a noun/pronoun or a clause. Common pattern: Me acuerdo de él/ella/usted; Me acuerdo de lo que dijiste.
target_language_example: No me acuerdo de su nombre.
native_language_example: I don’t remember his/her name.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase acordarse de (to remember). It uses a reflexive pronoun: me acuerdo = “I remember,” and it takes de before the person/thing: me acuerdo de ti. Often used to reassure someone you still remember them, especially with claro que / por supuesto (“of course”) or todavía (“still”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todavía me acuerdo de ti.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I still remember you.

additional_notes: Uses the verb agradar: the thing/person you like is the subject (e.g., "Ella me agrada" = "I like her"). Often sounds a bit more formal or restrained than "me gusta". You can also use it with an infinitive: "Me agrada trabajar aquí" (I like working here).
target_language_example: Me agrada mucho tu idea.
native_language_example: I really like your idea.

additional_notes: Used to express that something makes you happy or glad. Literally “it makes me happy/pleased,” so it’s often followed by an infinitive (me alegra verte = I’m glad to see you) or by a clause with que (me alegra que estés bien = I’m glad you’re well). Similar expressions: me alegro (I’m glad, more directly “I’m happy”), nos alegra (we’re glad).
target_language_example: Me alegra que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m glad you came today.

meaning: “I’m very happy (to hear/see/that…)” / “That makes me very happy.”
additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness about something. It literally means “it makes me very glad,” with an implied “it” (the situation). Common patterns: “Me alegra mucho + infinitive” (Me alegra mucho verte = I’m very happy to see you), “Me alegra mucho que + verb” (Me alegra mucho que estés aquí = I’m very happy that you’re here), and “Me alegra mucho por ti” (= I’m very happy for you). You can swap “mucho” for “tanto” (Me alegra tanto) or make it formal with “Nos alegra mucho…” (We’re very happy…).
target_language_example: Me alegra mucho que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m very happy you came today.

additional_notes: Used to react positively to news or information. It’s often followed by "eso" (that), "de" + noun (e.g., "de tu éxito"), or "que" + a full clause ("me alegra oír que..."). You can also say "Me alegra oírlo" = "I’m glad to hear it."
target_language_example: Me alegra oír que te sientes mejor.
native_language_example: I’m glad to hear that you’re feeling better.

meaning: “I’m happy/glad that …” (followed by a verb in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express your feelings about a situation or someone else’s action/state. It’s most commonly followed by the subjunctive: Me alegra que estés aquí. It can also be adjusted for different people: Nos alegra que…, Le alegra que…, etc.
target_language_example: Me alegra que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m glad you came today.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness or satisfaction about something. It’s followed by **que** + a verb in the **subjunctive** (digas, hayas logrado, lo veas, etc.) because it expresses an emotional reaction. **Lo** usually refers to “it/that” (something already mentioned or understood from context). You can change the indirect object: *Me alegra…* (I’m glad), *Nos alegra…* (we’re glad), *Le alegra…* (he/she is glad).
target_language_example: Me alegra que lo entiendas ahora.
native_language_example: I’m glad you understand it now.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness about something that happens to the other person (“you”). It’s often followed by the subjunctive because it expresses an emotion: me alegra que te ayude (that it helps you), me alegra que te diviertas (that you’re having fun), me alegra que te encuentres bien (that you’re doing well). In the past, you’ll often see: me alegra que te haya gustado (“I’m glad you liked it”).
target_language_example: Me alegra que te guste la comida.
native_language_example: I’m glad you like the food.

additional_notes: A common greeting when you see someone (often someone you haven’t seen in a while). Literally “it makes me happy to see you.” You can add emphasis or time words: “Me alegra mucho verte” (I’m very glad to see you), “otra vez” (again).
target_language_example: ¡Me alegra verte de nuevo!
native_language_example: I’m glad to see you again!

additional_notes:
Common way to express happiness about news or someone’s situation. Often followed by:
- "me alegro de + noun/infinitive": "Me alegro de verte" (I’m glad to see you)
- "me alegro de que + subjunctive": "Me alegro de que hayas venido" (I’m glad you came)
You can add intensity with "mucho", "tanto", etc., and use "por" to mean "for" someone: "Me alegro por ti" (I’m happy for you).
target_language_example: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
native_language_example: I'm glad you're here.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **alegrarse de** (“to be glad about”). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive (**Me alegro de verte.**) or by **que** + verb (**Me alegro de que hayas venido.**).
target_language_example: Me alegro de verte otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m glad to see you again.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness about a situation. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (me alegro de que + subjunctive), because it expresses an emotion/reaction: “Me alegro de que hayas empezado” (I’m glad you started). Often used with present subjunctive for past events with present relevance, and imperfect subjunctive after past contexts: “Me alegré de que vinieran” (I was glad they came).
target_language_example: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
native_language_example: I’m glad you’re here.

me alegro de que estés aquí

target_language_multi_word_term: me alegro de que estés aquí
additional_notes: Used to express happiness that someone is present. It uses the structure “alegrarse de que + subjunctive” (here: “estés”) because it expresses an emotion about a situation. You can swap “aquí” with another place: “Me alegro de que estés en casa” (I’m glad you’re home).
target_language_example: Me alegro de que estés aquí conmigo.
native_language_example: I’m glad you’re here with me.

meaning: “I’m glad that you have…” (about something you did).
additional_notes: Used to express happiness about someone else’s action or situation. After "Me alegro de que…" Spanish uses the subjunctive; "hayas" is the subjunctive of "haber" and is normally followed by a past participle (e.g., "hayas llamado", "hayas regresado"). It often refers to something that already happened but is still relevant.
target_language_example: Me alegro de que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m glad you came today.

meaning: "I’m glad that you (to me)…" / "I’m happy that you … for me."
additional_notes: Used to express happiness about something someone did involving you. It’s the start of the larger pattern: "Me alegro de que" + subjunctive verb. After "que", Spanish uses the subjunctive (e.g., "me hayas llamado" = "that you called me"). "me" is an object pronoun meaning "me/to me" and can attach to many verbs: "me hayas ayudado" (helped me), "me hayan escuchado" (listened to me).
target_language_example: Me alegro de que me hayas avisado a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m glad you warned me in time.

meaning: I’m happy to see you / I’m glad to see you.
additional_notes: Common friendly greeting when you meet someone (again). Literally “I rejoice to see you,” but in everyday English it’s “I’m glad/happy to see you.” You can change the pronoun: “me alegro de verlo/la verla” (formal you) or “me alegro de verlos/las verlas” (plural). Often followed by “de nuevo” (again) or used with “yo también” (me too).
target_language_example: ¡Qué bueno verte! Me alegro de verte de nuevo.
native_language_example: It’s great to see you! I’m glad to see you again.

meaning: “I’m very happy/glad (to hear that / for you).”
additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness about someone else’s good news or a situation. Common patterns: **me alegro mucho de + [noun/that]** (“I’m very glad about…” / “I’m very glad that…”), **me alegro mucho por ti** (“I’m very happy for you”), and **me alegro mucho de verte** (“I’m very happy to see you”). Often works as a stand-alone response to good news.
target_language_example: ¡Me alegro mucho por ti! Te lo mereces.
native_language_example: I’m so happy for you! You deserve it.

meaning: "I’m very happy/glad about" / "I’m really pleased to".
additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness about something. Follow it with a noun/pronoun: "Me alegro mucho de eso" (I’m very glad about that), or with an infinitive: "Me alegro mucho de verte" (I’m very happy to see you). If what follows is a full clause, use "me alegro mucho de que" + subjunctive: "Me alegro mucho de que se haya acabado..." (I’m very glad that ... is over).
target_language_example: Me alegro mucho de que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I’m really glad that you came today.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or show you’re pleased about someone else’s good news. It’s polite and common in conversation. You can change the person: “me alegro por usted” (formal), “me alegro por vosotros” (Spain), “me alegro por ustedes” (plural). Also common: “me alegro de que…” + verb (“I’m glad that…”).
target_language_example: ¡Qué bien! Me alegro por ti.
native_language_example: That’s great! I’m happy for you.

additional_notes: From the verb "amar" (to love): "amas" = "you love" (informal singular "tú"), and "me" = "me". Used to talk about romantic love, often in questions like "¿Me amas?" (Do you love me?). Compare: "te amo" = "I love you," and "me quieres" is often a softer/more common way to say "you love me" in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Dime la verdad: ¿me amas?
native_language_example: Tell me the truth: do you love me?

meaning: “I feel like … / I’m in the mood for …” (I’d like …).
additional_notes: Used to express a spontaneous desire, often for food, drinks, or an activity. Structure: "Me apetece" + infinitive (Me apetece beber...) or + noun (Me apetece un café). Verb agrees with what you want: "Me apetece" (singular thing) / "Me apetecen" (plural things).
target_language_example: Me apetece un café ahora.
native_language_example: I feel like a coffee now.

additional_notes:
Used to express regret about an action or decision. It’s followed by:
- **de + infinitive** (often **haber + past participle**): *Me arrepiento de haber dicho…* = “I regret having said…”
- **de + noun/phrase**: *Me arrepiento de lo que dije* = “I regret what I said.”
Negative: *No me arrepiento de…* = “I don’t regret…”.
target_language_example: Me arrepiento de no haberte llamado antes.
native_language_example: I regret not calling you earlier.

additional_notes: Used to express regret about a past action. Structure: (no) me arrepiento de haber + past participle (comido, gastado, ido, perdido). You can negate it: No me arrepiento de haber… (“I don’t regret having…”).
target_language_example: Me arrepiento de haber dicho eso.
native_language_example: I regret saying that.

additional_notes: Used to promise or commit to checking/arranging something so a result happens. It’s the future of “asegurarse de” (“to make sure”), followed by “que” + a verb (often in the subjunctive: sea, reciba, etc.). You can change the subject: “te asegurarás de que …” (you’ll make sure), “se asegurará de que …” (he/she will make sure).
target_language_example: Me aseguraré de que tengas todo lo que necesitas.
native_language_example: I’ll make sure you have everything you need.

additional_notes: Used to say someone helped you do an action. Structure: [person] + me ayudó a + infinitive (e.g., llevar, hacer, pintar). In speech, English often drops “to”: “He helped me carry…”. You can change the pronoun: te ayudó a (helped you), le ayudó a (helped him/her), nos ayudó a (helped us).
target_language_example: Mi amiga me ayudó a estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: My friend helped me study for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your impression of someone (how they come across to you), often after meeting them. Common with people: “(No) me cae bien” = “I (don’t) like them.” You can name the person: “Tom me cae bien” (I like Tom). With usted: “Usted me cae bien” (I like you / I find you likable).
target_language_example: Tiene unos defectos, sin embargo me cae bien.
native_language_example: They have some flaws; however, I like them.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb "casarse" (to get married), used to talk about a completed event. Often followed by "con" + the person ("Me casé con ella/él"), or used with time expressions like "hace ocho años" (eight years ago) or ages ("cuando tenía diecinueve años").
target_language_example: Me casé con mi pareja en 2018.
native_language_example: I got married to my partner in 2018.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of the reflexive verb caerse (to fall). It uses the reflexive pronoun me. Often followed by de/del/de la + place/vehicle to say where you fell from: Me caí de la moto (I fell off the motorcycle).
