target_language_example: Me caí de la bicicleta y me lastimé la rodilla.
native_language_example: I fell off the bike and hurt my knee.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: (yo) me cepillo = “I brush” (for myself). It’s commonly used with time expressions like cada mañana (“every morning”) or después de… (“after…”). You can also say: Me cepillo los dientes con un cepillo de dientes (“…with a toothbrush”).
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, me cepillo los dientes.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, I brush my teeth.

additional_notes: "Me comí" is the preterite (completed past) of "comerse" (to eat). The "me" is a reflexive pronoun often used to emphasize finishing or consuming something (similar to "ate it all" / "ate it up"), though in everyday Spanish it can also simply mean "I ate". Common pattern: "Me comí + (un/una/unos/unas) + food".
target_language_example: Ayer me comí una pizza entera.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ate a whole pizza.

additional_notes: From the verb **contar** (“to tell”). **Me** = “to me.” Used when someone told you information or a story. Often followed by **que + clause** (“me contó que…” = “told me that…”) or by a noun (“me contó una historia” = “told me a story”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana me contó que mañana no viene.
native_language_example: My sister told me that she’s not coming tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common way to say you accidentally injured yourself. Uses the reflexive pronoun “me” + past tense “corté” (from cortar). Often followed by how it happened with “con…” (with) or “haciendo…” (while doing).
target_language_example: Me corté el dedo y me salió sangre.
native_language_example: I cut my finger and it started bleeding.

meaning: "it was hard for me" / "it cost me" (past).
additional_notes: From the verb "costar" (preterite: costó). It’s used in two very common ways: (1) with an infinitive to talk about difficulty: "Me costó encontrar..." = "It was hard for me to find..."; in the negative, it means it was easy: "No me costó..." = "It wasn’t hard for me...". (2) with a price or amount to talk about cost: "Me costó trescientos dólares" = "It cost me 300 dollars."
target_language_example: Me costó mucho aprender a pronunciar la "rr".
native_language_example: It was really hard for me to learn to pronounce the “rr.”

meaning: 'I grew up in' (I was raised in).
additional_notes: Used to say where you spent your childhood and were raised. It can refer to a country, city, neighborhood, or even a specific house. Common contrast with where you were born: “Nací en…, pero me crié en…”. The verb is “criarse” in the past tense (preterite): me crié, te criaste, se crió, etc.
target_language_example: Aunque nací en Colombia, me crié en Miami.
native_language_example: Although I was born in Colombia, I grew up in Miami.

meaning: “(it/he/she) gives me” / “it causes me” (used in many set expressions).
additional_notes: From **dar** (“to give”) + **me** (“to me”). Often appears in common patterns: **me da para + [time/money/etc.]** = “it’s enough for me to…” / “it lasts me…” (e.g., *me da para una semana*), **me da igual** = “I don’t care / it’s all the same to me,” and **me da + [something]** = “it gives me / it causes me” (e.g., *me da alegría*, *me da un infarto*). You can swap **me** for other people: *te da, le da, nos da…*
target_language_example: No me da tiempo para hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to do it today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "dar asco" (to disgust/to gross out). The thing that disgusts you can be the subject ("Me da asco la comida") or you can just say "Me da asco" by itself. It can also be followed by an infinitive to say you feel disgusted about doing something: "Me da asco volver con él" (Going back with him disgusts me).
target_language_example: Me da asco ese olor.
native_language_example: That smell grosses me out.

meaning: "It gives me a headache" / "I get a headache (from it)."
additional_notes: Used when something causes you to have a headache (literal) or when something is mentally exhausting/annoying (figurative). Structure: [something] + me da dolor de cabeza (e.g., El ruido me da dolor de cabeza). Often you’ll also hear the shorter phrase Me duele la cabeza = “My head hurts” (you already have a headache).
target_language_example: Tanta tarea me da dolor de cabeza.
native_language_example: So much homework gives me a headache.

additional_notes: Literally “it gives me pleasure,” used to express happiness about what you hear/see or about meeting someone. Common patterns: “Me da gusto + infinitive” (Me da gusto verte = I’m glad to see you) and “Me da gusto + noun/pronoun” (Me da gusto tu llamada = I’m happy about your call). Often interchangeable with “Me alegra…”.
target_language_example: Me da gusto verte de nuevo.
native_language_example: I’m glad to see you again.

meaning: “I’m happy to see you.” / “It’s nice to see you.”
additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say you’re glad to see someone. Literally “it gives me pleasure to see you.” You can add time words like “de nuevo” or “otra vez” (“again”), or intensifiers like “mucho” (“Me da mucho gusto verte”). You’ll also hear “Me da gusto” by itself when the rest is understood.
target_language_example: Me da gusto verte hoy; ¿cómo has estado?
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you today; how have you been?

meaning: "I don’t care" / "it’s all the same to me".
additional_notes: Used to say something makes no difference to you. Often followed by "que" + subjunctive (Me da igual que...) or "si" (Me da igual si...). You can also say it alone as a complete answer: "Me da igual." Depending on tone, it can sound blunt or dismissive.
target_language_example: ¿Pizza o pasta? Me da igual, elige tú.
native_language_example: Pizza or pasta? I don’t care—you choose.

meaning: "I don't care" / "it’s all the same to me."
additional_notes: Used to say you have no preference between options or that something doesn’t matter to you. It can be followed by a noun (Me da lo mismo la pizza), or by a clause with "que" or "si" (Me da lo mismo que vengas / Me da lo mismo si vienes). Very similar to "me da igual."
target_language_example: Me da lo mismo si vamos en coche o en bus.
native_language_example: I don’t care whether we go by car or by bus.

additional_notes: Literally “it gives me fear.” Used with a person/thing as the subject: “(Él/Ella/Eso) me da miedo” = “He/She/That scares me.” Also common with an infinitive to say you’re afraid to do something: “Me da miedo + infinitive” (e.g., “Me da miedo caer” = “I’m afraid of falling”).
target_language_example: Me da miedo hablar en público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: Used to express strong pleasure or happiness about something. Very common in greetings: “Me da mucho gusto conocerlo/la” = “Nice to meet you” (formal); “Me da mucho gusto verte” = “I’m very happy to see you.” You can add an infinitive to say what you’re happy about (e.g., “haber ordenado…”), or use “por + someone” to mean you’re happy for them: “Me da mucho gusto por ella.”
target_language_example: Me da mucho gusto verte otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you again.

meaning: "they give me" / "they make me feel" (used for reactions like fear, disgust, etc.).
additional_notes: “Me” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me.” “Dan” is the 3rd-person plural of “dar” (they give). It’s very common in expressions where something causes a feeling or reaction: “me dan miedo” (they scare me), “me dan asco” (they disgust me), “me dan igual” (I don’t care about them). The verb agrees with the thing causing the feeling: singular “me da…” vs plural “me dan…”.
target_language_example: Las arañas me dan miedo.
native_language_example: Spiders scare me.

additional_notes: From the verb dar (to give): “me” = “to me,” “das” = “you give” (informal singular tú). It can mean literally giving something (Me das eso / Me das un beso) or causing a feeling/reaction (Me das lástima = You make me feel sorry for you; No me das miedo = You don’t scare me; Me das envidia/asco = You make me feel envy/disgust). For formal “you,” use me da (usted).
target_language_example: ¿Me das tu número de teléfono, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number, please?

meaning: “you owe me” (money, something, or a favor).
additional_notes: Used with the verb deber (to owe). Common patterns: “Me debes + noun” (Me debes dinero/una disculpa/un auto) and “Me debes una” = “You owe me one” (a favor). With “nada,” it means “You don’t owe me anything.”
target_language_example: Me debes cincuenta dólares.
native_language_example: You owe me fifty dollars.

additional_notes: From dejar + indirect object pronoun me (“me”). Commonly used to ask for permission (“¿Me dejas…?” = “Will you let me…?”) or to complain about what someone allows or causes (“Nunca me dejas hacer nada” = “You never let me do anything”). It can also mean “you leave me” in the sense of abandoning/keeping someone alone (“Siempre me dejas sola” = “You always leave me alone”). Usually followed by an infinitive (hacer, ir, salir) when it means “let me.”
target_language_example: ¿Me dejas salir un rato?
native_language_example: Will you let me go out for a while?

meaning: "(he/she/it) let me" or "(he/she/it) left me"; sometimes "(it) left me (in a state)" or "(he/she) left me (something)."
additional_notes: "Me" = "me". "Dejó" is the past tense (él/ella/usted) of "dejar". Common uses: (1) permission: "me dejó + infinitive" (me dejó pasar/entrar/ir) = "let me"; (2) abandon/leave: "me dejó" (me dejó solo) = "left me"; (3) leave someone waiting: "me dejó esperando" = "left me waiting"; (4) cause a result/state: "me dejó + adjective" (me dejó inconsciente) = "left me unconscious"; (5) leave/give (inherit): "me dejó + noun" (me dejó algunos bienes/esto) = "left me (something)."
target_language_example: El profesor me dejó salir temprano.
native_language_example: The teacher let me leave early.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of despertarse: “to wake up.” The “me” shows it’s reflexive (you woke yourself up / you woke up). Common with time words (temprano, ayer) and with “y…” to continue the story. Also used with “de…” to describe your mood: “Me desperté de mal humor.”
target_language_example: Me desperté a las siete y salí de casa.
native_language_example: I woke up at seven and left the house.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "darse cuenta (de)" = "to realize / to notice." It’s usually followed by "de" + noun/infinitive ("Me di cuenta de mi error", "Me di cuenta de que estaba enfermo"), though many speakers also say "me di cuenta que...". In the past tense "me di" is the preterite of "dar" and "cuenta" literally means "account," but the expression means becoming aware of something.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: I realized I had forgotten my keys.

additional_notes: Past tense of "darse cuenta de" (to realize/notice). Very commonly followed by "que" + a clause: "Me di cuenta de que...". You can change the indirect object pronoun to match the person: "me/te/se/nos/os/se di cuenta" (e.g., "Te diste cuenta de que..." = "You realized that...").
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado mis llaves.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten my keys.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of darse cuenta de (“to realize/notice”). Often used with time expressions like de repente (“suddenly”) or hoy (“today”). Can be followed by an added detail with que (“I realized that…”) or acerca de (“about…”).
target_language_example: Anoche me di cuenta de algo: había olvidado mis llaves.
native_language_example: Last night I realized something: I had forgotten my keys.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of darse cuenta de: "to realize/notice." Often used when something suddenly becomes clear (De repente/De pronto) or when you realize it later (Recién). It’s followed by que + a full clause (verb). You can change the person: "me di cuenta", "te diste cuenta", "se dio cuenta", etc.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten my keys at home.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “darse cuenta (de)”. In more careful/standard Spanish it’s very common to say “me di cuenta de que …” (with “de”), especially before a clause, but in everyday speech many people also say “me di cuenta que …”. It’s used when you suddenly understand or become aware of something.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta que había dejado mi bolso en el tren.
native_language_example: I realized I had left my bag on the train.

meaning: "(he/she/it) tells me that…" / "it tells me that…"
additional_notes: Used with the verb **decir** to report what someone (or something, like your face/body/intuition) communicates to you: **[subject] + me dice que + [clause]**. Often translates as **"tells me that"** (not usually "says me"). Note: **me dice qué** (with an accent on **qué**) means **"tells me what"**; many texts omit the accent by mistake, e.g. *Él no me dice qué hacer* = "He doesn't tell me what to do."
target_language_example: Mi amigo me dice que mañana llega tarde.
native_language_example: My friend tells me that tomorrow he’ll arrive late.

additional_notes: “Me” = “to me,” and “dieron” is the simple past (preterite) of **dar** for **ellos/ellas/ustedes** (“they/you all gave”). Spanish often drops the subject, so **me dieron** can mean “they gave me” without saying who. It’s also used in common patterns like **me dieron ganas de + infinitive** (“I felt like / got the urge to …”).
target_language_example: Me dieron una cita para el lunes.
native_language_example: They gave me an appointment for Monday.

meaning: "you tell me" (to me), usually after "que" (that) or in requests/commands.
additional_notes: "Me" = to me, and "digas" is the present subjunctive of "decir" (to say/tell). It commonly appears after expressions like "necesito que...", "quiero que...", "te ruego que..." and means "(that) you tell me...". It can also be used in negative commands: "No me digas..." = "Don’t call me / don’t tell me ..." (depending on what follows).
target_language_example: Quiero que me digas tu nombre.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me your name.

meaning: "they told me that" / "I was told that".
additional_notes: Used to report information someone else gave you. Literally: "to me" (me) + "they said/told" (dijeron) + "that" (que). In conversation it often implies you’re repeating what you heard (not necessarily confirming it’s true). You can also change the person: "me dijo que" (one person told me that).
target_language_example: Me dijeron que la reunión empieza a las ocho.
native_language_example: They told me that the meeting starts at eight.

additional_notes: Used when reminding someone of what they said in the past (dijiste = you told [informal tú, preterite]). Follow it with a statement ("…era un ladrón"), or with a verb in the subjunctive after giving instructions/requests ("…que hiciera esto", "…que regresara").
target_language_example: Me dijiste que hoy no venías, ¿recuerdas?
native_language_example: You told me you weren’t coming today, remember?

additional_notes: From the verb "decir" (to say/tell). "Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to me". "Dijo" is the simple past (pretérito) 3rd person singular: "he/she told" (also used for "you" formal: "usted"). Often followed by "que" + a clause: "Me dijo que..." = "He/She told me that..."
target_language_example: Mi jefe me dijo que llegara temprano.
native_language_example: My boss told me to arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you. It’s the indirect-speech pattern: "decir" (to tell) + indirect object "me" (to me) + "que" (that) + the reported sentence. The speaker can be anyone; context tells you who (él/ella/usted).
target_language_example: Mi jefe me dijo que mañana no hay reunión.
native_language_example: My boss told me that there’s no meeting tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report someone’s advice or recommendation. "Me dijo" = "told me"; "que" introduces what they said; "debería" (conditional of "deber") expresses “should/ought to” (often softer than "debo"). The subject (who told you) is understood from context or can be added: "El médico/ella/él me dijo que debería…".
target_language_example: Mi madre me dijo que debería dormir más.
native_language_example: My mom told me that I should sleep more.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. It’s the preterite of “decir” (dijo = told) + indirect object pronoun (me = to me) + “que” (that) + imperfect “ser” (era = was). After “me dijo que…”, Spanish often uses the imperfect (era) to describe a state/identity at that time (e.g., pobre, canadiense, feliz).
target_language_example: Mi jefe me dijo que era importante llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: My boss told me that it was important to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a state/condition in the past: **decir + me + que + estaba + adjective/noun**. The subject of **estaba** is usually the same person who spoke (“She told me she was pregnant”), but it depends on context.
target_language_example: Me dijo que estaba cansado y que se iba a casa.
native_language_example: He told me he was tired and that he was going home.

meaning: “(He/She) told me that I…” (introducing what someone said to you).
additional_notes: Used to report speech: **me dijo** = “(he/she) told me,” and **que** = “that.” The second **me** is a pronoun that belongs to the next verb (often reflexive), e.g. **me amaba** (“loved me”), **me odiaba** (“hated me”), **me pusiera** (“put on”), **me debería comprar** (“should buy”), **me podía quedar** (“I could keep”). You can add the speaker for clarity: **Tom/Mary me dijo que me…**
target_language_example: Mi hermano me dijo que me calmara.
native_language_example: My brother told me to calm down.

meaning: “(He/She) told me no”; “(He/She) told me not to …”.
additional_notes: Used when someone refuses a request ("He/She said no") or gives you a negative instruction ("told me not to"). Structure: "me dijo" = "told me" + "que no" + verb (often in the subjunctive): "Me dijo que no nadara" = "He/She told me not to swim."
target_language_example: Le pedí ayuda, pero me dijo que no.
native_language_example: I asked him for help, but he told me no.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said (reported speech). After "me dijo que…" (“he/she told me that…”), Spanish often drops the subject pronoun; "me dijo que él" adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., “he told me that HE…”). The verb after "que" follows normal tense rules (present, past perfect, etc.).
target_language_example: Me dijo que él no tenía tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: He told me that he didn’t have time today.

additional_notes:
Used with the indirect object pronoun me (“to me”) + dio (he/she/it/you-formal “gave,” past tense). Common patterns:
- me dio + a thing: “(someone) gave me…” (Me dio un beso. / Me dio permiso. / Me dio estas monedas.)
- me dio + a feeling/need: “It made me…” or “I got…” (Me dio sed = “I got thirsty”; El mal olor me dio asco = “The bad smell disgusted me.”)
The subject (who/what caused it) is often mentioned before, but can be omitted if understood.
target_language_example: Esa película me dio miedo.
native_language_example: That movie scared me.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "dar las gracias" = "to say thank you / to give thanks." Use it to report that someone thanked you; you can add "por..." to say what for ("Me dio las gracias por el regalo"). The subject is often a person (e.g., "Jenny me dio las gracias"), but it can also be implicit.
target_language_example: Al final de la cena, me dio las gracias por ayudar.
native_language_example: At the end of dinner, he/she thanked me for helping.

additional_notes: Used to say someone gave you a masculine singular thing: me (to me) + dio (gave, preterite of dar) + un (a). For feminine nouns, use “me dio una” (e.g., “me dio una camisa”). For plural, “me dio unos/unas” or more commonly “me dio algunos/algunas”.
target_language_example: Mi amiga me dio un regalo.
native_language_example: My friend gave me a gift.

meaning: “(He/She) gave me a…” or “(He/She) gave me one…”
additional_notes: From the verb **dar** (“to give”), in the **preterite**: **dio** = “gave.” **Me** means “to me.” You use it before a noun: **Me dio una naranja** (“He/She gave me an orange”), **Me dio una llave** (“…a key”). With some nouns it means delivering an action to you (often negative): **Me dio una patada** (“…a kick”), **Me dio una paliza** (“…a beating”).
target_language_example: Me dio una botella de agua porque tenía sed.
native_language_example: He/She gave me a bottle of water because I was thirsty.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite tense of "dar" (to give): "diste" = "you gave" (tú). "Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to me" or "me." Common with things you give (un beso, tu teléfono, tu palabra, una alternativa, una contusión). For the formal 'you,' say "me dio" (usted).
target_language_example: Me diste tu palabra, y yo te creí.
native_language_example: You gave me your word, and I believed you.

additional_notes: Used with "de" + noun/pronoun or "de que" + clause: "Me doy cuenta de eso" (I realize that), "Me doy cuenta de que..." (I realize that...). You can negate it: "No me doy cuenta" (I don’t realize / I don’t notice). Often used when you suddenly understand or become aware of something.
target_language_example: Me doy cuenta de que estaba equivocado.
native_language_example: I realize that I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used with **de** + noun (“me doy cuenta de la verdad”) or **de que** + clause (“me doy cuenta de que estaba equivocado”). It often implies you understand something now (sometimes after thinking about it or after something happens). You can change the person: *te das cuenta de*, *se da cuenta de*, *nos damos cuenta de*, etc.
target_language_example: Me doy cuenta de que hoy es lunes y tengo una reunión.
native_language_example: I realize that today is Monday and I have a meeting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about pain in a body part. Structure: Me duele + singular thing (Me duele la cabeza) / Me duelen + plural things (Me duelen los pies). You can add intensity: mucho, un poco, bastante.
target_language_example: Me duele la garganta cuando trago.
native_language_example: My throat hurts when I swallow.

meaning: “my … hurts” / “I have pain in my …” (for a masculine body part).
additional_notes: Used to say you feel pain in a specific body part: **me duele el + [masculine body part]** (el diente, el pecho, el pie, el tobillo, el codo). For feminine body parts, use **me duele la** (e.g., *me duele la cabeza*). You can add a side: *me duele el pie izquierdo/derecho*.
target_language_example: Me duele el estómago desde ayer.
native_language_example: My stomach has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shoulder pain. "Me duele" literally means "it hurts me" and is followed by the body part with "el/la": "Me duele la cabeza" (my head hurts), "Me duelen los brazos" (my arms hurt—plural). You can add sides like "derecho" (right) or "izquierdo" (left): "Me duele el hombro derecho/izquierdo".
target_language_example: Me duele el hombro desde ayer.
native_language_example: My shoulder has been hurting since yesterday.

meaning: "My ___ hurts" / "I have pain in my ___" (before a feminine body part).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **doler** to say something hurts. The pattern is **Me duele la + [feminine noun]** (e.g., *la garganta, la cabeza, la tripa*). Literally it’s like “**The ___ hurts me**,” so Spanish often puts the body part after the verb. For masculine body parts, use **Me duele el...** (*Me duele el estómago*). If more than one thing hurts, use **Me duelen...** (plural): *Me duelen las piernas*.
target_language_example: Me duele la cabeza.
native_language_example: My head hurts.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel pain in your head. Structure: "me" (to me) + "duele" (hurts, from doler) + "la cabeza" (the head). You can add a reason with "de" (e.g., "de tanto trabajar" = "from working so much") or use it as a request/complaint ("Paren de gritar, me duele la cabeza").
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme; me duele la cabeza desde esta mañana.
native_language_example: I can’t concentrate; I’ve had a headache since this morning.

meaning: it hurts a lot / I’m in a lot of pain.
additional_notes: Used to say that a body part hurts a lot. Pattern: "Me duele mucho + el/la + [body part]" (e.g., Me duele mucho la cabeza). You can also put the body part first for emphasis: "La cabeza me duele mucho" or "Mi pierna me duele mucho". For more than one thing hurting, Spanish often uses "me duelen" (plural): "Me duelen mucho los pies".
target_language_example: Me duele mucho la muela.
native_language_example: My tooth hurts a lot.

meaning: “my … hurt” / “I have pain in my …” (used with a masculine plural body part).
additional_notes: Used to say that a plural body part hurts. Structure: me (to me) + duelen (hurt, plural) + los + masculine plural body part. For feminine plural you use “me duelen las …” (e.g., Me duelen las rodillas). For a singular body part you use “me duele el/la …” (e.g., Me duele la cabeza). Common completions with “los”: los pies, los brazos, los dientes, los ojos, los músculos.
target_language_example: Caminé tanto que me duelen los pies.
native_language_example: I walked so much that my feet hurt.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of enamorarse de (“to fall in love with”). Use it with a person (me enamoré de ella/él/ti) or with a quality/thing (me enamoré de su encanto = “I fell in love with his/her charm”). Other persons: te enamoraste de (you), se enamoró de (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Me enamoré de él cuando lo vi por primera vez.
native_language_example: I fell in love with him when I saw him for the first time.

additional_notes: Used to express strong liking or enjoyment. Literal structure is "it enchants me": the thing you like is the subject (often after the verb), e.g., "Me encanta el té". For plural things, use "me encantan" (e.g., "Me encantan los libros"). You can negate it: "No me encanta" = "I don’t love it / I’m not crazy about it."
target_language_example: Me encanta esta canción.
native_language_example: I love this song.

additional_notes: Used to say you love or really like a masculine noun or a singular masculine idea. Structure: me (to me) + encanta (is pleasing) + el + noun. For feminine nouns use “me encanta la…”, and for plural use “me encantan los/las…”.
target_language_example: Me encanta el café por la mañana.
native_language_example: I love coffee in the morning.

meaning: “I love this …” / “I really like this …” (referring to a feminine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking. Literally it’s like “this … enchants me,” so the thing you love is the grammatical subject: Me encanta esta música. Use **esta** with feminine singular nouns (esta música, esta parte, esta temporada, esta bicicleta). With masculine singular, use **este** (Me encanta este libro).
target_language_example: Me encanta esta película; es muy divertida.
native_language_example: I love this movie; it’s really fun.

meaning: “I love this …” / “I really like this …” (talking about a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: Literally “this enchants me,” but it’s used to say you love/really like something. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: Me encanta este móvil. For feminine nouns use “me encanta esta …” (Me encanta esta canción). For plural: “me encantan estos/estas …”.
target_language_example: Me encanta este restaurante.
native_language_example: I love this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to express strong liking for a singular feminine noun. "Me" = to me, "encanta" = (it) delights/charms, "la" = the (feminine). For a masculine noun use "Me encanta el..."; for plural use "Me encantan las/los...".
target_language_example: Me encanta la música latina.
native_language_example: I love Latin music.

additional_notes: Used to say you really like something that belongs to the person you’re talking to. Grammatically it works like “(It) enchants/delights me, your …”: the thing you love is the subject (tu vestido/tu acento/tu sombrero), and “me” means “to me.” Often followed by a noun; if the noun is plural, use **Me encantan tus …**.
target_language_example: Me encanta tu camisa.
native_language_example: I love your shirt.

meaning: “I love (them)” / “I’m delighted by (them)” (used with plural nouns).
additional_notes: From the verb "encantar" (“to love/to really like”). "Me" marks who feels it (me), and "encantan" agrees with the thing(s) loved, so it’s used when what you love is plural: "Me encantan las naranjas". With a singular noun, use "me encanta": "Me encanta el café". It’s stronger than "me gustan" (“I like”).
target_language_example: Me encantan tus ideas.
native_language_example: I love your ideas.

additional_notes: Used to say you really like something. It takes an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les) and the verb agrees with what you love: encantan + plural noun (e.g., las bodas). Use "me encanta la" for a singular feminine noun, "me encantan los" for plural masculine, and "me encanta el" for singular masculine. Similar to "gustar": the thing you love is the grammatical subject.
target_language_example: Me encantan las canciones en español.
native_language_example: I love songs in Spanish.

additional_notes: Use this to say you love movies in general. Grammatically, "encantar" works like "to really please": movies (plural) are the subject, so you use "encantan" (plural) and the indirect object pronoun "me" (to me). You can add an adjective or nationality after "películas" (e.g., "americanas", "francesas"). For one movie: "Me encanta la película".
target_language_example: Me encantan las películas de terror, pero no me gustan las comedias románticas.
native_language_example: I love horror movies, but I don't like romantic comedies.

additional_notes: Used to express that you really like/love something. Grammatically, the thing you love is the subject, so you use **encantan** with plural nouns (vs. **me encanta** with singular). **Los** is used before plural masculine nouns (or mixed-gender groups); for plural feminine, use **me encantan las**.
target_language_example: Me encantan los libros de misterio.
native_language_example: I love mystery books.

meaning: “I’d love to” / “I would really like to.”
additional_notes: A polite, enthusiastic way to say you would like to do something (often in response to an invitation or suggestion). It’s the conditional form of “encantar” (“to love/delight”), so it often implies “I’d be delighted.” Use it with an infinitive (me encantaría ir) or with a noun (me encantaría una pizza).
target_language_example: Me encantaría ir contigo al cine.
native_language_example: I’d love to go to the movies with you.

additional_notes: Used to say you will be responsible for doing something in the future. It’s the future tense of “encargarse de” + the reflexive pronoun “me.” It can be followed by a noun/pronoun (de eso, de este problema) or by “que” + subjunctive to mean you will make sure something happens (Me encargaré de que la conozcas…).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: me encargaré de hablar con el profesor mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll take care of talking to the teacher tomorrow.

meaning: “I’ll take care of it.” / “I’ll handle it.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase “encargarse de” (to take charge of / be responsible for something). It often implies volunteering to do a task: “De eso me encargo yo” = “I’ll take care of that (myself).” You can say it alone (“Me encargo.”) to mean “I’ve got it.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes, yo me encargo de la cena.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of dinner.

meaning: “I ran into / met up with (someone),” often by chance.
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of reflexive "encontrarse con". Used when you unexpectedly meet someone (or happen to see them) in a place. Common pattern: "Me encontré con + person"; you can also add where/when: "Me encontré con Ana en el metro."
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré con mi profesor en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my teacher at the supermarket.

meaning: “I ran into her / met her (by chance) in …”.
additional_notes: Used for an unplanned meeting with someone (often with clues like “por casualidad”, “de casualidad”, “accidentalmente”). The place comes after “en” (en la calle, en la estación, en la tienda). Literal “I found myself with her in …” isn’t how you’d say it in English.
target_language_example: Me encontré con ella en el supermercado por casualidad.
native_language_example: I ran into her at the supermarket by chance.

meaning: "I ran into my..." / "I met my... (by chance)."
additional_notes: Used with a person you unexpectedly meet in a place: *me encontré con mi vecino/profesor/amigo...* It often goes with *por casualidad* (“by chance”). In the past tense it’s commonly *me encontré con...*; you can also say *me encuentro con...* for present (“I run into...”).
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré con mi hermana en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my sister at the supermarket.

me encontré con un viejo amigo

target_language_multi_word_term: me encontré con un viejo amigo
meaning: I ran into an old friend; I met up with an old friend (by chance).
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "encontrarse con" to mean "to run into/come across (someone)"—often unexpectedly. "Me" indicates "I" as the person who had the encounter (past tense: "I ran into"). "Viejo amigo" means "old friend" (a friend from the past, not necessarily elderly). You can swap in other people: "me encontré con mi jefe" (I ran into my boss).
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré con un viejo amigo en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into an old friend at the supermarket.

meaning: “I ran into him” / “I met up with him (by chance).”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **encontrarse con** = “to run into / bump into / come across (someone)” usually **unexpectedly**. Here **me** means “I (to myself)” and **con él** means “with him.” In the past, it often describes a chance encounter: **Me encontré con él en la calle.**
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré con él en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into him at the supermarket.

meaning: "I ran into him / I met up with him" (by chance) in/at/on...
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "encontrarse con" to talk about unexpectedly meeting someone. "Me" = I (to myself), "con él" = with him, and "en" introduces the place or time (e.g., en Tokio, en el tren, en enero). In conversation, it often implies it wasn’t planned.
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré con él en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into him at the supermarket.

meaning: “I meet up (with)” (me encuentro con…) or “I feel” (me encuentro bien/mal).
additional_notes: With **con** + person, it means to meet up: **Me encuentro con ella** = “I meet up with her.” Without **con**, it often describes how you feel: **Me encuentro bien/mal/muy bien** = “I feel well/bad/very well.” (It can also mean where you are: **Me encuentro en…** = “I’m in…”.)
target_language_example: Hoy no me encuentro bien.
native_language_example: I don’t feel well today.

additional_notes: “Me” = “to me.” “Enseñó” is the past tense (preterite) of “enseñar.” It’s used for a completed action in the past. It can mean teaching a skill or lesson (often with “a” + infinitive: “me enseñó a hacer…”) or showing something (“me enseñó la cámara”).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo me enseñó a manejar.
native_language_example: My grandpa taught me to drive.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone taught you how to do an action. "Me" = to me, "enseñó" = (he/she) taught (past), and "a" is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., leer, manejar, usar). You can change "me" to another indirect object pronoun (te/nos/le/les) and "enseñó" to another tense/person (me enseña, me enseñaron, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi mamá me enseñó a cocinar.
native_language_example: My mom taught me to cook.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "enterarse (de)" = to find out / to learn (about). It’s usually used when you learn new information (often unexpectedly). Common patterns: "me enteré de + noun" (Me enteré de su éxito = I found out about his/her success) and "me enteré (de) que + clause" (Me enteré que estaba enfermo = I found out that he was sick). Often appears with time words like "en cuanto" or "tan pronto" to mean “as soon as I found out.”
target_language_example: Me enteré de la reunión ayer y por eso no fui.
native_language_example: I found out about the meeting yesterday, so I didn’t go.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of the reflexive verb "enterarse" = to find out. Common patterns: "me enteré de + noun/thing" (I found out about…) and "me enteré de que + clause" (I found out that…). Often implies the information was new to the speaker, sometimes unexpectedly.
target_language_example: Me enteré de que la tienda ya cerró.
native_language_example: I found out that the store already closed.

meaning: "I am" (right now), used to form the present progressive with a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb in the gerund (-ando/-iendo) to talk about something happening now: me estoy + [verb]-ando/-iendo (e.g., me estoy quedando, me estoy poniendo). It’s the reflexive pronoun me + estar (yo): estoy. Common with verbs like quedarse (me estoy quedando dormido = I'm falling asleep), ponerse (me estoy poniendo viejo = I'm getting old), imaginarse (me estoy imaginando = I'm imagining), divertirse (me estoy divirtiendo = I'm having fun).
target_language_example: Me estoy preparando para salir.
native_language_example: I'm getting ready to go out.

meaning: “It’s killing me” (it’s hurting me / exhausting me / really bothering me).
additional_notes: Usually a figurative, exaggerated way to say something is causing you a lot of pain, discomfort, stress, or annoyance. It commonly refers to physical pain (e.g., a tooth, your back) or something draining (stress, heat/cold, tight clothing/wig). Grammar: “estar” + gerund (matando) = ongoing effect; you can add the cause as the subject: “El aire acondicionado me está matando.” = “The air conditioning is killing me.”
target_language_example: El aire acondicionado me está matando.
native_language_example: The air conditioning is killing me.

meaning: "it’s driving me crazy" / "it’s making me go crazy."
additional_notes: Used to complain that something is really annoying, stressful, or overwhelming. Literally it’s “(it) is turning me crazy”: *volver(se)* + adjective. Change the pronoun/person as needed: *me/te/le/nos/les está(n) volviendo loco/loca/locos/locas*.
target_language_example: ¡Ese pitido constante me está volviendo loco!
native_language_example: That constant beeping is driving me crazy!

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "irse" = "to leave". It often means you left a place: "Me fui de la fiesta" (I left the party). It can also be used with a destination using "a": "Me fui a tu escuela" (I went to your school). You can add how you left: "Me fui corriendo" (I ran off / I left running).
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, me fui a casa.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, I went home.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb "irse" (to leave/go away): "me fui" = "I left/I went away". It’s commonly followed by a destination with "a" ("me fui a la playa"), or by "a" + infinitive to say you went to do something ("me fui a acostar" = "I went to bed").
target_language_example: Me fui al supermercado después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I went to the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of ir: "me fui" = "I went/I left." Often used to say you left a place and headed home. You can add details after it: "a cambiarme de ropa" (to change clothes), "corriendo" (running).
target_language_example: Me fui a casa temprano porque mañana trabajo.
native_language_example: I went home early because I work tomorrow.

meaning: "I went to sleep" / "I went to bed."
additional_notes: Common way to say you decided to go to bed (often after finishing something or because it’s late). Literally "I went myself to sleep": *me fui* is the preterite of *irse* (to leave/go away) used like "I went," and *a dormir* means "to sleep." You’ll often hear variations like *me voy a dormir* (I’m going to bed / I’m going to sleep) and *me fui a la cama* (I went to bed).
target_language_example: Me fui a dormir temprano porque estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: I went to bed early because I was very tired.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of irse (me fui) to talk about going to bed at a specific moment in the past. Often appears with time words like temprano (early) or after another action: después de…, en cuanto… (as soon as…). Also common: irse a la cama (to go to bed) / ir a la cama (to go to bed, more neutral).
target_language_example: Anoche me fui a la cama a las diez porque estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: Last night I went to bed at ten because I was very tired.

meaning: I make a living (earn my livelihood).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how you earn money to live. It often appears with "como" to say what you do for work ("Me gano la vida como profesor") or with "con" to say what you earn money with ("Me gano la vida con esto"). You can change the pronoun/verb: "te ganas la vida" (you make a living), "se gana la vida" (he/she makes a living), "nos ganamos la vida" (we make a living).
target_language_example: Me gano la vida reparando bicicletas.
native_language_example: I make a living repairing bicycles.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gustar**. In Spanish, the thing you like is the grammatical subject: **Me gusta esa camisa** = “I like that shirt” (literally “That shirt pleases me”). Use **me gustan** with plural nouns: **Me gustan estos libros** (“I like these books”). You can add **a mí** for emphasis/contrast: **A mí me gusta**, pero a él no.
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho tu música.
native_language_example: I really like your music.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar: literally "eating is pleasing to me." The thing you like is the subject (comer + food/activity). You can add what you like to eat after comer: "Me gusta comer pizza." For emphasis, you can add "a mí": "A mí me gusta comer..."
target_language_example: Me gusta comer pasta los domingos.
native_language_example: I like to eat pasta on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that happens in a particular situation or at a particular time. It’s a common pattern: (No) me gusta cuando + verb (present tense). You can also change the person: te gusta cuando… (“you like it when…”), le gusta cuando… (“he/she likes it when…”).
target_language_example: Me gusta cuando me llamas por mi nombre.
native_language_example: I like it when you call me by my name.

additional_notes: Used to say you like the way someone does something or the way something looks/sounds/feels. Structure: Me gusta cómo + verb (present tense): “Me gusta cómo caminas” = “I like how you walk.” You can also use it with something: “Me gusta cómo suena” = “I like how it sounds.”
target_language_example: Me gusta cómo cocinas.
native_language_example: I like how you cook.

meaning: "I like the" (for a singular masculine noun).
additional_notes: Use "me gusta" + singular noun when the thing you like is one item/thing. "El" is the masculine singular article (the), so it’s followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., el sushi). For feminine nouns, use "me gusta la". For plural nouns, use "me gustan los/las".
target_language_example: Me gusta el café.
native_language_example: I like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you like a particular color or the color of an object. The grammar is literal: me (to me) + gusta (is pleasing) + el color (the color). You can add a specific color (Me gusta el color azul.) or use "de" to say whose/which item’s color you like (Me gusta el color de tu falda.).
target_language_example: Me gusta el color de esta camisa.
native_language_example: I like the color of this shirt.

meaning: “I like that …” (for a feminine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used with **gustar** to say you like something. Literally it’s like “That … pleases me,” so the thing you like is the subject: **Me gusta esa + [feminine singular noun]** (e.g., *esa bandera/esa idea*). For plural things, use **Me gustan esas + [plural noun]**. To say you don’t like it: **No me gusta esa …**.
target_language_example: Me gusta esa camiseta.
native_language_example: I like that T-shirt.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern "me gusta" + infinitive to talk about something you like doing. Literally, "listening to music pleases me" (me = to me). You can add details like the type of music ("música de Beethoven", "música japonesa") or when you do it ("mientras hago cualquier cosa").
target_language_example: Me gusta escuchar música cuando estudio.
native_language_example: I like listening to music when I study.

additional_notes: Used with an implied or stated masculine singular noun: ese concepto, ese tiro, ese coche. In Spanish, gustar literally works like “to be pleasing”: me gusta = “it pleases me / I like it.” For feminine nouns, use “me gusta esa …” (esa idea).
target_language_example: Me gusta ese plan; vamos mañana.
native_language_example: I like that plan; let’s go tomorrow.

meaning: “I like this …” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you like a specific thing close by or just mentioned. "Me gusta" literally means "(it) pleases me" and is followed by the thing you like. "Esta" is the feminine singular form of "this"; use it with feminine nouns (esta camisa, esta manzana, esta oficina, esta chica). For masculine nouns, use "me gusta este" (este libro). To say you don’t like it: "No me gusta esta ..."
target_language_example: Me gusta esta casa, pero no me gusta esta calle.
native_language_example: I like this house, but I don’t like this street.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar. Literally, “being … is pleasing to me.” It’s followed by an infinitive (estar) and then an adjective/state: Me gusta estar ocupado (I like being busy). You can change the person: te gusta estar… (you like to be…), le gusta estar… (he/she likes to be…).
target_language_example: Me gusta estar tranquilo los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I like to be relaxed on weekends.

meaning: "I like this ..." (for a singular masculine thing/person).
additional_notes: Used to say you like something: "Me gusta" + singular masculine "este" + noun. The verb agrees with what is liked (gusta = one thing). For feminine nouns use "me gusta esta" (e.g., "Me gusta esta camisa"), and for plural use "me gustan estos/estas" (e.g., "Me gustan estos zapatos"). Often translates to English "I like..." but literally means "This ... is pleasing to me."
target_language_example: Me gusta este restaurante.
native_language_example: I like this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy the activity of studying. "Me gusta" literally means "it pleases me" and is followed by an infinitive (here, "estudiar"). You can add what you study after the verb (e.g., "Me gusta estudiar historia").
target_language_example: Me gusta estudiar español por la noche.
native_language_example: I like studying Spanish at night.

meaning: I like to talk / I like speaking.
additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy talking or speaking (in general, or about something specific). Pattern: “Me gusta + infinitive (hablar, comer, viajar…)”. To add a topic, use “hablar de…” (Me gusta hablar del amor). To say a language, use “hablar + idioma” (Me gusta hablar francés) or “hablar en + idioma” (Me gusta hablar en francés).
target_language_example: Me gusta hablar contigo después de clase.
native_language_example: I like talking with you after class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about activities you enjoy. The verb after hacer is usually an infinitive (e.g., hacer investigación, hacer reír a alguien). The person who likes it is the indirect object: me/te/le/nos/os/les gusta. Example: "A María le gusta hacer deporte."
target_language_example: Me gusta hacer ejercicio por la mañana.
native_language_example: I like to exercise in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy playing something. Grammar: "me gusta" + infinitive (jugar). You can add what you play: "Me gusta jugar al ajedrez" (games often use "a"/"al"), or a sport/instrument can appear without it in some regions (e.g., "jugar golf"). You can also add a place with "en": "Me gusta jugar en el jardín". For liking multiple activities, you often hear "Me gusta jugar a..." / "Me gusta jugar al..." (or "Me gusta jugar deportes" in casual use).
target_language_example: Me gusta jugar al fútbol los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I like to play soccer on the weekends.

meaning: 'I like the' (talking about a singular feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say you like something. "Me" = to me, "gusta" = is pleasing, "la" = the (feminine singular). Put the thing you like after it: "Me gusta la miel". For plural things, use "Me gustan las ...". For masculine nouns, use "Me gusta el ...".
target_language_example: Me gusta la comida mexicana.
native_language_example: I like Mexican food.

meaning: “I like the food” / “I like (a type of) food.”
additional_notes: Used to say you like food in general or a specific cuisine/type of food. Structure: "me gusta" + singular noun ("la comida"). With plural nouns, use "me gustan" (e.g., "Me gustan las tapas"). You can add an adjective or nationality to specify: "comida chatarra" (junk food), "comida coreana" (Korean food), "comida picante" (spicy food).
target_language_example: Me gusta la comida italiana, pero no me gusta la comida muy picante.
native_language_example: I like Italian food, but I don’t like very spicy food.

me gusta la forma en que

target_language_multi_word_term: me gusta la forma en que
additional_notes: Used to say you like how someone does something or how something is (speaks, thinks, behaves, makes you feel, etc.). It’s followed by a verb clause: “me gusta la forma en que + [verb]”. You can change it for person/number: “me gusta / te gusta / le gusta / nos gusta…”. Similar options: “Me gusta cómo…” (more direct) and “Me gusta la manera en que…”.
target_language_example: Me gusta la forma en que me escuchas cuando hablo.
native_language_example: I like the way you listen to me when I talk.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "gustar" (literally, "to be pleasing"). "Me" = to me, and "gusta" stays singular because the thing you like ("la música") is singular. You can add details after it (e.g., "moderna", "especialmente el rock").
target_language_example: Me gusta la música, pero hoy prefiero el silencio.
native_language_example: I like music, but today I prefer silence.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say you like doing an activity. Literally “reading is pleasing to me,” so the grammar is different from English: gusta agrees with the thing you like (leer). You can add details after it: Me gusta leer antes de dormir / Me gusta leer novelas.
target_language_example: Me gusta leer en el parque los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I like to read in the park on weekends.

meaning: I like it a lot / I really like it.
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to express strong liking. The thing you like is the subject: Me gusta mucho esta fotografía. With plural nouns, use gustan: Me gustan mucho las películas. You can also use it before an infinitive to say you really like doing something: Me gusta mucho estudiar idiomas.
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho este lugar.
native_language_example: I really like this place.

meaning: "I like ... a lot" (for a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: Use "me gusta" + singular noun to say you like something; add "mucho" to emphasize "a lot." "El" is the masculine singular article (el béisbol, el helado, el japonés, el olor, el tenis). For feminine nouns, use "me gusta mucho la" (e.g., la música). For plural nouns, use "me gustan" (e.g., me gustan mucho los libros).
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho el café.
native_language_example: I like coffee a lot.

additional_notes: Used with comparisons to say you like one thing more than another. Common patterns: (1) "Me gusta más X que Y" = I like X more than Y. (2) "De + plural group + me gusta más + singular" = Of the group, I like this one the most. (3) "Cada vez me gusta más + (noun/clause)" = I like it more and more / increasingly.
target_language_example: Me gusta más esta película que la otra.
native_language_example: I like this movie more than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare preferences. With a masculine singular noun you often use "el": "Me gusta más el tenis". To make the comparison explicit, add "que": "Me gusta más el tenis que el fútbol". With feminine nouns you use "la" ("Me gusta más la pizza"), and with plural nouns use "los/las" ("Me gustan más los zapatos negros").
target_language_example: Me gusta más el café que el té.
native_language_example: I like coffee more than tea.

additional_notes: Used to express a preference. It often appears in comparisons with “que” (“more than”): “Me gusta más la X que la Y.” The “la” must match a feminine singular noun (e.g., la casa, la bicicleta); for masculine use “me gusta más el…”, for plural “me gustan más los/las…”.
target_language_example: Me gusta más la camiseta azul que la roja.
native_language_example: I like the blue T-shirt more than the red one.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that belongs to or is associated with someone. Structure: "Me gusta su + singular noun" (because "gusta" matches the singular thing you like). "Su" can mean his, her, your (formal), or their—context clarifies. For plural nouns, use: "Me gustan sus + plural noun".
target_language_example: Me gusta su acento.
native_language_example: I like his/her/your/their accent.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that belongs to the person you’re talking to. The full pattern is: "Me gusta" + singular noun + "tu" + noun (e.g., "Me gusta tu collar"). With plural nouns, use "Me gustan": "Me gustan tus ideas". Literally it’s closer to "Your ___ pleases me," so the verb agrees with the thing you like (gusta/gustan), not with "me."
target_language_example: Me gusta tu estilo.
native_language_example: I like your style.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy watching or seeing something. "Me gusta" = "I like" (literally "it pleases me"), and it’s followed by an infinitive verb like "ver" (to watch/see). With people, you often add "a": "Me gusta ver a las personas" (I like watching people).
target_language_example: Me gusta ver series por la noche.
native_language_example: I like watching series at night.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar. Literally it means “traveling is pleasing to me,” so the grammar is different from English: gusta agrees with the thing you like (viajar = an action, so singular), and me means “to me.” You can add details with en (in), por (by/through), etc.: Me gusta viajar en verano / por tren.
target_language_example: Me gusta viajar a otros países.
native_language_example: I like to travel to other countries.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "gustar" (literally "to be pleasing"). "Me" = "to me"; "gustaba" is imperfect past, used for ongoing states in the past, repeated past feelings, or "used to". The thing/person you liked is the grammatical subject: "Me gustaba eso" = "That used to please me" → "I liked that." Often used with emphasis: "A mí me gustaba..." (= "I" as opposed to others).
target_language_example: No me gustaba el café, pero ahora me encanta.
native_language_example: I didn’t use to like coffee, but now I love it.

meaning: "I like" (for plural things) / "they appeal to me."
additional_notes: Used with plural nouns (or an infinitive phrase treated as plural) and the verb gustar: "me" = "to me" and "gustan" agrees with what is liked (plural). Contrast: "me gusta" for one thing. You can add emphasis or comparison: "me gustan más... que..." (I like ... more than ...), "me gustan de veras" (I really like).
target_language_example: Me gustan más las manzanas que las naranjas.
native_language_example: I like apples more than oranges.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to express likes. Grammatically, the thing you like is the subject: “Las frutas me gustan” = “I like fruit.” Use me (to me) + gustan (they please) + las + a plural feminine noun (e.g., las frutas, las galletas, las faldas). For singular feminine, use “me gusta la …”. For plural masculine, use “me gustan los …”.
target_language_example: Me gustan las películas románticas.
native_language_example: I like romantic movies.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar to express preferences. Literally “girls are pleasing to me.” The thing you like (las chicas) is grammatically the subject, so the verb is plural: gustan. You can add adjectives after chicas (e.g., chicas japonesas) to specify what kind of girls you like.
target_language_example: Me gustan las chicas inteligentes.
native_language_example: I like smart girls.

meaning: "I like" (for plural masculine nouns; also used for mixed-gender groups).
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say you like things. Literally closer to "(they) are pleasing to me." Use it before a plural noun with los (e.g., los pasteles). For plural feminine nouns, use "me gustan las" (e.g., Me gustan las flores). For a singular thing: "me gusta el/la".
target_language_example: Me gustan los libros de misterio.
native_language_example: I like mystery books.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar: literally “men are pleasing to me.” "Me" = “to me,” and the thing you like ("los hombres") is the grammatical subject, so the verb is plural: "gustan." It can mean you like men in general, or in context it can imply romantic/sexual attraction.
target_language_example: Me gustan los hombres que son amables.
native_language_example: I like men who are kind.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar: the thing you like is the grammatical subject. Because perros is plural, you use gustan (not gusta). You can add a mí for emphasis/contrast: A mí me gustan los perros (As for me, I like dogs). Also note perro can be part of a food name (e.g., perros de maíz = “corn dogs”).
target_language_example: A mí me gustan los perros, pero a mi hermano le gustan los gatos.
native_language_example: I like dogs, but my brother likes cats.

meaning: I like them a lot / I really like them.
additional_notes: Used with gustar to say you like something a lot. The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so you use gustan with plural nouns (Las películas me gustan mucho) and gusta with singular nouns (La película me gusta mucho). The pronoun me means “to me.” Word order can vary: Me gustan mucho las películas / Las películas me gustan mucho.
target_language_example: Me gustan mucho estos libros.
native_language_example: I really like these books.

meaning: "I like all the ..." (for masculine plural nouns).
additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar. The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: gustan + plural (Me gustan todos los colores). If the noun is feminine plural, use: Me gustan todas las.... For a singular noun: Me gusta todo el / toda la.... You can add exceptions with excepto / menos (e.g., excepto la col).
target_language_example: Me gustan todos los libros de esta autora.
native_language_example: I like all the books by this author.

meaning: "I like your" (talking about plural things you own/do).
additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar. "Me" = "to me." "Gustan" is used because the thing liked is plural (your movies/shoes/etc.). "Tus" means "your" and is used with plural nouns (tus zapatos, tus perros). For one thing, use "me gusta tu ..." (singular).
target_language_example: Me gustan tus ideas.
native_language_example: I like your ideas.

additional_notes: From "gustar". Commonly used to politely ask for something (Me gustaría + noun) or to express a wish (Me gustaría + infinitive). Often followed by "un/una" for ordering: "Me gustaría un café".
target_language_example: Me gustaría hablar con el gerente, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak with the manager, please.

additional_notes: A polite way to request a conversation with a specific person. Uses the conditional "gustaría" to sound courteous (less direct than "quiero"). Follow it with a person’s name, a title ("el señor / la señora"), or a formal pronoun ("usted" or abbreviated "Ud.").
target_language_example: Me gustaría hablar con usted un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: I would like to speak with you for a moment, please.

meaning: “I would like to go to …” (to a place).
additional_notes: A polite way to express a wish or preference. Use it with a destination after "a": countries/cities (a Japón, a Egipto) and most plural country names take "a + los/las" (a los Estados Unidos). You can add time words like "algún día" (someday) or "un día" (one day).
target_language_example: Me gustaría ir a España algún día.
native_language_example: I’d like to go to Spain someday.

meaning: "I would like to be able to" / "I'd like to be able to."
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire about having the ability or opportunity to do something. It’s polite and a bit more tentative than "quiero" (I want). Follow it with an infinitive: "me gustaría poder + infinitive" (e.g., "viajar", "comprar", "hablar").
target_language_example: Me gustaría poder ayudarte más.
native_language_example: I'd like to be able to help you more.

meaning: “I would like (it) that…” / “I wish that…” (followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or preference about a situation, often hypothetical or not true right now. It’s commonly followed by the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., estuviera/estuviese, fuera, hubiera/hubiese, tuvieras). Often refers to someone else’s actions or a change in circumstances: “Me gustaría que vinieras” = “I’d like you to come.”
target_language_example: Me gustaría que me ayudaras mañana.
native_language_example: I’d like you to help me tomorrow.

meaning: 'I would like to know' / 'I'd like to find out.'
additional_notes: Polite way to express curiosity or a wish to know something. Often followed by a question word (por qué, cuánto, cómo, dónde, etc.) or by an infinitive to talk about knowing how to do something (e.g., saber bailar/tocar). You can also say it alone (“Me gustaría saber.”) to mean “I’d like to know.”
target_language_example: Me gustaría saber cómo se dice esto en español.
native_language_example: I’d like to know how you say this in Spanish.

meaning: “I would like to know how (to)… / I’d like to know how (to)…”.
additional_notes: A polite way to ask for instructions or an explanation. Often followed by an infinitive (cómo instalar…, cómo hacer…) or by a full clause (cómo el cuerpo absorbe…). More formal/indirect than “¿Cómo…?” and similar in tone to “Quisiera saber cómo…”.
target_language_example: Me gustaría saber cómo llegar al centro en autobús.
native_language_example: I’d like to know how to get downtown by bus.

meaning: "I would like to be" (I wish I were).
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or wish about becoming something or being different. It’s a polite/soft way to say what you want for the future or hypothetically. Often followed by a noun/job ("médico"), an adjective/comparison ("más joven"), or a longer phrase ("lo suficientemente rico como para...").
target_language_example: Me gustaría ser más paciente.
native_language_example: I would like to be more patient.

meaning: "I would like to have" / "I'd like to have."
additional_notes: A polite way to express a wish or desire. It uses the conditional of gustar (gustaría) + infinitive (tener) + the thing you want. Often used for hypothetical wants (e.g., better memory, more time) as well as polite requests or wishes.
target_language_example: Me gustaría tener una semana libre para descansar.
native_language_example: I’d like to have a week off to rest.

meaning: 'I would like to see' / 'I'd like to see'.
additional_notes: A polite way to say what you want to see. Uses the conditional "gustaría" (from "gustar") to sound softer than "quiero ver" ("I want to see"). Often followed by a person or thing: "ver a + person" ("ver a la señorita"), or just "ver + thing" ("ver mi dibujo").
target_language_example: Me gustaría ver el menú, por favor.
native_language_example: I'd like to see the menu, please.

additional_notes: Often used to express romantic interest/attraction (similar to “I’m into you”), though it can also be friendly depending on context. With gustar, the person you like is the grammatical subject: “me gustas (tú)” literally means “you are pleasing to me.” Contrast: “te gusto” = “you like me.” You can add emphasis: “A mí me gustas” (I like you) or “Me gustas tú” (I like you, not someone else).
target_language_example: Me gustas, pero quiero ir despacio.
native_language_example: I like you, but I want to take it slow.

meaning: I liked it / I liked him/her (in the past).
additional_notes: Past (preterite) form of "gustar" for a specific moment or completed experience. Literally it’s closer to “it pleased me,” so the thing/person you liked is the grammatical subject: "Me gustó la película" (the movie pleased me). You can add emphasis with "mucho": "Me gustó mucho".
target_language_example: Me gustó la comida, pero no me gustó el postre.
native_language_example: I liked the food, but I didn’t like the dessert.

additional_notes: Used when someone/something (él/ella/usted) has done something that affects you: "me" = "to me" / "for me" (e.g., me ha sorprendido = it has surprised me). It’s very common in the present perfect: me + ha + past participle. "Me" usually goes before the conjugated verb (ha).
target_language_example: El profesor me ha dado mucha tarea.
native_language_example: The teacher has given me a lot of homework.

meaning: "has given me" / "has done to me" (with dar).
additional_notes: "Me ha dado" is the present perfect of dar with the indirect object pronoun me: "(he/she/it) has given me". It often introduces what someone gave you (Me ha dado un libro / una carta), but dar is also used in common set phrases like "me ha dado un susto" ("it gave me a scare") and "me ha dado por + noun/infinitive" meaning you suddenly got into something or started doing it ("Me ha dado por la música" = "I’ve gotten into music").
target_language_example: Mi amiga me ha dado un consejo muy útil.
native_language_example: My friend has given me very useful advice.

meaning: "has left me"; also "has left (something) for me" or "has left me (in a certain state)."
additional_notes: From the verb "dejar" (to leave). It’s the present perfect: "ha dejado" = "has left" (with "me" = "me"). Common uses: (1) relationship: "Mi novia me ha dejado" = "My girlfriend left me" (broke up with me). (2) leaving something for you: "me ha dejado un mensaje" = "(she) left me a message." (3) causing a result/state: "me ha dejado embarazada/hecha polvo" = "(he) left me pregnant / left me exhausted" (i.e., caused that result). Context tells which meaning fits.
target_language_example: Juan me ha dejado una nota en la mesa.
native_language_example: Juan left me a note on the table.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decir (“to say/tell”): (él/ella/usted) me ha dicho = “he/she/you (formal) has told me.” Used to report what someone said, often with who said it: “Eso me ha dicho Manuela.” Can also appear in questions or negatives: “No es eso lo que me ha dicho.”
target_language_example: Mi jefe me ha dicho que mañana no hay reunión.
native_language_example: My boss told me that tomorrow there is no meeting.

additional_notes: From the verb "gustar" in the present perfect: "ha gustado" = "has/have pleased." Spanish often frames likes as something pleasing you: "Me ha gustado" literally means "It has pleased me." Use it to say you liked something (a book, movie, food, etc.), often with "mucho" (a lot). You can add the thing you liked as the subject: "Este libro me ha gustado" (This book, I liked it).
target_language_example: La película me ha gustado mucho.
native_language_example: I liked the movie a lot.

additional_notes: Present perfect of hacer with the indirect object pronoun me (“to me”). Often used for cause/result: (1) me ha hecho + adjective (“has made me [adjective]”), (2) me ha hecho + infinitive (“has made me [do]”), or (3) me ha hecho + noun/role (“has made me [something]”). In exclamations like "¡Mira lo que me ha hecho!", it means “Look what he/she did to me!” (something done to you).
target_language_example: Esa experiencia me ha hecho más fuerte.
native_language_example: That experience has made me stronger.

meaning: "I had" (past perfect), used with a past participle.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect form of haber (había) + the pronoun me. It’s used to form the past perfect: me había + participle (e.g., me había dormido = I had fallen asleep). The pronoun me can be reflexive (about yourself: me había levantado = I had gotten up) or an indirect object with se (se me había caído = it had fallen (on me)/I had dropped it). It describes an action that happened before another moment in the past.
target_language_example: Cuando llegaste, ya me había ido.
native_language_example: When you arrived, I had already left.

additional_notes:
"Me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me.” It’s used with hacer in many common expressions: 
- hacer una visita = to pay a visit (De vez en cuando él me hace una visita.)
- hacer una pregunta = to ask a question (Tom me hace la misma pregunta cada día.)
- hacer ruido = to make noise (Me hace ruido el estómago.)
A related and very common pattern is "se me hace" = “it seems to me / it feels (to me)” (Esto se me hace familiar.)
target_language_example: Mi jefe me hace muchas preguntas en la reunión.
native_language_example: My boss asks me a lot of questions in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is necessary or missing for you. It’s the pattern “hacer falta + noun” (e.g., Me hace falta harina = I need flour) or just “Me hace falta” when the thing is understood from context. Often interchangeable with “necesito,” but “hacer falta” emphasizes lack/need.
target_language_example: Me hace falta tiempo para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: I need time to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone causes an emotion or physical feeling in you. It comes from "hacer sentir" (to make someone feel). The subject can be a thing (Esto/La música) or a person (Tom), and you can add an adjective or phrase after it: "bien", "incómodo", "viejo", "como en casa", etc.
target_language_example: Esa canción me hace sentir feliz.
native_language_example: That song makes me feel happy.

meaning: 'they have (done to me)' / 'I have been …' (with a past participle).
additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "to me" or "me." "Han" is the "they/you all" form of "haber" used to make the present perfect: han + past participle (ofrecido, atacado, insultado, mantenido). It’s used when someone (often an unspecified "they") has done something to you: "Me han insultado" = "They’ve insulted me" / "I’ve been insulted."
target_language_example: Me han llamado esta mañana, pero no pude contestar.
native_language_example: They called me this morning, but I couldn’t answer.

meaning: I've been told that / they told me that.
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard from other people. It’s the present perfect of "decir" (han dicho = "have said/told"), with "me" = "to me". Often implies the source isn’t important or you don’t want to name who said it. Similar: "Me dijeron que" (they told me; simple past).
target_language_example: Me han dicho que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I've been told that it's going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Future tense of “hacerse cargo de” (to take responsibility for something/someone). Use it to volunteer or promise that you will deal with a task or be responsible for a person/thing. Often followed by a pronoun like “esto/eso/ello/ellos” or a noun (e.g., “me haré cargo del problema”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: me haré cargo de la reserva.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll take care of the reservation.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about something you have done to the speaker: me has ayudado (you’ve helped me), me has confundido (you’ve confused me). Word order: object pronoun + has + participle. In questions: ¿me has llamado? = have you called me?
target_language_example: Me has ayudado mucho hoy.
native_language_example: You’ve helped me a lot today.

meaning: “you have made me …” / “you’ve caused me to …”.
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (haber + hecho) to say someone has caused you to feel or do something. Common patterns: “Me has hecho + infinitive” (Me has hecho reír = You’ve made me laugh) and “Me has hecho + adjective/feelings” (Me has hecho sentir triste = You’ve made me feel sad). Often implies responsibility/blame when used in arguments: “Mira lo que me has hecho hacer” = “Look what you made me do.”
target_language_example: Me has hecho cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: You’ve made me change my mind.

meaning: "I have" (used with reflexive verbs in the present perfect).
additional_notes: Used to form the pretérito perfecto with reflexive verbs: **me he + past participle** (e.g., *me he despertado* = “I’ve woken up”, *me he ido* = “I’ve left”). **Me** is the reflexive pronoun (“myself”) and it goes before **he** (from *haber*). It’s common in Spain and also used elsewhere when talking about something that has happened recently or is still relevant now.
target_language_example: Me he duchado y ya estoy listo.
native_language_example: I’ve showered and I’m ready now.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "acostumbrarse a" (to get used to). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive ("...a vivir") or a noun phrase ("...a su forma de hablar"). Uses the present perfect ("me he...") to emphasize a change up to now: "I’ve gotten used to...". You can also say "ya me he acostumbrado a..." (I’m already used to...) or "todavía no me he acostumbrado a..." (I still haven’t gotten used to...).
target_language_example: Me he acostumbrado a levantarme temprano.
native_language_example: I’ve gotten used to getting up early.

additional_notes: From the verb enterarse de = “to find out about / to hear about.” It’s commonly followed by de + noun/phrase: Me he enterado de lo que ha pasado (“I found out what happened”). You can add time expressions (hace nada = “just now”) or emphasis like ya (“already”): Ya me he enterado (“I already know / I’ve already heard”).
target_language_example: Me he enterado de que mañana no hay clase.
native_language_example: I found out that there’s no class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present perfect of the reflexive verb levantarse (“to get up”). Used for something that happened earlier today or recently, especially in Spain (e.g., this morning: Me he levantado tarde). In many Latin American contexts, people often use the simple past instead: Me levanté tarde.
target_language_example: Hoy me he levantado a las siete.
native_language_example: Today I got up at seven.

meaning: "I've felt" / "I have felt" (how I’ve been feeling).
additional_notes: Present perfect of sentirse (“to feel” in the sense of physical/emotional state). It’s commonly followed by an adjective: Me he sentido mejor/feliz/triste. The adjective agrees with the speaker: me he sentido gordo (male) / gorda (female). You can change the pronoun and verb for other people: te has sentido (you’ve felt), se ha sentido (he/she has felt), nos hemos sentido (we’ve felt).
target_language_example: Últimamente me he sentido muy cansado.
native_language_example: Lately I’ve felt very tired.

meaning: “I hurt myself in/on (a body part)” / “I injured my (body part).”
additional_notes: Used with a body part to say you got hurt there: “Me hice daño en el pie” = “I hurt my foot.” Common with en + el/la + body part. In the past tense (hice), it refers to a specific moment when the injury happened; the infinitive is “hacerse daño (en) …”.
target_language_example: Me hice daño en la rodilla jugando al fútbol.
native_language_example: I hurt my knee playing soccer.

meaning: “(he/she/it) made me …” or “(he/she) did … to/for me” (past tense).
additional_notes: "Me" is an indirect object pronoun (“to me”), and "hizo" is the preterite of "hacer" (“made/did”). Common patterns: (1) "me hizo" + infinitive = “made me” do something: "me hizo esperar" (made me wait), "me hizo acostar" (made me lie down). (2) "me hizo" + noun = “did/made [something] for/to me”: "me hizo un cumplido" (gave me a compliment), "me hizo la cortesía de…" (did me the courtesy of…).
target_language_example: El jefe me hizo repetir el informe.
native_language_example: The boss made me repeat the report.

additional_notes: Past tense of hacer (“to make/do”) with an indirect object pronoun: me = “to/for me”. It’s commonly used for things someone makes or prepares for you (food, drinks, clothing, objects). Use un (masculine) or una (feminine): Me hizo un té / Me hizo una sopa.
target_language_example: Mi abuela me hizo un pastel para mi cumpleaños.
native_language_example: My grandma made me a cake for my birthday.

meaning: “(He/She) made me a …” / “(He/She) did a … for me.”
additional_notes: From the verb **hacer** (“to make/do”). **Me hizo una + noun** means someone made something for you or performed an action toward you. The noun after **una** is feminine (e.g., *una torta*, *una tarta*, *una reverencia*, *una jaula*). For masculine nouns, you’ll hear **me hizo un + noun**.
target_language_example: Mi amigo me hizo una comida deliciosa.
native_language_example: My friend made me a delicious meal.

meaning: "I would have liked (to)…" / "I wish I had…" (past regret).
additional_notes: Used to express that something did not happen, and you regret it or would have preferred it in the past. Often followed by an infinitive (me hubiera gustado ir, verlo) or by "que" + past subjunctive (me hubiera gustado que vinieras). It’s a common, polite way to talk about missed opportunities.
target_language_example: Me hubiera gustado llamarte antes, pero no tuve tiempo.
native_language_example: I would have liked to call you earlier, but I didn’t have time.

meaning: "I was going to" / "I was about to" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ir (iba) + a + infinitive to talk about an intention, plan, or something that was expected to happen in the past (often "future in the past").
