additional_notes: Used to add an improved option, suggestion, or piece of information compared to what was just said. Often follows a statement and can introduce a new idea: "Podemos ir mañana; mejor aún, el sábado". You may also see "aún mejor" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Podemos pedir pizza; mejor aún, cocinamos en casa.
native_language_example: We can order pizza; better yet, we’ll cook at home.

meaning: "better than" (used to compare with what you expected or with another action/ability).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons, often with a verb after "lo que": "mejor de lo que creí/esperaba" = better than I thought/expected. It can also compare two abilities/actions: "mejor de lo que corren" = better than they run. Very common with past expectations (creer, pensar, imaginar) or with "poder" + verb.
target_language_example: La película fue mejor de lo que esperaba.
native_language_example: The movie was better than I expected.

meaning: better to leave / it’s better to go.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or advise that leaving is the best option. Often appears as a standalone recommendation (like “We’d better leave”) or with a subject for clarity: “Mejor nos vamos” / “Mejor me voy.” You can also use it after a reason: “Si no hay taxis, mejor irse.”
target_language_example: Está muy tarde; mejor irse ya.
native_language_example: It’s very late; we’d better leave now.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to compare two things: "X es mejor que Y" (“X is better than Y”). In conversational Spanish it can also introduce advice or a warning, often with the subjunctive: "Mejor que + subjunctive" ≈ “It’d be better if…” / “You’d better…”.
target_language_example: Es mejor que me llames mañana que hoy.
native_language_example: It’s better for you to call me tomorrow than today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone knows/understands/can do something more than anyone else. It often appears after verbs like conocer (to know), saber (to know), entender (to understand), or with deberías saber (you should know): “Tú lo sabes mejor que nadie” = “You know it better than anyone.”
target_language_example: Ella entiende a su hermano mejor que nadie.
native_language_example: She understands her brother better than anyone.

meaning: "better than me" (I do/know/understand it less well).
additional_notes: Used to compare abilities, knowledge, or understanding with yours. Very often follows a verb or phrase like hacerlo (to do it), saber (to know), or comprender (to understand): hacerlo mejor que yo = do it better than me. In careful Spanish, some speakers prefer "mejor que yo" (implying "...que yo [lo hago/lo sé]") rather than "mejor que mí".
target_language_example: Nadie conoce esta ciudad mejor que yo.
native_language_example: Nobody knows this city better than me.

additional_notes: Plural form of *mejor amigo/a*. Common with a possessive (*mis mejores amigos*) to mean “my best friends,” or with an article (*los mejores amigos*) to mean “the best friends.” Singular: *mejor amigo* (male/mixed) / *mejor amiga* (female).
target_language_example: Tom y Mary son mis mejores amigos.
native_language_example: Tom and Mary are my best friends.

meaning: underage; a minor (not legally an adult).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is below the legal age of adulthood (often 18, depending on the country). Often appears with the verb “ser”: “Es menor de edad.” The opposite is “mayor de edad” (of legal age).
target_language_example: No puede entrar al club porque es menor de edad.
native_language_example: He/She can’t enter the club because he/she is underage.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or how long ago something happened. You’ll often see it with verbs like durar (to last), tardar (to take), or hacer + time + que (ago): Hace menos de una hora = “Less than an hour ago.”
target_language_example: La reunión dura menos de una hora.
native_language_example: The meeting lasts less than an hour.

additional_notes: Used to express relief that something bad didn’t happen or that a situation turned out well. Common patterns: (1) on its own: “Menos mal.” = “Thank goodness.” (2) with que + clause: “Menos mal que…” = “It’s a good thing that…” / “Luckily…” Often said at the end of a sentence as a reaction.
target_language_example: Menos mal que llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thank goodness you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to express relief about something that happened (or didn’t happen). It’s often followed by a verb phrase: "Menos mal que vino" (Good thing he came), "Menos mal que no pasó nada" (Luckily nothing happened). You can also hear it without "que" as a standalone reaction: "¡Menos mal!" (Thank goodness!).
target_language_example: Menos mal que llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: Good thing you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities (numbers, fractions, prices, time) or to say someone/something is inferior or not as good as another. Often followed by a number or a noun phrase: "menos que 10", "menos que un medio", "menos que una cucaracha" (figurative/insulting).
target_language_example: Este libro cuesta menos que el otro.
native_language_example: This book costs less than the other one.

additional_notes: Used for a message sent/received by phone text. Very common with verbs like enviar (to send), recibir (to receive), and ignorar (to ignore): “Te envié un mensaje de texto.” Also shortened in everyday speech to “mensaje” when context is clear.
target_language_example: Te mando un mensaje de texto cuando llegue.
native_language_example: I’ll text you when I arrive.

additional_notes: Used for messages sent by phone. Common with the verb "enviar" (to send): "enviar mensajes de texto" = "to text" / "to send text messages". Often appears in plural (mensajes).
target_language_example: Enviar mensajes de texto mientras se conduce es muy peligroso.
native_language_example: Sending text messages while driving is very dangerous.

additional_notes: Used to describe being willing to consider new ideas or different opinions. Common with the verb "tener" (to have) or "mantener" (to keep): "tener la mente abierta", "mantener la mente abierta". You may also hear the adjective form "de mente abierta" (“open-minded”).
target_language_example: Trata de mantener la mente abierta cuando escuches otras opiniones.
native_language_example: Try to keep an open mind when you listen to other opinions.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying or selling goods or currency illegally or unofficially, often to avoid regulations, taxes, or price controls. Common with things like dollars/foreign currency, stolen goods, or restricted items. Often used with verbs like comprar/vender (to buy/sell) and prepositions like en (in) or al (to the).
target_language_example: No compres medicamentos en el mercado negro.
native_language_example: Don’t buy medicine on the black market.

additional_notes: Mostly used in the fixed phrase «a merced a» meaning “thanks to” or “due to,” often in more formal or written Spanish. In everyday speech, «gracias a» is more common. Don’t confuse it with «a merced de» (“at the mercy of”).
target_language_example: A merced a tu ayuda, terminamos el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: Thanks to your help, we finished the project on time.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, cost, or risk. Often followed by an infinitive: “Merece la pena ver/ir/hacer…” (It’s worth seeing/going/doing…). You can also use it alone: “Merece la pena.”
target_language_example: Aunque está lejos, merece la pena ir.
native_language_example: Even though it’s far, it’s worth going.

additional_notes: Used to specify where a month falls within the calendar year, often with ordinal numbers: el primer/segundo/último mes del año. Note the contraction: de + el → del.
target_language_example: Marzo es el tercer mes del año.
native_language_example: March is the third month of the year.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the month immediately before the current one. Often appears with prepositions like «el mes pasado» (last month), «desde el mes pasado» (since last month), and «a finales del mes pasado» (at the end of last month).
target_language_example: Nos mudamos el mes pasado.
native_language_example: We moved last month.

additional_notes: Refers to the table located in the kitchen (often where people sit to eat, talk, or place things). You’ll also commonly hear it without "la": "mesa de cocina". With verbs: "sentarse a la mesa de la cocina" = to sit down at the kitchen table; "poner/dejar algo en la mesa de la cocina" = to put/leave something on the kitchen table.
target_language_example: Deja el correo en la mesa de la cocina, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the mail on the kitchen table, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s main long-term purpose or ambition (often with the verb ser: “Mi meta en la vida es…”). You can also use it in plural: “metas en la vida” (life goals).
target_language_example: Mi meta en la vida es aprender español.
native_language_example: My goal in life is to learn Spanish.

meaning: to mess up; to put your foot in it (say/do something embarrassing).
additional_notes: Common idiom used when you make a mistake, especially a social blunder (e.g., saying the wrong thing). Often used with phrases like "perdón" or "creo que" to soften it: "Perdón, creo que voy a meter la pata." Although it’s a fixed expression, it conjugates normally (voy a meter la pata / meto la pata / metí la pata).
target_language_example: Perdón, creo que voy a meter la pata con este comentario, pero necesito decirlo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I’m going to put my foot in it with this comment, but I need to say it.

meaning: to get into; to put oneself into (a place or a situation, often trouble).
additional_notes: Used for entering a physical place (e.g., a pool) or getting involved in a situation (very commonly: "meterse en problemas" = "to get into trouble"). It often implies doing it oneself (sometimes carelessly or as a result of one’s actions).
target_language_example: Los que hablan mucho suelen meterse en problemas.
native_language_example: People who talk a lot often get into trouble.

additional_notes: Used with the accidental/reflexive pattern: se me/te/le/nos/les metió algo en el ojo ("something got in my/your/his/her/our/their eye"). You can also use plural: se me metieron cosas en los ojos. Common in everyday situations (dust, eyelash, sand).
target_language_example: Dice que se le metió algo en el ojo.
native_language_example: He/She says something got in his/her eye.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an object’s length. It often follows a number and the verb ser/tener: "Es de ocho metros de largo" (It’s eight meters long), "Tiene treinta metros de largo" (It’s thirty meters long). You can also say "de X metros de largo" after a noun: "un escritorio de dos metros de largo" (a desk two meters long).
target_language_example: El puente es de cien metros de largo.
native_language_example: The bridge is one hundred meters long.

additional_notes: “Mi” means “my” and “abogado” is “lawyer/attorney” (male; for a female lawyer: “mi abogada”). Often used with verbs like hablar con (to speak with) and llamar a (to call). In formal address you may see “Ud.” = “usted” (“you”).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar con mi abogado antes de firmar.
native_language_example: I want to speak with my lawyer before signing.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your grandmother. Spanish family words usually take a possessive adjective (mi, tu, su, nuestro/a). You can also say "mi abuelita" for an affectionate "my granny/grandma".
target_language_example: Voy a visitar a mi abuela este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my grandmother this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your grandfather (your father’s or mother’s dad). Often followed by a verb: “Mi abuelo es… / Mi abuelo sale…”. You can also emphasize who someone is: “Él es mi abuelo.”
target_language_example: Mi abuelo vive cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: My grandfather lives near here.

additional_notes: A common way to state that someone passed away. **Murió** is the **preterite** (simple past) of **morir** and is used for a completed event. Often followed by time expressions like **hace tres años** (“three years ago”) or **poco después de…** (“shortly after…”).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió el año pasado.
native_language_example: My grandfather died last year.

meaning: "my soul"; also an affectionate way to address someone (like "dear").
additional_notes: Most literally refers to your soul/spirit (often in emotional, religious, or poetic contexts: "save my soul"). In some places it’s also used as a term of endearment when speaking to someone directly ("Lo siento, mi alma" = "I’m sorry, dear").
target_language_example: No te preocupes, mi alma, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, dear, everything is going to be fine.

additional_notes: “Mi” means “my.” “Amiga” is a female friend (or you use it if the friend is a woman/girl). It can also be used to address a woman directly in a friendly way (like “my friend”), depending on tone and context. For a male friend, use “mi amigo.”
target_language_example: Hoy voy a cenar con mi amiga.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to have dinner with my (female) friend.

meaning: "my friend" (male friend; also used for a mixed group).
additional_notes: Used with a noun + possessive: mi amigo / mi amiga. You can add details with an adjective after it (e.g., mi amigo francés, mi amigo gay). To introduce someone, Spanish commonly says “Este/Éste es mi amigo…”.
target_language_example: Éste es mi amigo Carlos.
native_language_example: This is my friend Carlos.

meaning: "my love" (a term of affection; also literally "my love" as a feeling).
additional_notes: Used as an affectionate way to address a partner (like “honey,” “sweetheart”). It can also mean “my love for (someone)” as a noun phrase: "Mi amor por ella...". Common in romantic contexts; tone depends on relationship and can sound overly intimate if used with strangers.
target_language_example: Mi amor, ¿puedes esperarme un momento?
native_language_example: My love, can you wait for me a moment?

additional_notes: Common in much of Latin America. In Spain, "mi coche" is more common. Used to talk about your personal vehicle (ownership or the one you use).
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy porque mi auto está en el taller.
native_language_example: I can’t go today because my car is at the mechanic’s.

additional_notes: Used to say that a bicycle belongs to you. "Mi" changes with the owner (mi = my, tu = your, su = his/her/your/their).
target_language_example: Voy a ir al trabajo en mi bicicleta.
native_language_example: I’m going to go to work on my bike.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: "mi" (my) + "brazo" (arm). Used when talking about your own arm, especially in everyday situations (pain/injury) or when someone is holding your arm. Common with verbs like "agarrarse a/de" (hold on to), "doler" (to hurt), and commands like "Suelta/Suelte" (let go) or "Toma" (take).
target_language_example: Me duele mi brazo derecho.
native_language_example: My right arm hurts.

additional_notes: Literally refers to your head (body part), often used when talking about pain: “Ay, mi cabeza” = “Ow, my head.” It can also be used more figuratively to mean thoughts or imagination, especially with “en”: “en mi cabeza” = “in my head.”
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme; tengo demasiadas cosas en mi cabeza.
native_language_example: I can’t concentrate; I have too many things in my head.

additional_notes: Means the place where you live. Often used with the preposition "a" to show movement toward home: "voy a mi casa" (I'm going to my house/home). You can also use it to describe location relative to your home: "cerca de mi casa" (near my house).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, voy a mi casa.
native_language_example: After work, I go home.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to talk about your house’s **location or position** (not a permanent characteristic). Common patterns: **mi casa está en** + place (“in/at…”), **mi casa está a** + distance/time (“… away”), **mi casa está lejos/cerca** (“far/near”), **mi casa está situada en** (“is situated on/in…”).
target_language_example: Mi casa está cerca del parque.
native_language_example: My house is near the park.

additional_notes: Use it to say your home is located near a place. After “cerca de” you normally use a noun (la escuela, la estación) or a place name. You can swap “mi casa” for other subjects (Mi trabajo está cerca de…, El hotel está cerca de…).
target_language_example: Mi casa está cerca de un supermercado.
native_language_example: My house is close to a supermarket.

meaning: my hometown (the city where I was born/grew up).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the place you’re from. Often appears with verbs like recordar (to remind), volver (to return), and ser (to be): «Mi ciudad natal es…». You can change the possessive: «tu/su/nuestra ciudad natal».
target_language_example: Quiero volver a mi ciudad natal este verano.
native_language_example: I want to go back to my hometown this summer.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective **mi** (“my”) before the noun **coche** (“car”). Common in everyday contexts to talk about your own car, including describing it (*Mi coche es azul*), saying something is wrong (*Le pasa algo a mi coche*), giving permission (*Puedes coger mi coche*), or telling someone to get out (*Sal de mi coche*).
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy; mi coche está en el taller.
native_language_example: I can't go today; my car is at the mechanic.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used to talk about your preferred color. Word order can vary: “El rojo es mi color favorito” and “Mi color favorito es el rojo” both mean the same thing. You can swap in any color after “es”.
target_language_example: Mi color favorito es el morado.
native_language_example: My favorite color is purple.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the person you share a room (or sometimes an apartment) with. Often said as "compañero/a de habitación" depending on the roommate’s gender (compañera for a woman). In many places, "roommate" can also be "compañero/a de piso" (someone you share an apartment with).
target_language_example: Mi compañero de habitación y yo compartimos el baño.
native_language_example: My roommate and I share the bathroom.

additional_notes: Used to offer or refer to advice you gave. Often appears with verbs like seguir (to follow): «seguir mi consejo» = “follow my advice.” Also common in formal commands: «Siga mi consejo.»
target_language_example: Mi consejo es que hables con el profesor cuanto antes.
native_language_example: My advice is that you talk to the teacher as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective mi (“my”) + corazón (“heart”). Very common in emotional or romantic phrases (e.g., con todo mi corazón = “with all my heart”), and also in metaphors like mi corazón está roto (“my heart is broken”).
target_language_example: Gracias por estar aquí; significa mucho para mi corazón.
native_language_example: Thank you for being here; it means a lot to my heart.

additional_notes: Used to describe your heartbeat, often with an adverb like rápido (fast), muy rápido (very fast), or más rápido (faster). It can be literal (after running) or emotional (nervous/excited, e.g., when you see someone).
target_language_example: Cuando hago ejercicio, mi corazón late más rápido.
native_language_example: When I exercise, my heart beats faster.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective mi (“my”) + cuarto (“room”). In many contexts, mi cuarto specifically refers to your bedroom in a home. Cuarto can also mean “quarter” (1/4) in other contexts, but with mi and sentences about keys/cleaning/location, it means a room.
target_language_example: Voy a estar en mi cuarto estudiando.
native_language_example: I’m going to be in my room studying.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “my account” (user account, bank account, etc.): *Borré/cerrare mi cuenta*, *bloqueó mi cuenta*. In restaurants or bars it can mean “my bill/tab,” especially in phrases like *La cuenta, por favor* (“The bill, please”) or *Póngalo en mi cuenta* (“Put it on my tab / charge it to my account”).
target_language_example: No puedo entrar a mi cuenta porque olvidé la contraseña.
native_language_example: I can’t log into my account because I forgot the password.

additional_notes: A common possessive phrase: **mi** (my) + **cuerpo** (body). Used to talk about your physical body, health, sensations, or injuries. It can also refer to your body as a whole (e.g., after death: *quemen mi cuerpo* = “burn my body”). In Spanish you may also hear **el cuerpo** instead of **mi cuerpo** when speaking generally about the body.
target_language_example: Me duele mi cuerpo después de correr.
native_language_example: My body hurts after running.

additional_notes: Very informal/vulgar. Can be literal (talking about your butt) or used as a rude way to show disbelief/contempt, similar to English “my ass!” (meaning “yeah, right / no way”). Because it’s crude, avoid it in polite or formal situations.
target_language_example: ¿Que él es muy honesto? ¡Mi culo!
native_language_example: That he's very honest? My ass!

additional_notes: Used to take responsibility or blame for something. Often appears in set phrases like "(No) es mi culpa" (It’s (not) my fault) and with "por" to mean "because of me / due to my fault" ("por mi culpa"). You can swap "mi" for other possessives: "tu culpa" (your fault), "su culpa" (his/her/their fault).
target_language_example: Perdón por llegar tarde; fue mi culpa.
native_language_example: Sorry for being late; it was my fault.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the date you were born and the yearly celebration. With dates you’ll often see: “Mi cumpleaños es el 20 de julio” (specific day) or “Mi cumpleaños es en noviembre” (month). It can also be used figuratively for an anniversary, e.g., “mi cumpleaños de sobriedad” = “my sobriety anniversary.”
target_language_example: ¿Qué quieres hacer por mi cumpleaños?
native_language_example: What do you want to do for my birthday?

meaning: my duty; what I’m supposed/obligated to do.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a responsibility or moral/legal obligation you personally have. It often appears with verbs like cumplir con (to carry out/fulfill) and ser (it was my duty). In Spanish you can also simply say Es mi deber + infinitive (e.g., Es mi deber informarle).
target_language_example: Es mi deber decirte la verdad.
native_language_example: It’s my duty to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used when something good or unexpected happens and you feel lucky. Very common with "Hoy es..." or "Debe de ser..." ("It must be...") to express surprise or excitement about your luck.
target_language_example: ¡Encontré mi cartera! Hoy es mi día de suerte.
native_language_example: I found my wallet! Today is my lucky day.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your female spouse. "Mi" changes with the owner (mi = my, tu = your, su = his/her/your formal/their). You can also say "la esposa de + name/pronoun" (e.g., "la esposa de Tom").
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi esposa esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my wife tonight.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: **mi** (my) + **esposa** (wife). It agrees with the noun (**mi** is used with singular nouns of any gender). Often used when talking about your spouse; with prepositions: **por mi esposa** = “for my wife / because of my wife.”
target_language_example: Voy al supermercado con mi esposa.
native_language_example: I'm going to the supermarket with my wife.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male spouse. Often appears after prepositions (e.g., para mi esposo, con mi esposo) or in the phrase "a mi esposo" as a personal-direct-object form (the "a" is used with people).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi esposo esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my husband tonight.

additional_notes: "Mi" is the possessive adjective "my" (before a noun). "Familia" means "family" and can refer to your relatives as a group. Use it with verbs like "ser" (Ellos son mi familia) and with objects like photos (una foto de mi familia).
target_language_example: Voy a visitar a mi familia este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my family this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own pet cat. "Mi" means "my" (before a masculine singular noun), and "gato" means "cat" (male cat, or cat in general). For a female cat you can say "mi gata."
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; mi gato está enfermo.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; my cat is sick.

meaning: "my people" (my group: family, friends, community, or team).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the people you identify with or feel loyal to—often your close circle (family/friends) or your group/community. It can sound warm and personal, and it doesn’t imply literal ownership.
target_language_example: Hoy salgo con mi gente después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I'm going out with my people (my friends) after work.

meaning: my room (bedroom or a room you’re staying in).
additional_notes: “Mi” means “my” and “habitación” is “room.” It’s commonly used for your bedroom at home or your room in a hotel (“mi habitación de hotel”). Use it with location/description verbs like “estar” (Mi habitación está arriba / está llena de…).
target_language_example: Voy a dejar mi maleta en mi habitación.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave my suitcase in my room.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your (female) sibling. In Spanish, possessives like "mi" agree with the thing owned ("hermana" is singular), not with the owner. You can add a name after it: "Mi hermana, Aynur".
target_language_example: Mi hermana vive en Nueva York.
native_language_example: My sister lives in New York.

meaning: "my sister is" (to describe who/what your sister is).
additional_notes: Used with "ser" to state identity, job, or a general characteristic about your sister. Follow it with a noun (often without an article for jobs: "Mi hermana es enfermera") or an adjective ("Mi hermana es famosa").
target_language_example: Mi hermana es estudiante.
native_language_example: My sister is a student.

additional_notes: Used to specify that your sister is older than you. You can swap the possessive: "tu/su/nuestra hermana mayor" (“your/his-her/our older sister”). "Mayor" goes after the noun ("hermana").
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi hermana mayor esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my older sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your sister who is younger than you. Often contrasts with "mi hermana mayor" (my older sister). "Menor" literally means "younger" (not "smaller").
target_language_example: Voy a visitar a mi hermana menor este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my younger sister this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your younger sister (not necessarily physically small). In Spanish, the possessive (mi) comes before the noun, and the adjective (pequeña) usually comes after: mi hermana pequeña. You can also hear mi hermana menor with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Voy a recoger a mi hermana pequeña al colegio.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my little sister from school.

meaning: “my sister” + “se” (a reflexive/pronominal pronoun used with certain verbs).
additional_notes:
You’ll often see **se** right after a subject like **mi hermana** before a verb. **Se** is used with:
- **Reflexive actions**: *Mi hermana se ducha* (“My sister showers”).
- **Pronominal verbs** that require **se** and can change meaning: *Mi hermana se comprometió* (“My sister got engaged”).
- With **dedicarse a**: *Mi hermana se dedica a la natación* (“My sister dedicates herself to swimming”).
In English, **se** isn’t always translated directly; it often corresponds to “(her)self” or is simply part of the verb.
target_language_example: Mi hermana se llama Ana.
native_language_example: My sister’s name is Ana.

additional_notes: Uses **tener** (“to have”) to talk about having things (classes, a job, good handwriting, etc.). In Spanish, **age is expressed with tener**: *Mi hermana tiene tres años* = “My sister is three (years old)” (not “has three years” in natural English). You can also use it for age differences: *tiene tres años menos que yo* = “she’s three years younger than me.”
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene 25 años y tiene un buen trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister is 25 years old and has a good job.

additional_notes: “Mi” means “my” and “hermano” means “brother.” It’s used to talk about your brother in general. Use “a mi hermano” when he is the indirect object (e.g., ‘I gave it to my brother’), and “a mi hermano”/“a mi hermano” after certain verbs like “ver” when the direct object is a person (e.g., “Veo a mi hermano”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: My brother lives in Madrid.

meaning: “my brother is …” (to describe or identify your brother).
additional_notes: Use it to say what your brother is like (adjective) or what he is (job/identity). After “es,” use an adjective (Mi hermano es rico/fuerte) or a noun with an article (Mi hermano es un doctor / Mi hermano es profesor—both are common for professions). You can also compare: “Mi hermano es más … que yo” = “My brother is more … than me.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano es muy amable, pero a veces es impaciente.
native_language_example: My brother is very kind, but sometimes he’s impatient.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your oldest/older brother. In Spanish, "mayor" means "older" (not "bigger"); it agrees with the noun: "hermano mayor" (older brother) / "hermana mayor" (older sister). You can also say "mi hermano mayor" by itself as a short answer or when introducing him.
target_language_example: Mi hermano mayor trabaja en una oficina cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: My older brother works in an office near here.

meaning: "my brother" + "(to) me" ("me" as an object pronoun before the verb).
additional_notes: Used when your brother is the subject and you are the person receiving the action. Spanish object pronouns like "me" normally go before a conjugated verb: "Mi hermano me ayuda" (My brother helps me), "Mi hermano me compró..." (My brother bought me...). With infinitives/gerunds, "me" can also attach to the end: "Mi hermano va a ayudarme" / "Mi hermano está ayudándome".
target_language_example: Mi hermano me llama todos los días.
native_language_example: My brother calls me every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your younger brother. In Spanish, "menor" means younger (opposite of "mayor" = older). It can describe siblings and also minors (under 18). You can swap "mi" for other possessives: "tu hermano menor" (your younger brother), "su hermano menor" (his/her/their younger brother).
target_language_example: Voy a recoger a mi hermano menor después de la escuela.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick up my younger brother after school.

additional_notes: A common way to talk about your younger brother. In Spanish, family members are often referred to with a possessive (mi/tu/su) + noun, and adjectives like pequeño usually come after the noun. "Hermano pequeño" can mean either the younger brother (relative age) or simply the smaller/younger kid brother; if you mean strictly “the youngest,” you can also say "mi hermano menor".
target_language_example: Mi hermano pequeño estudia en la universidad.
native_language_example: My younger brother studies at the university.

additional_notes: "Mi hermano" means "my brother." The "se" is a pronoun that goes with certain verbs (pronominal/reflexive verbs), so the full meaning depends on the verb that follows. Common patterns in the examples: "se muere" (from "morirse" = to die / be dying), "se compró" (from "comprarse" = to buy oneself / buy), "se parece" (from "parecerse" = to look like / resemble), "se unió" (from "unirse" = to join), "se va" (from "irse" = to leave/go away). In sentences like these, you can often translate "mi hermano" as the subject "my brother" and treat "se" as part of the verb.
target_language_example: Mi hermano se levanta temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: My brother gets up early every day.

meaning: "my brother lives in" (followed by a place).
additional_notes: Used to say where your brother lives. After "en" you can use a city (Boston), a country (Inglaterra), or a more general place (el extranjero = abroad). To add duration, Spanish often uses "desde hace + time" or simply "hace + time": "Mi hermano vive en Inglaterra desde hace/hace más de treinta años" = he has lived in England for more than 30 years.
target_language_example: Mi hermano vive en Madrid desde hace cinco años.
native_language_example: My brother has lived in Madrid for five years.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your (female) child. It’s possessive: mi + hija. With a verb like "ver" (to see), you usually add the personal "a": "ver a mi hija".
target_language_example: Voy a recoger a mi hija a la escuela.
native_language_example: I'm going to pick up my daughter from school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your (male) child. In Spanish, family words change for gender: "mi hijo" = my son; "mi hija" = my daughter. You can use it as the subject ("Mi hijo..."), or after prepositions like "con" (with) and "por" (for/because of).
target_language_example: Mi hijo tiene diez años.
native_language_example: My son is ten years old.

additional_notes: Used to describe a fact, identity, job, or characteristic about your son. After "es" you can use a noun ("periodista"), an adjective ("honrado"), or a phrase ("chico para su edad"). Adjectives usually agree with "hijo" (masculine singular): "mi hijo es alto", "mi hijo es inteligente".
target_language_example: Mi hijo es muy tímido en clase.
native_language_example: My son is very shy in class.

meaning: "my son is" (talking about his current state, condition, or location).
additional_notes: Uses **estar**, which is commonly used for temporary states/conditions ("is tall", "is very thin", "is still alive") and for location ("is up a few cars", "is out there"). **Mi hijo** means "my son" (male child); for a daughter, say **mi hija está**. Often followed by an adjective (alto, delgado, vivo) or a place phrase (aquí, ahí, afuera, arriba).
target_language_example: No sé dónde está mi hijo; mi hijo está afuera con sus amigos.
native_language_example: I don't know where my son is; my son is outside with his friends.

meaning: "my home" (the place you live, often with an emotional sense of belonging).
additional_notes: "Hogar" can mean your physical home, but it often emphasizes warmth, family, and the feeling of belonging more than "casa". You can use "mi hogar" to talk about where you live now or a place you consider home (including your hometown or country).
target_language_example: Después de viajar, por fin vuelvo a mi hogar.
native_language_example: After traveling, I’m finally coming back home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your life when you were a child. It often appears with memories and nostalgia verbs like recordar (to remember), pensar en (to think about), or phrases like durante/todo el día de mi infancia (during/all through my childhood). It can be used in emotional descriptions: Mi infancia fue feliz/triste/difícil.
target_language_example: A veces extraño mi infancia.
native_language_example: Sometimes I miss my childhood.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the person who is your superior at work. In many workplaces you can also hear it used more generally for the person in charge (e.g., a leader), but the most common meaning is “boss.” If you’re speaking directly to your boss, you’d usually say "mi jefe" only when talking about them to someone else (not to their face).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo una reunión con mi jefe.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a meeting with my boss.

meaning: "my side" (my perspective, or on my team).
additional_notes:
Often used in set phrases:
- "mi lado de la historia" = my side/version of the story.
- "de mi lado" = on my side (supporting me, allied with me). With "estar" it means someone supports you ("¿Estás de mi lado?"). With "tener" it means you have someone’s support ("Te necesito de mi lado").
target_language_example: Quiero escuchar tu lado, pero también necesito decir mi lado de la historia.
native_language_example: I want to hear your side, but I also need to tell my side of the story.

additional_notes: Used to say what your first language is. Spanish often uses the article with languages after “ser” (el turco, el japonés, el portugués), though in some contexts you may also hear it without the article (Mi lengua materna es turco). Make sure the language name agrees in gender/number when needed.
target_language_example: Mi lengua materna es el inglés, pero también hablo español.
native_language_example: My native language is English, but I also speak Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your mother. "Madre" is a bit more neutral/formal; in everyday speech many people also say "mi mamá" (more common and affectionate). Use "mi" before a singular family member (mi madre, mi padre).
target_language_example: Mi madre trabaja en un hospital.
native_language_example: My mother works in a hospital.

additional_notes: Used to describe your mother with a profession (often without an article: "Mi madre es profesora"), an adjective ("Mi madre es activa"), or nationality/origin ("Mi madre es griega"). You can also add more information after it (e.g., family relationships or job type).
target_language_example: Mi madre es enfermera.
native_language_example: My mother is a nurse.

meaning: "my mother is" (using estar: location or a state/condition).
additional_notes: Use "mi madre está" with "estar" to talk about where your mother is (location) or how she is (health, mood, condition): "Mi madre está muy bien." You can also use it with opinions/stances using expressions like "estar en contra de" (to be against). "Mi madre está en el cielo" is a common, polite way to say someone has passed away (literally "in heaven").
target_language_example: Mi madre está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: My mother is at home now.

additional_notes: Used to say that your mother isn’t available because she’s doing something. Often followed by a gerund to say what she’s busy doing (e.g., "está ocupada cocinando" = "she’s busy cooking") or by a place with "en" (e.g., "está ocupada en la cocina" = "she’s busy in the kitchen"). "Ocupada" agrees with "madre" (female); for a man you’d say "mi padre está ocupado."
target_language_example: Ahora no puede venir; mi madre está ocupada trabajando.
native_language_example: She can’t come now; my mother is busy working.

meaning: “my mother … me” (my mom does something to/for me).
additional_notes: Often used with the pronoun **me** before the verb to show that **I** am the person affected by the action. In sentences like *Mi madre me regaló… / me preparó… / me regañó*, **me** usually means **“to me/for me”** (indirect object), though with some verbs it can be closer to **“me”** as a direct object (e.g., *Mi madre me regañó* = “My mom scolded me”). Word order: **Mi madre me + verb**.
target_language_example: Mi madre me llamó anoche.
native_language_example: My mother called me last night.

meaning: "my mother made me (do something)" / "my mother made (something) for me."
additional_notes:
Used with two common patterns:
1) **Mi madre me hizo + infinitive** = she *made/forced* me do something: *Mi madre me hizo estudiar*.
2) **Mi madre me hizo + noun** = she *made* something (often handmade) for me: *Mi madre me hizo un vestido*.
In both cases, **me** means “to/for me.”
target_language_example: Mi madre me hizo terminar la tarea antes de salir.
native_language_example: My mother made me finish my homework before going out.

additional_notes: Past tense statement using the verb "morir" (to die) in the preterite: "murió" = "(she) died" (a completed event). Often used with time expressions like "cuando..." (when...) or "hace..." (ago).
target_language_example: Mi madre murió en 2018.
native_language_example: My mother died in 2018.

additional_notes: "Mi madre" means "my mother." The "se" is a very common little word that goes with certain verbs: (1) reflexive actions (she does something to herself: "se estaba preparando" = she was getting herself ready), (2) change of state/emotion ("se alegrará" = she’ll be happy/glad), and (3) verbs that simply require "se" ("se preocupa" = she worries). In English, "se" is often not translated as a separate word.
target_language_example: Mi madre se levanta temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: My mother gets up early every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your suitcase/luggage. Common in travel situations (airports, hotels). Often appears with verbs like robar (to steal), llevar (to carry/take), dejar (to leave), and with location phrases (aquí/allá). "Mi maleta está hecha" means "My suitcase is packed."
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mi maleta? No la encuentro.
native_language_example: Have you seen my suitcase? I can’t find it.

additional_notes: A common, affectionate way to say “my mother.” “Mamá” is used much more in everyday speech than the more formal “madre.” You can swap the possessive to talk about other people’s moms (e.g., “tu mamá” = your mom, “su mamá” = his/her/their mom).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi mamá esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my mom tonight.

meaning: "My mom (to/for) me..." (introduces an action your mom did for you or to you).
additional_notes: Used when "mi mamá" is the subject and "me" is an object pronoun. With many verbs (like comprar, hacer, dar), "me" is often an indirect object meaning "to me" or "for me": "Mi mamá me compró..." = "My mom bought me..." / "bought ... for me." With other verbs, "me" can be a direct object meaning "me" (e.g., "Mi mamá me llamó" = "My mom called me").
target_language_example: Mi mamá me hizo la cena ayer.
native_language_example: My mom made me dinner yesterday.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mi** (my) + **mano** (hand). Used for physical touch/holding and also in set expressions like **tomar/agarrar mi mano** (“take/hold my hand”). Note: **mano** is feminine in Spanish, so adjectives agree: *mi mano derecha/izquierda*.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes sostener mi mano un momento?
native_language_example: Can you hold my hand for a moment?

additional_notes: Used by a woman to refer to her spouse. Often appears with the verb “ser” (identity: “Mi marido es alemán”) or “estar” (temporary states/mood: “Mi marido está de muy buen humor hoy”).
target_language_example: Mi marido trabaja desde casa los lunes.
native_language_example: My husband works from home on Mondays.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your closest female friend. You can also say "mi mejor amigo" for a male friend. "Mejor" is the comparative form of "bueno" (good), so it’s literally "my better friend" → "my best friend."
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi mejor amiga esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my best friend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the closest friend. For a female friend, say "mi mejor amiga". In Spanish you can drop the subject pronoun: "Es mi mejor amigo" = "He is my best friend."
target_language_example: Él es mi mejor amigo desde la escuela.
native_language_example: He has been my best friend since school.

additional_notes: Refers to your thoughts, memory, imagination, or mental state. Common in expressions like "liberar mi mente" (to free my mind), "mi mente está en blanco" (my mind is blank), and with verbs like "venir a mi mente" / "vino a mi mente" meaning "to come to mind".
target_language_example: Necesito descansar; mi mente no para.
native_language_example: I need to rest; my mind won’t stop.

additional_notes: Literally means “my woman,” but in everyday Spanish it commonly refers to your wife (especially when speaking about her to others). Depending on the country and context, it can sometimes also mean “my girlfriend/partner,” so if you want to be very explicit you can say "mi esposa" (my wife).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi mujer para avisarle que llego tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my wife to let her know I’m arriving late.

additional_notes: Means a typewriter that belongs to the speaker. It uses the possessive adjective "mi" (my) + the noun phrase "máquina de escribir" (typewriter). "De escribir" literally means "of writing" (a machine for writing).
target_language_example: Mi máquina de escribir está en el escritorio.
native_language_example: My typewriter is on the desk.

additional_notes: "Nieto" means a grandson (male grandchild). For a granddaughter, use "mi nieta". It’s used to talk about your child’s child. In Spanish, family words are often used with a possessive like "mi" (my), "tu" (your), "su" (his/her/their).
target_language_example: Mi nieto vive con mis hijos.
native_language_example: My grandson lives with my children.

additional_notes: Used to say who you are (“Mi nombre es…”), or to refer to your name in general (written somewhere, on a list, etc.). In “en mi nombre,” it means “in my name / on my behalf.”
target_language_example: Hola, mi nombre es Laura.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Laura.

additional_notes: A common, polite way to introduce yourself. Often used with "Hola" (Hello): "Hola, mi nombre es..." In everyday conversation you can also say "Me llamo..." (I’m called/I’m named...).
target_language_example: Hola, mi nombre es Ana.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Ana.

meaning: "my girlfriend" (or "my bride" in a wedding context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “my girlfriend” (your female romantic partner). It can also mean “my fiancée/bride” when talking about marriage or a wedding (novio/novia = engaged couple or bride/groom). Used with a feminine partner; for a male partner, say “mi novio.”
target_language_example: Ella es mi novia desde hace dos años.
native_language_example: She’s been my girlfriend for two years.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male romantic partner. "Novio" can mean "boyfriend" (or "fiancé" if you’re engaged), so context matters. The feminine form is "mi novia" (my girlfriend).
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi novio esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to have dinner with my boyfriend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to give or refer to your personal phone number. Often appears with verbs like dar (to give), pedir (to ask for), or estar (to be located): “Te doy mi número de teléfono” (I’ll give you my phone number), “Me pidió mi número de teléfono” (He asked me for my phone number). You can swap the possessive: tu/su/nuestro número de teléfono.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres mi número de teléfono?
native_language_example: Do you want my phone number?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s office or workspace (a room at work, or a home office). It’s possessive: mi (my) + oficina (office). Often used with estar/ser for location or identification: “Está en mi oficina” (It’s in my office) / “Esta es mi oficina” (This is my office).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo una reunión en mi oficina.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a meeting in my office.

additional_notes: Used to give your personal view or judgment. Often appears after verbs like pedir (to ask for): "Me pidieron mi opinión." You can also use it in the pattern "Mi opinión es..." to compare or state your view.
target_language_example: En mi opinión, es una buena idea.
native_language_example: In my opinion, it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mi (my) + padre (father). Often used with family members: mi madre (my mother), mis padres (my parents), mi papá (my dad, more informal). You can also say el padre (the father) when not talking about your own.
target_language_example: Mi padre trabaja en el centro.
native_language_example: My father works downtown.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past tense (era) to describe what your father was like, his profession/role, or a past state/background description. Often followed by a noun or adjective: “Mi padre era escritor / un gran hombre”.
target_language_example: Mi padre era maestro cuando yo era niño.
native_language_example: My father was a teacher when I was a child.

additional_notes: Used to describe your father with an adjective or noun. With jobs/roles, Spanish often drops the article: "Mi padre es profesor" (not *un profesor*). With other nouns, you usually include an article or other determiner: "Mi padre es un poco anticuado" / "Mi padre es un diccionario ambulante".
target_language_example: Mi padre es muy paciente.
native_language_example: My father is very patient.

additional_notes: Used to describe your father with an adjective or noun after it (e.g., “un hombre honrado/noble/orgulloso/práctico”). You can swap “padre” for another person (mi madre/mi hermano) and/or change the description: “Mi padre es médico.”
target_language_example: Mi padre es un hombre amable.
native_language_example: My father is a kind man.

meaning: "my father is" (using *estar* for location or a temporary state/condition).
additional_notes: Use **mi padre está** with **estar** to talk about where your father is (**está en casa**, **está afuera**) or how he is/what condition he’s in (**está ocupado**, **está interesado en...**). For more permanent characteristics, Spanish often uses **ser** instead (*Mi padre es alto* = “My father is tall”).
target_language_example: Mi padre está cansado hoy.
native_language_example: My father is tired today.

additional_notes: Used when your father does something to/for you. In Spanish, the pronoun **me** usually goes **before** the conjugated verb: *Mi padre me ayudó* (“My father helped me”). It can be a **direct object** (“me” = the person receiving the action, e.g., *me mima*) or an **indirect object** (“to/for me,” e.g., *me hizo un almuerzo*, *me llevó*).
target_language_example: Mi padre me llamó esta mañana.
native_language_example: My father called me this morning.

additional_notes: A complete sentence using the preterite (murió) to talk about a finished event in the past. Often used with time expressions like "hace tres aos" (three years ago) or "cuando yo tena..." (when I was...).
target_language_example: Mi padre murió en 2018.
native_language_example: My father died in 2018.

meaning: "my father doesn't / my dad doesn't" (introduces a negative statement about your father).
additional_notes: "Mi padre" means "my father" (you can also say "mi papá" for "my dad"). "No" goes before the verb to make it negative: "Mi padre no bebe" = "My father doesn't drink." Often used with "ni... ni..." to mean "neither... nor...": "no bebe ni fuma" = "doesn't drink or smoke."
target_language_example: Mi padre no trabaja los domingos.
native_language_example: My father doesn't work on Sundays.

meaning: "my father" + "se" (a pronoun used with many verbs; often like "my father *got/left/recovered*...").
additional_notes: "Mi padre" = "my father." The "se" here is a pronoun that goes with *pronominal/reflexive* verbs (verbs that commonly appear with "se"). It doesn’t translate as a separate word in English in many cases, but it’s required in Spanish and can change the verb’s meaning: **enterar** = to inform vs **enterarse (de)** = to find out; **retirar** = to withdraw something vs **retirarse** = to retire/step away; **recuperar** = to recover something vs **recuperarse** = to recover (get better). Word order: subject + se + verb ("Mi padre se enterará...").
target_language_example: Mi padre se fue a casa temprano.
native_language_example: My father went home early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your father possessing/owning something, or having something as a characteristic. "Tiene" is the 3rd-person singular form of "tener" (to have). Often followed by a noun: "Mi padre tiene un restaurante."
target_language_example: Mi padre tiene dos perros.
native_language_example: My father has two dogs.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **ir** (“to go”) in the **he/she/you (formal)** form: **va**. Common patterns: **va a + place** (Mi padre va a París), **va en + transport** (va en bici / en bicicleta), and **va rumbo a + destination** (“is headed toward”).
target_language_example: Mi padre va al supermercado después del trabajo.
native_language_example: My father goes to the supermarket after work.

meaning: my father and my mother (my parents).
additional_notes: A straightforward way to refer to both of your parents together. Often you can also just say "mis padres" = "my parents". The verb that follows is usually plural (e.g., "Mi padre y mi madre estaban...").
target_language_example: Voy a visitar a mi padre y mi madre este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my father and mother this weekend.

additional_notes: "Papá" is a common, warm way to say "dad" (often more casual than "padre"). Use it with possessives like "mi" (my), "tu" (your), "su" (his/her/their). It can be the subject ("Mi papá es...") or show possession with "de" ("Era de mi papá" = "It was my dad's").
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi papá hoy.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my dad today.

meaning: "my dad" + "(to/for) me" (he did something to me or for me).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to say what your dad did, with "me" showing that *you* are the person affected. The "me" can mean he did something *to you* (Mi papá me mandó… = My dad sent/ordered me…) or *for you* (Mi papá me compró… = My dad bought me…). It’s very common with verbs like "dijo" (told), "compró" (bought), "regaló" (gave as a gift), "mandó" (ordered/sent).
target_language_example: Mi papá me ayudó con la tarea.
native_language_example: My dad helped me with my homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the portion that belongs to you (your share of something) or the responsibility/task you are supposed to do (“I did my part”). In music or performance, it can also mean “my part” (the part you play/sing): “No va a tocar mi parte.”
target_language_example: Yo ya hice mi parte; ahora te toca a ti.
native_language_example: I already did my part; now it’s your turn.

additional_notes: Use it to say what you do (or what you spend time on) for fun. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (leer, pintar, nadar) or by a noun (la fotografía, mi acuario).
target_language_example: Mi pasatiempo es cocinar comida italiana los fines de semana.
native_language_example: My hobby is cooking Italian food on weekends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your hobby. You can add what you collect right after: "Mi pasatiempo es coleccionar monedas" (coins), "...botellas" (bottles), "...insectos" (insects). Often you can also say "Me gusta coleccionar..." (I like to collect...).
target_language_example: Mi pasatiempo es coleccionar sellos.
native_language_example: My hobby is collecting stamps.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the country you belong to (by nationality/citizenship) or feel you come from. It’s a possessive phrase: mi (my) + país (country). In Spanish, the possessive changes with the owner (mi/mis, tu/tus, su/sus, nuestro/a/s, etc.), not with the noun’s gender.
target_language_example: Echo de menos mi país cuando estoy en el extranjero.
native_language_example: I miss my country when I'm abroad.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: mi (my) + perro (dog). Use it to talk about your own dog. In insults/jokes, comparing someone to "mi perro" can be rude (e.g., implying they look ugly).
target_language_example: Mi perro es muy tranquilo en casa.
native_language_example: My dog is very calm at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your cousin who is a woman/girl. Spanish distinguishes gender: mi primo = my (male) cousin, mi prima = my (female) cousin. Often used with a name in apposition: “Mi prima, Sandra.”
target_language_example: Mi prima vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun to say it’s the first one you have/had (mi primer hijo, mi primer viaje). It’s the shortened form of "primero" that’s used before a masculine noun; with feminine nouns use "mi primera" (mi primera vez).
target_language_example: Mi primer día en la universidad fue emocionante.
native_language_example: My first day at university was exciting.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male cousin. For a female cousin, use "mi prima". You can also add a name after it: "mi primo Balin" = "my cousin Balin".
target_language_example: Mi primo vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something/someone belongs to you or is personally yours. It must agree with a feminine noun: mi propia casa, mi propia familia. For masculine nouns use **mi propio** (mi propio plan). Often adds emphasis like “my very own.” It also appears in set phrases like **de mi propia cosecha** (“of my own making / my own invention”) and **a mi propia salud** (“to my own health,” as in a toast).
target_language_example: Quiero abrir mi propia tienda.
native_language_example: I want to open my own shop.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs to you personally or is done by you (not borrowed, shared, or someone else’s). It agrees with the noun: mi propio + masculine singular noun (mi propio plan), mi propia + feminine singular noun (mi propia casa), mis propios/mis propias for plural.
target_language_example: Necesito mi propio espacio para estudiar.
native_language_example: I need my own space to study.

additional_notes: Means “my watch” when you’re talking about a wristwatch, and “my clock” when it’s a clock (for example, an alarm clock). Used with verbs like ser/estar/parecer (“is/seems”), adelantarse/atrasarse (“runs fast/slow”), and arreglar (“to fix”).
target_language_example: No encuentro mi reloj; creo que lo dejé en casa.
native_language_example: I can’t find my watch; I think I left it at home.

additional_notes: Often refers to a personal goal or hope (not only a dream you have while sleeping). You can use it with verbs like "cumplir" (to achieve/fulfill) or in expressions like "hacerse realidad" / "convertirse en realidad" (to come true).
target_language_example: Mi sueño es viajar por el mundo.
native_language_example: My dream is to travel the world.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal dream, hope, or long-term goal, followed by a noun or (very commonly) an infinitive verb: "Mi sueño es vivir..." / "Mi sueño es conocer...". In everyday speech, "sueño" can also mean "sleepiness," but in this structure it means a dream/aspiration.
target_language_example: Mi sueño es tener mi propio negocio algún día.
native_language_example: My dream is to have my own business someday.

additional_notes: Use this to talk about an ambition or long-term goal. After "convertirme en" you usually say a noun for a job/role/identity (often with an article: "un/una"), e.g., "mi sueño es convertirme en un artista". "Convertirme" means “to become” (literally “to convert myself into”).
target_language_example: Mi sueño es convertirme en ingeniera.
native_language_example: My dream is to become an engineer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a personal dream or long-term goal. Follow it with what/where you want to study (e.g., “Mi sueño es estudiar en el extranjero / en Madrid”). In Spanish, “mi sueño es + infinitive” is a common pattern to express “my dream is to + verb.”
target_language_example: Mi sueño es estudiar medicina algún día.
native_language_example: My dream is to study medicine someday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an aspiration for the future. Follow it with a profession/role (often with an article: ser médico / ser un bombero) or another identity. You can swap in other nouns too: Mi sueño es ser famoso/a. Common variation: "Mi sueño es llegar a ser..." (to become).
target_language_example: Mi sueño es ser veterinaria y trabajar con animales grandes.
native_language_example: My dream is to be a veterinarian and work with large animals.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to school homework. It’s made of mi (my) + tarea (task/homework). You’ll also hear "hacer la tarea" = to do homework. With animals, both "El perro comió mi tarea" and "Mi perro se comió mi tarea" mean the dog ate it; "se comió" often emphasizes that it ate it up.
target_language_example: No puedo salir; todavía no termino mi tarea.
native_language_example: I can’t go out; I still haven’t finished my homework.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mi" (my) before the noun. In context it usually means a mobile phone. Common with "estar" for states/conditions: "Mi teléfono está mojado" (is wet) and "Mi teléfono está muerto" (is dead = has no battery / isn’t working).
target_language_example: No encuentro mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I can’t find my phone.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mi" (my) with "trabajo" (job/work). "Trabajo" can mean your occupation (job) or the tasks you do (work), depending on context. Often used to talk about doing your duties: "hacer mi trabajo" = "do my job."
target_language_example: Hoy tengo mucho, pero voy a hacer mi trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I have a lot, but I'm going to do my job.

meaning: 'my job/work is…' (used to describe your job or what your job involves).
additional_notes: Often followed by an adjective (Mi trabajo es aburrido/sencillo) or by an infinitive to say your responsibility (Mi trabajo es mantener el orden). You can also use it more broadly to mean 'my task/role is…' in a specific situation, not only your employment.
target_language_example: Mi trabajo es ayudar a los clientes.
native_language_example: My job is to help customers.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your aunt (your parent’s sister, or sometimes your uncle’s wife). You can change the possessive: mi tía (my aunt), tu tía (your aunt), su tía (his/her/your formal/their aunt). The accent matters: tía (aunt) vs tia (not correct).
target_language_example: Mi tía vive en México.
native_language_example: My aunt lives in Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your uncle (your mother’s or father’s brother, or your aunt’s husband). You can swap in other possessives: mi (my), tu (your), su (his/her/your formal/their), nuestro (our), etc. In Spanish, family words often use an article when speaking generally (e.g., "Mi tío" = my uncle; "El tío" = the uncle / my uncle in some contexts).
target_language_example: Mi tío vive en México, pero nos visita en verano.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in Mexico, but he visits us in the summer.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence when your uncle is the subject, and **me** is the object pronoun (usually an **indirect object**: “to me/for me”). It commonly appears with verbs like **dar** (to give), **regalar** (to gift), **llevar** (to take), etc.: *Mi tío me dio...* = “My uncle gave me...”. Spanish uses the pronoun even if English might use “to me/for me.”
target_language_example: Mi tío me compró un helado.
native_language_example: My uncle bought me an ice cream.

additional_notes: Uses the indirect object pronoun “me” (“to me”) and the preterite tense “dio” (he gave), from the verb “dar” (to give). You usually add what was given after it: “Mi tío me dio + [something]”.
target_language_example: Mi tío me dio dinero para el viaje.
native_language_example: My uncle gave me money for the trip.

additional_notes: Use this to say where your uncle lives. "Vivir en" is followed by a location (country, city, neighborhood, etc.). With masculine singular places that take an article, you often use "en el" (e.g., "en el centro").
target_language_example: Mi tío vive en Barcelona.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in Barcelona.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your life in general (your experiences, situation, or how things are going). It also appears in emotional phrases like “arruinó mi vida” (“ruined my life”) or “pasar mi vida con…” (“spend my life with…”). In some contexts, especially in conversation, it can also be used as an affectionate way to address someone (“mi vida” = “my love”), but that’s not the meaning in the examples.
target_language_example: No quiero cambiar mi vida ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to change my life right now.

meaning: "my last day" (the final day somewhere or doing something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the final day of a period of time in a place or situation: mi último día en la escuela/en el trabajo/aquí. The adjective último changes for gender/number: mi última noche (my last night), mis últimos días (my last days).
target_language_example: Hoy es mi último día en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Today is my last day at work.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning you have just one person/thing you’re counting on. Often used with forms of "ser" (eres/es/son/sois): "Tú eres mi única esperanza" = "You are my only hope." "Única" agrees with the feminine noun "esperanza."
target_language_example: Sin ti, no tengo nada: eres mi única esperanza.
native_language_example: Without you, I have nothing: you’re my only hope.

additional_notes: Used to say you have just one friend. It agrees with the noun: mi única amiga (female friend); mis únicos amigos / mis únicas amigas (plural). Often used for emphasis in emotional contexts (loneliness, closeness).
target_language_example: No salgo mucho; eres mi único amigo.
native_language_example: I don’t go out much; you’re my only friend.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tener (“to have”), tenerle (“to be afraid of”), superar (“to overcome”), and conquistar (“to conquer”). You may also hear: (tener) miedo a la oscuridad / (tenerle) miedo a la oscuridad.
target_language_example: De niño, tenía miedo a la oscuridad.
native_language_example: As a kid, I was afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Used after tener/sentir (and similar verbs) to say what you fear: tener miedo de + noun (miedo de las arañas) or de + infinitive (miedo de herir sus sentimientos). With people, it can mean being afraid of someone: miedo de mi jefe. In many contexts, Spanish also uses "miedo a" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Tengo miedo de hablar en público.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to a club or organization. Often with verbs like ser (“to be”) or hacerse (“to become/join”): «Soy miembro del club» / «Me hice miembro del club». You can also specify the type of club: «miembro del club de música / tenis».
target_language_example: Mi hermano es miembro del club desde 2020.
native_language_example: My brother has been a club member since 2020.

meaning: "members of the" (masculine singular: del = de + el).
additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to a group, organization, or body. It appears before a masculine singular noun with el (el comité, el Congreso, el gabinete, el consejo). For feminine singular, use "miembros de la" (de + la), and for plural, "miembros de los/las".
target_language_example: Somos miembros del club desde 2022.
native_language_example: We’ve been members of the club since 2022.

additional_notes: Used to set the background of an event that happened during an ongoing action. "Mientras" = "while" and "caminaba" is the imperfect tense of "caminar" (to walk), suggesting something in progress in the past. "por el" usually means "through the" or "along the" (masculine singular), and it needs a noun after it (e.g., "bosque", "parque", "río"). For a feminine noun, use "por la" (e.g., "por la calle").
target_language_example: Mientras caminaba por el centro, empezó a llover.
native_language_example: While I was walking through downtown, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happened during the time a person was asleep. It’s commonly followed by an action in the past (often pretérito): *pasó/hice/ocurrió… mientras dormía*. You can change the subject: *mientras dormías* (you), *mientras dormía* (he/she/I—context tells who), *mientras dormíamos* (we).
target_language_example: Me desperté varias veces mientras dormía.
native_language_example: I woke up several times while I was sleeping.

additional_notes: Uses **mientras** (“while”) to show two actions happening at the same time. **Leía** is the imperfect past of *leer* (“to read”), suggesting an ongoing/background action. The subject is understood from context (e.g., *mientras leía...* = “while he/she/I was reading...”); add it if needed: *mientras él/ella/yo leía la carta*.
target_language_example: Me quedé en silencio mientras leía la carta.
native_language_example: I stayed quiet while I was reading the letter.

additional_notes: Often used to contrast two people/things or two situations: "X..., mientras que Y..." = "X..., whereas Y...". It can also mean "while" in the time sense: "...mientras que yo estaba fuera" = "...while I was out."
target_language_example: Yo trabajo de noche, mientras que mi esposo trabaja de día.
native_language_example: I work at night, whereas my spouse works during the day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the time before another event happens, or at the same time as something else. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence and followed by a comma: “Mientras tanto, …”.
target_language_example: Mientras tanto, voy preparando la cena.
native_language_example: Meanwhile, I’ll start preparing dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money: 1,000 dollars. In Spanish, large numbers are often written with a space or a period (1.000 or 1 000) rather than a comma. You can also use it with time phrases like “por día” (per day).
target_language_example: Ese celular cuesta mil dólares.
native_language_example: That cellphone costs a thousand dollars.

additional_notes: In most Spanish-speaking contexts, "mil millones" is the unambiguous way to say 1,000,000,000 (a thousand millions). This avoids confusion because "un billón" in Spanish usually means 1,000,000,000,000 (a trillion in US English). Used in news, money, and statistics: "mil millones de dólares" = "one billion dollars."
target_language_example: La empresa vale mil millones de dólares.
native_language_example: The company is worth one billion dollars.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express a quantity of 1,000,000,000. In Spanish, "mil millones" = 1 billion (not "un billón," which usually means 1 trillion in most Spanish-speaking countries). Often followed by a currency, people, years, etc.: "mil millones de dólares", "mil millones de habitantes".
target_language_example: El gobierno invertirá mil millones de euros en el proyecto.
native_language_example: The government will invest one billion euros in the project.

additional_notes: Used to talk about prices, costs, allowances, or amounts of money in Japanese yen. You often see it with another number before it: dos mil yenes (2,000 yen), diez mil yenes (10,000 yen), cincuenta mil yenes (50,000 yen). With larger numbers, Spanish also uses mil as part of the number phrase: cinco mil yenes = 5,000 yen.
target_language_example: Este bolso cuesta tres mil yenes.
native_language_example: This bag costs three thousand yen.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to express a very large number: miles de años (thousands of years), miles de cosas (thousands of things). Often implies “a lot,” not an exact count.
target_language_example: Hay miles de personas en el concierto.
native_language_example: There are thousands of people at the concert.

additional_notes: Uses the plural noun "miles" (thousands) + "de" + a plural noun to express a large number. Common with past-tense events: "Miles de personas fueron/visitaron...". You can swap "personas" for other nouns: "miles de dólares", "miles de años".
target_language_example: Miles de personas asistieron al concierto.
native_language_example: Thousands of people attended the concert.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about an amount: millones de años (millions of years), millones de estrellas (millions of stars). It agrees only in the word millones (plural) and uses de before the noun. In Spanish you can also drop de when a number directly modifies a noun (vendió millones de copias).
target_language_example: Hay millones de personas que usan internet todos los días.
native_language_example: There are millions of people who use the internet every day.

additional_notes: Used to state amounts of money. With numbers: “dos/tres/diez millones de dólares” = “two/three/ten million dollars.” In Spanish, “millón” is singular and “millones” is plural, and it’s commonly followed by “de” before a noun like “dólares” (or “euros,” etc.).
target_language_example: Ganó millones de dólares con su empresa.
native_language_example: He/She made millions of dollars with his/her company.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a very large number of stars, often in astronomy contexts. The pattern is common: “millones de + plural noun” (millions of + noun). You may also hear “miles de millones de estrellas” for “billions of stars.”
target_language_example: En esta galaxia hay millones de estrellas.
native_language_example: In this galaxy there are millions of stars.

additional_notes: Used to talk about very large numbers of people. Often appears in big-picture statements (news, statistics, disasters). You can add modifiers like “muchas” or “varias” (muchas/varias millones de personas), and you can specify context with “en el mundo / en este país / en la ciudad”.
target_language_example: Millones de personas vieron el partido en la televisión.
native_language_example: Millions of people watched the game on TV.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to express quantity: "un millón de + noun" (un millón de palabras = a million words). In everyday speech it’s also an exaggeration meaning “a lot” (Tengo un millón de cosas que hacer = I have tons of things to do). Common emphatic phrase: "Ni en un millón de años" = “Not in a million years.”
target_language_example: Tengo un millón de cosas que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I have a ton of things to do today.

meaning: “a million dollars” (literal); also “great/amazing” in the phrase sentirse/verse como un millón de dólares.
additional_notes: Literally it refers to the amount of money: un millón de dólares (1,000,000 dollars), medio millón de dólares (half a million dollars). Figuratively, in expressions like “Me siento como un millón de dólares” or “(Me) veo como un millón de dólares,” it means you feel or look really good.
target_language_example: Después de dormir bien, me siento como un millón de dólares.
native_language_example: After sleeping well, I feel great.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money in Japanese currency. You can swap in other numbers (dos millones de yenes) or fractions (medio millón de yenes = half a million yen). With large figures, Spanish often uses singular “millón” after “un”: un millón de yenes.
target_language_example: Necesito un millón de yenes para el viaje.
native_language_example: I need a million yen for the trip.

meaning: Look, no… / Listen, no… (used to start a refusal or correction).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a sentence to get attention and introduce a negative response (disagreeing, refusing, or clarifying). Often sounds a bit firm or defensive depending on tone. Very common in spoken Spanish; you can also hear “Mira, es que…” or “Oye, no…”.
target_language_example: Mira, no puedo ir hoy; tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: Look, I can’t go today; I have a lot of work.

additional_notes: Imperative phrase used to tell someone to observe their surroundings (often to notice what’s happening or what’s nearby). You can also say "Mira alrededor" (less common) or "Mira a su alrededor" (formal: "look around you," addressing usted).
target_language_example: Antes de decidir, mira a tu alrededor y piensa.
native_language_example: Before you decide, look around you and think.

additional_notes: Used to draw someone’s attention to something you’re about to show or point out. Common in conversation as a lead-in (e.g., Ahora/Bien/Pero/Vaya, mira esto...). You can also use it to express surprise: “Mira esto, ¡un cigarro entero!”
target_language_example: Ven aquí y mira esto: encontré tus llaves.
native_language_example: Come here and look at this: I found your keys.

additional_notes: Used to call someone’s attention to something you’re about to show or point out: “Mira lo que he encontrado.” With verbs like “te digo,” it can also mean “listen to what I’m telling you / pay attention,” not necessarily literally “look.” Often followed by a verb in the present perfect (he encontrado, ha hecho) or another clause.
target_language_example: ¡Mira lo que compré en el mercado!
native_language_example: Look what I bought at the market!

meaning: "Watch what you're doing!" / "Look what you're doing!"
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to be careful or to scold them because they’re making a mistake or causing a problem. It's an informal/neutral command in the tú form (mira = "look/watch"). You can also hear variations like “¡Mira lo que has hecho!” (Look what you’ve done!).
target_language_example: ¡Mira lo que haces! Vas a romper el vaso.
native_language_example: Watch what you're doing! You're going to break the glass.

meaning: "Look what you’ve done." (said to blame or scold someone for the result of their actions).
additional_notes: Uses the informal command "mira" (look) plus "lo que has hecho" (what you have done). Often said in an annoyed or disappointed tone after something goes wrong. You can add words like "ahora" (now) for emphasis. In sentences like "Mira lo que has hecho a tu madre", it means "Look what you’ve done to your mother" (i.e., the effect you caused).
target_language_example: ¡Mira lo que has hecho! Ahora tenemos que limpiar todo.
native_language_example: Look what you’ve done! Now we have to clean everything.

meaning: “Look what … did/has done to him/her (or to you formal).”
additional_notes: Used to call someone’s attention to an effect or event involving a person. **Mira** is the tú imperative of *mirar* (“look”). **Lo que** means “what/that which.” **Le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her/to you (formal),” and it goes before the verb: *Mira lo que le pasó* (“Look what happened to him/her”). Often followed by verbs like *hacer* (do to), *pasar/suceder* (happen).
target_language_example: Mira lo que le pasó a tu hermana.
native_language_example: Look what happened to your sister.

additional_notes: Used to call someone’s attention to the result of an action involving them. It’s a common pattern: **Mira** (imperative “look”) + **lo que** (“what/that which”) + **te** (“to you/for you”) + a verb.
