With **hacer**, it often means “Look what he/they did to you.” With **traer**, it means “Look what I/they brought you.”
target_language_example: Mira lo que te compré.
native_language_example: Look what I bought you.

additional_notes: Used to point out who someone is or who has arrived/is present. Often expresses surprise, recognition, or irony (e.g., "Look who's being dramatic now"). Usually followed by a verb (mira quién ha venido, mira quién está ahí) or a clause (mira quién se pone dramático).
target_language_example: ¡Mira quién apareció de repente!
native_language_example: Look who showed up all of a sudden!

additional_notes: A common spoken phrase when someone arrives or appears. It can be friendly and welcoming, but it’s also often used sarcastically/teasingly (like “Well, look who decided to show up”). You’ll often hear it with fillers like "bueno", "oye", "vaya".
target_language_example: Vaya, mira quién está aquí; ¡pensé que no venías!
native_language_example: Well, look who's here; I thought you weren’t coming!

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (mirando) to describe an action in progress (“was looking…”), or something you’re doing while another action happens (“Looking out the window, I saw…”). “Por la ventana” is the common way to say “out the window.” You can also say “mirar por la ventana” (infinitive) or “estar mirando por la ventana” (to be looking out the window).
target_language_example: Estaba mirando por la ventana cuando empezó a llover.
native_language_example: I was looking out the window when it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used with the personal "a" when the direct object is a specific person (or personified being): "mirar a Ugolin", "mirar a los niños". With things, the "a" is usually not used: "mirar el reloj" (to look at the clock).
target_language_example: No dejaba de mirar a Ugolin.
native_language_example: He wouldn’t stop looking at Ugolin.

meaning: to look (someone) in the eyes; to make eye contact.
additional_notes: Used to express making direct eye contact with someone. Common in requests/commands like "Mírame a los ojos" or "No me mires a los ojos." You can specify the person with an indirect object pronoun: "mírame" (look at me), "míralo" (look at him), etc. As an infinitive phrase, it often appears after another verb (e.g., "quiero", "puedes", "debes").
target_language_example: Tienes que mirar a los ojos cuando hables con alguien.
native_language_example: You have to look people in the eyes when you speak with someone.

additional_notes: Used when you turn your head/eyes to see what’s nearby or to take in a place. Common in directions and when exploring: “Vamos a mirar alrededor” (Let’s look around).
target_language_example: Cuando llegues, puedes mirar alrededor y buscar la entrada.
native_language_example: When you arrive, you can look around and look for the entrance.

additional_notes: Used for physically directing your gaze upward (e.g., to the sky, a sign, the ceiling). In instructions, it can also mean to look at something located above (for example, on a page or screen). Often you’ll also hear: "mirar hacia arriba" (look upward).
target_language_example: Tienes que mirar arriba: hay un avión en el cielo.
native_language_example: You have to look up—there’s a plane in the sky.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want to find out or verify: mirar qué + verb/clause (e.g., mirar qué pasa = see what happens). You may also see it as an instruction in signs/notes using the infinitive (Mirar qué...) or as a command: Mira qué... / Mire qué... (Look what... / See what...).
target_language_example: Vamos a mirar qué opciones hay.
native_language_example: Let’s see what options there are.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "mirar" in 3rd person singular: "miró" = "he/she looked." "A su alrededor" means "around (him/her) / all around (them)." Often used when someone checks their surroundings, sometimes with adverbs like "frenéticamente" (frantically).
target_language_example: Miró a su alrededor y luego salió corriendo.
native_language_example: He looked around and then ran away.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "mirar hacia atrás". Used for a physical action (turning your head/body to see what’s behind you), and also figuratively meaning to think about the past (e.g., "nunca más miró hacia atrás" = he didn’t look back/regret it). Often appears with "sobre su hombro" (over his/her shoulder).
target_language_example: Cuando oyó un ruido, miró hacia atrás y vio a su amigo.
native_language_example: When he heard a noise, he looked back and saw his friend.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "mis" (my, plural) + "abuelos" (grandparents). It can refer to both grandparents together, or to grandparents in general. For an indirect object like "to my grandparents," use "a mis abuelos" (often with "les" as in "A mis abuelos nunca les gustó...").
target_language_example: Siempre llamo a mis abuelos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I always call my grandparents on weekends.

additional_notes: Plural of “mi amiga” (my female friend). “Mis” = my (plural), and “amigas” is the feminine plural form, used when the group is all women/girls (or a group of mixed genders that you’re referring to with feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Esta noche voy a cenar con mis amigas.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to have dinner with my (female) friends.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mis** = “my” (plural) + **amigos** = “friends” (masculine plural). **Amigos** can refer to a mixed-gender group; for an all-female group you can say **mis amigas**. It’s used to talk about your friends as a group or to introduce them (e.g., *Ven a ver a mis amigos*).
target_language_example: Esta noche voy a cenar con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to have dinner with my friends.

additional_notes: “Mis amigos” is the subject (“my friends”). “Me” is an object pronoun that comes before the verb and means the action is directed at you (the speaker): they congratulate me, invite me, are waiting for me, etc. In English you usually just say “My friends invited me…”, but in Spanish the “me” is required in these kinds of sentences.
target_language_example: Mis amigos me llamaron anoche.
native_language_example: My friends called me last night.

meaning: “my friends call me” (they refer to me as / my name is, to them).
additional_notes: Used to say what name or nickname people use for you. Pattern: [People] + me llaman + [name/nickname]. It can mean they literally phone you (“my friends call me”), but with a name after it, it usually means “they call me X.”
target_language_example: En el trabajo, mis amigos me llaman Dani.
native_language_example: At work, my friends call me Dani.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the people who are in your class at school or in a course. You can change the possessive to match the person: mis (my), tus (your), sus (his/her/their), nuestros (our). Singular: mi compañero/mi compañera de clase (my male/female classmate).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a estudiar con mis compañeros de clase.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to study with my classmates.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your belongings or personal items. In context it can mean physical objects (clothes, a bag, etc.) or more generally “my personal business/private matters” (e.g., “Don’t get into my stuff”). Often used with verbs like recoger (pick up), traer (bring), dejar (leave), or meterse en (mess with/get into).
target_language_example: Tengo que ir por mis cosas antes de irme.
native_language_example: I have to go get my things before I leave.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mis** (“my”, plural) + **hermanos** (“brothers”; can also mean “siblings/brothers” in mixed groups depending on context). Used to say who someone is to you (e.g., *Ellos son mis hermanos*) or to talk about your brothers in general (*Amo a mis hermanos*).
target_language_example: Voy a ver a mis hermanos este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to see my brothers this weekend.

additional_notes: "Mis" is the plural form of "my" (used with plural nouns). "Hijas" is the plural of "hija" (daughter). Use "mis hijas" when talking about your daughters; if you have one daughter, say "mi hija".
target_language_example: Voy a recoger a mis hijas a la escuela.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my daughters from school.

additional_notes: "Mis" means "my" (plural), and "hijos" can mean "sons" or "children" depending on context. Use it to talk about your kids in general or your sons specifically. For daughters only, say "mis hijas."
target_language_example: Mis hijos van a la escuela en autobús.
native_language_example: My kids go to school by bus.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mis" (my) with the plural noun "libros" (books). It agrees in number: "mi libro" (singular) vs. "mis libros" (plural). Often contrasted with other possessives: "tus libros" (your books), "sus libros" (his/her/their books), or with the possessive pronouns "los míos/los tuyos/los suyos" (mine/yours/his-hers-theirs).
target_language_example: No encuentro mis libros; ¿los viste?
native_language_example: I can’t find my books; did you see them?

additional_notes:
Literal meaning: your own hands (body part): "Mis manos están temblando" (My hands are shaking). It also appears in common expressions: 
- "(No) está en mis manos" = "It’s (not) in my hands" / "(I) can’t do anything about it".
- "De mis manos" can mean "from my hands" (someone took something away from you).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero la decisión final no está en mis manos.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but the final decision isn’t in my hands.

additional_notes: Literally the plural possessive phrase “my eyes.” Used both literally (opening your eyes, something getting in your eyes, seeing through someone’s eyes) and in the common expression “como a las niñas de mis ojos,” meaning “like the apple of my eye” (to protect/care for something very much).
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! Me entró polvo en mis ojos.
native_language_example: Careful! Dust got into my eyes.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: **mis** (my, plural) + **padres** (parents). It refers to both mother and father together. For one parent, use **mi padre** (my father) or **mi madre** (my mother).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mis padres esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my parents tonight.

meaning: "my parents" + "(to/for) me" (introduces what your parents do to you).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence where the subject is mis padres (“my parents”) and me is the object pronoun meaning “me” (often “to me” or “for me,” depending on the verb). It’s very common before verbs like dejan (let), dieron (gave), están esperando (are waiting for), prohibieron (forbade), etc. Example pattern: Mis padres me + verb + ...
target_language_example: Mis padres me compraron un regalo.
native_language_example: My parents bought me a gift.

additional_notes: You’ll often see this at the start of sentences with verbs that use **se**. With plural subjects like **mis padres**, **se** commonly shows a **reciprocal** action (they do it to each other), e.g. **se aman** = “they love each other,” **se conocieron** = “they met (each other).” It can also appear with certain verbs that are typically used with **se**, like **divorciarse** (to get divorced) and **separarse** (to separate).
target_language_example: Mis padres se ven todos los domingos.
native_language_example: My parents see each other every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify your parents. The verb "son" is from "ser" (to be) and is used with permanent/defining traits (nationality, identity, relationship) and many descriptions. Follow it with a name, an adjective, or a noun: "Mis padres son españoles / ancianos / médicos."
target_language_example: Mis padres son de México.
native_language_example: My parents are from Mexico.

additional_notes: Use this to say where your parents live. Follow it with a place name (Mis padres viven en Australia), a city (…en Kioto), or a general location with an article (…en el campo = in the countryside; …en la ciudad = in the city).
target_language_example: Mis padres viven en México, pero yo vivo en Canadá.
native_language_example: My parents live in Mexico, but I live in Canada.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **mis** = “my” (plural), **pies** = “feet” (plural of *pie*). Used for physical descriptions (*Mis pies están fríos*) and in expressions like **bajo mis pies** = “under my feet/beneath my feet.”
target_language_example: Después de caminar mucho, mis pies me duelen.
native_language_example: After walking a lot, my feet hurt.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis: doing something yourself, not someone else’s. It modifies a feminine plural noun: mis propias manos (“my own hands”), mis propias batallas (“my own battles”), mis propias cosas (“my own things”). With masculine plural nouns it becomes mis propios (e.g., mis propios problemas). Note: propia looks like English “proper,” but here it usually means “own.”
target_language_example: Quiero hacerlo con mis propias manos.
native_language_example: I want to do it with my own hands.

meaning: my own (emphasizing that they belong to me / I do them myself).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun (e.g., mis propios planes) to stress independence, personal ownership, or doing something without help. Singular forms are mi propio (masc.) and mi propia (fem.). Often appears with phrases like por mis propios esfuerzos (“by my own efforts”).
target_language_example: Prefiero tener mis propios objetivos y trabajar por mis propios medios.
native_language_example: I prefer to have my own goals and work by my own means.

additional_notes: Refers to dreams you have while sleeping or your hopes/aspirations for the future. It uses the possessive adjective "mis" (my) with the plural noun "sueños" (dreams). In phrases like "hacer realidad mis sueños", it means goals/wishes coming true.
target_language_example: Quiero cumplir mis sueños algún día.
native_language_example: I want to achieve my dreams someday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shoes that belong to you. It’s the plural possessive: mi (my) → mis (my, plural) + zapatos (shoes). Often appears as a full sentence in context (e.g., pointing: “Mis zapatos.” = “My shoes.”).
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mis zapatos?
native_language_example: Have you seen my shoes?

additional_notes: Used when someone in authority (a boss, officer, commander, etc.) is giving commands that must be followed. Common with verbs like **recibir** (to receive), **seguir** (to follow), **obedecer** (to obey), and **hacer caso a** (to pay attention to). In more formal or military-style speech you may also hear **a mis órdenes** meaning “at your service / ready to obey.”
target_language_example: Quiero que sigas mis órdenes al pie de la letra.
native_language_example: I want you to follow my orders exactly.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the same age as another person. It often appears with a possessive (mi/tu/su): “de mi misma edad” = “(someone) my age” / “the same age as me”, and with tener: “tiene mi misma edad” = “he/she is the same age as me.” Often paired with “más o menos” to mean “around/about the same age.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano y yo tenemos la misma edad.
native_language_example: My brother and I are the same age.

meaning: the same time; the same amount of time.
additional_notes: Used to compare timing or duration: el mismo tiempo que… = “the same time as… / the same amount of time as…”. With weather, it often appears as hacer el mismo tiempo (que…) = “to have the same weather (as…)”. You’ll also commonly see al mismo tiempo = “at the same time.”
target_language_example: Llegamos en el mismo tiempo que ellos.
native_language_example: We arrived in the same amount of time as them.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things are in, going to, or coming from an identical location. Very often appears with the article: "el mismo lugar" (to the same place / in the same place).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el mismo lugar de siempre.
native_language_example: See you at the same place as always.

meaning: 'half of' (an amount, size, distance, time, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to express 50% of something: la mitad de + noun/pronoun (la mitad de la habitación, la mitad de esa distancia). Often appears with “a” to mean “at the halfway point” or “half price”: a la mitad (halfway), a mitad de precio (at half price). It can also refer to the middle of a time period: a mitad de abril (mid-April).
target_language_example: Llegamos a la mitad del camino y descansamos.
native_language_example: We got halfway along the الطريق and rested.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening very late at night, while people are usually sleeping. Often used with "en": "en mitad de la noche" = "in the middle of the night." You may also hear "a mitad de la noche" with the same meaning. In Spanish, "mitad" = "half" and "noche" = "night".
target_language_example: Me desperté en mitad de la noche por un ruido.
native_language_example: I woke up in the middle of the night because of a noise.

meaning: in the middle of (the); halfway through (the).
additional_notes: Common in location and time/event contexts. For location: “en mitad del + [place]” = “in the middle of the + [place]” (e.g., en mitad del parque). For events/time periods: “a mitad del + [event/period]” = “halfway through the + [event/period]” (e.g., a mitad del concierto). Note: “del” is the contraction of “de + el”; with feminine/plural nouns it becomes “de la / de los / de las.” Often appears as “en mitad de” or “a mitad de,” depending on nuance.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en mitad del desierto.
native_language_example: We ran out of gas in the middle of the desert.

meaning: "moment of truth" (the decisive moment when you find out what’s really true or whether something will work).
additional_notes: Used when results are about to be revealed or a crucial test/decision is happening: an exam result, trying a plan, giving a presentation, asking an important question, etc. Often appears with verbs like "llegó" (it arrived) or "es" (it is): "Llegó el momento de la verdad."
target_language_example: Llegó el momento de la verdad: vamos a ver si el coche arranca.
native_language_example: The moment of truth has arrived: let’s see if the car starts.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the specific point in time when something happens. Often appears in patterns like "Es el momento en que..." (It’s the time when...) and "En el (mismo/este) momento en que..." (At the (same/this) moment when...). You can also say "Llegará un momento en que..." to mean "A time will come when...".
target_language_example: En el momento en que termine la reunión, te llamo.
native_language_example: The moment the meeting ends, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about coin collecting (coleccionar monedas antiguas). "Monedas" = coins; "antiguas" = old/ancient (feminine plural to match "monedas"). Depending on context, it can mean historical coins or just old coins.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo colecciona monedas antiguas desde hace años.
native_language_example: My grandpa has been collecting old coins for years.

meaning: to ride a bicycle; to bike.
additional_notes: Used with saber/enseñar/aprender to talk about having (or learning/teaching) the skill: “saber montar en bicicleta” (to know how to ride a bike), “aprender a montar en bicicleta” (to learn to ride a bike), “enseñar a montar en bicicleta” (to teach someone to ride a bike). Also commonly said as “montar en bici” in casual speech.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes montar en bicicleta?
native_language_example: Do you know how to ride a bike?

additional_notes: Used with estar + cubierto/a de + noun to describe a temporary or visible condition (“covered with/in”). In real sentences you usually include an article or demonstrative: “La montaña…” / “Esta montaña…”. Because montaña is feminine, it’s cubierta (not cubierto).
target_language_example: En invierno, la montaña está cubierta de nieve.
native_language_example: In winter, the mountain is covered in snow.

meaning: roller coaster; (figuratively) an emotional roller coaster.
additional_notes: Most commonly means the amusement-park ride. It can also be used figuratively to describe strong ups and downs in emotions or experiences: “una montaña rusa emocional”.
target_language_example: Este año mi trabajo ha sido una montaña rusa.
native_language_example: This year my job has been a roller coaster.

meaning: a lot of; lots of (a large amount/number of).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say you have many things or a large quantity: un montón de comida, un montón de bodas. It can be more literal as “a pile of” with physical items (un montón de papeles), but it’s very commonly used figuratively to mean “a lot of.”
target_language_example: Hay un montón de gente en la calle hoy.
native_language_example: There are lots of people in the street today.

meaning: a lot of people; lots of people.
additional_notes: Used to say there are many people (a big crowd) or many people in general. Very common in spoken Spanish. You can also use it with other nouns: un montón de trabajo (a lot of work), un montón de cosas (a lot of things).
target_language_example: En el concierto había un montón de gente, así que llegamos temprano para encontrar sitio.
native_language_example: There were lots of people at the concert, so we arrived early to find a spot.

meaning: to starve (to death); to be extremely hungry.
additional_notes: Literally “to die of hunger.” It can be used literally (lack of food, potentially life-threatening) or more loosely/hyperbolically depending on context. Common with estar a punto de (“to be about to”): estar a punto de morir de hambre.
target_language_example: Sus hijos están a punto de morir de hambre.
native_language_example: Their children are about to starve to death.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "mostrar" (to show) with the indirect object pronoun "te" (to you). It commonly appears after phrases like "Déjame..." (Let me...), "Necesito..." (I need...), "Voy a..." (I’m going to...), or "Estoy a punto de..." (I’m about to...). Word order can also be "mostrar algo" + "a ti" for emphasis, but "mostrarte algo" is the most natural.
target_language_example: Ven un momento; quiero mostrarte algo.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment; I want to show you something.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large quantity of water (for drinking, watering plants, or describing how much water there is somewhere). It’s the feminine form: mucha + agua (agua is feminine, but takes el in singular: el agua; in plural: las aguas). You can also use it in questions: ¿Hay mucha agua?
target_language_example: No hay mucha agua en la botella, pero podemos comprar más.
native_language_example: There isn’t much water in the bottle, but we can buy more.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general. It can be the subject of a sentence (Mucha gente asistió…) or an object after a preposition (hablar con mucha gente). It agrees in feminine singular because the key noun is gente (treated as singular).
target_language_example: En verano, hay mucha gente en la playa.
native_language_example: In summer, there are a lot of people at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say that a large number of people are located in a place or belong to a group/area (country, neighborhood, the world, etc.). It’s typically followed by a place noun: "mucha gente en + lugar" (e.g., "mucha gente en mi ciudad").
target_language_example: Mucha gente en mi ciudad usa el transporte público.
native_language_example: Many people in my city use public transportation.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what a large number of people are doing or how they are. It’s followed by: (1) a gerund to describe an ongoing action ("mucha gente está diciendo/saliendo"), or (2) an adjective to describe a state ("mucha gente está interesada").
target_language_example: Mucha gente está esperando el autobús ahora.
native_language_example: Many people are waiting for the bus right now.

meaning: very hungry; a lot of hunger.
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener: "tener mucha hambre" = "to be very hungry." "Hambre" is feminine, so you say "mucha" (not *mucho*). You can add emphasis: "tengo muchísima hambre" = "I'm extremely hungry."
target_language_example: No he comido en todo el día; tengo mucha hambre.
native_language_example: I haven’t eaten all day; I’m very hungry.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having been lucky (tener/tener + mucha suerte) or to wish someone luck (desear + mucha suerte). As a standalone phrase ("Mucha suerte."), it’s a common way to say “Good luck.”
target_language_example: ¡Mucha suerte en tu examen!
native_language_example: Good luck on your exam!

additional_notes: Used to talk about multiple items, activities, facts, or experiences in a general way. Often followed by an infinitive with para ("muchas cosas para hacer" = "many things to do"). Uses feminine plural agreement: muchas + cosas.
target_language_example: Tengo muchas cosas que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I have many things to do today.

meaning: "many things that" / "a lot of things to".
additional_notes: Used to introduce a list or set of tasks, objects, or ideas that are then described with a clause starting with que. Often followed by an infinitive for things you need/want to do (muchas cosas que hacer, muchas cosas que empacar) or by a full clause (muchas cosas que Edison inventó).
target_language_example: Tengo muchas cosas que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has many tasks/errands/obligations. You can change the number or person: “tengo muchas cosas que hacer” (I have…), “teníamos…” (we had…), “tiene…” (he/she has…). Often implies being busy and sometimes explains why someone can’t do something else.
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; tengo muchas cosas que hacer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I have a lot of things to do.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has faced or is facing many problems/challenges. Often appears with verbs like superar (to overcome) and pasar por (to go through). Usually refers to serious obstacles (life, work, health, etc.).
target_language_example: Hemos tenido muchas dificultades, pero seguimos adelante.
native_language_example: We’ve had many difficulties, but we’re moving forward.

additional_notes: Used with tener: "tener muchas ganas de + infinitive" (to really feel like doing something) or "tener muchas ganas de + noun" (to be very eager for something). Common for anticipation: "Tengo muchas ganas de verte" = "I can’t wait to see you."
target_language_example: Tengo muchas ganas de ir al concierto esta noche.
native_language_example: I really want to go to the concert tonight.

additional_notes:
A very common, polite way to thank someone. Often followed by:
- "por" + noun/infinitive: "Muchas gracias por venir" (Thanks for coming).
- "a" + person: "Muchas gracias a usted/a todos/a Tom" (Many thanks to you/all/Tom).
You can also add a name or title after it (e.g., "Muchas gracias, profesor").
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por tu ayuda, señora.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help, ma'am.

additional_notes: Use this to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It’s followed by a noun (Muchas gracias por la cena), a pronoun (por esto), or an infinitive/perfect infinitive to thank for an action (por llamar, por haberme invitado). In formal situations you may use "su" (Muchas gracias por su ayuda).
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por venir tan rápido.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for coming so quickly.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely for something that belongs to them or that they did for you. "Su" is the formal "your" (for usted/ustedes), so it’s common in emails, customer service, and professional situations: "Muchas gracias por su mensaje/tiempo/ayuda." With friends you’d usually say "Muchas gracias por tu…"
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por su ayuda.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

meaning: many people; a lot of people.
additional_notes: Plural phrase used to talk about a large number of people in general or in a place/event. It often comes at the beginning of the sentence as the subject ("Muchas personas..."), or after a verb to say an event attracted/required many people ("atrajo a muchas personas", "se requieren muchas personas"). "Muchas" agrees in gender/number with the noun (many = "muchos/muchas").
target_language_example: Muchas personas quieren un trabajo mejor.
native_language_example: Many people want a better job.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has (or is asking) many questions. It often implies curiosity, but depending on tone it can also suggest someone is asking too many or being a bit interrogative. In Spanish you can also say “tengo muchas preguntas” (I have a lot of questions) or “hacer muchas preguntas” (to ask a lot of questions).
target_language_example: Antes de empezar, tengo muchas preguntas.
native_language_example: Before we start, I have a lot of questions.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence ("Muchas veces..." / "...muchas veces").
target_language_example: He visto esa película muchas veces.
native_language_example: I’ve seen that movie many times.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true to a high degree (mucho) and then add a limitation or exception with pero. The comma often matches a pause in speech: "Te quiero mucho, pero…". You can use it with verbs (te quiero, me gusta), reactions (me asustaste), or what someone can do/knows (puedo hacer, sé).
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho, pero es demasiado caro.
native_language_example: I like it a lot, but it’s too expensive.

meaning: a lot about; a great deal about.
additional_notes: Used to say you have/read/know/learned/thought/talked a lot about a topic. It’s built from "mucho" (a lot) + "acerca de" (about/regarding). In everyday Spanish, "mucho sobre" often works similarly ("sé mucho sobre flores").
target_language_example: No sé mucho acerca de ese tema, pero puedo investigar.
native_language_example: I don’t know much about that topic, but I can research it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happened significantly earlier than another time/event. Often followed by “de” + infinitive or noun (“mucho antes de conocernos”), and it can also appear in comparisons with “de lo que…” (“mucho antes de lo que creéis” = much sooner/earlier than you think).
target_language_example: Llegamos mucho antes de que empezara la reunión.
native_language_example: We arrived much earlier than the meeting started.

additional_notes: Often used in patterns like “No fue/No pasó/No será mucho antes de que…”, meaning “It wasn’t/It didn’t take/It won’t be long before…”. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., llegara, saliera, empiece).
target_language_example: No será mucho antes de que te acostumbres a la ciudad.
native_language_example: It won’t be long before you get used to the city.

meaning: 'a lot / very much' (used with *echar de menos* = 'to miss').
additional_notes: You’ll most often hear this as **echar mucho de menos**: *Te echo mucho de menos* = “I miss you a lot.” The key expression is **echar de menos** (“to miss”); **mucho** intensifies it. Word order is usually *echar* + (object pronoun) + *mucho de menos*: *Te echamos mucho de menos*.
target_language_example: Echo mucho de menos a mi familia.
native_language_example: I miss my family a lot.

meaning: "a lot about you" or "a lot from you" (depending on the verb).
additional_notes:
Very common with verbs like:
- **aprender mucho de ti** = to learn a lot **from** you
- **saber mucho de ti** = to know a lot **about** you
- **(he) escuchado / oído mucho de ti** = (I’ve) heard a lot **about** you
You’ll also see **oír hablar mucho de ti** (“to hear a lot about you”). The exact English translation changes with context, but the core idea is “a lot” + “about/from you.”
target_language_example: Mis amigos me han hablado mucho de ti.
native_language_example: My friends have told me a lot about you.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/situations. It’s the comparative “mejor” (better) + “que” (than), and “mucho” intensifies the comparison (“much”/“a lot”). Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or a whole phrase: “mucho mejor que el mío / que tú / que antes”.
target_language_example: Este hotel es mucho mejor que el otro.
native_language_example: This hotel is much better than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare and emphasize improvement or a higher level: something is better than before or better than someone/something else. Often appears with comparison words like “que” (better than): “mucho mejor que él”.
target_language_example: Con este mapa, es mucho mejor llegar al centro.
native_language_example: With this map, it’s much better to get to downtown.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, people, or moments in time. It can compare with another noun/pronoun (Mucho mejor que ella), with time expressions like antes/ayer/la última vez, or in set phrases like mucho mejor que antes (“much better than before”). In sentences like “sabe mucho mejor que…”, saber means “to taste,” not “to know.”
target_language_example: Con esta medicina me siento mucho mejor que ayer.
native_language_example: With this medicine I feel much better than yesterday.

additional_notes: Often used to intensify a negative statement: “not X, much less Y” (Y is even harder/less likely). Common patterns: “no…, y mucho menos …” / “no…, mucho menos …”. It can also mean simply “much less/a lot less” with verbs like gastar, trabajar, estudiar.
target_language_example: No puedo pagar el alquiler, y mucho menos comprar una casa.
native_language_example: I can’t pay the rent, much less buy a house.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a comparison (more than expected or more than something else). Often followed by "de" + a clause: "mucho más de lo que..." (= much more than what/how...). Also common as "mucho más que" + noun/pronoun (= much more than).
target_language_example: Este hotel es mucho más caro que el otro.
native_language_example: This hotel is much more expensive than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison with más fuerte (“stronger” or, for sounds, “louder”). Common patterns: mucho más fuerte que… (“much stronger/louder than…”) and mucho más fuerte de lo que… (“much stronger/louder than what…”).
target_language_example: Con el micrófono, su voz suena mucho más fuerte que antes.
native_language_example: With the microphone, his voice sounds much louder than before.

additional_notes: Used to compare two situations: something is easier than before/than something else. Often followed by "de lo que..." ("than...") or said on its own when the comparison is understood. You can change the adjective to match what you mean: "mucho más difícil" (much harder), "mucho más rápido" (much faster).
target_language_example: Con tu ayuda, será mucho más fácil terminar hoy.
native_language_example: With your help, it’ll be much easier to finish today.

meaning: “much more than” (by a large amount); also “a lot more than” (not only).
additional_notes: Used to make a strong comparison. Often appears in patterns like: (1) comparison of degree/amount: “A ... mucho más que B” = “A ... much more than B”; (2) “mucho más que + verb” to emphasize that something went beyond what’s mentioned: “Hiciste mucho más que buscar...” = “You did more than just look...”.
target_language_example: Este trabajo es mucho más que un hobby para mí.
native_language_example: This work is much more than a hobby for me.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is bigger, more important, or more serious than what was just mentioned (eso = “that”). Often comes after a statement to correct or add emphasis: “It’s not just X; it’s much more than that.” Works with different tenses: es/era/fue.
target_language_example: No es solo un trabajo; es mucho más que eso.
native_language_example: It’s not just a job; it’s much more than that.

meaning: "a lot to me"; "means a lot to me."
additional_notes: Used to express that someone/something is very important or valuable to you, often with verbs like "significar" (to mean) or "valer" (to be worth). The verb changes with tense/person: "significa" (means), "significó" (meant), "vale" (is worth).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda; significa mucho para mí.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help; it means a lot to me.

meaning: a lot of heat; very hot (weather).
additional_notes: Used to talk about hot weather/conditions ("Hace/Hizo/Hará mucho calor" = "It’s/It was/It will be very hot"). With people, "Tengo mucho calor" means "I’m very hot" (feeling hot), not "I’m warm" as a general state.
target_language_example: Mañana va a hacer mucho calor, así que lleva agua.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it’s going to be very hot, so bring water.

additional_notes: Used as a warning to tell someone to be careful. Often said with the verb tener: (tú) ten mucho cuidado, (vosotros) tened mucho cuidado, (usted) tenga mucho cuidado. You can also use it after a preposition: con mucho cuidado = "very carefully."
target_language_example: Ten mucho cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: Be very careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has/earns/owes/spends a large amount of money. "Mucho" agrees with "dinero" (masculine singular), so it stays "mucho" (not *mucha*). Often appears with verbs like tener (to have), ganar (to earn/win), deber (to owe), pedir (to ask for/charge), and costar (to cost).
target_language_example: Ese coche cuesta mucho dinero.
native_language_example: That car costs a lot of money.

meaning: "a lot of money on" (spend/invest a lot of money in/on something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like gastar (to spend), invertir (to invest), and ganar (to earn). With gastar/invertir, en introduces what the money was spent/invested on: Gasté mucho dinero en el viaje. With ganar, en often indicates the place where the money was earned: Ganó mucho dinero en Nueva York. In English you’ll usually translate en as “on” (spend money on) or “in” (invest money in), depending on the verb.
target_language_example: No quiero gastar mucho dinero en ropa este mes.
native_language_example: I don’t want to spend a lot of money on clothes this month.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the weather expression “Hace…”: “Hace mucho frío” = “It’s very cold.” You can also contrast it with “mucho calor” (very hot). “Frío” is a noun here (“cold”), and “mucho” intensifies it (“a lot of”).
target_language_example: En invierno, aquí hace mucho frío por la noche.
native_language_example: In winter, it’s very cold here at night.

meaning: “Nice to meet you.”; also “good taste” (in art/style/choices).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a polite greeting when you meet someone (often short for “Mucho gusto en conocerte”). You can also use it literally to talk about someone’s taste: “tener mucho gusto” = to have good taste. In that sense, it’s about preferences/style, not pleasure.
target_language_example: Encantado, mucho gusto. ¿Cómo te llamas?
native_language_example: Nice to meet you. What’s your name?

additional_notes: Used to say something is very noisy. Often with verbs like hacer (to make): “Hace mucho ruido” = “It makes a lot of noise.” You can also use it to explain why you can’t hear/understand: “Hay mucho ruido aquí” = “There’s a lot of noise here.”
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme; hay mucho ruido en la calle.
native_language_example: I can’t concentrate; there’s a lot of noise in the street.

meaning: a long time; a lot of time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about duration (how long something takes, lasts, or how long you’ve been doing/been somewhere). Common with verbs like pasar (to spend), llevar (to have been doing/been somewhere for), and costar (to take/require). Often translates as “for a long time” or “a long time” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: No te he visto en mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in a long time.

mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a la vida

target_language_multi_word_term: Lleva/Cuesta mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a la vida (en pareja/de casado/a)
meaning: It takes a long time to get used to (married/couple) life.
additional_notes: Common pattern: **Llevar / costar / requerir + mucho tiempo + infinitivo** (“to take a long time to do”). Here, **acostumbrarse a** means “to get used to,” and it’s often followed by **la vida en pareja** (life as a couple) or **la vida de casado/a** (married life). You can swap **mucho tiempo** for **un tiempo** / **bastante tiempo** and change the situation: *acostumbrarse al trabajo*, *a la ciudad*, etc.
target_language_example: Cuesta mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a la vida en pareja.
native_language_example: It takes a long time to get used to life as a couple.

meaning: “a lot of time to/for” (a long time to do something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about having (or needing) plenty of time to do something, or waiting a long time for something. Often followed by an infinitive: mucho tiempo para + infinitivo (e.g., mucho tiempo para hacerlo). With nouns, it can mean “a long time for”: mucho tiempo para esa batalla (“a long time to wait for that battle”). In negatives it can mean “not much time to”: No tengo mucho tiempo para estudiar.
target_language_example: No tenemos mucho tiempo para decidir.
native_language_example: We don’t have much time to decide.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has had plenty of time to reflect/consider something. Often followed by what you’re thinking about: “mucho tiempo para pensar en/ acerca de + noun” (about a problem) or “mucho tiempo para pensar en eso” (about that). You can also use it with “tener” (to have) or “haber” (there is/are): “Tengo mucho tiempo para pensar” / “Hay mucho tiempo para pensar.”
target_language_example: Tuve mucho tiempo para pensar en lo que dijiste.
native_language_example: I had a lot of time to think about what you said.

additional_notes: Used to say there is a large amount of work to do. It can refer to being busy at a job (Tenemos mucho trabajo) or to effort required in general (Necesita mucho trabajo). Common patterns: “hay mucho trabajo” (there’s a lot of work), “tener mucho trabajo” (to have a lot of work), “mucho trabajo por delante” (a lot of work ahead), and “causar/ahorrar mucho trabajo” (to cause/save a lot of work).
target_language_example: Esta semana tengo mucho trabajo, así que no puedo salir.
native_language_example: This week I have a lot of work, so I can’t go out.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many topics to discuss, often after something happened or when two people need to have a conversation. Common patterns: “tener mucho de qué hablar” (to have a lot to talk about) and “hay/no hay mucho de qué hablar” (there is/isn’t much to talk about).
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, tenemos mucho de qué hablar.
native_language_example: After the meeting, we have a lot to talk about.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (“to have”): tener mucho en común (con alguien) = “to have a lot in common (with someone).” You can also say algo en común (“something in common”) or nada en común (“nothing in common”).
target_language_example: Creo que tenemos mucho en común.
native_language_example: I think we have a lot in common.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern **mucho que + infinitive** to express that there is a lot to do/say/etc. Common with **tener/haber/dar**: **Tenemos mucho que hablar** (“We have a lot to talk about”), **No hay mucho que hacer** (“There isn’t much to do”), **Nos dieron mucho que comer** (“They gave us a lot to eat”).
target_language_example: Hoy tengo mucho que hacer, así que no puedo salir.
native_language_example: Today I have a lot to do, so I can’t go out.

additional_notes: Used to say someone still needs to learn a lot (often with todavía/aún = “still”). The structure is “mucho” + “que” + infinitive (aprender), meaning “a lot to [verb]”: e.g., mucho que hacer (a lot to do), mucho que decir (a lot to say). You can add “de” + person/thing: Tengo mucho que aprender de ti (“I have a lot to learn from you”).
target_language_example: Todavía tenemos mucho que aprender.
native_language_example: We still have a lot to learn.

meaning: “a lot to do” / “many things to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re busy or have many tasks ahead. Often appears with tener (“to have”): Tengo/Tienes/Tenemos mucho que hacer. It can also be used with hay (“there is/are”): Hay mucho que hacer. Also common with time words like hoy (“today”).
target_language_example: No puedo salir ahora; tengo mucho que hacer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out now; I have a lot to do.

meaning: a lot to do with (something/someone); a lot to see.
additional_notes: Used mainly in two ways: (1) "tener mucho que ver con" = to be closely related to, or to have a lot to do with someone/something (often about connections, causes, or relevance). (2) "hay/no hay mucho que ver" = there is/isn't much to see (for example, in a place or situation).
target_language_example: Esto tiene mucho que ver con lo que dijiste ayer.
native_language_example: This has a lot to do with what you said yesterday.

additional_notes: "Muchos" agrees in gender and number with the noun (muchos amigos, muchas amigas). Often used with the verb "tener" (to have): "Tengo muchos amigos." You can also say "hacer amigos" (to make friends) or "hacer muchos amigos" (to make many friends).
target_language_example: En la universidad hice muchos amigos.
native_language_example: In college I made many friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long period of time, often with verbs like pasar (to pass) or llevar (to have been doing something for). It agrees in gender and number: muchos años (masc. plural); manyas would be muchos años anyway because año is masculine.
target_language_example: Viví en México muchos años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for many years.

additional_notes: "Muchos" means "many" (masculine plural) and "errores" means "mistakes/errors". Commonly used after verbs like "cometer" (to make/commit): "cometer muchos errores" = "to make many mistakes." You can also use it as the subject: "Muchos errores se podrían evitar..." = "Many mistakes could be avoided..."
target_language_example: Si no practicas, vas a cometer muchos errores.
native_language_example: If you don’t practice, you’re going to make many mistakes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of students (plural). You can place it before the verb as the subject ("Muchos estudiantes están...") or after "a" with an indirect object pronoun to mean "to many students" ("A muchos estudiantes les gusta..."). "Muchos" must match the noun: muchos estudiantes (masculine plural); muchas estudiantes (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Muchos estudiantes estudian en la biblioteca después de clase.
native_language_example: Many students study in the library after class.

additional_notes: "Muchos" agrees with the noun: muchos (masculine plural) + libros. You can use it after verbs like tener (to have), comprar (to buy), leer (to read), or with hay to say something exists: "Hay muchos libros...". For feminine nouns, it changes to "muchas" (e.g., "muchas revistas").
target_language_example: En mi casa hay muchos libros, pero no tengo tiempo para leerlos.
native_language_example: In my house there are many books, but I don’t have time to read them.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many children in a place (hay/había muchos niños...). With "tener" (tiene muchos niños), it means "to have many children" (to be the parent of many kids). "Muchos" agrees with the plural masculine noun "niños"; if it’s all girls, you can say "muchas niñas".
target_language_example: En esta escuela hay muchos niños.
native_language_example: There are many children at this school.

additional_notes: Plural phrase: "muchos" (many, masculine plural) + "países" (countries). Common after verbs like "hay" (there are) and with phrases like "en muchos países" (in many countries) or "de muchos países" (from many countries).
target_language_example: Esta costumbre existe en muchos países.
native_language_example: This tradition exists in many countries.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has lots of difficulties or issues. Often appears with tener (to have): “tener muchos problemas.” Can also be followed by de + noun (“problemas de planificación” = planning problems) or con + noun (“problemas con sus dientes” = problems with her teeth).
target_language_example: Últimamente tengo muchos problemas en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Lately I’ve been having a lot of problems at work.

meaning: "many of the" (many from a specific group).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say that a large number of people/things within a particular, known group have a certain quality or did something. It agrees in gender/number: muchos de los (masc. plural), muchas de las (fem. plural). With nouns like estudiantes/trabajadores, use "los" by default unless you specifically mean an all-female group ("las").
target_language_example: Muchos de los invitados llegaron tarde.
native_language_example: Many of the guests arrived late.

additional_notes: A very strong, enthusiastic way to say thanks. Common in both formal and informal situations. Often followed by something like "de verdad" (really) or "por..." (for...).
target_language_example: Muchísimas gracias por la ayuda.
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for the help.

additional_notes: Very common exaggeration to say you’re extremely hungry (not usually literal). You’ll also hear it with other subjects and tenses: "me muero de hambre" (I’m starving), "nos morimos de hambre" (we’re starving), "me moría de hambre" (I was starving). Often used with "¡Tengo hambre!" as a stronger alternative.
target_language_example: Después del gimnasio, me muero de hambre.
native_language_example: After the gym, I’m starving.

additional_notes: Often used as an exaggeration to mean “really hungry.” It agrees with the person: muerto (male) / muerta (female). You can also hear “medio muerto de hambre” = “half-starved,” often describing someone who looks underfed or very thin.
target_language_example: Después del viaje, yo estaba muerto de hambre y pedí pizza.
native_language_example: After the trip, I was starving and ordered pizza.

meaning: “sample of” / “specimen of”; sometimes “a token/show of” (a little bit to represent something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say what kind of sample or representative thing it is: muestra de orina = “urine sample,” muestra de agradecimiento = “a token of appreciation,” muestra de fotos = “a selection/display of photos.” In everyday Spanish, you’ll also see “una muestra de + noun” meaning a small sign or example of something (e.g., una muestra de cariño = “a sign of affection”).
target_language_example: Gracias por el regalo; es una muestra de tu apoyo.
native_language_example: Thanks for the gift; it’s a sign of your support.

meaning: “woman who/that …” (introduces a description of a woman).
additional_notes: Used when a noun (“mujer”) is followed by a relative clause introduced by “que” (“who/that”). It’s very common to describe or identify which woman you mean: “la mujer que vive aquí” = “the woman who lives here.” You can also say “una mujer que …” (“a woman who …”).
target_language_example: Ella es la mujer que trabaja en recepción.
native_language_example: She is the woman who works at reception.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** (son = “are”) to describe women with nouns/adjectives: *Las mujeres son fuertes.* Often appears with determiners like **algunas** (some), **estas** (these), **esas** (those), **todas** (all). Adjectives usually agree in feminine plural: *fuertes, altas, hermosas*.
target_language_example: Algunas mujeres son inteligentes.
native_language_example: Some women are smart.

additional_notes: A fixed pairing meaning “women and children,” often used when talking about a group of people (e.g., victims, evacuees). In Spanish it’s common to omit the article in lists or general statements (“Mujeres y niños…”), though you may also hear “las mujeres y los niños” when referring to specific people.
target_language_example: Primero evacuaron a mujeres y niños.
native_language_example: They evacuated women and children first.

meaning: the whole world; the entire world.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize totality (“all of it”), often in comparisons or big statements: el más X del mundo entero (“the most X in the whole world”), amar/salvar al mundo entero (“love/save the whole world”). It’s also common as “el mundo entero” with the article.
target_language_example: La noticia sorprendió al mundo entero.
native_language_example: The news surprised the whole world.

meaning: the real world (everyday life, outside of fantasy/online/a protected environment).
additional_notes: Used to contrast real life with an imaginary world, a virtual/online space, or a sheltered environment (like school). Often appears with “en el mundo real” (“in the real world”) and in expressions like “volver/al mundo real” (“to return to the real world”) or “te veo en el mundo real” (“see you in real life”).
target_language_example: Cuando termine la universidad, tendré que enfrentarme al mundo real.
native_language_example: When I finish university, I’ll have to face the real world.

meaning: (be) starving / very hungry (literally: dying of hunger).
additional_notes: Used with estar + (me/te/se/nos/os) + muriendo de hambre to emphasize strong hunger. It can be literal (someone is actually starving) or exaggerated in everyday speech (“I’m starving!”).
target_language_example: ¿Podemos comer ya? Estoy muriendo de hambre.
native_language_example: Can we eat now? I’m starving.

additional_notes: “Murió” is the past tense (preterite) of *morir* (“to die”) for él/ella/usted. Use **morir de + illness/cause** to say what someone died from: *murió de cáncer*, *murió de un infarto*. You can specify the type: **cáncer de + body part** (e.g., *cáncer de estómago*). For plural or other persons: *morí* (I died), *murieron* (they died).
target_language_example: Mi tía murió de cáncer hace dos años.
native_language_example: My aunt died of cancer two years ago.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of *morir*: **murió** = “died” (a completed event). **Morir de** is used to say the cause of death (“die of/from”). Often used with a person: *Mi padre / Ella / Él / Su tía murió de…*.
target_language_example: Su abuelo murió de cáncer de pulmón el año pasado.
native_language_example: His grandfather died of lung cancer last year.

additional_notes: "Murió" is the simple past (preterite) of "morir" (to die). You’ll often also hear "Se murió el año pasado"—very common in everyday speech and usually the same meaning. Use "el año pasado" to say "last year" (also common: "el año pasado" after the verb).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió el año pasado.
native_language_example: My grandfather died last year.

additional_notes: “Murió” is the preterite (simple past) of “morir” (to die), used for a completed event. “En” introduces where or when the person died: a country/city (Murió en Vietnam / en Madrid), a place (en el hospital), or a year/date (Murió en 1998 / en enero).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió en 2005.
native_language_example: My grandfather died in 2005.

meaning: “(he/she) died in the …” or “died during the …”.
additional_notes: Used to say someone died in a specific event, situation, or circumstance: *murió en el incendio* (in the fire), *murió en el parto* (in childbirth), *murió en el cumplimiento de su deber* (in the line of duty). The noun after it changes the article as needed: *murió en la* (feminine), *murió en un/una* (indefinite).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió en el hospital.
native_language_example: My grandfather died in the hospital.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "morir" in the simple past (pretérito): "murió" = "(he/she) died". It’s followed by "en" + a noun to say what event or situation caused/contained the death (e.g., "en la avalancha", "en la explosión"). Spanish often omits the subject pronoun: "Murió en la explosión" = "He/She died in the explosion."
target_language_example: Murió en la explosión.
native_language_example: He/She died in the explosion.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of morir: murió = “he/she died.” Used to say someone died during a war (often while serving as a soldier, but it can be any death connected to the war). To specify who, you can add a subject: Mi padre/Él/Ella murió en la guerra.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió en la guerra cuando era joven.
native_language_example: My grandfather died in the war when he was young.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone died because of an accident. The verb is in the simple past (pretérito): "murió" = “(he/she) died.” You can add details after "accidente" (e.g., "en un accidente de coche" = “in a car accident”). For other people: "morí" (I died), "moriste" (you died), "murieron" (they died).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió en un accidente de coche.
native_language_example: My grandfather died in a car accident.

murió en un accidente de tránsito

target_language_multi_word_term: murió en un accidente de tránsito
additional_notes: Used to state that someone’s cause of death was a road/traffic accident. It’s neutral in tone and often used in news or serious contexts. The subject can change (e.g., *Mi amigo murió...*, *Murieron...*). In Spain, you’ll also commonly hear *accidente de tráfico* instead of *accidente de tránsito*.
target_language_example: Lamentablemente, el actor murió en un accidente de tránsito.
native_language_example: Sadly, the actor died in a traffic accident.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago someone died. Pattern: "murió hace" + time expression (e.g., un año, dos años, unas horas, millones de años). "Murió" is the past tense of "morir" (to die), and "hace" means "ago" in this time expression.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo murió hace tres meses.
native_language_example: My grandfather died three months ago.

additional_notes: "Murió" is the simple past (pretérito) of "morir" for he/she/you-formal: "murió" = "he/she died." "Hace + time" expresses how long ago something happened: "hace tres años" = "three years ago." You can replace the time: "murió hace dos días" (died two days ago), "murió hace mucho" (died a long time ago).
target_language_example: Mi perro murió hace tres años.
native_language_example: My dog died three years ago.

additional_notes: You repeat "muy" to strongly intensify an adjective or adverb. In writing it’s often separated by commas ("muy, muy"), and in speech it’s said with emphasis. You can repeat it more times for even stronger emphasis ("muy, muy, muy importante").
target_language_example: Estoy muy, muy cansado hoy.
native_language_example: I’m very, very tired today.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens with high frequency. It commonly goes near the verb (before or after it): “La llamo muy a menudo” / “Muy a menudo voy a esquiar.” You can negate it with “no” to mean “not very often.”
target_language_example: Muy a menudo llego tarde al trabajo.
native_language_example: Very often I arrive late to work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has good luck or is in a favorable situation. It can describe a person (Eres muy afortunado) or an event/situation (un encuentro muy afortunado). You can change the gender/number: muy afortunada, muy afortunados, muy afortunadas.
target_language_example: Me siento muy afortunado de tener amigos como ustedes.
native_language_example: I feel very lucky to have friends like you.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude or appreciation for something you have. It’s typically followed by a noun phrase (una familia, amigos) or someone/something you possess (un amigo como tú). Adjective agreement matters: "muy afortunado" (masc. singular), "muy afortunada" (fem. singular), "muy afortunados/afortunadas" (plural).
target_language_example: Soy muy afortunado de tener un amigo como tú.
native_language_example: I’m very lucky to have a friend like you.

additional_notes: Used to describe experiences, places, weather, or people as pleasant/enjoyable. Often used politely about someone ("Es una persona muy agradable") or about an event/visit ("Fue muy agradable hablar contigo").
target_language_example: Fue muy agradable conocerte.
native_language_example: It was very nice to meet you.

meaning: very tall; very high (also: very loud, for sound/volume).
additional_notes: Describes height/level: "Es muy alto" = "He/She is very tall"; "un precio muy alto" = "a very high price." For sound/voice, Spanish typically uses "hablar muy alto" meaning "to speak very loudly" (more natural than "hablar inglés muy alto"). Agreement changes with gender/number when used as an adjective (alto/alta/altos/altas); the fixed term here is the masculine singular form "muy alto".
target_language_example: El árbol creció muy alto.
native_language_example: The tree grew very tall.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s friendly, considerate behavior (“He/She is being very kind”). It’s also a polite way to thank someone: “(Es) muy amable (de tu parte)” = “That’s very kind of you.” You may hear it alone as a short, formal-sounding thanks: “Muy amable.”
target_language_example: Muchas gracias, es muy amable de su parte.
native_language_example: Thank you very much, that’s very kind of you.

additional_notes: A polite, somewhat formal way to thank someone for a favor, help, or a nice gesture. Uses the formal “su” (you, formal), so it’s common with strangers, customers, older people, or in professional settings. Often said on its own, or after “Gracias”: “Gracias, muy amable de su parte.”
target_language_example: —Le guardé un asiento. —Gracias, muy amable de su parte.
native_language_example: —I saved you a seat. —Thank you, that’s very kind of you.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone or recognize a kind gesture. You’ll often hear it as a full sentence (¡Muy amable de tu parte!) or with “Eso es/fue…” depending on time: “Eso es…” (present) and “Eso fue…” (past). Similar in tone to “That’s very kind of you,” polite and common.
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por ayudarme; es muy amable de tu parte.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me; that’s very kind of you.

additional_notes: Used to describe people’s behavior as kind, polite, or helpful. Often appears after a form of "ser" (son/fueron/han sido): "Son muy amables" = "They are very kind." It can also be said by itself as a brief polite comment (e.g., after someone helps you): "Muy amables."
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por su ayuda; han sido muy amables.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help; you’ve been very kind.

meaning: 'very well' / 'really well'; also 'all right' (to agree or move on).
additional_notes: Use it to say someone does something well (Hablas muy bien español), to agree or transition in conversation (Muy bien, empecemos), or to say something looks/sounds good (Te queda muy bien; Suena muy bien).
target_language_example: Muy bien, entonces nos vemos mañana a las ocho.
native_language_example: All right, then I’ll see you tomorrow at eight.

additional_notes: Often repeated for emphasis in speech. It can mean "very good" (showing approval), but in many situations it works like "okay/alright" to move things along, get attention, or transition to the next point (e.g., addressing a group: "Muy bien, muy bien, damas y caballeros..."). Tone depends on context (it can sound encouraging or a bit impatient).
target_language_example: Muy bien, muy bien, empecemos con la primera pregunta.
native_language_example: Alright, alright, let’s start with the first question.

meaning: “Alright/OK, but…” (agreement followed by an objection or condition).
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what someone said (“muy bien” = OK/fine) and then introduce a limitation, disagreement, or next requirement with “pero” (but). Common in conversation to soften a contradiction. You’ll often hear it at the start of a reply.
target_language_example: Muy bien, pero primero necesito tu dirección.
native_language_example: Alright, but first I need your address.

meaning: "Alright/okay, let's…" (to introduce what you’re going to do next).
additional_notes: Used to transition and move the conversation or activity forward. "Muy bien" means "very well/alright," and "vamos a + infinitive" literally means "we’re going to + verb," but in this setting it often works like English "let’s + verb" (especially when the speaker is guiding a group).
target_language_example: Muy bien, vamos a empezar con una pregunta.
native_language_example: Alright, let’s start with a question.

meaning: “Alright then / OK, now…” (often: “OK, I get it.”)
additional_notes: Used as a transition or reaction before continuing: *Muy bien* can mean “alright/OK,” and *ya* often means “now” or “already.” Together, it commonly introduces what comes next (“OK, now I’m done / now I see…”). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral and practical, or slightly impatient/firm (especially when responding to someone’s attitude).
target_language_example: Muy bien, ya entendí; no hace falta que lo repitas.
native_language_example: Alright, I get it now; you don’t need to repeat it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something looks good or does well in a specific context or medium. Common with verbs like "salir" (to come out/appear in a photo), "verse" (to look/appear), and "pasarlo" (to have a good time): e.g., "Sales muy bien en estas fotos" (You look great in these photos), "Se ve muy bien en televisión" (It looks very good on TV). "En" can mean “in” or “on,” depending on what follows (en la foto, en televisión, en la cena).
target_language_example: Mi hermana sale muy bien en todas las fotos.
native_language_example: My sister looks very good in all the photos.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (or a woman/girl) as very pretty/beautiful. It agrees in gender and number: muy bonito (masc.), muy bonitos / muy bonitas (plural). Can describe people, things, places, or qualities like handwriting: “una letra muy bonita”. With people you’ll also hear “Qué bonita” or “Te ves muy bonita” (“You look very pretty”).
target_language_example: Tu casa es muy bonita.
native_language_example: Your house is very pretty.

additional_notes: Used to compliment how something looks (a place, an object, a scene) and can also describe how someone does something in an appealing way (e.g., singing). Note agreement: when modifying a feminine noun or plural nouns, it becomes "muy bonita/muy bonitos/muy bonitas." Often interchangeable with “muy lindo” or “muy hermoso,” depending on region and intensity.
target_language_example: Es un lugar muy bonito.
native_language_example: It’s a very nice/beautiful place.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: muy buen + noun (e.g., muy buen público, muy buen salario). It’s the shortened form of "bueno" → "buen" when it comes right before a masculine singular noun. For feminine nouns, use "muy buena" (muy buena idea). For plural, use "muy buenos/muy buenas".
target_language_example: Es un muy buen restaurante.
native_language_example: It’s a very good restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s work or performance. Often said on its own as a compliment (“¡Muy buen trabajo!”) or with “hacer” (“Hizo un muy buen trabajo”). You can also specify what it was good on: “Muy buen trabajo en + [task/part]”.
target_language_example: ¡Muy buen trabajo con la presentación!
native_language_example: Very good job with the presentation!

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun/person (Ella/María, una idea, una película, etc.). Often followed by "en" + activity/field ("muy buena en matemáticas") or "para" + infinitive ("muy buena para tocar la flauta"). For a masculine subject, use "muy bueno".
target_language_example: Mi hermana es muy buena para explicar las cosas.
native_language_example: My sister is very good at explaining things.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective "buenas" (feminine plural of "bueno") to describe plural feminine nouns (e.g., carreteras, chances, comidas, líneas, ideas). With masculine plural nouns you use "muy buenos" (e.g., "muy buenos amigos"). Not to be confused with the greeting "¡Muy buenas!" meaning "Hi/Good day!".
target_language_example: Tus razones son muy buenas, pero todavía no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: Your reasons are very good, but I still don't agree.

additional_notes: Used to strongly praise a person, thing, or situation. It agrees in gender/number with the noun it describes: muy bueno (masc. sing.), muy buena (fem. sing.), muy buenos (masc. plural), muy buenas (fem. plural). With verbs like ser/estar: Es muy bueno. / Está muy bueno (often means “it tastes really good”; when talking about a person, it can also mean “really attractive” in some contexts).
target_language_example: Eres un niño muy bueno.
native_language_example: You are a very good boy.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has skill or ability in a subject or activity. It’s followed by a noun (muy bueno en matemáticas), a pronoun (muy bueno en eso), or sometimes a clause with "lo que" (muy bueno en lo que hago). You can change gender/number: "muy buena en", "muy buenos en", "muy buenas en".
target_language_example: Soy muy bueno en lo que hago.
native_language_example: I am very good at what I do.

additional_notes: Used with estar or parecer to describe how someone feels/looks right now: "Estoy muy cansado" (I’m very tired), "Pareces muy cansado" (You look very tired). Agree in gender/number: muy cansado (masc. sing.), muy cansada (fem. sing.), muy cansados/cansadas (plural).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy muy cansado.
native_language_example: Today I’m very tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something costs a lot or is overpriced. It agrees in gender and number with the noun: muy caro (masc. singular), muy cara (fem. singular), muy caros/muy caras (plural).
target_language_example: Este coche es muy caro.
native_language_example: This car is very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about physical distance (Muy cerca de + place: “very close to…”) or being close to reaching a goal (“We’re very close”). It can also be used by itself as an adverbial phrase (“Muy cerca, ya.” = “Very close now/almost there.”).
target_language_example: Estamos muy cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: We’re very close to the station.

meaning: very happy/glad to (do something); very pleased about (something).
additional_notes: Used to express strong happiness or satisfaction. It’s commonly followed by **de + infinitive** (e.g., *muy contento de verte* = “very happy to see you”) or **de + noun/pronoun** (e.g., *muy contento de tu visita* = “very happy about your visit”). Note: Spanish *contento* usually means “happy/pleased,” not the same as English “content” in all contexts.
target_language_example: Estoy muy contento de estar aquí contigo.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to be here with you.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective difícil (“difficult/hard”) with muy (“very”). It describes tasks, situations, or experiences that are hard to do or deal with. You can also use it with other adjectives in the same pattern (muy importante, muy fácil, etc.).
target_language_example: Fue muy difícil tomar esa decisión.
native_language_example: It was very difficult to make that decision.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as highly entertaining or enjoyable. Can be said on its own ("Muy divertido.") or with ser ("Es/Fue/Será muy divertido"). "Divertido" changes to agree with the noun it describes (divertida, divertidos, divertidas), but the fixed term here is the masculine singular form "muy divertido."
target_language_example: Ha sido muy divertido.
native_language_example: It has been very fun.

meaning: "very sweet" (taste) or "very sweet/kind" (about a person or gesture).
additional_notes: Used literally for sweet flavors (food/drinks) and figuratively to describe someone as kind, affectionate, or thoughtful. Common pattern: "Es/Fue muy dulce de tu parte" = "That’s/That was very sweet of you" (a polite way to thank someone for a kind gesture).
target_language_example: ¡Qué detalle tan bonito! Fue muy dulce de tu parte.
native_language_example: What a nice gesture! That was very sweet of you.

meaning: very hard (a lot); very hard/strongly (with impact).
additional_notes: "Muy" intensifies "duro". With verbs like trabajar/estudiar, it means putting in a lot of effort ("work/study very hard"). With verbs like golpear/caer, it means with great force ("hit very hard"). It can also describe something physically hard (e.g., "La cama es muy dura" = "The bed is very hard/firm").
target_language_example: Tengo un examen mañana, así que estoy estudiando muy duro.
native_language_example: I have an exam tomorrow, so I’m studying very hard.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something or someone stands out as particularly important or different in a positive way. Often describes events (una noche muy especial), people/groups, or a purpose/role in life. In conversation you can also say it alone (“Muy especial.”) as a short, emphatic comment.
target_language_example: Para mí, este día es muy especial.
native_language_example: For me, this day is very special.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that feels unusual, odd, or hard to explain (a situation, sound, dream, person, moment, etc.). "Extraño" can also mean "foreign" or "I miss" (as in "Te extraño") in other contexts, but in this phrase it means "strange/weird." Note: Spanish adjectives agree in gender/number; you’ll also see "muy extraña" (feminine) and "muy extraños/extrañas" (plural).
target_language_example: Esto es muy extraño.
native_language_example: This is very strange.

additional_notes: “Muy” is an adverb meaning “very.” “Felices” is the plural form of “feliz” (happy) and is used with plural subjects (nosotros/nosotras, ellos/ellas, ustedes, etc.). You’ll often see it after verbs like ser, estar, parecer, or verse: “Somos/Estamos/Parecen/Se ven muy felices.”
target_language_example: Mis amigos y yo estamos muy felices hoy.
native_language_example: My friends and I are very happy today.

additional_notes:
Used to strongly express happiness. Often appears with:
- "estar muy feliz" = to be very happy (temporary state)
- "estar muy feliz de + infinitive" = very happy to have done/to do something ("Estoy muy feliz de haber salido...")
- "estar muy feliz por ti" = very happy for you (happy about someone else’s good news).
target_language_example: Estoy muy feliz de verte otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you again.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to mean “very strong” (e.g., a strong wind, a strong person/animal). With verbs it often means “very hard/intensely,” describing how something is done: soplar muy fuerte = “to blow very hard,” abrazar/besar muy fuerte = “to hug/kiss very tightly.”
target_language_example: Agárralo muy fuerte para que no se caiga.
native_language_example: Hold it very tightly so it doesn’t fall.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is easy. With verbs like "ser" or "parecer," it describes how easy something is: "Fue muy fácil" (It was very easy). In phrases like "Lo tiene muy fácil," it means someone has it easy / is in a very easy situation. "Ponerlo muy fácil" means to make it very easy for someone (often by simplifying things or helping).
target_language_example: Con esta guía, el examen será muy fácil.
native_language_example: With this guide, the exam will be very easy.

additional_notes: Used to intensify size/extent: "muy" (very) + "grande" (big/large). It can describe physical size (un cuarto muy grande, un país muy grande) or more general magnitude. In some contexts it can imply something figurative or important (e.g., "Te debo una muy grande" = "I owe you a big one / a big favor" for helping me out).
target_language_example: Ese perro es muy grande, pero es muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: That dog is very big, but it’s very calm.

additional_notes: “Guapa” is the feminine form of “guapo” and is used to compliment a girl or woman on her looks (pretty/attractive). It agrees with the person described: “muy guapa” (female), “muy guapo” (male). You can use it with “ser/estar” (e.g., “Ella es…” / “Estás…”).
target_language_example: ¡Qué vestido tan bonito! Estás muy guapa hoy.
native_language_example: What a nice dress! You look very pretty today.

meaning: "very beautiful" (talking about a woman or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Muy = “very” and hermosa = “beautiful” in the feminine form. Use it to compliment a woman/girl (“Eres muy hermosa”) or to describe a feminine noun (“La casa es muy hermosa”). For a man/masculine noun, use “muy hermoso”.
target_language_example: La playa es muy hermosa al atardecer.
native_language_example: The beach is very beautiful at sunset.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something matters a lot (a day, call, meeting, announcement, etc.). It often appears after the noun it describes: “una llamada muy importante” (a very important call).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar contigo; es muy importante.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you; it’s very important.

additional_notes: Use it to express that someone or something matters a lot to you. It agrees with the thing that is important: "importante" stays the same for masculine/feminine singular (él/ella/esto), but changes for plural: "muy importantes para mí". You can swap in other pronouns too: "para ti", "para él/ella", "para nosotros".
target_language_example: Tu apoyo es muy importante para mí.
native_language_example: Your support is very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly describe a person, animal, or idea as smart. It goes before the adjective: muy + adjective (muy inteligente, muy interesante, etc.). Often said as a compliment: Eres muy inteligente. Note the different forms of “you are” in the examples: ella es…, tú eres…, vos sos… (common in Argentina/Uruguay), vosotros sois… (Spain).
target_language_example: Tu hermana es muy inteligente y aprende rápido.
native_language_example: Your sister is very intelligent and learns quickly.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is interesting. "Muy" is an intensifier meaning "very" and goes before adjectives like "interesante." You can use it to describe things (a book, a movie, a class, a person’s idea).
target_language_example: La clase de hoy fue muy interesante.
native_language_example: Today's class was very interesting.
