additional_notes: Used to say that no person wants something. Often followed by an infinitive ("Nadie quiere morir"), a noun ("Nadie quiere una guerra"), or "que" + subjunctive to express what nobody wants to happen ("Nadie quiere que pase eso").
target_language_example: Nadie quiere esperar tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: Nobody wants to wait that long.

additional_notes: Commonly followed by a question word or clause describing what is unknown: nadie sabe + dónde/qué/cuánto/si... You can also use it with a noun: Nadie sabe su nombre. It’s a straightforward statement (not a question) and is often used to emphasize that information is unknown or secret.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe cuándo va a llegar el tren.
native_language_example: Nobody knows when the train will arrive.

additional_notes: Used to say that a fact is unknown to everyone (often implying it’s secret or not widely known). It’s followed by a clause introduced by que + a verb (usually in the indicative): Nadie sabe que vivo aquí.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe que estoy estudiando español.
native_language_example: No one knows that I’m studying Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to express that nobody knows what to say/what happened/what became of someone. It’s often followed by an infinitive ("Nadie sabe qué decir") or by a verb clause ("Nadie sabe qué le pasó"). Note the accent in “qué” when it means “what” in an indirect question.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe qué hacer ahora.
native_language_example: No one knows what to do now.

additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence/clause meaning “nobody/no one …” when the verb uses **se**. The **se** can be reflexive or part of a pronominal verb (a verb that commonly goes with se), and it comes before the conjugated verb: *Nadie se rió* (Nobody laughed), *Nadie se dio cuenta* (Nobody realized). If there are extra pronouns like **lo/la/los/las**, they also go before the verb: *Nadie se lo cree* (Nobody believes it).
target_language_example: Nadie se acordó de llamarme.
native_language_example: Nobody remembered to call me.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of "darse cuenta (de)" = "to notice/realize". Often followed by "de" + noun/phrase: "Nadie se dio cuenta de mi nuevo corte de pelo" (Nobody noticed my new haircut). You can also leave it implied: "Nadie se dio cuenta" (Nobody noticed).
target_language_example: Nadie se dio cuenta de que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Nobody realized that we arrived late.

additional_notes: "Nadie" is a negative pronoun meaning "no one." "Te" is the object pronoun for "you" (tú), meaning "you" as the person receiving the action ("you," "to you"). It’s commonly followed by another object pronoun: e.g., "Nadie te lo ha dicho" = "No one has told you (it)." With "nadie" before the verb, you normally don’t add "no" ("Nadie te obliga," not *"No nadie te obliga").
target_language_example: Nadie te entiende cuando hablas tan rápido.
native_language_example: No one understands you when you talk so fast.

meaning: “no one is going to (to you) / nobody will …”
additional_notes: Used to reassure or predict that no person will do something to you (or that nobody will be able to do something involving you). It’s typically followed by an infinitive: "nadie te va a decir" (no one is going to tell you), "nadie te va a hacer" (no one will do to you), "nadie te va a poder" (no one will be able to). Often implies “don’t worry.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, nadie te va a juzgar.
native_language_example: Relax, no one is going to judge you.

additional_notes: Used to say that nobody will do a future action. It’s formed with nadie (“no one”) + ir a + infinitive (a very common way to talk about the near future). Often used to reassure someone (Nadie va a buscarte) or to emphasize that something won’t happen.
target_language_example: Nadie va a ayudarte si no lo pides.
native_language_example: No one is going to help you if you don’t ask for it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a vehicle that travels in space. Most common with the article (la/una) and with verbs like aparecer (to appear) or estar a bordo de (to be on board). You may also see the more technical synonym “nave espacial” = “spacecraft” in news/science contexts.
target_language_example: Vimos una nave espacial en el museo.
native_language_example: We saw a spacecraft in the museum.

additional_notes: Used to express a necessity or strong requirement. "Necesidad de + infinitive" = need to do something (La necesidad de aprender). "Necesidad de + noun" = need for something (necesidad de amor). "Verse en la necesidad de + infinitive" means "to find yourself having to" (often because of circumstances).
target_language_example: Tengo necesidad de descansar un poco.
native_language_example: I need to rest a bit.

additional_notes: "Necesita" is the usted (formal you) form and also the he/she form of "necesitar" (to need). Used to say someone needs help or to politely offer help: "Si necesita ayuda, dígame" = "If you need help, tell me." For "I need help": "Necesito ayuda." For "Do you (informal) need help?": "¿Necesitas ayuda?"
target_language_example: Si necesita ayuda, puedo explicárselo otra vez.
native_language_example: If you need help, I can explain it to you again.

additional_notes: Used with the verb necesitar in the third-person singular (necesita) to say that someone or something needs one of something. Usually followed by a masculine singular noun (un trabajo) or by a noun phrase like "un poco de" (un poco de aire). For feminine nouns, use "necesita una" (e.g., "necesita una pausa").
target_language_example: Mi coche necesita un lavado.
native_language_example: My car needs a wash.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group (including the speaker) needs a greater amount of something. It’s “necesitamos” (we need) + “más” (more), and it’s usually followed by a noun (más dinero, más tiempo) or can stand alone if the thing is understood from context.
target_language_example: Para terminar hoy, necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: To finish today, we need more time.

additional_notes: Used to say that you (a group including the speaker) need one thing: Necesitamos un + noun (usually a masculine singular noun). If the noun is feminine, use "necesitamos una" (Necesitamos una habitación). With plural nouns, use "necesitamos unos/unas" (Necesitamos unos datos). You can also use it with some quantity phrases: "necesitamos un poco de..." (we need a bit of...).
target_language_example: Necesitamos un taxi para ir al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We need a taxi to go to the airport.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people (ellos/ellas/ustedes) needs assistance. From necesitar (to need) in the present tense: necesitan = “they/you all need,” plus ayuda = “help.” Often the subject is omitted: “Necesitan ayuda.”
target_language_example: ¿Necesitan ayuda con esto?
native_language_example: Do you need help with this?

additional_notes: From necesitar (to need) + algo (something). Often used as a statement about what someone requires, but it can also be a question just by changing intonation: ¿Necesitas algo? = “Do you need anything?” In Spanish, subject pronouns are often omitted, so “(tú) necesitas algo” still means “you need something.”
target_language_example: ¿Necesitas algo del supermercado?
native_language_example: Do you need anything from the supermarket?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "necesitar" (to need) in the tú form: "necesitas". It can be a statement (Necesitas ayuda.) or a question (¿Necesitas ayuda?). Often used to offer help or to point out that someone needs assistance; you can add names or softeners like "¿...?," "si..." (e.g., "Llámame si necesitas ayuda").
target_language_example: ¿Necesitas ayuda con la tarea?
native_language_example: Do you need help with the homework?

additional_notes: Used to ask for assistance. Often followed by **con** + noun (necesito ayuda con mi trabajo = I need help with my work) or **para** + infinitive (necesito ayuda para entender = I need help to understand). You can also specify the type of help: *ayuda médica* (medical help).
target_language_example: Necesito ayuda con esta tarea, por favor.
native_language_example: I need help with this homework assignment, please.

meaning: "I need to talk to / speak with" (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you must speak with a specific person or group. Follow it with a person, pronoun (él/ella/ellos/ellas/usted/ustedes), or an institution (la policía, mi abogado). You can add time/urgency words like "primero" (first) or "ahora mismo" (right now).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con usted un momento.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you for a moment.

meaning: I need to speak with you. (formal)
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone formally (usted), such as a stranger, an older person, a customer/client, or someone in authority. You can add details like en privado (in private) or acerca de algo importante (about something important). In many contexts it can also sound like “I need to talk to you,” implying something serious.
target_language_example: Disculpe, necesito hablar con usted un momento.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need to speak with you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say you want a conversation with someone. It can sound serious depending on tone and context. You can add details: de algo (about something), en privado (in private), un minuto (for a minute), or a place (en mi oficina). Also common with a name: "Tom, necesito hablar contigo".
target_language_example: Necesito hablar contigo en privado, por favor.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you in private, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need a greater amount of something. Typically followed by a noun (necesito más práctica) or a quantity/measure (necesito más tiempo). You can also add "de" before an uncountable noun: "necesito más de agua" (though "necesito más agua" is more common).
target_language_example: Necesito más tiempo para terminar el trabajo.
native_language_example: I need more time to finish the work.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone else to do something. It’s followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: "Necesito que firmes", "Necesito que veas", "Necesito que te quedes". With "yo" (I), the subjunctive form often looks different from the normal present (e.g., "hagas" not "haces").
target_language_example: Necesito que me llames mañana.
native_language_example: I need you to call me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for you. It uses the present subjunctive after “necesito que” because it expresses a need/wish about another person’s action. “Hagas” is the tú form of “hacer” (to do/make). You can add details like “por mí” (for me) or “primero” (first).
target_language_example: Necesito que hagas algo hoy, por favor.
native_language_example: I need you to do something today, please.

meaning: "I need you to" (do something to/for me).
additional_notes: Used to ask for something you need, followed by a verb in the present subjunctive because it comes after "necesitar que". The "me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to/for me" (or sometimes the person affected). Common patterns: "Necesito que me + verb" (Necesito que me ayudes / llamen / dejen / lleven). You can often drop "me" if the action isn’t directed at you: "Necesito que respondas" vs. "Necesito que me respondas" (answer me).
target_language_example: Necesito que me ayudes con esto, por favor.
native_language_example: I need you to help me with this, please.

meaning: I need you to help me.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for help. After “necesito que…”, Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive: “ayudes” (from “ayudar”). You can add what you need help with using “a + infinitive” (e.g., “a encontrarlo/a hacerlo”).
target_language_example: Necesito que me ayudes con esta tarea.
native_language_example: I need you to help me with this homework assignment.

additional_notes: Used to express that you require some information. Often followed by a question word like dónde (where), por qué (why), qué (what), quién (who), or a noun phrase: Necesito saber su nombre (I need to know his/her name).
target_language_example: Necesito saber a qué hora empieza la reunión.
native_language_example: I need to know what time the meeting starts.

additional_notes: Used when you’re asking for an explanation of what happened or what something is. It’s typically followed by a verb or clause: qué pasó/ocurrió/sucedió (what happened), qué significa (what it means), qué quieres (what you want). Note that the accent matters: qué = "what" (question/indirect question).
target_language_example: Necesito saber qué estás haciendo aquí.
native_language_example: I need to know what you’re doing here.

additional_notes: Use “su” to be polite or formal (usted). Common with strangers, customers, or older people. With friends/family you usually say “necesito tu ayuda.” You can also soften it: “Necesito su ayuda, por favor.”
target_language_example: Disculpe, necesito su ayuda para encontrar la estación.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help to find the station.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone directly for help. "Necesito" = "I need" (from necesitar), and "tu ayuda" = "your help." You can swap in another possessive: "necesito su ayuda" (formal or plural "your"), "necesito nuestra ayuda" (I need our help).
target_language_example: Lo siento, necesito tu ayuda con esta tarea.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need your help with this assignment.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: "Necesito un + noun". Use "un" with masculine singular nouns (un cable, un bolígrafo, un visado). For feminine nouns, use "necesito una" (e.g., "Necesito una silla"). You can also add adjectives after the noun: "Necesito un cable nuevo".
target_language_example: Necesito un taxi, por favor.
native_language_example: I need a taxi, please.

additional_notes: Use it to ask for or state you need a small amount of something. It’s followed by a noun (usually uncountable: jabón, papel, información; but it can also be abstract like tiempo). You can make it more polite by adding “por favor”: “Necesito un poco de agua, por favor.”
target_language_example: Necesito un poco de ayuda con esta tarea.
native_language_example: I need a little help with this homework.

additional_notes: Used to ask for assistance politely. You can add location or detail: “Necesito un poco de ayuda aquí” (here). You can also say who you need help from: “Necesito un poco de ayuda tuya” (I need a little help from you). In more urgent situations you might say “Necesito ayuda” without “un poco de.”
target_language_example: Perdón, necesito un poco de ayuda con esta puerta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need a little help with this door.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: necesito (I need) + una (a/an). Use it before feminine singular nouns: una ambulancia, una bicicleta, una habitación. For masculine nouns, use "necesito un" (e.g., necesito un médico). You can drop "yo" because the verb form already shows who needs it.
target_language_example: Necesito una mesa para la cocina.
native_language_example: I need a table for the kitchen.

additional_notes: Uses the "vosotros" form (Spain) to address a group informally. It can be a statement (Ne-ce-si-TÁIS a-YU-da.) or a question when said with rising intonation: «¿Necesitáis ayuda?». The accent in «necesitáis» marks the stress.
target_language_example: ¿Necesitáis ayuda con las maletas?
native_language_example: Do you all need help with the suitcases?

additional_notes: Used to deny a past action or experience: **negar + haber + past participle**. The verb **negar** is conjugated (here, **negó** = 'he/she denied'), and **haber** introduces a completed past action (like English 'having done'). Common after this: *negó haber dicho* (denied having said), *negó haber sabido* (denied having known).
target_language_example: Ella negó haber tomado el dinero.
native_language_example: She denied having taken the money.

additional_notes: Used with **negar** (to deny) + **haber** + past participle to deny a past action: *negó haber robado…* = “denied having stolen…”. The noun that was allegedly stolen comes after **el** (or **la/los/las**): *negó haber robado el dinero / la cartera*.
target_language_example: El hombre negó haber robado el reloj.
native_language_example: The man denied having stolen the watch.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to show that something doesn’t happen or isn’t true in the most basic/expected case. It often appears before the verb ("ni siquiera me acuerdo") or before what is being emphasized ("ni siquiera de eso").
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo; ni siquiera he desayunado.
native_language_example: I don’t have time; I haven’t even had breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is far from being true/achieved. Very common in comparisons like “no estar ni cerca de + noun/infinitive” (to be nowhere near + noun/doing something). It can also appear in contrasts like “ni cerca ni lejos” (neither close nor far).
target_language_example: Todavía no está ni cerca de terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: He’s still not even close to finishing the project.

meaning: "No way!" / "Not a chance." (also: "Don’t even talk/mention it.")
additional_notes: Common, colloquial expression used to strongly reject an idea or proposal: “De eso, ni hablar” = “Absolutely not / No way.” It can also mean “let’s not even talk about that” or “don’t mention that,” often with “de” + topic: “ni hablar de eso.”
target_language_example: ¿Prestarte mi coche? Ni hablar.
native_language_example: Lend you my car? No way.

additional_notes: Common, informal-sounding way to say you don’t know or had no knowledge about something. Often used alone as a short answer (“¿Sabes quién fue?” “¡Ni idea!”) or in longer phrases like “no tener ni idea de…” (to have no idea about…) and “no tener ni idea que…” (to have no idea that…).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora llega? Ni idea, todavía no me han dicho nada.
native_language_example: What time is it arriving? No idea—they still haven’t told me anything.

additional_notes: Used with a negative (often "no") to emphasize that someone doesn’t know or understand something at all: "no tengo ni idea de..." / "no tienes ni idea de...". It’s commonly followed by a noun ("ni idea de la hora") or by "lo que / quién / qué / cuál(es)" + a clause ("ni idea de quién fue").
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de dónde está mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my phone is.

meaning: not at all; far from it.
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a negative idea or to correct an assumption: “not even close.” Often follows a negative statement (e.g., “no…, ni mucho menos”) or can stand alone as a firm reply meaning “Definitely not.” Also common in the pattern “(no) … ni mucho menos …” = “(not) … much less … / let alone …”.
target_language_example: ¿Te molesta? No, ni mucho menos.
native_language_example: Does it bother you? No, not at all.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse something or shut down an idea. Often appears after a suggestion or request: "¿Me prestas tu coche? —Ni pensarlo." It’s also common as "¡Ni lo pienses!" (same idea).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo salir hoy aunque tenga examen mañana? —Ni pensarlo.
native_language_example: Can I go out today even though I have an exam tomorrow? —Don’t even think about it.

meaning: "as if" / "like" (showing disbelief or rejecting an idea).
additional_notes: Usually followed by the subjunctive and often used in exclamations to say something is NOT true or NOT a good excuse: "¡Ni que fuera tonto!" = "As if I were stupid!" It can also appear in shortened/elliptical phrases like "Ni que lo menciones" meaning "Don’t even mention it." This use is common in spoken, informal Spanish.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué corres? ¡Ni que llegáramos tarde!
native_language_example: Why are you running? It’s not like we’re late!

meaning: "Don’t you dare" / "Don’t even think about it."
additional_notes: A strong warning or command telling someone not to do something. Often followed by an infinitive: "Ni se te ocurra decirlo" (Don’t you dare say it). You may also hear "Que ni se te ocurra" for extra emphasis. Uses the verb "ocurrirse" (for an idea to occur to someone) with an indirect object pronoun: "se te" = "to you."
target_language_example: Ni se te ocurra tocar eso.
native_language_example: Don’t you dare touch that.

meaning: 'not even' (emphasizes that something doesn’t happen or isn’t true).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something is surprising or less than expected: not even the most basic/obvious thing. It often comes before the verb ("Ni siquiera se levanta") or before what is being emphasized ("ni siquiera sabes dónde vive").
target_language_example: Ni siquiera tengo tiempo para comer.
native_language_example: I don't even have time to eat.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something doesn’t happen at all: not even trying/thinking/reading it. "Ni siquiera" = "not even"; "lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him/that"). Often followed by a verb: "Ni siquiera lo + verb".
target_language_example: Ni siquiera lo entiendo.
native_language_example: I don’t even understand it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something doesn’t happen at all, not even in the most basic or expected way. It’s often followed by a verb: “ni siquiera me conoces” (you don’t even know me), “ni siquiera me miras” (you don’t even look at me), “ni siquiera me estás escuchando” (you’re not even listening to me). You can move it for emphasis: “Tú ni siquiera me conoces.”
target_language_example: Ni siquiera me llamaste para avisar.
native_language_example: You didn’t even call me to let me know.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you can’t do something basic/expected, often showing frustration, disbelief, or being overwhelmed. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., dormir, recordar, decir). You can change the verb to match the subject: ni siquiera puedo (I), ni siquiera puedes (you), ni siquiera puede (he/she/you formal), ni siquiera podemos (we).
target_language_example: Estoy tan cansado que ni siquiera puedo pensar con claridad.
native_language_example: I’m so tired that I can’t even think clearly.

additional_notes: "Ni siquiera" adds emphasis: something didn’t happen at all, not even the minimum you’d expect. The "se" is the pronoun used with reflexive verbs (e.g., despedirse = to say goodbye, cambiarse = to change clothes, esconderse = to hide) or with impersonal/passive constructions like "se puede" ("you/one can"). Word order: "ni siquiera" usually comes right before the verb phrase: "Ni siquiera se despidió" / "Ni siquiera se puede nadar".
target_language_example: Ni siquiera se acordó de llamarme.
native_language_example: He/She didn’t even remember to call me.

meaning: "I don't even know" / "I don't even know (that...)"
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you don’t know something at all, often showing surprise, frustration, or that you lack basic information. It’s commonly followed by a question word or clause: "ni siquiera sé qué...", "ni siquiera sé lo que...", "ni siquiera sé cómo...", "ni siquiera sé a qué...".
target_language_example: Ni siquiera sé dónde dejé las llaves.
native_language_example: I don't even know where I left the keys.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a negative idea (often with another negative like “no”): “Eso no te lo crees ni tú” = “Not even you believe that.” It also appears in “ni... ni...” structures to mean “neither... nor...” (“Ni tú ni yo” = “Neither you nor I”), and can be used alone as a short, emphatic reply (“Ni tú.” = “Not even you.” / “You neither.”).
target_language_example: Eso no lo entiendes ni tú.
native_language_example: Not even you understand that.

meaning: not even one; not a single (one).
additional_notes: Used with negation to emphasize zero quantity: no/none at all (often with "no" or alone as a fragment: "Ni un sonido"). It can be followed by a noun ("ni un correo") or by intensifiers like "solo/sólo", "poquito", etc. It agrees for gender/number: "ni una" (not even one, feminine).
target_language_example: No comí ni un bocado en todo el día.
native_language_example: I didn’t eat even a bite all day.

meaning: “not a cent; not even one cent” (nothing at all).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero amount of money. Common in phrases like “ni un centavo más” (“not a cent more”) or “no tener ni un centavo” (“to not have a cent / to be broke”). “Centavo” is the smallest coin unit in many Spanish-speaking countries.
target_language_example: No pienso pagarte ni un centavo más.
native_language_example: I’m not going to pay you one cent more.

meaning: not even a single; not a single (one).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero quantity, often with a negative idea (no, nunca, nadie, etc.) or in negative contexts. It’s a strong way to say “not one” of something: “No vi ni un solo… / Nunca… ni un solo…”. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: ni un solo día (masc.), ni una sola vez (fem.).
target_language_example: No tengo ni un solo minuto libre hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have a single free minute today.

meaning: not even one; not a single (feminine).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero amount of something, often after a negative word like "no" (e.g., "No queda ni una..."). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number: "ni una gota" (fem.), "ni un minuto" (masc.). It can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “not one.”
target_language_example: No tengo ni una idea de cómo hacerlo.
native_language_example: I don’t have even one idea of how to do it.

meaning: not a word; not a single word.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize total silence or that someone said nothing at all, often with negatives like "no" ("No dijo ni una palabra"). It can also be used as a command: "Ni una palabra más" = "Not another word."
target_language_example: No digas ni una palabra hasta que lleguemos a casa.
native_language_example: Don’t say a word until we get home.

additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis to mean “not even one.” It agrees in gender/number with the noun: ni un solo día (not a single day), ni una sola persona (not a single person). Often appears with other negatives like no/nunca, and can also be used with time expressions: ni una sola vez (not once).
target_language_example: No vi ni una sola señal de vida.
native_language_example: I didn’t see a single sign of life.

meaning: not a single word (none at all).
additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis with negatives like no, jamás, sin, or questions/short answers. Can refer to understanding (“I didn’t understand a thing”), speaking (“without saying a word”), believing (“I didn’t believe a word he said”), or the absence of something said (“not a single word of thanks”). Often works as a standalone comment: “Ni una sola palabra.”
target_language_example: No entendí ni una sola palabra de la película.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand a single word of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero quantity (often as a short answer: “Ni uno.” = “Not one.”). You’ll also see it with emphasis words: “ni uno más” (not one more), “ni uno solo” (not even one). In comparisons, it can mean “not … either”: “ni uno ni lo otro” (neither one nor the other).
target_language_example: No tengo ni uno solo.
native_language_example: I don't have even one.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something doesn’t happen or isn’t true in the most minimal/expected case. It often goes right before the verb or the thing being emphasized: "ni siquiera existía" (didn’t even exist), "ni siquiera mires" (don’t even look). Sometimes it starts the sentence for emphasis: "Ni siquiera sé..." (I don’t even know...).
target_language_example: Ni siquiera tengo tiempo para comer.
native_language_example: I don't even have time to eat.

additional_notes: Used with negatives (no, nadie, nunca, etc.) to mean “nowhere / not anywhere.” Common patterns: **a ninguna parte** with movement verbs (ir, salir, llevar) = “(to) nowhere / not anywhere,” and **en ninguna parte** for location = “nowhere.” Also appears in the set phrase **en medio de ninguna parte** = “in the middle of nowhere.”
target_language_example: No encuentro mis llaves en ninguna parte.
native_language_example: I can’t find my keys anywhere.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to say that zero items in a group apply: "Ninguna de las ventanas..." = none of the windows. You’ll also see it with a number: "ninguna de las tres" = none of the three (when the group is feminine or implied feminine). With a noun directly after it, Spanish often omits "de": "No respondí ninguna de las cartas" = I didn’t reply to any of the letters.
target_language_example: Ninguna de las respuestas es correcta.
native_language_example: None of the answers is correct.

additional_notes: Used when talking about two feminine things (e.g., dos cartas, dos opciones) to say that not one of them applies/was done. It can also be used alone as a short answer: “¿Cuál prefieres?” — “Ninguna de las dos.” For masculine nouns, use “ninguno de los dos”.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres té o café? — Ninguna de las dos; prefiero agua.
native_language_example: Do you want tea or coffee? — Neither; I prefer water.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people/things in a group apply. It’s followed by a noun phrase (often with a definite/possessive: "ninguno de los...", "ninguno de mis...") or by a pronoun: "ninguno de ellos". Often appears with "no" when it comes before a verb: "No conozco a ninguno de..." (double negation is normal in Spanish). "Ninguno" can change to feminine "ninguna" if the noun is feminine: "ninguna de las...".
target_language_example: No he visto a ninguno de mis vecinos hoy.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen any of my neighbors today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a group of people/things and say that zero of them do something or apply. Often appears with “no” in the sentence (double negative in Spanish): “No conozco a ninguno de ellos.” You can also use it as a subject: “Ninguno de ellos sabe…”. For feminine groups, use “ninguna de ellas” (none of them, women/things).
target_language_example: Ninguno de ellos quiere ir hoy.
native_language_example: None of them want to go today.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people/things in a specific group meet a condition. It’s normally followed by a plural noun: "ninguno de los candidatos". You can also use it with pronouns like "ninguno de los presentes" (“none of the people present”). With feminine plural nouns, it changes to "ninguna de las" (e.g., "ninguna de las opciones").
target_language_example: Ninguno de los estudiantes llegó a tiempo.
native_language_example: None of the students arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero out of two people/things apply. It agrees in gender/number with what it refers to: masculine singular is most common (ninguno), but with feminine nouns you often use “ninguna de las dos” (e.g., Ninguna de las dos opciones es buena). Often answers a choice between two: “¿Té o café?” — “Ninguno de los dos.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres pollo o pescado? — Ninguno de los dos; soy vegetariano.
native_language_example: Do you want chicken or fish? — Neither; I’m vegetarian.

meaning: none of us; not one of us.
additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in the group “we/us” did something or are something. It’s normally followed by a singular verb (Ninguno de nosotros es / puede / tiene), although plural agreement can appear in some contexts. For mixed genders, Spanish typically uses the masculine form ninguno; for an all-female group you may hear ninguna de nosotras (“none of us [women]”).
target_language_example: Ninguno de nosotros entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: None of us understand the question.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in that group (their children) did something or exist in the situation. Pattern: "ninguno/ninguna de + [possessive] + plural noun". It often goes with a singular verb (e.g., "Ninguno de sus hijos quiere...") even though "hijos" is plural. "Sus" can mean "his", "her", "their", or formal "your"—context tells you which.
target_language_example: Ninguno de sus hijos vive cerca.
native_language_example: None of his/her/their children lives nearby.

additional_notes: Means “no place.” It’s commonly used with negation words like no, nadie, nunca (e.g., “No voy a ningún lado” = “I’m not going anywhere”). You’ll also hear it after “ni” in the pattern “Ni aquí ni en ningún lado” (“Neither here nor anywhere”).
target_language_example: Hoy no salgo a ningún lado porque tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I’m not going anywhere because I have a lot of work.

additional_notes: Used with negation (ningún = “no/any” before a masculine singular noun). Common patterns: **sin ningún motivo** (“for no reason”), **no hay ningún motivo (de...)** (“there’s no reason (to...) / no grounds for...”), **por ningún motivo** (“under no circumstances / for no reason whatsoever”).
target_language_example: No lo hice con ningún motivo en particular.
native_language_example: I didn’t do it for any particular reason.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t an issue or to reassure someone you won’t cause trouble. Usually appears with negation (no / no hay / no es / no tenemos) because ningún means “no/none” before a masculine singular noun (problema). For feminine nouns, use ninguna (e.g., ninguna duda).
target_language_example: No hay ningún problema; puedo hacerlo mañana.
native_language_example: No problem; I can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a negation (no, ya no, no le encuentro, etc.) to mean “it doesn’t make any sense” or “it makes no sense.” It can also refer to a type of “sense,” like an ability: “sentido de la orientación” = “sense of direction.” Common patterns: “no tiene ningún sentido…”, “no le encuentro ningún sentido (a algo)”.
target_language_example: No tiene ningún sentido discutir ahora.
native_language_example: It doesn’t make any sense to argue now.

meaning: a little girl; a young girl.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a female child. "Niña" means "girl" and "pequeña" means "small/little"; together it’s a common way to emphasize that the girl is young. You can also say "una niña" or "una niña chica" in some regions.
target_language_example: Esa niña pequeña está jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: That little girl is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used to say what children are doing or what state they’re in right now. "Están" is the present tense, ellos/ellas/ustedes form of "estar" (to be). It’s often followed by a gerund (-ando/-iendo) for actions in progress: "Los niños están nadando" = "The children are swimming."
target_language_example: Los niños están jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: The children are playing in the park.

additional_notes: Refers to children who are very young (often toddlers or early elementary age). Used as a noun phrase ("the little/young kids"). You can also say "los niños pequeños" = "the young children."
target_language_example: En este parque hay muchos niños pequeños.
native_language_example: In this park there are lots of young children.

additional_notes: Used to say what (male or mixed-gender) children are like or what they are (identity/description) using **ser**. **Niños** is masculine plural, and **son** is the **they/you (plural) are** form of **ser**. Often appears after a subject like **Estos/Esos/Todos los niños son...**
target_language_example: Todos los niños son diferentes.
native_language_example: All children are different.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to answer “no” and then immediately negate/deny something with a second “no.” It can sound emphatic (“No, absolutely not”) or simply natural in speech. In writing, the comma often separates the initial answer from the following clause: “No, no tengo…”
target_language_example: No, no quiero ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I don't want to go today.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or correct something, often after someone suggests the opposite: “No, no lo comprendo” = “No, I don’t understand it.” The "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that,” referring to a masculine noun or to an idea/statement already understood from context. With forms like "no lo soy" or "no lo está," "lo" can mean “that” (e.g., “I’m not that,” “it’s not that/like that”).
target_language_example: —¿Lo entiendes? —No, no lo entiendo.
native_language_example: —Do you understand it? —No, I don’t understand it.

meaning: “can’t take it anymore” / “can’t stand it anymore.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve reached your limit (physically or emotionally). Often followed by what you can’t tolerate: “No aguantar más el ruido” (to not be able to stand the noise anymore), or used alone. Very close in meaning to “¡No puedo más!” depending on context.
target_language_example: No aguantar más este calor es imposible; vámonos a casa.
native_language_example: Not being able to take this heat anymore is impossible; let’s go home.

meaning: "not like that" / "not so" (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to say that a statement applies to one thing/person but does NOT apply to another. It often appears in contrast structures like: “X sí…, no así Y” (“X does…, but Y doesn’t”) or “X es…, no así Y” (“X is…, but Y isn’t”). It can sound a bit formal/literary in this contrastive use.
target_language_example: A Ana le encanta viajar; no así a su hermano.
native_language_example: Ana loves to travel; her brother doesn’t.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or written Spanish to mean that one action happens immediately after another. It typically introduces a clause with a past tense verb: "No bien + preterite/compound past…, (ya) + verb…". It does NOT mean "not well" in this use.
target_language_example: No bien llegué a casa, me llamó mi madre.
native_language_example: As soon as I got home, my mom called me.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand something (an idea, situation, or what someone said). Often followed by a question word like cómo (how) or por qué (why): “No comprendo cómo…” / “No comprendo por qué…”. You can add nada for emphasis: “No comprendo nada” = “I don’t understand anything.”
target_language_example: Perdón, no comprendo lo que dices.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand what you’re saying.

meaning: "I don't know" / "I'm not acquainted with" (a person/people).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "conocer" to say you are not familiar with a person. Spanish uses the personal "a" before a direct object that is a specific person (e.g., "No conozco a Tom", "No conozco a su hermana"). With indefinite pronouns like "ninguno/ninguna" it means you don’t know any of them ("No conozco a ninguno de ellos"). "Casi no conozco a..." = "I barely know...".
target_language_example: Lo siento, no conozco a tu amigo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know your friend.

meaning: “I don’t know (or: I don’t know of) anyone.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know any people in a place or in general. Often followed by a relative clause with "que" to add information: "No conozco a nadie que..." = “I don’t know anyone who...”. "Conocer" is for knowing people/being familiar with places (not for knowing facts). The "a" is the personal "a" used before direct objects that are people ("conozco a María", "no conozco a nadie").
target_language_example: Lo siento, no conozco a nadie en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anyone in this city.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., No creo que sea…, No creo que haga…). Often you can drop “que” in English: “I don’t think it’s necessary.”
target_language_example: No creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

meaning: "I don’t think that" / "I don’t believe that."
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement about what was just mentioned. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (e.g., pase, sea, suceda, vaya a pasar) because you’re talking about something uncertain or not confirmed.
target_language_example: No creo que eso funcione.
native_language_example: I don’t think that will work.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt/uncertainty. After a negative opinion like “no creo que…”, Spanish normally uses the subjunctive. Here, “haya + participle” is the present perfect subjunctive (haya dicho/hecho/entendido/salido, etc.). Often translates naturally as “I don’t think (he/she/they) has…” or “I don’t think there has been…”.
target_language_example: No creo que haya terminado el trabajo todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t think (he/she/they) has finished the work yet.

meaning: "I don’t think there is/are" (I doubt there’s…).
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or belief that something doesn’t exist or isn’t the case. "Haya" is the present subjunctive of "haber" (impersonal “there is/are”), triggered by "no creo que". It’s commonly followed by: alguien/nadie (someone/no one), ningún/ninguna (any/none), mucho/a (much/many).
target_language_example: No creo que haya suficiente tiempo para hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t think there’s enough time to do it today.

meaning: "I don’t think (that) … it" / "I don’t believe (that) … it."
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disbelief. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., entienda, hagan, haya hecho, supiera) because the speaker is not stating it as a fact. "Lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" or "him" (sometimes "her"), referring to something already mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: No creo que lo sepan todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t think they know it yet.

additional_notes: Used to say you doubt you’re able to do something. After expressions like “creo que / no creo que”, Spanish uses the subjunctive (here, “pueda” from “poder”). Often followed by an infinitive: “No creo que pueda hacerlo/ir/volver.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no creo que pueda ir mañana.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t think I can go tomorrow.

meaning: "I don’t think it is" / "I don’t believe it is" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disbelief about something. Because "creer" is negated ("no creo"), Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive after "que" (here: "sea" from "ser"). Often followed by an adjective or a noun clause: "No creo que sea correcto" / "No creo que sea eso."
target_language_example: No creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of deber (“should/ought to”) with no to say something is not recommended, not appropriate, or not expected. Often followed by an infinitive: no debería hacerlo (“I/you/he/she shouldn’t do it”). The subject can be clear from context or added (Yo/Tú/Él/Ella no debería...).
target_language_example: No debería decir eso en voz alta.
native_language_example: You/I shouldn’t say that out loud.

meaning: "I/you/he/she/etc. shouldn’t have" (regret about a past action).
additional_notes: Used to say something was a mistake in the past. Structure: no + deber (in conditional) + haber + past participle (aceptado, esperado, vuelto, tirado, etc.). The subject is often implied: "No debería haber vuelto" = "I shouldn’t have come back."
target_language_example: No debería haber dicho eso.
native_language_example: I shouldn’t have said that.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, a recommendation, or a mild warning/reproach. It uses the conditional of deber (deberías), which often sounds like a suggestion rather than a strict order. Followed by an infinitive: “No deberías + infinitive” (e.g., no deberías decir, venir, hacer).
target_language_example: No deberías conducir tan rápido.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t drive so fast.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not supposed to be in a place (because it’s not allowed, it’s unsafe, or it’s not the right time). Commonly followed by a time clause like “cuando…” (when…) or “durante…” (during…). Uses the conditional of deber (deberías) to give advice/soft obligation; stronger alternatives include “no puedes estar aquí” (you can’t be here).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no deberías estar aquí ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, you shouldn’t be here right now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something is not allowed or not advisable. It’s the negative of “debes” (from deber), and it’s often followed by an infinitive: “No debes fumar.” It can sound like a rule/obligation (“must not”) or advice (“shouldn’t”), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: No debes hablar durante la prueba.
native_language_example: You mustn’t/shouldn’t talk during the test.

meaning: to not say anything; to stay quiet.
additional_notes: Uses the infinitive after another verb or expression (e.g., es mejor / prometí / sabía que era mejor). Often implies choosing to keep silent (sometimes to avoid problems or keep a secret).
target_language_example: En la reunión, preferí no decir nada.
native_language_example: In the meeting, I preferred not to say anything.

meaning: to not say a word; to stay completely silent.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize total silence, often in situations where someone refuses to speak, is upset, or is shocked. Very similar variants include “no decir ni una palabra” (not to say even one word) and “sin decir palabra” (without saying a word). Neutral in tone and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Cuando le preguntaron qué había pasado, decidió no decir palabra.
native_language_example: When they asked him what had happened, he decided not to say a word.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to prevent something from happening. It’s the negative command (tú) of **dejar** (“to let/allow”) + **que** + a verb in the **subjunctive**: *No dejes que entre.* (“Don’t let him/her come in.”).
target_language_example: No dejes que te hablen así.
native_language_example: Don’t let them talk to you like that.

additional_notes: Negative tú command of decir (“to say/tell”), used to tell one person not to say something: No digas eso (“Don’t say that”). It can also be an exclamation meaning “No way!” or “You don’t say!” (showing surprise), often said as ¡No digas! or ¡No me digas! (“You’re kidding!”).
target_language_example: No digas eso, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t say that, please.

additional_notes: Negative command (tú) used to tell one person to stay quiet or keep a secret. Often used with names or “por favor”: “No digas nada, por favor.”
target_language_example: No digas nada cuando llegue mi mamá.
native_language_example: Don’t say anything when my mom arrives.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of decir: no + dijo + nada. Often used to describe someone staying silent or not commenting in a specific moment. You can add context with phrases like “en absoluto” (at all) or “con respecto a…” (regarding…).
target_language_example: Le pregunté qué pasó, pero no dijo nada.
native_language_example: I asked him/her what happened, but he/she didn’t say anything.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand something (a question, explanation, situation, etc.). You can add what you don’t understand: “No entiendo las preguntas” (I don’t understand the questions). With “nada” it means “I don’t understand anything at all”: “No entiendo nada.”
target_language_example: Perdón, no entiendo. ¿Puedes repetirlo?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand. Can you repeat it?

additional_notes: Used to express confusion or disagreement about the reason for something. Often followed by a clause (por qué + subject + verb): “No entiendo por qué lo hiciste.” It can also be used before a noun phrase to mean “why so much/so many”: “No entiendo por qué tanto alboroto.” (Note: “por qué” = “why” in questions/indirect questions; “porque” = “because”.)
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué no me lo dijiste antes.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you didn’t tell me earlier.

additional_notes: *No era* is the negative of **era** (imperfect past of **ser**, “to be”). Use it to say someone/something **was not** a certain identity, description, or characteristic in the past (often background info or a continuing past situation): *Tom no era bueno* (“Tom wasn’t good”). For plural, use **no eran** (“they weren’t”).
target_language_example: De niño, no era muy alto.
native_language_example: As a kid, I wasn’t very tall.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb **ser** in the **tú** form (**eres**). It’s commonly followed by a noun or adjective: **No eres estudiante** (“You’re not a student”), **No eres creativo/a** (“You’re not creative”). For emphasis you may see **no eres más que...** (“you’re nothing more than...”).
target_language_example: No eres mi jefe.
native_language_example: You're not my boss.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they aren’t alone in a situation, feeling, ability, or claim. Often followed by “que…” or by a description: “No eres el único que piensa eso” (You’re not the only one who thinks that) or “No eres el único con…” (You’re not the only one with…). You can change it for gender/number: “no eres la única” (to a woman), “no son los únicos/las únicas” (to a group).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no eres el único que está nervioso.
native_language_example: Relax, you’re not the only one who’s nervous.

meaning: "you are not a" (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *ser* to say someone is not a certain type of person/thing (identity or description): *No eres un Nazi / un asesino / un sucesor adecuado.* For a feminine noun, use *no eres una* (e.g., *No eres una doctora*). With plural, use *no eres* + plural noun/adjective (e.g., *No eres mi amigo* / *No eres mi amigo* vs. *No eres mi amiga*).
target_language_example: No eres un problema; eres parte de la solución.
native_language_example: You’re not a problem; you’re part of the solution.

additional_notes: Negative form of the verb **ser** (to be) in the **he/she/it/you (formal)** present tense: **no + es**. Used to say something isn’t true about someone/something (e.g., identity, description, origin): *No es cierto*, *No es médico*, *No es de aquí*.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero eso no es verdad.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that isn’t true.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t happen often, isn’t normal/acceptable, or isn’t possible. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive: "No es algo que se haga" (It’s not something people do), "No es algo que se pueda enseñar" (It’s not something that can be taught).
target_language_example: No es algo que puedas resolver en un día.
native_language_example: It’s not something you can solve in a day.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t concern you or isn’t your responsibility. Often implies you shouldn’t get involved. You may also hear: “No es asunto tuyo” (none of your business, to you) or “No es asunto nuestro” (none of our business, for us).
target_language_example: Si ellos quieren discutir, no es asunto mío.
native_language_example: If they want to argue, it’s none of my business.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone something doesn’t concern them. Often sounds firm or rude, especially said alone (“No es asunto tuyo.”). You can also use it with a clause: “No es asunto tuyo dónde estoy” = “Where I am is none of your business.” Variations: “no es asunto mío” (none of my business), “no es asunto nuestro” (none of our business).
target_language_example: No es asunto tuyo con quién salgo.
native_language_example: It’s none of your business who I’m dating.

meaning: “it’s not like that / that’s not true.”
additional_notes: Used to disagree or correct someone (“No, that’s not how it is”). It can also be used as a tag question (often with ¿…?) to ask for confirmation: “..., isn’t that right?” In questions it’s common to add the person’s name: “no es así, Damien?”
target_language_example: No, no es así; lo entendiste mal.
native_language_example: No, that’s not true; you misunderstood it.

meaning: “it’s not good” / “it’s not a good idea.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is bad quality (a road, a referee, a product) or to warn that an action is unhealthy, unsafe, or inappropriate. Often followed by an infinitive: “No es bueno + verb” (No es bueno fumar). You can add “para” to specify for whom: “No es bueno para ti.”
target_language_example: No es bueno conducir cuando estás cansado.
native_language_example: It’s not good to drive when you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something has a negative effect on a person, thing, or situation. Follow it with a noun or pronoun (para el bebé, para mí, para los negocios). You can also use it with an infinitive as the subject: "Fumar no es bueno para la salud."
target_language_example: Comer demasiada azúcar no es bueno para los dientes.
native_language_example: Eating too much sugar isn’t good for your teeth.

no es bueno para la salud

target_language_multi_word_term: no es bueno para la salud
additional_notes: Used to warn or advise that an action or habit is unhealthy. Often follows an activity: “Fumar no es bueno para la salud.” You can also add “tu/su” for “your/his/her/their”: “No es bueno para tu salud.”
target_language_example: Comer tanta azúcar no es bueno para la salud.
native_language_example: Eating that much sugar isn’t good for your health.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct something that was said or implied. Often appears with a tag question like “¿verdad?” or “¿no es cierto?” (similar to “right?” / “isn’t that so?”). You can also say “Eso no es cierto” = “That isn’t true.”
target_language_example: No es cierto; yo nunca dije eso.
native_language_example: That’s not true; I never said that.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is not responsible for a bad situation. Very commonly followed by **de + person/pronoun**: *No es culpa de Madame Blanche.* You’ll also often hear it as **No es culpa tuya / mía / nuestra** (“It’s not your/my/our fault”), and it can be emphasized with **No es tu culpa**.
target_language_example: No es culpa mía; fue un accidente.
native_language_example: It’s not my fault; it was an accident.

meaning: "is not (from / belonging to)" or "is not the kind/type to".
additional_notes: Used with **ser + de** to say something/someone doesn’t belong to a person or group (**El bebé no es de él** = he isn’t the father / the baby isn’t his), isn’t from a place (**No es de por acá** = not from around here), or isn’t the type to do something or have a trait (**No es de opiniones precipitadas** = he/she doesn’t make rash judgments; **no es de esos** = not one of those kinds). What comes after **de** can be a person/pronoun, a place, or a noun phrase describing a type/group.
target_language_example: Tranquilo: ella no es de mentir.
native_language_example: Relax: she’s not the type to lie.

meaning: “is not the …” / “it’s not the one who …”.
additional_notes: Used to negate an identity with the verb *ser*: *no es el/la/los/las + noun* (“is not the …”). It’s also common in contrast/emphasis structures: *No es el/la + noun/pronoun + quien/que + verb* (“It’s not the … who …”), often followed by *sino* (“but rather”). Gender/number changes: *no es el* (masc. singular), *no es la* (fem. singular), etc.
target_language_example: No es el profesor quien decide eso, sino el director.
native_language_example: It’s not the teacher who decides that, but the principal.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is difficult. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., “No es fácil estudiar”) or a clause about an activity (“No es fácil hablar una lengua extranjera”). You can also use it to comment on a person or situation: “No es fácil lidiar contigo.”
target_language_example: No es fácil levantarse temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to get up early every day.

meaning: "it is not the" (before a singular feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to negate an identification/description with a feminine singular noun: "No es la manera..." = "It’s not the right way...". The article "la" is for feminine singular nouns; for masculine singular, use "no es el" (e.g., "No es el problema"). Often followed by a noun or noun phrase (la manera, la vida real, la nación).
target_language_example: No es la respuesta correcta.
native_language_example: It’s not the correct answer.

no es la primera vez que

target_language_multi_word_term: no es la primera vez que
additional_notes: Used to say something has happened before (it’s a repeated situation). It’s typically followed by a verb clause (often in the present tense even if referring to past events): “No es la primera vez que + [verb]”. You can change the tense: “No fue/No era la primera vez que …” depending on the story/time frame.
target_language_example: No es la primera vez que llegas tarde.
native_language_example: It’s not the first time you’ve been late.

meaning: “it’s not what…” / “it’s not the same as…” (often: “it’s not what it used to be”).
additional_notes: Used to say something has changed or isn’t as good as before: “No es lo que era” = “It’s not what it used to be.” Also used to correct someone or clarify a misunderstanding: “No es lo que pregunté/oí” = “That’s not what I asked/heard.” It’s typically followed by a clause (e.g., “no es lo que pensé”) or by “era / solía ser.”
target_language_example: Este restaurante ya no es lo que era.
native_language_example: This restaurant isn’t what it used to be anymore.

meaning: “it’s not my …” (to say something doesn’t belong to you or isn’t your responsibility).
additional_notes: Used with a noun after it: “No es mi culpa” (It’s not my fault), “No es mi día” (It’s not my day), “No es mi especialidad” (It’s not my specialty). Often the full phrase is “Eso/Esa/Este/Esta no es mi …” = “That/This isn’t my …”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no es mi problema.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it’s not my problem.

additional_notes: Used to deny responsibility or blame. Often followed by "que" + a clause to explain what you’re not responsible for: "No es mi culpa que...". You can change the person: "no es tu/su/nuestra culpa".
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no es mi culpa que el autobús llegue tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it’s not my fault that the bus arrives late.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or sometimes an adverb) to soften a negative evaluation: *no es muy + adj.* It can mean “not very” or, depending on tone, “not particularly.” You can change **es** to match the subject: *no soy muy*, *no eres muy*, *no somos muy*, etc.
target_language_example: La película no es muy buena, pero vale la pena verla.
native_language_example: The movie isn’t very good, but it’s worth watching.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something, often followed by a noun: No es más que + un/una + noun. Can sound dismissive depending on context (e.g., “No es más que una niña” = “She’s just a girl”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: no es más que un rumor.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a rumor.

meaning: “it’s nothing more than a” / “it’s just a”.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or reduce something/someone to what the speaker considers its true or lesser nature. Often has a dismissive tone. It agrees with gender/number: no es más que un (masc. sing.), no es más que una (fem. sing.), no es más que unos/unas (plural).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: no es más que un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to downplay something or reassure someone. Common in phrases like “No es nada personal” (“It’s nothing personal”) and as a response to thanks (“No es nada” = “You’re welcome / It’s nothing”).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda. — No es nada.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help. — It’s nothing / You’re welcome.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t required. Often followed by a noun (No es necesario el algodón.) or by “que” + subjunctive to talk about an action (No es necesario que estés sola.). You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: No era necesario…, No será necesario….
target_language_example: No es necesario que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: You don’t need to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something cannot happen or cannot be done. Often followed by an infinitive (No es posible + verbo: “No es posible concebir…”) or by “que” + clause (No es posible que…: “It’s not possible that…” / “You can’t possibly…”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no es posible terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s not possible to finish the project today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t meet a need, requirement, or expectation. Often followed by “para” + someone/something: “No es suficiente para mí” (It’s not enough for me). Can also be used alone as a complete sentence: “No es suficiente.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero eso no es suficiente para aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that’s not enough to pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to make comparisons or soften a statement. Often followed by an adjective/adverb and sometimes by "como" to compare: "no es tan + adjective + como…" ("not as… as…"). It can refer to something (no es) or a person (él/ella no es), depending on context.
target_language_example: No es tan difícil como parece.
native_language_example: It isn’t as difficult as it seems.

meaning: “isn’t as tall as” (not as tall as).
additional_notes: Used to compare height and say someone/something is less tall than another. Pattern: [subject] + no es tan alto como + [comparison]. You can swap in other adjectives: no es tan grande como (not as big as), no es tan caro como (not as expensive as). For past/then-vs-now comparisons, you may see additions like: no es tan alto como lo era (not as tall as he/she used to be).
target_language_example: Mi hermano no es tan alto como Jiro.
native_language_example: My brother isn’t as tall as Jiro.

additional_notes: Used to say something is harder than it seems or to gently push back against someone’s suggestion. Often followed by comparisons with "como" ("No es tan fácil como...") or used as a standalone comment; you may also hear it with a tag question like "¿no?" to seek agreement.
target_language_example: Lo intenté, pero no es tan fácil.
native_language_example: I tried, but it’s not that easy.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty and say something is harder than it seems/than something else. Often followed by "parece" (it seems) or by another thing to compare with (e.g., "ese", "pensé").
target_language_example: Aprender español no es tan fácil como creía.
native_language_example: Learning Spanish isn’t as easy as I thought.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things and say the first one is less big than the second. Structure: [thing 1] + no es tan + adjective + como + [thing 2]. You can swap in other adjectives: no es tan caro como (isn’t as expensive as), no es tan rápido como (isn’t as fast as).
target_language_example: Este apartamento no es tan grande como el otro.
native_language_example: This apartment isn’t as big as the other one.

meaning: "It’s not that bad." / "He’s not that bad."
additional_notes: Used to downplay something negative or reassure someone. Often followed by a comparison with "como" ("not as bad as..."): "No es tan malo como crees/parece". Change "es" depending on the subject (e.g., "no soy tan malo", "no eres tan malo", "no es tan mala").
target_language_example: Tranquilo, el examen no es tan malo como parece.
native_language_example: Relax, the exam isn’t as bad as it seems.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to say something does not belong to the person you’re talking to (possession/ownership) or that something is not their role/strength. It’s followed by a **singular noun**: *No es tu taza / No es tu fuerte.* For plural nouns, use **no son tus**: *No son tus llaves.* Note agreement with **es** (singular) vs **son** (plural), not with the owner.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no es tu asiento.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it isn't your seat.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone they are not to blame. Often said directly to someone (with a name or term like amigo/niña) and can be contrasted with blame: “No es tu culpa, es mía” (“It’s not your fault, it’s mine”). You can also add emphasis: “Quiero que sepas que no es tu culpa” (“I want you to know it’s not your fault”).
target_language_example: No es tu culpa; hiciste lo mejor que pudiste.
native_language_example: It’s not your fault; you did the best you could.

additional_notes: Used to negate an identification or classification: “X no es un Y.” Use **no es una** for feminine nouns (e.g., *una idea*), and **no son** for plural (e.g., *no son unos/unas*). Often appears in contrasts with **sino** (“but rather”): *No es un lujo, sino una necesidad.*
target_language_example: Esto no es un juego.
native_language_example: This is not a game.

additional_notes: Often used to stress that something is serious and shouldn’t be taken lightly (a warning or emphasis), not necessarily about an actual game. It can also be literal when talking about something that isn’t a game or isn’t easy/fun. You’ll also hear it alone as a strong statement: “No es un juego.”
target_language_example: Conducir borracho no es un juego.
native_language_example: Driving drunk is not a game (this is serious).

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone does not belong to a category or is not described by a certain label: “No es una opción / excepción / vergüenza…”. It’s the negative form of “es una …”. For masculine nouns, you say “no es un …” (e.g., “No es un problema”).
target_language_example: Eso no es una buena idea.
native_language_example: That isn’t a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say something is false or to contradict what someone said. Often followed by what isn’t true: “Lo que dijiste no es verdad” (“What you said isn’t true”). You can also use it on its own as a direct denial: “No es verdad, señor.”
target_language_example: No es verdad; yo no dije eso.
native_language_example: That’s not true; I didn’t say that.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar in the first person singular (yo) to say you are not in a certain state/condition (busy, interested, working, etc.), often temporary. Common patterns: no estoy + adjective (No estoy ocupado.) or no estoy + gerund (-ando/-iendo) for an action in progress (No estoy trabajando.). For more permanent identity/traits, Spanish often uses no soy (ser) instead.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no estoy disponible ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not available right now.

additional_notes: Used to express disagreement. Often followed by **con** + a person/idea: *No estoy de acuerdo con eso / con lo que dices.* You can soften it with phrases like *Con todo respeto,* before it.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no estoy de acuerdo contigo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I don’t agree with you.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty. It often appears by itself (“No estoy segura.”), with a time word like “todavía” (not yet), or followed by “de + infinitive” to mean you’re not sure about doing something: “No estoy segura de querer…” (I’m not sure I want to…). For a man: “No estoy seguro.”
target_language_example: No estoy segura de poder ir mañana.
native_language_example: I’m not sure I can go tomorrow.

meaning: "I’m not sure that..." (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to express doubt/uncertainty about what follows. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "sea", "pueda", "tenga"). You can also say "No estoy seguro de que" if the speaker is a man. Often interchangeable with "No sé si..." in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No estoy segura de que podamos ir mañana.
native_language_example: I’m not sure we can go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty. You can leave it alone (“No estoy seguro.” / “No estoy segura.”) or follow it with information like “pero…” (but…), “todavía” (yet), or an embedded question (“No estoy seguro qué…” / also common: “No estoy seguro de qué…”). “Seguro/segura” agrees with the speaker’s gender.
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de la hora, pero puedo preguntar.
native_language_example: I’m not sure about the time, but I can ask.

additional_notes:
Used to express uncertainty. It’s followed by:
- a noun/idea: No estoy seguro de la hora.
- an indirect question: No estoy seguro de cuándo / qué / cómo…
- an infinitive: No estoy seguro de poder / ir / ganar…
- “que” + verb (often subjunctive): No estoy seguro de que me guste… (very common in speech). You can change the subject/person: No estamos seguros de…, ¿Estás seguro de…?
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de si mañana tenemos clase.
native_language_example: I’m not sure if we have class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say something is not in a certain state/condition, not located somewhere, or not available (e.g., “not for sale”). Often contrasts with “no es” (from ser), which is more for identity or defining characteristics.
target_language_example: Lo siento, el profesor no está en la oficina.
native_language_example: Sorry, the professor isn’t in the office.

meaning: "It’s not OK / it’s not right" or "it’s not well (in good condition)."
additional_notes: Used for (1) things that aren’t working or aren’t in good condition: "La mira no está bien" (the sight/scope isn’t working right), "La carretera no está bien" (the road isn’t in good condition); (2) people who don’t feel well: "No está bien, no quiere comer" (he/she isn’t well; he/she doesn’t want to eat); and (3) to say something is wrong or unacceptable: "No está bien mentir" (it’s not right to lie).
target_language_example: Lo que hiciste no está bien.
native_language_example: What you did isn’t OK.

additional_notes: Used to give mild praise or to say something is okay/acceptable, often with an understated tone. Common with comparisons like “para ser…” (“for being…”): “No está mal para ser la primera vez.” It can also react to news or results: “No está mal, ¿eh?/¿verdad?” = “Not bad, huh?/right?”
target_language_example: Tu español no está mal; te entiendo bien.
native_language_example: Your Spanish isn’t bad; I understand you well.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is prohibited by a rule, law, or policy. Often followed by an infinitive (No está permitido fumar / aparcar / nadar) or by a clause with que + subjunctive (No está permitido que nadie vaya allá). Also common as a short standalone answer: No está permitido.
target_language_example: No está permitido entrar sin identificación.
native_language_example: It’s not allowed to enter without ID.

meaning: “isn’t / is not (here/there)” or “isn’t (in a certain state/condition)” (about someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** to say someone/something is not present or not in a specific place/state. Often implies absence: **No está aquí** = “He/She isn’t here.” Can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “He/She/It isn’t (here/available).” In some contexts (like **No está ni ahí**) it can be part of an idiom meaning someone doesn’t care.
target_language_example: Lo busqué, pero no está en casa.
native_language_example: I looked for him, but he isn’t at home.

additional_notes: Uses **estar** (not *ser*) to talk about someone’s location. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., *El gerente no está aquí* or just *No está aquí*). **Aquí** means “here” (near the speaker); compare **allí/ahí** for “there.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor no está aquí ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor isn’t here right now.

meaning: “is not in” / “is not on” (it isn’t located there; it isn’t included).
additional_notes: Used with location words (en la habitación, en casa, en Madrid) to say someone/something isn’t there. Also used with lists/documents to mean “not included/on” (no está en la lista, no está en el documento). The verb changes with the subject: no estoy en…, no estás en…, no están en….
target_language_example: Mi pasaporte no está en mi bolso.
native_language_example: My passport isn’t in my bag.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t at home right now (present tense of estar). You can add a subject for clarity: “Mi mamá no está en casa.” Often paired with time phrases like “en este momento” (at the moment). In questions, “¿verdad?” works like “right?” to confirm.
target_language_example: Lo siento, el señor no está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the man isn’t at home right now.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb "estar" for "tú" (you). Common with adjectives or states/conditions: "No estás listo" (You’re not ready), "No estás seguro" (You’re not sure). You can also use it to negate an ongoing action with the gerund: "No estás comiendo" (You’re not eating). Often appears without the subject "tú" because it’s understood.
target_language_example: Ahora no estás en casa.
native_language_example: You’re not at home right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not real, not present, or not available. Often followed by a noun: “No existe la persona perfecta” (“The perfect person doesn’t exist”). Also used with ideas/concepts (“Dios no existe”) or things that used to exist (“ya no existe” = “no longer exists”).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad no existe el metro.
native_language_example: In this city, there is no subway.

additional_notes: “No fue” is the negative preterite (simple past) of **ser** (“to be”) and **ir** (“to go”), so meaning depends on context. Commonly it means **“it/he/she wasn’t…”** with adjectives or nouns: *No fue agradable* (“It wasn’t pleasant”). It’s also used in set time expressions like **“No fue hasta que…”** = “It wasn’t until…” and **“No fue mucho antes de que…”** = “It wasn’t long before…”.
target_language_example: No fue mi culpa.
native_language_example: It wasn’t my fault.

additional_notes: Used as an infinitive phrase after many verbs (e.g., aconsejar, preferir, prometer) to say that someone should/chooses/promises not to smoke. It can also appear on signs as a prohibition (e.g., «No fumar» = “No smoking”).
target_language_example: En este restaurante está prohibido no fumar.
native_language_example: In this restaurant it’s forbidden not to smoke.

additional_notes: Used with devices, machines, services, or systems to say they aren’t operating properly (e.g., elevator, phone, printer, TV). Also used more generally to mean “it doesn’t work” in the sense of “it won’t work / it doesn’t work out” (an idea, method, relationship, plan). Present tense of funcionar; for a temporary situation you can also hear “no está funcionando.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, mi tarjeta no funciona aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry, my card doesn’t work here.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "haber" ("ha") to form the present perfect in the negative: "no ha" + past participle (e.g., "no ha resuelto", "no ha faltado", "no ha funcionado"). Refers to something that has not happened up to now (or up to a point in time).
target_language_example: Ella no ha terminado el trabajo todavía.
native_language_example: She hasn't finished the work yet.

additional_notes: Present perfect negative: "no" + "ha" (has) + "cambiado" (changed). Used for something that has not changed up to now. With "nada" it emphasizes: "No ha cambiado nada" = "Nothing has changed." You can replace the subject depending on context (e.g., "La tarifa... no ha cambiado").
target_language_example: El plan no ha cambiado desde ayer.
native_language_example: The plan hasn't changed since yesterday.

meaning: "there hasn’t been" / "there haven’t been" (there has not been).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "haber" to say something did not exist or did not occur up to now (present perfect). It’s often followed by a noun: "no ha habido noticias" (there hasn’t been any news), "no ha habido agua caliente" (there hasn’t been hot water). For plural nouns, English uses "haven’t," but Spanish still uses "ha": "no ha habido problemas".
target_language_example: Hoy no ha habido clases.
native_language_example: There haven’t been classes today.

additional_notes: Negative form of the present perfect of ir (to go): no + ha + ido. Used to say someone hasn’t gone somewhere or hasn’t attended an event up to now (often with words like nunca, hoy, ayer). With things/events (not a person), ir can mean “to go” in the sense of “to turn out”: No ha ido bien = “It didn’t go well.”
target_language_example: María no ha ido a clase esta semana.
native_language_example: María hasn’t gone to class this week.

additional_notes: Negative present perfect of **ser** for **él/ella/usted** (and also used with things: **esto/eso**). Common in polite set phrases like **No ha sido molestia** = “It wasn’t any trouble.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no ha sido mi intención.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, it hasn't been my intention.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has not come (often meaning "not yet" up to now). It’s built with haber (ha) + past participle (venido). Common with negatives like "nadie" (no one): "No ha venido nadie" = "No one has come," and "nada" (nothing): "No ha venido nada" = "Nothing came/was included" (e.g., in a newspaper).
target_language_example: Todavía no ha venido el médico.
native_language_example: The doctor still hasn’t come.

meaning: “to just have to” / “there is/was nothing but” (only).
additional_notes:
Used mainly in two common patterns:
1) **No hay (no había / no habrá) más que + infinitive** = “You just have to…” / “All you have to do is…”.
2) **No hay (no había) más que + noun** = “There is/was nothing but…” (only that thing exists/was there). In phrasebook form it’s often listed as **no haber más que**, but in real sentences it appears conjugated (e.g., **no hay más que**, **no había más que**).
target_language_example: En este caso, no haber más que llamarme si necesitas ayuda.
native_language_example: In this case, you just have to call me if you need help.

additional_notes: Used with an implied subject (él/ella/usted) or with a named subject: “Mi madre no habla inglés.” For “I don’t speak English,” say “No hablo inglés.” For “we/they don’t,” use “no hablamos / no hablan.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no habla inglés.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she/you (formal) doesn’t speak English.

additional_notes: Use this to tell someone you can’t speak English. You can swap in other languages: “No hablo español/francés/alemán.” If you’re addressing someone formally, you can add “(lo) siento” to be polite: “Lo siento, no hablo inglés.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hablo inglés. ¿Habla español?
