Refers to “tú” (informal singular “you”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no tienes nada de qué preocuparte.
native_language_example: Relax, you have nothing to worry about.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t know or understand something, or to emphasize how surprising/important something is. Often followed by a noun or an indirect question: "no tienes ni idea de cavar" (about digging), "no tienes ni idea de lo que..." (what...), "no tienes ni idea de lo importante que..." (how important...), "no tienes ni idea de qué..." (what...). Can sound critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: No tienes ni idea de lo difícil que fue para mí.
native_language_example: You have no idea how hard it was for me.

meaning: "you don’t have to" / "there’s no need for you to".
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not obliged to do something, or that there’s no reason/need to do it. It’s often followed by an infinitive (no tienes por qué + decir/hacer/quejarte) and can sound reassuring or slightly firm depending on tone. You can change the person: no tengo por qué, no tienes por qué, no tiene por qué, etc.
target_language_example: No tienes por qué preocuparte; yo me encargo.
native_language_example: You don’t have to worry; I’ll take care of it.

meaning: you don’t have to (you’re not required to).
additional_notes: Used to tell one person informally (tú) that something is not necessary or not required. It’s the negative of "tienes que" (“you have to”). Commonly followed by an infinitive: "no tienes que + infinitive" (e.g., hacer, decir, escuchar, faltar, preocuparte). For a formal "you": "no tiene que"; for "you all": "no tienen que".
target_language_example: No tienes que venir si no quieres.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come if you don’t want to.

meaning: "you don't have to do it" / "you don't need to do it."
additional_notes: Used to say something is not necessary (it removes an obligation). It’s the negative of "tener que" (to have to). You can add timing or conditions: "No tienes que hacerlo ahora" (not now), "No tienes que hacerlo si no quieres" (if you don’t want to).
target_language_example: No tienes que hacerlo hoy; puedo encargarme yo.
native_language_example: You don’t have to do it today; I can take care of it.

additional_notes: Used to say a statement isn’t true for all people. Often followed by a verb: “No todo el mundo puede…” = “Not everyone can…”. Uses singular verb (“es”, “puede”, “quiere”) because “todo el mundo” is treated as singular.
target_language_example: No todo el mundo entiende esta broma.
native_language_example: Not everyone understands this joke.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement doesn’t apply to every member of a group. It’s typically followed by a plural noun ("no todos los errores") or by "que" + verb ("No todos los que vienen..."), and often contrasts with a generalization.
target_language_example: No todos los estudiantes tienen tiempo para estudiar hoy.
native_language_example: Not all (the) students have time to study today.

no tuvo nada que ver con

target_language_multi_word_term: no tuvo nada que ver con
meaning: “had nothing to do with”; “had no involvement in”; “was not connected to.”
additional_notes: Used to deny responsibility, involvement, or any connection to an event, situation, or wrongdoing. Pattern: “X no tuvo nada que ver con Y.” You can change tense/person as needed (e.g., “no tengo nada que ver con…”, “no tenía nada que ver con…”, “no tendrá nada que ver con…”).
target_language_example: Tom no tuvo nada que ver con el robo.
native_language_example: Tom had nothing to do with the robbery.

meaning: “is not going to” (negative of *ir a* + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about a future plan or something expected to happen (often in the near future). Conjugate **ir** for the subject: *no voy a*, *no vas a*, *no va a*, *no vamos a*, *no van a* + infinitive. Example: *No va a llegar* = “He/She isn’t going to arrive / won’t make it.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no va a poder venir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she isn’t going to be able to come today.

meaning: “it’s not going to work” / “it won’t work.”
additional_notes: Used to say something won’t succeed or won’t have the desired result (a plan, an idea, a relationship, a device, etc.). Very common in conversation. Often said emphatically on its own: “No va a funcionar.”
target_language_example: Si seguimos así, no va a funcionar.
native_language_example: If we keep going like this, it’s not going to work.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **(no) va a pasar** = “(it’s not) going to happen.” Often said to predict or insist that something won’t occur. With **de + time** it can mean “won’t last past…”: **No va a pasar de esta noche** = “It won’t last past tonight.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, eso no va a pasar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, that’s not going to happen.

additional_notes: Idiomatic phrase meaning that nothing else can be added or done—there’s no room/time for more. Common in the context of gambling (roulette/casino) as “no more bets,” and also used more generally to mean “that’s it, end of story” or “it can’t get any better / any further.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no va más: ya no aceptamos más pedidos hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s it: we’re not taking any more orders today.

meaning: “it’s not worth it / it’s not worth the trouble.”
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t worth doing (because it’s too much effort, risk, time, money, etc.). Often followed by an infinitive: “No vale la pena + infinitive” (No vale la pena discutir / hablar). You can also use it alone as a reaction: “¡No vale la pena!”
target_language_example: No vale la pena preocuparse por eso.
native_language_example: It’s not worth worrying about that.

meaning: “we’re not going to …” / “we’re not going to (do something).”
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about a future plan/intention that won’t happen, or to refuse/deny doing something: no vamos a + infinitive (ir, trabajar, volver, etc.). In speech it can sound like a firm decision (“we won’t…”).
target_language_example: No vamos a hablar de eso hoy.
native_language_example: We’re not going to talk about that today.

meaning: "you’re not going to..." (near future; tú form).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something will not happen (or someone won’t be able to do it): no vas a + infinitive. It’s the negative of the common future structure ir a + infinitive (“to be going to”). This is for tú; other forms include: no voy a (I’m not going to), no va a (he/she isn’t going to), no vamos a (we aren’t going to), no van a (they aren’t going to).
target_language_example: No vas a entender si no escuchas.
native_language_example: You’re not going to understand if you don’t listen.

additional_notes: Used to reassure or apologize after a mistake or problem, often as part of a promise: "Te/Le prometo que no volverá a suceder" (I promise you it won’t happen again). Literally it’s "it will not happen again" (future tense). You can also say "no volverá a pasar" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Perdón por el error; no volverá a suceder.
native_language_example: Sorry about the mistake; it won’t happen again.

additional_notes: Used to say you do not intend to do something (near-future plan) or to refuse/decide not to do something. It’s the negative of "voy a" + infinitive. For other subjects: "no vas a" (you), "no va a" (he/she/you formal), "no vamos a" (we), "no van a" (they/you all).
target_language_example: No voy a hablar de eso ahora.
native_language_example: I’m not going to talk about that now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to repeat an action. It’s a negative command with "volver a" (to do something again). After "a" you use an infinitive: "No vuelvas a decir...", "No vuelvas a hacer...". It can sound strict or threatening depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: No vuelvas a hablarme así.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that again.

meaning: "No, the…" (correcting/clarifying which masculine thing you mean).
additional_notes: Used when you say “no” and then specify the correct option with a masculine noun: “No, el metro”, “No, el grande”. It often answers a misunderstanding and is said with a short pause (written with a comma). Use **el** with masculine nouns; for feminine nouns you’d use **no, la**. You can also add an adjective or pronoun after **el** when the noun is understood from context (e.g., **No, el mío** = “No, mine”).
target_language_example: —¿Quieres el pequeño? —No, el grande.
native_language_example: —Do you want the small one? —No, the big one.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to contradict what was just said or assumed, then give the correct information. Often followed by a noun/adjective clause: “No, es de…”, “No, es en serio”, “No, es que…”. In speech it’s a common correction/clarification marker.
target_language_example: No, es que no tengo tiempo ahora.
native_language_example: No, it’s just that I don’t have time right now.

meaning: "No, I am…" (used to correct or contradict).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is NOT the case and then state your situation with the verb estar (yo estoy). Common patterns: (1) + adjective: "No, estoy cansado" (I’m tired). (2) + en + place/location: "No, estoy en…" (I’m in/at…). (3) + gerund to describe what you’re doing right now: "No, estoy hablando…" (I’m speaking…).
target_language_example: No, estoy ocupado ahora.
native_language_example: No, I’m busy right now.

meaning: "No, it’s…" / "No, he/she is…" (correcting someone: "No, it is/isn’t…").
additional_notes: Used to correct or contradict what someone just said, followed by a description of the situation or someone’s state/location. "Está" is from **estar** (temporary state, location, condition): *No, está bien / cerca / preocupado / roto.* Don’t confuse **está** (verb, with accent) with **esta** ("this" feminine, no accent): *No, esta puede ser nuestra única oportunidad…* ("No, this might be our only chance…").
target_language_example: No, está en casa; no puede venir ahora.
native_language_example: No, he’s at home; he can’t come right now.

additional_notes: A polite way to refuse or decline an offer or invitation. Often said as a full response by itself, or followed by a reason (e.g., “No, gracias. Estoy bien.”). You may also hear it without the comma: “No gracias.”
target_language_example: No, gracias. No quiero nada más.
native_language_example: No, thanks. I don’t want anything else.

additional_notes: "No," is often used to answer or correct someone, followed by a sentence. "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or "him"), referring to something already known from context. It usually goes right before a conjugated verb: "No, lo hice" = "No, I did it." (In "No, lo que...", "lo que" means "what/that which"—a different use of "lo".)
target_language_example: No, lo compré ayer.
native_language_example: No, I bought it yesterday.

meaning: “No, …” followed by “me” (“me / myself”) starting the next clause.
additional_notes: This isn’t a set phrase; it’s just a very common pattern in conversation: you say “No,” and then your next sentence begins with the object/reflexive pronoun **me**. You’ll see it with verbs like **gustar** (**No, me gusta…** = “No, I like…”), with accidents/things happening to you (**No, me lo perdí** = “No, I missed it”), or with reflexive verbs (**No, me voy** = “No, I’m leaving”). The comma is a pause in speech; in writing it may or may not appear.
target_language_example: No, me siento bien hoy.
native_language_example: No, I don’t feel well today.

additional_notes: Repeating “no” is very common in spoken Spanish to sound firmer, more certain, or to correct/deny something quickly (similar to “No, no…” / “No, not at all…” in English). It can be followed by an explanation (No, no puedo, porque…) or used alone (No, no mucho.). Intonation matters: it can sound polite but definite, or strongly insistent depending on tone.
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy; tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: No, I can’t go today; I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to correct or deny a statement about what something is. Often followed by a noun (No, no es gato.), an article + noun (No, no es la verdad.), or a negative word like nada/ninguno for emphasis (No, no es nada. / No, no es ninguna prueba.). In Spanish, double negatives are normal and correct.
target_language_example: —¿Es tuyo este libro? —No, no es mío.
native_language_example: —Is this book yours? —No, it isn't mine.

meaning: "No, I don’t / I haven’t / don’t (do) it." (with "lo" = "it/that").
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: the first “No,” answers/contradicts what someone said or asked, and the second “no” is the normal negation inside the sentence. “Lo” is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that” (often referring to a previously mentioned thing; grammatically masculine or unspecified). It can be used with different tenses (“no lo he visto” = “I haven’t seen it”) and with commands (“no lo subas” = “don’t upload it / don’t raise it”).
target_language_example: No, no lo sé.
native_language_example: No, I don’t know it / No, I don’t know.

meaning: “No, no…” (a firm or emphatic “no”; also used to correct or disagree).
additional_notes: Repeating “no” adds emphasis. It can sound like: (1) a stronger refusal (“No, no, eso no va a pasar.”), (2) a correction/clarification (“No, no, eso es lo que no quiero que hagas.”), or (3) mild disagreement, sometimes with a surprised/admiring tone depending on context (“No, no, ese sí que es un buen truco…”). Intonation matters: it can be friendly or more forceful.
target_language_example: No, no, gracias; prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: No, no, thanks; I’d rather stay home.

additional_notes: Repeating “no” is a common way to make a refusal stronger, show disagreement, or stop/correct someone (similar to “No, no, no!” in English). The number of “no”s varies with emotion/urgency. Often followed by a term of address like “cariño” (honey) or “hombre” (man/dude) to soften it or make it more conversational.
target_language_example: No, no, no, gracias; hoy no puedo.
native_language_example: No, no, no, thanks; I can’t today.

additional_notes: Repeating “no” shows strong refusal, disagreement, or alarm (like “No, no, no!” in English). Tone matters: it can mean “Don’t do that,” “That’s not true,” or “This is going badly.” Often used in speech; in writing it can be followed by a reason (e.g., “...nos hemos quedado sin opciones”).
target_language_example: No, no, no, no—eso no es lo que dije.
native_language_example: No, no, no, no—that’s not what I said.

meaning: “No, but …” (a refusal/disagreement followed by a contrast, correction, or extra point).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to reject or disagree with what was said or implied, then add a contrasting idea or important detail. Often sets up a correction (“No, pero…”), an exception (“No, pero…”), or a request after saying no (“No, pero dame detalles.”). In speech it’s usually said with a brief pause after “no”.
target_language_example: No, pero mañana sí puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: No, but tomorrow I can help you.

meaning: "No, please." (a polite refusal, or a plea for something not to happen).
additional_notes: Used when you want to say “no” politely (declining an offer, letting someone go first, refusing a role), or to protest/beg: “No, please!” In speech it can sound more urgent depending on tone and repetition (e.g., “¡No, por favor!”).
target_language_example: No, por favor, no me llames tan tarde.
native_language_example: No, please, don’t call me so late.

meaning: “No, because …” (a negative reply followed by the reason).
additional_notes: Used to answer a question or reject an idea, then immediately explain why. In speech it often has a slight pause after “no” (shown by the comma), and the reason comes after “porque.” You can also hear it used defensively or to correct someone’s assumption: “No, porque…” = “No, that’s not it—because…”.
target_language_example: ¿Vienes hoy? No, porque tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Are you coming today? No, because I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to answer "no" and then add a small correction/clarification: you’re saying it’s not what the other person thinks—it's only this. In these examples, **solo** means **only/just** (not "alone"). You may also see **sólo** with an accent in older writing, but **solo** is standard now.
target_language_example: No, solo quiero ayudarte un momento.
native_language_example: No, I just want to help you for a moment.

meaning: “No, I’m…” (used to deny or correct who/what you are).
additional_notes: Used to correct an assumption about your identity, job/role, relationship, nationality, etc. It uses **soy** (1st person singular of **ser**, “to be”). Often followed by a noun or adjective: *No, soy doctor.* / *No, soy español.* The comma is optional in writing: *No soy…*
target_language_example: No, soy tu profesor; soy tu compañero de clase.
native_language_example: No, I’m not your teacher; I’m your classmate.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to correct what someone assumed or to downplay something. It’s often followed by an explanation: “No, sólo quería charlar” (“No, I just wanted to chat”). Note: Spanish “sólo/solo” usually means “only/just” in this use, not English “solo” (alone), so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: No, sólo estaba preguntando.
native_language_example: No, I was just asking.

meaning: “No, you…” / “No, to you…” (starting a reply and addressing someone directly).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to contradict or correct someone: “No, te…” + verb. The comma is common in writing because it’s like “No, listen…” “Te” is an object pronoun meaning “to you” (or sometimes just “you” depending on the verb), and it normally goes right before the conjugated verb: “No, te entiendo” = “No, I understand you.”
target_language_example: No, te lo dije ayer.
native_language_example: No, I told you yesterday.

meaning: “No, I have to …” (I must / I need to).
additional_notes: Used to refuse or decline (often an invitation, request, or suggestion) and then give a reason with an obligation. After “tengo que” you normally use an infinitive: tengo que estudiar, tengo que ir, tengo que marcharme. In speech it can sound like: “No, es que tengo que…” (“No, it’s just that I have to…”).
target_language_example: No, tengo que trabajar mañana.
native_language_example: No, I have to work tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to start an answer that corrects or reassures someone by saying something has already happened or is already true (often with the sense of “don’t worry/it’s taken care of”). Common with verbs like: “No, ya he comido” (I’ve already eaten), “No, ya lo sé” (I already know), “No, ya los tengo” (I already have them). It can also introduce something expected soon: “No, ya vendrá …” (She’ll come later / She’ll show up). The comma reflects a pause; in speech it’s the intonation that matters.
target_language_example: —¿Te llamo un taxi? —No, ya viene mi hermano.
native_language_example: “Should I call you a taxi?” “No, my brother is already coming.”

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct someone and emphasize that *you* (not someone else) will/won’t do something. In Spanish you can omit the subject pronoun, so adding "yo" here is for emphasis or contrast: "No, (yo) no..." = "No, *I* don't..."
target_language_example: No, yo no dije eso.
native_language_example: No, I didn't say that.

additional_notes: Used to strongly contradict or refuse, often to emphasize that *you* specifically do not do something ("Not me"). It’s commonly followed by a verb ("No, yo no voy") or can stand alone when the verb is understood from context ("—¿Vienes? —No, yo no."). Word order adds emphasis: "yo" highlights the subject.
target_language_example: —¿Quieres café? —No, yo no tomo café.
native_language_example: —Do you want coffee? —No, I don’t drink coffee.

additional_notes: Used to deny something and immediately ask for the reason behind the question or accusation. Often sounds a bit defensive or surprised, like “No, why would I?” or “No, why are you asking?” In full sentences, it’s commonly followed by a verb: “¿por qué dices eso?”, “¿por qué harías eso?”
target_language_example: No, ¿por qué me preguntas eso?
native_language_example: No—why are you asking me that?

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny, disagree, or correct what was just said or suggested. The second "no" adds emphasis and can also sound reassuring in replies like "No, no fue nada" ("No, it was nothing"). Common in conversation.
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I can't go today.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to assume something or not to believe something. It’s the negative tú command of "creer" and is often followed by "que" + a clause: "No creas que…" (= "Don’t think that…"). It can also sound like a mild correction ("Don’t get the wrong idea").
target_language_example: No creas que estoy enojado; solo estoy cansado.
native_language_example: Don’t think I’m angry; I’m just tired.

additional_notes: Literally the negative command (tú) of empezar: “don’t start.” It can be literal (don’t begin an activity yet: No empieces antes de que llegue papá.) or used to stop someone from complaining/arguing/bringing something up: No empieces con eso / No empieces otra vez (= “Don’t start (that again)”). Often said directly to someone by name.
target_language_example: No empieces con las quejas, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t start with the complaints, please.

meaning: “there isn’t/aren’t any more” or “so there won’t be any more.”
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of **haber** (**haya**) after **no**. Common after expressions of purpose or prevention: **para que no haya más + noun** (“so there won’t be any more + noun”), e.g., problems, mistakes, confusion. It can also be used in firm instructions with **que**: **¡Que no haya más ruido!** (“No more noise!”).
target_language_example: Hablemos ahora para que no haya más malentendidos.
native_language_example: Let’s talk now so there won’t be any more misunderstandings.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important or not a problem. Often followed by "si" + clause ("No importa si...") meaning "It doesn’t matter if...". You can also say "No importa" by itself to reassure someone or to brush something off (similar to "It’s okay").
target_language_example: No importa si llegas tarde; te espero aquí.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter if you’re late; I’ll wait for you here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will not change the outcome, regardless of what happens/what someone says/thinks/does. It’s followed by a verb phrase: "No importa lo que diga" (no matter what he/she says), "No importa lo que cueste" (no matter what it costs). Often paired with "o" to list possibilities: "No importa lo que cueste o lo que necesites".
target_language_example: No importa lo que pase, te llamaré mañana.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I’ll call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Negative tú command (informal singular) from the verb "llorar" (to cry). Used to tell one person not to cry, often to comfort them. You may also see it in the proverb "No llores sobre la leche derramada" (“Don’t cry over spilled milk”). For a formal or plural command: "no llore" (usted) / "no lloren" (ustedes).
target_language_example: No llores; todo va a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t cry; everything is going to be okay.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. With numbers it means “only/just” (No tengo no más diez dólares = I only have ten dollars). It can also be used to stop something: “¡No más!” = “No more!/That’s enough!” In some regions (especially Mexico/Central America) you may hear it meaning “just/only” even without a number.
target_language_example: Tengo no más cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I only have five minutes.

meaning: to not stop; to keep (doing something).
additional_notes: Often used with **de + infinitive**: **no parar de + verb** = “to keep on / can’t stop (doing something)”. It can describe repeated actions, activity, or movement.
target_language_example: Esta semana prometí no parar de trabajar hasta terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: This week I promised not to stop working until I finish the project.

additional_notes: Very common, friendly phrase used to reassure someone or downplay an issue (after an apology, a small mistake, bad news, or an inconvenience). Literally “nothing happens,” but it usually means “it’s not a big deal.” Often used on its own as a complete response.
target_language_example: Perdón por llegar tarde. —No pasa nada.
native_language_example: Sorry for arriving late. —No problem.

meaning: to not be able to take it anymore; to be at your limit (often: exhausted).
additional_notes: Used to express that you’ve reached your physical or emotional limit. Often followed by a cause: “No puedo más con este calor” (I can’t take this heat anymore) or used alone: “No puedo más” (I can’t go on / I can’t take it anymore). With “ya” it emphasizes “anymore”: “Ya no puedo más.”
target_language_example: Después de tantas horas sin dormir, ya no poder más me tenía desesperado.
native_language_example: After so many hours without sleep, not being able to take it anymore had me desperate.

meaning: “Don’t look/see.” Also (informal): “Wow / you wouldn’t believe…” (to emphasize something).
additional_notes: Literally it’s the negative tú command of “ver” (to see): “no veas + noun” = “don’t look at/watch …” (e.g., no veas la televisión). In casual speech, “¡No veas!” can be an exclamation meaning something like “wow!” or “you should’ve seen…” to stress how intense/large/strong something was (often followed by “lo que…”: “No veas lo que gritaba”).
target_language_example: ¡No veas el calor que hace hoy!
native_language_example: Wow, it’s so hot today!

additional_notes: Used to refer to the night of a wedding (often the first night the couple spends together as married partners). It’s usually said with a possessive: "mi/tu/nuestra noche de bodas". "Bodas" is plural in Spanish here.
target_language_example: Reservaron una suite para su noche de bodas.
native_language_example: They booked a suite for their wedding night.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to tell you their name, often in formal/service situations (reception, forms, phone calls). It can be a full question (“¿Su nombre, por favor?”) or just said on its own as a prompt. You can also hear “Nombre y apellido, por favor” (“First and last name, please”).
target_language_example: Perdón, su nombre, por favor.
native_language_example: Excuse me, your name, please.

additional_notes: Used on forms and in official contexts to ask for or state your full legal name (first name + both last names in many Spanish-speaking countries). You may see it as a label by itself: “Nombre completo:”.
target_language_example: Por favor, escriba su nombre completo aquí.
native_language_example: Please write your full name here.

meaning: "name of"; used to identify what someone/something is called.
additional_notes:
Common in fixed expressions like:
- "el nombre de X" = "X’s name / the name of X"
- "bajo el nombre de X" = "under the name of X" (i.e., known as X)
- "responder al nombre de X" = "to go by the name of X" (to respond when called X)
Note: "nombre" looks like English "number" but means "name" (false friend).
target_language_example: Lo conocí bajo el nombre de Miguel.
native_language_example: I knew him under the name Miguel.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s given name (the name you receive at birth/baptism), as opposed to surnames (apellidos). Common in more formal contexts; in everyday speech people also say “nombre” when it’s clear they mean first name.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu nombre de pila?
native_language_example: What is your first name?

meaning: proper name / proper noun; (on forms) first name (given name).
additional_notes: In grammar, a "nombre propio" is a name that identifies a specific person, place, organization, etc. (e.g., Ana, Madrid) and is usually capitalized. In everyday contexts (especially on forms), "nombre propio" can mean your given name (first name), often contrasted with "apellido" (last name).
target_language_example: Escribe tu nombre propio y tu apellido aquí.
native_language_example: Write your first name and your last name here.

additional_notes: Used on forms, registrations, deliveries, and official requests when someone needs your identifying info. Often appears as a prompt by itself (e.g., “Nombre y dirección, por favor.”).
target_language_example: Para enviar el paquete, necesito tu nombre y dirección.
native_language_example: To send the package, I need your name and address.

additional_notes: From the verb **acercarse (a)** = “to get close / to approach.” **Nos acercamos** is 1st-person plural (“we”) in the present tense, often used while moving toward a place or target: **Nos acercamos a la meta / a la zona / al espacio aéreo…**. It can describe literal movement or getting closer in time/effort (e.g., toward a goal).
target_language_example: Nos acercamos al centro de la ciudad, así que hay más tráfico.
native_language_example: We’re getting closer to downtown, so there’s more traffic.

additional_notes: From the verb casarse (to get married). Nos is the “we/us” reflexive pronoun here (“we marry ourselves” → “we get married”). Often used with time phrases like hace siete años (seven years ago) or with places like en Las Vegas. Without context, it can mean either past (“we got married”) or present/future for a planned event (“we’re getting married”).
target_language_example: Nos casamos el próximo sábado.
native_language_example: We’re getting married next Saturday.

additional_notes: Used when two people are familiar with each other (not “I know you” in the sense of knowing information). It’s the reciprocal form of conocer: conocer = to meet/know (a person), conocerse = to know each other. Often used with time/degree words: Hace mucho que nos conocemos (We’ve known each other for a long time), Apenas nos conocemos (We barely know each other).
target_language_example: ¿De verdad? Pensé que nos conocemos desde la escuela.
native_language_example: Really? I thought we’ve known each other since school.

meaning: "we've known each other for" (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long two people have known each other. It’s typically followed by a duration (e.g., "cinco años", "mucho tiempo"). "Desde hace" combines: "desde" (since) + "hace" (ago) to express “for (how long)”. You can change "nos" to other pronouns: "se conocen desde hace..." (they’ve known each other for...), "os conocéis desde hace..." (you all have known each other for...).
target_language_example: Mi mejor amiga y yo nos conocemos desde hace tres años.
native_language_example: My best friend and I have known each other for three years.

meaning: “we met” (we got to know each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "conocerse" for "we" (nosotros). Use it to talk about the moment two people first met: "Nos conocimos ayer/en la universidad". Often used with time expressions like "desde el día en que nos conocimos" (“since the day we met”) or "aquí es donde nos conocimos" (“this is where we met”).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos en una fiesta hace dos años.
native_language_example: We met at a party two years ago.

meaning: "we met in/at/on" (a place, event, or platform).
additional_notes: Used with the verb conocerse in the simple past (pretérito) to say where two people first met. Use en for countries/cities (en Australia, en Boston), venues or groups (en un grupo de teatro), and also platforms/apps (en Facebook).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos en una fiesta de un amigo.
native_language_example: We met at a friend's party.

additional_notes: "Nos" is the indirect object pronoun meaning "to us." It’s used with the verb "dar" (to give): "(alguien/ algo) nos da + noun". In Spanish the subject can be omitted, so "Nos da..." often means "It gives us..." or "He/She gives us..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Nos da las llaves mañana.
native_language_example: He/She will give us the keys tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to the speaker and other people (nos = “to us”). The verb is usually in past tense (dijo = “said/told”), and que introduces the message/clause. You’ll often need to infer who the subject is from context (e.g., Ella/Tom).
target_language_example: El profesor nos dijo que no había clase hoy.
native_language_example: The teacher told us that there was no class today.

meaning: we realized / we noticed (we became aware).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the phrase "darse cuenta de" = "to realize/notice." "Nos" means "we (to ourselves)," and it’s often followed by "de" + a noun/what-clause: "nos dimos cuenta de algo" (we realized something) or "nos dimos cuenta de que..." (we realized that...). "De repente" commonly appears with it to mean "suddenly."
target_language_example: En cuanto lo vi, nos dimos cuenta de que era la misma persona.
native_language_example: As soon as I saw him, we realized it was the same person.

additional_notes: From the verb dar (to give) in the simple past (preterite): dio = “gave”. Nos is an object pronoun meaning “to us / us.” Often followed by a thing (Nos dio todo) or used more generally for what something caused (Eso nos dio motivos... = “That gave us reasons...”).
target_language_example: La película nos dio muchas ideas para el proyecto.
native_language_example: The movie gave us many ideas for the project.

meaning: “we had a lot of fun” / “we really enjoyed ourselves.”
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "divertirse" = "to have fun". "Nos" shows it’s "we" (reflexive: "we enjoyed ourselves"). "Mucho" intensifies it: "a lot"/"really". Often used to talk about a completed event (last night, on vacation, at a party).
target_language_example: En el concierto nos divertimos mucho.
native_language_example: We had a lot of fun at the concert.

additional_notes: Used with **de** to say your group will be responsible for something or someone: *Nos encargaremos de X.* It often appears with object pronouns like **ello/eso/esto** (“it/that/this”) or **él** (“him”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: nos encargaremos de todo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll take care of everything.

additional_notes: From the verb "encontrarse" (to meet). It often implies meeting in a place or bumping into each other unexpectedly. You’ll commonly add a location with "en" (Nos encontramos en...).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos en la estación a las seis.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the station at six.

additional_notes: From enseñar (to teach, to show) + nos (us). Used when someone or something teaches a group that includes the speaker. Often followed by: a + infinitive (nos enseña a ver...), a subject clause with que (nos enseña que...), or a direct object (nos enseña francés / historia). The subject can be a person (Ella nos enseña...) or a thing/field (La gramática nos enseña...).
target_language_example: El profesor nos enseña a usar estas palabras.
native_language_example: The teacher teaches us how to use these words.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say what “we” like. The thing liked is the grammatical subject: Nos gusta el jazz. (“We like jazz.”) With verbs/activities you usually use an infinitive: Nos gusta compartir. If you like more than one thing, use the plural: Nos gustan los perros. To say “we don’t like,” add no: No nos gusta.
target_language_example: No nos gusta levantarnos temprano.
native_language_example: We don’t like getting up early.

additional_notes: "Nos" is an object pronoun meaning "us" (the people receiving the action). "Ha" is the present perfect helper verb (haber) for él/ella/usted: "has". Together they often appear in the present perfect when someone has done something to/for us: "(Someone) nos ha + past participle" (e.g., nos ha olvidado = has forgotten us).
target_language_example: Mi jefe nos ha llamado esta mañana.
native_language_example: My boss has called us this morning.

meaning: "we need" / "we're lacking" (something is needed by us).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "hacer falta" = "to be needed". "Nos" marks who needs it (us). The thing needed usually comes after: "Nos hace falta agua". You can also use it for what’s missing/needed in a situation: "Lo que nos hace falta es..." ("What we need is..."). Often interchangeable with "necesitamos", but "hacer falta" emphasizes necessity or lack.
target_language_example: Nos hace falta una silla más para todos.
native_language_example: We need one more chair for everyone.

meaning: "have" (to us): they have + past participle (present perfect).
additional_notes: "nos" is the object pronoun meaning "us" (to/for us). "han" is the 3rd person plural of "haber" used to form the present perfect: "(ellos/ellas/ustedes) han" = "they/you all have". Together, "nos han" is used before a past participle: "nos han dicho" (they’ve told us), "nos han robado" (they’ve robbed us).
target_language_example: Nos han llamado esta mañana.
native_language_example: They called us this morning / They’ve called us this morning.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about something “we” have done/recently did. It’s the present tense of the auxiliary verb haber (hemos) plus the object/reflexive pronoun nos. Common with reflexive/pronominal verbs: nos hemos mudado (we’ve moved), nos hemos perdido (we got lost), nos hemos divertido (we had fun), no nos hemos decidido (we haven’t decided). Word order: Nos hemos + participle; in questions you can invert: ¿Nos hemos perdido?
target_language_example: Nos hemos levantado temprano hoy.
native_language_example: We got up early today.

meaning: we became friends / we made friends.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of hacerse amigos: it means that a friendship started. You’ll often see it with time expressions like rápido, inmediatamente, desde el principio. You can add a person with con (Nos hicimos amigos con ella) or sometimes de (Nos hicimos amigos de ellos), depending on region; con is generally safer for beginners.
target_language_example: En el curso de español nos hicimos amigos muy rápido.
native_language_example: In the Spanish course we became friends very quickly.

meaning: “invited us to” (an event/place), or “invited us to” + do something.
additional_notes: “Nos” = “us” (direct object), “invitó” is the past tense (pretérito) of “invitar” for he/she/you formal, and “a” introduces what you’re being invited to (a party, a wedding, a house) or an action (e.g., “nos invitó a cenar” = “invited us to have dinner”). You can add people for clarity: “nos invitó a Tom y a mí …” = “she invited Tom and me …”.
target_language_example: Mi vecina nos invitó a cenar el sábado.
native_language_example: My neighbor invited us to dinner on Saturday.

additional_notes: Future tense of ir (“to go”). It’s used when you’re talking about you + others leaving a place or going somewhere in the future. Common patterns: nos iremos pronto (we’ll leave soon), nos iremos de aquí (we’ll get out of here), nos iremos a casa (we’ll go home), nos iremos en cuanto... (we’ll leave/go as soon as...).
target_language_example: Si no mejora el clima, nos iremos mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: If the weather doesn’t improve, we’ll leave tomorrow morning.

meaning: "we had a good time" / "we enjoyed ourselves."
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "pasárselo" (to have fun). It’s commonly used with an adverb like "bien", "genial", "fatal", etc.: "Nos lo pasamos bien" = we had a good time; "Nos lo pasamos genial" = we had a great time. The "lo" doesn’t translate directly into English; it’s part of the Spanish structure.
target_language_example: En el concierto nos lo pasamos genial.
native_language_example: We had a great time at the concert.

additional_notes:
From the verb "mudarse" (to move/relocate). "Nos" indicates "we" (we moved ourselves). Often used with:
- "nos mudamos a + place" = we moved to...
- "nos mudamos de + place" = we moved from...
Depending on context, it can be past (preterite: "we moved") or present ("we’re moving" / "we move").
target_language_example: Nos mudamos a Madrid el mes pasado.
native_language_example: We moved to Madrid last month.

additional_notes: Future tense of the reflexive verb phrase "ocuparse de" (to take care of, to deal with). It’s commonly followed by a person or thing (often a pronoun): nos ocuparemos de eso/esto/él/ellos/ustedes. Not related to English "occupy" in meaning here.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, nos ocuparemos de todo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll take care of everything.

meaning: we agreed; we came to an agreement.
additional_notes:
From ponerse de acuerdo = “to agree / reach an agreement,” often after talking or negotiating. You can add details with:
- ponerse de acuerdo en + noun/gerund: Nos pusimos de acuerdo en compartir los gastos. (agree on sharing)
- ponerse de acuerdo para + infinitive: Nos pusimos de acuerdo para salir temprano. (agree to do something)
You can also specify the people involved: nos pusimos de acuerdo entre nosotros (among ourselves). The verb changes with the subject: me puse / te pusiste / se puso / nos pusimos / se pusieron.
target_language_example: Al final, nos pusimos de acuerdo y compramos el más barato.
native_language_example: In the end, we agreed and bought the cheapest one.

additional_notes: Used to say what remains for “us” (time, options, things, feelings). Common patterns: “nos queda + noun” (Nos queda un minuto), “sólo nos queda + infinitive / cosa” (Sólo nos queda esperar / una cosa), “ya no nos queda otra alternativa” (we have no other choice). Verb is "quedar" in the sense of “to remain.”
target_language_example: Nos queda poco tiempo, así que vamos rápido.
native_language_example: We have little time left, so let’s go quickly.

additional_notes: From the verb **quedarse** (to stay, to remain). **Nos** is the reflexive pronoun used with **quedarse**. In the present tense, **nos quedamos** often means a decision/plan to stay: *If we stay here...* In some contexts it can also be the simple past (**pretérito**): *we stayed / we ended up staying*, depending on the surrounding sentence and time clues.
target_language_example: Hace tarde, así que nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: It’s late, so we’re staying home.

meaning: “we ran out of” / “we were left without.”
additional_notes: Used to say that “we” no longer have something because it was used up, lost, or unavailable. Pattern: quedarse sin + noun (e.g., agua, comida, gasolina). In the past, common forms are nos quedamos sin… (we ran out of…) and me quedé sin… (I ran out of…).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin batería y no pudimos llamar a nadie.
native_language_example: We ran out of battery (our phone died) and we couldn’t call anyone.

additional_notes: Future tense of quedarse (“to stay,” “to remain”). It can mean staying in a place (Nos quedaremos en casa) or staying together (Nos quedaremos juntos). With “con + noun,” it often means “to keep/hold onto something” (Nos quedaremos con tu pasaporte = We’ll keep your passport).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: nos quedaremos aquí hasta que termine la reunión.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll stay here until the meeting ends.

additional_notes: Future tense of quedarse (“to stay/remain”) with nos (“we/us”) and aquí (“here”). Used to say that a group plans to remain in this place, often with a time phrase: hasta el domingo (until Sunday), por un tiempo (for a while).
target_language_example: Si empieza a llover, nos quedaremos aquí.
native_language_example: If it starts to rain, we’ll stay here.

additional_notes: From the verb **reírse** (“to laugh”). **Nos** is the reflexive pronoun for **nosotros** (“we”), used when the action applies to the subject: **nos reímos** = “we laugh / we laughed.” Depending on context, **reímos** can be present (“we laugh”) or preterite past (“we laughed”).
target_language_example: Nos reímos mucho en la fiesta.
native_language_example: We laughed a lot at the party.

meaning: we sat down; we sit (ourselves) down.
additional_notes: Form of the verb sentarse (“to sit down”), with nos (“ourselves / us”). It can describe the action of taking a seat in the past (preterite: “we sat down”) or a routine/present action (present: “we sit down”), depending on context. Often followed by en + place (“in/on/at”) or next to someone (uno al lado del otro).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos cerca de la ventana para hablar.
native_language_example: We sat down near the window to talk.

meaning: “we separate / we split up / we go our separate ways.”
additional_notes: From the verb "separarse" (to separate). It can be used literally (two people part ways at a place: "Here is where we separate") or about a relationship ending ("We broke up"). In the past, it’s often "nos separamos" = "we separated/we broke up."
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, nos separamos y cada uno se fue a su casa.
native_language_example: After the meeting, we split up and each one went home.

meaning: we have to leave (we need to go).
additional_notes: Used to say you (a group including the speaker) must leave, often because of time, an obligation, or urgency. Common with time words like ya (now), enseguida (right away), or with a softener like bueno (“well”). Equivalent to “tenemos que irnos,” with the pronoun attached to the verb.
target_language_example: Lo siento, nos tenemos que ir ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Sorry, we have to leave right now.

meaning: “is going to (do something) to/for us” (near future).
additional_notes: Built with the verb phrase **ir a + infinitive** to talk about the near future: **va a + infinitive** = “is going to + verb.” **Nos** is the pronoun for “us” (often an indirect object: to us/for us). Word order is typically **nos + va a + infinitive**. You’ll also see it with **se** as in **se nos va a + infinitive** (“it’s going to + verb on us / it’s going to end up happening to us”), e.g., **Se nos va a acabar** (“We’re going to run out of it”).
target_language_example: Si no salimos ya, se nos va a hacer tarde.
native_language_example: If we don’t leave now, we’re going to be late.

meaning: “we’re going to …” (we are leaving/going to do something).
additional_notes: Uses irse (to leave/go away) in the “near future” structure: nos vamos a + infinitive. Often means “we’re going to (do something soon)”, and can also imply “we’re leaving to go (do it)” depending on context. Common in plans and decisions: Nos vamos a casar / Nos vamos a mudar / Nos vamos a quedar. The next verb stays in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Nos vamos a cenar a las ocho.
native_language_example: We’re going to have dinner at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group (including the speaker) will enjoy themselves. It’s the near future with **ir a + infinitive**: *vamos a* (we’re going to) + *divertir* (to have fun). Often intensified with *mucho*: *Nos vamos a divertir mucho* = “We’re going to have a lot of fun.”
target_language_example: En la fiesta nos vamos a divertir mucho.
native_language_example: At the party we’re going to have a lot of fun.

additional_notes: From the verb ir (to go): “(nosotros) nos vamos.” Common for announcing that you’re leaving now (“We’re off / Let’s go”). It can also be used with a destination or activity: “Nos vamos de Japón” = “We’re leaving Japan,” “Nos vamos de cacería” = “We’re going hunting.”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; nos vamos.
native_language_example: It’s late; we’re leaving.

additional_notes: Used with the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**. **Nos** is an object pronoun meaning “to us / us,” and the subject (“they”) is often implied: **(Ellos/Ellas) nos van a + infinitive**. Common in warnings or predictions: *Nos van a descubrir* (“They’re going to find us out”).
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! Nos van a ver si hacemos ruido.
native_language_example: Careful! They’re going to see us if we make noise.

meaning: “we see each other again” / “we meet again.”
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of "ver" (veamos) because it refers to a future or uncertain time (often after "cuando", "hasta que", "espero que", "puede que"). Common in farewells like "Hasta que nos veamos de nuevo" (“until we meet again”).
target_language_example: Hasta que nos veamos de nuevo, cuídate mucho.
native_language_example: Until we meet again, take good care of yourself.

additional_notes: Common, casual way to say goodbye, often implying "see you later". You can add a time/place: "Nos vemos por la noche" (see you tonight). Literally it means "we see each other" (present tense used with future meaning). Not to confuse with "te ves..." (you look...), where "verse" means "to look".
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Alright, I'm leaving. See you tomorrow.

meaning: "See you in" (a time) / "See you at" (a place or event).
additional_notes: Common casual way to say goodbye and arrange the next meeting. Use **en + time** (Nos vemos en dos semanas / en un mes) and **en + place/event** (Nos vemos en el puente / en la boda). With parts of the day you’ll also hear **en la noche** (“at night”), though **por la noche** is also very common.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la entrada a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the entrance at eight.

meaning: “See you at the…” (to say you’ll meet someone at a place).
additional_notes: Used when saying goodbye and agreeing to meet at a specific location: Nos vemos en el + place (usually a masculine noun). For feminine places, use “nos vemos en la…”. “En” here often means “at” for locations (e.g., en el cole, en el karaoke). You can also add a time: “Nos vemos en el ensayo a las seis.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el café después del trabajo.
native_language_example: See you at the café after work.

additional_notes: A common, friendly goodbye. Literally “we see each other later” (from ver = to see). You can say it on its own, or after “vale / bueno / sí / muy bien” when ending a conversation. Similar options: “nos vemos” (see you), “hasta luego” (see you later).
target_language_example: Tengo que irme; nos vemos luego.
native_language_example: I have to go; see you later.

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say goodbye when you expect to meet again the next day. Literally means “we’ll see each other tomorrow,” but it’s used like English “see you tomorrow.” Often paired with time/place details (e.g., en la escuela, en la noche).
target_language_example: Bueno, me voy. Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Okay, I’m leaving. See you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Future tense of "ver(se)" used to talk about meeting again. Often used as a goodbye meaning “see you later/soon,” and it can be followed by a place or time ("nos veremos allí", "nos veremos esta noche"). "Ya nos veremos" can sound like “we’ll see about that / we’ll meet again” depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Nos veremos mañana en el café.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow at the café.

meaning: "(that) we see each other again" / "(that) we meet again."
additional_notes: This is the subjunctive form of "volver a ver" (“to see again”), used with expressions like "espero que..." (I hope...), "quizá..." (maybe...), and "hasta que..." (until...). It often appears in goodbyes: "Hasta que nos volvamos a ver" = “Until we meet again.”
target_language_example: Espero que nos volvamos a ver muy pronto.
native_language_example: I hope we see each other again very soon.

additional_notes: Future tense of “volver a ver(se)” (to see again). “Nos” means “each other / ourselves,” so it’s commonly used when saying goodbye or when you expect to meet again. Often with time expressions like “algún día” (someday) or “pronto” (soon).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, nos volveremos a ver pronto.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll see each other again soon.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you mean exactly two people: you and one other person. It often appears after a preposition (e.g., entre nosotros dos = between the two of us; a nosotros dos = to the two of us) or as the subject (Nosotros dos tenemos… = The two of us have…).
target_language_example: Entre nosotros dos, podemos resolverlo.
native_language_example: Between the two of us, we can solve it.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis or to show that the subject and object are the same group ("we" = "us"). Often appears after prepositions like "a" (a nosotros mismos = "to ourselves") or "con" (con nosotros mismos = "with/by ourselves"), and in phrases like "ni siquiera nosotros mismos" ("not even we ourselves").
target_language_example: Tenemos que ser honestos con nosotros mismos.
native_language_example: We have to be honest with ourselves.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is "nosotros" (we) and the verb takes the pronoun "nos". The pronoun goes right before a conjugated verb (Nos sorprendimos) or can attach to an infinitive/gerund/affirmative command (sorprendernos, sorprendiéndonos). Often translates as "we ... ourselves" (reflexive) or "we ... each other" (reciprocal), depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Nosotros nos levantamos temprano.
native_language_example: We got up early.

additional_notes: Future tense of "encargarse de" (to take care of / handle / be in charge of). It’s used to reassure someone that you will handle a task or responsibility, often followed by "de" + thing: "Nosotros nos encargaremos del resto/de todo."
target_language_example: No te preocupes: nosotros nos encargaremos de la reserva.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll take care of the reservation.

additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun nosotros (“we”) plus the verb ser in the present tense (somos). Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so Somos ingleses is also very common. Use ser for identity, origin, profession, and essential characteristics (e.g., Somos ingleses, Somos la realeza).
target_language_example: Nosotros somos estudiantes, pero ellos son profesores.
native_language_example: We are students, but they are teachers.

additional_notes: Used to say that the same thing is true for “we/us” as well. Often said as a short standalone reply (e.g., “Bueno, nosotros también.” = “Well, us too.”). Placement: it’s commonly “Nosotros también + verb” (Nosotros también seremos…), or “y nosotros también” to add “and we too.”
target_language_example: Si ustedes van, nosotros también vamos.
native_language_example: If you all go, we’ll go too.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the friendship relationship shared by the speaker and another person (or a group). Common with verbs like "ser" (describe it), "durar" (last), and "terminarse" (end), and in requests like "Hazlo por nuestra amistad" (“Do it for our friendship”).
target_language_example: Quiero cuidar nuestra amistad.
native_language_example: I want to take care of our friendship.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "nuestra" agrees in gender and number with the noun (casa is feminine singular). Often used with "ser" (Nuestra casa es pequeña) or "estar" (Nuestra casa está lista).
target_language_example: Nuestra casa está cerca del centro.
native_language_example: Our house is near downtown.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the city where you and your group (family, friends, community) live or are based. It agrees with the feminine noun "ciudad" → "nuestra" (not "nuestro").
target_language_example: Me encanta vivir en nuestra ciudad.
native_language_example: I love living in our city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the class (group of students) or the class session/lesson that you and others belong to. Uses the feminine singular possessive adjective "nuestra" to agree with "clase" (feminine). For plural: "nuestras clases" = "our classes."
target_language_example: Nuestra clase tiene un examen el viernes.
native_language_example: Our class has a test on Friday.

additional_notes: “Compañía” usually means a company/business. It can also mean “company” as in “companionship,” but in these examples it’s about a workplace/organization (“work for our company,” “our company needs people,” “join our company”). “Nuestra” agrees with a feminine singular noun like “compañía.”
target_language_example: Nuestra compañía ofrece buenos beneficios a sus empleados.
native_language_example: Our company offers good benefits to its employees.

additional_notes: “Nuestra” is the feminine singular form of “our,” used because “escuela” is a feminine noun (la escuela). It can refer to the building or the institution/community. Common with location verbs like “estar” and with “ir a / venir a” (to go/come to).
target_language_example: Nuestra escuela está cerca del parque.
native_language_example: Our school is near the park.

additional_notes: Used to say where your school is located. In Spanish, "estar" is commonly used for location (where something/someone is). It’s usually followed by a place phrase like "cerca de..." (near), "en..." (in/at), "en el centro" (in the center), "en el sur" (in the south), or a comparison like "más lejos que..." (farther than).
target_language_example: Nuestra escuela está al lado del parque.
native_language_example: Our school is next to the park.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s family. It’s a noun phrase with the possessive adjective "nuestra" (feminine singular) + "familia". You’ll also see: "nuestro" (masc. singular), "nuestros" (masc. plural), "nuestras" (fem. plural). Often used with "en" to say how many people are in the family: "Somos cinco en nuestra familia."
target_language_example: En nuestra familia siempre cenamos juntos los domingos.
native_language_example: In our family we always have dinner together on Sundays.

meaning: our native language; our mother tongue.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the language you grew up speaking. It agrees with the subject: nuestra (our, feminine) + lengua (language, feminine) + materna (native/mother). You can change it to mi lengua materna (my), tu lengua materna (your), su lengua materna (his/her/their/your formal), etc.
target_language_example: Aprender otro idioma me ayuda a valorar más nuestra lengua materna.
native_language_example: Learning another language helps me appreciate our native language more.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the trip/vacation (or period) right after a wedding. It’s a possessive phrase: nuestra = “our” + luna de miel = “honeymoon.” You can swap the possessive: mi luna de miel (my), tu luna de miel (your), su luna de miel (his/her/their/your formal).
target_language_example: Vamos a Italia para nuestra luna de miel.
native_language_example: We’re going to Italy for our honeymoon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the relationship between two people (romantic partners, friends, family, etc.). It’s feminine: la relación, so it becomes nuestra relación (“our relationship”). You’ll often see it with verbs like seguir (continue), arruinar (ruin), trabajar en (work on), and terminar (end/break up).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar de nuestra relación y de cómo podemos mejorarla.
native_language_example: I want to talk about our relationship and how we can improve it.

additional_notes: Used to say this is the one and only possibility to do something (often urgent or high-stakes). It’s typically followed by de + infinitive: "nuestra única oportunidad de + verb" (e.g., de salir, de arreglarlo). "Oportunidad" can mean either "chance" or "opportunity" depending on context.
target_language_example: Si fallamos ahora, perdemos nuestra única oportunidad de ganar.
native_language_example: If we fail now, we lose our only chance to win.

additional_notes: Used to talk about life in general from the speaker’s point of view (shared with others). Common in phrases like “en nuestras vidas” (“in our lives”) and “por/para el resto de nuestras vidas” (“for the rest of our lives”).
target_language_example: A veces las mejores decisiones cambian nuestras vidas.
native_language_example: Sometimes the best decisions change our lives.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend of the speaker and their group (family, team, etc.). It can be sincere (“he’s our friend/ally”) or ironic/sarcastic (“our friend here…”) depending on tone and context. Grammar note: possessives agree with the thing possessed: nuestro amigo (male, singular), nuestra amiga (female, singular), nuestros amigos / nuestras amigas (plural).
target_language_example: No te preocupes; es nuestro amigo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; he’s our friend.

additional_notes: Can mean either (1) your shared fate/future (“destiny”) or (2) the place you’re going (“destination”). Context usually makes it clear: with travel/arrival verbs like llegar, ir, estar cerca de → “destination”; with aceptar, cambiar, creer en → “destiny.”
target_language_example: Finalmente llegamos a nuestro destino.
native_language_example: We finally arrived at our destination.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a group you belong to (sports team, work team, project team, etc.). It agrees with a masculine singular noun: nuestro + equipo (even if the team has women and men). For a feminine noun like “selección” you’d say “nuestra selección.”
target_language_example: Nuestro equipo juega mañana, ¿vienes a apoyarnos?
native_language_example: Our team plays tomorrow—are you coming to support us?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a son shared by the speaker and at least one other person (often the other parent). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone you both care for like a son ("como nuestro hijo"). In Spanish you can drop the subject pronoun and just say “nuestro hijo…”.
target_language_example: Nuestro hijo tiene seis años y le encanta el fútbol.
native_language_example: Our son is six years old and he loves soccer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s own country (for example, your homeland). It agrees with a masculine singular noun: nuestro país. Variations: “nuestra nación” (our nation), “nuestros países” (our countries). Often used in formal or political contexts (defend, crisis, peace, international relations).
target_language_example: Nuestro país necesita unidad en tiempos difíciles.
native_language_example: Our country needs unity in difficult times.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "nuestro" = "our" (used with a masculine singular noun like "plan"). It can refer to a plan shared by the speaker and others (a team, family, friends). In many contexts you can also say "el plan" if it’s clear whose plan it is.
target_language_example: Mañana presentamos nuestro plan al cliente.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we present our plan to the client.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a teacher or professor who is male, from the speaker’s point of view. "Nuestro" agrees with a masculine singular noun (profesor). For a female teacher/professor, say "nuestra profesora."
target_language_example: Nuestro profesor nos dejó mucha tarea hoy.
native_language_example: Our teacher gave us a lot of homework today.

additional_notes: "Pueblo" can mean a small town or village, or the people/community of a place. "Nuestro" changes to match the noun: nuestro pueblo, nuestra ciudad, nuestros amigos, etc. Often used when welcoming someone to where you live or talking about your hometown.
target_language_example: Me encanta vivir en nuestro pueblo.
native_language_example: I love living in our town.

additional_notes: "Nuestro" means "our" and agrees with a singular masculine noun like "viaje". Used to talk about a trip you and others are taking or took; common with verbs like preparar (to prepare), continuar (to continue), and phrases like "nuestro viaje llegó a su fin" (our trip came to an end).
target_language_example: Disfrutamos mucho de nuestro viaje a México.
native_language_example: We enjoyed our trip to Mexico a lot.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: nuestros (our, masculine plural) + amigos (friends). Use for a mixed group or all-male friends; for all-female friends, say “nuestras amigas.” You can also use it to refer to friends you and someone else share (e.g., you and your family/partner).
target_language_example: Vamos a cenar con nuestros amigos esta noche.
native_language_example: We’re going to have dinner with our friends tonight.

additional_notes: Literally means “our hearts” (nuestro = our, corazones = hearts). Very common in emotional or poetic contexts to mean someone is remembered or loved (“in our hearts”), or to talk about inner feelings/intentions (“from the bottom of our hearts,” “the secrets of our hearts”). Can also be used metaphorically (e.g., “we carry weapons in our hearts” = anger/hatred).
target_language_example: Siempre te llevaré en nuestros corazones.
native_language_example: I will always carry you in our hearts.

additional_notes: Refers to what “we” (a group including the speaker) are doing to try to achieve something. Often used with set phrases like: juntar nuestros esfuerzos (join forces/work together), nuestros esfuerzos fueron en vano / para nada (our efforts were in vain/for nothing), nuestros esfuerzos no dieron resultados (our efforts didn’t produce results). You can change the possessive to match the group: mis esfuerzos (my efforts), tus esfuerzos (your efforts), sus esfuerzos (his/her/their efforts).
target_language_example: Si seguimos con nuestros esfuerzos, lo lograremos.
native_language_example: If we keep up our efforts, we’ll achieve it.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase used to talk about children belonging to “us” (the speaker and at least one other person). Use "nuestros" with masculine plural "hijos"; it can refer to a mixed group of boys and girls, or to sons specifically. For girls only, say "nuestras hijas".
target_language_example: Nuestros hijos están en la escuela hoy.
native_language_example: Our kids are at school today.

meaning: "our guests" (people invited to a place or event).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the group of guests that belong to or are hosted by “us.” Agreement matters: invitados (masculine plural or mixed group); invitadas (all women). In formal writing you may see nuestras/os invitados/as to include both forms.
target_language_example: Voy a saludar a nuestros invitados en la entrada.
native_language_example: I'm going to greet our guests at the entrance.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used to talk about the parents of “us” (the speaker and at least one other person). It can be the subject or object of a sentence (e.g., Nuestros padres viven…, Cuidar a nuestros padres). Often matches “our mom and dad.”
target_language_example: Nuestros padres no pueden venir hoy.
native_language_example: Our parents can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a house/home you have recently bought, rented, or moved into. It agrees in gender and number: nueva casa (feminine singular), nuevas casas (feminine plural). You can add a possessive: mi nueva casa (my new house), nuestra nueva casa (our new house).
target_language_example: Te invito a cenar en mi nueva casa este viernes.
native_language_example: I’m inviting you to dinner at my new house this Friday.

meaning: “new life” (a fresh start or new stage of life).
additional_notes: Often used when someone is starting over or entering a new phase (moving, a new job, recovery, a relationship change, etc.). It usually takes a possessive (mi/tu/su/nuestra) depending on who is starting the new life: “mi nueva vida” = “my new life.”
target_language_example: Con el nuevo trabajo, siento que empiezo una nueva vida.
native_language_example: With the new job, I feel like I’m starting a new life.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or a point in the past: "nueve años" (nine years), "hace nueve años" (nine years ago). It agrees with the number: "un año" (one year) vs. "dos/tres/nueve años" (plural).
target_language_example: Viví en México nueve años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for nine years.

additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened at any time prior to the moment being talked about. Often placed before the verb ("Nunca antes había...") or at the end for emphasis ("no ha ido nunca antes...").
target_language_example: Nunca antes había probado una comida tan picante.
native_language_example: I had never before tried food this spicy.

additional_notes: Used to say that up to that point in the past, something had never happened. It’s the past perfect: nunca antes + había + past participle (e.g., había visto, había hecho, había estado). Often used for emphasis; you can also say “nunca había…” without “antes.”
target_language_example: Nunca antes había visto una ciudad tan grande.
native_language_example: I had never seen such a big city before.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no prior experience of seeing something up to that moment. It’s built from: nunca (never) + antes (before) + había visto (had seen). You can change the last part to match the subject/verb: “nunca antes había hecho” (I had never done), “nunca antes habíamos visto” (we had never seen).
target_language_example: Nunca antes había visto una ciudad tan tranquila por la noche.
native_language_example: I had never seen a city so quiet at night.

additional_notes: Used to say that even if something seems impossible now, it could still happen. Often said as advice or encouragement when someone is being too certain that they won’t do something or that something can’t happen.
target_language_example: Crees que no vas a volver a enamorarte, pero nunca digas nunca.
native_language_example: You think you won’t fall in love again, but never say never.

meaning: "I never said that…" (denying you said something).
additional_notes: Used when you want to correct someone or clarify that you did not claim something. It’s often followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (fuera, fueran, fueras, fuéramos) because it refers to an unasserted/denied statement: “Nunca dije que fuera…” = “I never said (that) it was…”. You can also use it with a full idea: “Nunca dije que no.”
target_language_example: Nunca dije que quisiera ir contigo.
native_language_example: I never said that I wanted to go with you.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb “ha” (from haber) + a past participle to form the present perfect: “nunca ha + participle” = someone has never done something up to now. Example pattern: “Ella nunca ha viajado” = “She has never traveled.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano nunca ha visitado España.
native_language_example: My brother has never visited Spain.

meaning: “has never been” / “has never been to” (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: nunca + ha + estado (estar). It says something has not happened at any time up to the present. Common with places (nunca ha estado en España = has never been to Spain) and states/conditions (nunca ha estado casado = has never been married; nunca ha estado herido = has never been injured). For tú/yo/ellos, the form changes: nunca he/has/hemos/han estado.
target_language_example: Mi hermano nunca ha estado en México.
native_language_example: My brother has never been to Mexico.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the past perfect: “nunca había + participle” = “had never + participle.” It talks about something that had not happened up to a point in the past (often with antes / en mi vida / hasta entonces). The verb “haber” here is the auxiliary (había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían).
target_language_example: Yo nunca había visto esa película antes.
native_language_example: I had never seen that movie before.

meaning: “I/he/she had never been” (had never been to / had never been in a state).
additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (haber + estado) with nunca to say that up to a point in the past, the person had not experienced something. Often followed by en + place (“had never been to/in…”) or tan + adjective (“had never been so…”), e.g., “nunca había estado tan asustada” = “she had never been so scared.”
target_language_example: Cuando llegué a Madrid, nunca había estado allí antes.
native_language_example: When I arrived in Madrid, I had never been there before.

additional_notes: Used to say that up to that moment in the past, you had not heard something before. It’s the past perfect: nunca + había + oído (from oír). With a direct object: “Nunca había oído esa expresión.” With de: “Nunca había oído de él/ellos” = “I’d never heard of him/them.”
target_language_example: Nunca había oído esa palabra hasta hoy.
native_language_example: I had never heard that word until today.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (haber in imperfect: había + past participle: visto) with nunca to say that up to some point in the past, something had not happened. Often followed by an object (esto, algo así) or by a person/thing (a alguien, un árbol). You can change the subject: yo nunca había visto, ella nunca había visto, Tom nunca había visto.
target_language_example: Antes de viajar, nunca había visto la nieve.
native_language_example: Before traveling, I had never seen snow.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect: "había visto" = "had seen". "Nunca" makes it "had never seen". The "a" is the personal "a", used before a specific person (and often pets/animals) as the direct object: "Nunca había visto a Tom…". You can also use it before a thing treated like a person (e.g., "a tanta gente"). Often followed by an adjective or action: "Nunca había visto a Jimmy tan contento" (so happy), "Nunca había visto a Tom actuar así" (act like that).
target_language_example: Nunca había visto a mi hermana tan nerviosa.
native_language_example: I’d never seen my sister so nervous.

meaning: "I had never seen a" / "I had never seen one".
additional_notes: Uses the past perfect ("había visto") with "nunca" to say that up to that moment in the past, you had not had the experience of seeing something. Often followed by a noun ("un panda") or by "tan + adjective" to emphasize: "Nunca había visto un arcoíris tan bonito." You can change the article/gender/number as needed: "nunca había visto una..." / "nunca había visto unos..."
target_language_example: Antes de venir a España, nunca había visto un castillo tan grande.
native_language_example: Before coming to Spain, I had never seen such a big castle.

meaning: "you have never" (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect: "nunca has" + past participle (e.g., "nunca has ido" = "you have never gone"). It’s a common way to say someone has not done something at any time up to now. In questions, Spanish keeps the same word order: "¿Nunca has…?" = "Have you never…?/You’ve never…?"
target_language_example: ¿Nunca has probado la paella?
native_language_example: Have you never tried paella?

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (haber + visto) to say that up to now, in your life/experience, you haven’t seen something. Often used for emphasis or to highlight something new or shocking: "como nunca has visto" = "like you’ve never seen (before)." You can change the person: "nunca he visto" (I’ve never seen), "nunca hemos visto" (we’ve never seen).
target_language_example: Nunca has visto una playa tan tranquila como esta.
native_language_example: You’ve never seen a beach as calm as this.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done something up to now. It’s the present perfect in Spanish: nunca + he (from haber) + past participle (ido, oído, hablado, escrito, etc.). The subject pronoun (yo) is often omitted: “Nunca he ido…” = “(Yo) nunca he ido…”. Note: Spanish “he” is not the English pronoun “he”; it means “I have.”
target_language_example: Nunca he probado comida japonesa.
native_language_example: I have never tried Japanese food.

meaning: "I have never been" (have never been in a place/situation).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: nunca + he (haber) + estado (past participle of estar). Commonly followed by en/dentro de/bajo + noun to say you’ve never been somewhere or in a particular condition: “Nunca he estado en México”, “Nunca he estado sola”.
target_language_example: Nunca he estado en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: I have never been in this city.

meaning: “I have never been to …” / “I’ve never been in …”
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **nunca** (never) + **he estado** (I have been) + **en** (in/to). Often used to say you’ve never visited a place: *Nunca he estado en Inglaterra.* With situations/states it can mean “I’ve never been in/under…”: *Nunca he estado en fuga de la ley antes* (“I’ve never been on the run from the law before”). You can also say **Yo nunca he estado en…** for emphasis; word order is flexible in Spanish.
target_language_example: Nunca he estado en México, pero me gustaría ir.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Mexico, but I’d like to go.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no knowledge or awareness of a person, group, or thing. It’s the present perfect: "he oído" = "I have heard" (from oír). Usually followed by "de" + a noun/pronoun: "de ella" (of her), "de ellos" (of them), "de eso" (of that), "de ti" (of you).
target_language_example: Nunca he oído hablar de ese restaurante.
native_language_example: I've never heard of that restaurant.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (he tenido) with nunca to talk about something you have not experienced up to now. Often followed by a noun (nunca he tenido coche) or by que + infinitive to mean “I’ve never had to…” (nunca he tenido que pagar…).
target_language_example: Nunca he tenido un trabajo así.
native_language_example: I've never had a job like this.

additional_notes: Used to say that up to now, you have not had the experience of seeing something. It’s built from: nunca (never) + he (I have, from haber) + visto (seen, past participle of ver). Often followed by a noun or by "que" + a verb: "Nunca he visto una película" / "Nunca he visto un perro que hable."
target_language_example: Nunca he visto una ciudad tan bonita.
native_language_example: I've never seen such a beautiful city.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: "he visto" = "I have seen." "Nunca" goes before the verb phrase. The "a" is the personal "a" used before a direct object that is a specific person (and often animals): "Nunca he visto a este hombre…" If the direct object is a thing, you normally drop "a": "Nunca he visto este lugar."
target_language_example: Nunca he visto a nadie tan amable.
native_language_example: I've never seen anyone so kind.

additional_notes: An emphatic way to say something has not happened at any time and will not happen. Uses two near-synonyms (nunca + jamás) for extra force; it can also be said on its own as a strong refusal or denial (“Nunca jamás.”). Often sounds dramatic or literary, but it’s understood in everyday speech too.
