target_language_example: Nunca jamás voy a olvidar ese día.
native_language_example: I will never, ever forget that day.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): “había visto” = “had seen.” “La” is a direct object pronoun meaning “her” (or “it” for a feminine noun). Often followed by “antes” (before) or “en mi vida” (in my life) for emphasis, or used with “así” to mean “like that” (I’d never seen her like that).
target_language_example: Nunca la había visto tan contenta.
native_language_example: I had never seen her so happy.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never seen a specific female person before. It uses the present perfect (he visto = “I have seen”) and the direct object pronoun la (“her”). Common expansions: “nunca la he visto antes” (never seen her before), “nunca la he visto en mi vida” (never in my life).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero nunca la he visto.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I’ve never seen her.

meaning: 'never (to him/her/you formal)'—used before a verb with the indirect object pronoun le.
additional_notes: "Nunca" means "never" and usually comes right before the verb. "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him," "to her," or "to you" (formal). It’s used with verbs like decir (to tell/say), contar (to tell), mentir (to lie), and oír (to hear): e.g., "Nunca le dije..." = "I never told him/her..."
target_language_example: Nunca le dije la verdad.
native_language_example: I never told him/her the truth.

additional_notes: "Nunca" means "never." "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (often a previously mentioned thing/idea). It goes right before the conjugated verb (e.g., "nunca lo hice," "nunca lo he hecho," "nunca lo habría imaginado"). In "para que nunca lo encuentren," "lo" refers to what they won’t find (e.g., the body).
target_language_example: Nunca lo vi.
native_language_example: I never saw him/it.

additional_notes:
Used with a verb to say something never happened to you or someone never did something to you. 
- With a direct/indirect object: “Nunca me dijo…” = “She never told me…”, “Nunca me contaste…” = “You never told me…”.
- With experiences (pasar/sentir): “Nunca me había pasado…” = “This had never happened to me.”, “Nunca me había sentido…” = “I had never felt…”.
Often appears with the present perfect or past perfect (había + participle) to talk about something that had never happened up to that point.
target_language_example: Nunca me ayudaron cuando lo necesité.
native_language_example: They never helped me when I needed it.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar, which is often structured as “(Something) me gusta” = “I like (something)” (literally, “it pleases me”). So “Nunca me ha gustado X” means “I’ve never liked X,” and the subject is what comes after (Tom, biology, etc.). In this phrase, “ha gustado” is the present perfect (have liked), commonly used to talk about your experience up to now: “never liked.” You can add emphasis with “mucho”: “Nunca me ha gustado mucho” = “I’ve never liked it much.”
target_language_example: Nunca me ha gustado el café.
native_language_example: I have never liked coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve never experienced something up to that point in the past. It uses the past perfect ("había" + past participle "pasado") and often appears with words like "antes" (before), "esto" (this), or "algo así" (something like that).
target_language_example: Me asusté porque nunca me había pasado algo así.
native_language_example: I got scared because something like that had never happened to me.

meaning: "I had never felt" (about myself/my feelings, up to that point).
additional_notes: Uses the past perfect ("había" + past participle) to talk about an experience that had *not* happened before a past moment. Often followed by "así" (like this), "tan..." (so...), or "de esta manera" (in this way). The verb is reflexive: "sentirse" = to feel (emotionally/physically), so it’s about how you felt, not what you touched.
target_language_example: Hasta ese día, nunca me había sentido tan seguro de mí mismo.
native_language_example: Until that day, I had never felt so sure of myself.

meaning: “couldn’t have said it better” / “well said” (literally: “never better said”).
additional_notes: Used as a comment after a statement to emphasize that it was especially accurate, well-worded, or perfectly timed—often as a quick agreement or a witty remark. It can stand alone or follow what someone just said.
target_language_example: —Este café está buenísimo. —Nunca mejor dicho.
native_language_example: —This coffee is amazing. —Couldn’t have said it better.

additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen again (often with a strong, final tone). It can go at the end of the sentence for emphasis: “No lo haré nunca más.”
target_language_example: No voy a llegar tarde nunca más.
native_language_example: I'm never going to be late again.

additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis with negatives. Spanish commonly uses multiple negatives together (e.g., "no" + "nunca" + "nada"), and they still mean a single negative in English: "No me cuenta nunca nada" = “He never tells me anything.” You may also see it without "no" when it starts the sentence: "Nunca nada está realmente perdido" = “Nothing is ever really lost.” Word order can vary depending on what is being emphasized.
target_language_example: No dije nunca nada.
native_language_example: I never said anything.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something surprising or unexpected, followed by a verb clause. Often refers to what you believed in the past (pensé is the past tense of pensar, “to think”).
target_language_example: Nunca pensé que llegaríamos tan lejos.
native_language_example: I never thought we’d get this far.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) with impersonal **se** to make a general statement: **Nunca se sabe…** = “You never know…”. (2) with a reflexive verb (**acordarse, olvidarse, quejarse**, etc.) where **se** is part of the verb: **nunca se acuerda** = “he/she never remembers.” The subject can change: **yo nunca me… / tú nunca te… / él/ella nunca se…**
target_language_example: Nunca se sabe lo que va a pasar.
native_language_example: You never know what’s going to happen.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect: nunca + se + ha + past participle. It means something has not happened at any time up to the present. The "se" can be part of a reflexive verb (e.g., enamorarse) or a passive/impersonal construction (e.g., se ha intentado = "it has been tried").
target_language_example: Nunca se ha visto algo así aquí.
native_language_example: Something like this has never been seen here.

additional_notes: Used to say something is uncertain or unpredictable, often as a reason to be cautious, prepared, or open to possibilities. It can stand alone (“Nunca se sabe.”) or be followed by a clause with cuándo/lo que/cuánto, etc. Literally it’s “one never knows” (impersonal se).
target_language_example: Lleva un paraguas; nunca se sabe.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella; you never know.

additional_notes: Used to say something has never happened (or will never happen) to/with “you,” where **te** is the object pronoun (“you”). **Nunca** goes before **te + verb**: *Nunca te dije…* (I never told you…), *Nunca te he querido* (I’ve never loved you), *Nunca te dejaré* (I’ll never leave you).
target_language_example: Nunca te olvidaré.
native_language_example: I will never forget you.

meaning: "I’ve never seen you" / "I’ve never seen you (do/be) …"
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (he visto) to talk about your experience up to now: “I have never seen you…”. Often followed by a place (ahí/allí/por allí) or an action with an infinitive (fumar = smoke), or an adjective phrase (tan impresionado = so impressed). Word order can change slightly for emphasis (Nunca te he visto vs. No te he visto nunca).
target_language_example: Nunca te he visto tan contento.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen you so happy.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t get the chance to do something (often because there wasn’t time or the situation didn’t allow it). Commonly followed by "de" + infinitive: "Nunca tuve la oportunidad de conocerla" (…to meet her). Uses past tense "tuve" (from "tener") to talk about a completed past period.
target_language_example: Quise despedirme, pero nunca tuve la oportunidad de hablar con ella.
native_language_example: I wanted to say goodbye, but I never had the chance to talk to her.

additional_notes: Used to talk about quantity: el número de + plural noun (el número de personas, el número de estudiantes). It can also introduce an identifying number for something: número de cuenta (account number), número de habitación (room number), número de teléfono (phone number). Often appears in common phrases like un buen número de (quite a few), el mayor número de … posible (the greatest number of … possible), and cierto número de (a certain number of).
target_language_example: Necesito tu número de teléfono y el número de invitados.
native_language_example: I need your phone number and the number of guests.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s telephone number (mobile or landline). Often appears with possessives: mi/tu/su número de teléfono, or with verbs like dar (to give), anotar (to write down), and olvidar (to forget).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono?
native_language_example: What is your phone number?

additional_notes: Used to label something as second (e.g., a person who is second-in-command: "la mujer número dos") or to introduce the second item in a list/argument (like "Second, ...": "Número dos, ..."). In some contexts, "hacer el número dos" is a common euphemism meaning "to poop," but that meaning usually needs the verb ("hacer").
target_language_example: Número dos: mañana revisamos el plan con más calma.
native_language_example: Second: tomorrow we’ll review the plan more calmly.

additional_notes: Used in math to describe a whole number greater than 1 that has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself (for example, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11). Often appears with "ser" ("es un número primo" / "no es un número primo").
target_language_example: El 13 es un número primo.
native_language_example: 13 is a prime number.

meaning: number one; the top/best; the main/prime (suspect, rule, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for rankings ("el jugador número uno" = the #1 player), for ordering items ("regla número uno" = rule number one), and for identifying someone or something as the primary/most important one ("el sospechoso número uno" = the prime suspect). In some contexts it can also be used like "#1" to refer to a specific position or station (e.g., "en la número uno").
target_language_example: Ella es la chef número uno del restaurante.
native_language_example: She’s the restaurant’s number-one chef.

meaning: “or something” (to be vague / suggest an alternative).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a suggestion or list to mean “or something like that,” when you don’t want to be too specific or you’re giving an approximate idea. Very common in casual speech. You’ll also hear: “o algo por el estilo” = “or something like that.”
target_language_example: Podemos tomar un café o algo después de clase.
native_language_example: We can have a coffee or something after class.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a phrase to be vague or to soften what you just said, suggesting the idea is approximate (you’re not sure, or you don’t want to be too exact). Common in casual speech after an example or guess: “una tienda… o algo así.”
target_language_example: Podemos ver una película o algo así.
native_language_example: We can watch a movie or something like that.

meaning: “or two” (used to mean a small, approximate number, usually after “uno/una”).
additional_notes: Common in expressions like “uno o dos” / “una o dos” / “un mes o dos” to mean “one or two” or “a month or two,” suggesting an estimate or “just a few.” The verb usually agrees with the main noun (e.g., “uno o dos pasos”).
target_language_example: Dame un minuto o dos y te llamo.
native_language_example: Give me a minute or two and I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used after a number or amount to mean “at most” or “no more than” (e.g., “30 minutos o menos”). With “más o menos” it forms a common expression meaning “more or less / about / kind of.” Use “menos” with amounts, time, distance; for countable things you can think “fewer,” though Spanish still uses “menos” (e.g., “10 personas o menos”).
target_language_example: Necesito diez dólares o menos para el autobús.
native_language_example: I need ten dollars or less for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to present two possibilities: something is true/does happen, or it isn’t/doesn’t. Often appears after a verb like saber/preguntar/ver (“to know/ask/see”) as in “si … o no” = “whether … or not.” It can also be used by itself as a short reply meaning “Or not.”
target_language_example: Dime si vienes o no.
native_language_example: Tell me whether you're coming or not.

meaning: 'I mean,' 'that is (to say),' or 'so' (to clarify or rephrase).
additional_notes: Very common filler used to explain, clarify, correct yourself, or add emphasis—often placed at the start or in the middle of a sentence. It can introduce a rephrasing or conclusion: “..., o sea, ...” = “..., that is, ...”. In “o sea que ...”, it often means “so/which means that ...”.
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy; o sea, tengo que trabajar hasta tarde.
native_language_example: I can't go today; I mean, I have to work late.

meaning: "I mean, no…" / "I mean, it’s not like…" (used to clarify or soften a negative statement).
additional_notes: A very common conversational filler in informal speech. You say it before a negation to correct, explain, or tone down what you’re saying (often like "I mean" or "like" in English). It can introduce a clarification: "O sea, no X" = "I mean, not X" / "It’s not like X".
target_language_example: O sea, no es que no quiera ir; es que no puedo.
native_language_example: I mean, it’s not that I don’t want to go; it’s that I can’t.

additional_notes: Used in conversation to draw a conclusion or restate what follows as the result/implication of what was just said (similar to “so…” or “so, you’re saying…”). Often comes after an explanation and before the takeaway; can also sound like a filler/hedge in informal speech.
target_language_example: O sea, que no vienes mañana, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: So, that means you’re not coming tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used to draw a conclusion or restate what was just said (often like “so…” or “in other words…”). Common in conversation to connect ideas; it can sound a bit like a filler while the speaker is thinking.
target_language_example: O sea que llegamos tarde y ya empezó la película.
native_language_example: So we arrived late and the movie already started.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an alternative possibility or to soften what you’re saying. Often followed by “sí” or “no” (“o tal vez sí/no”), or by a full clause (“O tal vez no fuera culpa de nadie.”).
target_language_example: Podemos ir al cine, o tal vez quedarnos en casa.
native_language_example: We can go to the movies, or maybe stay at home.

meaning: "or three"; often used to mean "a couple/a few" (as in "dos o tres" = "two or three").
additional_notes: Used after a number to give an approximate quantity: "dos o tres" (two or three), "una o tres" (one or three). It can also be said alone to add or correct a number someone just said ("O tres." = "Or three."). With time, it means around that hour: "a las dos o tres" = around 2 or 3 o’clock.
target_language_example: Trae dos o tres vasos, por favor.
native_language_example: Bring a couple of glasses, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about complying with rules or instructions (often in sports, school, games, or law). You can also say “seguir las reglas” (to follow the rules). In the examples, “deben/tiene la obligación de” expresses obligation: “must/has the obligation to.”
target_language_example: Si quieres jugar, tienes que obedecer las reglas.
native_language_example: If you want to play, you have to obey the rules.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive: "estar/verse/sentirse obligado(a) a + infinitive". It expresses having a duty, requirement, or strong pressure to do something. Changes for gender/number: obligado/obligada/obligados/obligadas. Often used in negatives to reassure someone: "No estás obligado(a) a..." / "No te sientas obligado(a) a...".
target_language_example: No estás obligado a quedarte; puedes irte cuando quieras.
native_language_example: You’re not required to stay; you can leave whenever you want.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of **obligar**: **obligó** = “(he/she/it) forced/made/compelled.” Usually used in the pattern **obligar a alguien a + infinitive**: *La lluvia nos obligó a cancelar* (“The rain made us cancel”). It can also be reflexive (**se obligó a + infinitive**) meaning “(he/she) forced themself to…”.
target_language_example: El jefe me obligó a quedarme hasta tarde.
native_language_example: My boss made me stay late.

meaning: 'work by' (an artist/creator) or 'work of' (something important you’ve done).
additional_notes: Used to identify who created something: *la obra de Van Dyck* = “Van Dyck’s work / a work by Van Dyck.” It can refer to a specific piece (a painting, book, play, etc.) or someone’s body of work. In *la obra de mi vida*, it means “my life’s work” (your most important achievement).
target_language_example: En el museo hay una obra de Picasso que me encanta.
native_language_example: In the museum there’s a work by Picasso that I love.

additional_notes: Used for paintings, sculptures, etc., and also figuratively to describe something (or someone) seen as a masterpiece. Often appears with adjectives like auténtica (“genuine/real”) or una verdadera (“a real”).
target_language_example: Este cuadro es una obra de arte.
native_language_example: This painting is a work of art.

additional_notes: Used for a scripted story performed on stage. You can describe its structure (actos = acts, escenas = scenes) or roles/parts (papel = role). It can also be used more generally to refer to the play as a piece of writing or as the performance.
target_language_example: Vamos a ver una obra de teatro esta noche.
native_language_example: We’re going to see a play tonight.

additional_notes: Used for an outstanding work of art, music, literature, film, etc., often considered someone’s greatest achievement. Usually feminine: "la obra maestra"; plural: "obras maestras." Can also be used figuratively for something done extremely well (sometimes jokingly).
target_language_example: Muchos consideran esta novela una obra maestra.
native_language_example: Many consider this novel a masterpiece.

meaning: eight years (as an age or a length of time).
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s age with "tener" ("cuando tenía ocho años" = "when I was eight") or a duration with "hace" ("hace ocho años" = "eight years ago"), "por" ("por ocho años" = "for eight years"), and "llevar" ("lleva ocho años..." = "has been ... for eight years"). It can also appear in phrases like "en ocho años" meaning "in eight years" (over an eight-year period / not for eight years).
target_language_example: Viví en Madrid por ocho años.
native_language_example: I lived in Madrid for eight years.

additional_notes: A time expression used to say how long something happens each day. You can swap the number: “seis horas al día” (six hours a day), “diez horas al día” (ten hours a day). Common with verbs like trabajar (to work), dormir (to sleep), estudiar (to study).
target_language_example: Estudio ocho horas al día durante la semana.
native_language_example: I study eight hours a day during the week.

additional_notes: Used to say an object is too big for the available room. The verb is "ocupar" (to occupy/take up), here in 3rd person singular: "ocupa" = "it takes up". You can swap the subject: "Esta mesa/El sofá/Este armario ocupa demasiado espacio."
target_language_example: No compres esa cama; ocupa demasiado espacio en el cuarto.
native_language_example: Don’t buy that bed; it takes up too much space in the room.

additional_notes: Used with estar to describe someone being occupied with an activity happening now or around now: "estar ocupada + gerundio" (e.g., "ocupada preparando"). "Ocupada" is feminine; use "ocupado" for a man, and "ocupados/ocupadas" for plural. "La cena" is dinner/supper.
target_language_example: Estoy ocupada preparando la cena, ¿me llamas más tarde?
native_language_example: I’m busy preparing dinner—can you call me later?

additional_notes: Uses the verb **ocurrir** (“to happen/occur”) in the **simple past** (**ocurrió** = “it happened”). **Ocurrió** agrees with the thing that happened (here, **el accidente**). Common in telling where/when/how something happened: **Aquí fue donde ocurrió…** (location), **Así es como ocurrió…** (how it happened), **Hace un año que ocurrió…** (“It’s been a year since it happened”).
target_language_example: Nadie vio cómo ocurrió el accidente.
native_language_example: Nobody saw how the accident happened.

meaning: "I hate" (used before the thing/person you hate).
additional_notes: Spanish often uses the "personal a" before a specific person (and sometimes pets) as a direct object: "Odio a Tom", "Odio a mi hermana". With groups/animals it can also appear, especially if they’re seen as animate: "Odio a los reptiles". The base verb is "odiar" (to hate), and "odio" is the "I" form (yo odio).
target_language_example: Odio a ese hombre.
native_language_example: I hate that man.

additional_notes: Used to complain strongly about a type of person, followed by a verb phrase describing what they do. Pattern: "Odio a la gente que" + verb (usually in present tense): "dice", "miente", "habla", etc. Often sounds harsh; in polite situations you can soften it with "No soporto a la gente que..." (I can’t stand people who...) or "No me gusta la gente que..." (I don’t like people who...).
target_language_example: Odio a la gente que no respeta a los demás.
native_language_example: I hate people who don’t respect others.

additional_notes: A formal/standard way to refer to a member of the police. Often used with an article: "un/una oficial de policía" (a police officer) or "el/la oficial de policía" (the police officer).
target_language_example: ¿Puede llamar a un oficial de policía, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you call a police officer, please?

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for the place where you send mail/packages and buy stamps. Often used with location phrases like "hay una oficina de correos cerca" (there’s a post office nearby) or "ir a la oficina de correos" (to go to the post office).
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la oficina de correos a enviar un paquete.
native_language_example: I have to go to the post office to send a package.

additional_notes: Used to react to something (surprise, realization, interest) and then state what something is. "Es" is from the verb "ser" (to be) and is commonly followed by an adjective or a noun: "Oh, es genial" (adjective), "Oh, es una larga historia" (noun phrase). Often you’ll also hear "Oh, es que..." to introduce an explanation.
target_language_example: Oh, es mi culpa.
native_language_example: Oh, it’s my fault.

meaning: "Oh, that's…" / "Oh, that is…" (reacting to what someone just said or showed).
additional_notes: Used to react in the moment before adding an opinion or description: "Oh, eso es genial/lindo/patético". With just "Oh, eso es.", it can mean "Oh, that's it" or "Oh, that's right" depending on context and tone. "Oh" is an interjection and is optional; you can also say "Eso es genial".
target_language_example: Oh, eso es interesante; no lo sabía.
native_language_example: Oh, that's interesting; I didn't know that.

additional_notes: An interjection used just like in English. Punctuation matters: “Oh, no!” is a reaction (“Oh no!”), but “Oh, no estoy…” means “Oh, I’m not…” (here “no” is the normal negation of the verb). You can also use it to object to someone/something: “Oh, no, tú no.” = “Oh no, not you.”
target_language_example: Oh, no, se me olvidó la contraseña.
native_language_example: Oh no, I forgot my password.

meaning: "oh, please" (used to beg, insist, or show exasperation).
additional_notes: Often said with emotion. It can be a sincere plea ("Oh, please, not so fast") or a sarcastic/annoyed reaction depending on tone. You’ll also hear it repeated ("por favor, por favor") to emphasize urgency.
target_language_example: Oh, por favor, ayúdame un momento.
native_language_example: Oh, please, help me for a moment.

additional_notes: Used as a strong, often immediate agreement/confirmation, sometimes with a tone of remembering or realization (like “Oh, right!”). Common in conversation and can be followed by words like claro, definitivamente, es verdad, por favor.
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Oh, sí, claro.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Oh yes, of course.

meaning: “I wish it were…” (a wish about an unreal/imaginary situation).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish about something that is not true (or seems unlikely) right now. It uses the imperfect subjunctive of ser (fuera = “were”), similar to English “If only…” / “I wish I were…”. Often followed by adjectives or nouns: “Ojalá fuera + adjective/noun…”.
target_language_example: Ojalá fuera más alto.
native_language_example: I wish I were taller.

meaning: “I wish (that) I had…” (regret about the past).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish or regret about something that did not happen in the past. It’s followed by the past perfect subjunctive (hubiera + past participle): hubiera escuchado, hubiera estado, hubiera hecho, etc. Often corresponds to English “If only I had…” / “I wish I had…”.
target_language_example: Ojalá hubiera llamado antes.
native_language_example: I wish I had called earlier.

meaning: “I wish I could …” (expressing a wish, usually about something not possible right now).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish or regret. After ojalá, Spanish commonly uses the imperfect subjunctive (pudiera/pudiese), often implying the speaker thinks it’s unlikely or impossible. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (ir, venir) or a perfect infinitive to talk about the past (haber venido = “have come”).
target_language_example: Ojalá pudiera quedarme más tiempo.
native_language_example: I wish I could stay longer.

meaning: “I wish I had…” / “If only I had…”
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about something you don’t have (or that isn’t true) in the present. It uses the imperfect subjunctive (tuviera) after ojalá. You can add what you wish for: ojalá tuviera + noun, or ojalá tuviera + infinitive phrase (e.g., más tiempo para viajar).
target_language_example: Ojalá tuviera más tiempo para descansar.
native_language_example: I wish I had more time to rest.

meaning: 'eyes open' / 'keep your eyes open' (stay awake or be alert).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "mantener" or "tener": "mantén/mantenga los ojos abiertos" = "keep your eyes open". It can be literal (not closing your eyes) or figurative (pay attention, watch out). You may also hear "con los ojos abiertos" = "with my eyes open."
target_language_example: Mantén los ojos abiertos por si ves a Ana.
native_language_example: Keep your eyes open in case you see Ana.

additional_notes: A descriptive phrase for eye color. Often used with tener (to have): Tengo ojos azules. You may also see it in noun phrases with de: la chica de ojos azules (the blue-eyed girl). Azules agrees in number with ojos (plural).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene ojos azules.
native_language_example: My brother has blue eyes.

meaning: to forget (about); to forget to do something.
additional_notes: Reflexive form of "olvidar" used with "de" + noun or infinitive. Conjugates as "olvidarse" (e.g., "me olvido de", "me olvidé de", "se ha olvidado de"). Often interchangeable with "olvidar", but "olvidarse de" is very common and can emphasize forgetting something that was supposed to be remembered or done.
target_language_example: No te vayas a olvidarse de llamar.
native_language_example: Don’t go forgetting to call.

additional_notes: Refers to what most people in society think about an issue or person. Often used with verbs like "apelar a" (appeal to), "influir en" (influence), "temer" (fear), or to talk about someone’s reputation/image among the general public (e.g., "bajar/subir en la opinión pública").
target_language_example: La opinión pública está en contra de la medida.
native_language_example: Public opinion is against the measure.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the possibility of an outcome or the chance to do an action. It’s usually followed by a noun (oportunidad de éxito) or an infinitive verb (oportunidad de viajar). Common patterns: "tener una oportunidad de..." (to have a chance to...), "no tener ninguna oportunidad de..." (to have no chance of/to...), "una gran oportunidad de..." (a great chance of/to...).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes la oportunidad de hablar con ella hoy?
native_language_example: Do you have the chance to talk to her today?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what the opportunity is for. Most commonly followed by an infinitive (oportunidad para + verb): "una oportunidad para aprender". It can also be used with a noun or person: "una oportunidad para ti" (= for you). Note the common pattern "cada oportunidad para..." (= every opportunity to...).
target_language_example: Es una buena oportunidad para practicar español.
native_language_example: It’s a good opportunity to practice Spanish.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine subject (ella/yo as a woman). With a masculine subject, use "orgulloso de". Follow it with a noun ("orgullosa de su hija") or an infinitive/perfect infinitive ("orgullosa de ser...", "orgullosa de haber sido...").
target_language_example: Estoy orgullosa de mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm proud of my work.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine subject (ella, María). It’s the feminine form of "orgulloso". "De" introduces what she’s proud of, and "su" means "her" (or sometimes "his/your/their" depending on context). Common pattern: "estar/ser orgullosa de su + noun" (orgullosa de su talento, de su escuela, etc.).
target_language_example: Ella está orgullosa de su trabajo.
native_language_example: She is proud of her work.

additional_notes: Used with estar: "estar orgulloso/a de + person". "Orgullosa" is feminine; a man would say "orgulloso de ti". You can add emphasis with "muy": "Estoy muy orgullosa de ti."
target_language_example: Estoy orgullosa de ti por tu trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm proud of you for your work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *estar* or *sentirse* to express pride in someone/something, or in having done something: *estar/sentirse orgulloso de + noun/pronoun/infinitive/past infinitive (haber + participle)*. It changes for gender/number: *orgulloso, orgullosa, orgullosos, orgullosas*. Common pronouns after *de*: *de eso*, *de él/ella*, *de ello* (more formal/literary).
target_language_example: Estoy orgulloso de ti por tu esfuerzo.
native_language_example: I'm proud of you for your effort.

additional_notes: Used to express pride in someone’s actions or achievements. Note agreement: if the speaker is female, use "orgullosa de ti" instead. Common with verbs like estar ("Estoy orgulloso de ti") and sentirse ("Me siento orgulloso de ti").
target_language_example: Estoy tan orgulloso de ti.
native_language_example: I’m so proud of you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different topic, object, or situation than the one being discussed. Very common after verbs like decir (to say), hablar de (to talk about), and hacer (to do). In phrases like "No tengo otra cosa que + infinitive", it means "I have nothing else to + verb".
target_language_example: Prefiero hacer otra cosa esta tarde.
native_language_example: I’d rather do something else this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say there is an alternative way to do something, or to ask/suggest finding an alternative. Very common with "hay"/"debe haber"/"tiene que haber" (there must be another way) and with "otra forma de + infinitive" (another way to do something). Also appears in "de otra forma" meaning "in another way / differently".
target_language_example: Tiene que haber otra forma de llegar sin tomar la autopista.
native_language_example: There has to be another way to get there without taking the highway.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an alternative method or option. Very common in phrases like “Debe haber otra manera” (“There must be another way”) and “De una u otra manera” (“One way or another”). Related: “de otra manera” often means “otherwise.”
target_language_example: Tiene que haber otra manera de resolver este problema.
native_language_example: There has to be another way to solve this problem.

meaning: "another woman" (often: a different woman, sometimes implying a mistress/romantic rival).
additional_notes: Uses the adjective "otra" (feminine form of "otro") before the noun: "otra mujer" = "another woman" / "a different woman". In relationship contexts, it can strongly suggest “the other woman” (someone a partner is involved with).
target_language_example: Creo que está saliendo con otra mujer.
native_language_example: I think he’s dating another woman.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an alternative. Very common in the negative: “no (tener/dejar) otra opción” = “to have/leave no other choice,” and often followed by “que + infinitive” (e.g., “no tenemos otra opción que esperar” = “we have no choice but to wait”).
target_language_example: No me queda otra opción que irme ahora.
native_language_example: I have no choice but to leave now.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering a new chance to try again (often after a mistake). In "En otra oportunidad", it commonly means "another time" / "on another occasion" (a polite way to postpone something).
target_language_example: Lo siento; ¿me puedes dar otra oportunidad?
native_language_example: I’m sorry; can you give me another chance?

additional_notes: Often used with prepositions: **a otra parte** (“to another place/elsewhere”), **en otra parte** (“in another place/elsewhere”), **por otra parte** (“on the other hand”). It can mean a different section of something (**otra parte del rompecabezas**) or a different location (**en la otra parte de la ciudad**).
target_language_example: Si no está aquí, debe de estar en otra parte.
native_language_example: If it’s not here, it must be somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used when you mean a different person from the one mentioned or expected. Common with verbs like ser/estar ("Eres otra persona" = "You’re a different person") and pensar ("Pensé que eras otra persona" = "I thought you were someone else"). Often takes the feminine form "otra" because "persona" is grammatically feminine, even when referring to a man.
target_language_example: Lo siento, me equivoqué: pensé que eras otra persona.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was mistaken: I thought you were someone else.

additional_notes: Used to ask for one more cup of coffee (a refill or a second cup). "Otra" agrees with the feminine noun "taza" (so it’s not *otro*). Very common with polite requests like "por favor" and "me trae...".
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar otra taza de café, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me another cup of coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is done again. Very common with verbs like repetir (repeat), volver (return/do again), and empezar (start). In phrases like “No empieces otra vez”, it can mean “not again” (often expressing annoyance). It can also be used when reintroducing yourself (e.g., “Soy yo otra vez” = “It’s me again”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes explicármelo otra vez, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me again, please?

additional_notes: Used to add extra items beyond what was mentioned (like “and other things/stuff”). It can also mean “other matters” someone is thinking about or dealing with (e.g., Tener otras cosas en la cabeza = to have other things on your mind). Often appears as “y otras cosas” or “entre otras cosas.”
target_language_example: Hoy no puedo; tengo que hacer otras cosas.
native_language_example: I can’t today; I have other things to do.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re busy or have different priorities right now. It often implies “not this” or “I can’t because I have other things to do.” You can change it for the person/number: tengo/tienes/tiene/tenemos… otras cosas que hacer.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir; tengo otras cosas que hacer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go; I have other things to do.

meaning: “other people” (people who are not you/us/the ones already mentioned).
additional_notes: “Otras” is the feminine plural form of “otro” and agrees with “personas” (feminine plural). It’s commonly used to talk generally about people besides yourself or besides a particular group: “lo que otras personas piensen” = “what other people think.”
target_language_example: No escuches a otras personas; confía en ti.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to other people; trust yourself.

additional_notes: Usually means an additional day ("one more day") or a different day/time ("some other day"). In the phrase "el otro día," it means "the other day" = recently (not necessarily exactly one day ago). Common in: "otro día más" (one more day), "tal vez otro día" (maybe another day), "lo del otro día" (what happened the other day).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir otro día?
native_language_example: Can you come another day?

additional_notes: Often used with movement or direction: “mirar hacia/para otro lado” = to look the other way (sometimes implying ignoring something on purpose). With “ir a otro lado” it means going somewhere else. You’ll also hear “al otro lado” (on the other side) and “del otro lado” (from/on the other side).
target_language_example: Si no te gusta este asiento, nos sentamos en el otro lado.
native_language_example: If you don’t like this seat, we’ll sit on the other side.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to indicate the opposite side of something physical ("del espejo", "del valle") or the opposing/alternative perspective in a discussion ("del argumento"). "Del" is a contraction of "de + el"; with feminine nouns you use "de la" (e.g., "el otro lado de la calle").
target_language_example: Nos encontramos en el otro lado del río.
native_language_example: We’ll meet on the other side of the river.

additional_notes: Used to say a different location from the one you’re in or talking about. Often appears with verbs like estar/ir/buscar: “estar en otro lugar” (to be elsewhere), “ir a otro lugar” (to go somewhere else), “buscar otro lugar” (to look for another place). You may also hear “algún otro lugar” = “some other place,” and with “adonde/al que ir” to mean “somewhere else to go.”
target_language_example: Si no te gusta aquí, podemos ir a otro lugar.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it here, we can go somewhere else.

additional_notes:
Often used with a preposition: 
- **de otro modo** = “in another way / otherwise” (e.g., *No podía ser de otro modo* = “It couldn’t be otherwise”). 
- **no hay otro modo de + infinitive** = “there’s no other way to…” 
Used to suggest an alternative or to say something could not have happened differently.
target_language_example: Tenemos que encontrar otro modo de hacerlo.
native_language_example: We have to find another way to do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you should go to a different location. Often appears with verbs of going/moving (ir, entrar, irse, buscar) and can be followed by a relative phrase like “adonde/al que” (e.g., “No tengo otro sitio adonde ir” = “I have nowhere else to go”).
target_language_example: Si aquí no hay mesa, vamos a otro sitio.
native_language_example: If there’s no table here, let’s go somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used to refer to children different from the ones already being talked about (often with an implied comparison). Common patterns: "otros niños" = other children (in general), "los otros niños" = the other children (a specific group). You can also say "otros chicos" in some countries for "other kids/boys".
target_language_example: Mi hijo juega con otros niños en el parque.
native_language_example: My son plays with other children in the park.

meaning: other plans; something else in mind.
additional_notes: Often used to suggest that someone (a person, fate, God, circumstances) intends a different course of action than expected. Common patterns: "A menos que tengas otros planes" (unless you have other plans) and "Parece que X tiene otros planes" (it seems X has other plans), implying events will go differently than you hoped or planned.
target_language_example: Podemos vernos el sábado, a menos que tengas otros planes.
native_language_example: We can see each other on Saturday, unless you have other plans.

meaning: "Hey, don’t…" / "Listen, no…" (used to stop or correct someone).
additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention and immediately disagree, correct them, or tell them to stop doing something. Very common in spoken Spanish; often followed by a verb in the tú command form: “Oye, no hagas eso.”
target_language_example: Oye, no me interrumpas, por favor.
native_language_example: Hey, don’t interrupt me, please.

meaning: "Hey, why…?" (used to ask for a reason, often to get someone’s attention first).
additional_notes: "Oye" literally means "listen" (from *oír*, “to hear”), but in conversation it often works like "hey" or "listen" to grab attention. Use "oye, ¿por qué…?" to question why someone is doing/saying something; it can sound surprised, concerned, or slightly challenging depending on tone.
target_language_example: Oye, ¿por qué estás tan callado hoy?
native_language_example: Hey, why are you so quiet today?

meaning: “Hey, what…?” (used to get someone’s attention before a question).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish. Use it to call someone’s attention (“oye” = “listen/hey”) and then ask a question: oye, ¿qué haces? / oye, ¿qué pasa? It can sound a bit direct depending on tone; for a more polite option, you can use “disculpa” or “perdón” instead of “oye”.
target_language_example: Oye, ¿qué quieres comer hoy?
native_language_example: Hey, what do you want to eat today?

meaning: “I heard that …” (I found out / I was told that …).
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard from someone or somewhere. It’s the preterite (completed past) of **oír** (“to hear”), so it often implies you heard it at some point in the past. It’s followed by **que** + a full clause: **Oí que + [subject] + [verb]**.
target_language_example: Oí que mañana no hay clases.
native_language_example: I heard that there are no classes tomorrow.

meaning: "(to have) heard of" (to be aware of someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb haber in perfect tenses: he/ha/hemos/habían oído hablar de + noun/pronoun. It means knowing about someone/something (not necessarily hearing them speak). Often used in negatives: Nunca he oído hablar de eso ("I've never heard of that").
target_language_example: ¿Has oído hablar de esta película?
native_language_example: Have you heard of this movie?

meaning: heard of her (heard about her / know of her).
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "haber oído hablar de" to say you have (or haven’t) heard of someone/something—i.e., you’re aware of their existence. Very commonly used in the negative: "No/Nunca he oído hablar de ella" = "I’ve never heard of her." The pronoun changes with the person/thing: "de él" (him), "de ellos/ellas" (them), "de eso" (that), "de esto" (this), "de ti" (you).
target_language_example: ¿Has oído hablar de ella? Dicen que es muy famosa.
native_language_example: Have you heard of her? They say she’s very famous.

meaning: “(have) heard of him” (know about his existence).
additional_notes: Used with the verb haber to say you’ve heard about a person (or thing): "he/has oído hablar de...". Often implies only general awareness, not knowing them personally. The "de él" means “about him” (for a woman: "de ella"; for something: "de eso"). Common in questions and with "nunca".
target_language_example: ¿Has oído hablar de él antes?
native_language_example: Have you heard of him before?

meaning: '(have) heard that…' (introduces something you’ve heard/been told).
additional_notes: Used with haber + oído to report information you heard from someone else (a rumor, news, secondhand info). Common forms: «he oído que…» (I’ve heard that…), «hemos oído que…» (we’ve heard that…), «había oído que…» (I had heard that…). Often implies you’re not claiming it’s definitely true—just that you heard it.
target_language_example: He oído que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I’ve heard that it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: to hear about; to have heard of.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve heard information or talk about someone/something, even if you don’t know them/it well. Often followed by a noun, topic, or person: "He oído hablar de ese restaurante". With people, it’s very common as "¿Has oído hablar de…?" (= "Have you heard of…?"). In everyday speech you’ll also hear "he escuchado hablar de" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: ¿Has oído hablar de Frida Kahlo? Yo he oído hablar de ella, pero nunca he visto una exposición suya.
native_language_example: Have you heard of Frida Kahlo? I’ve heard of her, but I’ve never seen an exhibition of her work.

additional_notes: Used to express that you’re happy or relieved to hear someone speaking (often on the phone or after time apart). You can also say it with other possessives: oír su voz (hear his/her/your formal voice), oír mi voz (hear my voice). Note: oír is “to hear” (perceive sound), not “to listen” (escuchar).
target_language_example: ¡Qué alegría oír tu voz otra vez!
native_language_example: What a joy to hear your voice again!

additional_notes: Written abbreviation of «por ejemplo». Common in lists, notes, textbooks, emails, and formal writing. In speech, you usually say «por ejemplo» instead of «p. ej.».
target_language_example: Puedes traer una bebida, p. ej., agua o jugo.
native_language_example: You can bring a drink, e.g., water or juice.

additional_notes: Common Catholic/Christian prayer title. Often said as a set prayer (“Reza el Padre Nuestro”) or used to refer to the prayer itself (“el Padre Nuestro”). Capitalization varies, but it’s often written with capitals as a title.
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, mi abuela reza el Padre Nuestro.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, my grandmother says the Our Father.

additional_notes: Used for paying the monthly cost of renting a home/apartment (el alquiler). Often appears with tener que (“have to”) and time words like este mes (“this month”), mañana (“tomorrow”). You can also say pagar el alquiler + de + place: “pagar el alquiler del piso/de la casa.”
target_language_example: Tengo que pagar el alquiler antes del viernes.
native_language_example: I have to pay the rent before Friday.

additional_notes: Used for paying what you owe after a meal at a restaurant (the check) or for an invoice/service (a bill). Often used with tener que (“have to”) or insistir en (“insist on”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo pagar la cuenta con tarjeta?
native_language_example: Can I pay the bill/check with a card?

additional_notes: Used for paying rent for housing (an apartment/house). Often refers to the regular monthly rent payment: "Tengo que pagar la renta" (I have to pay the rent). In some regions people may say "pagar el alquiler" instead of "pagar la renta".
target_language_example: Tenemos que pagar la renta el lunes.
native_language_example: We have to pay the rent on Monday.

meaning: to pay in advance; to pay upfront.
additional_notes: Used when payment must be made before receiving a service or product (common with hotels, reservations, subscriptions, or deposits). Often appears with obligation phrases like "tener que" or "hay que": "Tienes que pagar por adelantado" / "Hay que pagar por adelantado".
target_language_example: Para reservar la mesa, tenemos que pagar por adelantado.
native_language_example: To reserve the table, we have to pay in advance.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is repeated or translated with the exact same words, without changing the phrasing. Common with verbs like repetir (to repeat), traducir (to translate), and citar (to quote).
target_language_example: Necesito la traducción palabra por palabra para entenderlo.
native_language_example: I need a word-for-word translation to understand it.

additional_notes: Common food word, especially for movie snacks. You can also hear just palomitas (popcorn), and in some countries crispetas, pochoclo, or rosetas. Often used with verbs like querer (to want), gustar (to like), hacer (to make), and comprar (to buy).
target_language_example: Voy a comprar palomitas de maíz para la película.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy popcorn for the movie.

additional_notes: Refers to a device that captures sunlight to produce electricity (or sometimes heat). Often used when talking about home energy, roofs, and renewable power. Plural: "paneles solares".
target_language_example: Vamos a instalar un panel solar en el techo.
native_language_example: We’re going to install a solar panel on the roof.

additional_notes: Refers to the flat devices that capture sunlight to produce electricity. Common with verbs like "instalar" (to install), "poner/colocar" (to put/place), and locations like "en el techo/tejado" (on the roof) or "en el patio" (in the yard). Often discussed together with "baterías" (batteries) for storing energy.
target_language_example: Vamos a instalar paneles solares para ahorrar electricidad.
native_language_example: We’re going to install solar panels to save on electricity.

meaning: French fry; fried potato (often used in the plural: papas fritas).
additional_notes: Although the singular "papa frita" can refer to a single French fry, it’s much more common to hear the plural "papas fritas" for a serving/order. In much of Latin America, "papa" = potato; in Spain, you’ll often hear "patatas fritas" instead. You may see it as a side dish: "con papa frita" / more commonly "con papas fritas" (with fries).
target_language_example: Quiero una hamburguesa con papa frita, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a hamburger with a French fry, please.

additional_notes: Common food phrase. In much of Latin America, papas fritas usually means French fries (like at a restaurant). Depending on the country/context, it can also mean potato chips (crisps). You’ll also see papas a la francesa for “French fries.”
target_language_example: Quiero una hamburguesa con papas fritas, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a hamburger with French fries, please.

additional_notes: Used for the paper you use in the bathroom. Often said with a quantity word like "un rollo de papel higiénico" (a roll of toilet paper). You can also use it figuratively to mean someone is being treated as disposable or disrespected (like "used like toilet paper").
target_language_example: ¿Puedes comprar papel higiénico cuando vayas al supermercado?
native_language_example: Can you buy toilet paper when you go to the supermarket?

meaning: "Dad, can I…?" (asking your dad for permission).
additional_notes: Used to get your father’s attention and ask permission to do something. Commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., entrar, salir, hablar) or by a verb phrase. For a more formal/less childlike option, you can say: "Papá, ¿puedo...?" is fine in families; "Padre, ¿puedo...?" is much less common and can sound very formal or religious.
target_language_example: Papá, ¿puedo quedarme despierto un poco más?
native_language_example: Dad, can I stay up a little longer?

meaning: “Dad, what…?” (starting a question to your father).
additional_notes: Used to get your dad’s attention and then ask a question. In writing, a comma often separates the person you’re addressing (Papá) from the question. You can follow it with many common question phrases: ¿qué es…? (what is…?), ¿qué pasa? (what’s wrong/what’s happening?), ¿qué significa…? (what does … mean?), ¿qué hay de…? (what about…?).
target_language_example: Papá, ¿qué vamos a hacer hoy?
native_language_example: Dad, what are we going to do today?

meaning: a pair of; a couple of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean (1) "a pair of" two matching items (un par de calcetines, un par de esposas, un par de gemelos), or (2) "a couple of" a small number/amount, often with time or distance (un par de noches, un par de kilómetros). Also used for small counts like "a couple of mistakes" (un par de errores).
target_language_example: Necesito un par de minutos para terminar.
native_language_example: I need a couple of minutes to finish.

additional_notes: Used when talking about buying/owning boots; "un par de" means "a pair of" + the item (often things that come in twos). You can add details after "botas" (e.g., "nuevas", "de esquiar").
target_language_example: Necesito un par de botas para el invierno.
native_language_example: I need a pair of boots for the winter.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a short amount of time, usually around two days. Common with “un” (un par de días) and with “más” to mean “a couple more days.” Also used with “hace” to mean “a couple of days ago” (hace un par de días).
target_language_example: ¿Me das un par de días para pensarlo?
native_language_example: Can you give me a couple of days to think about it?

additional_notes: Used when talking about gloves as a set of two. You’ll often see the pattern “un par de + [plural noun]” to mean “a pair of …” (e.g., un par de zapatos = a pair of shoes).
target_language_example: Necesito un par de guantes para el invierno.
native_language_example: I need a pair of gloves for the winter.

meaning: a couple of hours (about two hours).
additional_notes: Very common way to say an approximate short amount of time. Often used with “un”: “un par de horas” = “a couple of hours.” You can also add “más” for “a couple more hours” (Dame un par de horas más). In time expressions like “Hace un par de horas,” it means “a couple of hours ago.”
target_language_example: Vuelvo en un par de horas.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a couple of hours.

meaning: a couple of months (about two months).
additional_notes: Used to mean an approximate short period of time, usually around two months. Very common with time expressions like “hace un par de meses” (a couple of months ago) or with “solo/sólo” to emphasize it wasn’t long: “solo un par de meses.”
target_language_example: Nos mudamos aquí hace un par de meses.
native_language_example: We moved here a couple of months ago.

meaning: 'a couple of minutes' (a short amount of time).
additional_notes: Usually used with "un": "un par de minutos" = "a couple of minutes." It often means approximately two minutes, or just “a few minutes” in casual speech. Common with requests ("Dame...") or to say something will happen soon ("en un par de...").
target_language_example: Espera un par de minutos, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait a couple of minutes, please.

meaning: a couple of questions; a few questions.
additional_notes: Used to say you have a small number of questions (often 2, but it can also mean “just a few”). Very common with “solo/sólo” and “más”: “Solo tengo un par de preguntas” / “Un par de preguntas más.” You can make it polite with “para usted” or “para ti”.
target_language_example: Antes de empezar, tengo un par de preguntas para ti.
native_language_example: Before we start, I have a couple of questions for you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one set of two matching shoes. With numbers it often appears as “un par de zapatos” (a pair of shoes) or “dos pares de zapatos” (two pairs of shoes). “Par” can be used for other things that come in twos (e.g., “un par de calcetines” = a pair of socks).
target_language_example: Necesito comprarme un par de zapatos para la boda.
native_language_example: I need to buy a pair of shoes for the wedding.

additional_notes: Used for direction with verbs like mirar (to look) or caer (to fall): mirar para abajo = look down, caer para abajo = fall down. It can also describe a decline in situation, health, mood, or success: va/vas para abajo = things are going downhill. In phrases like “de cintura para abajo,” it means “from the waist down.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: hoy estás cansado, pero mañana vas a estar mejor y no vas para abajo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re tired today, but tomorrow you’ll be better and you’re not going downhill.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like venir, traer) to indicate movement in the direction of the speaker or the place where the speaker is. Often interchangeable with "hacia acá". You can also hear "para aquí" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ven para acá, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement toward the front ("Mueve tu silla para adelante") or looking/progressing into the future ("mirar para adelante"). As an encouragement/command, it means "go ahead / keep going" ("Dale para adelante", "Para adelante"). Often interchangeable with "hacia adelante" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Aunque estés cansado, sigue para adelante.
native_language_example: Even if you’re tired, keep going.

meaning: 'to catch/reach the' (so you don’t miss it).
additional_notes: Uses para + infinitive to express purpose (“in order to…”). With transportation (el tren, el autobús/el bus), alcanzar often means “to catch” (get there in time). The article el changes with the noun (para alcanzar la estación, para alcanzar los trenes).
target_language_example: Salí temprano para alcanzar el autobús.
native_language_example: I left early to catch the bus.

additional_notes: Used to point to or refer to a place away from the speaker (often farther than "ahí"). Very common with verbs of movement like ir, venir, caminar, mandar, and with commands: "Mira para allá" (Look over there), "Vete para allá" (Go over there). It can describe direction/destination rather than a precise location.
target_language_example: Si quieres hablar, vamos para allá.
native_language_example: If you want to talk, let's go over there.

additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive** to express purpose (why you do something): *Leo para aprender* = “I read to learn.” It can also follow a noun/idea: *Me enviaron aquí para aprender sus costumbres.* In sentence 1, many speakers prefer **difícil de aprender** (“hard to learn”) rather than *difícil para aprender*. Also note **aprender** means “to learn,” not “to apprehend.”
target_language_example: Escucho podcasts para aprender más vocabulario.
native_language_example: I listen to podcasts to learn more vocabulary.

additional_notes: Used to express purpose: para + infinitive. It’s usually followed by the person/thing receiving the help (often introduced by "a"): "para ayudar a mi hermano". If the object is not a person, Spanish may still use "a" in some cases: "para ayudar a crecer a las plantas".
target_language_example: Estoy aquí para ayudar a mis amigos con la mudanza.
native_language_example: I’m here to help my friends with the move.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for drinking. Often follows a noun like "algo" or "agua": "algo para beber" (something to drink), "agua para beber" (drinking water). You can also use it in questions: "¿Quieres algo para beber?"
target_language_example: ¿Tienes algo para beber?
native_language_example: Do you have something to drink?

meaning: for better or for worse; whether the outcome is good or bad.
additional_notes: Used to express acceptance that something is true or will happen no matter what, with good or bad consequences. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as a comment on what follows ("Para bien o para mal, ..."), or after the main idea.
target_language_example: Para bien o para mal, ya tomé mi decisión.
native_language_example: For better or for worse, I’ve already made my decision.

additional_notes: Used to explain the purpose of doing something (often waking up early): para + infinitive (“in order to …”). In Spain, coger el tren is the common way to say “catch/take the train.” In much of Latin America, people often prefer tomar/agarrar el tren because coger can be vulgar in some places.
target_language_example: Salimos de casa a las seis para coger el primer tren.
native_language_example: We left the house at six to catch the first train.

additional_notes: Uses para + infinitive to express purpose or function: something is intended/available “to eat” (tienen algo para comer), a place is good “to eat” (lugar para comer), or a break is “for eating” (pausa para comer). It can also contrast ideas like vivir para comer vs. comer para vivir.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes algo para comer?
native_language_example: Do you have something to eat?

additional_notes: Used after an amount, resource, or condition to say it’s enough/necessary for the purpose of buying something (e.g., "suficiente para comprar"). It can also describe something intended for purchase (e.g., "nada para comprar" = nothing to buy).
target_language_example: No tengo dinero para comprar comida hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have money to buy food today.

meaning: 'toward' / 'towards' (in relation to a person or group), especially about duties, behavior, or attitudes.
additional_notes: Used before a person, group, or institution to express your duty, responsibility, attitude, or behavior toward them. Common in more formal contexts (e.g., deber para con..., obligaciones para con...). Often interchangeable with "hacia" or "con" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Debes ser más amable para con tus compañeros.
native_language_example: You should be kinder toward your classmates.

additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive** to express purpose: you do one action **so that** you can get/obtain/achieve something. **Conseguir** often means “to get” (obtain), “to manage” (succeed in doing), or “to achieve,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Voy a llamar para conseguir más información.
native_language_example: I'm going to call to get more information.

additional_notes: Used when "para" (for/to/in order to) is followed by the masculine singular article "el" (the). It often expresses purpose or destination: "espacio para el televisor" (space for the TV), "para el frente" (toward the front), "para el evento" (for the event).
target_language_example: Compré flores para el cumpleaños de mi mamá.
native_language_example: I bought flowers for my mom’s birthday.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for lunch (food, money, plans) or that something will happen by lunchtime. Often used with "volver" (to go back) and "terminar" (to finish): "volver a casa para el almuerzo", "terminar para el almuerzo".
target_language_example: Tengo una ensalada para el almuerzo.
native_language_example: I have a salad for lunch.

meaning: for the exam (in preparation for it).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like estudiar, prepararse, repasar, and practicar to show the purpose/goal: studying or doing something in order to be ready for an exam. Often translated as “for the exam,” “for my exam,” or “for the test,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Estoy repasando mis apuntes para el examen de mañana.
native_language_example: I’m reviewing my notes for tomorrow’s exam.

meaning: "by/for the weekend" (no later than the weekend; planned for the weekend).
additional_notes: Used with "para" to set a deadline or a plan tied to the weekend. Often means something should be finished by the time the weekend arrives (deadline): "Terminarlo para el fin de semana". In other contexts it can mean something is intended for the weekend (plans/preparation): "Preparar comida para el fin de semana".
target_language_example: Necesito comprar comida para el fin de semana.
native_language_example: I need to buy food for the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say you will do something at the end or save something until the end (often implying “save the best for last”). It can refer to the end of an activity/event (e.g., la fiesta) or the last item in an order/sequence.
target_language_example: Dejemos los postres para el final.
native_language_example: Let’s leave dessert for last.

meaning: by Monday (deadline: no later than Monday).
additional_notes: Used to set a deadline. It means the task or situation should be completed/ready no later than Monday. Common with verbs like estar hecho/hacerse, terminar, estar bien, volver. Contrast: "el lunes" = on Monday (the day it happens); "para el lunes" = by Monday (deadline).
target_language_example: Necesito el informe para el lunes a primera hora.
native_language_example: I need the report by Monday first thing.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is suitable or intended for a specific job/role (often in hiring or workplace contexts). You’ll often see it after adjectives like adecuado/a (“suitable”), perfecto/a (“perfect”), ideal (“ideal”), or phrases like ser bueno/a para (“to be good for”).
target_language_example: Creo que ella es perfecta para el puesto.
native_language_example: I think she’s perfect for the position.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is suitable, qualified, or the right choice for a particular job/task (often with ser/estar + adecuado/a, indicado/a, cualificado/a). It can also simply mean “for work” in other contexts (e.g., ropa para el trabajo = work clothes).
target_language_example: Creo que ella es la persona ideal para el trabajo.
native_language_example: I think she’s the ideal person for the job.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans, preparations, money saved, or things you need in order to take a trip. It commonly follows verbs like preparar (to prepare), ahorrar (to save), buscar (to look for), and decidir (to decide). Often expanded with a destination/type of trip: para el viaje al espacio (for the trip to space) / para el viaje de Lois (for Lois’s trip).
target_language_example: Necesito comprar unas cosas para el viaje.
native_language_example: I need to buy a few things for the trip.

meaning: “to make matters worse” / “to make things worse.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an additional problem or bad event that happens after something already negative. Very common at the start of a sentence, often followed by a comma: “Para empeorar las cosas, …”.
target_language_example: Perdí el autobús y, para empeorar las cosas, olvidé mi cartera en casa.
native_language_example: I missed the bus and, to make matters worse, I forgot my wallet at home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the first step, first point, or a minimum/initial amount. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence: "Para empezar, ..." (= "To start with, ..."). It can also mean "enough to get started" ("Con eso tendrás para empezar" = "With that you’ll have enough to start").
target_language_example: Para empezar, vamos a revisar el plan y luego hablamos del presupuesto.
native_language_example: To start with, we’re going to review the plan and then we’ll talk about the budget.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific moment in the past or future relative to another event. Often appears with "ya" and with future or perfect tenses to show something will have happened before that point (e.g., "habrá + participio").
target_language_example: Para entonces, ya habremos terminado el trabajo.
native_language_example: By then, we’ll have finished the work.

meaning: "for that" / "for it" (to do that; for that purpose).
additional_notes: Used to talk about purpose or suitability for a specific thing: lack of ability/time/patience (“no tengo talento/paciencia/tiempo para eso” = “I don’t have the talent/patience/time for that”). It’s also common in offers of help: “Para eso estamos/estoy” = “That’s what we’re here for / That’s what I’m here for.”
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo para eso ahora.
native_language_example: I don't have time for that right now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the purpose of an action: you do something so that an unwanted result doesn’t happen. Often followed by a noun (para evitar el desastre) or by “que” + subjunctive (para evitar que se cayera = to keep her from falling).
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta para evitar el ruido.
native_language_example: Close the door to avoid the noise.

meaning: "to prevent" / "in order to stop" (something) from happening.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: you do an action *so that* another action or situation does not happen. It’s followed by a verb, often in the subjunctive: "para evitar que + (someone) + verb" (e.g., "para evitar que entren"). Often translates as "to prevent (someone) from..." or "so that ... doesn’t...".
target_language_example: Cerré la ventana para evitar que entrara el humo.
native_language_example: I closed the window to prevent the smoke from coming in.

meaning: to make/earn money; in order to make money.
additional_notes: Uses para + infinitive (ganar) to express purpose: the reason someone does something. Ganar dinero means “to earn money” (also “to make money”). You’ll often see it after a verb (Trabajamos para ganar dinero) or at the start of a sentence (Para ganar dinero, debes...).
target_language_example: Se mudó a la ciudad para ganar dinero.
native_language_example: He/She moved to the city to make money.

meaning: to speak; in order to talk.
additional_notes: Uses para + infinitive to express purpose (“in order to”). Often followed by more detail: para hablar en privado (to talk in private), para hablar sobre algo (to talk about something). Can also be a short answer meaning “to talk / to speak.”
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un minuto para hablar?
native_language_example: Do you have a minute to talk?

additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to…”). **Hablar con + person** means “to talk with/to,” and is commonly used for speaking directly to someone: *para hablar con nosotros / para hablar con mi mujer*.
target_language_example: Llamo para hablar con el médico.
native_language_example: I’m calling to talk to the doctor.

additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive** to express purpose: **for/to** do something. Common in phrases like **cosas para hacer** (“things to do”). The verb **hacer** can mean “to do” (tasks, work) or “to make” (something you create), depending on context.
target_language_example: Tengo mucho para hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today.

meaning: to do that; in order to do that.
additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to...”) or what something took time/effort/reason/courage to do. Often appears after expressions like *tomar (tiempo)*, *esperar*, *ser demasiado + adjective*, *ser lo suficientemente + adjective*, *tener razón*.
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo para hacer eso hoy.
native_language_example: I don't have time to do that today.

meaning: 'to make/do a…' or 'in order to make/do a…' (expresses purpose).
additional_notes: Used to say what something is intended for or why someone does something. It’s followed by an infinitive (hacer) + a masculine singular noun (un + noun): para hacer un picnic / un reportaje / un hogar. With a feminine noun, you’d say: para hacer una + noun (e.g., para hacer una reserva). In many contexts it translates naturally as “to” or “in order to” rather than literally “for.”
target_language_example: Necesito tiempo para hacer un plan.
native_language_example: I need time to make a plan.

additional_notes: Used with "para" + infinitive to express purpose: "para ir" = "in order to go" (often followed by a destination/activity: "para ir a trabajar", "para ir al cine"). In questions, "lugares ... para ir" means "places to go". Common with obligations/plans: "tengo que... para ir...", "haré lo posible para ir".
target_language_example: Necesito un taxi para ir al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: I need a taxi to go to the airport.

meaning: 'to go to' / 'in order to go to'.
additional_notes: Uses "para" to express purpose or what something is meant for, followed by "ir a" (to go to) + an infinitive or place. Common patterns: "(Alguien) me llama para ir a + infinitivo" (someone calls me to go and do something), and "es/era para ir a + lugar" (it’s only good for ending up going to that place).
target_language_example: Te llamo para ir a comprar pan.
native_language_example: I’m calling you to go buy bread.

meaning: to go to school (in order to go to school).
additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive (ir)** to express purpose (“in order to”). Often appears after another verb to explain why someone does something (e.g., *cogió el autobús para ir...*, *dejó su trabajo para ir...*) or after an adjective to show what someone is able/ready to do (e.g., *suficientemente mayor para ir...*, *demasiado enfermo para ir...*).
target_language_example: Me levanto temprano para ir a la escuela.
native_language_example: I get up early to go to school.

meaning: for the (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to show purpose, destination, recipient, or what something is intended for: *para la CBS* (for CBS), *para la realeza* (for royalty), *para la diarrea* (for diarrhea), *para la buena suerte* (for good luck). It’s simply **para** + **la** (feminine “the”); unlike **para el → para el** (often shortened to **pa’l** in speech), **para la** doesn’t contract.
target_language_example: Este regalo es para la profesora.
native_language_example: This gift is for the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for the dinner meal (what you ate, what you’re making, or whether someone will stay/eat at dinnertime). Often used with verbs like comer (to eat), hacer/preparar (to make/prepare), and quedarse (to stay).
target_language_example: Voy a preparar pasta para la cena.
native_language_example: I’m going to make pasta for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for a party (purpose/occasion). With verbs like comprar (to buy), ponerse (to put on/wear), and preparación (preparation): “compró… para la fiesta” = “she bought… for the party.”
target_language_example: Traje unos bocadillos para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I brought some snacks for the party.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you’ll do in the next opportunity/occasion (next class, next meeting, next edition, etc.). Often said alone as a reminder or suggestion: “Para la próxima.” = “(Do it) next time.”
target_language_example: Se me olvidó hoy; lo traigo para la próxima.
native_language_example: I forgot today; I’ll bring it next time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is good, bad, harmful, or important for health. Very common with phrases like “bueno/malo para la salud” (good/bad for your health) and “(ser) perjudicial para la salud” (to be harmful to your health). Often the meaning is general (“for health” / “for your health”) rather than a specific person’s health unless the context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Dormir bien es importante para la salud.
native_language_example: Sleeping well is important for your health.

meaning: 'for cough' / 'for a cough' (cough medicine or remedy).
additional_notes: Used with medicines, remedies, and treatments to say they are intended to relieve a cough (tos = cough). Often appears after nouns like medicina, jarabe, or remedio: "medicina para la tos". In English you might also say "cough medicine"; Spanish commonly uses "para" (for) in this context.
target_language_example: ¿Tiene algo para la tos seca?
native_language_example: Do you have anything for a dry cough?

meaning: to get to; in order to reach/arrive at.
additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive** to express purpose: *para llegar a X* = “(in order) to get to X.” **Llegar a** is used with places (*llegar a la estación*) and can also be figurative, meaning “to reach/get to (someone)” (*para llegar a mí* = “to get to me”).
target_language_example: ¿Qué metro tengo que tomar para llegar al centro?
native_language_example: Which subway do I have to take to get downtown?

meaning: in order to arrive on time.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: you do something (often quickly or with effort) so that you will be on time. Commonly followed by a destination or event: "para llegar a tiempo al tren / a la reunión". "Llegar a tiempo" means "to arrive on time" (not late).
target_language_example: Salimos temprano para llegar a tiempo a la cita.
native_language_example: We left early to arrive on time for the appointment.

meaning: "to go" (takeout); also "to take/carry" (for taking something somewhere).
additional_notes: In cafés/restaurants, you can answer "Para llevar" to mean you want the order to take away (not to eat there). Outside of food contexts, it often keeps its literal meaning: "para" + infinitive = "in order to..." / "for...", so "para llevar" can mean "to take/carry" (e.g., para llevarlo a casa = to take it home). Don’t confuse it with "llevar a cabo" (= to carry out), where "llevar" is part of a different expression.
target_language_example: ¿Es para llevar o para comer aquí?
native_language_example: Is it to go or to eat here?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "prepararse" or "estar preparado" to mean expecting or getting ready for the worst possible outcome. Often appears as "prepararse para lo peor".
target_language_example: Trae una linterna por si acaso; es mejor estar preparado para lo peor.
native_language_example: Bring a flashlight just in case; it’s better to be prepared for the worst.

additional_notes: Used to show purpose, recipient, or intended group before a masculine plural noun: para los principiantes (for beginners), para los productos (for the products), para los estudios (for studies). If the noun is feminine plural, use para las; masculine singular para el; feminine singular para la. "Para" can also mean "in order to" before an infinitive (para estudiar), but "para los" is specifically "para" + "los".
target_language_example: Este curso es para los estudiantes que quieren practicar más.
native_language_example: This course is for the students who want to practice more.

additional_notes: Uses para (“for”) + los niños (“the children/kids”) to say something is intended for them, given to them, or suitable for them. Often follows a noun (regalos para los niños) or a description (ideal para los niños).
target_language_example: Este juego es para los niños.
native_language_example: This game is for kids.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (when you’re bored or waiting).
additional_notes: Used after an activity to say you’re doing it mainly to fill time, not because it’s important or deeply enjoyable. Common pattern: hacer algo para matar el tiempo (e.g., leer, jugar, mirar videos).
