additional_notes: Used to say someone no longer believes they will achieve a goal (often a profession). It’s in the past tense (perdió). You’ll often see it as: “perdió las esperanzas de volverse + [noun/adjective]” (e.g., médico, actor).
target_language_example: Después de muchos rechazos, perdió las esperanzas de volverse cantante.
native_language_example: After many rejections, she lost hope of becoming a singer.

additional_notes: Used with a singular possessed noun: perdió su pasaporte (he/she lost their passport). “Su” can mean his, her, your (formal), or their—context tells you which. With abstract nouns it can mean “lost” in a figurative sense (perdió su interés = lost interest; perdió su memoria = lost their memory). In the expression “perdió su corazón por …”, it means “fell in love with …”.
target_language_example: Perdí mi teléfono y mi hermana perdió su cartera.
native_language_example: I lost my phone, and my sister lost her wallet.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of perder: “perdió” = “lost.” “Su” means “his/her/your(formal)/their,” so who it refers to depends on context. Often used for being laid off or fired (the cause may be unclear unless the sentence adds it).
target_language_example: María perdió su trabajo la semana pasada.
native_language_example: María lost her job last week.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of perder + masculine singular noun (el tren, el final, el interés, el conocimiento, el sentido...). Use it for (1) losing something or a quality ("Perdí el interés", "Perdí el conocimiento") and (2) missing a scheduled thing or part of something ("Perdí el tren", "Perdí el final"). For missing an event, English often prefers "missed" even though Spanish uses "perder".
target_language_example: Perdí el autobús y llegué tarde.
native_language_example: I missed the bus and arrived late.

additional_notes: Used when you didn’t realize how much time had passed (often because you were distracted, relaxed, or very focused). It’s in the past tense (perdí = “I lost”); you can change the person/tense: “perdimos la noción del tiempo” (we lost track of time), “he perdido la noción del tiempo” (I’ve lost track of time).
target_language_example: Estaba leyendo y perdí la noción del tiempo.
native_language_example: I was reading and I lost track of time.

additional_notes: Used to say you lost something that belongs to you. “Perdí” is the past tense (preterite) of “perder” (to lose). Add a noun after “mi”: “Perdí mi llave” (I lost my key). Often used with location phrases like “cerca de aquí” (near here), “por aquí” (around here), or “de camino a…” (on the way to…).
target_language_example: Perdí mi teléfono en el autobús.
native_language_example: I lost my phone on the bus.

meaning: “Sorry for …” / “Excuse me for …” (apologizing for something you did).
additional_notes: Used to apologize for an action or situation you caused. It’s commonly followed by a noun (perdón por la molestia = sorry for the inconvenience) or an infinitive verb (perdón por llegar tarde = sorry for arriving late). You can also say “Perdona por …” or “Perdón por …”.
target_language_example: Perdón por interrumpir, ¿puedo hacerte una pregunta?
native_language_example: Sorry for interrupting—can I ask you a question?

meaning: a low profile; to stay unnoticed.
additional_notes: Often used with the verb "mantener" (mantener un perfil bajo) to mean keeping a low profile: acting quietly, not drawing attention, and avoiding standing out—often for safety or to avoid problems. Also common as an instruction: "Mantené/Mantén un perfil bajo" (Argentine/Spain forms).
target_language_example: Cuando lleguemos, mejor mantén un perfil bajo y no hables con nadie.
native_language_example: When we get there, it’s better to keep a low profile and don’t talk to anyone.

meaning: to remain silent; to stay quiet.
additional_notes: Common in legal/police contexts (Miranda rights): "Tiene derecho a permanecer en silencio" = "You have the right to remain silent." Formed by the verb "permanecer" (to remain/stay) + "en silencio" (in silence). Neutral/formal register.
target_language_example: Usted tiene derecho a permanecer en silencio.
native_language_example: You have the right to remain silent.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the official document that allows you to drive. Common in formal situations (police checks, car rental, paperwork): “Su permiso de conducir, por favor.” In Spain this is the standard term; in many Latin American countries you’ll also hear “licencia de conducir” or “licencia de manejo.” The phrase “sacarse el permiso de conducir” means “to get/earn your driver’s license” (by passing the required tests).
target_language_example: Si vas a alquilar un coche, necesitas el permiso de conducir.
native_language_example: If you’re going to rent a car, you need a driver’s license.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about permission to do an action. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive (permiso para entrar / hablar / usar) or by a clause with "para que" + subjunctive when a different person will do the action (pedir permiso para que se quede). In formal contexts you may hear it alone as a request: "Permiso para...".
target_language_example: ¿Me das permiso para salir un momento?
native_language_example: Do you give me permission to step out for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to question or challenge something that was just said, often with a tone of disbelief: "But how did you…?" / "But how can we…?". A common related pattern is "¿cómo que + statement?" meaning “What do you mean (that)…?” / “Wait, you’re doing what?” (more colloquial).
target_language_example: Pero, ¿cómo que te vas tan pronto?
native_language_example: But what do you mean you're leaving so soon?

meaning: “But why?” (used to question or challenge a reason).
additional_notes: Used when you’re surprised, confused, or disagree and want an explanation. It often sounds more insistent than just “¿por qué?” because of “pero” (“but”). You can use it with any verb tense: “Pero, ¿por qué lo haces?” (present), “Pero, ¿por qué lo hizo?” (past).
target_language_example: Pero, ¿por qué no me lo dijiste antes?
native_language_example: But why didn’t you tell me earlier?

meaning: “But… who?” (used to ask who someone is, often with surprise or confusion).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or clarify someone’s identity: "¿Quién es (usted)?" = “Who are you/Who is he/she?” Adding "pero" (“but”) makes it sound like “Wait, but who…?” and can express surprise, doubt, or a request for explanation. Often used with "Disculpe, pero…" (“Excuse me, but…”). Punctuation and commas vary in writing; the meaning is the same.
target_language_example: Perdón, pero, ¿quién es él exactamente?
native_language_example: Sorry, but who exactly is he?

meaning: “But what…?” / “What (on earth)…?” (expresses surprise, protest, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Used to react to something unexpected or to object to what someone said/did. Often has an exasperated or shocked tone, similar to “But what are you doing?!” It’s usually followed by a verb phrase: “Pero, ¿qué haces?” / “Pero, ¿qué he hecho?”
target_language_example: Pero, ¿qué dices? ¡Eso no es verdad!
native_language_example: What are you talking about? That’s not true!

additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting point that happens occasionally. Often followed by a verb or clause: "..., pero a veces + [verb/clause]". You can also start a sentence with it to contrast with what was just said: "Pero a veces..."
target_language_example: Quiero salir hoy, pero a veces prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: I want to go out today, but sometimes I prefer to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to contrast a past situation or expectation with what is true at the present moment. Often comes after talking about how things were before: "Antes..., pero ahora..." It can also introduce a change in the conversation: "Pero ahora debemos...".
target_language_example: Antes no tenía tiempo, pero ahora puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: Before I didn’t have time, but now I can help you.

additional_notes: Used after mentioning a reason, obstacle, or negative fact, to show that what follows happens anyway. Often introduces a decision or action that goes against what you’d expect from the first part. You may also see it written as “pero aún así” (very common), though “pero aun así” is generally preferred when it means “even so.”
target_language_example: Estaba lloviendo mucho, pero aun así salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: It was raining a lot, but we still went for a walk.

meaning: "Well, anyway..." / "Come on!" (shows surprise, mild annoyance, or resignation).
additional_notes: A very common conversational filler. You can use it to react to something unexpected ("Come on!"), to lightly complain or question someone (often before a rhetorical question), or to move on/close a topic ("Well, anyway..."). Intonation and context change the exact feeling. Sometimes it’s said alone: “Pero bueno.”
target_language_example: Pero bueno, ¿en serio vas a salir con este frío?
native_language_example: Come on, are you really going out in this cold?

additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting opinion or a correction: you acknowledge something, then give what you believe. "Creo que" can also be translated as “I believe (that)” or “I think (that)”. Often you can drop "que" in English: “But I think you’re right.”
target_language_example: Pero creo que hoy no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: But I think I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to contrast appearances, assumptions, or what someone says with what is truly the case. Often follows something like parece/aparenta/creía/pensaba (“it seems/appears/I thought”).
target_language_example: Creí que era fácil, pero en realidad era bastante difícil.
native_language_example: I thought it was easy, but actually it was pretty hard.

additional_notes: Used to add a contrast after a previous statement. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: “pero es interesante” (but it’s interesting), “pero es un hombre honesto” (but he’s an honest man). The verb “es” (is) must match the subject (it/he/she).
target_language_example: No es barato, pero es de buena calidad.
native_language_example: It’s not cheap, but it’s good quality.

additional_notes: Used to contradict, limit, or correct what was just said. It’s often followed by a verb (e.g., "pero eso no explica...", "pero eso no cambia...") or by "era/es" + something ("pero eso no era...", "pero eso no es..."). In speech you may also hear "pero eso no" as a complete interruption meaning “but no/that’s not it.”
target_language_example: Entiendo tu punto, pero eso no resuelve el problema.
native_language_example: I understand your point, but that doesn't solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what happens now with what happened before or what usually happens. Often implies a change in result, plan, or intention ("this time it will be different"). Can appear at the start of a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Siempre llego tarde, pero esta vez llegué a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m always late, but this time I arrived on time.

meaning: "but this is..." (used to emphasize a reaction or contrast).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an evaluation or comment about something you’re seeing/experiencing, often with surprise or emphasis: "Pero esto es bueno" = "But this is good" / "This is really good." You’ll usually continue with an adjective or description (bueno, increíble, de primera, etc.).
target_language_example: Pero esto es increíble, no me lo esperaba.
native_language_example: But this is incredible—I wasn’t expecting it.

additional_notes: Used after describing an attempt to emphasize that nothing worked or no result was achieved. Often follows verbs like intentar (to try), esforzarse (to make an effort), or llamar (to knock/call). You can change the tense/person depending on context: “pero es en vano” (but it’s in vain), “pero será en vano” (but it will be in vain).
target_language_example: Busqué mis llaves por toda la casa, pero fue en vano.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys all over the house, but it was in vain.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast and point out that something exists or is available. Often followed by a noun ("pero hay muchas cosas…" = "but there are many things…"). Very common with the structure "pero hay que + infinitive" to mean "but you/we/they have to…" or "but it’s necessary to…" (e.g., "pero hay que hacerlo").
target_language_example: Quiero ir, pero hay un problema.
native_language_example: I want to go, but there’s a problem.

meaning: “but there’s something that…” (introduces an important point or exception).
additional_notes: Used to add a caveat or important detail after what was just said. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb: “pero hay algo que + (debes/deberías/puedes/es) …”. In speech, you’ll also hear “pero hay algo:” (“but there’s something: …”) without “que.”
target_language_example: Pero hay algo que necesito decirte antes de irme.
native_language_example: But there’s something I need to tell you before I leave.

meaning: “but the line was busy” (the phone line was in use).
additional_notes: Used after saying you called/tried to call someone to explain you couldn’t get through because they were already on another call. Also heard as: “pero estaba ocupado” or “pero daba ocupado” (dial tone), depending on region.
target_language_example: Intenté llamarte, pero la línea estaba ocupada.
native_language_example: I tried to call you, but the line was busy.

meaning: “but I’m afraid that…” (polite way to introduce bad news or a refusal).
additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re about to say, often when disagreeing, saying something is impossible, or refusing a request. Very common in polite conversation. Grammar note: "me temo" is from "temer" (to fear), but it usually means "I’m afraid" in this set phrase rather than literal fear.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero me temo que no puedo ayudarte hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I’m afraid I can’t help you today.

meaning: "but not" / "but (it) doesn't/didn't" (introduces a contrast with a negative idea).
additional_notes: Used to contrast what comes next with what was just said, where the second part is negative. Very common with verbs: "..., pero no puedo" (but I can’t), "..., pero no lo hará" (but he/she won’t). It can also contrast nouns/ideas: "Tengo X, pero no tengo Y" (I have X, but I don’t have Y).
target_language_example: Quería ayudarte, pero no pude.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but I couldn't.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a doubt or disagreement after something already said. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "pero no creo que puedas", "pero no creo que acepte"). In casual speech you may also hear "pero no creo" without "que" when the rest is implied.
target_language_example: Podemos intentarlo, pero no creo que funcione.
native_language_example: We can try, but I don’t think it will work.

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct what was just said: **X..., pero no es Y** (“X..., but it’s not Y”). Spanish often omits the subject (**él/ella/eso**), so **pero no es** can mean “but he/she/it isn’t,” depending on context. You’ll also see it before another phrase like **momento/para...**: **Pero no es momento para...** (“But it’s not time to...”).
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no es mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but it’s not my job.

additional_notes: Used to contradict or qualify what was just said by pointing out that something does not exist, is not available, or is not possible. Very common in phrases like “pero no hay que + infinitive” (“but you don’t have to / you shouldn’t + verb”) and “pero no hay + noun/adjective” (“but there’s no + noun / there isn’t + adjective”), e.g., “pero no hay vuelta atrás” = “but there’s no going back.”
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no hay tiempo.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but there isn’t time.

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct what was just said, with **lo** referring back to an idea, situation, or action mentioned before. It often replaces repeating the whole phrase: *Las notas son importantes, pero no lo son todo* (“…but they aren’t everything”). It can also stand for a previous verb or description: *Quería ayudar, pero no lo logró* (“…but he didn’t manage to”). The verb after **lo** changes with the subject/tense (e.g., *no lo era/estaba*, *no lo somos*, *no lo conocí*).
target_language_example: Pensé que iba a llover, pero no lo hizo.
native_language_example: I thought it was going to rain, but it didn’t.

meaning: "but I don't…" / "but I didn't…" or "but don't … me" (before a verb).
additional_notes: A very common, fully literal combination: pero = "but", no = "not", me = "me". It’s used right before a verb. Two frequent patterns: (1) "pero no me + verb" where me is part of the verb (often reflexive), meaning "but I don't/didn't…" (e.g., "pero no me esperaba…" = "but I wasn't expecting…"). (2) "pero no me + verb" where me is the object, meaning "but (someone) didn't … me" or an imperative "but don't … me" (e.g., "pero no me olvides" = "but don't forget me"). Context tells you which one it is.
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no me digas mentiras.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but don’t lie to me.

meaning: “but you can’t” (but you’re not able/allowed to).
additional_notes: Used to contrast what someone wants or expects with a limitation. Often followed by an infinitive ("pero no puedes ir / jugar / publicar") or used on its own when the verb is understood ("...pero no puedes."). It can mean lack of ability or lack of permission, depending on context.
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no puedes entrar sin una cita.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but you can’t enter without an appointment.

meaning: "but I can't" / "but I’m not able to."
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or objection: you want to do something (or something is expected), but you’re not able to. Very often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "pero no puedo ir", "pero no puedo decirlo"). You can also use it by itself as a response: "—¿Puedes venir? —Pero no puedo."
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no puedo hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but I can’t do it today.

meaning: "but" + "not" + a verb that uses "se" (e.g., "but it doesn’t…", "but they can’t…", "but it hasn’t…").
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression by itself: **se** belongs to the following verb. You’ll often see it with (1) **reflexive/pronominal verbs** like *hundirse* (“to sink”): *no se hunde* (“(she/it) doesn’t sink”), and (2) **impersonal/passive se** with forms like *se puede* (“it can be / it’s possible”), *se ha perdido* (“it has been lost”). Word order: *pero no se + verb…*
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no se puede ahora.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but it’s not possible right now.

additional_notes: Used after sharing information (often a secret) to ask someone not to repeat it. "se" = "to them" (indirect object), "lo" = "it" (the thing/secret), and "digas" is the tú command (negative) of "decir": "no digas" = "don’t say/tell". You can add who not to tell: "pero no se lo digas a tu madre / a nadie".
target_language_example: Te lo cuento, pero no se lo digas a nadie.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you, but don’t tell anyone.

meaning: "but I don't know" / "but I'm not sure".
additional_notes: Used to add a doubt or limitation after what you just said. Very common before a question word (qué, cómo, en qué, etc.) or a noun: "pero no sé el código" (but I don’t know the code), "pero no sé qué es" (but I don’t know what it is). Often followed by an infinitive: "pero no sé hacerlo" (but I don’t know how to do it).
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no sé cómo explicarlo.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but I don't know how to explain it.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or doubt after a contrast ('pero'). It’s often followed by a verb or clause: "pero no sé si + (verb/clause)". In questions it can also be "pero no sé si..." meaning "but I’m not sure whether...".
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero no sé si tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but I don't know if I have time today.

meaning: "but don’t (you)…" / "but I didn’t … you" (depending on the verb that follows).
additional_notes:
This is a very common start to a sentence. It combines:
- **pero** = “but”
- **no** = “not / don’t”
- **te** = “you” (informal singular object pronoun, often reflexive)

You’ll usually see it right before a verb:
- **Pero no te + verb** as a negative command or suggestion: *Pero no te alejes…* (“But don’t go far…”) / *Pero no te vas a morir* (“But you’re not going to die.”)
- **Pero no te + verb (past)** where **te** is the object (“you”): *Pero no te mentí* (“But I didn’t lie to you.”)

It uses **te** (informal “you”); with **usted**, it would be **pero no le…**.
target_language_example: Pero no te preocupes, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: But don’t worry, everything is going to be fine.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone after mentioning a problem or something negative. It’s addressing one person informally (tú). You can also say “pero no se preocupe” (formal, usted) or “pero no se preocupen” (to multiple people).
target_language_example: Llegaré un poco tarde, pero no te preocupes: te aviso cuando esté cerca.
native_language_example: I’ll be a little late, but don’t worry: I’ll let you know when I’m close.

additional_notes: Used after stating a desire or need to contrast with the fact that you don’t possess something. Often followed by what’s missing ("pero no tengo dinero") or left implied when context is clear ("Me gustaría tener uno, pero no tengo"). In speech you can add the subject for emphasis: "pero yo no tengo".
target_language_example: Necesito un cargador, pero no tengo.
native_language_example: I need a charger, but I don’t have one.

additional_notes: Used to contrast an expectation or statement with something that has *never* happened. Common before a verb phrase ("pero nunca + verb"), often emphasizing refusal, denial, or impossibility: "...pero nunca me rindo" (but I never give up).
target_language_example: Quise llamarte, pero nunca encontré el momento.
native_language_example: I wanted to call you, but I never found the right moment.

meaning: "but if" / "but (it) is/was...!" (often to contradict or insist).
additional_notes: Often used in two ways: (1) Literal conditional: "pero si + clause" = "but if..." ("But if there’s no ticket, you have to pay a fine."). (2) Very common conversational/emphatic use to correct someone, show surprise, or insist on a fact: "¡Pero si...!" ≈ "But it is...! / But I did...!" ("But we’ve looked a hundred times!"). The "si" here doesn’t really mean "if" in English; it’s more like emphasis.
target_language_example: ¡Pero si ya te lo dije!
native_language_example: But I already told you!

additional_notes: Used to set a condition and warn what will happen if it isn’t met. It often introduces a consequence: "Pero si no + (present tense), + (future/imperative)". Common in spoken Spanish to add emphasis or urgency, like "But if you don’t…, then…" / "Otherwise…".
target_language_example: Pero si no vienes ahora, me voy sin ti.
native_language_example: But if you don’t come now, I’m leaving without you.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said ("pero" = but) and then state something you’re certain about ("sé que" = I know that + a clause). Often follows a disclaimer like "No soy…, pero sé que…" (“I’m not…, but I know that…”).
target_language_example: No entiendo todo, pero sé que esto no está bien.
native_language_example: I don’t understand everything, but I know that this isn’t right.

meaning: “but yes” / “but actually (yes/it does)” (a contrast or correction).
additional_notes: Used to contradict or qualify what was just said or implied (similar to “but yes,” “but actually,” “but I do,” “but it is/they are”). Often followed by a verb or pronoun for emphasis: “pero sí lo tienen” = “but they do have it.” It can also stand alone as a brief reluctant agreement: “..., pero sí.” As a stronger emphatic form you may hear “pero sí que …” (e.g., “Pero sí que está enfermo” = “He really is sick”).
target_language_example: No es barato, pero sí vale la pena.
native_language_example: It’s not cheap, but it is worth it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce doubt, an alternative possibility, or a softer correction after what was just said. Very common when you want to reconsider or qualify a statement. Often followed by the imperfect/subjunctive in more speculative sentences (e.g., "pero tal vez sería/mejor...", "pero tal vez sea...").
target_language_example: Quiero ir contigo, pero tal vez no pueda mañana.
native_language_example: I want to go with you, but maybe I can’t tomorrow.

meaning: “but I have to…” (I need to / must…).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or a polite excuse before saying an obligation or necessity. Commonly followed by an infinitive: “pero tengo que + preguntar/salir/recoger/decir/hacer…”. You can change the subject: “pero tienes que…”, “pero tenemos que…”.
target_language_example: Quiero quedarme más, pero tengo que irme.
native_language_example: I want to stay longer, but I have to go.

meaning: “but you have to / but you need to.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast (“pero” = “but”) and then state an obligation or necessity with “tienes que” + infinitive: “pero tienes que + hacer/decir/ir…”. The subject is “tú” (you, informal singular).
target_language_example: Entiendo que estás cansado, pero tienes que terminar la tarea.
native_language_example: I understand you’re tired, but you have to finish the homework.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what was just said with what *you* did/are/need, often with strong emphasis on “tú” (you). It commonly appears at the start of a sentence to object, correct, or point out an exception: “Pero tú no estabas…” = “But you weren’t there…”. In speech, it can also be left hanging to show surprise or protest: “Pero tú…” = “But you…!”.
target_language_example: Quería irme, pero tú me convenciste de quedarme.
native_language_example: I wanted to leave, but you convinced me to stay.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or objection, often correcting someone or pointing out a fact about them. It’s usually followed by a noun or adjective: "Pero tú eres mi amigo" (noun phrase) / "Pero tú eres soltero" (adjective). The stress on "tú" emphasizes that *you* (not someone else) are.
target_language_example: Pero tú eres el que lo dijo primero.
native_language_example: But you’re the one who said it first.

meaning: "but you don't / didn't" (contrasting what someone else did).
additional_notes: Used to correct or contrast someone’s situation/actions with another person’s. In Spanish you often include the subject pronoun “tú” for emphasis (“you, specifically”). The verb is usually understood from context: e.g., “Yo puedo, pero tú no (puedes)”; “Él estuvo allí, pero tú no (estuviste)”.
target_language_example: Yo ya terminé, pero tú no.
native_language_example: I already finished, but you didn’t.

meaning: "but it's worth it" / "but it's worth the effort."
additional_notes: Used to contrast something difficult, annoying, or risky (introduced by "pero" = "but") with a positive outcome. "Vale la pena" literally means "(it) is worth the pain/effort," and is followed by an infinitive when you say what is worth doing: "vale la pena intentarlo" = "it's worth trying." Often used to encourage someone or justify continuing.
target_language_example: Es cansado, pero vale la pena hacerlo.
native_language_example: It's tiring, but it's worth doing.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what you just said with the fact that something has already happened or is true now. Often introduces a correction or an objection: "Pero ya me asignaron..." (but they already assigned me...), "Pero ya es tarde" (but it’s already late). In some contexts it means "but now" or "but by now" (things have changed since before).
target_language_example: Quería ayudarte, pero ya lo resolviste.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but you already solved it.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with something that used to be true but isn’t now. Often refers back to a previously mentioned action or situation: "Lo era, pero ya no" = "I/he/she used to be (that), but not anymore." You’ll also see it before a verb: "pero ya no lo hace" = "but he/she doesn’t do it anymore."
target_language_example: Antes vivía aquí, pero ya no.
native_language_example: I used to live here, but not anymore.

meaning: 'but I…' (contrasts what you say about yourself with someone/something else).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or exception focused on the speaker (yo). Often appears in comparisons like “Ellos no, pero yo sí” (“They don’t, but I do”), or to push back/clarify your own point: “No sé tú, pero yo…” (“I don’t know about you, but I…”). Spanish often includes “yo” here for emphasis, even though the verb ending already shows who the subject is.
target_language_example: No sé ustedes, pero yo prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: I don’t know about you all, but I’d rather stay home.

meaning: "but I don't" / "but I didn't" (in contrast to someone else).
additional_notes: Used to disagree or contrast your situation/actions with what was just said. The verb is often understood from context and left out: *Yo sí, pero yo no* (“I did, but I didn’t”). It can sound emphatic, especially when said alone: *Pero yo no.*
target_language_example: Ellos quieren ir, pero yo no.
native_language_example: They want to go, but I don’t.

meaning: "But why?" (asking for a reason, often with surprise or protest).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or question something someone just said/did. "Pero" adds contrast or objection (“but...”), so it often sounds like “Wait, why?” or “But why would you...?” You can follow it with a noun/phrase ("pero ¿por qué en mi auto?") or with "no" + verb ("pero ¿por qué no paras ya?").
target_language_example: Pero ¿por qué te vas ahora?
native_language_example: But why are you leaving now?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to react to something unexpected or confusing. It often expresses surprise, disbelief, impatience, or concern, and is usually followed by a verb: “pero ¿qué pasa?” (what’s going on?), “pero ¿qué pasó?” (what happened?), “pero ¿qué harás?” (what will you do?).
target_language_example: Pero ¿qué estás diciendo?
native_language_example: But what are you saying?

additional_notes: This is the noun perro (“dog”) + the verb está (3rd person singular of estar, “is”). Use estar for temporary states and locations: está sediento (is thirsty), está aquí/allí (is here/there). In real Spanish you usually include an article or possessive: el perro está…, mi/tu/su perro está… (just “perro está” by itself is uncommon). Note the accent: está (he/she/it is) vs esta (this).
target_language_example: Mi perro está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: My dog is at home now.

meaning: “the person whom/that …” (a person who is the object of a verb or preposition).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that refers back to a specific person. The "a" is the personal "a" used with people when they are the direct object (or after certain verbs/prepositions): "la persona a la que conocí" = “the person (whom) I met.” You’ll often see pronouns inside the clause too, e.g. "a la que le di" (“to whom I gave”), where "le" shows the indirect object (“to him/her”).
target_language_example: Ella es la persona a la que llamé ayer.
native_language_example: She is the person (whom) I called yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing a person. It usually follows an article or determiner (la/una/cualquier persona que…) and then a verb: "la persona que ayudó…". "Que" doesn’t change for gender or number (la persona que…, las personas que…).
target_language_example: Busco a una persona que hable inglés.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a person who speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to say that some number of people died. You’ll often see it with a quantity (muchísimas/cientos/doscientas/miles/muchas) and/or with details like cause (de cólera, de hambre) or place/event (en la guerra, en ese accidente). The verb is **morir** (to die); **murieron** is the **they** form in the simple past (pretérito).
target_language_example: En el incendio, varias personas murieron.
native_language_example: In the fire, several people died.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes which people you mean. It’s often followed by a verb: “personas que trabajan” (people who work). You’ll also see singular “persona que” (a person who/that).
target_language_example: Busco personas que hablen inglés.
native_language_example: I’m looking for people who speak English.

additional_notes: Used to show ownership (who something belongs to) or membership/classification (what group, category, or place someone/something is part of). It’s the verb "pertenecer" + "a". With people/pronouns: "pertenece a Tom", "pertenece a ella".
target_language_example: ¿Este paraguas pertenece a alguien?
native_language_example: Does this umbrella belong to anyone?

meaning: to go fishing at the river.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **ir a pescar al río** (“to go fishing at the river”). Here **al** = **a + el** (“to the”), emphasizing going to that place to fish. You may also hear **pescar en el río** (“to fish in the river”), which focuses more on the location where you fish rather than the trip there.
target_language_example: Los fines de semana vamos a pescar al río.
native_language_example: On weekends we go fishing at the river.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast: something is true even though there is an obstacle or opposing fact. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (pese a la lluvia, pese a su edad), an infinitive (pese a ser muy viejo), or a clause with que (pese a que era prudente…). Common related phrase: pese a todo = “despite everything.”
target_language_example: Pese a la lluvia, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("pidiendo" = "asking/requesting") to describe an action happening at the same time as another action, often after verbs like gritar (to shout), llorar (to cry), or llamar (to call). Common in emergencies: "gritó pidiendo ayuda" = "he shouted for help."
target_language_example: Corrí hacia ellos cuando los oí pidiendo ayuda.
native_language_example: I ran toward them when I heard them asking for help.

additional_notes: “Pidió” is the past tense (preterite) of “pedir” = “to ask for / to request.” It often uses “a” before a person: “pidió a sus amigos ayuda” = “he asked his friends for help.” Very common pattern: “pidió a [person] que + verb (subjunctive)” to say someone asked another person to do something: “pidió a la niñera que cuidara…”. Pronouns can be added: “le pidió a ella…” or “les pidió a todos…”.
target_language_example: El jefe me pidió a mí que llegara temprano.
native_language_example: The boss asked me to arrive early.

additional_notes: Common pattern: "pedir consejo a + person" = to ask someone for advice. "Pidió" is the simple past (preterite) of "pedir" (to ask for/request). "Su" means "his/her/your(formal)/their"—the owner is understood from context. You’ll usually continue with a noun like "amigo/a", "profesor/a", etc.: "le pidió consejo a su amigo".
target_language_example: Le pidió consejo a su hermana antes de aceptar el trabajo.
native_language_example: She asked her sister for advice before accepting the job.

additional_notes: Used to report a request in the past (preterite of pedir). After “pidió que”, Spanish typically uses the imperfect subjunctive: pidieron que fuéramos / hiciéramos / ayudáramos. Often followed by an object pronoun: “Nos pidió que…”, “Me pidió que…”.
target_language_example: El jefe pidió que llegáramos temprano.
native_language_example: The boss asked that we arrive early.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "pedir" to make a request: "pidió que" + verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "pidió que le llamara"). "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him," "to her," or "to you" (formal), depending on context. Often the full pattern is "[Someone] le pidió a [someone] que le + [subjunctive verb]".
target_language_example: El jefe le pidió que le enviara el informe hoy.
native_language_example: The boss asked him/her to send him/her the report today.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to apologize. Literally “I ask (for) apologies,” often used in customer service, speeches, or when speaking respectfully. Common patterns: “(Le/Les/Te) pido disculpas” (I apologize to you), and “Pido disculpas por…” (I apologize for…).
target_language_example: Le pido disculpas por la demora.
native_language_example: I apologize for the delay.

additional_notes: "Piensa" is the tú (informal singular) command form of pensar. Use "piensa en + noun/pronoun/thing" to tell someone to think about something or someone (e.g., "Piensa en mí", "Piensa en esto"). It can also imply "consider" or "keep in mind," especially in advice or reminders.
target_language_example: Piensa en lo que vas a decir antes de hablar.
native_language_example: Think about what you're going to say before you speak.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person informally (tú) to consider or reflect on something, usually followed by a clause: piensa en lo que dije/haces/vas a hacer (“think about what I said/you’re doing/you’re going to do”). You can change the verb form for other people: piense en lo que… (usted), piensen en lo que… (ustedes).
target_language_example: Piensa en lo que vas a decir antes de hablar.
native_language_example: Think about what you’re going to say before you speak.

additional_notes: Used to introduce someone’s opinion or belief. "Piensa" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "pensar" (he/she/it thinks). Often followed by a full clause: "piensa que + [sentence]". You can change the subject: "Yo pienso que..." (I think that...), "¿Piensas que...?" (Do you think that...?).
target_language_example: Mi hermano piensa que vamos a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: My brother thinks that we’re going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what a group of people believes or assumes. "Piensan" is the present tense of "pensar" (to think) for "ellos/ellas/ustedes"; the subject is often implied, and "que" introduces the clause that follows.
target_language_example: Piensan que no entiendo, pero sí entiendo.
native_language_example: They think I don't understand, but I do.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **pensar en** (“to think about”). **Piense en** is the **usted** imperative (formal), used to tell someone to think about or consider something. You’ll often see it followed by a noun (**Piense en su familia**) or by **lo que…** (**Piense en lo que gana** = “Think about what you gain”).
target_language_example: Piense en las consecuencias antes de decidir.
native_language_example: Think about the consequences before deciding.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pensar + en + noun/pronoun to say what someone has in mind (a person, thing, memory, idea). It can be general/habitual ("I think about...") or right now ("I’m thinking of..."). With an infinitive, it often means "to plan/intend to": No pienso en ir = "I’m not planning to go."
target_language_example: Pienso en mi familia cuando estoy lejos.
native_language_example: I think about my family when I’m far away.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is on your mind. The verb is pensar + en + person/thing: “pienso en ti” (I think about you), “pienso en eso” (I think about that). Often implies remembering, missing, or having someone in your thoughts. Negative form: “No pienso en ti (de ese modo)” = “I don’t think of you (like that).”
target_language_example: Pienso en ti cuando te extraño.
native_language_example: I think about you when I miss you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about a statement. Often followed by a verb in the indicative (e.g., "deberíamos", "había estado", "va a ser"). You can also say "Creo que…" with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Pienso que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion. Often followed by an adjective or noun: “Pienso que es lo mejor” (I think it’s the best). You may also see the pattern “Pienso que es + adjective + que + subjunctive” when what follows is a reaction or judgment: “Pienso que es extraño que no haya…” (I think it’s strange that there isn’t…).
target_language_example: Pienso que es importante hablar con el profesor hoy.
native_language_example: I think it’s important to talk to the teacher today.

additional_notes: Used to describe a picture/painting that is hanging or placed on a wall. Very often you’ll see it with verbs like colgar (to hang): "Colgué una pintura en la pared" / "Está colgando una pintura en la pared."
target_language_example: Esa pintura en la pared es nueva.
native_language_example: That painting on the wall is new.

meaning: "plans for" (intentions/arrangements for something in the future).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone intends to do or has arranged, often followed by a time period (mañana, este fin de semana) or a noun (vacaciones, su vida). Very common with tener: "No tengo planes para mañana" / "Ya tengo planes para el fin de semana". Also appears in broader contexts like "planes para la humanidad" (big goals/intentions).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes planes para el verano?
native_language_example: Do you have plans for the summer?

meaning: the main course; the main event (highlight).
additional_notes: Most commonly used on menus and in meals to mean the main dish served after an appetizer (la entrada) and before dessert (el postre). It’s also used figuratively to introduce the most important or anticipated part of something (a show, presentation, announcement): “And now, the main event.”
target_language_example: De plato fuerte pedí pollo con arroz.
native_language_example: For the main course I ordered chicken with rice.

additional_notes: Very informal, spoken-style shortening where the final -r in “por” and the final -r in “favor” may be dropped. You’ll hear it in casual speech (and sometimes see it written playfully), but in writing and formal situations use “por favor”.
target_language_example: Po favó, ¿me puedes ayudar un momento?
native_language_example: Please, can you help me for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to minimize the importance, value, or amount of something: "Es poca cosa" = "It’s not much" / "It’s no big deal." It can also describe a person as insignificant or weak (often a bit negative): "Es una poca cosa" = "He/She is a nobody."
target_language_example: No te preocupes, es poca cosa.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s not much.

additional_notes: Used to say a small number of people do something or are in a place. Often followed by a verb: “Poca gente sabe…” (“Few people know…”). You can intensify it with “muy”: “muy poca gente” (“very few people”).
target_language_example: Poca gente entiende este acento.
native_language_example: Few people understand this accent.

additional_notes: Used to say that only a small number of people do something or have something. Often appears as (muy) pocas personas + verb. Because it's an adjective + noun, it changes for gender/number (e.g., pocas cosas, pocos hombres).
target_language_example: Pocas personas entienden este tema.
native_language_example: Few people understand this topic.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that doesn’t happen often. It usually goes near the verb: "Pocas veces voy al cine". You can also use it with "muy" for emphasis: "muy pocas veces" = "very rarely".
target_language_example: Pocas veces salgo a cenar entre semana.
native_language_example: I rarely go out to dinner during the week.

additional_notes: Used literally in fantasy stories (a drink that causes a special effect). It can also be used figuratively to mean a “miracle cure” or “quick fix” that doesn’t really exist. Often appears with an article: "la/una poción mágica".
target_language_example: Se terminó el efecto de la poción mágica.
native_language_example: The effect of the magic potion wore off.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens slowly over time or step by step. Often placed at the start of a sentence (“Poco a poco, …”) or after the verb (“Se recuperó poco a poco”).
target_language_example: Poco a poco, voy aprendiendo español.
native_language_example: Little by little, I’m learning Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens soon after a previous event or time. It can refer to an earlier action (Poco después, murió.) or to a specific time marker (poco después del mediodía = shortly after noon). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence with a comma (Poco después, ...), or after the verb (llegó ... poco después).
target_language_example: Terminamos de comer y, poco después, empezó a llover.
native_language_example: We finished eating and shortly after, it started to rain.

meaning: little time; not much time (a short amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to say there isn’t enough time or that the available time is short. Common patterns: “me queda poco tiempo” = “I have little time left”; “poco tiempo para + infinitive” = “little time to do something”; “por poco tiempo” = “for a short time.”
target_language_example: Nos queda poco tiempo para llegar al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We have little time left to get to the airport.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about a small quantity: un poco de + noun (un poco de frío, un poco de champaña). With some expressions, it refers to a small degree/amount of something abstract (un poco de mal gusto).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes darme un poco de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little bit of water, please?

additional_notes: Means a small amount of water. Very common with requests (Dame un poco de agua.) or to describe what’s in something (Hay un poco de agua en la botella.). Often used with un: un poco de agua. With only/just: sólo/solamente un poco de agua.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un poco de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water, please?

meaning: a little (bit) of money; some money.
additional_notes: "Un poco de" means “a little (bit) of” and is used with uncountable nouns like dinero (money). In requests, "Dame un poco de dinero" is common but can sound direct; "¿Me das un poco de dinero, por favor?" is more polite.
target_language_example: Necesito un poco de dinero para el autobús.
native_language_example: I need a little money for the bus.

meaning: a slight fever; a little fever.
additional_notes: Almost always used as "un poco de fiebre" with the verb "tener" (to have): "Tengo un poco de fiebre". It means you have a mild temperature—not a high fever. You can also use it with "llevar" to say how long you’ve had it: "Llevo desde esta mañana con un poco de fiebre".
target_language_example: Creo que tengo un poco de fiebre, así que voy a descansar.
native_language_example: I think I have a slight fever, so I'm going to rest.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small amount of milk. Very common with drinks ("con un poco de leche" = "with a little milk"). For quantities with an uncountable noun like leche, Spanish uses "un poco de" (or just "poco de").
target_language_example: ¿Me pones un poco de leche en el café?
native_language_example: Can you put a little milk in the coffee for me?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a small amount of time. Very common with verbs like necesitar (Necesito un poco de tiempo), dar (Dame un poco de tiempo), or tener (No tengo mucho tiempo). You can add more detail with phrases like a solas (“alone”) or para + infinitive (un poco de tiempo para pensar).
target_language_example: Dame un poco de tiempo para pensarlo.
native_language_example: Give me a little time to think about it.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate a small additional amount (more time, money, food, etc.). It can also mean a small additional distance (“un poco más lejos”). Often appears with “solo/sólo” to mean “just a little more.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes esperar un poco más, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little longer, please?

meaning: “a little more (of)”; “just over / a little more than”.
additional_notes: Used before a noun or quantity. With nouns it means “a little more of” (Necesito un poco más de espacio). With numbers, time, age, etc., it often means “a little more than / just over” (un poco más de cuarenta años; un poco más de una hora).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes darme un poco más de agua?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more water?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a small extra amount of time to finish something or make a decision. Common with verbs like "dame" (give me) and "necesito" (I need): "Dame/Necesito un poco más de tiempo." You can also say it by itself as a brief request: "Solo/Sólo un poco más de tiempo."
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco más de tiempo para terminar?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more time to finish?

additional_notes:
Used to say that only a small number of students understood something. 
- **pocos** = few (emphasizes that the number is small).
- Often you’ll also hear **(solo) unos pocos estudiantes entendieron…** (“only a few students understood…”), which sounds a bit more neutral.
- **entendieron** is the **preterite** (simple past) of *entender* (“to understand”), used for a completed action in the past.
target_language_example: Pocos estudiantes entendieron la explicación.
native_language_example: Few students understood the explanation.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about a short amount of time. Common patterns: "cada pocos minutos" = "every few minutes" (repeatedly); "hace (unos) pocos minutos" = "a few minutes ago"; "quedan pocos minutos" = "there are a few minutes left".
target_language_example: Llegamos en pocos minutos.
native_language_example: We’ll arrive in a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say that “we” (nosotros) can trust or rely on someone/something. It’s the present tense of the verb phrase “confiar en” (to trust in/rely on). Often followed by a person: “confiar en él/ella/ellos/ella” or “en alguien/en nadie”.
target_language_example: Podemos confiar en ellos para terminar el trabajo a tiempo.
native_language_example: We can rely on them to finish the work on time.

additional_notes: From poder (we can) + hablar (to talk). Used to suggest discussing something now or later (“We can talk about that later”), or as a direct request/question (“Can we talk?”). Often followed by de + topic: “podemos hablar de eso…”.
target_language_example: ¿Podemos hablar un minuto en privado?
native_language_example: Can we talk for a minute in private?

additional_notes: Used to suggest or offer discussing a topic. Common with a pronoun or noun after de: de eso/esto (about that/this), de lo que quieras (about whatever you want). It can be polite and practical (“We can talk about it later”) or, depending on tone, a challenge (“We can talk about this, man.”).
target_language_example: Si quieres, podemos hablar de tus planes mañana.
native_language_example: If you want, we can talk about your plans tomorrow.

additional_notes: From poder (to be able to) + hacer (to do/make). Use it to talk about what “we” are able to do, offer help, or propose solutions: ¿Qué podemos hacer? (“What can we do?”). With que + verb, it often means “we can make/ensure that…”: Podemos hacer que el mundo se detenga (“We can make the world stop”).
target_language_example: No se preocupe: podemos hacer algo para ayudar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we can do something to help.

additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (“to be able to/can”) in the present tense for nosotros (“we”): podemos + infinitive (hacer). The pronoun lo (“it”) is attached to the infinitive: hacer + lo → hacerlo. You can add emphasis or details after it, e.g., “podemos hacerlo solos” (“we can do it alone/by ourselves”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: podemos hacerlo juntos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we can do it together.

additional_notes: Form of "poder" (to be able to/can) + "ir" (to go). Used to say that it’s possible/allowed for us to go somewhere or do something next. In questions like "¿Podemos ir...?" it often means "Can we go...?" or "Are we allowed to go...?" You’ll usually add a destination with "a" ("podemos ir a cenar", "podemos ir a casa") or use time words like "después" (later).
target_language_example: ¿Podemos ir a casa ahora?
native_language_example: Can we go home now?

meaning: "we can go to" / "can we go to?"
additional_notes: Used to talk about the possibility/permission of going somewhere. In questions (¿Podemos ir a...?) it often means asking for permission: “Can we go to…?” After "a" you can use a place (a casa, al parque) or an infinitive to say an activity (a nadar, a cenar).
target_language_example: ¿Podemos ir a la playa mañana?
native_language_example: Can we go to the beach tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (can/to be able to) + an infinitive. It’s used to express ability/possibility to change something (plans, clothes, settings) or to switch/modify something. Conjugate poder to match the subject (e.g., puedo cambiar, puedes cambiar, podemos cambiar), but the base multi-word term is poder cambiar.
target_language_example: Quiero poder cambiar mi asiento si hay disponibilidad.
native_language_example: I want to be able to change my seat if there’s availability.

meaning: to be able to wait; can wait.
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder + infinitive (esperar). Often appears in polite questions/requests with conjugated poder (e.g., “¿Puede esperar…?” = “Can you wait…?”). Note that esperar can also mean “to hope” or “to expect” depending on context, but with poder it most commonly means “to wait.”
target_language_example: No sé si voy a poder esperar mucho más.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I’m going to be able to wait much longer.

meaning: to be able to speak; to be able to talk.
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (“to be able to/can”) + an infinitive (hablar, “to speak/talk”). It expresses ability/permission/possibility to speak or talk, often after verbs like querer/esperar/necesitar (e.g., “Quiero poder hablar…”). With languages, it means “to be able to speak [a language]” (poder hablar francés). With con + person, it means “to be able to talk with [someone]” (poder hablar con Tom).
target_language_example: Quisiera poder hablar inglés fluidamente.
native_language_example: I would like to be able to speak English fluently.

additional_notes: Used with the modal verb **poder** + an infinitive (**hacer**) to talk about ability, possibility, or having the means to do something. **Poder** is conjugated (puedo, puedes, puede, etc.) and **hacer** stays in the infinitive: *No puedo hacer esto.* It often translates naturally as “can do” or “be able to do,” depending on the tense and context.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poder hacer eso hoy?
native_language_example: Can you do that today?

meaning: to be able to go; can go.
additional_notes: Used to talk about having the ability/possibility/permission to go somewhere. It’s built from the verb poder (can/to be able to) + infinitive ir (to go). Often appears after another verb or preposition (e.g., antes de poder ir...) and is very common in the negative with future meaning: no voy a poder ir = “I won’t be able to go.”
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de poder ir con vosotros.
native_language_example: I’m not sure I can go with you (all).

meaning: to be able to hear (to manage to hear).
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder + an infinitive (oír). It expresses ability/possibility to hear something (often affected by volume, noise, distance, connection quality, etc.). Common with object pronouns: poder oírte (to be able to hear you), poder oírlo/la (to be able to hear it/him/her). Note: oír = to hear (passively); escuchar = to listen (actively).
target_language_example: No puedo poder oír bien con tanto ruido; ¿puedes repetirlo, por favor?
native_language_example: I can’t manage to hear well with so much noise; can you repeat it, please?

additional_notes: "Poder" (to be able to/can) + infinitive. Conjugate "poder" to match the subject (puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden) and keep "trabajar" in the infinitive. Often used to talk about availability, permission, or capability (e.g., after an injury: "No puedo trabajar" = I can't work).
target_language_example: Para pagar el alquiler, necesito poder trabajar esta semana.
native_language_example: To pay the rent, I need to be able to work this week.

additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (to be able to/can) + venir (to come). Common in invitations, requests, and stating availability: ¿Vas a poder venir? (Are you going to be able to come?) / No voy a poder venir. (I’m not going to be able to come.) Can be made more polite with conditional forms (e.g., ¿Podrías venir? = Could you come?).
target_language_example: No voy a poder venir mañana.
native_language_example: I’m not going to be able to come tomorrow.

meaning: to be able to see (or to be able to watch/see someone).
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (“to be able to/can”) + an infinitive. With objects like la cámara, el reflejo, or bien, it means being able to see clearly. With people (ver a + person), it often means being able to see/visit them (meet up). Also common in purpose phrases: para poder ver = “in order to be able to see.”
target_language_example: Me acerco a la pantalla para poder ver mejor.
native_language_example: I move closer to the screen so I can see better.

meaning: to be able to return / come back.
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (can/to be able to) + infinitive. You conjugate poder (puedo, puedes, puede, etc.) and keep volver in the infinitive. Volver can mean “to return” or “to come back,” depending on context (returning somewhere vs. coming back here).
target_language_example: Si termino temprano, voy a poder volver hoy.
native_language_example: If I finish early, I’m going to be able to come back today.

meaning: to be able to handle / cope with (something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun/pronoun to say you can (or can’t) manage something physically, mentally, or emotionally. Very common in the negative: "No puedo con..." = "I can’t handle..." It can also mean being strong enough for a task (e.g., lifting/carrying) or being able to deal with a situation.
target_language_example: A veces no puedo con tanto trabajo.
native_language_example: Sometimes I can’t handle so much work.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + estar to express a possibility about someone’s location, state, or condition: "Podría estar en casa" (He/She could be at home), "podría estar cansado" (might be tired). In the negative, "no podría estar" often means "couldn’t be" (it’s not possible) or "wouldn’t be able to be," depending on context.
target_language_example: Ahora no contesta; podría estar conduciendo.
native_language_example: He’s not answering right now; he might be driving.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something may be in a place, but you’re not sure. It’s the conditional of poder (podría = might/could) + infinitive estar (to be) + en (in/at). Often used with uncertainty phrases like “por lo que sé/sabemos” (as far as I know/we know).
target_language_example: Mi teléfono podría estar en la cocina.
native_language_example: My phone might be in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past possibility or missed opportunity, often in conditional sentences (Si..., podría haber...). It’s the conditional of poder (podría) + haber + past participle (ganado, decidido, conseguido) to form the conditional perfect: “could have + done.”
target_language_example: Lo siento: podría haber llegado antes, pero había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: I could have arrived earlier, but there was a lot of traffic.

meaning: "could have done" (possibility/ability in the past, often implying a missed chance or a different option).
additional_notes: This is the conditional of poder (podría) + haber + past participle (hecho). It talks about an action that did not happen (or is uncertain) but was possible: "I/you/he/she could have done..." Often used to express regret, criticism, or hindsight ("I could have asked more" / "He could have done more"). You can replace hecho with another past participle: podría haber dicho (could have said), podría haber ido (could have gone).
target_language_example: Lo siento, podría haber hecho las cosas de otra manera.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I could have done things differently.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + haber + past participle (sido) to talk about something that was possible, but did not happen or is uncertain in hindsight. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: “podría haber sido cualquiera/cualquier cosa” = “it could have been anyone/anything.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: podría haber sido un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it could have been a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of poder: podría (would/could) + haber + past participle (hecho). It talks about a past possibility/ability, often implying it was possible in theory (or under certain conditions). “lo” means “it” and attaches to haber (haberlo). Often used with negatives or conditions: “No podría haberlo hecho sin…” = “I couldn’t have done it without…”.
target_language_example: Yo podría haberlo hecho, pero no tenía tiempo.
native_language_example: I could have done it, but I didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Conditional of ser (“to be”). Used to express possibility or a hypothetical situation. Often followed by an adjective or noun: podría ser útil (could be useful), podría ser su espía (might be his/her spy). With a subject pronoun, it can mean “I/you/he/she could be …”: Yo podría ser tu amigo.
target_language_example: No estoy seguro, pero podría ser verdad.
native_language_example: I’m not sure, but it could be true.

additional_notes: Used to warn about a possible risk. It’s the conditional of poder (podría = could/might) + ser (to be) + peligroso (dangerous). Often followed by para + person (“for someone”).
target_language_example: No entres ahí; podría ser peligroso.
native_language_example: Don’t go in there; it could be dangerous.

meaning: "could be a" / "might be a" (expressing a possibility).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + ser to say something is possible or uncertain. It’s commonly followed by a masculine singular noun with un; for feminine use "podría ser una" (e.g., "podría ser una mentira"). With plural: "podrían ser" (e.g., "podrían ser unos errores").
target_language_example: Con ese acento, podría ser un turista.
native_language_example: With that accent, he could be a tourist.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + ser to suggest something is possible rather than certain. The article changes with the noun: podría ser un / podría ser una. Common for guesses, hypotheses, or polite/soft statements: "Podría ser una buena idea".
target_language_example: No estoy seguro, pero podría ser una buena idea.
native_language_example: I’m not sure, but it could be a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. Often followed by a noun or clause (e.g., “Podría ser así” = “It could be like that”), or used alone as a hesitant “Maybe.” It’s the conditional form of “poder” (can/could), so it can also sound like a polite, tentative suggestion.
target_language_example: ¿Podría ser mañana?
native_language_example: Could it be tomorrow?

meaning: 'you could have' (had the possibility to do something in the past).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the conditional perfect: podrías haber + participle (e.g., podrías haber venido = you could have come). It often talks about a missed possibility, an alternative past, or a mild criticism/suggestion about what someone should have done.
target_language_example: Podrías haberme llamado ayer, pero no lo hiciste.
native_language_example: You could have called me yesterday, but you didn’t.

additional_notes: Uses the Spain-only plural “you” form (vosotros/vosotras): podéis = “you all can/are able to.” It often appears with a direct-object pronoun before the verb (la = “it” feminine, lo = “it” masculine/neuter): “La/lo podéis poner ahí” = “You can put it there.” “Ahí” means “there” (near the listener).
target_language_example: ¿Lo podéis poner ahí, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you (all) put it there, please?

additional_notes: Uses the vosotros form (common in Spain) to address a group in an informal context: podéis = “you all can/are able to.” Often a direct object pronoun comes before the verb: la podéis poner allí (“you can put it there” referring to a feminine noun), lo podéis poner allí (masculine/neuter). Allí means “there/over there” (not here).
target_language_example: La podéis poner allí.
native_language_example: You all can put it there.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (podía) to talk about a past belief/assumption or an ongoing ability to trust someone. Often appears after verbs like dije/pensé/sabía (“I said/thought/knew”) in sentences like “Pensé que podía confiar en ti.” Note: “confiar en” usually means “to trust,” not “to confide” (though in some contexts it can mean “to confide in”).
target_language_example: Creí que podía confiar en ti, pero me mentiste.
native_language_example: I thought I could trust you, but you lied to me.

meaning: "could do" / "was able to do" (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of poder (podía) + infinitive (hacer) to talk about past ability, what was possible, or what someone was allowed to do. Often implies an ongoing situation in the past (not a single completed attempt). For a specific one-time successful action, Spanish often uses "pude hacer".
target_language_example: No podía hacer nada sin ayuda.
native_language_example: I couldn't do anything without help.

additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the reflexive construction ponerse nervioso/a (“to get nervous”): (él/ella) se pone nervioso/a. It can also be used non-reflexively with an indirect object to mean “to make (someone) nervous”: Eso me pone nervioso/a. Adjective agreement: nervioso (masc.), nerviosa (fem.).
target_language_example: Mi padre siempre se pone nervioso.
native_language_example: My father always gets nervous.

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals that reproduce by laying eggs (birds, insects, reptiles, etc.). It’s the present tense, third-person plural of "poner" (to lay/put): *ponen* = “they lay.” With a singular animal, use *pone huevos* (“lays eggs”).
target_language_example: Las tortugas ponen huevos en la playa.
native_language_example: Turtles lay eggs on the beach.

meaning: to test; to put (someone/something) to the test.
additional_notes: Used when an experience, situation, or action tests a person’s abilities, patience, or the quality of something: "poner a prueba la paciencia" (test someone’s patience), "poner a prueba un plan" (test a plan). You can also use the reflexive form "ponerse a prueba" = to challenge oneself / test oneself.
target_language_example: Este trabajo va a poner a prueba tu paciencia.
native_language_example: This job is going to test your patience.

additional_notes: Used to indicate placing something in a specific location (“allí” = “there,” typically more specific/farther than “ahí”). Commonly appears with direct object pronouns (lo/la = “it”) and with polite/neutral forms like puede/pueden.
target_language_example: Lo puede poner allí.
native_language_example: You can put it there.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay close attention.
additional_notes: Commonly used as an instruction or request. Often followed by **a** + noun or clause: *poner atención a la explicación* / *poner atención a lo que dices*. You may also hear **prestar atención**, which means the same thing.
target_language_example: Tienes que poner atención a lo que te digo, por favor.
native_language_example: You have to pay attention to what I’m telling you, please.

meaning: to drive someone crazy; to get on someone’s nerves (to make them very nervous/irritated).
additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: "Me/Te/Le/Nos/Os/Les pone de los nervios" (or with a noun: "A Juan lo/le pone de los nervios"). It often describes repeated annoying behavior or a stressful situation. Stronger than "poner nervioso/a" (more like "make me lose patience").
target_language_example: Ese ruido me pone de los nervios.
native_language_example: That noise drives me crazy / gets on my nerves.

meaning: to start; to set in motion; to get going (a plan, project, machine, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for initiating something that will run or develop—like starting a machine/engine, launching a project, or implementing a plan. Very common in formal and everyday contexts. Often appears with nouns like: un proyecto, un plan, una iniciativa, una campaña, una máquina, el motor. Similar idea to “arrancar” for machines, but “poner en marcha” is broader and can be used for plans/projects too.
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a poner en marcha el nuevo proyecto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to launch/get the new project started.

meaning: to put (someone/something) in danger; to endanger.
additional_notes: Used to talk about causing risk or harm. Common patterns: "poner en peligro a alguien" (to endanger someone) and "poner en peligro algo" (to jeopardize something). You can also use it in passive-like statements: "Se puso en peligro la vida de..." (Someone’s life was put at risk).
target_language_example: No debes poner en peligro a tus amigos; maneja con cuidado.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t put your friends in danger; drive carefully.

additional_notes: Used for preparing the table before a meal (placing plates, cutlery, glasses, napkins, etc.). Common with verbs like ayudar a (to help), dejarme (let me), and expressions of time (me tomó unos minutos…).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner la mesa mientras yo cocino?
native_language_example: Can you set the table while I cook?

meaning: to cheat on (a partner); to be unfaithful.
additional_notes: A common idiom meaning to have an affair while in a relationship. It’s used with a direct object (the person being cheated on): "Le puso los cuernos a Ana" = "He cheated on Ana." You may also hear the noun phrase "los cuernos" alone ("Me puso los cuernos" = "She cheated on me").
target_language_example: Dicen que él suele poner los cuernos a sus parejas.
native_language_example: They say he tends to cheat on his partners.

meaning: to get in touch with; to contact.
additional_notes: Used when you want to communicate with someone (by phone, email, etc.). It’s the reflexive form of “poner en contacto con” (to put someone in contact with). You can change “me” to match the person: “ponerte / ponerse / ponernos / ponerse en contacto con”.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ponerme en contacto con tu jefe, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you get me in touch with your boss, please?

meaning: to contact him; to get in touch with him.
additional_notes: Literally “to put myself in contact with him.” Used for making communication (call, message, email, etc.). You can change the pronoun and person: ponerme/ponerte/ponerse/ponernos/ponerse en contacto con + persona (con ella, con ellos, con usted). Often used with intentar, poder, querer, or in the past: Me fue imposible ponerme en contacto con él.
target_language_example: No puedo ponerme en contacto con él hoy, pero le escribiré mañana.
native_language_example: I can’t get in touch with him today, but I’ll write to him tomorrow.

meaning: to catch up; to get up to date.
additional_notes: Used for catching up on missed information, work, messages, news, or someone’s life: "ponerse al día con el trabajo / con las noticias / con alguien". It’s reflexive (me/te/se/nos/os/se) and the verb changes with the subject (pongo/pones/pone/ponemos/ponéis/ponen).
target_language_example: Es importante ponerse al día con el trabajo antes del lunes.
native_language_example: It’s important to catch up on work before Monday.

meaning: to agree; to come to an agreement.
additional_notes: Used when two or more people reach an agreement after discussing something. Very common with "con" (with someone) and "en/sobre" (on/about something): "ponerse de acuerdo con alguien" / "ponerse de acuerdo en algo". Can also mean to coordinate plans: "Nos ponemos de acuerdo" = “We’ll work it out / we’ll agree on a plan.”
target_language_example: Tenemos que ponerse de acuerdo en la hora para vernos.
native_language_example: We have to agree on the time to meet.

meaning: To stand up (to get to a standing position).
additional_notes: Uses reflexive "ponerse" to mean "to get" into a new state/position. Often used when someone moves from sitting/lying down to standing. Common with requests and instructions: "Ponte de pie" (stand up) and formal "Póngase de pie" (stand up).
target_language_example: Es hora de ponerse de pie.
native_language_example: It's time to stand up.

additional_notes: Imperative of poner + direct object pronoun lo (“it”) + en (“on/in”). Used to tell someone where to place an object: en un sobre (in an envelope), en la mesa (on the table), en la pared (on the wall), en la mano (in your hand). With “tú” commands: Ponlo en…, and in negative: No lo pongas en….
target_language_example: Ponlo en la mochila, por favor.
native_language_example: Put it in the backpack, please.

meaning: "for God's sake" / "oh my God" (an exclamation for emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to show frustration, surprise, or urgency, often when asking someone to do something: “Por Dios, dime…” It can also be used more literally in religious contexts meaning “by God” or “from God,” e.g., “enviado por Dios” (“sent by God”).
target_language_example: Por Dios, por lo menos contéstame.
native_language_example: For God's sake, at least answer me.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally (not on purpose). Common with verbs like tirar (throw away), borrar (delete), encontrar (find), golpear/pegar (hit), and with reflexive constructions like “me encontré con…” (I ran into…).
target_language_example: Lo hice por accidente, perdón.
native_language_example: I did it by accident, sorry.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a place near where the speaker is, often a general area rather than an exact spot: "vive por acá" = "lives around here." It can also be used to guide someone: "Venga por acá" = "Come this way." Contrast with "por allá" (over there / that way, farther from the speaker).
target_language_example: Si pasas por acá mañana, llámame.
native_language_example: If you come by here tomorrow, call me.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens before the expected time. Common with thanks and apologies: “Gracias por adelantado” = “Thanks in advance,” and “disculparse por adelantado” = “to apologize in advance.” Also used with payments: “pagar por adelantado” = “to pay in advance/upfront.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes enviarme la información por adelantado?
native_language_example: Can you send me the information in advance?

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or will be done temporarily, up to a later change or decision. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (Por ahora, ...), or after what it modifies (Es suficiente por ahora.).
target_language_example: Por ahora, vamos a esperar aquí.
native_language_example: For now, we’re going to wait here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an indefinite or not-important place. Common with verbs like ver (to see): "lo vi por ahí" = "I saw him somewhere/around"; andar/estar: "anduve/estuve por ahí" = "I was around"; preguntar: "preguntaré por ahí" = "I'll ask around" (asking different people/places).
target_language_example: Creo que dejé mis llaves por ahí.
native_language_example: I think I left my keys around here somewhere.

meaning: for some reason; for something (a specific thing).
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) "for some reason" (often implying there’s a reason behind it): "Por algo preguntas" = "You’re asking for a reason."
2) "for something" meaning “to get/to fetch something”: "Fue a la cocina por algo de café" = "He went to the kitchen for some coffee."
Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Si estás nervioso, por algo será.
native_language_example: If you’re nervous, there must be a reason.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the exact reason, or when you suggest there may be a (possibly meaningful) reason. It can go at the beginning of the sentence ("Por alguna razón, ...") or after the verb ("... por alguna razón"). In expressions like "Todo pasa por alguna razón," it can imply "everything happens for a reason."
target_language_example: Por alguna razón, hoy estoy de buen humor.
native_language_example: For some reason, I’m in a good mood today.

meaning: 'over there' / 'over that way' (in that direction, at some distance).
additional_notes: Used to point out a place or thing that’s not close to the speaker. Often goes with gestures or words like "mira" (look). "Allá" implies farther away than "aquí" (here) or "ahí" (there/near you). You’ll commonly hear it at the end of a sentence: "Está… por allá."
target_language_example: El baño está por allá, al fondo.
native_language_example: The bathroom is over there, at the back.

meaning: over there; around there (in that area).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an imprecise location or direction away from the speaker, often when pointing or giving directions. It can also mean “around there” in the sense of “in that area/nearby,” and with verbs of movement it means going/passing “through/that way” (e.g., pasar por allí = to pass by there).
target_language_example: La tienda queda por allí, cerca de la plaza.
native_language_example: The store is over there, near the plaza.

meaning: “for God’s sake” / “for the love of God” (used to show frustration, disbelief, or to beg).
additional_notes: Common exclamation used to emphasize what you’re saying—often when you’re annoyed, shocked, or pleading. It can appear alone (“¡Por amor de Dios!”) or before/after a request (“Por amor de Dios, vístete.” / “Vístete, por amor de Dios.”). Can sound dramatic or rude depending on tone; not necessarily religious in intent.
target_language_example: Por amor de Dios, baja la música, que estoy trabajando.
