"Su" is formal/polite "your" (to one person) or can mean "his/her/their" depending on context. You’ll also hear "por tu ayuda" when speaking informally to someone you address as "tú."
target_language_example: Gracias por su ayuda, señor.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, sir.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without help, supervision, or support from others. It can also suggest acting independently of a group or instructions. Variants with other possessives are common (por mi cuenta, por tu cuenta, por nuestra cuenta), but "por su cuenta" is used for he/she/you formal/they.
target_language_example: Tom investigó por su cuenta.
native_language_example: Tom investigated on his own.

meaning: because of him/her/them; it’s his/her/their fault.
additional_notes: Used to blame someone for a bad result. It often introduces the cause: “Por su culpa, …” or appears after the statement: “Todo esto es por su culpa.” The “su” is formal “your” (usted) or “his/her/their,” so the exact person comes from context. Similar options: “por tu culpa” (because of you / your fault, informal-singular), “por mi culpa” (my fault).
target_language_example: Llegué tarde por su culpa.
native_language_example: I was late because of him/her/them.

additional_notes: Used to say something is being done to help or protect the person it affects (even if they don’t like it). Often said as a warning or justification. The possessive changes with the person: por mi propio bien (for my own good), por tu propio bien (for your own good), por nuestro propio bien (for our own good), por su propio bien (for his/her/their/your formal own good).
target_language_example: Vinimos a decirle algo por su propio bien.
native_language_example: We came to tell you something for your own good.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or that something turned out well. Common at the start of a sentence (Por suerte, …). In some regions you may hear/see it followed by "que" ("Por suerte que…") with the same meaning: "Luckily, …".
target_language_example: Por suerte, llegamos a tiempo.
native_language_example: Luckily, we arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to show obvious agreement, certainty, or to confirm something politely. Often placed at the start or end of a sentence (“Por supuesto, …” / “…, por supuesto.”).
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Por supuesto.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: Used to show strong agreement or that something is obvious/expected. Common as a short reply (“—¿Puedes ayudarme? —Por supuesto.”). Also used parenthetically to emphasize a statement (similar to “of course” in English).
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Por supuesto.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or agree with what was just asked or said. It’s often followed by a full sentence (por supuesto que + verb), but in conversation you can also answer simply: “Por supuesto.”
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Por supuesto que sí.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

additional_notes: “Por supuesto” means “of course/certainly.” Adding “que” introduces the clause, and “lo” is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (or sometimes “him/that”), referring to something already known from context: Por supuesto que lo conozco. = “Of course I know him/it.” You can swap the verb to fit the situation: por supuesto que lo tengo (I have it), lo era (it was), lo ha hecho (he/she has done it), etc.
target_language_example: Por supuesto que lo entiendo.
native_language_example: Of course I understand it.

additional_notes: Used to strongly and confidently deny something (often as an immediate reply). "Por supuesto" means "of course," and adding "que no" makes it an emphatic negative. It can sound polite or firm depending on tone (e.g., "No, por supuesto que no, señora"). You can also attach an object/pronoun after it: "Por supuesto que no lo hizo" = "Of course he/she didn’t do it."
target_language_example: —¿Te molesta si abro la ventana? —Por supuesto que no.
native_language_example: —Do you mind if I open the window? —Of course not.

additional_notes: Used to give a very definite, confident “yes,” often as a warm reassurance or strong agreement. You can say it by itself (“Por supuesto que sí.”) or after another agreement word like “claro.” The tone depends on context: it can be affectionate with terms like “cariño/amorcito,” or sarcastic/insulting if paired with an insult.
target_language_example: —¿Vienes mañana? —Por supuesto que sí.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Of course.

meaning: for his/her/their; because of his/her/their; by his/her/their.
additional_notes: "Por" has several common meanings (often "for," "because of," or "by"), and "sus" means "his/her/their" (plural: used with plural nouns, or with singular nouns in some regions). Together, "por sus" introduces the reason/cause ("because of their..."), what someone is fighting/doing something for ("for their..."), or the means of identification ("by their..."). The exact translation depends on context: e.g., "luchar por sus derechos" = "fight for their rights"; "identificar por sus huellas" = "identify by their fingerprints."
target_language_example: Lo conocen por sus buenos modales.
native_language_example: They know him for his good manners.

additional_notes: Used to say someone acts/thinks independently or alone. Common patterns: “pensar por sí mismo/a” (think for oneself), “hacerlo por sí solo/a” or “ir por sí solo/a” (do/go alone), and “hablar por sí solo(s)” (speak for itself/themselves—be self-explanatory). The reflexive pronoun changes to match the person: por mí, por ti, por sí (él/ella/usted), por nosotros/as, por vosotros/as, por sí (ellos/ellas/ustedes).
target_language_example: Algunas personas parecen nunca aprender a pensar por sí mismas.
native_language_example: Some people seem never to learn to think for themselves.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone/independently, without help or influence from others. It’s the feminine form; for a man: “por sí mismo,” for a group: “por sí mismos/as.” It can also mean “in itself” (e.g., “La victoria por sí misma…” = “Victory in itself…”).
target_language_example: María aprendió a cocinar por sí misma.
native_language_example: María learned to cook by herself.

meaning: by himself; on his own; for himself (i.e., independently).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone acts independently, without help or outside direction; also used for thinking/deciding independently (“for himself”). It agrees with gender/number: por sí misma (she), por sí mismos (they, masc./mixed), por sí mismas (they, fem.). Common with verbs like hacer, decidir, pensar.
target_language_example: Tom lo hizo por sí mismo.
native_language_example: Tom did it by himself.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without help, or that something is so clear it needs no explanation (e.g., "Los resultados hablan por sí mismos" = "The results speak for themselves"). The pronoun changes to match the person/number: por mí mismo/a, por ti mismo/a, por sí mismo/a, por sí mismos/as.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: ellos pueden hacerlo por sí mismos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: they can do it by themselves.

meaning: by himself/itself; on his/its own; (also) speaks for itself.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone/without help, or that something is self-evident (“it speaks for itself”). It agrees with the subject: por sí solo (masc. sing.), por sí sola (fem. sing.), por sí solos / por sí solas (plural). Often corresponds to “alone” or “on your own” in English.
target_language_example: Tom pintó la casa por sí solo.
native_language_example: Tom painted the house by himself.

meaning: by phone; on the phone (using a phone call).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like llamar (to call) and hablar (to talk) to say something is done via a phone call, not in person or by text. With estar, it often means someone is currently on a call: Está por teléfono / Está hablando por teléfono.
target_language_example: ¿Podemos hablar por teléfono esta tarde?
native_language_example: Can we talk on the phone this afternoon?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “por” + “ti” (the informal form of “you” after prepositions). Common when saying you did something on someone’s behalf or because of them (Lo hago por ti = I do it for you), and also in set feelings like “feliz por ti” = happy for you. For a formal or plural “you,” use “por usted” or “por ustedes.”
target_language_example: Hice esto por ti porque te quiero ayudar.
native_language_example: I did this for you because I want to help you.

additional_notes: Used when telling a woman to do something herself (to see/check/understand/decide from her own experience), often meaning “don’t rely on what others say.” It’s feminine because of "misma"; for a man: "por ti mismo." You’ll also hear "por mí mismo/a" (for myself) and "por sí mismo/a" (by itself / on its own, or for himself/herself).
target_language_example: No te lo puedo explicar: tendrás que descubrirlo por ti misma.
native_language_example: I can’t explain it to you: you’ll have to figure it out for yourself.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you personally do something, decide, or experience something without relying on others (“see for yourself,” “decide for yourself,” “do it yourself,” “think for yourself”). It can also mean “for yourself” in the sense of self-respect ("respeto por ti mismo"). Variation by gender/number: por ti misma (female), por vosotros mismos/mismas (you all, Spain), por ustedes mismos/mismas (you all, Latin America).
target_language_example: No te lo creas; compruébalo por ti mismo.
native_language_example: Don’t just believe it; check it for yourself.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (la + noun) to mean either (1) spread across an area: por toda la cara = “all over the face”, or (2) lasting for an entire time/extent: por toda la eternidad = “for all eternity”. For a masculine noun, use por todo el.
target_language_example: Tenía pintura por toda la camiseta.
native_language_example: He had paint all over his T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something lasts without end (often in dramatic, religious, or poetic contexts). It commonly follows a verb like estar, vivir, sufrir, or durar: “estar en paz por toda la eternidad.”
target_language_example: Te amaré por toda la eternidad.
native_language_example: I will love you for all eternity.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is in many places, spread around, or happening in many areas. Often follows verbs like "hay" (there is/are), "estar" (to be), or "ver" (to see): "Hay ___ por todas partes" = "There are ___ everywhere."
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, había vasos por todas partes.
native_language_example: After the party, there were cups everywhere.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (el + noun) to say something is spread across a place ("por todo el piso", "por todo el pasillo") or lasts for an entire period of time ("por todo el verano"). For feminine nouns, use "por toda la" (e.g., "por toda la casa").
target_language_example: Busqué mis llaves por todo el apartamento.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys all over the apartment.

meaning: all over the world; around the world.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens/exists in many places worldwide. Common with verbs like viajar (to travel), conocer (to know), haber (there is/there was), and tener (to have): “viajó por todo el mundo” = “she traveled around the world,” “había paz por todo el mundo” = “there was peace all over the world.”
target_language_example: Hay fans de esa banda por todo el mundo.
native_language_example: There are fans of that band all over the world.

meaning: all over the country; throughout the country.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or exists in many places across the entire country (distribution or spread). Often follows verbs like "viajar" (to travel), "extenderse" (to spread), or "tener" (to have) when talking about locations (branches, offices, influence, rumors, etc.).
target_language_example: Hay festivales por todo el país durante el verano.
native_language_example: There are festivals all over the country during the summer.

meaning: for everything that (…); because of all that (…).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or basis for something, referring back to all the things mentioned or understood from context. Often followed by a verb phrase: “por todo lo que + (someone) has done/said/been through.” In apologies it’s very common: “Perdón/Lo siento por todo lo que…”.
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho por mí.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you’ve done for me.

por todo lo que has hecho

target_language_multi_word_term: por todo lo que has hecho
additional_notes: Used to thank someone or show appreciation, often after help or support. You can add who it was for with "por mí" (for me), "por nosotros" (for us), etc. It can also stand alone as an incomplete phrase when the rest (like "gracias") is understood from context.
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho por mí.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you have done for me.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like gracias/perdonar/preocuparse/pagar to refer to “everything” in a broad, general way (often implying “everything you did” or “everything that happened”). In phrases like “gracias por todo” and “perdóname por todo,” it commonly means “for everything (overall)” rather than listing specific things.
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que hiciste por mí.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything you did for me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is present in many places, or that you looked in every place you could. Often with verbs like buscar (to look for) or hay (there is/are).
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, había vasos por todos lados.
native_language_example: After the party, there were cups everywhere.

meaning: “by/for/through all the …” (por + todos los + plural noun).
additional_notes:
The meaning depends on context:
- **by all the …** (who does something): *entendido por todos los humanos* (“understood by all humans”).
- **for all the …** (reason/charge): *por todos los crímenes* (“for all the crimes”).
- **through all the … / past all the …** (movement): *pasaron por todos los hoteles* (“they went through/past all the hotels”).
Also appears in fixed exclamations like **“¡Por todos los cielos!”** = “For heaven’s sake!” (more dramatic/old-fashioned).
target_language_example: Te lo digo por todos los motivos posibles.
native_language_example: I’m telling you for every possible reason.

meaning: by all means; by any means possible.
additional_notes: Used to say you will do everything possible to achieve something (sometimes with a sense of urgency or determination). Often follows a verb like intentar, hacer, conseguir, salvar, evitar. It can also be used alone as an emphatic reply meaning “Absolutely / By all means.”
target_language_example: Tengo que encontrar mis llaves por todos los medios.
native_language_example: I have to find my keys by any means possible.

additional_notes: Used with a duration of time to say how long something lasted. Often used with the preterite to describe a completed period in the past (e.g., Estudié…, Fui…, Estuvimos…), and also with quedarse/estar to describe how long someone stayed/was somewhere or in a state.
target_language_example: Viví en Madrid por tres años.
native_language_example: I lived in Madrid for three years.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **por** + possessive **tu** (“your”). **Por** is very common and changes meaning with context. With **por tu + noun**, it can express: reason/cause (**Gracias por tu ayuda** = “Thanks for your help”), topic (**preocupado por tu futuro** = “worried about your future”), exchange/value (**por tu dinero** = “for your money”), purpose/occasion (**por tu cumpleaños** = “for your birthday”), or a route/means (**mira por tu ventana** = “look through/out your window”).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu tiempo.
native_language_example: Thanks for your time.

meaning: for your help; because of your help.
additional_notes: Used to express gratitude ("Gracias por tu ayuda", "Estoy agradecido/a por tu ayuda") or to say that something happened thanks to someone’s help ("De no haber sido por tu ayuda..." = "If it hadn’t been for your help..."). "Por" here can mean both "for" (reason/thanks) and "because of" (cause).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda; no podría haberlo hecho sin ti.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help; I couldn’t have done it without you.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing/saying something to benefit the other person, often as advice, a warning, or even a mild threat (“you’d better… for your own good”). It can sound caring or controlling depending on tone and context. You can change the person: por mi bien (for my own good), por su bien (for his/her/your formal/their own good), por nuestro bien (for our own good).
target_language_example: No salgas solo de noche, por tu bien.
native_language_example: Don’t go out alone at night, for your own good.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a bad result. Often has an angry or accusatory tone. You can change the person: por mi culpa (my fault), por su culpa (your fault—formal / his/her fault), por nuestra culpa (our fault). Similar: es tu culpa (it's your fault).
target_language_example: Llegamos tarde por tu culpa.
native_language_example: We’re late because of you / It’s your fault we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to say you did or said something to help someone, even if it feels unpleasant or they don’t like it. Often appears with advice or warnings (e.g., “Te lo digo por tu propio bien”). You can change the person: “por mi propio bien” (for my own good), “por su propio bien” (for his/her/their own good), “por nuestro propio bien” (for our own good).
target_language_example: Tienes que descansar un poco; es por tu propio bien.
native_language_example: You have to rest a bit; it’s for your own good.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **por** followed by **un** (“a/an”), so it’s usually the start of a longer phrase: **por un + noun**. Common uses include: **cause/agent** (“because of / by”): *por un ruido* = “because of a noise”; **movement through** (“through”): *por un cielo* = “through a sky”; **duration** (“for”): *por un par de meses* = “for a couple of months”; **exchange/distribution** (“for/each”): *Tú por un hermano, yo por el otro* = “You for one brother, me for the other.”
target_language_example: Me desperté por un ruido extraño.
native_language_example: I woke up because of a strange noise.

additional_notes: Used to introduce one side of an argument, comparison, or situation. It’s often paired with "por otro lado" ("on the other hand") to show contrast, but it can also appear alone to present a first point before adding more context.
target_language_example: Por un lado quiero ir, pero por otro lado no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: On the one hand I want to go, but on the other hand I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration. Often follows a verb to say how long something lasted (e.g., estar, quedarse, vivir). You can also hear close variations like “durante mucho tiempo” or “por mucho tiempo.”
target_language_example: No te he visto por un largo tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you for a long time.

meaning: 'for a minute' (for a short time; sometimes 'by a minute').
additional_notes: Used to say something will last a short time: Déjame pensar por un minuto. It can also mean 'only for a moment' when asking for someone’s time: Solo necesito a Tom por un minuto. With times/being late, it can mean 'by a minute' (difference of one minute): Se me pasó el tren por un minuto (I missed the train by a minute).
target_language_example: Espera por un minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for a minute, please.

meaning: for a moment; for a short time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that lasts briefly. Often with commands/requests (Quédate..., Espera...) meaning “for a moment.” In negative expressions like “ni por un momento,” it means “not even for a moment” (not at all).
target_language_example: Espera por un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for a moment, please.

meaning: for a couple of days (for a few days).
additional_notes: Used to say something will last a short time, usually around two days (but it can also mean “a few days” in casual speech). Often used with verbs like irse, quedarse, estar, dejar, or vivir to talk about being somewhere temporarily.
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme aquí por un par de días.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay here for a couple of days.

meaning: for a while; for a short time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts temporarily. It can refer to minutes or longer, but it usually implies “not permanently.” Common with verbs like estar, quedarse, sentarse, esperar, dejar (a alguien) solo. You can add “más” to mean “a little longer”: por un rato más.
target_language_example: Quédate conmigo por un rato, por favor.
native_language_example: Stay with me for a while, please.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts/continues for a period of time (often temporary). Common with past or ongoing actions: "funcionó por un tiempo" (it worked for a while), "ha estado... por un tiempo" (has been... for some time), "sólo será por un tiempo" (it’ll only be for a while).
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme aquí por un tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a while.

additional_notes: Used to express duration (how long something lasts). It often appears with activities or states: "leer por una hora" (read for an hour), "descansar por una hora" (rest for an hour). In everyday speech, "durante una hora" is a very common alternative with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Estudié por una hora antes del examen.
native_language_example: I studied for an hour before the exam.

meaning: for a reason; for a purpose.
additional_notes: Used to say that something has a specific cause, explanation, or purpose—often implying it’s not accidental. Very common in reflective phrases like “Todo pasa por una razón” (“Everything happens for a reason”). You can also use it to emphasize why something is the way it is: “Es el número dos por una razón.”
target_language_example: Todo pasa por una razón, aunque no lo entendamos ahora.
native_language_example: Everything happens for a reason, even if we don’t understand it now.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions after "por" to say how long something lasts or has lasted (duration). Often used with estar + past participle/adjective: "He estado aquí por una semana". In many situations, especially with "llevar" or in some regions, you may also hear "una semana" or "desde hace una semana" depending on whether you mean duration vs. since a starting point.
target_language_example: He trabajado aquí por una semana.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for a week.

meaning: for once; just this one time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something should happen at least one time, especially if it usually doesn’t. Often appears in commands or complaints: “Hazlo por una vez” (do it for once). It can sound frustrated or critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: Por una vez, escúchame antes de decidir.
native_language_example: For once, listen to me before you decide.

meaning: 'defeated' (in the phrase “darse por vencido” = 'to give up').
additional_notes: Almost always used with the reflexive verb “darse”: “me doy por vencido” (I give up), “se dio por vencido” (he/she gave up). It means to stop trying because you think you can’t win or succeed.
target_language_example: No me doy por vencido; voy a intentarlo otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m not giving up; I’m going to try again.

meaning: 'yet to come' / 'still to come' (in the future).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that hasn’t happened yet. Common patterns: **estar por venir** (“to be yet to come”): *Lo peor está por venir.* It can also describe a future thing like an adjective after a noun: *una tarea por venir* (“a task still to come”). Note: **por + infinitive** can also mean “for + -ing” in other contexts (e.g., *Gracias por venir* = “Thanks for coming”), but **por venir** in *está por venir* means “yet to come,” not “for coming.”
target_language_example: Lo más difícil todavía está por venir.
native_language_example: The hardest part is still to come.

additional_notes: Used to say how many things happen or are done in each single occasion. Often appears with a number: "dos por vez" (= two at a time) or in instructions/limits: "solo una persona por vez" (= only one person at a time). In many contexts, Spanish also uses "a la vez" for “at the same time,” but "por vez" focuses on a per-occasion limit.
target_language_example: Solo se permite una persona por vez.
native_language_example: Only one person is allowed at a time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you won’t ask/say/do something again (often as a warning or to show impatience). Common with verbs like pedir (to ask for/request), preguntar (to ask), and hablar (to talk).
target_language_example: Te lo digo por última vez: no entres aquí.
native_language_example: I’m telling you for the last time: don’t come in here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the final point in a list, sequence, or explanation (similar to “lastly” or “and finally”). It can stand alone as a short transition (“Por último.”). Often followed by a comma: “Por último, …”.
target_language_example: Y por último, vamos a pagar la cuenta.
native_language_example: And finally, we’re going to pay the bill.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, followed by a description/identity of “you” with the verb **ser** (eres = “you are”). It introduces a cause: **[result] + porque eres + [adjective/noun]**. (Don’t confuse **por qué** = “why?” with **porque** = “because”.)
target_language_example: No voy a cambiar de plan porque eres mi invitado.
native_language_example: I’m not going to change the plan because you’re my guest.

meaning: 'because that's what…' (explaining a reason for something).
additional_notes: Used to justify or explain a statement by saying that something is simply the case or is what people do. It’s followed by a verb phrase (e.g., es, hacemos, hace la gente, tiene que pasar) and often has a tone of “that’s just how it is.”
target_language_example: No voy a discutir, porque eso es lo que quiere.
native_language_example: I'm not going to argue, because that's what he/she wants.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason/explanation. "Porque" = "because" and "estaba" is the imperfect of "estar" (I/he/she was), often used for temporary states or conditions (e.g., oscuro, sediento, avergonzado, decaído). It’s usually followed by an adjective or phrase describing the situation: "porque estaba cansado/a".
target_language_example: No salí porque estaba cansado.
native_language_example: I didn’t go out because I was tired.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason for an action in the past. "porque" = "because" (introduces the cause), and "estaba lloviendo" is the past continuous/imperfect form meaning it was raining (ongoing background situation). You can swap the subject/action: "Me fui temprano porque estaba lloviendo".
target_language_example: Cancelamos el picnic porque estaba lloviendo.
native_language_example: We canceled the picnic because it was raining.

meaning: “because I …” / “because (of) me …” (giving a reason that involves the speaker).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reason clause: **porque** + **me** (object pronoun) + verb. Often followed by more pronouns, like **porque me lo dijo** (“because he/she told me”). In English you usually translate the whole clause, not word-for-word (“because me” is not natural in English).
target_language_example: No fui porque me sentía cansado.
native_language_example: I didn’t go because I felt tired.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason that includes a negation (no). Often followed by a verb phrase: “porque no hay…” (because there isn’t…), “porque no tenía…” (because he didn’t have…). Don’t confuse with “¿por qué no?” (with accent and question marks), which means “why not?”
target_language_example: No salimos porque no tengo dinero.
native_language_example: We’re not going out because I don’t have money.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s no clear reason or explanation, or that someone did/feels something without a specific cause. It can also be a short, slightly dismissive answer to “¿Por qué?” (Why?): “—¿Por qué? —Porque sí.”
target_language_example: No quiero salir hoy, porque sí.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out today, just because.

additional_notes: Used to talk about whether something might happen or be true. It’s usually followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., “posibilidad de sobrevivir” = “chance of surviving”). In questions and comparisons, it often means “who has a better chance of…?”.
target_language_example: No hay mucha posibilidad de encontrar entradas hoy.
native_language_example: There isn’t much chance of finding tickets today.

meaning: “I’d rather die.” (used to strongly reject something).
additional_notes: From preferir (to prefer) in the conditional: preferiría = “I would prefer.” It’s often followed by antes que / que (“rather than”) + infinitive: Preferiría morir antes que levantarme temprano. This is usually hyperbole for emphasis, not a literal wish to die.
target_language_example: Preferiría morir antes que mentirte.
native_language_example: I’d rather die than lie to you.

additional_notes: Used to express a personal preference. You can follow it with a comparison using either "a" or "que": "Prefiero X a Y" or "Prefiero X que Y" (both mean “I prefer X to Y / rather than Y”). "Quedarme" is the reflexive infinitive of "quedarse" (“to stay/remain”), so it literally means “to stay myself (here).”
target_language_example: Hoy hace frío; prefiero quedarme en casa que salir.
native_language_example: It’s cold today; I’d rather stay home than go out.

meaning: '(the) question, please' (used politely in requests like 'Answer the question, please.')
additional_notes: Often appears after an instruction involving a question: "Responde/Responda a la pregunta, por favor" = "Answer the question, please." You’ll usually hear it with the article ("la pregunta") or with "esta pregunta" ("this question"). Note: "pregunta" means "question"—it is not related to English "pregnant."
target_language_example: Responde a la pregunta, por favor.
native_language_example: Answer the question, please.

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to someone you address as usted. Structure: preguntarle + algo + a + [person] (optional). The "le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to you (formal), to him, to her.” For an informal “you,” use preguntarte algo.
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿puedo preguntarle algo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you something?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question (often polite or a bit serious). It’s the infinitive phrase “preguntar” (to ask) + “-te” (to you) + “algo” (something). Commonly appears after verbs like “quiero/debo/tengo que” (I want/must/have to) or in questions like “¿Puedo preguntarte algo?”
target_language_example: ¿Te puedo preguntarte algo rápido?
native_language_example: Can I ask you something quickly?

meaning: to ask you the same thing.
additional_notes: Used when you were going to ask the same question as someone else, or to turn a question back on the other person (often with iba a / estaba a punto de / podría / puedo). The structure is preguntar + te (to you) + lo mismo (the same thing).
target_language_example: ¡Qué casualidad! Iba a preguntarte lo mismo.
native_language_example: What a coincidence! I was going to ask you the same thing.

additional_notes: Used with the verb preguntar + si to introduce an indirect yes/no question. With a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se pregunto si) it usually means “to wonder if” (thinking to yourself). Without reflexive (te/le pregunto si) it means “to ask (someone) if”.
target_language_example: Me pregunto si hoy va a llover.
native_language_example: I wonder if it’s going to rain today.

additional_notes: Preterite (past) of **preguntar** (“to ask”) + **a**, which often introduces the person being asked (**preguntó a María** = “he/she asked María”). It’s also used before embedded question words: **preguntó a dónde**, **preguntó a quién**, **preguntó a con quién** (“asked where/who/with whom”). Spanish needs **a** here even though English usually doesn’t say “asked to…”.
target_language_example: El profesor me preguntó a qué hora llegué.
native_language_example: The teacher asked me what time I arrived.

additional_notes: Used to report an indirect question in the past. "Preguntó" is simple past (preterite) of "preguntar" (to ask). "Dónde" introduces “where.” "Vivía" is imperfect of "vivir" (to live), common after "preguntó" to describe a situation that was true at that time. You can add who lived: "Me preguntó dónde vivía mi tío" (He asked me where my uncle lived).
target_language_example: El policía me preguntó dónde vivía.
native_language_example: The police officer asked me where I lived.

additional_notes: “Preguntó” is the simple past (preterite) of preguntar: “(he/she) asked.” With “por qué” it introduces an indirect question: “asked why + clause” (e.g., “preguntó por qué estaba llorando”). If you add “se” (se preguntó por qué), it often means “wondered why” to yourself.
target_language_example: Me preguntó por qué no fui a la fiesta.
native_language_example: She asked me why I didn't go to the party.

meaning: "(he/she) asked if / whether" (introduces an indirect yes/no question).
additional_notes: Used when reporting a yes/no question in the past: *X preguntó si...* = “X asked if/whether...”. After **si**, Spanish typically uses normal statement word order (not question word order). **Preguntó** is the preterite (simple past) form of *preguntar* for él/ella/usted.
target_language_example: La profesora preguntó si teníamos tarea.
native_language_example: The teacher asked if we had homework.

additional_notes: "Pregúntale" is the tú command form of "preguntar" plus the indirect object pronoun "le" (“to him/her/you-formal”). "A" introduces the person you’re asking (e.g., "a Tom", "a tu madre", "a un policía"). In some contexts it can be playful/figurative (e.g., "Pregúntale a mis labios" = “ask my lips,” implying a kiss).
target_language_example: Pregúntale a tu profesor qué significa esta palabra.
native_language_example: Ask your teacher what this word means.

meaning: to catch fire; to set on fire.
additional_notes: Used for something starting to burn on its own (La casa prendió fuego = “The house caught fire”) or for causing something to burn (Prendió fuego a la basura = “He/She set the trash on fire”). Often appears as "prenderse fuego" (to catch fire) and with "a" before the thing set on fire: "prender fuego a + noun".
target_language_example: La sartén empezó a prender fuego, pero la apagamos rápido.
native_language_example: The frying pan started to catch fire, but we put it out quickly.

additional_notes: Used with estar (or sentirse) to describe feeling worried/anxious about a situation or thing. It’s often followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., preocupado por tener que...).
target_language_example: Estoy preocupado por el examen de mañana.
native_language_example: I'm worried about tomorrow's exam.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is ready to face something or to do something. Common with estar: estar preparado para + noun ("para lo peor", "para todo") or + infinitive ("para hacer..."). It agrees with the person: preparado (m.), preparada (f.), preparados/as (plural).
target_language_example: No estoy preparado para hablar en público todavía.
native_language_example: I'm not ready to speak in public yet.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (preparando) to talk about an action in progress, often with estar (está preparando la cena = is preparing dinner). It can also appear with time expressions or other tenses (había llevado dos horas preparando la cena = had spent two hours preparing dinner).
target_language_example: Estoy preparando la cena, ¿puedes poner la mesa?
native_language_example: I’m preparing dinner—can you set the table?

additional_notes: Used with the verb presentar when you introduce a person. Structure: (Yo) le/les presento a + person (the person being introduced) (often followed by: a + the person(s) they’re being introduced to). The indirect object pronoun shows who you’re introducing them to: le (to you/him/her), os (to you all), les (to you all/them).
target_language_example: Te presento a mi hermana, Laura.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my sister, Laura.

additional_notes: Command form (tú) of "prestar atención". Use it to tell someone to focus/notice something. Often followed by "a" + noun/pronoun: "Presta atención a ella" (Pay attention to her), or used by itself: "Presta atención" (Pay attention). In the negative: "No presta atención" = "He/She doesn’t pay attention".
target_language_example: Presta atención a lo que dice el profesor.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what the teacher says.

additional_notes: Common command form (tú) of the verb phrase "prestar atención a". It’s followed by "a" + the person/thing you should focus on: "a ella", "a él", "a ellos", "a las bicicletas". You can also use it in other forms, e.g., "Presto atención a..." (I pay attention to...), "Presta atención" (Pay attention).
target_language_example: Presta atención a lo que dice el profesor.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what the teacher is saying.

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase **prestar atención** (“to pay attention”). Often used with **estar** to describe what someone is doing right now: **estás prestando atención** = “you’re paying attention.” You can add **a** to say what you’re paying attention to: **prestar atención a algo**. Negative is very common: **no estás/no estaba prestando atención** = “you’re/I wasn’t paying attention.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no estaba prestando atención a lo que dijiste.
native_language_example: Sorry, I wasn’t paying attention to what you said.

additional_notes: Common construction: (subject) + prestar + atención. Often followed by “a” to specify what you’re paying attention to: “Prestar atención a las instrucciones / a lo que dice.” Frequently used with “tener que” (to have to): “Tienes que prestar atención.” Imperatives use “presta atención” (tú) or “presten atención” (ustedes).
target_language_example: Tienes que prestar atención a lo que te digo, por favor.
native_language_example: You have to pay attention to what I’m telling you, please.

meaning: to pay attention to; to notice; to listen to carefully.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or with "lo que" + a clause: "prestar atención a su historia" (to his/her story) / "prestar atención a lo que dice" (to what he/she says). Often appears in advice or commands with "deberías" or "tienes que". Negative form: "no prestar atención a" = not to pay attention to / to ignore.
target_language_example: Deberías prestar atención a su historia.
native_language_example: You should pay attention to his/her story.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "prestar" (to lend) in the set phrase "prestar atención" = "to pay attention." It’s followed by "a" + a noun/pronoun or "a lo que" + verb ("to what..."). You can change the amount: "prestar mucha/poca atención a" (pay a lot/little attention to).
target_language_example: Tienes que prestar más atención a las señales de tráfico.
native_language_example: You have to pay more attention to the traffic signs.

additional_notes: Refers to the first person you ever loved romantically (often your first serious crush or relationship). Common in phrases like “Mi primer amor” (my first love) and “nunca se olvida al primer amor” (you never forget your first love).
target_language_example: Nunca voy a olvidar a mi primer amor.
native_language_example: I’m never going to forget my first love.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first day of something: a job, school, being somewhere new (primer día aquí / en la unidad), etc. You can also use it for the first day of a period: “primer día de la regla” (Spain) or more generally “primer día del período/menstruación.”
target_language_example: Hoy es mi primer día en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Today is my first day at work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone ranked #1 in a contest, race, competition, etc. Often appears with verbs like ganar (to win) and obtener (to get/earn): “ganó/obtuvo el primer lugar”. It can also describe the top spot being reserved or assigned: “El primer lugar está reservado para…”.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ganó el primer lugar en el torneo de ajedrez.
native_language_example: My sister won first place in the chess tournament.

additional_notes: Title for the head of government in many countries (not the same as the president/monarch). Used with or without an article: “el primer ministro” (the prime minister) or as a direct form of address: “Bienvenido, primer ministro.” Often capitalized in English; in Spanish it may appear in lowercase unless used as part of an official title in context.
target_language_example: El primer ministro dará un discurso esta noche.
native_language_example: The prime minister will give a speech tonight.

meaning: "first step" (the first action in a process).
additional_notes: Used literally for the first physical step, but very often figuratively for the first stage/action toward a goal or change ("el primer paso para..." = "the first step to..."). It can appear with or without the article: "el primer paso" (the first step) or "un primer paso" (a first step, one initial step).
target_language_example: Hablar con ella es el primer paso para arreglar el problema.
native_language_example: Talking to her is the first step to fixing the problem.

meaning: the first train (of the day / earliest train).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the earliest train on a route, often in the morning. It commonly appears with verbs like tomar/coger (to take), alcanzar (to catch), llegar a tiempo para (to arrive in time for), and perder (to miss).
target_language_example: Si quieres llegar temprano, toma el primer tren.
native_language_example: If you want to arrive early, take the first train.

meaning: (1) first class (travel/service); (2) first class / first lesson (in a course).
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: in transport/hospitality it refers to a higher, more expensive category of service (often said as "en primera clase" or "boleto en primera clase"). In school or a course, "mi/nuestra primera clase" means the first session/lesson with a teacher or group.
target_language_example: Compré un boleto en primera clase para el tren.
native_language_example: I bought a first-class ticket for the train.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the Catholic sacrament/ceremony when a child receives Communion for the first time. It’s commonly preceded by "la" (la primera comunión) and used with "de" to say whose it is (la primera comunión de mi hermana). People often talk about preparing/studying for it and about special clothes (e.g., a dress or suit).
target_language_example: Mis primos vienen a mi primera comunión este sábado.
native_language_example: My cousins are coming to my First Communion this Saturday.

additional_notes: Used for the head of government when the person is a woman. Often appears with the definite article: "la primera ministra". Capitalization varies, but in news and formal writing you may see it capitalized when used as a title before a name (e.g., "la Primera Ministra Ana Pérez").
target_language_example: La primera ministra dará un discurso esta noche.
native_language_example: The prime minister will give a speech tonight.

additional_notes: Used in grammar and storytelling. In Spanish, "primera persona" refers to speaking from the point of view of the speaker (yo/nosotros). Common phrases: "en primera persona" (in the first person) and "narrado/escrito en primera persona" (told/written in the first person).
target_language_example: La novela está escrita en primera persona.
native_language_example: The novel is written in the first person.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing/experiencing something for the first time. Often appears with "la" (la primera vez) or in the pattern "Primera vez que..." (= "First time that..."). Can also refer to someone’s first sexual experience, depending on context.
target_language_example: Es la primera vez que vengo aquí.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come here.

meaning: "the first to" (do something) / "first in" (a place or list).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone is the first person to do something: "el primero en + infinitive" (e.g., "el primero en moverse"). It can also be used with places/lists to mean first in a location or order ("el primero en la escena", "el primero en la lista"). Changes for gender/number: "el primero / la primera / los primeros / las primeras en".
target_language_example: Hayes es el primero en moverse.
native_language_example: Hayes is the first to move.

additional_notes: Usually appears as **lo primero que** + verb (“the first thing that I…”) or **el/la primero/a que** + verb (“the first person who…”). It introduces what happens first or what you remember/notice first. For people, Spanish often uses **que** (not *quien*) after *el/la primero/a*.
target_language_example: Lo primero que quiero hacer hoy es descansar.
native_language_example: The first thing I want to do today is rest.

additional_notes: Used for basic medical help given right away in an emergency (before a doctor/ambulance). Often appears with words like curso (course), equipo/kit (kit), or maletín (case): “un curso de primeros auxilios”, “un kit de primeros auxilios”. Usually plural in Spanish.
target_language_example: ¿Hay alguien que sepa dar primeros auxilios?
native_language_example: Is there anyone who knows first aid?

meaning: "(it’s) likely/probable that…" (followed by a verb in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used after expressions like Es probable que…, Es muy/poco probable que…, No es probable que…, Parece probable que…. Because it expresses likelihood/uncertainty, Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive after que: Es probable que venga. (If you state it as a fact, you might use the indicative: Es probable que viene is generally avoided in standard Spanish.)
target_language_example: Es probable que lleguemos tarde por el tráfico.
native_language_example: It’s likely we’ll arrive late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the specific issue or reason something isn’t working as expected. Often appears with a possessive: "Mi/Su/Tu problema es que...". You can also add emphasis with "El único problema es que..." ("The only problem is that...").
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero el problema es que no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but the problem is that I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: tener problemas para + infinitive. It means you have difficulty doing an action (often because it’s hard, confusing, or there’s an obstacle). In the negative (no tener problemas para), it means it was easy for someone to do it. Also common: tener problemas para + noun (e.g., problemas para el trabajo = problems at work), but with verbs it’s usually infinitive.
target_language_example: Tengo problemas para entender este acento.
native_language_example: I have trouble understanding this accent.

additional_notes: Used to say what subject someone teaches. After "profesor de" you usually name the subject (e.g., español, italiano, literatura). "Profesor" can mean a school teacher or a university professor, depending on context. Feminine form: "profesora de".
target_language_example: Soy profesor de español.
native_language_example: I am a Spanish teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say someone teaches the English language. For a female teacher, say "profesora de inglés." Often used with "ser" to talk about someone’s job ("Soy profesor de inglés"), or with "tener" to talk about having a teacher ("Tengo un profesor de inglés").
target_language_example: Mi hermano es profesor de inglés en una escuela secundaria.
native_language_example: My brother is an English teacher at a high school.

additional_notes: Used on signs and in rules to say that smoking is not allowed. Often appears as a standalone sign: “PROHIBIDO FUMAR”. With a person, you’ll often hear “tener prohibido + infinitive”: “Tienes prohibido fumar aquí” = “You’re not allowed to smoke here.”
target_language_example: En este edificio está prohibido fumar.
native_language_example: In this building, smoking is prohibited.

additional_notes: Used to make a strong commitment about what you will do (or what will happen). You can add an object pronoun: "te prometo que…" = "I promise you that…" (informal you), "le prometo que…" = "I promise you that…" (formal you). Often followed by a verb in the future or a negative statement: "Prometo que no…"
target_language_example: Te prometo que mañana te llamo.
native_language_example: I promise you that I’ll call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the forecast for upcoming weather (rain, temperature, wind, etc.). Very common in news and everyday conversation: “¿Cuál es el pronóstico del tiempo?” You can also say “el pronóstico” when the context is clearly weather.
target_language_example: Según el pronóstico del tiempo, mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place or object belongs to a private person or company and is not public. Common on signs and warnings (often implying “no trespassing” or “no public access”). You can say: Es/Esto/Esta es propiedad privada ("This is private property") or Estás en propiedad privada ("You’re on private property").
target_language_example: No entres: es propiedad privada.
native_language_example: Don’t go in: it’s private property.

additional_notes: Use "proteger" with the personal "a" before a direct object that is a person (or a pet): "proteger a mi hijo", "proteger a Tom". With things, you usually don’t use "a": "proteger la casa". You can add "de" to say what you’re protecting someone from: "proteger a alguien de algo".
target_language_example: Quiero proteger a mis amigos de cualquier peligro.
native_language_example: I want to protect my friends from any danger.

additional_notes: Used in politics and government for a law that is being proposed and discussed/voted on, but hasn’t become law yet. You’ll often see it with verbs like aprobar (to pass/approve), votar (to vote), and estar en contra / a favor (to be against / in favor).
target_language_example: El Congreso debatirá el proyecto de ley mañana.
native_language_example: Congress will debate the bill tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used in two main ways: (1) **la prueba de + noun** = 'a test of' (e.g., *una prueba de fe*, *una prueba de sonido*). (2) **la prueba de que + clause** = 'proof/evidence that' (e.g., *la prueba de que está vivo*). Also appears in the fixed expression **a prueba de + noun** meaning '…-proof' (resistant to), as in *a prueba de fallos* ('fail-safe').
target_language_example: Este mensaje es la prueba de que todo salió bien.
native_language_example: This message is proof that everything went well.

additional_notes: Used as a holiday greeting/wish around New Year’s (often in the set phrase “Feliz y próspero año nuevo”). You can say it on its own or after a greeting like “¡Que tengas un…!”
target_language_example: ¡Feliz y próspero año nuevo para ti y tu familia!
native_language_example: Happy and prosperous New Year to you and your family!

additional_notes: Used to talk about the week after the current one. Often appears with the feminine article because semana is feminine: la próxima semana. Common with time prepositions like para (for/by next week) and hasta (until next week).
target_language_example: Nos vemos la próxima semana.
native_language_example: See you next week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next occasion something will happen. Often appears with articles: "la próxima vez" = "the next time" (often a specific next occasion), "una próxima vez" = "a next time" (some future time, not necessarily scheduled). Common in goodbyes and promises: "Hasta la próxima vez" (Until next time), "para la próxima vez" (for next time).
target_language_example: La próxima vez, avísame con tiempo.
native_language_example: Next time, let me know ahead of time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was possible in the past, often when you’re not sure what really happened. It’s the past tense of “poder” (pudo) + “haber” + past participle: “pudo haber sido” (could have been), “pudo haber pasado” (could have happened). Also used in questions about unknown causes or responsible people: “¿Quién pudo haber…?” (Who could have…?).
target_language_example: Pudo haber sido un error, pero no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: It could have been a mistake, but I’m not sure.

meaning: “could have done” (it was possible in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the preterite of *poder* (*pudo*) + *haber* + past participle to express past possibility or speculation: *pudo haber hecho…* = “might/could have done…”. Often used to guess who did something (*La única persona que pudo haber hecho esto…*) or to say someone was/wasn’t capable of doing it (*Ella no pudo haber hecho tal cosa*). It can also appear with reflexives and other participles, e.g., *se pudo haber hecho daño* (“could have hurt himself/herself”).
target_language_example: Pudo haber hecho la tarea anoche, pero se quedó dormido.
native_language_example: He could have done the homework last night, but he fell asleep.

meaning: “could have been” (it’s possible that it was).
additional_notes: Uses the verb poder in the past (pudo) + haber + past participle (sido). It expresses possibility about a past situation or identity, often like a guess or speculation: “It might have been…” / “It could’ve been…”. Often followed by a noun or description: “pudo haber sido una buena persona”, “pudo haber sido Anglade”.
target_language_example: Pudo haber sido un error, pero ya no importa.
native_language_example: It could have been a mistake, but it doesn’t matter anymore.

meaning: (he/she) was able to solve the problem; managed to solve the problem.
additional_notes: Uses the preterite of poder (pudo) + infinitive to show that someone succeeded in doing something at a specific time. In negatives, it means someone was not able to: Nadie pudo resolver el problema = Nobody could solve the problem.
target_language_example: Por fin, Juan pudo resolver el problema después de intentarlo varias veces.
native_language_example: Finally, Juan was able to solve the problem after trying several times.

additional_notes: Formed with the present subjunctive of poder (pueda) + infinitive hacer. It’s commonly used after expressions like "algo/nada que..." (something/nothing that...), and after verbs/phrases of doubt, fear, or uncertainty (e.g., dudo que..., me temo que...). In these contexts Spanish uses the subjunctive because it’s not stated as a certain fact.
target_language_example: Si hay algo que pueda hacer, dímelo.
native_language_example: If there's anything I can do, tell me.

meaning: "Can you help me?" / "Could you help me?" (formal); also "(he/she/it) can help me."
additional_notes: Form of poder + ayudar + me. With a capital letter and/or question marks, it’s commonly a polite request to a stranger: «¿Puede ayudarme…?» (usted). Without question marks it can also be a statement about ability/possibility: «Nadie puede ayudarme» = “Nobody can help me.”
target_language_example: ¿Puede ayudarme a encontrar la estación, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me find the station, please?

additional_notes: Formed with the verb poder in the present tense (puede) + an infinitive (cambiar). It’s used to say something is possible: “can change.” The subject is often “él/ella/eso” or “esto” (it/this), and it can also be used with an indirect object like “te” (“puede cambiarte la vida” = “can change your life”).
target_language_example: Todo puede cambiar de un día para otro.
native_language_example: Everything can change from one day to the next.

additional_notes: Used with **confiar en + person/thing** (trust/rely on someone/something): *Puede confiar en Mary.* Also common with **confiar en que + clause** to mean **“trust that…”**: *Puede confiar en que todo saldrá bien.* Note: **confiar** is usually “to trust,” not “to confide (a secret).”
target_language_example: Puede confiar en mí; no se lo diré a nadie.
native_language_example: You can trust me; I won’t tell anyone.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: **tan + adjective/adverb + como** = “as + adjective/adverb + as.” Here it’s **rápido** (fast) used as an adverb with **correr**. Change **puede** for other forms (e.g., **puedo/puedes/pueden correr tan rápido como...**) or swap the verb/adverb (e.g., **puede hablar tan claro como...**).
target_language_example: Ella puede correr tan rápido como su hermano.
native_language_example: She can run as fast as her brother.

meaning: "might be" / "could be" (it/he/she might be in a place or state).
additional_notes: Present tense of poder + estar (3rd person singular). Used to express possibility about someone’s location or condition/state: Puede estar en casa. / Puede estar enfermo. It can also mean "can be" in general statements: Puede estar en cualquier parte. Negative: No puede estar lejos ("It can’t be far").
target_language_example: No contesta; puede estar durmiendo.
native_language_example: He’s not answering; he might be sleeping.

meaning: “there may be / there can be” (it’s possible that there is/are).
additional_notes: From "poder" (can/may) + "haber" (there is/are). Used to express possibility about existence or occurrence: "puede haber cambios" = “there may be changes.” In negative form: "no puede haber" = “there can’t be / there must not be.” "Haber" stays in the singular even if what follows is plural: "puede haber doce cadáveres" (not *pueden haber*).
target_language_example: Puede haber un problema con la reserva, así que llega temprano.
native_language_example: There may be a problem with the reservation, so arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability to speak (in general) or to speak a particular language. "Puede" is the present tense of "poder" (can/to be able to) for él/ella/usted. For other subjects: "puedo hablar" (I can speak), "puedes hablar" (you can speak), "podemos hablar" (we can speak). Often followed by a language: "puede hablar español".
target_language_example: ¿Usted puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak more slowly, please?

additional_notes: “Puede” is from poder (to be able to/can) and is also used as a polite formal “you” (usted). Use “hablar + language” to say you speak a language: “hablar francés/inglés/español”. For other subjects: “puedo hablar francés” (I can), “puedes hablar francés” (you informal), “podemos hablar francés” (we can).
target_language_example: ¿Usted puede hablar francés?
native_language_example: Can you speak French?

meaning: "can do" / "is able to do" (also: "may do" in the sense of permission).
additional_notes: Formed with poder (to be able to / can) + infinitive hacer (to do / to make). "Puede" is for él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). Often followed by "lo que" to mean "whatever" (e.g., "Puede hacer lo que quiera" = He/She can do whatever he/she wants). In negative form, "no puede hacer" means "can’t do" (or "mustn’t" depending on context).
target_language_example: ¿Puede hacer una copia de este documento?
native_language_example: Can you make a copy of this document?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “poder + infinitive” (here, hacer). It expresses ability/possibility: “(he/she/you formal/it) can do that.” Often used after a subject like alguien, nadie, todo el mundo, cualquier niño, etc. You can swap the subject: “Yo puedo hacer eso” (I can do that), “¿Puedes hacer eso?” (Can you do that?).
target_language_example: ¿Crees que él puede hacer eso solo?
native_language_example: Do you think he can do that alone?

meaning: “can do it” / “is able to do it.”
additional_notes: Made of "puede" (he/she/you-formal can) + "hacerlo" (to do it). Used to say someone has the ability or permission to do something. The subject can be explicit (Él/ella/usted) or implied by context.
target_language_example: ¿Crees que ella puede hacerlo sola?
native_language_example: Do you think she can do it by herself?

additional_notes: From poder (can/may) + irse (to leave/go away). Often used to give permission or to dismiss someone politely, usually addressing usted. Common with a destination: “Puede irse a casa” (You may go home). With “ya” it means “you can leave now / you may go now.”
target_language_example: Gracias, ya puede irse.
native_language_example: Thank you, you may leave now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability to swim. It’s the verb poder (to be able to/can) + nadar (to swim). Puede is the “he/she/you (formal)” present-tense form: él/ella/usted puede nadar. For “I can swim,” say: Yo puedo nadar. You can add adverbs or comparisons: puede nadar bien (swim well), puede nadar más lejos (swim farther), puede nadar una milla (swim a mile).
target_language_example: Él puede nadar bien.
native_language_example: He can swim well.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is possible or might occur. It can be general (Todo puede pasar. = Anything can happen.) or refer to someone (Le puede pasar a cualquiera. = It can happen to anyone.). Often appears in set phrases like "Nunca se sabe qué puede pasar" (You never know what might happen).
target_language_example: No te preocupes; puede pasarle a cualquiera.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; it can happen to anyone.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or a potential result. Often followed by a noun/adjective/phrase: "Puede ser útil" (It can be useful), "Puede ser peligroso" (It can be dangerous). Also used with "pero" to mean "may be ... but": "Puede ser joven, pero..." (He/She may be young, but...). In impersonal form with "se" it means "one/you can't...": "No se puede ser rápido..." (You can't be fast...).
target_language_example: Puede ser verdad, pero no tenemos pruebas.
native_language_example: It may be true, but we don’t have proof.

additional_notes: Used to say something is possibly (sometimes) a certain way: *X puede ser muy + adjective* (bitter, cold, complex, etc.). It’s the verb **poder** (“can/may”) + **ser** (“to be”) + **muy** (“very”). The subject can come before or after, and extra location info can go at the end: *El invierno puede ser muy frío en Nueva York.*
target_language_example: Este trabajo puede ser muy difícil.
native_language_example: This job can be very difficult.

meaning: "it can be / it could be"; also "maybe."
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "poder ser" ("to be able to be"). It’s used (1) to express possibility about what something is or might happen: "Puede ser esta noche" (It could be tonight); (2) in the pattern "Puede ser que + subjunctive" to mean "It may be that...": "Puede ser que eso tenga..."; and (3) as a short reply meaning "maybe" or "could be": "Puede ser, sí." In negatives like "no puede ser", it often means "it can’t be" or "that can’t be" (sometimes like "no way").
target_language_example: —¿Es verdad? —Puede ser, no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: —Is it true? —Maybe, I’m not sure.

meaning: "it may be that" / "it could be that".
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "Puede ser que venga"). You’ll also hear the shorter version "puede que" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Puede ser que lleguemos tarde por el tráfico.
native_language_example: We might arrive late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Formed with the verb poder + infinitive: puede (he/she/it/you formal) + tener (to have). Use it to express possibility, ability, or permission to have something. In negative form (no puede tener), it often means "cannot have" (impossible or not allowed), and it can also be used for logical deduction: "Él no puede tener hambre" = "He can’t be hungry" (it doesn’t make sense given the situation). For other subjects: puedo/podemos/pueden tener, etc.
target_language_example: El estrés puede tener un gran impacto negativo en tu salud.
native_language_example: Stress can have a big negative impact on your health.

additional_notes: Form of **poder + infinitive**: **puede ver** is 3rd person singular (“he/she can see”) and also the **usted** form (“you can see,” formal). Common in the impersonal/passive **se puede ver** = “you can see / it can be seen.”
target_language_example: Desde aquí, puede ver toda la ciudad.
native_language_example: From here, you can see the whole city.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility/uncertainty. It is typically followed by the subjunctive: puede que + (yo) llegue, (ella) sepa, (ellos) hayan salido. Often used at the start of a sentence, but it can also come after the subject (e.g., Ese plan puede que funcione).
target_language_example: Puede que mañana llueva, así que llevo paraguas.
native_language_example: It might rain tomorrow, so I’m bringing an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty about a past event. It’s the structure "puede que" + present subjunctive; with "haya" (from "haber") it’s followed by a past participle to form the present perfect subjunctive (e.g., "puede que haya llovido" = "it may have rained"). Often interchangeable with "quizá(s)" or "tal vez" in similar meanings.
target_language_example: Puede que haya olvidado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: I may have forgotten my keys at home.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s the structure: "puede que" + verb in the present subjunctive; here "haya" is the subjunctive of "haber" (to exist/there to be). Often followed by a noun: "puede que haya una salida" (there may be an exit), "puede que haya otros" (there may be others).
target_language_example: Puede que haya un error en la dirección.
native_language_example: There may be a mistake in the address.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility in the negative. It’s short for the structure **puede que + subjunctive**: *Puede que no estemos...*, *Puede que no esté...*. Common in conversation to hedge or show uncertainty, like “might not.”
target_language_example: Puede que no tenga tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I might not have time today.

meaning: "it may not be" / "it might not be".
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or possibility that something is NOT the case. It commonly introduces the subjunctive (here, sea from ser). You can also change the subject: Puede que él no sea… / Puede que no sea… (implied “it”). Often followed by an adjective or noun: suficiente, feliz, verdad, un resfriado, etc.
target_language_example: Puede que no sea la mejor idea.
native_language_example: It might not be the best idea.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s built from **puede que** (“it’s possible that”) + **sea** (subjunctive of *ser*, “to be”), so it’s normally followed by the **subjunctive**: *Puede que sea así.* You can change the verb to match the meaning: *Puede que esté…* (from *estar*), *Puede que tenga…* (from *tener*), etc.
target_language_example: Puede que sea verdad, pero no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: It might be true, but I’m not sure.

meaning: "I/you/he/etc. might have to" (it’s possible that someone will need to).
additional_notes: Combines possibility + obligation: **puede que** (“it may be / it’s possible that”) + **tener que** (“to have to”). After *puede que*, Spanish normally uses the **subjunctive**, so you’ll see forms like *tenga que, tengas que, tenga que, tengamos que, tengan que* (depending on who). Often followed by an infinitive: *tenga que ir / ayudar / despedir...*
target_language_example: Puede que tenga que quedarme en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: I might have to stay home tonight.

additional_notes: "Pueden" is the present tense of "poder" for "they" or "you (plural, Spain)", and it’s followed by an infinitive like "hacer". It talks about ability or possibility: "pueden hacer eso" = "they can do that." Often used in phrases like "pueden hacer mucho" (they can do a lot) or "¿qué pueden hacer?" (what can they do?).
target_language_example: Mis amigos pueden hacer la tarea después de cenar.
native_language_example: My friends can do the homework after dinner.

additional_notes: Formed by **pueden** (they/you-plural can) + **ser** (to be). Used to talk about possibilities or general truths about a plural subject: *Las gaviotas pueden ser…* You can often translate it as “can be” (ability/possibility) or “may be” (possibility).
target_language_example: Las reglas pueden ser diferentes en cada país.
native_language_example: The rules can be different in each country.

additional_notes: Formed with **poder** (to be able to/can) + infinitive: **pueden + ver**. It can refer to **they** (e.g., *Los gatos pueden ver...* = “Cats can see...”) or **you all** (Spain: *ustedes pueden ver...*). Very often it appears with **se** in an impersonal/passive sense: **se pueden ver...** = “you can see...” / “...can be seen.”
target_language_example: Desde aquí pueden ver el mar.
native_language_example: From here, they/you all can see the sea.

meaning: “can you help me?” / “could you help me?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for help. Often said as a question: «¿Puedes ayudarme?». You can make it more polite by adding «por favor» (¿Puedes ayudarme, por favor?) or more formal by using «¿Puede ayudarme?» (usted).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ayudarme a encontrar la estación, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me find the station, please?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is trustworthy. It’s the verb phrase "confiar en" (to trust in/on) with "puedes" (you can). Add a person or pronoun after "en": "puedes confiar en mí / él / ella / ellos". You can also limit it with phrases like "hasta cierto punto" (up to a point).
target_language_example: Puedes confiar en nosotros; no vamos a decir nada.
native_language_example: You can trust us; we won’t say anything.

meaning: "you can count on" (you can rely on / depend on).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is reliable or will be there to help. It’s the tú form of the verb phrase "contar con"; you can change it to other people: "puedo contar con..." (I can count on...), "pueden contar con..." (you all/they can count on...). Often followed by a person ("Puedes contar con Jack") or a pronoun/thing ("Puedes contar con ello" = you can count on it).
target_language_example: No te preocupes; puedes contar con nosotros.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; you can count on us.

meaning: "you can be sure" / "you can be certain."
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or emphasize certainty. Common patterns: "De eso puedes estar seguro" and "Puedes estar seguro de (algo)" (= you can be sure about something), or "Puedes estar seguro de que..." (= you can be sure that...). Often implies a promise or strong confidence.
target_language_example: Puedes estar seguro de que te llamaré mañana.
native_language_example: You can be sure that I’ll call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Formed from poder (to be able to) + hacer (to do/make). Used to say what someone is allowed or able to do. It’s often followed by an infinitive or by “lo” (it): “Lo puedes hacer…” = “You can do it…”. You’ll also see it in fixed phrases like “puedes hacer uso de…” = “you can make use of…”, and in role/option lists: “Puedes hacer de…” = “You can play/act as…”.
target_language_example: Si tienes tiempo, lo puedes hacer mañana.
native_language_example: If you have time, you can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (puedes = “you can”) + hacer (“to do/make”) + lo que quieras (“whatever you want”). It’s commonly used to give permission, say someone is free to choose, or express “it’s up to you.” The phrase can sound supportive (“Of course, do whatever you want”), but depending on tone it can also sound dismissive or annoyed (“Fine, do whatever you want”). You’ll often hear it with more options added: “puedes hacer lo que quieras, ir donde quieras” (“you can do whatever you want, go wherever you want”).
target_language_example: Si terminas tu tarea, puedes hacer lo que quieras.
native_language_example: If you finish your homework, you can do whatever you want.

meaning: "you can do it" / "you can do that".
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone or say they’re capable of doing something. "Puedes" can be "you can" (ability) or "you may" (permission), but in this phrase it’s usually about ability/encouragement. "Hacerlo" = "do it" (hacer + lo). You can add emphasis with the subject pronoun: "Tú puedes hacerlo."
target_language_example: No te rindas: puedes hacerlo.
native_language_example: Don’t give up: you can do it.

additional_notes: From poder (to be able to / can) + ir (to go). Used to give permission or say something is possible. Often followed by a condition: “Puedes ir si…” (You can go if…). With a reflexive pronoun (te puedes ir), it commonly means “you can leave/go home now.”
target_language_example: Puedes ir al baño, pero vuelve rápido.
native_language_example: You can go to the bathroom, but come back quickly.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is allowed/able to go somewhere. "Puedes" is the tú form of "poder" (can/to be able to), followed by "ir" (to go) + "a" (to/at). Often followed by a place ("puedes ir a la estación") or by an infinitive to mean "you can go to do something" ("puedes ir a visitar el Louvre").
target_language_example: Puedes ir a mi casa después de clase.
native_language_example: You can go to my house after class.

meaning: “you can leave” / “you can go (away)” (also: “you may leave”).
additional_notes: From poder (you can/are allowed to) + irte (to go away/leave; ir + te). Used to give permission (“Puedes irte ahora.”), to say it’s possible to leave, or in the negative to forbid it (“No puedes irte.” = “You can’t/you’re not allowed to leave.”). Often implies leaving the place or going away from the speaker. Can be followed by details: “por…” (by/through a route), “si quieres” (if you want).
target_language_example: Si ya terminaste, puedes irte.
native_language_example: If you’re done already, you can leave.

meaning: “you can call me …” or “you can phone/call me.”
additional_notes: From poder (you can) + llamar (to call) + me (me). With a name or nickname, it means how you’d like to be addressed: “Puedes llamarme Vanya” = “You can call me Vanya.” With time/conditions (cuando, esta tarde, si necesitas ayuda), it means to call on the phone: “Puedes llamarme cuando quieras” = “You can call me whenever you want.” Often softened with por favor.
target_language_example: Si tienes alguna pregunta, puedes llamarme mañana.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, you can call me tomorrow.

additional_notes: From poder (you can) + quedarte (to stay/remain). Often used to give permission or offer: Puedes quedarte conmigo/hasta esta noche/el tiempo que quieras (“You can stay with me/until tonight/as long as you want”). With "con + person/thing" it can mean “you can keep it / you can have it”: Puedes quedarte con mi camión (“You can keep my truck”).
target_language_example: Puedes quedarte aquí si quieres.
native_language_example: You can stay here if you want.

meaning: "you can stay here" / "you may stay here."
additional_notes: Used to give permission or allow someone to remain in a place. "Puedes" can mean either "can" (ability) or "may" (permission); in this phrase it usually means permission. Often followed by extra details like "conmigo" (with me), "en casa" (at home), "el tiempo que quieras" (as long as you want), "si quieres" (if you want), or conditions like "siempre que..." (as long as/provided that...).
target_language_example: Si no tienes dónde ir, puedes quedarte aquí esta noche.
native_language_example: If you have nowhere to go, you can stay here tonight.

additional_notes: Used to give someone permission to keep something or take possession of it. Very common with objects and money: “Puedes quedarte con el cambio” = “Keep the change.” With people, it can mean “you can stay with” or “you can take care of” someone (“Puedes quedarte con Colin” = “You can stay with Colin / You can keep Colin (with you)”), depending on context.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, puedes quedarte con mi paraguas.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you can keep my umbrella.

additional_notes: Used to offer permission (“You may use…”) or describe an available option (“You can use…”). Often followed by a thing (puedes usar el diccionario) or by “o” to present choices (puedes usar X o Y). In more formal Spanish, “puede usar” can be used for “you can use” (formal you).
target_language_example: Si no tienes efectivo, puedes usar mi tarjeta.
native_language_example: If you don’t have cash, you can use my card.

meaning: "you can use my..." (giving permission to use something of mine).
additional_notes: Used to offer or allow someone to use something that belongs to you. It’s typically followed by a noun: “Puedes usar mi coche/bolígrafo/ordenador…”. You can add “cuando quieras” (whenever you want) or “si quieres” (if you want) to soften it.
target_language_example: Puedes usar mi cargador si quieres.
native_language_example: You can use my charger if you want.

additional_notes: From poder (to be able to / can) + venir (to come). It can mean ability (“can you come?” / “if you can come”) or permission (“you may come”), depending on context. Used with conditions like si… (“if…”) and siempre que… (“as long as / provided that…”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a mi casa esta tarde?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house this afternoon?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "poder" (you can/are able to) + "ver" (to see). It can refer to physical sight (what is visible from a place, seeing in the dark, etc.) or to understanding/realizing something, especially with "que": "Puedes ver que es un error" = "You can see/tell it’s a mistake."
target_language_example: Desde aquí puedes ver el mar.
native_language_example: From here you can see the sea.

meaning: “I can help you.” / “Can I help you?”
