You can change **te veo** to match who you see: **lo/la veo** (him/her), **los/las veo** (them), **te veo** (you).
target_language_example: Cada vez que te veo, pienso en mi infancia.
native_language_example: Every time I see you, I think of my childhood.

additional_notes: Most commonly appears in the structure **tener que + infinitive**. With **tener**, it becomes **tener que tener + noun** (“to have to have … / must have …”), expressing necessity or requirement: *Tienes que tener dinero*, *Había que tener valor*. In comparisons, **que tener** can also mean “than to have”: *mejor X que tener Y* (“better to X than to have Y”).
target_language_example: Tienes que tener un boleto para entrar.
native_language_example: You have to have a ticket to get in.

meaning: "that he/she/you have..." (subjunctive), or "may you have..." (a wish).
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive of tener (tenga) after expressions like asegurarse de que (make sure that), decirle a alguien que (tell someone to), esperar que (hope that), and until/time phrases like hasta que (until). Also very common as a polite wish: "Que tenga(s) un buen..." = "Have a good..." (formal: tenga; informal: tengas).
target_language_example: Que tenga un buen viaje.
native_language_example: Have a good trip.

meaning: “have a nice day” (polite: “may you have a good day”).
additional_notes: Used as a polite goodbye or well-wish, often in customer service or formal situations. It uses the formal “usted” form (tenga = usted has), so it fits with señor/señora. It’s commonly preceded by “Gracias” or followed by a title: “Que tenga un buen día, señor/señora.”
target_language_example: Gracias por su ayuda; que tenga un buen día.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help; have a nice day.

meaning: Have a good day. (to you all)
additional_notes: A polite, common goodbye/well-wish addressed to more than one person (ustedes). Literally it uses the subjunctive meaning “may you have a good day.” For one person you can say: “Que tengas un buen día” (informal tú) or “Que tenga un buen día” (formal usted). Often used at the end of a conversation, e.g., when leaving a store or finishing a visit.
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; que tengan un buen día.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; have a good day.

meaning: “that you have” / “may you have” (subjunctive, used in wishes).
additional_notes: Used with the present subjunctive of tener (tengas) after expressions of emotion or desire (e.g., lamento, deseo) and in set phrases to wish someone well: “Que tengas buen día” = “Have a nice day” (literally “May you have a good day”). Often followed by a noun/adjective: que tengas hambre, que tengas suerte, que tengas un gran futuro.
target_language_example: Espero que tengas tiempo mañana.
native_language_example: I hope you have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: A common polite goodbye/well-wish. Literally “may you have a good day,” using the subjunctive (tengas) after que to express a wish. You can add a person or place: “Que tengas un buen día en el trabajo.”
target_language_example: ¡Hasta mañana! Que tengas un buen día.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow! Have a nice day.

que tengas un buen día en

target_language_multi_word_term: que tengas un buen día en
meaning: “Have a nice day at/in …” (a friendly wish).
additional_notes: Used to wish someone well as they go somewhere (work, school, the office, etc.). It uses the subjunctive ("que tengas") to express a wish. You typically add a place after "en": "Que tengas un buen día en el trabajo / en la escuela / en la oficina".
target_language_example: Que tengas un buen día en el trabajo.
native_language_example: Have a nice day at work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing something someone/ something possessed or contained in the past. Very common after verbs like saber (to know), ver (to see), demostrar (to show/prove): “No sabía que tenía…” = “I didn’t know (that) I had/it had…”. The verb tenía is the imperfect of tener, so it often implies an ongoing state or a background description in the past.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que tenía las llaves en el bolsillo.
native_language_example: I realized that I had the keys in my pocket.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect statement about an obligation in the past. It often follows verbs like darse cuenta de (to realize), decir (to tell), sentir (to feel), etc.: "Me di cuenta de que tenía que...". "Tenía que" is the imperfect of "tener que" and often suggests a felt/ongoing necessity at that time (not necessarily a single completed event).
target_language_example: Me dijo que tenía que levantarme temprano.
native_language_example: He told me that I had to get up early.

additional_notes: Often used after another clause with tan/tanto… que to mean “that everyone…”, or at the start of an instruction/wish with the subjunctive (Que + subjuntivo) to mean “Let everyone… / I want everyone to…”. Usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive in commands (Que todo el mundo esté / mantenga…).
target_language_example: Que todo el mundo apague el móvil durante la película.
native_language_example: Everyone, turn off your phone during the movie.

meaning: “(have) to take” (when used in “tener que tomar …”).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears after **tener que**: **tener que tomar + noun** = “to have to take + (something)”. **Tomar** often means “to take” (a bus, a decision, precautions, etc.). By itself, **que tomar** is usually just part of a longer phrase, not a standalone expression.
target_language_example: Tengo que tomar una decisión hoy.
native_language_example: I have to make a decision today.

meaning: to have to work; need to work.
additional_notes: Usually used as part of the structure **tener que + infinitive** to express obligation/necessity: **tener que trabajar** = “to have to work.” On its own, **que trabajar** is incomplete and depends on a previous verb like **tener** (e.g., **sin tener que trabajar** = “without having to work”).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to work.

meaning: "than your mother" or "that your mother…" (depending on context).
additional_notes:
This is a very common pattern with **que**:
- **Comparisons:** *más/menos… que tu madre* = “more/less … than your mother.”
- **Subordinate clause:** *quería que supieras que tu madre…* = “I wanted you to know that your mother…”
- It can also appear in **nadie más que tu madre** = “no one but your mother / nobody other than your mother.”
target_language_example: Eres más alto que tu madre.
native_language_example: You’re taller than your mother.

meaning: "that you" / "so that you" (introduces a clause where the subject is "you").
additional_notes: Used when the conjunction "que" starts a subordinate clause and you explicitly say the subject "tú" (often for emphasis or contrast). Common patterns: "para que tú + subjunctive" = "so that you..." (e.g., "para que tú pases"); and "y que tú + imperfect subjunctive" to add an idea about what you were/should have been (e.g., "y que tú fueras..."). Often Spanish drops the subject pronoun, so "que tú" can feel emphatic.
target_language_example: Lo hice para que tú estuvieras más tranquilo.
native_language_example: I did it so that you would be calmer.

meaning: "that you are" (introduces a clause explaining something).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions like demostrar (to show), imaginar (to imagine), descubrir (to discover), etc. "que" introduces a subordinate clause. "tú" is often optional in Spanish ("que eres"), but it’s included for emphasis or contrast. "eres" is the present tense of "ser" for "tú" (you are).
target_language_example: Me alegra saber que tú eres feliz aquí.
native_language_example: I’m happy to know that you are happy here.

additional_notes:
Used with **que** in two very common patterns:
- **Conjunction (subordinate clause):** after verbs like *asegurar, querer, decir, pedir*, etc. → *Quiero que usted…* = “I want you to…” (literally “I want that you…”).
- **Comparisons:** **más/menos… que usted** or **antes que usted** → “more/less… than you” / “before you.”
Also appears in the set phrase **Yo que usted…** = “If I were you…” (giving advice).
target_language_example: Yo que usted, le pediría perdón.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d ask for forgiveness.

meaning: “that you two …” / “I see/assume that you two …”.
additional_notes: Used when addressing two people (formal or plural “you”) and introducing a clause about them. Often appears after verbs like asumir/creer/ver (“to assume/believe/see”) or querer (“to want”)—e.g., “Quiero que ustedes dos…” = “I want you two to…”. With “que” here, English often drops “that.”
target_language_example: Necesito que ustedes dos lleguen temprano mañana.
native_language_example: I need you two to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like hacer (“to make”) to express making something worth the effort or suffering: hacer que valga la pena = “to make it worth it.” Literally “that it be worth the pain/effort,” so it often implies sacrifice or hard work. You can refer to living, doing a task, a trip, etc.
target_language_example: Vamos a hacer que valga la pena el viaje.
native_language_example: Let’s make the trip worth it.

meaning: “that you’re going to …” (introduces a clause about someone’s plan or intended action).
additional_notes: Common after verbs/expressions like decir, saber, entender, pensar, decidir, etc. to introduce what someone intends to do. Typically followed by an infinitive: que vas a + infinitivo (e.g., que vas a hacer, que vas a comer). Often appears inside longer statements and questions.
target_language_example: Tengo entendido que vas a pasar tus vacaciones en Nueva Zelanda.
native_language_example: I understand you’re going to spend your vacation in New Zealand.

meaning: “that (someone) go/goes” (subjunctive of ir, used after verbs like querer, necesitar, hacer).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause where the speaker wants/needs/makes someone go somewhere: “Quiero/Necesito/Haré que vaya…”. It often follows expressions of desire, necessity, influence, or purpose. Also appears in wishes like “Que vaya bien” = “I hope it goes well / Hope it goes well.”
target_language_example: Necesito que vaya contigo a la reunión.
native_language_example: I need him/her to go with you to the meeting.

meaning: "that you go" / "for you to go" (present subjunctive of "ir").
additional_notes: Used after expressions like "es hora de", "quiero que", "necesito que", "te aconsejo que", etc., to talk about someone going as something desired, required, recommended, or best. In "adondequiera que vayas" it means "wherever you go" (subjunctive after "wherever"). "Vayas" is the tú-form of the present subjunctive of "ir" (to go).
target_language_example: Quiero que vayas conmigo al mercado.
native_language_example: I want you to go with me to the market.

meaning: 'that you go to…' / 'that you’re going to…' (subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (wishes, worries, recommendations, time expressions), like: *Es hora de…*, *Me preocupa…*, *Esperamos…*. It introduces what you want/worry/hope will happen: *Me preocupa que vayas a la ciudad* = “I’m worried that you’ll go to the city.”
target_language_example: Quiero que vayas a casa temprano.
native_language_example: I want you to go home early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with **venga** (present subjunctive of *venir*). It commonly follows expressions that trigger the subjunctive, such as **necesitar que...** (“to need/want that...”) or time clauses like **después de que...** (“after...”), when the action is not yet certain or is in the future. It can also appear as a standalone wish/command: **¡Que venga!** (“Let him/her come!” / “Have him/her come.”).
target_language_example: Dile que venga mañana, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell him/her to come tomorrow, please.

meaning: "that you come" / "for you to come" (subjunctive, used after verbs like "want" or "prefer").
additional_notes: Used with verbs/expressions that introduce a desire, request, preference, or necessity (quiero, prefiero, necesito, te pido, es importante, etc.). It’s a que-clause + present subjunctive: venga(s) = "you come" (tú). Often appears in full phrases like "Quiero que vengas" (I want you to come).
target_language_example: Es importante que vengas temprano.
native_language_example: It’s important that you come early.

meaning: “that you come with us” / “for you to come with us.”
additional_notes: Used after verbs like necesitar (to need) and querer (to want) to ask or insist that someone come along with the group. It uses the subjunctive vengas (from venir) because it expresses a desire/need about someone else’s action. Often corresponds to English “I want/need you to come with us.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes confirmar que vienes? Queremos que vengas con nosotros.
native_language_example: Can you confirm you’re coming? We want you to come with us.

meaning: "that you come with me" (used to ask/insist that someone come with you).
additional_notes: Often follows verbs/expressions like querer (to want), pedir (to ask), ser mejor (it’s better), tener ganas de (to feel like). It uses the present subjunctive vengas (from venir) because it talks about what you want/request/suggest another person to do. Conmigo means “with me.”
target_language_example: Te ruego que vengas conmigo al médico.
native_language_example: I beg you to come with me to the doctor.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions that trigger the **imperfect subjunctive** in the past (wishes, requests, expectations, waiting): *querer que…*, *pedir que…*, *esperar que…*, *no esperaba que…*, *estar esperando a que…*. **Viniera** is the imperfect subjunctive of **venir** (to come), expressing something desired, expected, or uncertain rather than a simple past fact.
target_language_example: Yo le pedí que viniera temprano.
native_language_example: I asked him/her to come early.

meaning: 'that you would come' / 'for you to come' (imperfect subjunctive of venir).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions that trigger the subjunctive (wishes, preferences, emotions, etc.), especially in the past: esperaban/preferían/les molestaba + que + vinieras. It often implies an expected or desired action, not a simple statement of fact. Also appears after an implied verb of saying/requesting ("(Dijo) que vinieras").
target_language_example: Me alegró mucho que vinieras a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I was really happy that you came to the party.

meaning: to have to go back/return; to have to do again.
additional_notes: Almost always used after an obligation phrase like **tener que** (to have to) or **hay que** (one must): **tener que volver (a + infinitive / a + place)**. It can mean returning to a place (**volver al pueblo**) or repeating an action (**volver a hacerlo** = do it again).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero voy a tener que volver mañana.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I’m going to have to come back tomorrow.

meaning: "(that) you go back to" / "(that) you come back to" (followed by a verb or place).
additional_notes: Used after expressions like "es hora de...", "quiero que...", or "con la condición de que..." to introduce a clause in the present subjunctive: "que" + "vuelvas" (you return/go back) + "a" + infinitive/place. In English it’s often translated with "that you..." or just "you..." depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Necesito que vuelvas a intentarlo.
native_language_example: I need you to try again.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause and emphasize that something is already true or has already happened. Common patterns: **Ahora que ya + verb…** (“Now that you already…”), **…que ya no…** (“…that no longer…”). In reassuring statements like **Tranquilo, que ya vendrá**, **que ya** can mean “(don’t worry,) it’ll happen/they’ll come soon.”
target_language_example: Ahora que ya tienes el recibo, puedes devolver el producto.
native_language_example: Now that you already have the receipt, you can return the product.

additional_notes: Used when **que** introduces a subordinate clause and **ya no** signals a change from before: something used to happen/be true, but it isn’t now. Very common after verbs like *decir, ver, saber, acordar, decidir* (e.g., *Veo que ya no…*, *Decidimos que ya no…*). Word order can vary with the rest of the clause: *que ya no + verbo*.
target_language_example: Me dijo que ya no trabaja aquí.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn’t work here anymore.

additional_notes:
Used in two very common patterns:
1) After verbs/adjectives + que to introduce a clause with the subject “I”: Es imposible/Me molesta/No quiero que yo… (often followed by the subjunctive: que yo termine, que yo lea).
2) In comparisons: más/menos/mejor/peor … que yo = “... than I” (Spanish keeps “yo” after que in comparisons). Often “yo” is only used when you want to emphasize the subject; otherwise Spanish may omit it (Es imposible que termine…).
target_language_example: No creo que yo pueda ir hoy; hace más frío que yo pensaba.
native_language_example: I don’t think I can go today; it’s colder than I thought.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause after verbs like creer (to believe), saber (to know), pensar (to think), darse cuenta de (to realize), etc. Here, "era" is the imperfect of "ser" (to be), often used to describe what something/someone was like in the past or a past situation/background.
target_language_example: No sabía que yo era tan importante para ti.
native_language_example: I didn’t know that I was so important to you.

meaning: "that I ... it/him" (a clause introduced by *que* with *yo* as the subject and *lo* as the direct object pronoun).
additional_notes: *Que* often introduces a dependent clause: *para que yo lo + verb* (“so that I + verb + it/him”), usually with the **subjunctive**: *para que yo lo lea / resuelva*. In other contexts, *que yo lo + verb* can follow verbs like *olvidar, pensar* (“that I + verb + it/him”): *No olvides que yo lo traje*; *Pensabas que yo lo amaba*. Here *lo* refers to a masculine thing (*it*) or a man (*him*). Word order: *que* + subject (*yo*) + object pronoun (*lo*) + verb.
target_language_example: Te lo explico otra vez para que yo lo entienda bien.
native_language_example: I’ll explain it to you again so that I understand it well.

meaning: "as far as I know" / "to my knowledge".
additional_notes: Used to soften a statement and show you’re not 100% sure. Often appears in answers like “No, que yo sepa” (= “Not that I know of”) and can go at the beginning or end of a sentence: “Que yo sepa, …” or “…, que yo sepa.” It uses the subjunctive (sepa) after que.
target_language_example: Que yo sepa, no hay clases mañana.
native_language_example: As far as I know, there are no classes tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often appears after "que" to introduce a clause about a man/boy ("...that he..."): "Es cierto que él...", "Reconozco que él...", "después de que él...". It can also be used in comparisons after "mejor/peor/más/menos ... que" meaning "than him": "mejor que él". In many cases, Spanish can drop the subject pronoun and just use the verb ("Es cierto que va...") unless you need emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Me sorprende que él no haya llamado todavía.
native_language_example: It surprises me that he hasn’t called yet.

meaning: "that he was" (introduces what someone believed/said/proved about him).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions like creer (to believe), parecer (to seem), saber (to know), sospechar (to suspect), probar (to prove). It starts a subordinate clause: main clause + que + subject (él) + verb. Here, "era" is the imperfect of "ser" (he was), often used for descriptions or ongoing past situations. Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so you may also hear "que era" when the subject is clear.
target_language_example: Pensé que él era mi profesor, pero era el director.
native_language_example: I thought that he was my teacher, but he was the principal.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "decir" (to say), "pensar" (to think), "demostrar" (to prove), and "convencer" (to convince) to introduce what someone said/thought/proved. It’s a subordinate clause introduced by "que" = "that". In everyday Spanish, the subject pronoun "él" is often omitted if it’s clear: "Pensé que era inocente."
target_language_example: El informe confirmó que él era inocente.
native_language_example: The report confirmed that he was innocent.

meaning: "that he is" (introduces a clause about him).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions like admitir, pensar, parecer, olvidar, probar to introduce a statement about a male person. In Spanish, the subject pronoun (él) is often optional, so you’ll very commonly hear just “que es …”. Word order stays: que + (él) + es + description (adjective/noun phrase).
target_language_example: Sé que él es muy trabajador.
native_language_example: I know that he is very hardworking.

additional_notes: A very common subjunctive clause used after expressions of hope, desire, requests, doubt, or in time/condition phrases that refer to the future or something uncertain. Examples: “Espero que…”, “Nadie quiere que…”, “en caso de que…”, “la próxima vez que…”. You’ll often see it without the subject pronoun: “que venga”.
target_language_example: No creo que él venga hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t think he’ll come today.

additional_notes: Used to make a question sound more emphatic or specific than plain "qué". Very common before a verb: "¿Qué es lo que pasa?" = "What’s going on?" In indirect questions (after verbs like preguntar/saber), it appears without question marks: "Deberíamos preguntarle a Tom que es lo que piensa" = "We should ask Tom what he thinks." In standard spelling, the interrogative "qué" takes an accent ("qué es lo que"), but you may also see it written without the accent in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Que es lo que pasa?
native_language_example: What’s going on?

meaning: “what is it that…?” (an emphatic way to ask “what…?”)
additional_notes: Used to add emphasis or insistence in questions, often when you want a clearer or more specific answer. It’s commonly followed by a verb: “Que es lo que haces?” = “What is it that you’re doing?” In standard Spanish spelling, this is typically written with accents and opening question marks in questions: “¿Qué es lo que…?”; “qué” takes an accent when it’s interrogative.
target_language_example: Que es lo que piensas?
native_language_example: What is it that you think?

meaning: "How’s it going?/How are you?" (as a greeting); also used to propose an idea: "que tal si…" = "what if…?/how about if…?"
additional_notes: In standard Spanish spelling this is usually written with an accent and question marks: "¿qué tal?" and "¿qué tal si…?". You may still see it without punctuation/accents in casual texting ("que tal"). As a greeting it’s typically informal.
target_language_example: Que tal, Georg?
native_language_example: How’s it going, Georg?

meaning: "What are you going to do?" / "What will you do?"
additional_notes: Common question using the near-future construction **ir a + infinitive**: **vas a hacer** = “you’re going to do.” In standard written Spanish, the interrogative **qué** takes an accent when it means “what” (e.g., **¿qué vas a hacer?**). The version without accent (**que vas a hacer**) is often seen in informal texting, or when punctuation/accents are omitted.
target_language_example: No hay dinero; que vas a hacer ahora?
native_language_example: There’s no money; what are you going to do now?

additional_notes: Used with indirect object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/les) to say that clothes (and sometimes colors/styles) fit or look good on someone. Common patterns: “me queda bien” = it fits/suits me; “te queda bien” = it fits/suits you. For plural items you say “quedan bien” (e.g., “Estos zapatos me quedan bien”). Often used when trying on clothes or giving opinions.
target_language_example: ¿Esta chaqueta me queda bien?
native_language_example: Does this jacket fit/suit me well?

additional_notes: Used with clothing (and sometimes hairstyles/colors) to say something suits someone or looks flattering on them. It comes from the verb "quedar" (how something looks/turns out). The person it looks good on is an indirect object: me/te/le/nos/les queda muy bien. Common with "te" (you) or "le" (him/her/you formal).
target_language_example: Ese color te queda muy bien.
native_language_example: That color looks great on you.

meaning: to stay here; to remain here.
additional_notes: Used with the verb quedarse + aquí to express that someone will stay in this place for a period of time. Common with time phrases (un par de días, por una noche, hasta que...) and with permission/prohibition (¿Te vas a quedar aquí?, No os podéis quedar aquí.).
target_language_example: Entonces, ¿te vas a quedar aquí?
native_language_example: So, are you going to stay here?

meaning: to meet up with; to make plans to see (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a person to talk about arranging a meeting: "Quedar con Ana" = "to meet up with Ana" / "to make plans to see Ana." Often implies a planned appointment (time/place may be mentioned). In some contexts it can carry a romantic sense: "Está quedando con alguien" = "He/She is seeing/dating someone." Don’t confuse with "quedarse con", which means "to keep" (a thing) or "to stay with" (a person), e.g., "Me puedo quedar con el libro" = "I can keep the book."
target_language_example: He quedado con mi amigo a las seis para tomar un café.
native_language_example: I’m meeting up with my friend at six to have a coffee.

meaning: to stay/remain in; to meet up at (a place).
additional_notes: With the reflexive form ("quedarse en"), it means "to stay" somewhere: "quedarse en casa" (stay at home), "quedarse en la cama" (stay in bed). Without reflexive, "quedar en + place" often means "to arrange/agree to meet" at a place: "Quedamos en una cafetería" (We’re meeting at a café).
target_language_example: Quedamos en la plaza a las seis, pero yo me voy a quedar en casa si llueve.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at the plaza at six, but I’m going to stay home if it rains.

meaning: to be free/available; to become vacant.
additional_notes: Uses: (1) For time/plans: "¿Te queda libre el viernes?" = “Are you free on Friday?” / “Do you have Friday free?” (2) For places/things: "Quedó libre una mesa" = “A table became available.” In some contexts it can also mean “to go free” (e.g., after being detained or accused).
target_language_example: ¿Te queda libre esta tarde o mañana?
native_language_example: Are you free this afternoon or tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "quedarse" (to stay/remain). "-me" indicates the subject is "I" ("quedarme" = "to stay" for myself → "for me to stay"). Often used after another verb like "quiero" (I want): "Quiero quedarme aquí" = "I want to stay here."
target_language_example: Prefiero quedarme aquí un rato más.
native_language_example: I’d rather stay here a little longer.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "quedarse" (to stay/remain) + "en casa" (at home). "Quedarme" is the reflexive infinitive with the object pronoun "me" (I stay). You can change the pronoun depending on who stays: "quedarte" (you), "quedarse" (he/she/you formal), "quedarnos" (we), "quedarse" (they/you all). Often used with "tener que" (to have to) or "preferir" (to prefer).
target_language_example: Hoy no puedo salir; voy a quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: Today I can’t go out; I’m going to stay at home.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb quedarse + con. With people/places, it commonly means “to stay with” someone (remain together, stay over): Puedes quedarte con nosotros. With objects, it can mean “to keep”: Me quedo con el cambio (“I’ll keep the change”).
target_language_example: ¿Te puedes quedarte con nosotros esta noche?
native_language_example: Can you stay with us tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "quedarse" + adjective "dormido" (“asleep”). Very common for dozing off while doing something: "quedarse dormido viendo la televisión". It can also mean “to end up asleep” or “to oversleep” depending on context (e.g., being late because you fell asleep).
target_language_example: Mi padre suele quedarse dormido viendo la televisión.
native_language_example: My father often falls asleep while watching TV.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "quedarse" (to remain/to stay) + "en casa" (at home). Often used for plans or decisions not to go out: "Quiero/puedo/debo quedarme en casa". In past narratives you’ll also see "quiso quedarse" (he decided/wanted to stay) or "quería quedarse" (he wanted/was wanting to stay).
target_language_example: Él planea quedarse en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: He plans to stay at home tonight.

meaning: to run out of; to be left without.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say you no longer have something (often unexpectedly): "Me quedé sin dinero". It’s common in the past ("me quedé sin...") for something that happened, and in the present ("me quedo sin...") for what will happen if something continues.
target_language_example: Es fácil quedarse sin batería si dejas el GPS encendido todo el día.
native_language_example: It’s easy to run out of battery if you leave the GPS on all day.

meaning: 'to stay here' (telling one person to remain in this place).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "quedarse" (to stay/remain). "Quedarte" is the informal "tú" form meaning "for you to stay" or used after phrases like "deberías" (you should), "tienes que" (you have to), and "más te vale" (you’d better). To address someone formally, use "quedarse aquí" (usted).
target_language_example: Tienes que quedarte aquí hasta que vuelva.
native_language_example: You have to stay here until I come back.

additional_notes: Future tense of quedarse (“to stay/remain”). It often implies deciding to remain in a place for some time (temporarily or permanently). Common with reasons or time limits: “me quedaré aquí para…” (I’ll stay here to…), “no me quedaré aquí por mucho” (I won’t stay here for long).
target_language_example: Está lloviendo, así que me quedaré aquí un rato más.
native_language_example: It’s raining, so I’ll stay here a little longer.

additional_notes: Past tense (yo) of “quedarse dormido”: to fall asleep, often unintentionally or sooner than expected. Very common with “me”: “me quedé dormido” (masc.) / “me quedé dormida” (fem.). You can also use other persons: “se quedó dormido” (he fell asleep).
target_language_example: Me quedé dormido en el sofá viendo la tele.
native_language_example: I fell asleep on the couch watching TV.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of quedarse: quedé = “I stayed / I remained.” Use it for a completed action in the past (often implying you decided not to go out). You can add time expressions like todo el día (“all day”) or una semana (“a week”).
target_language_example: No tenía ganas de salir, así que quedé en casa.
native_language_example: I didn’t feel like going out, so I stayed at home.

meaning: 'ended up in/was left in' (a state or condition) or 'was supposed to/agreed to' (do something).
additional_notes: From the verb *quedar* (preterite: *quedó* = “he/she/it ended up/was left”). Common patterns: 1) *quedó en* + noun/state: *quedó en shock* (“he was left in shock”), *quedó en ruinas* (“it ended up in ruins”). 2) *quedó en* + infinitive: *quedó en darme una respuesta* (“you were supposed to give me an answer”). The exact meaning depends on context: a resulting condition vs. an arrangement/commitment.
target_language_example: Usted quedó en darme una respuesta.
native_language_example: You were supposed to give me an answer.

meaning: was left without; ended up without; went without (as a result).
additional_notes: Form of **quedar(se) sin + noun**. It indicates that someone/something ends up lacking something, often because it was lost, removed, or used up. **Quedó sin** is 3rd-person singular preterite (he/she/it/you-formal was left without). Common collocations: **quedó sin dinero** (was left without money), **quedó sin electricidad** (was left without electricity), **quedó sin explicación** (was left without an explanation), **quedó sin gasolina** (was left without gas). Reflexive variant: **se quedó sin** (e.g., *Él se quedó sin dinero*).
target_language_example: La ciudad entera quedó sin electricidad.
native_language_example: The entire city was left without electricity.

meaning: “we want to talk to (someone)” / “we’d like to speak with (someone).”
additional_notes: Used to say that “we” (queremos) want to talk/speak (hablar) with/to someone (con + person/pronoun). Often followed by a name (con Tom/Tomás) or a pronoun: con él (with him), con ella (with her), con usted (with you, formal). You can add a topic with “acerca de…” (about…).
target_language_example: Queremos hablar con usted sobre este tema.
native_language_example: We’d like to speak with you about this topic.

additional_notes: Used mainly with people (and pets) to express affection: "Quiero a mi familia" = "I love my family." It’s different from "querer + [thing]", which usually means "to want" ("Quiero un café" = "I want a coffee"). The "a" is the personal "a" used before a direct object that is a person (or pet).
target_language_example: Siempre voy a querer a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: I will always love my grandparents.

meaning: to love someone; to care about someone.
additional_notes: In Spanish, "querer" has two common uses: (1) "querer + infinitive" = "to want to do something" (Quiero comer.), and (2) "querer a alguien" = affection/caring for a person (Quiero a mi familia.). For romantic love, Spanish also commonly uses "amar", but "querer a alguien" is very frequent for family, friends, and sometimes partners. Don’t confuse "querer a alguien" (to love/care about someone) with the idea of "wanting" someone sexually/possessively—Spanish typically phrases that differently to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Es normal querer a alguien incluso a la distancia.
native_language_example: It’s normal to love someone even from afar.

meaning: to mean; to intend to say.
additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of a word/phrase ("¿Qué quiere decir...?" = "What does ... mean?") or to clarify what someone intended ("Quiero decir que..." = "I mean that..."). In the past: "Quise decir..." / "Quería decir..." = "I meant to say...".
target_language_example: ¿Qué significa esto? Es decir, ¿qué quiere decir "saltar"?
native_language_example: What does this mean? That is, what does "saltar" mean?

meaning: to want to talk; to want to speak.
additional_notes: Use it to express the desire to talk or discuss something. It often appears conjugated (quiero hablar, ¿quieres hablar?, quería hablar) and is commonly followed by “con” + person (Quiero hablar con Ana) or “de/sobre” + topic (Quiero hablar sobre el problema). As an infinitive phrase, it can be used after verbs like “deber”, “poder”, or “hacer” (e.g., No es fácil querer hablar de eso).
target_language_example: A veces cuesta querer hablar de lo que duele.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard to want to talk about what hurts.

additional_notes: This is the imperfect past of *querer decir* (“to mean / to want to say”). It often clarifies meaning: *Eso quería decir* (“That’s what I meant”). With an object pronoun, it can also mean “I’ve been wanting to tell you”: *Hace tiempo que te lo quería decir*.
target_language_example: Perdón, eso no era lo que quería decir.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s not what I meant.

meaning: "I wanted to tell you" / "I meant to tell you" (speaking to one person).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (quería) to sound softer/more polite than "quiero decirte". Common for introducing what you’re about to say: "Quería decirte algo/esto/eso" or "Quería decirte que...". "Decirte" = "to tell you" with "te" (informal singular "you").
target_language_example: Quería decirte que mañana no puedo ir.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I can’t go tomorrow.

meaning: 'I wanted to tell you that…' (often used as a polite/soft way to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect "quería" to sound less direct than "quiero" ("I want"). Very common for starting an apology, giving news, or sharing a thought. You can add "solo/sólo" for extra softness: "Solo quería decirte que…".
target_language_example: Quería decirte que mañana no puedo ir.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I can’t go tomorrow.

meaning: “I wanted to apologize for …” / “I just wanted to apologize for …”.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an apology for something specific. "Quería" is the imperfect of "querer" and often sounds softer/more polite than "quiero" (similar to “I wanted to…”). "Disculparme" is reflexive (“to apologize”), and "por" means “for” + the thing you’re apologizing about (por eso, por lo de anoche, por lo que pasó, etc.).
target_language_example: Quería disculparme por mi comentario; estuvo fuera de lugar.
native_language_example: I wanted to apologize for my comment; it was out of line.

meaning: "I wanted to talk" / "I wanted to speak."
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (quería) to express a past desire/intent (“I wanted to…”). Very common to soften what you’re about to say, similar to “I wanted to talk to you about…” (sometimes used even when the conversation is happening now). Often followed by: con + person (quería hablar contigo/con usted), de/sobre + topic (quería hablar de esto/sobre esto), or a solas (“in private”).
target_language_example: Perdona, quería hablar contigo un momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, I wanted to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of querer (quería) to express a past desire/intent to talk to someone. Very common before a person or pronoun: quería hablar con ella/él/usted/ustedes, or with nadie (“no one”) in the negative: no quería hablar con nadie (“didn’t want to talk to anyone”). Often followed by more details like al respecto (“about it”), antes de que… (“before…”), or cara a cara (“face to face”).
target_language_example: Quería hablar con mi jefe, pero estaba ocupado.
native_language_example: I wanted to talk to my boss, but he was busy.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (quería) to express a past intention or something you were planning to do: “I wanted to / I was wanting to…”. Often followed by por eso (“that’s why”), acerca de (“about”), or cara a cara (“face to face”). You can swap contigo for other people: quería hablar con él/ella/usted/nosotros.
target_language_example: Perdón, quería hablar contigo un momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, I wanted to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of querer (quería) + infinitive ir: used to talk about a past desire/intention, often as background information (not necessarily completed). Add a destination after a (a casa, a la izquierda, a Australia). Subject is understood from context or stated separately (Yo quería…, Tom quería…).
target_language_example: Quería ir a México, pero no pude.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to Mexico, but I couldn’t.

additional_notes: Used when one person wants another person to do something. After "quería que", Spanish typically uses the subjunctive: "quería que ganara" (wanted her to win), "quería que dejaras" (wanted you to leave…). "Quería" is the imperfect past, often describing an ongoing past desire or setting background context.
target_language_example: Quería que me llamaras cuando llegaras a casa.
native_language_example: I wanted you to call me when you got home.

additional_notes: Used to politely introduce a question or request for information. It’s the imperfect of "querer" (quería) + infinitive "saber" (to know). Often followed by "si" (if/whether) or a question word: "Quería saber si..." = "I was wondering if...". Can also be used with other subjects: "Ella quería saber..." = "She wanted to know...".
target_language_example: Perdón, quería saber si tienen mesa para dos.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was wondering if you have a table for two.

meaning: "I/they wanted to know if…" (a polite way to ask a question).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (quería) to sound softer/more polite than "quiero saber si". Often used to introduce an indirect yes/no question. You can change the subject: "Quería saber si..." (I wanted to know if...), "Ella quería saber si..." (She wanted to know if...).
target_language_example: Quería saber si hoy tienes tiempo para hablar.
native_language_example: I wanted to know if you have time to talk today.

meaning: "I/he/she wanted to be" (past desire to be something).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of querer (quería) + infinitive ser to talk about a desire in the past, often something ongoing or a background wish (e.g., childhood dreams). Change the subject by changing quería: yo quería ser, él/ella quería ser, nosotros queríamos ser. Often followed by a noun/adjective: quería ser periodista / quería ser alto.
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, quería ser médico.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I wanted to be a doctor.

meaning: "I wanted to see" / "I wanted to watch".
additional_notes: "Quería" is the imperfect past of "querer" (to want), often used to talk about a past desire, intention, or reason: "I wanted to..." (not necessarily completed). "Ver" means "to see" or "to watch" depending on context. With a person, it often means "to see/meet" someone: "quería ver a María" = "I wanted to see María."
target_language_example: Perdón que te molestara; quería ver si estabas bien.
native_language_example: Sorry to bother you; I wanted to see if you were okay.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of querer (quería) to talk about a desire in the past (“wanted to”). Add a place after en (a city, country, neighborhood, etc.). You can change the subject: yo quería, tú querías, él/ella quería, nosotros queríamos, etc.
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, quería vivir en España.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I wanted to live in Spain.

additional_notes: A common type of soft, mild cheese in Spanish-speaking countries, often used in salads, tacos, or with beans. In everyday speech it can also mean “freshly made cheese” in general (not aged). Note: in English “fresh cheese” isn’t a fixed product name, but in Spanish queso fresco is a common item you can ask for in a store.
target_language_example: ¿Me pone 200 gramos de queso fresco, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you give me 200 grams of queso fresco, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unknown or unspecified person, emphasizing that their identity doesn’t matter. It’s similar to "quienquiera que" and is often followed by a verb in the subjunctive when talking about something uncertain (e.g., "quien sea que llegue").
target_language_example: Quien sea que llame, dile que no estoy.
native_language_example: Whoever calls, tell them I’m not here.

additional_notes: A fixed expression used to express a strong hope or wish. Often appears as “¡Quiera Dios!” on its own, or in the pattern “Quiera Dios que + subjunctive” (e.g., “Quiera Dios que lleguemos a tiempo”). It’s somewhat formal/literary.
target_language_example: ¡Quiera Dios que todo salga bien!
native_language_example: God willing, everything will turn out well!

meaning: "(he/she/you formal) wants to buy a house."
additional_notes: Uses "querer" (to want) in the 3rd person singular present tense: "quiere" = he/she wants, or formal you (usted) wants. Followed by an infinitive phrase: "comprar" (to buy) + "una casa" (a house). You can change the subject or tense (e.g., "Quiero comprar una casa" = I want to buy a house; "Quieren comprar una casa" = they want to buy a house).
target_language_example: Mi hermana quiere comprar una casa este año.
native_language_example: My sister wants to buy a house this year.

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of a word/phrase or what something implies. Common patterns: “¿Qué quiere decir X?” = “What does X mean?” and “Eso quiere decir que…” = “That means that…”. It can also contrast words vs. intention: “dice una cosa y quiere decir otra” = “he says one thing and means another.”
target_language_example: No entiendo esta palabra: ¿qué quiere decir?
native_language_example: I don’t understand this word: what does it mean?

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning or implication of something (a conclusion from what was said or observed). Often follows a statement: "..., quiere decir que ..." It can also start a sentence to clarify: "Quiere decir que..." The verb changes with the subject: "eso quiere decir que...", "esto quiere decir que...", "no quiere decir que..." ("that doesn’t mean that..."). Common question: "¿Qué quiere decir (que)...?" = "What does it mean (that)...?"
target_language_example: No contesta mis mensajes; quiere decir que está ocupado.
native_language_example: He isn’t answering my messages; that means he’s busy.

meaning: "(he/she) wants to talk" / "(he/she) wants to speak."
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "querer + infinitive" (to want to + verb). "Quiere hablar" can be used on its own (“He/She wants to talk”) or followed by "con" + person (“…wants to talk with/to someone”) or "de" + topic (“…wants to talk about something”). For “I want to talk,” use "quiero hablar"; for “Do you want to talk?” use "¿Quieres hablar?"
target_language_example: Dice que quiere hablar con nosotros.
native_language_example: He says he wants to talk with us.

additional_notes: Used to say someone wants to have a conversation with a person or group. The verb is conjugated: quiere (he/she/usted), quiero (I), quieres (you), quieren (they/you all), etc. "con" is followed by an object pronoun or noun: conmigo (with me), contigo (with you), él/ella, ustedes, nosotros/as, vosotras, etc.
target_language_example: La profesora quiere hablar con nosotros después de clase.
native_language_example: The teacher wants to talk with us after class.

additional_notes: Uses the formal "usted" (you). "Quiere" is from "querer" (to want). Often used when passing along a message that someone wants to talk to you; the subject can be said (El jefe quiere...) or omitted (Quiere hablar con usted.).
target_language_example: Perdón, el doctor quiere hablar con usted.
native_language_example: Excuse me, the doctor wants to speak with you.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone wants to speak with the listener (“contigo” = “with you” informal singular). The subject is often implied from context (e.g., “Tom quiere hablar contigo”). For a formal “you,” use “quiere hablar con usted.”
target_language_example: Parece que el profesor quiere hablar contigo después de clase.
native_language_example: It looks like the teacher wants to talk to you after class.

additional_notes: Used to say that a third person (él/ella/usted) wants to go somewhere. The structure is: [subject] + quiere (querer, present tense) + ir a + place (often with a preposition/article: a Boston, a la playa, al cine).
target_language_example: Mi hermana quiere ir a Madrid mañana.
native_language_example: My sister wants to go to Madrid tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what one person wants another person (or something else) to do. After "quiere que", Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive: "quiere que vayas", "quiere que sepas". If the subject is the same person, Spanish often uses the infinitive instead: "Quiere ir" (He/She wants to go).
target_language_example: Mi jefe quiere que llegue temprano mañana.
native_language_example: My boss wants me to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is a common sentence frame: **querer que + subjunctive** (“to want someone to do something”). **quiere** = “he/she wants” or “you (formal) want”. **le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to/for him, her, or you (formal)”. It’s usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive: *quiere que le ayude / le diga / le dé…*
target_language_example: ¿Quiere que le ayude?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you?

additional_notes: From querer (to want) + saber (to know). Usually followed by a question word (qué, por qué, cuándo, cómo) or by “lo que …” to mean “what …”/“the thing that …”. It can refer to he/she/it or usted (formal you), depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi jefe quiere saber si puedes venir mañana.
native_language_example: My boss wants to know if you can come tomorrow.

meaning: “(he/she/you formal) wants to know the truth.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "querer + infinitive" (quiere saber = wants to know). "Quiere" is the present tense for él/ella/usted; it can also be used without the subject ("Quiere saber la verdad."). "La verdad" means "the truth."
target_language_example: ¿Por qué quiere saber la verdad?
native_language_example: Why does he/she/you (formal) want to know the truth?

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase "querer ser" (to want to be). "Quiere" is the 3rd person singular present tense of "querer" (he/she/it wants; also formal "you" want), followed by the infinitive "ser" (to be). Use it to talk about someone’s goals, intentions, or desired identity/state: "Quiere ser + noun" (profession/role) or "quiere ser + adjective" (a quality).
target_language_example: Mi hermano quiere ser médico.
native_language_example: My brother wants to be a doctor.

meaning: “wants to see you” (wants to meet with you).
additional_notes: From querer (to want) + verte (to see you). Used when someone is asking to meet/talk with you, often in person. It’s common in messages like “(Alguien) quiere verte” = “Someone wants to see you.” You can change the subject: “Mi mamá quiere verte,” “El jefe quiere verte.”
target_language_example: María quiere verte esta tarde.
native_language_example: María wants to see you this afternoon.

meaning: "(he/she) wants to go back to" or "wants to do again".
additional_notes: Used with a person as the subject (often omitted in Spanish). Structure: querer + volver a + [place/noun] to mean “return to (a place/thing)”, or querer + volver a + [infinitive] to mean “do again” (e.g., quiere volver a hablar = wants to talk again). Change "quiere" for other subjects: quiero (I want), quieres (you want), quieren (they want).
target_language_example: Quiere volver a intentarlo mañana.
native_language_example: He/She wants to try again tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say what “they” want someone else to do. It’s followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: quieren que vaya (they want me to go), quieren que lo ayudes (they want you to help him). You can include the person with an object pronoun before the subjunctive verb: quieren que les digas… (they want you to tell them…).
target_language_example: Quieren que me quedé un poco más para ayudar.
native_language_example: They want me to stay a little longer to help.

additional_notes: Literally “you want to say,” but it’s used to clarify meaning: to check you understood correctly or to restate what someone is saying. Often followed by what you think the person means: “¿Quieres decir (que)…?”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres decir que llegamos tarde?
native_language_example: Do you mean we’re arriving late?

additional_notes: Used to express what you want another person (or thing) to do. It’s typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive: “¿Quieres que vaya?” = “Do you want me to go?” You can add the subject after “que” (e.g., “quieres que ella regrese”).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres que te ayude con la tarea?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with the homework?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants you to do. It’s “quieres que” (you want that) + “haga” (I do, present subjunctive of hacer). Often appears inside questions like “¿Qué quieres que haga?” = “What do you want me to do?” You can swap the verb to fit the situation: “¿Quieres que vaya?” (…that I go?), “¿Quieres que te ayude?” (…that I help you?).
target_language_example: ¿Qué quieres que haga ahora?
native_language_example: What do you want me to do now?

meaning: “do you want me to … (to you)?” / “you want me to … (to you).”
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the subjunctive after que: ¿Quieres que te + verb(o)? = “Do you want me to + verb + you?”. Often used to offer to do something for someone (¿Quieres que te ayude?) or as a warning/threat depending on context (¿Quieres que te mate?). Can also appear in negatives: no quieres que te hagan… = “you don’t want them to do … to you.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres que te ayude con la tarea?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with the homework?

additional_notes:
Used to say you want to learn a skill or subject. Follow it with:
- "a" + infinitive for an action: "Quiero aprender a cocinar" (I want to learn to cook).
- a noun for a subject/language: "Quiero aprender español" (I want to learn Spanish). You can add what/with whom: "...con mis amigos" (with my friends).
target_language_example: Quiero aprender a cocinar comida mexicana.
native_language_example: I want to learn to cook Mexican food.

meaning: "I want to learn to…" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to acquire a new skill. After "aprender a" you use an infinitive verb (bailar, dibujar, manejar, tocar). You can add details after the verb (e.g., an instrument or "como vos/tú" = "like you").
target_language_example: Quiero aprender a cocinar comida mexicana.
native_language_example: I want to learn to cook Mexican food.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to confirm or verify something before continuing. After "de que," Spanish often uses the subjunctive when you’re talking about something uncertain or not confirmed yet (e.g., "Quiero asegurarme de que estés… / seas…"), but the indicative can appear when it’s treated as a future plan or something expected (e.g., "de que vas a…").
target_language_example: Quiero asegurarme de que tengas todo lo que necesitas.
native_language_example: I want to make sure you have everything you need.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you feel like eating or plan to eat: Quiero comer pizza. With an object pronoun (me/te/lo/la/los/las), it can mean “I want to eat it/him/her/them,” often with the sense of eating something up: Me lo quiero comer (“I want to eat it”). Word order can vary with time expressions: Quiero comer pizza esta noche / Esta noche quiero comer pizza.
target_language_example: Ahora quiero comer algo ligero.
native_language_example: Now I want to eat something light.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to purchase something. Structure: (Yo) quiero comprar + noun. You can add “una/un/este/esta” before the noun (e.g., quiero comprar una casa / este diccionario).
target_language_example: Quiero comprar un billete de tren.
native_language_example: I want to buy a train ticket.

meaning: "I want to buy a" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Use it to say what you want to purchase, followed by a masculine singular noun: "Quiero comprar un billete / un ordenador". For feminine nouns, use "una" ("Quiero comprar una camiseta"). With quantities, Spanish often still uses "un": "un kilo". You can also replace "quiero" with "quisiera" to sound more polite: "Quisiera comprar un billete".
target_language_example: Quiero comprar un regalo para mi mamá.
native_language_example: I want to buy a gift for my mom.

meaning: I want to thank you (formal) / I’d like to thank you.
additional_notes: A polite, formal way to express gratitude. Uses "darle" (to give to you/him/her) with the formal object pronoun "le" (often meaning "you" = usted). Commonly followed by "por" + noun/infinitive: "Quiero darle las gracias por su ayuda" (for your help). You can also specify who you’re thanking with "a": "Quiero darle las gracias al comité" (I want to thank the committee).
target_language_example: Quiero darle las gracias por todo lo que ha hecho.
native_language_example: I’d like to thank you for everything you’ve done.

additional_notes: Used in speech to clarify, correct yourself, add an explanation, or emphasize what you’re saying—often as a conversational filler at the start of a sentence. Literally "I want to say," but usually translates as "I mean."
target_language_example: Quiero decir, no es mala idea, pero necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: I mean, it’s not a bad idea, but we need more time.

meaning: “I mean that…” / “What I mean is…” (to clarify or explain).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation, clarification, or rephrasing of what you just said. Often functions like a filler similar to “I mean…” in English. You can also hear it as “Quiero decir…” without “que.”
target_language_example: Quiero decir que no es mala idea, pero cuesta mucho dinero.
native_language_example: I mean that it’s not a bad idea, but it costs a lot of money.

meaning: “I want to tell you” / “I want to say to you.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you want to tell someone. It’s made of quiero (I want) + decir (to say/tell) + te (to you, informal singular). Often followed by a noun (quiero decirte mi secreto) or by que + a full idea (quiero decirte que me gustas). For a formal “you,” use quiero decirle.
target_language_example: Quiero decirte algo importante.
native_language_example: I want to tell you something important.

meaning: “I want to be” (to be in a place/situation for now).
additional_notes: Uses estar (not ser) because it’s about being in a situation/state or being somewhere (often temporary), e.g., in a team, at home, in a meeting. Common pattern: quiero estar + en + place/group.
target_language_example: Quiero estar en casa temprano.
native_language_example: I want to be home early.

additional_notes: Often used in a romantic or committed sense (wanting to be together in a relationship), especially with phrases like “para siempre” (forever) or “el resto de mi vida” (the rest of my life). It can also simply mean wanting to be in the other person’s company.
target_language_example: Quiero estar contigo esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to be with you tonight.

meaning: "I want to talk" / "I want to speak."
additional_notes: "Quiero" = "I want" and "hablar" = "to talk/to speak." Often followed by "con + person" (Quiero hablar con tu tío = I want to talk with your uncle) or "de/sobre + topic" (Quiero hablar de eso = I want to talk about that). You can also use it on its own to mean you want to have a conversation (e.g., to discuss something or to clear things up).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar de lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: I want to talk about what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to speak with a person. Add the person after con: "Quiero hablar con Tom" / "...con mi hijo" / "...con un abogado". You can also add when or how: "ahora" (now), "en privado" (in private), or a topic with "acerca de" (about).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar con la doctora ahora.
native_language_example: I want to talk to the doctor now.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to speak with a specific male person (“él” = him). You can add time words like “ahora” (now) or “un momento” (for a moment), and topics with “sobre” or “al respecto” (about it). In polite situations you can soften it: “Quisiera hablar con él” (I’d like to talk to him).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar con él sobre el problema.
native_language_example: I want to talk to him about the problem.

additional_notes: Used to start a conversation, often to introduce a topic (quiero hablar contigo sobre...). You can soften it with un ratito (“for a little bit”) or add primero (“first”). Contigo is the special form of con + tú (“with you”).
target_language_example: Cuando tengas un momento, quiero hablar contigo sobre el trabajo.
native_language_example: When you have a moment, I want to talk to you about work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you want to discuss. After de you can put a person, thing, or subject: Quiero hablar de Michael / de ella / de una cosa. To say “talk to/with (someone)” use hablar con: Quiero hablar con tu madre.
target_language_example: Quiero hablar de esto contigo.
native_language_example: I want to talk about this with you.

meaning: “I want to do / I want to make.”
additional_notes: Formed from querer (to want) + infinitive. Use it before another verb to say what you want to do: “Quiero hacer + [infinitive/thing]”. With a person + an object, it can mean “I want to ask/tell/do something to you”: “Te quiero hacer una pregunta” = “I want to ask you a question.” Often interchangeable with “quiero” + another verb (e.g., “quiero hablar”).
target_language_example: Quiero hacer ejercicio mañana, pero hoy quiero descansar.
native_language_example: I want to exercise tomorrow, but today I want to rest.

additional_notes: Formed with **querer + infinitive**. **Hacerlo** = **hacer + lo** (“to do it”), where **lo** is a direct object pronoun (“it/him”). In context, **hacerlo + infinitive** can mean “to make him/it do (something)” (e.g., *No quiero hacerlo esperar* = “I don’t want to make him wait”). In the negative: **no quiero hacerlo** = “I don’t want to do it.”
target_language_example: Quiero hacerlo ahora, antes de que sea tarde.
native_language_example: I want to do it now, before it’s too late.

additional_notes: Literally "I want to do/make to you." It’s commonly used with a noun, especially in the pattern "Quiero hacerte una pregunta" (= "I want to ask you a question"). "Hacerte" is "hacer" (to do/make) + "te" (to you).
target_language_example: Quiero hacerte una pregunta sobre el trabajo.
native_language_example: I want to ask you a question about work.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to go somewhere or go do something. It’s often followed by **a + place/activity** (Quiero ir al cine / Quiero ir a su fiesta) or **con + person** (Quiero ir contigo). With a reflexive verb it can mean “I want to leave/go away” (Me quiero ir).
target_language_example: Quiero ir a casa ahora.
native_language_example: I want to go home now.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire to go somewhere. Conjugation: quiero = “I want”; ir = “to go”; a = “to/to the” (before a destination). You can follow it with a country/city (Quiero ir a Japón) or a place/activity like clase (Quiero ir a clase). For masculine singular places with el, Spanish contracts: a + el = al (e.g., Quiero ir al cine).
target_language_example: Quiero ir a la playa este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I want to go to the beach this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to leave and go back home. Often appears as (Yo) quiero ir a casa (subject “yo” is usually omitted). You may also hear me quiero ir a casa (“I want to go home / I feel like going home”), which adds the idea of wanting to leave.
target_language_example: Estoy cansado; quiero ir a casa.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I want to go home.

meaning: “I want to go to the …” (masculine singular place).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to go somewhere. It’s made of: quiero (I want) + ir (to go) + al (= a + el, “to the”). Use it with masculine singular destinations: al hotel, al centro, al dentista. For feminine singular places, use “quiero ir a la …” (a la playa). With plural, use “quiero ir a los/las …”.
target_language_example: Quiero ir al supermercado.
native_language_example: I want to go to the supermarket.

meaning: "I want to leave" / "I want to go away."
additional_notes: Uses the verb "irse" (to leave/go away), which is reflexive. You can add where you’re leaving from with "de" ("Quiero irme de Boston") and sometimes where you’re going with "a" ("Quiero irme a casa" = I want to go home). With times/activities, it can mean leaving to do something: "Quiero irme temprano a la cama" (I want to go to bed early).
target_language_example: Hace tarde; quiero irme ya.
native_language_example: It’s late; I want to leave now.

meaning: I want to go home / I want to leave and go home.
additional_notes: "Irme" = "ir" (to go) + "me" (myself), and is commonly used to mean "to leave" or "to go away" (from where you are now). "A casa" means "home" (literally "to (the) house"). You can add "ahora" (now) or "ya" to emphasize you want to go home now / you already want to leave.
target_language_example: Hace frío; quiero irme a casa.
native_language_example: It’s cold; I want to go home.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to head to bed (often because you’re tired or it’s late). "Irme" is "to go (leave)" with "me" = "myself" (I’m leaving), and "a la cama" literally means "to the bed." You can swap the time: "quiero irme a la cama temprano/tarde" (I want to go to bed early/late).
target_language_example: Es tarde; quiero irme a la cama ya.
native_language_example: It’s late; I want to go to bed now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you’re about to show someone. Structure: quiero (I want) + mostrarte (to show you; informal singular “you”) + algo (something). You can add details after algo: algo grandioso (something great), algo más (something else), algo primero (something first).
target_language_example: Ven conmigo; quiero mostrarte algo importante.
native_language_example: Come with me; I want to show you something important.

quiero pasar el resto de mi vida

target_language_multi_word_term: quiero pasar el resto de mi vida
meaning: “I want to spend the rest of my life.”
additional_notes: A romantic, very strong phrase often used when talking about a life partner (similar to proposing or expressing deep commitment). Commonly followed by: “contigo” (with you), “a tu lado” (by your side), or “con él/ella” (with him/her). Word-by-word: “quiero” (I want) + “pasar” (to spend) + “el resto de mi vida” (the rest of my life).
target_language_example: Quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo.
native_language_example: I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do or what you want to happen. It’s followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: quiero que te quedes, quiero que él vaya, quiero que ellos aprendan. For negatives: no quiero que + subjunctive.
target_language_example: Quiero que me llames cuando llegues.
native_language_example: I want you to call me when you arrive.

meaning: “I want you to meet …” / “I want you to get to know …”
additional_notes: Used when introducing someone or asking another person to become acquainted with someone. It’s built from quiero (I want) + que (that) + conozcas (you know/meet, subjunctive of conocer) + a (used before a specific person/people). If you’re introducing someone directly, you’ll often hear: “Quiero presentarte a …” (I want to introduce you to …).
target_language_example: Quiero que conozcas a mi hermano cuando llegue.
native_language_example: I want you to meet my brother when he arrives.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want another person to do. After "quiero que" (I want that…), Spanish uses the present subjunctive: "hagas" is the tú form of "hacer" (to do/make). Common pattern: "Quiero que + [verb in subjunctive]".
target_language_example: Quiero que hagas la cena hoy.
native_language_example: I want you to make dinner today.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do. After "quiero que" Spanish normally uses the subjunctive: "Quiero que lo digas" = "I want you to say it." "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "that" (referring to something already mentioned). Often followed by a verb: "quiero que lo + [verb]."
target_language_example: Quiero que lo hagas ahora.
native_language_example: I want you to do it now.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do, so the verb after que typically goes in the present subjunctive: quiero que me digas / esperes / hagas. The object pronoun me (“me,” “to me,” “for me”) comes before the second verb: quiero que me ayudes (not *quiero que ayudes me*).
target_language_example: Quiero que me ayudes con la tarea.
native_language_example: I want you to help me with the homework.

meaning: "I want you to tell me" (used to ask for information).
additional_notes: Used to request that someone tell you something. It’s followed by a clause with the information you want (cómo, qué, quién, dónde, etc.). It triggers the subjunctive: digas (from decir). You can swap the object pronoun: "quiero que le digas" (I want you to tell him/her), "quiero que nos digas" (tell us).
target_language_example: Quiero que me digas la hora, por favor.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me the time, please.

meaning: "I want (someone/it) to…" (introduces a clause with "se" + verb in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express what you want to happen: "quiero que" is followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "quiero que se entienda", "quiero que se cambie"). The "se" can be reflexive (someone feels/behaves a certain way: "que se sienta…"), impersonal (people in general: "que se entienda…" = "that it be understood"), or passive/"se" passive ("que se cambie" = "that it be changed"). In English you often translate it as "I want you/them/it to…" rather than literally "I want that…".
target_language_example: Quiero que se haga hoy mismo.
native_language_example: I want it to be done today.

meaning: “I want you to be …” (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to be/do. After “quiero que…”, Spanish uses the present subjunctive: “seas” is the tú form of “ser” (to be). Common pattern: “Quiero que seas + adjective/noun” (Quiero que seas honesto / mi novio) or “Quiero que seas tú mismo” (“I want you to be yourself”).
target_language_example: Quiero que seas paciente conmigo.
native_language_example: I want you to be patient with me.

meaning: "I want you to know" (said to make sure someone understands something important).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you want the other person to understand or remember. It’s often followed by a clause with "que" ("Quiero que sepas que...") or by a noun phrase ("Quiero que sepas la verdad / una cosa"). The verb after "que" is in the present subjunctive: "sepas" (from "saber").
target_language_example: Quiero que sepas que siempre puedes contar conmigo.
native_language_example: I want you to know that you can always count on me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you want the other person to know (often reassurance, praise, or important information). It uses the subjunctive after “quiero que” (sepas = “you know” in a “I want you to…” sense). You can change the person: “quiero que sepan que…” (I want you all to know that), “quiero que sepa que…” (formal you).
target_language_example: Quiero que sepas que estoy aquí para ayudarte.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m here to help you.

meaning: "I want you to..." (talking to someone informally, tú).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do: "Quiero que + [verb in the subjunctive]". The "te" is the informal object/reflexive pronoun for "you" and comes before the second verb (e.g., "quiero que te sientes", "quiero que te pongas..."). Often used with reflexive verbs like "disculparse", "levantarse", "meterse", "ponerse".
target_language_example: Quiero que te sientes aquí.
native_language_example: I want you to sit here.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern **querer que + subjunctive** to express what you want someone else to do. **Te quedes** is the present subjunctive of **quedarse** (“to stay / to remain”). Often followed by where/how long/with whom: *aquí* (here), *justo donde estás* (right where you are), *lejos de…* (away from…).
target_language_example: Quiero que te quedes aquí conmigo.
native_language_example: I want you to stay here with me.

meaning: “I want you to leave / go away.”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone you want them to go (often from the place you are). It uses the subjunctive after "quiero que" ("I want that...") → "te vayas" (from "irse", to leave/go away). It can sound firm or even rude depending on tone and context; adding "por favor" makes it softer.
target_language_example: Quiero que te vayas de aquí, por favor.
native_language_example: I want you to leave here, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do. Because it’s a request/wish directed at another person, Spanish uses the subjunctive: **quiero que** + **vayas** (from *ir*) + destination/action. You can follow it with a place (**a Boston**, **a la oficina**) or with an action (**a ver un doctor** = “to see a doctor”, **a presentarte** = “to introduce yourself”).
target_language_example: Quiero que vayas a casa ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I want you to go home right now.

meaning: "I want you to come to…" / "I want you to come and…"
additional_notes: Used to say you want someone else to come somewhere or to come do something. After "quiero que" (I want that…), Spanish uses the subjunctive, so "venir" becomes "vengas" (you come). "a" is the preposition "to" before a place ("a casa", "a Boston") or before an infinitive to express purpose ("a conocer", "a vivir").
target_language_example: Quiero que vengas a cenar con nosotros esta noche.
native_language_example: I want you to come have dinner with us tonight.

meaning: “I want you to go back to…” / “I want you to … again.”
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do (quiero que + verb). Here, vuelvas a can mean either “go back/return to (a place)” or “do again” (return to an action/state). It uses the subjunctive (vuelvas) because it’s a desire/request about another person. Often followed by a place (a casa, a tu asiento) or by an infinitive-like idea expressed after a (sonreír → ‘to smile again’: vuelvas a sonreír).
target_language_example: Quiero que vuelvas a intentarlo mañana.
native_language_example: I want you to try again tomorrow.

meaning: “I want to stay” / “I want to remain.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb combination querer + infinitive. Quedarme is the reflexive infinitive of quedarse (“to stay”), meaning “to stay/keep being somewhere or in some state.” It can be followed by a place (aquí, en Argel), by con + person (contigo), or by an adjective/state (vivo = alive).
target_language_example: No me quiero ir; quiero quedarme un poco más.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go; I want to stay a little longer.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire for information. Commonly followed by a question word (quién, qué, dónde, cuándo, por qué, cómo) or by “lo que” (“what/whatever”). You can emphasize it with “solo”: “Solo quiero saber…” = “I just want to know…”.
target_language_example: Quiero saber dónde está la estación.
native_language_example: I want to know where the station is.

additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation of the method or way something is done. It’s often followed by an infinitive ("cómo hacerlo") or by a full clause ("cómo lo hiciste", "cómo murió"). In questions it can also be "¿Quiero saber cómo...?" but more common is "Quiero saber cómo..." as a statement.
target_language_example: Quiero saber cómo llegar a la estación sin perderme.
native_language_example: I want to know how to get to the station without getting lost.

additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation or reason. Often followed by a clause (e.g., “...por qué pasó esto”), or it can stand alone as “Quiero saber por qué.” Note: in indirect questions like this, Spanish uses “por qué” (two words, with accent).
target_language_example: Quiero saber por qué no me llamaste ayer.
native_language_example: I want to know why you didn’t call me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity of a person. It’s followed by a verb or clause: “Quiero saber quién fue” (who it was), “quién inició esto” (who started this). In questions you might also hear: “¿Quiero saber quién…?” or more naturally “Quisiera saber quién…” (more polite) or “Quiero saber quién es” (present).
target_language_example: Quiero saber quién llamó anoche.
native_language_example: I want to know who called last night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question: *Quiero saber qué + (verb/clause).* **Qué** has an accent because it means “what” in a question (direct or indirect). You can follow it with many meanings depending on context: *qué piensas* (what you think), *qué pasó/ocurrió* (what happened).
target_language_example: Quiero saber qué quieres hacer mañana.
native_language_example: I want to know what you want to do tomorrow.

additional_notes: Use it to introduce an indirect yes/no question (something that can be answered with “yes” or “no”). After "si" you normally use the indicative: "Quiero saber si están...", "...si va a nevar". You can also use it politely as a request for information, similar to “I’d like to know if…”.
target_language_example: Quiero saber si mañana abren la tienda.
native_language_example: I want to know if the store is open tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you want to become or what role/identity you want to have. Follow it with a noun (quiero ser maestro/profesor), an adjective phrase (quiero ser una mejor persona), or sometimes “parte de…” (quiero ser parte de la solución). It’s the verb querer (to want) + ser (to be), and “ser” is used for more permanent identity/roles (job, friend, kind of person).
target_language_example: Quiero ser médico algún día.
native_language_example: I want to be a doctor someday.

meaning: "I want to be a" (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a goal or what you want to become (often a job/role) in the future. It’s made of quiero (I want) + ser (to be) + un (a, masculine). For feminine nouns, use “quiero ser una” (e.g., “quiero ser una doctora”).
target_language_example: De mayor, quiero ser un médico.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be a doctor.

meaning: "I want to see" / "I want to watch."
additional_notes: Used to say you want to see something (a person/thing) or watch something (a movie, show, game). It’s the present tense: "quiero" = "I want" + "ver" = "to see/watch". Often followed by a noun ("quiero ver la película") or by an indirect question with a question word like "cómo", "qué", "cuándo" ("quiero ver cómo acaba").
target_language_example: Quiero ver qué pasa mañana.
native_language_example: I want to see what happens tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when you want to meet or see a person. "Quiero" = "I want" and "ver" = "to see". The "a" is the personal "a", used before a direct object that is a specific person or pet (e.g., "Quiero ver a Tom", "Quiero ver a mi esposa"). You don’t use "a" with things: "Quiero ver la película" (no "a").
target_language_example: Quiero ver a mis amigos este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I want to see my friends this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say where you want to live. Follow it with a place (city/country) or a more specific location with an article: en Boston, en Brasil, en el mismo barrio. Note: vivir en + place (location); vivir con + person (to live with).
target_language_example: Quiero vivir en España cuando sea mayor.
native_language_example: I want to live in Spain when I’m older.
