Use "saber + infinitive" to say someone knows how to do something: "sé hablar francés" (I can speak French), "sabes hablar francés" (you can speak French), "saben hablar francés" (they/you all can speak French). You can also say "hablan francés" to mean "they speak French"; "saben hablar" emphasizes ability/knowledge.
target_language_example: Mis amigos saben hablar francés, pero yo no.
native_language_example: My friends can speak French, but I can’t.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people knows what happened/what something is/what they’re doing/what they have to do. It’s the 3rd person plural (ellos/ellas/ustedes) form of the verb saber in the present: saben + lo que (“what/that which”). Often followed by a verb phrase: saben lo que hicimos / saben lo que tienen que hacer.
target_language_example: No se preocupen: saben lo que tienen que hacer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: they know what they have to do.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people understands their actions and is acting deliberately. Often appears in the negative: “No saben lo que hacen” (“They don’t know what they’re doing”). You can also use it with other subjects: “sé lo que hago” (I know what I’m doing), “¿sabes lo que haces?” (Do you know what you’re doing?).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: los médicos saben lo que hacen.
native_language_example: Relax: the doctors know what they’re doing.

additional_notes: From the verb **saber** (“to know (a fact)”) in **3rd-person plural**: **ellos/ellas saben** = “they know”; **ustedes saben** = “you all know.” It’s usually followed by **que** + a clause: *Saben que estamos aquí* (“They know that we’re here”). As a question, **¿Saben qué?** can mean “You know what?” or “Guess what?” depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Saben que mañana es el examen.
native_language_example: They know that the exam is tomorrow.

meaning: know-how; the ability/skill to do something.
additional_notes: Often used as a noun phrase (usually with an article) to mean “expertise” or “practical skill,” especially in work or craft contexts: el saber hacer de la empresa. It can also be used more literally as “to know how to do (something)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Esta empresa tiene mucho saber hacer en diseño.
native_language_example: This company has a lot of know-how in design.

meaning: to know how (to do something); to find out how.
additional_notes: Used to talk about knowing the method/way something is done, or learning the details of how something happens. Often followed by an infinitive (saber cómo hacer algo) or by a verb in a clause (saber cómo se usa / cómo acaba). In questions and indirect questions: “Quiero saber cómo…” = “I want to know how…”.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes explicar para saber cómo se hace?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me so I know how it’s done?

meaning: to know about; to know of (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to express having knowledge or information about a topic, situation, or person: saber de política (to know about politics), saber de alguien (to know of someone / to have heard about someone). It also commonly appears with question words: saber de dónde vienes (to know where you come from). Often used in negatives (no saber de...) to mean not knowing anything about something/someone.
target_language_example: No parece saber de dónde viene ni adónde va.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t seem to know where he/she comes from or where he/she is going.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with dónde (with an accent). It’s commonly followed by a clause: saber dónde + verb (e.g., “saber dónde está…” / “saber dónde poner…”). Often appears with verbs like necesitar/querer: “Necesito/Quiero saber dónde…”.
target_language_example: Necesito saber dónde poner esto.
native_language_example: I need to know where to put this.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants or needs to find out what really happened or what is real. Often appears with verbs/phrases like querer/tener que/necesitar/merecer + saber la verdad. In conversation you may also hear "conocer la verdad" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Dime lo que pasó: necesito saber la verdad.
native_language_example: Tell me what happened: I need to know the truth.

additional_notes: Used before a clause to express knowing (or not knowing) what something is/means, what someone is doing/thinking, or what will happen. It’s typically followed by a verb phrase: "saber lo que estás haciendo" (to know what you’re doing), "saber lo que va a ocurrir" (to know what’s going to happen). In questions: "¿sabes lo que…?".
target_language_example: Tienes que saber lo que estás haciendo.
native_language_example: You have to know what you’re doing.

additional_notes: Used when you want more information about a person, thing, or topic. It’s built from saber (to know), más (more), and sobre (about). Typically followed by a noun or a pronoun: saber más sobre usted/ti, saber más sobre el país, saber más sobre los árboles.
target_language_example: Me gustaría saber más sobre tu trabajo.
native_language_example: I'd like to learn more about your job.

additional_notes: Used when you want an explanation or reason for something. Commonly followed by a clause: "saber por qué" + verb (e.g., "Quiero saber por qué te fuiste"). It can also stand alone when the reason is understood from context: "Tengo que saber por qué" (I have to know why).
target_language_example: Quiero saber por qué estás triste.
native_language_example: I want to know why you’re sad.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with information you know as a fact. Common after phrases like "me alegra" (I’m glad) or "ayuda" (it helps) to explain what you’re glad to know or what helps to know.
target_language_example: Es bueno saber que mañana no trabajas.
native_language_example: It’s good to know that you don’t work tomorrow.

meaning: to know who (someone is / who did something).
additional_notes: Used when you want to identify a person. It’s often followed by a clause with a verb: “saber quién + verb” (e.g., saber quién lo hizo = to know who did it). It can also introduce an indirect question: “Quiero/Necesito saber quién…” = “I want/need to know who…”.
target_language_example: Quiero saber quién llamó anoche.
native_language_example: I want to know who called last night.

additional_notes: Used when you want to express knowing (or finding out) what something is/was/will be. It’s typically followed by an indirect question clause: saber qué + verb (often in the subjunctive/future when it’s uncertain: No se puede saber qué pasará). Also common after phrases like estar impaciente por / tener ganas de: impacientes por saber qué había ocurrido.
target_language_example: Quiero saber qué piensas.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think.

meaning: to know if / to find out whether.
additional_notes: Used to ask for information about a yes/no question. Common patterns: “(no) saber si + clause” and polite inquiries like “Quería/Quisiera saber si…”. Often translated as “to know if” or “to find out whether,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Sólo quería saber si estás bien.
native_language_example: I just wanted to know if you’re okay.

additional_notes: Used to check that the other person understands your point or the implied meaning (sometimes a hint, joke, or something you don’t want to say directly). It’s often said as a tag at the end of a sentence, and it can also be rhetorical (you assume they understand). You may also hear it as: "¿Sabes a qué me refiero?" or "Ya sabes a qué me refiero."
target_language_example: No es exactamente barato, pero sabes a qué me refiero.
native_language_example: It’s not exactly cheap, but you know what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to say the listener understands the way something works, happens, or feels. Often followed by a clause (e.g., “sabes cómo se siente” = “you know how it feels”). In expressions like “Tú sabes cómo es” or “Sabes cómo son las cosas,” it means “you know how it is / how things are.”
target_language_example: ¿Sabes cómo llegar a la estación?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get to the station?

meaning: “you know what…” / “you know what (someone) is capable of…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize what someone knows about a situation (“de lo que estoy hablando” = “what I’m talking about”) or someone’s abilities/behavior (“de lo que es capaz” = “what (he/she) is capable of”). Often followed by a verb in the present: “eres/es/soy capaz” or “estoy hablando.”
target_language_example: ¿Sabes de lo que soy capaz si me ayudas?
native_language_example: Do you know what I’m capable of if you help me?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with information the speaker assumes the listener knows/understands, often with an implied “what to do/what it means/what I’m saying.” Typically followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., hacer) or a full clause (e.g., quiero decir). In questions it becomes “¿Sabes lo que…?” = “Do you know what…?”
target_language_example: Sabes lo que tienes que hacer, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: You know what you have to do, right?

meaning: “do you know what it is?” / “you know what it is.”
additional_notes: From saber (“to know”) + lo que es (“what it is”). Used either as a real question (often with rising intonation: ¿Sabes lo que es esto?) or as a statement meaning “you know what it is,” sometimes implying “you understand what I mean” or emphasizing something (e.g., Sabes lo que es capaz de hacer = “You know what he/she is capable of doing.”). Subject can change: ¿Sabes lo que es…? / No sabes lo que es… / Ya sabes lo que es…
target_language_example: ¿Sabes lo que es este botón?
native_language_example: Do you know what this button is?

meaning: “you know what I mean?” / “you know what I’m saying?”
additional_notes: Used to check that the other person understands you, often when you’re explaining something or being a bit vague. It can be said as a statement (“sabes lo que quiero decir.”) or as a question/tag (“…, ¿sabes lo que quiero decir?”). In very informal speech you may hear it shortened to “¿sabes lo que digo?” or “¿me entiendes?”.
target_language_example: Es un trabajo difícil, ¿sabes lo que quiero decir?
native_language_example: It’s a tough job, you know what I mean?

meaning: "you know very well" / "you know perfectly well".
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that the other person already knows something. It often introduces a clause or a question word: "Sabes muy bien que..." (you know perfectly well that...), "Sabes muy bien a quién/de qué..." (you know very well who/what...). Depending on tone, it can sound accusing ("You know very well...") or reassuring/romantic.
target_language_example: Sabes muy bien que no es tan fácil.
native_language_example: You know perfectly well that it isn’t that easy.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask that the other person knows the reason for something. Often used rhetorically before giving an explanation (especially in questions like “¿Sabes por qué?” / “¿Y sabes por qué?”). In writing you may see “porque” (because) vs. “por qué” (why).
target_language_example: ¿Sabes por qué no vine ayer?
native_language_example: Do you know why I didn’t come yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to introduce information the speaker assumes the listener already knows, or to remind/emphasize something. Often said in conversation and can sound like English “you know, …” before a statement. Comes from *saber* (to know): **(tú) sabes** = “you know” + **que** = “that”.
target_language_example: Sabes que mañana no trabajo, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: You know that I’m not working tomorrow, right?

meaning: “You know that … not / you know I/it/we can’t (etc.).”
additional_notes: Used to remind or insist that the listener already knows a negative fact. It’s often followed by a verb in the negative: “Sabes que no lo hice” (you know I didn’t do it), “Sabes que no podemos” (you know we can’t). In speech, it can sound like “You know I didn’t!”
target_language_example: Sabes que no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: You know I can’t go today.

meaning: "you know what?" (often used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Literally means “(you) know what?” and is usually used as a spoken, conversational phrase. It can introduce a new point or decision (“Pues, ¿sabes qué? Me voy.” = “Well, you know what? I’m leaving.”). It can also be used in a confrontational way before accusing someone (“¿Sabes qué hiciste?” = “Do you know what you did?”). Often said as a standalone: “¿Sabes qué?”
target_language_example: Pues, ¿sabes qué? Mejor lo hablamos mañana.
native_language_example: Well, you know what? We’d better talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unknown or uncertain, often with a tone of resignation: only God knows the answer. Literally it uses the future tense of "saber" ("will know"), but in everyday speech it means "God knows".
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora va a llegar? Sabrá Dios.
native_language_example: What time is he going to arrive? God knows / Who knows.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause explaining what someone knew. "Sabía" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), describing knowledge as a background/ongoing state in the past. Often followed by another verb phrase: "sabía lo que había pasado" (knew what had happened), "sabía lo que hacer" (knew what to do).
target_language_example: Yo sabía lo que querías decir.
native_language_example: I knew what you meant.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of saber: saber (to know) → sabía (I/he/she knew / used to know). Often introduces a clause with information someone already knew at that time: “Sabía que + [statement].” For other subjects: sabías que (you knew), sabíamos que (we knew), etc. (It can also mean “used to know” depending on context.)
target_language_example: Sabía que ibas a llamar.
native_language_example: I knew you were going to call.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of saber (sabía) + que + the imperfect of ser (era). It introduces a fact someone already knew at that time. The subject is often clear from context (yo sabía / él sabía / ella sabía). You can add what it was: “sabía que era un error / demasiado tarde / imposible.”
target_language_example: Sabía que era una mala idea, pero lo hice de todos modos.
native_language_example: I knew it was a bad idea, but I did it anyway.

additional_notes: Used when you recognize someone or reveal you already suspected their identity. Uses the imperfect tense sabía (“I knew / I was aware”), which suggests ongoing or prior knowledge. If you mean you realized it in that moment, you’ll often hear “supe que eras tú.”
target_language_example: Cuando escuché tu voz, sabía que eras tú.
native_language_example: When I heard your voice, I knew it was you.

meaning: "I knew that (he/she/it) was…" / "I knew I was…"
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you already knew in the past. "Sabía" is the imperfect tense (past background/ongoing), and "estaba" is also imperfect, describing a past state or an action in progress. The subject of "estaba" (I/he/she/it) is understood from context: e.g., "Sabía que estaba mintiendo" = "I knew he/she was lying" (or "I knew I was lying").
target_language_example: Sabía que estaba equivocado.
native_language_example: I knew I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to say you already expected someone (tú) would do something. It combines: sabía (imperfect of saber, “I knew”) + que (“that”) + ibas a + infinitive (“you were going to …”). The verb after a stays in the infinitive: Sabía que ibas a llegar / decir / preguntar.
target_language_example: Sabía que ibas a llamarme hoy.
native_language_example: I knew you were going to call me today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a negative statement you already knew or expected. "Sabía" is the imperfect of "saber" (I knew / I used to know), and it’s often followed by a clause with a verb in the conditional or future-in-the-past (e.g., "vendrías", "volvería") or another tense depending on context. "Que" = “that,” and "no" negates what follows.
target_language_example: Sabía que no ibas a estar de acuerdo.
native_language_example: I knew you weren’t going to agree.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of saber (sabía) to describe a past state of knowing/being able to figure out what to do. Very common in negatives: No sabía qué hacer (“I didn’t know what to do”). You can add more information with con + noun: no sabía qué hacer con la comida extra (“he didn’t know what to do with the extra food”).
target_language_example: Cuando empezó el examen, ya sabía qué hacer.
native_language_example: When the exam started, I already knew what to do.

additional_notes: An idiom used when someone or something makes you lose patience or self-control. It’s commonly used with a person as the object: “Me saca de quicio” (It drives me crazy). You can also use it with “poner” in some regions (“me pone de quicio”).
target_language_example: Tu actitud consigue sacar de quicio a cualquiera.
native_language_example: Your attitude can drive anyone crazy.

meaning: to take advantage of; to benefit from; to make the most of.
additional_notes: Used when someone gets a benefit from a situation, resource, or opportunity. Often followed by “de” + noun/infinitive: “sacar provecho de este curso” (benefit from this course), “sacar provecho de estudiar” (benefit from studying).
target_language_example: Quiero sacar provecho de mi tiempo aquí y practicar español todos los días.
native_language_example: I want to make the most of my time here and practice Spanish every day.

additional_notes: Imperative of the verb salir (“to leave/go out”) + de (“from/out of”). Used to tell someone to leave a place or get out of something: Sal de aquí (“Get out of here”), Sal de mi coche (“Get out of my car”). Very direct; can sound rude depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Sal de la habitación, por favor.
native_language_example: Get out of the room, please.

meaning: Get out of there. / Come out of there.
additional_notes: Imperative command (tú form) of the verb “salir” (“sal”). Used to tell one person to leave a place or come out from where they are, often urgently. You can add a reason with “antes de que…” (“before…”) or “quiero…” (“I want to…”). For a more polite request: “Salga de ahí” (usted).
target_language_example: ¡Sal de ahí ahora mismo, es peligroso!
native_language_example: Get out of there right now, it’s dangerous!

meaning: 'Get out of here' / 'leave here' (command, tú form).
additional_notes: Imperative of **salir** addressed to one person (**tú**). It’s a direct command and can sound rude or angry depending on tone, especially with insults or intensifiers like **ahora mismo** (“right now”) or **de inmediato** (“immediately”). For a more polite version: **salga de aquí** (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, sal de aquí y cierra la puerta.
native_language_example: Please, get out of here and close the door.

additional_notes: Imperative (tú) form of salir + de + possessive: used to order someone to leave a place or stop being in your way. Common with a noun: sal de mi apartamento/cama/camino/césped/vista. You can also say “sal de aquí” (“get out of here”). Add the accent in “mí” when it means “me.”
target_language_example: ¡Sal de mi habitación ahora mismo!
native_language_example: Get out of my room right now!

meaning: "(a) room for" / "(a) room of" (used to form room names).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to name what a room is used for or what kind of room it is: sala de juegos (game room/playroom), sala de control (control room), sala de interrogación (interrogation room), sala de clases (classroom). Often preceded by an article (una/la) and can be expanded with more words (sala de control de energía).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está la sala de control?
native_language_example: Where is the control room?

additional_notes: A common place in clinics, hospitals, offices, airports, etc. Used with articles like “la sala de espera” (the waiting room) or “una sala de espera” (a waiting room).
target_language_example: Por favor, espere en la sala de espera.
native_language_example: Please wait in the waiting room.

additional_notes: A common term for the main room in a home where you relax, sit, and spend time with others. In home listings or signs you may see it alone (e.g., “Sala de estar despejada”). Often interchangeable with “salón” depending on the region.
target_language_example: Nos sentamos en la sala de estar para ver una película.
native_language_example: We sat in the living room to watch a movie.

additional_notes: “Salgamos” is the present subjunctive form of “salir” used as a suggestion/encouragement (“let’s…”). “De aquí” means “from here.” Often used to urge someone to leave a place, sometimes because of danger, discomfort, or simply wanting to go elsewhere.
target_language_example: Hace mucho frío; salgamos de aquí.
native_language_example: It’s really cold; let’s get out of here.

additional_notes: Used for leaving a building/home and going outside into public space (often literally into the street). Common with verbs like querer/poder/necesitar: "quiero salir a la calle". It can also be used more broadly for going out (getting out of the house).
target_language_example: Hace frío, pero necesito salir a la calle un rato.
native_language_example: It’s cold, but I need to go out for a while.

meaning: to come to light; to be revealed (to become known).
additional_notes: Used for information, secrets, facts, news, or evidence that becomes public or is discovered. Common with time markers like “cuando” (when) or “después de” (after): “Cuando salió a la luz…”. It can also refer to something being published (e.g., a report, book, or story).
target_language_example: La verdad empezó a salir a la luz después de la investigación.
native_language_example: The truth began to come to light after the investigation.

meaning: to get by; to pull through; to move forward despite difficulties.
additional_notes: Used for overcoming hard situations (money problems, illness, setbacks) and continuing/progressing. Often expresses resilience: "Vas a salir adelante" = "You’ll be okay / You’ll get through it." It can also mean becoming self-sufficient or succeeding through your own effort ("salir adelante yo misma").
target_language_example: Aunque sea difícil, vamos a salir adelante.
native_language_example: Even if it’s hard, we’re going to get through it.

meaning: to go out with; to date.
additional_notes: Often means “to date” romantically ("salir con alguien" = to date someone). It can also mean “to go out with” in a non-romantic sense depending on context (friends, plans). Common forms include: present "salgo con", "sales con", "sale con"; past "salía con" (used to/would go out with/date).
target_language_example: Quiero salir con él.
native_language_example: I want to go out with him.

meaning: to leave when the phone rang / to be about to leave when the phone rang.
additional_notes: Often used with phrases meaning “to be about to” or “to be going to”: **estar a punto de salir**, **estar por salir** (common in some countries), or **ir a salir / iba a salir**. **Sonó** is simple past (preterite) of *sonar* (“to ring”), describing a completed event that interrupts what was about to happen.
target_language_example: Estaba a punto de salir cuando sonó el teléfono.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when the phone rang.

meaning: to leave; to get out of; to come out of.
additional_notes: Used with a place or situation you exit/escape from: “salir de aquí” (leave/get out of here), “salir de este lugar” (get out of this place), “salir de rehabilitación” (come out of rehab). With “de + noun” it can also form set phrases like “salir de juerga” = “to go out partying.”
target_language_example: Tenemos que salir de aquí ahora mismo.
native_language_example: We have to get out of here right now.

meaning: to get out of here; to leave this place.
additional_notes: Uses salir (to leave/go out) + de (from/out of) + aquí (here). Often implies leaving quickly or escaping, especially in urgent or dangerous situations (e.g., “salir de aquí con vida” = “get out of here alive”). You can change the place: salir de la casa (leave the house), salir de la ciudad (leave the city).
target_language_example: Tenemos que salir de aquí ahora mismo.
native_language_example: We have to get out of here right now.

meaning: to leave the house; to go out (from home).
additional_notes: Used for leaving your home to go somewhere else (work, school, errands, etc.). Common with "antes de" (before leaving), "cuando" (when leaving), or "decidir no" (decide not to). You can also say "no salir de casa" = "not leave the house" (e.g., to stay home).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; estoy por salir de casa.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m about to leave the house.

additional_notes: Used when a situation stops being manageable or predictable. Often appears conjugated (e.g., "se salió de control", "salió de control"). Can also be used in the infinitive as in "puede salir de control".
target_language_example: Si no intervenimos a tiempo, la situación puede salir de control.
native_language_example: If we don’t intervene in time, the situation can get out of control.

meaning: to leave the house; to go out (from home).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "salir" (to go out/leave) + "de" (from) + "la casa" (the house). Often used for physically stepping outside or going out in general (e.g., to get some fresh air). You’ll commonly see it as "al salir de la casa" (“upon leaving the house”) or "estar por salir de la casa" (“to be about to leave the house”).
target_language_example: Necesito salir de la casa un rato para despejarme.
native_language_example: I need to get out of the house for a while to clear my head.

meaning: to leave the room; to exit the room.
additional_notes: Used with "salir de" + a place to say you exit/leave it. Often appears with "dejar" (to let someone) or "permitir" (to allow): "Déjame salir de la habitación" = "Let me leave the room." You can also use it in instructions like "al salir..." (when leaving): "Cierra la puerta al salir de la habitación."
target_language_example: Por favor, no olvides apagar la luz al salir de la habitación.
native_language_example: Please don’t forget to turn off the light when leaving the room.

meaning: to leave (a place) / to get out of (a situation).
additional_notes: "Salir" means "to go out/leave". With "de" + masculine singular article "el" (contracted to "del"), it’s used for leaving a specific place (salir del baño, salir del metro, salir del teatro) or escaping/ending a situation (salir del embrollo, salir del juego, salir del matrimonio). With feminine singular you use "salir de la"; plural: "salir de los/las".
target_language_example: ¿Cómo puedo salir del problema sin hacer daño a nadie?
native_language_example: How can I get out of the problem without hurting anyone?

meaning: to go wrong; to turn out badly.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how a plan, situation, or attempt ends up. It’s the verb "salir" (to turn out) + "mal" (badly). Often appears with "va a" (is going to) or in the past: "salió mal" (went wrong), "ha salido mal" (has gone wrong). With an indirect object pronoun it can mean “go wrong for someone”: "me/te/le salió mal".
target_language_example: Si no revisamos los detalles, puede salir mal.
native_language_example: If we don’t check the details, it could go wrong.

meaning: to get your way; to get away with it.
additional_notes: Idiom used when someone manages to do what they wanted (often despite others disagreeing) or avoids consequences. It’s usually conjugated (me/te/se sale con la suya; nos salimos con la nuestra; etc.), but it can also appear in the infinitive as in the example below.
target_language_example: No podemos dejar que intente salirse con la suya otra vez.
native_language_example: We can’t let him try to get away with it again.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "salir" (to go out) in the simple past/preterite ("salió") + "a" + infinitive ("dar") to express going out in order to do something. "Dar un paseo" means “to take a walk / go for a stroll,” often for leisure (sometimes with someone or a pet). You can change the subject: "salí" (I went out), "saliste" (you went out), "salieron" (they went out).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, salió a dar un paseo por el barrio.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she went out for a walk around the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "salir corriendo": to leave a place quickly by running, often suddenly because of fear, urgency, or surprise. Literally "went out running". You can add where they ran (e.g., "del cuarto" = out of the room, "de su casa" = out of his/her house, "hacia el bosque" = toward the forest).
target_language_example: Cuando escuchó el grito, salió corriendo a la calle.
native_language_example: When he heard the scream, he ran out into the street.

meaning: “(he/she/it) left the” or “came out of the”.
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of **salir de + (place/source)**. Used for leaving a location (**salió de la casa/oficina/pieza**) or for something emerging from somewhere (**salió de la chimenea**, **salió de la oscuridad**). Related pattern: **salirse de** can mean “to come off/out of” (e.g., **se me salió de la camisa** = “it came off my shirt”).
target_language_example: Salió de la tienda sin comprar nada.
native_language_example: He/She left the store without buying anything.

meaning: “(He/She) left the room” / “went out of the room.”
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of salir: salió = “he/she left” (also “you left” in formal usted). Often followed by de + a place (salir de la habitación = to leave the room). You can add how someone left: “salió… sin decir adiós” (without saying goodbye), “salió… bailando” (left dancing).
target_language_example: Salió de la habitación muy rápido.
native_language_example: He/She left the room very quickly.

meaning: to jump out of bed; to get out of bed quickly.
additional_notes: Used when someone gets up suddenly or energetically (often because they’re in a hurry or excited). In everyday speech, “saltar de la cama” emphasizes speed, similar to “spring out of bed.”
target_language_example: En cuanto sonó la alarma, tuve que saltar de la cama.
native_language_example: As soon as the alarm rang, I had to jump out of bed.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "saltar" for he/she/it: "saltó". "Por la ventana" means going through/out via the window (often translated as "out the window"). You can change the subject: "Él/Ella/El gato saltó por la ventana."
target_language_example: El perro se escapó porque saltó por la ventana.
native_language_example: The dog escaped because it jumped out the window.

additional_notes: Used in medical, personal, and public-health contexts to talk about emotional and psychological well-being. Often contrasted with "salud física" (physical health).
target_language_example: Cuidar mi salud mental es una prioridad.
native_language_example: Taking care of my mental health is a priority.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of saludar: saludó = “he/she greeted.” Use it to describe how someone said hello in a friendly way. Often followed by an indirect object pronoun: me/te/nos/lo/la (e.g., Me saludó con una sonrisa = “She greeted me with a smile”).
target_language_example: El recepcionista nos saludó con una sonrisa.
native_language_example: The receptionist greeted us with a smile.

additional_notes: Used with people (or animals) as the direct object: salvar a + person/being. The "a" is the personal "a" used before a specific person (or pet): salvar a mis amigos, salvar a Fraga. In everyday Spanish, "salvar" can sound more formal or dramatic (e.g., rescue), while "salvar" is also common in set contexts like "salvar la vida" (save a life).
target_language_example: Tenemos que salvar a los niños antes de que sea tarde.
native_language_example: We have to save the kids before it's too late.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "salvar la vida". Typically used with an indirect object pronoun to indicate who was saved: "me/te/le/nos/les salvó la vida" = "saved my/your/his-her/our/their life." Can be literal (preventing death) or figurative (helping in a critical situation).
target_language_example: El medicamento le salvó la vida.
native_language_example: The medicine saved his/her life.

meaning: (Someone’s) nose is bleeding / to have a nosebleed.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "sangrar" (to bleed). In these examples, the person is shown with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les" + "sangra" + "la nariz" (literally, “the nose bleeds to me/you/him…”). In everyday English you usually say “My/your/his nose is bleeding” or “I have a nosebleed.”
target_language_example: Si te sangra la nariz, inclina la cabeza hacia adelante.
native_language_example: If your nose is bleeding, tilt your head forward.

additional_notes: Often used in set phrases like **tener sangre fría** (“to stay calm/keep your cool”) and **a sangre fría** (“in cold blood,” i.e., without emotion or mercy, often describing a crime).
target_language_example: Aunque todos estaban nerviosos, ella mantuvo la sangre fría.
native_language_example: Even though everyone was nervous, she kept her cool.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something) arrived/returned without injury or damage. Common with verbs like llegar, regresar, volver, venir, and can also be used for packages/items (e.g., un regalo).
target_language_example: Para mi alivio, vino a casa sano y salvo.
native_language_example: To my relief, he came home safe and sound.

additional_notes: A respectful Catholic title for the Pope. It’s most often used with the article and capitalized: "el Santo Padre". In everyday conversation you can also say "el Papa" (the Pope).
target_language_example: Mañana el Santo Padre dará una misa en Roma.
native_language_example: Tomorrow the Holy Father will celebrate a Mass in Rome.

additional_notes: Use this to say someone feels happy with how something turned out. "Satisfecho" agrees with the person: "satisfecho" (male), "satisfecha" (female), "satisfechos/satisfechas" (plural). Common with "estar" or "quedarse": "Estoy satisfecho..." (I’m satisfied), "Se quedó satisfecho..." (He ended up satisfied / was left satisfied).
target_language_example: No estoy del todo satisfecho con el resultado, pero está bien.
native_language_example: I’m not completely satisfied with the result, but it’s okay.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **acabar de + infinitive** to say something happened **a moment ago**. With **irse** (to leave/go away), it becomes **se acaba de ir** (“just left”). You can add who left (e.g., *Tom se acaba de ir*) or where to (e.g., *se acaba de ir de compras* = “just went shopping”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor se acaba de ir.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor just left.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has ended (a game, a show, a period of life, a situation). Often appears as a complete sentence for emphasis (“Se acabó.” = “That’s it / It’s over.”). You can also put the subject after it: “Se acabó el espectáculo.”
target_language_example: Ya discutimos suficiente; se acabó.
native_language_example: We’ve argued enough; that’s it.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, phase, or privilege has ended, often with a firm or final tone. It’s usually followed by a noun phrase: "Se acabó el recreo" (recess is over), "Se acabó el cuento de hadas" (the fairy tale is over). You can also hear it with feminine nouns: "Se acabó la fiesta".
target_language_example: Se acabó el descanso; volvamos al trabajo.
native_language_example: Break is over; let’s get back to work.

meaning: 'the ... is over' / 'the ... ran out' (for a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something has ended or there is none left. Common with feminine nouns like la batería (battery), la visita (visit), la discusión (discussion). In many contexts it’s an emphatic “That’s it—no more.” In full form you’ll often see: “Se acabó la + noun.”
target_language_example: Se acabó la paciencia.
native_language_example: We've run out of patience. / That's it—no more patience.

additional_notes: From the verb acercarse (“to approach / come closer”). Used for things, times, events, or weather that are coming soon: Se acerca el examen / el invierno / la hora. Often followed by a noun (Se acerca un tifón) or by "a" to show what something is getting close to (El día se acerca a su fin).
target_language_example: Se acerca el fin de semana.
native_language_example: The weekend is approaching.

additional_notes: Present tense, 3rd person plural of **acercarse** (to come closer/to approach). **Se** is reflexive here (the subject is moving closer by itself). Often used to warn that people/animals/enemies are getting nearer, and it can translate as “they’re approaching” or “they’re coming up.”
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! Se acercan demasiado rápido.
native_language_example: Careful! They’re coming closer too fast.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "acercarse a" = to move closer to or go up to a person/thing. It often implies physically coming near, and it’s commonly followed by a person/object: "se acercó a ella" (he came up to her), "se acercó a mí" (she came up to me). You can add an infinitive to show purpose: "se acercó a consolarla" (she approached to comfort her).
target_language_example: Me asusté cuando un perro se acercó a mí.
native_language_example: I got scared when a dog came up to me.

meaning: he lay down; he went to bed.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "acostarse" (a reflexive verb). Often used for going to bed to sleep: "Se acostó temprano". With context it can also mean lying down (e.g., on a bed or couch). For other subjects: "me acosté" (I went to bed), "te acostaste" (you went to bed), "se acostaron" (they went to bed).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, se acostó temprano.
native_language_example: After dinner, he went to bed early.

meaning: 'they feed on' / 'they eat' (as a regular diet).
additional_notes: Used to describe what an animal or creature eats as its main food source. It’s the verb "alimentarse de" in the third-person plural (they). You can change it to match the subject: "me alimento de" (I feed on), "se alimenta de" (he/she/it feeds on), "nos alimentamos de" (we feed on).
target_language_example: Los murciélagos vampiro se alimentan de sangre.
native_language_example: Vampire bats feed on blood.

additional_notes: From the verb **arrepentirse de** (“to regret/to be sorry about”). It’s reflexive, so you change **se** depending on the subject: **me arrepiento de** (I regret), **te arrepientes de** (you regret), **se arrepiente de** (he/she/you formal regrets), **nos arrepentimos de**, **se arrepienten de**. It’s commonly followed by **de + infinitive** (e.g., *de haber ido*, *de no estudiar*) or **de + noun/phrase** (e.g., *de la decisión*), or **de lo que + verb** (“what [someone] did”).
target_language_example: Él se arrepiente de no haber dicho la verdad.
native_language_example: He regrets not telling the truth.

meaning: looks like; resembles; is similar to.
additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things. The verb is pronominal: asemejarse a + noun/pronoun ("Ella se asemeja a su madre"). Often followed by “en…” to specify what is similar ("en muchos aspectos", "en todos los sentidos"). In the negative: “no se asemeja a…” (doesn’t resemble / isn’t like).
target_language_example: Esta ciudad se asemeja a la mía, pero es más grande.
native_language_example: This city looks like mine, but it’s bigger.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb phrase "bajarse de" in 3rd person singular: "se bajó" + "de el" = "del". Used for getting off public transport (bus, metro, taxi), getting out of a vehicle (car), or climbing down from something (e.g., a tree). Pattern: me/te/se/nos/se + bajé/bajaste/bajó... + de + el/la/los/las (del/de la/de los/de las).
target_language_example: Tom se bajó del taxi.
native_language_example: Tom got out of the taxi.

additional_notes: Used to say what something depends on or has as its foundation. It’s the reflexive verb basarse: (algo) se basa en (algo). You can change it for tense/person: se basan en (they are based on), se basaba en (was based on), se basará en (will be based on).
target_language_example: Esta decisión se basa en la información que tenemos ahora.
native_language_example: This decision is based on the information we have now.

additional_notes: Used to say that something depends on, is founded on, or takes its main support from something else. It’s the reflexive verb phrase "basarse en" (to be based on). Because it includes "la", it must be followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "la observación", "la adaptación"); with a masculine noun you use "se basa en el".
target_language_example: Este plan se basa en la experiencia del equipo.
native_language_example: This plan is based on the team’s experience.

additional_notes: From the pronominal verb “burlarse de” (to make fun of). It is used with “de” before the person/thing being mocked: “Se burla de mí” (He/She makes fun of me). You can also add a reason with “por”: “Se burla de John por su dialecto” (…because of his dialect).
target_language_example: Mi hermana siempre se burla de mí.
native_language_example: My sister always makes fun of me.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb phrase “burlarse de” + a person/thing: “to make fun of / to mock.” Often implies being unkind or humiliating. Other forms: “se burla de” (he/she makes fun of), “me burlé de” (I made fun of).
target_language_example: Se burló de mi acento, pero no me importó.
native_language_example: He/She made fun of my accent, but I didn’t care.

additional_notes: Form of the verb casarse (to get married). It’s reflexive: casarse con alguien = to marry someone. Use: (yo) me caso con, (tú) te casas con, (él/ella) se casa con, (nosotros) nos casamos con, (vosotros) os casáis con, (ellos) se casan con. Often used for future plans too: “María se casa con Pedro” can mean “María is marrying Pedro” (soon) or “María marries Pedro” depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi hermana se casa con su novio en junio.
native_language_example: My sister is getting married to her boyfriend in June.

meaning: "(that) [someone] marry" (imperfect subjunctive) / "(that) [someone] would marry" (in reported speech).
additional_notes: Imperfect subjunctive of "casarse con" (to marry). Used after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., pedir, querer, insistir, recomendar, sugerir, exigir, negar) and in reported speech to refer to a desired, requested, or hypothetical marriage. Common pattern: "[verbo que exige subjuntivo] + que + [persona] se casara con + [alguien]". Example: "Le pidió que se casara con él" = "He asked her to marry him."
target_language_example: Ella le pidió que se casara con ella.
native_language_example: She asked him to marry her.

meaning: they got married; they married (each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of casarse, used for a completed event: they got married. It’s often used with time expressions like hace tres meses (three months ago) or el mes pasado (last month). The "se" is part of the reflexive verb casarse (to get married).
target_language_example: Mis abuelos se casaron en 1975.
native_language_example: My grandparents got married in 1975.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: casarse = “to get married.” "Se casó" is the preterite (completed past action). Often used with "con" to say who someone married: "Se casó con él/ella." You can add time expressions like "ayer" or "cuando tenía...".
target_language_example: Mi hermana se casó en junio.
native_language_example: My sister got married in June.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb casarse (to get married). In the preterite, se casó is used for a completed past event: se casó con + person. It changes with the subject: me casé (I got married), te casaste, se casó, nos casamos, se casaron.
target_language_example: Mi primo se casó con su mejor amiga el año pasado.
native_language_example: My cousin got married to his best friend last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "casarse con" = “to marry / to get married to.” It’s used with "se" because it’s reflexive in Spanish: "casarse". You typically add a noun after "con un/una" (a person): "Se casó con un músico" / "Se casó con una doctora". For other subjects: "Me casé con…" (I married…), "Nos casamos con…" (we married…).
target_language_example: Se casó con una ingeniera el año pasado.
native_language_example: He/She married an engineer last year.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **casarse con** (“to marry” / “to get married to”). **Se casó** is the **preterite** (completed past) form: “he/she got married.” The subject is often implied (he/she/your friend, etc.). **Con una** introduces a feminine noun (e.g., *una chica, una canadiense, una viuda*).
target_language_example: Se casó con una médica en 2019.
native_language_example: He/She got married to a doctor in 2019.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of the reflexive verb **caerse** (“to fall down”). **Se** shows it happened to the subject (often accidentally). Commonly used for people/objects physically falling (*Se cayó en el tren*), and also for services or systems being down (*El servidor se cayó*).
target_language_example: Me asusté porque mi teléfono se cayó al suelo.
native_language_example: I got scared because my phone fell on the floor.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb "caerse" (to fall). "Se" changes with the subject (me/te/se/nos/os/se): "Me caí al suelo" = I fell to the ground. Used for people or objects accidentally falling.
target_language_example: El anciano se cayó al suelo.
native_language_example: The old man fell to the ground.

additional_notes: Used with the verb caerse (to fall, accidentally) in the past: se cayó = “(he/she) fell.” Add de + place to say where someone fell from (bed, stairs, roof, etc.). Often implies an accidental fall.
target_language_example: Se cayó de la bicicleta y se lastimó la rodilla.
native_language_example: He/She fell off the bike and hurt his/her knee.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the verb phrase “caerse (de)” = “to fall (from/off)”. “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“from/off the”). Used for falling from a place or vehicle: “del puente” (from the bridge), “del techo” (off the roof), “del camión” (off the truck). In some contexts “caerse del caballo” can also be figurative (suddenly realizing the truth), but it’s often literal too.
target_language_example: Mi hermano se cayó del árbol, pero está bien.
native_language_example: My brother fell from the tree, but he’s okay.

additional_notes: "Se cayó" is the past tense (preterite) of "caerse" = "to fall" (often accidental). "Del" = "de + el" ("from/out of the"). The subject changes with context: "El mono se cayó..." (the monkey fell), "Mi hermano se cayó..." (my brother fell). Often followed by what happened as a result: "pero no se rompió nada" (but nothing got broken) or "y se rompió una pierna" (and he broke a leg).
target_language_example: Ayer mi primo se cayó del árbol y se lastimó el brazo.
native_language_example: Yesterday my cousin fell out of the tree and hurt his arm.

additional_notes: Used with **se** to talk about what is generally eaten or what people eat somewhere, without naming who does it. Common in descriptions, recipes, and reviews: **Aquí se come bien** = “They/people eat well here.” It can also mean “it gets eaten” (passive sense): **El cuscús se come con carne** = “Couscous is eaten with meat.” Note: **come** means “(he/she/it) eats,” not “comes” (false friend).
target_language_example: Aquí se come muy bien.
native_language_example: People eat really well here.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of **comerse**. The **se** often adds emphasis that someone ate the whole thing or finished it (similar to “ate it all up”). Often used with a direct object: *Se comió mi almuerzo* = “He ate my lunch.”
target_language_example: Me distraje y mi hermano se comió toda la pizza.
native_language_example: I got distracted and my brother ate up all the pizza.

additional_notes: This is the preterite (completed past) of **comerse**: **se comió** = “he/she ate (it),” often implying eating it up/entirely. **una** is an indefinite article (“a”) when followed by a feminine noun (**una naranja**), or a pronoun meaning “one” when the noun is understood from context (**nadie se comió una** = “nobody ate one [of them]”).
target_language_example: Había muchas galletas, pero Ana se comió una.
native_language_example: There were many cookies, but Ana ate one.

additional_notes: Used to describe what something is made of or what parts/members it has. Structure: [thing] + se compone de + [components]. Often in the present tense, but can change for tense: “se componía de” (used to consist of), “se compondrá de” (will consist of).
target_language_example: El equipo se compone de jugadores de diferentes países.
native_language_example: The team is made up of players from different countries.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive pronoun “se” to show the subject bought something for themselves. It’s the preterite (past) form of “comprarse”. Often followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by “un”. You can change it to match the person: “me compré (un/una) …”, “te compraste …”, “nos compramos …”, “se compraron …” (plural).
target_language_example: Tom se compró un billete de lotería.
native_language_example: Tom bought himself a lottery ticket.

additional_notes: Future tense of “convertirse en” (to become/turn into). Used to say that someone or something will become a person/role/thing in the future. It’s reflexive (“se”) and is typically followed by a noun (often with an article): “se convertirá en médico / en un buen futbolista.”
target_language_example: Con práctica, se convertirá en un gran chef.
native_language_example: With practice, he/she will become a great chef.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a change or transformation into something else. It’s the verb phrase "convertirse en" (to become/turn into) in the 3rd-person singular (él/ella/eso/it). You can also use other persons: "me convierto en" (I become), "se convierten en" (they become).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, el problema se convierte en una oportunidad.
native_language_example: Over time, the problem turns into an opportunity.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of “convertirse en” = “to become.” Used for a completed change at a specific moment in the past. Pattern: “(subject) se convirtió en + noun/adjective” (often a new role/status/identity).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convirtió en un gran médico.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a great doctor.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "convertirse en" (to become/turn into). "Se" here is part of the verb, not a reflexive pronoun you can omit. Use "en un" with a masculine singular noun ("en una" for feminine, and no article before many jobs/roles: "se convirtió en fotógrafo"). It can describe a literal transformation (a frog turned into a prince) or a change in status/result (a book became a bestseller).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convirtió en un líder respetado.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a respected leader.

meaning: “(he/she) cut himself/herself” or “it got cut / was cut off.”
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of pronominal "cortarse". Often means someone accidentally cut themselves: "Se cortó con un cuchillo" (He/She cut himself/herself with a knife). With body parts, Spanish commonly uses the definite article: "Se cortó la mano" (not usually *su mano*). It can also be used for things like phone/internet: "La línea se cortó" = the line got cut / the call dropped.
target_language_example: Me asusté porque se cortó la llamada.
native_language_example: I got worried because the call dropped.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun "se" with "cortarse" to express that someone cut themselves (often accidentally). The subject can be specified ("Tom se cortó el dedo"). You can add details with "con" ("con el cuchillo") or a gerund phrase ("abriendo una lata").
target_language_example: Se cortó el dedo con el cuchillo.
native_language_example: He/She cut his/her finger with the knife.

meaning: "it is believed/thought that"; sometimes "who does (he/she) think (he/she) is...?"
additional_notes: Impersonal/passive "se" construction used to express a general belief or assumption without saying who believes it (common in news and formal writing): "Se cree que..." = "It’s believed/thought that...". In questions like "¿Quién se cree que es...?", it’s a reproach meaning "Who does he/she think he/she is...?".
target_language_example: Se cree que mañana lloverá en el norte.
native_language_example: It’s believed that it will rain in the north tomorrow.

meaning: “he/she thinks he/she is…” (often: “who does he/she think he/she is?”).
additional_notes: From creerse (to believe oneself to be / to think of oneself as). Common in the fixed question “¿Quién se cree que es?” to criticize someone acting important or interfering. Can also be a plain statement about someone’s self-image: “Se cree que es un héroe.”
target_language_example: ¿Quién se cree que es para hablarme así?
native_language_example: Who does he think he is to talk to me like that?

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb phrase "darse cuenta (de...)" = "to realize/notice (that/about...)". It often takes "de" before the thing you realize: "No se da cuenta de su felicidad" = "He doesn’t realize his happiness." You can change it by person/tense: "me doy cuenta" (I realize), "¿te das cuenta?" (do you realize?).
target_language_example: Por fin se da cuenta de que estaba equivocado.
native_language_example: He finally realizes that he was wrong.

meaning: he/she/it will realize; he/she will notice; one will realize.
additional_notes: Future tense of the pronominal expression "darse cuenta (de)" = "to realize/notice (that/of)." Typically followed by "de" + noun/infinitive or "de que" + clause: "Se dará cuenta de que..." It can mean suddenly noticing something or understanding it after reflection. The subject is often implied (he/she/you formal/one), and context clarifies who will realize it.
target_language_example: Si usted lo piensa bien, se dará cuenta de que está siendo egoísta.
native_language_example: If you think about it carefully, you'll realize you're being selfish.

meaning: (he/she) decided to; finally made up (his/her) mind to.
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb decidirse + a + infinitive to talk about making a decision to do something (often after thinking, hesitation, or difficulty). It changes with the subject: me decidí a, te decidiste a, se decidió a, nos decidimos a, se decidieron a.
target_language_example: Después de pensarlo mucho, se decidió a cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: After thinking about it a lot, he/she decided to change jobs.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb desmayarse (“to faint”). Used to say someone suddenly lost consciousness; often followed by a cause with de (Se desmayó de hambre = “He/She fainted from hunger”) or with al + infinitive to mean “upon/when doing something” (Se desmayó al ver la sangre = “He/She fainted when seeing blood”).
target_language_example: Se desmayó en el metro y llamaron a una ambulancia.
native_language_example: He/She fainted on the subway and they called an ambulance.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb despertarse (“to wake up”). Used for a completed event: se despertó = “he/she woke up.” Often followed by details like con... (“with...”), muy temprano (“very early”), or adjectives describing mood: se despertó malhumorado (“he woke up grumpy”).
target_language_example: Ella se despertó a las seis y no pudo volver a dormir.
native_language_example: She woke up at six and couldn’t go back to sleep.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) of reflexive verb detenerse (“to stop”). Used for a person, vehicle, or something more abstract: El auto se detuvo (“The car stopped”); Se detuvo y miró… (“He/She stopped and looked…”). Often followed by en/frente a/delante de to say where it stopped, or por/para + infinitive to say why/for what purpose: Se detuvo para mirar el auto.
target_language_example: El tren se detuvo en la estación.
native_language_example: The train stopped at the station.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression used to report rumors, common beliefs, or information from an unknown/general source (no specific subject). Very common in news and storytelling. Often followed by a statement: “Se dice que + [clause]”. Similar in meaning to “dicen que…”, but “se dice que” sounds more neutral/impersonal.
target_language_example: Se dice que este restaurante es el mejor de la ciudad.
native_language_example: They say this restaurant is the best in the city.

meaning: "it is said that the..." / "people say that the..."
additional_notes: Impersonal expression used to report a general belief, rumor, or common saying without naming who says it. Uses "se" (impersonal) + "dice" (is said) + "que" (that) + "el" (the, masculine singular). Often followed by a statement in the present tense.
target_language_example: Se dice que el café de Colombia es excelente.
native_language_example: It’s said that Colombian coffee is excellent.

additional_notes: This is the imperfect subjunctive form of **darse cuenta de** (“to realize/notice”). It commonly appears after expressions like **es como si...** (“it’s as if...”) and especially after **sin que...** (“without...”), as in **sin que nadie se diera cuenta** = “without anyone noticing.” It’s often followed by **de** + noun/idea: **darse cuenta del error** (“realize the mistake”), **darse cuenta de que...** (“realize that...” ).
target_language_example: Me fui sin que nadie se diera cuenta.
native_language_example: I left without anyone noticing.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "darse cuenta (de)". Use "se dio cuenta" by itself when the thing is understood (“He/She realized.”), or add "de" + noun/phrase (“He/She realized/noticed that…/about…”). Often used with time words like "por fin" (finally) or "en seguida" (right away).
target_language_example: Por fin se dio cuenta de su error.
native_language_example: He/She finally realized his/her mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "darse cuenta de". Used when someone suddenly understands something or becomes aware of a fact. Commonly followed by "que" + clause ("se dio cuenta de que...") or by a noun phrase / "lo que" ("se dio cuenta de lo que..."). Conjugates by person: "me di cuenta de" (I realized), "te diste cuenta de" (you realized), "se dio cuenta de" (he/she/you formal realized), "nos dimos cuenta de" (we realized), "se dieron cuenta de" (they realized).
target_language_example: Tom se dio cuenta de que no llevaba dinero consigo.
native_language_example: Tom realized that he wasn't carrying any money with him.

additional_notes: Third-person singular, preterite (simple past) of darse cuenta de (“to realize/notice”). It’s typically followed by que + a clause. Other persons: me di cuenta de que (I realized that), te diste cuenta de que (you realized that), nos dimos cuenta de que (we realized that), se dieron cuenta de que (they realized that).
target_language_example: Tom se dio cuenta de que había algo mal.
native_language_example: Tom realized that something was wrong.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "disfrazarse de" = to dress up/disguise oneself as someone/something. It’s reflexive ("se"). Pattern: [person] se disfrazó de + noun (often with an article depending on the noun: de policía / de una niña). Other persons: me disfracé de (I), te disfrazaste de (you), se disfrazó de (he/she/you formal), nos disfrazamos de (we), se disfrazaron de (they/you all).
target_language_example: El ladrón se disfrazó de policía.
native_language_example: The thief dressed up as a police officer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb divorciarse (to get divorced) in the past tense: se divorció = “(he/she) got divorced.” It normally takes de to say who the person divorced from: se divorció de su esposa/marido (“got divorced from his wife/husband”). su can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” so the context tells you whose spouse it is. Present tense: se divorcia de su … (“gets divorced from his/her …”).
target_language_example: Se divorció de su esposo el año pasado.
native_language_example: She got divorced from her husband last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "dormirse" (to fall asleep). Used for the moment someone transitions from awake to asleep (often unintentionally or gradually). Common patterns: "X se durmió" (X fell asleep) and "se durmió en + lugar" (fell asleep in/on + place).
target_language_example: Tom se durmió en la litera de arriba.
native_language_example: Tom fell asleep in the top bunk.

meaning: "(that) he/she/they realize" or "(that) he/she/they notice" (subjunctive form of *darse cuenta*).
additional_notes: Used after triggers that require the Spanish subjunctive, especially: **para que** (so that), **es mejor que** (it’s better that), **probablemente** (often with a negative like *ni/nunca*), and sometimes **cuando** when talking about a future moment (“when he realizes…”). It’s often followed by **de** + noun (*se dé cuenta de lo que hizo* = realize what he did) or **de que** + clause (*se dé cuenta de que la niñera se fue* = realize that the babysitter left).
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta despacio para que nadie se dé cuenta.
native_language_example: Close the door quietly so that nobody notices.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of enamorarse de. Use it to talk about someone falling in love with a person, or becoming very fond of a place/thing. Structure: [subject] se enamoró de + noun/person (e.g., Se enamoró de ella / de Alemania).
target_language_example: Tom se enamoró de Linda.
native_language_example: Tom fell in love with Linda.

meaning: is in charge of; takes care of.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase “encargarse de + noun/verb,” meaning to be responsible for something, manage it, or look after someone. It can refer to duties/tasks (Se encarga de las donaciones) or caring for a person (Se encarga de mí). Often implies an ongoing responsibility rather than a one-time action.
target_language_example: Mi hermano se encarga de hacer la compra los sábados.
native_language_example: My brother takes care of the grocery shopping on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb phrase "encogerse de hombros" = "to shrug (one’s) shoulders," often meaning “I don’t know,” “I don’t care,” or “what can you do?” You can swap the subject: "Me encogí de hombros" (I shrugged), "Se encogieron de hombros" (they shrugged).
target_language_example: No sabía la respuesta, así que se encogió de hombros.
native_language_example: He didn’t know the answer, so he shrugged his shoulders.

additional_notes: Pretérito (simple past) of "encontrarse con" (3rd person singular: él/ella/usted). Commonly implies meeting someone by chance ("ran into"), though it can also be a straightforward "met" in a specific context. Structure: [él/ella/usted] se encontró con + [persona].
target_language_example: Ella se encontró con él esta mañana.
native_language_example: She ran into him this morning.

meaning: "is located" / "is found"; also "is" (in a certain condition).
additional_notes: From the verb *encontrarse* (reflexive). Common in formal or neutral speech to say where something/someone is: *¿Dónde se encuentra…?* = “Where is it/he/she?”. It can also describe someone’s state or condition: *se encuentra bien/mal* = “is doing well/badly.” In some contexts it’s closer to “can be found” (availability): *No se encuentra en este momento* = “It’s not available right now.”
target_language_example: El museo se encuentra cerca de la plaza, y mi abuela se encuentra mejor hoy.
native_language_example: The museum is located near the plaza, and my grandma is doing better today.

additional_notes: Used to state where something is (a place, object, institution, or even an abstract idea). It’s a more formal, descriptive alternative to “está en.” The verb is “encontrarse” (to be found/to be located), and it agrees with the subject: “se encuentra” (he/she/it is located), “se encuentran” (they are located).
target_language_example: La farmacia se encuentra en la esquina.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is located on the corner.

additional_notes:
Preterite (completed past action) of the verb "enfadarse" = to get angry. Often used with:
- "enfadarse con + person" (to be mad at someone): "Se enfadó con María."
- "enfadarse por + reason" (to be upset about something): "Se enfadó por lo que dijiste."
target_language_example: Me equivoqué y mi jefe se enfadó conmigo.
native_language_example: I made a mistake, and my boss got angry with me.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb “enojarse” = “to get angry.” Often followed by “con” to say who someone was angry with: “Se enojó con María” = “He got angry with María.” You can add “mucho” to intensify it: “se enojó mucho” = “got very angry.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano se enojó conmigo por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: My brother got angry with me for arriving late.

additional_notes: From the verb "equivocarse" (to be mistaken). It’s used to say someone is wrong about something or made an error. Often appears with "no": "No, no se equivoca" = “No, you’re not wrong.” You can add "en" + topic: "Se equivoca en una cosa" = “You’re wrong about one thing.”
target_language_example: Creo que se equivoca en esto.
native_language_example: I think you’re wrong about this.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "escaparse". Used when someone or an animal manages to leave or flee (often unexpectedly), or when a person avoids a danger/problem: "escaparse de" + place/danger; "escaparse con" + something (to get away with it).
target_language_example: El perro se escapó de casa anoche.
native_language_example: The dog ran away from home last night.

additional_notes: Used with a gerund (-ando/-iendo) to talk about an action or process happening right now in a reflexive/impersonal or “se” passive construction (often like English “is being + past participle” or “is …-ing”). It’s very common in descriptions of ongoing changes: “se está calentando” (it’s warming up). With plural subjects, it becomes “se están” (e.g., “Las casas se están vendiendo”).
target_language_example: La cena se está preparando.
native_language_example: Dinner is being prepared.

additional_notes: Present progressive of comerse (to eat up). Used for someone currently eating something (often implies eating it all), or for things like rust/acid that are gradually consuming or eroding something: "El óxido se está comiendo el hierro" = "Rust is eating away at the iron."
target_language_example: ¡Date prisa! El perro se está comiendo mi sándwich.
native_language_example: Hurry up! The dog is eating my sandwich.

additional_notes: Used with something that is changing over time into a new state or situation. It’s the progressive form of "convertirse en" (to become/turn into), and it often implies the change is currently happening and may be gradual: "Esto se está convirtiendo en..." = "This is becoming/turning into...".
target_language_example: La situación se está convirtiendo en un problema serio.
native_language_example: The situation is becoming a serious problem.

meaning: "is getting / is becoming" (with hacerse); sometimes "is getting (something) done".
additional_notes: From the verb hacerse (reflexive). Common uses: (1) change over time: Se está haciendo mayor. / Nuestro mundo se está haciendo más pequeño. / Se está haciendo tarde. (2) with a noun phrase, it can mean "pretend to be": hacerse el tonto = to play dumb. (3) with a service/beauty item, it often means "get it done": hacerse las uñas = get your nails done. It’s usually followed by an adjective (más pequeño, mayor, tarde) or by a noun phrase (el tonto, las uñas).
target_language_example: Se está haciendo más frío.
native_language_example: It’s getting colder.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: estar + gerund (está moviendo) to talk about an action in progress. With "se" it often refers to something unspecified or already known from context (e.g., "Algo se está moviendo…" = “Something is moving…”). You can add details with phrases like "rápidamente" (quickly) or "hacia…" (toward…).
target_language_example: Algo se está moviendo en la oscuridad.
native_language_example: Something is moving in the dark.

additional_notes: Progressive form: **estar + muriendo** describes something happening right now/these days (“is dying”). **Se** is part of the verb **morirse** (to die), often used to emphasize the process/state. You’ll often see it with causes like **de hambre** (“from hunger”) or **desangrando** (“bleeding out”). It can be literal (a person) or figurative (e.g., **La tierra se está muriendo** = “The Earth is dying”).
target_language_example: El perro se está muriendo y necesitamos un veterinario.
native_language_example: The dog is dying and we need a veterinarian.

meaning: "is becoming / getting"; with the sun, "is setting."
additional_notes: This is the present progressive of "ponerse" (to become/get). It’s used for changes happening right now or developing: "Se está poniendo viejo" (It’s getting old), "Se está poniendo impaciente" (He’s getting impatient). With "el sol", "ponerse" commonly means "to set" (go down): "El sol se está poniendo". The reflexive "se" is part of the verb "ponerse."
target_language_example: La situación se está poniendo difícil.
native_language_example: The situation is getting difficult.

meaning: “is staying” / “is becoming; is getting (into a state)” / “is running out (of something)” / “is falling behind.”
additional_notes: This is the present progressive of quedarse (reflexive): estar + quedando. Common patterns: quedarse en + place = “to stay (somewhere)” (temporary lodging); quedarse + adjective = “to become/get” (e.g., calvo = bald); quedarse sin + noun or quedarse escaso de + noun = “to run out of / be short of”; quedarse atrás = “to fall behind.”
target_language_example: Nuestro país se está quedando atrás.
native_language_example: Our country is falling behind.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase volverse = “to become, to get” (often a noticeable change of state). Use it with adjectives (más frío, loca, difícil, calvo, descuidado) or with a noun phrase like “una locura.” It’s in the present progressive: se + está + volviendo, meaning the change is happening right now or lately.
target_language_example: La situación se está volviendo peligrosa.
native_language_example: The situation is getting dangerous.

meaning: "they are" / "are being" (used with a gerund to form the present progressive).
additional_notes: Used before a gerund (-ando/-iendo) to say something is happening right now: se están + gerund = “they are ___-ing.” The "se" often marks a reflexive/reciprocal action (e.g., people gathering) or a passive/impersonal idea (something is getting done/occurring). Which meaning it has depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Se están poniendo nerviosos antes del examen.
native_language_example: They’re getting nervous before the exam.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "irse" = "to leave" (to go away). Often used with a time expression: "Se fue hace un rato" (He left a little while ago), "se fue temprano" (left early), "se fue hace tres días" (left three days ago). You can add a place with "de": "Se fue del bar" (He left the bar). "Ya se fue" means "He/She already left."
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ya se fue.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he/she had already left.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb irse: irse = to leave/go away. Use it with a place (Se fue a París.) or with an infinitive to say someone went to do something (Se fue a acostar. = went to bed). Change the pronoun for other people: me fui a (I), te fuiste a (you), nos fuimos a (we), se fueron a (they).
target_language_example: Anoche se fue a casa temprano.
native_language_example: Last night he/she went home early.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "irse" (to leave/go away): "se fue" = "he/she/it left". Add a subject if needed: "Él se fue a casa" (He went home), "Ella se fue a casa" (She went home). Often implies leaving a place and heading home; you can add time or emotion: "se fue a casa al día siguiente" (went home the next day), "se fue a casa enojado/a" (went home angry).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, se fue a casa.
native_language_example: After work, he/she went home.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb phrase *irse a la cama* (“to go to bed”). The subject is often understood from context, so *Se fue a la cama* can mean “He went to bed” or “She went to bed.” You can add a time: *se fue a la cama a las once* (“went to bed at 11”).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, se fue a la cama temprano.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she went to bed early.

additional_notes: "Se fue" is the past tense (pretérito) of "irse" = to leave/go away. "Al extranjero" means "abroad" (literally, "to the foreign place/country"). The subject is often implied by context (él/ella/ellos/ellas/usted). You can add a reason with "a + infinitive": "se fue al extranjero a estudiar" = went abroad to study.
target_language_example: Mi hermana se fue al extranjero por trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister went abroad for work.

additional_notes: From the verb irse (to leave/go away). Use it to say someone left together with another person: Se fue con + person. The subject can be changed (me fui con…, te fuiste con…, nos fuimos con…). In some contexts it can also imply “ran off/went off with” someone, depending on the situation. Note: “se fue con paso ligero” uses se fue + manner (“left with a light/quick step”), which is a different use of con (with) than “with someone.”
target_language_example: Después del concierto, Marta se fue con sus amigos.
native_language_example: After the concert, Marta left with her friends.

additional_notes: Uses irse (to leave/go away) + gerund (corriendo) to describe leaving while doing the action (running). Often implies quickly/suddenly. With people, it can suggest hurrying away, sometimes because they’re scared, embarrassed, or in a rush.
target_language_example: Cuando sonó la alarma, se fue corriendo del edificio.
native_language_example: When the alarm went off, he ran out of the building.

additional_notes: Preterite of **irse de** (to leave a place). Use **de** for the place you leave: *Se fue de la playa* = “He left the beach.” You can add a destination with **a**: *Se fue de Japón a España* (“He left Japan for Spain”). Often implies leaving/going away (sometimes for good, depending on context).
target_language_example: Ella se fue de la oficina a las seis.
native_language_example: She left the office at six.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (se fue sin decir nada = “left without saying anything”) or with a past infinitive (se fue sin haber sido visto = “left without having been seen”). “Se fue” is the preterite of irse (to leave/go away). Note: Spanish “sin” means “without” (not the English noun “sin”).
target_language_example: Se fue sin avisar a nadie.
native_language_example: He left without telling anyone.

meaning: “(that) he/she/they leave” / “(that) he/she/they go away” (imperfect/past subjunctive of irse).
additional_notes: From irse (“to leave/go away”), in the imperfect subjunctive: (que) se fuera. Common after past-tense verbs and expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., querer, aconsejar, rogar, pedir, dejar, hacer), typically in a clause with que: “Ella le aconsejó que se fuera” = “She advised him to leave.” Refers to an unrealized, desired, requested, or allowed action in the past context (or reported speech).
target_language_example: Ella le aconsejó que se fuera más temprano.
native_language_example: She advised him to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "irse" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes". Used to say a group departed or went somewhere. Often followed by destination ("se fueron a casa") or manner/time ("se fueron en medio de la noche"). Also used with "por" to mean leaving/taking different routes: "se fueron por caminos separados".
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la fiesta, se fueron temprano.
native_language_example: When the party ended, they left early.

meaning: "they went to" / "they left for" (to a destination).
additional_notes: From the verb irse (to leave/go away) in the preterite: se fueron = “they left/went away.” It’s commonly followed by a + place/event to say where they went. Often implies leaving from where you are/speaking (stronger than just fueron a).
target_language_example: Se fueron a casa temprano porque estaban cansados.
native_language_example: They went home early because they were tired.

meaning: (someone) earns a living; makes a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how a person supports themself financially, usually by working. Often followed by a gerund ("trabajando", "cosiendo") to say how they earn a living. You can change the person: "me gano la vida" (I earn a living), "te ganas la vida" (you earn a living), "se ganan la vida" (they earn a living).
target_language_example: María se gana la vida cosiendo.
native_language_example: María earns a living sewing.

meaning: "has/have" in the present perfect (with "se" for passive/impersonal or reflexive actions).
additional_notes: Used as **se + ha + past participle**. Common in: (1) **passive/impersonal "se"** to mean “has been” without naming who did it: *Se ha producido un error* (“An error has occurred / has been made”). (2) **reflexive verbs** in the present perfect: *Tom se ha rendido* (“Tom has given up”), *Un tigre se ha escapado* (“A tiger has escaped”).
target_language_example: Se ha cancelado el vuelo por el mal tiempo.
native_language_example: The flight has been canceled because of bad weather.

meaning: "it’s over" / "it has ended" ("has run out" for supplies, patience, etc.).
additional_notes: Present perfect of acabar(se): something has finished or come to an end. Often used with no subject (Se ha acabado.) meaning “It’s over.” With a subject, it can mean that something has run out: Su paciencia se ha acabado = “His/Her patience has run out.” Common with ya: Ya se ha acabado = “It’s already over.”
target_language_example: Se ha acabado el café.
native_language_example: We’ve run out of coffee.

additional_notes: Present perfect of the reflexive verb "convertirse en" (to become/turn into). It describes a change up to the present: "X se ha convertido en Y".
