target_language_example: Te ves tan cansado hoy.
native_language_example: You look so tired today.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of **ver** (“to see”): **vi** = “I saw.” **Te** is the object pronoun “you” (informal singular). Often used to say you witnessed someone doing something: **Te vi + infinitive** (e.g., *te vi practicar* = “I saw you practice”).
target_language_example: Te vi en el parque ayer.
native_language_example: I saw you in the park yesterday.

meaning: “I would see you again” / “I’d see you again.”
additional_notes: From **volver a + infinitive** (“to do something again”): **volver a ver** = “to see again.” **Te** means “you” (object pronoun). Often used after a past belief/thought, especially with **nunca/jamás** (“never”): *Pensé que nunca te volvería a ver* = “I thought I’d never see you again.”
target_language_example: No pensé que te volvería a ver tan pronto.
native_language_example: I didn’t think I’d see you again so soon.

meaning: "I'm going to" (to you) — used before an infinitive to say what I’m going to do to/for you.
additional_notes: This is the near-future in Spanish: ir (voy) + a + infinitive. "Te" is the indirect/direct object pronoun meaning "you" (singular). It’s very common for promises, warnings, intentions, or plans directed at the other person: "Te voy a llamar" (I’m going to call you), "Te voy a ayudar" (I’m going to help you). For plural "you": "les voy a".
target_language_example: Te voy a llamar mañana.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you tomorrow.

meaning: "I’m going to give you" / "I’ll give you" (something).
additional_notes: From dar (to give) in the near future: voy a + infinitive = “I’m going to…”. Te is the indirect object pronoun “to you.” Often followed by what you’re giving: te voy a dar este libro (I’m going to give you this book). If it’s said by itself (“Te voy a dar.”) or in an argument, it can also be a threat meaning “I’m going to hit you / I’ll beat you up,” with the object implied.
target_language_example: Te voy a dar una oportunidad más.
native_language_example: I’m going to give you one more chance.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you’re about to share. Literally “to you (te) + I go (voy) + to (a) + say/tell (decir).” Often followed by what you’ll tell them: “lo que…” (what), “qué…” (what, in a question-like clause), “una cosa” (one thing), or a noun like “tus opciones” (your options).
target_language_example: Te voy a decir la verdad.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth.

meaning: "I’m going to teach you" / "I’m going to show you."
additional_notes: Uses **ir a + infinitive** to talk about the near future: **voy a enseñar** = “I’m going to teach/show.” **Te** means “to you.” **Enseñar** can mean “teach” (a skill or how to do something) or “show” (something you want the person to see). You can add: **a + infinitive** (te voy a enseñar a jugar...), **cómo** (te voy a enseñar cómo se hace), **qué** (te voy a enseñar qué cosas...), or a noun (te voy a enseñar algo/una cosa/helicópteros).
target_language_example: Te voy a enseñar a usar esta aplicación.
native_language_example: I’m going to teach you how to use this app.

meaning: “I’m going to take you” / “I’ll bring you (there).”
additional_notes: Very common near-future form: **ir a + infinitive** (“voy a llevar” = “I’m going to take”). **Te** means “you” (informal singular) as the direct object (“take you”). Often followed by **a + place/activity**: *te voy a llevar a la cama / a almorzar / a mi trabajo*. With direction words it can mean “take you back/out”: *te voy a llevar de vuelta* (back), *te voy a llevar afuera* (outside).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, te voy a llevar a casa después.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to take you home later.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure ir a + infinitive: (yo) voy a mostrar = “I’m going to show.” Te = “to you” (informal singular). Often followed by what you’ll show: “te voy a mostrar algo/lo que…” You can swap te for other indirect object pronouns: “le voy a mostrar” (to you formal / to him/her), “les voy a mostrar” (to you all / to them).
target_language_example: Espera un segundo, te voy a mostrar cómo se hace.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to show you how it’s done.

additional_notes: Used when you (speaker) will introduce the listener (te) to a person or group. Structure: (Yo) te voy a presentar a + person/people. Very common in social situations; you can change the pronoun and tense: “Te presento a…/Te presentaré a…/Les voy a presentar a…”.
target_language_example: Te voy a presentar a mi amigo Carlos.
native_language_example: I’m going to introduce you to my friend Carlos.

additional_notes: Used before a material or type to describe what a fabric is made of or what it’s for: "tela de algodón" (cotton fabric), "tela de lino" (linen fabric). It can also appear in set phrases like "tela de araña" (spider web/cobweb).
target_language_example: Quiero comprar tela de algodón para hacer una camisa.
native_language_example: I want to buy cotton fabric to make a shirt.

additional_notes: Common way to say “cell phone,” especially in Latin America. In Spain you’ll often hear “teléfono móvil” or simply “móvil.” You can say “mi/tu/su teléfono celular” to mean “my/your/his/her cell phone.”
target_language_example: No encuentro mi teléfono celular; creo que lo dejé en el coche.
native_language_example: I can’t find my cell phone; I think I left it in the car.

additional_notes: Common, neutral term for a mobile/cell phone (especially in Spain). In many places you’ll also hear “celular”. Uses the masculine article: el teléfono móvil; plural: los teléfonos móviles.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes tu teléfono móvil a mano?
native_language_example: Do you have your cell phone handy?

additional_notes: A fixed telephone in a public place (street, station, etc.) that anyone can use, usually by paying with coins or a card. Commonly used with verbs like "hay" (there is), "buscar" (to look for), and "llamar desde" (to call from).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar desde el teléfono público de la estación.
native_language_example: I’m going to call from the payphone at the station.

additional_notes: Temer means “to fear” and is usually followed by a (a person/thing): temer a algo / a alguien. Temen is the 3rd-person plural present tense (“they fear”). You may also see le temen a la muerte (“they fear death”), where le is an indirect object pronoun referring to what’s feared.
target_language_example: Muchas personas temen a la muerte, pero viven con valentía.
native_language_example: Many people fear death, but they live bravely.

additional_notes: Used to express worry or concern about what may happen or be true. It’s common as a polite, somewhat formal way to introduce bad news or an opinion the speaker thinks is negative. It’s followed by a clause (often in the future, or with subjunctive when expressing uncertainty/possibility). You can also use it alone: “Temo que sí” = “I’m afraid so.”
target_language_example: Temo que hoy no podamos ir.
native_language_example: I'm afraid we can't go today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ir/irse (to go) to say someone goes to bed earlier than usual or earlier than expected: "(me) fui temprano a la cama" = "I went to bed early." You can add a time word like "esta noche" (tonight).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo que madrugar, así que me voy temprano a la cama.
native_language_example: I have to get up early tomorrow, so I'm going to bed early.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very early during the morning hours (often soon after waking up or around sunrise). It can answer “when?” and is common with routines or plans: “Salimos / Nos vemos temprano por la mañana.”
target_language_example: Tengo que levantarme temprano por la mañana para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I have to get up early in the morning to go to work.

additional_notes: Informal command (tú form) used to warn someone to be cautious. Often followed by: **con + noun** (Ten cuidado con el perro.), **al + infinitive** (Ten cuidado al cruzar.), **de + noun** (Ten cuidado de tu entorno.), or **para no + infinitive** (Ten cuidado para no despertar al bebé.). You can also say **¡Cuidado!** as a shorter warning.
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con el coche; la calle está mojada.
native_language_example: Be careful with the car; the street is wet.

meaning: be careful with; watch out for.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone about something that could be dangerous or cause problems. It uses the tú command form (ten) of tener. You can follow it with a noun (Ten cuidado con el cuchillo) or with a clause using lo que (Ten cuidado con lo que dices). For formal you, use "tenga cuidado con"; for plural, "tengan cuidado con".
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con el tráfico al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: Be careful with traffic when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone to be cautious about the thing that follows (often with a verb): ten cuidado con lo que comes (what you eat), bebes (drink), deseas (wish for), dices (say). It’s the tú command form of tener cuidado (“to be careful”), commonly used as advice or a warning.
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con lo que publicas en internet.
native_language_example: Be careful what you post online.

additional_notes: Used to warn or advise someone to avoid doing something. It’s an affirmative command (tú) of "tener" (ten). Common pattern: "Ten cuidado de no" + infinitive (e.g., romper, despertar, quedarte). For a more formal command: "Tenga cuidado de no..."; for plural: "Tengan cuidado de no..."
target_language_example: Ten cuidado de no perder las llaves.
native_language_example: Be careful not to lose the keys.

additional_notes: Imperative form of tener: ten = “have” (you, informal singular). Used to ask someone to wait calmly or not get frustrated. You can add a person with con: Ten paciencia conmigo. For more than one person (Spain): Tened paciencia; for formal you: Tenga paciencia.
target_language_example: Ten paciencia, ya casi terminamos.
native_language_example: Be patient, we’re almost done.

additional_notes: Uses the **tú imperative** of *tener* (“ten”) to ask someone to show a bit more of a quality: *Ten un poco de paciencia/fe/empatía*. For a more polite/formal command, use **tenga un poco de** (usted). You can also hear **ten un poco más de** (“have a little more …”).
target_language_example: Ten un poco de paciencia, por favor.
native_language_example: Have a little patience, please.

additional_notes: Future of "tener que" + infinitive. Used to talk about an obligation or necessity in the future. Often followed by an infinitive verb: "tendremos que caminar" = "we’ll have to walk."
target_language_example: Si no llega el autobús, tendremos que ir a pie.
native_language_example: If the bus doesn’t arrive, we’ll have to go on foot.

meaning: 'will have to' (will need to; will be required to).
additional_notes: Future of obligation: "tener que" + infinitive. "Tendrá que" is 3rd-person singular (he/she/you-formal) and can also be used in general instructions. Often implies necessity/requirement rather than desire. Common subjects: "Él/ella tendrá que...", "Usted tendrá que...".
target_language_example: Ella tendrá que cocinar para todos.
native_language_example: She will have to cook for everyone.

meaning: 'will have to wait' / 'will need to wait'.
additional_notes: Uses the future of "tener que" (to have to) + infinitive: "tendrá que" = "he/she/you (formal) will have to". It’s used when someone must wait their turn or when something has to be postponed ("will have to wait" = "will have to be put off until later").
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor está ocupado; tendrá que esperar unos minutos.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor is busy; you'll have to wait a few minutes.

meaning: “they will have to” / “you (plural) will have to” (future obligation).
additional_notes: Form of "tener que" + infinitive to express that someone will be required/forced to do something in the future. "Tendrán" is the future tense of "tener" for "ellos/ellas" or "ustedes" (depending on context). Often followed by an infinitive: "tendrán que esperar". Can also be used with time expressions: "tendrán que pasar cinco años" = "five years will have to pass" (i.e., it will take five years).
target_language_example: Para entrar, tendrán que mostrar su pasaporte.
native_language_example: To enter, you (plural) will have to show your passport.

meaning: “you will have to / you’ll need to” (you are required to).
additional_notes: From "tener que" (to have to). "Tendrás que" is the future tense (tú form): it often gives advice, a strong suggestion, or states a requirement in the future. It is followed by an infinitive: "tendrás que + verbo" (e.g., "tendrás que estudiar").
target_language_example: Si quieres aprobar, tendrás que estudiar más.
native_language_example: If you want to pass, you’ll have to study more.

meaning: “I will have to” / “I’ll need to” (I’ll be required to).
additional_notes: Future of "tener que" + infinitive: expresses obligation or necessity in the future. Often used when something is unavoidable or required (by rules, circumstances, or someone else). Follow it with an infinitive verb: "Tendré que ir", "Tendré que decir...".
target_language_example: Mañana tendré que levantarme temprano.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll have to get up early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what would be necessary or what you should do, often as advice, a polite suggestion, or a regret about the past. It’s the conditional of tener que (to have to). With an infinitive: Tendría que estudiar más. With haber + past participle: Tendría que habértelo dicho = I should have told you / I would have had to tell you.
target_language_example: Tendría que levantarme temprano mañana.
native_language_example: I’d have to get up early tomorrow.

meaning: "should have" / "would have had to" (about something you didn’t do).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (tendría que haber + hecho/ido/traído/estado, etc.) to express a past obligation, often with regret or criticism: “I should have…” / “I would have needed to…”. It’s the conditional form of tener que (to have to), combined with haber to talk about the past.
target_language_example: Tendría que haber llamado antes.
native_language_example: I should have called earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say that two people share the same age. It’s most common when comparing yourself with someone else (often with “tú y yo…” / “él y yo…”). You can change the subject/verb: “tienen la misma edad” (they), “tenéis la misma edad” (you all, Spain), “tenemos…” (we).
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo tenemos la misma edad.
native_language_example: My sister and I are the same age.

meaning: "we have a lot of time" (we’re not in a hurry).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about how urgent something is. With "no" ("no tenemos mucho tiempo"), it means you should hurry because time is limited. You can add a time phrase like "esta noche" to specify when you have plenty of time.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, tenemos mucho tiempo antes de salir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we have plenty of time before we leave.

additional_notes: Used to say you and another person share many similarities (interests, tastes, experiences, opinions, etc.). The subject is “we” (nosotros/nosotras), so it often appears with “tú y yo” (you and I) or “usted y yo” (you and I, formal). You can also switch to other people: “tienen mucho en común” (they/you all have a lot in common).
target_language_example: Después de hablar un rato, me di cuenta de que tenemos mucho en común.
native_language_example: After talking for a while, I realized we have a lot in common.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It’s the present tense of "tener que" with "nosotros" (we): tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, tenemos que, tienen que + infinitive (verb). In questions it can mean "Do we have to...?"
target_language_example: Tenemos que salir ahora o llegaremos tarde.
native_language_example: We have to leave now or we’ll arrive late.

meaning: we have to find / we need to find.
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation: "tener que" + infinitive. "Encontrar" is "to find" (a thing/solution) or "to find"/"to locate" a person. Often followed by a direct object ("tenemos que encontrar la llave") or by "a" for people ("tenemos que encontrar a alguien").
target_language_example: Tenemos que encontrar una solución antes de mañana.
native_language_example: We have to find a solution before tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Tenemos que" expresses obligation/necessity ("we have to"). "Encontrar" means "to find." Use "a" before a specific person or people (the personal "a"): "a Mi-jin," "a ese tipo," "a esos dos niños," "a Tomás." If it’s not a person, you usually don’t use "a" (e.g., "Tenemos que encontrar las llaves" = "We have to find the keys").
target_language_example: Tenemos que encontrar a tu hermana antes de que oscurezca.
native_language_example: We have to find your sister before it gets dark.

additional_notes: Uses tener que + infinitive (“to have to” + verb) to express necessity/urgency. Often implies a serious or important conversation (e.g., about a problem or decision). You can add a topic with de (“about”) or sobre (“about”): Tenemos que hablar de/sobre esto.
target_language_example: Tenemos que hablar de lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: We need to talk about what happened yesterday.

meaning: "we have to talk about" / "we need to talk about".
additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic that must be discussed. Often implies importance, urgency, or that something serious needs to be addressed. Follow it with a noun ("de este tema") or with "algo" / "algunas cosas" ("de algo importante").
target_language_example: Tenemos que hablar de lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: We need to talk about what happened yesterday.

meaning: we have to do / we need to do.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that is necessary or required. It's the present tense of "tener que" (to have to) + infinitive "hacer" (to do/make). You can add an object after it: "tenemos que hacer esto" (we have to do this), or use it in questions: "¿Qué tenemos que hacer?" (What do we have to do?).
target_language_example: Tenemos que hacer la tarea antes de cenar.
native_language_example: We have to do the homework before dinner.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity/urgency: the speaker feels action is required. It can be followed by more detail with "con" (do something about/with): "Tenemos que hacer algo con la situación" and with "respecto a" (regarding/about): "Tenemos que hacer algo respecto a esto". Grammar note: "tenemos que" = “we have to / we need to” + infinitive.
target_language_example: Tenemos que hacer algo con este problema.
native_language_example: We have to do something about this problem.

meaning: “we have to go” / “we need to go.”
additional_notes: Used to say that going is necessary or required. Commonly followed by a destination ("para allá", "a casa") or by "con" to say who you’re going with or how ("con ellos", "con mucho cuidado"). In conversation it can also mean “we should go” (time to leave).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero ya es tarde: tenemos que irnos.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it’s late: we have to leave.

meaning: “we have to leave” / “we need to go (now).”
additional_notes: Used to say you (as a group) must leave, often because of time, urgency, or necessity. "Tenemos que" = "we have to" and "irnos" is "to go/leave" with "nos" (“ourselves/us”), so it implies leaving from the current place. Commonly followed by "de aquí" (from here) or time words like "ahora" / "ahora mismo" (right now).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tenemos que irnos ya.
native_language_example: Sorry, we have to leave now.

meaning: "we have to get to" / "we have to arrive at".
additional_notes: Used to say you (we) must reach a destination or event. "llegar" = to arrive; "a" is used before the place/event: "llegar a Berlín", "llegar a la reunión". Often implies needing to be on time.
target_language_example: Tenemos que llegar a tiempo al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We have to get to the airport on time.

meaning: we have to catch up / get up to date.
additional_notes: Used to say you need to update yourself on news, information, or pending tasks, or that two people need to talk and share what’s been happening. Common patterns: "ponerse al día con" (catch up with work/things), "ponerse al día de" (get up to date about something), and sometimes "ponerse al día en" (get up to date in an area/topic).
target_language_example: Después de las vacaciones, tenemos que ponernos al día con el trabajo.
native_language_example: After the vacation, we have to catch up on work.

meaning: we have to get out of here.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency or necessity to leave the current place. It’s built from: tenemos que (we have to) + salir (to leave/get out) + de aquí (from here). You can swap the subject: tengo que / tienes que / tienen que salir de aquí.
target_language_example: ¡Rápido! Tenemos que salir de aquí antes de que llegue la policía.
native_language_example: Quick! We have to get out of here before the police arrive.

meaning: we have to be / we must be.
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation for a group that includes the speaker ("we"). Pattern: "tenemos que ser + adjective/noun" (e.g., cuidadosos = careful, fuertes = strong, inteligentes = smart). In speech, "tenemos que" is often shortened to "tenemos que" → "tenemos que" (no change in writing, but said quickly).
target_language_example: Tenemos que ser pacientes y escuchar primero.
native_language_example: We have to be patient and listen first.

meaning: we have to go back to / we have to do (something) again.
additional_notes: "Tenemos que" means "we have to" (obligation/necessity). "Volver a" is used before an infinitive to mean "to do again" (volver a entrar = to go back in/enter again; volver a hacerlo = do it again). With a place, it often implies returning there (volver a Boston / volver a la nave = go back to Boston / back to the ship).
target_language_example: Tenemos que volver a intentarlo mañana.
native_language_example: We have to try again tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present tense of **tener** (to have) + **un** (a/an). Used to talk about possession or that something exists/has been obtained (e.g., “We have a problem,” “We have a TV”). Use **tenemos una** with feminine nouns (e.g., *una idea*).
target_language_example: Tenemos un minuto; vamos a hablar rápido.
native_language_example: We have a minute; let’s talk quickly.

additional_notes: Used to say that you and others are facing an issue or difficulty. Often said seriously (sometimes humorously), including the famous quote “Houston, tenemos un problema.” You can add details with con (“with/about”): “Tenemos un problema con eso” = “We have a problem with that.”
target_language_example: Si no llega hoy, tenemos un problema.
native_language_example: If it doesn’t arrive today, we have a problem.

meaning: “we have a …” (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: “Tenemos” is the nosotros (we) form of the verb “tener” (to have). Use “una” when the noun is feminine singular: “Tenemos una casa” (casa is feminine). For masculine nouns, use “un”: “Tenemos un coche.” It’s often used to state possession or to say something exists/has happened: “Tenemos una crisis.”
target_language_example: Tenemos una reunión mañana.
native_language_example: We have a meeting tomorrow.

meaning: to look down on; to disdain; to treat as inferior.
additional_notes: Used to express contempt or lack of respect toward a person or thing. It’s relatively formal/literary (you might also hear "menospreciar" or "mirar por encima del hombro"). Often appears with a direct object (e.g., "tener a alguien a menos").
target_language_example: No deberías tener a menos a tus compañeros por no pensar como tú.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t look down on your classmates for not thinking like you.

meaning: to have something to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Used to say there is a connection between two things. Very common in questions and negatives: “¿Qué tiene que ver X con Y?” (What does X have to do with Y?) / “No tiene nada que ver con…” (It has nothing to do with…). You can change “algo” to “mucho”, “poco”, or “nada”: “tiene mucho/poco/nada que ver con”.
target_language_example: Esto puede tener algo que ver con el trabajo.
native_language_example: This may have something to do with work.

meaning: to be (a certain age); to be years old (literally: to have years).
additional_notes: In Spanish, age is expressed with the verb tener (“to have”), not “to be.” The phrase is typically used with a number: “Tengo 20 años” (I’m 20). You can also ask: “¿Cuántos años tienes?” (How old are you?). In casual speech, “años” is sometimes omitted when the context is clear (“Tengo 20”).
target_language_example: Tengo 20 años; es decir, voy a tener años suficientes para votar.
native_language_example: I’m 20 years old; that is, I’m going to be old enough to vote.

meaning: to have enough; to have plenty (of something).
additional_notes: Used to say you have a sufficient amount of something. Often appears as “tener bastante (de) + noun” (e.g., tener bastante dinero = to have enough money), or by itself in questions like “¿Tienes bastante?” = “Do you have enough?” In some contexts, “bastante” can also mean “quite a lot,” but with “tener” it commonly implies “enough.”
target_language_example: Creo que voy a parar; ya voy a tener bastante.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to stop; I’m going to have had enough.

meaning: to be kind-hearted; to have a good heart.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone as genuinely kind, caring, or well-intentioned (even if they make mistakes). Commonly used with conjugations like: "tiene buen corazón" (he/she has a good heart), "tienes buen corazón" (you have a good heart).
target_language_example: Dicen que siempre intenta ayudar; de verdad, tener buen corazón importa más que quedar bien.
native_language_example: They say he always tries to help; truly, having a good heart matters more than looking good.

meaning: to have a good eye (good judgment, especially for noticing or choosing well).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is good at spotting details, quality, or the right choice (e.g., in art, clothes, bargains, people). Often followed by “para” + noun/infinitive: “Tiene buen ojo para la fotografía.”
target_language_example: Dicen que Marta tiene buen ojo para elegir regalos.
native_language_example: They say Marta has a good eye for choosing gifts.

meaning: to have a brain; to be sensible/smart.
additional_notes: Usually said as a comment or mild insult, often in the negative or as an imperative: “No tienes cerebro” (You have no brain) or “Usa el cerebro / Ten cerebro” (Use your brain). It’s fairly informal and can sound rude depending on tone.
target_language_example: Tener cerebro es pensar antes de hablar.
native_language_example: Having a brain means thinking before you speak.

meaning: to be clear about; to know for sure.
additional_notes: Used to say you understand something well or have made a firm decision/plan. Often followed by a clause with "que": "Tengo claro que..." It can also take a noun/pronoun: "No lo tengo claro" (= I’m not sure / I’m not clear on it).
target_language_example: Debes tener claro que mañana no puedo ir.
native_language_example: You should be clear that I can’t go tomorrow.

meaning: to have class; to be classy/elegant; (also) to have a class/lesson scheduled.
additional_notes: Commonly used figuratively to describe someone as elegant or refined ("Ella tiene clase"). It can also be used literally to mean you have a class/lesson ("Yo tengo clase").
target_language_example: Hoy no puedo salir; voy a casa temprano porque tengo que tener clase a las ocho.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I’m going home early because I have to have class at eight.

meaning: to have company; to not be alone (because someone is with you).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is with you (at home, at an event, etc.), often implying you have a guest or someone keeping you company. Commonly used in contexts like “No puedo hablar ahora; voy a tener compañía” (“I can’t talk now; I’m going to have someone with me”).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; voy a tener compañía.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m going to have company.

meaning: to be careful; to watch out.
additional_notes: Common advice/warning. Often followed by “con” + noun (“tener cuidado con el perro” = be careful with the dog) or “cuando / al” + verb (“tener cuidado cuando conduces” = be careful when you drive). It can also be used as a general reminder or caution in context.
target_language_example: Tenemos que tener cuidado con el tráfico al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: We have to be careful with traffic when crossing the street.

meaning: to be in pain; to have pain.
additional_notes: Used to talk about experiencing pain. Often you specify where: "tener dolor de cabeza" (to have a headache), "tener dolor de espalda" (to have back pain). In everyday Spanish, "me duele..." (it hurts...) is also very common: "Me duele la cabeza".
target_language_example: No quiero moverme porque tengo dolor.
native_language_example: I don't want to move because I'm in pain.

meaning: to take into account; to consider; to keep in mind.
additional_notes: Used to mean you should consider something before deciding or acting. Common patterns: "tener en cuenta + noun" (consider something/someone) and "tener en cuenta que + clause" (keep in mind that...). In "sin tener en cuenta", it means "without taking into account / regardless of".
target_language_example: Deberías tener en cuenta que ya no eres joven.
native_language_example: You should keep in mind that you’re not young anymore.

meaning: to keep in mind; to have in mind.
additional_notes: Used to say you are considering something, remembering it, or taking it into account. Often followed by a clause with “que” (e.g., “Tienes que tener en mente que…”), or used with an object (“tener en mente algo”). Conjugates normally (tengo/tienes/tiene/tenemos…).
target_language_example: Tienes que tener en mente que mañana cerramos temprano.
native_language_example: You have to keep in mind that tomorrow we close early.

additional_notes: Used to describe how you feel (temperature), not the weather. Spanish commonly uses "tener" (to have) with feelings/conditions: "Tengo frío" = "I'm cold". For the weather, you’d usually say: "Hace frío" (It’s cold). You can intensify it with "mucho": "Tengo mucho frío".
target_language_example: Si sales sin abrigo, vas a tener frío.
native_language_example: If you go out without a coat, you’re going to be cold.

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to want to.
additional_notes: Used to express desire/motivation, often with **de + infinitive**: *tener ganas de comer* (to feel like eating). In negative form: *no tener ganas de...* (to not feel like...). Also common with a noun: *tener ganas de pizza* (to feel like pizza).
target_language_example: A veces, lo único que quiero es tener ganas de salir.
native_language_example: Sometimes, the only thing I want is to feel like going out.

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to want to.
additional_notes: Used to express desire or inclination to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: "Tengo ganas de comer" (I feel like eating). You can also use it with a noun: "Tengo ganas de pizza" (I’m craving pizza / I feel like pizza). Common forms: "tengo ganas de" (I feel like), "tienes ganas de" (you feel like), "no tengo ganas de" (I don’t feel like).
target_language_example: A veces puedo tener ganas de salir, pero hoy prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: Sometimes I can feel like going out, but today I’d rather stay at home.

meaning: to have children; to have kids (to become a parent).
additional_notes: Used to talk about parenthood in general, either already having children or planning/being able to have them. Often appears after verbs like querer (want), decidir (decide), poder (can/be able to), or when discussing life plans (casarse y tener hijos = get married and have kids).
target_language_example: No sé si quiero casarme y tener hijos algún día.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I want to get married and have kids someday.

additional_notes: Common in Spain as a casual way to say someone has good luck: «¡Tienes leche!». More often you’ll hear it with an adjective: «tener buena leche» (to be good-natured / have good vibes) and especially «tener mala leche» (to be bad-tempered / mean). Literally it means “to have milk,” but the idiomatic meaning isn’t literal.
target_language_example: Dicen que Juan suele tener leche: siempre encuentra aparcamiento a la primera.
native_language_example: They say Juan is usually lucky: he always finds parking on the first try.

additional_notes: Used mainly for events, meetings, ceremonies, or situations happening at a specific time/place. Often appears in more formal contexts (news, announcements). Common patterns: "La reunión va a tener lugar el lunes" (is going to take place Monday), "El evento tuvo lugar en Madrid" (took place in Madrid).
target_language_example: La conferencia va a tener lugar mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: The conference is going to take place tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "tener" (to have) + the noun "miedo" (fear). It’s often followed by "de" to say what you’re afraid of: "tener miedo de + noun/infinitive" ("Tengo miedo de las arañas" / "Tengo miedo de hablar"). You may also hear "tener miedo a" with people, though "tener miedo de" is more common ("Tengo miedo de mi jefe").
target_language_example: No debes tener miedo del futuro.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t be afraid of the future.

meaning: to be very careful; to take great care.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone or emphasize caution. Often appears with obligation phrases like "tener que" (have to) or "hay que" (one must): "Tienes que tener mucho cuidado" / "Hay que tener mucho cuidado". You can add what to be careful about with "al" + infinitive ("al cruzar la calle" = when crossing the street) or with "con" ("con el cuchillo" = with the knife).
target_language_example: Deberías tener mucho cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: You should be very careful when crossing the street.

meaning: to be more careful; to take more care.
additional_notes: Used to warn or advise someone to act more cautiously. Common with deber/tener que (should/have to): “Deberías/Tienes que tener más cuidado…”. You can add “con + [thing]” (with/about something) or mention a danger: “Hay muchos peligros…”.
target_language_example: Tienes que tener más cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: You have to be more careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Almost always used in the negative: **no tener nada en contra de + noun/person/infinitive**. It means you don’t dislike or oppose someone/something, often followed by **pero...** to add a condition or preference.
target_language_example: No puedo decir que tenga nada en contra de Juan, pero prefiero trabajar sola.
native_language_example: I can’t say I have anything against Juan, but I prefer to work alone.

meaning: to seem/act effeminate (often said about a man).
additional_notes: Informal expression, especially common in Spain. Literally it means “to have a feather,” but idiomatically it refers to having feminine mannerisms (sometimes implying someone is gay). It can sound stereotypical or offensive depending on context, so use with caution.
target_language_example: Dice que no le importa tener pluma.
native_language_example: He says he doesn’t mind seeming effeminate.

meaning: to consider / to regard (someone or something) as.
additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or judgment about how you see someone/something. It’s often followed by an adjective or a noun: “tener por + adjective/noun” (e.g., tener por cierto = to consider true). It can also appear as “tener a alguien por + adjective/noun” (to consider someone as…).
target_language_example: Lo tengo por una persona honesta.
native_language_example: I consider him an honest person.

meaning: 'to keep in mind' / 'to bear in mind'.
additional_notes: Used to remind someone (or yourself) to remember an important fact while making a decision or considering something. Very common in advice and instructions. Often followed by "que" + a clause (e.g., "Hay que tener presente que...").
target_language_example: Hay que tener presente que mañana es feriado.
native_language_example: We have to keep in mind that tomorrow is a holiday.

meaning: to be wearing; to have on.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe clothes or accessories you are wearing: “tener + [item] + puesto/puesta/puestos/puestas”. The participle agrees in gender/number with the item: tengo puesto el abrigo / tengo puesta la chaqueta / tengo puestos los zapatos / tengo puestas las gafas. It can also mean something is “in place/installed” in some contexts (e.g., “tener puesto un programa”), but the everyday meaning is “to be wearing.”
target_language_example: Siempre tengo puesto el abrigo en invierno.
native_language_example: I always have my coat on in winter.

meaning: 'to have to' / 'must' (be required to do something).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. Structure: conjugated form of "tener" + "que" + infinitive (e.g., "tengo que ir", "tienen que salir"). It can also appear as the infinitive phrase "tener que" after another verb (e.g., "Odio tener que...", "Siento tener que..."). Often used to soften statements: "Siento tener que decirte...".
target_language_example: Odio tener que depender de usted.
native_language_example: I hate having to depend on you.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity to go somewhere or to leave. Common pattern: **tener que + infinitive** (e.g., **tengo que ir**, **tienes que ir**, **tenemos que ir**). You can add a destination with **a**: **Tengo que ir a casa** (I have to go home).
target_language_example: Lo siento, voy a tener que ir ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to have to go now.

meaning: to have to leave; to have to go (away).
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave because of an obligation or necessity. It combines (1) the structure “tener que + infinitive” = “to have to + verb” and (2) the reflexive verb “irse” = “to leave/go away.” In real conversation it’s more common to conjugate it (e.g., “Tengo que irme / Me tengo que ir”), but the dictionary form is “tener que irse.”
target_language_example: A veces es difícil decir "tener que irse" en medio de una reunión.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard to say “to have to leave” in the middle of a meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s opinion, statement, or guess is correct. It often follows verbs like creer (“to think/believe”) or poder (“can/might”): “Creo que puedes tener razón” = “I think you might be right”; “Podrías tener razón” = “You might be right.” Common reply: “Tienes razón” (“You’re right”).
target_language_example: Creo que puedes tener razón.
native_language_example: I think you might be right.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is logical/understandable (or not). Very common with "no": "no tener sentido" = "not to make sense." Also appears with verbs like "empezar a" or "comenzar a" (to start to): "empezar a tener sentido" = "to start making sense."
target_language_example: Entonces todo empezará a tener sentido.
native_language_example: Then everything will start to make sense.

additional_notes: A direct/explicit way to talk about sexual intercourse. Often used with "con" to specify the person ("tener sexo con alguien"). In many everyday situations, people may choose softer phrasing like "tener relaciones (sexuales)".
target_language_example: No quiero tener sexo sin protección.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have sex without protection.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Used to talk about luck as something you “have” (tener). Often appears with expressions like “quizás” (maybe) or “hay que” (you have to) to say you might need luck or be lucky to succeed. It can refer to luck in general or in a specific situation (e.g., “tener suerte en el trabajo”).
target_language_example: Hay que trabajar duro y tener suerte para adquirir riqueza.
native_language_example: You have to work hard and be lucky to acquire wealth.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel sleepy or drowsy (literally “to have sleep”). Common with conjugated forms like: tengo sueño (I’m sleepy), tienes sueño (you’re sleepy), tiene sueño (he/she/you formal is sleepy). Often used with “porque” to give a reason: Tengo sueño porque dormí poco.
target_language_example: Después de cenar, suelo tener sueño.
native_language_example: After dinner, I usually get sleepy.

meaning: to have a job; to have work (to do).
additional_notes: Often used to talk about being employed ("Tengo trabajo" = "I have a job"), but it can also mean you have tasks/work to do ("Tengo mucho trabajo" = "I have a lot of work"). You can also say "No tengo trabajo" for "I don’t have a job".
target_language_example: Ahora voy a tener trabajo, así que no puedo ir.
native_language_example: Now I’m going to have work, so I can’t go.

meaning: “to have a …” (to possess, have, or get something).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: tener un trabajo (to have a job), tener un jardín (to have a garden). For feminine nouns, use tener una. In questions/needs it’s also common: ¿Tienes un bolígrafo? (Do you have a pen?), Tengo que tener un plan. (I have to have a plan.)
target_language_example: Necesito tener un pasaporte para viajar.
native_language_example: I need to have a passport to travel.

meaning: to have a baby; to have a child (give birth / become a parent).
additional_notes: Used for becoming a parent or expecting a child, and it can refer to the mother giving birth or the couple having a child together. In the present or future it often implies pregnancy or plans ("Vamos a tener un bebé"). After birth, Spanish commonly uses "tener" where English might say "had": "Acaba de tener un bebé" = "She just had a baby."
target_language_example: El próximo año queremos tener un bebé.
native_language_example: Next year we want to have a baby.

meaning: to have a child (to become a parent).
additional_notes: Usually means to have a baby / become a parent (not possession). It can refer to planning or trying to conceive (“Están tratando de tener un hijo”) or expecting a baby (“va a tener un hijo”). The feminine equivalent is “tener una hija” when specifying a daughter.
target_language_example: Dime, ¿quieres tener un hijo conmigo?
native_language_example: Tell me, do you want to have a child with me?

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: tener + una + [noun]. Often means simply “to have a…,” but depending on context it can also mean “to need a…” (Necesitas tener una cuenta…). If you mean “one” (emphasis on the number), Spanish can stress it in speech (una, not just “a/an”).
target_language_example: Para entrar, necesitas tener una entrada.
native_language_example: To get in, you need to have a ticket.

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to talk about achieving your goal or doing well (in life, at work, in a project). Often used with "para" to mean "in order to succeed" (Para tener éxito, ...). You can also add context with "en" (tener éxito en la vida / en el trabajo).
target_language_example: Si quieres tener éxito, tienes que trabajar duro.
native_language_example: If you want to succeed, you have to work hard.

meaning: to have the guts / to have the balls (to do something).
additional_notes: Very informal and often vulgar (it literally refers to having your testicles “in place”). Used to talk about bravery or daring, often in challenges or confrontations. Commonly appears with an implied or explicit action: “A ver si tenerlos puestos te alcanza para decirlo en mi cara.” You may also hear “tenerlos bien puestos” (to really have guts).
target_language_example: Si de verdad dices tenerlos puestos, dímelo en la cara.
native_language_example: If you really claim to have the guts, say it to my face.

additional_notes: Formal command using the usted form of tener: “tenga” + “cuidado.” Used to warn someone or tell them to act cautiously. For an informal warning to one person, you’ll often hear “ten cuidado.” You can also say “¡Tenga cuidado!” for emphasis.
target_language_example: Tenga cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Used to say something is connected to a topic or situation. This is the present subjunctive form (3rd person singular) of “tener que ver con,” commonly triggered after expressions of doubt/negation/possibility (e.g., no creo que…, quizá…, es posible que…) or after indefinites like nada/algo/todo: “nada que tenga que ver con…”. Other forms you’ll also see: tiene que ver con, tenía que ver con, etc.
target_language_example: No creo que tenga que ver con esto.
native_language_example: I don’t think it has anything to do with this.

meaning: “Be careful.” (to more than one person, or formal “you” in some countries).
additional_notes: Imperative of tener + cuidado. Used to warn or advise people to act cautiously. Often followed by con + noun/phrase: tengan cuidado con lo que comen (“be careful with what you eat”). Can also be used alone as a warning.
target_language_example: Tengan cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: From the expression "tener miedo" (literally "to have fear"). "Tengas" is the present subjunctive form of "tener" for "tú" and commonly appears in: (1) negative commands: "No tengas miedo" = "Don’t be afraid", and (2) after phrases like "no quiero que...": "No quiero que tengas miedo" = "I don’t want you to be afraid." It often takes "de" (miedo de algo/alguien = afraid of something/someone).
target_language_example: No tengas miedo de la oscuridad.
native_language_example: Don’t be afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: This is the subjunctive form of "tener razón" (to be right). It’s commonly used after expressions of doubt, possibility, or hope like "quizá(s)", "puede que", and "espero que": "Quizás tengas razón" = “Maybe you’re right.” In statements of certainty, you usually use the indicative: "Tienes razón" = “You’re right.”
target_language_example: Quizás tengas razón, pero quiero pensarlo un poco más.
native_language_example: Maybe you’re right, but I want to think about it a bit more.

meaning: “I have something” / “I’ve got something” (often: “I have some…”).
additional_notes: Often used with **de** + noun to mean “I have some/a bit of…”: *Tengo algo de diarrea* (“I have a bit of diarrhea”), *Tengo algo de trabajo* (“I have some work”). Without **de**, it usually means you have something specific: *Tengo algo en el ojo* (“I have something in my eye”), *Tengo algo más para ti* (“I have something else for you”).
target_language_example: Tengo algo de fiebre, pero puedo ir.
native_language_example: I have a bit of a fever, but I can go.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an important message or topic before an infinitive verb (usually + decir, hablar, discutir): "Tengo algo importante que decir." You can add an indirect object pronoun to show who you’re talking to: decirte (to tell you), decirle (to tell him/her/you-formal), decirles (to tell you all/them). With a person, you can also use "con" + someone: "...que discutir con Ud."
target_language_example: Tengo algo importante que decirte.
native_language_example: I have something important to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a gift, message, or action you want to give/do for someone. Very common pattern: “Tengo algo para + ti/vos/vosotros/usted” and often followed by an infinitive to say what it is: “Tengo algo para darte/mostrarte/decirte.”
target_language_example: Tengo algo para ti: un regalo.
native_language_example: I have something for you: a gift.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to give someone a gift, a message, or show them something (often as a surprise or “wait—here”). Uses the informal “ti” (to you). For a formal version, say “tengo algo para usted.” You can add details after it: “Tengo algo para ti, un regalo / una sorpresa / una muestra de agradecimiento.”
target_language_example: Espera, tengo algo para ti: una pequeña sorpresa.
native_language_example: Wait, I have something for you: a little surprise.

meaning: “I have something to …” / “There’s something I need/want to …”.
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you’re going to say, show, do, or explain: Tengo algo que + infinitive (decir, mostrar, hacer). If there’s another verb after it, Spanish often uses que again: “Tengo algo que quiero que veas” (“I have something I want you to see”). You can change the person/tense: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, etc.
target_language_example: Tengo algo que contarte.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you.

meaning: “I have some things to …” (things I need/want to do).
additional_notes: Used to introduce tasks, errands, or topics you need or want to handle. It’s often followed by an infinitive: “tengo algunas cosas que hacer/terminar/poner en orden,” or by a verb phrase with a subject: “tengo algunas cosas que quiero aclarar.” You can swap “algunas” for “unas” (more casual) or change the number: “tengo una cosa que… / tengo muchas cosas que…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo algunas cosas que hacer antes de salir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have some things to do before I leave.

additional_notes: Used to announce something positive. Often followed by “para ti” (“for you”): “Tengo buenas noticias para ti.” You can change the verb to match the subject (e.g., “Tenemos buenas noticias” = “We have good news”). “Noticias” is plural in Spanish here (literally “good news” = “good pieces of news”).
target_language_example: Tengo buenas noticias: ¡aprobaste el examen!
native_language_example: I have good news: you passed the exam!

additional_notes: Use with people to talk about how you feel: "tener calor" = to feel hot. For things/places, use "hace calor" (it’s hot) instead. You can change the subject: "tienes calor" (you’re hot), "tenemos calor" (we’re hot).
target_language_example: Tengo calor; ¿puedes abrir la ventana?
native_language_example: I’m hot; can you open the window?

meaning: “I have things to do.” / “I have stuff to do.”
additional_notes: Common way to say you’re busy or to give a reason you can’t do something. Often used with a time or place word (e.g., "hoy", "mañana", "aquí"). "Que hacer" literally means “to do,” so the phrase is basically “I have things to do.”
target_language_example: No puedo salir ahora; tengo cosas que hacer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out now; I have things to do.

additional_notes: Used to say you are entitled/allowed to do something. Common in legal/formal contexts, but also used in everyday speech to insist on your rights. Structure: tengo derecho a + infinitive (e.g., hablar, saber, no contestar). You can change the person: tienes/tiene/tenemos derecho a…
target_language_example: Tengo derecho a pedir una explicación.
native_language_example: I have the right to ask for an explanation.

additional_notes: Used to say you possess/own two of something. Often followed by a noun (e.g., “Tengo dos libros” = “I have two books”). You can also use it alone when the noun is understood from context (e.g., “¿Cuántas entradas tienes?” “Tengo dos.”).
target_language_example: ¿Cuántos boletos tienes? Tengo dos.
native_language_example: How many tickets do you have? I have two.

additional_notes: Used to say how many children you have. In Spanish, “hijos” can mean “sons” specifically, or “children” in general when the gender mix isn’t specified. For clarity, you can say “dos hijos (sons)” vs. “dos hijas (daughters)” or “dos hijos y una hija.”
target_language_example: Hola, tengo dos hijos y vivimos en Madrid.
native_language_example: Hi, I have two children and we live in Madrid.

meaning: "I have a feeling that..." / "I have a hunch that..."
additional_notes: Used to express an intuition or gut feeling about something, without being sure or having clear proof. The verb changes with the subject: (yo) tengo, (tú) tienes, (él/ella) tiene el presentimiento de que + a full clause in the indicative (e.g., "va a suceder", "están").
target_language_example: Tengo el presentimiento de que hoy vamos a recibir buenas noticias.
native_language_example: I have a feeling that today we’re going to get good news.

meaning: 'as far as I understand' / 'I understand that' (based on what I've heard).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you believe is true because someone told you or you inferred it, but you’re not 100% sure. Common in polite conversation; it softens a statement and implies “correct me if I’m wrong.” Often followed by a verb in the indicative: “tengo entendido que + (buscas / eres / vives…)”.
target_language_example: Tengo entendido que mañana no hay clases.
native_language_example: I understand that there are no classes tomorrow (as far as I know).

meaning: 'I feel like' / 'I really want to' (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or urge. It’s followed by an infinitive (verb): "Tengo ganas de + comer/ir/verte". You can change the person: "tienes ganas de" (you feel like), "tiene ganas de" (he/she feels like), "tenemos ganas de" (we feel like). Often stronger/more immediate than "quiero" (I want).
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de salir un rato.
native_language_example: I feel like going out for a bit.

meaning: "I feel like going out" / "I want to go out."
additional_notes: "Tener ganas de" + infinitive means “to feel like doing” or “to want to do” (often a desire in the moment). Here, "salir" usually means “to go out” (leave the house, go out socially). You can change the subject: "tengo" (I), "tienes" (you), "tiene" (he/she/you formal), "tenemos" (we).
target_language_example: Esta noche tengo ganas de salir con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Tonight I feel like going out with my friends.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **tener** (“to have”) + **hambre** (“hunger”). In Spanish you say you “have hunger” (not *soy hambriento*). You can modify it with words like **no** (not), **ya no** (not anymore), **casi no** (hardly), **mucha** (very hungry), **un poco de** (a little hungry).
target_language_example: Tengo hambre, ¿podemos comer algo?
native_language_example: I’m hungry—can we eat something?

meaning: “I have the impression that… / I get the feeling that…”
additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or guess that you’re not 100% sure about (a personal sense or hunch). It’s followed by a clause with "que". You can change "tengo" to match the speaker: "tienes la impresión de que…" (you), "tiene la impresión de que…" (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Tengo la impresión de que no nos están diciendo toda la verdad.
native_language_example: I have the impression that they’re not telling us the whole truth.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a goal or plan. Follow it with an infinitive verb (de + verb): “Tengo la intención de + hacer/ir/estudiar…”. You can change the subject/person: “tienes la intención de…” (you intend), “tiene la intención de…” (he/she/you formal intends), “tenemos la intención de…” (we intend).
target_language_example: Tengo la intención de ahorrar dinero este año.
native_language_example: I intend to save money this year.

additional_notes: Used to express an intuition, impression, or suspicion (often without proof). It’s followed by a clause with "que" + a verb: "Tengo la sensación de que + (está/va a/es...)". In everyday speech you can also hear "Tengo la sensación de que..." meaning roughly the same as "Me da la sensación de que..." or "Siento que...".
target_language_example: Tengo la sensación de que hoy va a llover.
native_language_example: I have a feeling that it’s going to rain today.

additional_notes: Used with body parts in Spanish: you often use the definite article (las) instead of a possessive (mis). It’s commonly followed by an adjective (tengo las manos sucias = “my hands are dirty”) or used in set expressions like “tener las manos atadas” (“to have your hands tied,” meaning you can’t do anything about a situation).
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo las manos mojadas.
native_language_example: Sorry, my hands are wet.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel fear. Often followed by **de + noun**: *Tengo miedo de los payasos* (“I’m afraid of clowns”), or by a clause (very common in speech) expressing what you fear might happen: *Tengo miedo (de) que me den un tiro* (“I’m afraid they’ll shoot me”). You can also negate it: *No tengo miedo* (“I’m not afraid”).
target_language_example: Tengo miedo de perder mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of losing my passport.

additional_notes: Used to express fear. Common patterns: (1) tengo miedo de + noun: Tengo miedo de los perros. (I’m afraid of dogs.) (2) tengo miedo de + infinitive: Tengo miedo de ir/morir. (I’m scared to go/to die.) (3) tengo miedo de que + subjunctive for a feared possibility: Tengo miedo de que se haya perdido. (I’m afraid (that) it got lost.) In questions, use qué with an accent: Tengo miedo de qué vaya a decir el profesor. (I’m afraid of what the teacher might say.)
target_language_example: Tengo miedo de hablar en público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun (e.g., *muchas cámaras/monedas*). Often appears in the common expression **tengo muchas ganas de + infinitive / de + noun**, meaning “I’m really looking forward to…” or “I really feel like…” (e.g., *Tengo muchas ganas de verte* = “I’m really looking forward to seeing you”).
target_language_example: Tengo muchas ganas de ir al concierto.
native_language_example: I’m really looking forward to going to the concert.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a list of tasks or topics: **tener + (muchas) cosas que + infinitive** (e.g., *comprar, hacer, decir, meditar*). In everyday speech it often means you still need to do them (similar to “I still have a lot to do”). You may also hear an extra **tengo que**: *Tengo muchas cosas que tengo que comprar*—this is more repetitive but still natural.
target_language_example: Hoy tengo muchas cosas que hacer, pero primero necesito un café.
native_language_example: Today I have lots of things to do, but first I need a coffee.

meaning: "I have a lot of things to do."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re busy or have many tasks/errands. You can change the time phrase: "hoy" (today), "ahora" (now), "esta mañana" (this morning). The structure is literal: "tengo" (I have) + "muchas cosas" (many things) + "que hacer" (to do).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir; tengo muchas cosas que hacer esta tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go; I have a lot of things to do this afternoon.

meaning: "I really want to" / "I can’t wait to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb) to express strong desire or excitement: "Tengo muchas ganas de + infinitivo". You can also use it with a person pronoun to mean you’re eager to see someone: "... de verla" (to see her) / "... de verle" (to see him/you—formal).
target_language_example: Tengo muchas ganas de ir a la playa este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I really want to go to the beach this weekend.

additional_notes: Uses the verb tener (“to have”) to say you’re busy or have many tasks. You can extend it with que hacer (“to do”) or por hacer (“left to do”): Tengo mucho trabajo que hacer / Tengo mucho trabajo por hacer. You can change the subject too: Tienes mucho trabajo (you), Tiene mucho trabajo (he/she/you formal), Tenemos mucho trabajo (we).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo salir hoy; tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out today; I have a lot of work.

meaning: “I have a lot to …” (I have many things I need to do/say).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb) to express that you have a lot of something to do, say, tell, pay, etc.: “Tengo mucho que + infinitive.” It’s the present tense of “tener” (to have). You can change the subject/person: “tienes mucho que…”, “tenemos mucho que…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy tengo mucho que hacer.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I have a lot to do.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re busy or have many tasks. It’s the phrase "tener + mucho + que + infinitive" (to have a lot to + verb). You can change the subject/person: "tienes mucho que hacer" (you have a lot to do), "tenemos mucho que hacer" (we have a lot to do). You can also swap "mucho" for "poco" (little) or "tanto" (so much).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo salir; tengo mucho que hacer esta tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out; I have a lot to do this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a lot of friends. "Tengo" = "I have" (from *tener*), and it can be followed by details like where they’re from ("de Recife"), where they are ("en Boston"), or what kind they are ("extranjeros").
target_language_example: Tengo muchos amigos en la universidad.
native_language_example: I have many friends at the university.

meaning: (Usually with **no**:) “I have nothing / I don’t have anything.”
additional_notes: In correct Spanish, you normally say **no tengo nada**. Spanish commonly uses a **double negative**: **no** before the verb + **nada** after it. You can also add details after **nada**, e.g., **No tengo nada que decir** (“I have nothing to say”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo nada para ofrecerte ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have anything to offer you right now.

additional_notes: Used to strongly express trust in a person, their abilities, or something they will do. It’s formal/neutral and often followed by a person (en ti, en mi médico) or a noun phrase (en sus capacidades). You can change the verb for other people: tengo/tienes/tiene/tenemos plena confianza en…
target_language_example: Tengo plena confianza en que todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: I’m fully confident that everything will turn out well.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: "Tengo que + infinitive" (e.g., "Tengo que estudiar"). You can change the subject by conjugating "tener": "tienes que" (you have to), "tiene que" (he/she has to), "tenemos que" (we have to), etc.
target_language_example: Tengo que irme ahora.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest or slightly reluctant confession/opinion, often after thinking about it or despite expectations (sometimes like “I have to admit, you’re right”). You can change the subject: tengo/tienes/tiene/tenemos que admitir que…
target_language_example: Tengo que admitir que tenías razón.
native_language_example: I have to admit that you were right.

meaning: "I have to learn to..." / "I need to learn to..."
additional_notes: Used to say you feel obligated or it’s necessary for you to learn a skill or how to do something. Grammar: "tengo" is the 1st-person singular of "tener" (to have), "que" introduces the obligation (tener que = to have to), and "aprender a" is followed by an infinitive verb (aprender a + jugar/leer/ser). You can also use other persons: "tienes que aprender a..." (you have to learn to...), "tenemos que aprender a..." (we have to learn to...).
target_language_example: Tengo que aprender a cocinar mejor.
native_language_example: I have to learn to cook better.

meaning: "I have to fix/repair" (I need to fix).
additional_notes: Used to say you are obligated or need to repair something. Structure: tengo que + infinitive (arreglar). You can replace "tengo" with other forms: "tienes que arreglar" (you have to fix), "tenemos que arreglar" (we have to fix). "Arreglar" can also mean "to arrange/sort out" depending on context, but in these examples it means to repair an object or vehicle.
target_language_example: Tengo que arreglar mi bicicleta antes de mañana.
native_language_example: I have to fix my bike before tomorrow.

meaning: “I have to buy” / “I need to buy.”
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. The structure is: (yo) tengo que + infinitive (comprar = to buy). You can change the object after comprar: comprar algo/uno/una, comprar pan, comprar una camisa, etc.
target_language_example: Tengo que comprar pan antes de volver a casa.
native_language_example: I have to buy bread before going back home.

meaning: "I have to say" / "I need to say".
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you feel you must say. Often followed by what you’re going to say (e.g., "Te tengo que decir que..." = "I have to tell you that...") or used to close a statement ("Eso es todo lo que tengo que decir" = "That’s all I have to say"). Uses "tener que" + infinitive to express obligation/necessity; changes with the subject (tienes que decir, tiene que decir, etc.).
target_language_example: Te tengo que decir que no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: I have to tell you that I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity (tener que + infinitive). "Decirle" means "to tell to you/him/her"; the indirect object pronoun "le" can refer to usted, él, or ella, so the meaning depends on context. Common variations: "tengo que decirte" (informal "you": tú), "tengo que decirles" (to you all/them).
target_language_example: Tengo que decirle la verdad.
native_language_example: I have to tell you the truth.

meaning: "I have to tell you" / "I need to tell you."
additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker feels obligated or needs to say. It’s often followed by a noun (la verdad, adiós) or by "que" + a full statement (Tengo que decirte que no). The "te" means "to you" (informal singular); with formal "you" it becomes "tengo que decirle".
target_language_example: Tengo que decirte algo importante.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something important.

meaning: I have to tell you something.
additional_notes: Common way to introduce news or an important message. "Tengo que" expresses obligation/need (“I have to / I need to”), and "decirte" means “tell you” (informal singular "tú"). You can add emphasis with "muy importante" or soften it with "cuando puedas" (when you can).
target_language_example: Tengo que decirte algo, pero prefiero hablar en persona.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something, but I’d rather talk in person.

additional_notes: From **tener que + infinitive** (“to have to + verb”). **Tengo que** = “I have to,” and **encontrar** = “to find.” Often followed by what you need to find: *Tengo que encontrar mi teléfono.* Note: **encontrar** can also mean “to meet” (*Encontré a Ana en el supermercado* = “I ran into Ana at the supermarket”), and it can look like English “encounter.”
target_language_example: Tengo que encontrar mi pasaporte antes del vuelo.
native_language_example: I have to find my passport before the flight.

meaning: "I have to be" / "I need to be."
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It’s the verb phrase "tener que" (to have to) + "estar" (to be), and it’s commonly followed by an adjective or a location/state: "tengo que estar listo" (I have to be ready), "tengo que estar en casa" (I have to be at home), "tengo que estar con mi familia" (I have to be with my family). "Estar" is used for temporary states/conditions and location (not permanent identity—"ser").
target_language_example: Mañana tengo que estar en la oficina a las ocho.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to be at the office at eight.

meaning: “I have to study.” / “I need to study.”
additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation or necessity to study. Common pattern: "tener que" + infinitive (here, "estudiar"). You can add what you’re studying ("Tengo que estudiar matemáticas") or when/how much ("hoy", "mañana", "mucho").
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo salir; tengo que estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out; I have to study for the exam.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **tener que + infinitive** to express obligation/necessity. Very commonly followed by **con + person**: *tengo que hablar con mi jefe* (“I have to talk to my boss”). You can change it for other subjects: *tienes que hablar* (you have to talk), *tiene que hablar* (he/she has to talk).
target_language_example: Tengo que hablar contigo en privado.
native_language_example: I have to talk to you in private.

meaning: "I have to talk to..." / "I need to speak with..."
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or urgency to speak with someone. "Tengo que" = "I have to" and "hablar con" = "to talk with/to speak to." You change "tengo" to match the subject (e.g., "tienes que hablar con" = you have to talk to; "tenemos que hablar con" = we have to talk to). "con" is followed by a person or pronoun (e.g., "con él/ella/usted").
target_language_example: Tengo que hablar con mi jefe antes de la reunión.
native_language_example: I have to talk to my boss before the meeting.

meaning: “I have to talk to him.” / “I need to talk to him.”
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. "Tengo que" + infinitive = "I have to" + verb. "Con él" means "with him" (él = he/him; note the accent distinguishes it from "el" = "the"). You can add time words like "ahora" (now) or "ahora mismo" (right now).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tengo que hablar con él antes de irme.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I have to talk to him before I leave.

meaning: “I have to talk to you.” / “I need to talk to you.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an important or serious conversation. "Tengo que" means "I have to / I need to" and "hablar contigo" means "talk with you" (to one person you address as "tú"). Often followed by details with "acerca de" (about) or "en privado" (in private).
target_language_example: Oye, tengo que hablar contigo un momento.
native_language_example: Hey, I need to talk to you for a moment.

meaning: "I have to do" / "I need to do".
additional_notes: Used to talk about an obligation or something you must do. It’s made from: tener (to have) + que (to) + infinitive. Change "tengo" for the subject: "tienes que hacer" (you have to do), "tiene que hacer" (he/she/you formal has to do), "tenemos que hacer" (we have to do). Often followed by a noun ("hacer compras" = do shopping, "hacer llamadas" = make calls) or an action ("hacerte una pregunta" = ask you a question).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que hacer la tarea antes de salir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to do my homework before going out.

meaning: "I have to do something." / "I need to do something."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re obligated or need to do an unspecified task ("something"). Often refers to something you must do now or soon. You can change the subject and tense: "tienes que hacer algo" (you have to), "tiene que hacer algo" (he/she/you formal has to), "tenemos que hacer algo" (we have to), "tuve que hacer algo" (I had to).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que hacer algo primero.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to do something first.

additional_notes: Used to say you need/are required to make a phone call. "Tengo que" = "I have to" (obligation/necessity) + "hacer una llamada" = "make a call." You can change the verb/person: "tienes que..." (you have to), "tengo que hacer una llamada rápida" (a quick call).
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo que hacer una llamada antes de salir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to make a call before leaving.

meaning: "I have to do it." / "I need to do it."
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It’s the phrase "tener que" (to have to) + "hacerlo" (to do it). You can change the subject: "tienes que hacerlo" (you have to do it), "tenemos que hacerlo" (we have to do it).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tengo que hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I have to do it today.

meaning: "I have to go" / "I need to go."
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave or go somewhere. Often followed by **a + infinitive** for what you have to do ("tengo que ir a comprar" = I have to go buy something), or by a place/direction with **a/al/abajo** ("tengo que ir al aeropuerto" = I have to go to the airport; "tengo que ir abajo" = I have to go downstairs). You can add time words like **ahora mismo** (right now) or **solito** (alone/by myself).
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo que ir ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go right now.

meaning: "I have to go to" / "I need to go to" (in order to do something or go somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation or necessity to go somewhere or to go do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive (ir a hablar, ir a prepararme) or by a place (ir a la tienda). You can change the subject: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, etc.
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a estudiar ahora.
native_language_example: I have to go study now.

meaning: "I have to go get..." / "I have to go pick up..."
additional_notes: Used to say you must go somewhere to get someone or something. With people, Spanish typically uses the personal "a": "ir a buscar a mi hijo" (go pick up my son). With things, the "a" is usually not used: "ir a buscar mi sombrero" (go get my hat). "Buscar" can mean "look for," but in this structure it often means going to fetch/pick up.
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a buscar a mi amiga al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: I have to go pick up my friend at the airport.

meaning: "I have to go to the" (to a feminine place).
additional_notes: Used to say you must go somewhere: tengo que (I have to) + ir (to go) + a la (to the, feminine singular). It’s followed by a place noun that takes "la" (e.g., la comisaría, la mezquita, la ópera, la casa). For masculine places, you usually say "tengo que ir al" (a + el).
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a la farmacia antes de cenar.
native_language_example: I have to go to the pharmacy before dinner.

tengo que ir a ver a

target_language_multi_word_term: tengo que ir a ver a
additional_notes: Used to say you need/are obligated to go visit someone. The structure is: tengo que (I have to) + ir a (go to) + ver a (see/visit) + person. Use "ver a" (with "a") before a person: "ver a mi papá"; with groups it can be "ver a unos amigos". In a question or with another subject, it changes: "tienes que ir a ver a..." (you have to), "tiene que ir a ver a..." (he/she has to).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que ir a ver a mi abuela esta tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go see my grandma this afternoon.

meaning: “I have to go to the bathroom.” / “I need to use the restroom.”
additional_notes: Used to say you need to use the toilet. "Tengo que" = "I have to / I need to" + "ir" = "to go" + "al baño" = "to the bathroom." You can add "urgentemente" (urgently) to emphasize. In some places people also say "tengo que ir al servicio" or "tengo que ir al baño" as a polite, everyday way to excuse yourself.
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo que ir al baño ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go to the bathroom right now.

meaning: “I have to go / I need to leave.”
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave now (often to end a conversation). Literally “I have to leave”: tengo que (I have to) + irme (to leave/go away). You can add a destination with a: “tengo que irme al trabajo” (I have to go to work).
target_language_example: Perdón, tengo que irme ya.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re obligated or need to make a phone call. "Tengo que" = "I have to" + "llamar a" = "to call". Use "a" before a person (a Tom, a mi hermano) and also before some places you call (a casa). You can change the verb form: "tienes que llamar a..." (you have to call...), "tiene que llamar a..." (he/she has to call...).
target_language_example: Tengo que llamar a mi mamá esta noche.
native_language_example: I have to call my mom tonight.

meaning: “I have to take care of / deal with.”
additional_notes: Used to say you must handle a task, responsibility, or problem. "Ocuparme" is "to take care of" (reflexive: ocuparme = take care of it/myself), and it’s followed by "de" + a thing/issue: "ocuparme de esto" (take care of this). Often implies you need to attend to something now or that it’s your responsibility.
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que ocuparme de esto ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to take care of this right now.

meaning: I have to leave / I need to go out.
additional_notes: "Tengo que" expresses obligation or necessity (from "tener que" = "to have to"). "Salir" means "to leave" or "to go out"; context tells you which: leaving a place ("salir de la ciudad" = leave the city) or going out (e.g., out of the house). You can add a reason with "para" + infinitive: "tengo que salir temprano para tomar el tren" (I have to leave early to catch the train).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que salir ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to leave now.

meaning: "I have to take" / "I need to take."
additional_notes: "Tener que" + infinitive expresses obligation or necessity (something you must do). "Tomar" often means "to take" in Spanish (e.g., tomar un descanso = take a break; tomar una decisión = make/take a decision; tomar el autobús = take the bus). Depending on context, "tomar" can also mean "to drink" (e.g., tomar una cerveza = have a beer).
target_language_example: Tengo que tomar el autobús a las ocho.
native_language_example: I have to take the bus at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re obligated/required to work (often as an excuse or explanation). It’s the 1st-person singular of “tener que” + infinitive: “tengo que” (I have to) + “trabajar” (to work). You can add time phrases like “hoy,” “mañana,” “en la mañana,” “esta noche.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no puedo salir: tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out today: I have to work.

meaning: "I have to go back" / "I have to return."
additional_notes: Uses the structure **tener que + infinitive** to express obligation: *tengo que* = “I have to.” **Volver** means “to return/to go back,” and it’s often followed by **a** when you’re going back to do something: *tengo que volver a ir* = “I have to go again.” You can also use it with a place: *volver al centro* = “go back to downtown/the center.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo que volver a casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go back home.
