target_language_multi_word_term: todo lo que tenía que decir
additional_notes: Used to conclude a statement or discussion, meaning there’s nothing more you need or want to add. Common with verbs like decir (dije / he dicho / ya dije) and with “Es…” (“That’s…”): “Es todo lo que tenía que decir.” Literally “all that I had to say,” with tenía que = “had to / needed to.”
target_language_example: Para mí, es todo lo que tenía que decir.
native_language_example: For me, that’s everything I had to say.

todo lo que tienes que hacer es

target_language_multi_word_term: todo lo que tienes que hacer es
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple action or instruction that’s enough to achieve something. It’s often followed by an infinitive (mirar, obedecer, pulsar, seguir, sentarte). You can change the subject: "todo lo que tengo que hacer es..." (I), "todo lo que tienes que hacer es..." (you), "todo lo que tiene que hacer es..." (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Todo lo que tienes que hacer es escribir tu nombre aquí.
native_language_example: All you have to do is write your name here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the total set of things that follow in a relative clause. Often appears at the start of a sentence (“Todo lo que + verb...”) or before another clause (“...todo lo que el profesor dijo”). It can also be used with verbs like “hacer”, “decir”, “tener”, “necesitar”.
target_language_example: Anoté todo lo que dijiste.
native_language_example: I wrote down everything you said.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to all people in general (similar to "todo el mundo"). It usually takes singular verb agreement: "Todo mundo estaba..." / "Todo mundo ha...".
target_language_example: En esta ciudad, todo mundo se conoce.
native_language_example: In this city, everyone knows each other.

additional_notes: "Todo" = "all" + "su" = "his/her/their" + "dinero" = "money." It means the person’s entire amount of money. "Su" can be singular or plural (their), and the meaning depends on context. Often used with verbs like "robar" (to steal), "gastar" (to spend), "traer" (to bring), and "dar" (to give).
target_language_example: Perdió todo su dinero en el viaje.
native_language_example: He/She lost all his/her money on the trip.

meaning: all kinds of; every kind of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk generally about a wide variety within a category: todo tipo de deportes/personas/ropa. It often means “many different kinds of,” not necessarily literally every single kind.
target_language_example: En esta tienda hay todo tipo de regalos.
native_language_example: In this store there are all kinds of gifts.

meaning: “all kinds of things”; “all sorts of things.”
additional_notes: Used to be vague and general, meaning there are many different (often unspecified) things happening or available. Often appears with verbs like pasar/suceder (to happen), haber (there is/are), imaginar (to imagine), and can be used alone as a short answer. You may also hear the plural form “todo tipo de cosas” after “hay” or “suceden” without changing the meaning.
target_language_example: En ese trabajo hice todo tipo de cosas.
native_language_example: At that job I did all kinds of things.

additional_notes: Used to say you know, like, or tell all the details about someone or something. Often appears with verbs like saber (to know), contar (to tell), and gustar (to like). You’ll also commonly hear the shorter synonym “todo sobre…”.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de eso, pero te diré todo acerca del viaje mañana.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that, but I’ll tell you everything about the trip tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to check if someone is okay (“¿Todo bien?” / “¿Va todo bien?”) or to reassure that things are fine (“Está todo bien”, “Va a estar todo bien”, “Saldrá todo bien”). Very common in casual speech; you can answer simply “Sí, todo bien.”
target_language_example: ¿Todo bien? Si necesitas algo, dime.
native_language_example: All good? If you need anything, tell me.

additional_notes: Used to say the result or decision is determined by something else. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: «Todo depende de los resultados», «Todo depende de ti». You can also hear «Depende de…» without «todo» when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Todo depende de lo que diga el médico.
native_language_example: It all depends on what the doctor says.

additional_notes: Used to express optimism or to say that an outcome isn’t ruled out. Often appears after giving a reason or condition: “Con la tecnología, todo es posible” (with technology, anything is possible). Can also be said on its own to mean “you never know.”
target_language_example: Si trabajas duro, todo es posible.
native_language_example: If you work hard, anything is possible.

additional_notes: A reassuring phrase about the future (estar in the future tense: estará). Often said to comfort someone or express confidence that things will work out. You can also hear the near-future version: "todo va a estar bien."
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo estará bien mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be fine tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that everything is in a certain state or condition (Todo está bien/correcto/perdido) or in a certain place (Todo está en su sitio). It often introduces a description: Todo está + adjective (bien, correcto, perdido) or Todo está + preposition phrase (bajo control, en orden, en llamas).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo está listo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is ready.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to say a situation is under control. Often said on its own as a calming response (similar to “It’s okay”). You can also hear it as a check-in question: “¿Todo está bien?” = “Is everything okay?”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, todo está bien; ya llamé al médico.
native_language_example: Relax, everything is okay; I already called the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say that preparations are complete. Very common as a standalone statement ("Todo está listo.") or with emphasis like "Casi todo está listo" (almost everything) or "Creo que todo está listo" (I think everything is ready).
target_language_example: Ya podemos salir; todo está listo.
native_language_example: We can leave now; everything is ready.

meaning: “everything will be fine / everything will go well.”
additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or express confidence about the future. Uses the future tense of ir (irá = “will go”). Often said as a complete sentence, sometimes with a comma + a term of endearment (e.g., “cariño”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo irá bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Literally “everything together.” Used to mean things are combined/mixed in the same place (“put it all together”). It can also mean “overall / taken as a whole,” often at the start of a sentence: “Todo junto, no es muy complicado” = “All in all, it’s not very complicated.”
target_language_example: Metí la ropa y los zapatos todo junto en la maleta.
native_language_example: I put the clothes and the shoes all together in the suitcase.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the totality of things in a clause: “everything that + verb.” Very common in sentences like “Todo lo que (yo) sé es…” (“All I know is…”), “Todo lo que dijiste…” (“Everything you said…”). Note: “Todo lo que” (everything that) is different from “todo” alone (“everything/all”).
target_language_example: Todo lo que necesito es un poco de tiempo.
native_language_example: All I need is a little time.

additional_notes: Used to exclude one thing from “everything.” With people/adjectives it often means “anything but” (strong emphasis): “Es de todo menos tonto” = “He’s anything but stupid.” Often appears as “todo menos + noun” or “de todo menos + adjective/noun.”
target_language_example: Quiero ir a cualquier lugar, pero a casa todo menos.
native_language_example: I want to go anywhere, but home is the one place I don’t want to go.

additional_notes: Used to express an extreme choice with no middle ground: either complete success/commitment or complete failure/no commitment. Often said on its own as a slogan or attitude (e.g., in sports, business, relationships). You may also see it as "o todo o nada" for emphasis.
target_language_example: En este proyecto vamos a por todo: es todo o nada.
native_language_example: In this project we’re going for it: it’s all or nothing.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) emotional importance: “Eres todo para mí” = “You mean everything to me.” (2) practical meaning: “Tradujo todo para mí” = “He/She translated everything for me.” Often appears with the verb ser: “(Lo) eres / (él) era todo para mí.”
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme; eso significa todo para mí.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me; that means everything to me.

meaning: Everything will be fine / everything will work out.
additional_notes: Used to reassure or comfort someone when they’re worried. It’s in the future tense of “salir” (to turn out), so it literally means “everything will turn out well.” Commonly followed by phrases like “al final” (in the end) or “confía en mí” (trust me).
target_language_example: Tranquila, todo saldrá bien al final.
native_language_example: Relax, everything will work out in the end.

additional_notes: Used to say you know, tell, hear, or forget all the information/details about something. It’s often used after verbs like saber (to know), contar (to tell), oír (to hear), and olvidar (to forget): “Sé todo sobre…”, “Cuéntame todo sobre…”. You can also use “todo acerca de” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Cuéntame todo sobre tu nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Tell me everything about your new job.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you know (or want to know) all the details about a person. Often appears with verbs like saber (to know) or contar (to tell): “Quiero saber todo sobre ti.” You can also say “saberlo todo sobre ti” (“to know everything about you”), where “lo” refers to “everything.”
target_language_example: Quiero saber todo sobre ti.
native_language_example: I want to know everything about you.

additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or calm a situation. It’s often said with emphasis (e.g., “Te lo prometo” = “I promise you”) and can be placed at the start or end of a sentence (e.g., “Ahora todo va a estar bien”).
target_language_example: Tranquila, todo va a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be fine.

meaning: “Everything is going to be okay / turn out fine.”
additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or express optimism about the future. Very common in stressful situations; often said with “te lo prometo” (“I promise”) or as “va a salir todo bien” (same meaning).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is going to be okay.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that the situation is okay or progressing smoothly (at work, at home, during a trip, etc.). Often said as a response to questions like “¿Cómo va todo?” (How’s everything going?) or to confirm there are no problems.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo va bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is fine.

meaning: all of them (masculine or mixed-gender group).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific group of people or things already mentioned. For an all-female group, use "todas ellas". You can also say "todos" alone when "them" is understood from context.
target_language_example: Todos ellos llegaron temprano a la reunión.
native_language_example: All of them arrived early to the meeting.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to refer to a specific group/amount already known from context or pointed out: todos esos + noun (e.g., todos esos televisores). It can also refer to a period of time: todos esos años = “all those years.” Contrast: todos estos = “all these” (near the speaker).
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas guardado todos esos papeles.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you kept all those papers.

meaning: all these (plural, masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the whole set of things close by or just mentioned. It agrees with the noun: todos estos platos/factores/policías. Feminine: "todas estas" (e.g., todas estas ideas). Singular: "todo este" / "toda esta".
target_language_example: ¿Por qué todos estos problemas pasan al mismo tiempo?
native_language_example: Why do all these problems happen at the same time?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been true or happening for a long time up to now (often with emotion like surprise, frustration, or nostalgia). Common in phrases like “Después de todos estos años…” (“After all these years…”) and “Todos estos años creí que…” (“All these years I thought…”).
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas guardado ese secreto todos estos años.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you kept that secret all these years.

additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition: **en todos lados** = “everywhere” (location), **a todos lados** = “to everywhere / to all places” (movement). Common synonym: **en todas partes**. In many regions you may also hear **en todos lados** and **por todos lados** (“all around / everywhere”).
target_language_example: Busqué mi celular por todos lados, pero no lo encuentro.
native_language_example: I looked for my phone everywhere, but I can’t find it.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun: todos los + noun (e.g., todos los estudiantes = all the students). With feminine nouns it changes to todas las. It can refer to a whole group in general statements (Todos los mamíferos…) or to a specific set (una lista de todos los becarios). Also appears in fixed expressions like “¡por todos los cielos!” (an exclamation like “for heaven’s sake!”).
target_language_example: Todos los días estudio un poco de español.
native_language_example: I study a little Spanish every day.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of animals being talked about. Often used as the subject of a sentence: “Todos los animales son…” = “All animals are…”. In negative sentences you may see “No todos los animales…” = “Not all animals…”.
target_language_example: Todos los animales necesitan agua.
native_language_example: All animals need water.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or regularly once a year. Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also go near the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Mis abuelos nos visitan todos los años en verano.
native_language_example: My grandparents visit us every year in the summer.

meaning: all the boys / all the guys.
additional_notes: Means “all the boys/guys” in a group. It’s common in everyday speech to use chicos to mean “boys/guys” (not necessarily children). If it follows a noun phrase, you often see a + todos (e.g., A todos los chicos les gustó... = “All the guys liked...”/“All the boys liked...”).
target_language_example: Todos los chicos quieren ir al cine.
native_language_example: All the guys want to go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group, excluding the person/people already mentioned. It agrees in gender/number with the group: todos los demás (masc./mixed plural), todas las demás (fem. plural), todo lo demás (everything else, neutral/unspecified things), toda la demás (rare; feminine singular in specific contexts). Often follows a noun implicitly: "como todos los demás" = like everyone else.
target_language_example: No quiero ser como todos los demás.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be like everyone else.

additional_notes: Used to say you know/need/have every piece of information. Often appears with verbs like saber/conocer (to know), tener (to have), recordar (to remember), and escuchar (to listen to someone who has the information).
target_language_example: Si quieres ayudar, necesito todos los detalles.
native_language_example: If you want to help, I need all the details.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do regularly on Sundays. The plural "domingos" is used in Spanish to mean "every Sunday" (a repeated habit), not multiple specific Sundays. Often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Salgo a caminar todos los domingos.
native_language_example: I go for a walk every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens daily or as a regular routine. It often goes at the beginning or end of a sentence: “Todos los días estudio” / “Estudio todos los días.”
target_language_example: Trabajo todos los días, pero descanso los domingos.
native_language_example: I work every day, but I rest on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens daily, followed by the preposition **a**. **A** can introduce a **time** (*a las ocho*, *a la misma hora*) or a **destination/event** (*a misa*, *a casa*). Often it’s really the phrase **todos los días** (“every day”), with **a** starting the next part of the sentence.
target_language_example: Voy todos los días a las ocho.
native_language_example: I go every day at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Refers to the entire group of students. With a verb it often means “every student” in the sense that the statement applies to the whole group (e.g., “Todos los estudiantes aplaudieron.”). It can also be part of expressions like “a todos los estudiantes” (“to all the students”).
target_language_example: La profesora saludó a todos los estudiantes al entrar en clase.
native_language_example: The teacher greeted all the students when she walked into class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly on Saturdays and Sundays. It’s often used with routine verbs like "normalmente" or "soler" ("suele"). You can also say "cada fin de semana" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Trabajamos todos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: We work every weekend.

additional_notes: "Todos" means "all" and agrees in gender/number with the noun: todos los hombres (masculine plural). It’s used to make a general statement about men in a group or in general. For "all people" (mixed/unspecified gender), Spanish often uses "todas las personas" or "todo el mundo".
target_language_example: En esta empresa, todos los hombres y todas las mujeres tienen las mismas oportunidades.
native_language_example: In this company, all the men and all the women have the same opportunities.

meaning: “all men are …” (a general statement about men).
additional_notes: Used to make generalizations: “Todos los hombres son + adjective/noun.” The verb “son” is the plural form of “ser” (to be). You can soften/limit the statement with “No todos los hombres son …” (“Not all men are …”). The word after “son” usually agrees in masculine plural (e.g., “sabios,” “mortales”).
target_language_example: No todos los hombres son iguales.
native_language_example: Not all men are the same.

additional_notes: A set phrase meaning that every person (often understood as everyone, regardless of differences) should have the same rights or be treated the same. Common in legal, moral, and religious contexts: "ante" or "a los ojos de" (before / in the eyes of) + Dios; "de acuerdo a" (according to) + la ley. Note: "hombres" can mean "men" literally, but in older/formal usage it can also mean "human beings" (people).
target_language_example: En una democracia, todos los hombres son iguales ante la ley.
native_language_example: In a democracy, all people are equal before the law.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the entire human population as a group. Often appears in general statements (e.g., with verbs like "son" / "somos"). In Spanish you can also say "todos los seres humanos" (a bit more formal) or simply "todos" if the context makes it clear you mean people.
target_language_example: Todos los humanos necesitan agua para vivir.
native_language_example: All humans need water to live.

additional_notes: Uses **todo** in plural (**todos**) with a plural noun (**los libros**) to mean the complete set of books in a group. Often appears after **ya / he / hemos** to say you’ve finished reading everything (e.g., *Ya he leído todos los libros...*). With **no**, it means “not all the books” (not necessarily none): *No todos los libros...*.
target_language_example: En esta caja están todos los libros que compré ayer.
native_language_example: In this box are all the books I bought yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens regularly on Mondays. Place it after the verb ("Lo hago todos los lunes") or at the beginning for emphasis ("Todos los lunes lo hago").
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio todos los lunes.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every Monday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens monthly (a repeated habit or a regular payment). Also appears in comparisons like “De todos los meses…” = “Of all the months…”.
target_language_example: Pago el alquiler todos los meses.
native_language_example: I pay the rent every month.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every person in a group. It’s often followed by “de + [group]” (e.g., todos los miembros de la familia/del comité). With negation, “No todos los miembros…” means “Not all the members…”.
target_language_example: Todos los miembros del equipo llegaron a tiempo.
native_language_example: All the members of the team arrived on time.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of children being talked about. "Todos" is plural masculine and is used for mixed-gender groups; for an all-girls group you can say "todas las niñas". You’ll often see it with "a" when the children are the direct object: "a todos los niños" (e.g., "les gusta" / "vi a").
target_language_example: Todos los niños del barrio juegan en el parque después de la escuela.
native_language_example: All the kids in the neighborhood play in the park after school.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire group of passengers (people traveling on a plane, train, bus, ship, etc.). Often appears in announcements or reports: “Todos los pasajeros deben estar listos para abordar” (“All passengers must be ready to board”). Note: with a masculine plural noun like “pasajeros,” it can include mixed genders.
target_language_example: Todos los pasajeros deben permanecer sentados durante el despegue.
native_language_example: All passengers must remain seated during takeoff.

additional_notes: Means every problem in a given situation. Often used after verbs like resolver (“to solve”): resolver todos los problemas (“to solve all the problems”). You can also say todos mis/tus/sus problemas (“all my/your/his/her/their problems”).
target_language_example: No puedo resolver todos los problemas a la vez.
native_language_example: I can’t solve all the problems at once.

meaning: “all those who” / “everyone who” (refers to people who…).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by an action or description that follows. It’s often followed by a verb: “Todos los que viven aquí…” = “Everyone who lives here…”. You can also use it with other forms: “todas las que” (feminine plural), “todo el que / todos los que” depending on singular/plural.
target_language_example: Todos los que tengan boleto pueden entrar.
native_language_example: Everyone who has a ticket can come in.

additional_notes: Means “all beings/creatures” in a general sense. It’s often followed by an adjective like vivos/vivientes (“living”) to specify “all living beings” (todos los seres vivos). On its own (todos los seres), it can sound more broad or philosophical (all beings, including people/creatures).
target_language_example: Debemos respetar a todos los seres vivos.
native_language_example: We should respect all living beings.

additional_notes: Common in status checks or announcements (like “All systems go/ready”). Often used with verbs like estar, funcionar, or listo: “Todos los sistemas están bien / funcionando / listos.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, todos los sistemas están funcionando.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, all systems are working.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each summer (a habitual routine). Often used with the present tense for habits ("Voy todos los veranos...") or with the imperfect/past to describe a repeated action in the past ("Iba todos los veranos...").
target_language_example: Visitamos a mis abuelos todos los veranos.
native_language_example: We visit my grandparents every summer.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to say that every one of something belongs to you: todos mis + noun (e.g., todos mis exámenes). With feminine plural nouns, use todas mis (todas mis amigas). For singular, use todo mi / toda mi.
target_language_example: Ya terminé todos mis deberes.
native_language_example: I already finished all my homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your entire group of friends. It often comes before a verb: “Todos mis amigos están…” (All my friends are…). In comparisons you may see “De todos mis amigos…” = “Out of all my friends…”.
target_language_example: Todos mis amigos viven cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: All my friends live near here.

additional_notes: Uses the plural of "todo" + the subject pronoun "nosotros" for emphasis/clarity. Often appears after a preposition: "para todos nosotros" (for all of us), "entre todos nosotros" (among/between all of us), "por todos nosotros" (for all of us/on behalf of all of us). With "de": "el más alto de todos nosotros" = "the tallest of all of us".
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda; significa mucho para todos nosotros.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help; it means a lot to all of us.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean that every one of the things belongs to 'us': todos nuestros planes/asuntos. For feminine plural nouns, use "todas nuestras" (todas nuestras ideas).
target_language_example: Todos nuestros amigos llegaron temprano.
native_language_example: All of our friends arrived early.

additional_notes: “Todos” agrees with the noun being talked about (todos/todas), and “sus” means “his/her/your/their” (the owner is shown by context, not by the word itself). Used before a plural noun: “todos sus sueños” = “all his/her dreams.” If the noun is feminine plural, use “todas sus …” (e.g., “todas sus fotos”).
target_language_example: Perdió todos sus documentos en el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: He/She lost all his/her documents at the airport.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of someone’s friends. The pronoun "sus" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their" depending on context; often you clarify with "de él" or "de ella" (e.g., "todos sus amigos (de ella)"). Used frequently with preposition "a" when the friends are the indirect object: "Invitó a todos sus amigos".
target_language_example: Invitó a todos sus amigos a cenar.
native_language_example: He invited all his friends to dinner.

additional_notes: Means someone is trying as hard as they can. Often used with contrast like “a pesar de…” (despite) or with “en vano” (in vain): “A pesar de todos sus esfuerzos…” / “Todos sus esfuerzos fueron en vano.” You can change the possessive to match the person: “todos mis esfuerzos” (all my efforts), “todos nuestros esfuerzos” (all our efforts).
target_language_example: A pesar de todos sus esfuerzos, no consiguió el trabajo.
native_language_example: Despite all his efforts, he didn’t get the job.

additional_notes: Used to address a group of people with the pronoun "ustedes" (common in Latin America and also used formally in Spain). "Todos" agrees in gender/number: use "todas ustedes" for an all-female group. Often used for emphasis; you can also just say "ustedes" (= you all).
target_language_example: Gracias a todos ustedes por venir hoy.
native_language_example: Thank you all for coming today.

additional_notes: Used to say that all the people in a group were in a certain state or doing something. It’s the imperfect tense of estar (estaban), often describing an ongoing situation in the past (e.g., emotions, conditions, actions in progress). Typically followed by an adjective (felices, satisfechos) or a gerund (escuchando).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, todos estaban nerviosos.
native_language_example: When I arrived, everyone was nervous.

additional_notes: "Todos" refers to all people in a group, and "están" is the present tense of estar (used for states/conditions, locations, or temporary situations). Often followed by an adjective or phrase: "Todos están bien" (everyone is fine), "Todos están de acuerdo" (everyone agrees), "Todos están en casa" (everyone is at home).
target_language_example: En la reunión, todos están de acuerdo con el plan.
native_language_example: In the meeting, everyone agrees with the plan.

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group does something at the same time or stays/comes/returns as a group (not separately). It often goes with verbs like ir (to go), volver (to return), estar (to be), and vivir (to live).
target_language_example: Vamos a entrar todos juntos.
native_language_example: Let's go in all together.

additional_notes: Often appears as **a todos nos** + verb to mean “to all of us / for all of us”: *A todos nos pasa* (“It happens to all of us”). It can also be **Todos nos...** as the subject (“All of us...”): *Todos nos están mirando* (“They’re looking at all of us”). In an all-female group you may hear **todas nos**. With reflexive verbs you’ll see it before the verb: *todos nos reunimos* (“we all meet / we all get together”).
target_language_example: A todos nos gusta esa canción.
native_language_example: All of us like that song.

additional_notes: Used to include the speaker and a group ("we"). Often placed at the start for emphasis: "Todos nosotros..." You’ll also see it after a preposition as "de/para todos nosotros" ("of/for all of us"). Feminine group: "todas nosotras"; mixed/masculine group: "todos nosotros".
target_language_example: Todos nosotros tenemos que ayudar.
native_language_example: All of us have to help.

additional_notes: “Todos” means “everyone/all (people)” and “quieren” is the present tense of “querer” (to want/to love). It’s used to say that all people in a group want something: Todos quieren + noun (dinero), or Todos quieren + infinitive (creer, sentarse). With a person, “querer a + person” means “to love” or “to care about”: Todos quieren a Tom. You can negate it with “No todos quieren…” = “Not everyone wants…”.
target_language_example: No todos quieren lo mismo.
native_language_example: Not everyone wants the same thing.

additional_notes: Used to say the reason is obvious or already known by everyone. It can be neutral (“we all know why we’re here”) or slightly accusatory/pointed (“we all know why you did that”). Often followed by a clause: por qué + verb (por qué estamos aquí), or by something like “lo hiciste” (“you did it”).
target_language_example: No hace falta explicarlo: todos sabemos por qué pasó.
native_language_example: No need to explain it: we all know why it happened.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker presents as common knowledge or obvious to everyone. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Todos sabemos que + (he/she/it/they)…”
target_language_example: Todos sabemos que hoy no es el mejor día para discutir.
native_language_example: We all know that today isn’t the best day to argue.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something presented as common knowledge or obvious. Typically followed by a clause (indicative): “Todos saben que + [statement].” In speech you may also hear “Todo el mundo sabe que …” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Todos saben que mañana es el examen.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that the exam is tomorrow.

meaning: “everyone” / “they all” (used before a verb with se).
additional_notes: Use **todos** as the subject meaning “everyone/they all,” and **se** is the pronoun required by many verbs (often reflexive or describing a change of state): *levantarse* (to get up), *dormirse* (to fall asleep), *irse* (to leave), *reírse* (to laugh), etc. In English you usually translate it as **“everyone”** or **“they all,”** not word-for-word as “all themselves.”
target_language_example: Todos se fueron temprano.
native_language_example: They all left early.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement that includes everyone in a group (“all of us”). It’s often followed by an adjective or noun: “todos somos responsables” (we’re all responsible). You can also say “todas somos” if the group is all female, and “todos somos” can also be used for mixed groups.
target_language_example: En esta familia, todos somos importantes.
native_language_example: In this family, we are all important.

additional_notes: Used to say that every person/thing in a group has the same quality. It’s the plural of “todo es” (everything is). Often followed by an adjective or a noun: “Todos son altos” (They’re all tall), “Todos son hackers” (They’re all hackers).
target_language_example: En esta clase, todos son muy inteligentes.
native_language_example: In this class, they’re all very smart.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about everyone (including the speaker). Often followed by a noun ("todos tenemos problemas") or by "que" + infinitive to express obligation/inevitability ("todos tenemos que morir"). Spanish commonly drops the subject pronoun "nosotros" because "tenemos" already shows it's "we".
target_language_example: Todos tenemos días buenos y días malos.
native_language_example: We all have good days and bad days.

additional_notes: From "todos" (everyone/all) + "tienen" (they have). Used to say that something is true for every person in a group. Often followed by a noun ("Todos tienen secretos") or by "que" to mean "everyone has to" ("Todos tienen que saber...").
target_language_example: Todos tienen que llevar identificación.
native_language_example: Everyone has to carry ID.

additional_notes: Emphatic way to refer to every single person or thing in a group, highlighting individuals one by one. Often used with “de”: “todos y cada uno de ellos/de ustedes/de los sabores.”
target_language_example: Quiero agradecer a todos y cada uno de ustedes por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I want to thank each and every one of you for your help.

meaning: "have/take a little (of)" (informal command to one person).
additional_notes: Uses the tú imperative of tomar (“to take/have”). Common when offering something (food/drink) or telling someone to use/add a small amount. Often followed by a noun: toma un poco de café/agua/esto.
target_language_example: Toma un poco de agua, por favor.
native_language_example: Have a little water, please.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase from the verb "tomar una decisión" (to make a decision). Used with an auxiliary verb like "haber" to form the present perfect: "he/has/hemos/han tomado una decisión" = "I/you/he/we/they have made a decision." You can add adjectives after "decisión" (e.g., "una decisión importante/significativa").
target_language_example: Ya he tomado una decisión.
native_language_example: I've already made a decision.

meaning: to get some fresh air; to take a breath.
additional_notes: Used when you step outside or pause to breathe and recover (physically or emotionally). In Spanish it’s a common, natural expression; in English you usually say “get some air” or “take a breath” rather than “take air.”
target_language_example: Voy a salir un momento a tomar aire.
native_language_example: I’m going to step out for a moment to get some fresh air.

meaning: to have something (to drink); or to take/pick up something.
additional_notes: Very common phrase. With food/drinks, tomar means “to have” (especially “to drink”): Me gustaría tomar algo = “I’d like to have something (to drink).” With objects, tomar means “to take/grab/pick up”: Necesito tomar algo del auto = “I need to get something from the car.” Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, podemos tomar algo en un bar.
native_language_example: After work, we can have a drink at a bar.

additional_notes: Common polite phrase used by hosts, receptionists, or staff to invite someone to sit. Often said as an imperative: "Tome asiento" (formal you) or "Toma asiento" (informal you). Also used with "puede": "Puede tomar asiento".
target_language_example: Puede tomar asiento, por favor.
native_language_example: You can take a seat, please.

additional_notes: Common collocation with tomar (“to take”), but it usually translates as “to make decisions” in English. Often used with tener que (“to have to”): Tienes que tomar decisiones. You can also specify what kind of decisions: tomar decisiones importantes (to make important decisions).
target_language_example: No puedo tomar decisiones sin más información.
native_language_example: I can't make decisions without more information.

meaning: to go out for some fresh air.
additional_notes: Used when you step outside (often briefly) to breathe fresh air, get a break, or clear your head. Very common with ir/venir/salir: «Voy a tomar el aire», «Vamos a tomar el aire». It’s not about “taking” air literally; it means going outside for air.
target_language_example: Después de estar todo el día en casa, salí a tomar el aire.
native_language_example: After being at home all day, I went out to get some fresh air.

meaning: to tease someone; to pull someone’s leg (to joke/trick them).
additional_notes: Common in Spain and Latin America. It usually implies you’re joking or making someone believe something that isn’t true. Often used as a question or denial: “¿Me estás tomando el pelo?” / “No te estoy tomando el pelo.” It’s not literally about hair.
target_language_example: ¿Es verdad, o solo quieres tomar el pelo?
native_language_example: Is it true, or are you just pulling my leg?

additional_notes: Used to say you will consider a factor, suggestion, or information when making a decision. Very common with an object (e.g., “tomar en cuenta algo” = to take something into account). In many regions you’ll also hear “tener en cuenta” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vamos a tomar en cuenta tu opinión antes de decidir.
native_language_example: We’re going to take your opinion into account before deciding.

meaning: to take the floor; to speak up (in a meeting or group).
additional_notes: Used when someone begins speaking after being given a turn, or when they decide to address a group. Common in formal or semi-formal contexts (meetings, classes, presentations): “Ahora va a tomar la palabra…” = “Now … will speak.” Often contrasted with “pedir la palabra” (to ask to speak).
target_language_example: Al final de la reunión, Marta decidió tomar la palabra para hacer una pregunta.
native_language_example: At the end of the meeting, Marta decided to take the floor to ask a question.

meaning: to take note; to write down.
additional_notes: Used when you want to record information so you don’t forget it. Often followed by "de" + what you’re noting ("Tomé nota de su número"). In polite requests you’ll hear "Tome nota" (formal) or "Toma nota" (informal).
target_language_example: Voy a tomar nota de tu dirección.
native_language_example: I’m going to write down your address.

meaning: to take by surprise; to catch off guard.
additional_notes: Used when something happens unexpectedly and surprises someone. Commonly used in the past tense (e.g., "me tomó por sorpresa") with an event/person as the subject: "La noticia/lluvia/decisión me tomó por sorpresa." Similar in meaning to "sorprender" or "pillar desprevenido/a".
target_language_example: La lluvia nos tomó por sorpresa cuando salimos sin paraguas.
native_language_example: The rain took us by surprise when we went out without an umbrella.

additional_notes: Often used in an impersonal way: "Tomar tiempo + infinitive" or "Tomar tiempo + noun" ("It takes time to…" / "It takes time for…"). In some contexts, it can also mean “to time/measure” something (e.g., timing a race), but beginners most often see it as “to take time.” Related: "tomarse tiempo" = “to take your time.”
target_language_example: Aprender español puede tomar tiempo.
native_language_example: Learning Spanish can take time.

additional_notes: Common pattern: tomar + un/una + noun. Often means "to drink/have" with beverages (tomar un café, tomar un té, tomar un poco de leche). It can also mean "to take" in other contexts (tomar un vuelo = to take a flight; tomar un recado = to take a message). The exact translation depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres tomar un café conmigo?
native_language_example: Do you want to have a coffee with me?

meaning: to get some fresh air; to step outside for a bit.
additional_notes: Commonly used when you need a short break, often by going outside. You can use it with ir/venir/volver (e.g., “Voy a…”, “Vamos a…”) or as a command (“Ve a…”).
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, salí a tomar un poco de aire.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I went out to get some fresh air.

meaning: "to take/have a" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Very common pattern: **tomar + una + [noun]**. Depending on the noun, it can mean **take/grab** (tomar una valija), **take** (tomar una muestra, tomar una clase), or **have/drink** (tomar una taza de café). With abstract nouns it can mean **make** (tomar una decisión).
target_language_example: Voy a tomar una foto.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a photo.

additional_notes: Common with tener que / deber / es hora de to express obligation or urgency: “Tengo que / Debes / Es hora de tomar una decisión.” In the past, it’s often “tuve que tomar una decisión” (“I had to make a decision”).
target_language_example: Necesito más información antes de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: I need more information before making a decision.

additional_notes: Common way to say you nap, especially a short rest during the day (often after lunch). Uses the verb "tomar" (to take) + "una siesta" (a nap).
target_language_example: Después de comer, voy a tomar una siesta.
native_language_example: After eating, I'm going to take a nap.

meaning: to take a vacation / to go on vacation.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase meaning to take time off from work or school to rest or travel. Also very common: "ir de vacaciones" (to go on vacation). You can add a time expression: "tomar vacaciones en agosto" (take vacation in August) or a duration: "tomar dos semanas de vacaciones" (take two weeks of vacation).
target_language_example: Voy a tomar vacaciones la próxima semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a vacation next week.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of tomar: tomé = "I took" (a completed action). Used to say you used a taxi as transportation, often with phrases like "para" (in order to), "porque" (because), and location words like "enfrente de" (in front of). In everyday speech you can also say "cogí un taxi" (Spain) or "agarré un taxi" (some Latin America).
target_language_example: Tomé un taxi para llegar a tiempo al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: I took a taxi to get to the airport on time.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of "tomar" + "un". Common uses include: taking/grabbing something (Tomó un lienzo), having/eating/drinking something (Tomó un bocado), taking a class/course (Tomó un curso), and with time expressions meaning "it took (someone)" (Le tomó un tiempo...). The subject can be a person or sometimes a thing/situation depending on context.
target_language_example: Ana tomó un taxi para llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: Ana took a taxi to arrive on time.

meaning: curfew (a required time to be off the streets / at home).
additional_notes: Used to say that authorities have declared or imposed a restriction on movement at certain hours. Common verbs: haber (Hay toque de queda), declarar (Se ha declarado el toque de queda), imponer (Se impuso un toque de queda), cumplir (Tengo que cumplir con el toque de queda).
target_language_example: Durante la emergencia, impusieron un toque de queda a las 10 de la noche.
native_language_example: During the emergency, they imposed a curfew at 10 p.m.

meaning: "works as" (has the job of); also "works like" (in the manner of).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone’s role or profession: "Trabaja como cajero" = "He works as a cashier." With "como + un/una" it can also describe how someone works (a comparison): "trabaja como una hormiga" = "works like an ant" (works very hard). You can change the subject and tense: "Trabajo como…", "Ella trabajaba como…", etc.
target_language_example: Ella trabaja como profesora en una escuela primaria.
native_language_example: She works as a teacher at an elementary school.

meaning: 'works hard' (third-person singular: he/she/it works hard) or 'work hard' (as a command).
additional_notes: From "trabajar" (to work) + "duro" (hard). It can describe what someone does ("Él trabaja duro") or be used as an instruction/encouragement ("¡Trabaja duro!"). You can also change the subject: "Yo trabajo duro", "Nosotros trabajamos duro", "Ellos trabajan duro".
target_language_example: Mi hermana trabaja duro todos los días.
native_language_example: My sister works hard every day.

meaning: 'works in' / 'works at' (a place, company, country, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with "en" to say where someone works: a workplace (en una escuela), a company/store (en Walmart), a field/area (en la televisión), or a location (en Francia). For working *for* a person/company as an employer, Spanish often uses "trabajar para" (e.g., "Trabajo para Google").
target_language_example: Mi mamá trabaja en un hospital.
native_language_example: My mom works at a hospital.

meaning: "works at/in the" (she/he works at a place or in an industry).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone works. It’s the verb "trabajar" (to work) in the 3rd-person singular present tense: "él/ella trabaja" = "he/she works". Use "en" for workplaces and fields: "trabaja en la panadería" (at the bakery), "trabaja en la industria del cine" (in the film industry). With masculine nouns, it changes to "trabaja en el" (e.g., "trabaja en el hospital").
target_language_example: Mi papá trabaja en la escuela del barrio.
native_language_example: My dad works at the neighborhood school.

additional_notes: From the verb "trabajar" (to work). "Trabaja" can refer to he/she/you (formal: usted). "En un banco" means "at/in a bank". You can change the subject: "Yo trabajo...", "Él/Ella trabaja...", "¿Trabajas en un banco?"
target_language_example: Mi mamá trabaja en un banco cerca de casa.
native_language_example: My mom works at a bank near our house.

meaning: "(he/she) works at/in a …" (a workplace/activity, feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone works. The verb is from **trabajar** (to work) in the **él/ella/usted** form: *trabaja*. It’s followed by **en** + **una** when the workplace noun is feminine: *una escuela, una tienda, una oficina*. For masculine nouns, you’ll often see *trabaja en un …* (e.g., *un banco*). In English this can be “works at a” or “works in a,” depending on the place.
target_language_example: Mi hermana trabaja en una cafetería del centro.
native_language_example: My sister works at a café downtown.

meaning: working hard in the field (doing farm work).
additional_notes: Uses the gerund "trabajando" (working) plus the adverb "duro" (hard) to describe an ongoing activity. Common with forms of "estar" to express what someone is/was/will be doing: "está/estuvo/estará trabajando...". "En el campo" usually refers to the countryside or farm fields.
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando duro en el campo para terminar antes de que anochezca.
native_language_example: We’re working hard in the field to finish before it gets dark.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (or sometimes seguir) to form the present progressive: estar trabajando en + place/project. With a place, it usually means being employed there or doing work there (e.g., in Africa). With a thing/idea, it means focusing effort on it (working on something).
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando en un proyecto nuevo.
native_language_example: We are working on a new project.

meaning: to work as; to work like (very hard, like…).
additional_notes: Use **trabajar como + noun** to say someone’s job (**Trabaja como médico** = “He works as a doctor”) or to compare how someone works (**trabajar como esclavo** = “to work like a slave,” i.e., extremely hard). In comparisons, **como** means “like/as,” not a job title.
target_language_example: Es terrible verlos **trabajar como** esclavos en este calor.
native_language_example: It’s terrible to see them work like slaves in this heat.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for putting in a lot of effort at work or toward a goal. Uses the verb trabajar (to work) + duro (hard). You can change the subject/tense: Trabajo duro. / Trabajé duro. / Tengo que trabajar duro.
target_language_example: Si quieres aprobar el examen, tienes que trabajar duro.
native_language_example: If you want to pass the exam, you have to work hard.

meaning: to work in/at (a place); to work on (a task/project).
additional_notes: Use **trabajar en + place** to say where you work (city, company, building): *trabajar en Osaka / en un hospital*. Use **trabajar en + thing** to mean working on something (improving/preparing it): *trabajar en su discurso / en esto*. Often contrasted with **trabajar para** (to work for an employer), but **trabajar en** emphasizes location or the thing you’re working on.
target_language_example: Estoy feliz porque voy a trabajar en Osaka el próximo año.
native_language_example: I’m happy because I’m going to work in Osaka next year.

additional_notes: Used when two or more people cooperate or collaborate on a task or goal (often on a project). It can describe a one-time effort (Vamos a trabajar juntos en esto) or an ongoing situation (Solíamos trabajar juntos). You can also use it as advice/command: Debéis trabajar juntos.
target_language_example: Si queremos terminar a tiempo, tenemos que trabajar juntos.
native_language_example: If we want to finish on time, we have to work together.

meaning: “I work in/at/on …” (to say where you work or what you work on).
additional_notes: Used with places and organizations: “Trabajo en un supermercado” = “I work at a supermarket.” With projects/areas it can mean “work on/in”: “Trabajo en marketing” / “Trabajo en un proyecto.” Note: “Trabajo en equipo” means “teamwork” or “working as a team.”
target_language_example: Trabajo en una oficina cerca del centro.
native_language_example: I work in an office near downtown.

additional_notes: Used to talk about effort that is difficult and requires persistence. Often appears with verbs like "hacer" (to do) or "requerir" (to require), or in set phrases like "con trabajo duro" (with hard work). "Trabajo" is a noun and "duro" is an adjective meaning "hard/tough."
target_language_example: Con trabajo duro, puedes lograr tus metas.
native_language_example: With hard work, you can achieve your goals.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning people working together as a team toward a shared goal. Often used with verbs like existir (to exist), contar (to matter), and with adjectives like perfecto (perfect).
target_language_example: Para terminar el proyecto a tiempo, necesitamos trabajo en equipo.
native_language_example: To finish the project on time, we need teamwork.

meaning: work to be done; work left to do.
additional_notes: Used to say there is still pending work. Often appears with “hay” (there is/are): “Hay mucho trabajo por hacer.” The pattern “por + infinitive” can express something that remains to be done (pending/unfinished).
target_language_example: Todavía tenemos trabajo por hacer antes de irnos.
native_language_example: We still have work to do before we leave.

meaning: (some) work to do; tasks that need to be done.
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener to say you have work to do: "Tengo trabajo que hacer". You can add quantity/degree words like "mucho", "tanto", "un montón de", or adjectives like "importante": "Tengo mucho trabajo que hacer", "Tenemos importante trabajo que hacer". Similar to "cosas que hacer" (things to do).
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; tengo trabajo que hacer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I have work to do.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to swimwear in general. Used for both men’s and women’s swimwear (one-piece, bikini, swim trunks), depending on context. Plural: "trajes de baño".
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está mi traje de baño?
native_language_example: Where is my swimsuit?

additional_notes: Often used with the verb phrase “hacer trampa (en un examen)” = “to cheat (on an exam).” You may also hear “copiar en el examen” (to copy/cheat) or “hacer trampa en una prueba” (test/quiz).
target_language_example: Si haces trampa en el examen, puedes suspender la clase.
native_language_example: If you cheat on the exam, you might fail the class.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened following someone’s death. Common in more formal or written Spanish; in everyday speech you might also hear "después de la muerte de". It’s followed by a person (or sometimes an animal) or a noun referring to the deceased (e.g., "su madre").
target_language_example: Tras la muerte de mi abuelo, la familia se reunió en su casa.
native_language_example: After my grandfather’s death, the family met at his house.

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) **Tratar de + noun** = “to deal with / to be about” (often in definitions or explanations): *La ética... trata de la conducta humana.*
2) **Tratar de + infinitive** = “to try to (do something)”: *Trata de dormir*, *Él trata de ver...*. In commands, **Trata de...** means “Try to...”. (Very common with **no**: *Trata de no preocuparte* = “Try not to worry.”)
target_language_example: Trata de llegar temprano mañana.
native_language_example: Try to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a gentle command: trata de (infinitive) = “try to …”, and trata de no (infinitive) = “try not to …”. It’s the tú (informal singular) command form of tratar; for a more formal/polite version use “trate de no …”. Common with reflexive verbs: “trata de no preocuparte / ponerte tenso(a)” = “try not to worry / get tense.”
target_language_example: Trata de no contestar sin pensar.
native_language_example: Try not to answer without thinking.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the "to + verb" form): "tratando de + verbo" (e.g., tratando de ahorrar, tratando de averiguar). Often appears with "estar" for an action in progress: "estoy/está/están tratando de..." It can also follow time expressions to show ongoing effort: "Pasé toda la tarde tratando de..."
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de aprender español, pero es difícil.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn Spanish, but it's hard.

additional_notes: “Tratando de + infinitive” means “trying to …”. Here it’s followed by “encontrar” (to find). It often describes an ongoing effort and can translate as “trying to find” or “looking for,” especially when someone is searching for a person or thing.
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de encontrar mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I'm trying to find my phone.

meaning: to deal with (a person or situation).
additional_notes: Often used for handling a difficult person or managing a problem/situation. Common patterns: "tratar con alguien" (deal with someone) and "tratar con algo/esto" (deal with something/this).
target_language_example: No sé cómo tratar con este problema.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to deal with this problem.

meaning: 'to try to' / 'to attempt to' (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: tratar de + infinitive (e.g., tratar de entender = to try to understand). You’ll often see it after prepositions like al: al tratar de + infinitive = “while/when trying to…”. Don’t confuse it with tratar a/con, which relates to “to treat” or “to deal with (someone)”.
target_language_example: Voy a tratar de llegar temprano.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to arrive early.

meaning: 'try to' (usted form); also, in 'se trate de', 'be about / be a'.
additional_notes: From the verb "tratar de". "Trate de + infinitive" is often a polite/formal command to one person (usted): "Trate de comprender" = "Try to understand." It can also appear after expressions like "Es posible que..." with the present subjunctive: "Es posible que trate de hacerlo". With "se trate de + noun", it means "it may be about / it may be a": "Puede que se trate de un bandido" = "It might be a bandit."
target_language_example: Trate de llegar temprano, por favor.
native_language_example: Try to arrive early, please.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (trato de + verb) to talk about making an effort to do something. Often implies the action is difficult or not guaranteed: Trato de no pensar en eso. In many contexts you may also hear "trato" without "de" (Trato de ayudar / Trato ayudar), but "trato de" is very common.
target_language_example: Trato de llegar temprano, pero siempre hay tráfico.
native_language_example: I try to arrive early, but there’s always traffic.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that an agreement has been reached (often after negotiating). Similar to saying “Deal!” or “You’ve got a deal.” You’ll also hear it as a question: “¿Trato hecho?” = “Deal?”
target_language_example: Si tú traes la comida, yo pongo las bebidas: trato hecho.
native_language_example: If you bring the food, I’ll bring the drinks: it’s a deal.

additional_notes: "traté de" is the preterite (simple past) first-person singular of "tratar de" + infinitive. It describes an attempt you made at a specific moment in the past; it doesn’t necessarily imply success. Common pattern: "traté de" + infinitive (hacer, conseguir, escribir, no reírme, etc.).
target_language_example: Ayer traté de llamarte, pero no contestaste.
native_language_example: Yesterday I tried to call you, but you didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the phrase “tratar de + infinitive” = “to try to do something.” It’s followed by an infinitive: “trató de convencer”, “trató de consolar”. Often used when you want to say someone made an effort, whether or not they succeeded. Note: “tratar” can look like English “treat,” but “tratar de” usually means “to try to,” not “to treat.”
target_language_example: Ella trató de llamarte, pero no pudo.
native_language_example: She tried to call you, but she couldn’t.

additional_notes: "Trató de" is the preterite (simple past) of "tratar de" (= to try to). "Ocultar" means "to hide/conceal," and "su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their"—you know which from context. It’s typically followed by a noun, often an emotion or problem (e.g., "su confusión", "su dolor").
target_language_example: Él trató de ocultar su nerviosismo durante la entrevista.
native_language_example: He tried to hide his nervousness during the interview.

additional_notes: Used to say someone made an effort but didn’t succeed. It’s followed by an infinitive: “trató en vano de + infinitive.” Here “trató” is the preterite (past) third-person singular form of “tratar de” (= to try to). You can change it for other subjects/tenses: “traté en vano de…”, “trataba en vano de…”, “trataron en vano de…”.
target_language_example: Ella trató en vano de ocultar su temor.
native_language_example: She tried in vain to hide her fear.

additional_notes: Used mainly to talk about someone’s age with the verb "tener": "Tengo trece años" = "I’m thirteen." Also used with "cuando tenía trece años" to mean "when I was thirteen." In Spanish you generally say you "have" years, not "are" years old.
target_language_example: Tengo trece años y estoy en octavo grado.
native_language_example: I’m thirteen years old and I’m in eighth grade.

meaning: "thirty years" (an age or a length of time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s age (cumplir treinta años = to turn 30) or a duration (llevar treinta años + gerund = to have been doing something for 30 years; hace treinta años = thirty years ago).
target_language_example: Viví en México durante treinta años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for thirty years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time (how long something takes or how long you wait) or about how late/early someone is. Often appears with phrases like “en treinta minutos” (in thirty minutes), “por treinta minutos” (for thirty minutes), “treinta minutos o menos” (thirty minutes or less), or “treinta minutos atrasado” (thirty minutes late).
target_language_example: La reunión dura treinta minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting lasts thirty minutes.

additional_notes: The Spanish number 35. Used for ages, quantities, answers in math, or said by itself as a short answer (e.g., giving a number).
target_language_example: En mi oficina somos treinta y cinco personas.
native_language_example: In my office there are thirty-five people.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): “se había ido” (had left) to show the train left before another past action (e.g., arriving at the station). “ya” means “already,” emphasizing it was gone by the time you arrived.
target_language_example: Llegué tarde y el tren ya se había ido.
native_language_example: I arrived late and the train had already left.

additional_notes: Used to count down right before an action begins (starting a game, recording, jumping, etc.). Often said as part of a longer countdown (e.g., cinco, cuatro, tres, dos, uno) or after "en" to mean "in": "En tres, dos, uno" = "In three, two, one."
target_language_example: ¡En tres, dos, uno... acción!
native_language_example: In three, two, one... action!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a length of time (duration) or about time relative to another moment (e.g., “three years later/after”). Often appears with time expressions like “han pasado…” (have passed) and “durante…” (for/during).
target_language_example: Estudié español durante tres años.
native_language_example: I studied Spanish for three years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for three days) or a point in time in the past (about three days ago). With "en tres días," it can mean a deadline/time until something happens (in three days). "Ya van tres días" means three days have already passed.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes terminarlo en tres días?
native_language_example: Can you finish it in three days?

additional_notes: "Tres" = "three" and "hijos" is the plural of "hijo" (son/child). Often used when talking about family size: "tener tres hijos" (to have three children) or "ser padre/madre de tres hijos" (to be the father/mother of three children). If you specifically mean children of any gender, you may also hear "tres hijos" used generically, but "tres hijos y dos hijas" specifies sons and daughters.
target_language_example: Mis padres tienen tres hijos.
native_language_example: My parents have three children.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration (lasted three hours), a delay (delayed three hours), a frequency (every three hours), or a time difference (three hours earlier/before). You can also use it with "otras" to mean "another three hours" ("otras tres horas").
target_language_example: Esperamos tres horas en el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We waited three hours at the airport.

additional_notes: A time duration or time point measured in months. Common with expressions like: cada tres meses (every three months), en menos de tres meses (in less than three months), tres meses después (three months later), and for how long something lasts: Vivirá aquí tres meses (He’ll live here for three months).
target_language_example: Estudié español durante tres meses.
native_language_example: I studied Spanish for three months.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 3,000 (quantity, measurements, etc.). In Spanish, mil (“thousand”) doesn’t take a plural ending: you say tres mil, not *tres miles*.
target_language_example: El coche cuesta tres mil dólares.
native_language_example: The car costs three thousand dollars.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a short amount of time (duration) or a point in time (in three minutes / three minutes later). Common patterns: “por tres minutos” = for three minutes; “en tres minutos” = in three minutes (from now); “tres minutos más tarde” = three minutes later; “los últimos tres minutos” = the last three minutes.
target_language_example: Vuelvo en tres minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in three minutes.

meaning: "three or four"; used to mean "about/around a few" (an approximate number).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the exact number and are estimating. It can modify many things: amounts (tres o cuatro mil), time (tres o cuatro días / horas), frequency (tres o cuatro veces), or objects (tres o cuatro libros). You can also say it alone as a short answer: “¿Cuántos?” — “Tres o cuatro.”
target_language_example: Llegaré en tres o cuatro minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in three or four minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for three weeks) or a point in the future (in three weeks). With time expressions, Spanish often uses "durante" or "por" to mean "for" (e.g., "durante/por tres semanas"), and "en" to mean "in" (e.g., "en tres semanas").
target_language_example: Estudié español por tres semanas antes del viaje.
native_language_example: I studied Spanish for three weeks before the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens three times (quantity or frequency). Also used in comparisons to mean “three times as much/as old” (e.g., “tres veces tu edad” = “three times your age”). Often appears in phrases like “leerlo tres veces” (read it three times) or “pensárselo tres veces” (think twice/think carefully—literally “think it over three times”).
target_language_example: He visitado Madrid tres veces.
native_language_example: I’ve visited Madrid three times.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). You can swap the number: "dos veces a la semana" (twice a week), "cuatro veces a la semana" (four times a week). It’s often used with phrases like "al menos" (at least) or "unas" (about/around): "al menos tres veces a la semana", "unas tres veces a la semana".
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio tres veces a la semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens in one day, especially routines or instructions (meals, brushing teeth, taking medicine). You can also change the number: "dos veces al día" (twice a day), "cuatro veces al día" (four times a day).
target_language_example: Tengo que tomar esta pastilla tres veces al día.
native_language_example: I have to take this pill three times a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). You can change the number: “dos veces por semana” (twice a week), “cuatro veces por semana,” etc. You’ll often see it with routines and schedules, sometimes with “al menos / por lo menos” (“at least”).
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio tres veces por semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three consecutive times with no break in between. Often goes after the verb (Ganó tres veces seguidas / Perdimos tres veces seguidas). Similar phrases: dos veces seguidas (twice in a row), cuatro veces seguidas (four times in a row).
target_language_example: He llamado tres veces seguidas, pero no contesta.
native_language_example: I’ve called three times in a row, but they aren’t answering.

additional_notes: A money amount: "trescientos" = 300 and it agrees in gender with the noun ("trescientos dólares"; "trescientas" with feminine nouns). Used with verbs like "recibir" (to receive), "deber" (to owe), and "ganar" (to earn).
target_language_example: Tengo que pagar trescientos dólares por el coche.
native_language_example: I have to pay three hundred dollars for the car.

additional_notes: A literal phrase used when talking about farming or planting. "Trigo" = wheat, "en" = in, "su" = his/her/your/their (formal), and "campo" = field/countryside. "Su" changes depending on who owns the field (e.g., "trigo en mi campo" = wheat in my field).
target_language_example: El agricultor cultivó trigo en su campo este año.
native_language_example: The farmer grew wheat in his field this year.

meaning: a piece of; a chunk of.
additional_notes: Used with nouns to talk about a part cut/broken off or a portion of something (food, material, objects): un trozo de carne (a piece of meat), un trozo de hierro (a piece of iron). Often implies a fairly solid piece (compare: un pedazo de is very similar; una rebanada de = a slice; una porción de = a serving/portion).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres otro trozo de pastel?
native_language_example: Do you want another piece of cake?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a small piece of paper, often for quick notes or drawing. Very common with verbs like escribir (to write), anotar (to jot down), and dibujar (to draw).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un trozo de papel para apuntar la dirección?
native_language_example: Do you have a piece of paper to write down the address?

additional_notes: Used for an illusion performed by a magician (cards, disappearing objects, etc.). You can use it with verbs like hacer (to do), mostrar/enseñar (to show/teach), and entender (to understand how it works).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hacer otro truco de magia?
native_language_example: Can you do another magic trick?

additional_notes: Used to talk directly to someone about their grandfather. The possessive "tu" is informal singular "your" (used with friends, family, kids). With strangers or formal situations, use "su abuelo" (your [formal] grandfather).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se llama tu abuelo?
native_language_example: What is your grandfather's name?

additional_notes: Used with the possessive adjective **tu** (“your,” informal singular) + **alma** (“soul”). Common in religious, poetic, or emotional contexts to talk about someone’s spirit, inner life, conscience, or deepest feelings. With **tu**, it’s addressed to one person you speak to as **tú** (not formal **usted**).
target_language_example: Quiero cuidar tu alma, no solo tu cuerpo.
native_language_example: I want to take care of your soul, not just your body.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a friend who is female (“amiga”). It can mean the listener’s friend (“tu amiga está aquí”) or be used by the speaker to say they are the listener’s friend (“soy tu amiga”, “seré tu amiga”). For a male friend: “tu amigo.”
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu amiga?
native_language_example: Where is your (female) friend?

additional_notes: "Tu" means "your" (informal singular). "Amigo" is masculine; for a female friend, say "tu amiga". Often used to address someone warmly (e.g., "Soy tu amigo" = "I’m your friend").
target_language_example: Tranquilo, soy tu amigo.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m your friend.

additional_notes: Used to talk directly to someone about the help they give or could give. It often appears after verbs like apreciar (to appreciate), esperar (to hope for/expect), necesitar (to need), and with sin + tu ayuda (“without your help”). Note: 'ayuda' can mean both 'help' (noun) and 'help!' (as a cry), but 'tu ayuda' is the noun phrase.
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda; no podría hacerlo sin ti.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help; I couldn't do it without you.

additional_notes: Literally refers to someone’s head, but in many common expressions it means what someone is thinking or imagining: ¿Qué pasa por tu cabeza? (“What’s going through your head?”), Está en tu cabeza / Todo está en tu cabeza (“It’s all in your head”), Usa tu cabeza (“Use your head” = think). It also appears in physical actions: Inclina tu cabeza (“Tilt/bow your head”).
target_language_example: No sé qué tienes en tu cabeza, pero estás muy preocupado.
native_language_example: I don’t know what’s in your mind, but you’re very worried.

additional_notes: Refers to the listener’s face. Often used with prepositions: “en tu cara” = “in your face/on your face” (location) and can also be used as a confrontational expression (“¡En tu cara!” = “In your face!”).
target_language_example: Tienes algo en tu cara.
native_language_example: You have something on your face.

additional_notes: "Tu" is the informal singular "your" (used with friends, family, kids). "Casa" can mean both a house and a home; Spanish often uses "casa" where English would say "home." "Es tu casa" can be literal ("It’s your house") or a welcoming phrase meaning "Make yourself at home."
target_language_example: Cuando quieras, ven a tu casa a cenar.
native_language_example: Whenever you want, come to your place for dinner.

additional_notes: Often used literally for the physical heart (especially with verbs like abrir, mostrar, cuidar), and very commonly figuratively to talk about emotions, love, courage, or what your conscience/desires tell you (e.g., Sigue a tu corazón = “Follow your heart”; Haz lo que te mande tu corazón = “Do what your heart tells you”). As a romantic expression, perder el corazón por alguien means “to fall for someone.”
target_language_example: Escucha a tu corazón antes de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: Listen to your heart before making a decision.

additional_notes: Most often refers to someone’s bedroom in a home. Common in commands like “Vete a tu cuarto” (“Go to your room”). Note: “cuarto” can also mean “fourth” or “a quarter,” depending on context, but with “tu” it usually means “your room.”
target_language_example: Deja la ropa en tu cuarto, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the clothes in your room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk directly to someone about their physical body (health, injuries, sensations, physical contact). It can also be used figuratively in spiritual/philosophical contexts (body vs. soul). In some contexts it can sound intimate or even threatening depending on tone (e.g., sexual situations or “I’ll take care of your body”).
target_language_example: Escucha a tu cuerpo y descansa si lo necesitas.
native_language_example: Listen to your body and rest if you need to.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a problem or mistake: Es tu culpa. Very common in the phrase No es tu culpa (“It’s not your fault”). You can also contrast with es mía (“it’s mine”) or use past tense: No fue tu culpa (“It wasn’t your fault”).
target_language_example: Lo siento por lo que pasó, pero no es tu culpa.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about what happened, but it’s not your fault.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the day you were born or your birthday celebration. Often appears with prepositions like por/para/en (e.g., "un regalo por tu cumpleaños" = a gift for your birthday; "en tu cumpleaños" = on your birthday).
target_language_example: ¿Qué quieres hacer por tu cumpleaños?
native_language_example: What do you want to do for your birthday?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something good is happening to them now, or that they're about to get a lucky break. Often said as: "(Hoy/Este) es tu día de suerte"; can also be negated: "Hoy no es tu día de suerte" (today isn’t your lucky day).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: hoy es tu día de suerte, todavía quedan entradas.
native_language_example: Relax: today is your lucky day—there are still tickets left.

additional_notes: Literally means "your age" (tu = your, edad = age). It can refer to someone's current age (e.g., comparing ages), and in phrases like "A tu edad" it means "at your age"—often used to talk about what is typical or expected for someone of that age.
target_language_example: A tu edad, yo ya trabajaba.
native_language_example: At your age, I was already working.

additional_notes: Used to address someone and refer to their wife. Commonly appears with verbs like hablar con/de (to talk with/about), estar (to be), and irse (to leave): “Tu esposa está al teléfono” (Your wife is on the phone), “Tu esposa se fue” (Your wife left). Note: when speaking directly to your wife, you’d say “mi esposa” (my wife), not “tu esposa”.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu esposa ahora?
native_language_example: Where is your wife now?

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "tu" (your, informal singular) + "familia" (family). Used when speaking to one person you address as "tú". For formal "you" (usted), use "su familia". In many situations, "familia" can mean immediate family or relatives in general, depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo está tu familia?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive "tu" (“your,” for one person you address as tú). "Habitación" can mean “room” in general, but in everyday contexts like home it often means “bedroom.” You can use it with verbs of location and movement: "estar en tu habitación" (to be in your room), "ir/volver a tu habitación" (to go back to your room).
target_language_example: Deja tu mochila en tu habitación, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave your backpack in your room, please.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive adjective "tu" (“your”) + "hermana" (“sister”). It agrees with the noun (hermana = feminine singular). For a male sibling, use "tu hermano". With a more formal "you" (usted), you’d usually say "su hermana" (which can also mean “his/her/their sister,” depending on context).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se llama tu hermana?
native_language_example: What is your sister’s name?

additional_notes: Used to talk to someone about their brother. In Spanish, family words often take a possessive (tu = your) instead of saying the person’s name. It can be either literal (your actual brother) or used casually to refer to someone’s “brother” in conversation.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu hermano ahora?
native_language_example: Where is your brother now?

additional_notes: Used to address someone and refer to their female child. It can appear as the subject ("Tu hija es...") or after prepositions like de/con ("orgullosa de tu hija", "con tu hija"). You’ll also see it with emphasis: "Es tu hija."
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu hija ahora?
native_language_example: Where is your daughter now?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive “tu” (you = tú) + “hijo” (son). Use it when talking to one person you’re on tú terms with (friend, family, child). For formal “your,” use “su hijo.”
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu hijo?
native_language_example: Where is your son?
