additional_notes: Used for something you give someone for their birthday. You can say: comprar un regalo de cumpleaños (to buy a birthday present), mandar/enviar un regalo de cumpleaños (to send one), and buscar un regalo de cumpleaños (to look for one).
target_language_example: Le compré a mi hermano un regalo de cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I bought my brother a birthday present.

additional_notes: Used to say who will receive the gift. Very common with verbs like comprar (to buy), buscar (to look for), traer (to bring), escoger/elegir (to choose). Note: regalo can also be used figuratively, meaning someone/something is very helpful or “a gift” to a group (e.g., for the press).
target_language_example: Compré un regalo para mi hermano.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my brother.

additional_notes: Used when giving or presenting someone with a gift. "Regalo" means "gift/present" and "para ti" means "for you" (informal singular "you"; with a friend/child). For formal singular, use "un regalo para usted"; for plural "you," use "un regalo para ustedes".
target_language_example: Tengo un regalo para ti, pero no lo abras todavía.
native_language_example: I have a gift for you, but don’t open it yet.

additional_notes: “Reloj” is used for devices that tell time. It can mean a wristwatch (reloj de pulsera) or a clock (reloj de pared). Context usually makes it clear. Common phrase: “Un reloj roto tiene razón dos veces al día.” = “Even a broken clock is right twice a day.”
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un reloj? Necesito saber la hora.
native_language_example: Do you have a watch/clock? I need to know the time.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning a watch made of gold (or gold-colored). Often used as a gift or award: "regalar/dar/recibir un reloj de oro". Use "un" with a singular, countable object; plural: "unos relojes de oro".
target_language_example: Mi abuelo me regaló un reloj de oro por mi graduación.
native_language_example: My grandfather gave me a gold watch for my graduation.

additional_notes: A common way to say “watch” when you mean the kind you wear on your wrist (as opposed to a wall clock, “un reloj de pared”). Often used with colors/materials: “un reloj de pulsera de oro” (a gold wristwatch), “un reloj de pulsera dorado” (a golden/gold-colored wristwatch).
target_language_example: ¿Llevas un reloj de pulsera?
native_language_example: Are you wearing a wristwatch?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tener (to have), coger/agarrar/pillar (to catch/get): Tengo un resfriado. / Cogí un resfriado. Typically refers to a mild illness (runny nose, sore throat), not the flu (la gripe).
target_language_example: No voy a salir hoy; tengo un resfriado.
native_language_example: I’m not going out today; I have a cold.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular indefinite article “un” (“a/an”) + “restaurante”. Often appears after verbs like ir a (to go to), entrar en (to enter), buscar (to look for), and tener (to have/own).
target_language_example: Vamos a cenar en un restaurante cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: We’re going to have dinner at a restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something private or hidden that you don’t want others to know. Very common with verbs like decir/contar (to tell), tener (to have), and guardar/ocultar (to keep/hide): “Te diré un secreto” (I’ll tell you a secret), “Tengo un secreto” (I have a secret).
target_language_example: No se lo digas a nadie: es un secreto.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone: it’s a secret.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly. Common with verbs like "permíteme" (allow me), "dame" (give me), or on its own: "Un segundo, por favor."
target_language_example: Un segundo, ya vuelvo.
native_language_example: One second, I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person in a general, neutral way (often to emphasize someone’s humanity). With a specific person you can also say "el ser humano" (the human being) in a more abstract sense. In sentence 1, "todo un" adds emphasis (roughly: "a real/whole human being").
target_language_example: Antes de juzgarlo, recuerda que es un ser humano.
native_language_example: Before judging him, remember that he’s a human being.

meaning: a sign of; an indication of.
additional_notes: Used to describe what something shows or suggests (often an abstract quality): "un signo de salud" (a sign of health), "un signo de orgullo" (a sign of pride), "un signo de debilidad" (a sign of weakness). Note: "signo" can also mean a written symbol/mark, like "un signo de admiración" (!).
target_language_example: Su silencio fue un signo de desacuerdo.
native_language_example: His/Her silence was a sign of disagreement.

meaning: a system of (a set of connected parts/methods for something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe the type or purpose of a system: un sistema de alarma (alarm system), un sistema de ventilación (ventilation system), un sistema de localización (location/locating system). In weather, it can refer to a pressure system: un sistema de baja presión (a low-pressure system).
target_language_example: El edificio tiene un sistema de seguridad muy moderno.
native_language_example: The building has a very modern security system.

meaning: a place; a spot; a seat (a free place).
additional_notes: Very common, neutral word for “place/spot” in general. In contexts like transport, restaurants, or events, “un sitio libre” often means an available seat or open spot. Often followed by “para + infinitive” (purpose) or “donde + verb” (a place where…).
target_language_example: ¿Hay un sitio libre cerca de la ventana?
native_language_example: Is there a free seat near the window?

additional_notes: “Un” is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). Use “un soldado” when introducing or describing someone as a soldier (job/role): “Soy un soldado” = “I’m a soldier.” To describe the type of soldier, add “de …” (e.g., “un soldado de combate” = “a combat soldier”). Feminine: “una soldado” is often used; you may also see “una soldada” in some contexts, but it’s less common.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo fue un soldado valiente.
native_language_example: My grandfather was a brave soldier.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is exactly one (often with negation: “ni a un solo… / not a single…”). It can also mean “with a single…” in expressions like “de un solo trago” (“in one gulp”). Agreement changes with gender/number: un solo, una sola, unos solos/unas solas (rare).
target_language_example: No tengo un solo minuto libre hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have a single free minute today.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning “a hat.” It uses the masculine indefinite article “un” (like “a/an”). You can change it to “el sombrero” (“the hat”), or make it plural: “unos sombreros” (“some hats”), “los sombreros” (“the hats”). In everyday Spanish it can refer to different kinds of hats (e.g., a sun hat, cowboy-style hat, etc.).
target_language_example: Necesito un sombrero para el sol.
native_language_example: I need a hat for the sun.

meaning: a dream (while sleeping); also a dream/ideal (figuratively).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a dream you have while sleeping: "Desperté de un sueño" (I woke up from a dream), "Solo fue un sueño" (It was only a dream). It can also be used figuratively to mean something unreal or ideal, similar to "a dream" in English (e.g., "La vida es un sueño").
target_language_example: Tranquilo, solo fue un sueño.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it was only a dream.

additional_notes: Used to describe an unusual or odd dream someone had. Common with verbs like tener (to have) and soñar (to dream): "Tuve un sueño extraño" / "Soñé un sueño extraño". You can change the adjective to describe the dream (e.g., "un sueño raro", "un sueño horrible").
target_language_example: Anoche tuve un sueño extraño y me desperté temprano.
native_language_example: Last night I had a strange dream and I woke up early.

additional_notes: Common food word. It’s masculine: el sándwich / un sándwich. Plural: sándwiches.
target_language_example: Quiero un sándwich de jamón, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a ham sandwich, please.

meaning: somewhat; a bit. (Also: a point/goal in sports.)
additional_notes: Most commonly used as an adverb meaning “somewhat/a bit,” often before an adjective or a comparison: “un tanto cansada” (somewhat tired), “un tanto más cuidadoso” (a bit more careful). In sports contexts, “un tanto” can mean “a point” or “a goal”: “anotó un tanto” (he/she scored a goal/point).
target_language_example: Estoy un tanto preocupado por el examen.
native_language_example: I'm a bit worried about the exam.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "coger" (to take/catch) or "llamar" (to call) when you take or request a taxi. "Un" means "a/one"; for "the taxi," use "el taxi."
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a un taxi para ir al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: I'm going to call a taxi to go to the airport.

meaning: “a taxi to (do something / go somewhere)” (a taxi in order to…).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (para + ir/llegar/no llegar, etc.) to explain the purpose for taking/calling a taxi. You’ll often see it in patterns like “(Tomar/Llamar) un taxi para + infinitive.”
target_language_example: Vamos a tomar un taxi para llegar más rápido.
native_language_example: We’re going to take a taxi to get there faster.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a non-specific period of time. Common patterns: “desde hace un tiempo” = “for some time now”; “llevar + un tiempo + (adjective/past participle)” = “to have been (something) for a while” (e.g., “lleva un tiempo desaparecido”). You can add words like “al menos” (at least) to limit the time: “al menos un tiempo”.
target_language_example: No lo veo desde hace un tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him for a while.

meaning: a guy; a man; a person (often male).
additional_notes: Common, informal-ish way to refer to an unknown/unspecified man (“some guy”) or just “a person” in general. Can describe someone with an adjective: “un tipo emocionante” = “an exciting guy.” More formal/neutral alternatives: “un hombre” (a man), “una persona” (a person).
target_language_example: Vi a un tipo en la calle preguntando por direcciones.
native_language_example: I saw a guy on the street asking for directions.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe a category or variety of something: "un tipo de veneno" (a type of poison). It can also be used more loosely to mean “something like” or “a sort of,” especially when you’re not being very exact: "Es un tipo de cerradura" (It’s a kind of lock). Don’t confuse it with "un tipo" meaning “a guy.”
target_language_example: Necesito un tipo de adaptador para este enchufe.
native_language_example: I need a kind of adapter for this plug.

additional_notes: Uses the informal noun "tipo" (guy/dude) followed by "que" to introduce a description or relative clause about him. Common in spoken Spanish; in more formal contexts you might use "un hombre que" (a man who) or "una persona que" (a person who).
target_language_example: Vi a un tipo que siempre llega tarde.
native_language_example: I saw a guy who is always late.

additional_notes: Used for a single shot from a firearm: Oímos un tiro (We heard a gunshot). Common verb phrases: dar/pegar un tiro a alguien = to shoot someone; darse/pegarse un tiro = to shoot oneself. Also in the idiom un tiro en la oscuridad = “a shot in the dark” (a guess).
target_language_example: Oí un tiro y llamé a la policía.
native_language_example: I heard a gunshot and called the police.

meaning: a shot (a gunshot) to the head.
additional_notes: Used to describe being shot in the head, often in violent crime contexts. With verbs like "pegarle un tiro" (to shoot someone) or "pegarse un tiro" (to shoot oneself). "De un tiro en la cabeza" means "with a shot to the head" (how someone was killed or injured).
target_language_example: La policía dijo que murió de un tiro en la cabeza.
native_language_example: The police said he died from a shot to the head.

additional_notes: An insult used to call a man/boy stupid or foolish (can be harsh depending on tone). For a woman/girl, use "una tonta". It can also be used more lightly to mean “a silly person” in context.
target_language_example: No seas un tonto: mira a ambos lados antes de cruzar.
native_language_example: Don’t be an idiot: look both ways before crossing.

meaning: a job; work; a piece of work (a task/project).
additional_notes: Most often means “a job” (employment): conseguir/buscar un trabajo. It can also mean “work” or “a piece of work/project,” especially with descriptions like preciso, difícil, etc. In “un trabajo en progreso,” it refers to something still being developed (“a work in progress”).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un trabajo nuevo.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a new job.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a job with fewer hours than a full-time job. Often appears after verbs like "buscar" (to look for), "encontrar" (to find), or "querer" (to want).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un trabajo a tiempo parcial los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a part-time job on weekends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about work with fewer hours than a full-time job. Very common with verbs like conseguir (to get), encontrar (to find), or buscar (to look for): “conseguir/encontrar/buscar un trabajo de medio tiempo.” You may also hear “trabajo a medio tiempo” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un trabajo de medio tiempo para pagar la universidad.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a part-time job to pay for college.

additional_notes: "Trago" literally means a swallow/gulp, and in everyday speech it commonly refers to a drink of alcohol (like “a drink” or “a shot”). You’ll often hear it with verbs like "tomar" or "echarse": "tomar un trago" / "echarse un trago".
target_language_example: ¿Quieres un trago?
native_language_example: Do you want a drink?

additional_notes: Most commonly means a (men’s) suit (jacket + trousers) for formal occasions or work. In some contexts it can also mean an outfit or costume (especially with descriptive adjectives like “extraño” or in contexts like festivals, uniforms, or dressing up).
target_language_example: Para la entrevista, necesito comprarme un traje.
native_language_example: For the interview, I need to buy a suit.

additional_notes: Traje usually means “suit” (a matching jacket and pants/skirt), but in some contexts it can mean an “outfit” or “costume.” Nuevo agrees with traje (masculine singular). You can change the article depending on context: el traje nuevo (the new suit), mi traje nuevo (my new suit).
target_language_example: Para la boda, me compré un traje nuevo.
native_language_example: For the wedding, I bought myself a new suit.

additional_notes: Used when negotiating or agreeing on terms: hacer un trato (to make a deal), hacer un trato con alguien (to make a deal with someone). Also appears in set phrases like Es un trato. (“It’s a deal.”). Trato can also mean “treatment” (el trato), but in these examples it means “deal/agreement.”
target_language_example: Si me ayudas hoy, mañana te ayudo yo: es un trato.
native_language_example: If you help me today, I’ll help you tomorrow: it’s a deal.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like hacer/tener/llegar a (un trato con alguien) to mean you make/have/reach an agreement. In other contexts, trato can also mean “treatment” (how someone is treated), so the “deal/agreement” meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Llegamos a un trato con el dueño del apartamento.
native_language_example: We reached a deal with the owner of the apartment.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a part cut or broken off from something (food, wood, etc.). It’s followed by a noun: un trozo de tarta/pan/madera. For food, English often says “a piece of” (un trozo de pastel) and for larger/rougher things “a chunk of” (un trozo de madera).
target_language_example: ¿Me das un trozo de chocolate, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of chocolate, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single portion of cake. "Trozo" is a generic word meaning "piece/chunk" (you can also say "una porción" or "una rebanada" in some contexts). Often appears with serving verbs like "servirse" (help yourself) or "servir" (to serve).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres un trozo de pastel o prefieres helado?
native_language_example: Do you want a piece of cake, or would you prefer ice cream?

meaning: a piece/slice of cake (a portion of cake).
additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering a portion of cake. "Trozo" is a general word for a piece/chunk; for cake you’ll often also hear "un trozo" or "una porción" (and sometimes "una rebanada"). "Tarta" commonly refers to cake (often one you slice), and in some places can mean a tart/pie depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un trozo de tarta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of cake, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a single piece/stick of chalk. Common in classrooms. You can change the color with an adjective: "un trozo de tiza blanca/amarilla". In requests, it often follows verbs like "dar" (give), "traer" (bring), or "sacar" (take out).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un trozo de tiza, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of chalk, please?

meaning: a glass (a drinking container); also: a vessel/tube (e.g., blood vessel).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a drinking glass/cup: "un vaso de agua". In some contexts, "vaso" is used for tubes or vessels in the body, especially in the fixed phrase "vaso sanguíneo" (blood vessel).
target_language_example: ¿Me traes un vaso de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about one serving of a drink in a glass. Common pattern: "un vaso de" + drink (agua, té, jugo, leche). You can also change it for quantity/gender: "dos vasos de...", "medio vaso de...".
target_language_example: Quiero un vaso de agua, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or talk about a serving of water in a glass. Common with verbs like querer (to want), tomar (to drink), traer (to bring), and dar (to give). You can add details like con hielo (with ice).
target_language_example: ¿Me traes un vaso de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of water, please?

un vaso de agua, por favor

target_language_multi_word_term: un vaso de agua, por favor
additional_notes: A polite request you can use in restaurants or at someone’s home. "Un vaso de agua" means "a glass of water"; add "por favor" to make it polite. You’ll often hear it with formal commands like "Deme..." or "Tráigame..." (to a stranger/service staff) or with an informal request like "¿Me traerías...?" (to a friend).
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿me pone un vaso de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you get me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to order or ask for milk served in a glass. In requests, you’ll often hear it with verbs like “quiero”, “me das”, or “tráeme” (e.g., “Tráeme un vaso de leche”). By itself (“Un vaso de leche, por favor.”), it works as a short, polite order.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un vaso de leche, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a glass of milk, please?

additional_notes: Used when ordering, offering, or talking about drinking a single glass of wine. "Un vaso" is a drinking glass (not necessarily a wine glass). You can swap the drink: "un vaso de agua" (a glass of water), "un vaso de cerveza" (a glass of beer).
target_language_example: ¿Me pones un vaso de vino, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you get me a glass of wine, please?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone or something really fits the description: un verdadero patriota = 'a true patriot', un verdadero héroe = 'a real hero'. The adjective changes for gender/number: un verdadero, una verdadera, unos verdaderos, unas verdaderas. Common with abstract nouns too: Ha sido un verdadero placer = 'It’s been a real pleasure.'
target_language_example: Eres un verdadero amigo.
native_language_example: You’re a true friend.

meaning: a dress (a one-piece garment, usually for women).
additional_notes: A common clothing noun. Use it with verbs like llevar (to wear), ponerse (to put on), comprar (to buy), coser (to sew), and with descriptions: un vestido precioso (a beautiful dress), un vestido sin tirantes (a strapless dress), un vestido con la espalda descubierta (a backless/low-back dress). In plural: vestidos.
target_language_example: Me voy a poner un vestido para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I’m going to put on a dress for the party.

additional_notes: Commonly used to describe what someone is wearing. With clothing, Spanish often uses the verb phrases "ponerse" (to put on) and "llevar" (to wear/carry on your body): "Se puso un vestido blanco" (She put on a white dress) vs. "Lleva un vestido blanco" (She is wearing a white dress). "Vestido" is masculine in Spanish (el vestido), even though it refers to women’s clothing; the adjective agrees with it: blanco.
target_language_example: Hoy me voy a poner un vestido blanco.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to put on a white dress.

additional_notes: Means a dress that is new (recently bought or made). Common with verbs like ponerse/probarse (to put on/try on), comprar (to buy), and hacer (to make/sew). Word order: noun + adjective (vestido nuevo).
target_language_example: Me compré un vestido nuevo para la boda.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new dress for the wedding.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like hacer (to take/go on), tomar (to take), or ir de (to go on): hacer un viaje, tomar un viaje, ir de viaje. You can add details with adjectives (un viaje largo/corto/genial) or destinations (un viaje al extranjero / a España).
target_language_example: Vamos a hacer un viaje a México el próximo mes.
native_language_example: We’re going to take a trip to Mexico next month.

additional_notes: “Viejo” means “old.” With “un,” it can work in two common ways: (1) before a masculine noun to mean “an old …” (un viejo camino = an old road), and (2) by itself as a noun meaning “an old man/guy.” Depending on tone and context, calling someone “un viejo” can sound casual or slightly disrespectful (like “an old guy”). For feminine, use “una vieja,” and for plural, “unos viejos/unas viejas.”
target_language_example: Un viejo me pidió direcciones en la calle.
native_language_example: An old man asked me for directions in the street.

meaning: an old friend; a longtime friend.
additional_notes: Often means a friend you've known for a long time (not necessarily an elderly friend). Use "un" with masculine "amigo"; for a female friend, say "una vieja amiga". You can put it in sentences like "ver a un viejo amigo" (to see an old friend) or "una visita de un viejo amigo" (a visit from an old friend).
target_language_example: Mañana voy a cenar con un viejo amigo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to have dinner with an old friend.

meaning: an old friend of mine (a long-time friend).
additional_notes: "Viejo" here usually means you’ve known the friend for a long time (not that the person is elderly). The structure is: un/una + noun + mío/mía (of mine). You can change it for gender/number: "una vieja amiga mía", "unos viejos amigos míos", "unas viejas amigas mías".
target_language_example: Hoy me encontré con un viejo amigo mío en el centro.
native_language_example: Today I ran into an old friend of mine downtown.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "echar un vistazo" or "dar un vistazo" (“to take/have a quick look”). It can also mean recognizing something instantly: "de un vistazo" (“at a glance”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes echarle un vistazo a este documento?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at this document?

meaning: an angel; (figuratively) a very good, sweet person.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a spiritual being (“angel”), often in religious contexts (e.g., “un ángel del Señor”). It’s also commonly used as a compliment to say someone is kind, innocent, or well-behaved (e.g., “Tom es un ángel”).
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme; eres un ángel.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me; you’re an angel.

additional_notes: “Árbol” means “tree” (masculine noun). Use “un” for “a/an” with masculine singular nouns: un árbol. The plural is “unos árboles” (“some trees”). Common with adjectives: un árbol grande/alto.
target_language_example: Hay un árbol en el patio.
native_language_example: There is a tree in the yard.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or requesting emergency medical help. Often appears with verbs like necesitar (to need), enviar (to send), llamar (to call), or solicitar (to request). In many places you can say: "Llame a una ambulancia" (Call an ambulance).
target_language_example: ¡Rápido, llamen a una ambulancia!
native_language_example: Quick, call an ambulance!

additional_notes: Refers to a person, thing, or situation that could cause harm, danger, or problems. Often used with "ser" ("es una amenaza" = "it’s a threat") or "considerar" ("lo consideran una amenaza" = "they consider him/it a threat"). You can add an adjective: "una amenaza mortal" = "a deadly threat".
target_language_example: Ese virus es una amenaza para la salud pública.
native_language_example: That virus is a threat to public health.

additional_notes: Used for a friend who is female, or when you want to specify “a friend (who is a woman).” The masculine is “un amigo,” and the plural is “unas amigas” (all female) or “unos amigos” (mixed group or all male). In “una amiga de la familia,” it means “a family friend” (female).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con una amiga.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with a (female) friend.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one of your friends (female), often when you don’t need to say which friend specifically. Masculine equivalent: "un amigo mío". You can also use it with other people: "una hermana mía" (a sister of mine), "un compañero mío" (a classmate/coworker of mine).
target_language_example: Una amiga mía vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: A friend of mine lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Most commonly means an exciting experience or journey. In romantic contexts (e.g., “Tuve una aventura con ella”), it can mean an extramarital affair or a short romantic/sexual fling; context usually makes this clear.
target_language_example: El viaje por la montaña fue una aventura increíble.
native_language_example: The trip through the mountains was an incredible adventure.

meaning: a band (music group); sometimes a gang.
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a music group (una banda de rock). In some contexts it can mean a group of criminals (a gang). The article changes with gender/number: una banda, la banda, unas bandas.
target_language_example: Mi hermano toca la guitarra en una banda.
native_language_example: My brother plays guitar in a band.

meaning: a band/gang of; (informally) a bunch of.
additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to describe a group of people (often criminals: "una banda de ladrones" = a gang of thieves). In casual speech it can also mean "a bunch of" in a negative/insulting way ("una banda de idiotas").
target_language_example: La policía detuvo a una banda de ladrones.
native_language_example: The police arrested a gang of thieves.

additional_notes: Used for any drink (alcoholic or non-alcoholic): agua, café, cerveza, etc. Common in offers and invitations: "¿Quieres una bebida?" / "Vamos por una bebida" (= let’s go get a drink). In restaurants, "incluye una bebida" means one drink is included with the meal/entry.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres una bebida o prefieres agua?
native_language_example: Do you want a drink, or do you prefer water?

additional_notes: “Bella” is an adjective meaning “beautiful.” With “una,” it often refers to a beautiful female person (una bella mujer/una bella muchacha). It can also be used before a feminine noun more generally (una bella historia = “a beautiful story”), though “una historia bella” is also possible. Adjective agrees in gender/number: un bello libro, una bella casa, unas bellas flores.
target_language_example: Busco una bella foto para mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a nice/beautiful photo for my passport.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase: "una" (a/an, feminine) + "bicicleta" (bicycle). Use "una" for one bicycle in general; use "la bicicleta" for a specific bicycle. In Spanish, "bicicleta" is feminine, so adjectives agree: "una bicicleta vieja" (an old bike).
target_language_example: Voy al trabajo en una bicicleta.
native_language_example: I go to work on a bicycle.

additional_notes: "Una" means “a/an” (feminine), "bicicleta" is “bicycle/bike,” and "nueva" means “new” and agrees with the feminine noun (bicicleta). In Spanish, adjectives often come after the noun, so you say "bicicleta nueva" (not *nueva bicicleta* in most everyday cases).
target_language_example: Necesito una bicicleta nueva para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I need a new bike to go to work.

meaning: a bag; a sack; (also) a pouch/bag for a specific purpose (e.g., a vomit bag).
additional_notes: Commonly used for shopping bags and paper bags: una bolsa de papel. You can add an adjective for size (una bolsa grande) or use "bolsa de + noun" to say what kind of bag it is (una bolsa de patatas = a bag of potatoes).
target_language_example: ¿Me das una bolsa para llevar esto?
native_language_example: Can you give me a bag to carry this?

additional_notes: Used to say what kind of bag something is or what it contains: una bolsa de regalo (a gift bag), una bolsa de farmacia (a pharmacy bag), una bolsa de seda (a silk bag), una bolsa de papas fritas (a bag of chips), una bolsa de gimnasia (a gym bag). In Spanish you often keep the "de" even when English uses an adjective (e.g., "gym bag" → "bolsa de gimnasia").
target_language_example: ¿Me das una bolsa de plástico, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a plastic bag, please?

meaning: a bomb; (figuratively) something that could suddenly “explode” (cause trouble).
additional_notes: Most commonly a literal explosive device: “una bomba japonesa”, “una bomba de diez toneladas”, “el impacto de una bomba”. It’s also used in comparisons with “como una bomba” to describe emotions or situations that can suddenly explode (e.g., anger).
target_language_example: Encontraron una bomba cerca del edificio.
native_language_example: They found a bomb near the building.

meaning: “a bottle of” (used to say what’s inside the bottle).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to name the contents: una botella de agua/leche/vino. It’s a common container + “de” pattern: un vaso de (a glass of), una taza de (a cup of).
target_language_example: Quiero una botella de agua, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a bottle of water, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or asking for wine in a restaurant or store. "Una" is the feminine form of "a/one" because "botella" is feminine. You can swap the drink: "una botella de agua/cerveza".
target_language_example: ¿Nos trae una botella de vino tinto, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you bring us a bottle of red wine, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something was not serious ("It was just a joke"). It can also mean a practical joke/prank depending on context. Often used with ser: "Es/Solo es/Era una broma."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, solo es una broma.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a joke.

additional_notes: Literally “a witch” (female). Used in stories/fantasy (a magical witch), but it can also be said about a person as an insult meaning she’s nasty or cruel. Masculine: “un brujo” (wizard/warlock).
target_language_example: Dicen que en esa casa vive una bruja.
native_language_example: They say a witch lives in that house.

meaning: "a good" (before a feminine singular noun) / "a good one" (feminine).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: una buena historia (a good story), una buena señal (a good sign), una buena herramienta (a good tool). The adjective buena agrees with the noun (bueno for masculine: un buen libro). It can also be used on its own to mean “a good one” when the noun is understood from context (feminine).
target_language_example: Necesito una buena idea para el proyecto.
native_language_example: I need a good idea for the project.

additional_notes: Used to describe a girl/woman as well-behaved, kind, or “good” in a moral/social sense. It can be neutral (a compliment) but can also sound patronizing or controlling, especially when used as a command ("Sé una buena chica...") or about an adult woman. Often appears with "ser" (Es una buena chica) or as an instruction: "Sé una buena chica" (= Be a good girl).
target_language_example: María siempre ayuda a los demás; es una buena chica.
native_language_example: María always helps others; she’s a good girl.

additional_notes: Used to say something seems like a good plan or suggestion. Often after verbs like parecer (to seem): "Parece una buena idea"; or with es/era (it is/was): "Es/era una buena idea". You can also use it to agree: "Sí, es una buena idea".
target_language_example: Creo que es una buena idea salir temprano.
native_language_example: I think it’s a good idea to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as a good mom (or to talk about yourself as one). It agrees with a female noun: una buena madre (a good mother). Without “una,” it can be used as a description: Es buena madre = She’s a good mother. You can also use it with ser: ser una buena madre = to be a good mother.
target_language_example: Quiero ser una buena madre para mis hijos.
native_language_example: I want to be a good mother to my children.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action (verb in the infinitive) that’s a useful, effective, or polite method to achieve something: "una buena manera de + infinitive" (e.g., "una buena manera de ganar dinero"). You can also use it to suggest there’s a nicer/more tactful way to say something: "Hay una buena manera de decirlo".
target_language_example: Leer todos los días es una buena manera de aprender español.
native_language_example: Reading every day is a good way to learn Spanish.

meaning: a good night (as a wish: “Have a good night.”).
additional_notes: Commonly used to wish someone well in the evening/night, especially when saying goodbye. Often appears with commands or wishes: "Ten una buena noche" (tú), "Tenga una buena noche" (usted), or "Que pases/tenga/pasen/tengan una buena noche" (“May you have a good night”). It can also describe that the night is good for doing something: "Es una buena noche para...".
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; que tengas una buena noche.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; have a good night.

meaning: good news (a good piece of news).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or react to positive information. It’s a noun phrase; you can point to something just mentioned with "Esa/Esto/Eso es una buena noticia" ("That/This is good news"). Also common: "Tengo una buena noticia" ("I have good news").
target_language_example: Tengo una buena noticia: mañana no hay clases.
native_language_example: I have good news: there are no classes tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character or morals. It often means someone is kind, decent, and does the right thing (not just “good at something”). You can use it with different forms of “ser” (soy/eres/es) or “parecer” (seems).
target_language_example: Ella es una buena persona y siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: She’s a good person and she always helps others.

additional_notes: Used when you want people’s first reaction to you (or something you do) to be positive. Common with verbs like "dar" (to give/make) and "causar" (to cause/make): "dar/causar una buena primera impresión".
target_language_example: En la entrevista, intenté dar una buena primera impresión.
native_language_example: In the interview, I tried to make a good first impression.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a valid/convincing justification for an action or decision. Often appears with “por” to explain motivation: “por una buena razón” = “for a good reason.” You can also say “esa es una buena razón” (“that’s a good reason”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: lo hice por una buena razón.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I did it for a good reason.

additional_notes: Used to justify an action or a feeling. It’s often followed by an infinitive (para + verb): “una buena razón para no hacerlo” (a good reason not to do it). You can also use it with “estar” + adjective to explain emotions: “una buena razón para estar enojado” (a good reason to be angry).
target_language_example: No tengo una buena razón para mentir.
native_language_example: I don’t have a good reason to lie.

additional_notes: A common animal noun; "cabra" is feminine, so it uses "una" (indefinite article). Often used in farm contexts like "ordeñar una cabra" (to milk a goat).
target_language_example: En la granja hay una cabra y dos ovejas.
native_language_example: On the farm there is a goat and two sheep.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical box or container (cardboard, wood, etc.). It can also mean a case or housing for something (e.g., una caja musical = a music box). With "dar" or "enviar" it often implies giving/sending a packaged box. "Caja" can also mean "cash register" or "cash desk" in stores, but that’s not the sense in these examples.
target_language_example: Pon el libro en una caja, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the book in a box, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a quantity packaged in a box, followed by the plural item: una caja de dulces/galletas/clavos. You can change the article/number: una caja de… / la caja de… / dos cajas de….
target_language_example: ¿Me compras una caja de chocolates, por favor?
native_language_example: Will you buy me a box of chocolates, please?

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "canción" (song) is feminine, so it takes "una/la". Use "una canción" for an unspecified song ("I’m writing a song"), and "la canción" for a specific one ("the song"). Common verbs with it include "escribir" (to write), "cantar" (to sing), "escuchar" (to listen to), and "poner" (to play/put on music).
target_language_example: Estoy escribiendo una canción en alemán.
native_language_example: I’m writing a song in German.

additional_notes: Used with ser or become (convertirse en) to say that a person, responsibility, or situation creates extra work, worry, or expense for someone: “ser una carga para mis padres”, “una carga para él/ella”, “una carga para todos/nadie”. Often expresses guilt or stress (“Siento que soy una carga para todos”).
target_language_example: No quiero ser una carga para ti.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be a burden on you.

additional_notes: “Carrera” often means a profession/career path (e.g., *hacer/seguir/estudiar una carrera*, *una carrera en medicina*). It can also mean a competition where you run/drive (e.g., *estar en una carrera*, *una carrera alrededor del mundo*). Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Quiere hacer una carrera en medicina.
native_language_example: He wants a career in medicine.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a written letter (sent by mail): *una carta del colegio*, *mandar/enviar una carta*, *hay una carta para ti/vosotros*, *una carta para usted*. In games (like playing cards), *carta* can mean a card: *Elige una carta* (“Choose a card”). Don’t confuse with *tarjeta* (often used for bank/ID cards) or *menú / a la carta* (restaurant menu/ordering style, different use).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llevar una carta al correo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take a letter to the post office, please?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like escribir (to write) or mandar/enviar (to send) to indicate the recipient: escribir una carta a Judy. Very often you’ll also see the indirect object pronoun: escribirle una carta a Judy (“to write Judy a letter”).
target_language_example: Voy a escribir una carta a mi abuela mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to write a letter to my grandma tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say who the sender is. It’s often followed by a person (una carta de mi mamá) or a pronoun (una carta de él/ella). You can also use it with names: una carta de Mary.
target_language_example: Recibí una carta de mi abuelo ayer.
native_language_example: I got a letter from my grandfather yesterday.

additional_notes: Used for a letter (or sometimes a long message) written to someone to express romantic love. Often appears with verbs like escribir (to write) or recibir (to receive).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres que te escriba una carta de amor?
native_language_example: Do you want me to write you a love letter?

meaning: a written letter (a letter that has been written).
additional_notes: “Escrita” is the feminine past participle of “escribir” (to write), agreeing with “carta” (feminine). It often takes extra information with: **en** + language (una carta escrita en inglés/francés), **por** + person (una carta escrita por él = written by him), or a time phrase (una carta escrita hace una semana = written a week ago).
target_language_example: Tengo una carta escrita por mi abuela.
native_language_example: I have a letter written by my grandmother.

additional_notes: "Casa" is a feminine noun, so it uses "una" (indefinite article = “a”). It can mean the physical building (“house”) or, in many contexts, “home.” To say “one’s own house/home,” you can use "una casa propia."
target_language_example: Quiero comprar una casa cerca del trabajo.
native_language_example: I want to buy a house near work.

meaning: a (kind of) house of… / a house with…
additional_notes: Use **casa de + noun** to describe what a house is for or what type it is (**una casa de caridad** = a charity house), or to mention a defining feature/material (**una casa de techo/tejado rojo** = a house with a red roof; **una casa de madera** = a wooden house). In English this is often translated as “a house with…” or “a … house,” not literally “a house of…”.
target_language_example: Buscamos una casa de madera cerca del lago.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a wooden house near the lake.

meaning: “a house in …” (used to say where a house is located).
additional_notes: Use **una casa en + place** to give the location: *una casa en Australia / en Connemara*. You can also use it before a more specific description like *una casa en renta* (“a house for rent”). Often appears with verbs like **comprar** (to buy) or **buscar** (to look for).
target_language_example: Quieren una casa en la playa.
native_language_example: They want a house on the beach.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "una" (a) + "casa" (house) + "grande" (big/large). "Grande" usually goes after the noun and agrees in number (e.g., "unas casas grandes").
target_language_example: Quieren comprar una casa grande cerca del parque.
native_language_example: They want to buy a big house near the park.

meaning: a new house (a house that is newly built or new to you).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like comprar (to buy) and construir (to build): "comprar una casa nueva", "construir una casa nueva". "Nueva" agrees with "casa" (feminine singular), so it’s "una casa nueva" (not *nuevo*). It can mean brand-new construction or simply a different house you’re moving into, depending on context.
target_language_example: Estamos buscando una casa nueva cerca del trabajo.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new house near work.

additional_notes: Used to order or offer a single beer. With verbs like pedir/querer/dar/tomar: “Quiero una cerveza” (I want a beer). “Vamos por una cerveza” means “Let’s go (get) a beer” (often implying going out together).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes traer una cerveza, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a beer, please?

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to refer to a girl or (often) a young woman. It can sometimes be used loosely for an adult woman depending on context and region. Plural: "unas chicas" (some girls) / "las chicas" (the girls).
target_language_example: Estoy hablando con una chica de mi clase.
native_language_example: I’m talking to a girl from my class.

additional_notes: “Chica” commonly refers to a girl or young woman. In some contexts it can be like “girl” in English when talking about a woman informally (e.g., “una chica guapa” = “a pretty girl/young woman”). For an adult woman in a more neutral/formal way, you’ll often hear “una mujer”.
target_language_example: Vi a una chica en el parque.
native_language_example: I saw a girl in the park.

meaning: “a very (… ) girl” / “a girl who is very (… )”.
additional_notes: Common pattern: **una chica** (“a girl/young woman”) + **muy** (“very”) + an adjective. You normally need an adjective after **muy** (e.g., *una chica muy tímida* = “a very shy girl”). In some contexts, **chica** can mean “young woman” (not necessarily a child).
target_language_example: Conocí a una chica muy simpática en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I met a very nice girl at the party.

additional_notes: "Chica" means "girl"/"young woman". "Guapa" means "pretty" or "good-looking" (often about people; in some contexts it can also mean "handsome"). "Muy" intensifies it: "very." Because "chica" is feminine, the adjective is "guapa" (masculine: "guapo").
target_language_example: En la fiesta conocí a una chica muy guapa.
native_language_example: At the party I met a very pretty girl.

meaning: an appointment; a date; a quotation/citation.
additional_notes: Very common noun with three main meanings: (1) an appointment/meeting you scheduled (often with a doctor, director, accountant, etc.): "Tengo una cita (con el médico)"; (2) a romantic date: "tener una cita" / "invitar a alguien a una cita"; (3) a quote/citation from a text: "una cita de la Biblia". Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Tengo una cita con el dentista mañana a las nueve.
native_language_example: I have a dentist appointment tomorrow at nine.

meaning: a date with; an appointment with.
additional_notes: "Una cita" can mean either a romantic date or a scheduled appointment/meeting. "Una cita con + person" is used to say you have something scheduled with someone (often romantic in these examples). For medical/business appointments you’ll also hear "una cita con el médico / con el dentista" or "una cita en el banco".
target_language_example: Mañana tengo una cita con el dentista.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have an appointment with the dentist.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase: "una" = "a" (feminine singular) + "ciudad" = "city/town". Often followed by an adjective (e.g., "una ciudad pequeña" = "a small town/city"). With a name, use "la" instead: "la ciudad de Madrid" (the city of Madrid).
target_language_example: Quiero vivir en una ciudad grande.
native_language_example: I want to live in a big city.

meaning: a coincidence; something that happens by chance.
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser: "Fue una coincidencia" = "It was a coincidence." You can also say "Qué coincidencia" ("What a coincidence!") or "Es mucha coincidencia" ("That’s too much of a coincidence"). It can describe neutral, lucky, or even suspicious/dangerous chance events depending on context.
target_language_example: Encontrarnos aquí fue una coincidencia.
native_language_example: Running into each other here was a coincidence.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used with verbs like tener (to have) and tener/tuvimos (we had): «Tenemos una conversación» / «Tuvimos una conversación». It can be described with adjectives, e.g. «una conversación confidencial» (a confidential/private conversation).
target_language_example: Necesito tener una conversación contigo.
native_language_example: I need to have a conversation with you.

additional_notes: In everyday Spanish, "tomar/beber una copa" often means to have an alcoholic drink (like a glass of wine, a cocktail, etc.), especially in social situations: "Tomemos una copa" = “Let’s go for a drink.” It can also literally mean a glass/cup (the container), but with verbs like "tomar" and "beber" it usually refers to the drink.
target_language_example: Después de cenar, vamos a tomar una copa.
native_language_example: After dinner, let's go have a drink.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering wine by the glass. "Una copa" is the serving (a glass), and "de vino" specifies what it’s filled with. Commonly used with "por favor" in restaurants/bars: "Una copa de vino, por favor."
target_language_example: ¿Quieres una copa de vino?
native_language_example: Do you want a glass of wine?

additional_notes: Used to ask for, make, or send a duplicate of something (a book, report, image, letter, file, etc.). Often used with verbs like dar (give), hacer (make), enviar (send), tener (have).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar una copia de tu pasaporte?
native_language_example: Can you give me a copy of your passport?

additional_notes: A feminine noun used for clothing worn around the neck, usually with a dress shirt. Common with the verb llevar (to wear/carry): llevar una corbata. You can describe it with colors and patterns: una corbata negra (a black tie), a rayas (striped).
target_language_example: Necesito una corbata para la entrevista.
native_language_example: I need a tie for the interview.

meaning: a thing; (also) something I want to say/ask you.
additional_notes: Literally “a thing.” Very common as a general placeholder for an object, idea, or fact. Often used to introduce an important point or request: “Te diré una cosa” (I’ll tell you something), “¿Puedo pedirte una cosa?” (Can I ask you something?), “Prométeme una cosa” (Promise me one thing). Also used in fixed patterns like “Una cosa es cierta” (One thing is certain) and “Tenemos una cosa en común” (We have something in common).
target_language_example: Antes de irte, quiero decirte una cosa.
native_language_example: Before you leave, I want to tell you something.

meaning: “one more thing” / “one more thing to do.”
additional_notes: Used when adding an extra point or request at the end of what you were saying (“Oh, and one more thing…”). Also common to mean there’s one additional task left to do (“I have to do one more thing”). Often said on its own: “Una cosa más.”
target_language_example: Antes de irnos, una cosa más: apaga las luces, por favor.
native_language_example: Before we leave, one more thing: turn off the lights, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific thing/idea and then describe it with a relative clause using que (“that/which”). Very common in speech: “Te diré una cosa que…” = “I’ll tell you something that…”. You can change the noun: otra cosa que (another thing that), algo que (something that), una cosa que sí/no… (one thing I do/don’t…).
target_language_example: Te voy a decir una cosa que aprendí ayer.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you something that I learned yesterday.

additional_notes: Used for quantities of food, medicine, etc., especially in recipes or home remedies. It’s a noun phrase: una cucharada (a spoonful) + de (of) + ingredient. In many contexts it implies a tablespoon, but everyday speech can also mean just “a spoonful” in general.
target_language_example: Pon una cucharada de sal en la sopa.
native_language_example: Put a spoonful of salt in the soup.

additional_notes: Used to describe a friendly, affectionate reception. Common with verbs like dar (to give) and recibir (to receive): Darle/Dele una cálida bienvenida = “Give him/her a warm welcome” (informal/formal command).
target_language_example: Cuando llegó a la oficina, todos le dieron una cálida bienvenida.
native_language_example: When she arrived at the office, everyone gave her a warm welcome.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a photo/video camera. Use "una" because "cámara" is feminine. Plural: "cámaras". Related: "una cámara de fotos" (still camera) / "una cámara de video" (video camera).
target_language_example: Me gustaría comprar una cámara como esta.
native_language_example: I would like to buy a camera like this.

additional_notes: "Dama" is a more formal/polite way to refer to a woman, often implying respect, elegance, or good manners (e.g., "una dama encantadora"). It’s also used in set job phrases like "dama de oficina" (office worker/office lady, a somewhat old-fashioned term). For “female partner/date,” you can also hear "una dama" in formal contexts.
target_language_example: En la recepción vi a un señor y a una dama.
native_language_example: At the reception I saw a man and a lady.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb "tomar": "tomar una decisión" = "to make a decision". You can also say "tomar una decisión" in formal contexts (government, work) and everyday situations. In some countries (e.g., Argentina/Uruguay) you may see "tomá una decisión" (voseo) instead of "toma una decisión".
target_language_example: Necesito tomar una decisión hoy.
native_language_example: I need to make a decision today.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like deber (“to owe”) and ofrecer (“to offer”): “Te debo una disculpa” = “I owe you an apology,” and “Debo ofrecerle una disculpa” = “I should offer you an apology.” Also very common in Mexico to say “Una disculpa” by itself to mean “Sorry / My apologies.”
target_language_example: Perdón, te debo una disculpa por lo que dije ayer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I owe you an apology for what I said yesterday.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun or a quantity to mean exactly 12 (common for eggs, fruit, etc.), and often more loosely to mean “many” (e.g., “una docena de veces” = “a dozen times,” sometimes just emphasizing repetition).
target_language_example: Necesito una docena de huevos para la receta.
native_language_example: I need a dozen eggs for the recipe.

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like **tomar** (to take), **darse** (to give oneself), or **ducharse** (to shower): *tomar una ducha*, *darse una ducha*. You can add adjectives like *una ducha rápida* (a quick shower).
target_language_example: Voy a darme una ducha antes de salir.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a shower before going out.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "una" = "a" + "enfermedad" = "illness/disease." Use it to talk about being sick in general or about a medical condition (often with an adjective: "una enfermedad contagiosa" = "a contagious disease"). With "por" or "debido a" it expresses cause: "por una enfermedad" / "se debió a una enfermedad" = "because of an illness."
target_language_example: No pude ir a trabajar por una enfermedad.
native_language_example: I couldn't go to work because of an illness.

additional_notes: Used for both job-style interviews (a formal meeting where someone asks you questions) and media interviews (an article/TV/radio segment where someone is interviewed). Often used with “hacer una entrevista” (to do/conduct an interview) or “dar una entrevista” (to give an interview).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo una entrevista de trabajo a las diez.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a job interview at ten.

additional_notes: Used to describe something approximately or when you don’t know the exact name, or when it only partly fits the description. It agrees in gender/number with “especie” (usually stays as “una especie de” even with masculine nouns). Common in speech: “Es una especie de…” = “It’s kind of a…”.
target_language_example: Es una especie de sopa, pero con mucho ajo.
native_language_example: It’s a kind of soup, but with lots of garlic.

meaning: a star; also used for a (one-)star rating or as a compliment (“you’re a star”).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: a star (in the sky) or a star-shaped object (“me hizo una estrella” can mean “she made me a star,” e.g., a drawing/craft). Figurative meaning: “Eres una estrella” = “You’re a star” (you did great). In reviews/ratings, “una estrella” means “one star,” and you can add/remove stars (“Nos quitó una estrella…”).
target_language_example: Le di una estrella a ese restaurante.
native_language_example: I gave that restaurant one star.

meaning: a movie star; a film star.
additional_notes: Used to describe a famous actor/actress from movies. It’s a noun phrase: una (a) + estrella (star) + de cine (of cinema/film).
target_language_example: Mi abuela conoció a una estrella de cine en Madrid.
native_language_example: My grandmother met a movie star in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used for the brief streak of light you see crossing the night sky. Commonly appears with verbs like ver (“to see”) and atravesar (“to cross”), and in the expression pedir un deseo (“to make a wish”) when you see one.
target_language_example: Anoche vimos una estrella fugaz y pedimos un deseo.
native_language_example: Last night we saw a shooting star and made a wish.

additional_notes: Used (often with exaggeration) to say something is taking a very long time or that it has been a long time since something happened. Common patterns: “(Esto) está llevando una eternidad” = “This is taking forever,” and “Hace una eternidad (que)…” = “It’s been ages (since)…”. Also used alone as a short answer: “Una eternidad.”
target_language_example: Te estuve esperando una eternidad.
native_language_example: I was waiting for you forever / for ages.

additional_notes: Used to say there is a reason or cause for something (often with "hay" or "tiene que haber"). It can also mean a clarification someone gives to help you understand something.
target_language_example: Necesito una explicación, por favor.
native_language_example: I need an explanation, please.

additional_notes: Used when something seemed like an emergency/problem (fire, security threat, warning, pregnancy scare, etc.) but turned out not to be real. Often said after checking the situation: "Fue/era una falsa alarma" or "Tuvimos una falsa alarma".
target_language_example: Llamamos a los bomberos, pero fue una falsa alarma.
native_language_example: We called the firefighters, but it was a false alarm.

additional_notes: Refers to a family as a group of relatives (parents, children, etc.). Often used with adjectives: una familia pobre (a poor family), una familia numerosa (a big/large family), una familia adoptiva (a foster/adoptive family).
target_language_example: Ellos son una familia muy unida.
native_language_example: They are a very close-knit family.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a social gathering: "una fiesta" (a party). It’s often followed by "de" to say what kind of party: "una fiesta de despedida" (a farewell party), "una fiesta de disfraces" (a costume party), "una fiesta de Halloween". In some contexts it’s used figuratively to mean something is very enjoyable or abundant (e.g., "comer era una fiesta" = eating felt like a feast/a celebration).
target_language_example: Vamos a hacer una fiesta en mi casa el sábado.
native_language_example: We’re going to have a party at my house on Saturday.

additional_notes: Used to specify what kind of party it is. Very common with nouns like: despedida (farewell party), bienvenida (welcome party), disfraces (costume party), Halloween (Halloween party), cumpleaños (birthday party). Structure: una fiesta de + noun.
target_language_example: El sábado hay una fiesta de cumpleaños para mi hermana.
native_language_example: On Saturday there’s a birthday party for my sister.

additional_notes: "Flor" is a feminine noun, so it uses "una" for “a/one.” You’ll also see it after numbers (e.g., "solo una flor" = “just one flower”). Commonly used with verbs like "dar/entregar/ofrecer/traer" when giving a flower to someone ("le entregó una flor" = “he gave her a flower”).
target_language_example: Quiero comprarle una flor a mi mamá.
native_language_example: I want to buy my mom a flower.

meaning: a shape; a way (of doing something).
additional_notes: Common in two main senses: (1) physical shape: "una forma redonda" (a round shape). (2) method/way: "una forma de + infinitive" (a way to do something), e.g., "una forma de ahorrar" (a way to save). "Hay una forma" / "Tiene que haber una forma" means "There is a way" / "There has to be a way."
target_language_example: Buscamos una forma de llegar más temprano.
native_language_example: We're looking for a way to arrive earlier.

meaning: a way of; a form of.
additional_notes: Used to describe a method or manner of doing something (una forma de + infinitive: "una forma de recordar"), or a type/kind of something (una forma de pago/comunicación). In the set phrase "una forma de decirlo," it means "one way to put it" (a certain way of expressing an idea).
target_language_example: Busco una forma de aprender español más rápido.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a way to learn Spanish faster.

meaning: a fortune; a lot of money (very expensive).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like costar (to cost) to emphasize that something costs a very large amount of money: “cuesta una fortuna” = “it costs a fortune.” You can also use it with other verbs about money (e.g., ganar una fortuna = to make a fortune).
target_language_example: Ese coche me costó una fortuna.
native_language_example: That car cost me a fortune.

additional_notes: Very common in everyday Spanish. Used with verbs like tomar/sacar (to take): “Tomé/Saqué una foto.” You can add de to say what the photo is of: “una foto de mi papá.”
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes tomar una foto, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of me, please?

additional_notes: Used to say what or who appears in the photo. Common with verbs like tomar (to take), sacar (to take), mostrar (to show), tener (to have), and colgar (to hang). Also used with possessives: una foto de mi familia = “a photo of my family.”
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una foto de tu perro?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of your dog?

additional_notes: Used to say what the photo shows. **Su** means “his,” “her,” “their,” or formal “your,” so you often need context to know whose it is (e.g., *una foto de su instituto* = a photo of his/her/their school).
target_language_example: Tengo una foto de su familia en mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I have a photo of his/her family on my phone.

additional_notes: Uses a possessive adjective (tuya = “yours,” feminine singular) to say the photo shows the person you’re talking to. You can also hear: “una foto mía” (a photo of me), “una foto suya” (a photo of him/her/you-formal), “una foto nuestra” (a photo of us). Often used with verbs like mandar/enviar (to send) or dar (to give).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una foto tuya para el pasaporte?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of you for the passport?

additional_notes: Most commonly means a complete sentence (especially in writing or grammar exercises): "Escriba una frase..." It can also mean "a phrase" (a group of words), depending on context. Plural: "frases".
target_language_example: ¿Puedes escribir una frase en español?
native_language_example: Can you write a sentence in Spanish?

meaning: "a drop of" (a very small amount of).
additional_notes: Used with liquids and substances (agua, leche, aceite) to mean a tiny quantity: "una gota de agua". Often appears in negative expressions like "no había una gota de..." = "there wasn't a drop of..." and can be used figuratively for something very small (e.g., "una gota de vida" = not an ounce/sign of life). You may also see comparisons like "una gota de agua en el mar" to emphasize how insignificant something is compared to a larger whole.
target_language_example: Solo quiero una gota de limón en el té.
native_language_example: I only want a drop of lemon in the tea.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (una). Gran is a shortened form of “grande” placed before the noun; it usually means “great” (excellent/important) rather than physical size. If you mean literal size, you’ll often see “una noticia grande” (a big piece of news), but “una gran noticia” is the natural choice for “great news.”
target_language_example: Fue una gran experiencia para mí.
native_language_example: It was a great experience for me.

meaning: a large amount of; a great deal of.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a big quantity of something, often uncountable nouns (dinero, agua, vino). With plural countable nouns, Spanish often prefers “una gran cantidad de” or “una gran cantidad” rather than “muchos/muchas” when emphasizing the size of the quantity (e.g., una gran cantidad de coles). You can also use it without “de” if the thing is understood: “Una gran cantidad fue desperdiciada.”
target_language_example: Gastamos una gran cantidad de tiempo esperando el autobús.
native_language_example: We spent a large amount of time waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the sum is big (often a lot more than usual or expected). It’s a common, neutral phrase and can fit many contexts (saving, spending, losing, needing money). You can swap in other nouns: "una gran cantidad de tiempo" (a lot of time).
target_language_example: Gastaron una gran cantidad de dinero en la boda.
native_language_example: They spent a large amount of money on the wedding.

additional_notes: Used to describe a city as large (and often impressive). In Spanish, "gran" is a shortened form of "grande" that is placed before a singular noun ("una gran ciudad"; "una ciudad grande").
target_language_example: Madrid es una gran ciudad, pero es muy cara.
native_language_example: Madrid is a big city, but it's very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to say that two things are very different, or that something matters a lot (“it makes a big difference”). Often appears with: **Hay una gran diferencia (entre X y Y)** = “There’s a big difference (between X and Y)”, and **Hace una gran diferencia** = “It makes a big difference.”
target_language_example: Dormir bien hace una gran diferencia en cómo me siento.
native_language_example: Sleeping well makes a big difference in how I feel.

additional_notes: Usually means a family with many members (children, relatives). In some contexts it can also be a warm, figurative way to describe a close-knit group (e.g., a workplace) as “one big family.”
target_language_example: Tiene una gran familia, así que la casa siempre está llena.
native_language_example: He has a big family, so the house is always full.

additional_notes: Used to describe a large or very fun celebration. Common with verbs like "celebrar" (to celebrate), "hacer" (to throw/hold), or "ser" (to be): "Fue una gran fiesta". "Gran" is a shortened form of "grande" used before singular nouns (gran fiesta, gran día).
target_language_example: Vamos a hacer una gran fiesta este sábado.
native_language_example: We’re going to throw a big party this Saturday.

meaning: a large fortune; a lot of wealth/money.
additional_notes: Often used when talking about someone having or leaving (inheriting) a lot of money or assets. Common with verbs like dejar (to leave, as an inheritance), heredar (to inherit), and hacer (to make/earn): «dejó una gran fortuna», «hizo una gran fortuna».
target_language_example: Cuando murió, dejó una gran fortuna a sus hijos.
native_language_example: When he died, he left a large fortune to his children.

meaning: a large crowd; a big group of people.
additional_notes: Used to describe many people gathered in one place (at an event, in a park, waiting for something, etc.). It often goes with verbs like "había" (there was/were), "atraer" (to attract), and "esperar" (to wait). Feminine: "una" + "multitud" (even though it refers to many people).
target_language_example: En el concierto había una gran multitud.
native_language_example: There was a large crowd at the concert.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a very good chance or situation to do something (often followed by "para" + person or "para" + infinitive: "una gran oportunidad para ti" / "una gran oportunidad para aprender"). The adjective "gran" is a shortened form of "grande" used before singular nouns ("una gran oportunidad").
target_language_example: Es una gran oportunidad para aprender español.
native_language_example: It’s a great opportunity to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is very important and requires care or accountability. Often appears with verbs like "ser" (Es una gran responsabilidad) or "implicar" (implica una gran responsabilidad). The adjective agrees in gender/number: "una gran responsabilidad" (feminine singular) vs. "un gran reto" (masculine singular).
target_language_example: Ser jefe de equipo es una gran responsabilidad.
native_language_example: Being a team leader is a big responsibility.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very unexpected, or to introduce that you have a surprise for someone (often with "para ti"). You can change the adjective (e.g., "una sorpresa pequeña") but "gran" is a common way to say "great/big" before a singular noun.
target_language_example: Tenemos una gran sorpresa para ti.
native_language_example: We have a big surprise for you.

meaning: a large sum of money; a lot of money.
additional_notes: A common, neutral/formal way to talk about a big amount of money, often in contexts like banking, inheritance, donations, or losses. You can adjust the adjective: "una enorme suma de dinero" (an enormous sum), "una pequeña suma de dinero" (a small sum).
target_language_example: Gastaron una gran suma de dinero en la casa nueva.
native_language_example: They spent a large sum of money on the new house.

meaning: a wide/great variety of; many different kinds of.
additional_notes: Used to say there are many different types within a category. It’s followed by a plural noun (or a singular collective noun): una gran variedad de libros/productos/platos. Often used in stores, menus, and descriptions.
target_language_example: En el supermercado hay una gran variedad de frutas.
native_language_example: At the supermarket there’s a wide variety of fruit.

additional_notes: Used for a place where crops are grown and/or animals are raised. Often followed by “de + noun” to specify the type (e.g., “una granja de pollos” = a chicken farm).
target_language_example: Vamos a visitar una granja este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to visit a farm this weekend.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "guerra" (war) with the feminine indefinite article "una" (a). Use it to talk about a war in general or one not yet identified; for a specific war, use "la guerra" (the war). You’ll often see it with "con" (with) to mean “a war with [someone]”: "una guerra con Estados Unidos".
target_language_example: Nadie quiere una guerra.
native_language_example: Nobody wants a war.

additional_notes: Used for a room inside a building (e.g., bedroom, office). In travel/hotels, pedir/need “una habitación” usually means a hotel room. Note the difference: “habitación” (room) vs. “casa” (house) vs. “apartamento/departamento” (apartment).
target_language_example: Quisiera una habitación doble para dos noches, por favor.
native_language_example: I'd like a double room for two nights, please.

additional_notes: This is the feminine singular form of the adjective "hermoso/a" and it must agree with the noun: "una hermosa ciudad" (feminine). With masculine nouns you use "un hermoso" (e.g., "un hermoso día"). It’s usually followed by a noun; by itself it can sound incomplete unless the noun is implied (or it’s used to mean “a beautiful woman”).
target_language_example: Es una hermosa idea.
native_language_example: It’s a beautiful idea.

additional_notes: "Hija" is the feminine form of "hijo" (son/child). Use "una" for “a/one” with feminine nouns. Often paired with "un hijo" (a son) or "hijos" (children/sons, masculine plural).
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene una hija y un hijo.
native_language_example: My sister has a daughter and a son.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a story” (something you tell or write). It can also mean “history” in the sense of an account of past events (una historia sobre el médico = “a story/history about the doctor”). For “History” as a school subject, you’ll often see “la Historia” (capitalized).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes contarme una historia antes de dormir?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a story before bed?

additional_notes: Used to describe a story as interesting; often follows forms of "ser" (Es/Ésta es una historia interesante) or verbs like "contar" (to tell) (Me ha contado una historia interesante). You can change the article and adjective for gender/number: "una historia interesante" (feminine singular), "historias interesantes" (plural).
target_language_example: Ayer me contó una historia interesante sobre su viaje.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she told me an interesting story about his/her trip.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one single sheet of paper (not a page in a book). Often used when asking for or listing basic stationery items: un sobre (an envelope), un lápiz (a pencil), un bolígrafo (a pen).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar una hoja de papel para escribir la dirección?
native_language_example: Can you give me a sheet of paper to write the address?

additional_notes: Used to talk about how long something lasts or how long someone has been waiting, and also for delays: "Se retrasó una hora" = "It was delayed by an hour." Often appears with time expressions like "hace una hora" (an hour ago), "en una hora" (in an hour), and "una hora más" (one more hour).
target_language_example: Tengo una hora para terminar el informe.
native_language_example: I have one hour to finish the report.

meaning: an hour and a half (1.5 hours).
additional_notes: Used to state a duration or an amount of time. Often follows verbs like durar (“to last”), ser (“to be” for an event/length), or expressions like hace… (“…ago”) or sobre (“about/around”). In speech you may also hear: hora y media (without una) or like: una hora y media de espera (“an hour and a half of waiting”).
target_language_example: La reunión va a durar una hora y media.
native_language_example: The meeting is going to last an hour and a half.

meaning: an idea; a thought; a plan.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb tener (to have) or ocurrírsele a alguien (to occur to someone): “Se me ocurrió una idea” = “I had an idea / An idea occurred to me.” You can describe it with adjectives like buena/mala/tonta (good/bad/silly).
target_language_example: Tengo una idea para la cena.
native_language_example: I have an idea for dinner.

additional_notes: "Iglesia" is a feminine noun, so it uses "una" (indefinite article = “a/an”). You’ll often see it in location phrases like "hay una iglesia" (there is a church) or with "ver" (to see).
target_language_example: ¿Hay una iglesia por aquí?
native_language_example: Is there a church around here?

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "una" (a/an) + "isla" (island). Use "una isla" when introducing an island for the first time or when it’s not specific; for a specific island, use "la isla" (the island).
target_language_example: Vamos a visitar una isla este verano.
native_language_example: We’re going to visit an island this summer.

meaning: “a long …” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: This is the feminine singular form of the adjective **largo/a** (“long”). It agrees with the noun: **una larga noche** (fem.), but **un largo día** (masc.), **unas largas noches** (plural). In many cases the adjective can also go after the noun (**una noche larga**), but placing it before the noun is common and can sound a bit more descriptive/emphatic.
target_language_example: Tuvimos una larga conversación después de la clase.
native_language_example: We had a long conversation after class.

additional_notes: Used to describe a letter (carta) that is lengthy. Often appears with verbs like escribir (to write), enviar (to send), and recibir (to receive): “escribir/enviar/recibir una larga carta.” In “le escribió una larga carta,” le means “to him/her.”
target_language_example: Te escribí una larga carta ayer.
native_language_example: I wrote you a long letter yesterday.

additional_notes: Used either literally (a story/history that is long) or, very often in conversation, as a quick way to say “it would take a long time to explain” (sometimes implying it’s complicated). Common with the verb ser: “Es una larga historia.”
target_language_example: ¿Por qué llegaste tarde? —Es una larga historia.
native_language_example: Why were you late? —It’s a long story.

meaning: a language; also a tongue (including “sharp/poisonous tongue”).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “a language” (synonym: *un idioma*): *Aprender una lengua…* It can also mean the physical “tongue.” Figuratively, it can refer to someone’s way of speaking, especially if they say hurtful things: *tener una lengua afilada* (“to have a sharp tongue”), *una lengua cargada de veneno* (“a venomous/poisonous tongue”).
target_language_example: Aprender una lengua requiere practicar cada día.
native_language_example: Learning a language requires practicing every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about any language that is not your native/first language. Often appears with verbs like hablar (to speak) and dominar (to master): hablar una lengua extranjera, dominar una lengua extranjera. Note: lengua here means “language” (not just “tongue”).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo una lengua extranjera para mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language for my job.

meaning: a legend (a famous person), or a legend/story.
additional_notes: Most commonly means a legendary person (someone very admired or famous): “Eres una leyenda.” It can also mean a traditional story or myth (“una leyenda urbana” = an urban legend). Context tells you which meaning fits.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo es una leyenda en el barrio.
native_language_example: My grandpa is a legend in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to describe something as nice, lovely, or pretty (e.g., una linda historia, una linda manera). "Linda" agrees with the noun it describes: una linda + feminine singular noun; un lindo + masculine singular noun; unas lindas / unos lindos for plural.
target_language_example: Tienes una linda sonrisa.
native_language_example: You have a nice smile.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the items that follow (often with a noun or an infinitive clause): una lista de cosas, una lista de precios, una lista de lo que me debes. It’s also common with verbs like hacer (to make), tener (to have), mantener (to keep), and mostrar/enseñar (to show).
target_language_example: Necesito una lista de invitados para la fiesta.
