additional_notes: Used to identify someone by their role, title, or position. **Usted** is the formal/polite “you” (common with strangers, customers, officials, or in professional settings). **El** is the masculine singular “the,” so it’s used before masculine nouns/titles (el juez, el experto, el responsable). For a woman or a feminine title, use **usted es la** (e.g., “Usted es la doctora.”).
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿usted es el gerente?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are you the manager?

additional_notes: Uses the formal “usted” (“you”). “El único” agrees with a masculine person; for a woman, say “usted es la única.” Often followed by more information: “el único adulto aquí” (the only adult here) or “el único en quien puedo confiar” (the only one I can trust).
target_language_example: Usted es el único que puede ayudarme con esto.
native_language_example: You’re the only one who can help me with this.

additional_notes: Used with the formal “you” (usted) + the verb “to be” (es) + an indefinite article (un/una) + a noun (often a label or description): “Usted es un maestro.” Use “una” with feminine nouns (“Usted es una doctora.”). Often sounds direct/strong in Spanish, especially with insults (some examples like “dolor en el culo” are very vulgar).
target_language_example: Usted es un buen amigo.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the person addressed (usted) should do something personally, without help. Often appears in instructions or polite requests (e.g., Hágalo… / Sírvase…). The feminine form is “usted misma” when addressing a woman.
target_language_example: Puede llamarlo usted mismo si quiere.
native_language_example: You can call him yourself if you want.

additional_notes: Used to make a negative statement about someone you address formally (usted). It comes before the verb: “Usted no sabe” = “You don’t know.” With verbs like ser/estar, it often means “you are not”: “Usted no es…” = “You are not…”. You may also see it as “a usted no …” when “usted” is an indirect object for emphasis: “Yo pensé que a usted no le interesaba” = “I thought you weren’t interested.”
target_language_example: Usted no puede entrar aquí.
native_language_example: You can’t come in here.

meaning: formal: "you don’t have" / "you do not have."
additional_notes: Used with the formal subject pronoun "usted" when speaking politely to one person. "No" goes before the verb to make it negative. It can mean (1) not possessing something ("Usted no tiene niños") or (2) not having a certain quality/idea ("Usted no tiene idea..."). Note that "usted no tiene que + infinitive" means "you don’t have to + verb" (not obligation).
target_language_example: Usted no tiene que venir mañana.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the formal “usted” to address someone respectfully. Often introduces something the speaker assumes the listener already knows or understands (sometimes with emphasis: “usted sabe muy bien…” = “you know very well…”). Common before question words: “usted sabe dónde/qué/cuándo…”.
target_language_example: Usted sabe que no es fácil.
native_language_example: You know it isn’t easy.

additional_notes: Uses the formal pronoun "usted" (instead of informal "tú") to mean "you". Often used to emphasize that two specific people share something or should do something together; it can also appear alone as a fragment for dramatic emphasis ("You and I.").
target_language_example: Usted y yo tenemos que hablar en privado.
native_language_example: You and I need to talk in private.

additional_notes: Used to speak directly to two people at once, especially in Latin American Spanish where "ustedes" is the normal plural "you". It’s often used for emphasis or clarity (making it explicit it’s exactly two people). In Spain, you’ll more commonly hear "vosotros dos" in informal situations and "ustedes dos" in formal ones.
target_language_example: ¿Ustedes dos pueden venir conmigo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you two come with me, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe two or more people you’re addressing. “Ustedes” is the standard plural “you” in Latin America (formal/neutral), and it can also be used in Spain in formal situations (informal plural there is usually “vosotros”). “Son” is the “they/you all are” form of ser, used for identity, descriptions, relationships, and general qualities.
target_language_example: Ustedes son muy amables.
native_language_example: You all are very kind.

meaning: 'is going to' (he/she/it is going to + verb).
additional_notes: “Va a” is the 3rd-person singular of the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**. Use it to talk about plans, intentions, or something you expect will happen soon: **va a nevar** (“it’s going to snow”). With a question it often means “what is he/she going to…?”: **¿Qué va a decir?** (“What is he going to say?”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano va a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: My brother is going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**. **Va** is the 3rd-person singular present of **ir** (“to go”), so it matches **él/ella/usted/eso/esto** (and names like Tom). For other subjects: **voy a cambiar** (I), **vas a cambiar** (you), **vamos a cambiar** (we), **van a cambiar** (they). Often used for predictions or things expected to happen soon, but it can also mean “will” in general.
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, todo va a cambiar.
native_language_example: With time, everything is going to change.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future form "ir a + infinitive": (él/ella/usted) va a creer = he/she/you (formal) is going to believe. Often appears with object pronouns: "no lo va a creer" (he/she isn’t going to believe it) and "no se lo va a creer" (she isn’t going to believe it / she won’t believe it).
target_language_example: No te lo va a creer nadie.
native_language_example: No one is going to believe you.

meaning: “is going to give” / “will give” (and by extension: “will cause,” “will hit,” “will shock,” depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the near-future form **ir a + infinitive**: **(él/ella/usted) va a + dar**. The exact meaning of **dar** changes a lot with what comes after it. Common patterns include: **dar una oportunidad** (give a chance), **dar un consejo** (give advice), **dar una vuelta** (take a walk/turn), **dar sus frutos** (pay off, “bear fruit”), **dar en la cara / dar a la cara** (hit in the face), and **dar la corriente** (give an electric shock).
target_language_example: Ten cuidado: ese cable te va a dar la corriente.
native_language_example: Be careful: that wire is going to shock you.

additional_notes: Form of “ir a + infinitive” (near-future): “va a doler” = “it’s going to hurt.” Often used to reassure (“No te va a doler”) or as a warning. It can be made more specific with an indirect object pronoun: “te va a doler” (it’s going to hurt you). In the second example, “la puta madre” is a strong vulgar intensifier (very rude).
target_language_example: Te va a doler un poco, pero termina rápido.
native_language_example: It’s going to hurt a little, but it ends quickly.

additional_notes: Formed with **ir a + infinitive** to talk about something in the near/expected future. **Va** agrees with the subject (e.g., *va a durar, van a durar*). Often followed by a time expression: *toda la noche* (all night), *mucho tiempo* (a long time), or *hasta + day/time* (until...).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: la batería va a durar todo el día.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: the battery is going to last all day.

meaning: “is going to start” / “is about to begin.”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**. **Va** is the (he/she/it/you formal) form of *ir*; you change it for other subjects: *voy a empezar* (I’m going to start), *vamos a empezar* (we’re going to start), *van a empezar* (they’re going to start). Often used for something starting very soon: *Ya va a empezar* = “It’s starting any moment now.”
target_language_example: Date prisa: la reunión va a empezar.
native_language_example: Hurry up: the meeting is about to start.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **va a** + **encantar**. With **encantar**, the person who “loves it” is shown with an **indirect object pronoun**: **me/te/le/nos/les va a encantar** (“I/you/he/she/we/they are going to love it”). Often **it** is implied: *Te va a encantar* = “You’re going to love it.”
target_language_example: Este restaurante te va a encantar.
native_language_example: You’re going to love this restaurant.

meaning: “is going to be” / “will be” (future of estar).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure: ir (present) + a + infinitive. "Va" is the 3rd-person singular of "ir" (él/ella/usted), so it commonly refers to "it" (e.g., "Todo va a estar bien" = “Everything is going to be fine”). You can change "va" to match the subject: "voy a estar" (I’m going to be), "vas a estar" (you’re going to be), "van a estar" (they’re going to be). Often used to reassure someone.
target_language_example: Mañana va a estar nublado, pero no va a llover.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it’s going to be cloudy, but it isn’t going to rain.

meaning: “It’s going to be okay / (he/she/you) will be fine.”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **va a estar** = “is going to be / will be.” Often used to reassure someone. Subject can be implied (e.g., **Va a estar bien.**) or stated (e.g., **Ella/Usted va a estar bien.**).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, todo va a estar bien.
native_language_example: Relax, everything is going to be okay.

meaning: “it’s going to work” / “it will work” (it will function; it will succeed).
additional_notes: From **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to…”) + **funcionar** (“to work/function”). Used to say something will work in the future or as a plan: **Así es como va a funcionar** (“That’s how it’s going to work”). Very common in negatives: **(Esto) no va a funcionar** (“This isn’t going to work”). You can swap the subject: **voy/vas/va/vamos/van a funcionar**.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, el plan va a funcionar.
native_language_example: Relax, the plan is going to work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say someone will like something in the near future. Gustar works “backwards” compared to English: the thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person is an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les). Common patterns: “Te va a gustar” = You’re going to like it; “No le va a gustar” = He/She isn’t going to like it; “Les va a gustar” = They/You all are going to like it. The literal word-for-word idea is closer to “it is going to be pleasing to (someone).”
target_language_example: Estoy seguro de que te va a gustar esta película.
native_language_example: I’m sure you’re going to like this movie.

meaning: "there is/are going to be" (there will be).
additional_notes: Future of "haber" used in the sense of "there is/are": "va a haber" + noun. You can change it for other persons: "va a haber" (there is/are going to be), "van a haber" is commonly heard but in standard Spanish "va a haber" is used even with plural nouns ("Va a haber muchas personas"). Often used to announce events or say something will exist/occur.
target_language_example: Va a haber mucha gente en la fiesta.
native_language_example: There are going to be a lot of people at the party.

meaning: "is going to do" / "will do" (he/she/it is going to do).
additional_notes: This is the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **va a hacer** = “is going to do/make.” It’s the **third-person singular** form (for *él/ella/usted*). For other subjects: *voy a hacer* (I’m going to do), *vas a hacer* (you’re going to do), *vamos a hacer* (we’re going to do), *van a hacer* (they’re going to do). In questions you’ll often see: **¿Y qué va a hacer?** = “So what’s he/she going to do?”
target_language_example: Creo que va a hacer una llamada ahora.
native_language_example: I think he/she is going to make a call now.

meaning: “is going to go” / “will go” (also used in “(me/te/le) va a ir…” = “things will go…” for someone).
additional_notes: Most often it’s the near future of ir (“to go”): va a ir = “he/she/it is going to go.” In everyday Spanish it also appears in the pattern (me/te/le/nos/les) va a ir + adverb (bien/mal) to say how things will go for someone: “Te va a ir muy mal” = “Things are going to go very badly for you.” With se + indirect object, it can mean something is about to slip away or be missed: “Se me va a ir el avión” = “I’m going to miss the plane / the plane’s going to leave without me.”
target_language_example: Si no estudias, te va a ir mal en el examen.
native_language_example: If you don’t study, you’ll do badly on the exam.

meaning: 'is going to go to' / 'will go to' (near-future plan).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s planned or expected trip/action in the near future. It’s the verb "ir" in the near future ("va a" = "is going to") plus the infinitive "ir" (to go) + "a" (to/to). Often followed by a place ("va a ir a Europa") or an activity ("va a ir a acampar"). You can change the subject/person: "voy a ir a" (I’m going to go to), "vamos a ir a" (we’re going to go to), etc.
target_language_example: María va a ir a México este verano.
native_language_example: María is going to go to Mexico this summer.

meaning: “It’s going to go well.” / “Things will go well.”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **va a ir** = “is going to go.” Often said on its own to reassure someone. With an indirect object pronoun it can mean “(for me/you/us) it’s going to go well”: **Me/Te/Nos/Les va a ir bien** (“I/you/we/they will do well”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, en la entrevista te va a ir bien.
native_language_example: Relax, the interview is going to go well for you.

meaning: 'is going to arrive' / 'will arrive' (also: 'is going to reach/get').
additional_notes: Formed with **ir a + infinitive** to talk about the near future: **(él/ella/usted) va a llegar** = “he/she/you (formal) is going to arrive.” With things/ideas it can be figurative: **no nos va a llegar muy lejos** = “it won’t get us very far.” You can also add time words like **ya** (any moment now) or **cuándo** (when).
target_language_example: El tren ya va a llegar.
native_language_example: The train is about to arrive.

meaning: “is going to take” / “will take” (time), or “is going to take/bring/lead (someone/something)” (to a place or result).
additional_notes: This is the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **va a** (he/she/it is going to) + **llevar** (to take/bring/lead). Common uses: (1) with time expressions: **Esto va a llevar años** = “This will take years.” (2) taking someone somewhere: **Me va a llevar con Eboshi** = “He’s going to take me to Eboshi.” (3) leading to an outcome: **te va a llevar muy lejos** = “it’s going to take you far.”
target_language_example: El proyecto va a llevar mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: The project is going to take a lot of time.

additional_notes: Common weather phrase. Literally “(it) goes to rain,” using **ir a + infinitive** (va a + llover) to talk about the near future or a prediction. Often used with time words like **mañana** (tomorrow) or with sources like **según el pronóstico** (according to the forecast).
target_language_example: Creo que va a llover esta tarde, así que lleva un paraguas.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain this afternoon, so bring an umbrella.

additional_notes: Formed with **ir a + infinitive** to talk about a near-future action. **Va a matar** is 3rd-person singular (he/she/it is going to kill). Often used as a threat or warning (**Te va a matar** = “He/She’s going to kill you”), and it can also be figurative (**Tu adicción te va a matar** = “Your addiction will kill you”). Change **va** depending on the subject: **voy a matar** (I’m going to kill), **vas a matar** (you’re going to kill), **van a matar** (they’re going to kill).
target_language_example: Tu adicción te va a matar.
native_language_example: Your addiction is going to kill you.

additional_notes: Uses the construction **ir a + infinitive** (morir) to express an expected future event. **Va** is the 3rd person singular present of *ir* (él/ella/usted **va**). Change *ir* to match the subject: *yo voy a morir, tú vas a morir, él/ella/usted va a morir, nosotros vamos a morir*, etc. Can sound neutral and factual, or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Dice no, y es el día en que va a morir.
native_language_example: He says no, and it’s the day he’s going to die.

meaning: “is going to need” (he/she/it/you formal is going to need).
additional_notes: Future with ir a + infinitive: va a + necesitar. Used to predict a need in the near future. Subject can be a person or thing (e.g., Tom va a necesitar…, La casa no va a necesitar…). You can add an object after necesitar: ayuda, apoyo, un abrigo, etc.
target_language_example: Tom va a necesitar ayuda.
native_language_example: Tom is going to need help.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** (near future): **(something) va a pasar** = something is going to happen. Often used to talk about predictions or expectations. It can also mean "is going to pass (by)" in other contexts, but in these examples it means "happen." You can change the subject: **voy a pasar** (I’m going to happen / pass — usually "pass"), **te va a pasar** (it’s going to happen to you), **nos va a pasar** (it’s going to happen to us).
target_language_example: Si sigues así, algo malo va a pasar.
native_language_example: If you keep going like this, something bad is going to happen.

meaning: “is going to put/set” (or, with *se*: “is going to get/become”).
additional_notes: It’s the near-future form **ir a + infinitive**: **(él/ella/usted) va a poner** = “he/she/you (formal) is going to put.” Very common in fixed phrases like **va a poner fin (a algo)** / **va a poner punto final (a algo)** = “is going to put an end to (something).” With **se** (**se va a poner + adjective**), it changes meaning to “is going to get/become” (e.g., **se va a poner feo** = “it’s going to get ugly,” **se va a poner emocionante** = “it’s going to get exciting”).
target_language_example: Esto se va a poner difícil.
native_language_example: This is going to get difficult.

meaning: “is going to” + (stay/remain / fit / turn out / end up).
additional_notes: It’s the near-future form (ir a + infinitive) with quedar. Quedar is very flexible: (1) with clothes, means “to fit / to look good on” (Te va a quedar bien). (2) means “to stay/remain” (Va a quedar entre nosotros = it will stay between us). (3) can mean “to be left over” (Algo te va a quedar = you’ll have something left). (4) can mean “to end up / become” (Va a quedar ciego = he’s going to end up blind). With the reflexive form quedarse, meanings change: quedarse con can mean “to keep” (Se va a quedar con los elfos) or “to stay with” (Se va a quedar con nosotros).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo va a quedar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is going to be fine.

meaning: “is going to leave/go out/come out” (will exit, go outside, or turn out).
additional_notes: It’s the near-future: **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to …”). **Salir** commonly means “to leave/exit,” “to go out” (socially or outside), or “to come out” (be released, be published, appear). With **bien/mal**, **salir** often means “to turn out” (e.g., *Todo va a salir bien* = “Everything is going to turn out fine”). Context tells you which meaning fits.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is going to turn out fine.

meaning: it’ll turn out fine / it’s going to go well.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a plan, situation, or result will have a good outcome. It’s the near future construction (ir a + infinitive): "va a" + "salir". You can change the subject/person: "me/te/le/nos/les va a salir bien" (It’ll turn out well for me/you/him/her/us/them). Often used with "todo": "Todo va a salir bien" = Everything will be fine.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Relax, everything will turn out fine.

additional_notes: "Va a ser" is the near-future form of "ser" (to be): **ir (present) + a + infinitive** → "va a ser" = "he/she/it is going to be." It’s used to predict or state what something will be like in the future. You can change the form of **ir** to match the subject: **voy a ser** (I’m going to be), **vas a ser** (you’re going to be), **van a ser** (they’re going to be).
target_language_example: Creo que la reunión va a ser corta.
native_language_example: I think the meeting is going to be short.

meaning: “is going to be a …” (future: it will be a + noun).
additional_notes: Used to predict/announce what something will be in the near future. It’s the near-future construction ir (va) + a + infinitive (ser) + un/una + noun/adjective phrase. Change for the subject: voy a ser…, vas a ser…, van a ser…. Also change the article for gender/number: va a ser una…, van a ser unos/unas….
target_language_example: Mañana va a ser un día largo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is going to be a long day.

additional_notes: Form of the near-future: **ir (to go) + a + infinitive**. **Va** agrees with the subject (**él/ella/usted va**). Other common forms: **voy a ser** (I’m going to be), **vas a ser** (you’re going to be), **van a ser** (they’re going to be). Often appears in phrases like **A ver qué va a ser** = “Let’s see what’s going to happen / what it’s going to be.”
target_language_example: Mañana va a ser un día largo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is going to be a long day.

additional_notes: Form of the near future: ir (va) + a + infinitive (suceder). Used to predict or state what will happen soon or in the future. Often appears with negatives like “no va a suceder” = “it’s not going to happen.” In sentence 1, the insult “pedazo de mierda” is very vulgar; it’s not part of the phrase.
target_language_example: Si no estudias, va a suceder lo mismo otra vez.
native_language_example: If you don’t study, the same thing is going to happen again.

meaning: “is going to have” (near-future of tener: “to have”).
additional_notes: Formed with **ir a + infinitive**: **(él/ella/usted) va a tener** = “he/she/you (formal) is going to have.” Often used for near-future plans or predictions. With **que** it becomes an obligation: **va a tener que + infinitive** = “is going to have to …”. In pregnancy contexts, **tener un hijo / un niño** commonly means “to have a baby (a son/boy).”
target_language_example: Creo que ella va a tener que ir mañana.
native_language_example: I think she’s going to have to go tomorrow.

meaning: "will have to" / "is going to have to" (will be required to).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity in the near or expected future. It’s built from the near-future construction "ir a" + infinitive plus the obligation phrase "tener que": "va a" + "tener que" + infinitive. You can change "va" depending on the subject: "voy a tener que" (I’m going to have to), "vas a tener que" (you’re going to have to), "van a tener que" (they’re going to have to).
target_language_example: Si no estudia, va a tener que repetir el curso.
native_language_example: If he/she doesn’t study, he/she is going to have to repeat the course.

meaning: 'is going to have a baby' (is expecting).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure ir a + infinitive: va a + tener. It’s a common way to say someone is pregnant/expecting (ella va a tener un bebé = she’s going to have a baby). You can change the subject: voy a tener, vas a tener, van a tener, etc. Often followed by a time expression: este mes, el próximo mes, en junio.
target_language_example: Mi prima va a tener un bebé en abril.
native_language_example: My cousin is going to have a baby in April.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** to talk about the near future. **Va** is the “he/she/it/you (formal)” form of *ir* (to go) + **a** + **venir** (to come). Often used when you expect something to happen soon or you’re fairly sure. Can also appear with additions like **por mí** (“to pick me up”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a venir mañana.
native_language_example: My sister is going to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **(él/ella/usted) va a volver** = “he/she/you (formal) is going to return.” Often followed by a time phrase (**a las cinco**, **en tres horas**) or a clause with **cuando** (“when”). For other subjects: **voy a volver** (I’m going to return), **vas a volver** (you’re going to return), **vamos a volver** (we’re going to return).
target_language_example: Va a volver mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: He/She is going to come back tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Form of the verb **ir** (to go): **va** = “(he/she/it/you formal) goes.” Used as **ir + a + place** (“go to [a place]”): *Va a la oficina.* Also used as **ir a + infinitive** to talk about the near future (“going to do”): *Va a estudiar.* With **se** (**se va a ...**) it often means “leave/go away,” especially with a time: *Se va a las nueve* = “He leaves at nine.”
target_language_example: Marta va al supermercado y luego va a cocinar en casa.
native_language_example: Marta goes to the supermarket and then she’s going to cook at home.

meaning: “(he/she/it) goes to the” / “is going to the” (to a feminine place).
additional_notes: From **ir** (to go): **él/ella/usted va** = “he/she/you (formal) goes.” Use **a** for destination: **va a la + [feminine noun]** (e.g., *la embajada, la mezquita*). With masculine **el**, it contracts: **va al** (*va al museo*). Note that with **irse** (“to leave”), you’ll often see a similar pattern with time: *Se va a la una* = “He/She leaves at one.”
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a la escuela todos los días.
native_language_example: My sister goes to school every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s bedtime. With a person, it’s usually reflexive: “se va a la cama” (he/she goes to bed). The subject can change: “voy/vas/va/vamos/van a la cama.”
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a la cama temprano los días de escuela.
native_language_example: My sister goes to bed early on school days.

additional_notes: "Va" is the he/she/you(formal) form of "ir" (to go) in the present tense. "A" means "to," and "la escuela" means "the school." Use it to say that someone attends/goes to school (often as a routine).
target_language_example: Mi hermano va a la escuela todos los días.
native_language_example: My brother goes to school every day.

va a la escuela en bicicleta

target_language_multi_word_term: va a la escuela en bicicleta
additional_notes: Use "ir a" + place to say where someone goes, and "en bicicleta" to say the means of transport (like “by bike”). In the present tense, "va" is the "él/ella/usted" form of "ir" (to go). You can swap the subject: "Yo voy...", "Tú vas...", "Nosotros vamos...".
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a la escuela en bicicleta todos los días.
native_language_example: My sister goes to school by bike every day.

additional_notes: From the verb **ir** (to go): **va** = “he/she goes.” Used to talk about attending church services. You can change the subject and verb: **voy a la iglesia** (I go), **vas a la iglesia** (you go), **vamos a la iglesia** (we go). Often appears with time expressions like **los domingos** (on Sundays) or frequency words like **rara vez** (rarely).
target_language_example: Mi abuela va a la iglesia los domingos.
native_language_example: My grandmother goes to church on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ir** (to go) in the **él/ella/usted** present tense: **va** = "goes." **al** is a required contraction of **a + el** ("to the" + masculine singular noun): *va al supermercado, va al concierto*. For feminine singular nouns, you don’t use **al**: *va a la tienda*. It can also be used with places/directions: *Va al otro lado* ("He/She goes to the other side").
target_language_example: Mi hermano va al trabajo en autobús.
native_language_example: My brother goes to work by bus.

meaning: "(he/she) goes to the movies / goes to the cinema."
additional_notes: "Ir al cine" means to go to the movie theater to watch a film. "Va" is the present tense (él/ella/usted) form of "ir" (to go). You can add adverbs of frequency like "a menudo" (often), "rara vez" (rarely), "casi nunca" (hardly ever).
target_language_example: Mi hermano va al cine los viernes.
native_language_example: My brother goes to the movies on Fridays.

meaning: "(He/She) goes to school on foot" (walks to school).
additional_notes: Used to say someone goes to school by walking. "Va" is from "ir" (to go) in the present tense for él/ella/usted. "Al" = "a" + "el" (to the). "A pie" means "on foot" (by walking).
target_language_example: Mi hermano va al colegio a pie todos los días.
native_language_example: My brother walks to school every day.

additional_notes: "Va" is the present-tense form of *ir* (to go) for *él/ella/usted*. Use it to talk about someone’s regular habit or routine. "Al" = "a" + "el" and is used because you’re going *to* a place (destination). Often used with frequency words like *a menudo, frecuentemente, normalmente, todas las mañanas, los fines de semana*.
target_language_example: Mi papá va al parque después del trabajo.
native_language_example: My dad goes to the park after work.

meaning: 'goes to work by (transport)' / 'goes to work in (a vehicle)'.
additional_notes: Used to say how someone gets to work. Structure: [person] + va + al trabajo + en + [mode of transport]. Common options: en taxi, en coche/en auto/en carro (car), en tren, en autobús. "Va" is the present tense of ir for él/ella/usted; for I: "voy al trabajo en...", for they: "van al trabajo en...".
target_language_example: Ella va al trabajo en taxi.
native_language_example: She goes to work by taxi.

additional_notes: Used with "ir" to talk about how something is going (El negocio va bien; Me va bien; No va bien). With indirect object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/les) it means someone is doing well. With clothing or style it means something suits someone or fits them well: "Le va bien" (it looks good on them) and "Te va bien" (it fits you/looks good on you). You’ll also hear it alone as a short reply meaning “Okay / Sounds good / All right.”
target_language_example: ¿Cómo te va? — Me va bien, gracias.
native_language_example: How’s it going? — It’s going well for me, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to say something is contrary to a rule, law, belief, or what someone wants. It can also mean to oppose someone (e.g., "go against your parents"). The verb changes with the subject/tense: "voy/vas/va/vamos/van en contra de..."; "fue/iba/irá en contra de...".
target_language_example: Eso va en contra de las normas de la empresa.
native_language_example: That goes against the company’s rules.

meaning: (It) is going very well; (someone) is doing very well.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ir" to talk about how things are going for someone or something (work, life, a project, etc.). Common patterns: "me/te/le/nos/les va muy bien" = "it’s going very well for me/you/him-her/us/them".
target_language_example: Con el nuevo trabajo, me va muy bien.
native_language_example: With the new job, I’m doing very well.

additional_notes: Used to say something exceeds a limit, ability, understanding, expectations, or what’s normal. Very common with nouns like mi comprensión (my understanding), mi poder (my ability/power), lo que puedo imaginar (what I can imagine), or lo absurdo (the absurd). You can also conjugate it: va / van / iba / irá más allá de.
target_language_example: Lo que pasó ayer va más allá de lo que puedo explicar.
native_language_example: What happened yesterday goes beyond what I can explain.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or choosing something and you want one unit (a drink, a ticket, a portion, etc.). It’s common in casual speech: someone offers options and you respond with “va uno” to mean you want one. Often followed by what it is: “Va uno de pollo.” Although “va” literally means “goes,” here it functions more like “make it” / “I’ll have.” Note: In practice, speakers often match gender with the noun (e.g., “va una” for *cerveza*), but “va uno” is used when the implied item is masculine or generic (e.g., *uno* = one [item/order]).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres un boleto para el tour? —Sí, va uno.
native_language_example: Do you want a ticket for the tour? —Yes, I’ll take one.

additional_notes: Refers to the vacation period in summer (often the break from school or work). It’s commonly used with possessives (mis/tus/sus vacaciones de verano) and with verbs like pasar (to spend) or acabar(se) (to end): «Mis vacaciones de verano se están acabando».
target_language_example: Este año mis vacaciones de verano son en agosto.
native_language_example: This year my summer vacation is in August.

meaning: “it’s worth it / it’s worth the effort.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is worthwhile (the benefit is worth the time, cost, or effort). Often followed by an infinitive: “Vale la pena + verb” (Vale la pena estudiar). You can also say “No vale la pena” = “It’s not worth it.”
target_language_example: Vale la pena intentarlo otra vez.
native_language_example: It’s worth trying again.

additional_notes: Used to recommend a place or attraction by saying the visit is worth the time/effort. You can swap in other infinitives: vale la pena ver (to see), probar (to try), etc. Often followed by a noun (vale la pena visitar el museo) or a place name (vale la pena visitar Suiza).
target_language_example: Si tienes tiempo, vale la pena visitar el centro histórico.
native_language_example: If you have time, it’s worth visiting the historic center.

additional_notes: Used to compare value or importance. It can mean literal monetary value (e.g., “the frame is worth more than the painting”) or figurative importance (e.g., “health matters more than gold”). Common pattern: [thing] vale más que [other thing].
target_language_example: Tu amistad vale más que cualquier regalo.
native_language_example: Your friendship is worth more than any gift.

meaning: to be worth it; to be worthwhile.
additional_notes: Used to say that an effort, cost, or experience is worth doing because the result/benefit is good. Common patterns: “Valer la pena + infinitive” (Puede valer la pena esperar = It may be worth waiting) and “Valer la pena + noun” (Puede valer la pena el viaje = The trip may be worth it). Often used in questions/negatives: “¿Puede valer la pena…?” / “No puede valer la pena…”.
target_language_example: ¿Crees que puede valer la pena visitar este museo?
native_language_example: Do you think it might be worth visiting this museum?

additional_notes: Often used with something + “que valga la pena” (“something that’s worth it”). Uses the present subjunctive of valer (“valga”) because it’s commonly in relative clauses or after expressions like “nada/algo” (e.g., “nada que valga la pena”). You can also use it as a set phrase: “Vale la pena + infinitive” (“It’s worth + -ing”): “Vale la pena leerlo.”
target_language_example: No quiero perder tiempo en algo que no valga la pena.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time on something that isn’t worth it.

meaning: 'it was worth it' / 'it was worth the effort.'
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "valer la pena" = "to be worth it." Used to say that the effort, cost, or waiting was justified by the result. Often followed by an infinitive or a clause with "que": "Valió la pena esperar" (It was worth waiting), "No valió la pena que hiciera cambios" (It wasn’t worth it for him to make changes).
target_language_example: Aunque fue cansado, valió la pena hacerlo.
native_language_example: Even though it was tiring, it was worth doing.

meaning: “it was worth it / it was worth the effort.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **valer la pena** (“to be worth it”). **Valía** is the imperfect past (“was worth”), often used when looking back on something or describing a past situation: *No valía la pena* = “It wasn’t worth it.” Commonly followed by an infinitive: **valía la pena + infinitive** (*valía la pena intentarlo/probar* = “it was worth trying”).
target_language_example: Aunque fue difícil, valía la pena hacerlo.
native_language_example: Even though it was hard, it was worth doing.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about a plan or an intention (near future): vamos a + infinitive. In speech it can also be used to propose something or move the conversation/action forward ("Okay, let's...").
target_language_example: Vamos a comer ahora.
native_language_example: We’re going to eat now.

meaning: let’s look for / we’re going to look for.
additional_notes: From ir a + infinitive ("to be going to" + verb). "Vamos" can mean either "we go" or "let’s"; in context, "vamos a buscar" is often used to suggest an action together ("Let’s look for...") or to state an immediate plan ("We’re going to look for..."). You can replace what you’re looking for: "Vamos a buscar un restaurante / una salida / mis llaves".
target_language_example: Vamos a buscar tu teléfono; seguro que está aquí.
native_language_example: Let’s look for your phone; I’m sure it’s here.

meaning: “we’re going to look for” / “we’re going to go get (someone).”
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about going to find or pick up a person. The "a" is the personal "a" and is required before a direct object that is a person (e.g., "buscar a Zé", "buscar a las chicas"). In conversation, it often implies going to pick someone up or go meet them.
target_language_example: Vamos a buscar a mi hermana a la estación.
native_language_example: We’re going to pick up my sister at the station.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or announce that it’s time to eat. Literally “we go to eat” = “we’re going to eat,” but in conversation it often works like an invitation: “Let’s eat.” In a different context, it can also be literal (“We’re going to eat couscous / in the kitchen”). Related idiom: “No te vamos a comer” means “We’re not going to hurt you” (literally “We’re not going to eat you”).
target_language_example: Si ya estás listo, vamos a comer.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, let’s eat.

additional_notes: Used to suggest doing an activity together. Literally “we’re going to take a stroll,” but in conversation it often functions like an invitation or plan (similar to “let’s…”). You can also use it as a question: “¿Vamos a dar un paseo?” = “Shall we go for a walk?”
target_language_example: Hace buen tiempo; vamos a dar un paseo por el parque.
native_language_example: The weather is nice; let’s go for a walk in the park.

additional_notes: Uses ir a + infinitive (“vamos a” + verb) to talk about what you’re about to do. Often used as an invitation/suggestion (“Let’s start”), especially with con (“with”), desde (“from”), or por (“by/with”). In “Ya vamos a empezar,” ya can add emphasis like “Here we go again / We’re starting already,” depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Bueno, vamos a empezar con la primera pregunta.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s start with the first question.

meaning: "we're going to be" / "we will be" (future state or location).
additional_notes: This is the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **vamos a + estar**. Use it to talk about where you’ll be or how you’ll be later (state, condition, or location): *Vamos a estar aquí...*, *Vamos a estar ocupados...*. It often implies a planned or expected future, similar to English “going to.” With adjectives, make sure they agree in number/gender: *vamos a estar muertos* (not *muerto*) if talking about “we.”
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a estar en casa todo el día.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we're going to be at home all day.

additional_notes: Often used to start a conversation or to suggest discussing something. Literally it’s “we’re going to talk,” using **vamos a + infinitive** (near future). Depending on tone and context, it can also feel like “let’s talk (about this).”
target_language_example: Vamos a hablar de lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about what happened yesterday.

meaning: “we’re going to do/make” (we are going to do).
additional_notes: Formed from "vamos a" (we’re going to) + "hacer" (to do/make). Used to talk about a plan or what you and others will do next. In questions like "¿Qué vamos a hacer?" it means “What are we going to do?”
target_language_example: ¿Qué vamos a hacer mañana?
native_language_example: What are we going to do tomorrow?

meaning: “let’s do it” / “we’re going to do it.”
additional_notes: From "vamos a" (let’s / we’re going to) + "hacerlo" (do it). Often used to suggest starting an action together (“Let’s do it”), but it can also simply state a plan (“We’re going to do it”). Add-ons like "juntos" (together), "otra vez" (again), or "a tu modo" (your way) are very common.
target_language_example: Está bien, vamos a hacerlo ahora.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s do it now.

meaning: "we're going to go" / "we're going to leave".
additional_notes: Formed with **ir (to go)** in the present (**vamos**) + **a** + infinitive (**ir**). It often expresses a near-future plan or intention. Very commonly used to talk about leaving: **Nos vamos a ir** = “We’re going to leave / We’re heading out.” (Even though it’s literally “we’re going to go,” English usually uses “leave/ head out” in this context.)
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; vamos a irnos.
native_language_example: It’s late; we’re going to leave.

meaning: “we’re going to go to … / we’re going to …” (near future plan).
additional_notes: Uses ir a + infinitive for the near future with nosotros (vamos). With places, it’s often “vamos a ir a + place” (two a’s in a row: one from “ir a” + one introducing the destination). With an action, use “vamos a ir a + infinitive” (e.g., “vamos a ir a hablar…”). In casual speech, people may shorten it to “vamos a…” when the meaning is clear.
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a ir a comprar comida.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to go buy food.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure ir a + infinitive: vamos a + morir. It can be meant literally (a real danger) or used dramatically to express that a situation is very bad. Also common as nos vamos a morir (“we’re going to die”).
target_language_example: Si no encontramos agua pronto, vamos a morir.
native_language_example: If we don’t find water soon, we’re going to die.

meaning: “we’re going to get out of here / we’re going to leave (this place).”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **vamos a + salir** (“we’re going to leave”). **de aquí** means “from here/out of here.” Depending on tone and context, it can be a simple plan (“let’s leave”) or a strong statement of determination/encouragement (“we’ll get out of here”).
target_language_example: Tranquilos: vamos a salir de aquí juntos.
native_language_example: Relax: we’re going to get out of here together.

meaning: "we’re going to have to" (we must / we need to).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity/obligation for “we,” often because circumstances require it. It’s the near-future structure: vamos a + infinitive (tener que + infinitive). After it, use another infinitive: Vamos a tener que esperar / hacer / hablar.
target_language_example: Vamos a tener que salir más temprano para llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: We’re going to have to leave earlier to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Literally “we’re going to take.” Used to propose a shared plan. With transportation (el autobús, el barco), tomar = “to take/catch.” With drinks (té, una copa, cervezas), tomar = “to have/drink.” Often followed by the thing you’ll take/have: “Vamos a tomar + noun.”
target_language_example: Hace frío; vamos a tomar un café caliente.
native_language_example: It’s cold; let’s have a hot coffee.

meaning: "Let’s see" / "we’ll see" (used to pause, think, or introduce what comes next).
additional_notes: Often used as a conversational filler before explaining, deciding, or checking something: "Vamos a ver..." = “Let’s see…” It can also be literal: "vamos a ver a tu mamá" = “we’re going to see/visit your mom,” and "nos vamos a ver" = “we’re going to see each other.” In speech, it’s commonly followed by a comma: "Vamos a ver, escúchame."
target_language_example: Vamos a ver, ¿qué opciones tenemos?
native_language_example: Let’s see—what options do we have?

additional_notes: Used to introduce checking, finding out, or figuring out something next (often before making a decision or offering help). Very common in service situations or when examining something: “Vamos a ver qué podemos hacer” = “Let’s see what we can do.” In speech it can sound like a brief pause while you assess a situation.
target_language_example: Dame un momento: vamos a ver qué opciones hay.
native_language_example: Give me a moment: let’s see what options there are.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to end a conversation or to say you’ll stay in contact as plans develop. Often implies “we’ll check in and update each other.” You may also hear it as “vamos viendo” (“we’ll see / we’ll play it by ear”).
target_language_example: No sé si podré ir mañana, pero vamos hablando.
native_language_example: I’m not sure if I can go tomorrow, but we’ll keep in touch.

meaning: "Come on" / "let’s go" (urging someone to move or continue).
additional_notes: Repetition adds emphasis and impatience/encouragement, like “come on, come on” or “hurry up.” It’s common in speech when pushing someone to act, keep going, or speed things up.
target_language_example: Vamos, vamos, que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Come on, come on—we’re going to be late.

meaning: “Come on, come on!” (urging someone to hurry up or do something).
additional_notes: Repeated for emphasis, often said impatiently or to encourage someone (like “come on!” or “let’s go!”). You can repeat it more or fewer times depending on how strong you want it to sound. Common in speech and in excited/urgent situations.
target_language_example: Vamos, vamos, vamos, que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Come on, come on, we’re late.

additional_notes: From the verb "ir" (to go): "vamos" = "we go". Often used to suggest an action like “let’s…” when followed by a place (Vamos a tu casa = Let’s go to your house). It’s also used for the near future when followed by an infinitive (Vamos a comer = We’re going to eat). With "a por" it means “go get / go after” someone or something: "Vamos a por ellos" = Let’s go after them / Let’s go get them.
target_language_example: Vamos al parque.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the park.

additional_notes: Used to suggest that you and the other person (or group) go home. It’s the present tense of ir (“to go”) with the inclusive “we” form (vamos) + a (“to”) + casa (“home”). You can add words like pronto (“soon”) to say when.
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; vamos a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late; let’s go home.

meaning: “we go to the” / “let’s go to the”.
additional_notes: "Vamos" can mean either (1) "we go/are going" (present tense) or (2) "let’s go" as a suggestion/command. "Al" = "a" (to) + "el" (the), used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., al valle).
target_language_example: Vamos al supermercado después de clase.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the supermarket after class.

meaning: "are going to" (they are about to / will do something).
additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** to talk about a near future or planned action. **van** = "they go" (present of *ir*), **a** = "to". It’s followed by an infinitive: *van a quedarse* (are going to stay), *van a aumentar* (are going to increase). Object or reflexive pronouns often go before *van*: *se van a encontrar* (they’re going to meet), *no te van a sacar* (they’re not going to get you out).
target_language_example: Van a llegar tarde si no salen ya.
native_language_example: They’re going to arrive late if they don’t leave now.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to…”). **van** is from *ir* (to go) and matches **ellos/ellas/ustedes** (they/you all). **hacer** means “to do/make.” Often used to talk about plans or what will happen soon; in questions it can be **¿Qué van a hacer?** (“What are they/you all going to do?”).
target_language_example: ¿Qué van a hacer este fin de semana?
native_language_example: What are you all going to do this weekend?

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **van a + matar** (“they’re going to kill”). **Van** is the **ellos/ellas/ustedes** form of *ir* (“to go”), so the subject is usually “they” (or “you all,” in Latin America). The person in danger is shown with an indirect object pronoun: **me/te/nos/lo/la** etc. It can be literal (a real threat) or exaggerated/joking, e.g., **“Mis padres me van a matar”** = “My parents are going to kill me” (meaning “they’ll be furious”).
target_language_example: Si llego tarde otra vez, mis padres me van a matar.
native_language_example: If I’m late again, my parents are going to kill me.

additional_notes: This is the near-future construction **ir a + infinitive**. **Van** is the **ellos/ellas/ustedes** form of **ir** (to go), and **ser** is “to be.” It’s used to talk about what something/someone will be like: *Van a ser famosos* (They’re going to be famous).
target_language_example: Van a ser días muy largos.
native_language_example: They’re going to be very long days.

meaning: “you/they are going to see” (and sometimes “you’ll see.”).
additional_notes: Form of the near-future: **ir (van) + a + infinitive (ver)**. **Van** is used with **ustedes** (“you all”) or **ellos/ellas** (“they”). It can also be said on its own (**Van a ver.**) meaning “You’ll see.” to build suspense or as a warning/promise depending on tone.
target_language_example: Si no me crees, van a ver lo que pasa mañana.
native_language_example: If you don’t believe me, you’ll see what happens tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration of time (more than a couple of hours, but not exact). Often appears with duration phrases like "durante varias horas" (for several hours) or "me llevó varias horas" (it took me several hours).
target_language_example: Estuvimos esperando varias horas en el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We waited several hours at the airport.

additional_notes: Used to say an action happened repeatedly (more than once, not an exact number). It often comes after the verb ("Lo intenté varias veces") but can also appear earlier for emphasis ("Varias veces me pasó eso").
target_language_example: Te lo dije varias veces, pero no me escuchaste.
native_language_example: I told you several times, but you didn’t listen to me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future action: present tense of ir (vas) + a + infinitive. Often expresses a plan, intention, or a prediction: Vas a venir, vas a ser, vas a volver. Informal vs formal: 'vas a' (tú) vs 'va a' (usted/él/ella).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a estudiar hoy?
native_language_example: Are you going to study today?

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone (about their health, safety, or a situation). It’s the near future with **ir a + infinitive** (“vas a estar” = “you’re going to be”). Often said with a supportive tone: *Vas a estar bien, tranquilo/a.* As a question, it can check on someone’s condition: *¿Vas a estar bien?*
target_language_example: No te preocupes: vas a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—you’ll be fine.

meaning: "you are going to do" / "you will do" (informal singular).
additional_notes: From **ir a + infinitive** (near future): **vas a hacer** = **you’re going to do/make**. It’s used with **tú** (informal “you”); formal would be **va a hacer** (usted) and plural **van a hacer** (ustedes). **Hacer** can mean “to do” or “to make,” depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer mañana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tomorrow?

additional_notes: Formed with **ir (vas) + a + infinitive (ir)** to talk about a planned/near-future action. Very common in conversation (often like English “going to”). In questions/negatives: **¿Vas a ir?** (Are you going to go?) **No vas a ir.** (You’re not going to go.) With **te** it becomes **te vas a ir**, which usually means **“you’re going to leave”** (to go away).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a ir a la fiesta mañana?
native_language_example: Are you going to go to the party tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses **ir a + infinitive** (“vas a llegar”) to talk about something that will likely happen soon. **Llegar tarde a/al + place/event** = “to arrive late to…”. Often used as a warning or reminder: *Vete… o vas a llegar tarde* (“Leave… or you’ll be late”).
target_language_example: Si no sales ahora, vas a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: If you don’t leave now, you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Literally the near-future form of "morir" (to die): "vas a" + infinitive. Often used as a dramatic statement or a threat ("¡Vas a morir!"), and very commonly in the negative to reassure someone: "No te vas a morir" = "You’re not going to die" / "You’ll be fine."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no te vas a morir; solo es una inyección.
native_language_example: Relax, you’re not going to die; it’s just a shot.

additional_notes: From **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to…”) + **necesitar** (“to need”). **Vas** is the *tú* form of **ir**. It often appears with an object: **Vas a necesitar esto** (“You’re going to need this”), or with a pronoun before the verb: **La vas a necesitar** (“You’re going to need it/her”). Can also be used for emphasis like “You’re going to need more than that.”
target_language_example: Vas a necesitar ayuda para terminar a tiempo.
native_language_example: You’re going to need help to finish on time.

meaning: “you’re going to lose” / “you’re going to miss (it)”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **vas a + perder** (you’re going to lose). Often used as a warning about something that will happen soon: **Vas a perder el tren** = “You’re going to miss the train.” With things like **el tren / la oportunidad / el partido**, English often uses “miss” rather than “lose.”
target_language_example: ¡Date prisa o vas a perder el autobús!
native_language_example: Hurry up or you’re going to miss the bus!

meaning: “you are going to be” / “you will be.”
additional_notes: Formed with ir (vas) + a + infinitive (ser) to talk about the future. It can describe a future identity/state (“Vas a ser padre”) or a future event affecting you (“Vas a ser arrestado”). Often translates naturally as “you’ll be…” in English.
target_language_example: Si estudias mucho, vas a ser un gran médico.
native_language_example: If you study a lot, you’re going to be a great doctor.

meaning: 'you're going to have to' / 'you'll have to' (you must).
additional_notes: Common way to express obligation or necessity directed at "tú" (you, informal). It’s the near-future structure "vas a" + "tener que" + infinitive: "Vas a tener que confiar" = "You’ll have to trust." Can sound firm or like a warning depending on tone. For "usted": "va a tener que"; for "ustedes": "van a tener que".
target_language_example: Vas a tener que estudiar si quieres aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to study if you want to pass the exam.

additional_notes: Commonly used to predict what will happen next or to emphasize a warning, promise, or challenge (often like “just you wait”). It’s the informal (tú) form of the near-future: ir a + infinitive (ver). In context it can mean literally “you’re going to see (something/someone)” (e.g., Me vas a ver = “You’re going to see me”), or idiomatically “you’ll see (what I mean/what happens).”
target_language_example: Vas a ver que todo sale bien.
native_language_example: You’ll see—everything will turn out fine.

meaning: "a glass/cup of" (a serving in a glass/cup).
additional_notes: Used to say what the glass/cup contains: "un vaso de agua" (a glass of water), "un vaso de jugo" (a glass of juice). With a material, it can describe what it’s made of: "un vaso de papel" (a paper cup). "Vaso" can mean a glass or a cup depending on the context.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un vaso de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase: "vaso" is a drinking glass (not a cup), and "de" means "of." You can pluralize it: "dos vasos de agua" (two glasses of water).
target_language_example: ¿Me traes un vaso de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to one serving of milk in a drinking glass. You can modify it with quantities like un/medio/dos vasos de leche. In everyday Spanish, people often drop “de leche” if it’s clear from context: “Dame un vaso, por favor” (when you’re already talking about milk).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes traer un vaso de leche, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of milk, please?

meaning: 'is/are going to' (subjunctive) / 'might' (about something that may happen).
additional_notes: “Vaya” is the present subjunctive form of “ir” (to go). “Vaya a + infinitive” is used in dependent clauses—often after expressions like dudar que (to doubt), no creer que (to not think), tener miedo de que (to be afraid), esperar que (to hope)—to talk about a possible or expected action, often in the near future: “No creo que eso vaya a pasar” = “I don’t think that’s going to happen.”
target_language_example: No creo que ella vaya a venir hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t think she’s going to come today.

meaning: “(that I/you/he/she) go to…” (present subjunctive of ir); also “Go to…” (formal command).
additional_notes: “Vaya” comes from the verb “ir” (to go). It’s used as a subjunctive form after words like “que”, “cuando” (talking about the future), “quizá(s)”, “puede que”, etc.: “Quieren que vaya a ayudar”, “Cuando vaya a…”. It’s also the formal (usted) command: “Vaya a la parte de atrás” = “Go to the back.” Often followed by a place (a la cárcel, a tu fiesta) or an action with an infinitive (a ayudar).
target_language_example: Quizá no vaya a la reunión mañana.
native_language_example: Maybe I won’t go to the meeting tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Vayamos" is the present subjunctive of "ir" for "nosotros" and is commonly used to propose an action (“Let’s …”) or as a polite command. It’s usually followed by (1) a place: "Vayamos a la cocina" (Let’s go to the kitchen), or (2) an infinitive: "Vayamos a comer" (Let’s go eat / Let’s eat). You’ll also see it in phrases like "Es hora de que nos vayamos a casa" (“It’s time for us to go home”), where "que" triggers the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Vayamos a tomar un café.
native_language_example: Let’s go have a coffee.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of **ir** for **ustedes** (you all / you plural). Used to tell a group to go somewhere (**Vayan a la casa**) or to go do something (**Vayan a trabajar**). Often followed by a place (a + el/la/los/las) or an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: Chicos, vayan a dormir; mañana tenemos clase temprano.
native_language_example: Guys, go to sleep; tomorrow we have class early.

meaning: "(that) you go to"; in warnings with "no": "don’t you (go and)… / don’t…"
additional_notes: "Vayas" is the tú present subjunctive of *ir* (to go). It often appears after expressions like *para que* (so that) to express purpose: *para que vayas a…* = “so that you go to…”. With *no* it can be a negative command or a warning/threat: *No le vayas a decir…* = “Don’t you tell him…” / “Don’t go and tell him…”. It can also be literal movement: *No vayas a tu casa* = “Don’t go to your house.”
target_language_example: No vayas a contarle a nadie lo que pasó.
native_language_example: Don’t you tell anyone what happened.

additional_notes: Imperative (tú) form of **ir**: **ve**. Use **ve a + place** (Ve a casa) and often **ve a + infinitive** to tell someone to do something (Ve a lavarte la cara). For a more polite command, use **vaya a**.
target_language_example: Ve a tu cuarto y termina la tarea.
native_language_example: Go to your room and finish your homework.

meaning: “go to the” (addressing one person; feminine singular place/thing).
additional_notes: Command form of **ir** (to go): **ve** = “go” (tú). **a** = “to”. **la** is used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., *la enfermería*, *la consola*). Often used to give directions or instructions. (With masculine nouns: **ve al**.)
target_language_example: Ve a la puerta y espera aquí.
native_language_example: Go to the door and wait here.

meaning: "go and see" / "go check"; also "go watch" (TV, a movie).
additional_notes: Imperative (tú) form of **ir a ver**. Use it to tell someone to go look/check something (**Ve a ver quién es** = go see who it is), to go look somewhere (**Ve a ver al otro lado** = go look on the other side), or to go visit someone (**Ve a ver a tu hija** = go see/visit your daughter). With people, you often use **a**: **ver a + person**.
target_language_example: Ve a ver si la puerta está cerrada.
native_language_example: Go check if the door is closed.

additional_notes: Uses the tú imperative of ir (“ve”). It’s followed by a + ver (“to see/visit”) and then the personal a before a person (or pets treated like people): ve a ver a Tom / a mi madre. You can replace the person: ve a ver a María / ve a ver a los niños. More formal: vaya a ver a…; plural: vayan a ver a…
target_language_example: Ve a ver a tu abuela esta tarde.
native_language_example: Go see your grandmother this afternoon.

meaning: Go check (to see) if… / Go see whether…
additional_notes: Common way to tell someone to go and check something. It’s an informal-sounding but very normal everyday command. Uses the tú imperative of "ir" (ve) + "a ver" (to go see) + "si" (if/whether). Often implies “go find out” or “go make sure.”
target_language_example: Ve a ver si hay leche en la nevera.
native_language_example: Go check if there’s milk in the fridge.

additional_notes: A casual/vocative use addressing a girl: **ve** is the **tú** command of *ir* (“to go”). In natural writing, a comma is often used (*Ve, chica,*), but the phrase can also appear without punctuation as **ve chica**. Often followed by a destination or reason: *ve a casa*, *ve con tu mamá*, etc. Out of context, **ve** could be confused with forms related to *ver* (“to see”), but as a standalone command it most commonly means “go.”
target_language_example: Ve chica, que ya es tarde.
native_language_example: Go on, girl, it’s already late.

meaning: Go get… / go for… / go via (a place).
additional_notes: “Ve” is the tú command form of “ir” (to go). With “por”, it often means (1) go to fetch something or someone: “Ve por el libro” = “Go get the book,” or (2) go through/along a route: “Ve por el pasillo” = “Go down/through the hallway.” “Ve por ellos” can mean “Go get them” or “Go after them,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ve por agua, por favor.
native_language_example: Go get some water, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the next step: checking, finding out, or considering options before deciding what to do. It’s the nosotros (we) command form of "ver" (to see), followed by "qué" (what). Often followed by a clause like "podemos hacer" (we can do) or "tienes" (you have).
target_language_example: Veamos qué pasa si lo intentamos otra vez.
native_language_example: Let’s see what happens if we try again.

meaning: “times a day” (how many times per day).
additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one day, usually with a number: “cinco veces al día” (five times a day). Common in routines and instructions, especially medical directions: “Tome uno cuatro veces al día” (Take one four times a day). You can also use similar patterns like “una vez al día” (once a day) and “dos veces al día” (twice a day).
target_language_example: Revisa el correo dos veces al día.
native_language_example: He checks his email twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to compare sizes/amounts with a multiplier: [number] + veces más grande que + [thing]. It agrees in gender/number with what’s being described (grande doesn’t change; you can also hear “más grandes que” with plural subjects). Common numbers: dos/tres/cuatro veces…, veinte veces…, etc.
target_language_example: Este país es diez veces más grande que el mío.
native_language_example: This country is ten times bigger than mine.

additional_notes: Used to talk about age (tener veinte años = “to be 20 years old”) or a length of time (hace veinte años = “20 years ago”, en veinte años = “in 20 years / over 20 years”, llevo + gerundio + veinte años = “I’ve been … for 20 years”, han pasado veinte años = “20 years have passed”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene veinte años y yo llevo veinte años viviendo aquí.
native_language_example: My brother is 20 years old, and I’ve been living here for 20 years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration ("for twenty minutes," "twenty minutes ago") or an estimated time/distance ("It’s twenty minutes away" = by car/on foot depending on context). With "hace" it means "twenty minutes ago"; with "en" it means "in twenty minutes" (time needed to do something).
target_language_example: El restaurante está a veinte minutos de aquí.
native_language_example: The restaurant is twenty minutes from here.

additional_notes: Used to state a percentage in calculations, business deals, tips/commissions, discounts, or statistics. It often appears with verbs like "ser" (El veinte por ciento es...), "quedarse con" (keep/take), or written as "20%".
target_language_example: Me descuentan el veinte por ciento si pago hoy.
native_language_example: They give me a twenty percent discount if I pay today.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the physical constant (how fast light travels, especially in a vacuum). It can also be used figuratively to mean “very fast,” often with the phrase “a la velocidad de la luz” (“at lightning speed”).
target_language_example: Contestó a la velocidad de la luz.
native_language_example: He replied at lightning speed.

meaning: “Come, come!” (calling someone over / urging them to come).
additional_notes: Repeat of the imperative "ven" (from "venir") to sound more insistent, urgent, or encouraging. Often used when calling someone closer: "Ven, ven aquí". You can repeat it more times for emphasis ("Ven, ven, ven").
target_language_example: Ven, ven, no tengas miedo.
native_language_example: Come on, come—don’t be scared.

meaning: "come to" / "come and" (used to invite someone to do something or come somewhere).
additional_notes: Imperative of "venir" (tú): "ven" = "come". With a place/noun: "Ven a nuestra mesa" = "Come to our table." With an infinitive: "Ven a acostarte" / "Ven a jugar" = "Come (and) lie down" / "Come (and) play" (often like an invitation or suggestion).
target_language_example: Ven a cenar con nosotros esta noche.
native_language_example: Come have dinner with us tonight.

additional_notes: Used to invite or tell someone to come and meet a person (often for the first time). It’s an imperative: ven (“come”) + a + conocer (“to meet/get to know”) + a (before a person). You can change the verb form: Ven a conocer a mis amigos. / Venga a conocer a mis amigos. / Vengan a conocer a mis amigos.
target_language_example: Ven a conocer a mi hermana; acaba de llegar.
native_language_example: Come meet my sister; she just arrived.

additional_notes: An invitation/request using the tú command form of **venir** (“ven” = “come”). **A** means “to,” and **mi casa** is “my house/home.” You can add time phrases after it (e.g., *a las ocho*, *esta tarde*, *por la mañana*) or soften it with *por favor*.
target_language_example: Ven a mi casa después de la escuela.
native_language_example: Come to my house after school.

additional_notes: Informal command (tú) using the affirmative imperative of venir (ven) + a + infinitive (ver) + object pronoun (me). Used to invite/ask someone to visit you, often with time phrases like antes de…, antes de que…, or de vez en cuando (from time to time).
target_language_example: Si estás cerca, ven a verme esta tarde.
native_language_example: If you’re nearby, come see me this afternoon.

additional_notes: Informal command using "venir" (tú form: "ven") + "acá" (“here”). Used to call someone over; tone depends on context and can sound affectionate ("cariño") or aggressive/insulting.
target_language_example: Ven acá un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: An informal singular command (imperative) using "venir" (to come): "ven" = “come” (to one person). "Aquí" means “here,” near the speaker. Used to call someone closer or get their attention. For a more polite command, use "venga aquí"; for more than one person, "vengan aquí".
target_language_example: Ven aquí un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Uses the tú imperative of "venir" ("ven") + "aquí" ("here") + "y" ("and") to tell someone to come to where you are and then do something else. Often followed by another command: "Ven aquí y siéntate." You can also say "ven acá y" in many regions with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ven aquí y explícame qué pasó.
native_language_example: Come here and explain to me what happened.

additional_notes: An invitation/command telling someone to accompany you and your group. Uses the informal (tú) command form of venir: ven. You can soften it with por favor, or turn it into a question: ¿Vienes con nosotros? (Are you coming with us?).
target_language_example: Ven con nosotros al parque esta tarde.
native_language_example: Come with us to the park this afternoon.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) using **venir** (tú form): **ven**. Used to invite or tell someone to accompany you. You can add a destination: **Ven conmigo a la tienda.** You may also hear **Ven conmigo y hablamos de...** (“Come with me and we’ll talk about...”).
target_language_example: Ven conmigo al parque.
native_language_example: Come with me to the park.

meaning: would be good for (someone); would come in handy.
additional_notes: Conditional form of "venir bien" (to suit/to be good for someone). Often used with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les vendría bien" + noun/infinitive. Common for giving advice or making polite suggestions (e.g., "Le vendría bien una taza de té").
target_language_example: Me vendría bien un descanso después de clase.
native_language_example: A break would be good for me after class.

additional_notes: This is a polite/formal command or invitation using the usted imperative of **venir**: **venga**. You can soften it with **por favor** (“Venga a verme, por favor.”). With friends/family you’ll often hear **ven a verme** (tú).
target_language_example: Cuando tenga tiempo, venga a verme a la oficina.
native_language_example: When you have time, come see me at the office.

additional_notes: Used with places/origins to say where you are from. It’s the 1st-person singular present of "venir" + "de" (origin). You can also use it to mean "I’m not here as a visitor / I’m not just visiting" depending on context (e.g., "no vengo de visita").
target_language_example: Hola, vengo de México, ¿y tú?
native_language_example: Hi, I’m from Mexico—how about you?

meaning: “(have/has) come to” (a place) or “come to” (do something).
additional_notes: “Venido a” is the past participle of venir (“to come”) used with haber to form the present perfect: he/has/habíamos venido. It’s often followed by either a destination (a + place: “venido a Londres”) or by an infinitive to express purpose (a + infinitive: “venido a ayudar” = “come to help”). Word order with pronouns: “Han venido a verte” = “They’ve come to see you.”
target_language_example: He venido a estudiar español.
native_language_example: I’ve come to study Spanish.

meaning: 'to come to' (a place, event, or time).
additional_notes: Use "venir a" to say someone comes to a destination or event: "venir a Japón", "venir a la fiesta". With times it’s often "venir a + time" meaning "come at (that time)": "venir a las nueve" = "come at nine".
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a mi casa mañana a las ocho?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house tomorrow at eight?

meaning: to come see me / to come to see me.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to visit you. Structure: "venir a" + infinitive expresses coming somewhere in order to do something. "verme" = "to see me" (ver + me). Often said as a request or expectation: "Tienes que venir a verme" (You have to come see me).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a verme mañana por la tarde?
native_language_example: Can you come see me tomorrow afternoon?

meaning: to be relevant; to apply (to the situation).
additional_notes: Used to say something is (or isn’t) related to the topic or situation. Very often appears in the negative: “No viene al caso” = “That’s not relevant / That’s beside the point.”
target_language_example: Lo que dices no viene al caso; dejemos ese tema.
native_language_example: What you’re saying isn’t relevant; let’s drop that topic.

additional_notes: Used to invite, tell, or ask someone to come to the speaker’s location (“here”). Often followed by an infinitive to say the purpose: “venir aquí a + infinitive” (e.g., venir aquí a hablar = come here to talk). In commands, it commonly appears as “ven aquí” (informal tú) or “venga/vengan aquí” (formal usted/ustedes).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir aquí un momento, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you come here for a moment, please?

meaning: to be useful / to come in handy; to suit (someone) well.
additional_notes: Used to say something is convenient or helpful in a situation. Often appears as "me/te/le/nos/les viene bien" (it suits me/you/them) or in the conditional "me vendría bien" (it would come in handy). It can also mean something fits well (like clothes): "La camisa te viene bien".
target_language_example: ¿Te puede venir bien si te llamo mañana?
native_language_example: Would it work for you / would it be convenient if I call you tomorrow?

meaning: to come with (someone/something); to show up with (something).
additional_notes: Used for accompanying someone or bringing something when you come: "Vine con mi amiga" (I came with my friend). In set phrases like "venir con tan poco aviso/anticipación" it means coming even though you were told only shortly beforehand (“on such short notice”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir con tu pasaporte?
native_language_example: Can you come with your passport?

meaning: 'to come with us' / 'to come along with us'.
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to join your group or to say they must accompany you. The verb changes with the subject (e.g., ¿Quieres venir con nosotros? / Tienen que venir con nosotros). With other groups, swap the pronoun: venir con ustedes (with you all), venir con ellos/ellas (with them).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir con nosotros al cine?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us to the movies?

additional_notes: Used to invite, request, or tell someone to accompany you. The verb changes for the person (vienes/viene/vienen), while "conmigo" stays the same: "¿Vienes conmigo?" (Are you coming with me?). Often sounds like a command or strong insistence in statements like "Tienes que venir conmigo" or "Vas a venir conmigo."
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir conmigo al supermercado?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me to the supermarket?

meaning: 'to come from' (to be from; to arrive from a place; to originate from somewhere).
additional_notes: Used with a place or origin to say where someone/something comes from or originates (venir de + país/ciudad/alguna parte). It can refer to: (1) a person’s origin (Vengo de…), (2) a recent arrival (Acabo de venir de…), or (3) the source/origin of something (La señal/los ruidos pueden venir de…). Note: don’t confuse with "acabar de" + infinitive ("to have just done"), though you’ll often see "acabo de venir de …" meaning "I’ve just come from …".
target_language_example: Acabo de venir de Polonia.
native_language_example: I’ve just come from Poland.

meaning: to run in the family; to be a family trait/tradition.
additional_notes: Used to say that a quality, skill, habit, or even a health issue is common in a family (inherited or passed down). Often used as: “Eso viene de familia” (That runs in the family).
target_language_example: El talento para el deporte parece venir de familia.
native_language_example: The talent for sports seems to run in the family.

meaning: to come for; to come to pick up (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used when someone comes to get or pick up a person or thing: "Puedes venir por la comida" = "You can come pick up the food." With people, it can also mean "to come for" someone in a threatening sense (e.g., to arrest or attack): "Van a venir por nosotros." In directions, you may hear "venir por aquí" meaning "come this way / come through here."
target_language_example: Pueden venir por la comida.
native_language_example: They can come pick up the food.

additional_notes: Used with a following clause introduced by "lo que" (“what/that which”): "Veo lo que estás haciendo" = “I see what you’re doing.” It can mean literal seeing (with your eyes) or understanding someone’s point: "Veo lo que quieres decir" = “I see what you mean.”
target_language_example: Veo lo que dices, pero no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: I see what you’re saying, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand the reason for something. Often appears as **No veo por qué...** (“I don’t see why...”), meaning you don’t understand the reason or you disagree that there’s a good reason (e.g., **No veo por qué no...** = “I don’t see why not...” ).
target_language_example: Ahora veo por qué estás preocupado.
native_language_example: Now I see why you’re worried.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an observation or realization based on what you’ve just seen or learned. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Veo que + [clause]”. Depending on tone/context, it can sound neutral (“I see that…”) or slightly pointed/ironic (“Oh, I see you…”).
target_language_example: Veo que ya terminaste la tarea.
native_language_example: I see that you already finished the homework.

additional_notes: Used to start the classic guessing game where one person says “Veo veo…” and gives clues (often the color) about something they can see, and others guess what it is. You’ll often hear: “Veo veo.” “¿Qué ves?” “Una cosita…” “¿De qué color?”
target_language_example: ¿Jugamos al veo veo? Veo veo una cosita de color rojo.
native_language_example: Do you want to play I spy? I spy something red.

meaning: to see (a person); to meet with (someone).
