additional_notes: Used when the subject is explicitly "él" (he) and you want to make the sentence negative. In Spanish, "no" goes right before the verb: "Él no trabaja" = "He doesn't work." The exact English translation depends on the verb tense that follows (present: "doesn't"; past: "didn't"; perfect: "hasn't", etc.). Often Spanish drops the subject pronoun, so you may also see just "No trabaja".
target_language_example: Él no entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: He doesn't understand the question.

additional_notes: Used to negate a statement about a male subject (él). Often followed by an adjective or a noun: él no es feliz (he isn’t happy), él no es culpable (he isn’t guilty). In Spanish you can also drop the subject pronoun when it’s clear: No es feliz.
target_language_example: Él no es mi hermano, es mi primo.
native_language_example: He is not my brother; he’s my cousin.

él no es más que un

target_language_multi_word_term: él no es más que un
additional_notes: Used to minimize or dismiss someone by saying they are only a certain kind of person. Structure: (subject) + no + ser + más que + un/una + noun. Change the article and noun to match gender/number: “Ella no es más que una…” / “Ellos no son más que unos…”. It can be neutral (“just a poet”) but often sounds critical (“nothing but an egoist”).
target_language_example: Él no es más que un aprendiz; todavía le falta experiencia.
native_language_example: He's nothing but an apprentice; he still lacks experience.

meaning: "he is not a" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to negate someone’s identity/role/classification with the verb "ser" (él + no + es + un + noun/adjective-noun). For feminine nouns, use "él no es una". For plural: "ellos no son". Often paired with "sino" to correct something: "Él no es un X, sino un Y."
target_language_example: Él no es un turista; es un estudiante.
native_language_example: He is not a tourist; he is a student.

meaning: he couldn’t / he wasn’t able to (do something).
additional_notes: Past tense of "poder" (preterite): él pudo = he could. Commonly followed by an infinitive (pudo abrir, pudo ir, pudo resistir). With "haber" + past participle (no pudo haber dicho), it often expresses disbelief: "He couldn’t have said that."
target_language_example: Él no pudo llegar a tiempo por el tráfico.
native_language_example: He couldn’t arrive on time because of traffic.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say he is unable to do something or not allowed to do it: “Él no puede + infinitive” (Él no puede salir = He can’t go out). With “no puede haber + past participle,” it expresses logical impossibility/deduction: “He can’t have + past participle” (Él no puede haber ido a la escuela = He can’t have gone to school).
target_language_example: Él no puede venir hoy porque está enfermo.
native_language_example: He can’t come today because he’s sick.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person lacks something (an object, money, time, permission/eligibility, a quality, etc.). In Spanish you usually don’t need to include the subject pronoun (Él): more natural is often just “no tiene…”. With abstract nouns it often translates as “he has no…” (e.g., no tiene remordimiento = he has no remorse).
target_language_example: Él no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: He doesn't have time today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man (or “he”) does not do something at any time. In Spanish, the subject pronoun is often optional, so you’ll also see just “nunca …” or “nunca + verb.” Note the accent: “él” (he) vs “el” (the). Common pattern: “Él nunca + verbo” (e.g., “Él nunca llega tarde”).
target_language_example: Él nunca llega a tiempo.
native_language_example: He never arrives on time.

additional_notes: Preterite form of perder for completed past events. Used for losing things/people (perdió a su hijo), and common figurative uses like "perder la paciencia" (to lose patience), "perder la vida" (to lose one’s life), or "perder el corazón" (to fall in love).
target_language_example: Él perdió las llaves ayer.
native_language_example: He lost the keys yesterday.

meaning: "he thinks that" (he believes/has the opinion that).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what a man believes or thinks is true. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Él piensa que + [statement]”. In questions: “¿Él piensa que…?”
target_language_example: Él piensa que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: He thinks it's going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "he can" / "he is able to"; sometimes "he may" (permission/possibility).
additional_notes: Él = “he” and puede is the 3rd-person singular of poder (“to be able to / can”). Use it to talk about someone’s ability (Él puede correr...), permission (Él puede jugar... siempre que...), or possibility (Él puede estar allá = “He might be there”). In questions: ¿Él puede...?
target_language_example: Él puede venir mañana, pero no está seguro.
native_language_example: He can come tomorrow, but he’s not sure.

meaning: “he can speak” / “he is able to speak.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb **poder** (“can/to be able to”) in the **él/ella/usted** form (**puede**) + an infinitive (**hablar**). It can express **ability** (He can speak French) or sometimes **permission/possibility** depending on context. Often you’ll swap **él** for another subject: **yo puedo hablar**, **tú puedes hablar**, **nosotros podemos hablar**.
target_language_example: Él puede hablar con el director mañana.
native_language_example: He can speak with the director tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the verb querer (“to want”). Follow it with an infinitive to say what he wants to do (Él quiere aprender, ir, volver, ser) or with a noun to say what he wants (Él quiere una manzana, un diccionario). In sentences like “Si él quiere…”, it means “if he wants (to).”
target_language_example: Él quiere comprar un coche nuevo.
native_language_example: He wants to buy a new car.

additional_notes: "Él" = "he" and "sabe" is the present tense of "saber" (to know). With an infinitive (conducir, hablar, jugar, recitar), it usually means "he knows how to" or "he can" do something. You can also use it without a verb to mean he knows a fact: "Él sabe la verdad" (He knows the truth).
target_language_example: Él sabe cocinar muy bien.
native_language_example: He can cook very well.

meaning: "he knows how to speak" / "he can speak" (a language).
additional_notes: Used to say that a man has the ability to speak a language. Very commonly followed by a language name (español, japonés, ruso) or by “X lenguas/idiomas” (five languages). Often you’ll also see: “Él sabe hablar + [idioma] bien/muy bien” (he speaks it well/very well).
target_language_example: Él sabe hablar inglés y francés.
native_language_example: He can speak English and French.

additional_notes: Present tense of saber with the subject pronoun él (“he”). Use saber for knowing facts/information (Él sabe eso), knowing how to do something (Él sabe lo que hace), or knowing about a topic (Él sabe de física). Often the subject pronoun is dropped in Spanish: Sabe todo.
target_language_example: Él sabe hablar inglés.
native_language_example: He knows how to speak English.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy has the ability or knowledge to do something, usually followed by an infinitive verb: "Él sabe cómo + infinitive" (e.g., calcular, cambiar, contestar, hacer, subir). Often implies competence: he knows the right way to do it.
target_language_example: Él sabe cómo usar esta aplicación.
native_language_example: He knows how to use this app.

meaning: "He left the room." / "He went out of the room."
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **salir de** = “to leave/go out of (a place).” **Salió** is the **preterite** (simple past) form of *salir* for **él/ella/usted**. Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so you’ll also hear **Salió de la habitación**.
target_language_example: Él salió de la habitación y cerró la puerta.
native_language_example: He left the room and closed the door.

meaning: "he" + "se" (a pronoun used with reflexive/pronominal verbs: "himself", or a required "se").
additional_notes: "Él" is the subject pronoun “he.” "Se" is a clitic pronoun used in several common ways: (1) reflexive actions: Él se lava. (“He washes (himself).”); (2) pronominal verbs that normally use "se": Él se convirtió… (“He became…”), Él se va… (“He’s leaving/going…”), Él se quedó… (“He stayed…”); (3) with some verbs it can add a sense of completing the action: Él se leyó un libro. (“He read a whole book.”). Because "se" has multiple functions, "él se" isn’t translated as one fixed English phrase.
target_language_example: Él se levantó temprano para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: He got up early to go to work.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of casarse con = “to marry / to get married to,” used when the marriage happened at a specific time (e.g., el mes pasado). You must use con before the person: Se casó con Ana. (Not: *se casó Ana*). Casarse is reflexive; in other persons: me casé con, te casaste con, se casó con, nos casamos con, etc.
target_language_example: Él se casó con Laura en 2020.
native_language_example: He married Laura in 2020.

meaning: he decided to; he made up his mind to.
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb phrase "decidirse a" + infinitive. It emphasizes reaching a decision after thinking or hesitating (similar to “make up one’s mind”). It’s followed by an infinitive: "se decidió a ir", "se decidió a mantener".
target_language_example: Al final, él se decidió a hablar con su jefe.
native_language_example: In the end, he decided to talk to his boss.

additional_notes: From the verb ir (to go): "se fue" is the preterite (completed past) form meaning he went away/left. Often used with destinations: "él se fue a casa" (he went home), "él se fue de la ciudad" (he left the city), "él se fue a dormir" (he went to sleep), or by itself: "Él se fue" (He left).
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, él se fue sin decir nada.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, he left without saying anything.

meaning: “he went to / he left for” (a place), or “he went to” + infinitive (e.g., to bed).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **irse** (“to leave/go away”). **Irse a + place** means he left for/went to that place: *Él se fue a Londres.* It can also be **irse a + infinitive** to mean “to go and do something,” very commonly *irse a acostar* (“to go to bed”). Often implies leaving one location to go somewhere else (not just being in motion).
target_language_example: Él se fue a México el año pasado.
native_language_example: He went to/left for Mexico last year.

additional_notes: Uses the verb ir in the past (preterite): se fue = "he went" (also often implies "he left"). a casa means "home" (literally "to the house"). You can change the time expression at the end: ayer (yesterday), tres horas después (three hours later).
target_language_example: Él se fue a casa temprano porque estaba cansado.
native_language_example: He went home early because he was tired.

meaning: he earns a living (makes a living).
additional_notes: Used to say how someone supports themselves financially, often followed by a gerund (-ando/-iendo) or by "como" + a job: "Se gana la vida enseñando" / "Se gana la vida como escritor". The base phrase is "ganarse la vida" and it can change for other subjects (e.g., "me gano la vida", "nos ganamos la vida").
target_language_example: Él se gana la vida trabajando en un restaurante.
native_language_example: He earns a living by working in a restaurant.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb *levantarse*. It can mean getting out of bed (often with a time: *a las cinco*) or standing up from a chair (*de la silla*). Often used with adverbs like *lentamente* (slowly) or time phrases like *esta mañana* (this morning).
target_language_example: Cuando oyó su nombre, él se levantó y salió de la sala.
native_language_example: When he heard his name, he stood up and left the room.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man did not agree to do something (often something requested or expected). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: “se negó a + contestar / dar / decir / escuchar / hacer”. You can change the subject: “yo me negué a…”, “ella se negó a…”, “ellos se negaron a…”.
target_language_example: Él se negó a firmar el contrato.
native_language_example: He refused to sign the contract.

meaning: “he stood up / he put (something) on himself / he became (a state)” (from ponerse).
additional_notes:
"Ponerse" is a very common reflexive verb with a few everyday meanings:
- "ponerse de pie" = to stand up.
- "ponerse + [body part]" (often with "la mano") = to place it on yourself: "Se puso la mano en la boca" (He put his hand over his mouth).
- "ponerse + adjective" = to become (a temporary change): "Se puso pálido" (He turned pale).
target_language_example: Él se puso nervioso antes del examen.
native_language_example: He got nervous before the exam.

additional_notes: From the verb **quedarse** (“to stay, remain”). Common patterns: **se quedó en + place** (he stayed in a place), **se quedó + adjective** (he ended up/was left in a state: *despierto* = awake), and **se quedó en silencio** (he fell/kept silent). It can also mean “he stayed behind” depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando todos se fueron, él se quedó en casa.
native_language_example: When everyone left, he stayed at home.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “quitarse” (to take off/remove from yourself). It’s reflexive: "se" shows the action is done to oneself, usually with clothing or accessories. The thing removed is introduced with a direct object: "Él se quitó el abrigo / las gafas". Often used with body-related items too (e.g., "se quitó los zapatos").
target_language_example: Cuando llegó a casa, él se quitó los zapatos.
native_language_example: When he got home, he took off his shoes.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb sentarse (to sit down). It describes a completed action: he sat down (and then likely did something else). Often followed by en + place (él se sentó en el banco) or by a + infinitive to show purpose (él se sentó a leer = he sat down to read).
target_language_example: Él se sentó en la silla para esperar.
native_language_example: He sat down in the chair to wait.

additional_notes: Used to describe a habit or something that happens regularly with a male subject (él). Word order is often “Él siempre + verb” (Él siempre olvida...). You can also see “Él siempre que…” meaning “Whenever he…” (Él siempre que nos visita...). Accent matters: “él” (he) vs “el” (the).
target_language_example: Él siempre llega temprano a clase.
native_language_example: He always arrives early to class.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of tener (tener → tenía) used with él (“he”). It often describes an ongoing situation in the past (“he had...”) or gives background information. With age, Spanish uses tener (“to have”): Él tenía once años = “He was eleven (years old)”.
target_language_example: Cuando él tenía veinte años, él tenía dos trabajos.
native_language_example: When he was twenty years old, he had two jobs.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy was correct about something (often after checking facts or after events happen). You can add details with "en" or "sobre": "Él tenía razón en eso" (He was right about that), "Él tenía razón sobre el precio" (He was right about the price). Present tense is "él tiene razón" (he is right).
target_language_example: Al final, él tenía razón sobre el horario del tren.
native_language_example: In the end, he was right about the train schedule.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man possesses something or has a relationship/attribute: *Él tiene una casa / una hija / un coche.* Spanish often uses *tener* where English might use “to have,” and it’s the 3rd-person singular present form of *tener* (“he/she/it has”).
target_language_example: Él tiene dos hermanos.
native_language_example: He has two brothers.

él tiene algo que ver con

target_language_multi_word_term: él tiene algo que ver con
meaning: “he has something to do with” (he is involved/connected with).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is involved in or connected to something, often implying suspicion or responsibility (especially with scandals or problems). You can change the subject: "yo/tú/ella/nosotros tenemos algo que ver con…". Often heard as a question: "¿Qué tiene que ver él con eso?" (= What does he have to do with that?).
target_language_example: Creo que él tiene algo que ver con el robo.
native_language_example: I think he has something to do with the robbery.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man owns/has two items, animals, etc. The number comes right after "tiene" and the noun follows (sometimes omitted if it’s obvious from context). Often paired with "uno... y el otro..." or "uno... y uno..." to describe each one.
target_language_example: Él tiene dos hermanos: uno vive en Madrid y el otro en Valencia.
native_language_example: He has two brothers: one lives in Madrid and the other in Valencia.

meaning: he is afraid of / he is scared of.
additional_notes: Used to say what a man/boy is afraid of. After "miedo de" you can use: (1) a noun/person ("de papá", "de su padre"), or (2) an infinitive verb to talk about an action ("de nadar", "de equivocarse"). You can change the subject: "yo tengo miedo de", "ella tiene miedo de", etc.
target_language_example: Él tiene miedo de hablar en público.
native_language_example: He is afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: A common comparison setup: **Él tiene más dinero + de lo que / del que + verb** (“He has more money than he can/use/needs/etc.”). In speech you may hear **Él** dropped: **Tiene más dinero...**
target_language_example: Él tiene más dinero del que puede gastar.
native_language_example: He has more money than he can spend.

meaning: "he is right" (he has the correct answer/opinion).
additional_notes: Used to agree with a man’s statement, opinion, or decision. "tener razón" means "to be right"; you can change the subject: "ella tiene razón" (she’s right), "tú tienes razón" (you’re right), "tienen razón" (they’re right). Often used with emphasis like "Sí" or "Por supuesto".
target_language_example: Perdón, él tiene razón: esa calle es de un solo sentido.
native_language_example: Sorry, he’s right: that street is one-way.

additional_notes: Used with **tener** to say that a man has or possesses something, or has a certain characteristic: *Él tiene un acento… / un talento…*. In Spanish, the subject pronoun **él** is often optional because the verb form **tiene** already implies “he/she has.” Use **un** with masculine nouns and **una** with feminine nouns (*Él tiene una idea*).
target_language_example: Él tiene un perro muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: He has a very calm dog.

meaning: "he has a" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **tener** (to have). **Él** = he, **tiene** = has, **una** = a/an (feminine singular). You use **una** before feminine singular nouns (e.g., *una hermana, una piscina*). With masculine nouns, it’s **un** (*él tiene un hermano*).
target_language_example: Él tiene una bicicleta nueva.
native_language_example: He has a new bicycle.

additional_notes: "Él" means "he" (with the accent to distinguish it from "el" = "the"). "Trabaja" is the present tense of "trabajar" (to work). Use it to say where someone works ("en" + place) or who they work with ("con" + person).
target_language_example: Él trabaja en un hospital.
native_language_example: He works in a hospital.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy made an effort to do something, often with an infinitive verb after de: “trató de ayudar” (tried to help), “trató de hablar” (tried to speak). In conversation you can change the subject: “yo traté de…/ella trató de…/tratamos de…”. Also common: “intentar + infinitive” as a similar alternative.
target_language_example: Él trató de llamarte, pero no tenía tu número.
native_language_example: He tried to call you, but he didn’t have your number.

meaning: 'he had' / 'he got' (preterite of tener); also in 'él tuvo que…' = 'he had to…'
additional_notes: "Él" means "he" and "tuvo" is the simple past (preterite) of "tener" (to have). It’s used for completed actions/events in the past: "Él tuvo un sueño" (he had a dream), "Él tuvo un hijo" (he had a child). With "que" + infinitive, it expresses obligation in the past: "Él tuvo que vender…" = "He had to sell…". Note: "tuvo" is irregular (not *tenió*).
target_language_example: Él tuvo que salir temprano por trabajo.
native_language_example: He had to leave early for work.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person (él) was involved in an accident. Very common with details like what kind of accident it was (de coche, fatal) or what happened as a result (y se rompió la pierna). In everyday speech you’ll also hear: “Él tuvo un accidente” (past), “Él tiene un accidente” (present), “Él tuvo un accidente de camino a casa” = “on the way home.”
target_language_example: Él tuvo un accidente en la carretera, pero está bien.
native_language_example: He had an accident on the highway, but he’s okay.

meaning: 'he is going to' (near future) or 'he goes to' (destination).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (va a + infinitive) to talk about plans, intentions, or something expected to happen: "Él va a comprar..." = "He’s going to buy...". With places, "va a" can also mean "goes to": "Él va a Londres" = "He goes to London". Often shortened in speech to "Él va a" → "Él va a" (with the 'a' closely connected) before an infinitive.
target_language_example: Creo que él va a llamarte esta noche.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to call you tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite (*vino*) to talk about a completed action in the past. The accent matters: **él** = “he”, while **el vino** (no accent) means “the wine.” Often followed by **a** to show destination or toward someone: *Él vino a mi oficina*, *Él vino a mí*.
target_language_example: Él vino a mi casa anoche.
native_language_example: He came to my house last night.

meaning: "he came to" (a place) / "he came to" + verb (to do something).
additional_notes: “Vino” is the simple past (pretérito) of **venir** (to come) for **él**. Use **vino a + place** to say where he came: *Él vino a mi oficina ayer.* Use **vino a + infinitive** to say his purpose (what he came to do): *Él vino a pedirnos ayuda.* You may also see **vino a + place + para + infinitive**: *Él vino a Nueva York para buscar trabajo.*
target_language_example: Él vino a verme después del trabajo.
native_language_example: He came to see me after work.

additional_notes: Used to say where or how a man/boy lives. Often followed by places with en (in), cerca de/lejos de (near/far from), or with someone: con... (with...). In Spanish, the subject pronoun él is often optional because vive already implies “he/she/it lives”; él is used for emphasis or clarity (e.g., Él vive aquí, pero ella vive allá). Accent matters: él (he) vs el (the).
target_language_example: Él vive con sus abuelos.
native_language_example: He lives with his grandparents.

meaning: “he lives in” (he resides in a place).
additional_notes: Used to say where a man/boy lives. Follow it with a city/country (Él vive en Tokio) or a place with an article/demonstrative (Él vive en esa casa). Often the subject pronoun "él" is dropped in Spanish: "Vive en Tokio." Note the accent: "él" (he) vs "el" (the).
target_language_example: Él vive en Madrid desde hace dos años.
native_language_example: He has lived in Madrid for two years.

additional_notes: A complete sentence in the simple past (preterite). In Spanish you often drop the subject pronoun, so you can also say “Volvió a casa.” “Volver” = to return/come back; “a casa” = (to) home.
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, él volvió a casa muy tarde.
native_language_example: After work, he came back home very late.

meaning: "he and I" (just the two of us).
additional_notes: Used to talk about two people together: a male person (él) and yourself (yo). Often appears as the subject of a sentence: “Él y yo somos amigos.” In careful/standard Spanish, after a preposition you typically use “él y yo” (e.g., “entre él y yo”) rather than “entre él y yo” being the subject; some speakers say “sobre él y yo” where “sobre él y mí” might be expected depending on meaning. Word order can also be “yo y él,” but “él y yo” is common.
target_language_example: Él y yo vamos al cine esta noche.
native_language_example: He and I are going to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about you and another male person together (a group of two). It’s “él” (he) + “y” (and) + “yo” (I) + “somos” (we are, from *ser*). For a female person, you’d usually say “ella y yo somos …”. In conversation, Spanish often drops pronouns, so you may also hear “Él y yo somos…” shortened to “Somos…” when it’s clear who you mean.
target_language_example: Él y yo somos compañeros de clase.
native_language_example: He and I are classmates.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like poner/hacer (to place) or dar (to give): “poner énfasis en la importancia de + noun/infinitive” = “to emphasize how important it is to + verb / the importance of + noun.” Often followed by “de” to introduce what is important.
target_language_example: El profesor puso énfasis en la importancia de practicar todos los días.
native_language_example: The teacher emphasized the importance of practicing every day.

additional_notes: A classic fairy-tale/storytelling opener used to begin a narrative. It’s a fixed expression; the verb form (érase) is an old-fashioned past tense of “ser” and isn’t used much outside this set phrase.
target_language_example: Érase una vez un dragón que vivía en una cueva.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a dragon who lived in a cave.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point to something that was just mentioned. “Ésa” is the feminine form of “ese/esa” and takes an accent when it’s a pronoun (meaning “that one/that”). Often followed by a noun (“ésa es una decisión…”) or an adjective (“ésa es la correcta”).
target_language_example: Ésa es la respuesta correcta.
native_language_example: That is the correct answer.

meaning: “that’s the …” / “that is the …” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or explain something: **Ésa es la explicación** (“That’s the explanation”). **Ésa** refers back to something already mentioned or understood from context. In modern Spanish you’ll often see it written without the accent (**esa es la**), but it means the same here.
target_language_example: Ésa es la razón por la que llegué tarde.
native_language_example: That’s the reason why I arrived late.

meaning: "That is..." (pointing to a specific thing/person; masculine).
additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something: Ése es mi teléfono. The accent in «ése» marks it as a demonstrative pronoun ("that one/that"), and it normally refers to a masculine noun (often something implied). For feminine you’ll often hear «ésa es...», and for plural «ésos/ésas son...».
target_language_example: Ése es mi libro; el tuyo está en la mesa.
native_language_example: That is my book; yours is on the table.

meaning: 'That is the…' (pointing to a specific masculine thing).
additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize something: **Ese/Ése** = “that (one)” and **es el** = “is the” (masculine singular). Often followed by a masculine noun: *Ése es el núcleo / el mensaje / el secuestrador*. Modern Spanish usually writes **ese** without an accent, but you may still see **ése** to avoid confusion.
target_language_example: Ése es el problema.
native_language_example: That is the problem.

meaning: 'That is my…' (pointing out something/someone as yours).
additional_notes: Used to identify something/someone: ése = “that one” (masculine, singular), es = “is”, mi = “my”. It’s commonly followed by a noun (mi chico, mi secreto, mi regalo). Often written with accent marks as “ése”, though in modern Spanish it’s also common to write “ese” without an accent.
target_language_example: Ése es mi libro.
native_language_example: That is my book.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out a specific feminine noun: Ésta es la casa… (“This is the house…”). Often said while indicating something/someone nearby or the one being talked about. With nouns, you’ll usually see “Esta es…” (without accent) before the noun; “Ésta es…” (with accent) can be used when “this” stands alone (like “this one”), though in modern Spanish the accent is often omitted.
target_language_example: Ésta es la opción correcta.
native_language_example: This is the correct option.

meaning: “this is the” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or present something: “This is the …”. It’s feminine because it goes with a feminine noun (la obra, la inspiración, etc.). In modern Spanish, the accent is often omitted in demonstratives ("esta es la" is very common), but "ésta" may be used to emphasize “this one” or to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Ésta es la mejor opción para mí.
native_language_example: This is the best option for me.

additional_notes: Used to identify or introduce something that belongs to you: Ésta (this, feminine) + es (is) + mi (my). It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., mi idea, mi prima, mi bota, mi gata, mi mesa, mi respuesta). You’ll often see it without the accent in everyday writing: “esta es mi…”.
target_language_example: Ésta es mi casa.
native_language_example: This is my house.

additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize something that belongs to “you” (tú): **Ésta** (= “this one/this”) + **es** (= “is”) + **tu** (= “your”). **Ésta** is feminine and typically refers to a feminine noun mentioned or implied (e.g., *la llave, la noche, la película, la oportunidad*). Often you’ll also see **Esta es tu…** (without the accent) in modern spelling; both are understood.
target_language_example: Ésta es tu mesa; la mía está allí.
native_language_example: This is your table; mine is over there.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something: Ésta (this one) + es (is) + una (a). It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (una carretera, una caseta, una estación, una oración, una tradición). In modern Spanish, the accent in esta/ésta is often omitted (esta es una...), but you may still see it written with an accent for clarity.
target_language_example: Ésta es una idea muy buena.
native_language_example: This is a very good idea.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out several items/people that are grammatically feminine plural. It commonly introduces or labels what you’re showing: “Éstas son mis alumnas” (These are my students). Often followed by a noun (“éstas son las cosas…”) or by a possessive pronoun like “las mías” (mine). In everyday writing you may see “estas son” without the accent, but the accent can help distinguish the pronoun “éstas” from the determiner “estas” before a noun.
target_language_example: Éstas son mis llaves; las tuyas están en la mesa.
native_language_example: These are my keys; yours are on the table.

additional_notes: Used to point out or introduce someone/something: “Éste es mi amigo…” = “This is my friend…”. “Éste” is a demonstrative pronoun (“this one”) and “es” is “is”. In modern Spanish, the accent is often omitted (“este es”), especially in writing, but both are understood. It agrees in gender/number: “Ésta es…” (this is, feminine), “Éstos son…” (these are, masculine), “Éstas son…” (these are, feminine).
target_language_example: Éste es el restaurante que te recomendé.
native_language_example: This is the restaurant I recommended to you.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out a specific masculine noun: “Éste es el + [noun]…”. In modern spelling, the accent is often omitted (“Este es el…”), but “éste” may still appear to avoid ambiguity or for emphasis. For feminine, use “Ésta/Esta es la…”.
target_language_example: Éste es el lugar donde nació mi padre.
native_language_example: This is the place where my father was born.

meaning: 'This is my…' (pointing out something you own).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify a masculine singular noun that belongs to you (mi + noun): “Éste es mi caballo.” It often implies you’re indicating/pointing at something. In everyday writing, accents are often omitted (“Este es mi…”), but the meaning is the same; the accented form is the demonstrative pronoun (“this one”). For a feminine noun, use “Ésta/Esta es mi…” (e.g., “Esta es mi casa”).
target_language_example: Éste es mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: This is my passport.

additional_notes: Used to point out or introduce a specific masculine noun: Éste es un + [noun]. "Éste" (with accent) is a demonstrative pronoun meaning “this one/this,” and it agrees with what it refers to (masculine singular). In modern Spanish the accent is often omitted ("este"), but the meaning here is the same.
target_language_example: Éste es un problema fácil de resolver.
native_language_example: This is an easy problem to solve.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out a specific book you have or are referring to. In Spanish you often say it with emphasis when presenting something: “Éste es…” (this one is…). You’ll also commonly hear it without the accent in modern spelling: “Este es un libro.”
target_language_example: Éste es un libro para aprender español.
native_language_example: This is a book to learn Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify multiple masculine items close to the speaker. Often followed by an adjective (Éstos son buenos.) or a noun phrase (Éstos son los zapatos...). In modern Spanish, accents on demonstratives (éstos, ése, aquél) are often omitted: estos son.
target_language_example: Éstos son mis libros.
native_language_example: These are my books.

additional_notes: Used to say that certain things belong to you. "Éstos" refers to masculine plural items (people or things) close to you or being pointed out; in modern Spanish it’s very common to write it without an accent: "estos son míos". The possessive pronoun changes with gender/number: "estos son míos" (masc. plural), "estas son mías" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: No te confundas: éstos son míos y aquéllos son tuyos.
native_language_example: Don’t get confused: these are mine and those are yours.

meaning: “we were going to” (we intended/expected to do something).
additional_notes: Imperfect of ir + a + infinitive (“ir a” future), used to talk about plans, intentions, or what someone thought was going to happen. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive: íbamos a entrar, íbamos a jugar, íbamos a morir. Can also imply something was about to happen or was expected, even if it didn’t happen.
target_language_example: Íbamos a salir temprano, pero empezó a llover.
native_language_example: We were going to leave early, but it started to rain.

meaning: the last straw; the final thing that makes you lose patience.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the full phrase: “la última gota (que colma/colmó el vaso)” = “the last straw (that broke the camel’s back).” Literally it means “last drop,” imagining a glass that overflows after one final drop. You can also say “fue la última gota” (“that was the last straw”).
target_language_example: Cuando cancelaron el vuelo por tercera vez, fue la última gota.
native_language_example: When they canceled the flight for the third time, it was the last straw.

additional_notes: Used in time expressions like “a última hora” = “at the last minute / at the very end.” Also commonly used with news: “noticias de última hora” = “breaking news / latest news.”
target_language_example: Lo decidí a última hora.
native_language_example: I decided it at the last minute.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there won’t be another chance after this. Often appears with "para" + infinitive to say what the last chance is for (e.g., "última oportunidad para + hacer algo").
target_language_example: Esta es mi última oportunidad para hablar con ella.
native_language_example: This is my last chance to talk to her.

meaning: “the last word” (final say; to speak last, especially in an argument).
additional_notes: Often used with **tener la última palabra** (“to have the last word,” to insist on being the one who decides or speaks last) or **decir la última palabra** (“to say the last word”). Common in disagreements: *Siempre quieres tener la última palabra.*
target_language_example: No quiero discutir; no necesito tener la última palabra.
native_language_example: I don’t want to argue; I don’t need to have the last word.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent previous occasion (la última vez) or to emphasize doing something for the final time (una última vez). Often appears with de: el mismo de la última vez (“the same as last time”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes explicarlo una última vez, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you explain it one last time, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the final day of a period, event, job, trip, etc. Often appears as "el último día" (the last day) or "mi último día" (my last day), and can be followed by "de" to specify what it’s the last day of: "el último día del año" (the last day of the year).
target_language_example: Mañana es el último día de clases.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is the last day of classes.

additional_notes: Often used with an article: "el último momento" = "the last moment" (the very end). With "a": "a último momento" means "at the last minute" (done very late, with little time left). It can also be used as an adjective: "consejos de último momento" = "last-minute advice."
target_language_example: Compré el regalo a último momento.
native_language_example: I bought the gift at the last minute.

meaning: 'the last one who/that' or 'the last thing that'.
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause introduced by **que** to talk about the final person/thing in an order or sequence: **el último que llegó** (the last one who arrived), **la última que habló** (the last one who spoke), **lo último que dije** (the last thing I said). **Último** changes for gender/number: **el último que**, **la última que**, **los últimos que**, **las últimas que**.
target_language_example: Yo fui el último que llegó a casa.
native_language_example: I was the last one to get home.

meaning: "last resort"; the final option when nothing else works.
additional_notes: Used to describe a choice you make only after trying other possibilities. Often appears as "como último recurso" (as a last resort) or "ser el último recurso de..." (to be someone’s last resort).
target_language_example: Llama a la policía solo como último recurso.
native_language_example: Call the police only as a last resort.

meaning: the last train (of the day / final scheduled train).
additional_notes: Used when talking about the final train service available, often implying that if you miss it you’ll have no more trains until the next day. In travel contexts you’ll also hear similar phrases like "el último autobús" (the last bus) or "el último metro" (the last subway).
target_language_example: Si perdemos el último tren, tendremos que quedarnos aquí hasta mañana.
native_language_example: If we miss the last train, we’ll have to stay here until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to single out one thing as the only one that does something. Typically appears with an article: "la única cosa que…" (feminine) = “the only thing that…”. In everyday Spanish, "lo único que…" is more common than "la única cosa que…", but both are understood. Agreement can change with gender/number (único/única, cosa/cosas).
target_language_example: La gravedad es la única cosa que me mantiene aquí.
native_language_example: Gravity is the only thing that keeps me here.

meaning: "only hope" (the last/sole thing that might save a situation).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is the one and only chance for success or rescue. It agrees in gender/number: mi única esperanza, nuestra única esperanza; plurals are possible (p. ej., nuestras únicas esperanzas). Also common in the pattern “Eres/Sos/Usted es mi/nuestra única esperanza.”
target_language_example: Por favor, ayúdame: eres mi única esperanza.
native_language_example: Please, help me: you're my only hope.

additional_notes: Used after an article to single out one person or thing from a group: "el/la único/a que" (singular) or "los/las únicos/as que" (plural). It’s followed by a verb describing what that person/thing does or can do: "Es el único que puede hacerlo" = “He’s the only one who can do it.” Note agreement: "único" matches the gender/number of the noun or person (el único que, la única que, los únicos que, las únicas que).
target_language_example: Tú eres el único que lo sabe.
native_language_example: You’re the only one who knows it.

meaning: the only thing we have left.
additional_notes: Used to express that there are no other options left, often with a feeling of resignation. Commonly appears as “(Es) lo único que nos queda” (“It’s the only thing we have left”). You can change the indirect object to match the people involved: me queda (I have left), nos queda (we have left), les queda (they/you all have left).
target_language_example: Si el plan A falla, lo único que nos queda es esperar.
native_language_example: If plan A fails, the only thing we have left is to wait.
